## Volume front matter

### Series title page

# The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library

Of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated carefully with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the very extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers have commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they have done so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, uniform throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—one, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but now brought together for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and literary form.

## First Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [Christian poets of the fourth century]

## In the year of our Lord 329

### C. V. Aquilinus Juvencus, Hispanic presbyter

*(According to the Arevalian edition.)*

[Column 0009]

# Dedication

To the most illustrious and most reverend lord, the Lord Don Gregorio Alfonso Villagómez Lorenzana, knight of the distinguished royal Hispanic Order of Charles III, archdeacon of Calatrava, canon of Toledo, etc., Faustino Arévalo.

[Column 0009]

Gregory, most distinguished man, when I had resolved to revise against ancient copies the *Evangelical History* which the presbyter Juvencus rendered in Latin verse, and to illuminate it with notes, as I had recently done with Dracontius and not long before with Prudentius, and when I had already reached the point of considering its publication, I was suddenly deterred from the undertaking altogether by the difficulty no less than by the grandeur of the subject. I would certainly have abandoned this intention had you not intervened, in accordance with your devotion to every branch of learning, and especially to these more sacred studies, and urged me both to complete other works and, above all, to finish this one.

Therefore, as was fitting for a man bound to you by so many obligations, and who attributes as much to your judgment and affection as to those of very few others, I immediately obeyed you and handed my Juvencus, completed as best I could, over to the printers. Now, fresh from the press, I present him to you, dedicating the book—as that famous writer says—to your virtue and merits.

I freely admit that this edition was not perfected in every detail, nor completed in all its parts; nevertheless, I think no one will deny that it is the fullest of all those thus far prepared, and that, so far as I was able and in order to obey you, I have brought it to the degree of perfection, or even to the summit, that could reasonably be expected of me.

In this matter I wish not only to be recognized as most grateful toward you, but also hope—indeed, certainly desire—to appear mindful of the benefits bestowed upon me by the most eminent Cardinal Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, Archbishop of Toledo, your uncle and one who loves you most dearly—benefits which I shall cherish in everlasting remembrance.

What could have been more welcome and desirable to me, or more delightful, than that the most ancient monument of Christian poetry, composed by the most noble Hispanic presbyter Juvencus, thoroughly trained in both secular and sacred literature, during the very beginnings of the peace restored to the Church by the Emperor Constantine, and now at last revised by me under your encouragement and auspices—you who embody within yourself all those qualities in which Juvencus most excelled—should come to light for the common benefit of the Christian republic?

To pass over those splendid monuments and trophies of your ancestral nobility, still visible at Mogrovejo from the earliest battles of the Spaniards against the Moors, you certainly possess among your ancestors, in whom you may rightly and deservedly glory, two outstanding men enrolled in the calendars of the saints: Turibius Alfonso Mogrovejo, Archbishop of Lima, and Vincent Lorenzana, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose religious cult your mother’s family celebrates in its chapel with altar and sacred rites.

You possess two most distinguished bishops: Pedro Villagómez, who succeeded his uncle Saint Turibius in the archbishopric of Lima and commended many monuments of his genius and learning to posterity in writing; and Ferdinand Villagómez, Bishop of Tlaxcala, who played a major part in the Second Council of Mexico and arranged its decrees and canons in proper order and form.

You possess and behold, to say nothing of others, those two most brilliant lights of Spain, a noble pair of brothers and your uncles: the eminent Cardinal Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, whom I have just mentioned, and his brother, no less distinguished by merit than by birth, Thomas, Bishop of Gerona.

Inspired by so many and such illustrious examples within your own family, should we be surprised that you have acquired many other distinctions through virtue and talent, preferring by far to be commended by your own merits rather than by the praises of your ancestors?

I had formed a high opinion of you long before this. I knew that you possessed outstanding talent, were inflamed by an extraordinary desire to learn, had laid excellent foundations in childhood and adolescence, and were adorned with a reputation for eloquence, whose monuments—though not numerous, certainly illustrious—have been made public. I also knew that you had devoted yourself wholeheartedly to the more serious disciplines, and especially to theology, so that from the earliest years of your youth you have sustained, with great glory and esteem for your name, the grave responsibility of investigating every branch of theology and judging those who are to be appointed and advanced to the care of souls throughout the extensive diocese of Toledo.

Yet my opinion was far surpassed by the singular force of your intellect and the abundance of your sacred learning, which I came to know when, during your many months in Rome, I heard you almost every day, whenever the occasion arose, discoursing extemporaneously and subtly on the deepest mysteries of our religion, cutting every difficulty down to the quick and resolving the hardest questions in such easy and flowing speech that you seemed—if I may use Augustus’s expression—to have your intellect ready at hand.

Nor did all those eminent men, ornaments of the Church and of letters, think otherwise—men whose company you willingly sought, led by your love of learning, and to whom you yourself were exceedingly dear and welcome because of the excellence of your intellect and the candor of your well-ordered character.

[Column 0011]

It was also possible to admire in you an eager zeal for investigating Roman antiquities, both sacred and profane; refined judgment in assessing works of the liberal arts; and an ardent desire to examine all the works of piety which have been wisely established in Rome, numerous and varied as they are, to relieve human suffering. It is therefore greatly to be desired that men of this kind should come here from Spain, so that they might in turn bring a favorable opinion of our nation among foreigners, and, returning from here to their homeland, carry back something beneficial, as though from a commerce in the liberal arts.

Would that this study of mine on Juvencus, which must also be counted among the benefits of your Roman journey, corresponded to your other thoughts and cares! But if anything is lacking in it—or rather, whatever may be lacking, for much will indeed be lacking—I readily hope that you will pardon me, either because of the difficulty of the arduous work, which you yourself have long experienced while revising the Isidorian *Breviary*, Saint Martin of León, and the Toledan Fathers, in order partly to lighten the labor of the eminent editor Lorenzana; or because of that singular kindness with which you are accustomed to embrace devotees of good literature, and with which you have wished to embrace me, along with many others—or, lest I seem insufficiently grateful, among the first.

Farewell.

Rome, 28 September 1792.

[Column 0011]

# Prolegomena to C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus

## Chapter I

### The testimonies of Saint Jerome concerning Juvencus are examined. The opinion that Juvencus was once accorded religious veneration is rejected.

[Column 0011A]

### 1

After revising Prudentius and Dracontius against ancient copies and illuminating them as best I could, I must now explain not so much why I am publishing Juvencus with similar care as why I delayed so long or preferred others to him.

For Juvencus is not only the most ancient of all the Christian poets whom we know with certainty to have existed among the Latins; he is also the most distinguished in the brilliance of his language, the elegance of his style, and a certain ancient simplicity entirely suited to the divine subject of his poem.

In his poem one may admire not only the first harmony—at least among the Latins—of the four Gospels, in imitation of which innumerable others were later produced, but also certain distinctive interpretations of Sacred Scripture, commendable because of their antiquity, and, in addition, a variety of readings in the Gospel volume that he used in his own time, namely at the beginning of the fourth century.

### 2

Yet I do not now intend to deny or call into question Prudentius’s primacy among Christian poets, which I once gladly asserted with most others on account of his remarkable variety of subjects and poems, his exceptionally keen intellect, his immense poetic inspiration, and his extraordinary learning.

The reason that led me to publish Dracontius immediately after Prudentius was that I had found in manuscript codices his poems two-thirds more extensive than what had previously appeared. From these manuscripts an entirely different Dracontius emerges, and they seemed to me likely to bring much greater benefit to students of learning and sacred antiquity than any essays of mine on other Christian poets, in whose poetry there is scarcely anything else one can do except establish the ancient reading after examining manuscripts of the highest quality.

### 3

The grandeur of the subject itself also deterred me from publishing Juvencus. If by practice and experience in this genre I have made any progress, I understand that all of it must be brought to bear on narrating the deeds and sayings of our Savior; yet I readily perceive that this assistance is very slight for undertaking so great a burden, since even the most experienced person should approach such a task only timidly and step by step.

I shall therefore follow Juvencus as my guide—not indeed with equal strides, but as best I can. I shall defer my commentaries on Sedulius, Arator, and the other sacred poets to another time, lest someone reproach me with what Nicolás Antonio charged Antonio de Nebrija in *Bibliotheca vetus*, book II, chapter 4, part 1, no. 114:

> Yet I am all the more surprised that Juvencus has thus far had no one to hold a torch before him by the light of critical industry or explanation, which he requires, except Barthius to some extent, and Fabricius, who dealt with the matter in a superficial fashion; for our Antonio de Nebrija, who could and ought to have commended his fellow citizen Juvencus to pious readers, explained together with Sedulius and Arator, and who transmitted to posterity the fruits of his industry on Sedulius and somewhere testified that he had commentaries on Arator ready, is nevertheless reported to have provided no assistance to the Hispanic Juvencus.

Lest I fail in my customary practice, I shall gather in these Prolegomena whatever I have collected about him, his works, his manuscript codices, and his editions, although it was scattered in many places.

### 4

It is no small praise of Juvencus that Saint Jerome praised him more than once and not merely in passing. For we know nothing else securely about his life except what Jerome transmitted concerning him.

Thus this distinguished doctor writes in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 84, volume II, column 909:

> Juvencus, a presbyter of the noblest lineage, a Spaniard, transferring the four Gospels almost word for word into hexameter verse, composed four books, and also some pieces in the same meter pertaining to the order of the sacraments. He flourished under the Emperor Constantine.

In a certain codex of Juvencus this testimony is reproduced with some variation, as I shall report in no. 50.

### 5

Vallarsi observed in his notes that it is sufficiently apparent from the gentilicial name itself that Juvencus was of the noblest lineage, because in ancient books, according to Juret, he is called C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus.

Certainly Jerome’s testimony concerning Juvencus’s noble lineage requires no proof. Nevertheless, some evidence for the same nobility—though not entirely clear, at least probable—may be drawn from the four names by which Juvencus is designated in ancient parchments.

These names, however, are not pronounced in the same way by everyone. Johann Albert Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca Latina*, book IV, chapter 2, citing Juret, p. 273, on Symmachus, and Paul Colomesius in his *Paralipomena* to William Cave’s *Chartophylax*, as well as in relation to Gyraldus’s fifth dialogue on poets, says that Juvencus’s complete name was Aquilinus Caius Vettius Juvencus.

### 6

In the manuscript codices listed below, no. 306 and following, he is variously called C. Vectius Juvencus, Aquilinus Juvencus, Q. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, Gaius Vectius Aquilinus, C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, C. Vetius Aquilinus Juvencus, or C. Vectius Aquilinus Juvencus.

Remigius Ceillier, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume IV, states that in certain manuscripts his name is Aquilinus Caius Vettius.

Nor should it be omitted that two Florentine manuscript codices add the letters V. C., which signify *vir clarissimus*, “most illustrious man.” I discussed this title in the Prolegomena to Prudentius, no. 50 and following.

But, as I suspect, Juvencus was called *vir clarissimus* not by the ancients but by some recent copyist. In the Vatican codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, which I shall describe in no. 48, I find Juvencus’s name written as follows: *Gai Vetti Aquilini Juventi*; in the Ottobonian codex, which I shall discuss in no. 49, it is written: *Gai Vetti Aquilini Juvenci*.

The only difference concerns the names *Juventi* and *Juvenci*. For *Gai*, not *Cai*, is clearly read in both, and it is likewise read in another ancient exemplar, which I shall cite from Labbe in no. 36.

### 7

Accordingly, Juvencus’s praenomen could be written *Gaius*. For although this praenomen, which sometimes passes into a nomen, is usually written *Caius*, it is also found written with G, as in the Pisan cenotaph of Caesar:

> Let two gilded equestrian statues of Gaius and Lucius, the Caesars, be erected.

Quintilian, book I, chapter 7, teaches that *Gaius* is pronounced even when it is written *Caius*. The Greeks, indeed, always write it with G: Γάϊος (*Gaios*); and some wish to derive the word from γαίω (*gaio*), “I rejoice,” as though it arose from the joy of the parents.

Valerius Maximus—or, if the author was Titus Probus or Julius Paris—left this observation in the epitome on praenomina and noted a similar variation in the writing of *Gnaeus*:

> Some write *Neum*, others *Gneum*, others *Cneum*. Those who use the letter G in this name seem to follow antiquity, which made extensive use of that letter … Those who use C seem to delight in corrupting the syllable.

If you wish, compare Noris, *On the Pisan Cenotaph*, dissertation 4, chapter 5; the notes of Dionysius Gothofredus on Festus, under the word *Gaia Caecilia*; and Sigonius, *On Roman Names*.

### 8

The second name of Juvencus, which the ancient Romans simply called the *nomen*, just as the first was called the praenomen, is not *Vettus* but *Vettius*, unless someone should prefer *Vectius*.

This appears to be Juvencus’s gentilicial name; accordingly, it should be written *Vettius* or *Vectius*, although *Vettus*, *Vetus*, and *Vetuus* are also found in certain ancient monuments. For gentilicial names were commonly derived from other names, such as *Cornelius*, *Tullius*, *Claudius*, *Julius*, *Aemilius*, and so forth.

Concerning the name *Vettius* or *Vectius*, I have nothing else to cite from antiquity except that Glandorp, in *Roman Onomastics*, says that it was the name of a Roman plebeian family which eventually began, under the emperors, to attain public honors. He nevertheless names several distinguished Vectii.

In Juvencus’s case, as I have said, the name is more properly gentilicial than familial. Since such gentilicial names generally arose from some place or people—for example, *Tarquinius* from the Tarquinii—it is not an unreasonable conjecture that Juvencus derived his origin from the Vectones, or Vettones, peoples of ancient Lusitania between the Douro and Tagus.

This may perhaps have been why some people invented the claim that Juvencus’s homeland was Oliva, as I shall show shortly.

In Natalis Alexander’s *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 6, article 4, Juvencus’s name is given as *Vestius*, and placed third: *Caius Aquilinus Vestius Juvencus*. Labbe, following Peter Pithoeus, likewise reports this form in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although from another ancient exemplar he gives *Gaius Vectius Aquilinus*.

### 9

The Romans, not content with a praenomen and a nomen, added a cognomen. Cognomina of this kind were customarily assigned from a person’s character, body, or circumstances.

Thus, from color, people were called *Rutilus*, *Eburnus*, *Aquilinus*, *Albus*, *Niger*, *Rufus*, and *Flavus*, as Sigonius explains in *On Roman Names*.

Festus says that *Aquilius* is a praenomen:

> *Aquilius*, a praenomen, is said from the color *aquilus*, that is, black.

It would be better to interpret *aquilus* as a reddish or darkish color.

Nor is *Aquilius* always a praenomen, as can be seen in C. Aquilius, from whom the *Lex Aquilia* survives, in the *Digest*, book IX, title 2, which is entirely concerned with the *Lex Aquilia*, or law of Aquilius.

Glandorp, in *Roman Onomastics*, lists several Aquilii, among most of whom *Aquilius* is a nomen, not a praenomen. I observe the same thing in ancient inscriptions, in which *Aquillius* is sometimes written.

In the fourth century Aquilius Severus, a Hispanic writer, flourished; he is praised by Saint Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3, and by Nicolás Antonio, book II, chapter 2, part I, of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*. In some manuscripts he is called *Achillius*, in others *Acilius*.

### 10

According to the agreement of most codices, Juvencus’s agnomen is not *Aquilius*, a name more commonly used among the earlier Romans, but *Aquilinus*. Goldastus, however, calls him *Aquilius*, and I shall cite his words in no. 37.

Many persons named Aquilinus occur in the *Acts of the Saints* and in martyrologies; the same name is also found in ancient pagan inscriptions and other monuments.

But we must not omit the man who shares Juvencus’s first three names: C. Vettius Aquilinus, consul with Q. Junius Rusticus in the year 162 of Christ.

In the *Fasti* he is called only Vettius Aquilinus, but Gruter preserves an inscription belonging to the time of Marcus and Commodus Augusti, which Lipsius saw at Rome near the church of Saint Louis, in a private residence. In it, among the fifteen men of the *stlitibus iudicandis*—as it seems—or among the other members of a college of twenty, C. Vettius Aquilinus is named second. He was, as noted in the margin, consul in the year 914 from the founding of the City; and thus he is called by Pagius, who writes the praenomen of Junius Rusticus as Lucius.

There was another Q. Vettius Aquilinus, consul in the year 125 of Christ, and another Vettius Aquilinus, consul in 286. For all these men, see the notes of Mansi on Pagius, in the years 878, 915, and 1039 from the founding of the City.

### 11

Perhaps, in order to distinguish Juvencus from the consul C. Vettius Aquilinus, or from other members of the same Vettian gens and Aquiline family, this very name *Juvencus* was added to him. It is his fourth name and may properly be called his cognomen.

In fact, *Juventius* is a better-known and nobler Roman name. We might assert this form for our Juvencus on the authority of the very ancient Vatican codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, where the name appears in the genitive case as *Juventi*.

Barthius praises the ancient comic poet Juventius, citing Charisius, book II, in *Adversaria*, book XXI, chapter 5, column 1025.

But since all the other codices, and the Queen of Sweden’s codex itself at the beginning, present the form *Juvencus*, it would be wrong to depart from so established a word—especially since it accords with an ancient Roman custom by which many cognomina were derived from both kinds of livestock, large and small.

I shall quote Varro, book II of *On Agriculture*, chapter 1, according to Sigonius’s correction in *On Roman Names*:

> We have many names from both kinds of livestock, large and small: from the smaller, *Porcius*, *Ovinius*, *Caprilius*. Likewise from the larger, *Equitius*, *Asinius*. It must be understood that when we say *Goat*, *Bull*, or *Calf*, cognomina are being signified, since people are called the Capras of the Annii, the Bulls of the Statilii, and the Calves of the Pomponii. Thus many others are named from animals.

The published editions read this passage somewhat differently.

### 12

Juvencus, therefore, was given his cognomen from *juvencus*, “young bull,” just as the Greek poet Moschus was named from the Greek word μόσχος (*moschos*), which means “young bull.”

Barthius played on this word in book VIII of *Epidorpidum*, no. 74:

> The bull is more worthy than the man to hold the plow;  
> Here Juvencus places Arator beneath the yoke.

He is speaking of these two Christian poets, Juvencus and Arator.

Nor is the word *Juvencus* entirely unknown among Latin personal names. Saint Juvencus, Bishop of Pavia, is famously remembered at Pavia.

Concerning him I accept what Montfaucon reports in *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, p. 1245, column 2, among the manuscript books of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres. He says that there is a copy of Haymo’s exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul, etc., at whose beginning are hymns on the Passion of Christ, Saint Dionysius, and Saint Juvencus, Bishop.

### 13

It should nevertheless be noted that the Roman Martyrology reads, under 8 February:

> At Pavia, Saint Juventius, bishop;

and under 12 September:

> At Ticinum, Saint Juventius, bishop.

In other martyrologies, however, and in many manuscripts, the name is written *Juvencus*, although it is otherwise found corrupted in many ways: instead of *Juvenci* or *Juventii*, one often finds *Eventii*, *Inventii*, *Yventii*, *Hiventii*, *Quentii*, *Yentii*, *Hyventis*, and *Venuntii*.

Our Juvencus himself is not only called *Juventius* in some places but also *Hiventius*, and occasionally *Juvenis*. This can be gathered from Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, p. 508, where, from the Ambrosian Library of Milan, he lists a poem by *Aquilinus Juvenis* on the Acts of the Apostles.

I understand that this codex contains Aquilinus Juvencus’s poem on the four Gospels and Arator’s poem on the Acts of the Apostles. Perhaps, however, the error lies with Montfaucon, not with the ancient codex. In Montfaucon’s index, at least, the codex is clearly attributed to Juvencus.

### 14

There was another Juvencus, Coelius, a Dalmatian, whom Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca Latina*, book IV, chapter 2, observed to be different from the presbyter Juvencus.

He too was a Christian writer and composed the life of Attila in prose, which Barthius often mentions in his *Adversaria*, calling its author Juvencus Coelius Calanus.

For this Juvencus, the writer of the *Life of Attila*, and for its editions, see Johann Vogt, *On Rarer Books*. When Nicolás Antonio wrote about Juvencus, he did not know that this *Life* had been committed to the press; yet it had appeared much earlier, namely at Ingolstadt in 1604, in quarto.

Sidonius, book IX, letter 14, mentions the *History of Juvencus Martialis*, or, as others read it, of Juventius or Viventii.

Savaro, in his note on that passage, distinguishes Juvencus from Martialis and thinks that this person was Gargilius Martialis, whom Lampridius and Vopiscus mention.

Sirmondus, in a note, asserts that the writer was the same Juventius Martialis and conjectures that he was this very Gargilius Martialis mentioned by others.

### 15

Having explained Juvencus’s four names one by one, it is not superfluous now to add that Roman men often had four names: praenomen, agnomen, cognomen, and nomen. This indicated nobility of lineage, as I observed with Alexander ab Alexandro in the Prolegomena to Prudentius, no. 41.

In the same place I showed, together with Sirmondus and the Marquis Scipione Maffei, that this was in a certain sense the distinctive rule of names in the Middle Ages: each person’s proper name was placed last, as in Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator—for Maffei says that *Senator* was Cassiodorus’s proper name—and in Marcus Aurelius Clement Prudentius.

The same should therefore be thought concerning Caius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, although the order of the names in Juvencus, as in others, is sometimes found reversed. This used to happen even among the earlier Romans.

### 16

So much concerning Juvencus’s name, which Jerome expressed; the other three, which he omitted; and the nobility of his lineage, which he explicitly affirmed.

Another observation by Vallarsi must now be examined. To Jerome’s words, “four …,” he added:

> More accurately, following Fabricius, he should have said: “He arranged the evangelical history in four books, following Matthew’s sequence above all”; he did not devote one book to each evangelist.

I do not see why Fabricius and Vallarsi charge Jerome with having said, or seeming to have said, that Juvencus devoted one book to each evangelist.

For the assertion that, transferring the four Gospels, Juvencus composed four books is true, even though he did not devote one book to each evangelist, but set forth a harmony of the evangelists in his own order.

He certainly followed Matthew more than the others—not because he always preferred Matthew’s order, for he suitably arranges the sequence of Jesus Christ’s life from the four evangelists, but because he takes more material from Matthew than from the others. Matthew’s Gospel is richer than each of the other three.

Andreas Gallandi, who included Juvencus in volume IV of his *Library of the Fathers* and praises him very highly, observes in the Prolegomena to that volume, chapter 15, that Juvencus omitted many things because he wished to express all the deeds, but not all the sayings, of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

In Jerome’s notice on Juvencus, besides the history of the four Gospels, he indicates certain other pieces in the same meter—hexameter verses—belonging to the order of the sacraments.

These works still lie hidden or, as I am more inclined to think, have perished.

In Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, from the Vatican Library of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 1234, there is a note concerning “an anonymous concise book on the seven sacraments compiled in verse,” commonly called *The Decretal for the Instruction of Priests with Commentary*. As one may infer even from its title alone, this book certainly does not appear to be by Juvencus.

Let us also leave to their true author the verses of Hildebert which Montfaucon cites under Juvencus’s name from the same library, no. 88:

> The four books of Prosper of Aquitaine’s epigrams … Hildebert’s verses on the sacraments.

Peter Crinitus says in his *Life of Juvencus*:

> He composed several hymns, by which he clearly showed that he had rendered the greatest service to the Christian religion.

Paciandus, *On the Cult of Saint John the Baptist*, dissertation 4, chapter 6, reports that Georg Witzel, in his *Hagiologium, or On the Saints of the Old and New Testament*, Mainz, 1541, transcribed hymns in honor of Saint John the Baptist, which the presbyter Juvencus, under Constantine, and Adam of Saint Victor poured forth under the inspiration of heavenly thought and with an artistic arrangement of words.

In *Hymnodia Hispanica*, §23, p. 102, I stated that this was not sufficiently clear to me.

I have not yet been able to find Witzel’s *Hagiologium*. Nevertheless, I readily persuade myself that the hymn, or hymns, of Juvencus in honor of Saint John the Baptist were excerpts from book I of the *Evangelical History*, where Juvencus narrates that Elizabeth conceived from Zechariah in a miraculous manner, was subsequently visited by the Virgin Mary, and finally gave birth to John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner.

From the same book comes Juvencus’s hymn on the Annunciation, which Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca vetus*, book IV, chapter 2, no. 1, reports to have been inserted by Andreas Wilkius in the first part of his *Heortographia*, published in 1610, in octavo. See no. 85 on this matter.

Nor would I believe that Crinitus saw any other hymns except fragments of this kind, or portions excerpted from the *Evangelical History*.

For the poem on the Acts of the Apostles, which belongs to Arator but is mistakenly attributed to Juvencus in a certain manuscript codex, see nos. 13 and 41.

A greater controversy concerns the poem on Genesis, which is published under Juvencus’s name in Edmond Martène’s *Collection of Ancient Writings*, volume IX, columns 13 and following, from a Corbie codex written nine hundred—or by the present reckoning, a thousand—years ago. This attribution is confirmed by the codex which I shall identify below in no. 43.

The same matter may also involve the Juvencus codex on the Old Testament cited in no. 44, unless this is an error for “on the New Testament,” a matter to which we shall return at that place.

What I thought about this controversy I stated in the Prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 25, no. 220.

Some attribute the work to Tertullian, others to Cyprian; Elias Pinius, by conjecture, attributed it to Salvian of Marseille, as did Allixius.

Georgius Fabricius published the beginning of this poem among the Christian poets and assigned it to Cyprian.

Andreas Rivinus, who published Tertullian’s poetic short works with notes at Leipzig in 1651, in octavo, included in that collection this incomplete book on Genesis.

Source/review notes: Raw Terra review retained as complete=false solely for omitted anchors. Five substantive edits were applied; every source column transition was traced to its corresponding translated source paragraph.

[Col. 0018C] [Col. 0018D] [Col. 0019A] 17. The editor of the Pisaurian collection of poets not only places Cyprian’s name before the same poem, but also asserts in a note on the chapter concerning Cyprian by Johann Albert Fabricius in the Prolegomena to volume V that the manuscripts, according to the testimony of all editors, bear the name Cyprian, and that there is no reason for us to depart from the manuscripts. The Pisaurian collector was evidently unaware that the poem on Genesis had been published in a much fuller form under Juvencus’s name in the Collection of Ancient Writers of Edmund Martene, and that its beginning is reproduced from manuscripts in many editions of Tertullian. Martene, however, performed a commendable service with exemplary fidelity by reproducing the manuscript exactly. For the earliest editors of the Christian poets arrogated great license to themselves and recast the verses according to the rules of meter they had learned, without even indicating the older writing they had found on the parchment.

[Col. 0019B] Now anyone well acquainted with the style and metrical practice of the Christian poets across their various periods will readily assign the poem on Genesis, in the form in which Martene brought it forth from the Corbie manuscript, to the sixth century or later. Let this also be my judgment concerning the other poems commonly cited under the names of Tertullian and Cyprian: perhaps they had as authors one Tertullian and another Cyprian, not those who lived in the third century. I think it is not out of place here to show that among the Latins no sacred poet is demonstrably older than Juvencus.

[Col. 0019C] [Col. 0019D] For Lactantius lived at the same time, and many learned men judge that the poems commonly attributed to him are not his. Commodian scarcely deserves a place among poets, since he poured forth only what the Greeks call πολιτικοί [political, or popular, verses], while preserving the number of the hexameter but neglecting the quantity of the syllables. Add that Gennadius, in chapter 15 of On Ecclesiastical Writers, places Commodian after Lactantius, although some now conjecture that he flourished in the third century.

[Col. 0020A] G. Fabricius, in his Commentary on Christian Poets, reports from Jerome that Victorinus of Poitiers—whom others call Victorinus of Petavium—flourished before Lactantius and Juvencus, and attributes to him a poem on Jesus Christ, God and Man. But many others assign both this poem and other works published under Victorinus’s name to Marius Victorinus the African, who embraced the Christian faith in old age toward the end of the fourth century.

[Col. 0020B] Cuillier does not hesitate to affirm that Juvencus is the earliest of all the extant Christian poets. As for the poem on Genesis, since many call it a work of Juvencus, it must be listed among Juvencus’s doubtful works, and, in my judgment, among the spurious ones. No more effective argument for this position can be offered than the poem’s own conflict with the Evangelical History.

18. I would more willingly place among Juvencus’s doubtful works the poem by an unknown author, On the Praises of the Lord, which Fabricius published among the Christian poets on page 765. For its author was also writing under Constantine and approaches Juvencus in style; likewise, in a similar manner to Juvencus, he celebrates Constantine’s praises at the end of the poem. If these considerations are not sufficient to allow us to doubt whether Juvencus is the author, they at least establish that those few verses by an unknown poet, a contemporary of Juvencus, should be placed no more appropriately than after Juvencus.

19. In the Basel edition of Juvencus, Sedulius, and Arator by Theodorus Poelmannus, another little poem is added immediately after Juvencus, entitled *The Heroic Triumph of Christ*. In its margin there is this note: “In the author’s copy the author’s name was not written.” The same poem, under the same title, is found after Juvencus in the Basel edition of Sedulius and Juvencus by Bartholomaeus Westhemerus, published in 1541.

[Col. 0020C] These verses therefore seem to have been written in some old exemplar in the same form as Juvencus’s work. Yet they have been omitted from Fabricius’s collection of Christian poets and from other collections. The meter and Latinity of this poem are not without merit; but I fear that it may be the work of some later author who lived in the fourteenth century and wished to append this continuation to Juvencus’s Evangelical History. For I have no sufficiently clear knowledge of the antiquity of the manuscript from which such a poem was extracted together with Juvencus. Meanwhile, I shall have no hesitation in placing it among Juvencus’s doubtful or spurious works, especially since it is not readily available.

In the manuscript of the San-Germain library, number 43, which I shall describe, a poem of Juvencus on the Ascension is mentioned. I do not think that this has anything to do with *The Triumph of Christ*, or indeed with Juvencus. Perhaps some verses have been excerpted from the first book of Arator, and Juvencus’s name has been substituted for Arator’s. In the same number 43, another San-Germain manuscript attributes to Juvencus a preface to the *Paschal Work*, which ought to be restored to Sedulius.

[Col. 0020D] 20. After describing Juvencus’s works, Jerome establishes his period as follows: “He flourished under the emperor Constantine.” It is indeed an error that some editions read “under Constantius.” The same Jerome explicitly states that Juvencus composed the Evangelical History under that emperor in letter 70, elsewhere numbered 84, to Magnus, an orator of the city of Rome. There he explains why, in his own little works, he includes examples from secular literature, showing on whose example he acts. After praising many distinguished men, he continues:

[Col. 0021A] “Juvencus the presbyter, under Constantine, set forth the history of the Lord and Savior in verse, nor did he fear to subject the majesty of the Gospel to the laws of meter. Of the others, whether dead or living, I say nothing; their strength and their intention are evident in their writings.”

Thus Jerome defends himself by the authority of Juvencus.

21. In this eulogy, I find that Arntzenius notes in *Miscellanies*, chapter 5, drawing on Heumann’s *Poecile*, volume II, book III, page 349, that some manuscripts read “the truth of the Gospel” instead of “the majesty of the Gospel.” Arntzenius nevertheless prefers the latter reading, while Vallarsius recognized no textual variation. Nor should the common reading be disturbed, which many others retain, since they use Jerome’s very words in praising Juvencus. Fortunatus indicates this same reading at the beginning of book I of the *Life of Saint Martin*:

[Col. 0021B] “Juvencus sings the work of majesty through the art of meter.”

[Col. 0021C] [Col. 0021D] [Col. 0022A] 22. Jerome also gives evidence concerning the year in which Juvencus was writing his poem on the Gospels. In the addition to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, volume VIII of the works, column 787, under the year of the Lord 332, he says: “Juvencus the presbyter, a Spaniard by birth, sets forth the Gospels in heroic verse.” All this is wonderfully confirmed by the epilogue of the *Evangelical History*:

[Col. 0022B] “Christ’s peace has granted this to me; this peace of the age,

which Constantine, the indulgent ruler of the open earth,

fosters; he is present, worthy to receive fitting grace.”

This could have been said of Constantine especially at the time when he defeated Licinius, namely in the year 324, whom he ordered to be killed the following year. From that time almost until his death Constantine fostered peace throughout the Roman world. For this reason he was called “the founder of eternal security,” as Fabricius notes in his *Commentary on Christian Poets*.

I do not know what Fabricius means when he says that Juvencus recalled the emperor Constantine, the ruler of his own times, but omitted mention of the pontiff Silvester because the latter’s royal power and authority in the empire or in the Christian world had not yet been established. He is gravely mistaken if he wishes to infer from Juvencus’s silence that at that time the Roman pontiff had no primacy in the Christian world. There was no reason for Juvencus, when praising the peace of the age through which he had obtained leisure to devote himself to sacred poetry, to mention the authority of the Roman pontiff throughout the Christian world. See the notes on the epilogue of the *Evangelical History*.

23. Sextus Rufus, in his *Epitome*, describes the peace of that period in a similar manner: “Constantine, master of the world, prepared an expedition against the Persians at the end of his life. For, after the nations throughout the world had been pacified, and following his recent and more glorious victory over the Goths, he marched against the Persians with many armies.”

In Carlo Patin’s *Imperial Coins*, pages 465 and following, one may see several coins of Constantine whose inscriptions testify to the peace founded by Constantine:

“VICTOR EVERYWHERE.”

“FOUNDER OF PEACE.”

“BLESSED TRANQUILITY.”

[Col. 0022C] In Natalis Alexander’s *Ecclesiastical History* and in the dictionary of materials appended to that history, it is asserted that Juvencus dedicated his poem to Constantine. But since Constantine is mentioned only to indicate the period in which the poem was written, such an assertion rests on a weak foundation. Thus Virgil, at the end of book IV of the *Georgics*, which he had separately dedicated to Gaius Maecenas along with three other books, indicates that he was singing while

[Col. 0022D] “... mighty Caesar thunders against the distant

Euphrates,”

[Col. 0023A] and so forth.

[Col. 0023B] 24. Petrus Crinitus defines Juvencus’s period as follows: “He flourished especially under the emperors Constantius and Constans. At that time Tiberianus, Nazarius, and Flavius Vopiscus, who composed books on the deeds of the Roman emperors, were distinguished in Latin eloquence.”

[Col. 0023C] But Crinitus does not explain on whose authority he assigns Juvencus’s period to the emperors Constantius and Constans, nor do I think there is any reliable witness for this. Sixtus of Siena, in book IV of the *Bibliotheca Sancta*, can more easily be brought into agreement with Jerome’s view: “Juvencus, the most celebrated poet of his age ... under the emperor Constantine and his sons, who were ruling, in the year 330.” Either he expresses what Jerome said, or at least intended to express it. Otherwise, in the year 330 Constantine’s sons were indeed Caesars, but not emperors.

[Col. 0023D] [Col. 0024A] 25. It is therefore uncertain how long Juvencus lived. It is equally uncertain whether he held any office besides that of presbyter. Alcuin, whom I shall cite in number 94, calls him a presbyter and *scholasticus*. In former times *scholasticus* denoted someone practiced in forensic exercises, as I demonstrated in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, number 48, page 31. I do not think Alcuin calls Juvencus a *scholasticus* in that sense. The word was also applied to a rhetorician or learned man, and that meaning suits Juvencus better.

[Col. 0024B] No one now fails to ridicule, along with Nicolás Antonio, the episcopate of Salamanca which Pseudo-Haubert attributed to Juvencus under the year 337. Antonio likewise indicates that Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis, Marinus Siculus, and Eisengrein, in asserting that Juvencus was a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, rely on no foundation. For it cannot in any way be inferred that he was a presbyter of the Roman Church or that he ever came to Rome, to say nothing at present of the title or designation “cardinal,” which is much later.

[Col. 0024C] [Col. 0024D] But must we expose the other falsehoods found in the spurious *Chronicle of Dexter*? No one certainly gives them credence. They must nevertheless be exposed, because they have spread widely into the writings of otherwise reputable authors, and many unwary people are deceived unless they are warned of the danger. Thus, not many years ago, the noble Spanish poet Gregorio Salas, while listing his countrymen and mine—namely, the illustrious men of the province of Extremadura—assigned Juvencus to us as a native of the town of Oliva. He presumably found this in some good author, but it had been derived from the most polluted sources.

[Col. 0025A] The fictitious Dexter therefore says under the year 337: “At Salamanca in Vettonia, Saint Juvencus the presbyter dies; according to some, he took part in the Council of Iliberis.” The same Pseudo-Dexter mentions Juvencus again under the year 407: “At Caesarobriga, which is now called Oliva near Ambracia in Vettonia, Juvencus spends several years, and is said to have been born there. From there he goes to Salamanca, where the memory of the learned and holy man flourishes greatly.”

[Col. 0025B] 26. When these two testimonies are compared, Dexter seems to contradict himself. But the interpreter Bivarius comes to the rescue and observes that the splendid memory of Juvencus, which existed at that time, is what should be referred to the year 407; his other deeds are mentioned only incidentally.

Tamayus de Salazar confirms the same point in the *Hispanic Martyrology* under September 12, in an epigram which he produces from a manuscript in his possession:

[Col. 0025C] **An epigram in praise of Saint Juvencus the presbyter and confessor**

[Col. 0025D] “Behold, the city of Caesarobriga, thereafter venerable,

[Col. 0026A] recognizes Juvencus the presbyter as its own pledge.

Salamanca, then, held him, born there, illustrious

[Col. 0026B] in learning, a holy man in piety.

[Col. 0026C] The assembly of the fathers at Iliberis knew him,

[Col. 0026D] and his learned hand applied itself to its decrees.

[Col. 0027A] At last the holy confessor ascended Olympus,

[Col. 0027B] so that Vettonia herself might rejoice in his praises.”

[Col. 0027C] [Col. 0027D] 27. It is widely known that Tamayus deserves no credence in what he produces from manuscripts which he claims to possess—whether he received works of this kind by ancient writers, fabricated by others, in good faith, or whether he himself composed them maliciously.

[Col. 0028A] [Col. 0028B] Caesarobriga, now called Oliva, is a town eight miles from Placentia. The reason for conjecturing that Juvencus was born in Vettonia or derived his origin from there was mentioned by us in number 8. That very argument may have given the fabricators of the false chronicles an opportunity to invent that Oliva was Juvencus’s native soil.

[Col. 0028C] [Col. 0028D] A particular conjecture may be added, which can be drawn from an inscription in Gruter, page 938, number 7. For in that inscription, said to have been found in the village of Oliva and produced from Resende, a certain Vettus is praised:

“L. DOMITIUS, SON OF T., OF THE GALERIAN TRIBE, VETTO, OF OTOBESA, LIES HERE. MAY THE EARTH LIE LIGHTLY UPON HIM. T. L. DOMITIUS FORTUNATUS MADE THIS FOR HIS PATRON AT HIS OWN EXPENSE.”

In Gruter’s index of names, the name Vettus is clearly given in the nominative case.

28. In Resende’s *Lusitanian Antiquities*, which are included in the *Illustrated History of Spain*, the same inscription is confined to two verses and is explained by Resende as follows:

“Lucius Domitius Vetto, son of Titus, of the Galerian tribe, of Otobesa, lies here. May the earth lie lightly upon you. Domitius Fortunatus made this for his patron at his own expense.”

In the same place Resende publishes another inscription from the ruins of Caperensia in the same town of Oliva. In it, without any controversy, a certain Caecilius Vetto—not Vettus—is named.

Whichever form of the name is found engraved in the Olivan inscriptions, Vettus or Vetto, some suspicion—certainly a slight one—could arise from it that we should trace the origin of Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus to that town. But there is never any reason to fabricate or confidently assert what one does not know.

29. The religious veneration once rendered to Juvencus in Spain by some people must be discussed more carefully. I intend to deny such veneration in such a way that I shall not be displeased if at least some doubt about it is stirred up and remains in the minds of others.

For just as certain Spanish writers of the immediately preceding century showed themselves excessively ingenious in enlarging the catalogue of Spanish saints, so, on the other hand, I believe that our forebears did not show great diligence in transmitting to posterity the memory of the virtues by which the earliest Fathers of the Church in Spain were distinguished.

No one can doubt, however, that many monuments of the primitive Church perished not so much through the passage of time as through misfortune and a certain astonishing transformation of affairs, kingdoms, and regimes. Moreover, those men, however conspicuous for holiness, who flourished at a time when the cult of martyrs alone or chiefly prevailed—especially if they had not held episcopal rank—did not readily obtain public veneration and cult.

30. Tamayus de Salazar, in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, assigns the commemoration of Blessed Juvencus, as he calls him, to September 12, and refutes Hieronymus Roman de la Higuera, who in his manuscript *Hispanic Martyrology* had wished Juvencus to be venerated on June 1.

These two Hispanic Martyrologies, that of Tamayus and that of Higuera, together with the manuscript epigram in Tamayus’s possession mentioned shortly before, and the *Chronicle of Dexter*, must all be placed in the same category. They do more harm than good to the case for Juvencus’s cult. Certainly they make us more cautious, so that we may weigh with mature judgment the other evidence brought forward in its support.

31. Philippus Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue of the Saints* under September 12, writes: “In Spain, Saint Juvencus the presbyter.” In a note he says that Juvencus wrote that famous poem on the Gospels, and so forth. As witnesses to Juvencus’s sanctity he praises Franciscus Maurolycus and Constantius Felicius in their Martyrologies, as well as Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, in his *Catalogue of the Saints*.

The Bollandists list Juvencus among those omitted under September 12, although they acknowledge that he is called a saint in the German Martyrology. They add that Maurolycus and Felicius, because of the period in which they lived, do not possess sufficient authority to establish an ancient cult.

I do not think that Maurolycus intended to assert the cult of Juvencus the presbyter. For under September 12 he writes:

“At Pavia, formerly called Ticinum, the saints Syrus, bishop of Pavia, and Juvencus, who soon succeeded Syrus ... But Juvencus the presbyter, who wrote the Gospels in verse, flourished in Spain in the time of Constantine.”

He therefore mentions Juvencus the presbyter incidentally, not in order to number him among the saints, but to distinguish him from Juvencus the bishop.

Felicius, in his *Calendar*, or *Ephemeris*, published at Urbino in 1577, writes under September 12:

“Another Giovenco is mentioned, who was a priest; he wrote the Gospels in verse and was famous in Spain in the time of Constantine.”

32. The bishop of Equilio creates a greater difficulty; the Bollandists admit that he is sufficient to confirm an ancient cult. They reply, however, that in his catalogue he did not list only saints and was not so accurate that it is necessary to swear by his words.

The first reason is inadequate. For the bishop of Equilio speaks of Juvencus just as he does of the other saints. He mentions him twice. The first occurrence is in chapter 69 of book VIII, under the title “On Saint Hiventius the Presbyter”:

“Hiventius the presbyter flourished in Spain in the time of the emperor Constantine. This man, distinguished for holiness and renowned for wisdom, eloquent in rhetorical style and of most noble birth, translated the four Gospels almost word for word into heroic meter in four books, and rested in peace in Spain after a glorious end.”

He mentions him again in book XI, chapter 121:

“On Saint Juvencus the Presbyter. Juvencus the presbyter flourished in Spain. Possessing holy works, he rendered the four Gospels, and so forth. And in Spain he is celebrated under the name of confessor. The foregoing is taken from Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.”

This is how it is read in an old edition without place or year. In another similarly old edition, also without place or year, it reads: “This saint, distinguished by holy works.” The former reading is preferable.

33. There is therefore no doubt that Juvencus is counted among the saints by the bishop of Equilio, since his memory was evidently celebrated in Spain under the name of confessor.

A different judgment must be made concerning Petrus Crinitus, whom Tamayus de Salazar says gave Juvencus a place among Catholic priests—that is, among confessors, for so he interprets the term. Here are Crinitus’s words:

“There is also no doubt that he was one of the Christian priests, as the ancient authorities testify.”

What do these words mean? Nothing other than that Juvencus was a presbyter, as the ancient authorities commonly report.

Jacobus Faber agrees with the bishop of Equilio. In the letter to Faber Stapulensis prefixed to Aldhelm’s *On Virginity*, published at Deventer in 1512 in quarto, he writes: “When I considered that fruit which emerged from that edition of the blessed Juvencus ...” This is reported by Fabricius in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Bibliotheca of Ancient Latin Books*.

34. As for the bishop of Equilio, the Bollandists’ second reason is certainly valid: he was not so accurate that it is necessary to swear by his words. They also point out that it is impossible to understand how, if Juvencus’s cult had flourished in Spain in the time of Petrus de Natalibus, it could have failed to continue down to our own time.

Furthermore, it must be considered that, in the second place where Petrus de Natalibus mentions Juvencus, he cites Jerome as his authority, although nothing concerning Juvencus’s cult is found in Jerome. Since Petrus wrote in the fourteenth century outside Spain, and no Spanish authors of his time or of the immediately following period testify to veneration being rendered to Juvencus in Spain, nor is his memory commemorated in any Spanish Church Breviary that has come down to us, no solid argument for establishing an ancient cult of Juvencus can be drawn from the bishop of Equilio or from those who followed him.

35. In fact, in the earliest *Bibliothecae Patrum*, in which the title “Saint” was commonly and rashly given to many writers—and for that reason was ordered to be deleted in numerous places in the *Expurgatory Index of Brasichellensis*—Juvencus was nevertheless never called “Blessed” or “Saint.”

Some writers do praise Juvencus’s virtue, but are entirely silent about his public cult. Thus Franciscus Tarapha writes in *On the Kings of Spain*, under Constantine:

“Juvencus, a Spanish poet and presbyter, noble by birth but nobler in virtue and learning, was at this time exceedingly distinguished.”

Such piety and religion shine forth in Juvencus’s poems that it is reasonable to believe that he flourished in virtue. I wish, however, that I could confirm this through more reliable authorities who lived closer to his own time.

**20. CHAPTER II. The Manuscripts of Juvencus Are Listed**

36. In the *Introductory Dissertation* in volume I of Bernard Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, number 28, the following is mentioned among the handwritten books of the monastery of Zurich: “Juvencus’s fourth book”—perhaps “the four books”—“of the Evangelical History; Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*; Cicero’s invectives against Catiline, seven hundred years old.”

All these works seem to have been contained in a single manuscript that was seven hundred years old.

Ceillier, in volume IV, praises a manuscript of Juvencus in the library of the abbey of Monstier-Ramey in Champagne. It does not appear to differ from the one mentioned by Labbe in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, who says that in an old exemplar of the monastery of Aremac in Champagne there was written: “The four books of the Gospels of Gaius Vettius Aquilinus, presbyter.”

37. Martene, in volume I, page 65, of his *Literary Journey*, mentions that a manuscript of Juvencus was present in the monastery of Saint Benedict near the Loire, and in volume II, page 112, another similar one in the abbey of Saint Arnold at Metz.

Goldastus writes in a letter to Weitzius, prefixed to the edition of Dracontius prepared by the latter:

“I shall write back about Prudentius when I have obtained more leisure. I do not possess complete parchment copies of Quintus Vettius Aquilius Juvencus and Arator. Nevertheless, since you insist so greatly that I send them to you, I assign them to you and will arrange to have them delivered when an opportunity arises.”

In the catalogue of the manuscripts preserved in the monastery of Bobbio, drawn up around the tenth century and printed by Muratori in volume III of the *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, pages 818 and following, I find, from the old library: “One book of Juvencus,” namely, one manuscript of Juvencus.

From the new library—or from the books presented by Dungalus to the most blessed Columbanus, that is, to the monastery of Bobbio founded by Saint Columbanus—there is: “One book of Fortunatus, containing Paulinus, Arator, Juvencus, and Cato.” In the same place, among the books of Benedict the presbyter: “One of Juvencus ... One book of Sedulius, Juvencus, and Prosper, and of Prudentius and other versifiers.”

38. Montfaucon, in his *Bibliotheca of Manuscript Libraries*, page 219, number 21, lists from the Cassinese library a poem of Juvencus the presbyter from the eleventh century. He also lists, in the same place, his poems, six hundred years old.

On page 225, number 326, from the same library, he lists “the heroic poem of Juvencus the presbyter on the four Gospels”; and on page 229, number 509, “the verses of Juvencus on the four Gospels.” These two manuscripts do not seem to differ from the two Cassinese manuscripts mentioned above.

39. From the library of D. Valletta at Naples, Montfaucon, page 231, notes a parchment manuscript of C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus on the four Gospels.

40. In the library of the Dominicans of Saint Mark at Florence, Montfaucon, page 425, column 1, lists:

“C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, vir clarissimus, presbyter: poems on parchment.”

At the end: “A cento of Proba from the poems of P. Vergil.” At the foot of the book: “For Cosimo de’ Medici, Joannes Aretinus completed this book successfully at Florence on the Ides of February.” I do not find the year.

Another manuscript of the same library is mentioned by Montfaucon on page 497 as follows:

“An exposition of Aquilinus Juvencus the presbyter on the Gospels in hexameter verse.”

From a manuscript of the library of Saint Mark, Reinesius, as Schoettgen noted, copied the following title:

“G. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, vir clarissimus, presbyter.”

I believe this is the manuscript described by Montfaucon in the first place.

41. Among the books of the cathedral library at Padua, Montfaucon, page 485, records a manuscript of “Juvencus the Spaniard on the four Gospels.” Another may be added in the library that at that time belonged to the Lateran canons, according to Thomasinus in *On the Libraries of Padua*.

In the Ambrosian Library, page 508: “Aquilinus Juvenis’s poem on the Acts of the Apostles, parchment, twice.” This manuscript is attributed to Juvencus in the catalogue. I think it contains Juvencus and Arator. See above, number 13.

In the same Ambrosian Library, page 519: “Four books of Juvencus the presbyter on the Gospels, ancient parchment, twice, bombicinus.”

42. From the library of the King of England, Montfaucon, page 639, records: “Four books of Juvencus the presbyter’s poems on the Evangelical History.”

From the Bodleian Library, page 656: “Juvencus’s poem on the four Gospels.”

From the library of Saint Benedict’s College at Cambridge, page 671, column 1: “A manuscript of Juvencus”; and another, on page 685, among the manuscripts of Edward Bernard. In the Royal Library, page 686: “The four Gospels of Juvencus in verse.”

Reuschius says that the Cambridge manuscript preserved in one of the colleges is extremely ancient and written in uncial letters, and that another Cambridge manuscript exists in the university library.

43. The library of Saint-Germain, page 1135 in Montfaucon, contains among other things: “A preface of Juvencus the presbyter to the *Paschal Work.” I have no doubt that it should be read “of Sedulius the presbyter,” and so forth.

In manuscript 675, page 1136:

“JUVENCUS—or rather Cyprian’s—history of Genesis. Certain letters of Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine. Certain works of Saint Cyprian. JUVENCUS’s poem on the Ascension. The Sibyl’s verses on the day of judgment.”

Concerning the metrical history of Genesis, which most attribute to Cyprian or Tertullian, and some to Juvencus, see what was said in number 16. I explained my opinion concerning the poem on the Ascension in number 19. In the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, number 73, I explained which verses of the Sibyl on the day of judgment are meant.

44. A certain manuscript of the monastery of Moyenmoutier in the Vosges, of the Order of Saint Benedict, according to the same Montfaucon, page 1180, contains “the poems of Sedulius and the poems of Juvencus the presbyter.”

Another, in the library of Saint Benignus at Dijon, ibid., page 1286: “The four books of Juvencus the presbyter on the four Gospels in meter.”

In the same work, page 1373, from the library of Saint Victor in Paris, there is listed: “Juvencus in verse on the four Gospels.”

On page 1408, from the library of the monastery of Saint Peter at Corbie: “The poems of Juvencus on the Old Testament, followed by Aristotle’s *Categories*, parchment manuscript of the tenth century.”

Someone might conjecture that this refers to Juvencus’s poem on Genesis, which, against my wishes, some people attribute to Juvencus, as I noted in number 16. It is easier, however, to suspect an error and read: “The poems of Juvencus on the New Testament.”

45. Angelus Maria Bandini, in volume I of the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Laurentian Medicean Library*, column 722, notes in a parchment manuscript of the fifteenth century, page 161: “The four books of the Gospels of C. Vettius Juvencus in heroic verse.” In book IV the final verse, “Through the Lord,” and so forth, is missing.

In the same place, column 772, manuscript 22, fifteenth century: “The four Gospels in hexameter verse, by Juvencus, in four books.” At the beginning is Jerome’s testimony concerning Juvencus, taken from chapter 84 of *On Illustrious Men*. At the end: “The end. Three thousand seven hundred verses.”

I believe these are the two manuscripts described by Montfaucon on page 289, where he discusses the Laurentian Medicean Library: “The four books of the Gospels of C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, a most distinguished man, in heroic verse”; and on page 291, a paper manuscript: “The four Gospels of Juvencus the presbyter, of most noble Spanish birth, in hexameter verse, almost word for word, three thousand seven hundred verses.”

Unless there is an error in the numbers, this Juvencus manuscript is much fuller than the published copies. For in the printed editions there are approximately three thousand sixteen verses. In the edition published by us, Juvencus consists of 3,221 verses.

Concerning the second of these manuscripts, Reuschius writes: “The Florentine manuscript in the library of Saint Lawrence is not especially ancient, but is most elegantly adorned with initial letters in gold and purple. In the same parchment book are found the lyric poems of Prudentius, the *Acts of the Apostles* of Arator, and the works of Sedulius. Juvencus is called there ‘Gaius Vettus Juvencus,’ and at the end ‘Gaius Vettus Aquilinus.’”

I believe Omeisius refers to the same manuscript: “A certain distinguished patron copied the following title from a Florentine manuscript of Saint Lawrence: ‘The preface of Gaius Vettius Juvencus to the books of the Gospels.’ More fully, however, the poet’s name is read at the end of the same manuscript: ‘The fourth and final book of Gaius Vettius Aquilinus is happily completed. Thanks be always to God. Amen.’”

46. The catalogue of the manuscripts of the Bodleian Library presents us with manuscript 2219: “Juvencus’s poem on the four Gospels”; manuscript 5137: “A Latin-French glossary on Juvencus”—perhaps “against Juvencus”; manuscript 6463: “The four books of Juvencus the presbyter.”

The Oxford manuscript which Reuschius identifies from Spizelius may perhaps be one of those listed in this catalogue.

In volume IV of the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris, number 8321, a manuscript partly on paper and partly on parchment, formerly Colbert’s, is listed. Among other contents it contains “the Evangelical History of Juvencus the presbyter, in four books and heroic verse.” His poems are listed under number 544 of the same catalogue.

Concerning the Ghent manuscript with which Juvencus was compared by Poelmannus, see number 70.

Fabricius, under the word *Debilis* in his *Commentary on Christian Poets*, praises two manuscripts, one Ghent and one Merseburg. The manuscript used by Barthius, which Adversarius scarcely thinks any better manuscript exists, lay hidden at Zwickau while Reuschius was writing.

Another manuscript from Cologne is praised by Barthius in book XIII, chapter 19, of his *Adversaria*: “The Cologne parchments which we praise,” he says, “were written under Louis the Pious, son of the great Charlemagne. If anyone possesses older copies written differently, we shall yield to the truth.”

Compare Barthius’s words reported by us in the note on verse 9 of book I and on verse 2 of book II.

Juretus saw the Dijon manuscript in the monastery of Saint Benignus when commenting on Paulinus of Périgueux, *Life of Saint Martin*, book III, verse 62, pages 243 and 255.

Joachimus Zehnerus compared the Fulda manuscript with the greatest care, as Reuschius testifies. The same Reuschius calls the Florentine manuscript of Antonio Magliabecchi not especially ancient. Juretus used the Pithoean manuscript in his commentary on Paulinus of Périgueux, page 255.

47. In the Vatican Library I found only three manuscripts of Juvencus—or rather two, since the first contains only, after the works of Horace, the Lord’s Prayer under the title “Our Father of Juvencus.” It begins: “Thus the secret house ...,” and continues to “Nor is it hard to impose a heart yielding to errors,” as you can observe in book I from verse 620 onward.

This manuscript is on paper and of no great quality; it is among the manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden, number 1785.

Montfaucon listed, on page 45, number 1393, among the manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden: “The four books of Juvencus the presbyter on the Gospels in verse. The four books of Sedulius on the Old and New Testaments.”

In the same place, number 1396, Swedish Royal Library: “The poems of Juvencus the presbyter on the four Gospels.”

On page 50, number 1597, Swedish Royal Library: “Excerpts from councils, and so forth; several poems of Augustine, Plato, Avitus, Juvencus, and Fortunatus. A brief chronicle of Isidore of Seville.”

In the Vatican Library, in the collection of Alexander Petavius, page 67: “Juvencus the presbyter on the four Gospels, in verses: 903, 1095, 95.”

In the Ottobonian Vatican Library, page 190: “Sedulius, Juvencus, an old manuscript.”

Of these, only the manuscript I mentioned and two others now appear to be extant; I shall describe the latter immediately.

48. The parchment codex of the Queen of Sweden, in quarto, no. 333, contains the works of Juvencus and Sedulius. Juvencus begins as follows: “Here begins the preface of Juvencus the presbyter.” Eight verses follow, which we place as the first preface: “Matthew composed…” The other three manuscript codices agree, as I shall say in the note to this first preface. After these verses comes: “Likewise, the preface,” namely the commonly printed preface, “Nothing immortal …,” up to the verse “sweet Jordan,” after which is added: “The preface ends,” and, without any other title, there follows: “He was a king …” At the end: “Here ends Book IV of the Gospels, in the verses of Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus the presbyter.”

The orthography of this codex is generally as follows: *nanctus* for *nactus*, *Matheus*, *presbiteri*, *genetrix*, *inmortale*, *conjunx*, occasionally *ad* for *at*, and *competa* for *compita*. There are no commas and no punctuation, or only rare punctuation, in the first hand; diphthongs are written out. The Gospel chapters are not indicated, nor are there any titles of the kind found in most printed editions. There are some interlinear glosses, which will be of use to us. The codex should be assigned to the eighth or ninth century. We provide an engraved representation of its script.

In citing this codex in the variants of the Queen of Sweden, we shall call it, in abbreviated form, *Reg.* Eight verses, which this codex presents as the first preface, had previously been published by G. Fabricius in his *Commentary on Christian Poets*, under the word *Evangelistae*. He says that he found them in an ancient codex, but does not explain who the author of that codex was. I likewise find them after Sedulius in the Basel edition prepared by Poelmann, with this marginal note: “The author’s name had not been added in the exemplar.” They certainly are not by Sedulius, for at the end of his first book he had already concluded a similar thought in verse. Those verses must therefore be restored to Juvencus, although most codices begin with the second preface, “Nothing immortal …” On the practice by which ancient poets prefixed two prefaces to their poems, see the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 16. G. Fabricius rightly wonders with what rashness or negligence the second prologue, “Nothing immortal …,” was formerly inserted among the works of Ausonius.

49. The Queen of Sweden also possessed codex no. 1396, now listed among the Ottobonian codices as no. 35. It is a parchment quarto containing, likewise, the poems of Sedulius and Juvencus. The title of Juvencus here is: “Here begins the preface of Juvencus the presbyter,” namely the preface commonly found in printed editions, “Nothing immortal …” Then comes: “The preface ends,” and at this point an encomium of Juvencus by St. Jerome from the *De viris illustribus* is inserted, as we transcribed it in no. 4. *Competa*, *subolem*, and other forms are written much as in the preceding codex of the Queen of Sweden, except that this one has punctuation. The titles are also absent, and the Gospel chapters are not indicated.

At the beginning of the codex I find the following note: “A very ancient codex, before 700.” It seems to me to be approximately the same age as the preceding codex. At the end one reads: “It ends. Here ends Book IV of the Gospels, in the verses of Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus.” In the preceding codex Sedulius follows Juvencus; in this Ottobonian codex Sedulius precedes Juvencus, and between the two there is inserted a riddle without an author. For the name Arnulfus, which appears to have been erased, does not seem to have been written as the author’s name. I do not know whether this epigram has been printed anywhere; but precisely because I do not know, I shall appropriately publish it here:

> One word in its entirety gives four names simultaneously to things.
>
> For with the whole word it designates the Latin god;
>
> But when its first part is removed, it becomes the first offspring of Daunus;
>
> When the middle is removed, what remains is the opposite of sick;
>
> When the end is removed, what remains is what refuses all meals.

An explanation of the riddle is prefixed to the epigram, namely *Saturnus*, who is the Latin god: from this word comes *Turnus*, when the first part is removed; when the middle is removed, *sanus*; when the end is removed, *satur*. The third verse would proceed more clearly as follows: “But when the first part is removed, it becomes the offspring of Daunus.” This Ottobonian codex we shall call *Ott.*

50. Another codex that we used is preserved in the library of the Roman College and contains the poems of Arator, Juvencus, and Sedulius. Before Juvencus it gives Jerome’s testimony concerning him, as explained in no. 4, with this one difference: “Juvencus, a most noble Spaniard by birth, was a presbyter,” and so forth. The following title is supplied: “Here begins Book I of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter, also most noble by birth, and first the preface, ‘Nothing immortal …’” After this preface has ended: “Here begins the history and the first book.” Book IV concludes at verse 751, “Terror had shut off every feeling from the soldiers,” immediately after which is added: “Juvencus ends.”

The old codex from which this was copied was evidently defective, for this codex is paper and belongs to the fifteenth century. At the end of Sedulius it is noted: “This book belongs to the monastery of St. George Major of Venice, of the Congregation of St. Justina.” The script of Sedulius, however, differs from that of Arator and Juvencus, and perhaps these three Christian poets were bound together from different volumes. In the margins of Juvencus there are some notes and twenty-seven variant readings. We shall call this codex of the Roman College *Rom.*

51. After Reuschius had reviewed the manuscript codices of Juvencus of which he could have had knowledge, he says:

“Moreover, there is no doubt that more parchment codices exist here and there; for no codex from the Viennese, Roman, French, or other celebrated libraries has been recorded here. Let anyone who can obtain access to more of them therefore endeavor to prepare a better edition.”

Reuschius himself, however, used a paper codex from Trenchin, written in monastic script and copied from another exemplar that had belonged to Johannes Hadikius. Daniel Wilhelm Moller had shared this codex with Reuschius; but it had suffered the tyranny of a glossator, who had introduced many variant readings out of his own invention. For example, wherever Juvencus used the ancient word *plebes*, the glossator invariably substituted *turba* or a similar word. It is fortunate that Reuschius never trusted that codex alone. Yet *plebes* in the nominative singular should not be regarded as an ancient form of *plebs*, as I shall say at Book IV, verse 694.

Poelmann, in his edition, which I shall discuss in no. 70, appears to have used a manuscript that belonged to the library of Ghent. The Basel edition of 1545, discussed in no. 74, was collated with the Rottendorf codex. Saubertus had collected very many variant readings from an excellent Helmstedt parchment codex; Omeisius deserves praise for having used them in nos. 51 and 60. Some readings of the Fulda codex, transcribed by Zehner, were useful to the same Omeisius, who also received a collation of two Cambridge codices, as I shall report in the cited passage.

Joannes Fridericus Grunerus, in the *Acts of the Latin Society of Jena*, vol. III, treatise 2, Book I of the *Critical Observations*, chapter 6, carefully elucidates several passages of Juvencus from the manuscript codices *Cant.* and *Un.*, which Benzelius examined in England. He also cites codex *D.*, though I do not know whether it is different from the two English manuscripts *Un.* and *Cant.* Grunerus praises Reuschius’s industry, but adds:

“Those who know how great the labor is of reviewing ancient authors more accurately against manuscript codices will readily believe that Reuschius did not remove all the scribal faults in his excellent edition of that poet [Juvencus].”

## CHAPTER III. Editions of the Poems of Juvencus

52. First edition. Bayer, in his notes to Nicolaus Antonius’s *Bibliotheca veterum*, says that he possesses an old edition of Juvencus without title or inscription, place, or year, produced, in his opinion, around 1490 together with Cyprian, *On the Wood of the Cross*; Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*; Arator’s *Apostolic History*; Antonius Nebrissensis’s *Cosmographia*; Columella, *On the Cultivation of Gardens*; Palladius, *On Grafting*; and Valerius Probus, *On Abbreviations of Letters*, in quarto.

Joannes Albertus Fabricius, among other editions of Juvencus, records an old edition without place or year, in quarto, with the following title: “Juvencus the presbyter, enclosing the immeasurable majesty of the Gospel in heroic verses.” This appears to be the old edition preserved in the Vatican Library, which I shall discuss in no. 61.

53. Second edition, 1499, according to Fabricius, who says that Juvencus was printed at Paris in that year, in folio, together with Sedulius and five *Paeans for the Feasts of the Blessed Virgin* by P. Barri, edited by Jacobus Faber. In the letter to Faber Stapulensis prefixed to his edition of Aldhelmus, *On Virginity*, printed at Deventer in 1512, in quarto, Faber says:

“Considering the fruit that emerged from that edition of the divine Juvencus, whom I was the first of all to publish many years ago, and who had been mutilated and incomplete for me because of his antiquity, I restored him to the form in which he is circulated both here and elsewhere. I could not easily say what things in him were altered and what things were added to incomplete verses because of the corruption of the exemplar.”

Yet he ought certainly to have said so, in order that it might be clear to us what he published from the old, mutilated, incomplete, and corrupt exemplar, and what he added from his own ingenuity and resources.

Ceillier also records this Paris edition of 1499, in folio, with Sedulius and other pious works, prepared by Jacobus Le Fèvre. It is therefore distinct from another Paris edition, which I shall now describe. Reuschius notes that Nicolaus Heinsius owned this edition, as is clear from the catalogue of his books. Cornelius a Beughem also mentions it in *Typographical Incunabula*, p. 80. The title is:

“P. Barri’s five *Paeans for the Feasts of the Blessed Virgin*; the poems of Juvencus and Sedulius the presbyters; works by Beroaldus and others; and Propertius.”

54. Third edition, about 1500: “Juvencus the presbyter, enclosing the immeasurable majesty of the evangelical law in heroic verses.” Copies were available in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the Silver Lion. In quarto. There are nine gatherings, through *i*; in addition, *k* is a ternion and *l* a bifolium. On the title page is a device bearing the inscription “Jehan Petit.”

Three encomia of Juvencus from St. Jerome follow, as well as one from Johannes Trithemius, one from Baptista Mantuanus, and one from Francesco Petrarch.
