Then: “Here begins the prologue of Juvencus the presbyter on the four Gospels.” Next: “Book I of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter, who renders the four Gospels of Christ in hexameter verses.” Titles, or headings of the subjects explained in the poem, are present.

55. At the end is an epigram by Hermannus Busch of Münster on Juvencus the Spanish presbyter, addressed to the reader:

> Bind, Pierian goddesses, ivy wreaths, and pluck the laurels;
>
> Let lofty Castalia pour forth her clear waters,
>
> And let the grove raise its joyful ridges in unfamiliar green,
>
> Where the winged horse of Bellerophon once stood.
>
> Let Permessus sprinkle the grass with shining streams,
>
> And let lovely Thalia adorn the shores of your Cephissus.
>
> Let Cyrrha bring flowers, violets, and lilies;
>
> Let the Delphian fields breathe all around with countless roses.
>
> Let a breeze murmur through the whole region with a gentle breath;
>
> Let oak trees drip honey from Cecropian combs.
>
> Let the Spanish land applaud Juvencus on his return,
>
> Whose neglected work had been consumed by squalor.
>
> Now, with the whiteness gone from his face,
>
> He has put on again the blessed features and former limbs of his beauty.
>
> His hair, worthy once more of Apollo’s ivy wreaths, shines,
>
> And his ivory hand strikes the golden lyre.
>
> Cease to marvel if suppliant Orpheus has moved
>
> Tartarus and the mournful deity of the infernal realm.
>
> These things are indeed empty; but may such glory
>
> Fly to Juvencus, who moves the heavenly god with his voice.

56. Finally, Faustus, who was about to lecture on Juvencus at school, addresses the reader as follows:

**FAUSTUS GREETS THE READER**

“Take care, my reader—take care, I say—not to dishonor so chaste and so Catholic a poet with that ridiculous title. For the book should be titled as follows: *The First Book of Juvencus, the Spanish presbyter and most celebrated poet, on Evangelical History.* If anything else has been corrupted either through the neglect of time or through the carelessness of printers, I shall not leave it uncorrected in my public and daily reading.

“But since you were born a Christian of Christian parents, handle Juvencus—both the Christian poet and the expounder of the Christian faith—with your hand by night and with your hand by day, lest you always seem to read or hear only pagan poets and orators. Nothing is surely more beautiful or more pleasing than not to be ignorant of the divine mysteries illuminated by elegant verse.

“Moreover, thanks are due not only to me but also, and in no ordinary measure, to Brother Alphonsus, a Spaniard and a most learned theologian. For from him I received Juvencus, whom I had long sought; I published what I received; and what I published I shall interpret with the greatest diligence, so that my workshop may appear to have produced not so much secular as sacred literature. Farewell.”

57. It is not sufficiently clear how Faustus could have sought Juvencus for so long, when Jacobus Faber had been the first of all to publish him at Paris in 1499, to say nothing of the edition which Bayer, in no. 52, assigned to the year 1490.

In the copy of this edition preserved in the Angelica Library at Rome, the satires of Persius are bound together with the interpretation of Johannes Britannicus and Jodocus Badius Ascensius. In his preface Badius praises Faustus as “the foremost ornament of Gaul and bulwark of learning,” adding that he was “that royal musician and most renowned poet who educated Paris for so many years.” Ascensius signs from the Lyon workshop in 1499.

The type in which Juvencus was printed appears to be exactly the same as that in which the satires of Persius were printed. These are said to have been printed “in the most noble school of Paris” in the year 1500, on 12 May, through the skilled work of Thielmann Kerver. On the title page of Persius’s satires there is the same device as in Juvencus, with this note: “Sold at the Silver Lion and the Pelican in the district of Saint-Jacques, Paris.”

The edition is elegant but full of errors in many places. I do not consider the edition described in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris to be different from this Juvencus edition:

“Juvencus the presbyter’s evangelical history, described in heroic verse. Paris, Joannes Petit, in quarto.”

The year is not given. On Joannes Parvus, or Petit, see Michael Maittaire, *Annals of Typography*, vol. II, part I, p. 84.

58. Who that Faustus was who explained Juvencus, and who that brother Alphonsus the Spaniard was from whom Faustus received Juvencus, is less necessary to establish, but nevertheless ought to be investigated.

Publius Faustus Andrelinus of Forlì, a poet distinguished for his age, taught the humanities at the University of Paris from 1489 for thirty years, with great applause. He therefore is the Faustus who interpreted Juvencus. Mazzuchelli in *Italian Writers* and Tiraboschi in vol. VI of his *History of Literature*, part II, Book VI, chapter 5, no. 64, collect further information about his life. See also Maittaire in the cited place, p. 91.

Tiraboschi may perhaps have overlooked the words of Faustus that we quoted. They would certainly have enabled him to defend Faustus’s character against Erasmus’s jibes, for the other arguments he advances are weaker.

59. I would think that the Alphonsus from whom Faustus received Juvencus was Alphonsus de Cordova, of the Augustinian Order. After receiving the doctorate in Paris, he held at Salamanca the chair of Gregory of Rimini, which had formerly been established there because of Gregory’s fame for learning, and he died at Ávila in 1542, as Nicolaus Antonius reports.

Petrus Ciaconius, in the manuscript *History of the University of Salamanca*, which was in the possession of Petrus Madariaga, an Augustinian and recently an assistant, relates that in 1508 learned men were brought from Paris to Salamanca to teach the philosophy and theology of the Nominalists, and that at that time the chair in which Gregory of Rimini was read was established.

The chronology therefore encourages us to believe that Alphonsus de Cordova, or de Corduba, the patron of the Nominalists, was the man praised by Faustus.

60. Fourth edition, 1501. This is the edition produced by Aldus in quarto, which some assign to the year 1502 because it was published in that year, as is clear from Aldus’s letter to Daniel Clarius, dated June 1502.

This collection consists of several Christian poets divided into two volumes. The first contains Prudentius, as I explained more fully in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 104. It was reprinted in octavo without place or year, together with Aldus’s letter.

The second volume contains Sedulius; Juvencus; Arator; Proba Falconia’s *Cento*; Lactantius Firmianus, *On the Day of the Lord’s Resurrection* and *On the Passion*; Cyprian, *On the Wood of the Cross*; Tiphernius’s *Supplication to the Virgin*; *Prayer to the Blessed Virgin*; *Morning Prayer to Almighty God*, “Almighty, whom I worship in my mind …,” which is found among the poems of Ausonius; Damasus, *On the Praises of the Apostle Paul*; *Elegy on Jerusalem*; and several Sapphic hymns by Raphael Zovenzonius.

At the end: “Venice, at the press of Aldus, 1501, in January.” Aldus added, so that they might be included in the same volume, the *Life of St. Martin*, not in verse, as Ceillier thought, but in prose, composed by Sulpicius Severus; the *Life of St. Nicholas*, translated from Greek into Latin by Leonardo Justiniano; and the *Homerocentones* in Greek and Latin.

Reuschius assigns Aldus’s edition of Juvencus to 1502 and says that he had read that another Aldine edition of the same poet existed from the year 1582, unless the number had been altered by the printers. It certainly had been altered: Aldus did not publish Juvencus except in 1501.

Barthius’s judgment of Aldus is given in Book XXVI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 27:

“As Aldus and his followers often corrupted authors through the audacity of correcting them, so nevertheless, relying as they did on the assistance of the best Italian codices, they are not to be entirely despised by those who examine everything carefully.”

61. Fifth edition, about 1503. This edition is preserved in the Vatican Library, in quarto, without place or year. Its title is the same as that of the Paris edition mentioned shortly before, and it has the same encomia of Juvencus. The prologue and the beginning of Book I are likewise headed in the same manner. At the end is Hermannus Busch’s epilogue to the reader, or the epigram described above.

There are eight complete gatherings, from *a* to *h*. In this Vatican copy other works printed at Deventer in 1503 and approximately that year by Rithardus Pafraet are bound together; they appear to have been printed in the same type as Juvencus.

This edition seems to have been reproduced from the Paris edition of Joannes Petit. The titles distinguishing the subjects are different from those in the Aldine and Poelmann editions. The first titles, however, are:

“On the holy parents of John the Baptist and on the conception of that precursor of the Lord, Luke II”; “The Annunciation of Mary”; “The Visitation of Mary”; and so forth.

Omeisius possessed an edition of Juvencus without place or year, which he considered to have been produced at Cologne before the end of the fifteenth century, as I shall say in no. 85. But perhaps it is not different from this edition, which I consider to be the Deventer edition. Reuschius indeed asserts that the edition possessed by Omeisius is also found in the Vatican Library and in the Paulina Library at Leipzig.

62. Sixth edition, 1505, Leipzig, in folio, according to the catalogue of the Frankfurt-on-the-Oder Library cited by Fabricius. Ceillier mentions this edition, perhaps from Fabricius; Reuschius also mentions it, and, I think, had seen it.

63. Seventh edition, 1506, Paris, in quarto, from the Manarsian Library, p. 335, as cited by Fabricius. Ceillier agrees.

64. Eighth edition, 1509, Rouen, in quarto, with notes by Jodocus Badius Ascensius, according to Fabricius and Ceillier. G. Fabricius collated it, as appears from his commentary on the Christian poets under the word *compleo*. Reuschius also praises it.

65. Ninth edition, 1511, Leipzig, in quarto, by Melchior Lotter, with Hermannus Busch’s epigram on Juvencus appended. Fabricius had seen this edition without a date; Joannes Mollerus supplied him with the place and date. Ceillier also records it, but, I think, from Fabricius.

Christophorus Cellarius, in his *Later Studies* under the word *sanctifus*, cites two Leipzig editions, one from 1512 and the other from 1517. But perhaps in Cellarius’s Panormitan edition the year 1512 was printed by mistake for 1511. Reuschius gives 1511 as the year of this edition.

In the Paris edition of 1545, which I shall discuss shortly, the preface is by Wolfgang Gulden of Zweibrücken, Master, and so forth. He signs it at Leipzig on 2 January 1511. Wolfgang argues as though he himself had been the first of all to publish Juvencus; evidently he did not know of the other editions of Juvencus. The Leipzig edition of 1511 therefore appears to be the one prepared by Wolfgang.

66. Tenth edition, 1517, Leipzig, according to Cellarius, cited shortly before, and according to the catalogue of the Bunau Library, vol. I, col. 2018. From this it is clear that it is in quarto and was prepared by Jacob Thanner.

In that same year an edition of Juvencus was reprinted at Salamanca with the notes of Badius, which I mentioned in no. 64. Joseph Rodriguez de Castro, *Hispanic Library*, vol. II, p. 176, gives the following title:

“Juvencus the presbyter, enclosing the immeasurable majesty of the evangelical law in heroic verses, briefly elucidated by Jodocus Badius Ascensius.”

At the end: “The book of Juvencus has reached its desired conclusion. Salamanca, in the city, in the workshop of the venerable Joannes de Porras. In the year of the Lord 1517, on 17 January.”

In this edition the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ is in a certain way separated from the rest of the poem, almost as in the Paris edition of 1545, which I shall list in no. 73. The printer’s name is Joannes de Porres, or Porras.

67. Eleventh edition, 1419 [clearly 1519], Vienna, according to the Bodleian Catalogue cited by Fabricius. Maittaire describes it as follows in vol. II of the *Annals of Typography*, part I, p. 331:

“Four books of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter on Evangelical History, by Joannes Singrenius, at his own expense; in quarto, Vienna in Pannonia, 1519.”

68. Twelfth edition, 1537:

“Juvencus the Spanish presbyter and Christian poet, Book III [correct to IV], on Evangelical History, emended and purged of many errors. Two books of Arator the subdeacon, containing the Acts of the Apostles, previously unprinted in Germany. The *Enchiridion* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a consular man [correct to ‘most distinguished man’], of the Old and New Testament. Little books necessary for the Christian school. Basel, at the presses of Bartholomaeus Westhemerus and Nicolaus Brylingerus, in the year 1537, in small octavo.”

I used this edition from the select and richly furnished library of His Eminence Cardinal Valenti Gonzaga. It is also preserved in the Angelica Library. It appears to have been reprinted in 1542.

69. Thirteenth edition, 1537:

“The evangelical histories of Juvencus the Spaniard and Sedulius Scotigena, presbyters and most Christian poets, expressed with exactness in heroic verse; now published in a smoother form and much more carefully corrected through the collation of several ancient books. Cologne, at the press of Eucharius, 1537, in July. In octavo.”

The editor is Reinhardus Lorichius Hadamarius, although his dedicatory letter has been torn from the copy I use; it is preserved, however, in the edition of Poelmann, which I shall now describe. The printer is known by the name Eucharius Cervicornus.

70. Fourteenth edition, in the same year, 1537, or approximately then:

“Four books of Juvencus the Spaniard on Evangelical History. Four books of Caelius Sedulius’s *Miracles of God*, or *Paschal Poem*, together with several hymns. Two books of Arator on the Acts of the Apostles. Two hymns of Venantius Honorius Fortunatus restored to their integrity by G. Cassander. Everything reviewed by Theodorus Poelmannus of Kranenburg. Basel. In octavo.”

There is no date, but Reinhardus Lorichius Hadamarius signs his dedicatory letter to D. Joannes, Count of Vueda, at Marburg on 7 July 1537. He says that he published Juvencus and Sedulius after rescuing them from the injuries of numerous errors introduced by scribes or printers and restoring them through his own efforts.

Juvencus therefore appeared with Sedulius at Cologne in 1537, from the recension of Hadamarius. Poelmann later followed that edition at Basel, adding various readings in Juvencus and Sedulius, but especially in Juvencus.

In Poelmann’s Basel edition, without a date, besides these various readings and Hadamarius’s dedicatory letter, there are two epigrams, one by Poelmann and one by Hadamarius, on the usefulness of reading sacred poets. After Juvencus comes a poem entitled *The Heroic Triumph of Christ*, concerning which see no. 19.

Perhaps this edition should be assigned to 1551, as I shall explain in no. 75. G. Fabricius says of it in his commentary on Christian poets, under the word *Juvencus*:

“The diversity of readings in Juvencus printed at Basel had been collected by Theodorus Poelmann from an edition, if I am not mistaken, from Rouen, or from a manuscript that agreed with that edition. He later noted that this manuscript had come from the library of Ghent.”

71. Fifteenth edition, 1541:

“The paschal work, or five books of the divine miracles, of Caelius Sedulius the presbyter, both most devout and most learned, with the lucid explanations of Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis. We have also added the evangelical history of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter, on the same subject, together with commentaries on it. Everything collated with the most ancient exemplars and corrected. With a very full index. Basel, 1541, in octavo.”

After Sedulius appears the following title:

“Four books [printed as three] of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter and Christian poet on Evangelical History, emended and purged of many errors.”

After the encomia of Juvencus:

“Prologue of Juvencus the Spanish presbyter on the four Gospels of the Lord.”

The commentaries of Jodocus Badius Ascensius are appended or interspersed. After Juvencus comes the poem *The Heroic Triumph of Christ*, concerning which see no. 19. At the end: “Basel, at the press of Bartholomaeus Westhemerus, in the year 1541.”

Westhemerus himself supplies the preface; he was planning to publish other Christian poets as well.

The headings of the subjects in this edition differ from those in Aldus, the old Vatican or Deventer edition, Poelmann, and Hadamarius. Variant readings are written in the margin.

Westhemerus had already published Juvencus in 1537, as we have seen. Misled by the title of this edition, Kuhnius cited an edition of Antonius Nebrissensis, as I shall report in the variant readings at Book III, verse 340, saying that it was the first edition to give Juvencus together with his explanations. Nebrissensis’s explanations concern Sedulius; he never commented on Juvencus, as I observed with Nicolaus Antonius in no. 3.

72. Sixteenth edition, 1542, Basel, with the *Dittochaeon*, or *Enchiridion*, of Prudentius, reprinted from the Basel edition of 1537, as I reported from Ludewig in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 110. Neither Fabricius nor Ceillier mentions this edition in his catalogue.

73. Seventeenth edition, 1545:

“Juvencus the Spanish presbyter’s *Evangelical History*, described in heroic verse. Printed at Paris by Petrus Galterus for Joannes Barbaeus and Claudius Garamontius, 1545. In sixteenths, or duodecimo.”

The preface is by Wolfgang Gulden, and this Paris edition follows his Leipzig edition of 1511. See no. 65.

The end of Book IV is assigned after verse 403: “The Pharisees recount all the miracles of his deeds.” Then follows: “The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, composed metrically by Juvencus the presbyter.” But since verse 404 is connected with what precedes by the particle *ergo* (“therefore”), the end of Book IV is improperly placed before it.

Encomia of Juvencus from St. Jerome, Trithemius, Johannes Baptista Mantuanus, and Francesco Petrarch are added, as well as Lactantius’s poem on the Passion of the Lord. The titles are more numerous and fuller than in most editions; I presume that they were supplied by the editor.

74. Eighteenth edition, in the same year, 1545, Basel, in octavo, with Sedulius and Arator, collated with the Rottendorf codex and other manuscripts, according to Fabricius and Reuschius.

75. Nineteenth edition, 1551:

“Four books of Juvencus the Spaniard’s Evangelical History … everything reviewed and illustrated with various readings through the efforts of Theodorus Poelmannus. Basel, 1551, in octavo, with Sedulius, Arator, and two hymns of Fortunatus restored by G. Cassander.”

From the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. This edition appears to have been reprinted from the first Poelmann edition described in no. 70, which appeared without a date, as I said then—unless perhaps the true year of the first edition was added by hand in the copy of the Royal Library by someone who knew it.

Barthius, Book XLIX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, praises a Lyon edition of 1551 which presents three authors—Arator, Sedulius, and Juvencus—thoroughly renewed in accordance with manuscript readings. I do not know whether these editions are different, or whether Barthius wrote “Lyon” for “Basel.”

76. Twentieth edition, 1553:

“The sacred poetry of C. Juvencus, Caelius Sedulius, and Arator, reviewed and collated. Lyon, 1553. In duodecimo or sixteenths, at the presses of Joannes Tornaesius and Gulielmus Gazeius.”

Latinius had collated this edition, as is clear from his library. In the Royal Library of Paris there is a copy of this edition collated by P. Rupellensis against manuscript variant readings in C. Juvencus. This edition was reprinted in 1566, as I shall observe in no. 78.

77. Twenty-first edition, 1564, Basel, in quarto, among the Christian poets, with commentaries by Georgius Fabricius. Some say that this edition is in folio; others assign it to 1562. I discussed it at greater length in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 111. I shall give Barthius’s judgment of Fabricius in the note to Book I, verse 179.

78. Twenty-second edition, 1566:

“The sacred poetry of C. Juvencus, Caelius Sedulius, and Arator, reviewed and collated with the greatest care and diligence. Lyon, at the press of Joannes Tornaesius, 1566. In small format, or sixteenths.”

This edition is preserved in the Casanatense Library; I also used it from the library of His Eminence and most distinguished Cardinal Valenti Gonzaga. It is dedicated to Georgius Armagnacius, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1553, on 1 February.

It was therefore renewed from the first Tornaesian edition, published in 1553, unless it is altogether the same edition with only the title page changed—a fraud commonly practiced by booksellers.

Ceillier counts this edition of 1566 twice and says that it is in octodecimo. Nicolaus Antonius used a Tornaesian edition of 1564 in twenty-fourmo, which I do not consider different from the editions I have mentioned.

79. Twenty-third edition, 1569:

“The sacred poetry of Juvencus and Arator. Milan, printed by Pacificus Pontius, 1569. In octavo.”

At the end is Jacopo Sannazaro’s lamentation to mortals on the death of Our Lord Christ. The Gospel passages are indicated, but the titles are not explained.

At the end Juvencus is praised by St. Jerome, Trithemius, Petrus Crinitus, Johannes Baptista Mantuanus, and Francesco Petrarch, as in the Tornaesian edition, to which this Milanese edition appeared to me, on comparison, to conform.

It is preserved at Rome in the celebrated Barberini Library and in the library of the Roman College.

80. Twenty-fourth edition, 1573:

“Four books of Juvencus the Spaniard’s Evangelical History. Caelius Sedulius, and so forth. Everything reviewed by Theodorus Poelmannus of Kranenburg. Cagliari, 1573. Printed by Vincentius Sembeninus of Salò, printer to the Reverend Lord Nicolaus Canyelles, Vicar General during the vacancy of the see. In octavo.”

Bandini, in his catalogue of the manuscripts of the Medicean Library, suggests that Theodorus Poelmannus supervised this Cagliari edition. This should be understood to mean that Poelmannus supervised the Basel edition described in no. 70, according to whose standard this Cagliari edition was produced, even reproducing the first title of the work.

This Cagliari edition is sufficiently well corrected. It is preserved in the Sapienza and Angelica libraries at Rome.

81. Twenty-fifth edition, 1575, in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*, reprinted in other editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, such as Paris 1589, Cologne 1618, Paris 1624, 1644, and 1654, and Lyon 1677.

Whether all these editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* are in fact distinct from one another, I questioned in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 60, and have still been unable to discover the truth. The *Bibliotheca Patrum* published in 1589 was reviewed and expurgated in the index of the Brasichellan expurgatory catalogue, but Juvencus’s poems were left untouched.

Among the *Bibliothecae Patrum* one may place the work recorded by Thomas Ittigius in his book *On the Libraries and Chains of the Fathers*:

“Paraphrases and meditations on the Sunday Gospels, collected from the holy Fathers and Doctors of the Church who wrote in verse, by M. Johannes Zehner, 1602, Leipzig.”

Within this arrangement of sacred poems Juvencus, or something from him, was inserted.

The work published by Andreas Wilkius in 1610, the *Heortography* in octavo, belongs to the same category. In its first part there is a hymn of Juvencus on the Annunciation. See no. 16.

There also appeared the Benedictine Dominicus Schram’s *Analysis of the Works of the Holy Fathers and Ecclesiastical Writers*, in octavo, Augsburg; in volume IX, published in 1786, there is an analysis of Juvencus’s works from Gallandius’s edition. Schram wished to reform certain things, but corrupted most of them.

82. The twenty-sixth edition, in the year 1588: *The Sacred Poetry of C. Juvencus, Coelius Sedulius, and Arator; the Poem of Lactantius Firmianus on the Benefits of Christ: all revised and compared with various editions and manuscript codices. To these are added the Centos of Proba Falconia on certain chapters of sacred history* [Col. 0039C]. Lyon, Jean de Tournes, 1588. In 16mo. From the Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris and from Ceillier, who, I think, understands this edition when he praises the Lyon edition of 1588 in 8vo; nor perhaps is that edition different from the one Reuschius reports as published at Geneva in 1588, in 12mo, for he joins it with the other editions of de Tournes. He also records another Venetian edition in 12mo, without a date; it seemed appropriate to conjecture it into this place as well.

83. The twenty-seventh edition, in the year 1603, in the *Corpus of Latin Poets*, Lyon, in 4to. To this belong the other editions of Juvencus in the *Corpus* and *Choir of Latin Poets*, such as Geneva 1611, in 4to; Lyon 1616, in 4to; Geneva 1627 and 1640, in 4to; London 1713, in folio; and Pesaro 1766, in 4to, volume V. Ceillier records a Lyon edition of Juvencus from the year 1616, in 4to, but I do not think it is different from the edition of the *Choir of Latin Poets* produced that year by Alexander Fichet, with his own name suppressed.

84. The twenty-eighth edition, in the year 1710: *The Four Books of the Evangelical History of C. Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter, with the complete notes of Georg Matthias Koenig, Magnus Daniel Omeis, and Christian Schoettgen, as well as selected notes of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, Georg Fabricius, and others. Revised by Erhard Reusch, who added the memorial of Omeis and two indexes.* It is available at Frankfurt and Leipzig from Wolfgang Michaelles, bookseller of Nuremberg. MDCCX. In 8vo. In his preface Reusch says: “I did not wish to assume the right to remove or alter anything from the unpublished labors of such great men. For if I had permitted myself this, Juvencus would have appeared with his features slightly changed. I would have omitted certain discussions of commonplaces and everything that might seem to have been sought too far afield.” He adds that Omeis had been more sparing in examining variant readings and had been prevented by death from undertaking a second revision. Reusch says that he brought forward conjectures less than he weighed readings found in the manuscripts on the scales of judgment. He entered very few variant readings in the notes, because he intended to append to the notes a booklet of them collected by Omeis; but, with the fair approaching, he was unable to have it printed. He was also considering publishing a separate Dissertation on the character of the Christian poets [Col. 0040B], by which he would demonstrate Juvencus’ excellence.

85. In his preface Omeis reports that his uncle Johann Saubert had conceived the plan of publishing Juvencus long before, on the basis of an excellent parchment manuscript and a comparison of editions, as he stated in his *Various Readings on Matthew*, p. 259, and near the beginning of his preface to the reader of his theological-philosophical *Palaestra*. From this library collection Omeis acquired for himself an old edition of Juvencus in large octavo format, without place or year of printing, which he himself conjectured to have been completed at Cologne before the end of the fifteenth century. In the ample margin of this edition Saubert had added a great many variant readings from that famous and excellent parchment manuscript of Julia; to these he appended quite a few others, chiefly from the edition of Hadamar. Koenig, Omeis’s teacher, had publicly lectured on Juvencus at Altdorf and had dictated learned observations upon him, chiefly philological ones, which he shared with Omeis. In 1705 Omeis began interpreting Juvencus in his poetic lectures and proceeded to elucidate him with selected observations of Ascensius and Fabricius, and of Andreas Wilkius—who, in part I of his *Heortography*, p. 197, Leipzig 1676, adorned Juvencus’ account of the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary with philological notes—as well as with Koenig’s complete observations and his own, much more extensive ones. Among others, he also consulted Johann Price’s commentary on various books of the New Testament, London 1660.

86. Concerning the manuscript codices mentioned in Omeis’s various readings, apart from the Helmstedt manuscript [Col. 0040D]—which Saubert had used—he relates that he received a copy of Juvencus from Daniel Wilhelm Moller, who had himself carefully transcribed it at Trenčín, in a city of Hungary, from an ancient papyrus manuscript preserved in the library of Johann Hadik. In addition, Gottfried Thomasius had procured for Omeis, from the library of the people of Schleusingen, a *Corpus of Christian Poets*, in the margins of which Joachim Zehner had entered variant readings from a Fulda manuscript and from one or two editions. Johann Albert Fabricius had sent him a collation, accurately made by Erich Benzelius, with two Cambridge manuscripts. Fabricius himself relates this somewhat differently in his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus* [Col. 0041A]. He had intended to offer scholars a new edition of Juvencus, corrected against manuscript codices and old editions. Later he showed Omeis the collations of the Helmstedt manuscript, which he had received from the Reverend Abbot Johann Fabricius, and of the Cambridge manuscript, which he had received from Erich Benzelius. Fabricius mentions that a letter of Omeis to Abbot Johann Fabricius, in which he speaks of his commentaries on Juvencus, had been published. At his death Omeis entrusted the task of publishing Juvencus to Reusch, who added Schoettgen’s notes, unseen by Omeis, and appended a eulogy of Omeis himself. From this it is worth noting that Omeis took Maria Dorothea Rostia into the communion of his marriage: she had been born to pious and honorable parents in the celebrated Spanish commercial city now called Sanlúcar, and was the widow of Conrad Pilnhuber, distinguished for her virtues and beauty.

87. The twenty-ninth edition is in the *Bibliotheca of the Fathers*, edited and prepared by Gallandi, published at Venice from the year 1765 onward. In volume IV, in the Prolegomena, chapter 15, it discusses Juvencus. It presents a poem on Genesis as a certain work of Juvencus, taken from Martene together with his notes. At the end it adds, from Georg Fabricius and Barthius, Juvencus’ epigram on the four Evangelists. It appends brief notes to Juvencus’ *Evangelical History*. Therefore, although we have assigned all the other editions of Juvencus in the *Bibliothecae Patrum* to one place together, the Gallandian edition, prepared with particular study and care, deserved to occupy a distinct place.

## CHAPTER IV. Eulogies of Juvencus drawn from ancient writers and from certain more recent authors.

[Col. 0041C]

88. The praises with which St. Jerome celebrates Juvencus were mentioned in chapter 1. But what he says in his commentary on Matthew, book I, chapter II, 11, volume VII, column 14, should not be omitted here:

> Juvencus the presbyter has most beautifully comprehended the sacred significance of the gifts in a single verse:
>
> *Thus they offer gold, myrrh, and gifts to the King, the Man, and God.*

89. Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 331, is cited by some as having praised Juvencus. I find nothing of the kind in Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Perhaps they mean the continuation of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, by Jerome, whose words I quoted in no. 22 [Col. 0041D]. I also consider it false that Vasaeus states in his *Chronicle* that Juvencus was celebrated by Sulpicius Severus. Some infer that Juvencus and Sedulius were praised by Arator from Aldus’s account, who says this in the Life of Arator prefixed to the *Collection of Christian Poets*:

> Arator is said to have turned to writing the Acts of the Apostles in verse for this reason: he had seen that Juvencus and Sedulius had done the same in the Gospel.

This may be seen in that Arator which is bound in Venice, in the library of St. George, surnamed Major, and of the Ever-Virgin Mother of God.

90. Pope Gelasius, in the celebrated decree that he issued at the Roman council concerning canonical, ecclesiastical [Col. 0042A], and apocryphal books, which was edited under the name of Hormisdas from a certain manuscript by Francisco Juretus, says this about Juvencus:

> Likewise, we do not reject the laborious work of Juvencus, but marvel at it.

Fontanini compared this decree with the Vatican manuscript in the *Appendix to the Antiquities of Horta*, and later Joseph Blanchini compared it more carefully in a copy of Fontanini belonging to the distinguished Bishop of Reggio, who had added variant readings by hand and also inserted them in the Prolegomena to volume IV of Anastasius. Yet he notes nothing in these words except *lavoriosum* for *laboriosum* on the basis of a Florentine manuscript. In Gratian’s decree, chapter “The Holy Roman Church,” distinction 15, these words were formerly read as follows:

> Likewise, we do not reject the laborious work of Vincentius, but imitate it.

Padilla, in his *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, century 4, chapter 45, corrected *Juvenci* for *Vincentii*, and observed that some had wrongly explained the passage as referring to the *Historical Mirror* of Vincent of Beauvais, who flourished in the thirteenth century. Padilla, however, left the word *imitamur* (“we imitate”) untouched. The true reading had already been disclosed by Antonius Augustinus, and before him by Covarruvias, book IV of the *Various Resolutions*, chapter 16; it also appears in Burchard and Ivo, in the same decree of Gelasius, and in Chifflet, in his notes to Vigilius of Thapsus, p. 149.

91. Venantius Fortunatus, book I of *The Life of St. Martin*, at the beginning:

> For Juvencus was the first to distinguish verse in a teachable order  
> and to sing, with the art of meter, the work of Majesty.  
> From this, too, the conspicuous tongue of Sedulius shone forth. [Col. 0042C]

Fortunatus not only says that Juvencus was the first of all to enclose evangelical majesty within the laws of meter; he also implies that Sedulius fashioned his Paschal work in imitation of Juvencus. It is therefore all the more remarkable that Sedulius, in his preface to Macedonius, should in a certain sense have concealed that Juvencus was known to him, although he shows himself well acquainted with St. Jerome, who often praised Juvencus.

Aldus, in the Life of Arator prefixed to the *Collection of Christian Poets*, where he adds something about Sedulius, explains this conjecture as follows:

> Nevertheless, we infer from his letter to the presbyter Macedonius that Sedulius had not seen Juvencus’ books on the evangelical history. For when in that letter he gives the reason why he wrote the Gospel in verse, he makes no mention at all of Juvencus, who had done the same. If he had knowingly omitted this, he would not be free from blame, especially since the passage itself required him to say that he had Juvencus as his model. Certainly Sedulius had some occasion to name Juvencus explicitly when he said:
>
> “Rarely, best father—as your own learning also recognizes through the constant practice of reading—has anyone adapted the gifts of divine piety to a style of this kind of melody; and there are many whom the discipline of secular studies delights more through poetic pleasures and the charms of verse.”

One may wonder whether Orentius also imitated Juvencus, on the basis of Fortunatus’ judgment [44], who adds shortly afterward:

> And Orentius touched upon a few things with flourishing speech.

[Col. 0043A]

92. Isidore, in the verses that were formerly read in his library:

> Read through the learned poem of eloquent Avitus:  
> behold, Juvencus and Sedulius are here for you.  
> Both equal in language, both flourishing in verse,  
> they bring abundant cups from the evangelical spring.  
> Therefore cease to associate yourself with pagan poets:  
> while you can possess such great blessings, what need have you of Callirhoe?

I discussed these verses at greater length in my notes to Dracontius, book I *On God*, verse 176, p. 143. But, to add something new, it should be observed that the first six verses, which shortly before had been unjustly regarded as unpublished by Eugenius de Levis in his *Anecdotes* and attributed to St. Damasus, had been published by him in part in a more correct form. For the fifth verse in the Madrid edition of the works of St. Isidore reads:

> Here the venerable volumes of the law shine like gems.

Levisius’s manuscript gives the better reading, and in it those verses were attributed to St. Damasus:

> Here the venerable volumes of the twofold law shine.

The subject is the Old and New Law, as is clear from the following verse:

> Here the New has been established together with the Old.

In the verses I have now presented, I corrected another error of the Madrid edition, in which one reads: “Both equal in language.” Meter requires: “Both equal, in language.” For *gentilibus* I would prefer another reading as well, to satisfy the meter; but here perhaps the error belongs to the poet.

What he intends by these words, “What need have you of Callirhoe,” will be understood by anyone who understands the final verse of the first satire of Persius:

> In the morning, give him the edict; after dinner, Callirhoe.

[Col. 0043C] Some think Callirhoe is the name of a prostitute, others of some comedy. The latter view better suits the Isidorian verse.

93. Jonas Scotus, in the *Life of St. Columban*, chapter 14, elsewhere no. 22, cites Juvencus, book I, verse 44; I shall recall him at that passage.

94. Bede used verses of Juvencus more than once, as I shall explain in the variant readings on verse 340 of book III and in the notes on verse 632 of book IV, and elsewhere.

### 95.

Alcuin, in the preface to his seven books against Felix, addressed to Charlemagne, in Baluze, *Miscellanies*, book IV, p. 116:

> In this little work I have endeavored to prove the truth of the Catholic faith by the most certain testimonies of the holy Fathers, namely, of blessed Jerome . . . and also of Isidore of Hispalis and Juvencus, a scholasticus of that same province.

The same Alcuin, book II against Felix:

> But if you do not wish to believe the other teachers of the world, at least believe your own most learned men. Juvencus the presbyter and most learned Spanish scholasticus sang in his evangelical poem as follows: “For thine shall conceive,” etc. (See book I, verse 95.) This man flourished in the time of the emperor Constantine. You see these things clearly: the heresy of adoption or of naming had not yet arisen in Spain. Or judge as a heretic that man who stands among you as a most learned teacher, etc.

Again, in book II against Elipandus, the same Alcuin writes:

> Those Spanish Fathers had their own time, and they left us splendid traces of their labor in holy conduct; we praise and love them . . . Thus we have looked upon the evangelical poems of blessed Isidore . . . and also of the presbyter Juvencus, an excellent scholasticus whom blessed Jerome praises; in one of his verses he did not fear, with Catholic speech, to call Christ the proper Son of God.

The most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, to whose patronage and assistance our studies owe a very great deal, appropriately uses Alcuin’s authority in his highly learned preface to volume I of the *Toledan Fathers*, to demonstrate that the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt fell into error of fact when they believed that the Toledan Fathers had taught the heresy concerning Christ’s adoptive sonship. Elsewhere Alcuin imitated Juvencus, using a verse of his that he praised, as I shall note at book I, verse 30.

96. Among the ancients who used Juvencus’ authority and verses is also counted Lupus, abbot of Ferrières [Col. 0044B]; but I shall present his words at book I, verse 702.

97. Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, under Constantine:

> Reticius, bishop of Autun, is held in the highest renown, as is Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter who composed the four books of the Gospel in hexameter verse.

98. Freculphus, bishop of Lisieux, in his *Chronicle*, volume I, book III, chapter 21, discusses various teachers under the emperor Constantine and transcribes Jerome’s words about Juvencus from the *On Illustrious Men*. It appears in volume XIV of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 1171.

99. Eulogius of Córdoba, in *Memorial of the Saints*, book I, no. 3, cites a verse of Juvencus, calling it “philosophical,” as I shall mention more distinctly at book I, verse 30.

100. Theodulf of Orléans, book IV, poem I, verse 11:

> There was a fitting concern for the Fathers, nor was it the least concern of the devout,  
> whose names are written below; see them.  
> Sedulius, Rutilus, Paulinus, Arator, Avitus,  
> and Fortunatus, and you, thundering Juvencus.

Sirmond, in his note on this passage, does not know who the Christian poet Rutilus was. Some think that one should read: “Sedulius the radiant, Paulinus,” etc., so that *rutilus* is an adjective joined with Sedulius. This can be supported by Fortunatus’ verse, no. 91:

> From this, too, the conspicuous tongue of Sedulius shone forth.

For just as Fortunatus calls Sedulius conspicuous, Theodulf seems to call the same man red-haired, perhaps in imitation of Fortunatus, whom he likewise names. Arntzenius, in his preface to Sedulius, p. 9, does not approve this interpretation.

101. Notker Balbulus, volume I, column 9 of Bernard Pez’s *Treasure of Anecdotes*, chapter 7 of the book *On the Interpretation of Scripture*:

> I know that you have already committed Juvencus, Sedulius, Arator, and the Ambrosian hymns to memory.

The passage is corrupt. I read: “Juvencus and Sedulius, Arator and the hymns,” etc. Notker was writing to his pupil Solomon, later bishop of the Church of Constance.

102. Luitprand, in *Lives of the Pontiffs*, chapter 51, concerning Gelasius:

> He also praises the History of Orosius, and the work of Sedulius and Juvencus.

[Col. 0045A]

103. Honorius of Autun, book I, chapter 84, from Jerome:

> Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter of very noble birth, composed the four Gospels in hexameter verse, together with certain other works in the same meter relating to the order of the sacraments. He flourished under Constantine.

104. Francesco Petrarch, *Eclogue* 10, entitled “The Setting Laurel,” says this about many Christian poets and finally about Juvencus:

> Far away there, across the river, apart among the tombs of kings,  
> there was a radiant Arator of the divine field,  
> plowing the rich soil with a rough plowshare.  
> With him on one side Prudens, on the other a second Sedulius,  
> competed, as they plowed, to tear up the clods with the stiff rake.  
> The land was fertile and the oxen weary; nowhere were laurel,  
> ivy, or myrtle. For the green glory of the garland is not a fragile Muse’s pursuit or voice, but a threshing-floor fresh with a sacred spring, and a lofty house; then a green pinewood spread broadly,  
> with sweet olive trees; and on the bright threshold stood a Virgin,  
> nurturing in her rosy bosom a comely child.  
> This was the matron who consecrated to the temple golden fruits,  
> gathered in remote gardens, in wicker baskets.  
> I shall tell wonders, beyond belief; but here I saw the poems  
> of the Spanish Juvencus, who sang in our tongue alike  
> of the man, the eagle, the ox, and the lion.

105. Baptista Mantuanus, in the *Apology*, volume I of his works:

> I am certain that I would rather be criticized with these outstanding men than, together with you, my censors, be praised by the ignorant crowd. I wish to set before their eyes the Spanish Juvencus, whom Jerome lists among illustrious men and in the catalogue of the most learned, so that what Persius says may happen to them: “Let them see virtue and waste away because they have abandoned it.” Come forth, our Zoili: behold a man initiated into sacred mysteries, crowned with laurel, surrounded on every side by the Muses, holding a lyre. Hurry to this rare and great spectacle, but take care not to condemn him suddenly. He is praised by Jerome. This man, then, encloses the immense majesty of the evangelical law in heroic verse; and other Christians, men both most serious and most holy, have done the same.

106. Johann Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Juvencus the presbyter, Spanish by nationality, a noble man and a most learned philosopher, poet, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, venerable to the Church no less for his conduct than for his knowledge of Scripture, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in meter and in prose; but only a few of them have come to my attention. I have read a notable work that he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses: *Four Books on the Four Gospels*; *Nothing Is Immortal*; *Two Books on the Sacraments*. The other works he is said to have composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330.

I have not read elsewhere that Juvencus composed anything in prose. It is certainly false that the *Evangelical History*, as Trithemius implies, consists of hexameter and pentameter verses.

107. Petrus Crinitus, *On Latin Poets*, book V, chapter 89:

> Juvencus the poet was Spanish by nationality and was born into a distinguished and highly illustrious family, as Jerome relates. He flourished especially under the emperors Constantius and Constans; at that time Tiberianus, Nazarius, and Flavius Vopiscus were famous in Latin eloquence—the latter having composed books on the deeds of the Roman emperors. Among the other poems said to have been published by him, he wrote the four Gospels in hexameter verse. In this work he showed greater diligence in preserving the historical narrative than in displaying the elegance of his own talent. The same Juvencus composed several hymns, by which he clearly showed that he had rendered excellent service to the Christian religion. There is no doubt that he was counted among the Christian priests, as the ancient authors testify. The divine Jerome repeats Juvencus’ poems in places and commends him as a learned and elegant poet.

108. Reinhard Lorichius Hadamarius, in the dedicatory letter to Johann Count of Vueda prefixed to his edition of Juvencus:

> It is much safer and more prudent to cling to those authors who, according to what is said, have never been deprived of their position by the judgment of the most learned men, and who have flourished and become renowned for many centuries. If our Juvencus and Sedulius do not hold the first places among them, they will certainly, in my judgment, not be among the last. One of them the divine Jerome praised in more than one place, as though he were worthy, as they say, of an Argive shield; the other the reverent decrees of the holiest Fathers raised to the heavens with their praises. Even if they do not seem to satisfy minds that delight excessively in ornate verbal display, minds that flatter and indulge themselves in delicacies more through elegance of speech than through devotion—if they do not thunder everywhere with pompous verbal apparatus—they will compensate for everything by the abundant and conspicuous fruit of truth and holiness . . . Although nothing occurs here that, taken from these authors and instilled in purified ears, could cause offense. For there is nothing alien to pure Latinity, nothing alien to the laws of poetry, nothing barbarous, nothing unusual that, like a reef, he would say must be avoided. A lucid phrase shines forth, and the language is free from every fault. There is no lack of an ornate dignity of words and things in which even the more exacting critics would find satisfaction. All these features make the work more commendable and, as though bringing in the sun, illuminate the history of evangelical truth, expressed in verses full of venerable majesty.

109. Eustathius Swartius, *Analects*, book II, chapter 15:

> The sweetness of the Christian name in Paulinus makes one eager to take up another swan of the true Apollo. I know he will not be the greatest of poets. Yet he will be such a poet as the true judges of poets may prefer to love, even for the simplicity of his style, rather than certain swellings and affected—not grave, but leaden—difficulty of some other singers, who, while dreaming of nothing but eagles, become carrion vultures, handling every elegance with their foul claws, so that among the common people there follows a reputation for virtue, while among the learned there is nothing but contempt for ugly, rapacious disorder. The man we have said we will take up is the good Juvencus, the pious and gentle herald of the pious emperor Constantine.

110. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLIII, chapter 23, column 1973:

> Juvencus is a poet considerably more learned than people generally think, although he restrains his style and strives to retain the very words of Sacred Scripture.

And book LXIX, chapter 5, column 2777:

> With the assistance of an excellent manuscript of Juvencus, we have discussed certain matters concerning the *Evangelical History* in the preceding books. We shall add more in this chapter to the ancient writer, esteemed by the ancients, and to his work. Nor should we be deterred by the ravings of cloistered men who condemn this kind of author for the reason that, when speaking of divine matters, they do not speak with Maro, Ovid, or even Lucan rather than with Paul, Isaiah, and Matthew—obviously so that they may make themselves seem princes of Roman eloquence by such contempt. For these men, having read scarcely a third of the three writers, claim the right to judge them all; and the style of true piety proves its own simplicity even in the chairs of the Tullians. We shall discuss this matter elsewhere in such a way, I think, that those censorious lemures will voluntarily surrender a large part of their arrogance out of shame at their own stupidity.

It must also be counted to Juvencus’ credit that not only Barthius and Swartius, just mentioned, have illuminated many passages of his, but also Grunerus, Arntzenius, Vonckius, and others. Some also attempted an edition of Juvencus but did not complete it, such as Johann Weitz, concerning whom see the note on book I, verse 13.

111. It is easy to add further testimonies, but it is by no means necessary. It will suffice to indicate some others: Platina, in the Life of Pope Mark I; Lil. Gregorius Gyraldus, *History of the Poets*, dialogue 5; Johann Peter Lonchius, *Poetic Library*, part I, p. 76; Andreas Wilkins, *Heortography*, part I, p. 201; Gerardus Johannes Vossius, *On Latin Poetry*, chapter 4; Johann Gottfried Olearius, in the *Abacus of Patrology*, p. 283; Olaus Borrichius, *Academic Dissertation on Poets*, p. 69. Add to these Volaterranus, Eisengrein, Bergomensis, Sixtus of Siena, the Centuriators, Baronius, Scaliger, Possevinus, and countless others [Col. 0047C]. Nor should one omit those whose words in praise of Juvencus we have cited in their appropriate places: Barthius, Prolegomena no. 12; Gallandi, no. 16; Felicius, Ferrarius, and Maurolycus, no. 31; the bishop of Equilium, no. 32; Tarafa, no. 36; Busch, no. 55; Faustus, no. 56; Barthius, on book I, verses 9, 245, 399, and 683; book II, verses 2 and 61; book IV, verses 62 and 93; Badius, on book I, verse 9, and elsewhere.

112. It should therefore matter little to us that some seem to judge Juvencus’ style incorrectly, since even these men themselves do not at all deny the benefit that can be gained from reading him. Johann Ludwig Vives, book III *On the Transmission of Learning*:

> Juvencus, Sedulius, Prosper, and Paulinus are muddy and troubled waters, yet health-giving, as they say of certain rivers.

Philippus Brietius, book IV *On Latin Poets*, on Juvencus and his style:

> He is somewhat lowly because he clings too closely to the words of the Gospel, and because he is more a lover of truth than of poetry; he confines himself too much in a poem more devout than elegant.

Alphonsus García Matamoros, *On the Academies and Learned Men of Spain*:

> Prudentius and Juvencus, if I may exercise free judgment in this matter, seem better versifiers than poets.

Dupin, in the *New Library*, volume I, calls Juvencus a poet of great value and the first of the Christians. He recognizes poetic spirit in his poem and praises the rhythm of its verses, but says that the words are not always poetic and sometimes not even Latin. Nevertheless, he adds that it could scarcely have been possible to enclose the Gospel words in verse more effectively or faithfully [Col. 0048A]. Ceillier, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume IV, says that Juvencus is charged with a low style, neglect of poetic ornament, and faults of meter and Latinity.

113. This place would call for a discussion of Juvencus’ prosody and Latinity. But I have said a good deal about the style and poetry of Christian poets generally in the Prolegomena to Dracontius, and perhaps even too much in the Prolegomena to Prudentius. I shall therefore abstain from that discussion all the more willingly at present, because the supposed faults of meter and Latinity that the ignorant—or, which amounts to the same thing, the half-learned—judge to be present are far rarer in Juvencus than in Dracontius, Prudentius, or any other Christian poet.

## CHAPTER V. A passage of Matthew, chapter XX, verse 28, read differently by Juvencus from the way it is now read in the Vulgate.

[Col. 0048B]

114. Peter Sabatier, against Bentley and Casley, learnedly and forcefully confirms in the preface to volume III of the ancient Italian version, drawn from old manuscripts, that a Latin translation of Sacred Scripture, called the *Itala*, existed before St. Jerome and perhaps originated as early as the times of the Apostles. Juvencus, as I shall say more fully later, followed this old Latin version rather than the Greek copies of the New Testament; at any rate, he often agrees with it. The notable passage that I shall now present is from Matthew, chapters XX, verses 27–29.

115. The Vulgate reads:

> And whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant. Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many. And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him.

The old Itala version from the Colbertine manuscript reads:

> And whoever wishes . . . for many. But you seek to grow from the little and to become smaller from the greater. When entering and being invited to a dinner, do not recline in the more distinguished places, lest someone more eminent than you should arrive; and when the one who invited you to dinner approaches, he says to you: “Move farther down”; and you are put to shame. But if you recline in a lower place, and someone humbler than you arrives, the one who invited you to dinner says to you: “Move farther up,” and it will be more advantageous for you. And as they were going out from Jericho, many crowds followed him.

116. As is well known, Juvencus chiefly follows Matthew. Accordingly, take his verses from book III, verse 608:

> No one can be first unless he serves all,  
> nor can anyone alone be first. Thus the Son of Man, as a servant in obedience to you,  
> alone performs his own pious duties,  
> and for many lays down his life in precious blood.  
> But you wish to rise from the least possessions,  
> and, thus falling from the highest, you grasp the lowest.  
> If anyone invites you, setting out a dinner banquet,  
> let no one who has understanding place his limbs  
> in the highest seats, etc.

It is clear from Juvencus that the words missing from the Vulgate formerly existed in the Itala. Many other manuscripts of the ancient version confirm the same point.

117. There is, however, some difference in these words: “But you seek to grow from the little and to become smaller from the greater.” Thus it is read in the Colbertine manuscript, except that Sabatier corrected the error *minor esse* (“to be smaller”) to *minores esse* (“to become smaller”), for, as he says, it was plainly a slip of the pen. Corbeiensis 2 and Claromontanus read exactly:

> But you seek to grow from the little and to become smaller from the greater.

Corbeiensis 1 alone changes *quaeritis* (“you seek”) to *quaeretis* (“you will seek”), and *de majore minores fieri* (“to become smaller from the greater”) for *esse* (“to be”). The Cambridge manuscript has:

> But you seek to grow from the least and to become less from the great,

which amounts to the same thing. The sense is clearer in Sangermanensis 1:

> But you seek to grow from the little and to become greater from the lesser,

and in the index of chapters, article 58:

> Concerning the sons of Zebedee: and concerning becoming greater from the least; and concerning the two blind men.

The manuscript of the monastery of St. Andrew near Avignon supports this:

> But you seek to grow from the little and to be greater from the great.

118. St. Leo seems to have read it both ways. In letter 18, to Dorus, bishop of Beneventum, when rebuking presbyters who rashly surrendered their rights and honor, he says:

> For you were not unaware that the Lord said, “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted,” and that he also said, “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled.” But you seek to grow from the little and to become smaller from the greater. For both things are disordered, both are contrary to proper sequence.

So he read the passage, and Quesnellus defends this reading against others, who had published: “to grow from the little and to become greater in honor.” The same St. Leo, in letter 79 to Pulcheria, chapter 2, writes:

> These things were then being impressed upon those who wished to grow from the little and to pass from the lowest to the highest.

Quesnellus denies that the words “to pass from the lowest to the highest” are an explanation of “to become greater from the lesser.” Rather, he says, it seems certain that they are nothing other than a repetition of the earlier words in different terms; he attempts to prove this from the sequence and context of the letter. Richard Simon, in his *Observations on the Text and Versions of the New Testament*, chapter 21, disagrees with Quesnellus. The critical dissertation of Simon, at the end of the same work, should also be consulted; there he responds to the difficulties raised by Antoine Arnauld concerning the Cambridge manuscript. Against Simon, however, there appeared a *Critical Dissertation Concerning the Greek Copies on Which Mr. Simon Claims that the Ancient Vulgate Was Based, and Concerning the Judgment to Be Made of the Famous Manuscript of Beza*—in French, *Dissertation critique touchant les exemplaires grecs, sur lesquels M. Simon prétend que l’ancienne Vulgate a été faite, et sur le jugement que l’on doit faire du fameux manuscrit de Bèze*—Cologne, 1691.

[Col. 0049D]

119. Juvencus follows and explains the reading of the Colbertine manuscript:

> But you wish to rise from the least possessions.

That is: “But you seek to grow from the little.”

> And thus, having fallen from the highest, you grasp the lowest.

That is plainly: “And to become smaller from the greater.”

Sabatier comments as follows:

> This verse plainly renders the sense of our Colbertine manuscript: “And to become smaller from the greater”; indeed, it makes it clearer. For although this may at first sight have some obscurity in the Latin manuscript, as Juvencus now expresses it, it offers nothing that impedes the sense. It can be understood as though it said: “With the very ambition by which you seek to rise from the little, you seek to fall, and to become smaller from the greater.” Or: “By the very means by which you seek to rise from the little, you fall by those same means, and you are smaller from the greater.”

This interpretation is confirmed by the example that follows, of the man who, when invited to dinner, takes the first place and is thrown down from it.

120. The Anglo-Saxon version of Matthew in four manuscripts, cited by Thomas Marescallus, is not far removed from this sense:

> You desire to grow in small matters and to become less in great matters.

In the London Polyglot Bibles, volume VI, almost exactly the same words as in the Colbertine manuscript are also given in Greek from three copies:

> But you seek, etc.

Joseph Blanchini, in the *Fourfold Gospel*, likewise reads the passage from the Veronese and Vercelli manuscripts together with the Colbertine manuscript and Juvencus:

> But you seek to grow from the little and to become greater from the lesser;

and he states that this reading exists in two Bodleian manuscripts, as others also report. The Vercelli manuscript, said to have been written by the hand of St. Eusebius, was also collated by Andrea Irici, who discusses this very addition in his preface and notes.

121. What follows in the ancient Italic version of the Colbertine manuscript—“But when entering, and when invited to the dinner,” etc.—has likewise been expressed by Juvencus: “If any one of you invites,” etc. Although similar words are read in Luke, chapter 14, verses 8 and following, Sabatier nevertheless proves that Juvencus took this from Matthew. For, after expressing the former addition in two verses, he immediately added: “If any one of you invites,” etc. And, leaving aside the following verses of Matthew chapter 20, in which the healing of the two blind men is narrated, he proceeds at once to Matthew chapter 21, which corresponds to Luke chapter 19, and not to what follows in Luke chapter 14, where the first place at table is discussed.

122. Two Corbie manuscripts, the manuscript of the Monastery of Saint Andrew near Avignon, the Clermont manuscript, and the Cambridge manuscript agree with the Colbertine manuscript. Of the Sangerman manuscripts, the larger one, no. 15, has the earlier addition: “But you seek,” etc.; no. 55, however, does not have this second one, “But when entering, and when invited,” etc. Conversely, the smaller Sangerman manuscript, without a numerical designation, records this second addition, “But when entering,” while omitting the earlier one, “But you seek.” All these manuscripts differ from the Colbertine in the second addition only in wording or in the order of the words; in substance and sense they agree with it.

This same parable at the place cited in Matthew is read in the Greek text of the London Polyglot Bibles, volume VI, and in the Anglo-Saxon version translated by Marescallus. The same passage is indicated by three chapter lists prefixed to the Gospel of Matthew in the Colbertine manuscript and in two Corbie manuscripts. Hilary also, in his commentary on Matthew, although he passes over the earlier addition, “But you seek,” explicitly explains this other one; and in the chapter headings prefixed to Hilary’s commentary on Matthew, no. 20, we read: “Concerning the sons of Zebedee; concerning the first place at table; concerning the two blind men.”

Two old manuscripts used by Blanchinius in the *Fourfold Gospel* present this second addition together with the earlier one: “But when entering, and when invited to the dinner,” etc. Two other Latin manuscripts of the Bodleian Library, cited by Blanchinius, agree with them.

In the library of the most sacred prince, Our Lord Pius VI, filled with rare and select books, I consulted the Greek New Testament with variant readings and commentary by Johann Jakob Wettstein, Amsterdam, 1751; then the *Four Gospels in Greek with Variant Readings from the Manuscript Text*, Copenhagen, 1788, prepared by Andreas Birch; and further the Greek and Latin New Testament from manuscripts never previously examined, for the most part from Moscow manuscripts, edited by Christian Friedrich Matthaei at Riga, in octavo. The volume containing the Gospel of Matthew appeared in 1788.

The manuscripts of Friedrich Matthaei and Birch agree with the Vulgate. Birch alone indicates, from the margin of manuscript Assemanianus 1 of the Philoxenian Syriac version: “But you seek to be increased from the least and to be diminished from the great,” together with the following parable. Wettstein found: “But you seek to grow from the least and to become less from the greater,” together with the remaining addition, in the Royal manuscript 3935, the Colbertine 4051 and 1895, and in the manuscript of the College of Louis the Great, then belonging to the Jesuits.

## CHAPTER VI. The usefulness of collating the manuscript codices of Juvencus. The method of this edition.

123. Those who were the first to commit ancient authors to print, having obtained one or another manuscript exemplar—often faulty, sometimes mutilated—frequently corrected and supplemented the works themselves as the sense seemed to require, without warning readers at which points they had departed from the manuscript codices. Worth reading is the dissertation of Johann Michael Heusinger, part 1 of the *Acta of the Latin Society of Jena*, p. 40: “Concerning Greek and Roman authors not yet sufficiently emended according to the authority of ancient exemplars.” What Barthius thought in this matter of the Aldine editions, we saw above, no. 61. The same Barthius argues, p. 2778, against the grammatical fastidiousness of Georg Fabricius in publishing and correcting Christian poets at will; we shall cite him at book I, verse 179.

Arntzenius, together with Johann Albert Fabricius and Daumius, observed in the preface to his edition of Sedulius—and Gretserus had observed it long before—that G. Fabricius was excessively ingenious in works belonging to others that he edited. In publishing Juvencus, Faber Stapulensis likewise confesses this about himself, as I noted in no. 53: “For what has been altered in it, and what has been added to the imperfect verses because of the corruption of the exemplar, I cannot easily say.” Re-read, in no. 51, Gruner’s judgment on the edition of Juvencus prepared by Reusch.

124. If any other author needs a careful recension, Juvencus above all does. For from the alteration of a single word a substantially different interpretation of Sacred Scripture may arise. Thus Barthius, in book 29 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, having observed that in book I, verse 171, an old philologist had written *dedecus oppressum* (“disgrace oppressed”) in the margin of the parchment, added *dedecus oppressae* (“the disgrace of the oppressed woman”): “For by this reading violence is indicated as having been inflicted upon the Virgin, as it seemed to that good Joseph; and this made the betrothed Virgin more excusable in his mind, which was wandering from the truth of the matter, yet even in that falsehood excusable.”

Readings of this kind must therefore be examined more carefully than if one were dealing with some other author, especially in such sacred mysteries. Moreover, many scribes and early editors, accustomed to our Vulgate reading, often brought Juvencus’s words into conformity with it, although he himself followed the ancient Italic version and sometimes said something entirely different from what now appears in printed editions, as I shall demonstrate from manuscripts in many places.

125. Some maintain that by recording such variant readings everything is rendered uncertain and turned upside down. Whether they sufficiently understand what they are saying is uncertain to me. For what of it? Since it is established that the writings of the ancients have been corrupted in many places by the ignorance, carelessness, or perversity of copyists, and also by the ravages of time, is it not better, insofar as possible, to distinguish the true from the false, the certain from the uncertain, the probable from the absurd, than to accept everything without any examination?

Nor would I deny that one can also err in this undertaking. Barthius’s judgment should by no means be despised, book 36 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 20, column 1669: “And indeed I shall say this once for all: too much is attributed by most people devoted to these studies to those blind books. I do not indeed think that the judgments of variant readings are to be blamed, but that they should be assessed by everyone is plainly the source of boundless uncertainty. And matters have now reached the point that no one wishes to belong to any one of them; so much do they all seem to want to have dreamed upon that two-headed mountain.”

126. For my part, in recording the variant readings of old editions, and especially of the manuscript codices that I have examined, I have resolved to employ the greatest diligence. This may perhaps seem excessive to those occupied with other matters, but it is by no means useless, so that critical scholars may form a judgment about the whole matter.

Among differing scriptural readings, after collating manuscript exemplars, I generally select the one that comes closest to the ancient Italic version of the Gospels used by Juvencus; nor do I regret spending time explaining it. Both in the variant readings and in the notes appended below, apart from matters relating to Latin and prosody, I undertake especially to elucidate those passages that contain some distinctive interpretation of Sacred Scripture adopted by Juvencus.

His authority must be regarded as highly important both in establishing the true reading of Sacred Scripture and in explaining its meaning. For Juvencus flourished at a time when the copies of Sacred Scripture were less corrupt; and since he deliberately undertook the difficult task of harmonizing the Gospels, it is reasonable to believe that he had highly approved exemplars before his eyes and adopted those interpretations that at that time prevailed most strongly in the Church among its holiest and most eminent men.

Although among the Greeks the heretic Tatian, Ammonius of Alexandria, and Theophilus of Antioch are said to have composed a harmony of the four Gospels, among the Latins before Juvencus we read of no one who undertook such an arduous and difficult work. Calmet provides a sufficiently extensive catalogue of those who prepared evangelical harmonies after Juvencus in the *Bibliotheca sacra*, before the *Biblical Dictionary*.

127. Since old editions and manuscript codices are generally indicated by the first letters of their names, it will be useful to add the following table for the convenience of readers:

**ALD.** Aldus’s edition. See no. 60.  
**BARTH.** Barthius’s *Adversaria*.  
**BAS.** Basel edition of 1537. See no. 68.  
**CA. CANT.** Cambridge manuscripts in Reusch. See no. 86.  
**DAVENTR.** Daventry edition, as I believe. See no. 61.  
**FABR.** Fabricius (Georgius), in the *Corpus of Christian Poets*. See no. 77.  
**FAUST.** Faustus’s edition. See nos. 54 and following.  
**FULD.** Fulda manuscript. See no. 86.  
**GALLAND.** Gallandi’s edition. See no. 87.  
**HAD.** Hadamar’s edition. See no. 69.  
**HELMST.** Helmstedt manuscript. See no. 86.  
**OTT.** Vatican Ottobonian manuscript. See no. 49.  
**POELM.** Poelmann’s edition. See no. 70.  
**REG.** Vatican manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden. See no. 48.  
**ROM.** Manuscript of the Roman College. See no. 50.  
**TORN.** Tornaesius’s edition. See nos. 76 and 78.  
**WESTHEM.** Westhemer’s edition. See no. 71.

128. I shall often have occasion to cite, through Sabatier, the manuscripts of the ancient Italic version of the Gospels: the Colbertine, the two Sangerman manuscripts, likewise the two Corbie manuscripts, the Cambridge, the Clermont, the manuscript of Fosses-Saint-Maur, those of Saint Gatianus, Saint Martin, and the Major Monastery of Tours. This much it is sufficient to have noted, so that when the designations or initial letters of these manuscripts occur, the reader may readily understand them for himself.

Sabatier labels the Italic version “the ancient version” and our Vulgate “the new Vulgate”—not because the latter is actually new; for it is ancient, as the Council of Trent says, session 4, decree on the edition and use of the sacred books, and has been approved in the Church by the long usage of so many centuries—but Sabatier likes to speak in this way in order to distinguish the Vulgate from the more ancient Italic version.

The question may be raised here whether Juvencus then used the Italic version, which was commonly employed, or Greek exemplars of the New Testament. Calmet, under the entry “Latin Bibles,” writes as follows:

“These Latin versions were needed only by uneducated people; for the educated, being distinguished by birth and status and knowing the Greek language, had no need to resort to a translation. Moreover, there were many Latin versions, not even produced by the most learned men, as Saint Augustine testifies, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 11, no. 16: ‘Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted; but the Latin translators cannot be counted at all. For as soon as a Greek codex came into anyone’s hands in the earliest times of the faith, and he seemed to possess some ability in both languages, he ventured to translate it.’”

Hence arose astonishing confusion and disorder, so that there were almost as many exemplars as codices, as Jerome says in the preface to the four Gospels.

Nevertheless, I believe that Juvencus did consult Greek exemplars but chiefly followed the Italic version. Although there were several other Latin versions, the one called Italic surpassed the others and was valued even by learned men because it was more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning, as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 15, book II.

Indeed, Juvencus often openly departs from the Scripture found in the Greek codices in order to preserve a reading that is retained in most of the ancient manuscripts of the Italic version. The variation found among the old Latin exemplars, however, does not prove that there were different versions, just as similar variation in the Greek text does not prove that the text itself was different.

129. In the notes I often refer the reader to the notes on the commentary on Prudentius and to the notes on Dracontius, so as not to repeat what has already been done and cause the work to expand by useless bulk. For I edit Juvencus in such a way that, together with Prudentius and Dracontius, he forms a continuous part of one body of Christian poets.

## C. VETTIUS AQUILINUS JUVENCUS, HISPANIC PRESBYTER, FOUR BOOKS OF EVANGELICAL HISTORY

### Preface

**[Note: [Col. 0053]]**

*(Verse 1).* The manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden and Barthius write *Matheus*, and some teach that it should be written in that form. Poelmannus and Reuschius wrongly established *Mathaeus*. Fabricius, by conjecture, I think, reads: “Matthew established the morals of virtue by a path.”

**[Note: [Col. 0053]]**

*(Verse 1).* I discussed this first preface in the *Prolegomena*, no. 48. Sabatier, in the *Bibliotheca sacra of the Latin versions*, at the beginning of the Gospel of Saint Mark, brought forth from a very old Sangerman manuscript the first two verses:

“Matthew established,” etc.,

which are immediately followed by two others concerning Saint Mark, in this sense:

“Mark roars from his mouth like a lion, and like one bellowing—  
He thunders forth, opening the mysteries of eternal life.”

Sabatier entirely omits the remaining verses concerning the other two Evangelists. That verse, however, “Mark roars,” etc., is abnormal and corrupt. Barthius, book 11 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 23, transcribed almost eight complete verses from a manuscript of Juvencus, nearly as they appear in Poelmannus. Reusch likewise testifies that the same epigram is found in the Cambridge and Helmstedt manuscripts of Juvencus.

He also observes that in the first two verses Juvencus wishes to indicate, although he does not express it, that Matthew is signified in the form of a man on Ezekiel’s wheel; he chiefly infers this from the words of the following verse, “in proper order.”

### 61

Matthew established the morals of virtue by a path,

And gave laws for right living in proper order.

**[Note: [Col. 0055A]]**

3. See *Reg.*, above *volare*, whether it is a gloss or a correction. Fabricius: “Mark roars from his pious mouth, resembling a lion—He resounds, opening the mysteries of eternal life.” Fabricius, verses 7 and 8, assigns the eagle to John, as do many others.

6. Poelmannus reads corruptly *jura sacer*. Fabricius: “the calf, which is carried beside the walls.” Poelmannus: “the calf, which speaks beside the walls.” *Reg.* and Barthius: “the calf, which speaks the ancestral walls.” So also the Cambridge manuscript, but with *quia* for *qui*. By conjecture: “which speaks the duties of Abijah,” or “which speaks the gifts of Abijah,” with *Abia* used adjectivally; or *moenera* in the old manner for *munera* (“gifts”), or *moenia* for *munia* (“duties”). Perhaps *Abia* is also used indeclinably, as in book I, verse 141: “Elizabeth,” and in Luke: “of the division of Abijah.”

7–8. Fabricius: “John loves to fly between earth and heaven—And the powerful eagle cuts through everything in its swift descent.”

**[Note: [Col. 0055B]]**

The figure of the lion is customarily assigned to Mark and that of the eagle to John, also in ancient paintings. Juvencus judges otherwise. An ancient glossator in Barthius’s manuscript adds the following interpretation:

“Matthew, because he was more concerned with morals than the other Evangelists, is therefore designated by a rational animal, that is, a man. Mark is said to fly between heaven and earth. Since he did not describe the birth of the Word, in which the deity assumed the earth of our flesh, as Matthew and Luke did, he seems not to have touched the earth. And because he said little about divinity, he did not penetrate heaven as John did. He is compared to an eagle because of the speed of his narrative, since he is brief in everything.

“Luke bears the figure of a calf, which is accustomed to be slaughtered in the temple, because he describes more fully what the Lord did in the temple and around the temple, and speaks more extensively about the Lord’s passion. John is expressed by a lion, because he uttered something like a lion’s roar when he said, ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ No one, so far as I know, denies the calf to Luke.”

Thomasius also affirms in his dissertation on the four insignia of the Evangelists that everyone assigns the figure of an ox to Luke. Augustine, in *On John*, chapter 8, tractate 36, assigns a lion to Matthew, not a man; and it can be confirmed that a few others made the same assertion. Most, with Jerome, assign a man to Matthew. Barthius says that some attach an angel to Matthew. Yet among the four commonly accepted insignia of the Evangelists, an angel has no place.
