Irenaeus, book 3 of *Against Heresies*, chapter 11, held the opinion of Juvencus, who assigns the lion to John and the eagle to Mark; Augustine indicates the same opinion in book 1 of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 6, although he approves it less. Thomasius, in the work cited, attacks the same view and rails against this epigram of ours, as though it had been composed by some trifler after Augustine. But I shall attach little weight to the judgment of a man who thought he had produced something substantial when he concluded his attack with the words, “But hands off the tablet,” and signed at the very bottom: “Erasmus, in the *Adages*.”

4. By “swift descent” I understand rapid descent, just as a tightly stretched or drawn rein is called *stricta*. *Stricto* may also be taken to mean “brief”; the following verse suggests this.

5. Luke is more expansive than Mark. “The battles of Christ” are perhaps mentioned here because, as Petrus Aurorarius, or of Riga, says in the prologue to the Gospels, cited by Barthius in the place mentioned, Luke is designated by the sacrificial ox, which “took special matter from your cross, O Christ.”

6. Luke, chapter 1, verse 5: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah,” etc. Abijah was one of the descendants of Eleazar, son of Aaron, and head of the eighth priestly class in David’s distribution, 1 Chronicles 24:21. Since Luke therefore begins with a sacrifice and with the priest of the division of Abijah, the sacred calf is said to “speak the duties of Abijah,” or “because it speaks the duties of Abijah,” as Reinesius corrected it, cited by Thomasius in the place mentioned.

7. Some think that the first syllable in *rugio* must necessarily be long. Perhaps for this reason Fabricius omitted this word in his version of Mark. Following his example, the verse could be recast as:

“John roars from his pious mouth, resembling a lion.”

But “resembling one who roars” is satisfactory, either because the verse may be spondaic, with synaeresis in *rugienti*, or because the first syllable of *rugio* is in fact short. The author of the poem on Philomela, among Ovid’s poems, has in some editions, verse 49:

“Untamed tigresses snarl, and lions roar,”

where either the first syllable is shortened or synaeresis occurs in *rugiunt*.

8. It should be noted that the four Evangelists are listed in this epigram in the order in which they now appear in the sacred Scriptures. In the Cambridge manuscript of the Gospels and in another Corbie manuscript cited by Sabatier, at the beginning of the Gospel of Saint Mark, the order of the Evangelists is changed: Matthew appears first, then John, then Luke, and finally Mark.

The Gospels are listed in the same order in the very ancient Vercelli manuscript, in which *Lucanus* is written instead of *Lucas*. Iricius demonstrates in his preface, drawing on Garbellus in a letter to Blanchinius and on others, that this arrangement was once customary in many churches.

This has led me to suspect whether this same order may have been observed by Juvencus and later inverted by someone who wished to arrange the names of the Evangelists according to the customary order. It could thus have happened that Juvencus assigned the eagle to John and the lion to Mark, but that later, after the order of the names had been reversed, the figures too were applied in a different manner, as the author of the epigram intended.

The variation among the readings, which I have recorded from Fabricius and other manuscripts and printed editions, supports this view. On the figures of the four animals by which the four Evangelists are distinguished, see Barthius, book 11 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 23; Jacobus Thomasius, in the dissertation held under his presidency at Leipzig in 1667 and printed in 1671, *On the Insignia of the Four Evangelists*; and his program on the Four Animals of Ezekiel, among the *Dissertations on Various Subjects*, no. 38, and in the *Theological-Philological Thesaurus*, or *Collection of Dissertations*, volume II, p. 57.

Ambrose, in the prologue to Luke, expresses the sense of our epigram in nearly the same way:

“And thus in the individual books the form of the animals is represented, so that the course of each book seems to correspond to the nature, virtue, grace, or miracle of the animal proposed. Although all these qualities are present in all of them, nevertheless in each there is a certain fullness of its particular virtue. One author described the origin of the man more fully and instructed human morals with richer precepts. Another began with an expression of divine power: the king from the king, the strong one from the strong, the true one from the true, who in living power despised death. A third set forth the priestly sacrifice first and unfolded the very slaughter of the calf in a fuller style. The fourth expressed more abundantly than the others the divine miracles of the resurrection.”

Ambrose, however, does not depart from the common view in assigning the insignia of the Evangelists.

### 62

Mark loves to fly between earth and heaven,

And the powerful eagle cuts through everything in swift descent.

[5] Luke describes the battles of Christ more fully;

Rightly the sacred calf, which speaks the duties of Abijah.

John roars from his mouth like a lion, resembling one who roars;

He thunders forth, opening the mysteries of eternal life.

10. The Ottobonian manuscript has *orbes*, correctly emended by another hand.

12. The old edition of Faustus has *non* in place of *nam*, incorrectly.

13. Aldus, the manuscript of the Roman College, and the Tornaesian edition have *rapiat*, which are supported by *Reg.* and *Ott.*; others have *rapiet*.

15. Faustus’s edition has *frequentent*, incorrectly.

16. Faustus’s edition has *quorum et famam*.

17. *Reg.* has the corrupt reading *fluentae*. The copyist perhaps intended *fluente*.

19. Poelmannus and Fabricius have *decurrit*. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, Barthius, Aldus, and others have *discurrit*, which also appears in Faustus and Poelmannus as a variant reading. *Discurrit* is preferable, also in Barthius’s judgment: for Juvencus says that fame is diffused through all the spaces of the world, spreading the glory of poets.

**[Note: [Col. 0057B]]**

9. Barthius explains these verses in book 11 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 23. He begins as follows:

“I possess old parchment manuscripts of the four books of Aquilius Juvencus, in which he chiefly followed Matthew and embraced evangelical history in simple meter. Yet he did not write so un-Latinly that there are not in him many traces even of the ancient language used before the age of Maro; hence I am led by conjecture to think that many barbarisms found in this author belong to barbarous monks. Our book is an excellent one, and from it many corrupt passages in this ancient and pious poet can be corrected.”

He observes that *compage* designates a firmly joined connection, as in Sedulius, book 5, verse 266:

“The infernal roads lay open, and, split apart, gape—  
The rocks divided in their solid structure.”

Badius Ascensius says that the author in this prologue easily shows what kind of talent he possesses and how golden a vein he has for poetry, unless he prefers to restrain it by the faith that captivates every understanding and by evangelical sobriety. One can scarcely find anything either more sententious or more delightful than this proem.

Bede, *On Meter*, in the chapter on scansion, gives this verse as an example: “The connected scansion,” he says, “which is considered more praiseworthy than the others, is that in which a foot nowhere ends with a word, as in ‘Nothing immortal,’ etc.”

10. In Barthius’s very old book there was a gloss: “This is joined because Rome was commonly called the eternal city.” Nothing could be more appropriate, as Barthius notes. Juvencus set down the three greatest things that he could, and those which possess—or rather once possessed—the greatest appearance of eternity.

On old coins bearing the inscription “Eternal Rome,” see the commentary on Prudentius, book 1 *Against Symmachus*, verse 219. There exists a book by Gabriel Barri Francicanus—under whose name the most learned Cardinal Sirletus is said to be concealed—*One Book on the Eternity of the City*. Rome, in the buildings of the Roman people, 1571.

Virgil, who so greatly proclaims the eternity of the Roman empire, nevertheless acknowledged that it would finally perish, book 2 of the *Georgics*, verse 498: “The Roman state and kingdoms destined to perish,” etc. Rome, called by Virgil in book 2 of the *Georgics*, verse 534, “the fairest of things,” is likewise called “golden” by others, with no dissimilar meaning. Ovid, *Art of Love*, book 3, verse 113:

“Once there was rustic simplicity; now golden Rome—  
She possesses the great wealth of the conquered world.”

Ausonius, *On Cities*:

“First among cities, glory of the gods, golden Rome.”

12. Lucretius, book 1, verse 469: “Past time, beyond recall.” In Juvencus, however, *irrevocabile* rather signifies something certainly determined and incapable of change. Livy, book 42, chapter 62: “He would surrender himself to an irreversible fate.” Pliny the Younger, book 3, letter 7: “He hastened toward death with irreversible constancy from weariness of illness,” with an alternative reading *decurrit*, which is better.

13. Among the pagans there was an opinion that the world would finally be consumed by flames, evidently derived from sacred authors, as I observed in the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn 11 of the Catholic Hymns*, verse 106. At that passage Weitzius cites Sophocles’ verses on the conflagration of the world, which, he says, he is adducing in his preface to Juvencus. From this it appears that he was preparing commentaries on Juvencus. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 37.

15. “For long ages,” but ages that will eventually have an end; for “nothing immortal is held together by the structure of the world.” The use of the verb *frequentant* in the sense of “celebrate” should be noted; Barthius had already noted it in the place cited. The same verb in this unfamiliar sense occurs in book I, verse 152; book II, verses 693 and 727; book III, verse 202; and book IV, verse 222.

Wittekind, book I: “They celebrated the name of the new king with a loud cry.” Nor is this without the support of better Latin usage, as Barthius proves from the author of the *Priapeia*, poem 76: “The daughters-in-law of Aetna celebrate Ceres.” More relevant to our subject is Sulpicia in the *Satire*: “Muse, with what meters do you celebrate heroes and arms?” So too *frequentare memoriam alicuius* (“to celebrate someone’s memory”) occurs in Seneca, *Consolation to Marcia*, chapter 3. *Frequentare* in the sense of “narrate” or “repeat” was also used by Vopiscus, Spartianus, and in the Theodosian Code, as Ducange demonstrates.

17. Smyrna was one of the cities that claimed Homer as a citizen. Statius, *Silvae*, book 4, poem 2, verse 9:

“Both Smyrna and Mantua weave garlands for the revered.”

Perhaps the reading is *odoratas* (“fragrant”) rather than *adoratas* (“revered”). Hence Homer was called the Smyrnaean poet. See Aulus Gellius, book 3, chapter 11, and Leo Allatius’s dissertation on Homer’s birthplace.

18. *Minciades*, *Minciadae*: a name formed by Juvencus from the river Mincius, which flows past Mantua. Juvencus mentions the spring of Smyrna and the river of Mantua so that at verse 34 he may conclude that the waters of the Jordan are superior for bringing eternal life to the flesh.

Nothing immortal is held together by the structure of the world,

[10] Neither the world, nor the kingdoms of men, nor golden Rome,

Neither the sea, nor the earth, nor the fiery stars of heaven.

For the Father of all things has established an irreversible time,

When the final torrent of flame shall carry away the entire world.

But nevertheless exalted deeds and virtue’s honor

[15] Celebrate countless men through long ages;

[65] Poets augment their fame and praises.

The lofty songs flowing from the spring of Smyrna celebrate these men;

The sweetness of the Mincian Maro celebrates those men.

Nor does the glory of those poets spread less widely,

[20] [Col. 0059A] [Note: [Col. 0059A]]

20. Barthius’s manuscript has *aeternum similis* (“like the eternal”), which Barthius rejects in book 11 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 23, because it would be harsher if *aeternum* were used for *aeternorum*. But in book 34, chapter 13, he prefers the poetic *aeternum similis*, because in this way Juvencus agrees better with other poets who say that the glory of poets is eternal. He understands *aeternum*, I think, as an adverb. I prefer *aeternae similis* (“like the eternal [glory]”); for that is what Juvencus means.

22. *Reg.*, *Ottob.*, Barthius, and the Roman manuscript have *jusso moderamine* (“by ordered governance”); most have *justo* (“by just governance”). Tornaesius had already printed *jusso*.

27. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, Barthius, and the Roman manuscript have *erit* (“will be”); commonly *erunt* (“will be,” plural).

28. In *Reg.*, *in* is absent. Poelmannus has *in populos* instead of *in populis*.

31. The manuscript of the Roman College has: “Here, when he descends flame-bearing.” *Reg.* has *coruscus* (“flashing”).

**[Note: [Col. 0059B]]**

20. Barthius observed, from this passage of Juvencus and by comparison with other passages by other authors, that it is the custom of poets to consider eternal whatever they sing, book 34 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 13, column 1568.

Propertius, book 3, elegy 1, concludes after much else:

“But the name won through genius does not fall away with time—  
Glory founded on genius stands without death.”

Ovid, book 1 of the *Amores*, elegy 15, verse 31:

“Though flint-stones, though the teeth of the enduring plow,  
Perish with time, poems are untouched by death.”

And in book 4 of the *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 8, verses 47 and following, he brings forward more in the same sense. Horace, book 4, ode 8:

“The Muse forbids the man worthy of praise to die;  
The Muse blesses him with heaven.”

So also Lucan and other poets everywhere.

21. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 2, verse 70:

“Add that heaven is carried along in constant rotation,  
And draws the high stars, turning them in swift revolution.”

*Polus* (“pole”) is derived from Greek πολέω (*poleō*, “I turn”).

22. *Aethera* is the singular accusative, frequently used by Latin poets in the Greek manner instead of *aetherem*. *Jussum* is said of *moderamen* so that we may understand the world to be governed by divine providence. Omeisius, who prefers *justo*, understands weight, measure, and number. Soon, at verse 41: *moderaminis aequi* (“of equal governance”); and book II, verse 577: *justo moderamine legis* (“you govern by a just law”).

23. These verses, up to the end of the prologue, are found in a certain Vatican manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 29, containing various works, especially metrical ones, including a poem by Petrus Aurorarius on both Testaments. First there is an elegiac epigram in praise of the sacred subject treated by poets:

“Let the golden songs of the Maeonian poet yield,” etc.;

then these verses of Juvencus, but without the author’s name. Strabo, *On the Life of Blessed Blaitmaicus*, section 3, part 2, in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*:

“If they earned such fame for their song,  
Who carried the morals and deeds of wicked men  
To heaven in praises,” etc.

25. Bede, *On Meter*, chapter on scansion, observes in this verse a mixed scansion, which contains both arrangements, so that in some places the foot is joined and in others separated.

26. Above he affirmed that nothing immortal is held together by the structure of the world. Now, however, he promises himself immortal glory from his evangelical poem, because, even when the world perishes in fire, he hopes to obtain eternal life in return for time so well spent.

It was customary for profane poets to promise themselves immortality of name through their poems. Lucan, book 9, verse 985:

“Our *Pharsalia* will live,  
And will be condemned to darkness by no age.”

Horace, book 3, final ode:

“I have built a monument more lasting than bronze,  
And higher than the royal structure of pyramids;  
Which neither consuming rain nor the unrestrained north wind  
Can destroy, nor the innumerable succession  
Of years and the flight of time.  
I shall not wholly die,” etc.

Ovid at the end of the *Metamorphoses*:

“And now I have completed a work which neither Jove’s anger nor fires,  
Nor iron nor devouring age will be able to destroy.  
When that day shall come which has power over nothing but this body,  
Let it end the uncertain span of my life.  
Yet in my better part I shall be borne eternal above the lofty stars,  
And my name shall be indestructible.”

Juvencus, imitating the pagan poets, directed the thought toward the goal to which all Christians ought to look exclusively: he desires only the glory that is established in eternal life and that we can attain through good works.

28. “Among the peoples,” because that gift had already been displayed to all nations; and therefore the expression is more meaningful than if we read *in populos*, as Reusch believes. “Without the guilt of falsehood,” because he derives his subject from the Gospels. Pagan poets and other profane writers generally weave lies into the deeds of men.

Dio Chrysostom wrote a speech on Troy not having been captured. Many call Virgil’s history into question and show that it is largely false with certainty. These two, Homer and Virgil, nevertheless obtained the chief glory among poets; for that reason Juvencus mentions them before all others.

30. Alcuin echoes Juvencus in a letter to a certain transalpine bishop, in Mabillon’s *Ancient Analecta*, Paris edition, 1733, p. 403:

“This is your work in the present light; this is your reward in eternal glory. For, as a certain poet says concerning the work of evangelical song:

‘This work—for perhaps it rescues me from the fire (read: “will rescue”)—  
When the flame-vomiting judge descends from his citadel.’

I too shall say:

‘This work—for it not only rescues you from the fire,  
But will make you ascend to the citadel of heaven.’”

Our own Saint Eulogius of Córdoba likewise writes at the beginning of the *Memorial of the Saints*:

“And just as I confess myself unworthy of so great a work, so also I trust that through its perfection I shall not only be freed from sins, but, drawn away from punishments, hope to find through its intervention with the Lord a more excellent grace; as in that philosophical saying:

‘This work will perhaps one day rescue me from the fire.’”

Here *olim* (“one day”) is used instead of *etenim* (“for indeed”), so that the thought may be concluded by this verse. Eulogius commonly calls Christians who excelled in learning, or who were teachers in the Church, “philosophers,” as Ambrosius Morales observes in his scholia on book I, no. 8.

Omeisius brings here Ovid’s verses from book 1 of the *Amores*, elegy 15, at the end:

“Therefore, even when the highest fire has consumed me,  
I shall live, and a great part of me shall survive.”

But Ovid is plainly speaking of the highest fire by which human bodies were formerly burned after death. I have collected more concerning such prayers, by which ancient ecclesiastical writers customarily sought pardon for the final day of judgment, in the *Prolegomena* to Prudentius, chapter 19, and in the notes on Dracontius, book 3, verse 681.

31. I do not know of any writer older than Juvencus who used *flammivomus* (“flame-vomiting”). Arator used the word in Book II, verse 531: “He lies beneath the flame-vomiting sun.” Some read *flammivolo sub sole* (“beneath the flame-flying sun”), as though it meant “flying with flames”; but *flammivomo* is more elegant. I find it not only in old printed editions but also in the Vatican manuscript codices. Likewise, the Roman College codex containing Arator, Juvencus, and Sedulius, which I collated with Juvencus, reads: “He lies beneath the flame-vomiting sun.” Rabanus Maurus—or whoever was the author of the old hymn for the Ascension of Christ—imitates Juvencus:

> When you return with the flame-vomiting cloud.

This hymn was published by Brower among other works of Rabanus.

> Which remains like the eternal one while the ages fly,  
> And the vault of heaven, by ordained command,  
> Rolls the starry ether around lands and seas.

**66** But if songs have earned such long-lasting fame,  
which bind falsehoods to the deeds of men of old,  
[25] certain faith will grant us the immortal distinction  
of eternal praise through the ages, and will repay our merit.

For my song will be the life-giving deeds of Christ,  
a divine gift among the peoples, free from the crime of falsehood.

**67** Nor is there fear that the world’s fires will carry away with them  
[30] this work: for perhaps this very work will rescue me from the fire,  
when Christ, the Judge, the glory of the Father enthroned on high,  
will descend from the shining flame-vomiting cloud.

The Barthius codex reads *sanctificans* (“sanctifying”).

40. The Poelman manuscript reads *Cujus* instead of *Hujus* (“whose” instead of “this man’s”).

32. Book II, verse 62: “By the name of the Father enthroned on high,” etc.; and Book III, verse 409: “The face of the Father enthroned on high.” Venantius Fortunatus, I think, borrowed this word from Juvencus in Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*, verse 1. Bishop Engelmodus imitates it more clearly in his verses to Abbot Ratbert, volume IX, part II of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 897, Cologne, 1618:

> When the king enthroned on high has distinguished the world  
> By the urn of judgment, etc.

Barthius interprets Juvencus as alluding to what the voice of God said above the Jordan, Matthew 3:17: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Juvencus translates this in Book I, verse 398, as follows:

> You, my son, today amid rejoicing I proclaim  
> Begotten from me: this glory of offspring pleases me.

See also the Epistle to the Hebrews 1:3: “Who, being the brightness of his glory, and the image of his substance,” etc.

33. In *sanctificus*, the final syllable is lengthened by the rule of caesura. Barthius, Book XI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 230, and Cellarius, *On Barbarisms in Later Works*, should not be heeded when they assert that the meter requires *sanctificans*. Both words, *sanctificus* and *sanctifico*, are used only by ecclesiastical writers, such as Tertullian and Prudentius. An uncertain author, *On the Baptism of Bebianus*, writes:

> Therefore, as one sanctified, he shone again, renewed from the water.

Paulinus of Petricord, Book V of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> Which preserve such gifts of sanctifying touch.

The word is quite common in the liturgy.

34. He sets the pure stream of the sweet Jordan against the waters of Helicon, the fountain of Smyrna, and the river Mincius. He longs to draw from Jordan’s waters so that he may speak songs worthy of Christ. But why does he praise the Jordan for this purpose? A gloss in Barthius’s codex explains the allegory as follows:

> By the Jordan he wishes the Holy Spirit to be understood. Jordan derives its name from two rivers, one called Jor and the other Danis; by flowing together they form the Jordan. So too the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. For it is not said either that the Father is the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s, or that the Son is the Father’s and the Holy Spirit’s. Rather, we truly confess that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son, and proceeds from both. Jordan is interpreted as “descent,” a name fitting the Holy Spirit, because when those who humble themselves in the waters of Baptism do so, there occurs a descent of divine grace and kindness, which is especially attributed to the Holy Spirit.

Barthius corrects the wording to: “for when he humbles himself in the waters of Baptism, there occurs in him.” The etymology of *Jordan* supplied here is also uncertain. Critical writers deny that the Jordan is formed from two rivers, or that there is any river called Dan.

Juvencus mentions the water of the Jordan to express the grace of Baptism. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 2, verse 61:

> Command us to remain such as you once ordered us  
> To shine, cleansed of our stains,  
> When we were washed in the river Jordan.

I have written more extensively in my commentary on this passage of Prudentius about the eagerness with which ancient Christians sought to be baptized in the Jordan, because Christ was baptized there. Paulinus imitated this pious invocation of Juvencus in *The Life of Saint Martin*, Book IV:

> Let hearts thirsting for cleansing ask for Castalian waters;  
> Other [waters] befit men reborn in the Jordan.

35. Perhaps this is imitated from Virgil, Book VI, verse 662:

> And the pious prophets, and those who speak words worthy of Phoebus.

Statius, Book IV, satire 21, verse 10: “I shall speak things worthy of,” etc. Other verses of Juvencus answer these in Book IV, verse 803, in the epilogue:

> My mind has received these powers of faith and holy fear,  
> And the grace of Christ has shone so greatly upon me  
> That my earthly tongue willingly receives  
> The adornments of the divine law in my verses.

36. Most editions provide headings for the subject matter and indicate the passages of the Evangelists whom Juvencus follows. Such headings are absent from our manuscripts. We shall therefore insert them in their proper places from Aldus’s edition. Although it seems certain to us that Juvencus composed his poem without these inscriptions, they are nevertheless useful and may perhaps have been prepared through the diligence of ancient writers or glossators.

38. **CHAPTER I.—On the parents and conception of John the Baptist, the Lord’s precursor (Luke 1:26).** He explains Luke’s words, “of the course of Abia,” which he later, at verse 45, explains by the word *sorte* (“by lot”). Barthius, Book XI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 12, observes that these courses were daily rotations, or successions of priests assigned by day, for administering the sacrifice and the prescribed rites in the Temple, on the basis of 3 Esdras 1:1–2:

> And Josiah celebrated the Passover … appointing the priests by daily courses, clothed in vestments, in the Temple of the Lord.

This Third Book of Esdras is outside the canon of our sacred books. First Chronicles 24 lists the twenty-four classes, or courses, assigned by David for the ministry of the Lord. There, verse 3 says:

> And David divided them … according to their courses and their ministry.

And verse 7:

> The first lot came out for Jehoiarib, etc.

Then, verse 10:

> The eighth lot was for Abia.

Again, verse 19:

> These were their courses according to their ministries.

Eucherius, in his *Instructions*, or *Questions on the New Testament*, writes:

> What is meant by what is written in Luke concerning Zacharias the priest, that he was of the course of Abia? The priests had been distributed into twenty-four lots for the ministry of the Temple, so that each might perform his priestly office in the order of his course. In this order Abia held the eighth lot, and Zacharias the priest belonged to that course.

39. Juvencus often calls priests “prophets,” as here, verses 221 and 327; Book III, verse 292; and Book IV, verses 405 and 524.

41. *Moderamen* is used for *moderatio* (“moderation”). Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 274:

> But the virtue of gentle moderation.

42. Barthius interprets *annexos*, in Book XLIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 23, as meaning “devoted exclusively to that one concern, pursuing no other occupation,” because Juvencus alludes to the ancient Roman law by which *nexi* were acquired by *mancipatio* through bronze and scales, as persons bound to another’s authority. On this subject see Turnebus, Book XX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 19.

It seems to me that Juvencus intended to explain Luke’s words, “without reproach.” In the Greek text this is expressed by **ἄμεμπτοι** (*amemptoi*), which most translate “without blame”; in the Cambridge manuscript of the Gospels, cited by Sabatier, “without blemish.” But since nearly all the ancient versions and the Latin Fathers, together with the Vulgate, render it “without reproach,” and since this corresponds very well to the Greek word—for **ἀμεμφία** (*amémphia*) means “the absence of reproach”—Juvencus explained it by *annexos*, that is, “united,” never quarrelling or disagreeing among themselves.

A similar sense appears here, verse 341:

> Always binding him to his proper love.

The phrase is common in ancient inscriptions to signify harmony between spouses: “With whom she lived without reproach.” In Gruter, page 1145, number 8:

> To his dearest wife, with whom he lived without reproach for twenty years.

Many other similar examples may be seen in Gruter, and in Manutius and Cellarius, *On Orthography*. Fabretti, pages 256 and following, cites fifteen inscriptions in which the formula *sine querela* (“without reproach”), *sine ulla querela* (“without any reproach”), or, as it appears on stones, *querella*, signifies the enduring harmony of spouses.

Apuleius uses the expression in this sense, Book II of the *Florida*:

> Therefore he would carefully take precautions lest afterward he should incur a cause for reproach.

Thus Crates warned Hipparchia, a maiden who desired marriage. Horace speaks similarly of the harmony of lovers, Book I, Ode 13:

> Thrice happy, and more than thrice,  
> Are those whom an unbroken bond holds fast,  
> And whom no bitter complaints tear apart,  
> Before the final day dissolves their love.

Although the word *querela* is not, as Petrus Clovius maintains in his commentary on the cited passage of Apuleius, properly used of an offense affecting conjugal love, it cannot be denied that it is very frequently understood in this way. When the subject is spouses, that meaning should therefore be preferred.

Critical interpreters who examine this passage partly say that the words are obscure, as Valla does; others explain them as “harmless,” “undefiled,” “whole,” “innocent,” “irreproachable,” “without reproach before God and men”—that is, possessing not merely a pure conscience but also an untarnished reputation.

Yet the Greek word itself could be translated “not quarrelsome,” and the Latin translator should not be blamed for using the more common phrase *sine querela*. Petrus Chrysologus, Sermon 89, appears to adopt Juvencus’s interpretation, for he says of these spouses:

> This is a new happiness and a singular marriage, when one mind remains in two, one holiness in two; what was separated in sex was united in mind, and what the eyes saw as two was one in conduct; virtue made equal those whom nature had made unequal.

It is especially worth noting that these spouses lived in harmony and without reproach because both had advanced in years, and they had no son. For among women, especially Jewish women, sterility was counted a disgrace and a reproach.]

> The Judge, Christ, the glory of the Father enthroned on high.

Therefore, let the sanctifying Spirit, author of my song, be present to me,

[Col. 0062A] **68** and refresh the mind of the singer with the pure stream  
[35] of the sweet Jordan, so that we may speak things worthy of Christ.

45. Irenaeus likewise says, Book III, chapter 10:

> According to the custom of the priesthood, he went out by lot to offer incense, and entered the Temple of the Lord to make the sacrifice.

So too the Vulgate and the ancient Italic version in many manuscripts read *sorte exiit* (“he went out by lot”). The sanctuary was the more secluded part of the Temple, which only the high priest was permitted to enter. A veil separated the Holy Place from the sanctuary; ordinary priests, but not laymen, entered the Holy Place. The pagans called it an *adytum*, or *adyta*, a word also used by Christian writers.

Paulinus, poem 35, *On the Death of Celsus*:

> Then, when the altar had been stripped bare by the torn veil—  
> Or: when the veil had been torn and the altar uncovered—  
> The sacred places lost the reverence of the sanctuary.

Within the Holy Place stood a golden altar on which fragrances were burned. Laymen approached the enclosure of this place in order to present sacrifices and offerings, but they did not enter within.

48. I think *foribus sancti* (“at the doors of the Holy Place”) is intended. This refers to the common reading *astrata*, *adstrata*, or *prostrata*, as found in Barthius’s manuscript codex. Ovidius used *asterno* in this sense, Book II of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 343:

[Col. 0069C] **89.** “Betrothed” (*desponsa*) is more Latin than “affianced” (*deponsata*), although the latter, which the Vulgate uses, is also correct. Many understand the Blessed Virgin to have already been married at that time, and take “betrothed” or “affianced” in a less exact sense. Juvencus, whose authority certainly ought not to be dismissed, suggests—or even clearly maintains—the contrary view. Even if we explain Juvencus, so as to bring him into agreement with the common opinion of the Fathers and theologians, as referring to the solemn celebration of the wedding, which he understands to have been postponed even after the true marriage contract, he still differs from most on this point: he believed that she had not lived in the same house with Joseph, even after she had been betrothed to him or had contracted marriage with him.

It cannot be denied that probable arguments for either opinion may be drawn from the Gospels, as may be gathered from what St. Thomas excellently discusses in the third part, question 29, article 2:

> To the third objection it must be said that, as Chrysostom says in his commentary on Matthew, the Blessed Virgin was betrothed to Joseph in such a way that she was also living in his house. For just as, in the case of a woman who conceives in her husband’s house, the conception is understood to be marital, so in the case of one who conceives outside the house, the conception is suspect. Thus the reputation of the Blessed Virgin would not have been sufficiently protected merely by her betrothal, unless she had also been living in the house. Therefore what is said—“He did not wish to take her home”—is better understood to mean that he did not wish to expose her to public disgrace, rather than that it refers to bringing her into the house. Hence the Evangelist also adds that he wished to dismiss her privately. Nevertheless, although she was living in the house because of the initial bond of betrothal, the solemn celebration of the marriage had not yet taken place, and for that reason they had not yet come together carnally. Therefore, as Chrysostom says, the Evangelist does not say, “Before she was brought into the house of the bridegroom,” for she was already inside. It was customary among the ancients for brides to be kept in the houses of their betrothed. Hence the Angel also says to Joseph, “Do not fear to take Mary as your wife,” that is, do not fear to celebrate her wedding solemnly—although others say that she had not yet been brought into the house, but was merely betrothed. The former view, however, is more consonant with the Gospel.

The opinion more pleasing to St. Thomas is confirmed by Suárez, *Disputation* 7, volume XVII. The other interpretation, which is closer to Juvencus, is held by Anselm, Abulensis, Cajetan, Baronius, and others. Juvencus seems to me to narrate the whole matter in this order. The Blessed Virgin had already been betrothed to her kinsman, perhaps even before she was marriageable; but, at her parents’ command, she was secluded in virginal dwellings, where she grew to maturity and awaited the proper time for contracting marriage. At that very time the Angel appeared to her, and, after she had conceived by the Holy Spirit, she immediately contracted a true marriage with her bridegroom Joseph and went to greet Elizabeth. For if she had been kept in seclusion in virginal dwellings while awaiting the wedding day, once we know that she immediately came out of those dwellings and went in haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah, we readily understand that this occurred after the wedding day. With the matter explained in this way, scarcely any difficulty remains that cannot easily be resolved. For what Juvencus relates afterward, at lines 168 and following, can suitably be understood of Joseph already as the husband and spouse of the Blessed Virgin, who considered dismissing his wife Mary.

**90.** Martial, book I, epigram 71, calls the dwelling of the Vestal Virgins a “virginal house.” In a similar way, we can explain “virginal dwellings” as referring to some house in which virgins lived together and were educated. P. Canisius, book I of *On the Virgin Mother of God*, chapter 12, and Suárez, in the third part, question 29, article 2, disputation 7, prove from the Fathers that there was in the Temple of Jerusalem a place where virgins dedicated to God lived, and that the Blessed Virgin spent her life in these virginal dwellings from the third year of her age—when, as is piously believed, she was presented by her parents in the Temple—until her betrothal.

The following passage in 2 Maccabees 3:49 may be understood of such an ascetic residence of virgins:

> And the women, girded with sackcloth around their breasts, flocked through the streets; and the virgins who had been confined came running to Onias.

Thus the Blessed Virgin, secluded in such virginal dwellings, lived chastely and piously until the time of puberty. But the annunciation of the divine Word certainly did not take place there, since the Angel was sent by God to a city of Galilee called Nazareth. We must therefore understand either that there was also in the city of Nazareth some place suited to the education of virgins, or that the “virginal dwellings” mentioned by Juvencus were nothing other than a private room in the paternal house of the Mother of God, where she devoted herself solely to God and, with the door closed, prayed to the Father in secret.

Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, section I, chapter 1, article 2, explains the passage in 2 Maccabees about the virgins “who had been confined” as referring to girls who were being piously educated and who remained secluded in their own rooms or inner chambers of the paternal house, not being permitted to go outside. Juvencus should therefore reasonably be explained as referring to these dwellings of the paternal house. See the note on line 620 of this work.

**91.** The gloss in the Regius manuscript reads, “to await the day—the future wedding.” Others, especially Koenigius, interpret the passage in this way. If we maintain that the marriage had already been contracted at that time, we will understand this as referring either to the day on which the public and solemn marriage ceremonies were to be performed, or to the day on which Joseph was going to take her into his house. *Servare* is sometimes used in the sense of “to observe,” “to keep watch,” or “to await.” *Dies* can also mean an indefinite period of time, so that “to await the day” has the same meaning as “to await the proper time.” Accordingly, the Blessed Virgin was permitted, at her parents’ command—that is, given or handed over, for the verb *permitto* has that meaning here—to grow to maturity in virginal dwellings and await the day.

This is how the sense of these verses proceeds, not as Wilkius explains it: “she was hidden away in order to mature and to await the day.” Juvencus suggests that the Virgin was betrothed to Joseph while her most holy parents, Joachim and Anna, were still alive. Many, however, assert that the parents of the Virgin Mary had died when she was about fourteen years old, and that she was consequently given in marriage to Joseph by the priests. The matter is uncertain, and there are not lacking ancient writers who affirm that both parents, or at least St. Anna, survived until the fourth year of the life of our Savior. I take the word “parents” in its proper sense, not in the less exact sense that became common in a later age, when relatives are called parents; I discussed this at Dracontius, book III, line 586.

[Col. 0071A] **92.** Poelman, Aldus, and others read *nuntius infert* instead of *infit*.

**93.** Poelman in the text, Romanus, Ottobonianus, and Fabricius: “Hail, destined to make the earth safe through your offspring.” Aldus, Tornesius, Poelman in the variant apparatus, Faustus, and the manuscript of Deventer: “Hail, destined to bear a saving offspring for the earth.” The Regius manuscript: “Hail, saving offspring destined for the earth,” so that the Virgin is called a saving offspring. Grunerus, citing the passage from the manuscripts of Un. and Cant., reads *progenie terris futura salubri* (“through an offspring destined for the earth’s welfare”), a reading rightly disliked by Gallandius, who prefers *progenie terras jutura salubri* (“through an offspring destined to make the earth safe”); and in fact the meter does not allow *futura*, while *paritura* (“about to bear”) appears to be a gloss.

**94.** Tornesius has *conspecta*, incorrectly.

**95.** Alcuin, book II against Elipandus, incorrectly reads *Non* instead of *Nam*.

**96.** Alcuin, in the cited passage, has *per saecula*; in book II against Felix he incorrectly reads *per singula*.

**97.** The Roman manuscript reads *ut propriam*.

**98.** Poelman, Faustus, Gallandius, Tornesius, and Fabricius: “To him, when you have brought him forth into the light, let the name Jesus be given.” The Un. manuscript in Grunerus: “To him, when you have brought him forth into the light, let the name Jesus be given.” The manuscript of Barthius, Grunerus in the cited passage, Alcuin against Elipandus, Romanus, and Ottobonianus: “To him, when you have brought him into the light, let him be named Jesus.” The Regius manuscript likewise; the Canterbury and Aldine editions, however, have *nomen Iesus*.

**99.** Aldus, Tornesius, Faustus, Romanus: *sic incipit* (“thus it begins”). Poelman, Fabricius, and others: *sic inchoat* (“thus it commences”).

**101.** Romanus, the manuscript of Barthius, Regius, Ottobonianus, and Gallandius: *mihimet*, which is preferable to *mihi nunc* in Aldus, Poelman, Tornesius, and others.

**102.** Tornesius, Faustus, Romanus, Aldus, Fabricius, and Poelman in the variant apparatus: *profatur*; the Regius and Ottobonianus manuscripts, with others: *fatetur*.

**104.** The manuscript of Barthius: *Spiritus adveniet*. Romanus: *Spiritus ac veniet*.

**106.** Most printed editions punctuate *gigni: populis* (“to be born: for the peoples”). Aldus, Romanus, and Faustus have *gigni populis quem* (“to be born for the peoples, whom”), a reading followed by Gallandius from Isaiah 9:6, “For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us,” and from Luke 2:11, “Today a Savior has been born for you.” Reuschius approves *gigni: populis quem* from Acts 4:12.

[Col. 0071D] **92.** Virgil, book XI, line 242: “Thus he began to speak.” So others commonly use *infit* with an infinitive; but one will not easily find *infit* with an accusative, as in *sermonem infit*.

**93.** From *juvo* (“I help”) comes the participle *jutus* and *juturus* in Tacitus, Palladius, and Columella, who in book X, line 121, says: “And rue, destined to make the berries of Pallas flavorful.” Others read *victura* instead of *jutura*.

**95.** In these verses Alcuin proves, against Felix and Elipandus, that Christ is the natural Son of God, as I have shown in the *Prolegomena*, no. 94.

**98.** Juvencus generally uses *Iesus* as a trisyllable; accordingly, *nomen Iesus* may be read. Yet even in this wording I understand *nomine Iesus*, with *Iesus* remaining trisyllabic through elision of the final syllable of *nomine*.

**101.** The Blessed Virgin was conscious of her virginity and had vowed it to God. Hence she says, “I shall hope for myself,” and so forth; this is more forceful than “I shall now hope for myself.” See line 292 of this work, and book II, lines 301 and 617, where the word *sibimet* occurs.

**103.** Luke’s words are chapter 1, verse 35: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Arnulf of Lisieux imitated Juvencus in poem I, or rather retained the very words of the sacred text, as Barthius observes in book IX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 17, column 449. Arnulf’s verse is: “And the sacred power of the Father, overshadowing the virginal womb.” All the older versions and most of the Fathers use this verb. Victorinus of Africa, book I against Arius, used both *obumbrabit* (“will overshadow”) and *inumbrabit* (“will shade”). Both are good Latin words.

Hugo Grotius thinks the expression was taken from birds brooding over their young. Gregory the Great, *Moralia* XVIII, on Job XVII: “As though he will spread a certain shadow around you, by cooling and protecting you from the heat of lust.” Theophylact first offers the comparison of a bird covering its young or overshadowing them with its wings; then, as though uncertain, he proposes the comparison of a painter who first sketches and applies shadows, and afterward adds the finished color. Maldonatus rejects this comparison and reformulates the first one as follows: “Perhaps he would have spoken more aptly by saying that it is like a bird’s customary practice of covering its eggs, so that by its warmth the chicks may be generated and hatched.” Grotius adopted this explanation.

**107.** Attention should be paid to the interpretation of Luke 1:35: “Therefore also the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” Juvencus seems to have punctuated it as follows: “and what will be born from you will be called holy, the Son of God.” Tertullian states this plainly in book IV against Marcion, page 701: “Therefore what will be born in you will be called holy, the Son of God.” Juvencus explains the verb *vocabitur* (“will be called”) with *vocitare necesse est* (“must be called”). For in sacred Scripture “to be called” often means simply “to be,” in the Hebrew idiom, as in Isaiah 1:26: “After this you will be called the city of the just, the faithful city,” and here in Luke 1:32: “He will be called the Son of the Most High.” Homer uses it similarly in the *Iliad*, book IV, line 6, where he reports Juno’s words to Jupiter: “Both in lineage and as your wife—I am called,” that is, “I am both your sister and your wife.”

Juvencus’s interpretation is this: “By the word and power of the Holy Spirit, a child will be generated from you who will be holy and the Son of God.” Some interpreters point out that *sanctum* (“holy”) should be joined with *nascetur* (“will be born”), because this is how the punctuation stands in corrected Bibles. Joannes Albertus Bengelius, in his *Gnomon of the New Testament* on this passage, inclines, together with Tertullian, the Syriac interpreter, and the author of the sermon *Against All Heresies* preserved by Athanasius, toward Juvencus’s interpretation, so that *sanctum* is treated as part of the predicate.

Mazochius, volume III of the *Spicilegium*, on this passage, conjectured that it should be punctuated as in Luke 2:23: “As it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” Maldonatus does not approve this manner of punctuation and observes that it had also been rejected by Bede. Still less persuasive is the view of Maldonatus himself, who, with a few others, thinks that *sanctum* has rather the force of an adverb than of a noun.

To this calm speech the messenger began to reply:

“Hail, destined through your offspring to make the earth safe;

cease to trouble your mind at the sight of one who inspires fear.

[95] For by heavenly command your womb will conceive

the one whom God rejoices and commands to be believed

79 as his own offspring, destined to reign throughout all ages.

When you have brought him into the light, let him be named Jesus.”

Then the Virgin began to speak to him in a timid voice:

[100] [Col. 0072A] “They say that no conception occurs without a husband.

How, then, may I hope that offspring will come to me alone?”

The messenger replied in rapid speech:

“The lofty power of God will fly around you, overshadowing you,

and the pure Spirit will come, most excellent Virgin,

[105] and soon by a chaste utterance will command that a child,

80 magnificent, be born for the peoples, whom it is necessary

to believe and to call the offspring of the Most High God.”

[Col. 0073A] **108.** Perhaps: “Thus your kinswoman is barren.”

**110.** The Regius manuscript has *hauxit*, which seems to have been in the Ottobonian manuscript, perhaps instead of *hausit*. But *auxit* (“increased”) is good.

[Col. 0073B] **112.** Some printed editions have *nunc esse*. Fabricius, with Aldus and Faustus, printed *nunc ecce*, which I find confirmed in the Regius, Roman, and Ottobonian manuscripts, where the error is *nunc et ecce*. So also Luke: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord,” and so forth.

**117.** The Ottobonian manuscript has *prolis*, with *proles* written by a second hand; this is not correct.

**119.** Ottobonian, Regius, Aldine, Tornesian, and Faustine editions: *exsiluit*; others: *exiliit*.

**120.** Romanus, the manuscript of Barthius, and the Regius manuscript: “She was filled with the holy breath.” The Un. manuscript in Grunerus likewise. From this one might conjecture: “The divine utterance, completed also by the holy breath,” since in this way the word *afflamen* (“breath, inspiration”) is omitted; I will discuss it in the note on line 126. The Ottobonian manuscript has *vocis, completa affamine*, but it seems originally to have read *afflamine*. Grunerus would read *completa est famine* from manuscript D, perhaps Canterbury, and emend it to *affamine*, as in line 126, *affamina sensit*. Gallandius considers this repetition of the same word defective. Most have *Divinae vocis completa afflamine sancto*. Luke says: “And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. And she cried out with a loud voice and said.” This, then, is the holy *afflamen*. I join *divinae vocis* with *tremore* (“with trembling”), namely, “as soon as she heard the greeting,” and so forth.

**122.** Romanus reads incorrectly: *uteri sinu animae*.

[Col. 0073C] **108.** Since the Latin Vulgate, the Old Latin version, and other Fathers read *cognata tua* (“your kinswoman”), I will not object if someone reads in Juvencus: “Thus your kinswoman, believed barren by all,” with the final syllable of *tua* lengthened before the *st* of the following word. Some report that St. Elizabeth was the sister of St. Anna, the mother of the Virgin Mary. Others explain the kinship of the Mother of God with St. Elizabeth differently.

**109.** “From mortal seed,” so that the distinction between the conception of Christ and that of St. John the Baptist may be indicated.

[Col. 0073D] **110.** *Aevum* (“age”) can also mean old age, or the final part of old age.

**111.** “They obey everything at the command,” because “no word will be impossible with God.” Victorinus, book I of *Genesis*, line 73: “It should always be enough for you to believe that God can do whatever is thought impossible.”

**113.** By these words the Virgin Mary gives her consent: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word.” In the old Old Latin version: “May it happen to me according to your word.” In Juvencus, “according to your word” is expressed as “as your words sound,” that is, “as your words signify,” for the verb *sonare* has this meaning. Cicero, book III of *On Duties*, chapter 21: “These two words seem to differ from one another, although in reality they appear to signify one thing”; and book II of *On the Ends*, chapter 2, section 6: “Sometimes not to understand what this word ‘pleasure’ signifies.”

The Blessed Virgin Mary shows that she is ready to serve God, specifically in the work that the Angel had explained. Once this consent had been given, the Word immediately became flesh. Some think that the words “Let it happen to me according to your word” imply desire in the Virgin. Juvencus recognizes only consent, as do most others who follow him. It is equivalent to the Blessed Virgin’s saying: “Behold, I offer myself as the handmaid of the Lord, so that it may happen to me according to your word.”

[Col. 0074B] **115.** **CHAPTER III.** Mary visits Elizabeth. Luke 1:31–56. The city of Judah, namely Hebron, as most believe. The Evangelist says, “into a city of Judah,” and in the old Old Latin version, *Judae* or *Judaeae*.

**119.** Gifanius, in his *Index to Lucretius*, maintains that the ancients very often used *dissilui*, *exsilui*, and *prosilui*, not *dissilii*, *exsilii*, and *prosilii*. Forcellinus also asserts in his *Lexicon* that *exsilui* is safer and more customary than *exsilii*. Omeisius, on the contrary, maintains that *exsilii* should be read, because it stands for *exsilivi*, just as *audii* is said for *audivi*.

**120.** Similar examples occur at line 150 and following: “Soon also the accustomed inspirations penetrate the mind,” and “Filled, he sings the words conscious of what is to come”; and at line 250.

**121.** *Magnum* is used adverbially, as I will explain at line 128.

**122.** A gloss in the Regius manuscript reads *sinuamine—gremio* (“sinuamine—womb”). Badius explains it as “a curved embrace.” Juvencus again uses *sinuamen* in book III, line 56; Prudentius and Sidonius also use this word.

[Col. 0074D] **123.** Again at line 135: “And the just God wished to be regarded throughout the ages.” See the note on line 713.

**125.** *Viscus* is any internal organ of an animal; it is used specifically for the womb, especially in the plural, by Ovid, Seneca, Ulpian, and others. The Church also sings: “Blessed are the wombs that bore the Son of the eternal Father,” and so forth.

**126.** *Affamen* is used once and again by Apuleius in book XI of the *Metamorphoses*. Therefore, just as Juvencus says *affamen* and *sinuamen*, so we should believe that he wrote *afflamen* at line 120. Koenigius supplies several similar forms: *allegamen, eructamen, frustramen, imprecamen, irrigamen, micamen, picturamen, quassamen, scrutamen, surculamen, temperamen, veteramen*. But many of these are drawn from later writers and are not worthy of imitation.

“Thus your kinswoman, believed barren by all,

the wife of Zachariah, has recently increased the wonders

[110] of mortal birth in limbs wearied by age.

Her sixth month is here; thus everything obeys the command.”

81 Then the Virgin said: “Behold, now I am a handmaid to the Lord who commands,

ready, as your words sound, to serve.”

The messenger departed and concealed himself from her emptied ears.

[115] Then she quickly made her way to a city of Judaea,

entered the house of Zachariah, and greeted the pregnant Elizabeth.

[Col. 0074A] At once Elizabeth’s anxious womb, whose offspring was confined within it,

resounded with a greater movement;

and at the same time the mother leapt up, shaken with trembling

[120] at the divine voice, filled with holy inspiration,

82 and crying out loudly: “Hail, happy woman,

bearing a blessed fetus in the hollow of your womb.

Why did the just God wish to honor my house

so greatly, that the mother of the exalted Godhead

[125] should visit me? Behold, my offspring rejoices

within my womb, as soon as it sensed Mary’s first utterance.”

[Col. 0075A] **127.** The Un. manuscript: “Blessed is she who believes.” Grunerus would conjecturally prefer *quae credis* (“you who believe”), following *Beata, quae credidisti* (“Blessed are you who believed”). The Vulgate, Poelman in the variant apparatus, and Fabricius: “who, having trusted, will soon bring forth the fulfillment.” Most have: “who believes that the fulfillment will soon come to the words.” Fabricius has *verbo* instead of *verbis*, and in the following verse *quod* instead of *quae*.

**128.** Although Barthius read *verbis* with his manuscript, he now reads *quod*. He rejects *locutus* (“having spoken”), found in Fabricius, because the former declares faith only in the past, whereas the latter directs the same faith also toward what follows. Fabricius, as I suppose, inserted *locutus* on his own initiative to express Luke 1:45: “And blessed is she who believed.” In the old edition of Faustus, however, *quod* is also found, with *verbis* above it and *loquetur* (“will speak”) shortly afterward.

Reuschius reads: “What God, in graciously deeming it great, spoke to the handmaid,” following the Greek text:

> Ὅτι ἔσται τελείωσις τοῖς λελαλημένοις αὐτῇ παρὰ Κυρίου  
> “For there will be fulfillment of the things spoken to her by the Lord.”

Omeisius had made the same observation. At least *locutus* should be retained. Some manuscripts of Luke omit *illi* (“to her”) or *tibi* (“to you”).

**129.** The manuscript of Barthius and the Regius manuscript, written by the first hand: “She, drawing into her mind through joys mingled with shame words spoken in a subdued voice, tremblingly turns them over.” The Tornesian manuscript likewise, although it incorrectly reads *suppresse* for *supressae*, as I think. Romanus: “She, drawing into her mind through joys mingled with shame—of a subdued voice.” Omeisius found the reading of Barthius’s manuscript in the Fulda manuscript and preferred it to the others. Reuschius agrees, interpreting the shame as arising from recognition of her unworthiness; yet this sense of unworthiness was mingled with the joy that the Lord had looked upon her.

The Cologne edition of Hadamarius, 1537: “She, drawing into her mind through many joys her shame—with suppressed voice,” a reading accepted by Poelman in the text. The Regius manuscript, second hand, and the Ottobonian manuscript: “She, drawing into her mind through joys mingled with shame—the words of a suppressed voice.” This reading pleases me, although Reuschius thinks the expression too colloquial and unworthy of Juvencus, for which judgment he gives no reason. See Virgil, book IV of the *Aeneid*, line 285.

Poelman in the variant apparatus, Daventria, Aldus, and Faustus: “She, drawing into her mind through many joys, with shame suppressed, trembling words of the voice.” Fabricius has the same, but *mixta* (“mingled”) instead of *multa* (“many”); Barthius says that this reading of Fabricius is far better. I would prefer: “with voice suppressed.”

[Col. 0075C] **127.** Barthius says that *finis* is the purpose for which something is given; by this statement he confirms the printed reading. Juvencus again uses the word in book I, line 238: “And may he deign to impose an end upon his words, with peace for his own.”

**128.** *Magnum* is used adverbially for “very greatly.” Valerius Flaccus, book I, line 263: “And sounding loudly.” Add Plautus, Gellius, and others.

**130.** *Suppressae vocis dicta* means words spoken in a lowered voice. This could have been said more clearly, and, as I conjecture, Juvencus wrote: “With voice suppressed, she turns over trembling words,” with the final syllable of *voce* lengthened for the sake of the caesura. This is unusual among the ancients, but frequent among poets of the later period; it would appear still more frequent if bold copyists, ignorant of this practice, had not corrupted many verses. The modesty of the Virgin in conversation is indicated. Cicero, *Pro Sulla*, chapter 10: “When he had spoken in a subdued voice about the crime of Publius Lentulus and the audacity of all the conspirators, merely so that you who approved those things might hear him, he spoke about the punishment of Publius Lentulus and the prison in a loud and lamenting voice.” *Pavitantia* (“trembling”) is a word proper to poets, though to good poets—Virgil, Lucretius, Terence, Valerius Flaccus, and Seneca the tragedian.

**132.** “Of the boundless world,” as in the speech of Eugenius of Toledo, from the best copies: “God the King, with whom the structure of the boundless world consists,” not, as others read, “God the boundless King, whom the structure of the world consists.” See the *Prolegomena* to Dracontius, no. 66, page 49 and following. Reuschius confirms this, since if the world is boundless, how great must be the one who created it? Prudentius, book I against Symmachus: “And he created the immeasurable expanse of the great universe.” Ovid, book II of the *Metamorphoses*, line 35: “He replies: O light, common to the boundless world.”

[Col. 0076C] **134.** Most understand the words of the Mother of God, “because he looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid,” as referring to the virtue of humility. Maldonatus, with Juvencus and others, understands them as referring to her lowly and humble condition.

**136.** “He cast down the proud” is an elegant expression, like “to break enemies” or “nations.” Cicero, *First Catiline*, chapter 9: “Can anything break you? Can you ever correct yourself?” On the word *thronus*, see the commentary on Prudentius, line 102 of the *Apotheosis*.

**137.** *Largifluus* (“flowing generously”) is a word used by the ancient writers Lucretius and Pacuvius.

[Col. 0076D] **138.** In the Vulgate we have *quasi mensibus tribus* (“about three months”). In many copies of the Old Latin, *quasi* is absent, as here in Juvencus and in St. Ambrose, book II on Luke. The numeral adjective *trinus* (“threefold”) frequently occurs in Juvencus. It is distributive, but is sometimes used outside a distributive sense, as here and elsewhere in Juvencus. *Ternus* likewise has the same meaning and is used either distributively or outside a distributive sense. Consequently, in the manuscripts not only of Juvencus but also of other writers, one word is often substituted for the other, and the ancient copies disagree among themselves.

**139.** Fabricius, in the *Christian Poetic Commentaries*, says that *repedare* means to return home on foot. The origin of the word seems indeed to be something like “to draw back the foot,” but it is simply used for “to return.” This word, used by Lucilius and Pacuvius, then placed among obsolete expressions, was finally restored to use by writers of declining Latin, including Juvencus, Ammianus, Damasus, and others. See Cellarius, *Curiae Posteriores*, and Joannes Ludovicus de la Cerda, *Adversaria Sacra*, chapter 21, no. 6. The Mother of God returned to her home already certain of what was to come—not because she had previously been uncertain, but because experience had taught her that what the Angel had declared concerning Elizabeth was true.

Blessed is she who believes that the fulfillment will soon come

of the words that God, in graciously deeming it great, spoke to the servants.

She, drawing into her mind joys mingled with shame,

[130] 83 turns over the trembling words of a subdued voice:

“My spirit celebrates magnificent praises

and gives thanks to the Lord of the boundless world. Scarcely can

[Col. 0076A] this spirit contain such great joys, because he has deigned

to raise me, lowly as I am, to a lofty place, and has wished me

[135] 84 to be regarded as blessed by all nations and throughout the ages.

Behold, he has removed the throne from the cruel,

and has broken the proud; with lavish wealth he has enriched the humble needy.

Then she remained there for three full months,

and returned home, now certain of what was to come.”

[140] [Col. 0077A] **140.** The Regius, Ottobonian, and Roman manuscripts, Reuschius with five manuscripts, Barthius, and Poelman in the variant apparatus: “until the appointed day should compel Elizabeth to bring forth the fetus, as the days rolled toward the light, the crowd of relatives, gathered in expectation of the birth, hastened together; they celebrate the remarkable joys and command that the child bear the father’s name.” Tornesius has the same, but punctuates: “should compel her. Gathered in expectation of the birth,” which is less satisfactory; worse still, with others he writes *Elizabeth* instead of *Elisabeth*, as the meter requires.

Aldus, Faustus, Fabricius, Poelman in the text, Daventria, and others: “until the burden should leave Elizabeth’s womb, to be released into the clear light; the rumor of so great a birth gathered them together.” Barthius, who elsewhere judged this reading false, as though it had arisen from the mistake of treating the name *Elisabeth* as indeclinable, later, in book LVI, chapter 17, seems to admit the same reading. But instead of *deserat* he reads *deseret*, from the verb *deserare*, “to open” or “to unseal,” which is required by the word *solvenda* (“to be released”) in the other verse. Barthius likewise corrects *reserate* to *deserate* in Fulgentius, book I of the *Mythologies*; and in Apuleius, book I of the *Metamorphoses*, some read *deseratus* instead of *reseratus*.

**143.** Poelman in the variant apparatus has *per gaudia*. The manuscript of Barthius has *frequentans* instead of *frequentes*.

**145.** Reuschius punctuates: “The mother refuses this; but let him be called John—she repeats.” Others have *sed Joannes* without the comma.

**146.** The Ottobonian manuscript has *ingemuit*, correctly emended to *ingeminat*. The edition of Hadamarius, Romanus, and Poelman in the text have *cunctis tunc*; most have *muti tunc*.

**147.** The Regius and Ottobonian manuscripts, Poelman in the variant apparatus, Tornesius, and Fabricius: “They consult him and ask in writing that he declare the name,” which is good, with the final *e* of *consulere* lengthened because of the two consonants in the following word. The manuscript of Barthius: *consulerent, scriptoque rogant*. Romanus: *consulere, et scriptoque rogant*. Aldus, Faustus, and Poelman in another reading: “They consult him and ask in writing that he declare the name.” Poelman in the text and Hadamarius: *in scriptoque rogant*.

**148.** Barthius somewhere reads *dum* instead of *cum*.

**149.** I believe *sonentia* in Fabricius is an error for *sonantia*, although the ancients used *sonere* for *sonare*, along with many similar forms collected here by Schoettgenius.

**150.** Fabricius incorrectly has *penetrans*. The manuscript of Barthius: “The passages penetrate the tongue.” Tornesius has *essuetam*; Hadamarius, *assueta*, which Westhemerus also printed in the variant apparatus instead of *assuetam*. Romanus: “The accustomed spiritual passages penetrate the mind”; but perhaps *spiracula* stood originally, which alone I approve. *Assueta*, with its final syllable lengthened for the sake of the caesura, would not be bad. Yet *assuetam* is confirmed by book II, line 720.

[Col. 0077C] **140.** **CHAPTER IV.** The birth of John the Baptist. Luke 1:56, 80. The phrase *fundere foetum* (“to pour forth the fetus”) suggests the ease of giving birth. Dracontius, book II, line 682, concerning the same birth of St. Elizabeth: “The boy is poured forth from the womb under a blessed destiny.”

**141.** *Elisabeth* is indeclinable; that is, “the rolling days would compel Elisabeth to bring forth the fetus.” *Volvenda dies* has the force of an imminent time, as Gifanius observed in his *Index to Lucretius*, under *volvenda*. Virgil, book IX, line 6: “Turnus, what no one of the gods would dare promise to one who desired it, the rolling day has now brought of its own accord.” Avitus, book V, line 411, or 416: “The greater part had already spent the hours of night, and the rolling day was approaching, its appointed lot near at hand.”

**142.** We should note the custom common among Greeks, Romans, and Jews: relatives were accustomed to gather to visit women who had given birth and to be present when, after eight or nine days, the infant was given a name.

**145.** He takes the particle *sed* (“but”) from the Gospel: “He said, ‘By no means, but he shall be called John.’”

**147.** Maldonatus says of this passage in the Evangelist: “Juvencus thinks that Zachariah was questioned in writing.” Juvencus’s meaning seems different to me: namely, that Zachariah was asked by gestures to declare the child’s name in writing.

**148.** The Vulgate has: “And asking for a writing tablet.” The Old Latin likewise in most manuscripts, but the Canterbury manuscript has: “And when he had asked for a tablet, he wrote: ‘John is his name.’” Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, has: “And he received writing tablets,” and so forth, which is more Latin, since the singular neuter is *pugillar*. A tablet may be understood with *pugillarem*. For *pugillares* is also an adjective, with *tabellae*, *codicilli*, or something similar understood. Prudentius, hymn 9, *Peristephanon*, concerning St. Cassian, line 15: “From which the writing tablets, accustomed to run over wax.” Forcellinus says: “Here Prudentius shortens the first syllable; he is a bad authority for prosody.” I do not see, however, why Prudentius should be censured, since *pugillar* comes from *pugillus*, or “fist,” and the first syllable of *pugillus* is short. Ausonius likewise shortens it in the iambic dimeter of epigram 146: “Open up the tablet with two leaves.” On such wax-coated tablets, on which the ancients wrote, see the commentary on the cited hymn of St. Cassian.

Juvencus’s meaning should be explained so that Zachariah both wrote the name and, having recovered the power of speech, pronounced it. The Evangelist suggests this: “He wrote, saying, ‘John is his name.’ And they all marveled.” The better reason for their astonishment seems to have been that he pronounced the name, rather than that he wrote it. Zachariah and Elizabeth could already have agreed by signs or in writing that the name John should be given. I do not sufficiently understand St. Ambrose’s reasoning in his commentary on this passage: “Indeed, the mute man could not make his son’s name known to his wife; but through prophecy Elizabeth learned what she had not learned from her husband.” Ambrose’s reasoning could be confirmed if we say that Zachariah was mute in such a way that he could not only speak or hear, but could not even write. Yet this is stated neither by Ambrose nor, in my judgment, implied by the Evangelist.

The time was now at hand when the rolling days,

[Col. 0077D] moving toward the light,

would compel Elizabeth to bring forth the fetus at the appointed time.

A crowd of relatives, gathered in expectation of the birth, hastened together.

Then they celebrate the wondrous joys and command that he bear his father’s name.

[145] The mother refuses this, but repeats: “Let him be called John.”

[Col. 0078A] Then they agree to consult the mute father’s command

and ask him in writing to declare the name.

But—O wondrous faith!—when he attempts to write on the tablets,

86 he releases his bound tongue through resounding words.

[150] Soon also the accustomed inspirations penetrate the mind,

[Col. 0079A] **151.** The parchment manuscript of Barthius has: “And, filled with God, conscious of the words to come,” from which Barthius wishes to restore: “And, conscious of the words of the coming God, he dictates.” Tornesius has *ventura*, incorrectly.

**152.** The Ottobonian manuscript has *concelebrant et frequentant*, less well.

**154.** Tornesius, Romanus, Regius, and Ottobonianus have *quod*; others have *qui*.

[Col. 0079B] 160. Poelman, Roman, Aldine, and Fabricius read *Et tu*. Regius and Ottobonianus, together with Tornacensis, read *At tu*. The Vulgate and Old Latin versions read *Et tu, puer* (“And you, child”). The Canterbury manuscript reads *Et tu autem, infans* (“And you, however, infant”).

161. Tornacensis, Regius, and Ottobonianus read *Dicere, et Dominum mox praegrediere viando* (“to proclaim, and you will soon go before the Lord on his way”). Aldine has the same, but reads *progrediere*. Roman follows Aldine, though incorrectly reading *progredire*. Poelman reads *Diceris, Dominum mox praegrediere viando* (“you will be called, and you will soon go before the Lord on his way”), and, in place of the alternative reading, *progrediere*. *Praegrediere* is preferable on the basis of Luke 1:76: *Praeibis enim ante faciem Domini* (“For you will go before the face of the Lord”). [Col. 0080A] And in the Canterbury manuscript, in Sabatier, it reads: *Antecedes enim ante faciem Domini* (“For you will go before the face of the Lord”). Faustus follows Aldine; others follow other witnesses, with *praegrediere*.

162. Aldine, Roman, and Tornacensis read *per limen* (“through the threshold”). Most read *per lumen* (“through the light”), which corresponds more closely to the words of Luke 1:79.

[Col. 0080B] 165. Most write *Exhinc* (“from here onward”); Sabatier, in place of the alternative reading, has *Exin*.

168. Roman and Barthius’s manuscript read *Mariae sponsi* (“of Mary’s betrothed”), which, as Barthius says, amounts to the same thing, in chapter 5 of book 69 of his *Adversaria*.

171. In the margin of Barthius’s manuscript there was the conjecture of an earlier philologist, *Dedecus oppressae* (“the disgrace of the violated woman”), indicating that Saint Joseph thought force had been used against the Virgin. In Roman, *cedet* is an error for *celet* (“he should conceal”).

[Note: [Col. 0079B]

154. *Visere* and *visitare* (“to visit”) are often used in explaining the mystery of the Incarnation. Compare the commentary on Prudentius’s *Cathemerinon*, hymn 11, verse 32: *Dignatus orbem viseret* (“He deigned to visit the world”).

155. *Cornu salutis* (“horn of salvation”) comes from the sacred text. In Hebrew idiom, *horn* signifies power and kingship.

[Col. 0079C] 156. Luke’s words are: *Et erexit cornu salutis in domo David pueri sui* (“And he raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant”). The Old Latin version from the Colbert manuscript reads *in domum* (“into the house”). Thus God raises up power and salvation and grants light from the family of David.

161. I discussed the verb *viare* (“to travel,” “to go on one’s way”) in the commentary on Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, preface 2, verse 15. Add Cerda, *Adversaria sacra*, chapter 144, no. 34.

164. *Abrumpent, discutient, dispellent* (“they will break through, disperse, drive away”): they will emerge from the darkness.

166. In the thirtieth year of age, the Jews customarily admitted those who belonged to the priestly order to priestly service. See Numbers, chapter 4, verses 3 and 47.

167. *Pleno aevo*, *plena aetate*, *plenis annis* (“in full maturity,” “at full age,” “in full years”), as Virgil said of Lavinia: *Jam plenis nubilis annis* (“Now marriageable in full years”). See our notes on verse 384 of book 1 of Dracontius.

168. CHAPTER V. Joseph considers leaving Mary. Matthew 1:19–24.

169. They use *onus uteri* (“the burden of the womb”) in this same way: Ovid, Gellius, Sidonius, Avitus, and Sedulius, whose passages Omeisius has annotated. Ovid, *Fasti*, book 3, verse 42: *Coelesti tumidus pondere venter erat* (“Her belly was swollen with a heavenly burden”). Consult Arntzenius on Sedulius, book 1, verse 96.

171. The gloss in the Regius manuscript is *thalamos—sponsalia* (“marriage chamber—betrothal”). Properly speaking, *sponsalia* are the promise and stipulation of a future marriage. Juvenal, satire 6, verse 25: *Conventum tamen, et pactum, et sponsalia nostra / Tempestate paras* (“Yet you are preparing our meeting, agreement, and betrothal in due season”). The gloss may be confirmed by verse 178: *Haec praecepta sequens servat sponsalia pacta* (“Following these commands, he keeps the betrothal agreements”).

Matthew’s words are: *Joseph autem vir ejus, cum esset justus, et nollet eam traducere, voluit occulte dimittere eam* (“But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly”). The Greek word for *traducere* (“to expose”) is παραδειγματίσαι (*paradeigmatísai*), meaning “to expose to disgrace,” “to display as an example,” or “to defame.” For *dimittere* (“to dismiss”), which all the witnesses present, the Greek text has ἀπολῦσαι (*apolŷsai*). If the subject is a wife, it could be translated “to divorce her”; if a betrothed woman, “to repudiate” would be better, since a future marriage too can be repudiated. In the Canterbury manuscript: *Et nollet eam praepalare* (“and was unwilling to put her forward”). Hilary, on Matthew 1: “And this saying was spoken of Joseph, who wished to cast her away, because, being righteous, he did not wish the law to be applied against her.” Augustine, letter 153: “And he was unwilling to make her public.” Vigilius of Thapsus, book 12 *On the Trinity*: “And he was unwilling to expose her.”

Joseph was therefore considering within himself how he might conceal Mary’s disgrace and dismiss her, or reject his marriage with her. This is Juvencus’s interpretation; for that reason he does not approve the view of some who explain *nollet eam traducere* as “he did not wish to bring her into his house.” Barthius, book 44 of his *Adversaria*, chapter 9, proves that *traducere* is a nuptial term, drawing, I think, on Prudentius the Younger, a Spaniard, in the *Life of Blessed Mary the Virgin*. But this author used *traducere*, as I understand it, to explain that a newly married woman had passed into another family, because already at that time some understood Matthew’s words, *Et nollet eam traducere*, in this way.

Others think that Joseph judged nothing evil concerning the Blessed Virgin, either because he understood that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit, or because he was so moved by the Virgin’s extraordinary holiness that he suspended all judgment. Juvencus also dissents from these, and instead agrees with Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Justin, and other Fathers and interpreters that Joseph had persuaded himself that Mary had conceived through adultery. Menochius is not far from the opinion of the earlier philologist who conjectured *Dedecus oppressae* in Juvencus. “Perhaps,” he says, “Joseph thought that force had been used against Mary, and that she was therefore pregnant without any fault of hers.” A dissertation by Francis Baringius, *On paradigmatism, or the repudiation of an adulterous betrothed woman*, has been included in the *New Theological-Philological Treasury*.

172. “This is divine,” says Barthius, page 2778, “indicating not merely a dream, but sleep itself sent upon the man by God.
