173. In place of the alternative reading, Poelman and Fabricius read this verse: *Mox stertente, Dei vox est audita monentis* (“Soon, as he snored, the voice of God admonishing him was heard”). Barthius rightly judges this line spurious in the passage cited above.

174. Tornacensis reads *pactum* (“agreement”); the others, *pactae* (“of the betrothed woman”). Poelman, in place of the alternative reading, has: *Tu sponsam capias, vacat omni pactio fraude* (“Take your betrothed woman; the agreement is free from all deceit”).

175. Barthius’s manuscript has *sanctus* (“holy”), which Barthius prefers to *sancto* (“holy,” ablative), asserting that the latter was introduced by ignorant correctors, though he gives no proof. The reading *sanctus* is supported by Matthew: *Quod enim in ea natum est, de Spiritu sancto est* (“For that which has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit”). Nevertheless, our text itself suggests *sancto* in the words *sancto foetu* (“with holy offspring”). [Col. 0081B]

177. Roman and all the printed editions I have seen have: *Nobiscum Deus est cui nomen, protinus ille* (“God is with us, whose name he is, immediately he”). The Regius and Ottobonianus manuscripts have: *Nobiscum Deus est nomen cui protinus ille* (“God is with us; his name is immediately he”). In the first hand of the Regius it seems to have been written so as to be understood as *cui*, namely, “to whom,” referring to the virgin; but the second hand added punctuation in Regius: *nomen cui: protinus*, with the gloss *cui—proli* (“to whom—to the offspring”). [Col. 0082A]

179. Poelman and Hadamar, in the alternative reading, have: *Sed tum forte novi capitum discussio census* (“But then perhaps the review of the new census of heads”). Barthius approves this reading from his manuscripts, and it appears in Ottobonianus and Tornacensis, where *furte* and *discussia* are written incorrectly, and in Aldine, which has *cum* for *tum*. Roman follows Aldine, but in the margin *capitibus* is corrected to *capitur*. In the Regius manuscript the variant *novo capitum discussio censu* (“the review of heads by a new census”) is not to be despised. Fabricius, Faustus, and Poelman have *novus, capitum discussio, census* (“new: a review, a census, of heads”), which is expressed by Poelman in place of the alternative reading as *Sed cum forte novus*, and by Barthius, book 11 of his *Adversaria*, chapter 20.

180. Regius has *Caesaris Augusti ex jussis* (“by the commands of Caesar Augustus”). Faustus and Poelman, in place of the alternative reading, have: *Caesareque Augusto jussus per plurima scribi* (“and ordered by Caesar Augustus to be recorded through many [regions]”), which appears spurious. Most have *Caesaris Augusti jussis per plurima terrae* (“by the commands of Caesar Augustus through many parts of the earth”), which interprets Luke 2:1: *Ut describeretur universus orbis* (“that the whole world should be registered”). Fabricius published *jussu* (“by the command”) for *jussis* and was followed by Sabatier.]

[Note: [Col. 0081B]

173. In Barthius’s manuscript there was this gloss: *Horrida somnia*—“that which was oppressed by the sleep of doubt.” It speaks of the suspicion Joseph held concerning his wife’s violation, and therefore has little or nothing to do with this passage, as Barthius observes. Barthius likewise calls *horrida* (“dreadful,” “horrid”) a poetic word, arising from the matter itself, some kind of horror having given occasion for the alteration. Juvencus again uses it in this book, verse 286, of the Magi: *Totam mox horrida somnia noctem / Sollicitant* (“Soon dreadful dreams trouble the whole night”). Add that *horror* is used of religious fear and is often joined with reverence. Valerius Flaccus, book 2, verse 432: *Threiciis arcana sacris: hic numinis ingens / Horror* (“The secrets of Thracian rites: here there is great awe of the godhead”). [Col. 0081C] Compare the commentary on Prudentius, book 1 *Against Symmachus*, verse 199.

174. In Barthius’s manuscript there was a gloss: “It could be concluded from this that they were merely betrothed, though the marriage was nevertheless firm.” I do not know what this refers to, unless perhaps it suggests that Joseph and Mary did not yet have a true marriage. Most, however, think that when Joseph was turning this thought over in his mind, a valid marriage had already been contracted, and they interpret Matthew’s words, *Accipere conjugem tuam* (“to take your wife”), as meaning “to retain her,” not “to dismiss her”; and because he had already considered dismissing her, the angel commanded him to abandon that thought.

A girl was properly called *pacta* when she had agreed to marriage on fixed terms; *sponsa* (“betrothed woman”) when the solemn stipulations called *sponsalia* had been added. Reuschius demonstrates, however, that good writers do not always observe this distinction, and he also maintains that *conjugium pactae* (“the marriage of the betrothed woman”) can be used for *conjugem pactam* (“the betrothed wife”), following Greek usage.

Jerome seems doubtful to me on this matter in chapter 1 of Matthew. The martyr Ignatius adds a fourth reason why Christ was conceived of a betrothed woman: “So that,” he says, “her child might be concealed from the devil, while he thought that it had been begotten not from a virgin but from a wife.” Here a valid marriage is asserted. For the devil, who is not present everywhere and does not know what happens where he is absent, seeing that Mary was Joseph’s wife, could have thought that the child had been begotten not from a virgin but from a wife.

Jerome adds: *Antequam convenirent, inventa est in utero habens de Spiritu sancto* (“Before they came together, she was found to have in her womb a child from the Holy Spirit”). She was found by no one other than Joseph, who, with almost marital permission, knew everything concerning his future wife. I understand *almost marital permission* because he was a betrothed man, not a husband, as is more clearly expressed by the words *futurae uxoris* (“future wife”). Mary therefore was not yet a wife.

Later, however, Jerome adds: “How is Joseph, when he concealed his wife’s crime, called righteous?” But this testimony concerns Mary: Joseph, knowing her chastity and wondering at what had happened, silently concealed what he did not know the mystery of. Here he simply calls Mary “wife,” although shortly before he had called her “future wife.” I do not know whether Jerome can be understood by the term *future wife* to mean “future mother” or “mother of a household”; for in *future wife* Jerome indicates the reason why Joseph knew everything.

177. Matthew 1:23: *Et vocabunt nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod est interpretatum, Nobiscum Deus* (“And they shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us”). In Barthius’s manuscript there was the gloss *Homo-Deus* (“God-man”). The relative *cui* (“to whom,” “whose”) at the end of a sentence is unusual, but it is nevertheless sometimes used, as in Prudentius, hymn 2 *Peristephanon*, verse 299: *Gemmas corusci luminis, / Ornatur hoc templum quibus* (“With gems of flashing light, with which this temple is adorned”). This verse closes the stanza.

178. *Sponsalia pacta* (“the agreed betrothal”): if one attends to the proper meaning of the words, one will again judge that Juvencus held the opinion that the Blessed Virgin had not yet married Joseph, since he was considering refusing her marriage chamber and withdrawing from the betrothal. But it is not necessary to retain the precise meanings of words in Juvencus any more than in the Gospel. Compare the note on verse 174.

179. CHAPTER VI. The Edict of Caesar Augustus. Luke 2:1–7. Juvencus calls it a *novus census* (“new census”) in order to explain Luke’s words in the cited chapter, verse 2: *Haec professio prima facta est* (“This registration was the first one made”), and so forth.

From these verses, as Barthius says in book 69, chapter 5, we are taught with complete clarity both what *discussio* means in such passages of authors and what that enrollment of peoples under Augustus was—an enrollment which others have described only in many extended sentences. He adds that it is called the review of a new census because no such review of a census had ever been heard of throughout the world in the memory of humanity.

He then attacks Georg Fabricius for either having himself changed the true reading or having wished to follow a corrupt old edition. “Certainly,” he says, “I suspect that excessive license toward the authors whom the schools commended caused him to be mocked by scholastic pride. There is scarcely any class of men among whom the editing of good authors has not always taken on something of culpable arrogance.” Catholic writers who judged Fabricius in this way can easily defend their judgment by the authority of the non-Catholic Barthius.

Barthius explains *discussio* in the passages cited. There was a particular office of the *discussor*, namely, an inspector, censor, or assessor; accordingly, *discussio* means inspection, assessment, census, more careful examination, or investigation. See book 10 of the *Code*, title 30, law 1, and elsewhere. Macrobius, Symmachus, and Julius Firmicus use the word *discussio* in this sense.

180. *Plurima terrae* (“many parts of the earth”), like *amoena locorum* (“pleasant places”), *aspera belli* (“the hardships of war”), below, verse 262, *per longa viarum* (“along the length of the roads”), and similar expressions. *Plurimus* with a genitive occurs in Silius, book 16, verse 362: *Insignis multa cervice et plurimus idem / Ludentis per colla jubae* (“Conspicuous with its many-necked mane, and equally abundant in the playful mane flowing over its necks”).]

89 “Accept the marriage of your betrothed, which is free from all guilt;

[175] the Spirit has filled her womb with holy offspring.”

The prophet sang that this offspring would come from a virgin;

[Col. 0082A] GOD IS WITH US is his name.” Immediately he,

90 following these commands, keeps the betrothal agreement.

But then perhaps the review of the new census of heads,

[180] ordered by Caesar Augustus throughout many parts of the earth,

181. Roman: *Syria hoc tum jure regebat* (“Syria at that time ruled by this authority”). Omeisius, together with one Canterbury manuscript, has *Describebatur Syriam tunc jure* (“Syria was then being registered by this authority”), a reading approved by Reuschius. But because of the unnecessary repetition of *tunc* (“then”), he published, with Poelman, Aldine, Tornacensis, Hadamar, and Fabricius, *Syriae*, so that it may be understood as “the land of Syria.” Regius has *Syria*, though it seems to have originally been *Syriae*. Ottobonianus correctly has *Describebatur, Syriam cum jure regebat* (“Syria was being registered; he ruled it with authority”), since *plurima terrae* (“many parts of the earth”), that is, places or something similar, suggests the words of Luke, *universus orbis* (“the whole world”). Faustus published *Describebatur Syrie: quam*, so that *Syrie* stands for *Syria*.

182. Poelman, in place of the alternative reading, has *proprii*, so that peoples may be understood; this is also held by Aldine and Tornacensis. In both Canterbury manuscripts and Regius: *Cyrinus proprio*, less correctly, as though it meant “by his own authority.” The reading should be refined to *proprios*, namely, “their own territories.”

183. Poelman, Aldine, Tornacensis, Hadamar, Fabricius, and others have *Addebant* (“they added”). The true reading is *Edebant* (“they declared,” “they registered”), which appears in Barthius’s manuscript and in our Ottobonianus. *Edere* is the proper verb in a census and recurs shortly afterward, where some read *Obtulit hic illum* (“he presented him here”). Roman incorrectly has *vires, genusque, nomenque* (“strength, race, and name”).

185. Ottobonianus has *quae genuit: Mariae quae censum* (“which she bore: Mary, who [gave] the census”). Regius has *quae genuit, generis quae censum* (“which she bore, who [gave] the census of her lineage”). Aldine, Roman, and others have *quae genuit, generis censum quae* (“which she bore, who [gave] the census of her lineage”).

186. Daventer has: *Obtulit hic illam: genus hinc uterque trahebat* (“Here he presented her: from this source each derived his lineage”). Tornacensis, Poelman, Hadamar, and Fabricius have: *Obtulit hic illum, genus hinc quod uterque trahebat* (“Here he presented him, from whom each derived his lineage”). Ottobonianus: *Edidit hic illam Davidis origine Joseph* (“Here Joseph, of David’s lineage, brought her forth”). Regius: *Edidit Mariam Davidis origine Joseph* (“Joseph, of David’s lineage, brought forth Mary”); the second hand adds *hic Mariam* (“Mary here”) as a gloss at *Bethlehem*. Aldine, Roman, and others have *Edidit hic Mariam. Davidis origine Joseph* (“Here he brought forth Mary. Joseph, of David’s lineage”); but the point after *Mariam* seems to have been incorrectly added.

Barthius’s manuscript has the text without a point, as does Roman and the two Canterbury manuscripts. Sabatier made two verses from the two readings:

*Edidit hic Mariam: Davidis origine Joseph—  
Obtulit hic illam, genus hinc quod uterque trahebat—  
Desponsamque* (“Here he brought forth Mary: Joseph, of David’s lineage—Here he presented her, from whom each derived his lineage—His betrothed woman”), and so forth.

Schoettgenius wished to restore:

*Obtulit hic illum Davidis origine Caesar* (“Here Caesar presented him, of David’s lineage”),  
*Addidit et Mariam, genus hinc quod uterque trahebat* (“And he added Mary, from whom each derived his lineage”),

namely, *hic* (“here”) at Bethlehem and *illum* (“him”) for the census. Thus he arranges the order of the following verses: *Desponsamque*—“his betrothed woman”—with the following two verses—*Hospitium* (“lodging”)—*Augusti* (“of Augustus”)—*Circa* (“around”).

188. Regius, together with Barthius’s manuscript and Roman, has *hospitio amborum* (“the lodging of both”). Aldine incorrectly has *Hospitum amborum* (“the lodgings of both”).

189. Most printed editions and Roman have *perparva* (“very small”). Regius has *praeparva* (“exceedingly small”), and the same seems to be found in Ottobonianus. Barthius’s manuscript has *praeparva habitacula arvi* (“exceedingly small dwellings of the field”); Barthius thinks that another word lies hidden at the end. He was considering a cave. To humor him, I am inclined to conjecture: *Angusto fuerant praeparva habitacula in antro* (“In a narrow cave there had been exceedingly small dwellings”). Aldine has *faerat*.

190. Ottobonianus, Regius, Barthius’s manuscript, the Lyon edition of 1551, Poelman in place of the alternative reading, Tornacensis, and Aldine have the following:

*Illic virgo novo completo in tempore foetu—  
Solvitur, et puerum veteri cunabula textu—  
Involvunt, duroque datur praesepe cubili.*

(“There the virgin, the time having been completed with new offspring, is delivered, and the ancient woven cradle wraps the child, and a manger is given to the hard bed.”)

In Ottobonianus the first hand has *cubile* (“bed”), and it seems to have had *completa*, which is clearly read in Regius and Roman. To avoid the clash of two genitives, Reuschius published *completa in tempora* (“the times having been completed”), but he holds the true reading to be:

*Illic virgo novum completo in tempore foetum—  
Solvitur* (“There the virgin, the time having been completed, is delivered of new offspring”),

by synecdoche. Tornacensis, and Poelman’s second hand, have *completo in tempore*. Aldine, Hadamar, Fabricius, and Poelman in the text have:

*Illic Virgo novum completo tempore foetum—  
Edidit, et leni pannoso tegmine motu—  
Texit, cui durum cunas praesepe ministrat.*

(“There the Virgin, when the time was complete, brought forth a new child, and with gentle movement covered him with a woolen cloth; a hard manger served as his cradle.”)

Fabricius has *fotu* (“with warmth”) for *motu* (“with movement”); Hadamar incorrectly has *complures* for *completo*. Daventer has *cui cunas durum* (“for whom the hard [manger served as] a cradle”). Schoettgenius: *Edidit, atque levi pannoso tegmine fotu* (“She brought forth, and with gentle warmth of a woolen covering”). Barthius rightly rejects this entire reading as spurious.]

[Note: [Col. 0083C]

183. *Edebant*, that is, “they declared,” “proclaimed,” or “set forth.” It is a forensic term. Ulpian, *Digest*, book 2, title 13, which is entirely about *edere*, law 1: “To publish also means to make an opportunity for copying, or to set forth in a written document and give it, or to dictate it.” Pliny, book 10, letter 22: “When I was publishing his years and census, as you had instructed, I was warned by more experienced men,” and so forth. Others read *crederem* (“I would believe”), less well.

[Col. 0083D] 184. You could explain it in this way: Bethlehem is a city of Judea. But perhaps Juvencus read *In Bethlehem Judaeae* (“in Bethlehem of Judea”); this is how it is read in the old Canterbury manuscript version and in the Greek text. Mazochius defends this reading in volume 3 of *Spicilegium Biblicum*, on Matthew 2:5, against Saint Jerome, who considered *Judaeae* an error of copyists for *Juda* or *Judae*. *Davida canorum* (“singing David”), as in book 2, verse 572: *Legistis certe in templo Davida canorum* (“Surely you have read in the temple of singing David”). Some vary in the quantity of the syllables in *Davidis*.

187. *Desponsa* (“betrothed woman”) here certainly refers to a wife. Luke, verse 5: *Ut profiteretur cum Maria desponsata sibi uxore praegnante* (“to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant”). *Profiteri* (“to declare,” “to register”) is a census term.

189. I discussed the word *habitaculum* (“dwelling,” “lodging”) in the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 10, verse 40. Sannazarius perhaps imitated Juvencus in book 2 *On the Birth of the Virgin*: *Est specus haud ingens parvae sub moenibus urbis* (“There is a not very large cave beneath the walls of a small city”).

Juvencus follows the opinion of those who maintain that the Savior was born in the outskirts of Bethlehem. He suggests that the lodging of which Luke speaks was some kind of cave or hollow in the earth; others too report this. Some teach that the Lord was born within the city of Bethlehem itself. Bede, chapter 8 *On the Holy Places*, says that the lodging was a kind of natural half-cave situated in the eastern corner of Bethlehem.

Juvencus’s view was both more common among the ancients and is now sufficiently accepted among Catholics. Nothing certain, however, can be derived from sacred Scripture to confirm such opinions. See Suárez, volume 17, question 35, disputation 13, section 3, to omit the many Protestants who have written special dissertations on the birthplace of Jesus Christ: Strauch, Gottfried Wegner, Johann Heinrich Krause, and Samuel Scherff. Among Catholics, Tillemont, Serry, and others support the suburb; Petavius, Sandinus, and many others support the city.

190. The sacred text reads: “While they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she bore her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the lodging.” One may consult Johann Christoph Letsch’s *Philological Exercise on the Cradle of Christ*; Daniel Vogel’s dissertation *On the Bethlehem Stable in Which the Redeemer of the Human Race Was Born*; Ernst Salomon Cyprian’s dissertation *On the Swaddling Clothes of Christ*; Georg Goet’s *Study on Christ’s Manger*; and Francesco Bianchini’s dissertation *On the Translation of the Holy Cradle and the Lord’s Manger, as well as of the Body of Blessed Jerome, from the Bethlehem Church to the Liberian Basilica*, volume 3 of Anastasius.]

191. The fact that the cradle should have wrapped the child in an ancient woven covering created difficulty for ancient copyists, who therefore altered this passage. It should be observed, however, that *cunabula* (“cradle”) can also mean the infant’s own little bed, or the swaddling clothes in which infants are wrapped.

Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act 5, scene 1, verse 51: “But that child whom I washed—how big he is, and how strong! No one could tie him up in a cradle.” Some read *quivit incunabulis* (“could in the cradle”), as in *Truculentus*, act 5, scene 1, verse 11: “Now there is need of coals, there is need of swaddling clothes, there is need of cushions, cradles, and cradles for infants.” Thus one might also read in the old Juvencus: *incunabula textu* (“a cradle of woven material”), and so forth.

Bede, *On Orthography*: “Cradles are the cloths of infancy,” but John, bishop of Constantinople, writes that Lazarus was wrapped in *cunabula* (“cradle-cloths”) in the tomb. On these words Cerda, *Adversaria*, chapter 121, number 68, says: “Here investigate what they are. I think that some take *cunabula* for any kind of swaddling clothes.” *Veteri textu* (“with an old woven covering”) denotes poverty, which some unjustly try to remove from the parents of Jesus Christ. Sedulius echoes Juvencus in book 2, verse 57: “He who clothes all things at birth with his own gifts had coverings of scanty cloth.”

192. Juvencus calls the bed or manger in which the Lord lay *durum* (“hard”). This by no means proves that it was not wooden, as I demonstrated against Basnage in the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 9, verse 77, where, at verse 80, page 374, I reproduced an ancient engraved image of the Savior’s wooden manger, which the highly esteemed Cardinal Borgia, out of his exceptional devotion to the study and preservation of sacred literature, generously shared with me from his rich museum.

The syntax of *pecorum custodia sollicitae noctis* (“the anxious night-watch of the flocks”) is somewhat complicated. In the sacred text: *Custodientes vigilias noctis super gregem suum* (“keeping the watches of the night over their flock”). Reuschius acknowledges that the two genitives, *pecorum* (“of the flocks”) and *sollicitae noctis* (“of the anxious night”), are governed by one noun, as in book 3, verse 369: *Incubuit, mentisque simul convulsa venena / Daemonis horrendi, purgato corde, fugavit* (“He attacked and at the same time drove away from the cleansed heart the convulsing poisons of the dreadful demon”). Omeisius arranges the words thus: “The night-watch held the shepherds of the flocks,” and so forth.

197. *Viridi terrae* (“of the green earth”), as in verse 194, *pascua laeta* (“joyful pastures”). There is no reason for Schoettgenius to doubt whether the ground in the Bethlehem countryside could have been green, although the Savior was born in winter, since the climate of that region is temperate. Still less would this one word compel us to abandon the common opinion about the day and month of the Lord’s birth, although opinions on this matter differ so greatly that, except for July, I know of no month that lacks some defender. Trombellius examines all these opinions in *The Life of the Mother of God*, volume 3, part 1, dissertation 18, chapter 1 and following; many others may be consulted there.

In most manuscripts of the Greek text one reads ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία (*en anthrṓpois eudokía*), “good will among human beings.” In some, however, as in the Vulgate and Old Latin version, one reads ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκίας (*en anthrṓpois eudokías*), “among people of good will.” The Fathers echo the Vulgate with great agreement. When Juvencus speaks of righteous people, he too understands “peace on earth to people of good will.” Menochius explains the sense of the Latin text as: “On earth, peace to people of God’s good will and divine pleasure—that is, peace to people whom God loves, already regards as pleasing, and in whom he delights.” Maldonatus had held the same view, referring the passage to the predestined. 210. The Vulgate: *Discesserunt ab eis angeli in coelum* (“The angels departed from them into heaven”). The Greek text is similar. But in some manuscripts of the old Latin version, in the singular: *Discessit angelus* (“The angel departed”). *Coeli secreta* (“the secrets of heaven”) is a phrase also used by other poets, as I noted concerning Dracontius, book 2, verse 4: *Quae coeli secreta tegunt* (“which conceal the secrets of heaven”). Other poets adopted it from them, such as Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book 2, chapter 33: *Coeli secreta penetrare* (“to penetrate the secrets of heaven”). It is also appropriate to revisit the statement concerning angels who return to their own place, from which they came. Virgil uses this verb more than once with that meaning.

212. *Gremium* (“lap,” “bosom”) is elegantly transferred and is also said of inanimate things, such as *gremium terrae* (“the bosom of the earth”), *gremium urbis* (“the bosom of the city”), and *gremium Graeciae* (“the bosom of Greece”). Silius, book 8, verse 192, of a river: “Until Numicius, as the story goes, received her into his sandy bosom and hid her in his glassy caves.” In our passage, since the subject is a child, *Praesepis gremio cernunt puerum jacentem* (“They see the child lying in the bosom of the manger”) has greater elegance.

213. Juvencus has captured the force of the Greek verb. διεγνώρισαν (*diegnṓrisan*) is ambiguous and means both “they recognized” and “they made known to others”; Juvencus expressed both meanings.

214. *Constupuerunt* (“they were utterly astonished”) comes from *constupeo*. I do not know whether this verb has any author other than Juvencus. He could indeed have said *laetantes obstupuerunt* (“rejoicing, they were astonished”), but he preferred *constupuerunt*, so as to declare that they were all astonished together.

[Col. 0087D] 215. The shepherds were astonished because everything corresponded to the nocturnal commands and was truly what they had been told during the night. This astonishment seems here to be narrated as occurring on the day itself or on the following days. For when the shepherds had seen the child lying there, they afterward, as verse 212 says, scattered the wandering seeds of swift report. Then follows: *Laetantes obstupuerunt—Omnia nocturnis monitis quod vera recurrant* (“Rejoicing, they were astonished—because everything returned as true in accordance with the nocturnal commands”). The same order seems to be set out in the sacred text: *Vera recurrant* (“that they return as true”), as in book 2, verse 769: *Ut dictum Isaiae merita de plebe recurrat* (“so that Isaiah’s saying may rightly return concerning the people”).

216. CHAPTER VIII. The Circumcision of the Lord. Luke 2:21.

217. Special dissertations *On the Circumcision of the Lord* have been written by Wilhelm Lyser, Antonius Bynaeus, and Daniel Gerdes. The Evangelist’s words do not clearly state that the child Jesus was circumcised: *Et postquam consummati sunt dies octo, ut circumcideretur puer, vocatum est nomen ejus Jesus* (“And when the eight days were completed, so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called Jesus”). Circumcision is indicated more clearly in the Greek text, where, after *puer* (“child”), there is the conjunction “and,” by which circumcision is in a certain sense asserted, with the giving of the name added afterward.

Juvencus certainly asserts the circumcision, which must be believed with divine faith, since the whole Church has understood Luke’s words in this way. The necessity for Christ to be circumcised according to the custom of the Law should be explained with a suitable distinction. Christ was not subject to the commandment of circumcision, and therefore his parents were not obliged to circumcise him. Besides the fact that he was God, he had not been generated from male seed. Nevertheless, Suárez, volume 17, disputation 15, section 1, teaches that although it was not in itself necessary for Christ’s parents to circumcise the child, it could reasonably have been regarded as necessary in consequence, in order to avoid scandal.

Moreover, it was supremely fitting that Christ be circumcised. Saint Thomas, part 3, question 37, article 1, with his theological gravity and exceptional intellectual acuity, by which he habitually cuts matters to the quick, lists seven distinct reasons why Christ ought to have been circumcised. This is sufficient for it to be said, in some sense, that it was necessary for Christ to be circumcised according to the custom of the Law. The phrase “to adapt the name” seems to have been borrowed by the Pseudo-Cyprian in the treatise *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, chapter *On the Meaning of Circumcision*: “Since this was commanded to be celebrated on the eighth day, and the name was to be applied to the circumcised man,” and so forth.

218. “His name was imposed on him,” as the voice commanded, and so forth—namely, Jesus.

219. “Sent by God” (*missa Deo*) instead of “by God” (*a Deo*): a dative used for an ablative, a usage familiar to Juvencus in passive constructions of this kind. On the expression *missa a Deo*, see verse 98. Luke, who entirely omits the history of the Magi, immediately after the circumcision recounts Mary’s purification: “His name was called Jesus,” the name that had been given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. “And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord.” Matthew, however, who passes over Mary’s purification in silence, immediately after the Savior’s birth records the arrival of the Magi, and then his flight into Egypt: “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem,” etc. “When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Rise, and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.”

This difficulty has long troubled interpreters: did the purification precede the arrival of the Magi, or did the arrival of the Magi precede the purification? If we say that the Magi came first, before Christ was presented in the Temple, it is not clear how Christ could have been presented in the Temple after their arrival, since Herod, having been deceived by the Magi, sought him in order to destroy him, and Joseph, after the Magi had departed, was warned by the angel to flee into Egypt. Moreover, Herod’s command that all male children two years old and under should be killed shows that the Magi did not come to Jerusalem immediately after the child’s birth.

Conversely, if we maintain that Christ’s presentation and Mary’s purification took place before the arrival of the Magi, it must be explained how it happened that the Magi worshiped the infant Jesus in the city of Bethlehem. For after mentioning the offering in the Temple, Luke adds, in chapter 2, verse 39: “And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.”

Undeterred by this difficulty, Juvencus first relates the presentation in the Temple and then the arrival of the Magi. Since Mary’s purification took place on the fortieth day after Jesus’ birth, according to the law, what Luke says about Jesus’ parents’ return to Galilee may indeed be understood to mean that they returned immediately; but afterward, when the year had turned, at approximately the season in which the Savior had been born, they may have returned to the city of Bethlehem. Luke himself relates the same at verse 41: “And his parents went every year to Jerusalem for the solemn feast of the Passover.”

Saint Epiphanius, who in book I of *Against Heresies*, chapter 30, no. 29, states that the Magi came to worship Christ after two full years had passed, also reports that Joseph and Mary came with the infant to Bethlehem every year—or at least in the first and second years—at the time when the child had been born.

Others, however, rather suppose that Luke, after recounting the purification, immediately stated that Jesus’ parents returned with the child to Galilee because he was not going to mention the flight into Egypt. Joseph was warned of that flight in a dream after the presentation in the Temple, but before they had returned to Galilee. This is the view of Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, chapter 5; Bede; Jansenius of Ghent; Cajetan; and many others.

Although most therefore believe that the Magi’s adoration occurred either on the thirteenth day after the Savior’s birth or at least before the fortieth day, the solution to the difficulty adopted by Juvencus, a very ancient interpreter, should not be dismissed. On this subject one may consult Hermann Rombach’s work, *The First Fruits of the Nations, or the History and Praise of the Three Holy Magi*; Petrus de Marca’s dissertation, *On the Arrival of the Magi to Christ, and Whether They Were Kings*; Florentinius’s *Exercise 3, On the History of the Magi Who Came to Christ and the Time of Their Journey*; Alphonsus de Mendoza, *On the History of the Magi*; Stephanus Salazar, *On the Arrival of the Magi*; Leichnerus, *On the Time of the Magi*; Augustine Calmet’s dissertation, *On the Magi*; Balthasar Stolberg; Daniel Roden, *On Those Same Magi*; and Laurentius Benedictus Triebel, *On the Magi Who Arrived after Jesus Had Been Presented in the Temple*, in the new *Theological-Philological Treasury*.

Hardouin and Berruyer hold a peculiar opinion. They imagine that Christ’s offering in the Temple took place when he was already three years old, at approximately the age when Anna brought her son Samuel to the Temple. Trombellius fully explains and refutes their interpretation in *On the Life of the Mother of God*, volume III, part I, dissertation 22.

And at the same time, after these words, they revisit the secrets of heaven.

The shepherds hasten and see the child lying

They praise in amazement; rejoicing, they stand astonished,

According to the custom of the law, and his name must be assigned.

## Notes

**219.** Sabatier: “And among the first,” and, instead of *pro d. s.*, “Among which the first,” which is the reading I find in one manuscript and in the printed editions.

**221.** Aldine, Tornesian, Roman, Reginensis, and Ottobonian manuscripts: *sed a sec. m.*, apparently also Barthius’s manuscript and others, *sensu—Coelestes voces*. Hadamar, Poelmann, and Fabricius: *sensum—Coelestis vocis*. Barthius’s manuscript writes *coelesteis* instead of *coelestes*, from which perhaps *coelestis vocis* arose, with *sensum* first produced from *sensu*. Poelmann also has, instead of *pro d. s.*, *sensu—Coelesteis voces*. In the Ottobonian manuscript there is an error, *dignis* for *dignus*, as appears from the correction made there.

**231.** Reginensis and Roman manuscripts: *palumbes*. Ottobonian, Tornesian, Aldine, Poelmann, and, instead of *pro d. s.*, Fabricius: *palumbos*. Poelmann in the text, Hadamar, *columbas*.

## Notes

**220. Chapter IX. Mary’s purification. Luke 2:9–39.** The title *Christ’s presentation in the Temple* would be more accurate, for Juvencus scarcely speaks of Mary’s purification.

**221.** The construction is obscure and the sentence insufficiently clear. The Evangelist has, verse 23: “As it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord. And to offer a sacrifice, according to what was said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” The sense of Juvencus’s words can therefore be extracted as follows: among the regulations of the ancient law, Moses gave this command for observance, that those descended from the ancient priestly stock should offer the firstborn for consecration to God. The law itself is worded in Leviticus 12:6: “And when the days of her purification have been completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a yearling lamb as a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove as a sin offering to the door of the tent of meeting, and she shall hand it to the priest. He shall offer it before the Lord and shall pray,” etc.

**222.** *Observare dedit*, “he gave for observance,” is a Graecism, like *Ferre sui dederat monumentum*, “he had given a memorial to be carried,” and *pignus amoris, Magnum dat ferre talentum*, “a pledge of love; he gives a great talent to be carried.” Virgil and other writers use the same construction. See below, verse 309.

**224.** Although neither Christ was included under the law of presentation in the Temple nor Mary under the law of purification, it was nevertheless especially fitting that Mary should observe that law for her son and for herself, as we said concerning the circumcision at verse 217. The theologians discuss this matter in the third part of Saint Thomas, questions 37, articles 3 and 4.

**225.** *Simeon* means “hearing” or “obedient.” Juvencus perhaps has this etymology in mind when he says that Simeon was worthy to grasp the heavenly voices with understanding.

**227.** He calls the body a “prison” in a phrase familiar to sacred and ecclesiastical writers. On this, see more in the commentary on Prudentius, verse 44 of the preface, page 233.

**228.** “He would see death” is taken from the sacred text, “he would not see death,” which is expressed in the same way in the Greek text. Perhaps this expression belongs to the figure by which one sense, or one of its acts, is sometimes substituted for another. *To see* is used for *to experience*, as in Psalm 15:10: “Nor will you give your holy one to see corruption.”

**229.** “The praise of heaven,” namely, the one whom heaven praises.

**230.** Below, verse 272: “All the oracles of the seers promise that he will come.” The verb *spondere*, “to promise,” is often used of prophets and prophecies.

**231.** The law stated: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons”; and shortly before Juvencus says, “and likewise to carry fledgling pigeons to the shrines.” Why, then, does he now say *palumbes*, “wood-pigeons”? I suppose that he wished thereby to make the Virgin’s poverty more evident. For a *palumbes*, or *palumbus*, is a wild pigeon that nests in trees and hedges. From the Gospel itself it is not clear whether the Mother of God offered turtledoves, pigeons, or wood-pigeons.

Suarez, in the third part, question 37, disputation 16, section 1, says: “It is worthy of notice why the Evangelist did not state their offering definitely, but reported it disjunctively. The law itself was framed disjunctively because it wished to leave this to the will of those making the offering; nevertheless, in practice the requirement was not fulfilled unless one of the two was offered specifically. Since Luke is acting not as a legislator but as a historian, why did he not state specifically what the Virgin offered? In truth, there is no other reason except that he wished only to signify the Virgin’s poverty, which could be useful to us. For whether she offered a turtledove or a young pigeon had no bearing on our instruction.”

97 Moses had written the ordinances of the ancient law,

98 Among which he ordained that the firstborn, of the ancient stock of seers,

Should be offered for consecration,

And that fledgling pigeons likewise should be carried to the shrines.

When these things, observed by Mary, are brought to the Temple,

[225] Behold, the old man Simeon, worthy to grasp

The heavenly voices with understanding, to whom once the power

That knew the future had revealed that, after laying aside

The prison of his ailing body, he would see death freely

And rest, when first he had seen the praise of heaven

And the salvation of earth—

[230] 99 Christ, whom all the oracles of the prophets promise—

He saw the wood-pigeons being solemnly carried into the Temple.

[Note]

**232.** Trombellius, in *The Life of the Blessed Virgin*, volume III, dissertation 22, reads *Ipse ubi curvato*; instead, *pro d. s.*, *Isque ubi*, which others prefer. I believe Juvencus wrote *Is ubi*, with the monosyllable *is* lengthened, as I shall explain elsewhere in similar cases. The Tornesian edition incorrectly has *ubi curato*. The sense requires *curvato*.

**233.** Trombellius, in the same work, dissertation 22, question 7, chapter 1, reads *movit*; instead, *pro d. s.*, *monvit*. He approves *movit*, namely, that God added strength to Simeon’s body. The common reading *monuit* is also more correct. The Evangelist’s words are: “And he came in the Spirit into the Temple.”

**237.** The Tornesian edition has *Nunc me famulum*, contrary to the meter. Gruner prefers the reading of manuscript Un., *Nunc, nunc jam famulum*. Aldine and Poelmann in the text, Reginensis, Roman, and Hadamar: *atris*. Tornesian and Fabricius: *arctis*. In the Ottobonian manuscript *arctis* was deleted and changed to *atris*. *Arctis* is preferable. In the Roman manuscript there is the error *Deus* for *Dominus*. Sabatier has *liberat arctis*; but afterward, verse 239, *Dignetur*. The manuscripts and printed editions give *liberet*, followed by *Dignetur*. Yet *liberat … Dignatur* agrees better with Luke’s words. The ancient versions and the Fathers consistently have: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.” Ambrose, however, in book *On Joshua*, chapter 3, reads: “Now, Lord, dismiss your servant in peace,” and likewise in book II of his commentary on Luke. Elsewhere he agrees with the others.

**238.** In the Ottobonian and Reginensis manuscripts, *vinculis* has rightly been corrected to *vinclis*.

**240.** Aldine, Tornesian, Fabricius, Reginensis, and Poelmann, instead of *pro d. s.*, have *radiisque refulget*. Hadamar and Poelmann in the text have *radiusque refulget*. The Ottobonian manuscript, against the metrical reasoning, has *radiisque renitet*, unless one corrects it to *renidet*, as seems to have been done in the Roman manuscript. Koenigius produced *renidet* from Barthius’s manuscripts; Reuschius also printed it.

**241.** Poelmann, instead of *pro d. s.*, and the Roman, Ottobonian from the first hand, Tornesian, Aldine, and Fabricius have *addet*. Reginensis, Hadamar, and others have *addit*. The Aldine edition has *mentibus* for *gentibus*.

**242.** Perhaps *cumulata* or *cumulate*. After this verse, Poelmann, Aldine, Tornesian, Fabricius, and the Daventrian edition contain another verse: “Hence he says: ‘Virgin, why do these things seem so wondrous to you?’” It was inserted by some ignorant person so that Simeon’s speech would appear to turn toward the Virgin, as in the Evangelist. It is absent from Barthius’s manuscript and from our Reginensis, Roman, and Ottobonian manuscripts. It was also omitted from Reuschius’s edition, which Gallandius incorrectly suspected had happened through a typographical error.

**243.** The Aldine edition lacks this verse: “Why so greatly [did] Mary’s …” Barthius, book LVIII, chapter 5, says that *viscera matris*, “the mother’s inward parts,” was commonly written; but I do not find it even in Fabricius, whose edition Barthius usually corrects at that passage.

**244.** Barthius’s manuscript and the Roman manuscript have *ad casum populi datur*, which Tornensis printed. Others have *ad populi casum*. The Aldine and Daventrian editions have *ad casum populis datur*.

**245.** Reginensis has *Concedet populos*, with Tornensis. Most have *populis*. Gruner, together with the English manuscripts, prefers *populos*. Tornesian, Aldine, Fabricius, and Daventrian, after *populos* or *populis*, read as follows:

“They will deny that he is a sign to them;
But these will hold that he came from heaven.
Ravenous envy will bring it about that bitter death
Will run its course;
And the soul …”

Poelmann likewise has this reading, but with Aldine and Tornesian reads: “And your soul, flashing with the sword, believe me, with the sword,” instead of the others’ “And the soul of the mother with the sword flashing from iron.” Barthius’s manuscript, Poelmann in the text, the Roman, Ottobonian, and Hadamar have:

“*populis*, a sign spoken against;
This one will come, running through what is owed to death;
And the soul of the mother with the sword flashing from iron;
So that …”

The Reginensis has the same, but, as I said above, *populos* and soon afterward *percurret debita*, as the Ottobonian also has. The Roman has *animum* for *animam*. Barthius leaves the reading of his manuscript for consideration by those who, as he says, will someday adorn the finest Christian poet, valuable for antiquity, with a new recension. Gallandius considers the same reading less correct in Reuschius’s edition. I retain the shorter wording, for the longer seems to have been produced to make Juvencus’s somewhat obscure verses clearer.

## Notes

**232.** Simeon’s old age is described. With advancing age the body becomes bent. They think that a decrepit person was called *silicernium*, as though he “looked upon a flint.” That Simeon was old can be inferred from the Gospel, and the Church sings it in the antiphon to the Magnificat at the First Vespers of the Purification. In the readings of the second nocturn of the same feast, from a sermon attributed to Saint Augustine but now not believed to be his, it is asserted: “He was presented in the Temple and recognized by the old man Simeon, renowned, aged, approved, and crowned.” More certainly, Saint Augustine says in Sermon 20 *On the Season*: “That old man Simeon had lived a long time.”

**233.** *Gremium* differs from *sinus*: the *sinus* is within the breast and arms, whereas the *gremium* is the embrace formed by the belly and thighs when one is seated. If the words were used with strict propriety, *sinus* should be written here instead of *gremium*. But one is often used for the other, whatever Valla argues against this in *Elegantiae*, book IV, chapter 37; Badius seems to follow him. Nevertheless, Badius interprets the passage to mean that the lower part of the child could have been warmed in the lap while the upper part rested in the arms.

**238.** “From the bonds of the body,” as in verse 227, “the prison of the body.” See also Barthius, *Adversaria*, page 1064, where he proves that *vincula* can be used for bodies, or rather for life, as he says.

**239.** The Evangelist says “in peace.” This formula, taken from the Psalms and other passages of Holy Scripture, was always used by Christians and was frequently inscribed in funerary epitaphs. Compare Lupius, Dissertation 1, *On Baptisteries*, no. 138 and following.

**241.** *Lustratis*: purified, cleansed from sin, or illuminated. See verse 280.

**242.** Koenigius disputes the quantity of the third syllable in *Israelitarum*, as though it necessarily had to be long. But apart from the fact that there would be no fault if the second and third syllables were both shortened, the two vowels may also be contracted by synaeresis, so that the first foot is a spondee. Koenigius himself seems to concede this when he observes that a diphthong can be formed from *a* and *e*. In exactly the same way Dracontius, Fortunatus, Drepanius, and others pronounced *Israelitarum* in their hexameters.

**243.** *Tantum*: “so greatly,” “to such an extent,” as above at verse 79.

**245.** Luke’s words are: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed.” Juvencus’s verses correspond to these words: “This child, until he will come.” Luke continues: “And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” The Old Latin version in the Colbert manuscript has: “And your soul, and his own, will pass through,” etc.; the Cambridge manuscript has: “And your own soul, however.” Juvencus renders this as follows: “The sword, flashing from iron, will run through what death claims, and the soul of the mother.”

I understand *debita letho*, “owed to death,” to mean the son’s life, which was owed to death, as in the expression “to pay the debt of nature.” This is Reuschius’s interpretation. This same sword, however, will be the sign by which it is shown that this child is the Messiah; but some will deny that the sword is the sign of the Messiah. *Signum dicta in contraria* is taken from the Greek text, **σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον**, that is, “a sign concerning which dispute will be made on both sides.” This is also Reuschius’s view, following his own reading.

More correctly, however, with Maldonado, I interpret Christ as having been appointed as a sign against which nearly all the Jews would cast not only their words but also their weapons. They were not content merely to blaspheme often; they also crucified him. In his Passion Christ was like a target at which people commonly contend by opposing, striking, and piercing. His Passion itself brought such intense grief to Mary that, as it were, a sword pierced her soul. And while Christ suffered in this way, it became apparent what disposition and what faith each person held toward him.

And when he, weary in his bent body, now more heavily burdened by age, enters the Temple—as the guiding Spirit had instructed him—

Behold, he at once perceived that the little Jesus had come to the Temple in his mother’s lap; with trembling arms

[235] 100 he received the child and joyfully uttered these words:

“Now, now, let the Lord release me, his servant, now,

From the narrow bonds of the body, and deign

To bring my words to their end in peace. Behold, your splendid light

[240] Surrounds our eyes and shines forth in its rays,

Which he will add to all the nations, illuminating them,

To the accumulated glory of the Israelite people.

101 Why did Mary’s motherly heart marvel so greatly?

This child is appointed for the fall of the people; he will grant

[245] The peoples rebirth; a sign spoken against.

This one will come; the sword will run through what death claims,

102 And the soul of the mother, with the sword flashing from iron,

So that the hidden, dark scrolls of the heart may be revealed.”

Thus God spoke in Simeon; and soon, behold, to the prophetess

[250] He filled the female mind with holy inspiration.

Anna was advanced in age; in the flower of youth

An untimely death had deprived her of her husband,

But chaste life and the worship of God took the place

Of a husband for her. Under divine command she recognized

[255] Christ and spoke with a corresponding utterance.

Then, when the mother had fulfilled the solemn law

For the child’s name, and Joseph marveled at everything,

They happily returned to their homeland and carried the child home.

[Note]

**249.** All the printed editions I have seen read: “God said these things in Simeon: behold, the voice of the prophetess.” Barthius found the passage corrupt in his manuscript: “Simeon said this; presently God, behold, the prophetess.” He hoped to restore the true reading from other manuscripts. Three manuscripts cited by Reuschius, and our Roman, Reginensis, and Ottobonian manuscripts, give: “God said these things in Simeon: presently, behold, the prophetess.” The feminine form is explained in a gloss in the Reginensis: “the prophetess—Anna the prophetess,” namely, God completed the female mind of Anna the prophetess. Since scribes did not understand that *prophetes* could be said of a woman, just as *sacerdos*, *vates*, and similar words can, they corrupted the verse by putting *vox* for *mox*.

**252.** Poelmann, instead of the divided reading, and the Aldine and Daventrian editions have *Constituit viduam*, “he appointed a widow.”

**253.** The printed editions read:

“Then she enjoys a chaste life in place of a dear husband,
And continuous worship of God; she, led by divine power,
Recognized him.”

Some manuscripts cited by Reuschius, as he indicates here, and our Reginensis, Roman, and Ottobonian manuscripts read:

“Chaste, but always in the Temple, in place of a husband’s life,
And the worship of God came to her; she, commanded by divine power,
Recognized him.”

The gloss in the Reginensis says: “*cessere*, they came to that woman; *jussa*, compelled.”

**257.** The Roman manuscript has *genitrix, Joseph*; *et* is absent.

**258.** Poelmann in the text and Hadamar have *redeunt*; most have *repedant*. Barthius’s manuscript has *repetunt*. Virgil, Gratius, and others use *repeto* with the preposition *ad*. The Roman manuscript has the erroneous reading *Ad primam laeti*, “joyful at the first.”

## Notes

**247.** In the Vulgate and the Old Latin version, *machaera* is called *gladius*, “sword”; by Paulinus, in letter 50, formerly numbered 43, it is called *framea* or *gladius*; by Augustine, in letter 149, *framea*; in the Greek text it is **ῥομφαία**, *rhomphaia*. A *machaera* is a long sword sharpened on one side; *framea* and *rhomphaia* are types of spear. In Augustine’s time, however, *framea* and *rhomphaia* also signified a certain kind of sword. See Augustine, letter 120, chapter 16, and Isidore, *Origins*, book XVIII, chapter 6.

**248.** Notice how Juvencus interprets the Gospel’s words “so that they may be revealed.” Here the particle *ut* is not causal. *Quo pateant* means the same as “then they will be revealed.” *Volumina cordis*, “the scrolls of the heart,” is perhaps a new but elegant expression. A *volumen* is anything bent into a circle. Compare Pliny, book VII, chapter 45: “The great cycles of human fortune.”

**249.** I see no adequate reason why *propheta* or *prophetes* could not be said of a woman. Reuschius would not have hesitated to follow our reading if this use of *prophetes* had been established for him. Yet Hilary plainly says in his commentary on Psalm 14, no. 4, *Anna prophetes*, “Anna the prophetess.” The Old Latin version in the Cambridge manuscript has *Anna prophetis*; *prophetis* will be either the genitive of *prophetes* or of *prophetis*. One could therefore read: “Then, behold, the prophetess.” But let us accept Hilary as the authority; we use the common word *propheta*, which by itself is restricted to a female prophet by the following expression *femineam mentem*, “a woman’s mind.” Vossius, book I of *On Analogy*, chapter 19, cites from Aeschylus **τὰς προφήτας**, “female prophets”; from Tertullian, *prophetes* more than once; and from Sidonius, *psaltes*.

**250.** See the note on verse 120.

**254.** *Cessere*: “succeeded,” “took the place of”; *evenere*: “came to her,” as though the best possible lot had entered into the place of a husband. Nepos, *Life of Datames*, chapter 1: “Those things which turned out favorably for him.” Virgil, book III of the *Aeneid*, verse 333: “With Neoptolemus dead, the kingdom passed to Helenus.” Ignorance of this meaning gave the scribes an occasion for corrupting the passage. *Numine jussa*: “commanded by divine will,” as in verse 299, *Divino numine jussus*, “commanded by divine will.”

**256.** *Pueri* is used for the name, or for the person of the child himself, as in Revelation, chapter 3, verse 4. Compare what I discussed on this subject in *Hymnodia Hispana*, in the note on the hymn of Saint Isidore, page 275.

**258.** “To his homeland,” namely Nazareth. Luke continues in chapter 2, verse 39: “And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.” How, then, could Christ have been worshiped by the Magi at Bethlehem after his presentation in the Temple? For Juvencus, Epiphanius may answer; as I said at verse 220, he supposes that Jesus’ parents came with him again to Bethlehem from Galilee.

A people farther away, familiar with the rising sun,

[260] 104 Skilled in observing the risings and settings of the stars.

The foremost men of this people bore the name of Magi.

From this people selected nobles arrive at Solymi by long roads,

Approach the king, and ask to be told

Which region of Judea held the child under royal rule,

[265] 105 Who had been born: they said that from the rising

Of the shining star they had been warned to travel,

So that with suppliant right hands they might worship

The venerable divine power that had arisen upon earth.

Herod, terrified, [asked] the foremost men of Jerusalem,

[Note]

**259.** Reginensis, Roman, Ottobonian, Poelmann, and, instead of *pro d. s.*, Tornensis: “There is a people farther away, familiar with the rising sun.” The Aldine edition has *proxima*, “nearest,” instead of *conscia*, “familiar.” Fabricius, Poelmann in the text, and Hadamar have: “There is a people of the eastern Phoebus, near the realm of the rising sun.” Perhaps the reading should be *surgentis conscia solis*, “familiar with the rising sun.”

**261.** Barthius, book LVII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 2, printed *Quorum primores*, “whose foremost men.” I do not know whether *Hujus primores* arose by chance.

**262.** Poelmann, instead of the divided reading, and the Ottobonian and Roman manuscripts have *Solymos*. The Reginensis has *Tunc hi delecti Solymos*, and previously seems to have had *dilecti*. Others have *Solymas*.

**265.** Hadamar, Poelmann in the text, and Fabricius have *Jam genitum: et sese*. Poelmann, instead of the divided reading, and Fabricius have *Progenitum; et sese*. The Aldine and Tornesian editions, together with the Reginensis and Ottobonian manuscripts, more elegantly have *Progenitum: sese* without *et*. The Roman and Daventrian manuscripts likewise have this. Compare again verse 274, *Progigni maneat*.

**266.** The Ottobonian manuscript from the first hand has *via*. *Viam* is better. Trombellius, in *On the Life of the Mother of God*, volume III, part I, dissertation 23, inexplicably printed *venisse diem*, “that the day had come”; instead, the divided reading indicates *viam*, “the road.”

**268.** Poelmann in the text, Aldine, Hadamar, and Fabricius have: “Herod, skilled in the prophetic utterances and laws.” Tornesian, Poelmann instead of the divided reading, Reginensis, Roman, and Ottobonian have: “Herod, the heights of the Solymi, the prophets.”

## Notes

**259. Chapter X. The Magi come with gifts. Matthew 2:1–12.** Reuschius favors the interpretation that this people is called “familiar with the rising sun” because it knew its rising. I think it is better understood as meaning that the people was, as it were, adjacent to the rising sun.

A speech on the Magi from the East, delivered by Samuel Durrie under the direction of Omeisius, was printed at Altdorf in 1686. Many authors have written about these same Magi; I listed them at verse 220. Antonius Collinus most impudently denied the historical truth of the Magi, attempting to prove that their story had been inserted into Matthew’s Gospel. This intolerable error is refuted by the authority not only of other ancient Fathers but also of Juvencus, whose authority is by no means suspect. See the learned dissertation of Liberatus Fassonius, *On the Truth and Divinity of the History of the Magi Found in Matthew*, Rome, 1758.

Juvencus thinks that the Magi came from the remote regions of the East, since he calls their people “farther away” and “familiar with the rising sun.” Shortly afterward, at verse 276, he calls them Persians. In Juvencus’s time this name was applied to all the eastern nations outside the Roman Empire, as Barthius thinks in book LVIII, chapter 2. Yet I readily believe that Juvencus regarded them as actual Persians. Indeed, I think Prudentius imitated Juvencus when he sang in hymn 12 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 25:

“Behold, from the heart of the Persian world,
Where the sun takes its gate,
The Magi, skilled interpreters,
See the royal standard.”

Compare our commentary on this passage of Prudentius.

**260.** “Skilled at observing.” Horace, book IV, ode 8, verse 7: “One skilled now in portraying a man on stone, now a god in liquid colors.” Ovid, Silius, and other poets use similar language. The wise men of various peoples, who presided over sacred rites, directed ceremonies, and devoted themselves to hidden disciplines, were called Magi.

Juvencus attributes astronomy and mathematical contemplation to them. Tertullian, Saint Leo, Sicardus of Cremona, Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, and Saint Thomas held the same view, as did most scholastic writers who follow him. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 617, says of the Magi: “The astrologer, trembling, stiffened through the sleepless night upon the Chaldean summit.” At this passage Weitzius cites the verse: “Among the Persians he is a Magus who knows the stars.”

In ancient times whatever was secret and beyond the understanding of the common people was called *magic*. Thus Lucan, book III of the *Pharsalia*, calls the hieroglyphic carvings of the Egyptians “magical languages”; for at verse 223 he says: “And in stones only, birds and beasts, and animals carved, preserved magical languages.”

**261.** It is also disputed whether the Magi were kings. This is commonly believed, but the opinion lacks certain support from ancient authority. Juvencus calls them “the foremost men” of that people. Barthius says that this title arose from the reverence in which the Magi were held by the eastern peoples because of their studies of wisdom. In fact, Juvencus suggests rather that they were not kings than that they were. Fabricius, in his *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, believes that the Magi held a dignity immediately below that of kings.

**262.** Juvencus suggests that the Magi came as envoys, chosen by their peoples to worship Christ. Gaudentius of Brescia, *Sermon 19 to Paul the Brother*: “Herod persecutes the little one, but the splendor of the obedient star declares the great God; the Magi, envoys of all nations, humbly worshiped him and brought to the heavenly king the honor due to him by offering mystical gifts.”

This too is obscure, for the Magi were not actually sent by all nations. Nevertheless, the nations are signified through them. “Through long roads,” as above at verse 180, “through many lands.” Jerusalem, the chief city of Palestine, was also called *Solyma*, or *Solymi*. The peoples of Palestine were called Solymi. Tacitus, book V of the *Histories*, chapter 2: “The Solymi, a people celebrated in the poems of Homer, gave the city founded by them the name Jerusalem from their own name.” Hence the adjective *Solymus*. Juvenal, satire 6, verse 543: “An interpreter of Solymian laws.”

**264.** Schoettgen explains the phrase as: “Which region of Judea, which part of Judea, would hold the child under royal rule,” apparently against the Muses. I explain it as: “Which region of Judea, etc.”

**265.** A speech on the star that guided the Magi, delivered by Wilhelm Fritzius under the direction of Omeisius, was printed at Altdorf in 1683.

**266.** *Venisse viam*, “to have traveled a road,” like *ire iter*, “to go a journey,” *vivere vitam*, “to live a life,” and *servire servitutem*, “to serve a servitude.” Cicero, *Philippic* II, chapter 25: “To have traveled a journey of so many days.” In truth, Cicero’s expression is more elegant because *tot dierum*, “of so many days,” is added. Similarly, “I live an unhappy life” is more elegant than simply “I live a life”; and below Juvencus has *Gaudia magna Magi gaudent*, “the Magi rejoice with great joy,” which is more graceful than if he had said *Gaudia Magi gaudent* without an adjective serving the function of an adverb.

**267.** “Let them worship the divine power.” Thus at verse 277: “To show what must be worshiped”; and at verse 285: “And they gave gifts to the king, the human being, and God.” Juvencus and other Fathers therefore read in the Gospel that Christ was worshiped by the Magi as God.

Accordingly, Joannes Franciscus Buddeus, *Sacred Meditations*, page 56; Honoratus of Saint Mary, volume II of *Observations on the Rules of Criticism*, book III, dissertation 4, article 5; and Fassonius, in his special dissertation *On the Worship Given to Jesus Christ by the Magi*, Rome, 1736, rightly expose and refute the impudent rashness of Basnage, Le Clerc, and Richard Simon, to mention no others.

**268.** The priests of the pagans were called seers and prophets. Macrobius, book VII of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 13: “So much so,” he says, “that, as you say the Egyptians believe, when I had seen their priests, whom they call prophets,” etc. When Juvencus says at verse 279 *Imperio accitos*, “summoned by command,” he changes the grammatical gender because he is attending to the sense, not the words. See the commentary on Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 504, and the note on Dracontius, *Elegies*, verse 153.

274. “Let it remain,” that is, “let it be fixed.” Cicero more than once has *Maneat ergo* (“Let it therefore remain”) and *Illud maneat* (“Let that remain”); others imitate him.

276. *Pertendere gressum*, as *tendere iter* (“to pursue a journey”) and *tendere cursum* (“to pursue a course”).

278. *Iteris* for *itineris*, the more usual form. *Obliquis iteris*, etc., is used by Lucretius, Propertius, Accius, Varro, Naevius, and Julius Hyginus. On the star that appeared to the Magi, see the dissertations of Johann Friedrich Frenzel, Elias Bertrand, and Jacob Elsner.

279. *Sulcantem auras*, an elegant metaphor. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.694 ff.:

> A star, leading a torch with abundant light, ran on . . .  
> Then, along a long track, a furrow—  
> Gives light.

Lucan, Valerius Flaccus, Prudentius, and other good poets have similar expressions.

280. *Lustrata*, namely, “as though illuminated” by the star itself. For the simple verb is often used for a compound one, as *verto* for *everto*. Nor do I assign any other meaning to *lustro* when Virgil says, *Aeneid* IV.607:

> The sun, which with your flames illuminates all the works of the earth;

and VII.148:

> When the following day was illuminating the lands  
> With its first lamp.

281. *Gaudia magna gaudent*, “they rejoice with great joy,” an elegant expression, as I observed at verse 266. In Cicero’s *Letters to Friends* VIII.2, a letter of Caelius to Cicero, we read: *Ut suum gaudium gauderemus*, “that we might rejoice in his joy.” Terence, *Andria* V.5, at the end:

> For I know that he alone will rejoice wholeheartedly in my joys.

Add Aulus Gellius IX.9: *Gaudium gaudeat genuinum et intimum*, “May he rejoice with genuine and profound joy.”

282. *Videre* deserves notice. Although the Vulgate has *invenerunt*, “they found,” *viderunt*, “they saw,” occurs in most Greek manuscripts cited by Wetstein, Birch, and Matthaei. The oldest Vatican manuscript, 1209, likewise has *viderunt*, as does the Latin version of the ancient Cambridge codex and the author of the *Incomplete Commentary on Matthew*.

285. Since the gifts offered by the Magi mystically signify God, king, and man, there is no doubt that frankincense signifies God, gold the king, and myrrh the man, whatever order in which those gifts may ultimately be mentioned. Prudentius assigns the same meaning to these gifts in the *Dittochaeon*, although he does not preserve the order:

> Here the Magi bring precious gifts to Christ,  
> A child beneath the Virgin’s breast: myrrh, frankincense, and gold.  
> The mother marvels at so many honors of her chaste womb,  
> And that she has borne God, man, and also the supreme king.

I have said more about this offering of gifts in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 12 *Cath.* verse 69.

> Who recount the predictions foretold by the ancient prophets,
>
> [270] He orders all things to be sought out from the law by those summoned under his authority,
>
> So that it may become clear which city is Christ’s birthplace;
>
> All the oracles of the prophets promise that he will come.
>
> [106] Then it is revealed that he is destined to be born  
> [275] within the walls of Bethlehem;  
> He must lead the sacred people of the Israelites

>

>

>
> [295] [Col. 0100A] He ordered a dreadful slaughter throughout Bethlehem’s streets,
>

>
> Be torn away by the sword, though guilty of no offense.

>

>
