### Notes

286. Ottobonian, Reginensis, Poelmannian: *Dona dabant*, “they were giving gifts,” for *d. s.* (“for the reading”). Perhaps *Donabant* should be read, since *munera* has preceded. Aldine, together with most copies: *Dona ferunt*, “they bring gifts,” as it is also read by Jerome and Alcuin.

287. Roman manuscript: *Sollicitant, scevumque jubent*, “they disturb and command the savage one”; thus the Roman manuscript commonly writes *scevus* for *saevus*, and these words are often confused in manuscripts, namely *scaevus* and *saevus*.

289. Aldine: *rediere latenter*, “they returned secretly.” Roman manuscript, incorrectly: *magi redire laetantes*, “the Magi return rejoicing.”

293. Roman manuscript, in the margin: *Quae* for *Quem*.

295. Reginensis, Roman, and Ottobonian:

> Horrible slaughter throughout Bethlehem’s streets he ordered,  
> Commanding that all the infants and the tender population at the breast  
> Be torn away by the sword, though guilty of no offense.

In the Roman manuscript *cunctos* occurs for *mandans*, and *evelli* for *avelli*. In Ottobonian there is *teneram sub*, but *-que* must be added to satisfy the meter. Poelmannian, in the text, and Hadamarian:

> He stained Bethlehem’s streets with cruel slaughter,  
> Tore away all the infants and the tender population at the breast  
> With the sword, though guilty of no offense.

Aldine, Tornesian, and Fabrician have the same, but:

> commanding the tender population at the breast  
> To fall innocent beneath the rigid sword in their bosoms.

Fabricius reads *teneroque*, and shortly afterward *in sinubus*. Poelmannian, for the reading, combined both versions:

> Horrible slaughter, etc.; the infants, etc.,

as in Reginensis, and afterward *innocuam*, as in the Aldine.

299. Ottobonian and Roman: *Quam bonus Hieremias divino numine jussus*, “How good Jeremiah, commanded by divine power”; this agrees with Reginensis, which writes *Heremias*. The printed editions that I have been able to consult read:

> For the pious prophet, instructed by divine power, [lamented] this.

Tornesian has *jussus* for *doctus*. Likewise at verse 348:

> Isaiah the prophet sang what, commanded by divine power,

and at verse 254: *Numine jussa*, “commanded by divine power.” It is clear that Juvencus is fond of the word *jussus*. I retain the reading of the Vatican and Roman manuscripts, which perhaps was altered by those who did not understand that the meter proceeds correctly with *Jeremias*, through contraction of the first two vowels, as Prudentius often did with *Jesus*.

300. Sabatier has *Complerat*, “had filled,” and, for the reading, *Complorat*, “laments,” which is the only form I find in the printed editions and manuscripts. Aldine and Poelmannian, for the reading: *miserae*, “wretched”; Reginensis, Roman, and others: *misero*, “wretched.” In Ottobonian the first hand perhaps had *miserae* or *miseras*; the second hand has *misera*, which cannot be maintained. Aldus understands *miseras* to refer to the mothers, as is clear from the following verse of Scripture.

301. Aldine and Poelmannian, for the reading:

> Dreadful cries will heavily strike the ether.

Others:

> To strike heaven heavily with dreadful laments.

302. Roman manuscript: “and the tyrant’s savage [violence].”

### Notes

288. *Diversis Herodis callibus aulam*: a transposition of words, somewhat intricate, for *diversis callibus aulam Herodis*, “the palace of Herod by various paths.” Similar expressions often occur among poets.

290. **CHAPTER XI. Joseph, warned by an angel in a dream, flees with the child and his mother into Egypt, and the infants are killed. Matthew II.19.** The Herodian massacre of the infants—which some impiously rejected as apocryphal and patched onto Matthew’s Gospel—is shown to be something to be believed with certain and divine faith by Johann Fidalke, in *The History of the Herodian Massacre of the Infants*; Carl Gottlieb Hoffmann, in the dissertation *Why Josephus Was Silent about the Slaughter of the Bethlehemite Infants*; and Castus Innocens Ansaldi, in *Defenses of the Herodian Massacre of the Infants*—for that is how he wished to title his defense of the history of the Herodian massacre.

291. *Aegyptum* for *in Aegyptum*, “into Egypt.” Poets not infrequently omit this kind of preposition, and historians sometimes do so as well. In ordinary usage *transportare* is said of things carried by ship across the sea or a river. Juvencus uses it for “carry.”

292. *Sibimet* has emphatic force, as at verse 101: *Unde igitur sobolem mihimet sperabo venire?*, “From where, then, shall I hope that offspring will come to me?” Juvencus changes the tense, using *succedere*, “to succeed,” for *successurum*, “that he would succeed.” This change of tense was familiar to Christian poets and was occasionally used by earlier writers, as I noted in my commentary on Dracontius III.76. In a similar way, when it had been announced at Augustus’ birth that nature was bringing forth a king for the Roman people, the terrified Senate decreed that no one born in that year should be reared. Suetonius reports this in *Augustus* 94 and adds that those who had pregnant wives took care that the decree of the Senate should not be conveyed to the treasury, so that each man might draw hope to himself.

293. Virgil, *Against Eutyches* IV, borrowed this verse from Juvencus, p. 42:

> The same man, attacked by Herod’s plots,  
> whom the Magi’s care, skilled in the stars, sought, etc.

*Callere*, “to know thoroughly,” is more properly joined with the accusative than with the ablative. Nevertheless, it is found with the ablative in Justin, Solinus, Valerius Maximus, and Apuleius. The construction is figurative: *cura callens magorum* for *cura magorum callentium*, “the care of the Magi who knew.” *Astris*, “by the stars,” is likewise used figuratively for astrology.

295. *Jussit caedem*, “he ordered slaughter,” just as one orders tribute. Tacitus, *Annals* IV.72: *Tributum iis Drusus jusserat*, “Drusus had ordered tribute from them”; XIII.15: *Neque jubere caedem fratris palam audebat*, “nor did he dare openly to order his brother’s death”; and *Agricola* 45: *Nero jussit scelera, non spectavit*, “Nero ordered crimes; he did not merely witness them.”

296. Juvencus readily repeats the same phrases. Shortly before, at verse 282: *Videre sub ubere matris*, “they saw [him] at his mother’s breast.”

297. *Crimen* here may be understood as “cause” or “pretext.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.339:

> Scatter the peace that has been arranged; sow the causes of war.

Cicero also said, as Reusch notes, *Suscipere crimen culpae*, “to assume the charge of guilt.”

299. *Bonus* means “upright,” and perhaps here “merciful,” as the verb *complorat* indicates. *Bonus* also often means beneficent, gentle, or merciful.

300. *Funere*, “by death”; this meaning is obvious.

301. *Pulsare* is governed by *complorat*. Jeremiah is evidently lamenting that a voice was heard in Ramah, etc. Reusch says that *jubens*, “commanding,” must be understood here. Virgil describes a similar woman’s wailing, drawing on Ennius, *Aeneid* II.486:

> Within the house, everything is mingled  
> With groaning and miserable turmoil.

Statius, *Silvae* V.1.22:

> It was consolation to strike the heavenly gods  
> With furious laments against injustice.

Maldonado suggests that Juvencus had in mind the meaning of the name *Ramah*, “high,” as though the voice had reached the heavens. See the note on Book III, verse 142.

302. [The note belongs to the following textual variant.]

303. Aldine and Poelmannian, for the reading: *roseo*, “rosy”; most copies: *horribili*, “dreadful.”

304. Reusch printed *unus, et alter*, “one and another,” which König and Schoettgen explain as referring to two, although philologists dispute whether this expression denotes the number two or three. Our manuscripts have *primus, et alter*, “the first and another,” together with other printed editions, as in Book IV, verse 236: *Tum primus, et alter*, “then the first and another.”

305. Poelmannian in the text, Hadamarian, and Fabrician: *misere suppresserat*, “had pitifully crushed.” Aldine, Ottobonian, and Roman: *miseros oppresserat*, “had crushed the wretched ones.” Tornesian: *miseros suppresserat*. Reginensis: *miserandus presserat*, “the pitiable one had crushed.” Perhaps it would be preferable to read *lethiferi miserandos presserat*, “had crushed the pitiable victims of the death-bringing age.”

306. Poelmannian: *rursum*; Reginensis, Roman, Ottobonian, and others: *rursus*, both meaning “again.” Reusch, for the reading, has *devictus*, “overcome,” which he does not consider absurd, as in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.684, concerning Mercury:

> He tries to overcome the watchful eyes of Argus,

and verse 685:

> He struggles to conquer gentle sleep.

307. Reginensis and Roman: *Urgetur monitis Mariam, puerumque Joseph*, “Joseph is pressed by warnings to [take] Mary and the child”; Ottobonian likewise, but incorrectly has *quae* for *que*. Perhaps *puerumque Josephus* should be read, or a hiatus must be admitted in *puerumque Joseph*, with synaloepha disregarded; Reusch thinks Juvencus admitted this deliberately. The printed editions read: *Joseph urgetur monitis Mariam, puerumque*, “Joseph is urged by warnings [to take] Mary and the child.”

308. Poelmannian incorrectly has *victare*.

309. Aldine, Tornesian, Poelmannian, and Fabrician, for the reading: *praedictum*, “foretold,” which also appears in Reginensis and Ottobonian, and signifies the foretold name: *Quoniam Nazaraeus vocabitur*, “because he will be called a Nazarene.” Hadamarian and Poelmannian in the text have *praedicto*, less well. In the Roman manuscript there is the error *puro* for *puero*, “child.”

311. Aldine and Poelmannian, for the reading: *instructa*, “instructed,” instead of *instincta*, “inspired”; the latter is much better. Roman manuscript, corruptly: *Mox instincta*.

314. Roman manuscript: *Procurrens*, “running forward”; Aldine and Fabrician: *Praecurrens*, “running before”; others: *Occurrens*, “coming to meet.” In Aldus and the Roman manuscript *proveniebat* is erroneous.

315. Poelmannian, for the reading: *Omniaque in vultu et verbis veneranda micabant*, “and everything venerable shone in his face and words.”

316. Aldine, Tornesian, Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman: *Et jam*, “and now.” Others: *At jam*, “but now.”

317. Aldine, Tornesian, and Roman: *servando*, “by observing,” instead of *servare*, “to observe.” Reusch calls this a Greek construction, using the infinitive for the gerund.

318. Aldine and Ottobonian: *laeti*, “joyful”; others: *laetis*, “joyful” in the ablative or dative.

### Notes

305. He calls the age of the infants *lethiferum*, “death-bringing,” because Herod had ordered all those from two years old and younger to be killed.

306. **CHAPTER XII. Joseph, warned in a dream, brings the child and his mother back to their homeland. Matthew II.19–23.**

307. *Urgeo* with the infinitive; on this see the note on Dracontius III.446.

308. *Aegypto* without the preposition *ex*, “from,” as in a similar matter I said above at verse 308. *Nazara*, or Nazareth, means “fortunate,” as again in Book II, verse 106, because Jesus lived there and thereby received, or rather acquired, the name Nazarene.

309. *Dedit addere*, “gave to add,” has a similar syntax to that above, verse 222: *Observare dedit*, “he gave to observe.”

310. Juvencus joins together these two predictions, which are mentioned separately by the Evangelist. At Matthew II.15 he says:

> So that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: “Out of Egypt I called my son,”

which is taken from Hosea XI.1. Again Matthew II.23 says:

> So that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He will be called a Nazarene.”

The Evangelist uses the plural for the singular, as Juvencus explains it together with other interpreters. Many understand Isaiah XI.1. Perhaps Juvencus saw a copy of Matthew in which *per prophetam*, “through the prophet,” was written; for the old version in the Colbertine and Corbie manuscripts, and the Greek text in Bodleian manuscript 1, have the singular *per prophetam*.

311. *Instincta* is a word used by the best writers and often employed when speaking of divine inspiration, which Cicero also calls *instinctus divinus*, “divine inspiration.” *Instincta Deo*, “inspired by God,” means *a Deo*, “by God,” as above, verse 219: *Vox missa Deo*, “a voice sent by God.”

312. *Aegypto ex alta*, “from lofty Egypt.” Perhaps he refers to Upper Egypt, namely the Thebaid, where many, including ancient writers, believed that the Lord had taken refuge. Or he calls Egypt “high,” that is, “deep,” or lower than Judaea, following the scriptural expressions “to descend into Egypt” and “to ascend from Egypt.”

313. These three verses are taken from Luke II.40. Juvencus arranges the narrative as follows. From Luke he takes and continuously narrates Christ’s birth, circumcision, and presentation in the Temple up to Luke II.39:

> And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city.

He then inserts from Matthew the arrival and worship of the Magi, the massacre of the infants, the flight into Egypt, and the return to the city of Nazareth. Afterward, from Luke II.40, he continues to narrate the events of Jesus’ childhood.

316. **CHAPTER XIII. Jesus, sought by his parents, is found disputing among the teachers. Luke II.42–51.**

317. *Cum*, “when,” and afterward *ferebant*, “they were carrying,” are in the indicative because a reference to time has preceded. See the note on Book II, verse 6.

319. *Omnibus annorum vicibus*, namely, “through every year,” as the Evangelist says. *Vices* often means succession or alternation. Pliny XII.14: *Per vices annorum*, “in alternate years.” Sometimes, however, *vices* denotes the times at which something occurs. Horace, *Odes* IV.14.13:

> He struck down the fierce man more than once.

Columella, Book III, final chapter: *Annua vice*, “year by year.” It is not entirely certain that Christ went up to Jerusalem every single year. The Evangelist indicates this to some extent, and Bede agrees with Juvencus on the point.

321. *Patriam* for *in patriam*, “to their homeland,” as was observed at verse 291. Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.793: *Patriam remeabo inglorius urbem*, “I shall return inglorious to my native city.” See also Statius, *Silvae* III, final poem, verse 12.

> Or am I to suppose that, wearied, I shall return to the Euboean household gods?

> [112] When the child, among the crowd of companions, left his mother’s footsteps
>
> And willingly sought the hidden places of the Temple,
>
> His mother searched for him through the city’s streets and hidden houses,
>
> [325] Along the paved roads, among acquaintances and relatives.
>
> But when the third day arrived,
>
> [113] She hastened back to the Temple and found him inserted among the choirs
>
> Of the prophets, handling the obscure laws
>
> In an assembly of elders. Scarcely could the elders
>
> [330] [Col. 0104A] Worthily marvel at the boy’s words. But the pious mother said:
>
> “My son, I seek you, lost, with abundant tears,
>
> Anxious and lamenting with your supposed father. What reason
>
> Separates you from your parents in your journey
>
> And keeps you in the Temple’s dwelling?”
>
> But he replied: “Why do you trouble yourselves so much? Why do you seek me?
>
> [335] Do you not yet understand, mother, that by right I must dwell
>
> In the seats and house of my Father, since I was born for them?”
>
> [114] He said this, joined his steps to theirs, and returned to his homeland.
>
> Yet his mother did not fully grasp the weight of the saying;
>
> Nevertheless she kept all these matters hidden in her heart.
>
> [340] But the boy, by suitable and very sweet acts of obedience,
>
> Always drew both of them into his own love.
>
> Meanwhile, the succession of ages, running its appointed course,
>
> Was bringing all the promises of the ancient Scripture to fulfillment.
>
> [115] The offspring of Zechariah called everyone in the deserted valleys
>
> [345] With a cry to lay aside their stains,
>
> So that they might receive the wondrous washings of the clear river,
>
> By which the beauty of the soul, cleansed of its filth,
>
> Might shine. Isaiah the prophet sang what he had been commanded by divine power:
>
> “A voice resounds far and wide in the deserted valleys:
>
> [350] Make the broad roads ready; let every path of the roads be straight,
>
> So that it may worthily bear the footsteps of the Lord.
>
> The hills will sink down, and every valley will be filled;
>
> He will straighten the winding paths of the journey into a good line of rectitude,
>
> And the Father and Lord of salvation grants everyone
>
> [355] [116] To behold the clear light with bodily eyes.”
>
> Therefore the crowds were present, rushing everywhere here and there,
>
> Filling the banks, and eagerly seeking the washings.
>
> Their garments were woven from camel hair,

### Notes

322. Poelmannian, for the reading, and Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman: *Cum puer*, “when the boy.” Aldine and others: *Dum puer*, “while the boy.”

324. Reginensis: *per vicos, urbes*, with the gloss *et urbes*, “through the streets, cities.” Ottobonian, Aldine, Tornesian, and Roman: *per vicos urbis, perque*, “through the streets of the city and through.” Poelmannian and Fabrician: *per vicos, urbisque per abdita*, “through the streets and the city’s hidden places.” Hadamarian, against the meter: *per vicos urbisque perque abdita tecta*, “through the streets of the city and through hidden roofs.”

325. Aldine: *perque viae*; read *perque iteris* with most copies. In Westhemerus, *perque itineris* in the margin is an error or gloss. Sabatier conjectured *Perque vias stratas*, “along paved roads,” but this is unnecessary, since at verse 350 Juvencus likewise reads *stratas* without *vias*.

327. Fabrician and Poelmannian, for the reading: *vatumque coronae*, “and the circles of the prophets,” preferred by König and Schoettgen because *corona* denotes an assembly.

331. Westhemerus, for a variant spelling: *te quaeso*, “I beg you,” an ancient word meaning *quaero*, “I seek,” as noted at verse 284.

333. Tornesian: *secrevit*, “separated,” which I find in Reginensis with the gloss *separavit*, “separated.” But perhaps the first hand had *secernit*, “separates,” found in Ottobonian, Roman, and others.

336. Aldine, Tornesian, Hadamarian, Daventrian, and others:

> It is necessary for one born to dwell in seats and houses.

Reginensis and Ottobonian, the older manuscripts, together with the more recent manuscript of the Roman College:

> It is necessary for one born to dwell in seats and houses.

Fabricius printed this, except that he initially read *aedibus atque domo*, “in buildings and a house.” *Sedibus*, “seats,” is better, since the Temple is called the seat of the Lord, and shortly before we read *templique in sede*, “in the seat of the Temple.” Fabricius also notes in his index, or commentary, under *inhabitare*, “to dwell,” that the first syllable of this word is long in Juvencus, as in Fortunatus, *On the Joys of Eternal Life*:

> Rejoicing to dwell in the virginal house.

Barthius, Book XXI, chapter 17, shows with similar examples from Ausonius, Aldhelm, and Jonas Aurelius that among writers, especially those of the declining Latin period, the letter *h* had force in verse and helped lengthen a syllable; he praises this very verse of Juvencus. Becman, chapter 4 of *A Guide to the Latin Language*, proves that *h* is improperly removed from the system of letters, among other reasons because it often creates positional length, as in Virgil, *Eclogues* 6.53:

> He, reclining on his snow-white side, supported by soft hyacinth.

### Notes

322. *In populo*, “among the people,” “in the multitude,” or “in the crowd.” *Populus* also has this meaning, as I showed in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* XI *Peristephanon*, verse 5. Omeisius less aptly refers *in populo* to the Evangelist’s words *in comitatu*, “in the company.” Schoettgen criticizes Juvencus for supposing that Christ had already set out on the journey and then returned to Jerusalem, which conflicts with the Evangelist, who expressly says that Christ remained immediately in the Temple. Yet a careful reading of the Gospel plainly proves that Juvencus agrees perfectly with the Evangelist. Luke II.43 ff. says:

> When the days were completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. But supposing him to be in the company, they traveled a day’s journey.

Juvencus says that the boy left his mother’s footsteps among the company and willingly sought the secluded parts of the Temple. This could have happened either because the boy left his mother’s footsteps in the Temple and sought its more secluded places, or because he withdrew from his mother outside the Temple in the city and then went into the Temple—the latter possibility being suggested by both the Evangelist and Juvencus. For it is false that the Gospel establishes that the boy remained immediately in the Temple. When Juvencus says that the boy left his mother’s footsteps, he may perhaps intend to indicate the boy’s singular love for his mother, whose footsteps he never otherwise left. The Jews report that it was formerly customary for men and women to travel separately when going to Jerusalem or returning from it. Boys, as is reasonable to believe, stayed close to their mothers. The boy Jesus, when he was already twelve years old, left his mother’s footsteps in order to go to the Temple. His mother, apparently, thought that he had done this in order to join the men.

325. *Strata*, *stratae*, “road,” from which Italians and Spaniards call a road *strada* and *estrada*. Earlier Latins said *strata via*, “a paved road.” Virgil uses it poetically in *Aeneid* I.426: *Strata viarum*, “the paved roads,” just as he says *opaca locorum*, “the shaded places.” Writers of the later age commonly used *strata* and *stratae* in this sense, including Eutropius; the emperors Honorius and Theodosius in the *Theodosian Code*; Victor of Vita; Alcuin; and others. See Cellarius, *On the Barbarous Usage of the Later Age*, and Ducange.

326. The Evangelist’s word, *Requirebant eum inter cognatos et notos*, “they were seeking him among their relatives and acquaintances,” suggests greater attentiveness than the simple verb *quaerebat*, “she sought.” Juvencus nevertheless adds *Perque iteris stratas*, “along the paved roads,” to signify diligence and perseverance.

327. *Chorea* here means a chorus, from which *chorea* is derived; that is, a gathering or company. If one reads *vatumque coronae*, “the circles of the prophets,” it can be explained by the Evangelist’s words, “in the midst of the teachers.”

328. *Legum obscura*, “the obscure matters of the laws”; see verse 180.

329. *Tractantem*, “handling” or “discussing,” is an ecclesiastical word. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* 13.101.

330. Fabricius, in his *Commentary on Christian Poets*, takes *senibus* adjectivally and interprets it as “with words suited to an old man.” Nothing more inept could be said. The true sense is: “The elders could scarcely admire the boy’s words adequately.” The Evangelist says: “All who heard him were astonished,” etc.

332. Just as Saint Joseph is called the supposed father of Jesus Christ, so Juvencus calls him the supposed begetter. This designation should not easily be used outside the meter: Saint Joseph could be called “father” for other reasons as well, but “begetter” only because he was commonly thought to be so. See Suárez, volume XVII, part II, *On the Incarnation*, question 29, disputation 8, section 1.

333. *Retentare*, a frequentative verb from *retineo*, “to retain,” is used by many good writers with nearly the same meaning. In another sense *retentare* means “to attempt again.”

334. *Tantum*, “so much” or “so greatly,” as above at verse 79.

336. The words of the Vulgate are:

> “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

The Old Latin agrees in most manuscripts, but the Corbie manuscript has:

> “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s things?”

Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*:

> “That I must be in the things of my Father?”

Ambrose:

> “That I must be in the house of my Father?”

Saint Leo the Great, letter 16, in a certain manuscript of Saint Vedastus at Arras:

> “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”

This signifies that he was the son of him whose Temple it also was. The Armenians, Syrians, and Persians likewise read, “In the house of my Father.” Nor do the words of the Greek text, *ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου* (“in the things of my Father”), have any other sense, as Lamy confirms with suitable examples in his *Harmony* on this passage. Spencer should also be consulted, *On the Hebrew Laws and Rites*, p. 1186. Most interpreters explain the words thus: “Did you not know that I must be engaged in those affairs which have been entrusted to me by my Father?” I willingly dissent from them in order to follow Juvencus’ interpretation.

> [338. The force of the word should be noted, as in Cicero, *On the Orator* II.17: “One must employ the gravity of all meanings and the weight of all words.” In this sense Horace, *Art of Poetry* 319: “A tale without charm, without weight and art.”]

339. Daventrian: *reservant*, “they preserve”; most copies: *reservat*, “she preserves.” I scarcely doubt that *reservant* should be read, so that the meaning is that all the words which the Virgin had heard were preserved in the secrets of her heart. *Mentis secreta* and *cordis secreta* occur more than once in Juvencus. In the Vatican and Reginensis manuscripts there appears to be a certain mark above *reservat*, from which another reading, *reservant*, may be inferred. Someone might conjecture *secreto corde reservat*, “she preserves in her secret heart,” but this differs too greatly from the manuscript wording. Omeisius nevertheless found in the Uncial manuscript *corde secreto reservat*, with an uncertain meter. He also conjectured *cuncta intra cordis secreta reservat*, “she preserves everything within the secrets of her heart.” Westhemerus printed *reservant* in the text and *reservat* in the margin.

341. Poelmannian, for the reading: *vectabat*, “was carrying.” Westhemerus in the margin: *vectebat*; in the text, together with others: *nectebat*, “was binding,” which is better. Hadamarian, incorrectly: *semperque cogens*, “and always compelling.” Roman: *nectabat* for *nectebat* or *vectabat*.

344. Some punctuate: *Zachariae soboles, desertis vallibus, omnes*, “the offspring of Zechariah, in the deserted valleys, all [called].” This cannot be maintained. John was crying out in the deserted valleys themselves, or in the deserted places.

347. Reginensis: *Queis animae virtus*, “by which the soul’s virtue.” Tornesian has the error *specie*, “appearance.”

348. Some write *Esaias*, others *Isaias*, “Isaiah.”

350. I prefer the reading of the Vatican, Reginensis, and Ottobonian manuscripts, together with the Roman: *Instruite stratas*, “make the roads ready.” It is certainly better to *instruere stratas*, namely, to construct, adorn, or prepare the roads, than to *sternere stratas*, “spread out the roads.” In the printed editions alone I find *Sternite jam stratas*, “now pave the roads,” which seems to have arisen from scribes who thought the meter did not work with *Instruite stratas*. Yet it is established that the final syllable of *instruite* can be lengthened and, according to some, must be lengthened because of the *st* at the beginning of the following word. Through ignorance of this fact, some verses in Prudentius had been corrupted. See my notes in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, p. 186 ff.

351. Aldine and Poelmannian, for the reading:

> which the blessed feet of the Lord are to tread.

Reginensis, Roman, and Ottobonian, together with most copies:

> which may worthily bear the footsteps of the Lord.

353. Reginensis, Roman, Ottobonian, and Tornesian: *iteris*; others, with Aldus: *callis*, “paths.”

354. Roman manuscript, corruptly: *tractate sereniter*, “handle serenely.”

### Notes

338. The force of the word, as in Cicero, *On the Orator* II.17: “One must employ the gravity of all meanings and the weight of all words.” In this sense Horace, *Art of Poetry* 319: “A tale without charm, without weight and art.”

340. *Praedulcibus*, “very sweet”; Lucretius, Virgil, and other excellent writers use this word.

341. *Ad proprium cogens amorem*, “compelling [them] toward his own love,” means “impelling them to love him.” *Cogere* is commonly used for *compellere*, “to compel,” or “to use force to make someone do something.” *Nectebat* may have the meaning which I explained from Barthius at verse 42. It appears that the accusative with the preposition *ad* is governed both by the verb *nectebat* and by the present participle *cogens*. See the textual variants at Book III, verse 304.

342. **CHAPTER XIV. John’s baptism in the Jordan, and his food and clothing. Christ is also baptized, heaven is opened, and the Father’s voice is heard. Matthew III.1 ff.; Mark I.1 ff.; Luke III.1 ff.; John I.19 ff.**

343. The order of the words is: “Meanwhile the succession of ages, running its appointed course, was bringing all the promises of the ancient Scripture to fulfillment.” *Per debita currens* means “running to completion,” fulfilling what had been foretold in the Old Law, or approaching at the appointed time. *Veteris scripti* means the Old Testament.

344. Matthew III: “John came preaching in the desert of Judea.” Mark I: “John was in the desert, baptizing and preaching.” Juvencus, following the practice of poets, uses *desertis vallibus*, “in deserted valleys,” without the preposition *in*. Again at verse 349: “A voice resounds far and wide in the deserted valleys.”

346. Antonius Maria Lupi discusses excellently the word *lavacrum*, by which baptism is usually called, in an Italian dissertation on sacred baptisteries, completed and furnished with learned notes by the distinguished Francesco Antonio Zaccaria.

347. *Species animae*, “the beauty of the soul.”

348. *Numine jussus*, “commanded by divine power,” as at verse 299.

354. Luke III.6: *Et videbit omnis caro salutare Dei*, “and all flesh will see the salvation of God.” The expression *oculis tractare lumen*, “to handle the light with the eyes,” should be noted as meaning “to see” or “to receive light.” *Tractare* here belongs to the sense of touch. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V.38:

> The things that we taste, smell, touch, and hear are located in that very part where we perceive them.

One sense, however, is often used for another.

356. *Passimque hinc inde*, “everywhere here and there.” Reusch says that this example can enlarge the *Index of Equivalent Expressions* which Vechner provides in *Hellenolexicon* I.6, pp. 91 ff. *Ruere* sometimes means “to go eagerly and hurriedly.” Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* VII.19, or 20: *At illum ruere nuntiant, et jam jamque adesse*, “They report that he is rushing forward and is already, already at hand.” This is familiar among poets. Below, verse 363: *Irruere ad fluvium*, “to rush toward the river.”

358. Matthew, in the cited passage: *Ipse autem Joannes habebat vestimentum de pilis camelorum*, “John himself had a garment made of camel hair.” Some explain this as meaning that John used a camel’s hide for clothing. Juvencus’ interpretation is more accurate: he represents John’s garment as woven from camel hair. Hilary likewise says in his commentary on Matthew: *Pilis camelorum vestis adtexta*, “a garment woven from camel hair.” Paulinus, in poem VI on Saint John the Baptist:

> His garment was woven from the bristles of a crooked camel,

or, in another reading, “stitched together.” One may also consult the dissertations or treatises of Balthasar Holberg on the clothing and food of John the Baptist; Conrad Oldius on his dwelling, food, and clothing; Friedrich Spanheim on the same subject; Solomon Deyling on the birth, upbringing, and other matters of John the Baptist; and Paul Rabe on his food and clothing. Against some interpreters, one must maintain that his clothing and food were poor.

### Notes

359. Reginensis: *pelles*, “skins”; Ottobonian: *pellis*, “skin,” but this was changed by an older hand to *pelles*. Thus *zonae* will be a singular genitive. Others have:

> And a skin belt.

The Evangelist Matthew says:

> And a leather belt around his waist.

360. Reginensis, Daventrian, Ottobonian, Roman, and Aldine:

> He was accustomed to eat locusts from the rural fields.

In Ottobonian the verse is written by the same old hand at the bottom of the page, since it is entirely absent in its proper place. In the same manuscript *hedere* occurs for *edere*. Tornesian, Hadamarian, Poelmannian, Fabrician, and others:

> He, who was accustomed to eat locusts in the rural fields.

This wording seems more correct to me, for the first syllable of *edere*, “to eat,” would have to be shortened, whereas Latins used *esse*, not *edere*, for “to eat.” Perhaps because most people believe the first syllable of *locusta* to be short, some substituted *Edere locustas*, etc. Yet although *locusta*, the feminine noun, occurs among the ancient Latins with its first syllable long, it is not easy to show that the first syllable of *locusta*, the insect, must necessarily be lengthened. Prudentius shortened it in the *Dittochaeon*, verse 117. See my commentary on that passage. Nevertheless, the manuscript reading may be defended by the authority of Rusticus Helpidius, *On the Old and New Testaments*, verse 17:

> The table has what the Father commands Peter to eat.

361. Tornesian, Fabrician, and Poelmannian, for the reading:

> He made his food by eating wild honey.

Reginensis, Ottobonian, Roman, Aldine, and others:

> Wild honey supplied his food.

One may conjecture *Cui tenuem*, “for whom [he made] a slender [food],” instead of *Et tenuem*, “and slender.”

362. Aldine: *Usque ubi tot populos*, “until where so many peoples,” less satisfactorily. Perhaps Juvencus wrote *Is ubi*, “when he,” or “there where.” See the textual variants at verse 232.

362. Roman manuscript begins: *sic incipit ore*, “thus he begins with his mouth.”

367. In Ottobonian, for the reading, it seems to be *vestras tollat*, “may he raise your [things].”

368. Reginensis, Ottobonian, Tornesian, and Poelmannian, for the reading:

> For even from the rocks he can make peoples  
> Succeed in your place, since a degenerate offspring wanders.

In Reginensis *sobolis* is written, and in Ottobonian *plebis*, but the latter was made from *plebes*. Aldine and others:

> For the king of the powers above can easily create from a hard rock  
> A lineage, when its offspring is degenerate.

Schoettgenius preferred this reading because it comes closest to the Evangelist’s words, while Reusch disagreed, considering the phrase *Superum rex*, “king of the powers above,” an unacceptable paganism in Juvencus. Sabatier printed *rex caute*, “the king cautiously,” and, for the reading, *degener erat*, “was degenerate”; this does not fit the meter.

371. Tornesian and Poelmannian in the text, Hadamarian: *aciesque levata*, “and the axe raised.” Aldine, Westhemerus in the text, Fabrician, and Poelmannian, for the reading: *acies sublata*, “the axe lifted.” Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman: *acies levata*, which conflicts with the meter, as does *aciesque elevata* in Daventrian. Reginensis has the gloss *subrecta* for *levata*. Perhaps *subrecta* was the earlier reading, with *levata* as its gloss; for the latter word has the appearance of a gloss that later migrated into the text. One may conjecture *acies elata*, “the raised axe,” or:

> Before everyone’s eyes, and the axe’s face raised.

372. Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman: *caeduntur*, “they are cut down”; read *caedentur*, “they will be cut down,” since *fovebunt*, “they will cherish,” follows. The Vulgate has:

> “It will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

The Cambridge manuscript, Sangermanensis 1, and Lucifer of Cagliari, *Book II Against Saint Athanasius*, have:

> “It is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

360. Again, at verse 378, *ruralis* occurs. Macrobius, Nemesianus, Ammianus, Julius Firmicus, and—on the authority of certain copies—Caesar, *Gallic War* III.14, use this word; most readers in Caesar read not *ruralium* but *muralium*. In the Reg. manuscript there is a gloss, *locustas—azillas*, “locusts—small birds”; perhaps *acridas* should be read, from the Greek word by which locusts are denoted. On such locusts and the wild honey on which John fed, see our commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn 7, verse 69.

366. “Produce fruit”: Schoettgenius says that this is a Hebraism, as in Genesis 1:11. Works of this kind belonging to repentance are enumerated more distinctly by Paul, Ephesians 5:9: “For the fruit of the light,” etc.

367. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.136: “Has such confidence in your lineage held you?”

370. *Roboreis*: a species of tree used for the genus. The Evangelist says: “For already the axe has been placed at the root of the trees.”

373. Maldonatus refutes the objection that Prudentius and Juvencus seem to have equated John’s baptism with Christ’s Baptism as follows: “I could answer—not subtly, but poetically—that they spoke poetically. But there is no need to excuse the statement on poetic grounds, since we can interpret it favorably. For many ancient authors spoke in the same way . . . They say that John’s baptism was given for repentance, for the remission of sins, Luke 3—not because sins were remitted through it, but because it aroused people to repentance. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 76.”

375. He explains the Evangelists’ words in this way. Matthew says: “Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” Mark: “Whose sandal-strap I, stooping down, am not worthy to loose.” Luke: “Whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loose.” Balduinus, *De Calceo antiquo*, chapter 11, proves that poets use *vincula* (“bindings”) for any footwear, but especially for sandals. Hebrew footwear covered only the soles of the feet and was fastened above with rounded straps or thongs; thus it resembled the Roman sandal. Lamy displays a drawing of such footwear in his *Harmony of the Gospels* at this passage. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 35, says of Moses: “Commanded to loose the bindings tied around his feet.” Arator, II.81: “The lowly thong that binds the lofty soles.” Cicero calls them “shoe-straps,” and Petronius “the bindings of shoes.” It was the duty of servants not only to loosen the bindings of shoes, but also to carry them wherever their masters ordered, since at banquets and elsewhere they might use different kinds of footwear. This was indeed a most menial service, as may be seen in Johann Christoph Wolf’s *Philological Observations on the New Testament* and the other authors cited there. Sometimes masters also removed their shoes because of a sacred place, and the servant was meanwhile ordered to carry them; or, at any rate, when the master entered sacred places, the servant loosened the shoe-thongs and kept them. Among the Hebrews, disciples customarily removed the shoes of their teachers, and inferiors those of their superiors, as a mark of honor; so also the first Christians removed the shoes of bishops, and even now the subdeacon removes those of a bishop celebrating Mass. In the letter of the Smyrnaeans concerning the martyrdom of Saint Polycarp, we read: “He even tried to remove his own shoes—something he had never previously been accustomed to do, since each of the faithful daily vied ambitiously with the others to see who would first touch his body’s skin.” It is conjectured that the custom of kissing the feet of the Roman Pontiff succeeded this practice. Besides Balduinus and Bynaeus’s writings on ancient footwear, one may consult Johann Adam Koenig’s dissertation *On the Custom of Carrying Shoes*.]

378. A *pala* is an iron implement with which earth is turned and removed, but it is wider and flatter than a mattock. By imitation of this implement there were other wooden *palae*, which Cato mentions in *On Agriculture*, chapter 11; they were useful for winnowing grain on the threshing floor. Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 3: “He carries a shovel in his hand to cleanse his threshing floor.” Isidore, *Etymologies* XX.14: “The shovel, commonly called the winnowing-fan, is named from winnowing away the chaff.” Some manuscripts of Tertullian have *ventilabrum*, “winnowing-fan,” but Pamelius prefers *palam* on the basis of the same Tertullian’s *On Flight in Persecution*, as well as Cyprian and Jerome.

380. *Secreti*, “separated” from the chaff. *Secretus* is also used by Quintilian, book IX, chapter 3, for “excellent” or “select.”

381. *Populor* (“I ravage”) is used quite frequently of consuming fire, for example by Florus II.2 and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.319. Add Seneca the Tragedian, Virgil, and others.

383. Juvencus and others lengthen the *a* in *Jordanis*. Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III, shortens it: “With the Jordan struck by his feet, the way made, he returned.” John’s baptism is called “venerable washing,” as at verse 346, “wondrous washing.”

384. *Increpitans*: crying out, proclaiming, thundering; it has nearly the same meaning as *increpo*, which Propertius uses for “proclaim” in book III, elegy 8, verse 9: “Let the mouths of the halcyons, their complaints laid aside, rest— / Let the mother not rebuke her perished Itys.” Juvencus below, verse 456: “Announces, proclaiming abundant heraldings of salvation.”

388. Matthew’s words are: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Reuschius doubts whether Juvencus understood the sacraments, but would prefer to think that he referred to all the precepts of the Law.

390. Poets often apply the epithet *vitreus*, “glassy,” to waters in the sense of “transparent.”

391. A gloss in Reg.: *Surgenti—elevanti caput Christo*, “rising—raising Christ’s head.” Juvencus distinctly affirms three things: that God’s manifest presence shone forth, that the heavens were opened, and that the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove. It therefore appears that he had read something in the Gospels that no longer survives. Matthew reports: “But when Jesus had been baptized, immediately he went up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.” Mark: “And he was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately, as he was coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him.” Luke: “And when Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened. And the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon him.” Juvencus may therefore have encountered a copy of Saint Matthew’s Gospel resembling Sangermanensis 1 in Sabatier and Martianay: “And when Jesus was baptized, a great light shone from the water, so that all who had gathered were afraid.” A manuscript of the Gospels, believed to have been written by Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, agrees with this in column 2: “And when he was baptized, a great light surrounded the water, so that all who had come were afraid.” “The manifest presence of God, which shone forth,” and “a great light shining from the water” do not differ greatly from one another, or are perhaps one and the same thing. Millius should be consulted at this passage in the *Prolegomena to the Greek New Testament*, no. 766, p. 73, where he discusses Juvencus; also Grotius at this place, who observes that the same event is related in the Syrians’ liturgy; Johann Andreas Iricius in his preface and notes to the Vercelli manuscript; and especially Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, §88. Fabricius, *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament* I, p. 347, together with Dodwell, denies that Justin derived his account from the Gospel of the Ebionites. For it differs somewhat and seems to have been taken from another tradition. I would not object, however, if someone interpreted Juvencus in such a way that this verse were an explanation of the following one, in which the Gospel text is expressed more literally: “And behold, the heavens were opened above him.” Suarius, in part III, question 39, disputation 27, section 1, interprets this as a change occurring in the air above the Savior, manifest to all who were present. For what the Vulgate has, “they were opened to him,” could be translated from the Greek as “they were opened above him,” and in many manuscripts of the old version it simply says, “the heavens were opened,” without *to him*. Schoettgenius thinks that Juvencus, in this manifest presence, referred to an ancient tradition still preserved in images: namely, that God the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, made himself visible. He says that God’s presence was seen after the Savior rose from the waters.]

392. I have explained why the heavens were called “sevenfold” by the ancients in the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 5, and in the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 36: “Not yet before the ruler of the sevenfold heaven.” I find no writer older than Juvencus who used the word *auricolor*, “golden-hued,” but it is correctly formed and follows the analogy of *versicolor*, “many-colored,” and *unicolor*, “single-colored.”

[Col. 0111C] 394. Saint Thomas, whom many Scholastics follow, teaches in III, question 39, article 7, that the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared was a real animal. Ambrose explicitly denies this in *On the Sacraments* I.5: “It was not a dove that descended, but something like a dove. Christ assumed flesh, not something resembling flesh, but the reality of flesh. The Holy Spirit, however, appeared in the form of a dove, not in the reality of a dove.” Suarius at the cited passage, disputation 27, section 2, favors this interpretation; Saint Thomas himself had followed it in I, distinction 16, article 3, single question, and many interpreters embrace it. Juvencus anticipated them, depicting this manifestation of the Holy Spirit with great elegance and vividness, as Augustine Varenus says in his dissertation *On the Dove Descending upon Christ’s Head*.

395. “He drenched the body of Jesus,” because he descended upon him and remained in him.

396. *Inane*, “void,” in the sense of air. See the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 152.

[Col. 0111D] 397. “Anointed with breath,” just as above he “drenched the body with breath.” Jerome found the following in the Gospel written in Hebrew, which the Nazaraeans read, in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 11, volume III: “But when the Lord had ascended from the water, the whole spring of the Holy Spirit descended and rested upon him.” Hilary, commenting on this passage in Matthew, writes: “The order of the heavenly mystery is also expressed in him: for after he was baptized, when the entrances of heaven had been opened, the Holy Spirit was sent forth and recognized as visible in the form of a dove, and he was drenched with the anointing of such paternal affection; then a voice from heaven speaks.”

398. Someone may ask where Juvencus derived this: “You, Son, today amid rejoicing I testify that you were begotten from me.” Matthew has only: “And behold, a voice from heaven saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’” Mark: “And a voice came from heaven, ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.’” Luke: “And a voice came from heaven, ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.’” The answer is that the old Itala manuscript at Cambridge has this reading in Luke: “Now when all the people had been baptized, and when Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended bodily in the form of a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” The Greek text in the same manuscript agrees with this. The Colbert manuscript likewise has: “And a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” In the Vercelli manuscript, after the word *complacui* in Matthew, something has been worn away by age; Iricius reasonably conjectures that it belonged to this very wording. Hilary had likewise read it in book VIII of *On the Trinity*, no. 25, and again in book XI, no. 18: “As he ascended from the Jordan, the voice of God the Father was heard: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’ so that through this testimony the spiritual anointing of the flesh sanctified in him might be recognized”; and also in his commentary on Psalm 2, no. 29, and in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 2. Justin Martyr agrees in his *Dialogue against Trypho*: “For after Christ had ascended from the river Jordan, a voice was uttered concerning him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” Lactantius also recognized this wording in book IV, chapter 15, as did Faustus the Manichaean in Augustine, book XXIII *Against Faustus*. Augustine himself, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* II.31, writes: “As for the fact that some copies according to Luke have the voice sounding with the words written in the Psalm, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’—although it is said not to be found in the older Greek copies—if it can be confirmed by certain trustworthy copies, what else should we understand than that both formulations, in whatever order of words, sounded from heaven?” Whether these same words, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” once existed in Matthew’s Gospel is less certain. For although it is clear from Epiphanius, heresy 30, that the Ebionites read them in Matthew’s Gospel, the only Gospel they used, Epiphanius himself notes that this Gospel of the Ebionites had been interpolated and corrupted in many places. See Sabatier’s notes on Matthew and Luke, and Fabricius, *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament* I, pp. 347 ff., where he transcribes a fragment of the Gospel of the Ebionites from Epiphanius and lists several writers who discuss the subject.

399. Barthius, *Adversaria* XLVIII.9, explains Matthew’s verse, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” which the German translator had rendered poorly, since it means only that the Father delights in the Son. According to Matthew’s meaning, the Father was pleased in the Son, and so pleased that through him—who is his wisdom and power—he had previously created and now preserves all things, and through him had blessed the human race. “The paraphrast,” he adds, “a poet indeed, but one whom I remember finding satisfactory in many places as an excellent interpreter, Juvencus Aquilius, expressed the meaning of this verse most elegantly.” Barthius therefore rightly regarded Juvencus’s words, “This glory of offspring pleases me,” as an excellent explanation of Matthew’s verse.]

419. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXVI.7, corrects the passage to *properat, quam moenibus urbis—Mox inferre pedem tendit: vis*, etc., because Matthew reports that the Lord was taken by the devil to the holy city, not that he himself entered it. He understands a tmesis in *quam mox*, which the scribes failed to recognize and therefore corrupted the true reading. Shortly afterward Aldus has *tendit* for *suasit* or *fecit*. But Barthius’s correction is unnecessary: the devil perceived that Christ, after being taken up by him, had set foot in the city. Nor was Christ led or taken as though compelled, but willingly, as many interpreters hold, with whom I readily agree; and Juvencus may perhaps have intended to suggest this interpretation. The same verb *sensit* returns at verse 434, together with the same controversy.]

[Note: [Col. 0113C]]

400. Chapter XV. After fasting for forty days and nights, Jesus is tempted by the devil. Matthew 4:1 ff.; Mark 1:12 ff.; Luke 4:1 ff. Juvencus’s phrase “and the haunts of wild beasts” is taken from Mark’s Gospel: “He was tempted by Satan, and he was with the wild beasts,” which some less appropriately interpret of demons. Ancient tradition establishes that Mount Quarantana was a deserted place where Christ fasted. For the history of Christ’s temptation, see Salomon Deyling, *Sacred Observations* II.27, and the other dissertations preserved in the *Theological-Philological Treasury*.

402. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII.19, observes that the ancients customarily called everything unpleasant or contrary “black” and “dark,” especially Christian poets.

403. Envy dragged the demon’s mind here and there, as he suspected Christ’s divinity and the redemption of the human race. *Aeger* here means anxious, envious, or sorrowful; this meaning is sufficiently common, especially among poets and other reputable authors, as Reuschius observes.

405. “Forty suns”: days, in a phrase used by good poets.

407. *Contexta*: continued through divine power, or even commanded by God the Father and, as it were, prepared. The former interpretation is more pleasing, as in book III, verse 380: “And many fasts ward off the strength of his robust breast.”

408. Prudentius, on Christ’s same fast, *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 189: “Strengthening, evidently, with health-giving fasting / the vessel too weak for pleasures it desires.” A gloss in Reg.: “For the kingdom of the earth”—for destroying the devil’s kingdom—“they held, they strengthened.” One may also interpret it as “for obtaining the kingdom of the earth,” or “for beginning the kingdom of grace on earth.” Perhaps *mentis secreta* is nominative, governing *tenebant*, rather than depending on *jejunia*; the sense would then be: “The secret recesses of the mind held or observed continued fasts of the heart for the kingdom of the earth.” *Mentis secreta*, as at verse 339, *Cordis secreta*.

410. *Sceleris fallacia*, figuratively for “the deceit of the wicked one.” See the textual variants at book IV, verse 644.

411. These expressions are well known: “to know for certain,” “to regard as certain,” “to think for certain,” “to believe for certain,” “to state for certain,” “to deny for certain,” “to promise for certain.” Yet *pro certo genuit* differs somewhat, where *pro certo* means simply “certainly”; it is nevertheless not very different from *pro certo polliceri*, “to promise with certainty.”

415. *Quoniam* in the sense of *quia*, “because.” Saint Ambrose, book IV on Luke: “He answered, saying: ‘It is written: Because man does not live by bread alone.’” Instead of *vivit*, some copies of the Itala in Luke, and most in Matthew, read *vivet*, “will live,” as Juvencus read it. The Greek likewise has ζήσεται, “will live.” Augustine, book II *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, and Arnobius in his *Annotations on the Gospels*, likewise have *vivet* instead of *vivit*. “Will sustain life”: will preserve and maintain it. Martial XIV.108: “Which an untroubled servant may hold and preserve— / Take cups fashioned from Saguntine clay.”

416. “The substance of bread,” as in this book, verse 631: “And today the life-giving substance of holy bread.” Prudentius also uses *substantia* for food in *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 40: “That he might see one deprived of every substance,” where Iso adds the gloss “food, provisions.” Compare the Theodosian Code, title 3, final law, *On the Custody of Prisoners*, and title 27, law 2, *On Food*, as well as Ducange under *Substantia*, “nourishment.”]

Then he seeks the shadowy mountains and the haunts of wild beasts,

and the servants strive to offer him the obedience of the Father.

123 Soon the raging demon’s envy, with black terror,

seizes his mind; nor did deceitful cunning fail

to tempt Christ meanwhile.

[405] Forty suns had passed for him in succession,

since no nourishment of food or drink had been supplied;

but the fasts of a steadfast heart, joined together,

held the secret recesses of his mind toward the kingdom of earth.

Then at last he warned the body to seek food.

[410] [Col. 0114A] Meanwhile, attempting him with the deceit of dreadful wickedness,

“if God truly begot you,” he says,

“you can command these stones with a powerful utterance

to assume the use and form of wheaten bread.”

Christ replies: “Such things no longer terrify me.

[415] For I remember what is written: ‘Because not bread alone

will sustain the believer’s life—the readily available substance of bread—

but the power of God’s word fills devout hearts.’”

Again the tempter hastens to weave deceit

with his crafty arts. For from the walls of the city

420. Ott. seems to punctuate: *sensit vis livida Christum*, “the envious power perceived Christ,” which is less satisfactory; for *vis livida* is better attached to the single verb *suasit*.

421. Ald., Daventr., Poelm., for the alternative reading, *marmoreo tendit*. Torn., Ott., *marmoreo fecit*, with *suasit* above it in Ott. Reg. and Rom., *marmoreo suasit*. Fabr. and Poelm. in the text, together with Had., as usual, *marmorei suasit*.

422. This verse and the following were absent from Reg., but were added in an old hand in the margin.

426. Torn., Ald., Poelmann., for the alternative reading, *id esse* instead of *tale*. Rom. has, not ineptly, *tale, ministri—Ut lapsum studeant*. In Torn. the error has been corrected.

427. Torn., *descendere corpus*; correct to *defendere*.

430. Ald., Torn., *his dictis Christus*. Others, *his Christus dictis*.

431. Rom., *Te meminisse*. Others, *Me meminisse*. In Reg. *Ne vires*, etc., is placed first, then *Me meminisse*. Rom. lacks the verse *Ne vires*.

434. Ald., Poelm., for the alternative reading, *magis* instead of *jugis*. Regarding the verb *sensit*, the same conjecture may be raised here as was proposed above from Barthius concerning verse 420. Rom. reads *scensit*. Here I would more willingly read *suasit*, *fecit*, or *tendit*, as at verse 421. Badius interprets the Evangelist’s words, “Again the devil took him,” in the same way as “Jesus took his disciples,” namely, not as carrying them, but as taking them along as companions.

435. Reg., Ott., Ald., Torn., *illi*. Hadamar., Poelm., and others, *olli*, which amounts to the same thing.

437. Ald., Poelmann., for the alternative reading, Fabr., *tibi* instead of *tuo*, and *regna* instead of *regno*.

438. Sabatier with Ald., *si me*; for the alternative reading he assigns *me si*, which is found in the others.

441. Ott., *Haereat, ut nobis semper*; afterward *factum ut semper nobis*. Reg. incorrectly has *Haereat semper ut nobis*. In Ott., *donum*, with *jussum* above it.

442. Reg., *Dominum coeli*.

443. Reg., Rom., Ott., with Ald., *numen*. In Ott., first hand, *nomen*, which most printed editions have.]

[Note: [Col. 0115C]]

420. Most think that Christ was carried by the devil either in his hands, upon his shoulders, or in such a way that the devil’s force impressed an impulse upon Christ’s body, by which he was conveyed to the pinnacle of the temple. Maldonatus, with Origen, Euthymius, and Anselm, believes that Christ was led by the devil in such a way that he traveled on his own feet. *Vis livida*, as at verse 402, *rabidi mox livor daemonis*. This manner of expression is often used by poets: *vis equi* for “horse,” *vis animi* for “mind,” *vis flammea* for “flame” or “a very great fire,” *vis canum* for “dogs.” Compare Gifanius’s index to Lucretius under *vis*.

422. Poison is often attributed to the tongue of the envious and malicious. Ovid, on envy, *Metamorphoses* II.777: “Their breasts are green with bile, their tongue is drenched with poison.” Silius VII.260: “With the poison of deceit / he attacks their minds.” Prudentius, *Dittochaeon* 1: “Eve was a dove, then white; afterward she became black / through the evil-minded poison of the serpent’s deceit.” So also many others.

424. *Jaculari*, “to hurl forth by force.” Book III, verse 406: “And may he hurl himself headlong into the waves of the sea.” Florus I.14: “He hurled himself amid the thickest weapons of the enemy.” Pliny II.25: “Toward what regions he may hurl himself.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII.19, observes that, following the philosophy of Democritus, Latin poets speak of “empty air”; the chorus of Christian poets followed them.

427. The proper meaning of *defendo* is “to prohibit, ward off, repel,” which it would be superfluous to confirm with examples.

428. The adjective *famulus*, as in Ovid more than once and in Prudentius, verse 80 of *Hamartigenia*.

429. *Offensio lapidis*: striking against a stone, or the injury resulting from such a collision. For *offensio* has both meanings; but the first fits this passage better.

430. Above, verse 245: *Dicta in contraria*, “words in reply.”

434. *Furibunda fallacia*, figuratively for “the furious and deceitful demon,” as at verse 410, *sceleris fallacia*, and verse 420, *vis livida*.

436. An imitation of Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.272: “If no glory of such great things moves you.”

440. This too is expressed figuratively, as at verse 434, *furibunda fallacia*.

442. *Devotus*: devoted, dedicated, addicted, consecrated by a vow; in this sense the word is used by the best writers. In the sense of “pious” or “religious,” it is a specifically Christian word, used by Arnobius, Lactantius, Prudentius, Jerome, and their contemporaries, and much more frequently by later authors.

444. *Excussus*: cast out and thrown down by force, as though shaken off. Hilary, on Matthew 4: “After this flight of the devil, angels minister to Christ.” The Gospel merely says, “The devil left him,” or “released him,” or “departed from him,” or “withdrew from him.” Prudentius expressed the demon’s same flight in *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 195: “But, his deceit rebuked, he falls backward.” Mazochius thought that Prudentius affirmed the devil’s actual fall backward; I explained the passage in that way in my commentary. Compare Proba’s *Cento*.

445. Chapter XVI. Jesus, after John’s arrest, withdraws into Galilee. Matthew 4:12 ff.; Mark 1:14; Luke 4:14. Lamy, contrary—as he states—to the opinion of all interpreters, argues that the prison mentioned here was not Herodian. He thinks that John was delivered to prison twice: first by the leaders of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, and later, after some interval, by Herod. He therefore arranges the historical sequence as follows: After Christ’s fast, John declared to the Jews that he was Christ’s forerunner and bore witness concerning Jesus Christ the Messiah. On hearing this testimony, Peter and Andrew, John’s disciples, followed the Savior. When, shortly afterward, or on the day following John’s testimony concerning him, he heard that John had been cast into prison—namely, by the leaders of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin—he withdrew into Galilee. As you see, Juvencus constructs the history differently; and we gladly follow him, lest we depart from the common opinion of all interpreters.]

Immediately the envious power perceived Christ and urged him

125 to set foot upon the marble summit of the temple.

Then it attacks him with a voice deceiving through poison:

“If God is truly your father, from the summit of the temple

you will hurl your body by a leap through the empty air.

[425] Scripture will be your witness, openly promising

that the servants of the supreme Father have been commanded

to protect the body from a fall,

and to lift your limbs with ministering hands,

lest the impact of the stone injure the soles of your feet.”

[430] To these words Christ returned words in reply:

126 “Rather, I must remember the heavenly writing,

[Col. 0116A] lest presumptuous confidence test the Lord’s powers.

Again the furious deceit perceived Christ standing

on the lofty ridges of a precipitous mountain,

[435] showing him kingdoms shining throughout the world.

‘Do you see,’ he says, ‘what glory belongs to such great things?

I can now and immediately grant them all to your kingdom,

if you worship me, their giver, in adoration.’

Then Jesus rejected him as he pressed these words:

[440] “Flee, mad fury of pestilential poison,

so that we may always hold fast to the fixed command:

that the just and devoted man should worship the Lord of heaven,

and, serving him, venerate the divine power of the One forever.”

Shaken out by such words, the demon fled through trackless ways.

[445] 127 When he learned that John, amid the shadows of prison,

[Col. 0117A] [Note: [Col. 0117B]]

446. Hadam., Poelman., Ald., Fabric., *Submersum*. Torn., Reg., *Demersum*. Ott., Rom., *Immersum*. Poelm., in the text, Hadam., Fabr., Reg., Ott. by a later hand, *tristi compressit corda dolore*. Ald., Torn., Ott. first hand, Rom., *corde dolorem*: as though he had not manifested grief by signs and words, which Reuschius thinks was not the poet’s intention. In any case, *comprimere corda dolore*, for “to conceive” or “receive” grief, is an unusual phrase.

449. Hadam., Reuschius, Poelman. in the text, Fabr.: *Terra Zabulon, et regio cui Nephthala nomen*. Ald., Daventr., and Torn. likewise, but with *Zabulonum* for *Zabulon*, and Torn. incorrectly *Nephthalia*. Rom. and Vatt. Reg. and Ott. have: *Terra Zabulonum, et regionis Nephthala nomen*. In each of these readings, the quantity of *Zabulon* is pronounced with a different interval in this verse and in verse 447, as it is clear Juvencus did with other proper names. Since, however, *Zabulon* is indeclinable in the sacred writings, and the second syllable of the name is written in Greek with a diphthong, these verses could be restored as follows: “And he appointed Zabulon’s borders as the place of his dwelling. / The land of Zabulon, the region called Nephthala.” It should also be noted that the *a* in *terra* is lengthened because of the *z* of the following word, which has the force of a double consonant.

450. Barthius’s manuscript, Rom., Reg., Ott., Basil., Ald., *Galilaeaque arva*, from which Barthius correctly conjectures *Galilaeiaque arva*. Most printed editions have *Galilaeaque rura*. Torn., incorrectly, *Galilaeaeque rura*. Some write *Galileaque*.

451. Reg. distinguishes: *Jordanem. Gentes.* Others: *Jordanem gentes*.

453. Rom., *In morteque illius umbra*, which is corrupt.

454. Reg., and Ott. first hand, *splendens*, but the meter opposes it.

455. Ott., first hand, *munere*; second hand, *munera*, with many others. Rom., Bas., Ald., *munia*.

457. Rom., *vidit*; *videt* should be retained. Sabatier printed *geminos* and, for the alternative reading, *ponti*, which other printed editions and manuscripts exhibit.]

458. In the Roman manuscript, *Prosolidum*: read *Praesolidum*. Aldus printed: “Simon the Praesolidus, worthy of the surname Peter”; in the Errata he corrected it to: “and Simon the Praesolidus, worthy of the name Peter.” But perhaps he intended to correct it to: “and Simon the Praesolidus, worthy of the name Peter,” shortening *si*, as others commonly do; or else *Praesolidumque Simon*, treating the name as indeclinable. Elsewhere Juvencus always shortens the first syllable of *Simonis* and lengthens the second. See the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 230, where I discussed the quantity of the first and second syllables in this word. One could read: “Simon the Praesolidus, worthy of the name.”

461. The Regius manuscript has *altos*, with the gloss *profundos* (“deep”).

463. The Roman manuscript has *perpulchra* (“very beautiful”); most copies have *praepulchra*, which Gallandius says, according to Juvencus’s usage, stands for *perpulchra*, just as in verse 458 *praesolidum* stands for *persolidum*.

466. Aldus, the Roman, Basel, and Tornesian manuscripts: “After the twin brothers, Jacob and John, amid the sea.” So too the Ottobonian manuscript in its second hand, unless *fratres* (“brothers”) is an apposition reflecting a different reading or a gloss. Most copies: “After the brothers Jacob and John, amid the sea.” Poelman, as a variant reading; Reuschius: “After the twins Jacob, etc.” Badius says that in this spelling *Jacobum* is a four-syllable word, with the third syllable long. So too Claudian—or rather someone else—writes: “Do not tear apart my verses, leader Jacob.” Yet *Jacobum*, as well as *Joannem*, may be trisyllabic, with the first two syllables of *Jacobum* lengthened. It is remarkable how greatly Christian poets vary in the quantity of the syllables of this name.

> 448. The phrase “to converge” occurs in the same sense in book II, verse 346: “When he recognized that the appointed time had come together”; and in the same book, verse 828: “By the order of the ages, for things to converge according to commands.”
>
> 452. “Enclosed”: immersed. In a similar way, in this book, verse 163: “All will break through the darkness of death.”
>
> 456. “Rebuking”: preaching, thundering forth. See the notes on verse 384.

> 457. CHAPTER XVII. He calls Peter and Andrew, John and James, fishermen. Matthew IV, 18 ff.; Mark I, 16 ff.
>
> [Column 0118C] 458. “The Praesolidus”: he alludes to the name Peter and to Christ’s words: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”
>
> [Column 0118D] 459. “Winding coils”: Virgil spoke of a serpent in book XI, verse 753: “But the wounded serpent twists its winding coils.” For the fishing line from which the hook hangs, *linum* (“flax,” “thread”) is sometimes used in a simple sense, as in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, verse 923: “Now, seated on a mound, I guided the line with my rod,” and shortly afterward: “I sat down on the turf while the dripping lines dried.” Add Juvenal, Sedulius, Fortunatus, and Sulpicius Severus.
>
> 460. Poets often use *marmor* (“marble”) for the sea, as I noted in my commentary on Dracontius, verse 578, book I.
>
> 463. *Indago* is properly a hunters’ term: thus they call the enclosing of wild animals in a place from which they cannot escape; this enclosure is made in various ways. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 121: “While the wings tremble and they surround the forest with a hunting enclosure.” Here it has the sense of investigation. It should also be noted that *fortia lucra* means “great gains.”
>
> [Column 0119B] 467. “Sea-herds”: fish, which Proteus is said to drive in herds. “Spots” are the openings in a net—*mallas* in Spanish—as I explained in my note on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 42. Hence *maculosus textus* means “a spotted fabric,” that is, a net; yet I do not find anyone else using *maculosus* in this sense.

> 469. In some printed editions *Zebedaeum* is incorrectly written.

Poelman, as a variant reading, has *sancta ferebat* (“he carried holy things”); this reading is not unsuitable, but *serebat* (“he sowed”) is better.
>

>

>

The Roman manuscript has *Monstrabant: Christus facili sed murmure cunctos* (“They showed them: Christ, with an easy but murmuring…”), which should be corrected to *Christus facile sub munere cunctos* (“Christ easily, beneath his gift, all…”). All the others I have seen have: “They showed them to Christ; by an easy gift he quickly restored them all.”
>
> 480. The Roman manuscript has *sanctos* (“holy”); correct it to *sanos* (“healthy”).
>
> 494. The Regius manuscript: “In this way those who mourn will follow things worthy of consolation.” The Roman has the same, but *solatia* (“consolations”) seems more likely than *solatio* (“consolation”). The gloss in the Regius manuscript is: “In this way”—that is, “in such a way”; “solatio”—that is, “consolation.” Perhaps one should read: “In this way consolation worthy of those who mourn will follow.” All the others I have seen have: “Here consolations worthy of those who mourn will follow.”

> [Note: [Column 0119B]]
>
> 469. *Zebedeus* occurs again with the same syllabic interval in book III, verse 316: “Peter and the two sons born of Zebedee through the byways,” a reading I do not reject.
>
> 471. CHAPTER XVIII. Jesus travels through Galilee, preaches repentance, and cures various human illnesses. Matthew IV, 23 ff.; Mark III, 7; Luke VI, 17.
>
> 474. Servius, commenting on verse 10 of book VI of the *Aeneid*, thinks that *procul* has a twofold meaning: both “near” and “far,” as though it meant “far from the eyes” or “before the eyes.” Others more correctly believe that *procul* can signify both a small and a great distance. Here Juvencus uses *procul* in the sense of “far and wide,” for Matthew’s words are: “And his fame went throughout all Syria.” Reuschius explains it in another sense: “His fame was spread through nearby or surrounding Syria”; this is less convincing.
>
> 475. “A thousand tongues of fame,” that is, many tongues are attributed to it. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 181, concerning Fame: “A dreadful, monstrous thing, with as many feathers on its body … as there are watchful eyes beneath—wondrous to say—as many tongues, as many mouths resounding, as many ears raised.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XII, verse 47, concerning Fame: “All the land roars, reports the voices, and repeats what it hears.” Poets commonly use “a hundred” and “a thousand” for “very many,” just as orators and historians use “six hundred.”
>
> 478. “The strength of the limbs”: limbs, or the power of the limbs. Thus Lucretius, for rock or the hardness of rock, writes in book I, verse 889: “the strength of the rock.” Virgil, for iron, has in book VII, verse 609: “the strength of iron.” See Gifanius, *Index Lucretianus*, under *robur saxi* (“strength of rock”) and *vis morbi* (“power of illness”).
>
> 481. In Latin, “illnesses of the mind” sometimes means desires, mental disturbances, and vices, although Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III, chapter 4, regards this metaphor less favorably. He himself nevertheless often uses it. Juvencus calls those things “illnesses of the soul” that cast the mind down from its natural condition, such as madness, frenzies, or mental vices contracted through the prolonged presence of a demon.
>
> 482. The illness of lunacy is described. Some interpret it as epilepsy. Isidore, *Etymologies* IV, 7: “The common people call epileptics lunatics because their madness accompanies the course of the moon”—a statement perhaps taken from this passage of Juvencus. For the preceding passage in Isidore reads: “The term epilepsy arose because, seizing the mind, it likewise possesses the body.”
>
> 483. Juvencus often uses this verb to display the force of divine authority. Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 844; III, 105 and 130. The opposite is *injussus*, used of things that occur spontaneously.
>
> [Column 0120C] 486. *Plebes* is nominative singular; I will discuss it at book IV, verse 694, in the variants.
>
> 488. CHAPTER XIX. Who will be blessed. Matthew V, 1 ff.; Luke VI, 20 ff. Juvencus seems to suggest that this sermon was delivered on a mountain. There is considerable disagreement among interpreters on this matter; their differing opinions can be read in Nicholas Albertus, *On the Life of Christ*, part 2, no. 101. Some think that Christ delivered the sermon to the disciples on the mountain, as Matthew says, and later repeated it to the crowds in a level place, as Luke says.
>
> 489. Ovid, book IV of the *Ex Ponto*, elegy 9, verse 17: “While a crowd of the sacred senate surrounds your side.” Thus one may say *cingere sinum* or *cingere gremium* (“to encircle the bosom” or “lap”), although I have found no one else speaking in this way. Badius explains *gremium cingentibus* as “sitting around.”
>
> 490. Many authors of Gospel harmonies think that the Lord delivered this sermon later. Lamy agrees almost entirely with Juvencus. “He who had come,” he says, “to bring forth a new law, as soon as he had gathered a larger number of disciples and had secured belief through his miracles, why would he not have promulgated that law, instructing the disciples and the people who followed them in excellent teaching?” It has also been debated among interpreters whether in this first beatitude “the poor in spirit” means all those who lack inward pride, or those who truly suffer poverty but nevertheless are content with their lot. Juvencus expresses the former interpretation, as do Augustine, Jerome, Chrysostom, Hilary, Basil, Gregory, and many other Fathers. Compare Heinsius, *Sacred Exercises* on this passage of Matthew, chapter IV, page 23.
>
> 491. *Receptat*, perhaps in imitation of Lucretius, book II, verse 998: “What was sent forth from the regions of the ether—the heavens receive it back again, restored to their temples.”
>
> 492. It should be observed that Juvencus does not follow the Greek text, in which this beatitude is placed after the next one, but the old Italic version, which preserves the same order as the Vulgate.

> whom the Jordan separates with its stagnant stream.
>
> Seeing these peoples, he sat down on a lofty crag,
>
> and thus addressed the disciples encircling his lap:
>
> [490] “Blessed are the humble, whom poverty of spirit encompasses;
>
> for the lofty kingdom of heaven receives them.
>
> Likewise blessed are the meek, whom gentleness crowns,
>
> to whom the fairest earth is owed by right.
>
> Now consolations worthy of those who mourn will follow them.”

> [Note: [Column 0121B]]
