> 495. “Nourishment and drink” is a metaphor indicating intense desire. Horace, book I, *Epistle* 18, verse 23: “Whom an unrelenting thirst and hunger for silver possesses.”
>
> 497. *De pectore* (“from the heart”) is sometimes superfluous, as I noted in my commentary on Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 3; sometimes it is used in the sense of *ex* (“from”), as in Propertius, according to Koenigius.
>
> 499. The old Italic version and the Vulgate have: “Blessed are the pure in heart.” Saint Cyprian, Letter 46, says: “Blessed are those pure in heart”; and Saint Augustine, sermon 12, volume V: “Blessed are those who are pure in heart.” *Tueri* often means to look upon eagerly and with the greatest attention.
>
> 501. This verse is an example of mixed scansion in Bede, *On Meter*, in the chapter on scansion. See above, the note on verse 25.
>
> 502. *Insectatio* occurs again in verse 507. Decimus Brutus, in Cicero’s *Letters to Friends* XI, letter 1: “So great is the arrogance of men, and their persecution of us.” Other excellent writers have spoken in the same way.
>
> 504. *Operum justa* for *opera justa* (“righteous works”): this manner of speaking is familiar in Juvencus. Schoettgenius wished to call it a hendiadys.
>
> 505. Lucan, book I, verse 262: “And pressing goads add their spurs to the doubtful mind in battle.” Juvencus uses *stimulos* (“goads”) for trouble, harassment, and persecution; Cicero and others likewise speak of “the goads of pain.” Juvencus expresses Matthew V, verse 11: “Blessed are you when they curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely on my account.” Sabatierius unjustly declares that Juvencus has been silent about all these matters, assigning to verse 12 of the same chapter these words: “Rejoice, you who uphold righteous deeds, when swift injustice presses upon you with savage goads,” together with the following two verses. Juvencus follows the old version as it appears in the Colbert manuscript: “They will speak every evil against you on account of righteousness”; the Sangerman manuscript 1, Cambridge manuscript, Hilary, Ambrose, Ambrosiaster, Pope Symmachus, and the others cited by Sabatierius agree with it.
>
> 506. He uses the Evangelist’s word: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven.” Through the grace of God, glory—or eternal life—is granted as a reward for the good works of the righteous. This was explicitly defined at the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 33: “If anyone says that the good works of a justified person are gifts of God in such a way that they are not also the good merits of the justified person; or that the justified person, by the good works performed by him through the grace of God and the merit of Jesus Christ, whose living member he is, does not truly merit an increase of grace, eternal life, and the attainment of that eternal life—provided he dies in grace—and also an increase of glory, let him be anathema.” Although the fitting merit of eternal life has not been defined in these precise words, it is nevertheless most clearly gathered from the sacred Scriptures, councils, and Fathers. It is sufficient to have indicated this against Koenigius’s note on this passage.
>
> 508. CHAPTER XX. He calls the Apostles the salt of the earth. Matthew V, 13; Mark IX, 49; Luke XIV, 34. By Juvencus’s expression “on this earth,” I understand “in this world.” The Evangelist has: “You are the salt of the earth,” and shortly afterward: “You are the light of the world.” The savor of salt is used for salt itself, just as below “the substance of salt” is used for salt. On this subject there is a dissertation by Valerius Greissengius entitled *Salt That Has Lost Its Savor*. Schoettgenius, together with Lomeierus, explains “on this earth” as “in Judea,” not “throughout the whole earth.”
>
> 510. “The substance of salt” is said in the same way as in verse 416 of this book: “the substance of bread.”
>
> 511. The Italic version and the Vulgate have: “But if the salt should lose its savor”; yet the Italic version in some manuscripts and many Fathers have: “But if the salt should become foolish”—that is, lose its savor.
>
> 512. *Vestigia* (“footprints”) is used metonymically for the sole of the foot and for the feet themselves.
>
> 513. CHAPTER XXI. The same Apostles are called the lights of the world. Matthew V, 14; Mark IV, 21; Luke VIII, 16, and XI, 33.
>
> 517. *Cunctis* for *a cunctis*: Juvencus often uses the dative for the ablative in these passive constructions.
>
> 518. *Thronus*: I discussed this word in my note on Prudentius, verse 102 of the *Apotheosis*.

> 519. CHAPTER XXII. That he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Matthew V, 17 ff.

> I have not come to overturn the ancient commands
>
> that the prophets set forth.
>
> For all things will remain for you to fulfill through me.
>
> I speak the truth: until the destruction of heaven, earth, and sea comes,
>
> [525] not even the letter of the law, or the fine distinction of a small mark,
>
> will be lacking before all things are accomplished in the order of the age.
>
> For if anyone dares to loosen even the smallest part of a commandment
>
> and teaches human beings to do the same by persuasion,
>
> 135 he will hold the name of “least” in the heavenly dwelling.
>
> But whoever, preserving the disciplines of his own conduct,
>
> [530] faithfully hands on the commands of his ancestors,
>
> will be great and bear a great name beyond the stars.
>
> You have heard the command of the ancient law:
>
> if anyone stains his hands with human blood,
>
> he will pay the penalty under the avenging sword.
>
> [535] But I will command that no one rise up in anger
>
> or be moved by burning hatred of his brother.
>
> 136 For this man will pay penalties before a just judge.
>
> Nor will a lesser flame pursue the insults
>
> of those who call their brother foolish or wretched.

> [Column 0123B] 521. “All things will remain to be completed by me for you,” so that you too may fulfill them. For God, through his supernatural grace, causes us to fulfill the law.
>
> 523. The meaning of the particle *saltem* (“at least”) should be noted: here it means “only,” “merely,” or “just.” Cellarius disputes this meaning against Borrichius in the appendix to his *Miscellaneous Notes*. Borrichius thinks Virgil and Ovid spoke in this way; Cellarius scarcely concedes that the usage began in the Silver Age. He confirms that later Latin was not far removed from it by the example of Jerome and Apuleius. Forcellini argues that all the passages cited for this meaning can be explained otherwise. For my part, I do not see what other sense *saltem* can have here in Juvencus.
>
> 524. “A slender distinction of a small mark”: the *apex* was a slender stroke placed above a vowel to distinguish a short syllable from a long one, as Scaurus teaches at the end of his *Orthography*. Quintilian, book I, chapter 7, or 13: “Whether *malus* signifies a tree or a bad man is distinguished by the mark.” Some have thought that the Hebrew vowel points are meant; this opinion must be entirely rejected.
>
> 528. “Will hold the name of least”: will be called least, which means the same as “will be least,” that is, the last, almost nothing, or rather nothing. Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*: “Declaring that those who loosen the smallest commandments will be least—that is, last and almost nothing.” Koenigius says that *minimus* for “none,” or “having no place,” is a Hebraism.
>
> 529. *Moderamina* (“disciplines,” “regulations”): Juvencus frequently uses this word, though its meaning is not immediately obvious. Shortly afterward, in verse 532: “the discipline of the law.” Here “preserving the disciplines of his own conduct” means the same as “who fulfills the commandments.”
>
> 530. *Priorum* (“of former people”), meaning “of ancestors”: this usage is sound and familiar from Virgil, Tacitus, and Pliny the Younger.
>
> 531. “Beyond the stars”: in the kingdom of heaven, says the Evangelist.
>
> 532. CHAPTER XXIII. On murder. Matthew V, 21 ff.
>
> 535. “I”: taken from the Gospel, where it has emphasis. Donatus, commenting on Terence, *Eunuchus* V, 9: “By adding *I*, he used the expression customary among those who see more deeply into a matter.” “Rise up in anger,” as in book IV, verse 564: “Let religion rise up in anger.”
>
> 536. The old Italic version in many manuscripts has: “But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment.” In the Vulgate and the best Greek manuscripts, *without cause* is absent; Augustine appears to approve this reading in book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 19, and Jerome explicitly defends it in his *Commentary on Matthew*. In some manuscripts *WITHOUT CAUSE* is added; nevertheless, the true and settled judgment is that anger is entirely removed, since Scripture says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable,” and so forth. Therefore *WITHOUT CAUSE* should be deleted. These verses of Juvencus, venerable for their antiquity, confirm this reading. Some explain the Gospel’s words so that one who is angry with his brother is worthy to have his case examined at the judgment. Maldonatus prefers Juvencus’s and Euthymius’s interpretation: that he is liable to the capital punishment which was decreed in judgment against murderers. Christ means that the person who kills in the Gospel by will alone is worthy of no lesser punishment than one who kills in fact.
>
> 537. “Will pay the penalties”: will give them. Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, chapter 17: “Let him pay the heavy penalties for his impiety toward our father.” The Evangelist’s words are: “He will be liable to judgment,” which interpreters refer to a certain tribunal called by the Hebrews *Mispat*, that is, “judgment.” Likewise, they explain “he will be liable to the council” as referring to another, more serious tribunal called the *Synedrion*. Thus the Evangelist means that the one who is angry with his brother in grave hatred will be punished by eternal punishment, while a heavier punishment is to be inflicted on those who break out into words of insult. Juvencus expresses the same thought, but says nothing specifically about the distinct tribunals of judgment and council, or Sanhedrin. For I understand the words “before a just judge” rather as referring to God.
>
> [Column 0124D] 538. “Nor lesser”: that is, “greater”; for I think these words have this force.
>
> 539. A gloss in the Regius manuscripts has *cient*—“they call.” Ovid, *Fasti* IV, verse 484: “He shouts and calls each name in turn.” Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 46: “A voice was heard calling him by name.” In Juvencus, *sub* is redundant in *sub nomine*, as often in Dracontius, whose word index records several instances under *sub*. Compare also the commentary on Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 102. In this verse Juvencus includes two kinds of insult, explained by the Evangelist as follows: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” Juvencus gives *fatuum* (“foolish”) first and then *Raca*, which he interprets as “wretched,” that is, afflicted and miserable. Others explain *raca* or *racha* as a brainless, vain person, a little man; others derive it from the Greek *ῥακός*, “rag,” and understand it as a poor and ragged man—an interpretation Juvencus may have had in mind. The Evangelist distinguishes three degrees of feeling and punishment: first, anger that does not break out into words, punished by judgment; second, an insulting word by which one calls his brother *raca*, light-minded, unstable, unfortunate, or miserable, making him liable to the punishment or sentence of the council; third, the more insulting word by which one calls his brother a fool, punishable by the fire of Gehenna. Although the kind of punishment is the same—namely, eternal death—the degrees of punishment are distinguished according to the differing gravity of the offense.

> 540. The Regius manuscript and, apparently, the first hand of the Ottobonian have *volens*; read *voles*. The Regius has *munus* (“gift”), and as a variant reading *donis* (“gifts”).
>
> 541. Aldus and the Basel manuscript have *tangent* (“they touch”); the Roman has *tangunt* (“they touch”). In the Regius and Ottobonian manuscripts, *tangent* has been corrected to *tanget* (“it will touch”).
>
> [Column 0125B] 542. The Roman manuscript, together with all the others, has *fratre* (“with your brother”); in the margin, *fraude* (“by deceit”).
>
> 543. Aldus has *cuncta adytis illic admota*, together with the Tornesian and Basel manuscripts. Other printed editions have *cuncta adytis illis admota*. The Regius, Ottobonian, and Roman manuscripts have *cuncta illic adytis admota*.
>
> 547. Aldus, the Roman manuscript, Poelman (as a variant reading), and the Daventrian edition have *semper contraria virtus* (“the opposing virtue always”); most copies have *virtus contraria semper* (“the opposing virtue always”).
>
> 548. The Roman, Regius, Ottobonian, Aldine, Daventrian, and Basel manuscripts have *Corporis: hoc casti*. Poelman, together with other printed editions, has *Corporis haec casti*, an punctuation preferred by Reuschius, because Juvencus connects this part of the sacred text with what follows, where Christ speaks about adultery. Reuschius understands the opposing virtue to be an evil thought, for which this remedy is provided.
>
> [Column 0126A] 549. The Ottobonian manuscript has *rapide*; but diphthongs are sometimes omitted and sometimes added in these codices. The printed editions have *rapidae*. The Roman has *Cum* for *Dum*.
>
> 550. The first hand of the Ottobonian manuscript has *Accusabat enim* (“for it was accusing”).
>
> 553. The Roman, Fabricius, and Aldus have *solveris* (“you will be released”); the Regius, Ottobonian, and Poelman have *mitteris* (“you will be sent”), in the first hand. From the preceding verse it can be inferred that *solveris* is the more genuine reading.
>
> 554. In the Roman manuscript, *Ultra quam minimi*; read *Ultima quam*.
>
> 557. The Ottobonian has *interne feriant*; correct it to *frenent* (“restrain”). The Roman likewise has *interne* for *internae*.
>
> 558. The Regius and Ottobonian have *luenda*; the Roman, together with the printed editions, has *luenda est*.

> [Note: [Column 0125C]]
>
> 540. CHAPTER XXIV. On offering. Matthew V, 23–24. *Offerre* (“to offer”), meaning to consecrate to God, is a word frequently used by Christians and commonly found in liturgical contexts. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 155: “Receive the light that I, your servant, offer.” In Juvencus, gifts or offerings may be understood, as in verse 546: “Offer pleasing gifts to God with a tranquil heart.” The Evangelist says: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” or, in the Italic version: “If you will offer your gift at the altar.” Christ is speaking about the ancient sacrifices of the Jews; but the passage should be understood much more especially of the Eucharist.
>
> 547. CHAPTER XXV. One must agree with one’s adversary—that is, with virtue and reason, which oppose vices—on the way, that is, in life. Matthew V, 25 ff. A gloss in the Regius manuscript reads: “The opposing virtue—the divine word to you while you go with your adversary on the way.” Saint Paulinus likewise interprets the Evangelist’s words. Matthew has: “Be reconciled with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the attendant, and you be thrown into prison.” Instead of “be reconciled,” some have “be well disposed” or “make peace with your adversary.” The common explanation is obvious. Juvencus seems to follow another interpretation: by the opposing virtue of the body he understands the desire of the flesh, which must be treated with the swift love of chastity or purity. Thus the reason for agreeing or making peace with this adversary is, according to Juvencus, that the love of chastity expels evil thoughts; in this way body and soul are brought into harmony. “Virtue of the body” is used for “body,” as in verse 478, “strength of the limbs” for “limbs.” See the note on that verse. Omeisius denies that Juvencus’s explanation is accepted today. Maldonatus offers several interpretations and admits that Juvencus’s view—that the adversary is the flesh which lusts against the spirit—is also held by Athanasius, *Question* 62, and seems to be approved by Jerome in his commentary on this passage.
>
> 549. The gloss in the Regius manuscript: “He walks—the opposing virtue.” That is, the body, or virtue of the body, as I interpret it. “Through the crossroads of life” explains Matthew’s “on the way.” Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*: “He commanded us to be reconciled quickly with our adversary through kindness on every path of our life.”
>
> 550. “The practice of an impure body”: your adversary resisting you. For the flesh lusts against the spirit unless it is cured by the love of chastity; then flesh and spirit agree with one another. Juvencus is hinting at lust and fornication, for he connects this part of the sacred text with what follows concerning adultery.
>
> 554. The Gospel’s words are: “Until you pay the last farthing.” Tertullian and Cyprian have “the final farthing.” Instead of “last” or “final,” “smallest” is not inappropriate. See the note on verse 528: “He will hold the name of least in the heavenly dwelling.” Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, verse 950: “To exact everything down to the smallest farthing.” Fortunatus, on the Last Judgment: “They will be compelled to pay the smallest farthing of coins.” So too the author of the book *On the Forty Dwellings*: “I tell you, you will not leave there until you also pay the smallest farthing.”
>
> 555. CHAPTER XXVI. Adultery must be avoided. Matthew V, 27 ff. The Vulgate has: “It was said to the ancients.” Most Greek manuscripts omit “to the ancients.”
>
> 556. Thus Juvencus renders Matthew’s words: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
>
> 557. *Molimina* is used chiefly by poets for an undertaking or attempt. Juvencus often uses the word. Book II, verse 18: “Thus are the undertakings of your race.”
>
> 559. CHAPTER XXVII. The eye must be removed and the hand cut off if they cause one to go astray. Matthew V, 29 ff. The verb *laqueo, laqueas* is absent from Forcellini and Ducange; but it is appropriately formed from *laqueus* (“noose”). Horace and Prudentius use the compound *illaqueo*, and Cicero *illaqueatus*, as do Columella and Solinus *laqueatus*. Hence, in the circus, *laqueatores* were those who had learned to entangle others with nooses. In another sense *laqueatus* means “adorned with a coffered ceiling.” Elsewhere Juvencus said *erroris laqueos* (“the snares of error”) for scandals. See book III, verse 12, with its note.
>
> [Column 0127C] 561. *Jaculare*: throw it away. See the note on verse 424 of this book. This construction should be noted: *refert perdere membrum* (“it is advantageous to lose a member”), with *quam* meaning “more advantageous than,” or “rather than.” The Vulgate and old Italic version likewise have: “For it is advantageous to you that one of your members perish rather than your whole body go into Gehenna.” Good Latin writers sometimes omit *magis* or *potius* in comparisons of this kind. Tacitus, *Annals* I, chapter 58: “I preferred peace to war.” Consult Forcellini under *quam* and *potius*. The first syllable of *refero* is common; many hold that this is due to the preposition *re*. The impersonal *refert* is always lengthened.

563. **With everlasting punishments:** because the Gospel mentions Gehenna, or everlasting fire. Sabatier suspects that Juvencus read *quam corpus totum tuum, et anima mittatur in gehennam* (“than that your whole body and soul be cast into Gehenna”), but this reading is found nowhere. In fact, Juvencus is doing nothing more than explaining the Vulgate reading.

567. **CHAPTER XXVIII. That a wife is to be divorced only on account of adultery.** Matthew V, 31; XIX, 7 ff.; Mark X, 11–12; Luke XVI, 18.

568. Matthew V, 31: “Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.” The words with which the bill of divorce was written are called *feralia*, that is, deadly, mournful, dreadful, and perhaps liable to litigation. Among other things, the husband handed his wife a bill of divorce on which was written: “I have given her a bill of divorce into her hand, a document of separation, a seal of division.” Otherwise, the bill of divorce granted the woman the right to contract another marriage. Compare the note on Book III, verse 475.

569. Matthew’s words are these: “Everyone who divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” Catholic interpreters explain this as follows. Only fornication, or adultery—or an offense equal or more serious than it—can provide sufficient grounds for separating a wife from her husband, insofar as the marriage bed and household are concerned. When this occurs, the bond of marriage is not dissolved, since by its nature it is indissoluble; and Christ has declared it indissoluble by his new laws. But a husband who divorces his wife without the cause of fornication, or another cause equal or more serious, makes her commit adultery, because without any fault of hers he exposes her to his own lust. Juvencus is somewhat obscure, but his words must certainly be referred to this interpretation.

571. A woman abandoned without sufficient cause, or driven from her husband’s house, if she marries another man—or commits adultery—will lose the rights of chaste modesty, that is, she will violate her modesty, with her husband as the responsible cause. In other words, the guilt will be assigned to the husband, because his wife violates her modesty. Badius explains: “She will lose, etc., [that is,] she will not be taken by another, because whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” Juvencus, Book III, verse 476, again treats this subject:

> For he who buys will pay the penalty, who takes away the rights  
> Of the chaste marriage-bed; and another wife, joined to his halls,  
> Will bear the charge of adultery before the eyes of the people.

Perhaps, therefore, the meaning of this passage is: A woman abandoned by a bill of divorce, with her husband as the responsible cause, will lose the rights of chaste modesty, or of the marriage-bed or marriage itself.

572. **CHAPTER XXIX. That one must not swear in any manner, but must say “Yes” and “No.”** Matthew V, 33 ff.

575. *Vestigia*: feet, or the lowest part of the feet. See the note on verse 512.

576. The Jews carefully avoided swearing by God, but readily and rashly swore by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and their own head, which they did not believe to be genuine oaths. Maimonides, in his treatise *Shebuoth*, or *On Oaths*, chapter 12, numbers 3 and 4: “If someone swears by heaven, earth, the sun, and similar things, even though he had in mind only the one who created them, the oath is nevertheless not an oath.” This is why Martial, Book XI, epigram 95, addresses the circumcised man—or Jew—as follows:

> Behold, you deny and swear to me by the temples of the Thunderer.  
> I do not believe you. Swear, circumcised one, by Anchialus.

He calls this an oath by God, which the Hebrews formulated in this way: *An chi alon*, “No: the Most High lives.” Others say that *Anchialus* means in Hebrew “by the living God,” or “by him who lives forever.” Isaac Vossius, in his commentary on Pomponius Mela, Book I, chapter 8, corrects *Anchialum* to *Ancharium*, that is, “the ass,” because the Jews were accused of worshiping an ass. Christ forbids all these oaths, declaring that they truly are oaths. I say, he forbids them not only when they are false, but also when they are uttered rashly and without cause. An example of swearing by the earth occurs in Theocritus: **Νὰ Δᾶν**, Doric for **νὰ Γᾶν**, “by Earth.”

> Hasten to tear away the author of miserable guilt,  
> And cast it far away. For it is better to lose one small limb  
> Than to give the whole body over to the flames,  
> And likewise plunge the soul into everlasting punishments.  
>   
> And if the right hand leads the mind along crooked paths,  
> [565] It is better to cut away the cause of error with steel  
> Than to surrender the whole body to eternal flames.  
>   
> The ancients prescribe that, if anyone breaks a marriage,  
> [Col. 0128A] He must write a divorce, the deadly words of the law.  
>   
> Only the adulterous woman may rightly depart from the husband’s house;  
> [570] But let the others remain: for the abandoned woman  
> Will lose the rights of chaste modesty, with her husband responsible.  
>   
> The ancient laws forbid perjury upon the tongue.  
> But let the boldness of swearing yield to our commands;  
> Nor is it permitted for a human being to swear by high heaven,  
> [575] Which is the seat of the Lord, nor by the earth  
> That bears the footsteps of God, nor by the venerable name  
> Of the city of Jerusalem, which belongs to the great King.

577. Rome and Ottobonianus read *propria est* (“is his own”); the Regina manuscript, together with most printed editions, reads *patria est* (“is his fatherland”). Gallandius prefers *propria est*, on the basis of Matthew V, 35: “Nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King,” and Psalm XLVII, 3: “The city of the great King.” These passages, however, support either reading equally. Koenigius, in place of *propria*, adds 2 Chronicles VI, 6, and Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 85: “Give me my own house, Thymbraeus,” that is, a dwelling which I may possess by right.

580. The Aldine edition reads *albumque, aut* (“white or”), and so forth.

581. Aldus: “Yes, yes; let what is be borne forth; what is not, say ‘It is not.’” Others have the reading printed here; but Tornacensis and Poelmannus, with a different division of the words, read *dicere non est* (“it is not to say”). See whether it is preferable to punctuate: “Is it? It is; let that suffice.”

584. Rome reads *tenebat* (“held”): retain *tenetis* (“you hold”).

585. Rome reads *sequetur* (“will follow”): retain *sequatur* (“let it follow”), in accordance with the Gospel’s wording.

587. Rome: *Te siquis partem*, which makes no sense. Aldus: *si tibi quis partem* (“if anyone [strikes] you on one cheek”). The Regina manuscript, Ottobonianus, and most printed editions: *Ac si quis partem* (“And if anyone [strikes] one cheek”). Barthius, Book XXVI, chapter 7, column 1265, says that the passage should be emended according to its meaning: *Hanc si quis partem* (“If anyone [strikes] this cheek”), which he declares both more elegant and more consonant with the Gospel’s words. Matthew V, 39 says: “But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.” Luke VI, 29: “And whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also.” Nevertheless, the reading of the manuscripts and editions, *Ac si quis*, seems to me to proceed satisfactorily.

589. The Regina manuscript: “If anyone takes away your cloak, or your tunic, let him immediately carry off everything; yield willingly,” with the gloss *cuncta—vestimenta* (“everything—that is, clothing”). The other witnesses have the reading printed here. Ottobonianus, in a later hand, writes *tonicam*. In Rome, *Aufert* is an error for *Auferat*.

592. The printed editions: *gravis atque oneris* (“heavy and burdensome”). Rome corruptly: *grandique oneris*. Regina: *gravidumque oneris*. Ottobonianus: *gravidique oneris*, which is more attractive, if *gravidus* is taken for *gravis* (“heavy”), since *gravidus* is derived from *gravis*.

593. Our manuscripts, together with some printed editions, read *aliudque iteris* (“and another journey”); Aldus, Poelmannus, and others read *aliudque viae* (“and another route”).

594. Regina, Ottobonianus in its first hand, Tornacensis, Basel, and Aldus read *vel si* (“or if”); Ottobonianus in its second hand, Rome, Poelmannus, and others read *vel se*.

596. Regina reads *et tristem* (“and the sad one”), but *et mitem* (“and the gentle one”) is better.

598. Aldus reads *Nec caecis* (“nor [are] the blind…”).

599. Daventria, Aldus, and other printed editions: *praecipiam semper blando esse* (“I shall always command that [you] be gentle”). Against them, the manuscripts Rome, Regina, and Ottobonianus read *praecipiam blando super esse*, with the gloss in Regina: *super esse—super eminere* (“to be above—to surpass”). Reuschius restores this reading, taking *super* as *insuper* (“moreover”) and *per omnes* as *in omnes* (“toward all”), which is more Latin.

578. Martial, Book IX, epigram 49: “You would swear by your sacred rights and by your head.”

583. *Obreptans* is a word used by Plautus and Cicero. “The deadly force of poison,” as at verse 420, *vis livida* (“the livid force”), and verse 440, “Flee the mad rage of the deadly poison.” Here too the subject seems to be the devil. Matthew says: “Whatever is more than these is from evil.” Maldonatus, together with Theophylact, defends the same interpretation. Others explain it differently.

584. **CHAPTER XXX. That whoever inflicted a punishment was compelled to suffer the same himself, because under the ancient law like was to be repaid with like.** Matthew V, 38 ff.

585. *Sequatur* (“let it follow”), as at verse 538: “Nor will a lesser flame follow their insults.” See the note on Dracontius, Book II, verse 470.

588. *Praebere* (“to offer”) is commonly used in similar contexts: “to offer one’s neck to the knife,” “to offer one’s throat,” “to offer one’s neck,” “to offer one’s mouth to insult.”

591. **CHAPTER XXXI. That one must obey a person who orders him to go a mile or carry a burden.** Matthew V, 41.

592. *Ire viam* (“to go a road”), as at verse 266 of this work: *venisse viam* (“to have come a road”).

594. **CHAPTER XXXII. That alms are to be distributed and a loan given freely.** Matthew V, 42. The Evangelist’s words are: “Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.” Some also explain the first words as referring to one who asks that something be lent to him. Juvencus expressly refers them to almsgiving, which must be performed even for those who pretend to be needy. For in some manuscripts of the Old Italic version these words are expressed: “To everyone who asks you,” or “To everyone asking.” Isidore, *Sentences* III, chapter 60, number 13: “Whoever asks without being in need, even if he pretends to be needy, ought nevertheless to be pitied with one’s whole heart. And although he may perhaps present the false appearance of a needy person, the one who gives simply does not lose the fruit of mercy.” Perhaps the reading should be: “Whoever in need asks,” or “Whoever asks, even if …,” and so forth.

597. **CHAPTER XXXIII. That enemies are to be loved.** Matthew V, 43 ff.; Luke VI, 27.

598. *Blind* is often applied to the emotions of the mind, which make people blind and headlong: blind desire, anger, greed, and the like.

601. *Excindere* (“to cut down”) is elegant, as though the destruction of some city were being described.

602. *To follow with hostile spirits and hatred* means to pursue and harass. Tacitus, Book IV of the *Histories*, chapter 29: “To pursue the enemy with the spear.” Virgil, Ovid, Caesar, and Florus use the expression in the same way.

604. Compare the note on Book II, verse 560.

> If we honor only our close friends,  
> What place can there be here for a just reward?  
> A people devoted to profit serves friendship alone.  
> But you must be like the perfect Father.  
>   
> Wherever a noble opportunity for righteousness appears,  
> [610] Avoid the eyes of men: for no reward  
> Will remain afterward to follow such an action.  
> Only the barren praise of the crowd will applaud.  
>   
> But when you do something with your right hand,  
> Let the left hand remain unaware; and then the one searcher  
> Of the hidden heart will repay just merits with worthy rewards.  
>   
> There are people whom the boastful display of an inflated mind exalts,  
> [Col. 0132A] And who rejoice in standing before crowds with their own prayers,  
> And wear out the day by prolonging it with many words.  
> To these pompous prayers succeeds an empty profit.  
>   
> But let the innermost chambers of a secret house  
> [620] Be closed for chaste prayers, and worship God with few words.  
> The Father himself knows what trembling moves your heart.  
> In God’s absence we say nothing; no hidden chambers  
> Of the heart conceal anything: God, being present, sees all.  
>   
> [625] Therefore let the prayer be concluded with these words:  
> “Father, seated upon the starry summit of heaven,  
> We pray that reverence for your name may be sanctified  
> [Col. 0133A] In us, exalted Father; and may your tranquil light  
> Come into the world, and the gracious light of your kingdom appear.  
>   
> [630] Thus, may your clear will be done in heaven and on earth;  
> May the life-giving substance of holy bread  
> Come to us today; may your gift soon release us,  
> In your indulgence, from the countless debts of our evil error;  
> And may it be lawful for us likewise to forgive debts.  
>   
> [635] May the fierce temptation of the deadly demon be kept far away,  
> And may your right hand lift us from evil into the light.  
> For thus the Father will forgive the offenses of the peoples,  
> If you wish each of you to forgive one another’s sins  
> And not harden your heart against errors.  
>   
> [640] The fasts of the people are also greatly pleasing to God.  
> [Col. 0134A] But many strive to disfigure their own face  
> In order to seek the vain reputation of fasting among men.  
> But you, with your hair made shining by pleasing olive oil,  
> Wash your cheerful face from pure springs,  
>   
> [645] So that the Father alone, seeing the fitting service  
> Of your devoted heart, may grant praise and reward.  
> It is vain to watch over talents buried in the earth:  
> There rust and devouring moths hold sway,  
> And thieves plunder everything extracted from its hiding places.  
>   
> [650] Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven’s summit.  
> Neither rust, nor moths, nor the dreadful band of thieves  
> Will plunder them. Wherever your wealth is stored,  
> [Col. 0135A] There your hearts too are held under the same dominion.”

605. Most Greek manuscripts, and the Fathers cited by Wetstenius, read *friends* in Matthew V, 47, instead of *brothers*.

607. This verse must be explained from the Gospel text: “Do not even the tax collectors do this?”—namely, love their friends. Thus a people devoted to profit, that is, tax collectors, serve friends alone.

608. *Perfectus* (“perfect”) means complete in every respect and is also said of a human being. Cicero, *On Duties* I, 15: “Since we live not with perfect and completely wise men,” and so forth.

609. **CHAPTER XXXIV. That empty ostentation in good works is to be avoided.** Matthew VI, 1 ff. Most interpreters teach that *righteousness* here means almsgiving, for the Hebrews called almsgiving by a similar word.

611. *Posterius*, used adverbially for “afterward” or “later,” is employed by Cicero, Nepos, Plautus, and others. As punishment follows crime, so reward follows a good work. Sallust, in the speech of Philippus against Lepidus, before the middle of Book I of the *Historical Fragments*, chapter 14: “When rewards follow wicked men, scarcely anyone is good without payment.”

616. **CHAPTER XXXV. That the solicitation of praise in speech is to be avoided.** Matthew VI, 5 ff. The word *praetumidus* (“excessively swollen”) occurs more than once in Claudian.

617. The gloss in Regina: *assistere—adesse sibi* (“to stand by—to be present to oneself”). This is the proper meaning of *assisto*, as though from *asto*: “I place myself nearby.” The dictionaries everywhere abound in excellent examples.

618. *Multifluus* (“flowing abundantly”), as at verse 137, *largifluus* (“flowing generously”). Arator, Book II, verse 1064: “He gives cups from his vessel and orders all to be watered with abundant speech.” Thus Dracontius coined *dulcifluus* (“sweet-flowing”) in Book I, verse 164. The subject is the *battology* of prayers, by which many things are requested in many words, or the same words are repeated again and again in empty sound.

620. It was customary among the Hebrews to have private rooms within their houses serving as prayer chambers. See Judith VIII, 5. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 737, “a secluded part of the house,” from which it may be inferred that the same custom existed among pagans. In connection with this passage of Matthew, the observations of Balthasar Holberg and Salomon Deyling on the *battology* of prayers deserve consideration. A distinction must be made between empty verbosity, which is rightly condemned, and persistent prayer conducted according to the rules of piety. Augustine, Letter 130, formerly 121, chapter 10: “Let there be no abundance of words in prayer, but let there not be a lack of abundant prayer, if fervent intention perseveres. For to speak much is to deal with something necessary in prayer through superfluous words. But to pray much is to knock upon the one to whom we pray through the prolonged and devout exercise of the heart.”

622. *Trepidatio* means trembling, or the beating of a heart moved by desire or fear of something. The heart is the seat of the emotions. Tibullus I, elegy 11, verse 11: “Nor would I know sad weapons, nor hear the trumpet with my heart beating.” Plautus, *Aulularia* IV, 3, 3: “At once my heart began to perform a comic act, and to leap into my breast.”

625. *Votum* sometimes means a wish, desire, or will; at other times, a prayer. It can be taken either way here, but it seems more correct to understand it as “prayers.”

626. **CHAPTER XXXVI. The Lord’s Prayer.** Matthew VI, 9 ff.; Luke XI, 2 ff.

627. *Sanctificetur* (“may it be sanctified”): concerning this word, recall the note on verse 33 of this work.

629. Ottobonianus, Poelmannus, and Fabricius: *lux ampla patescat* (“may the broad light appear”). Aldus and Regina: *alma patescat* (“may the nurturing light appear”), with a gloss—or variant reading—in Regina: *lux sancta redundet* (“may the holy light overflow”); in its first hand, the text seems to have read *lux ampla*. Rome and another Regina manuscript, no. 1785: *lux alma redundet* (“may the nurturing light overflow”). Reuschius considers *lux alma* more suitable.

630. Aldus punctuates: “Thus, in heaven, as on earth, may [your will] be done.” The words of the Gospel require the punctuation: “Thus, in heaven as on earth.” Regina, Ottobonianus, and Rome: *tua fiat* (“your will be done”). Another manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 1785: “In heaven and on earth may your will be done.” Most printed editions: “Thus, in heaven as on earth, may your will be done.”

634. Regina: *fenera fas est* (“it is right to forgive debts”), which is better than the reading of all the others, *fenera nostris* (“debts to our own”).

636. Fabricius: *Deque malis* (“and from evils”); others: *Eque malis* (“and from evils”).

637. Poelmannus, Hadamar, Fabricius, Aldus: “For then the Father will forgive the sins of his people.” Regina: “For thus the Father will forgive the sins of his people.” Ottobonianus: “For thus the Father forgives the sins of his people.” Another manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 1785: “For thus the Father will forgive the sins of his people.” Some read: “For then the Father will forgive the offenses.”

638. *Alternis* (“one another”) may be conjectured.

639. Badius, instead of *cedere* (“to forgive”), reads *credere* (“to believe”), with an interpretation referring to confession. Regina, Aldus, Fabricius, Tornacensis, and Basel read *intendere*, namely “to harden through hatred and anger”; other manuscripts and editions read *impendere* (“to direct” or “to impose”).

643. Aldus and Poelmannus, with a different division of the words, read *madefactus* (“moistened”). The manuscripts and most printed editions read *nitefactus* (“made shining”), which should be retained.

646. Ottobonianus, Aldus, and Rome in the margin: *laudet, meritumque rependat* (“may he praise and repay the merit”), which may perhaps be correct. Rome corruptly reads *meritumque rependet* (“and he will repay the merit”).

647. Regina and Tornacensis: *terrae* (“of earth”); others: *terra* (“earth”).

649. Ottobonianus writes *deripiunt* (“they plunder”).

652. Aldus, Poelmannus, Fabricius, Hadamar, Regina, and Ottobonianus: *Pactio* (“agreement”). Rome and Tornacensis: *Factio* (“band” or “faction”), which seems sound; Juvencus frequently uses this word. See the verbal index.

631. In some manuscripts of the Old Italic version one finds: “Give us today our supersubstantial bread,” instead of “our daily bread.” In Greek the word is **ἐπιούσιον**, which some translate as “coming upon us,” others as “for tomorrow,” others as “substantial,” others as “excellent,” and most as “supersubstantial.” Sabatier thinks that Juvencus is referring to this reading. But the matter is uncertain, for Juvencus used *substantia panis* (“the substance of bread”) for “bread” at verse 416, and *substantia salis* (“the substance of salt”) for “salt” at verse 510. Schoettgenius thinks that the bread is called “life-giving” because it gives spiritual life, since it is called holy.

633. *Debitum*, absolutely used, means something owed or a debt. It is rarely used in the plural by the older writers.

634. *Fenus* is profit arising from money; it is also used for the principal itself. The Gospel’s words are: “As we also forgive our debtors.” Koenigius says that *fenera* is used improperly for “debt,” and thinks that *fac* (“make”) or something similar is missing in the Vulgate wording. The passage as restored by us proceeds with good sense.

635. This explains the words: “And do not lead us into temptation.” In the Old Italic version: “And do not permit us to be led into temptation.” Hilary, on Psalm CXVIII: “Do not abandon us in temptation which we cannot bear.” Other Fathers agree, though they perhaps present the meaning rather than the actual words of the Lord’s Prayer.

636. Many explain the words of the Lord’s Prayer, “Deliver us from evil,” from the Greek as “Deliver us from the demon,” who is called “the evil one” by antonomasia. Juvencus, together with most interpreters, took *evil* in the neuter gender. Here and elsewhere *light* denotes a prosperous condition.

640. **CHAPTER XXXVII. That one must fast, but not in order to seek reputation, as hypocrites do.** Matthew VI, 16 ff.

641. *Foedare* (“to disfigure”) is used in place of *extermino*, which the Old Italic version and the Vulgate present. Jerome, in his commentary on this passage: “The word *exterminant*, which through the fault of translators has become common in ecclesiastical writings, means something quite different from what it is commonly understood to mean: for exiles are *exterminated*, that is, sent beyond the boundaries. Therefore, in this passage we must always understand *demoliuntur* (‘they destroy’) instead.” In fact, some manuscripts read *demoliuntur*. In Juvencus, *foedare* explains either word, whether *demoliuntur* or *exterminant*. Terence, *Phormio* I, 2, used the expression “to extinguish someone’s appearance.” The ancients had learned, through the action of certain medicines, to turn the natural color into pallor.

643. *Nitefactus* is derived from *nitefacio* (“to make shining”). Gellius XVIII, 11: “The wind makes the blue sea shine as it ruffles it.” Similar forms occur elsewhere: *inanefactus*, *cadefactus*, *aliefactus*, *ardefactus*. Koenigius did not know that *nitefacio* occurs in some places.

644. *De* is redundant, as often in Christian poets. These words either refer to private fasts or mean that those who fast should not deliberately make their faces pale.

647. **CHAPTER XXXVIII. That one must not devote oneself to an earthly treasure, but to a heavenly one.** Matthew VI, 19 ff.; Luke XII, 33.

648. Serenus Sammonicus, *On Medicine*, makes the first syllable of *tinea* long: “A *tinea* creeping within the inner organs by nature.” Compare Sedulius IV, 20: “Neither does biting rust devour, nor does the moth furrow.” Prudentius shortened it in *Psychomachia*, verse 600: “Material, purses too, with frequent moths.” Horace, Ovid, and Juvenal also shortened it, unless one prefers to recognize synaeresis, which must likewise be admitted in Juvencus and Prudentius. But it is preferable to maintain that the first syllable is short, for in Serenus one should read *taenia serpens* (“a creeping thread”).

652. *Res*, meaning household property, wealth, income, patrimony, or possessions, occurs frequently in poets and other writers.

> There your hearts too are held under the same dominion.  
> The body’s lamp is the means by which you see the public lights:  
>   
> [655] But if the eye’s vision is pure and clear,  
> All the limbs of the body will shine brightly.  
> But if it is corrupt and sees perversely,  
> Dark shadows will press upon all the limbs.  
>   
> And if the light is turned into black shadows,  
> [660] How great will be the horror of darkness itself without light?  
>   
> No one can serve two masters equally:  
> He will yield either to the hatred or to the love of one of them.  
> Nor will a servant endure both masters alike.  
> No one will ever be able to serve wealth  
> [665] [Col. 0136A] 149 And God at the same time. But hold fast to these commands.  
>   
> Do not let clothing concern you for the sake of your body,  
> Nor seek simple food with anxious care.  
> Do we not value the soul more highly than the body’s food?  
> Or could anyone hesitate to prefer the body to clothing?  
>   
> [670] Let us look at the birds of the air: they do not till  
> The surface of the soil with a pressed plow, nor cast seed of grain,  
> Nor cut down the stalks of crops with a curved sickle.  
> Yet sustenance and drink and food will come to them.  
>   
> Is not God’s care for human beings more deeply cherished?  
> [675] [Col. 0137A] 150 Nor was it fitting to defer concern for clothing.

676. Ottobonianus: *Pectoribus nostris non sicubitalia possent*, in which the division of *sicubitalia* is scarcely discernible. Regina: *necsicubitalia*, in nearly the same manner, but with the inept gloss *si ubicumque* (“if anywhere”); Rome: *nam sicubi talia possent* (“for if such things could anywhere…”). Fabricius, Poelmannus in the text, Hadamar, and others read: “If no one can by himself now exceed the bodily form he possesses, or add anything to a limb.” Koenigius conjectured: “Can men by thought add cubit-length increases to their own limbs?” Reuschius confirmed this conjecture from the Helmstedt and Fulda manuscripts. Our Vatican, Regina, and Ottobonianus manuscripts support it. Someone may suspect: “Can such cubit-increments…?” Reuschius reads from his manuscripts: “In our hearts: no, even if cubit-increments could [be added], etc.,” and comments: “It is not even fitting for my disciple to be troubled by cares, even if he could bring it about that he exceeded his stature and added a portion of another [cubit] to his bodily height.” *Pectoribus vestris* (“in your hearts”) seems preferable to *Pectoribus nostris*.

677. Thus Poelmannus in the text, Fabricius, Hadamar, and others, together with our manuscripts. Aldus and other printed editions read *Per se* (“by himself”), and so forth, as I have recently explained.

678. Regina: *lilia fulgent* (“the lilies shine”). I attempted to restore the order of these verses as follows:

> Is not God’s care for human beings more deeply cherished?  
> You know in your hearts whether men can add cubit-length increases  
> To their own limbs?  
> And was it fitting to burden the heart with concern for clothing?  
> Consider the lilies through the rich fields, and so forth.

I understand *pectoribus* (“with your hearts”) as “thinking” or “by thinking.” Although this is harsh, it nevertheless refers to the Gospel: “Can a thinking man…?” Juvencus put “hearts” for “thought” in Book II, verse 84.

679. Regina, Ottobonianus, Poelmannus, with a different division of the words, and Rome: *labores* (“labors”). Aldus, Hadamar, Fabricius, and others: *ligones* (“hoes”). Someone might conjecture *ligone* (“with a hoe”).

680. Aldus, Fabricius, Hadamar, Poelmannus in the text, Daventria, and others: *Nec Salomona gravem* (“Nor Solomon, weighty …”). Regina and Ottobonianus: *Nec Salomona illum* (“Nor [did he make] Solomon that”). Rome: *Nec Salomon illum*. From the Vulgate reading one may conjecture *Nec Salomona gravem*. Perhaps instead: *Nec Salomona tamen* (“Nor Solomon, nevertheless”). Poelmannus, in a different division of the words, placed *Nec Salomona illum*, a reading also adopted by Omeisius. See the variant readings on Book II, verse 712.

682. This verse is absent from the printed editions, including the Reuschian edition. But since it is present in our manuscripts, Regina, Ottobonianus, and Rome, why should we continue to tolerate its absence?

685. Rome: *Cur nobis potior non est fiducia praesens?* (“Why is present trust not more valuable to us?”). Retain the reading printed here.

689. Aldus and Basel: *currunt?* (“do they run?”); others: *current* (“they will run”).

693. Our manuscripts, Regina, Ottobonianus, and Rome: *juris vestri* (“of your right”). The printed editions: *vestri juris* (“of your right”).

694. Ottobonianus, Basiliensis, Tornacensis, Aldus, and Poelmann in the main text: “Whatever [things are] on earth.” Reginensis, Romanus, and others: “What you [do] on earth.” Aldus and Badius have *tempora* (“times”), while others read *tempore* (“time”). Badius displays and explains *tempora* as “temporal judgments”; *capti* (“captured”) means “by enticements and riches.” Reuschius prefers *statuetis, tempore capti* (“you will establish, captured by time”), where *time* is used metonymically for what is done badly in time, as in the phrase “O times, O customs!”

696. This verse is commonly punctuated incorrectly. Its meaning is: “You must bear the measure that you impose”—that is, that you impose on others.

[Note: [Col. 0137C]]

680. I understand the passage as referring to Solomon when he abounded in the court of a wealthy kingdom, so that *aula* is taken in the ablative of separation.

681. *Gratia* means elegance, charm, or beauty. Pliny, Celsus, Quintilian, Apuleius, and their contemporaries use the word in this sense. Hence the Three Graces (*tres Gratiae*) derived their name.

683. Barthius observes in *Adversaria*, book XXXV, chapter 12:

> No one who is not utterly ignorant fails to know that places called *culta* by poets are fertile, productive, and cultivated. But it is by no means a commonplace that *laeta* has the same meaning.

Juvencus, book I:

> But if God himself clothes the green abundance  
> of meadows and shrubs,

And such writers should not be despised—writers whom the common people rashly hold in contempt. They would possess greater authority if they had not reached us through so many barbarous monastic hands. I would ask Barthius: through what other, more learned hands could these poems have reached us? Or how would we possess them now, unless they had at last been conveyed to us through the hands of monks?

Nor do I approve Barthius’s claim that, in poets, *laeta* means fertile places on the basis of this passage in Juvencus. Since *laeta* is joined with *virentia*, it should rather be understood as an adjective used absolutely, as in book II, verse 817:

> And that it is less than all the green things in seed.

Columella, book I, chapter 5: “For herds, and green things, and their fruits.” And book III, chapter 8: “Nature has declared an equal law of fertility for green things, human beings, and the other animals.”

684. *Vestit* (“clothes”): for this metaphor, see the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 184, “Subject to our flames,” because the Evangelist Matthew says: “But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, etc.” Indeed, it is thrown into the furnace. The old Itala, more clearly, in manuscript 1 of Saint-Germain has: “And tomorrow it is thrown into the fire.” Badius explained Juvencus’s words about the sun’s burning in the wrong order.

689. *Spontaneus* is a word used by Seneca and later writers. Cellarius restored it to the Silver Age against Vossius; but the passage of Pliny that he cites from Borrichius has an uncertain reading.

690. Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 615:

> Let tomorrow’s affair not trouble you.

Columbanus:

> Let the surrounding abundance of things not trouble you,

which is taken from the cited passage of Prudentius, and from another passage in *Hamartigenia* 333:

> And the surrounding abundance of glittering things deceiving him.

691. The Gospel text is: “For tomorrow will be anxious for itself; sufficient for the day is its own evil.” In Greek, the word for “evil” is *κακία* (*kakia*), meaning affliction or distress. Juvencus therefore rightly uses *fraus* (“harm,” literally “deceit”), for *fraus* also signifies damage. Compare the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 326.

692. CHAPTER XL. One must not judge rashly. We see the speck in another’s eye but do not notice the beam in our own. Pearls must not be cast before swine. Matthew 7:1 and following; Luke 6:37; Mark 4:24.

693. “He will follow the evidence of your law”: he will judge you by the judgment with which you have judged others. He will return like for like.

> In our breasts. Can human beings add  
> an increase of cubits to their own limbs?  
> See how lilies bloom through the rich fields.  
> Yet no labors have ever weighed upon them.
>
> **[680]** Nor did the beauty of such a garment clothe Solomon,  
> when he flourished in the court of a wealthy kingdom.
>
> Natural goodness, common to the earth, will be pleasing.  
> But if God himself clothes the green abundance  
> of meadows and shrubs, subject to our flames,
>
> **[685]** why is your trust in the Father not greater?
>
> Therefore leave food, drink, clothing, and every empty concern  
> to faithless peoples, with their earthly anxiety.  
> Rather seek worthily the heavenly kingdoms  
> and the justice of God: the rest will run of itself.
>
> **[690]** Do not worry about tomorrow’s supply of things.  
> Each day is sufficient for itself because of its daily harm.
>
> Let harsh condemnation flee from your judgment.  
> For the Lord will follow the evidence of your law.  
> Whatever you establish on earth, captured by time,
>
> **[695]** the Father will preserve the same for you in heaven.
>
> You must bear the measure that you impose.

[Col. 0138A] [Note: [Col. 0138B]]

697. Ottobonianus writes *fistucam*.

698. Badius reads *lignum* (“wood”), but conjectured that *tignum* (“beam”) should be read, as the other witnesses have.

699. Romanus: *labores* (“you labor”); others: *laboras* (“you labor”). Poelmann and others print *laboras?* with an interrogation mark, which is also found in the Gospel. Some print *laboras* without interrogation.

700. Poelmann in the secondary reading: *Eripe* (“remove”); in the main text, *Diripe*, as in most witnesses. Ottobonianus: *Deripe*. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Aldus, Daventriensis, and Badius: *lumine trabem* (“the beam from the eye”), which is surprising, since the *a* in *trabem* is short. Romanus, Hadamarius, Poelmann, and others correctly have *tignum*.

702. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, read *Ne sanctum canibus* (“Do not give what is holy to dogs”). In our manuscripts and printed editions I find *Ne canibus sanctum* (“Do not give the holy thing to dogs”).

703. Reginensis and the second hand of Ottobonianus write *munilia* instead of *monilia*.

704. Hadamarius: *Namque illo in coeno*; read *illa* with the others.

705. The Basel edition has, erroneously, *conversique suos*. Fabricius and Tornacensis have *Conversique canes* (“and the dogs, having turned…”). Poelmann in the secondary reading: *Conversaeque sues* (“and the sows, having turned…”). In the main text, as in the manuscripts and most printed editions: *Conversique sues* (“and the swine, having turned…”).

707. Badius has *adytus* (“sanctuary”), to which Romanus’s *adytis* may perhaps refer. But *aditus* (“entrance”) is correct. In Romanus it is clearly written, and above it appears as a separate reading, *apertis*.

709. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, and Romanus: “You will not give a stone, or a serpent to those asking for a fish.” The printed editions have: “Will you give a stone, or a serpent to those asking for a fish?” This comes closer to the Gospel text, and the holy Fathers also generally express the sentence as a question.

711. Fabricius: *dabitis dona optima natis* (“you will give excellent gifts to your children”). I do not know from whom he borrowed this, for the manuscripts and printed editions have *dabitis semper bona natis* (“you will always give good things to your children”), which is sound.

713. Perhaps *poscentibus aequus* (“kind toward those asking”) or *poscentibus aequa* (“kind things toward those asking”).

714. Poelmann in the main text, as most witnesses: *hominum*; in the secondary reading: *homini*.

717. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, and Romanus: *supra sidera* (“above the stars”). The printed editions: *super aethera* (“above the heavens”).

718. Poelmann in the main text, with others: *Quam*; in the secondary reading: *Quod*.

721. Reginensis: *strictis*; above, in the secondary reading, *vastis*, which is found in Ottobonianus, Romanus, and the printed editions.

722. Reginensis, Romanus, and the second hand of Ottobonianus have *ducit*, which Tornacensis printed. Most others, together with Ottobonianus in the main text, have *ducet*. Ottobonianus and Romanus write *scropea*.

723. In the manuscripts Reginensis, Ottobonianus, and Romanus, *inlex* is written instead of *illex*.

[Note: [Col. 0139C]]

702. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, should be heeded here, in letter 8:

> Servius says that in the verse where Virgil contracted the syllable in the words “You know we have done it, and it is necessary to remember too much,” he shortened *ri*, he says, because of metrical necessity. Likewise Juvencus: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor wish…,” although some say that the perfect subjunctive and the future should be distinguished. Whatever the truth may be, the secure rule of grammar is that poetry may vary the *ri* of the subjunctive. Examples can be found in the very best poets.

703. *Monilia*: that is, pearls with which necklaces (*monilia*) are adorned.

705. *Rumpent* means “they will break apart” or “they will tear to pieces.” Ovid, *Ibis* 603:

> May the boar that killed Lycurgus’s son, the tree-born man,  
> and bold Idimon tear you too.

Add Martial, book XII, epigram 14.

706. CHAPTER XLI. One must ask, seek, and knock. Matthew 7:7 and following; 21:22; Mark 11:24; Luke 11:9; John 14:13.

711. *Durities* (“hardness”), because people are rigid and hard—that is, not inclined toward kindness.

713. *Quam magis gaudet* means “the more he rejoices,” or “the more greatly,” for *quam* properly means “how much” or “to what extent.” *Aequus* (“kind,” “just”) is used for “good” or “just.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 129:

> Few, whom just Jupiter loved.

See the note at verse 123 of that passage.

717. CHAPTER XLII. The way that leads to destruction is broad, while the way that leads to salvation is narrow. Matthew 7:13 and following; Luke 13:24.

718. *Quam lata* perhaps means “how very broad and spacious the way is.” The Evangelist says: “Enter through the narrow gate, because broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it.” But in the following verse, with an expression of wonder: “How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!”

Nevertheless, I would believe that even the mark of wonder may be absent from the sacred text. The sense is straightforward: “The gate is very narrow, and the way is constricted,” for that is the force of the particle *quam*. Thus, in expressing this very sentence, Hilary, Ambrose, Leo the Great, and others omit the particle. Most Greek manuscripts cited by Wetstenius, as well as Matthew, have not *ὅτι* but *τί*. This particle can also indicate a question or wonder in Juvencus.

720. *Per prona* means “down steep slopes,” because “the descent to hell is easy.” Silius, book XV, 234:

> The nature of the ground resisted, and above,  
> with little effort in the struggle,  
> they rolled everywhere down the slopes  
> and, with their bodies mutilated,  
> poured out unstable life.

Seneca, letter 123: “Those who go down a slope lean their bodies backward; those who go uphill lean forward.”

722. A *scrupus* is a rough rock; hence *scrupeus*, “full of rough rocks,” and *scrupea loca*, places difficult of access and bristling with huge rocks. *Celsa* (“lofty”) should be joined with *virtus* rather than with *scrupea*.

723. *Illex* comes from *illicere*, “to entice.” See the commentary on Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 328. With a genitive in Apuleius’s *Apologia*: “Venus, the enticer of the soul.”

724. *Suasit* is used with the accusative in place of the dative. Apuleius, Tertullian, and others spoke in the same way. If an infinitive follows, it is not particularly rare for *suadeo* to take the accusative of the person, as in *Suadeo te quiescere* (“I advise you to rest”). Nevertheless, *Suadeo tibi* (“I advise you”) is always preferable.

> Do you see the speck clinging to your brother’s eye,  
> yet do not perceive the beam standing in your own?
>
> And do you first labor to cleanse another’s eye?
>
> **[700]** But remove the deceptive beam from your own eye.  
> Then you will take care to remove the tiny splinter from another’s.
>
> Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor wish  
> to cast pearls shamefully before filthy swine.
>
> For those pearls, thrown beneath their feet in the mud, will lie there,
>
> **[705]** and the swine, turning, will tear you with a great wound.
>
> To the one asking, it will be given; the seeker will possess what is found;  
> to the one knocking, the entrances will be opened wide.
>
> You people, who give bread to all your children when they ask,  
> will you give a stone to those asking for bread, or a serpent to those asking for a fish?
>
> **[710]** You, I say, who are hard, whose hearts are deeply marked  
> by hardness, will always give good things to your children.
>
> How much more gladly will the merciful Father of humankind  
> worthily provide good and gentle things to those who ask?
>
> Whatever benefits of human beings you wish to come to you,
>
> **[715]** provide these same things to all through your own favor.
>
> This is the sum of the law; this is the right proclaimed by the prophets.  
> Go, righteous ones, through the narrow gate above the stars.
>
> How broad and spacious is the way that, along its left-hand track,  
> rolls its precipitous path into the darkness of death,
>
> **[720]** and countless crowds enter it down the slopes!
>
> The life-giving path is hemmed in by huge rocks,  
> and lofty virtue scarcely leads a few through the rugged places.
>
> But if the deceitful, enticing plain of evils has seduced any too deeply  
> into a shameful, slippery fall,

[Col. 0141A] [Note: [Col. 0141B]]

726. Fabricius has *effrenis*; the manuscripts and other printed editions have *effrenus*, which should not have been altered.

732. In Ottobonianus the reading is *cedentum*, perhaps derived from *credentum*, for something has been erased. I prefer *credentum*.

734. Ottobonianus has *videndum* without *est*, which is more elegant. Most witnesses, however, have *videndum est*.

735. In Ottobonianus this verse, *Quapropter*, is enclosed by a comma and marked off. In our other manuscripts and in the printed editions it appears without any mark. Omeisius and Schoettgenius, following Fabricius and the Helmstedt and Cambridge manuscripts, judged that the word could conveniently be absent. Reuschius, although hesitant, retained it and said that the passage concerns those who conceal a corrupt life: to guard against them, not only their doctrine but also their life must be examined.

736. Fabricius: *ficus, de sentibus* (“figs from thistles”). Others: *ficus, nec sentibus* (“figs, nor from thorns”).

738. Reginensis: *Utque arbor vestitur proprio*; correct to *Utque arbor proprio vestitur*.

740. Sabatier published *Non ergo* at Matthew 7, but the law of meter requires *Non ego*.

741. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Fabricius: *perblanda*. Aldus and other printed editions: *praeblanda*, a new word, as Omeisius observes. Reginensis writes *adolatio*, and this spelling fits the meter better than *adulatio*, which the other manuscripts and printed editions have, since the second syllable of *adulatio* is long. Omeisius maintains that Juvencus shortens it by poetic contraction. Romanus: *quae Dominum*; Aldus may have intended the same in the joined letters. Reginensis, from the second hand of Romanus: *dicet*; others: *dicit*.

743. Poelmann in the main text: *Olli*; most witnesses: *Illi*.

744. The Helmstedt manuscript has *volenter*, an adverb also used by Apuleius.

745. Badius: *qua*; read *quae*. In Reginensis it is not sufficiently clear whether *severo*, *severa*, or something else should be read.

748. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Poelmann in the secondary reading:

> Once, under our name, great powers  
> subdued everything for us by holy commands.

Aldus, Hadamarius, Fabricius, and other printed editions:

> Once virtue arose for us under our name,  
> and everything obeyed our commands.

Reuschius defends the former reading, saying that *nobis* is the dative of the person for whom something is acquired. The arrogance of these people is being noted: they do not hesitate to claim for themselves the virtues that God worked through them. The words *sanctis jussis* (“by holy commands”) in the following verse also refer to this.

753. Romanus: *genitis*; correct to *gestis*.

754. Reginensis: *meritis*; read *monitis*.

[Note: [Col. 0141C]]

725. *Pronosque*, as at verse 720, means “down the slopes.”

726. *Sonipes* is a poetic word for “horse.” Juvencus added this material to reinforce the Gospel’s meaning. Here he shows clearly how elevated his style could have been, had he wished to range more freely.

727. Horace, book III, ode 4, verse 45:

> Who rules the inert earth and the stormy sea.

728. CHAPTER XLIII. On false prophets and hypocrites. Matthew 7:15 and following; Luke 6:44. To observe someone sometimes means to revere and honor him, but at other times it means to examine and watch him, so that the observer may avoid his traps.

735. *Molitio* means an effort or undertaking; it is used indifferently of good and evil. The doctrine of those who lie in wait must be examined, but their conduct must also be investigated.

737. *Ruris per terga*: see the note on verse 671.

740. CHAPTER XLIV. Not those who say “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but those who do the commands of God. Matthew 7:21 and following. Omeisius explains the phrase *verbis et honore* by a hendiadys, namely “with honorific words.”

742. *Spontanea*: see the note on verse 689.

745. Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 324:

> The final day has come, and the inevitable hour.

749. *Virtutes*: in sacred writings and among ecclesiastical writers, this word is commonly applied to miracles.

753. *Res gestae* and *gesta* are more distinguished deeds or notable actions. For that reason Badius preferred *factis* (“deeds”), since the passage concerns private matters.

754. CHAPTER XLV. A house built upon rock remains unharmed, whereas one built upon sand collapses. Matthew 7:24 and following; Luke 6:47 and following. For the word *quisque* used for *quisquis*, see the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 719, and the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymns*, book 7, verse 216.

755. *Fundamina* is a poetic word used by Virgil, Ovid, and others.

> It seizes these men and drags them downward, like the rush of a river,  
> or a spirited horse, unrestrained when its reins are broken,
>
> or a ship without a helmsman over windy seas.
>
> It seizes them and drags them downward,
>
> Observe those who, under a false name,  
> set traps for you and are called prophets.
>
> **[730]** The appearance of sheep clothes them, but beneath it  
> they conceal the savage hearts of wolves by deceit,  
> tearing and dragging the unsuspecting flocks of believers,  
> whom cruel error deceives.
>
> Such monsters are recognized by their own fruits:  
> one must see what end the deceptive doctrine seeks.
>
> **[735]** Therefore the undertaking must be examined.
>
> For you have never noticed figs coming from thistles,  
> nor grapes from thorns, across the fields.
>
> As a tree is clothed by its own fruit-bearing growth,
>
> **[740]** so the deceit of those men is revealed by the fruit that displays it.
>
> I will not be moved by the words and honor of flatterers,  
> nor by the fact that excessively smooth flattery calls me “Lord.”
>
> He will receive the spontaneous rewards of the heavenly abode.
>
> But those who willingly do the commands of our Father  
> will rightly rejoice in the gift of the kingdom.
>
> **[745]** Soon the final day will come, which with strict justice  
> will assign rewards to righteousness and Gehenna to crime.
>
> Then the weeping of many will cry such things to me:
>
> “Did not great powers once, under your name,  
> subdue everything for us by holy commands?
>
> **[750]** Often our voice too was counted among the prophets,  
> and under your name a demon served us?”
>
> Then I will swear to them that no such life  
> of human beings, stained by unrighteous deeds,  
> has ever been known to me.
>
> Whoever devotes his ears and deeds to my warnings,
>
> **[755]** I will liken to a man laying foundations upon solid rocks,

[Col. 0143A] [Note: [Col. 0143B]]

756. Badius: *ponente*, incorrectly. Romanus: *super cui*, less well. Poelmann in the secondary reading: *surgunt*; others: *surgent*.

759. Aldus: *immoto*. Tornacensis and Badius: *immota*. Most: *immotae*. Aldus: *fundamine*; Badius and Tornacensis likewise. Others: *fundamina*. Poelmann in the main text: *immotaeque fundamina*; in the secondary reading: *immotoque fundamine*.

761. Reginensis: *pergit*; the others: *perget*.

762. Fabricius: *Hanc*; correct to *Hunc*.

763. Ottobonianus:

> The foundations of the house, when the wind  
> and rain began to press upon them  
> with torrents pouring forth.

Reginensis has the same, but *infusis* (“poured in”) instead of *effusis* (“poured out”), with a gloss on *venti*—“when they began to press upon them.” In Ottobonianus, the first hand perhaps had *flamina*, from which *flamine* arose. Romanus:

> The foundations of the house, when the wind came,  
> and rain began to press upon them  
> with rivers poured forth.

*Primo* is absent. The printed editions express it differently:

> The foundations of the house; as soon as the winds  
> and rain, with rivers pouring forth, began to press upon them.

766. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Aldus: *gravi*. Fabricius, Poelmann, and some others: *gravis*.

767. Reginensis: “When he had said such things, fixed amazement”; with the gloss *dicente*—“when the Lord was speaking.”

768. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, and Romanus: *transcenderat*; the printed editions: *transcenderet*.

775. Romanus: *Et*; in the margin, *Ut*. One may conjecture *Ut caream* (“that I may be free”). Matthew says: “He worshiped him, saying, ‘Lord, if you wish, you can cleanse me.’” Mark and Luke do likewise. I therefore follow the conjecture, although all the others have *careat*.

776. Poelmann in the secondary reading: *sufficiet*; most witnesses: *sufficiat*.

778. Reginensis and the second hand of Ottobonianus write *Incolomi*. Poelmann in the main text, Tornacensis, and Hadamarius:

> He ordered him to conceal these joys  
> and, obedient to the law, to offer gifts at the temple.

Poelmann in the secondary reading and Fabricius: *celaret gaudia … offerret*. Reginensis, first hand: *celare gaudia … offerret*. Reginensis after correction, Ottobonianus, Daventriensis, Aldus, Romanus, and Badius: *celare haec … offerret*.

781. Aldus: *projectis*.

783. Aldus, Daventriensis, Hadamarius, Poelmann, and most printed editions: *tepens*. Fabricius printed *repens*, perhaps meaning *repente* (“suddenly”), not from *repo*, a reading also found in Reginensis and Ottobonianus. Romanus agrees, though it has the error *reperis* for *repens* and *Ejus* for *Cujus*. Two manuscripts cited by Omeisius also have *repens*. Reuschius printed *tepens* and explained it as “relenting,” but observed that Prudentius also shortened the first syllable of *repo*, *Peristephanon* III, 161:

> A dove suddenly (*repens*) flashes forth from there.

I am not sufficiently convinced of this, for in that passage *repens* may perhaps stand for *repente*. An old gloss of Ison gives *repens* as “sudden.” In the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 288, “And the spotted serpent creeps through its scaly body,” I showed that there is some reason why the first syllable of *repo* may be shortened. Forcellinus confirms that *repo* derives by metathesis from the Greek verb *ἕρπω* (“to creep”).

[Note: [Col. 0141C]]

756. *Librata* means “placed as if on a balance,” “set level,” so that they cannot totter, leveled by the instrument called a *libella*. *Surgent* is from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 441:

> O fortunate ones, whose walls are already rising.

761. *Diversis* means “opposite” or “contrary,” for the noun *diversus* also has this meaning, as lexicographers confirm with many examples. Pliny, Macrobius, Ulpian, and others used *lubricum* as a substantive.

768. Sallust, Ovid, Tacitus, and others use *immensum* adverbially. *Stupuit* from the astonishment caused by wonder takes the accusative again in book II, verse 297:

> They were astonished at the teacher.

769. The Evangelist Matthew says: “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.” Thus Juvencus understands by “the elders” the scribes and Pharisees, or perhaps also the elders.

770. CHAPTER XLVI. Jesus descends from the mountain and cures a leper. Matthew 8:1 and following; Mark 1:40; Luke 5:12.

774. *Juvenis*: rather, a man full of leprosy, as Luke says. See the note on book II, verses 332 and 419, concerning this word *juvenis*.

776. *Voluisse tuum* means “your will.” See the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 367.

777. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 350:

> It rolls without being touched.

Varro also used the ablative *attactu*, and Forcellinus denies that examples occur outside the ablative case. *Purgare* (“to cleanse”) is the most suitable verb for this matter, as Arntzenius noted, *Observationes Specimen*, chapter 9. Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*: “To cleanse lepers.”

780. CHAPTER XLVII. The centurion’s paralytic boy is cured. Matthew 8:5 and following; Luke 7:1.

782. Matthew always calls him a boy, while Luke usually calls him a servant and sometimes a boy. Romans also called their slaves *pueri* even when they were old. Compare the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* 9, verse 1. I therefore do not see why Juvencus calls the centurion’s servant an underage boy. He often calls an adult man *juvenis*, but an underage *puer* must certainly refer to genuine childhood.

784. *Dissolvit* is the proper verb for describing paralysis. See the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 118: “With flesh loosened from bones and nerves laid bare.” I understand “the punishment, surviving life, held him” to mean that in limbs loosened and dead through paralysis there was a punishment that survived the life of the other limbs. Compare the note on book II, verse 605.

> above which level walls will rise.  
> That house will remain unharmed by rains and winds  
> and will withstand the threats of torrents with firm strength,
>
> because its unmoving foundations cling to rock.
>
> **[760]** But whoever merely holds my commands by hearing  
> and proceeds far away from them in contrary deeds along slippery paths,
>
> I will make him like one who supports  
> the foundations of his house upon shifting sand.
>
> As soon as the wind began to blow upon it  
> and rain, with torrents pouring forth, began to bear down,
>
> **[765]** the whole mass collapsed beneath its overturned weight,  
> and ruin followed with the heavy wreckage of the roof.
>
> When he had said these things, the crowd was struck  
> with great amazement and was immensely astonished,
>
> because the power granted to Christ had risen far above  
> the teaching of the elders.
>
> **[770]** At last, as he left the heights of the lofty mountain,  
> a rejoicing crowd of following peoples pressed around him.
>
> Behold, a young man whose vitals were afflicted by dreadful corruption,  
> disfigured by leprosy that covered his entire body,  
> fell prostrate in reverence and prayed to Christ:
>
> **[775]** “May I at last be free from the burden of such great disease;  
> let your will be sufficient.” Then Christ’s right hand,  
> by touch alone, cleansed his filthy limbs.
>
> Thereafter, when he was restored to health, Jesus ordered him  
> to conceal his joy and, obedient to the law, offer gifts at the temple.
>
> **[780]** From there, as he was departing, a centurion immediately  
> presented himself as a suppliant and prayed in these words:
>
> “The sick spirit of an underage boy is suffering;  
> a creeping disease has dissolved all the functions of his limbs,  
> and punishment, surviving, now holds his life.”

[Col. 0145A] [Note: [Col. 0145B]]

794. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, Aldus, Tornacensis, and Badius: *Quod multos*. Hadamarius, Fabricius, and Poelmann in the secondary reading: *Quam multos*.

796. Aldus: *vestris*; others: *nostris*.

797. Tornacensis and Fabricius write *demersa*; most have *dimersa*. Badius has *diversa*, less well, although it can be explained in some acceptable sense, namely “opposite” or “on the contrary side.” See the note on verse 761.

798. Ottobonianus, first hand: *fletamque*; in Reginensis, first hand, perhaps *flentumque*. The common reading is *fletumque*.

799. Reginensis: *poenae*; the others: *poenam*.

800. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Aldus: *At tibi*. Tornacensis and Badius likewise. Others, with Hadamarius and Poelmann in the main text: *Ac tibi*. Aldus, Fabricius, Romanus, Tornacensis, and Badius: *junvenis*. Others: *juveni*. In Reginensis *fidelis* has become *fideli*, evidently referring to *virtute*. Reuschius: “But to you, already young, faithful in the strength of your mind,” etc. That is: “To you, centurion, the fruit of your faith will come; the boy whom you described as so faithful and obedient to you will receive the light of healing or health.” In Reuschius’s reading and explanation, two datives are attached to the same verb.

803. Aldus, Badius, and Poelmann in the secondary reading: *percurrunt*; others: *transcurrunt*.

805. Romanus: *Provenisse*; the others more correctly: *Praevenisse*.

808. Reginensis: *Servator*; the others: *Salvator*.

809. After this verse Reginensis has: “Book I ends; Book II begins.”

[Note: [Col. 0145B]]
