791. *Dat dicta* sometimes means “he speaks,” not “he deceives.” I gave examples in the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 456.

792. *Memini me invenisse* (“I remember having found”) is elegant with the present infinitive, even when the subject is past. But the perfect infinitive is also found with Cicero, Virgil, and other good writers.

795. *The lofty kingdom of heaven* is figuratively used for “the lofty ruler of heaven.” Reuschius supplied either: “the one holding the kingdom of heaven will call,” or “the heavenly Father will call to the kingdom of heaven.” It should be noted that *vocabit* is joined with the infinitive *accumbere* (“to recline”) at the living table. Horace, book II, ode 18, at the end, concerning Charon:

> Called and uncalled, he hears  
> to lift up the poor man  
> who has completed his labors.

Some arrange the order as: “Charon, called and uncalled, hears to lift up…” Others, better: “Called to lift up the poor man finished with his labors, and uncalled, he hears.” That is, he lifts the poor man from his labors, whether summoned to do so or not summoned.

The verb *vocabit* itself should also be noted: used absolutely, it is a standard word for inviting someone to dinner. Hence *vocator* (“one who invites”) and *vocatio* (“invitation”). Examples may be read in Forcellinus and other lexicographers.

796. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 83:

> You grant the gods to recline at banquets.

797. Here, and in chapter XXII, verse 13, Matthew calls them “the outer darkness.” Mazochius, in his note on Matthew 8:12, volume III of *Spicilegium*, derives this expression from the fact that the prison was more secluded and darker, as though it were a prison outside a prison. The *Acts of Saint Vincent*, section 8:

> Seek a dark place, oppressed by a heavy roof, removed from all public light, condemned to perpetual night, proper to his guilt—namely, a prison outside the prisons.

798. *Horrendum* is used adverbially. Virgil, book VI, 288: “Horribly hissing.” I omit the other examples.

799. *Acta* means “driven,” “forced,” “impelled,” or “subdued.” The verb has these and other meanings.

802. *Cum voce*: see the variant note on book II, verse 597, *Cum dicto*.

804. *Recursus* properly means a return made by running. Matthew in the Vulgate has only: “And Jesus said to the centurion, ‘Go, and as you have believed, let it be done for you’; and the boy was healed in that hour.” The Itala in some manuscripts, most Greek manuscripts, the Ethiopian version, and the other Syriac version add: “And the centurion returned to his house and found the boy healed at that same hour.”

805. *Laetatur* with an infinitive is sufficiently common.

806. CHAPTER XLVIII. Peter’s mother-in-law is freed from fever by a touch. Matthew 8:14 and following; Mark 1:30 and following; Luke 4:38.

807. Sedulius, book III, verse 33:

> Perhaps fever, panting, scorched Peter’s mother-in-law  
> with the heat of a powerful lamp.

Strictly speaking, *anhela* means “panting,” as in “the panting mother-in-law.” Sedulius calls the fever itself *anhela* because it makes her pant. Consult the notes in Arntzenius’s edition. *Jacebat* (“she lay”) is also aptly used, for this verb is often used when the subject is ill.

808. *Salvator*: a word unknown to the ancients and begun to be used by Christian writers, by Tertullian, Lactantius, and others. Augustine therefore vigorously defended its use, *Sermon* 299, section 6. An old inscription is also cited from Gruter, page 15, number 5: “To Jupiter Custos Quirinus Salvator, for the safety of Caesar Nerva Trajan,” etc. Isidore, *Origins* VII, chapter 2, defends the same word together with Saint Augustine. Isidore’s annotator observes that *soter*, or “savior,” is not adequately expressed by the word *servator*.

809. Ulpian used the expression *ministerium praebere* (“to provide service”), as others used *ministerium praestare* and *ministerium facere* (“to perform service”).

> But, I beg you, have mercy by command, for our crimes  
> forbid us to enter the dwelling of the author of life and light.
>
> Now it is enough for you to order health to return by a word.
>
> I have often compelled men subject to me  
> to obey commands of duty by a word.
>
> **[790]** He had spoken; then Christ, moved by the man’s prayers and faith,  
> turned to the following crowd and spoke these words:
>
> “Never have I remembered finding such faith  
> among the people of our ancestors. But learn from true words  
> that the lofty kingdom of heaven will call many people,
>
> **[795]** born in different regions of the world,  
> to recline at the life-giving table with our fathers.
>
> Their descendants, submerged in blind darkness,  
> gnashing their teeth terribly and multiplying their weeping,  
> will undergo punishment driven by perpetual torments.
>
> **[800]** But to you, young man, faithful through the virtue of your mind,  
> as you believe, the fruit of salvation will come with the light of salvation.”
>
> He had spoken, and sooner than the spoken word,  
> with the voice of the speaker, the gifts of the word  
> ran swiftly to the boy.
>
> **[805]** The soldier entered the house in swift return  
> and rejoiced that the gifts of healing God had preceded him.
>
> Thereafter holy Jesus entered Peter’s house,  
> where his panting mother-in-law lay burning with fever.
>
> When Jesus the Savior touched her right hand,  
> the woman, made well, served at the tables.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0147]

[Col. 0147A] [Note: [Col. 0147A]]

2. Reginensis and Tornacensis: *Contigerat*, with *Inciderat* (“had fallen into” or “had entered”) written above in Reginensis as a gloss. The common reading *Inciderat* is sound. In Reuschius, some, following Aldus, have *aemula* (“rivaling”); but *caerula* (“blue”) is a highly appropriate epithet for night, as Koenigius aptly observed from Greek usage.

[Col. 0147B] 5. Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Poelmann in the secondary reading: *Devinctosque animam*, a commonly known Graecism. Most printed editions: *Devinctasque animas*. In Tornacensis, *Devictasque animas* appears to be an error.

7. Romanus: “They were carrying [them]—at the word of Christ, with sickness removed by his touch.”

8. In Poelmann, *munere* (“by a gift”) appears to be an error; the others have *munera* (“gifts”), with a gloss in Reginensis: “healings.”

9. Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Tornacensis: *exorta*. Reginensis: *extorta*, incorrectly. Aldus printed *exortas* in the errata but corrected it to *exortus*, which is found in Hadamarius, Poelmann in the main text, and others.

[Col. 0148A] 10. Most punctuate the passage: “Of the rejoicing people, when that anxious man was with the crowds,” which should be explained as “when he was anxious on account of the crowds.” I punctuate it: “Of the rejoicing people with the crowds: he was anxious.”

12. Most: *Discipulis*; some cited by Omeisius: *Discipulos*. Both are correct. Romanus: *profusus*; others more correctly: *profusis*.

13. Omeisius reports that some prefer *sancto* to *Sancti*, by which name Juvencus frequently refers to Christ through antonomasia. This is also the gloss in Reginensis: *Sancti*—“of Christ.”

14. Here and elsewhere the manuscripts and printed editions vary: sometimes *olli*, sometimes *illi* is written.

15. Reginensis and Ottobonianus write *rupis*. Reuschius observes that in the Fulda manuscript *rupes exesa* is not badly read, as in Seneca the Tragic’s *exesum antrum* (“a cave eaten away”) and Seneca the Philosopher’s *exesa saxa* (“rocks eaten away”).

[Note: [Col. 0147B]]

1. CHAPTER I. Many sick people are healed, and the words of the Lord to the scribe who wished to follow him. Matthew 8:16 and following; Mark 1:32; Luke 9:58. It should be noted that, in the division of Matthew’s Gospel chapters that we now use, Juvencus’s second book begins at verse 16 of chapter VIII. In earlier times, however, the chapters were indicated differently, as can be seen in Martianaeus and Sabatier. Thus Juvencus, following Matthew chiefly, carried his first book through chapter XX of Matthew according to the old division of chapters. From chapter XXI onward he began the second book of his poem, carrying it through chapter XL. He continued book III from chapter XLI through chapter LXII. The final book of the Gospel history encompasses the remaining chapters of Matthew, from chapter LXIII through the last chapter, LXXIV.

In the first verse of this book, *prono lumine* (“with the declining light”) should be noted. Poets elegantly speak of a “declining day,” “declining star,” or “declining light” when these are near setting. Badius says: “A description of evening time, than which nothing is more elegant.”

2. *Inciderat pontum* stands for *inciderat in pontum* (“had fallen into the sea”); likewise later, verse 591: “If perhaps your little sheep should have fallen into the pit.” Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 270:

> The horseman, carried in swift motion,  
> fell into this trick.

Nepos, *Life of Atticus*, chapter 10: “So that no danger might arise, which happened at night, he sent him a guard.” Some other passages of Virgil and Lucretius are cited, but their readings are uncertain.

*Super* seems to be used here for *desuper* (“from above”). Night is given a *palla*, a woman’s garment. See the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 521, and the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* 5, verses 27–28. In that passage Prudentius seems to have imitated Juvencus, according to Giselinus:

> And rival light drives away the absent day.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book X, chapter 20:

> Juvencus describes that veil of night not inelegantly at the beginning of book II: “And now…” Let no one think this unusual in a poet who professes Christ. Elegant indeed—and there are not a few passages in that poet that show a vigorous talent pressed into the service of his subject, as we shall someday demonstrate at greater length, especially when we are equipped with an excellent parchment exemplar, with which we believe no one has yet made a better collation—or even seen it.

3. The ancients, but especially poets, commonly attribute flame and fire to the stars. *Per inane* (“through the void”) is also poetic for “through the air.” See book I, verse 396.

6. *Caeca nocte* means “in the dark night.” *Ferebant* is a temporal adverb joined with the indicative when a temporal reference has preceded. See book I, verses 317 and following.

9. Book I, verse 801: “With the light of salvation.”

### 10

“Gratantis” means “rejoicing,” “congratulating,” or rather “giving thanks.” For *grator* also has this meaning, although some consider the reading doubtful in Ovid, *Fasti* III, verse 418, where they read *cratera* instead of *gratare*. “Anxius,” as others punctuate it, is construed with the dative. Ovid, *Heroides* XX, verse 198: “Our hearts are anxious for your life,” that is, “for the sake of your life.”

### 11

“Sea traversed under sail” (*mare velivolum*) comes from Virgil. See the note on Dracontius, Book II, verse 185, “to launch the ship” (*deducere puppim*), a nautical expression used when ships are brought from the shipyards or harbor out into the sea. Lexicographers indicate similar passages in other writers. The Evangelist says briefly: “When Jesus saw the great crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the lake.” The Old Latin version has: “He ordered his disciples to go across the lake.”

### 13

“Vessel” (*navigium*) is used of every kind of ship. Omeisius says that *navigio* is used for *navi* (“ship”), in the manner of writers of later Latin.

### 14

Matthew’s words are interpreted as follows: “And one of the scribes approached and said to him, ‘Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.’ And Jesus said to him, ‘Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’” Jerome explains it in a similar way, presenting Jesus as saying: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of riches and the profits of the world, when I do not even have a little lodging?” Juvencus, however, seems rather to be pointing out the treachery of the Jews who persecuted him; for at verse 18 he says: “Such are the schemes of your people.”

### 15

*Latebrae* is more usual in the plural; but there are so many examples of the singular *latebra* in the most authoritative writers that its use here ought not to be disputed.

**[162]** And now day, descending with slanting light, had fallen upon the sea, and blue-black night was drawing its dusky cloak, embroidered with starry flames, across the airless expanse. When many men, falling through weakness of mind,

**[5]** and bound in soul by the criminal art of the demon, were being carried by the people in their eagerness through the already blind night,

**[163]** the word of Christ, removing so great a weakness, graciously bestowed the Father’s gifts on all.

But behold, a greater tumult arose with the light: the thankful crowd was joined by multitudes. Anxious to launch the lofty vessel upon the sail-bearing sea, he ordered his disciples to do so. Then, with abundant prayers, the scribe likewise begged to depart in the vessel of the Holy One.

Christ said to him: “Scribe, where will you follow me?”

**[15] [164]** “A rock cut out in the wilderness affords foxes a hiding-place, and the forest gives rest to birds of the air; but the Son of Man is permitted to enter no dwelling: such are the schemes of your people.”

Then one of the disciples addressed him in these words:

**[20]** “The final rites are owed to my dead father. Therefore may your will, Holy One, grant us time, so that we may bury the body of my wretched parent.”

Christ replied: “Rather, you shall accompany our journey, and let the dead bury the dead in the earth.”

**[25] [165]** They go aboard the ship; the sails swell, filled by their wind, and the keel flies over the hissing waves. After the vessel had reached the deep, the sea began to rise in fury and to swell here and there with enormous winds, and it pressed to raise raging mountains toward heaven.

**[30]** Now it strikes the ship with its mass, now the prow with a whirlwind; the waves, crashing above, wash over the ship’s deck, and, when the deep is driven apart, land is laid bare.

Meanwhile Jesus was taking his sleep in the ship. His disciples and the terrified sailors together begged him to wake and pointed out the dangers of the sea.

He then said: “How little confidence you have! Fear has rushed upon your faithless hearts!” He commands the storms and spreads calm peace over the waters.

## Notes

### 16

In the Roman manuscript: “And the forest not ineptly gives quiet to the aerial birds”; perhaps *ac silva* should be read. The earlier reading was *silvam*. Others write *aeriis* or *aereis*.

### 17

In the Basle manuscript: *secedere tectis* (“to withdraw into dwellings”); the others more suitably have *succedere* (“to enter”).

### 18

In the Ottobonian manuscript, in place of the reading of the first edition: “Such is the intention of your people.” Others have: “Such are the schemes of your people.” Below, verse 310: “But he, perceiving the schemes within the mind.” Juvencus uses the same word elsewhere as well.

### 21

The Roman, Aldine, and Basle editions have *Sed* (“But”); others have *Hinc* (“Therefore”). The Ottobonian, Reginensis, Roman, Aldine, Tornesian, and Basle witnesses have *nobis tua* (“your [will] for us”); Hadamar, Fabricius, and Poelmann have *tua nobis* (“your [will] for us,” with the order reversed). Most have *sancta* (“holy”); in the Ottobonian manuscript it seems to be *Sancte* (“Holy One”), which I think comes from Juvencus’s own hand, for he commonly addresses Christ in this way. Thus below, verse 181: “There is no doubt, Holy One, that God’s abundant will [is directed toward] you.” If desired, consult the note on verse 96 of Prudentius’s third *Cathemerinon*: “Therefore your hands, Holy One, [have formed] us.”

### 23

The Ottobonian manuscript originally had *itener*, corrected to *itiner*, as most witnesses read. The Basle and Poelmann manuscripts, in place of the common reading, have *callem* (“path”); Aldus has *calcem* (“heel” or “track”). Fabricius reads *itiner* and observes in his commentary that Georgius Cassander regularly replaced *itineris* with *iteris* in Juvencus; he says that he found a different reading in his own ancient manuscript, namely *vide* or something else. See the textual variants at Book I, verse 325. The Roman manuscript corruptly has: “Christ says in reply: it is better to contract nature by the journey.” The Tornesian manuscript has: “It is better, on the journey, that you accompany ours.” Others have *potius* (“rather”) instead of *melius* (“better”).

### 24

The Roman, Tornesian, Basle, and Aldine editions have *terrae* (“of the earth”); others have *terra* (“earth”). See Book III, verse 69, where all read: “The disciples bury [him] in the earth.”

### 25

The Roman manuscript writes *navim* (“ship”).

### 26

The Ottobonian manuscript, in place of the common reading, has *flatuque volat* (“and it flies by the blast”).

### 28

The Reginensis has *et immissis hic*; the Tornesian, *et immissis hinc*; others, *et immensis hinc*. Reuschius prefers the latter, so that the repeated word may intensify the meaning of *tumescere* (“to swell”). Cicero said *pariter immensus aer* (“the equally boundless air”), and Virgil *immensae nubes* (“enormous clouds”).

### 29

The Reginensis has: “It presses and raises swiftly toward heaven.” Aldus, Basle, and Tornesius have: “It began and raised swiftly toward heaven.” The Roman, Ottobonian, Hadamar, and Poelmann manuscripts in the text, together with other witnesses, have: “It presses and raises raging [mountains] toward heaven.” Fabricius has: “It began and lifted the abrupt mountains toward heaven.” Poelmann, in place of the common reading, supplies three verses instead of this single verse:

“Raging winds, with storms mingled here and there—  
It began and raised swift mountains toward heaven—  
The sea lifts abrupt mountains beyond the stars.”

Omeisius says that *sustollere* (“to raise up”) is an excellent word, used both by earlier writers and by Juvencus in Book II, verse 599, and Book III, verse 336.

### 31

Poelmann, in place of the common reading, has *receptat* (“receives”); *receptant* (“receive”) is better, namely, the upper decks receive [the waves] from above. Reuschius also approved this, saying that *receptat* is found in some manuscripts. He does not, however, consider it absurd if *super*, following Greek usage, is construed with the genitive *laterum* (“of the sides”). See Vossius, *De Constructione*, chapter 65, p. 583.

### 32

Poelmann, in place of the common reading, and the Tornesian manuscript have *dissectoque* (“and when it has been cut apart”); others have *disjectoque* (“and when it has been scattered”), which is better.

### 33

The Roman manuscript has *capiebat* (“was taking”); the others *carpebat* (“was enjoying”).

### 36

The Reginensis, Ottobonian, Roman, and Poelmann manuscripts, in place of the common reading, have *quam nulla subest* (“in which no confidence exists”). Aldus and most printed editions have *quam parva subest* (“in which little confidence exists”). *Nullus* often means “light,” “small,” or “empty.” Terence, *Hecyra* V.3.2: “For no reason he sent [him].”

### 37

Fabricius has *timor arguit* (“fear proves”); the manuscripts and all other printed editions have *timor irruit* (“fear rushes upon [them]”), and the Reginensis gloss has “the voice of one who marvels.” Fabricius perhaps took *arguit* from Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 13: “Fear proves cowardly spirits.” Omeisius rightly considers the common reading, supported by the authority of the manuscripts, preferable. Some pronounce the verse with an interrogative mark: “Fear rushes upon faithless hearts?”

## Additional Notes

### 17

*Succedere*, “to enter,” used of someone who enters a house, is frequent. Cicero, *Pro domo sua*, chapter 44: “So he said that the man who, among the Marsi, where he was born, had no roof under which he could take shelter from the rain, had bought a most distinguished house on the Palatine.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 631: “Come, young men, enter beneath our roof.”

### 18

See Book I, verse 557, for *molimina* (“schemes,” “machinations”).

### 19

**CHAPTER II.** Jesus commands a disciple to follow him, leaving his father unburied. Matthew VIII, 21 and following; Luke IX, 59 and following.

### 20

“Final gifts,” or “last duties,” is an elegant expression for funeral rites. Virgil, Book VI, verse 213: “And he brought final offerings to the ungrateful ashes.” On *munera* (“gifts”), compare the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 10, verse 47: “The final honor receives the limbs.”

### 25

**CHAPTER III.** The disciples awaken Jesus, sleeping in the ship, so that he may calm the storm. Matthew VIII, 23 and following; Mark IV, 35 and following; Luke VIII, 22 and following.

### 26

He uses words especially proper to nautical matters—*conscendunt* (“they board”), *volat* (“it flies”), *stridente* (“hissing”), and so forth—whose explanation cannot be pursued at greater length here.

### 27

Book I, verse 535: “Lest anyone dare to rise into anger.”

### 31

A *tabulatum* is a surface covered with joined boards.

### 32

“Deep” is used for “sea.” See the note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 394.

### 36

These are the words of the Gospel: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?”

### 38

“To spread the sea” or “the waves” is a common expression. “He spreads peace,” that is, “he brings about tranquility.”

In fearful conversations they exchanged accounts of the miracles among themselves:

**[40]** “What power has been granted to him? What is the authority by which, at his command, the stirred waters bow before the winds, and the upraised storms submit their necks?”

The ship of the Gerasenes had now come to rest beneath the shore. But behold, as a young man came out—wondrous to tell—he encountered him; a dark spirit was tearing apart and filling the wretched man’s mind with the madness of its power.

**[45]** The man found it pleasant to dwell in grim tombs, and no one could restrain his raging fury. Indeed, he even broke strong iron chains and split heavy fetters as though they were threads of wool.

**[50]** Once freed from his shackles, it was a light game for him to mock them, and to crush his savage breast against stones.

When he saw Christ proceeding along the shore, he rushed forward with a cry, ran a long way, and worshiped him:

**[55]** “Most certain offspring of the Lord who reigns forever, we beg you not to drive us away from the borders of our accustomed region, tortured far away by torments.

**[168]** For ‘Legion’ is our name, and a single power of harming unites many spirits under one name.

**[60]** “Do you see how the unclean swine are rooting up these pasturelands? At least permit them to satisfy their rebuffed frenzy. We beg this in the sublime name of the Father enthroned on high.”

Christ commands them to release the man’s mind and allows them to bring their madness to an end in the herds of swine.

**[65]** Now, when the demon had been shaken off, the man’s dull mind reverently honors the unexpected gifts of his salvation.

Then the swine, rushing from the edge of the cliffs, plunged into the sea and hastened to destroy their lives. But the terrified swineherds, seeing so great a miracle from the watchtowers, fled and rushed to the roofs of the city; they spread the report and gathered the people to the shore.

**[169]** When the assembled crowd of spectators had been compelled to believe that the mad young man had returned to his senses, they anxiously begged that he leave the region.

**[75]** Jesus, the light of the world, then returned home. Behold, as he came back, they placed before Christ’s feet, lying on a bed, the young man whose limbs had been numbed and whose bodily function a harsh disease had destroyed.

Moved by compassion, Jesus addressed him:

**[80]** “Let firm confidence be present in your mind, young man, for the error of your past life will be forgiven you.”

The scribes, in the hidden recesses of their malicious minds, took exception to this saying, because he had uttered words that required divine power to be performed. But Christ, perceiving such thoughts, said:

**[85]** “The utterances of the scribes challenge this saying. How much easier it is to say this, they will prove alike by the power of the ensuing word and deed, and they will see that authority to forgive sins has been granted to me.”

---

## Notes

### 65

For *decusso* (“shaken off”), Koenigius conjectures *discluso* (“shut out”). Thus in Book III, verse 193, he reads: “The power of the Virgin and the mind, when the demon has been shut out.” Others have *discusso* (“shaken off”). Elsewhere Juvencus also uses *discludere* for “to drive out,” as in Book III, verse 162.

### 68

The Reginensis has “cast into the sea.” Aldus and Poelmann, in place of the common reading, have *vitam* (“life”); others have *vitas* (“lives”).

### 69

The Reginensis has “But from the cliffs”; the Roman, “But from the cliffs”; the Ottobonian, together with the printed editions, “But from the watchtowers.”

### 71

The Reginensis, Ottobonian, Roman, and Tornesian manuscripts have “And they kindle the report.” Most printed editions have “And they spread the report.” Poelmann, in place of the common reading, has “And they intensify the report,” a reading found in the Paris manuscript that did not displease Omeisius, as in Tacitus, “sluggishness is intensified,” that is, “increased.” Reuschius likewise printed this reading. Yet *accendunt* (“kindle”) seems more elegant in the same sense. One is said to kindle confidence, eagerness, thirst, hope, care, desire, vices, or price.

### 72

The Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman manuscripts, together with the Basle and Aldine editions and Poelmann’s edition made from the manuscripts, have: “After they had recognized that the mad young man had returned to his senses.” Hadamar, Tornesius, Fabricius, and Poelmann in his main text, as well as Reuschius, have: “They saw that the mad young man had returned to his senses.”

### 74

The Roman manuscript has: “so that he might leave that region.”

### 77

The Reginensis has *dissolverat aeger* (“the sick man had been paralyzed”).

### 78

The Reginensis, Ottobonian, and Roman manuscripts, together with Poelmann’s edition made from the manuscripts, have: “They placed him lying on a bed before Christ’s feet.” Aldus and nearly all other printed editions have: “They place before his feet, on a warm bed, limbs reclining.” Reuschius confirms that the former reading is genuine in Juvencus; by it, a very elegant change of grammatical gender is produced. That is, *juvenis torpentia membra* (“the young man’s numb limbs”) stands for “the young man possessing numb limbs.” See the note on Dracontius, *Satisfactio*, verse 153, concerning this kind of change of gender. The same figure also occurs elsewhere in Juvencus.

### 83

Sabatierius, I do not know from where, produces *virtute verenda* (“with a power to be feared”). The proper reading is *ferenda* (“to be borne”), that is, “to be uttered.”

### 84

The printed editions punctuate: “Christ had uttered: but hearts.” It seems better, with the Roman manuscript, to punctuate: “He had uttered. But Christ, seeing such hearts…”

### 85

Besides its other meanings, *retractare* also means “to disapprove,” “to criticize,” or “to reject.” Gellius, Book XIV, chapter 3: “They say that Plato was so deeply moved by this deed and writing of his that, in a certain book, after mentioning King Cyrus, he criticized and corrected that work,” namely, Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*.

---

### 90

A *stratum* properly means that with which a bed is covered, but it is commonly used for the bed itself.

### 91

*Fortibus* means “healthy,” “vigorous,” or “strong.” Although *fortis* usually refers to courage, the best writers sometimes use it of bodily strength.

### 92

Quintilian, Book IV, chapter 2: “Nor is it permitted to go through the middle.”

### 95

**CHAPTER VI.** Matthew is called to the apostleship. Matthew IX, 9 and following; Mark II, 13 and following; Luke V, 27 and following.

### 99

**CHAPTER VII.** Philip is called to the apostleship, and Christ’s words to Nathanael. John I, 43 and following. Immediately after narrating Peter’s call, John recounts Philip’s call: “Jesus looked at him and said, ‘You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas,’ which is translated ‘Peter.’ The next day he wished to depart for Galilee and found Philip. And Jesus said to him, ‘Follow me,’” and so forth.

Lamyus follows this same order. Although the other Evangelists say that Jesus withdrew into Galilee after hearing that John had been handed over to prison, he interprets the matter by saying that John was thrown into prison twice: first by the leaders of the Jerusalem council, and later, as time passed, by Herod.

Others, rejecting Lamyus’s opinion, believe that on the same day Christ migrated from Judea to Galilee, called the Apostle Philip, and, having been invited to the wedding, performed the miracle of changing water into wine. Juvencus narrated Peter’s call much earlier; afterward he added several miracles performed by Christ, and finally records the call of Matthew, Philip, and Nathanael.

He therefore did not think that the miracle at Cana in Galilee, by which Christ changed water into wine, was the first of all the miracles Jesus performed openly, but rather the first of those he performed in Cana of Galilee. Some interpret John in this way. Most, however, understand the transformation of water into wine at Cana of Galilee to have truly been the first of all the miracles Jesus performed publicly, at least, in order to show that he had been sent by the Father.

### 101

“Way” (*via*) means a manner of life, or even a law or custom; for in Scripture *via* has these and similar meanings.

### 102

“Meets Nathanael” (*concurrit Nathanaeli*) means “encounters Nathanael.” Terence, *Eunuchus* II.2.25: “The delicacy sellers happily meet me, eager to come toward me.”

### 105

Philip said to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth.” Philip then thought that Jesus had been begotten by Joseph. This is certainly what Juvencus attributes to Philip.

### 107

“I wonder whether this is Ciceronian.”

### 111

*Tendere* means “to travel,” “to proceed,” or “to come.” In this sense it often takes an accusative, which can easily be supplied here: “when he saw him coming toward him from far away,” and so forth.

### 113

The Reginensis and Tornesian manuscripts have *servant*, which seems also to have been in the Ottobonian manuscript, where *servans* (“preserving”) now appears, together with the Roman and printed editions. The Reginensis has *sine fraude nocendi* (“without the deceit of harming”); the Ottobonian and Roman have *sine fraude maligna* (“without malicious deceit”). Poelmann, in place of the common reading, has *maligni* or *veneni* (“of the malicious one” or “of poison”). Most printed editions have *maligna*. Reuschius printed *maligni* with Badius, who believes that the devil is indicated; but he says that the Paris reading *veneni* (“of poison”) is not unsuitable.

### 115

The Roman manuscript has “To whom God”; read “To whom the Lord.”

### 116

The Reginensis and Ottobonian manuscripts have *diffusa* (“spread out”), with the Reginensis gloss *expansa* (“extended”). The Roman manuscript, together with the printed editions, has *diffusae* (“spread out”), which may be retained.

### 121

The Reginensis, Roman, Aldine, Tornesian, and Basle editions have “You are the peoples”; the Ottobonian, with other witnesses, has “You are the people.”

### 125

In the Ottobonian manuscript, *Cernitis* (“you see”) was correctly changed to *Cernetis* (“you will see”).

### 126

The Ottobonian writes *celeris* (“swift”); *celeres* (“swift ones”) is clearer, namely, “swift ministers.”

### 129

The Tornesian, Basle, Aldine, and Fabrician editions have *mitis* (“gentle”); the manuscripts, together with Hadamar and Poelmann, have *clari* (“illustrious”), an epithet Juvencus also uses in Book III, verse 3.

### 130

The Roman and Ottobonian manuscripts have “When he was born, together with him”; the Reginensis has *Nato compariter*, with a gloss, “*nato*—with.” The printed editions have “Together with the child,” but Aldus and the Daventria manuscript corruptly read *concelebrabant* (“they celebrated together”).

If the verse is printed as “When he was born, together with him, she celebrated the wedding feast,” it is *fistularis*—a verse in which the number of syllables increases with each successive word. A similar example occurs in Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 86: “Nor is he capable of being tortured by human anxieties.”

I think Juvencus wrote *Nato cum pariter*, placing *cum* afterward, because Cicero in *Orator*, chapter 45, and Quintilian in Book VIII, chapter 3, with the approval of grammarians, forbid joining *cum* with words beginning with *n*, either because, as Cicero says, the letters would collide offensively, or rather because, as Quintilian says, the letter *m* must be pronounced with the lips coming together, and therefore makes us pause if it is followed by the letter *n*, which is pronounced with the lips open, or else is corrupted into the nature of that letter.

It has nevertheless been observed that Cicero said *cum nominibus* (“with names”) in chapter 9 of *Pro domo sua*. Tursellinus indicates other examples from Cicero in *Particulae*, chapter 40, no. 11: *Pro domo sua ad Pontifices*, “since neither a slave”; *In Verrem* V, “since nothing”; *De legibus* III, “since no magistrate.” It would be easy to cite many more from other writers.

## Additional Notes

### 116

Book III, verse 655: “The fig, spreading its shady canopy over the one approaching.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI, chapter 4: “Do you wish us to pursue what remains beneath those shades of the alder trees?” He quoted these words from Cicero to show that Virgil was not the first to use this word. He also cites Varro.

### 118

“Author of the spirit” means “the divine spirit that is in me.” Juvencus explains Nathanael’s calling in the same words as Philip’s calling above, verse 100: “And enrolled him as a companion among his friends.” John reports only this: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

Perhaps Juvencus held the opinion that this Nathanael was not distinct from the Apostle Bartholomew, whose calling is described nowhere else in the Gospel, whereas the calling of all the other apostles is separately reported. Rupertus, Abulensis, Jansenius, Cornelius a Lapide, and others indeed hold this view; Maldonatus, however, rejects their opinion together with Saint Augustine.

### 120

“Of the nation” (*gentis*) is used antonomastically for “of the Israelite nation”: “You are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” See Dilherr, *Farrago rituum sacrorum*, and *Saeculum*, Book II, chapter 6, and Carolus Hure’s *Dictionarium Sacrae Scripturae*, under *gens*.

### 122

“An easy power” means “an easy prodigy,” an easy or unarduous miracle. *Virtus* (“power”) is frequently used in Scripture and by ecclesiastical writers for “miracle.” Consult the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 211. Omeisius explained it as: “My power, present everywhere, by which I saw you beneath the fig tree, easily persuaded you to believe.”

### 123

John has: “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you beneath the fig tree,’ you believe. You will see greater things than these.” Ambrose, Book I *On Cain*, chapter 8: “Before you stood beneath the fig tree,” and so forth. Nathanael was indeed beneath a fig tree, but whether standing or reclining is unclear.

### 125

“To see the heaven split open.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 594: “The cloud splits itself and clears an open way into the ether.”

### 127

John’s words are: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.” Juvencus’s interpretation is noteworthy: the angels will ascend into heaven and, descending from there, will bring a crown to the Son of Man. In this way he explains the words “upon the Son of Man.”

When this occurred is uncertain. Some think the passage concerns the Lord’s Ascension, and that the ascending and descending angels signify the ministry of the angels who serve Christ, just as Jacob saw angels ascending and descending on the ladder—that is, ministering to God.

When ascending and descending are said of angels, they signify the ordinary ministry of angels, just as “entering” and “going out” signify the ordinary ministry of human beings; this expression is frequent in Scripture.

Others refer John’s passage to the final day of judgment, when Christ will come with the angels who serve him in order to judge the world. Jansenius, with others, believes that this vision truly occurred to Christ while he was on earth but was passed over in silence by the Evangelists.

Theophylact, commenting on this passage, says: “Moreover, these things occurred at the Cross and at the Ascension. For even before the time of the Passion an angel from heaven strengthened him; angels were seen at the tomb; and at his assumption, as Luke relates…”

### 128

**CHAPTER VIII.** Jesus, invited with his disciples to a wedding, changes water into wine. John II, 1 and following. I would not have noticed that *festa* is an adjective and *connubia* a noun, unless Omeisius had taught the opposite: that *connubia* is an adjective, meaning “nuptial.” I cannot approve this at all.

132. *Per talia dicta*: “by such words”; this is the more usual expression. Sedulius, book V, verse 217: “Another, having adored Christ through supplicating words.”

133. *The liquor of joy*: why wine is called this, see the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 172: “gifts of joy,” etc.

134. *Good tables*: friendly tables, sumptuous and cheerful ones. Plautus, *The Menaechmi* II.2, used the expression “a good dinner.”

136. John, at the cited passage: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” Augustine, *On True Religion*, book I, col. 757: “Depart from me, woman? What is there between me and you? My hour has not yet come.” Juvencus explains it: “You are hurrying, mother,” etc. But why did he not retain “woman”? For he could have said, “You are hurrying, woman.” Perhaps he wished to suggest Theophylact’s interpretation. For Theophylact says: “If wine is lacking, those themselves who lack it ought to come forward and ask, not you as mother. For when members of the household make requests, the matter becomes a scandal to those who see it; but when those who are in need ask, there is no room for suspicion.”

138. *She rejoiced*: although the son’s reply had been framed in a somewhat reproachful formula, as most interpreters teach, the Mother of God nevertheless understood that by her prayers she had moved her Son to provide wine. Maldonatus takes Juvencus’s verse in this sense. He says that she rejoiced at Christ’s reply because she recognized that he intended to perform a miracle. From this he concludes that Christ had not reproached his Mother.

140. *Very beautiful*, as at book I, verse 463, “Hewn from the rocks”: water jars, or vessels for water, were customarily made from hollowed stones, as may still be seen in many surviving examples. Compare the observations of Angelo M. Bandini on an ancient ivory tablet depicting this miracle of Christ. Juvencus reproduced the words of the Gospel: “Now there were six stone water jars there.” This rule should be applied when judging the vessels displayed among sacred treasures in certain churches as though they were the vessels used in the miracle at Cana of Galilee. In ancient paintings and monuments this miracle is often depicted, as may be seen in the work *Sacred sculptures and paintings extracted from the cemeteries of Rome*, 1737.

[Col. 0160C] 141. Matthew Hostus wrote about the capacity of the six water jars. See Joannes Tabingius, “On the Water Jars at Cana,” in the *New Theological-Philological Treasury*.

142. *In the bosom of the spring*, as though in its lap. Compare the note on book I, verse 212, and Gifanius’s index to Lucretius, under the word *gremium terrae* (“the lap of the earth”).

143. From Virgil, book I of the *Aeneid*, verse 728: “They set out great bowls and crown the wines,” that is, they fill them up to the rim. Another interpretation is that they encircle the cups with a garland or crown. Juvencus adhered to the former. Lucretius, book III, verse 925: “This also men do when they have reclined and hold—often they hold cups and shade their faces with garlands”; this rather concerns the second method, crowning the cups.

145. *Breezes mingled with the waves*: this is the physical explanation of why foam forms, because the breezes are mixed with the waves. He therefore uses a description to indicate foam.

146. *The chief servant*: the *architriclinus*, as John calls him. Some understand him to be the person who was steward, or master, of the banquet and tasted the food and wines beforehand. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 54, teaches that there were several table servants, some of whom poured water over the hands, while others carried in the dishes, being called bearers, and so forth. A slave placed in charge of the dining room is called a *tricliniarch* in an ancient epigram. Thus Juvencus calls this man the chief servant. There was another man who was master of the feast.

150. *Fine wines*: good wines. For *fine* is sometimes used for *good* in any category. Horace, book I of the *Epistles*, verse 41: “Since nothing is better than a fat thrush, nothing finer than a broad vulva.” Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 104: “The vinegar will be very sharp and very fine.” Below, verse 305: “fine foods,” and verse 317: “fine labor.”

151. *Through the tables*: he expressed this same idea adverbially as *mensatim*, book III, verse 214. This circumlocution for an adverb is common among both Greeks and Latins.

154. CHAPTER IX. Jesus drove the buyers and sellers from the temple. John II.13ff.; Matthew XXI.12; [Col. 0161C] Mark XI.15; Luke XIX.45. Juvencus continues to weave together the narrative from John, who reports that after the wedding celebrated at Cana Jesus went down into the city of Capernaum with his mother and disciples. “And there,” he says, “they remained not many days. And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem,” etc. Some interpret the words “and the Passover was near” so that the sense is, “and when the Passover drew near.” Others say that the evangelists often join events separated by considerable intervals in a continuous narrative when they have decided not to mention the time that intervened. So Lamy thinks that a long period and many deeds of Christ intervened between the wedding at Cana and this arrival of Christ in the city of Jerusalem. Theophylact distinguishes two events: one that John narrates at the beginning of the signs, and another that Matthew records near the time of the Passion. Toletus likewise holds this view in his commentary on John II.]**

155. Reg. and Ott. read *deflexit* (“turned aside”); in Ott. *direxit* (“directed”) is written above, as in Rom. and the printed editions. Reg. and Ott., with others, read *temploque*; Rom., with the others, *templumque*. Either form is correct.

158. Reg. and Ott. read: “One, intent on money, had leisure to count the trade.” Rom. agrees, with *arte* for *artem*. In Reg. there is the gloss *artem*—“of price, or of acquiring profit.” All the printed editions read: “One, intent on money, had burdened the tables with bronze.” Reuschius printed this common reading but does not conceal that the earlier reading, which in my opinion he found in the manuscripts, seems more learned. He understands *artem* by metalepsis to denote money acquired by deceit and fraud. Consider whether it may be restored as *arti numerare*, that is, “he had leisure for the art of counting.”

160. Rom. and Torn. read *proturbat* (“drives out”); others *perturbat* (“disturbs”). The former is preferable.

161. Rom. and Ott. read *ac* for *et*. Ott. has *menses*, corrected to *mensas*. Reg. has *aeres*, corrected to *aeris*. Reg., Ott., and Fabr. read *profundit*; Rom., Had., and Poelm. *profudit*; Ald., Torn., and Bas. *aerisque profudit*. Although the first syllable of *profudit* is shortened by Lucilius and others, it is lengthened by Catullus and many others. It is therefore better to read: “And, overturning the tables, he pours out heaps of bronze.”

156. *Locantem*: placing them, setting them out, or selling them by auction to those who bought them after paying the price.

[Col. 0161D] 157. *Corpora juvencum*: that is, “the bodies of young bulls.” *Great bodies of young bulls* means the same as *young bulls with great bodies*. Thus *corpora germana septem* (“seven German bodies”) means “seven Germans” here, verse 731. Virgil, book II of the *Aeneid*, verse 18: “Having selected the bodies of men by lot.” Thus also *the body of Turnus* in the same Virgil, book VII, verse 650, and *the body of the gods* in Lucretius, book I, verse 1014. Sometimes *bodies* is simply used for animals. The Greeks likewise speak of “the body of a river” and “the body of the wind.”

159. *The blows of the whip*: a hendiadys, as it is commonly called, one thing expressed through two.

161. John, at the cited passage: “And he poured out the money-changers’ bronze coins and overturned their tables.” The money-changers, or *trapezitai*, so called from their tables, kept heaps of small coins, or bronze, on the tables in order to make profit by exchanging money.

162. *Superincrepitans* (“rebuking further”) is formed by analogy with other similar verbs: *superincumbo*, *superingero*, *superimpono*. Those who were removed from sacred places were customarily called profane: “Away, away, you profane.” Virgil, VI.258.

167. *Venerable temple*. Badius observes that in the Gospel the temple is not called venerable, lest Christ seem to speak arrogantly about himself or boastfully about the temple.

168. *The sun’s third light*: for “the third day,” or “when the sun rises on the third day.” Lucretius, book VI, verse 1195: “And around the eighth bright light of the sun—” “Or even on the ninth lamp he restored life.”

169. He seems to assert that Christ rose from the dead at sunrise, or at least at the rising of dawn. There was darkness when he rose, as is clear from the sacred writings. Yet it is a plausible opinion that this occurred just as the morning star began to shine, amid darkness and light; I have supported this view in the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 542.

170. *With blind murmuring*: either with a sound that could not be heard, as Schoettgenius interprets it, or without deliberation.

171. *Forty*: that its final syllable is common in quantity is proved by definite examples. Badius rashly asserted, without any reason, that Juvencus shortened it.

172. It may be asked which ancient kingdom Juvencus is discussing. John merely says: “This temple has been built for forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” I think Juvencus understood these words of the temple begun by Zerubbabel under Cyrus and completed in the sixth year of Darius, after forty-six years—that is, following the explanation given by Sigonius, *On the Hebrew Republic*, book II, chapter 5. When the Jews wished to refute Christ, and knew that the first temple, built by Solomon, had taken seven years, the second, built by Zerubbabel, forty-six, and the third, built by Herod, one year and somewhat more, they mentioned neither the first nor the third, since these did little to support their case, but the second: for three days are much farther removed from forty-six years than from one. Some think that Herod enlarged the old temple rather than founding a new one after destroying the old, as Josephus relates. Others, unwilling to accuse Josephus of lying in so important a matter or to portray the Jews as so foolish that they would have spoken of the construction of Zerubbabel’s temple when the discussion concerned the temple then standing, attempt to prove that forty-six years elapsed from the year in which Herod began to restore the temple until the year when the Jews made this objection to Christ. During all that time something was continually being added to the temple, and it was not completed until the younger Agrippa. But this opinion fits Juvencus’s words poorly: he would not then have said, “by the construction of the ancient kingdom.”]**

Here *tribuit* means “does,” “provides,” “distributes,” “bestows,” or “exhibits.” Below, verse 641: “And thereafter he will bestow greater miracles of events.”

187. *Given back again*: a frequent pleonasm, discussed in the note on Dracontius, book I, verse 111.

189. *Astonished in heart*: a Graecism familiar to Juvencus.

192. *Correpo* means “I creep in,” secretly entering; *correpto* has the same meaning, though Forcellini rejected it as barbarous. Just as *repto* is formed from *repo*, so *correpto* is formed from *correpo*. But *repto* is supported by the authority of good writers and is elegantly used of infants who have already been born; Juvencus may perhaps have had this in mind. *Into the womb*, into the uterus. Cicero, book I of *On Divination*, chapter 20: “When, pregnant, she held this very Dionysius in her womb.” Add Plautus and others, who use *alvus* for the female womb.

196. Bas. and Ald. read *conscendit*. Ott. has *conscenderet*, or *conscendere*.

200. Poelm., *pro d. s.*, reads: “Here, when he wishes, he flies wherever he flies.” It may have the same meaning as: “Here, where he wishes, he flies wherever he flies.”

201. Ald. and Bas. read *quae sunt exordia*; most have *quae sint*.

202. Reg. reads *ejus concurrentia*, but it is not sufficiently clear whether *ejus* or *ei* is written.

204. Ottob., Rom., and Ald. read *reviviscere*. Reg. has *revisvescere*, from which *revisviscere* was made, with the gloss *renasci* (“to be reborn”). But *revisviscere* or *revivescere* does not fit the meter, nor does *reviviscere*, unless the second syllable is shortened contrary to its nature. Hence Hadam. and most printed editions have *revigescere*. Omeisius preferred this, although he had not found the word in an older writer than Juvencus. But Nonius, chapter 9, no. 12, in Cicero, book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, chapter 16, read *reviguit*, where others have *sic viguit*. Reuschius preferred by conjecture *revirescere*, a verb that certainly fits the meter and is used by many writers for “to be reborn,” “to be renewed,” or “to revive.”

205. Rom. reads *possim*; read *possum*.

206. In Reg. this and the following verse appear to have been added by a glossator’s hand.

John III.6: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” In the Vercelli codex there is added: “What is born of the Spirit is spirit, because God is spirit, and it is born of God.” [Col. 0165D] Juvencus, Hilary, book VII *On the Trinity*, and the Corbie codex had read this way. See Ivo, letter I, and Iricius, in the preface and notes to the Vercelli codex. Ambrose also defends the same reading, book II of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 7, and book III, chapter 10: “The Lord himself said in the Gospel: ‘For God is spirit.’ You Arians testify so explicitly that this passage concerns the Spirit that you remove it from your own codices; and would that you removed it from yours and not also from the codices of the Church . . . 205. *To see*: to understand. *Cerno* (“I discern”) is often transferred from physical sight to the mind. 208. *Snatched away*: carried off or blinded. Omeisius suspects that Juvencus was referring to the origin of the soul, with an allusion to the story of Prometheus.

215. *With respect to new matters*: that is, “about new matters.” *De* is sometimes redundant and sometimes understood. Or understand it rather as: “Receive what meaning lies beneath the new matters just spoken.”

222. Statius, book III of the *Silvae*, final poem, verse 56: “In the deepest inner chambers of the mind.”

223. *To establish faith in the deity*, an unusual expression for “to believe.” Reuschius understood verse 165 of this chapter in this way: “He would raise their minds to such deeds.”

224. *May trample underfoot*: in the manner of triumphal processions, discussed at verse 42 of this chapter.

229. *To summon the lands for examination*: to call them to judgment. Horace used this verb.

230. He explains John’s words: “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.” The Greek is ἵνα κρίνῃ, “so that he may judge,” that is, condemn the world and exact punishments from it. Christ’s first coming was to save the world; his second will be to judge the world. *To weigh out* means, as it were, to examine by weighing. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn 4 of the Peristephanon*, verse 11: “About to set before the nations a just balance with an even—weight.”

233. *Agitation*: disturbance. An “uncertain agitation of law” is properly said, just as one speaks of the agitations of waves and the like; it amounts to saying, “He will not be condemned.” John says: “Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged.”

237. *Wretched proud men*: proud sinners. Again, at verse 663 of this chapter: “And by severe judgment cause wretched sinners to rise.” I have shown in the notes on Dracontius, book I, verse 11, and book II, verse 150, that sinners are called *wretched* in the old ecclesiastical style.

238. *They embraced and held*: an emphatic expression. It should also be noted that the same accusative case is governed by two verbs, something that occurs more than once in Juvencus.

243. *Into the midst*: into the public light. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XV.2: “Nevertheless, before that time he had never brought the matter into the open because of fear of danger.” Related expressions are *to place in the midst*, *to take from the midst*, and so on.

254. Ald., Poelm., in the text; Bas., “To her Christ said: ‘Give me a drink of water, woman.’” Had., “To her Christ said more fully: ‘Give, woman, a drink,’” which is corrupt. Rom., “Thus formerly Christ: ‘Give me, woman, a drink of water.’” Westhem., in the text, “he said, ‘Give a drink of water’”; in the margin, “he said, ‘Give a drink of the side,’” which has no proper sense. Poelm., *pro d. s.*; Torn., “Christ asks her to give him a drink.” Reg. and Ott. join both verses: “Christ asks her to give him a drink—to her Christ said: ‘Give me, woman, a drink of water.’” Reuschius omits the latter and prefers the former, because Juvencus often speaks in this way, as in Book II, verses 259, 336, and 430. I hold another opinion.

256. Poelm. in the text; Reg., Hadam., Fabr., “a Samaritan woman gives a drink to a Jew.” Ald., Bas., “a Samaritan woman gives a drink to a Jew.” Poelm., *pro d. s.*; Ott., “a Samaritan woman gives a drink,” which is in no way admissible. In Rom. these two verses read: “That I may now give you a drink, Samaritan woman—scattering the commands of the ancient Samaritans, serving.”

258. Reg., Ott., Rom., in the text; Ald., Bas., “Savior.” [Col. 0169C] Poelm. and other printed editions, “Salvator,” which also appears in the margin of Rom. For *nosses*, Rom. and Torn. have *nosces*.

260. In Reg. and Ott. *traderet* was correctly made from *tradere*. Rom., “that he might give you living water.”

265. Ott., Rom., Ald., Bas., “Indeed, Jacob had this well.” Poelm. in the text; Hadam., Reg., Westh., in the margin, “For Jacob had this well.” Poelm., *pro d. s.*; [Col. 0170B] Torn., Fabr., “For Jacob had this well.” Westh., in the text, “Jacob indeed had this well,” with the first two syllables of *Jacob* lengthened and the last shortened. Reuschius prefers *puteum* to *puteo*, as in “to drink water,” “cups,” and similar expressions. Omeisius retains it. “For Jacob had this well” is taken from Varro, who used *puteum* in the neuter gender.

267. Bas., “ruler of Olympus on high.” Ald., “To him replied the ruler of Olympus on high.” Most have, “To him replied Jesus, ruler of the world.”

268. Reg., *plane*; and the gloss, *certe*; others, *plene*. Ald., corruptly, *plenae*.

270. Ott., *libendi*: correct to *bibendi*.

272. Ald., Torn., Bas., *unde*. Manuscripts and other printed editions, *inde*. Rom., *luet*; correct to *fluet*.

276. Torn., *prospector*: this word occurs in Apuleius and Tertullian. Omeisius prefers *perspector* with the better witnesses, although it is not found in the earlier Juvencus.

278. Reg., *vivorum*: correct to *virorum*.

281. In Reg. there is the gloss *praeceptum venerandum—adorandi*; from this I infer that *venerandi* should be read, namely: “It is clear to us that there is a command to venerate, or worship, on the summit of this mountain of ours.” Below, verse 286: “And from all Jerusalem worship will be far away.” *Venerari*, meaning “to honor” or “to pray,” is customary among reputable authors of Latin. In the received reading the sense is: “The command remained: that it must be venerated,” etc., as in verse 283, “You say that one must pray.” Some attribute the active verb *venero* to Plautus.

Ambrose, Sermon 27, otherwise Sermon 18 among the sermons attributed to him in the Appendix of the Maurist edition: “Let us by no means despise his commands.” *Samaritum* is either contracted from *Samaritarum*, from *Samarita* or *Samarites*, or comes from *Samarites* in the plural, like *Curetes, Curetum*. Again, verse 324: “Behold the people of the Samaritans,” where the second syllable is lengthened, although elsewhere it is shortened. See the variant readings at verse 436.

259. *Posco* with two accusatives. See the variant readings at verse 254 of this passage.

261. *Gremium* used of a well, as above, verse 142, “in the bosom of the spring.”

263. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXXV, chapter 16, p. 1616: “Among Christian poets,” he says, *vivus*, following other usages, denotes a man of free birth, flourishing in his resources, and vigorous. He cites Paulinus, Marius Victor, Tertullian, and Juvencus at this passage. But Juvencus follows the Gospel more closely: “And he would have given you living water.” Water is called “living,” as perennial springs are called living springs.

264. “By the virtue of our forefather,” that is, by our forefather Jacob, whose virtue is celebrated so greatly. Horace, *Satires* II.1: “When he withdraws from the crowd and the stage into seclusion—the virtue of Scipio’s descendant and the gentle wisdom of Laelius.”

274. *Excitus*: the second syllable is lengthened when derived from *excio*; it is shortened when derived from *excieo*.

[Col. 0170D] 277. *Veridicis*: a sound word, also used by Cicero. Catullus, poem 63, concerning the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, says *oraclum veridicum*, “truth-speaking oracle.”

278. *Nexa*, as above *revinctam*, signifies the bond of marriage and is more expressive than if he had said *juncta es*, “you are joined.”

279. Juvencus’ words should be compared with the Gospel: “Jesus says to her: ‘You have spoken well, because I have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband.’” That is, the man whom she uses to satisfy her lust is not her husband but her concubinary partner. Thus I understand Juvencus: “Now you bear, or carry upon yourself, another man’s marital bonds.” Perhaps he hints that the man with whom the Samaritan woman was involved had been another man’s husband. Schoettgenius and Reuschius explain it this way; they think that the Samaritan woman was the reason why her fornicator abandoned his lawfully married wife. *Super* means “upon” or “besides.”

281. *In arce*, “on the summit.” Poets especially often use *arx* [Col. 0171C] of a mountain peak. Virgil, concerning Rome’s seven hills, *Georgics* II.535: “and enclosed seven citadels with a single wall.”

283. Rom., “And you”; others, “But you.”

284. Rom., “Jesus returned,” as though *Iesus* were disyllabic, as often in Prudentius. Juvencus generally pronounces it as three syllables.

287. Reg., “comes from the shores.”

291. Ott., *Christus his*, corrected to *Spiritus his*. Others have *iis* for *his*.

292. Ott., Rom., Ald., Torn., Bas., *conquiret*; Reg. and others, *conquirit*.

297. Rom., *At*; others, *Et*.

298. Ott., *illius*, but changed to *illis*. In Reg., *illis*, with a gloss, in place of *illius*. Rom., *illis*, with many printed editions. Ald. and others, *piis*. Reuschius considers *illius* altogether necessary, on the basis of the Cantabrigiensis manuscripts; nevertheless, to avoid offending anyone by the contraction in *illius*, he placed *ejus* in the text, from Codex Unicus. From the gloss in Reg., “above the secrets,” namely, “alone,” one might infer *Quod sola illius*, “that she alone might possess his.” The manuscripts Reg., Rom., Ott., with many printed editions, have *potiretur*. But the meter requires *poteretur*, with Hadam. and others, from *potior, potiris*, of the third conjugation, not from *potior, potiris* as a fourth-conjugation form. For *secreta*, *secrete* or *secreto* would be preferable.

Manuscripts Reg., Rom., Ottob., Ald., Bas., *rogitabant sumeret escas*, “they were asking him to take food.” Hadam. and others, *rogitant ut sumeret escas*, “they ask that he take food”; Reuschius says that although this reading appears to conflict with the grammarians’ rules, it is not opposed to the authority of the ancient witnesses.

311. In Reg., *sociabitur* was changed correctly to *satiabitur*.

283. *Orandum*, simply concerning prayer, or petitions made to God. See the note on Book I, verse 48. Reuschius explains it as “to be worshiped.”

288. *Nunc jam* is a pleonasm, which occurs elsewhere as well.

289. The syntax is somewhat harsh: the meaning is that true worshipers, once error has been removed, should pray to the holy Father.

[Col. 0171D] 290. “The laws fortify and defend.” See the commentary on Prudentius, Book II, *Against Symmachus*, verse 179, where, among other passages relevant to this sense, the words of Trebellius Pollio are cited: “Imperial majesty ought to be adorned not only with arms but also armed with laws.” It may be asked why Juvencus says that true worshipers of God are “armed with just laws.” The sacred text reads: “But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” Juvencus explains “in truth” as “with error removed.” It remains, therefore, that “armed with just laws” is his interpretation of “in spirit,” as though the Spirit and Christian religion command this, so that true worshipers, armed and undaunted, will worship God everywhere. This may also be related to the statement that the Father seeks such hearts of worshipers on earth.

292. *Conquirit*, “seeks” or “requires.” “Such hearts of worshipers” means worshipers possessing such a heart, or such steadfastness among worshipers. See verse 84 of this passage: “But seeing such hearts,” and the note on verse 65.

295. *Miserator*: before Juvencus this word was used by Tertullian, Book V, *Against Marcion*, chapter 11.

297. *Stupeo*, meaning “to wonder greatly,” governs the accusative among poets; examples would be unnecessary.

300. Figuratively, “he led out the people through all the city walls,” meaning “the whole people,” etc.

[Col. 0172D] 303. *Fusae*, that is, “poured out,” “numerous.” Cicero, *On the Orator* II.38: “He introduces a style of speech that is not clear, not poured out and flowing, but meager, dry, compressed, and minute.”

305. “Beautiful foods”: see the note on verse 150.

307. *Inter se* is used reciprocally in place of the relative *inter illos*, “among them,” a usage sometimes employed despite Valla’s objections.

309. *Respuat*, “reject,” “repudiate,” “not admit”; for *respuo* has this meaning among others. Nor do I agree with Reuschius, who remarks: “A harsher word, which the more refined ears of the ancients would scarcely have tolerated.”

310. *Molimina mentis*: see verse 18.

311. “This breast”: it would have been preferable to say *pectus hoc*, “this breast,” since Christ is speaking of himself. Nevertheless, Cicero and others sometimes use *iste* for *hic*, “this,” and conversely *hic* for *iste.”

because the woman had obtained his secret words.

But the woman, hurrying, left her jar by the spring,

[300] and led the people out through the whole city.

For she recounts, in the prophet’s words, everything

that she herself had previously done, set out in order.

Then the throngs poured out and hastened toward Christ.

Meanwhile the disciples were asking him to take food.

[305] He replied that he had enough beautiful food.

But then, among the astonished disciples,

a hidden conversation ran back and forth:

191 “Perhaps someone earlier gave food to the master,

so that, being properly satisfied, he rejects our food.”

[310] But he, seeing the inward designs of their minds,

[Col. 0172B] said: “This is my food: this breast will be satisfied

if I carry out the commands of the great Father throughout the world.”

[Col. 0173A] [Note: [Col. 0173B]]

313. Ott., *hic*; Reg., Rom., and the printed editions, *hinc*.

314. Reg., Rom., Ott., *aestatis*: evidently “the beginnings of the fruit-bearing harvest of summer,” or the two genitives may be joined with *primordia*. See the note on verse 193 of this passage. Most printed editions have *aestati*, “until summer.”

319. Ald., *excipiet*, in place of *accipiet*.

320. Manuscripts with most printed editions, *Vos ego*. Poelm. and Fabr., *Hos ego*. Rom., above, *ergo* for *ego*, against the meter.

322. Reg., *a pr. m.*, *bona*: perhaps one should read, “The gifts of another’s good grain will enrich you,” namely, “with good grain.”

325. Manuscripts Reg., Rom., Ott., *impendere soles*, which is better than *expendere* for “to spend.” Suetonius, *Augustus* 98: “He spent four days in retreat at Capri.” Reuschius, from the Fulda manuscript, has *impendere*; and in one edition he conjectured, with Zehner, *illis geminos impendere soles*.

[Col. 0174B] 327. Ald. punctuates *verbis—Ipsos sed*.

329. Reg., Rom., Ott., *Servator*. Printed editions, *Salvator*.

330. Reg., “And again he had returned to the land of Galilee.” Ott., Rom., and the printed editions, “And he had returned again to the region of Galilee.”

331. Rom., *vinum*: perhaps the water “of the spring” had been changed into wine, or *vinum* in Rom. is nominative. I change nothing.

332. In Ottob., *morbis* was correctly changed to *morbus*.

333. Two manuscripts cited by Reuschius have *horis*, but *oris* is more poetic; and in manuscripts the aspirate is often added to or removed from vowels, as in *harundo* and *ymnus*. Below, verse 344: “the shores of the light.”

337. Ald., *Non erat ulla fides*; others, *erit*. In Virgil and others, *pius* and *prius* are interchanged. Reuschius chooses *prius* from the sacred codex, “before he dies.” I prefer another reading.

339. Rom., “There was no faith”; others, “there will be.”

340. Rom., *Sedibus*; others, *Aedibus*.

[Note: [Col. 0173C]]

313. John, in the passage cited: “Do you not say that there are still four months, and the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest.” So also the old Itala. Juvencus explains this as “the beginnings of the fruitful harvest of summer are still four months away.” Lamy, in his *Harmony of the Gospels*, explains the Greek *τετράμηνον* as a four-month period in this way: “The saying is proverbial, as though Christ had said: Among you the saying is common, ‘There are still four months during which the harvest can be gathered; the harvest is coming, but it has not passed.’ Thus there is no need for haste now.” Mazochius, on this passage, thinks that in Judea no more than four months intervened between sowing and harvest, and explains it thus: “After sowing, you use that familiar saying: ‘From what we have entrusted to the furrows, we shall reap the fruit after four months.’ But the fruit of spiritual sowing is much more premature, for the regions are already yellowing for harvest.” Maldonatus had preceded him, offering the similar Latin proverb: “The crop is still in the blade.”

315. “Whitening harvests,” that is, “becoming yellow.” He uses the Gospel’s word *albae*, “white.” Jerome, commentary on Micah VII: “See the regions, for they are already white for reaping.” Mazochius observes on this passage that there is a type of wheat in the kingdom of Naples commonly called “white,” whose crop, while awaiting harvest, whitens rather than yellows. I would not, however, infer from this that Judean wheat was of that kind.

[Col. 0173D] 317. “Beautiful labor,” like “beautiful freedom” in Virgil and similar expressions, concerning which see the note on verse 150.

319. John says: “So that both the one who sows may rejoice together, and the one who reaps.” These sowers are the prophets, who formerly cast the first seeds of the divine word.

320. Virgil, *Georgics* I.297: “But ruddy Ceres is cut down in the middle of the heat,” that is, harvested at midday and in the heat. Silius, Book XV, verse 536: “The unripe crop is cut down with the swift sword.”

324. Above he shortened the first two syllables more than once in *Samaritum* and *Samaritis*. Compare the variant readings at verse 436.

325. *Exorant*, “they obtain,” “they secure by prayer.” John, in the passage cited: “When the Samaritans had therefore come to him, they asked him to remain there, and he stayed two days.”

226. The phrase *multos plebis* should be noted, meaning “many from the people.”

330. CHAPTER XIII. The son of the royal official freed from death. John 4:46 and following.

332. The words of the Gospel are: “There was a certain royal official whose son was ill,” etc. In Greek, for *regulus* there is βασιλικὸς, or alternatively βασιλίσκος. Juvencus calls him a *regulus*, a royal young man, namely a man from the royal court, perhaps Herod’s. Juvencus often uses *juvenis* for a man or adult, as I said at verse 44 of this passage. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* II, to Curio, already fifty-four years old, as Gothofredus observes: “May our advancing age come to rest in your youth.” See also the note on Book III, verse 55.

333. Ovid, *Heroides*, final letter, verse 169: “But for me—alas, unhappy woman!—my limbs are scorched by fevers.” Likewise *aestus*, “fever,” in Book I, verse 799.

335. “For his fortune,” that is, “for his condition,” “for his salvation.” Perhaps Juvencus had in mind that a child was called the father’s fortune. Ovid, *Fasti* VI.29: “If one looks to lineage, I made Saturn my first ancestor; I was Saturn’s first fortune.”

337. “Bitter death,” an untimely funeral: a familiar elegance.

340. “In your homes,” for “in your home,” according to a manner of speaking that began to grow common as Latin declined. Or understand *vestris* as “your own and your family’s.”

Four months, you think, still remain from this point

until the beginnings of the joyful harvest

of fruit-bearing summer are surely here.

[315] “Lift up your eyes, then, and behold the whitening fields,

192 and all the countryside already calling for the ripened harvest.

Whoever now reaps will enjoy the reward of beautiful labor,

and thereafter rejoice, overflowing with life-giving grain;

the sower too will gladly receive the reapers’ joys.

[320] I have now sent you to cut a harvest heavy with grain

that was not planted in your furrows by your labor.

The gifts of another’s good grain will enrich you.”

While with such words he filled the hearts of his companions,

behold, the people of the Samaritans came, asking,

[325] and there they earnestly begged him to spend two days.

Already deep faith had established many of the people,

[Col. 0174A] and no longer did they entrust themselves only to a woman’s words;

rather, manifested power itself taught them in person

that Jesus the Savior had come into the world.

[330] And now he had returned to the region of Galilee,

193 where once he had changed the waters of the spring into wine.

Here a royal young man, whose son was being scorched by illness

with burning fever at the farthest limits of life,

when he learned that Christ had certainly returned,

[335] flew to him and, pouring out prayers for his son’s fate,

begged him, demanding the swift gifts of healing,

lest his dutiful son be dragged to bitter death.

At this Christ said: “Unless power persuades you of everything by signs,

there will be no faith at all. But go, and, with life preserved,

[340] embrace your dear son in your homes.”

[Col. 0175A] [Note: [Col. 0175B]]

341. Rom., *fratrem*: read *fructum*.

342. Rom., incorrectly, *animi* instead of *animum*. Ott., *laetanti pectore*, without *in*.

344. Ald., Bas., Poelm., *pro d. s.*, *puero resonatque jacenti*. Reg., Ottob., with other printed editions, *pueroque in luminis oras*. Rom., incorrectly, *puerumque*. “For the boy beneath the shores of light” would not be bad, etc. In the more common reading, *refert* or *narrat* may be understood: “he reports” or “relates that salvation had returned.”

347. Reg., *Sanati*. In Ott. there seems to have been *Sanatis*. Rom., *Sanantis*, with the printed editions.

349. Reg., Rom., Ott., Torn., Poelm., *pro d. s.*, *una*; others, *unus*. Manuscripts with most printed editions, *sociaverat*. Ald., Torn., Bas., *satiaverat*. In Daventr., *sociaverat unus*; but the manuscript gloss *repleverat* seems to have been made for *satiaverat*, which I approve less.

353. Manuscripts and printed editions consistently have *occulto reprehendere risu*. But what, I ask, is this “hidden laughter”? I have no doubt that one should read *occulto reprehendere nisu* [Col. 0175C], that is, “with hidden effort and exertion.” Above, verse 18: “Thus are the designs of your people,” and verse 310: “But he, seeing the inward designs of the mind.” In Book III, verses 152 and following, I likewise read: “That the hearts of the scribes may assail the speaker’s words with hidden effort.”

354. Reg., Ott., *vellet*; in Ott., above, *iniret*, which most printed editions have. Poelm., *pro d. s.*, Fabr., [Col. 0176B] *adiret*.

355. Ald., Fabric., Bas., Poelm., *pro d. s.*, *clausa*. Manuscripts with other printed editions, *saeva*, which I prefer, although *clausa*, “covered and feigned,” is not displeasing.

356. Un. in Reuschius, with a question: “Does he say, ‘Is there need of physicians?’” etc.

357. Rom., Reg., Ottob., Poelm., *pro d. s.*, *vegetat virtutis honore*. In Ottob., *pro d. s.*, *vegetat viresque ministrat*, which occurs in most printed editions. Reuschius adopted *virtutis honore*, “with the honor of virtue,” that is, “with virtue and strength.” A similar expression occurs in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.283, or 285.

358. Wopkensius, on Sedulius, Book I, verse 22, conjectured *miseris* for *miserans*.

359. Reg. writes *saltim*.

364. In Ott., *Joannes* was correctly made from *Joannes*.

366. Reg., Ott., Torn., Fabr., *ferret*. Rom., with Ald. and other printed editions, *ferrent*, which perhaps stood in Ott. in the first hand. But, in my view, *ferrent* was written by copyists who thought *plebes* was nominative plural. I would not deny that the plural verb *ferrent* can elegantly be joined with *plebes*, or “the people,” in the singular. But since this elegance is not established, I would be reluctant to admit it in Christian poets. Although *plebes* has sometimes been used in the plural, the singular is much more customary.

[Note: [Col. 0175C]]

342. “Beautiful faith” in the sense explained at verses 150 and 317.

346. *Concurrere*, “to agree,” “to correspond,” “to coincide.” See Book I, verse 448, and Book II, verse 831 of this passage.

348. The gloss in Codex Reg. reads: *Mancipat—subdit Christo*, “he subjects—submits to Christ.”

349. CHAPTER XIV. Jesus tells the Pharisees, who are murmuring about the publicans’ feast, that the healthy have no need of a physician. Matthew 9:10 and following; Mark 2:15 and following.

350. A beautiful description of the publicans, who, having professed to collect public taxes for profit, seize plunder for themselves in the name of the treasury. Jansenius of Ghent likewise maintains that the Jews hated the publicans because they acted through force and robbery.

[Col. 0175D] 351. He rightly calls the publicans’ profit “plunder.” Cicero, *Against Verres* V, otherwise Book III, chapter 50: “To have made the greatest profits and plunder.” See the note on Dracontius, Book II, verse 769.

352. This appears to be a hypallage, as though Juvencus meant: “These people received Jesus with the disciples at the feast.” But Juvencus may instead have wished to reproduce the words of the Gospel. Matthew: “And it came to pass, as he reclined at table in the house, that many publicans and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.” Mark adds: “For there were many, and they followed him.”

[Col. 0176C] 360. Again, verse 581: “For God would prefer not sacred things, but gentle hearts.”

363. CHAPTER XV. When John’s disciples ask why Christ’s disciples do not fast, the parable of the torn garment and the wineskins is presented. Matthew 9:14 and following; Mark 2:18 and following; Luke 5:33 and following.

368. “The bridegroom’s vows”: weddings are so called in the *Theodosian Code*, Book III, title 5, law 7. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, near the end: “Previously destined for him by nuptial vows and the marriage pact.” Matthew and Luke call the bridegroom’s companions, who accompanied him with joyful dances and led him to the bridal chamber, “the children of the bridegroom”; Mark calls them “the children of the wedding.” On this custom of escorting and accompanying the bridegroom with lamps or torches, dances, and songs, consult Martinus Roa, *Singularia*, Book II, chapter 21.

369. The received text of Matthew’s Gospel: “And Jesus said to them: ‘Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.’” The old Itala: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast?” Hilary on this passage: “He replies that, while the bridegroom is present, the disciples have no necessity of fasting … But once he has been taken away, he says that they will fast.”

By these words fair faith, soon to receive

the fruit of salvation, strengthens his spirit in his rejoicing heart.

As he set out on his journey, rushing servants came to meet him,

194 bringing news that salvation had suddenly returned to the boy, into the realms of light,

[345] from the threshold of death.

When he learned that the appointed time corresponded

with the words of Christ the healer, he devoted himself

and his household to him, embracing the venerable gift of faith.

By chance one day had brought many people together for a feast,

[350] men who, having undertaken the collection of public taxes for profit,

professed them and seized plunder in another’s name.

Jesus received these men together with his disciples.

Behold, the Pharisees secretly criticized him,

because, a teacher of the law, he entered such banquets.

[355] [Col. 0176A] 195 But he, perceiving what fierce thoughts held their hearts,

said: “The healthy limbs, where unimpaired health
