flourishes through the honor of strength, have no need of physicians.

But healing must rightly be applied to the sick in compassion.

Learn now at least what the prophet’s words command:

[360] ‘I seek not sacrifices more than gentle hearts.’

For I did not come to guide the righteous who walk rightly,

but to call the wicked back from the threshold of sin.”

Behold, from the number of the astonished at Christ’s gifts,

one of John’s disciples asked

[365] why they themselves observed frequent fasts according to the law,

and no fasting among the people was borne under Christ.

Christ answered him in this way, with calm voice:

“Those who accompany the bridegroom’s vows

with joyful dances do not, while he is present,

196 carry sorrowful fasts.”

[370] [Col. 0177A] [Note: [Col. 0177B]]

371. Poelm. in the text; Dauventr., Hadam., Ald., Fabr., “To him they will give themselves to sadness—Then they will give their spirits to tears because of the horror of food—They will receive languid fasts in their grieving minds—How foolish.” In Rom. and Poelm., second hand, *Spondebunt* instead of *Tuncque dabunt*. Ott. likewise has *Spondebunt*, but the verse *Languida* is absent. Reg. similarly has *Spondebunt*, but first places the verse *Languida*, then another *Spondebunt*. Certainly one of the two is superfluous; but *Spondebunt animos lacrymis horrore ciborum* seems to me the more spurious. Koenigius conjectured *Sponte dabunt animos*. In Codex Ca. it was written *Languida concupient*.

373. Reg., second hand, Ott., *pannis—Vestibus ut turpis pejus scissura patescat*: this seems a sound reading and punctuation. Others, *pannos—Vestibus, ut*.

374. Rom., Torn., *Vestibus, ut turpis pejor scissura patescat*. Codex Fuld., *ut pejor turpis*. Codex Cant., *ut ruptis pejor*. Poelm. in the text; Hadam., *ut veteris pejor scissura patescat*, which Reuschius explains as “a new tear worse than an old tear,” through the construction of a comparative with the genitive [Col. 0177C]. Ald., Poelm., *pro d. script.*, *ut turpis pejus scissura notetur*. I retain the reading indicated by the Reg. and Ott. manuscripts in the preceding verse.

375. The manuscripts Rom., Reg., Ott., *Aut utribus calidum*. Printed editions, *Utribus aut calidum*. Perhaps the editors made this change because they thought the first syllable of *utribus* necessarily long; but this lacks foundation, although no example from antiquity occurs showing that it can be shortened.

377. Ott., Rom., *Sed rudibus rectum est utribus spumantia musta*. Thus Reg., but without *est*, and with the gloss *rudibus—novis*. Printed editions, *Utribus est rectum rudibus spumantia musta*, so that the first syllable of *utribus* is not shortened, as I just stated.

380. In Ottob. it seems to have been changed to *ad oras* from *adorans*.

381. Rom., *Ut sibi defunctam*. Bas., *Et sibi defunctum*. Read *Et sibi defunctam*.

382. Koenigius conjectures *Complorat lacrymis*, “she laments with tears.”

383. This verse is absent from Rom. Reg., Ottob., *Defunctis etiam poscebat munera Christi*, which Poelm. printed *pro d. s.* Most printed editions, *Defunctae vita poscebat munere Christi*. Hadam., *Defuncto vita, poscebat munera Christi*.

384. Rom., first hand, Ald., Daventr., Reg., Ott., Bas., *Servator*; others, *Salvator*.

385. Manuscripts and most printed editions, *Progressi*. Hadamar., Poelm., in the text, *Progressos*; Reuschius says this reading can be tolerated, but prefers another syntax: “The woman, following and observing the Savior’s footsteps, follows,” so that the second accusative may be absorbed, which can easily be supplied. Or say that the same accusative, *vestigia*, is governed by both verbs.

387. Reg., Rom., Fabr., *Carpebat fluxus lacerans [Col. 0178C] sine fine cruoris*. Ald., Bas., Torn., *Torquebat fluxus macerans sine fine cruoris*. Rom., Hadamar., Poelm., *Carpebat fluxus lacerans sine fine cruoris*. In *macero*, the *a* is lengthened; for this reason I also rejected Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 8, verse 22: *Sordidus cultu macerare frontem*, as Nebrissensis reads it; others, better, have *Sordidus cultu lacerare frontem*. Koenigius suspects *manans sine fine*. After this verse Poelm., Hadam., and Torn. insert another: *Torquebat solvens morbus pallore virentem*; but Torn. and Poelm., *pro d. s.*, read *Torquebatque gravi morbus*. This verse is absent from most witnesses.

388. Ald., Torn., Bas., Rom., *fessa—Pectoris haec*, etc. Others, *fessam—Pectoris*. Reuschius, *fessa* in the sixth case, with *muliere* understood: “weary woman.” I do not approve this.

[Note: [Col. 0177C]]

370. *Turbine saecli*, as at verse 223 of this passage.

372. *Ferre jejunia*, “to bear” or “carry fasts,” used for “to fast.”

373. Matthew: “No one puts a patch of unprocessed cloth on an old garment, for it tears away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear results.” This sentence might perhaps be expressed better thus: “How foolish it is to sew new cloth onto old garments!” A new patch sewn onto old cloth usually takes away that part of the old garment to which it is attached by stitching. This happens whether a garment is made from two pieces, old and new, or whether a new and unprocessed patch is sewn onto an already worn garment. Juvencus therefore uses *subtexere* for *contexere*, “to join together”; and either way is grammatically sound, whether “to join new cloth to old” or “old cloth to new.” Reuschius thinks that the ancient method of sewing was not as skillful as ours, but that the *πλήρωμα*, “fullness,” which had to be inserted into the old garment was thicker, so that it stood out more and wore out the garment more quickly.

375. In place of “hot must,” the sacred text has “new wine.”

376. *Disperdere* is used for *disperdi* through enallage, as Reuschius says.

379. CHAPTER XVI. While going to raise the ruler’s daughter, Jesus heals a woman from an issue of blood. Matthew 9:18 and following; Mark 5:22 and following; Luke 8:41 and following. Concerning the verb *tracto*, used in ecclesiastical style for *dissero*, “I discuss,” see the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 13, *Peristephanon*, verse 101.

[Col. 0178D] 380. The Evangelists call him the *archisynagogus*, or ruler of the synagogue, namely, the head of the synagogue, by whose order the customary matters in the synagogue were determined.

382. *Implorat lacrymans* is a pleonasm, since tears are already implied in *implorat*. But the less obvious meaning of *imploro* should be noted here: *implorat natam* means “he names and calls upon his daughter with tears,” and repeats her name. Cicero, *Against Verres* VII, otherwise Book V, chapter 49: “Calling me his salvation, naming you his executioner, invoking the name of his son.” Reuschius explains *implorat lacrymans* as “he confirms with tears and sighs that what he says about his daughter’s death is true.” Sedulius imitates Juvencus, Book III, verse 298, *Imploratque gemens*, “and he invokes her groaning”; Wopkensius should be consulted there.

385. *Vestigia servans*, “observing” or “following the footsteps.”

387. *Sine fine*, “without end”: a phrase familiar to ecclesiastical writers. See the note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 21.

Now the day will come when the bridegroom will be snatched

from the midst of his companions by the upheaval of the age;

then they will take up languid fasts in their minds, weeping.

How foolish it is to sew new cloth onto old garments,

so that the ugly tear may gape worse?

[375] Or to put hot must into worn wineskins,

197 whose bursting causes all the wine to be lost?

But foaming musts are properly stored in new wineskins;

thus strong vessels preserve the wine.

[Col. 0178A] As he discussed these things, the chief of the priests, struck to the heart by grief,

[380] behold, fell down in worship,

and weeping implored for his dead daughter—a pitiable funeral—

that certain salvation might come; he sought Christ’s gifts

even for the dead.

Without delay, Jesus the Savior rose and went on.

[385] As they went, a woman followed, observing his footsteps,

198 whom, as twelve years passed by,

a flow of blood had consumed without end,

her strength exhausted and her whole body weary.

[Col. 0179A] [Note: [Col. 0179B]]

389. Ott., *hic*, correctly changed to *haec*.

### 390

In Reg., Daventr., Torn., Bas., and Poelm., instead of *d. s.* [the reading in the main text], [there is] *secumque fide*; Ald. and Fabr. have *Arcana, secumque fide*. In Ott., *Arcano, secumque fide*, and perhaps originally *fidem*. In Rom., *Arcanum secumque fides*. Hadam. and Poelm. in the text have *Arcanaque fide secum*. Someone might conjecture *Arcana secura fide*. In any event, the reading of Ott. seems better than the others. *Arcano* is an adverb used by Plautus, Caesar, and Cicero, although in the latter the reading is uncertain. One may punctuate either *mentem Arcano* or *mentem, Arcano*.

### 392

Rom. has *si posset*; others, *posset si*.

### 395

Reg. has *causam*, but it seems to have been *causas*.

### 398

Our manuscripts and others have *restricto*. Ald. and some printed editions have *constricto*; others, *constrictae*. Fabr. has *riguerunt* instead of *viguerunt*; I do not know whether this arose from conjecture or from the authority of some manuscript. Reuschius confirms this reading, although he himself adopts another, from Lucan, Book IV: “Dry blood, stiffening, constricted the wounds.” In Westh., in the margin, instead of *constricto* in the text appears *constantiae*, which seems to be an error.

### 399

Perhaps *funere*. Reg., with Ald. and others, punctuates *funera virginis, ingens*. But since *funera pompae* recurs below, at verse 401, it seems that this passage should be punctuated *ubi funera virginis, ingens*, that is, “where the great funeral of the virgin was.” It would be better, however, to read at verse 401 *munera pompae*.

### 401

In Reg. and Ott., *factum est celebrabat* has been corrected from *celebrabant*. The printed editions and manuscripts have *funera*, but I would willingly read *munera*. For what are “the final funerals of the supreme procession”? But *ultima munera* is aptly placed, in accordance with what was said at verse 20 of this book: “The final gifts are owed to the deceased father.” *Munera* is an accusative in apposition, and the sense is: “After they had arrived where the wailing of the people and the blaring of the trumpets were celebrating the funeral of the virgin, the final gifts,” and so forth. Moreover, this conjecture, which was once also Rivinus’s, is supported by the Cambridge manuscripts, and Reuschius followed it.

### 403

I prefer *demersa*, with our manuscripts, to *dimersa*, which is found in Ald. and others.

### 404

Poelm. has *fertur* instead of the main reading; but the sense requires *retur*.

### 405

Rom. has *relinquit*, which also seems to have been the first hand’s reading in Ott., instead of *reliquit*.

### 411

Our manuscripts and Poelm., instead of the main reading, have *Caecorum pariter gressu*. Most printed editions have *Lumine captorum gressu*. Juvencus perhaps wrote *gressu labante*, with the first syllable of *labante* long, as in this book at verse 437 and in Book III, verse 373: “He falters because in your breast—his steps waver with unstable faith over slippery ground.”

### 412

Fabr. and Westh. in the text have *Atque iis Christus ait*; in the margin, *Ollis Christus ait*. Ald. and Bas. have *Istis*; others, *Illis* or *Ollis*. In Reg. and Torn. the passage is elegantly presented as a question:

“What do your hearts believe?—Will the light taken away be restored by my power?”

This seems to have been the first hand’s reading in Ott. Most copies omit the question marks:

“If your hearts believe, the light taken away will now be restored by my power.”

Matthew says: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” Nevertheless, Reuschius prefers the non-interrogative form. Others add the question even when *si credunt* is written, because they take *si* in the sense of *num* (“whether”), as in Book IV, verse 355.

### Notes

**389.** *Pectoris* means the mind or thought. This is a hendiadys—one thing expressed through two words—as often elsewhere, unless one prefers *pectoris arcano*.

**391.** Fabricius, in his Commentary, under the word *Actutum*, says that this expression is comic and was also used by Alcimus in Book I: “Quickly bringing forth everything in delightful offspring.” Yet the same word was used by Cicero, Livy, Virgil, and other non-comic writers.

**393.** *Per populum*: Mark says, “He came behind in the crowd and touched his garment.” Barthius proves from this verse, in Book XXXIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 4, column 1552, that *peplum* can mean any cloak. Fabricius, in his Commentary under *Peplum*, says that it is a loose, ankle-length garment without sleeves, common to men and women. In general, *peplum* is used for any loose garment.

**394.** Description of the fringe: “The hanging threads of the upper garment.” The edges of clothing, especially when they have cut or slit borders, are called *fimbriae*. *Tractavit*, “touched,” has the same meaning in Book I, verse 354: “To touch the serene light with bodily eyes.”

**395.** *Causae* is sometimes used simply for diseases, as I established in my note on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn I, verse 20: “You seek the ailments of suppliants, which you moisten with remedies.”

**396.** *Tali cum voce*, as in this book at verse 597, *Cum dicto*.

**400.** Barthius argues from this passage, in Book XXXIV, chapter 5, that funeral music was embellished by the sound of trumpets. Although the use of the flute may have been more common at funerals, and although the evangelist Matthew mentions flute-players in the Vulgate, many passages nevertheless show that the trumpet too was used. Virgil, Book XI, verse 92, on the funeral of Pallas: “The cry of the men and the blaring of trumpets rises to heaven.” Add Ovid, Horace, Persius, and others. Gellius, Book XX, chapter 2, notes that those who were accustomed to play for the dead—that is, for those who had completed life and been buried—were called *siticines*, and had a kind of trumpet different from the others. Iricius found *tubicines* in the Vercelli manuscript of the Old Latin version at Matthew, but says that *tibicines*, with the Vulgate, is preferable, because funerals of those of lesser age were conducted with the flute, and those of greater age with the trumpet, according to Servius on *Aeneid* V: “And the desire for praise, aroused.” But even if this distinction is true, it does not follow from the Vulgate that the girl in question was of lesser age. The Greek text does support it with *puellula*, “little girl” or “little daughter”; but Mark plainly says that she was twelve years old. Servius, however, seems to understand “lesser age” as infancy. See Berald on Statius, *Thebaid* VI, 121.

**407.** Just as the devil is called the discoverer of death, so Christ, in contrast, is called the victor over death and the discoverer of life. See what I said on this subject in my Commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 4, verse 9.

**408.** *Frigentis*, that is, “of the dead woman.” Virgil, Book VI, verse 219: “They wash and anoint the body of the cooling corpse.” Hence *frigid death*, from its effect.

**410.** **CHAPTER XVII. Two blind men are healed.** Matthew IX, 27, etc.

**411.** *Gressu labente*, “with faltering step”: why so? Were they also lame? The Evangelist is silent. Their steps therefore faltered, or they stumbled or wavered, because, being blind, they could not walk with complete ease.

### Poem

The woman, believing, turned these words over silently in her heart,

[390] and already, with secret faith, held firmly in mind

that the wasting sickness would immediately flee her weakened body

if only she could touch the outermost garment of Christ.

When she touched with trembling hand through the crowd

the hanging threads of the upper garment, he immediately,

[395] seeing both the causes of the disease and the believing heart,

granted swift healing with these words:

“Receive the gift that the steadfastness of your faith has earned.”

And at once the veins, their blood constricted, grew strong again.

When they had arrived where the immense funeral procession of the virgin—

[400] the wailing of the grieving crowd and the blaring of trumpets—

was celebrating the final gifts of the supreme rite,

he said: “Let these sorrows withdraw from your homes.

For the girl lies plunged in peaceful sleep,

whom the ignorant crowd of mourners considers dead.”

[405] The crowd left the speaker, laughing,

because he had said that the girl taken by death was sleeping.

But Christ, victor over death and discoverer of life,

deigned to take the cold girl’s right hand in his own right hand,

and immediately ordered her to rise, to the father’s wondrous joy.

[410] From there, as he returned, a cry immediately met him:

two blind men, alike, with faltering step.

Christ said to them: “If your hearts believe, the light that was taken away will now be restored by my power.”

They declare that they believe with steadfast heart.

[415] Then Christ says: “You who believe, behold the light,

and after this disclose our name to no one.”

He spoke; but the insatiable zeal of those granted so great a joy of sight

was spreading the report everywhere.

Then a young man is brought forward, from whom the faculty of speech had been snatched

[420] by the assault of a resounding demon.

But when the demon, driven out, fled from his breast,

the powers of a sound tongue immediately returned.

He is surrounded by the pressing tumult of a wondering crowd;

but, seeing so many thousands of men,

[425] he groans, like the lord of the countryside, whose happy pastures

countless flocks crop, lacking a shepherd.

Then he addresses such words to the disciples:

“How happily the crops spread over the ridges of the fields!

[430] But the scanty reaper is overwhelmed by the heap of harvest.

It remains to entreat the lord of so great a harvest,

that he may wish to fill his fields with a multitude of cultivators.”

Having said this, he gathers brave hearts, selected apart from the whole people,

in a company of twice six.

Having chosen them, he equips them with such instructions:

[435] “Avoid the path that the faithless nations tread,

and the tracks of Samaritan deceit.

Proceed where the guardianship of the ancestral flock falters.”

### 414

Others have *Olli*; others, *Illi*.

### 415

Ott., Torn., Bas., Ald., and others have *lucem*. Reg., Rom., Had., and others have *lumen*.

### 416

Rom. has *Nec cuiquam vestrum*, apparently an error for *nostrum*. Ottob. has *post haec vos dicite*.

### 417

Reg., Torn., Rom., and Bas. have *sed propere*. Ott., with other printed editions, has *sed major*.

### 418

Rom. has *per cuncta serebat*; in the margin, a different reading or correction, *ferebat*.

### 419

Ald. and Poelm., instead of the main reading, have *Afferturque*; most have *Offerturque*. Ald. has *sonore*; correct to *sonorae*.

### 421

Reg., Rom., Ott., Ald., Torn., and Bas. have *Ast ubi propulsus*. Poelm. in the text and Fabr. have *Atque ubi propulsus*. Hadam. and Poelm., instead of the main reading, have *Atque propulsus ubi*. Both arrangements are permitted by the metre.

### 425

In Ott., *Ingemit* has correctly been made from *Ingemuit*.

### 427

Rom., Ald., and others have *talia dicta*.

### 428

Ald. and Bas. have *Quam late segetes ruris per terga latescunt*. Torn. has *En late segetes ruris per terga patescunt*, which Poelm. also has instead of the main reading. Most printed editions, with our manuscripts, have *Quam laetae segetes ruris per terga patescunt*.

### 431

Reg. has *numeros*, but it seems to have been corrected to *numero*, with a gloss on *numero*. In Ott., *colentem* has been made from *colentum*. Most have *numero complere colentum*.

### 432

In Ott., *delecta* has been made from *dilecta*. In the same manuscript, *seorum* is an error for *seorsum*. *Suorum* would not be inappropriate: “And summoning his twelve disciples,” Matthew says.

### 433

The printed editions and most manuscripts have:

“Fortia conglomerat bisseno pectora coetu,  
Bis sex consociat fidorum corda virorum.  
Hos ubi, etc.”

Ott. has the verse *Bis sex* first, followed by *Fortia*. In Torn. the verse *Fortia* is absent; it was also omitted by Fabricius and is certainly not very necessary. It could be retained here and the verse *Bis sex*, etc., omitted. I follow that arrangement.

### 434

Ott. has *dilegit*, corrected by the second hand to *delegit*.

### 435

The manuscripts and most printed editions have *Devitate itiner, quod*. Ald. and Fabr. have *Devitate viam, quam*.

### 436

Reg. and Ott. have *Et Samaritum*, although Reg. may originally have had *Et Samaritarum*. Rom., Ald., and Bas. have *Et Samaritarum*. Had. and Poelm. in the text have *Atque Samaritum*, as above at verse 324, *Ecce Samaritum*, unless one prefers to read there *En Samaritarum*. Juvencus often shortens the first two syllables. Others have different readings. Ott. has *fraudes* and Torn. *fraudibus*, instead of *fraudis*; the latter should be retained.

### 437

Our manuscripts Reg., Rom., and Ottob., together with Daventr. and Westh. in the text, have *labat*, with a gloss in Reg., *deficit*. In this same Reg. the reading may originally have been *balat*, which appears in Hadam., Poelm., and other printed editions. *Labat* seems preferable from the Gospel text, Matthew X, 6: “But go rather to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel.” The first syllable of *labat*, however, is short, which is an objection. But what is *custodia balat*? I have no doubt that *custodia* means “guardians.” I therefore retain *labat*, lengthening its first syllable contrary to the practice of the ancients. Koenigius retains *custodia balat* and takes *custodiam* passively, as “the thing guarded.” Even so, the Gospel’s meaning is not sufficiently expressed. One might conjecturally restore *custodia lapsat*, but this verb means less than *labat*. In Book IV, verse 501, our manuscripts likewise have *sed corpus debile labat*, for which some printed editions have *lapsat*. Compare also Book III, verse 373.

### Notes

**418.** *Per cuncta*: “through everything,” “everywhere.” I discussed this expression in my note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 292.

**419.** **CHAPTER XVIII. A mute demon is expelled, and the crowd flows together to Jesus.** Matthew IX, 32 and following; Luke XI, 14, etc. Juvencus calls the mute man who had a demon a young man, as Matthew says. See the note on Book I, verse 774, and on this book, verse 332.

**420.** *Substantia vocis*: “voice,” as *substantia salis* in Book I, verse 510. See the note on Book I, verse 631.

**423.** *Tumultus* here means a crowd, and a multitude moving about and making noise out of astonishment. Lucan, Book III, verse 102: “To imitate false voices in joyful tumult.”

**424.** *Tanta* for *tot*: see the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 554, where *quanti* occurs for *quot*.

**425.** *Pascua laeta*, as in Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 1: “What makes the fields fruitful,” etc.

**426.** *Tondent*: “crop,” “consume,” “graze”; this meaning of the verb is familiar to poets. See Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 15.

**428.** *Laetae segetes*, as I said at verse 425; *ruris per terga*, as in Book I, verse 671.

**430.** The sacred text says: “Ask therefore the lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest.” The use of *deposcere* would require “from the lord of the harvest.” *Orare* permits either construction; *rogare* takes an accusative.

**431.** *Numerus* is often used for “multitude” and “abundance,” as in *numerus frumenti*, “a quantity of grain,” and *numerus vini*, “a quantity of wine.”

**432.** **CHAPTER XIX. He instructs the disciples what they are to do.** Matthew X, 1, etc.; Mark III, 17, VI, 8; Luke VI, 13, IX, 1.

**433.** *Conglomerat*: Lucretius and Ennius used this verb; Celsus used *conglomeratus*, and the *Code of Justinian* *conglomeratio*. Juvencus uses *glomerandi* in this book at verse 579 and frequently elsewhere.

**436.** *Samaritarum fraudis vestigia*: “the deceptive tracks of the Samaritans,” or “the tracks of the Samaritans’ deceit.” There seem to be two genitives governed by the same noun. See above at verse 313.

### Poem

“Now, as you go, take a mind like mine,

so that holy faith may subject to you the powers of the black demon

[440] and adapt devoted care to the afflicted.

These powers will be given to you without any payment.

You too must distribute the gifts freely, in no other manner.

Let possession of gold or silver not master your mind,

nor let the wicked desire for money subdue you.

[445] Let the minister of unadorned virtue not wish to preserve

two garments or two coverings for his feet.

When you enter the walls of a city, always seek

those whose hospitality is suitable for the righteous to enter.

Then, when you have entered, summon peace beneath the roof.

[450] If the household is tranquil, that peace will remain there.

But if it is dreadful in the character of its inhabitants,

it will flee, and your peace will follow your departure.

Whoever, savage, excludes you from the threshold of his house,

or rejects the life-giving words with hardened ears,

[455] when you leave that house, shake its traces from your feet,

lest an unjust portion of life cling to you.

A punishment worse than that of Sodom will await them in torments

when the end comes upon the whole world.

Go, then, like sheep, the prey of savage wolves.

[460] But be vigorous with the clever heart of serpents;

yet, in your gentleness, surpass the sweet doves.

For violence will often rush upon you,

and your bodies will be brought before human tribunals.

The violence of the age will press you fiercely

[465] with scourges, savage chains, and harsh tyrants because of me.”

### 439

Poelm., instead of the main reading, has *virtutem*; in the text, with the others, *virtutes*.

### 441

Torn. has *vocis*; read *vobis*.

### 442

Ott. has *gravita pendite*, corrected to *gratuita pendite*. Reg. has *gratuita impendite*, although something seems to have stood in place of the final three letters of *impendite*. Rom. has *gratis impendite*. All the printed editions I have seen have *cunctis impendite*. I think *gratis impendite*, with Rom., is preferable, from Matthew X, 8: “You have received freely; give freely.”

### 445

Ald. has *Non geminas*. Ald. and Poelm., instead of the main reading, with the manuscripts Ott. and Rom., have:

“two coverings—  
let the minister wish to preserve unadorned virtue.”

Reg. likewise has this, but *portare* instead of *servare*. Hadam. and other printed editions have:

“two coverings—  
let the minister wish to serve unadorned virtue.”

### 452

Rom., Ott., and Reg. write *habitum*, with a gloss in Reg., *sanctitatis*. Among the printed editions, Ald., Daventr., and Vesth. in the text also prefer *habitum*. Hadam., Poelm., and others have *abitum*. This reading is sound and agrees with the words of the Gospel. Matthew X, 13: “And if that house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you.” Hilary, on this passage: “If it is worthy, and worthy of sharing in peace; if unworthy, let peace return in turn.”

### 453

Reg., Rom., Ott., and Poelm., instead of the main reading, have *ferus*; others, *ferox*. Rom. has *de limine*; better, with the others, *vos limine*.

### 454

Reg., Ott., Rom., Ald., and Daventr. have *spernet*. Hadam., Poelm. in the text, and some others have *penetret*. After this verse, the printed editions of Daventr., Poelm., and others insert two additional verses of the same meaning:

“Whether, turned away, it will forbid the servants of God to enter the house  
and, displeased, prevent them from sharing the fires of hospitality.”

They are absent from Ald. and from our manuscripts Rom., Reg., and Ott., as well as from other excellent manuscripts, according to Reuschius’s testimony. They must therefore be expelled from this place as spurious, especially since Juvencus has expressed the Gospel’s meaning very well without them. Matthew X, 14: “And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet”; and similarly Mark VI, 11: “And whoever does not receive you or hear you, when you leave there, shake the dust from your feet,” etc. In the first of the two verses that I reject, Poelm. notes the variant *Sive adversa* for *Sive aversa*.

### 455

Poelm., instead of the main reading, has *egressu*; in the text, with the others, *egressi*.

### 456

Ott. has *vobis ne*. Reg. and Rom., with the printed editions, have *ne vobis*.

### 457

In Koenigius, some have *Illos*, others *Illis*. Rom. has *horridior*; the others, *deterior*.

### 458

Sabatierius read *omnis*, which perhaps slipped from his text by accident; the others have *omni*.

### 459

Rom., Ald., and Bas. have *Pergite nunc, ut oves*. Others have *Pergitis en, ut oves*, which comes closer to the words of Matthew X, 16: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves,” and Luke X, 3: “Go; behold, I send you as lambs among wolves.” In this same verse Rom. and Reg., with many printed editions, have *saevorum*; Ott., with others, *durorum*.

### 461

Reg. and Ott., with Poelm. in the text, and Hadam., have *dulces*; Rom. has *dulci*, namely, “in simplicity.” Ald., with other printed editions, has *puras*. Fabricius likewise printed *puras* from a manuscript, as he says; he also observes that Ravisius read no differently.

### 463

Poelm., instead of the main reading, has *consistent*; in the text, with others, *statuentur*.

### 464

Ott. has *dirisque*, but it seems to have been *durisque*.

### Notes

**439.** *Daemonis atri*: above, at verse 45, *Spiritus ater*; and below, at verse 616, *Si daemone pellitur atro*.

**445.** *Tegmina bina*: this is how he explains Matthew, “neither two tunics nor shoes.” For Mark, chapter VI, says: “But be shod with sandals.” The disciples are therefore not forbidden shoes, but two shoes, just as two tunics. Juvencus’s opinion is followed by St Thomas, Cajetan, and Maldonatus, as Julius Nigronus noted in *De Caliga*, chapter 2, no. 32.

**446.** *Virtus nuda*: “simple virtue.” Lactantius, at the beginning of Book I of the *Institutes*: “So that they might follow naked and unencumbered only virtue”; others read *veritatem* for *virtutem*.

**448.** *Hospitio succedere*: compare the note on verse 17, *Succedere tectis*.

**450.** It may be understood as: “Peace will remain in that house.”

**456.** He gives the reason why the disciples are commanded to shake the dust from their feet.

**461.** Why the simplicity of the dove is praised, see Barthius, Book XXXIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11.

**462.** *Incumbet*: Scaliger, *Poetics* IV, chapter 16, notes that this verb, which Maro often uses, is weighty and sonorous. Juvencus likewise takes pleasure in it.

**463.** *Statuentur corpora vestra*: “you will be brought before the tribunal.” Juvencus often uses *corpora* for people, or for beings composed of body and soul. *Statuentur* is used for *sistere*, “to set up” or “to bring before”; *sistere* is a legal term.

### Poem

“But when they hand you over, do not be anxious about your words:

the grace of speech will be given to you, flowing of its own accord.

The Spirit within you will speak what is worthy on your behalf.

For the wicked madness of a brother will betray his brother,

[470] and children will hand over the bodies of their parents to death.

Hatred will always pursue you because of our name,

but the glory of life accompanies the completion of faith.

Flee from the houses of the city that will persecute you;

from one place seek another, and then another.

[475] For cities must always remain for you,

that may furnish a people under the name of Israelites.

A disciple never rises above the lofty heights of his teacher,

nor should a servant attempt to surpass his master.

It is enough for the disciple to equal the strength of his teacher,

[480] and for the servant to attain a power like that of his lord.

Let every fear always be absent from your hearts,

for everything stripped bare is brought forth from its hiding places.

Whatever is commanded you secretly in darkness,

proclaim in the bright and shining light of the sun.

[485] And whatever I whisper into your ears,

let it be spread publicly from the lofty roofs over the people.

Despise the fury of those who overthrow your bodies

with the sword: they have no power

to send the living mind down into death as well.

[490] Rather, let the heart’s secrets fear him, to whom belongs all power

over body and soul alike.”

### 494

The manuscripts Rom. and Reg., with most printed editions, have *Ni jussu*, with a gloss in Reg., *nisi cum jussione*. In Ott. *jussu* appears, while *ni* or another word has been erased. Ald. and Bas. have *Injussu*, which they prefer; Gallandius calls it excellent, and Reuschius elegant, as in *Injussu populi*. Yet the Gospel’s words are explained equally well whether we read *Injussu* or *Ni jussu*. Matthew X, 29: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father?”

### 495

Schoettgenius, on the words *Quis dubitet*, says that there is no difficulty at all in this verse if we read either *judicet* or *dicat*; but if *Credere* is read in the following verse, then *dubitet* is correct, since the metre does not permit *judicet*. Rom. has *multos*; correct to *multis*.

### 496

Gallandius rightly says that *Cedere*, with Omeisius, is preferable to *Credere*. I find *credere* in the manuscript Rom.; the printed editions have *cedere*. Ott. incorrectly writes *caedere*. Reg. has the gloss *cedere—antecedere*. The same Gallandius cites *prae milibus* from the Paris edition; most have *pro milibus*. Reg., Ott., Daventr., Ald., and Torn. have *hominem*, which is preferable to *hominum* in Rom., Poelm., and others.

### 502

Rom., Daventr., Hadam., and Poelm. have:

“And let him who in his mother’s breast separates the sweet daughter.”

Reg. and Ottobon. likewise have this, but *dulci* instead of *dulcem*. Ald., Torn., and Bas. have:

“And let him who in his mother’s breast separates the sweet mother from her daughter.”

### 504

Rom. has *Vel matris, sobolisve meum*; the clearer reading is *Vel matri, sobolive*. Rom. likewise has *postponit*; *postponet* is better in the other copies.

### 507

Rom. and Ald. have *florentem fruge salutem*. Reg. and Ott., with most printed editions, have *florentem fruge salutis*, explained by the gloss in Reg.: *florentem—animam vel vitam*. In Ott. the first reading may have been *salutem*.

### 509

Rom. has *itidem* instead of *idem*.

### 512

Ott., Rom., Ald., and Bas. have *caecis*. Reg., Had., and Poelm. have *caeci*, which Reuschius preferred.

### 516

Daventr. and Torn. have *Largitur terris*. The manuscripts and most printed editions have *Pollicita est terris*. Reg. and Ott. have *fulgens*; others, *fulges*.

### 517

Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr. have *An superest aliam posthac*. Reg. and Daventr. have *An aliam superest posthac*. Ott., Ald., and Bas. have *Anne aliam superest post haec sperare*. Torn. and Rom. have the same, but *posthac* instead of *post haec*. I prefer the reading of Reg., *An aliam superest posthac*. Nor is it an objection that *an* is usually shortened: there are examples in which it is lengthened, although some vary in writing it. I find it highly probable that such monosyllables, called short by most authorities, possess a common quantity that may be either long or short, as I said in my note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 357 of the *Carmina de Deo*. Juvencus also lengthens *an* elsewhere, at Book III, verses 326 and 682, and Book IV, verse 529.

### Notes

**492.** *Passeribus pretium*, etc. Manilius, on poor people carrying little birds about for sale, Book V, verse 380:

“Throughout the whole city  
those who carry birds in cages, prepared at command,  
whose entire wealth consists in a small sparrow.”

**496.** A similar verse is found in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 325:

“And he sees that one remains from so many thousands just now;  
and he sees that one remains from so many thousands just now.”

**502.** *Dulcis* is an epithet especially suitable for children; Juvencus uses it elsewhere as well.

**503.** Matthew: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me,” etc. Juvencus therefore has approximately this sense: “If anyone values a parent more highly than loving me,” etc. “My love” can mean either the love with which I love or the love with which another loves me. In the latter sense God says: “If anyone values a parent more highly than love for me.”

**507.** I find *invenio* used for “acquire” or “obtain,” as in *nomen invenit* and several similar expressions.

**510.** *Sibi gaudebit*: “he will rejoice to his own benefit.” *Sibi* is often redundant in this way, though it is elegantly used in expressions such as “what does he want for himself?” and “what does he seek for himself?” Christian poets often use *perpes* for *perpetuus*, “everlasting.” See the Index of Dracontius’s words.

**511.** **CHAPTER XX. John sends disciples to Jesus, and Jesus speaks to the crowds about John.** Matthew XI, 7, etc.; Luke VII, 24, etc.

**514.** *Portare*: “to carry” or “bear,” as in “to carry prayers,” “to bear salvation,” and so forth. Virgil, Book IX, verse 312: “He gave his father many messages to bear.”

**516.** *Sub* is either superfluous or is used for *in*. Dracontius, Book I, verse 230: *Sub tempore primo*, “at the first time”; Book II, verse 356: *Sub tempore parvo*, “in a short time.”

**517.** Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 354: “The sole safety of the defeated is to hope for no safety.”

### Poem

“The price of sparrows will scarcely amount to a small fraction of a coin;

yet not one is worthy of falling into your snares

without the Lord’s command.

[495] Who, wise beneath the Lord’s protection, would doubt

that one human being is to be trusted in place of many thousands of winged creatures?

Whoever acknowledges me before the judgment seat of the earth,

I shall likewise acknowledge before the Father.

So likewise before the Father I shall deny the one who denies me.

[500] I have not now come to bring peace upon the earth,

but a sword, which will divide a son from his father’s breast,

and a beloved daughter from her mother’s breast.

If anyone values a parent more highly than loving me,

or places a mother or a child before my love,

[505] he will feel the dreadful rejection issued from our abode.

Whoever scorns his soul because of our name

will find it flourishing with the joyful fruit of salvation.

Whoever receives you will have received me with kindly service;

he too will rejoice that he has received me in the place of the supreme Father,

[510] to his own benefit in everlasting life.”

When he had given these commands to the twelve disciples,

righteous John, from the shadows of the dark prison,

ordered chosen men from the number of his followers

to carry these words to Christ and report the truth:

[515] “Are you, in our present age, the rest for pious souls

which the kingdom of heaven promised to the earth?

Or does some other salvation still remain to be hoped for hereafter?”

With such words Christ sent back the message.

The darkness of the blind is changed into the light of daylight,

[520] and the limbs of the weak grow strong with renewed power.

Leprosy is driven away from the pale, scaly body,
523. In *Reg.* and *Rom.*, *amissae lethi post funera vitae*, which I retain; Davisius had restored it from a manuscript under chapter 70, section 6 of Caesar’s *Bellum Alexandrinum*. See Arntzenius on Sedulius, book IV, line 137: *Alii amissa lethi post funera vita* (“Others read: life lost after the funeral rites of death”). After this verse, *Reg.* and *Rom.* read:

> *Depositum repetens animae substantia corpus,*  
> *Ad corpus remeans animae jam libera virtus.*

“Recovering the body entrusted to it, the substance of the soul; the soul’s power, now free, returning to the body.”

In *Poelm.*, *Hadam.*, *Daventr.* and others, the same verses occur, but in reverse order: first *Ad corpus*, then *Depositum*. *Ott.*, *Ald.*, *Bas.* and Fabricius omit *Depositum* entirely and give only *Ad corpus*; that reading could be retained. Yet the verse beginning *Depositum* has a stronger air of antiquity and resembles Juvencus’ style; the other verse, *Ad corpus*, has the character of a gloss. Ancient Christians often called the bodies of the dead “the deposit,” that is, something entrusted until the day of judgment. Consult the note on Dracontius, book I, line 681. Juvencus uses *animae substantia* (“the substance of the soul”), as at line 420 of this work, *substantia vocis* (“the substance of the voice”), and book I, line 510, *substantia salis* (“the substance of salt”), etc. Reuschius, along with others, retained *Ad corpus* and rejected the other verse beginning *Depositum repetens*.

526. The manuscripts *Reg.*, *Rom.*, *Ott.*, and *Poelm.* read *nostri* (“of our”), instead of *d. s.*; Aldus and most printed editions have *terris* (“to the earth”), which Reuschius considers preferable.

[Col. 0189C] 529. *Rom.*, together with most printed editions, reads *Haec super* (“concerning this”); *Reg.* and *Ott.* have *Hoc super*, a reading approved by Omeisius and Gallandius. Gallandius says that it derives from the Gospel context. Matthew 11:7, in the Italic version, reads: “When they had departed, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John the Baptist: What did you go out into the desert to see?” etc. Hilary, commenting on this passage, has: “When they had departed, he spoke to the crowds about him: What did you go out into the desert to see?” etc. Thus *hoc super* means “about this teacher,” namely John the Baptist.

530. The manuscripts *Reg.*, *Ott.*, and *Rom.* read *deserto*, which Aldus also printed. *Desertis* is more strictly Latin, as in *Hadam.*, *Poelm.* in the text, and others; but *deserto* is preferable, since Hilary also uses that word, and the ancient version of Sacred Scripture apparently current in Juvencus’ time reads, according to Sabatier: “What did you go out into the desert to see?”

531. *Rom.* reads *stamen*; in *Ott.* too, *stamen* was formed from *stramen*. The same reading appeared in Barth’s codex, and he seems to approve it, since he wrote *Optime* (“excellent”) in the margin, as Koenigius reports. *Reg.*, together with the printed editions, reads *stramen*. The words of the Italic version are “a reed shaken by the wind”; those of the Vulgate, “a reed shaken by the wind.” Jerome, in *Ezekiel* 40, has “a reed shaken by the wind.” The author of the *Opus imperfectum* on Matthew, homily 27, has “a reed moved by the wind.” Most other Fathers distinctly name a reed. Juvencus seems to have wished to express both possibilities. *Stramen* means straw, a stalk, and similar material ordinarily used for strewing a rustic bed. *Stamen*, metaphorically, denotes the fibers in wood and the threads in grasses and flowers stretched lengthwise in a regular arrangement; therefore *stamen arundineum* (“the threadlike structure of a reed”) could in some fashion also be defended.

532. In *Ott.*, *videri* (“to be seen”) originally stood here; it was correctly emended to *videre* (“to see”).

534. Aldus, Basilius, and *Poelm.* read, instead of the received text:

> *Fatidicis longe praeponitur ille prophetis,*  
> *Ut veteris quondam cecinere oracula scripti.*

“He is placed far above the prophetic seers, as once the oracles of ancient Scripture sang.”

The manuscripts and most printed editions have:

> *Ille prophetarum solus transcendere vires*  
> *Indicio veteris scripti promittitur olim.*

“He alone of the prophets is promised of old, by the testimony of ancient Scripture, to surpass their powers.”

Reuschius found *socius* (“companion”) in place of *solus* in one source, but rejects it. Sigebert Havercampus noticed the same point in his *Index criticus* on Sallust, under *indicare* (“to indicate”): he restores *solus* from the best manuscripts. *Torn.* has *viris*, wrongly, for *vires*. *Reg.* and *Rom.* read *Judicio veteris* (“by the judgment of ancient Scripture”), which is not unattractive. It has been observed by others, and by me in the note on Dracontius, book II of *Carmen de Deo*, line 560, that *indicium* and *judicium* are often confused in ancient copies. In this passage, however, I prefer *Indicio*.

536. *Ott.* originally had *Hinc* (“hence”); a second hand, together with the other manuscripts and most printed editions, has *Hunc* (“him”). *Poelm.* reads *Nunc* (“now”) instead of the received text.

537. Aldus, *Rom.*, and Basilius read *mitto illum* (“I send him”); others have *mitto meum* (“I send my own”), which agrees better with the Gospel wording. Matthew 10:10: “For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face,” etc.

539. *Poelm.* reads, instead of the received text:

> *Qui major nostris Joanne hoc viribus esset.*

“Who would be greater in strength than our John.”

The text, together with the other witnesses, has:

> *Major Joannis nostri qui viribus esset.*

“He who would be greater in strength than our John.”

540. *Poelm.*, Fabricius, and others read:

> *Sed minimus coeli qui in regno est, major habetur.*

“But the least one who is in the kingdom of heaven is considered greater.”

The manuscripts and most printed editions have:

> *Sed minor hoc coeli fiet sublimior aura.*

“But one lesser than this will become more exalted in the court of heaven.”

In *Rom.* and *Ald.*, *haec* stands for *hoc*; in *Rom.*, the margin has *fecit* for *fiet*. The syntax is involved and should be explained as follows: “But the lesser one will become more exalted in the court of heaven than this one,” namely John. The Greek has “lesser,” not “least.” Reuschius arranges the sense thus: “He who is lesser than this John in the court of heaven will become, will exist, will be in that blessedness more exalted, more august, and more blessed.” This explanation is scarcely clearer than Juvencus’ own verse.

[Col. 0190D] 541. *Rom.* reads *Cujus* (“whose”); others, *Hujus* (“of this one”). The manuscripts *Rom.*, *Reg.*, and *Ott.* have *sentit* (“feels”); the printed editions have *sensit* (“felt”). *Sentit* is preferable. Thus Matthew 11:12: “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

[Note: 0189D]

522. *Vox aeria* (“airy voice”) is so called either from its cause or from its nature itself. Seneca, *Natural Questions* II.29: “Since a voice is nothing other than a blow of air.”

523. Sedulius, book IV, line 137: “And although he endured the dangers of a lost life.” *Lethi post funera*: Reuschius takes *lethi*, “of death,” abstractly for the concrete sense “deadly.”

533. Matthew: “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings.” Thus in Juvencus *molli cum veste* (“with soft clothing”) means the same as “those who wear soft clothing”: they are held, are, exist, or dwell there. Such less obvious meanings must be carefully noted.

[Col. 0190D] 539. *Joannis viribus* (“in John’s strength”) stands for *Joanne*, just as elsewhere one finds *virtus animae* (“the soul’s power”), *scribarum pectora* (“the scribes’ breasts”), *vis vulneris* (“the force of a wound”), and *robur saxi* (“the strength of a rock”).

541. Matthew’s Gospel: “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” The ancient version in the Colbert manuscript reads: “The kingdom of heaven is compelled, and those who compel it seize it.” Many others read similarly, and Ambrose consistently does so in numerous passages. Omeisius explains *vim* (“violence”) as meaning: “People in great numbers, as though violent, burst into heaven.” Maldonatus interprets it as meaning that the kingdom of heaven is open to all, so that whoever wishes may rush into it.

> The sound of an airy voice penetrates deaf ears.  
> Life is restored to the life lost after the funeral rites of death,  
> The substance of the soul reclaiming the body held in deposit,  
> And the shining glory of our radiant coming is revealed to its poor followers, not disdaining them.  
> Blessed will he be whom error has not deceived.

The disciples report these commands to the teacher. Concerning this, Christ proclaims such words to the people:

> Why lately did you wish to go out into the desert  
> To see a reed moved by the trembling wind?  
> Why also to see a man clothed in soft clothing?  
> In the houses of kings they are held in soft clothing.  
> He alone of the prophets is promised of old,  
> By the testimony of ancient Scripture, to surpass their powers.  
> For this reading of the venerable voice speaks of him:  
> “Behold, I send my minister to prepare the roads  
> Before your faces”—no woman has borne anyone  
> Who would be greater in strength than our John.  
> But the lesser one will become more exalted than this heavenly court.  
> From his rising the royal realm of heaven feels force,  
> And fierce violence seizes the kingdom of heaven.  
> All the Law received its fulfillment from the Baptist’s time,  
> And the same time brings the prophets’ end.  
> If you wish to know the inner mysteries of the swift-moving age,  
> Elias once assumed John’s blessed body as a dwelling,  
> Whom the representation of fire-footed four-horse teams, commanded by a flashing whirlwind, carried away.  
> Let him hear these things, opening his ears to life-giving words.  
> Now I confess to you, Father, whose glory shining heaven and fruit-bearing earths serve,  
> That you have now hidden these things from proud wise men,  
> And that this power can comprehend the little hearts of infants.  
> Now all things of the reigning Father have been handed over to me;  
> Nor can anyone know the Son of the Lord except the Father alone;  
> The Son will behold the Father in his mind, or the Son himself will reveal such things to whomever he chooses.  
> Let all come here whom the burden of a heavy load oppresses:  
> By the Father’s gift my power will be able  
> To restore their former strength in joyful rest.  
> Take up the yoke firmly; my burden is light for the righteous.

[Col. 0191A] 543. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, Aldus, and Basilius read:

> *Lex omnis summam, Baptistae a tempore cepit.*

“Every law received its completion from the time of the Baptist.”

*Hadam.* and *Poelm.* have this in the text, while Westhemerus places *ad tempora* (“unto the times”) in the margin. *Torn.* reads *a tempore coepit* (“began from the time”). *Poelm.* gives *in tempore* (“in the time”). Basilius has *Lex omni* (“for every law”). *Rom.* reads:

> *Vox omnis summa Baptistae a tempore coepit.*

“Every voice’s culmination began from the time of the Baptist.”

544. Aldus and Basilius have *conclusus eodem* (“closed by the same one”); the others have *concluditur idem* (“the same is brought to an end”).

545. In *Reg.*, this verse and the following verses, through *Quanto igitur nobis*, are missing and have been supplied on an appended leaf by a later hand.

546. After *Si vultis*, *Had.*, *Poelm.* read:

> *Ipse est Elias felix venturus in aevum,*  
> *Corpus Joannis felix habitabile sumpsit*  
> *Elias quondam.*

“He is Elias, blessed, who is to come for ever; Elias of old assumed John’s blessed body as a dwelling.”

*Daventr.* is similar, but has *Ipse est Joannes* (“He is John”) instead of *Ipse est Elias*. *Rom.* and *Reg.* have:

> *Corpus Joannes felix habitabile sumpsit,*  
> *Ipse est Joannes felix venturus in aevum,*  
> *Elias quondam.*

“John assumed a blessed body as a dwelling; he is John, blessed, who is to come for ever; Elias of old.”

*Ott.* and Aldus, after *Si vultis*, omit *Ipse est* entirely and immediately read:

> *Corpus Joannis felix habitabile sumpsit*  
> *Elias, quondam.*

“John assumed a blessed body as a dwelling—Elias of old.”

This seems more likely to derive from Matthew 11:14: “And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elias who is to come.” Reuschius thinks that the poet, through hypallage and reversed order, expresses Christ’s testimony concerning Elias of the New Covenant. He adds that this device displeased a glossator, who, attempting to reproduce the Gospel text more exactly, inserted the verse:

> *Ipse est Elias, felix venturus in aevum.*

“He is Elias, blessed, who is to come for ever.”

I suspected the following reconstruction:

> *Si vultis volucris penetralia noscere saecli,*  
> *Ipse est Joannes felix venturus in aevum,*  
> *Elias quondam quem...*

“If you wish to know the hidden places of the swift age, he is John, blessed, who is to come for ever—Elias of old, whom...”

[Col. 0192A] 547. *Rom.* reads *missa* (“sent”), which in *Ott.* was made from *misso*. *Reg.*, together with most printed editions, has *jussa* (“commanded”); Juvencus is fond of this word. It is suitable for expressing the representation of the four-horse chariot, which took place by divine command. Aldus, however, printed *missa*.

548. *Rom.* has *quadrigarum* (“of chariots”); others have *quadrijugorum* (“of four-horse teams”), which better agrees with *Flammipedum* (“fire-footed”).

551. *Hadam.*, *Poelm.*, Fabricius, and others have *frugiferarum* (“fruit-bearing”). All our manuscripts, together with Aldus and *Daventr.*, have *frugiferentum*, which also pleased Gallandius because the word occurs in Lucretius, book I, line 3: “which [rules] the sea-bearing ships and the fruit-bearing lands.”

552. *Torn.* and *Poelm.* read, instead of the received text, *Namque abscondisti* (“for you have hidden”). Westhemerus has this in the text and *Coelesti nunc quod* in the margin, incorrectly, instead of *Celasti nunc quod*, which is found in the manuscripts and most printed editions. In *Ott.*, after this verse, another is inserted:

> *Occulis haec quondam parve sapientibus orsa,*  
> *Parvulaque, etc.*

“Once you hid these things from the supposedly wise, and from the little ones...” Perhaps it should read *prave sapientibus* (“from those perversely wise”).

553. *Reg.* reads *Parvula qui infantum* (“the little things which belong to infants”), a reading obscurely indicated in *Rom.*, where *vix* appears incorrectly for *vis*.

554. From the Gospel text, someone might conjecture *Jam mihi regnanti sunt omnia tradita Patri* (“Now all things have been handed over to me, the reigning Father”) instead of *a regnante Patre* (“by the reigning Father”). Juvencus often uses the dative for the ablative. In the present passage, however, the syntax would become too involved and the sense insufficiently clear.

[Col. 0192C] 559. *Poelm.* and *Ott.* originally had *munera* (“gifts”); in *Ott.* this was correctly changed to *munere* (“by the gift”), in agreement with the other manuscripts and printed editions.

561. Schoettgenius suspects *ferre* (“to bear”) instead of *forte* (“strongly”): that is, “for bearing.” Reuschius retains *forte*, either meaning “good and salutary” or, adverbially, “firmly, with steadfast courage.”

[Note: 0191C]

542. *Atrox*, in a favorable sense, means “vigorous, steadfast.” Horace, book II, ode 1, line 23: “And all the lands subdued, except Cato’s steadfast spirit.” Silius, book VI, line 378: “That steadfast faith.”

543. *Summam* means “end, completion.” Quintilian, book III, chapter 2: “Utility gave him zeal and growth; reason and practice gave completion.” Compare Barthius and Burmannus on Gratius, *Cynegeticon*, line 317.

545. Matthew has only: “And if you are willing to receive it.” The old version in the Colbert manuscript, together with Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 35, reads: “And if you are willing to hear.” Manuscript Sangermanensis 1, together with the Clermont manuscript, has: “And if you are willing to know.”

[Col. 0191D] 546. Matthew’s words are: “He is Elias who is to come.” The claim that Elias assumed John’s body as a dwelling-place has the flavor of metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls. This doctrine was sufficiently common among the Jews in Christ’s time; for that reason they thought that Christ was John the Baptist, or Jeremiah, or Elias, or one of the other prophets. The same idea appears in Herod’s words at Matthew 14:2: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead.” Christ speaks of John in the same way: “He is Elias”; but by adding, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” he clearly declares that the statement is to be understood mystically. The same interpretation suits Juvencus, who immediately adds: “Let him hear these things, opening his ears to life-giving words.” Reuschius nevertheless suspects from this passage, and from line 524, that Juvencus came from the school of Plato, since at line 524 he openly acknowledges metempsychosis, reading it thus: “The soul’s free power returning to the body.”

548. *Flammipes* (“fire-footed”) is a new word formed by Juvencus by analogy. *Simulatio* sometimes means likeness or imitation; Forcellinus confirms this meaning in the present verse of Juvencus. The gloss in the *Reg.* manuscript is *simulatio—sicut visus est* (“representation—as he appeared”). In book III, line 265, on the same subject:

> “Whom, on a swift chariot,  
> Through the heavenly whirl once represented by four-horse chariots,  
> He inserted among the stars, the swift force of burning flame.”

Sedulius, book I, line 163: “Carried into the stars in a golden, fire-bearing chariot.” Arntzenius, on this passage, says that Juvencus’ expression is not dissimilar, but reads *Flammigerum rapuit* (“the fire-bearing one carried him away”). Muncker on Fulgentius, book I of the *Mythologies*, page 616, should also be consulted.

549. Above, line 454: “Or will reject the life-giving words with hardened ears.”

550. Chapter XXI: Jesus’ confession to the Father, and that the Lord’s yoke is easy. Matthew 11:25 and following; Luke 10:21 and following.

554. *Omnia Patris* means “all things belonging to the Father,” as in book I, line 199, *Omnia mundi* (“all things of the world”), and book IV, line 218, *Omnia pompae* (“all things of pomp”). Matthew says: “All things have been handed over to me by the Father.”

560. Matthew: “And I will refresh you.” Sangermanensis 2 has: “And I will refresh you; I will make you rest.” Jerome, on Isaiah 58, has: “And I will give you rest,” for, he says, this is what the Greek *ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς* means, “I will give you rest.” Predestinatus, book III, volume I of Sirmondus, the author of the *Opus imperfectum* on Matthew, and Juvencus at this passage agree with one another. Schoettgenius observes that Juvencus elegantly paraphrased *ἀναπαύσω* with the Syriac interpreter. A similar point is noted on Matthew 5:45: “Who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil.”

561. *Forte* should perhaps be understood adverbially, meaning “firmly.” Since the burden is called light, the yoke can scarcely be called “strong” in any satisfactory sense, although Reuschius thinks otherwise.

> For I will bestow sweet salvation upon the humble in heart.

These words having been spoken, he passes through the burdened cultivated fields, and the crowd of accompanying disciples was plucking the full grain of the ears in the field. That day demanded rest according to the ancient law, for the Sabbaths prescribed repose in accordance with the old commands. Behold, the Pharisees publicly reproach Christ because the disciples, while harvesting, were trampling upon the commands of the holy law. But Jesus, its fulfiller, begins to unfold to them the memorials of the ancient Scripture:

> Surely you have read that once, in the temple,  
> The melodious David took the consecrated bread with the people  
> And satisfied his own hunger and that of his companions;  
> Yet it was unlawful for anyone to touch the loaves,  
> Which by law the priest alone was permitted to take.  
> The same thing is written in the just ordering of the law:  
> “The prophets profane the Sabbaths in the temple without guilt.”  
> Nor is your gathering here any less  
> Than the power of the temple. If your hearts understood  
> That God preferred not sacred rites but merciful hearts,  
> The faction would not so often have condemned holy men,  
> Who are free from guilt. But now I, sovereign over all the Sabbaths,  
> Will keep them voluntarily under the law’s authority.

Then, after saying these things, he enters their synagogue. At the entrance he immediately sees a young man whose withered hand hung uselessly from his shoulder. They test him with deceitful questions, asking whether it is lawful to bring healing on the Sabbaths, so that the penalty for violating the law might remain. Christ replies:

> If your little sheep should perhaps fall into a pit,  
> Surely you would pass beyond the Sabbath’s rest of the law  
> And lift the worthless animal from the broken-down depth.  
> How much greater, then, should the healing of human beings  
> Rouse and kindle our minds toward good works!

“Come, then, young man, stretch out your sound right hand.” At the word, the healed man extended both palms.

At this sign, which could scarcely have been raised with fitting reverence by the astonished people, they loudly proclaim in their hostile councils that he must be destroyed. Perceiving these schemes of the leaders, Christ departs and applies healing, granted by his ancestral power, to the various maladies of the people.

A man was brought there whose dreadful demonic power had wanted him to live deprived of tongue and sight and to be food for his own torments. When he had been cured and was vigorous in sight and voice, the blind faction of the Pharisaic people recognized that he had done this with the help of the demon who alone, as prince of the demons, held the powers of wickedness under his dominion. But Christ opens their hearts to the truth and refutes them with convincing words:

> If a kingdom, divided into two parts, should gape apart,  
> And division, split against itself, should fight,  
> Everything will quickly fall, its inner parts torn apart.  
> And if a dreadful demon is driven out by a dark demon,  
> It is divided against itself and fights with hostile power.  
> Who could carry off prey from a strong man’s house  
> Unless he first attacked and bound the arms of its guardians  
> With cords, so that the seizure of the prey might be easy?  
> Whoever is separated from my weapons is not my soldier;  
> He will stand as an enemy in the opposing battle-line.  
> Whoever wanders free from gathering my flocks,  
> Scatters my sheep’s pasture along the pathless ways.  
> But whatever human error there may be concerning all these things  
> Can be forgiven—only let the Holy Spirit never be torn  
> By words poured forth from an irrational mind.

[Col. 0191C] 562. I understand the passage thus: “I will bestow sweet salvation upon the one who is humble in heart.”

563. Chapter XXII: The disciples pluck ears of grain. Matthew 12:1 and following; Mark 2:23; Luke 6:1. *Culta* (“cultivated fields”), used absolutely, means cultivated fields not only among poets but also among other writers. In *Reg.* the gloss is *gravatae—maturae* (“burdened—ripe”).

564. *Praeterit per culta* (“he passes through the cultivated fields”). Plautus, *Mercator* V.4.46: “Who pass along the roads.” *Populus* (“people”) means a multitude, as in book I, line 322, and elsewhere.

565. Virgil, *Georgics* III.176: “But you will pluck the planted grain by hand.” Others use *carpo* (“pluck”) in the same sense. Juvencus adds *in ordine* (“in orderly fashion”), because this was permitted to the Jews. Deuteronomy 23:24–25: “When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, eat grapes as much as you wish, but do not carry any away with you. If you enter your friend’s standing grain, break off the ears and rub them with your hand, but you shall not cut with a sickle.” Omeisius thought the phrase meant something else. *In ordine*, he says, means that the disciples were not wandering outside the path.

570. *Completor* (“fulfiller”): as far as I know, no one earlier than Juvencus used this word.

571. *Retexens* (“unfolding again”) means explaining anew, reviewing, or going through again. Claudian, Ausonius, Apuleius, and other writers of the same period assign this meaning to *retexo*; indeed, Cicero does so as well.

572. Book I, line 184, similarly: *Davida canorum* (“melodious David”).

576. *De lege* (“from the law”) instead of *ex lege* (“according to the law”); or *de* may be superfluous, as often happens.

[Col. 0194C] 577. *Justo moderamine* (“in the just ordering”): see the textual variants and note on book I, line 22.

579. Consider Matthew’s words: “Amen I say to you, here is one greater than the temple.” Thus the old version in the Colbert manuscript. Sangermanensis 1, together with Clermont and Corbie 2, reads: “Because here is one greater than the Sabbath.” Corbie 1: “Because this is greater than the temple.” Cambridge: “Because here is one greater than the temple.” Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 9: “For here is something greater than the temple.” Hilary, on Matthew: “He indicates himself as the temple... because he himself is greater than the Sabbath.” Jerome, on Matthew: “Here” should be read not as a pronoun but as an adverb of place, because the place that contains the Lord of the temple is greater than the temple.

In the Greek text some manuscripts have “greater,” others “greater” in the neuter. Juvencus therefore seems to have read, “Because here something greater than the temple is,” and interprets it to mean: “Because in this place there is something greater than the temple,” namely the crowd of disciples itself, which is to be preferred to the temple; for the righteous are the living temple of God. Thus, though hungry, they could pluck ears of grain on the Sabbath without sinning, just as the priests did not sin when on the Sabbath they performed the duties necessary for the worship of the temple. Reuschius also supports this interpretation. In Pliny, book VIII, chapter 42 at the end, *glomeratio* means the act of gathering into a ball; here it means “gathering,” since *glomero*, like *conglomero* and *agglomero*, is used for “collect” or “assemble.” Compare lines 433 and 723 of this book and lines 581 and 756 of book III.

581. Recall line 360 of this book, where the same thought is expressed.

582. Juvencus often uses *factio* (“faction”) in a negative sense; shortly afterward, at line 608, *Caeca pharisaeae cognovit factio gentis* (“the blind faction of the Pharisaic people recognized”).

[Col. 0193A] 562. *Torn.*, with all our manuscripts, reads *largibor* (“I shall bestow”). Most printed editions have *largitur* (“he bestows”). Plautus uses *largibor*, *Bacchides* IV.7.30. The ancients formed fourth-conjugation verbs in this way. Gallandius printed *largibor*, but records *praebebo* (“I shall grant”) as a variant from a Paris edition.

567. *Ott.* has *Sabbati*, correctly emended to *Sabbata*.

568. *Poelm.* in the text, together with *Hadam.* and Fabricius, reads *curant* (“they attend to”). All our manuscripts, with the best printed editions, have *coram* (“publicly”), since *coeperunt* (“they began”), or some similar verb, is understood. Others write *reprehendere* or *reprendere* (“to reproach”).

569. Aldus has *Qui*; read *Quod*.

571. *Poelm.* has *iis*; Aldus, with the manuscripts, *his*.

574. *Reg.* and *Rom.* read *Et comitum, propriamque famem* (“and that of his companions, and his own hunger”); *Ott.*, with the printed editions, has *Et propriam comitumque famem* (“and his own hunger and that of his companions”).

577. *Reg.* has *scriptum justo*; the others, *scriptum est justo*.

578. *Ott.*, *Torn.*, and *Hadam.* read *Sabbata profanent templo sine crimine vates* (“let the prophets profane the Sabbaths in the temple without guilt”). *Reg.* and *Rom.* read the same, but have *profanant* (“profane”); Westhemerus places *Sabbata profanet* in the margin. *Poelm.* and Fabricius read *Vates in templo sine crimine festa profanent* (“let the prophets profane the festivals in the temple without guilt”); Westhemerus, Aldus, and Basilius have the same, but with *profanant*. *Profanant* accords better with the Gospel’s wording than *profanent*. Matthew 12:5: “Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” Although the first syllable of *profano* is usually short, I judge our manuscripts’ reading *Sabbata profanant* to be sound: I do not see why it could not be lengthened, as it often is in *propino*, *profundo*, and *procuro*, and sometimes in *profari*, *profiteor*, *profugio*, and *profectus*. Indeed, in Latin it is mostly lengthened, as in *promoveo* and *profero*.

579. *Rom.* has *ista*; the others *istic* or *isthic* (“here”). In the same manuscript *minorem* stands incorrectly for *minor est*.

581. *Reg.* and *Torn.* have *malit*; *Ott.* *malet*; above, correctly, *mallet*, with the others.

582. *Ott.* has *vires*; above, correctly, *viros*. The same *Ott.*, together with Aldus, *Daventr.*, Basilius, and *Rom.*, has *factio sacros*, which Reuschius dislikes because *Expertes culpae* follows. *Reg.* has *factio praeceps*, with the gloss or variant *vestra*. *Poelm.* in the text, with *Hadam.*, has *factio vestra*.

[Note: Col. 0193C]

562. I understand: “I shall bestow sweet salvation upon him who is humble in heart.”

563. CHAPTER XXII. The disciples pluck ears of grain. Matthew 12:1 ff.; Mark 2:23; Luke 6:1. *Culta*, used absolutely, means cultivated fields, not only among poets but also among other writers. In *Reg.* the gloss is *gravatae—maturae* (“laden—ripe”).

564. *Praeterit per culta*: “he passes through the cultivated fields.” Plautus, *Mercator* V.4.46: “who pass along the roads.” *Populus* means a multitude, as in book I, line 322 and elsewhere.

565. Virgil, *Georgics* III.176: “But you will pluck the sown grain by hand.” Other writers use *carpo* in the same sense. Juvencus adds *in ordine* because this was permitted to the Jews. Deuteronomy 23:24 ff.: “When you enter your neighbour’s vineyard, eat grapes as much as you please, but do not take any away with you. If you enter your friend’s grain-field, break off ears and rub them with your hand, but do not reap with a sickle.” Omeisius thought otherwise: *in ordine*, he says, means that the disciples were not wandering off the path.

570. *Completor*: so far as I know, nobody earlier than Juvencus used this word.

571. *Retexens*: explaining again, recounting, unfolding. Claudian, Ausonius, Apuleius, and other contemporaries—even Cicero—assign this sense to *retexo*.

572. Book I, line 184, similarly: *Davida canorum* (“melodious David”).

576. *De lege* for *ex lege*; or *de* is superfluous, as often happens.

[Col. 0194C] 577. *Justo moderamine*: see the variants and note on book I, line 22.

579. Take Matthew’s words: “Amen, I tell you, this one is greater than the temple.” So too the old version in the Colbert manuscript. Sangermanensis 1, with Clermont and Corbie 2, has: “This one is greater than the Sabbath”; Corbie 1: “This is greater than the temple”; Cambridge: “This one is greater than the temple”; Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 9: “For this one is greater than the temple.” Hilary on Matthew: “He indicates himself as the temple . . . because he himself is greater than the Sabbath.” Jerome on Matthew: *hic* is to be read not as a pronoun but as an adverb of place, because the place which contains the Lord of the temple is greater than the temple. In the Greek text some manuscripts have the masculine “greater,” others the neuter. Juvencus therefore read, “For here there is something greater than the temple,” and interprets it: “In this place there is something greater than the temple,” namely the very gathering of disciples, which is to be preferred to the temple; for the righteous are God’s living temple. The hungry disciples could therefore pluck ears on the Sabbath without sin, just as priests did not sin when they performed on the Sabbath what was necessary to the temple’s worship. Reuschius also accepts this interpretation. In Pliny, book VIII, chapter 42 at the end, *glomeratio* is the act of forming a ball; here it is a gathering, because *glomero*, like *conglomero* and *agglomero*, may mean to collect or assemble. Compare lines 433 and 723 of this book, and book III, lines 581 and 756.

581. Recall line 360 of this book, where the same thought is expressed.

582. Juvencus often uses *factio* in a bad sense; shortly below, line 608: *Caeca pharisaeae cognovit factio gentis*.

[Col. 0195B] 585. Aldus and *Poelm.* read *illorum*; the manuscripts and other printed editions, *ipsorum*.

586. *Rom.* has *pro lumine*; *Poelm.* has *de limine* instead of the received text; in its text, with most witnesses, *pro limine*, in the sense noted at line 299 of this book.

587. *Rom.* has *Caecatum*; correct it to *Siccatum*. *Siccatae* would not be bad either.

592. *Reg.* and *Ott.* have *Inciderent*. Above, *Ott.*, and *Rom.* with the editions, have *Inciderint*. Others cited by Omeisius read *Inciderit*, making *pecuscula* a feminine singular, an unusual usage.

595. Koenigius suspects *tollens* and therefore conjectures *molles*. Reuschius thinks *tollens* refers to *tolletis* in line 593.

596. The manuscripts *Rom.*, *Reg.*, and *Ott.* have *juvenis, sanam protendito dextram*, as *Poelm.* indicates among its variant readings. Other editions have *Juvenis, redivivam extendito dextram*, which is less pleasing.

597. *Poelm.* has *Cum dixit*; the other manuscripts and editions, *Cum dicto*, which is sound and is used four times by Apuleius in book I, as Barthius observed in *Adversaria* XXXV.14, col. 1612, where he cites Juvencus, book IV, line 512: *Cum dicto Judas numero stipante catervae—Advenit*. Martianus Capella also uses *cum dicto* for “without any delay,” book IX, at the beginning, p. 302. Thus, although *Quo dicto* might be conjectured, the old reading should be retained. Juvencus uses the same phrase at book I, line 802: *Dixerat, et dicto citius cum voce loquentis*, etc. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, Fabricius, *Poelm.*, and *Hadam.* have *palmam sanus porrexit utramque*. Reuschius reports that *Rom.* has *palmam sanam porrexit utramque*. Aldus, *Daventr.*, *Torn.*, and Basilius have *palmas sanas porrexit utrasque*. Reuschius finds some emphasis in the repetition *palmam sanam*. But, since *utramque* is added, this is not really repetition. Better, then, is *palmam sanus porrexit utramque*: he extended both the hand that had been healed and the other, which had always been sound.

598. *Reg.* and *Ottob.* have *His tum pro signis*, which I prefer to the other readings, as Gallandius also preferred it from the Helmstedt manuscript. Reuschius inserted *Justum pro signis*, which *Poelm.* gives among its variants. In *Rom.*, Aldus, and apparently *Daventr.*, is *Istum pro signis*. *Poelm.* in the text, with *Hadam.* and Fabricius, has *Istis pro signis*. Badius conjectures *Christum pro signis*; Reuschius, *Isti pro signis*, namely the Pharisees. Reuschius likes Badius’s conjecture, but wholly rejects *Istis*. Further, Aldus and Basilius have *signis quem vix*; most witnesses, *signis, quae vix*; *Rom.*, less aptly, *signis quaevis veneratio*. Retain *quae vix*.

600. For *Conciliis* perhaps read *Consiliis*, the word used by the Evangelist. Sabatier printed *Consiliis*, perhaps accidentally or conjecturally. *Ottob.* in the first hand has *despiciendum* or *dispiciendum*; among the variants, *decipiendum*, which appears in most manuscripts and editions. Gallandius, with *Torn.*, printed *deripiendum* and does not approve *decipiendum*. But I prefer the latter to the other readings. Matthew 12:54 reads: “But when the Pharisees went out, they took counsel against him how they might destroy him.” Here *decipere* is used in the sense of ensnaring and taking by fraud.

601. *Reg.* has *Perspiciens*, but perhaps it was *Prospiciens*, for something has been erased.

602. *Hadam.*, Fabricius, and *Poelm.* in the text have *Decedens*; *Poelm.* among the variants, *Decessit*. Our manuscripts *Rom.*, *Reg.*, and *Ott.* have *Discedens*, which Westhemerus places in the margin. Aldus, *Torn.*, Basilius, and Westhemerus in the text have *Discessit*, preferred by Reuschius, who thinks the change from past tense to participle arose from a change of tense not uncommon in poets.

603. Aldus, Basilius, and *Poelm.* have *in populis*; *Rom.*, *in populo*; most, *in populos*. Aldus has *prima*; *Rom.* in the text obscurely *patria*, in the margin *propria*; the other manuscripts and editions have *patria virtute*, which is correct.

604. *Daventr.* has *Oblatusque ibidem mox daemonis*; Aldus, *Oblatusque ibidem nox daemonis*; *Ott.* and *Rom.*, *Oblatusque ibidem est, quem daemonis*; *Reg.*, with many printed editions, *Oblatusque illi est, quem*. The latter perhaps arose to avoid shortening the second syllable of *ibidem*. But all our manuscripts, and the best editions, establish that Juvencus shortens it in book III, line 80: *Ille jubet cunctis ibidem convivia poni*, although some even there substitute *illic* or *itidem* for *ibidem*. In the poem of Claudianus Mamercus, or Mamertus, also attributed to Paulinus of Nola, line 84: *Cognosces ibidem, ne pergas tradere fatis*. Vossius, part I of *De arte grammatica*, book II, chapter 20, thought this Juvencus line should be restored as: *Oblatusque ibi mox, quem*. Wasius, *Senarii*, chapter 15, demonstrates from Plautus that *ibidem* may be shortened.

[Note: Col. 0195D]

585. CHAPTER XXIII. The healing of the man’s withered hand. Matthew 12:9 ff.; Mark 3:1; Luke 6:6. *Conventiculum*, and its plural *conventicula*, is the Latin equivalent of the Greek *synagoga* (“synagogue”).

589. *Per sabbata*: on the Sabbath day.

591. *Pecusculum* is a diminutive not found before Juvencus.

593. *Profundum*, used absolutely, means a deep place or pit.

595. *Tollens* should rouse our minds, raising them toward good works. Juvencus very often governs the same accusative with two verbs.

598. CHAPTER XXIV. A man possessed by a demon, blind and mute, is healed; and those who think he acts through the prince of demons are refuted. Matthew 12:14 ff.; Mark 3:22 ff.; Luke 11:15.

601. *Molimina*: see the variant reading on line 18 of this book.

604. *Daemonis horrida virtus*: compare book I, line 420, *vis livida*, of a demon.

[Col. 0197B] 605. Aldus has *vivere pene*, with *pene* meaning “almost,” or rather “scarcely,” as Spaniards say *apenas*, perhaps derived from this adverb. In some people’s opinion *paene* is more correctly spelled. *Rom.* perhaps refers to this with *vivere pone*. Most have *vivere poenae*, which suits the sense and is more clearly explained by the following line. *Poelm.* among the variants, and Basilius, have *afflixit amare*, which seems alien to Juvencus’ hand.

608. *Reg.* has *Pharisaeae cognoscunt pectora plebis*; the others, *pharisaeae cognovit factio gentis*, which better resembles Juvencus’ style.

614. Fabricius has *distractio*; *Reg.*, *divulsio*, but something else stood there earlier, and *divisio* is offered among the variants. Most editions and manuscripts have *divisio*.

615. *Rom.* has *Diruptis*; the others *Disruptis*. Both *dirumpo* and *disrumpo* are customarily written and may be written.
