617. *Rom.*, not badly, has *repugnet* for *repugnat*. Above, *labentur*.

619. *Reg.* has *aggressus*, as though *aggrediens*; the others *aggressor*, which Omeisius calls a rare word, used by no ancient author. But he is mistaken: Ulpian often uses it in the *Digest*, specifically for a robber or plunderer, book XLVII, title 9, law 3. Nevertheless, I prefer *aggressus*. *Rom.* has *nobis*; correct *nodis*.

620. Aldus and Basilius have *et facilis* for *ut facilis*. Matthew 12:29 reads: “Or how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he has first bound the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.” This supports Aldus’s reading. Reuschius too would prefer *et facilis veniet*.

623. The manuscripts and most editions have *aberrat*; Aldus and Basilius, *oberrans*; *Torn.*, *oberrat*. Reuschius chooses *oberrat*, that is, wanders here and there, and rejects *aberrat*. Westhemerus incorrectly has *cogentibus* in the text, and *cogendis* in the margin.

624. *Reg.* and *Ott.* have *Dissicet*, which recalls *Rom.*’s *Dissitet*. More printed editions have *Disjicit*; Aldus, *Disjicet*; Basilius, *Dejiciet*, contrary to the metre. Matthew 12:30: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” The old Colbert manuscript version in Sabatier reads: “And whoever does not collect with me disperses.” I therefore retain *Disjicit*, though I do not deny that *Dissicit* may also be written, as it appears in many old copies of other writers. On *dissicit* or *disicit* with one *s*, for which some write *dissecat*, see the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 97, and hymn 2 of the *Peristephanon*, line 209; and Priscian, book XIV, p. 1002 of Putsch’s edition.

625. *Rom.* has *horror*; retain *error*, in the sense “sin.”

629. *Rom.* has *Ingeret*; *Reg.*, *Ingerat*; the others, *Ingerit*. *Ingeret* or *Ingerat* seems preferable, from Matthew 12:32: “And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven.” So at line 625, *fuerit*, and line 631, *violabitur*. In *Ott.* the first hand had *relinqui*, corrected to *remitti*.

630. Sabatier printed only *tantum a quocumque* and, among the variants, *tantum cuicumque*, which alone I find in manuscripts and editions; *Rom.* incorrectly has *cujuscumque*. It is a characteristic phrase of Juvencus: a dative is used for the ablative of agency with a passive verb. *Cuicumque* for *a quocumque* is indeed a fairly common usage, at least among late writers.

[Note: Col. 0197C]

605. Pliny, book XVI, chapter 1: “Fortune spares many as a punishment,” taken from Laberius: “Fortune is accustomed to spare many as a punishment.” Paulinus, *On the Death of Celsus*, line 569: “For them life will be to die without end, and death to live in punishments.” Juvencus, book I, line 784: *Vitamque tenet jam poena superstes*, “and punishment, surviving, holds life,” for “surviving life,” by hypallage, as Omeisius explains.

610. *Nequitiae vires*: the other demons.

615. *Medullis*: from the comparison of a kingdom with the human body. Maximus of Tyre, discourse 41, also elegantly compares a city with the human body.

616. *Daemone atro*: above, lines 45 and 439.

622. In his commentary Fabricius explains *duellum* as a conflict between two persons, which this line confirms. But Juvencus uses *duellum* simply for “war,” when he says *in fronte duelli*, namely in the enemy’s front line; this is the true sense of *duellum*. The ancients sometimes used *du* for *b*; this usage remained in *duellum*, and both *bellum* and *duellum* are said. Later writers began to restrict *duellum* to war between two persons, and this sense passed into the vernacular languages.

623. Juvencus’ interpretation should be noted. Matthew merely says: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Juvencus rightly explains it of the flocks which the Lord had come to gather.

627. The Holy Spirit is torn by words uttered from a mad mind when his works are attributed to a demon; this is what the Jews did when they said that Christ cast out demons through Beelzebub, prince of demons. This wrongdoing is so great that it is scarcely ever, and only with the greatest difficulty, forgiven; since it admits of no excuse such as is usual in other sins, it does not by its nature deserve pardon. This is the sense in which the Saviour’s words must be understood. Others explain them differently.

628. *Sive* is formed from *si* and *vel*, and in fact is sometimes used for *vel si*, “or if”; that meaning suits this passage.

> Free from guilt. But now I, sovereign over all the Sabbaths,  
> Will keep them voluntarily under the law’s authority.  
> Then, after saying these things, he enters their synagogue.  
> At the entrance he immediately sees a young man,  
> Whose withered hand hung uselessly from his shoulder.  
> But then, testing him with deceitful words,  
> They ask whether it is lawful to bring healing on the Sabbaths,  
> So that the penalty for violating the law might remain.  
> Christ replies: If your little sheep should perhaps fall  
> Into a pit, surely you would pass beyond the Sabbath’s rest  
> Of the law and lift the worthless animal from the broken-down depth.  
> How much greater, then, should the healing of human beings  
> Rouse and kindle our minds toward good works!  
> Come, then, young man, stretch out your sound right hand.  
> At the word, the healed man extended both palms.  
> At this sign, which scarcely any reverence  
> Could raise with fitting honor before the astonished people,  
> They loudly proclaim in their hostile councils that he must be destroyed.  
> Perceiving the schemes of the leaders, Christ departs  
> And applies healing, granted by his ancestral power,  
> To the various maladies of the people.  
> A man was brought there whom the dreadful power of a demon  
> Had wanted to live deprived of tongue and sight  
> And to be food for his own torments.  
> When he had been cured and was vigorous in sight and voice,  
> The blind faction of the Pharisaic people recognized  
> That he had done this with the aid of the demon  
> Who alone, as prince of the demons, held  
> The powers of wickedness under his dominion.  
> But Christ opens their hearts to the truth  
> And refutes them with convincing words:  
> If a kingdom, divided into two parts, should gape apart,  
> And division, split against itself, should fight,  
> Everything will quickly fall, its inner parts torn apart.  
> And if a dreadful demon is driven out by a dark demon,  
> It is divided against itself and fights with hostile power.  
> Who could carry off prey from a strong man’s house  
> Unless he first attacked and bound the arms of its guardians  
> With cords, so that the seizure of the prey might be easy?  
> Whoever is separated from my weapons is not my soldier;  
> He will stand as an enemy in the opposing battle-line.  
> Whoever wanders free from gathering my flocks  
> Scatters my sheep’s pasture along the pathless ways.  
> But whatever human error there may be concerning all these things  
> Can be forgiven—only let the Holy Spirit never be torn  
> By words poured forth from an irrational mind.

If anyone hurls abuse in a frenzy against the Son of Man,

even these sins can be forgiven.

[630] But whoever profanes the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199B]

632. *Reg.*, “he will be burned by fire,” a reading published by Fabricius, which pleases me because it agrees more closely with Matthew XII, 32: “But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” Others read: “Now and forever he will be burned by fire in punishments.”

633. *Rom.*, *venenifici*; others, *veneniferi*, which is more Latin and is used by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, verse 85. Fabricius has printed, incorrectly, *suae* for *saeva*.

634. *Ott.*, first hand, *mitiscere*; second hand, *mitescere*.

635. *Reg.*, *promuntur congrua justis*.

637. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and *Bas.* transmit this verse: “By the merits of their words life will be given before the Judge,” and omit the following verse. *Ott.* alone has: “By the merits of their words punishment will be given before the Judge”; above it has *poena*, and at the beginning of the page the same verse is written with the word *poena*. This single verse, with *sub judice poena*, appears in *Torn.* In *Reg.* there are these two: “By the merits of their words life will come before the Judge— / By the merits of their words punishment will be given before the Judge.” In *Daventr.*, with the order reversed: “By the merits of their words punishment will come before the Judge— / By the merits of their words life will be given before the Judge,” but incorrectly *sub indice vita*. *Poelm.*, *Hadam.*, and Fabr.: “By the merits of their words life will be given before the Judge— / By the merits of their words punishment will come before the Judge.” Matthew XII, 37: “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Hence the reading of *Reg.* or *Hadam.* is to be preferred. Besides, repetitions of this kind were frequent among ancient poets.

639. *Bas.*, *faciat*: read *faciet*.

641. *Ottob.*, first hand, *tribuit*; second hand, *tribuet*, as in the other manuscripts and printed editions.

642. *Ott.*, *Ald.*, and *Bas.*, *emortua*. *Reg.*, *Hadam.*, and most printed editions, *demortua*. *Rom.*, incorrectly, “The Begetter [Genitor] his dead bodies.” *Demortuus* is Cicero’s word; nevertheless, I would not object to *emortua* in Juvencus. On this word, if desired, compare what I noted on Dracontius, Book II, verse 623. It is customary among our Christian poets to lengthen a short syllable because of the caesura; perhaps, to avoid this, some scribe changed *Genitor emortua* into *Genitor demortua*. But since we can support *demortua* by the authority of manuscript *Reg.*, we retain it willingly. *Ott.*, *reddet*; others, *reddit*.

644. *Reg.*, *ad lumen surgentia*. *Ald.*, *ducit*, which was in *Ott.*, and from which *ducet* seems to have arisen; this is the common reading. If the manuscripts allowed it, I would read: “The bodies that he wills, rising to the heavenly powers, he leads,” from John V, 21: “So also the Son gives life to those whom he wills.” Reuschius admits that the Greek text has the present tense, but thinks that Juvencus referred it to the final judgment.

645. *Reg.*, *Rom.*, and *Poelm.*, instead of *d. s.*, *quemquam vestri*. *Ott.*, *quicquam vestri*. Several printed editions, *quemquam vestrum*. *Reg.*, *quaerit*; the others, *quaeret*. *Quaerit* is closer to the words of the Gospel. John V, 22: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

650. Fabr., *figit*, with *Poelm.* and *Ottob.*, first hand; from this *figet* seems to have arisen in *Ott.*, which is found in the other manuscripts and printed editions. John says: “Who hears my word and believes him who sent me.” Reuschius, following the sacred text, and abandoning the change of tense that he had admitted in the preceding passages, accepted the present instead of the future. It makes no difference that the following verse has *patescent*. Thus Latins like to speak: “If you give, you will receive.”

651. Codex *Un.*, “Soon the gifts of the one who sends me will be revealed.” Reuschius restored from the manuscripts *dona patescent*, which our manuscripts—*Rom.*, *Reg.*, and *Ott.*—support. The old editions have *dona videbit*. Juvencus omitted the dative *ei*, “to him”; this is familiar in other writers as well.

652. In *Ottob.*, first hand, *Aeternumque* seems to have stood; as an adverbial form, it would not be objectionable.

654. *Torn.* and *Rom.*, *lumina*, a reading that Schoettgen dislikes. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *limina*. Nevertheless, I will not conceal that at this place, verse 519, Juvencus uses *lumine lucis*.

655. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, and *Rom.*, *tempus cum mortua*. *Ald.*, *Hadam.*, *Poelm.*, and Fabricius, *tempus quo mortua*. *Cum* seems more suited to the Gospel text than *quo*. John V, 25: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God”; and in the old version, from the Cambridge manuscript, apud Sabatier: “For the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear,” etc. Nevertheless, *quo* is not unsuitable; some Fathers present the passage in a similar way.]

[Note: [Col. 0199D]

631. Horace and Ovid use the word *irrevocatis*. Juvencus uses *irrevocatis* for *irrevocabilibus*, “irrevocable.”

635. *Thesauris justis*: the Evangelist says, “from the good treasure.”

636. *Venenum* is often taken in a bad sense; but in its primary meaning the word is neutral and can be understood in either sense. *Digest* L, title 16, *On the Meaning of Words*, law 236: “When someone says *venenum*, he must add whether it is bad or good; for medicines too are poisons.” Cicero, *For Cluentius*, chapter 54, from the ancient law: “Whoever made or shall have made a bad poison.”

637. Sabatier observes that Juvencus omitted Matthew’s verse 36: “But I say to you that for every idle word which people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.” But Juvencus sufficiently embraces this very thought in this and the following verse.]

[Col. 0200D] 639. CHAPTER XXV. Jesus tells the Jews that whatever the Father has done, the Son will also do; that the hour is now at hand when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and many other things. John V, 19. *Sectabitur* means the same as “will do,” “will imitate,” or “will carry out.”

645. The absolute ablative *se judice* should be noted, that is, “with himself as judge.” Arntzenius offers several similar examples from Avitus, Arator, and Fortunatus in his notes on Sedulius IV, verse 8, *Se judice praestat*. In inscriptions, *se vivo, fecit* is not uncommon. *Quaerit* means “summons for questioning” or “inquires into” someone. This meaning of *quaero* is quite common; hence *quaestio* and *quaesitores*.

648. *Repulsus honore* means “repelled from honor.” Ovid, *Amores* III, elegy 11, verse 9: “So often repelled from the doors,” etc. Add Horace, *Satires* II, satire 7: “And, repelled from the doors— / He drenches him with cold water.”]

But the Holy Spirit, when profaned by anyone’s blasphemous frenzy of words,

[Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199B]

will, by irrevocable

punishments, will now and forever be burned in fire.

When will the savage offspring of the venom-bearing serpent

be able to grow mild through the sweet fruit of speech?

[635] For good things are drawn forth from good treasures for the righteous,

and evil poisons proceed from a deadly mouth.

222 By the merits of their words, life will come before the Judge;

by the merits of their words, punishment will be given before the Judge.

Whatever the Begetter will do, the Son will carry out in all things.

[640] For the Begetter reveals to the Son all things that must be seen,

and thereafter will grant him greater miracles of mighty deeds.

For just as the Begetter restores dead bodies

to the bright light of life, so the Son will lead

[Col. 0200A] whatever bodies he wills, rising to the heavenly realms.

[645] 223 Nor does the Begetter, with himself as judge, inquire into any of you,

but has given these rights of inquiry throughout the world to the Son,

so that equal glory may remain with the Son and with the Father.

For if the Son is rejected by you in honor,

with equal wickedness you will despise the Begetter.

[650] But grace establishes faith in our message;

soon the gifts of the Begetter who sends me will be revealed.

His present constancy will also grant eternal life.

He does not undergo judgment, but departs far away

from black death and, vigorous with light, advances to its threshold.

[655] The time will come when dead bodies

[Col. 0201A] [Note: [Col. 0201B]

657. *Rom.*, “The Begetter possesses life for himself”; others, “The Begetter possesses life in himself.”

659. *Reg.*, *Rom.*, and *Poelmann.*, instead of *d. s.*, *In terras*, which Reuschius published because John wishes to indicate the guilty person, not the place of judgment. *Ott.*, with most printed editions, *In terris*, which Gallandius retained. Some punctuate it thus: *jus dicere jussit. In terras hominis*, or *In terris hominis*. *Ald.*, *Daventr.*, *Bas.*, *Torn.*, and Gallandius, *cum corpore*. Our manuscripts, with *Hadamar.* and many other printed editions, *de corpore*. The sense is the same.

662. These two verses, *Justorumque* and *Judicioque*, had been omitted in *Ott.*, but were supplied by the same old hand [Col. 0201C] at the bottom of the page.

663. *Torn.*, *Judicioque gravi*: correct to *Judicioque*.

664. *Torn.*, with manuscripts *Reg.* and *Rom.*, *tribuit*; *Ott.*, *tribuat*; several printed editions, *tribuet*. *Reg.*, *voluntas*; others, *potestas*. Either reading can be defended. John V, 30: “I can do nothing of myself. As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me.” *Tribuit* is preferable to *tribuet*; *tribuat* must be rejected.

668. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, *Daventr.*, and *Ald.*, *Falsa loquar, aliusque itidem quia*. So *Rom.*, but there *itidem* is less good than elsewhere. *Hadam.*, *Poelm.*, and Fabr.: *Falsa loqui possem: ast alius quia*. So *Torn.*, but with *est* for *ast*. Sabatier published: *Falsa loqui possem: est alius, qui testis habetur*, I do not know whether by chance or deliberately; for in the manuscripts and printed editions I find only *quia testis*. The words in John V, 31 are: “If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true.” Therefore I retain *Falsa loquar*. Immediately in the following verse: “There is another who bears witness of me, and I know that the witness which he bears of me is true.” Perhaps one should read: *Falsa loquar, alius itidem quia testis habetur*, with the conjunction *-que* after *alius* omitted, since it is superfluous. By the rules of caesura, the second syllable in *loquar* and the third in *alius* may be lengthened; scribes who failed to notice this corrupted the true reading.

669. *Ald.*, *Pro vobis*: correct to *Pro nobis*. In *Bas.*, *tum vero* is an error for *temnere*. *Reg.*, *semper* for *recte*, not badly. *Rom.*, *temnere talia*, but corruptly *tenere* for *temnere*. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *talia temnere*.

672. *Ott.*, *testes*, correctly emended there to *testis*.

673. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and Fabr., *demisit*; others, *dimisit*, with the same meaning.

676. *Rom.*, *poterat*; *Ott.*, with most others, *poterit*, instead of *d. s.*, *potuit*. *Potuit* is correct; but I suspected *potis est*, a phrase which some scribes, not understanding it, replaced with another reading in certain manuscript copies. John V, 38 indicates the present tense: “And you do not have his word remaining in you.”

679. *Reg.*, *Perpetuam cuncti vita quam*, with a gloss at *putatis*: *vobis*, which is either obscure or corrupt. *Rom.*, *Perpetuam cuncti vitam qua ferre putatis*. This agrees sufficiently with John V, 39: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life.” The common reading comes to the same thing: *Perpetuam cunctis vitam quam ferre putatis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0201D]

656. “They will receive, hear, and understand.” This is an obvious meaning of *accipio* in Cicero and others. *Tenebunt*: “they will obtain,” “they will attain.” The usage of *teneo* extends astonishingly far. Here it means “they will possess.” Therefore they will possess life together with the voice, together with the utterance, as above, verse 597.

659. John, at the cited passage: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” Christ is the Son of Man because he was born of the Virgin Mary, and therefore came from the body of a human being.

663. *Miseros pravos*: compare Book IV, verse 304: “The wretched wicked will be pierced by eternal punishment.” See the variant reading at verse 237 of this book: “The wretched proud fled.”

666. John: “Because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

669. *Talia temnere*: the calumnies of the Jews and the false speeches, or false judgments, of people concerning me.

[Col. 0202D] 671. *Testatio*: the utterance of testimony. The word is frequent in the books of the jurists.

672. *Adhaeret*: “he stands by me,” “he supports my side.” Reuschius calls it a most elegant metaphor.

675. John, at the cited passage: “Nor have you seen his appearance.” The old version in some manuscripts, and certain Fathers, have it somewhat differently: “nor his figure,” or “nor his form,” or “nor his face.”

676. *Per vestra sedere pectora*: “to sit in your breasts,” “to dwell in your breasts,” “to be implanted in them.”

677. John: “For the one whom he sent, him you do not believe.” The substantive *substantia* has various uses in Juvencus. See Book I, verse 416. Cyprian, *On the Advantage of Patience*, p. 216, calls patience the *substantia* of enduring and bearing.]

224 They will receive our word, and with the voice they will possess life.

For just as the Begetter possesses life in himself,

so he grants life to the Son and ordered him to pronounce judgment

on earth, because he came from the body of a human being.

[660] Nor should it seem astonishing to you that all bodies

should rise from their own tombs at the hearing of a voice,

that the souls of the righteous should be joined to a restored body,

and that the wretched wicked should rise for severe judgment.

Nor does my own power alone grant judgment to me;

[665] for all things are commanded by the will of the Begetter,

who ordered me to seek out justice on earth.

For if I rise as my own witness on my own behalf,

[Col. 0202A] I shall speak falsely; and another, likewise, is regarded as a witness.

225 On our behalf, therefore, it is right for me to disregard such things.

[670] For, by the true signs of my deeds, my present testimony

shines more clearly than every light.

The Begetter, granting such things, stands by me as witness,

the one who sent me to set his commands upon the earth.

For you have never been able to grasp his voice,

[675] nor has he allowed you to see his own appearance.

Nor could his speech settle within your breasts,

because there is no substance of faith in you.

Let the reading of the ancient writings be sought by you,

the eternal life which you think you can possess.

[680] [Col. 0203A] [Note: [Col. 0203B]

682. Manuscripts *Rom.*, *Reg.*, and *Ott.*, *Contingat gratia vitae*. Printed editions, *contingant gaudia vitae*.

684. *Reg.*, *Rom.*, and *Ottobon.*, *Namque ego quod summi*; this very reading seems to have been intended by Aldus in the joining of the letters. Others, *Namque ego, qui summi*.

685. Our manuscripts, with *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and *Daventr.*, *Respuitur vobis*, with a gloss in *Reg.*, namely, “my preaching.” Or understand it as “it is rejected by you,” namely, that I came, etc. Others have *Respuor a vobis*, which agrees with John V, 43: “I came in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me.” *Poelm.* and Fabr., *veniet sed dyscolus alter*; so *Ald.*, *Daventr.*, *Bas.*, Badius, and *Hadam.*, who write *discolus*. Our manuscripts, *Rom.* and *Ott.*, second hand, or, instead of *d. s.*, with *Torn.* and Reuschius, *veniet sed discolor alter*, which is more pleasing, as though meaning “varied,” “different,” or “unlike.” The cited chapter of John, verse 43, has: “If another comes in his own name, him you will receive.” There is no place here for the word *dyscolus*, “wicked” or “difficult,” which Forcellini rejected as barbarous. In the Vatican parchments *Reg.* and *Ottob.*, first hand: *veniet sed decolor alter*, as though “ugly.” So also one Cambridge manuscript.

687. Printed editions and manuscripts, *Alternae in vobis*. The true reading in my view is *Alternae vobis captatur*, as in verse 683: “The glory of earthly praise is not sought by me.” The sacred text says: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” Perhaps: *Alternis vobis*.

689. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and *Hadamar.*, *Nec vos*; *Poelm.* with others, *Ne vos*, instead of *d. s.*, *Nec vos*. Choose whichever you prefer.

691. Some write *Moyses*, others *Moses*. *Ald.* and *Poelm.*, instead of *d. s.*, *servastis*; most have *servatis*.

693. *Reg.*, *Mosei*; *Ott.*, *Moysei*; *Rom.*, *Moysi*; others, *Mosi*, which appears especially in the printed editions.

697. *Ott.*, *Polluta malis*, published by Fabricius after *Daventr.*; the others, *Polluta magis*. Matthew: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign,” etc. Koenigius conjectured *Polluta malis* as well, from Book IV, verse 564: “Polluted by evils, let Religion rise into anger.”

700. *Reg.*, *absumit*: retain *absumpsit*. *Ott.*, *penetrabilibus*; likewise *Reg.*, but in this passage it has been correctly emended to *penetralibus*.

701. *Ald.*, *diversa*, which seems to be an error for *demersa*.

[Col. 0204C] 702. *Poelm.*, *Advenit tempus*; *Rom.* with most others, *Adveniet tempus*, which agrees with the words of Matthew XII, 41: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation,” etc. Hence *surgit* in *Rom.* must be rejected, and *surget* read with the others.

704. *Rom.*, *Nec istam*: read *Haec istam*.

705. *Rom.*, *Sed maris*: correct to *Quod maris*.

706. *Bas.*, *Communita*, incorrectly, for *commonita*.

707. *Rom.*, *Sic et*; others, *Hic et*.

709. In *Ott.*, *surgit* has properly been changed to *surget*, in accordance with the sense of the Gospel. In *Rom.*, in the margin, *auras* is given as a different reading or correction for *oras*; but the others prefer *oras*.]

[Note: [Col. 0203C]

688. The sacred text: “And the glory that is from God alone you do not seek.” The Cambridge manuscript: “And you do not seek the glory from the one God.” Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book X: “And you do not seek the honor of him who is the only God.” Juvencus favors this reading.

[Col. 0203D] 690. John: “In whom you hope.”

692. *Si crederet error*: “If you, who now err because you do not believe, were to believe, you would also believe us, and therefore error would cease.”

694. CHAPTER XXVI. To the Pharisees asking for a sign, he gives the sign of Jonah and of the Ninevites. Matthew XII, 38ff.; Luke XI, 29; Mark VIII, 11.

695. *Comitor* takes the dative, as in Book IV, verse 219: “And the wise company attends only the bridegroom.” Consult the variant readings at that verse.

699. *Cetus*, genitive *ceti*, singular; *cete* in the plural.

703. *Gens hominum*: the Ninevites. Omeisius observes that the Rabbis count the Ninevites among the nations of the earth. *In fletum dedita*: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 384: “And gives his spirit over to mourning.”

[Col. 0204C] 704. *Crimine*: “accusation”; for *crimen* is not rarely used in this sense.

706. Those who wish to obtain something through tears generally weep prostrate or cast down. Caesar, *Gallic War* VII, chapter 26: “The matrons suddenly rushed into public view, and, weeping, threw themselves at the feet of their own people”; and *Civil War* III, chapter 98: “With palms outstretched and prostrate on the ground, weeping, they begged him for safety.” Reuschius cites from Livy: “To throw oneself into womanly tears”; but explains it as “he turned back,” “recalled his mind to the Lord,” or “in his mind looked back to the Lord.” *Reflecto* properly means “to bend back.”

707. John: “And behold, something greater than Jonah is here.” Hilary, on Psalm II: “And behold, one greater than Jonah is here.” But the Greek text makes clear that *hic* in the Latin versions is not a pronoun but an adverb, meaning “in this place.” Juvencus therefore correctly renders it by an adverb and explains it: “Here also greater things than Jonah’s warnings are commanded.”

709. The Old Latin version and the Vulgate consistently have *regina austri*, “queen of the south.” The same wind that is called *auster* in Latin is known in Greek by the corresponding term, which Latin poets frequently use. What Juvencus says, *vitales surget in oras*, the sacred text gives as “she will rise in judgment.”]

226 This reading also bears witness to our gift.

Yet you do not dare draw nearer to us,

lest the grace of true life come to you.

The glory of earthly praise is not sought by me.

For I have come in the name of the highest Begetter,

[685] and you reject me; but another, unlike me, will come,

supported by his own name, and your people will follow him.

You seek the glory of fame from one another,

and avoid seeking the praise of the One alone.

Nor will I accuse you before the Begetter; but there

[690] the one whom your hope now celebrates will be your accuser,

227 Moses, whom you preserve without any honor of faith.

For if your error, because of which you do not believe, believed his writings,

it would also believe us, whose writings Moses’ writings frequently mention.

Then these words follow in reply to the scribes:

[695] Undoubted faith will accompany these utterances,

if power confirms them by unmistakable signs.

Then he said: “A generation polluted by evils seeks

signs for itself; but signs will stand for future events.

For as long as the prophet remained beneath the hollow breast of the whale,

[700] so long will the offspring of man remain submerged

in the deep recesses of the earth.”

The time will come when the race of men, restored to life,

will rise, devoted to weeping over its own deeds.

It will condemn this people on a deserved charge,

[705] 228 because, warned by the voice of the prophet rising from the depths of the sea,

it turned in tears, prostrate, toward the Lord.

[Col. 0204B] Here too greater things than Jonah’s warnings are commanded,

yet the impious people, with savage hearts, despise the light.

And the queen of the South will rise in the life-giving regions.

[710] [Col. 0205A] [Note: [Col. 0205A]

710. *Reg.* and *Ott.*, *speciem*, instead of *d. s.*, *specimen*, with *Rom.* and the printed editions. *Speciem* can be defended, but *specimen*, “example,” is preferable. In *Rom.*, *plebes* appears to have been corrected to *proles*. The others have *plebes*.

712. *Reg.*, *Ut Salomona regem*: the law of meter prevents this; it may perhaps be better to read *Ut Salomon regem*. But since the same *Reg.*, instead of *d. s.*, transmits *Ut Salomona pium*, in agreement with the other manuscripts and printed editions, we should certainly retain it and understand *pium* as “peaceful” or “mild.” I discussed this meaning of the word more fully in the notes on Dracontius, Book I, verse 11. Some write *Solomona*, and shortly afterward *Solomone*, as also occurs in certain old copies of the Bible, evidently from the Greek text. Compare the variant readings at Book I, verse 680.

714. *Reg.*, *Et tamen obtuso caecatur pectore plebes*. Others, *Et tamen obtusae caecantur pectora plebis*; but in *Ott.* it is written *obtunsae*, which amounts to the same thing. I would not object to: *Et tamen obtusa caecantur pectora plebis*. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 571: “The Carthaginians do not carry hearts so dull.”

715. In *Ott.* there was *expulsis*, from which *expulsus* was correctly formed.

716. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, *Rom.*, *purgato pectore*. *Ott.*, instead of *d. s.*, *Daventr.*, *Ald.*, *purgato corpore*. *Rom.*, *purgato e pectore*. *Poelm.* and other printed editions, *purgato e corpore*. Codex *Un.*: “Whom the holy breath cleanses, issuing from the body,” where perhaps *proluto e corpore* should be read, as Reuschius conjectures; he nevertheless denies that a satisfactory sense can be extracted from it, to say nothing of the pleonasm.

717. *Torn.*, *venenatus*; Aldus likewise published this, but in the *Emendata* correctly changed it to *venenatis*, which is much more elegant.

719. Aldus with other printed editions: “If, burning, it finds no rest in a peaceful seat.” Manuscripts *Reg.*, *Ott.*, and *Rom.*: “Nor, burning, did it find for itself rest in a peaceful seat”; but *Reg.* has *placitae* for *placidae*. The reading of our codices agrees more closely with the Gospel’s words, Matthew XII, 43: “He travels through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” Reuschius prefers *Si* in the sense of “after,” with *cum*, because Juvencus concluded in rhetorical form what Christ expressed in simple grammatical diction.

[Col. 0206B] 720. *Reg.* repeats *suetae quaerens habitacula*, but corruptly has *habicula* for *habitacula*; all the others have *repetit suetae sitiens habitacula*.

721. In *Ott.* there seems first to have been *Ac si* for *At si*. *Rom.*, *Et si*.

723. *Poelm.*, *Had.*, *similis*; *Rom.* with most printed editions, *similes*.

724. Printed editions, *homini*. Manuscripts *Rom.* and *Reg.*, *hominis*; this may also have been in *Ottob.*, where *homini* now appears. I prefer *homini*. *Rom.*, *penetrat qui viscera serpens*: retain *penetratque in viscera serpens*.

725. *Ott.*: *Sic genus hoc vero mentis cum degener errat*; others, *sensu* for *mentis*. I suspect *hoc veri sensu cum*. Reuschius found in his manuscripts *etiam vero mentis*, a reading he calls not inelegant, namely, “from what is true, from truth.” Before this verse, *Sic genus* is followed in *Rom.* by another anomalous verse: *Sic erit haec generatio deteriora priorum*. The same verse, with only the difference *Sic ista generatio*, etc., occurs in *Reg.* after this verse beginning *Sic genus*. Perhaps a verse was added by the poet to explain Matthew XII, 45: “And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” For what follows, *Sic erit et generationi huic pessimae*, is contained in these two verses, *Sic genus* and *Vincula*.

727. *Poelm.*, instead of *d. s.*, *Atque haec*; in the text, *Atque ea*. *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and *Rom.*, *dum*; others, *cum*.

729. *Ott.*, first hand, *misceri*; correctly changed to *miscere*.]

[Note: [Col. 0205C]

710. *Ad specimen*: a comparison is made with her. Omeisius explains it as “with regard to her,” “as a test,” or “as an example.”

[Col. 0205D] 711. Matthew says: “Because she came from the ends of the earth.” Juvencus identifies Libya. Many relate that this queen, named Nicaula, went from Ethiopia to Jerusalem. Others say that she was queen of Arabia and report that the Arabs called her Balkis. Juvencus follows the former opinion and understands all Africa by the name Libya, as Virgil does, *Georgics* I, verse 240: “When the world rises toward Scythia and the lofty Rhipaean heights, Libya slopes down and is pressed toward the southern winds.” From the Books of Kings it is established only that she was called the queen of Sheba.

713. Matthew: “And behold, something greater than Solomon is here,” where *hic* is an adverb, as shortly before, verse 707. Juvencus could indeed have written: “She would hear: here is a power greater than Solomon.” The sense would be nearly the same as it is now. But if Juvencus had written the verse in the other way I mentioned, copyists ignorant of the matter would nevertheless have corrupted it.

716. *Turbat*: “drives out,” a simple verb used for a compound. *Sanctus flatus*, “holy breath,” because Christians customarily blow upon demons during exorcisms. On this see the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 10, *Peristephanon*, verse 920: “He blows upon them, as though he saw the demons themselves.”

720. *Suetae mentis*, as in Book I, verse 150: “Soon they also penetrate the accustomed recesses of the mind.”

722. *Ridentia*: a familiar but elegant metaphor.

723. *Glomerando*: compare the note at verse 579. *Furores*: “more wicked spirits,” as Matthew says, or “furious spirits,” just as *scelus* can mean “wicked” for “wicked person.”

727. CHAPTER XXVII. He teaches that those are his mother and brothers who hear and do the word of God. Matthew XII, 46ff.; Mark III, 31; Luke VIII, 20.

728. *Pro foribus*: consult the variant readings at verse 299 of this book.

728. “And outside they ask to exchange words with him face to face.” Matthew: “They stood outside, seeking to speak with him.”]

While he was repeatedly uttering these life-giving sayings to the peoples, his mother stood there outside the doors with his brothers and asked to speak with him face to face. Then he sent back these words in reply to his mother’s message:

“Here with me sit my mother and my kindred bodies. For whoever fulfils the Father’s will joins a body related by blood to mine and is counted under the name of my mother and my family.”

[735] Jesus, the light of the world, goes forth from the temple

and sits at the edge of the sea, on the shore of the land.

Countless throngs of people flowed there.

He, climbing into the lofty boat nearest the shore,

sets forth these words for the crowd filling the coast:

[740] [Col. 0208A] Behold, the sower entrusts seeds to his own field.

They fall upon different soil, and according to the quality

of the places they bear their allotted result. For wherever the trampled earth of the roads

is compacted beneath feet into a solid surface,

232 the seeds, lying bare, give prey to the birds of the air.

[745] But where rocks are covered with a very thin layer of dust,

the grain indeed brings forth the green growth of a shoot;

but because no substance lies beneath the dry clods,

the threads of its roots wither when heat has set in.

Soon all the tips of the ears slide into death,

and other seeds fall upon rough ground:

here the crop rises more swiftly than from thorns

[Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209B]

752. *Bas.*, *augens*: this must be emended to *angens*.

753. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and Fabr., *dantur quae*; others, *quae dantur*.

754. In *Reg.* and *Ott.* the first hand seems to have written *frequentant*. But the sense requires *frequentat*. In *Rom.* *frequentant* is quite clear, though with this punctuation: *cui laeta frequentant—Incrementa sui, centeno copia foetu*.

755. *Torn.*, *centena*: read *centeno*, to satisfy both meter and sense.]

### 759

Rom., “having dismissed the believing crowd, he spoke.” Someone might suspect that *amota* (“having removed”) ought to be read. Later, at the end of the parable, a distinction is indeed made between the disciples and the crowd, verse 796: “Then he adds these things to the disciples and the crowd”; and more clearly, Book III, verses 74ff.: “When he sees the believing crowds gathered in a remote valley . . . .” The disciples advise Christ to dismiss the crowds. Reuschius in fact reads *amota* and judges that this is more correct according to the poet’s intention. Nevertheless, I would not dare change *admota* to *amota*, especially since what follows in the Gospel and in Juvencus does not suitably apply to a believing crowd, unless those who, at verse 772, “stand by with closed ears and heavy eyes,” are called believers. Juvencus often uses *plebs* and *populus* of the disciples. Compare Book II, verse 564; Book III, verse 494; Book IV, verse 52.

### 763

Reg., Rom., Poelm., for *d. s.*, “the lights of the mind” (*lumina mentis*). Ottob., “the thresholds of the mind” (*limina mentis*). Ald., together with most printed editions, “the thresholds of life” (*limina vitae*). “The lights of the mind” is more consistent with the Gospel’s meaning. Matthew 13:11: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; but to them it has not been given.” In other ancient versions: “to know the secrets of God,” “to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven.” Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 22: “To them it was given to know the secrets, which the people were not permitted to understand.” Koenigius prefers *limina vitae*, because *consistere adytis* (“to stand within the inner sanctuaries”) has preceded, and in Book IV, verse 443, Juvencus says: “If he had never touched the thresholds of life with his feet.”

### 764

Mss. Reg., Rom., Ott., with Ald. and Daventr., “If anyone has worth” (*Si quis habet dignus*). Hadam. and other printed editions, “If anyone has something worthy” (*Si quid habet dignus*). I prefer *Si quis*, on the basis of the passage cited above, Matthew 12: “For whoever has, to him it will be given.” In Reg. the verse is read: “If anyone has, worthy in merits, he will receive better things”; *mentis* (“of the mind”) seems to have been corrected to *meritis* (“in merits”).

### 768

All printed editions: “It is disclosed to the people” (*Promitur in populum*). Our mss. Reg. and Ott.: “He lightly touches the people” (*Praestringit populum*); Rom.: “He lightly grazes the people” (*Perstringit populum*). On the differing spelling *praestringo* and *prestringo*, I spoke in the note on Prudentius, verse 507 of the *Psychomachia*. Here *praestringit* means “he lightly touches,” as when one touches something in passing or brushes against it briefly, because the grace of the speech was not communicated fully to the people. Copyists, unaware of this meaning, transcribed the reading according to their own judgment as *Promitur in populum*. Schoettgenius and Reuschius print *Perstringit* or *Praestringit*, but explain it as “he dulls, blunts, or blinds.”

### 769

Ott., *recurrant* (“may they return”); this could be upheld only if *dicta* (“the things said”) were read instead of *dictum* (“the thing said”).

### 770

Ald., *populi mentis* (“of the people’s mind”); more correctly, *populi mentes* (“the minds of the people”).

### 771

In our mss. and in Ald. it is written *Obicibus*, not *Objicibus*.

### 775

Ald., Torn., Bas., *veterum* (“of the ancient”); others, *veteres* (“the ancient”). Rom., “the ancient, holy, and righteous prophets.”

### 776

The reading *optarunt cernere* (“they desired to see”), as it stands in Had., is not displeasing.

### Note: 752–776

**752.** In Reg. there is a gloss, *angens*—“strangling.” The increase of the thorns, strangling or choking, plainly destroys the crop. The same accusative, *frugem* (“the crop”), is governed both by the verb *internecat* (“destroys”) and by the participle *angens* (“strangling”); this is often observed in Juvencus. Barthius, *Adversaria* 35.19, column 1621, observes that in this verse of Juvencus *internecare* means “to kill” or “to destroy.” Prudentius uses the same verb, *Apotheosis*, preface 2, verse 49: “Lest the empty fiber of the stalk, torn away, should at once destroy the grain-bearing ear.” The same Barthius discusses *angens* in place of *suffocans* (“choking”) in book 24, chapter 19, column 1272ff. Columella, book 10, calls a plant *angens* (“choking”). Properly, *angere* means “to strangle” or “to choke,” but figuratively it is used for “to be distressed” or “to trouble.” Something similar occurs with *suggillo*, which means “I strangle” or “I choke,” and figuratively “I afflict with trouble” or “I constrain.” From this one understands what Luke 18:5 says: “Yet because this widow troubles me, I will vindicate her, lest by coming continually she wear me out.” Compare, if desired, Ducange under *suggillo*, and the note on Book III, verse 448.

**754.** *Pulchram segetem* (“a beautiful crop”): see the note on that epithet at verse 150.

**756.** *Gestat* has nearly the same meaning as *gerit* (“he bears”).

**761.** *Dei penetralia* (“the inner chambers of God”): Matthew has “the mystery of the kingdom of heaven.” In some mss. of the ancient Italic version: “the secrets of God,” or “the secrets of the kingdom of heaven.”

**766.** *Retentant* is a frequentative formed from *retineo* (“I retain”) and has the same meaning. It is also used for “I draw back” or “I take up again.”

**769.** *Recurrat* means “may it prove to be true.” See Book I, verse 215.

**770.** *Crassis objicibus* (“with thick obstacles”), from Matthew’s text: “For the heart of the people has grown dull,” etc. Apuleius, at the beginning of Book I of the *Metamorphoses*: “But you, with thick ears and an obstinate heart, reject things that perhaps are truly reported.”

**771.** Gloss in Reg.: *Objicibus*—“with obstacles of doubt.” Matthew has: “Lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn back, and I heal them.” Hence *munera vitae* (“the gifts of life”), that is, life.

**776.** *Clarent* means “they are manifest.” Book IV, verse 148: *clarebunt* (“they will shine”). I do not know why Koenigius calls it an ancient verb. Lucretius, Book VI, verse 937: “Which shines in the very first line.” Claudian, *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*, verse 191: “The coming power shone forth in Ascanius.” In another sense *clarere* means “to shine”; in another, “to be distinguished, celebrated, or renowned.”

### 777

Reusch., Ald., *quis sit* (“who he may be”); others, *qui sit*. Copyists sometimes did not double a letter *s* when it occurred at the end of one word and the beginning of the next, although it ought properly to be doubled, as Reuschius says.

### 778

Our mss. read *dimittit*; the printed editions variously have *dimittit* and *demittit*. Hadam., Fabr., Poelm., in the text, *in auras* (“into the breezes”); our mss., with Ald., *in aures* (“into the ears”). This is the genuine reading. Matthew 13:19: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes,” etc. This means to cast the Lord’s word into the outermost ears. For speech to be properly understood, it must penetrate the inner ears and not remain on the outside. In this sense Seneca, *On Anger* 1, final chapter: “Evil does not come from the depths, but clings, as they say, to the surface of the mind,” that is, it does not penetrate. Virgil, Book XII, verse 434: “And, grazing his kisses over the top of the helmet, he speaks.” Hence the proverb, “to taste something with the tips of one’s lips.” In explaining the same parable, Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, verse 1055: “He does not understand the Father’s heavenly law with the outermost ear, but at the same time prepares the crop and soil of his heart, so that his inward breast may shine no less with cultivation.” Consult the commentary on that passage.

### 779

Reg.: “Nor does a swift mind receive it,” with the gloss “burning with desire.” The same reading occurs in Rom. Reg.: *Nec sensus recipit* (“nor does understanding receive it”), which I understand as “with steady strength of understanding,” whether of inner hearing, or of the mind and intelligence. Matthew: “Everyone who hears the word of God and does not understand it.”

### 780

Reg.: “The demon will snatch away all of it from him.” Matthew has the present tense, “snatches away.”

### 781

The mss. and several printed editions: “This is like a field, hard, which brings forth shoots along a path”; this is a sound reading, for the seed that falls beside the road is indicated. Ald.: “Such is like a hard field, which produces shoots of grain.” The Basel edition agrees with Ald., but in it *qui* is missing.

### 785

Reg.: *mentem tribulatio cordis* (“tribulation of the heart [afflicts] the mind”), apparently written by someone who did not know what *strictura coercens* (“constraining compression”) meant, or who introduced a gloss into the text. The reading is nevertheless supported by Matthew’s Gospel text: “When tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately scandalized.” Properly, *strictura* is an unworked mass of iron hammered by a mallet; hence Prudentius uses it, *Against Symmachus* II, verse 286, for the striking of the glowing mass itself, and other writers metaphorically use it for any constriction or compression, as does Caelius Aurelianus, Book I of the *Acutae*, and elsewhere. In Juvencus, however, I think *tritura* (“threshing” or “grinding,” from the Greek θλῖψις, *thlipsis*, “tribulation”) should be restored from the Greek text.

### 786

Reg., Ottob., Rom., Poelm., for *d. s.*, *credita letho* (“entrusted to death”); old age and death are commonly attributed to plants. Others, with Ald. and Daventr., *credita farra* (“entrusted grain”).

### 792

In Reg. it now reads *stant viribus arva* (“the fields stand in strength”), but something else appears to have been erased.

### 793

Ott. clearly has *clara*; in Rom. and Ald. it is also written *clare*, not *clarae*, as found in most printed editions. *Clare*, or *clara*, is certainly preferable.

### 794

Rom., *animam* (“soul”); others, *animum* (“mind”). Reg. and Rom., *tractata*; the same reading was formerly in Ott., but here *tractante* (“handling”) has been printed with the editions.

### 795

Rom., *Centiplicemque*; this is also written for *Centuplicem*. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, final verse: “And the fruit enriches the fruitful field a hundredfold,” where some likewise write *centiplex*.

### 798

Poelm., erroneously *jacet* (“lies”) for *jacit* (“casts”).

### 799

Rom., *Quod post* (“which afterward”); others, *Sed post* (“but afterward”). Ald. and most printed editions, *subripiens* (“stealing away,” by lying in wait for the man) *saporem* (“the flavor”); Poelm., for *d. s.*, Torn., *hominum insidiando sapori* (“lying in wait for the taste of men”). Ott. and Rom., *hominum insidiando sopori* (“lying in wait for the sleep of men”); this is reflected in Reg., *hominum insidiare sopori*. Sabatier printed *homini insidiando soporem* (“lying in wait for the man’s sleep”), but perhaps intended to print *saporem*. The genuine reading is *hominum insidiando sopori*, from Matthew 13:25: “But while the men were sleeping, his enemy came,” etc. However, *subrepens* (“creeping in”) is conjectural in place of *subripiens* (“stealing away”). Reuschius understands the common reading *surripiens* (“stealing away”) to mean the good seeds, which is not established by the Gospel; or, in the other reading, *surripiens saporem*, “stealing away the taste,” that is, the meaning and understanding.

### 800

Hadam., Fabr., Poelm. write *inspargit*; the mss. and other printed editions have *inspergit*.

### 801

Hadam., Fabric., Poelm.: “When the stalk with its grain-bearing ear—roughness—has come forth.” Our mss., Ald., Daventr., Bas. correctly have: “When the roughness of the grain-bearing ear has come forth with the stalks”; and the gloss in Reg. explains *horror* as “roughness.” See above, verse 791.

### Translation of verses 804–831

Then the servants of the Lord, marveling at such things, spoke:

“Did you not scatter good seed across the land?

[805] Why, then, are your fields burdened with foul darnel?

But now, if you command it, we shall cleanse the entire harvest,

and the wheat’s brightness, separated from the filth, will remain.”

Then the Lord answered in a gentle speech:

“This is your deceit, enemy; but let us allow the grain

[810] to grow together with the darnel. For when harvest-time is full,

I shall command the separated darnel, tied into a bundle,

to be burned up in the fires; but from our seed the reaper

will afterward fill our granaries with cleansed grain.

Likewise, if you open the ears of your heart, the heavenly kingdom is like a very small mustard seed,

[815] which its cultivator plants in his own little field.

It is believed to be smaller than all growing seeds;

but soon, when it has taken on an increase of vigorous greenness,

[820] it rises with uplifted head above all the crops of the fields,

so that a feathered throng may play among its branches

and be able to inhabit green shades.

The life-giving heavenly gift is like leaven,

which a woman puts beneath a great mass of flour.

Thereafter, mixed with a little warmth of leaven,

[825] it comes together into the body of a single mass.

Such things he then brought forth to the people, concealed in perplexing words,

so that the sayings of the ancient prophet might correspond

in the sequence of ages with the events ordained:

‘I shall deign to open my mouth; the image of varied speech,

[830] belching forth, will unfold the things hidden since the world’s creation.’

Then he returns home late and leaves the crowds behind.

## BOOK THREE

### Notes on Book III

**Verse 1.** Ott., Rom., *in terris* (“on the earth”); Reg., with the printed editions, *in terras* (“onto the earth”).

**2.** Ott., *velit* (“may he wish”), apparently formed from *vellet* (“he might wish”). The meter requires *vellet*.

**3.** Reg., *Et segetis, Christus quibus* (“and of the crop, Christ, to whom”); the others, *clarus* (“bright”) instead of *Christus*.

**10.** Mss. Reg., Ott., Rom., with Torn. and Poelmann., and Gallandius, for *d. s.*, *patrii* (“native”). Ald., Daventi., Hadam., *patris* (“of the Father”). For *venient* (“will come”), Ald. and Bas. have *veniunt* (“come”). I retain *venient*.

**12.** Ott., *Corrigere* (“to correct”); in Reg. perhaps *Corrigere* also formerly stood, but it now has *Colligere* (“to gather”), which is shown by both the subject matter and the Gospel’s meaning to be the only correct word.

**14.** Rom., Reg., Ald., Poelm., for *d. s.*, *fletusque perennis* (“and everlasting weeping”). Others, with Ott., *luctusque perennis* (“and everlasting mourning”). Both the Vulgate and the ancient versions use the word *fletus* here. I had thought that *Dentibus* (“of teeth”) belonged here.

**17.** Reg., Rom., *Servator* (“Savior”); others, with Ott., *Salvator*. In Rom., *primamque* appears to be an error for *patriamque*.

**20.** Rom., *primas*; read *patrias* (“native”).

**24.** Ott., Rom., *sese musitanti voce volutant* (“they roll themselves along with a murmuring voice”). Reg., *sese mussanti voce susurrant* (“they whisper to one another with a murmuring voice”). Ald., Hadam., Poelm., in the text, Reusch., Torn., *sese summissa voce volutant* (“they roll themselves along with lowered voice”). Fabricius and Poelmann, for *d. s.*, Gallandius, *sese mussanti voce volutant*. The reading of Reg. is preferable: *sese mussanti voce susurrant*. *Mussare* means “to murmur secretly,” in Virgil and others. From it comes the frequentative *mussito*, which in Ott. and Rom. is wrongly represented by *musitanti*; nor does the meter permit *mussitanti*. *Susurrare* likewise means to utter words secretly. Ovid, *Heroides*, final letter, verse 233: “He too, I do not know what, now—as wandering rumor whispers—complains that he has neglected faith as a witness.” Hence Christian writers called secret slanderers *susurrones*, people who secretly speak evil and foment disagreements among others by whispering.

**25.** Rom., *Nun hic*; perhaps the copyist intended to write *Numne hic* (“Is this not?”). Ald., Bas., *soboles fabri* (“the offspring of the craftsman”); others, *fabri soboles*.

**26.** Ott., *Non Maria genetrix?* (“Is Mary not the mother?”), with *est* omitted. Rom., Ald., *Num Maria est genitrix? num fratrum nota propago est?* (“Is Mary the mother? Is he not known as the offspring of brothers?”). Others, *Non Maria est genitrix? non fratrum nota propago est?* (“Is Mary not the mother? Is he not known as the offspring of brothers?”). I omit Valla, who thinks *Mariam* should always be read in the nominative, like *Adam* and *Abraham*.

### Editorial notes on Book III

**Verse 1.** **CHAPTER I.** He interprets the parable of the darnel to the disciples. Matthew 13:36ff. Juvencus added this first verse on his own. Matthew says only: “Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house; and his disciples came to him, saying, Explain to us the parable of the darnel of the field.” In Book IV, verse 151, stars are called *ignicomae* (“fire-haired”). Ausonius and Nemesianus used *ignicomus* (“fire-haired”), and Avienus also said *ignicomans*. Poets commonly attribute hair to the sun, stars, and even fire. Hence also *auricomus* (“golden-haired”) for the sun.

**7.** Virgil, *Eclogue* 5, verse 37: “Unhappy darnel and barren oats rule.” Isidore, *Etymologies* 17.9.132: “Darnel, which poets always call *infelix lolium*, ‘unhappy darnel,’ because it is useless and unfruitful.” The syntax is: “People covered by the demon’s art are unhappy, useless darnel.” The Evangelist calls those covered by the demon’s art “children of the wicked one.”

**8.** The meaning is: “The enemy will be the demon, a dreadful force.” *Vis horrida* (“dreadful force”) is an apposition. In Book I, verse 420, the demon is called *vis livida* (“a livid force”).

**12.** In this book, verse 38: “the stain of error”; and verse 402, “the snares of error”; and again Book IV, verse 732, “the snares of error.” Thus he explains the word *scandala* (“stumbling-blocks”), as in Book I, verse 559: “If error should perhaps ensnare you through your right eyes”; and Book IV, verse 98: “Let credulity be hurled down by the snares of those who err.”

**15.** *Secretis* means “separated” or “set apart.” Soon afterward, verse 96: “And thereafter, set apart, he worships the divine power of the Father.” Virgil, Book VIII, verse 670: “And the pious set apart, with Cato giving them laws.”

**16.** The sacred text: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” In place of *fulgent* (“they shine”) stands *vibrantur* (“they are shaken or flashed forth”), for which others read *vibrant* (“they flash”), with an accusative understood, *flammas* (“flames”) or something similar. Properly, *vibrare* means “to cast forth” or “to shake.” Virgil, *Aeneid* 7, verse 524: “The flash hurled from the sky.”

**17.** **CHAPTER II.** The prophet is without honor in his own country. Matthew 13:53ff.; Mark 6:1; Luke 4:16; John 6:42.

**18.** *Expediens* means “explaining” or “expounding.” This is an elegant usage.

**20.** *Insinuare se* means “to make an entrance for oneself into a matter.” Sometimes *insinuare* is used like an intransitive verb without an accusative, which is easily understood. Here the same accusative, *virtutes* (“miracles” or “powers”), may serve with *insinuando* (“introducing”) and *docebat* (“he taught”), as often happens in Juvencus. Cicero, *On Invention* 1.15, explains what rhetorical insinuation is.

**21.** *Suorum* means “of his own people,” that is, of his fellow citizens. On a similar manner of expression, consult the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 255.

### Translation of Book III, verses 1–26

The fire-haired sun had poured its rosy radiance upon the earth.

The disciples ask what question about the darnel and the crop might mean,

and Jesus, bright, explains these things to them:

“He who commits the best grain to the fields

[5] is the Son of Man. Understand the world under the name of ‘field’,

and righteous people as the pure seed.

But the unhappy darnel—people covered by the demon’s art—

are human beings; the enemy will be the demon, a dreadful force.

The end of the world is the time of harvest.

[10] The Father’s ministers will come through the fields,

and the Son of Man will command them to gather from his kingdom

the snares and stain of error,

and together to burn what has been gathered in rapid flames.

[15] Here there will always be the gnashing of teeth and everlasting weeping;

but for the separated righteous there will come the golden light of life,

so that the lights of the sun may flash forth in the seats of heaven.”

Having taught these things, the Savior returns to his native city.

There, explaining to the people—wonderful to say—

the laws of righteousness and the life-giving commands,

[20] he also taught by introducing native miracles.

Then the crowd of his own people, stirred by heavy envy,

turning over in mind the miracles of the Lord who was present,

and considering the lineage of the well-known man in due order,

whisper these things to one another in murmuring voices:

“Is this not the craftsman’s son, whose name is Joseph?

[25] Is Mary not his mother? Is he not known as the offspring of brothers?”

### Notes on verses 27–53

**27.** Reg., Ottob., Daventr., *tantaeque minister* (“and minister of such great [things]”). Rom. and most editions, *tantaeque magister* (“and teacher of such great [things]”). Matthew says only: “From where, then, does this man have all these things?” This encompasses both teaching and the power of miracles. I therefore read *minister*, which Reuschius also preferred.

**28.** Reg., Rom., *labes cuncta* (“all stain”); the editions with Ott., *labes victa* (“overcome stain”). Reg., Ottob., Hadam., Poelm., in the text, *laborum* (“of labors”). Rom., Ald., and others, *malorum* (“of evils”). Reuschius retains *laborum*, because *labors* is often used for evils and diseases themselves. Compare below, verse 209, and Book IV, verse 282.

**29.** Reg., *Gazara*; read *Nazara*. In Ott. *sit* (“may it be”) was written; above, it was made thus.

**31.** Rom., *patria* (“native”), with the others, but in the margin *propria* (“own”).

**34.** Our mss., with the editions, *illic* (“there”), and the gloss in Reg., “in his kingdom.” Cantabr., *illi* (“to him”), which Reuschius preferred: namely, that divine power might subject all evils to Christ, or for Christ’s sake. For this construction, see the grammarians Scioppius and Sanctius. It is preferable to read *illius* (“of him”), with the final two syllables contracted by synaeresis, as was said of the same word in Book II, verse 298. Matthew’s words are 14:1: “Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus”; and Mark 6:14: “King Herod heard—for his name had become known—and he said.” In an ancient version from the Colbert manuscript: “When King Herod had heard—for his name had become known to him—and he said”; from another Corbie manuscript: “King Herod heard—for his name had become known to him—and they said.” Thus Sabatier: perhaps *et dicebat* (“and he said”) ought to have been written.

**36.** I would think that *Tantae Joannes* (“John of such great [power]”) should be read. Here Matthew says: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him.” The common reading may express this meaning: “Herod thinks that he possessed such great gifts of power that John had been released from the law of death.”

**42.** Ott. *subegit* (“he subjected”); corrected to *subigit* (“he compels”), which the others have. Rom., *subiit* (“he underwent”), less well.

**44.** Reg., Ald., Torn., Bas., Reusch., *casto* (“chaste”); Ott., Rom., with the other editions, *sancto* (“holy”).

**45.** Reg., Torn., *Sanctus Joannes* (“holy John”); others, *Doctus Joannes* (“learned John”). Ott. likewise has the latter, although it was formerly written *Dotus*. One may suspect *Castus Joannes* (“chaste John”) after *sancto quod jure vetabat* (“which the holy man rightly forbade”). I conjectured *nescia flecti* (“ignorant of yielding”), but everywhere I find *nescia recti* (“ignorant of right”), and that reading does not displease me.

**47.** The mss. and most printed editions have *ipsumque* (“and him himself”); Ald., Hadam., and others, *justumque* (“and the righteous man”). Hadam. reads *qui* (“who”) instead of *quia* (“because”), and Poelm. has it in the text.

**48.** Ott., *gravabit* (“will burden”); read *gravavit* (“burdened”).

**49.** Poelm., for *d. s.*, *justi promotio pressa timore* (“the advancement of the righteous man, pressed by fear”). The reading of all the others is clearer and truer: *justi primo compressa timore* (“the righteous man, at first restrained by fear”). Reuschius hints at another reading, *promoto pressa timore* (“with fear advanced and pressing”), that is, with fear prolonged; thus he conjectures.

**51.** Ott., Rom., with most printed editions, *suscipiebat* (“he received”); Reg., *suspiciebat* (“he suspected”), which was printed in Torn. and seems preferable to me. These two words, *suscipere* and *suspicere*, are easily confused in mss. Matthew 14:5 has: “And wishing to kill him, he feared the people, because they held him as a prophet.” Compare this book, verse 685.

**53.** Reg.: *celsis instrueret convivia mensis* (“he would furnish banquets on lofty tables”); above, as a different reading, *tectis* (“under roofs”); but *instrueret* does not fit the meter.

### Editorial notes on verses 31–53

**31.** *Sub* in place of *in*: this has been noted more than once in Juvencus and Dracontius, and is certainly worth noting.

**32.** *Pressit* means “suppressed”; a simple verb is used for a compound, as *vertere* for *evertere* (“to overthrow”).

**33.** **CHAPTER III.** John’s head placed on a dish. Matthew 14:1ff.; Mark 6:14; Luke 3:19.

**35.** *Lethi lege* (“by the law of death”). Albinovanus, on the death of Drusus, addressed to Livia, verse 360: “Black death summons all things under its own laws.” Thus *lex tartari* (“the law of Tartarus”), “the laws of the underworld.”

**39.** “Demon, a savage pest, inflamed by the harms of evils,” etc. Orcus is insatiable. Dracontius, Book II, verse 531: “Unhappy Tartarus, never satisfied with shades.” Consult the note on that passage.

**42.** *Subigit* means “he compels Herod.” By “impious crimes” lust is indicated; by “savage deeds,” cruelty. Again, verse 61: “But she, preserving the impious crimes of her dreadful mother.” Later writers frequently use *scelus* (“crime”) of sexual intercourse.

**46.** Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 491: “And he placed all fears and inexorable fate beneath his feet.”

**47.** Perhaps from that same Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 84: “Because he forbade the wars”; Juvencus takes many other expressions from the foremost of poets, some of which we point out whenever the occasion presents itself. To pursue all of them would be endless.

**52.** Birthdays were formerly celebrated with great preparation and pomp. Censorinus wrote *On the Birthday*; among more recent authors, Martinus Roa also wrote a special book entitled *On the Sacred and Profane Birthday*.

**53.** *Struere* and *instruere* are proper words for banquets and tables. Thus one says “to arrange provisions, a table, or altars with gifts.” Tacitus, *Annals* XV.37, also said *struere convivia* (“to arrange banquets”). Compare the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 140.

### Translation of verses 27–53

“Whence, then, comes this teacher of the law and minister of such great power, to whom the conquered affliction of sufferings yields?”

Thus the crowds of Nazara spoke; Jesus answered them:

“Miracles are always despised in one’s own lands,

[30] and prophets remain without honor in their native dwelling.”

Christ, indignant at such things, restrained his gifts.

Meanwhile, fame flew to the proud king,

that his divine power subdued all evils.

But Herod thinks that he possessed such great gifts of power

[35] that John had been released by the law of death.

For once, when the demon saw with an envious heart

that righteous John was loosening the stain of error

with pure waters, the savage pest, inflamed by evil’s harms,

then sought Herod the king,

[40] and, easily penetrating the dwellings of the unjust heart,

compelled him to heap up impious crimes through savage deeds.

Herod had burned with illicit love,

inflamed for his brother’s marriage-bed, which holy John

rightly forbade. But a savagery ignorant of right

[45] placed laws beneath its feet, and enjoyed forbidden unions;

and, because he forbade them, he even plunged John

into the darkness of prison and burdened him with chains.

For his thirsty savagery, at first restrained by fear, held back from the righteous man’s blood, because the people

[50] greatly revered John as a prophet.

But once, on a certain birthday, the joyful tyrant Herod

was arranging banquets beneath lofty roofs,

### Notes on verses 55–75

**57.** Our mss. Reg., Ottobon., Rom.: *Compositas lusit cantu modulante choreas* (“he played arranged dances to accompanying song”). All printed editions: *Compositas cithara jungit modulante choreas* (“he joins arranged dances to the modulating lyre”).

**58.** Reg., *miratus virginis artem* (“admiring the maiden’s skill”), which is more elegant than *mirata virginis arte* (“admired by the maiden’s skill”). But since the latter is consistently asserted in the other mss. and editions, there is no reason to disturb the common reading, especially since among the ancients, Varro and Pomponius, *miro* and *miras* were in use, as often happens with similar deponent verbs. Below, verse 85: *Genitore precato* (“with the father entreated”).

**59.** Poelm., Fabr., *nunc* (“now”); the others with Rom., more suitably *tunc* (“then”). The editions with Reg. have *patere* (“to be open”). Ott., Rom., *parare* (“to prepare”), which three codices cited by Reuschius also present, in place of “about to be open.” Yet he does not depart from the Vulgate. Cicero speaks in this way, *For Balbus* 9: “with these rewards . . . which are open to tributaries, open to enemies, often open to slaves.”

**60.** Poelm., *Iratus spondet* (“angry, he promises”); read *Juratus spondet* (“having sworn, he promises”).

**63.** Reg., Ott., *poscens* (“demanding”), not absurdly, if punctuated as follows: “He urges John’s head to be torn from his neck, demanding that the present gifts be brought on a platter.” Rom., with the printed editions, *poscit* (“he demands”).

**65.** Poelm., for *d. s.*, *aeger* (“sick”); in the text, with the others, *aegre* (“reluctantly”). Some punctuate it thus: “Yet, mindful of his oath and sworn obligation, he nevertheless commands reluctantly.”

**67.** Almost all editions publish the verse as: “She, criminal, carries the crime to her mother’s guilty pleasures.” Fabricius aptly punctuated it: “She carries—an abomination!—the crime to her mother’s guilty pleasures,” and in the second Index observed that here *nefas* (“abomination”) is an interjected particle expressing indignation. Just as *malum* (“evil”), so *nefas* is sometimes inserted into speech like an interjection. Virgil, Book VIII, verse 688: “He carries Bactra, and—horror!—the Egyptian wife follows.” In Ott. *matri* (“to the mother”) is now read, but perhaps *matris* (“of the mother”) stood there originally. The meaning is the same whether we read *matri* or *matris*. It is nevertheless more probable that Juvencus wrote *matris*, as in Book II, verse 409: “Soon he ordered the father’s wondrous pleasures to arise.”

**68.** Ald., *ac* (“and”), instead of *at* (“but”).

**71.** Reg., Ott., Hadam., Poelmann., in the text, and Reuschius, *insonti* (“innocent”); Rom., Ald., Torn., Bas., *insontis* (“of the innocent”).

**72.** Reg., *secreta* (“separate”), from which *secretae* (“of the separate [one]”) arose. *Frondosa* (“leafy”) has already preceded.

**75.** Ott., *vidit* (“saw”); above, correctly, *videt* (“sees”).

55. Matthew gives this briefly: “On Herod’s birthday the daughter of Herodias danced in the midst and pleased Herod.” Concerning the word *young men* instead of *men* or *people*, see what was said at verse 332 of Book II. Here it may signify nobles, from verse 64: “Herod beneath the burden of the assembled nobles.” Lipsius, *Electorum* II.1, notes that knights are sometimes called *young men*. “Virgin daughter” means a maiden daughter, as she is called by Mark.

56. An elegant description of the girl dancing skillfully. In former times, as now, girls were taught to dance. Horace, Book III, Ode 6:

> “The mature maiden delights to be taught Ionian movements—  
> and even now is fashioned in her limbs,  
> and from her tender nail meditates  
> upon illicit loves.”

Compare Juvenal, Satire 11, verses 162 ff.; Statius, Book I, *Silvae*, final poem, verse 71; and Martial in many passages concerning girls, especially Gaditanian girls.

60. *She had asked.* The verses which Ovid sang concerning the oath by which Phoebus bound himself to Phaethon may be compared here, *Metamorphoses* II, verses 44 ff.

61. *Observing*, that is, keeping watch over: “impious crimes,” above, verse 42.

64. The sacred text of Matthew reads: “And the king was grieved; but because of the oath, and those who reclined with him, he ordered it to be given.” Juvencus seems to indicate that Herod was grieved because of the nobles present, unless the words are arranged thus: “Herod, sad, yet beneath the burden of the nobles present, and mindful of his oath,” etc. It may also be understood that Herod was grieved because of the nobles and the oath, since he felt himself impelled by those very circumstances to order the killing of John the Baptist.

67. In the Vulgate Matthew continues thus: “He ordered it to be given; and he sent and beheaded John in the prison. And his head was brought on a platter, and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.” The Colbert manuscript of the Old Latin version condenses the narrative thus: “He ordered it to be given to the girl. But the girl brought it to her mother.” Juvencus confirms this condensed narrative, as does Hilary, who says only concerning this passage: “And Herod, although sad, fulfilled his oath. And the girl presented the gift to her mother.”” Although Hilary later says, “Amid the other joys of the dissolute people, John’s head is brought on a platter,” this has been taken from the preceding material, verse 8: “But she, instructed beforehand by her mother, said, ‘Give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter.’”

68. A gloss in Reg. reads: “without a name—or knowledge.” Juvencus imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 557:

> “The huge trunk lies upon the shore,  
> the head torn from the shoulders, and the body without a name.”

See the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 473. Reuschius thought that this might refer to the disciples, whose names had not become known.

69. “They commit [him] to the earth”: see verse 24 of Book II.

70. CHAPTER IV. Jesus satisfies five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. Matthew XIV, 13 ff.; Mark VI, 31; Luke IX, 10; John VI, 1.

72. *Separated, withdrawn, hidden.*

73. “The gifts follow,” namely, the author of the gifts himself. Or, “they seek the gifts,” for *sequor* also has this meaning.

76. “Many bodies,” that is, many people. He frequently uses *body* for *person*. “He subjected [them] to healing” instead of “he healed” or “cured”; this appears to be an unusual expression used by Juvencus elsewhere when the subject is salvation granted by divine power.

> Since pride rejoices whenever it is joined with luxury,

[55] In the midst of the young men, the queen’s virgin daughter,

Quickening the alternating movements of her flanks,

Played dances composed to the accompaniment of song.

But he himself, especially astonished,

[60] Amazed at the maiden’s skill, marveled; then, having sworn,

He promises that all rewards would be available,

Whatever the girl might ask.

But she, observing the impious crimes of her dreadful mother,

Urges that John’s head be torn from his neck

And brought on a platter; she demands the present gift.

Herod, sad beneath the burden of the nobles present,

[65] [Col. 0220A] Yet mindful of his sworn oath, reluctantly commands

The innocent man’s head to be brought

And handed over to the girl.

She—ah, sacrilege!—carries it to the wicked joys of her mother.

246 Weeping, the disciples commit the mangled, nameless trunk

Of the body to the earth, and follow Christ.

[70] When he learned of the pitiable death of the righteous man,

He abandoned the land polluted with innocent blood

And hid beneath the leafy shade of a secluded valley.

But the people followed the gifts of his immense power.

When he saw that crowds of believers

[75] Had gathered in a remote valley, he compassionately subjected many bodies, with the corruption of disease driven back, to healing.

In compassion he subjected many bodies to healing.

[Col. 0221A]

[Note: [Col. 0221B]]

79. Reg., Ott.: *competa*. Rom.: *compita*.

80. Ald., Daventr., Torn., Bas., and Reusch, with our manuscripts, have *ibidem*; the other editions have *illic*. Concerning this variant reading, see the note to Book II, verse 604. Vossius should be consulted, *De arte grammatica* II, p. 249, chapter 20, who asserts that some likewise read this form.

81. Reg. has *nil*; Rom. has *nihil*, which the printed editions report. In Rom., incorrectly, *condunt* instead of *ostendunt*.

82. Ald., Bas.: *Quam pisces*; the others: *Ni*.

83. Rom. has *inquam*; in the margin, *inquit*, with the others. Some write *tunc*, others *tum*.

85. Ott. has *Suscipiensque*, correctly emended from the second hand’s *Suspiciensque*.

90. Ald.: “And they fill twelve baskets with fragments.” Others: “They fill the folds of the baskets with fragments.” Fabricius likewise printed this, and in his commentary notes that *fragminis* is a Graecism, as in this same book, verse 760, *compleo* is found with the genitive: “The tables are filled by a mingled, countless crowd.” Fabricius nevertheless remarks that both passages were altered in the Rouen edition. I would believe that the Rouen edition follows the Aldine. Virgil used *impleo* with the genitive in *Aeneid* I, verse 219: “They are filled with old wine and rich game.” Likewise, *compleo* with the genitive occurs more than once in Plautus, and *completus* similarly occurs in Juvencus at this place, verses 253 ff.: “You saw the baskets brought back—again filled with the remnants.” One might also conjecture: “They fill [the baskets] with a fragment of the baskets.”

93. Reg.: “Then he himself orders”; and a gloss: “he himself—Christ.” All the others: “Then he orders them from there.” Rom., together with some printed editions, writes *navim*.

95. Ott.: *In sua quaeque viros*; but this seems to have been corrected to *In sua quemque viros*, which is more elegant. It was observed that others had tried in vain to alter it in this way: *In sua quaeque viros*: “Each man has his own property,” hence *sua* in the plural. John XIX, 27: “The disciple received her into his own [home].” The Greek text has “into his own things.” See Vulpia’s note on Catullus, poem 63, verse 277. It is also elegantly said: “all men, each into his own.” Ovid, *Tristia* III.4, verse 64: “To name each one whom I desire by his own name.” In Reg., *montis*; emend to *montes*.

96. Reg., Ott., Daventr., Ald., Torn., Bas.: *nomen*. Rom., with Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr.: *numen*, which I think should be retained, although *nomen* also does not displease me, as though he were praying to the name of the Father; for *adorat* may be used for *orat*, and the Evangelists Matthew and John use the verb *orare*.

98. Ott.: *fluctum*; above, correctly, *fluctus*.

[Note: [Col. 0221C]]

77. Book III, verse 564: “The final portion of the failing light remained.”

79. *Through the crossroads*: Matthew says, “Going into the villages.” A *compitum*, more often in the plural *compita*, is a place where several roads converge or meet. But since country people in villages gathered at crossroads when summoned by trumpet, either to hold assemblies or for games or sacrifices, the term may reasonably be extended to designate villages. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 382:

> “And around the great villages and crossroads  
> the sons of Theseus established prizes.”

Koenigius maintains that Juvencus uses *compita* abusively for hamlets and villages.

80. *Convivia poni*, that is, “to be set out” or “served.” Martial, Book VIII, epigram 22: “You invite me to boar; you set before me, Gallicus, a pig.” Cato, Juvenal, and others use the verb in this way. Arntzenius, in his note on Sedulius’ prologue, verse 11, page 29, supplies several further examples of *appono* in this sense.

82. *Fragments.* Schoettgenius thinks that Juvencus is alluding to the loaves of the Hebrews, which were prepared in such a way that they could be broken more easily than ours.

84. Virgil, Book VIII, verse 176:

> “He orders the food and the cups, once lifted, to be set back,  
> and himself seats the men on a grassy bench.”
