85. *Having prayed*, passively, just as *precantur* is used passively in Nonius, chapter 7, no. 104, from Varro’s *Eumenides*. Priscian too, Book VIII, testifies that the ancients said *preco* for *precor*. Ausonius, in the *Ephemeris*: “God must be prayed to by me.”

86. *In due order*: Matthew says, “And he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds.”

87. Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 133: “He loaded the tables with unpurchased delicacies”;” and *Aeneid* III, verse 224: “We build couches and feast on rich food.”

88. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 630: “For as soon as he was filled with food.” Compare the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 71: “The guest filled with food.”

90. *Of fragments*, that is, “of pieces,” as it is read in the Gospel. Concerning the word *basket*, see the note on verse 249 of this book.

92. *People*, a great multitude. See the note on Book I, verse 322: women and children were not usually counted. Consult the note on verse 219 of this book: “No one counted the mothers and children.” It is well known that poets include any women whatever under the term “mothers.”

93. CHAPTER V. Jesus walks upon the sea and grasps Peter, who is sinking. Matthew XIV, 22 ff.; Mark VI, 45; John VI, 15.

96. *Withdrawn*: see the note on verse 15 of this book.

97. *Soporata* will fit better with *omnia* than with *nocte*, although in that arrangement the final syllable of *soporata* must be lengthened by reason of the caesura alone; Koenigius considers this no objection. Omeisius cites from Lucan, Book II, *nox sopora*; Virgil likewise has, in *Aeneid* VI, verse 390: “Here is the place of shades, of sleep, and of sleep-giving night.” But *nox soporata* would be something different.

98. *To cleave* is aptly attributed to a ship cutting through waves. *Middle* is what is equally distant from two extremes; but it is commonly taken to mean what lies between two or more things, even if it is not equally distant from all of them. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 270: “Now wooded Zacynthus appears in the middle of the wave”; and Book X, verse 305: “He is released and sets the men down amid the waters.”

> And now, beneath the final light of the failing day,

The disciples urge Christ to dismiss the crowds,

So that each may seek provisions for himself through the villages.

[80] 247 He orders food to be set out for everyone there.

The disciples show that no more food is available

Except two fish and five fragments of grain-bread.

“This is enough,” he says. Then immediately he orders the crowd

To recline and arrange their limbs upon grassy couches.

[85] Then, looking up to heaven, having prayed to the Father,

He himself divides the two fish and the five loaves in due order,

And loads the tables with abundant food.

And now the crowd lies filled—wondrous to say—

[Col. 0222A] And then the attendants gather the leftovers from the tables,

[90] And fill twelve baskets with the fragments.

248 The number of those who had eaten was then five thousand men;

Besides them there was a crowd of mothers and children.

Then he orders the disciples to board the ship

And cross the strait, until he should dismiss them all,

[95] Each man to his own place. Then he sought the mountain’s heights,

And afterward, withdrawn, worshiped the Father’s divine power.

And now everything lay torpid in the sleeping night,

While the stern cleaved the waves in the middle of the sea,

[Col. 0223A]

[Note: [Col. 0223B]]

101. Ott.: *attollit*; read *attollens*.

103. Reg.: *mirabile dictu*; the others more suitably have *mirabile visu*.

106. Ald.: *confusa mente*.

107. Manuscripts: *Tum*; printed editions: *Cum* or *Tum*.

108. Reg.: *Credentum regat*; meter requires *Credentumque regat*. Ott. and the first hand of Reg. write *vegitans*.

110. Rom., Ald.: *respondit*; the others: *respondet*.

113. Reg.: *non mersos*; the others: *immersos*, with a gloss or explanation, “not sunk.” In fact, *immersus* in most writers means the same as *mersus*. But the preposition *in* in such compounds sometimes negates; hence a double and contrary meaning arises, as *intectus* may mean “covered” and “not covered.” In Torn. there was an error, *vigere*, which Latinus corrected in his library to *figere*.

114. Reg.: *post* instead of *mox*. Rom. writes *navim*.

119. Rom.: *aequore*; the sense requires *aequora*.

121. Reg., Ott., with many printed editions: *deripe*; Rom., with others: *diripe*.

122. In Ottob. the first hand seems to have had *praetenditur*, which is certainly not displeasing. The common reading is *protenditur*.

124. Ott. and Rom. write *Ascenseque*, not *Ascensaeque*; perhaps one should read *Ascensaque rati* in the ablative of means. In Reg. the gloss is “*Ascensaeque*—by Christ.” Matthew XIV, 32: “And when they had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased.” In the ancient version from the Colbert manuscript: “And when he had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased.” Other ancient manuscripts have this or something similar; but the Cambridge manuscript has: “And when they had gone up into the ship, the wind rested.” Sabatier, in the printed editions, presents *flamina*, and himself prefers *flumina*, though I do not know where he found it: for the manuscripts and printed editions I have seen have *flamina*, and the Gospel text requires *flamina*.

126. Ald.: “All the companions whom the misfortune had made associates in the voyage”; the others have *socios*, which is better, although in most copies the punctuation is less suitably placed: “All the companions whom the misfortune had made associates in the voyage.”

130. Rom.: *adjungere*; read *attingere*.

[Note: [Col. 0223C]]

100. Matthew: “But in the fourth watch of the night.” There were four watches of the night, each consisting of three hours; these three hours, however, were shorter in summer and longer in winter. A *station* is a place where soldiers stand for purposes of defense, and the term is used for the soldiers themselves, for a guard, and for a watch. From this comes the origin of the name of the ecclesiastical stations, concerning which the most learned Gaspar Bertalazone, Canon Regular of the Lateran and perpetual abbot, gives a great deal of instruction in *Dissertation on Feasts*, Part II, chapter 5, and again in his work *On Fasting*.

103. *Suspended*, lifted up, not sunk. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, verse 810:

> “Or through the middle of the sea, suspended above the swelling wave,  
> it might carry its course.”

Pliny, Book VIII, letter 20: “The root was suspended in the water as well as submerged.”

105. “The sailors’ hearts trembled with fear” seems to be figuratively expressed for “fear trembled in the sailors’ hearts.” Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpine* III, verse 152: “Trembling vibrates in the innermost marrow.” Ovid, *Heroides* 11, verse 77: “You would see my pale limbs trembling.”

107. “Let all fear be gone” is from Virgil, Book XI. See also Prudentius, Book II against Symmachus, verse 736.

108. Matthew: “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” Juvencus had seen another version, found in the manuscripts Sangermanensis I, Corbeiensis I and II, Claromontanus, and Constantiensis: “Stand firm; do not be afraid; it is I.” But in Corbeiensis I alone it reads: “Stand firm, and do not be afraid.” Hilary, on this passage: “The Lord immediately spoke to them and ordered them to stand firm”; and later: “He will say, ‘It is I.’” “Life-giving steadfastness” is faith, which in Book II, verse 677, is called “the substance of believing.”

117. *They terrify*: a verb used by Lucretius, Virgil, Statius, and other poets. *To grow frequent*, or, as others write, *to become numerous*, is likewise a proper word.

118. *Melted*, because they had previously supported Peter, as though they were solid.

119. *The strong strength of faith*: faith when it was firm and powerful. A similar phrase occurs in this book at verses 191 and 277. See the note on Book I, verse 478.

122. Matthew: “Stretching out his hand, he seized him.” Juvencus names the right hand, by which aid is more often given; it is also a sign of faith and power.

123. *Doubted*, that is, doubtful. Others have used this participle with a similar meaning. Albinovanus, *Elegy to Livia* I, verse 84: “And harmonious devotion, and love not doubted.” But *is soothed* and *with bitter words* seem contrary to one another. In the very rebuke Juvencus praises the Savior’s clemency.

125. *They marveled*, they admired, as has been said elsewhere. But what does *rogantes* mean? Matthew merely says: “Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, ‘Truly you are the Son of God.’” Juvencus therefore uses *rogantes* for *adorantes*, “worshiping.” Concerning the verb *rogare* used alone for “to pray to God,” see the note on Book I, verse 48.

127. *Fervid* is a proper epithet of a strait, derived from *fervere*, “to boil,” as Varro teaches, Book VI, chapter 3 of *On the Latin Language*, section 15.

130. *The outermost threads of the garment*, the fringe, as Matthew calls it. See Book II, verse 393 and following.

249 Carried and tossed by the adverse blast of the rising wind.

[100] But when the fourth watch of the night

Was already pressing on its course, the morning-bringing light rising,

He, suspended above the liquid waves, traversed the path

With dry footsteps—wondrous to see!

And now he was approaching the stern, but the sailors, unaware,

[105] Struck with terror, felt their hearts tremble with shuddering fear,

And together they raised a cry in confused voices.

Then Christ speaks to the frightened men: “Let all fear be gone,

And may life-giving steadfastness guide the mind of believers.

Behold, it is I; recognize me as the teacher of your light.”

[110] 250 Trusting, Peter answers him with these words:

“If your power truly deigns to look upon us,

Permit me likewise, at your command, to set my feet

[Col. 0223B] Upon the liquid waves, immersed in the waters.”

The Lord assents to these words; Peter immediately dares

[115] To leave the ship, and, relying upon the sea, sets down his footsteps.

[Col. 0224A] But when the miracles of such great things terrify his mind,

And he sees the threats of the wind growing stronger,

The waves gradually yield, melted by wavering fear—

The waves that had borne the strong support of faith.

[120] And now Simon, submerged to the middle of his body, cries:

“Christ, rescue me as I perish amid dreadful waves.”

At once the right hand is extended to meet Peter,

And his doubting faith is soothed with bitter words;

The contrary winds yield to the boat that has taken him aboard.

[125] 251 All who were companions in the boat, whom fortune had gathered together,

Marveled as they worshiped the present offspring of God.

At last the stern had crossed the seething straits,

And the heavy anchor had taken hold of the desired harbor.

[Col. 0224B] The people gather along the shores in swift haste,

[130] Carrying the sick; and to touch the threads of his garment

[Col. 0225A]

[Note: [Col. 0225A]]

131. The manuscripts, with many printed editions, have *miroque*; Ald., with others, *mirumque*. Fabricius printed this as well, but, as he observes in his commentary, by placing *exoptant* parenthetically—“and they all desire this wondrous gift”—and he supplies similar examples from Tertullian and Paulinus. Reuschius prefers *miroque* because of the added *-que*.

132. Hadam. has *plena*; correct to *plenam*.

135. Poelm., in the text together with others: *patitur doctrina labare*; in place of the doubtful reading, *lapsare ferunt documenta*. Badius read this and explains *lapsare* as “to totter frequently,” and *ferunt* as “they suffer.” Reuschius says that this reading is not bad and preserves traces of genuine antiquity; he observes that neither *documentum* nor *doctrina* is read in the Evangelists. Elsewhere Juvencus lengthens the first syllable in *labat*, as I shall say at verse 373 of this book.

136. Rom.: “to totter—by the hands of the ancient commandment.” The others: “to totter—by the commands of the elders? by their hands,” or “to totter?—by the commands of the elders’ hands.” Reg. has *quos cura*; perhaps it was *nam cura*, as the others have. *Quos* is clearer.

139. Ald., Poelm., according to the printed edition: *mandata*. The manuscripts and other printed editions: *praecepta*. Ott. has *quod*, but it was corrected to *quid*, which the arrangement of letters in Rom. seems to suggest. Most have *quod*.

140. Hadam. and Poelm.: *defixa morte*; the other printed editions, together with the manuscripts: *defixa lege*. Matthew XV, 4: “Honor your father and mother; and whoever curses father or mother shall die the death,” from Exodus XX, 12, and Deuteronomy V, 16. Hence some perhaps devised: “For God threatens death with fixed death,” but *defixa lege*, “with a fixed law,” is better.

141. Reg.: *cujusquam*; correct to *cuiquam*. Juvencus uses this phrase more than once, using *cuiquam* for “by anyone.”

143. Rom.: *ista haec*; Reg., Ott., Ald.: *ista* instead of *isthaec*, which most printed editions have. In *ista* the final syllable would be lengthened by reason of the caesura.

[Note: [Col. 0225B]]

131. Omeisius says that there is neither a command of God nor a promise that the relics of the saints benefit us after their death by driving away diseases. But since God is the author of miracles, what prevents us from acknowledging that the relics of the saints can benefit us even after their death? Indeed, it is established from sacred Scripture, apostolic tradition, and the common practice of the Church that the saints existing in heaven are rightly and usefully invoked by us, and that their relics are most honorably venerated with religious devotion. See Pichler, *Theological Polemics*, Part II, Controversy 2.

133. CHAPTER VI. That hands should be washed; and that the things proceeding from the mouth, not those entering it, defile a person. Matthew XV, 1 ff.; Mark VII, 1, etc. The first part is better explained as follows: Christ defends the disciples when they are accused of not washing their hands.

134. *Seeking to entrap Christ*, attempting to snare him with deceptive words. Plautus, *Amphitryon* I.1.269: “Why are you trying to trap me, executioner?” See the note on verse 684 of this book.

136. Matthew’s words are: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” Koenigius explains *cura praeterit* as “it passes them by,” namely, the disciples, or *praeterit* as meaning “is neglected” or “is omitted.” Juvencus does not explain the sense very clearly; perhaps the passage is corrupt.

139. “Having transgressed, you betray the commandments of God.” The same accusative is governed by two verbs. *Prodere* means “to abandon.” Cicero, *Academica* IV, chapter 8: “The good man, who has determined to endure every torture and to be torn apart by unbearable pain rather than betray either duty or faith.” Matthew says: “You transgress the commandment of God.” Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 9: “You frustrate the commandment of the Lord.” Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 29: “You pass over the commandment of God.” Augustine, on Galatians, volume III: “Dissolving the commandment of God.” Pope Siricius, letter 10: “You have rejected the commandment of God.”

142. *To strike*, to harass and, as it were, to accuse. Seneca, *Hercules Oetaeus*, verse 1671: “Striking the gods, and Jupiter himself, with cries.” Claudian, in the prologue to Book II against Eutropius, verse 51: “Wretch, why do you assail the stars with womanish complaints?” See the notes on Book I, verse 301, and on verse 172 of this book.

143. The Gospel passage, which Juvencus abridges, must now be explained. Matthew XV, 5–6: “But you say: Whoever says to father or mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ and does not honor his father or mother, has made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition.” Mark VII, 11–13: “But you say: If a man says to father or mother, ‘Corban’—which is a gift—‘whatever is from me will benefit you,’ and you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, abolishing the word of God through your tradition, which you have handed down; and you do many similar things.”

Sabatier thinks that Juvencus did not render Matthew verse 5 and Mark verses 11 and 12. But Juvencus embraces the whole meaning in this verse: “You make these things void by teaching perversely.” God had said in Exodus XX, 12: “Honor your father and mother,” etc. The scribes and Pharisees made this commandment of God void through their perverse teaching. What, then, was that perverse teaching? They maintained that a son who had vowed to God those goods from which he was bound to support his parents was neither obliged nor permitted thereafter to support his parents from such consecrated goods. Clear traces of this sacrilegious doctrine still exist in the Talmud.

Maldonatus, who reports several other interpretations, explains the passage differently, along with Strabo, Hugh, and Lyra: “Whatever is from me,” that is, “whatever I shall offer to God, will benefit you; it will be as though I had given it to you.” For those on whose behalf a sacrifice was offered consumed the sacrifice, unless it was a burnt offering. Therefore, the person who said this and thereafter did good to his parents in no other ways would be free from guilt—namely, according to the perverse doctrine of the Pharisees.

There is a distinctive reading in the very ancient Tridentine Gospel Book, at this place in Matthew: “But you say: Whoever says to father or mother, ‘My gift will benefit you,’ has not honored his father. And you have emptied the word of God for the sake of your tradition.” The distinguished prelate Simon de Magistris, bishop of Cyrene, most courteously shared with me a copy of this Gospel Book, which will be of some use to me in the future.

The autograph manuscript is described in the preface by Bonellus of Cavalesio, of the Reformed Province of Saint Vigilius, who signs himself at Trent, at Saint Bernardino, 11 May 1762. The codex is therefore made of parchment, differing from other parchment codices even in its thinness; it has no binding and is wrapped only in a silk veil. As a result, the Gospel of Matthew, which is first, and the Gospel of Mark, which is last, are defective and incomplete. Its shape is midway between oblong and square, arranged in two columns on each side, all of whose initials are a cubit high. It is purple in color, though now in most places somewhat darkened by age, with silver letters and some gold ones. Bonellus himself had provided a specimen of it in volume II of his work *Historical-Critical Notices*, page 62. The order of the Gospels is extremely ancient: according to Matthew, according to John, according to Luke, and according to Mark—for that is how it is written. It also consistently preserves ancient orthography. Contracted words are absent or rare. Bonellus produced a copy according to the autograph with the greatest possible fidelity, care, and reverence; however, he omitted certain notes added in a second hand in the margin, though they were written before the year 1000.

> They all desire to touch the outermost threads, and through this wondrous gift

All believers receive complete health throughout their limbs.

Behold, the Pharisees and scribes, deceitful on every side,

Seeking to entrap Christ, bring forth deceptive words:

[135] 252 “Why does your teaching allow the disciples to totter

From the commands of the elders? They neglect the care of washing their hands,

And at the same time take food with its uncleanness.”

At this he speaks: “This is more worthy of inquiry:

You have all transgressed and betrayed the commandments of God.

[140] For God threatens death by a fixed law

If anyone wounds a father with an injurious word,

Or a mother is struck by her child’s bitter words.”

253 “You make these things void by teaching perversely.”

[Col. 0227A]

[Note: [Col. 0227B]]

144. In Reg. there seems to have been *urgent* instead of *vigent*.

146. Rom.: *pererrat*; retain *pererrant*.

148. Poelm., according to the printed edition: *homines*, namely, “things cast out do not sprinkle people with uncleanness,” etc. The manuscripts, with other printed editions, have *homini*.

150. Reg., Ott.: *penetrabilibus*; this error also occurs elsewhere in our manuscripts instead of *penetralibus*.

153. Reg.: *Occulto carpant*, with the gloss “they disparage.” Others: *Occulto traherent*. For *risu*, which all have, I restore conjecturally *nisu*, in accordance with what was said at Book II, verse 353. Matthew says: “When they heard this saying, they were offended.”

154. Reg. had *plantatarum*, but it was corrected to *plantarum*.

155. Reg.: *suo*, from which *sui* arose.

156. Rom.: *Penitus abjiciet*; emend to *Abjiciet penitus*. Westh. has *longa*; in the margin, *longe*, which is better.

157. Reg. writes *nanctus*, which appears to have been written by the first hand in Ott. For *oberret*, Ald. and Bas. have *oberrans*.

158. Reg. and the first hand of Ott.: *Decidit*. Rom., with the printed editions: *Decidet*. Read *demersus*, with the manuscripts, rather than *dimersus*, found in some editions.

159. Ott.: *velit*, but it seems to have been *vellet*, which is unquestionably correct.

163. Some place a question mark after *lucem*, others do not. Matthew: “Are you also still without understanding?”

164. In the first hand of Reg. there seems to have been *oris* instead of *ori*.

166. Rom.: *concepta pectore*; read *concepta e pectore*, so that the verse scans. Aldus punctuates *promunt*—“the mouths of men bring forth the mind”; the others more suitably punctuate *promunt*—“the mouths of men bring forth the mind.”

170. Reg.: *Concilia*; the others: *Consilia*.

[Note: [Col. 0227D]]

145. *Raises aloft*: a verb of Ennius and Cato which writers of the declining Latin age, against Erasmus’ judgment, brought back into use—Apuleius, Mamertinus, Macrobius, Prudentius, and others.

146. *The secrets of the heart*: Book II, verse 490.

147. *The ears of the heart*: Matthew: “Hear and understand.” Paulinus, in the *Panegyric of Celsus*: “Therefore let us open the eyes of the mind and the ears to Christ.”

151. *Brought out*, sent forth, made public.

153. *The breasts of the scribes*, that is, the scribes. Juvencus likes to speak in this way.

155. *The level sea* designates a plain. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 11 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 185. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, verse 781:

> “Meanwhile, across the level of the burning plain,  
> the son exercised the horses.”

And without an added noun, *of the plain* or *of the countryside*, *Georgics* I, verse 97:

> “And he who, having split the level earth, raises ridges,  
> again breaks through them with the slanting plow.”

159. *To be resolved*, defined, demonstrated. Solinus, chapter 2, elsewhere section 8: “Bocchus resolved that the lineage of the ancient Gauls was Umbrian.” Barnabas Brissonius observes from the law, section 59, paragraph 1, *On Testamentary Manumission*, that *absolvere* is a legal term meaning “to answer the question proposed.” The words of the Digest at the cited place are: “He seems to have resolved even the matter about which inquiry is made.”

160. *Soon* in the sense of “a little earlier” is rare. Columella, Book III, chapter 20: “I have no doubt concerning the other matter which I had proposed shortly before.”

162. *You shut out*, you exclude. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI, chapter 4, asserts that the word *discludo* strikes the ears as new; but its authority is defended by Virgil and Lucretius. Add Caesar, Cicero, and others. Forcellinus carelessly attributes to Macrobius the claim that he had asserted the word *discludo* to be new.

169. *In the secrecy of the heart*, as elsewhere in the plural: “the secrets of the heart.”

170. *Thefts*: illicit intercourse among poets generally. Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 183: “The incestuous are aflame; the adulterers’ thefts burn.”

171. *The deceptive error of men*, instead of “false witnesses” or “false testimonies,” as Matthew puts it.

254 How clearly the prophet’s words about you are in force!

[145] “The people honor me with the highest praise of their lips,

But far away their hearts’ secrets wander in another direction.

Therefore listen, all of you, and turn the ears of your heart:

Whatever things enter a person from outside

Cannot sprinkle him with shameful uncleanness,

Nor will they lodge in his life or spirit.

[150] But the things that burst forth from the inner chambers of the mouth of men

Will miserably stain the inward mind when uttered.

The disciples tell Christ that the words of the speaker

Secretly offend the breasts of the scribes.

Then he says: “Our Father, the planter, will utterly cast away

[155] The seeds which he himself did not sow in the level of his field,

Uprooted from their roots and thrown far away.

[Col. 0227B] If a blind man happens to find a blind guide, he will wander,

[Col. 0228A] 255 And both will fall together, plunged into a pit.”

Then Peter asks that the question be explained,

[160] The question which he had shortly before put to the Pharisees and scribes.

Then the sower of eternal life answered as follows:

“You too, with a hardened heart, shut out all the commands,

And does the mind’s doubt not admit the light?

For whatever comes from outside to the human mouth

[165] Passes into the stomach and runs on, unknown to the spirit.

But the things conceived in the inner heart, which the mouths of men bring forth, can besprinkle the mind

With the stain of corruption and defile a person with unclean guilt.

From the secrecy of the heart are brought forth counsels harmful to life,

[170] Murders, and wicked thefts from marriage beds,

[Col. 0228B] Frauds, and the deceptive error of men as witnesses,

[Col. 0229A] [Note: [Col. 0229B]]

172. Reg., Rom., with several printed editions: “And the rapid madness of the voice, striking heaven.” The first hand of Ott.: “And the raging madness, striking heaven with its voice”; the second hand: “And the raging madness of the voice, striking heaven,” which Ald., Bas., Torn., and Poelm. print according to the received text. In the Gospel, blasphemies are spoken of, and they are explained by this verse; therefore *raging voice* seems more appropriate than *rapid voice*.

173. Fabr.: *maculent*; correct to *maculant*.

174. Reg. and Ottob. write *Inlotis*. Daventr. incorrectly has *palluit* instead of *polluit*.

177. Aldus printed, with most others, *Sidonem, Tyrumque petit*, but in the Errata corrected it to *Sidonemque, Tyrumque petit*, which Omeisius followed, with Gallandius’ approval. This reading is confirmed by our Reg. manuscript, where *Sydonemque* is written. In fact, it better satisfies the meter, for the first syllable of *Tyrus* is shortened by Avienus, Priscian, and Prudentius, verse 496 of the *Hamartigenia*: “Not him, the queen of Tyre.” The more common reading, *Sidonem, Tyrumque petit*, could be defended, for in proper names whose quantities are pronounced at differing intervals neither Juvencus nor other Christian poets—or even pagan poets contemporary with the Christian poets—were excessively strict. But here Juvencus seems to have intended to shorten the first syllable of *Tyrum*; otherwise he would have said *Tyrum, Sidonemque petit*, following the Evangelist’s order: “He withdrew into the territory of Tyre and Sidon.” Rom., Ald., Bas.: *tum femina*; the others: *cum femina*.

179. Rom.: *Solvitur*; retain *Volvitur*, with the others, unless it is understood as “she is released with loosened hair and prayers,” as in this book, verse 354: “Loosened by weeping,” etc. Rom., Reg., Ottob.: *desinit*, printed by Fabricius. Most editions: *deserit*.

181. Ott.: *Resipire*; above, according to the printed edition, *resipisse*. I think Rom. also originally had *resipire*, written by the first hand. The common reading is *resipisse* and is more to be approved. *Resipio* and *resipisco* sometimes mean “to return to one’s former state of mind”; but *resipio* is used in this sense chiefly in past tenses, whereas in other tenses *resipisco* is more frequent. See the note on Book II, verse 72: “But after the mad young man had recovered his senses.”

184. Rom.: *Corrigere, quas*, contrary to the meter. Ott.: *quos*; according to the printed edition, *quas*; the sense requires *quas*.

185. Ott.: *tum Jesus talia fatur*; the erasure indicates that this was also in Reg., third hand. The printed editions, together with Rom., have *tum talia fatur Iesus*, which should be retained. Although Ottob.’s reading can be defended, it does not resemble Juvencus’ style, since Juvencus always makes the name *Jesus* trisyllabic.

186. Rom.: *panes* instead of *panem*. Ald., Bas.: *detrahit*; most: *detrahet*.

187. Reg.: *Et canibus jaciat*; Rom., Ald., Bas. more suitably: *Ut canibus jaciat*. The reading of Ott. and other printed editions proceeds correctly: *Et canibus jaciet*.

189. Ott., Poelm., in the text, Torn., Hadam., [Col. 0230C] *Decidet, et nihilo dominorum coena gravatur* (“It falls, and the masters’ dinner is burdened in no respect”). Ald., Bas., *Decidit, atque nihil dominorum coena gravatur* (“It has fallen, and the masters’ dinner is burdened in no respect”). Poelm., as an alternative reading, *Decidit, et nihilo dominorum coena gravetur* (“It has fallen, and let the masters’ dinner be burdened in no respect”); so Rom., but with *gravatur*. Reg.: *Decidit, et nihil dominorum coena gravator* (“It has fallen, and nothing of the masters’ dinner is burdened”), above which stands *gravatur*. Reuschius published *Decidit, et nihilo dominorum coena gravatur* in this sense: portions are thrown from the masters’ tables to the little dogs, and therefore no greater expense needs to be incurred, nor does the table need to be burdened with more food. He nevertheless does not reject Badius’s reading: *Decidat, atque mihi dominorum coena gravetur* (“Let it fall, and let the masters’ dinner be burdened for me”). As though the woman were saying: “I desire to gather, like a dog, the crumbs falling from the masters’ tables.”

192. Reg. prints *verbis coelestibus* (“with heavenly words”), which is also found printed in Torn. The others have *verbis, et voce locutus* (“having spoken in words and with his voice”).

[Note: [Col. 0229C]]

172. A fine description of blasphemy. On the word *pulsans* (“striking”), compare the note at verse 142 of this book.

176. CHAPTER VII. The daughter of the Syrophoenician woman healed of a demon. Matthew 15:21 and following; Mark 7:25.

[Col. 0229D] 177. *Fusis crinibus, et precibus* (“with loosened hair and prayers”): these two dissimilar things are elegantly attached to the same verb. Ovid, *Heroides* 2, verse 25: “Demophoon, you gave both words and sails to the winds— / I complain that the sails lack return, the words lack faith.”

178. *Causata*, “putting forward as a cause.” *Causor* means “to bring forward as a cause”; this may occur whether the cause is true or false. *Natam jacentem*, “the daughter lying ill,” for Juvencus often uses *jacere* in this sense. The girl’s illness, however, was that she was held or tormented by a demon, as the Evangelist says and Juvencus explains afterward. Juvencus sometimes adds details resembling the truth, though they are not clearly related by the Evangelists.

179. *Volvitur*, “she throws herself upon the ground” or “is violently agitated.” Matthew says only: “Having gone out from those regions, she cried out, saying,” etc. Later: “His disciples came to him, saying: Send her away, because she cries out after us.”

183. *Bidentes*: Juvencus uses this word elsewhere as well; other writers likewise call sheep by this name.

[Col. 0230D] 184. *Cogere*: the proper word for shepherds gathering scattered sheep. Virgil, *Eclogues* 3, verse 20: “Tityrus, gather the flock”; and verse 98: “Gather the sheep, boys.” Juvencus often uses the same word in a similar way.

187. The sacred text has *mittere canibus* (“to give to the dogs”). To throw bread to dogs—namely, to cast it down and, as it were, make a waste of it—is more expressive. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 8: “He was not yet throwing the children’s bread to the dogs.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* 7, near the end: “The entrails thrown to our dogs.” Phaedrus, *Fables* 3.7: “From his table the master gives bones, the scraps thrown to the household.” Thus *jactare pecuniam, opes* means “to squander money or wealth.”

191. Above, verse 119: “The mighty strength of faith.”

256 And a raging madness of voice striking heaven.

“These are the things that defile a person, that fill him with impurities.

But with unwashed hands he never defiles

[175] the earthly food taken at the body’s discretion.”

When he had said these things, he makes for the fairest lands of the Syrians,

and Sidon and Tyre; while a woman, with loosened

hair and prayers, pleading that her daughter lay ill,

throws herself down and anxiously does not cease imploring

[180] 257 silent Christ to restore the mind tormented by a savage demon,

[Col. 0230A] and at last to allow the wretched girl to recover her senses.

Then he also answered the prayers of the disciples who followed,

saying that he preferred to gather his Father’s own sheep,

which vain error had scattered widely.

[185] More insistently she pressed him; then Jesus speaks thus:

“No one will ever take bread away from his own children

and throw it to dogs.” Then the woman speaks thus:

“At least a portion of the crumbs falls to the dogs from the masters’ table,

and the masters’ dinner is burdened in no respect.”

[190] 258 Then the Lord speaks: “May worthy rewards of salvation come to you,

for such great strengths of faith have earned them.”

Having spoken such things in words and with his voice,

[Col. 0231A] [Note: [Col. 0231A]]

193. Reg., Ott., *decusso daemone* (“the demon having been struck down”), which is preferable to *discusso* (“the demon having been dispersed”) in Rom. and the printed editions. Thus Prudentius, preface to Book 1 *Against Symmachus*, verse 37: “and having struck down the serpent far away.” Earlier writers—Livy, Propertius, Ovid, and Pliny—use the same verb. Reuschius printed *discluso* (“having been shut out”); Omeisius approved this because Juvencus uses the verb more frequently. See Book 2, verse 65.

194. Reg. has *secunda* (“favorable”), with the gloss *prospera* (“prosperous”). But the meter requires *foecunda* (“fruitful”), which is also more appropriate to the sense.

195. Reg., *Galileae repedat Salvator* (“the Savior returns to Galilee”); Ott., *Galileas repedat Servator* (“the Preserver returns to Galileas”). Others also vary between *Salvator* and *Servator*.

196. Ald., Bas., Reusch., *consedit in arce* (“sat in the citadel”), which I think was also written by the first hand in Reg. In Rom., by the first hand, stands *conscendit in arce* (“climbed into the citadel”); by the second hand, *consedit in arce*. Most have *conscendit in arcem* (“climbed into the citadel”). Matthew says: “And going up onto the mountain, he sat there.”

198. Our manuscripts have *et crurum debile vulgus* (“and a crowd weak in its legs”); among the printed editions, some have this, while others have *et vulgus debile crura* (“and the crowd, its legs weak”), a reading adopted by Reuschius with Koenigius. To me, *et crurum debile vulgus* appears to be from Juvencus’s hand, in the manner of *Integer vitae, scelerisque purus* (“upright in life and free from wickedness”) and other similar adjectives that especially take a genitive among poets. Fabricius followed this reading from the Mersburg and Ghent manuscripts, as he states in his commentary under *Debilis*.

199. Rom., Hadam., Poelm., in the text, *alios* (“others”). Reg., Ott., Ald., Bas., *alii* (“others”), namely, “others were saying that the speechless were being brought.” So below, verse 267: “Others said that Jeremiah was one of the prophets.”

200. Reg., *acerbos* (“bitter”); others, *amaros* (“bitter”).

201. Reg., *mirando* (“wonderful”), but perhaps it was *venerando* (“venerable” or “worthy of reverence”).

204. Ott., *Discipulos Christus agens* (“Christ addressing the disciples”); above, *Discipulos tunc Christus agens* (“Christ then addressing the disciples”): the latter is required by the metrical rule and agrees sufficiently with the sense. See verse 420 of this book.

[Col. 0232B] 205. Reg., *Secreto alloquitur* (“he addresses them privately”). The printed editions, together with other manuscripts, have *Secrete alloquitur* (“he addresses them secretly”). Both are Latin, but *secreto* is preferable to *secrete*, which is used by Tertullian and other later writers. *Secreto* is employed by better authors.

206. Rom., *remeantia lumina* (“returning lights”): read *remeant jam lumina* (“the lights are now returning”).

207. Reg., by the first hand, *sumant* (“let them take”); by the second hand, correctly *sumunt* (“they take”).

213. Reg., Ott., *discerpere* (“to tear apart”); Rom., with the printed editions, *decerpere* (“to pluck off”). *Discerpere* is more suitable to this passage, meaning “to tear into separate portions”; *decerpere* properly means “to remove by plucking,” as fruit is plucked from a tree.

214. Reg., *curam* (“care”), which can be defended if *coepit* (“he began”) is supplied; Gallandius supplied it in the preceding verse with *discerpere*. Reg., Ottob., Rom., *dedere plebi* (“to give to the people”). The printed editions, *tradere plebi* (“to hand over to the people”). In all manuscripts and printed editions I find *mensatim* (“portion by portion”); in Rom., *ex mundo, mensantim* has been changed to *mensatim*. One might conjecture *per mensas* (“through the tables”), but *mensatim* should be retained, since Forcellini placed it among the Latin adverbs on the authority of our Juvencus. There are several similar adverbs: *vicatim* (“by neighborhoods”), *ostiatim* (“from door to door”), *tributim* (“by tribes”), *properatim* (“hastily”).

216. Some write *Ad saciem*; most, *Ad satiem*. An old edition apud Omeisius has *Ad faciem*, which is erroneous.

[Note: [Col. 0231C]]

195. CHAPTER VIII. Near the Sea of Galilee, the blind, lame, and mute are healed, and four thousand men are fed with seven loaves and a few fish. Matthew 15:30 and following; Mark 8:1 and following.

199. *Vocabula*, “names.” Virgil, Book 7, verse 337.

203. Tacitus also joins praises and thanks, as in *Annals* 1.69: “to offer someone praise and thanks”; and *Annals* 12.37: “to venerate someone with praises and thanks.” To say *celebrare grates alicui* (“to celebrate thanks to someone”) certainly seems unusual, but *laudes gratesque celebrare* (“to celebrate praises and thanks”) can more easily be defended as a combined expression. Latin writers more commonly say *celebrare aliquem laudibus* (“to celebrate someone with praises”).

[Col. 0231D] 204. *Cogens* (“gathering”), in the sense explained at verse 184.

205. *Multa est*, “it is great.” See the note on Dracontius, Book 2, verse 63.

207. *Sibi* (“for themselves”) is superfluous, but is added for elegance.

209. *Viantes* (“travelers”): compare the note on Book 1, verse 161.

211. Matthew’s words are: “And Jesus said to them: How many loaves do you have? And they said: Seven, and a few small fish.” Juvencus interprets this as meaning that they had seven loaves and a few small fish prepared by them for their immediate nourishment; these were few even for them or their immediate companions. Reuschius takes it this way and says that *sibi* (“for themselves”) was added meaningfully. At least Juvencus implies that the seven loaves and few fish had been brought by the Apostles so that they might be fed. Some, however, think that those loaves and fish were for sale among the crowd.

212. *Terrae per terga* (“upon the back of the earth”). See the note on Book 1, verse 671. *Cubare* (“to recline”), following the custom of the ancients, who ate while reclining.

213. Matthew’s text reports: “He broke them and gave them to his disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.” Juvencus sets out all these actions distinctly. Christ himself undertakes to tear the food apart with his hands and to give it portion by portion to the entire people through the disciples, who set out the meal. *Dedere* may also be understood as standing for *dari*, that is, “to be given” or “to be handed over.” Schoettgenius explains *curat discerpere* as “he tears apart,” that is, *discerpit*. Reuschius takes it either as an enallage, *discerpere*, that is, “he was tearing apart.”

215. *Ponunt* (“they set out”), a verb commonly used at banquets, as noted at verse 80 of this book. On the verb *repletur* (“is filled”), see likewise the note at verse 88 of this book.

216. *Ad satiem* (“to satiety”): compare Book 1, verse 673.

The power, after the demon had been cast out, filled the maiden’s mind, which it had embraced, with fruitful gifts of salvation.

[195] From there the Savior returns to the regions of Galilee,

and climbs from afar into the citadel of the lofty mountain.

Without delay the peoples gather, and with them they drag

some who are blind, and a crowd weak in its legs,

and others who are speechless, and a thousand names of diseases.

[200] Yet he removed bitter maladies from them all,

and grants them strength through a venerable gift.

Then the peoples together celebrate such great miracles

259 and celebrate praises and thanks to the eternal Father.

[Col. 0232A] Christ, gathering the disciples on the summit of the mountain,

[205] addresses them privately: “The people’s compassion is great;

for the sun’s light has now returned to the earth for the third time

since they have taken no food for themselves.

I do not wish to send away such a great crowd fasting,

lest weariness afflict the people traveling over long distances.

[210] The disciples show Christ that they have seven loaves

and a few small fish as food for the immediate need.”

Then he ordered the people to recline upon the back of the earth,

and he himself undertakes to tear apart with his own hands

whatever food there was,

260 and to give it portion by portion to the entire people.

[215] The disciples set out the food, and the people are filled

to satiety with provisions; soon they gather up the fragments of bread

[Col. 0233A] [Note: [Col. 0233B]]

217. Ott. writes *comulato*; above, *cumulato*.

218. Reg., *plebe* (“by the people”); Ott., *plebi* (“to the people”); Rom., with most printed editions, *plebis* (“of the people”). Fabricius printed *plebe*: either that or *plebi*, in the ablative or dative case, must be retained. I do not accept Reuschius’s interpretation, namely, “from every region they had been, or were present.” In Torn. there is the error *fuerat* for *fuerant*.

220. Reg., Rom., Torn., Ald., *Magedarum*. Hadam., Poelm., *Mageddarum*. Ott., *Magidarum*. Bas., *Magedorum*. *Magedarum* is preferable, because in the Vulgate and most ancient versions this place is called Magedan.

224. Rom., Ald., Bas., *Connexum* (“joined”): it is hardly doubtful that *Convexum* (“arched”) should be read. Hence *convexa caeli* (“the arched vaults of heaven”); on this matter see the note on Dracontius, Book 1, verse 136.

225. Reg., by the second hand, and apparently Ott., *procedet* (“will proceed”). The printed editions, with Rom., *procedit* (“proceeds”).

227. Reg., *solis ubi tristia* (“where the sun’s [things are] sad”), not badly, with the final syllable of *solis* lengthened according to the caesura.

229. Ott., *fragosa* (“rough”); read *fragosa[m]*.

233. Others have *suis* (“its own”), without an interrogation.

241. Ott., *Illud Pharisei* (“that of the Pharisee”); others, *Illa Pharisaei* (“that of the Pharisee”), which is better, as at verse 221: *Ecce Pharisaei* (“Behold the Pharisees”).

243. Reg., *tacitam volvit cunctatio mentem* (“hesitation turns a silent mind”); Ott., *tacita volvit cunctatio mentes* (“silent hesitation turns minds”); Rom., with the printed editions, *tacitas volvit cunctatio mentes* (“hesitation turns silent minds”). For *cunctatio*, others write *conctatio* or *contatio*.

[Note: [Col. 0233B]]

219. It was customary not to count women and children. Jerome, on this passage: “Women and little children, the weaker sex and the lesser age, are considered unworthy of enumeration. Therefore, whenever priests, Levites, armies, or crowds of combatants are described in the Book of Numbers, servants, women, little children, and the common multitude are omitted from the count.”

220. CHAPTER IX. On the sign of the prophet Jonah. Matthew 16:1 and following; Mark 8:11; Luke 12:54.

221. *Sadducaei*: the first syllable is lengthened, though in Book 4, verse 14, some shorten it.

224. *Convexum coelum, nox humida* (“the arched heaven, the damp night”). Both epithets are appropriate and are drawn from Virgil. *Convexum* means rounded, though for others it means hollow. It should be noted that the second and third verses of Matthew, which Juvencus explains from *Convexum* through verse *Fallaces*, are absent from some copies. Indeed, Jerome, in his commentary on this passage, after giving the first four verses of Matthew 16, adds: “This is not found in most manuscripts, and the meaning is clear: from the order and regularity of the elements, both clear and rainy days can be predicted.” Hilary also read this passage in the same way: “He replied that they were accustomed to infer many things about the nature of the sky, declaring it clear or stormy according to whether it reddened at sunrise or sunset.”

[Col. 0233D] 225. *Astrifer* (“star-bearing”) is a word used by Statius and Martial; *astriger* (“star-bearing”) by Statius, Claudian, and Solinus. *Procedit vesper olympo* (“evening advances from Olympus”) is from Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, final verse: “And evening advanced from reluctant Olympus.”

226. *Ventura luce* (“with the coming light”): the author of the *Moretum*, verse 4: “fearing the sad fasts of the coming light.” *Serenum* (“clear”) is used for “clearness.” See the note on Dracontius, Book 1, verse 586.

227. *Tristia*, etc. Matthew says: “For the sky is reddened with sadness.”

229. *Fragosam*, “full of crashing noise and tumult,” or also “harmful to farmers and sailors.” Koenigius says the word is rare; but besides Valerius Flaccus and Quintilian, whom he cites, it is used by Virgil, [Col. 0234B] Claudian, Ovid, Gratius, and other ancient writers.

231. A *facies* (“appearance” or “face”) is attributed to the sky, the sea, the mountain, and other inanimate things.

234. *Profundo* (“depth”), used substantively. Dracontius, Book 1, verse 151: “The earth is drawn up, submerged in the vast depth.”

[Col. 0234C] 235. By the term *bellua* (“beast”) a whale is understood, as I explained in my note on Dracontius, Book 2, verse 159: “Horrid monsters swim, and a huge beast rejoices.”

238. It is asked why Juvencus calls the place *arva Philipporum* (“the fields of the Philippi”), since Matthew, in the singular, says in chapter 16, verse 13: “But Jesus came into the regions of Caesarea Philippi.” And Mark 8:27: “And Jesus went out, and his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi.” Near the sources of the Jordan, Philip the tetrarch either founded or embellished this city, and called it Caesarea after the name of Tiberius Caesar. Later Juvencus recalls the same city in verse 258: “The lands that flourish with the famous name of Philippaeus.” Here he has used the plural *Philipporum* for the singular *Philippi*, unless one prefers to emend it to *Arva Philippaea, sociisque* (“the Philippaean fields, and to his companions”). It was customary for poets of this period to lengthen a short vowel solely by reason of the caesura. This would now be detected more often if bold scribes, ignorant of this practice, had not corrupted many verses.

239. *Vobis*, “from you”: this is familiar in Juvencus.

[Col. 0234D] 242. Let us hear the evangelist Matthew: “Who said to them: Observe and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. But they reasoned among themselves, saying: Because we have taken no bread.” In manuscript Corb. 1: “But they reasoned among themselves, saying: He says this because we have not brought bread.” The old Tridentine Evangelistary: “Then they considered among themselves, saying: Because we did not buy bread.” To explain that under the name of the Pharisees’ leaven the disciples understood the bread which the Pharisees displayed or perhaps sold, Juvencus adds: “That they mix into foods and deceive under the name of bread.” *In the name of bread* is the same as *in bread*. Badius restores: “He would have said *under the name*, if the verse did not forbid it.” But Juvencus uses *in* for *sub* and *sub* for *in* indiscriminately.

And they bring back seven baskets, with the weight heaped up.

Then there were four thousand people in all,

and no one counted either the mothers or the children.

[220] From there he crosses by ship to the regions of Magedarum.

Behold the Pharisees and deceitful Sadducees,

persisting in trying to demand heavenly signs.

But Christ, seeing their deceitful hearts, speaks:

“Whenever the damp night closes the arched heaven,

[225] 261 if a red evening advances from the star-bearing Olympus,

you say: ‘With the coming light there will be clear weather.’

And now, when at sunrise red clouds mingle

with a confused light of color,

you say that a rough fury of winds

[230] [Col. 0234A] and storms is coming for farmers and sailors.

Hypocrites, you know how to discern the appearance of the sky,

but you do not know how to examine the seasons of the ages

by their own signs? Yet signs will be given you,

which once came from the immense depths of the sea,

[235] when the beast held the prophet in the prison of its belly.”

He said this, and quickly loosing the ship’s ropes,

he hastened across the straits in rapid course

262 to reach the fields of Philippi, and speaks these things to his companions:

“Carefully avoid harmful grain for yourselves,

and turn fierce leaven away from your tables.

[240] The Pharisees and deceitful Sadducees

mix that into foods and deceive under the name of bread.

Why does hesitation turn your silent minds?”

[Col. 0235A] [Note: [Col. 0235A]]

244. Reg., Ottob., Rom., *Pro qua* (“for which”); and the Reg. gloss, *pro qua cunctatione* (“for which hesitation”). Hadam. likewise printed this. Ald., Daventr., *Pro quo* (“for which,” masculine/neuter). Fabr., Poelm., *Proh quam parva* (“Alas, how little”). For *torpente* (“being numb”), Ott. erroneously has *torpenti*. The same Ott. writes *fatescit* (“crumbles”), instead of *fatiscit* (“decays”). In Rom., *facessit*; this appears to be an error for *fatescit* or *fatiscit*.

245. Reg., Rom., Torn., *adversi* (“being opposed”); Ott., with Ald., Hadam., Poelm., and Daventr., *aversi* (“turned away”). Reuschius has *aversi*, but acknowledges the same sense in *adversi*. They were turned away, opposed, or alienated from the boat in mind and thought. If *aversi, navi* is distinguished as in the Paris manuscript, *tollere panes navi* then means “to take the loaves into the boat.” Badius interpreted *adversi navi* as “brought up against the boat”; Schoettgenius, *adversi* as “toward one another.” Matthew says: “But they reasoned among themselves, saying: Because we have taken no bread.” The phrase may be explained as *dicitis adversi*, that is, “you speak with hostile minds.”

248. Our manuscripts Reg., Rom., and Ottob. have *Quod panes quinque plebis mihi millia quinque* (“that five loaves for me [filled] five thousand of the people”). This is the genuine reading, with the final syllable of *quinque* lengthened either because of the caesura, or rather because the mute and liquid in the following word have the power to lengthen or make common the short vowel of the preceding word. Not understanding this, scribes altered the line in various ways. Poelm., in the text, Torn., Hadam., Fabr., *Quod panes quini plebis mihi millia quinque* (“that five loaves for me [filled] five thousand of the people”). Poelm., as an alternative reading, Ald., Daventr., Bas.: *Panes quinque mihi plebis quod millia quinque* (“five loaves for me, because five thousand of the people”).

[Col. 0236A] 249. Rom., Ottob., and Reg., by the first hand, *Implerent* (“would fill”); the printed editions, *Implerint* (“have filled”). *Implerint* is more appropriate to the sense.

252. Rom., *Quod facile implerent quinque sportasque referri* (“which five could easily fill, and the baskets be brought back”). The true reading is *septem* (“seven”), not *quinque* (“five”): the reference is now to the seven loaves, which sufficed for four thousand people. *Implerint* should also be retained here, as in most copies.

253. Rom., *completa* (“filled”); emend to *completas*.

254. Rom., *caveri* (“to be guarded against”); Reg., Ott., *cavere* (“to beware”); the printed editions, *cavenda* (“things to be guarded against”).

257. Reg., Ott., *perventum liquidi* (“having reached the fluid [depth]”); Rom., with the printed editions, *perventum est liquidi* (“the fluid [depth] has been reached”).

258. Reg., Ott., by the first hand, and Rom., *quae* (“which”), namely, *perventum est rura* (“the fields have been reached”), instead of *ad rura* (“to the fields”). See Book 1, verse 291, and verse 381 of this book. Among the printed editions, Ald. and Bas. have *quo* (“where”); Hadam., Fabr., and Poelm. have *qua* (“by which way”), which also appears in Ott. by the second hand; Badius explains it as *qua parte* (“by which route”). The same Ott. has *pallent* (“grow pale”), correctly emended there to *pollent* (“flourish”).

259. Torn., less well, *consilium* (“counsel”) instead of *concilium* (“assembly”).

260. Rom., *quem discipulorum fama putarent* (“whom the disciples’ report would suppose him to be”); the others, *quem se populorum fama putaret* (“whom the report of the peoples supposed him to be”), which is sound.

[Col. 0236C] 261. Torn., incorrectly, *Respondens* (“answering”). Reg. and Ott., *Respondent multi* (“many answer”); the Reg. gloss, *multi—discipulorum* (“many—of the disciples”). But *multas* (“many [opinions]”), with Rom. and the printed editions, is more suitable here. In Ott., *ex plebes* has correctly been changed to *plebis*.

[Note: [Col. 0235C]]

246. *Vacuum fuerit*, “it would have been free” or “it would have been possible.” Tacitus, *Histories* 2.38: “After the world had been subdued and rival cities and kings destroyed, it was possible to desire secure wealth.” Sallustius, quoted by Gellius, Book 9, chapter 12: “After the Punic fear had been removed, it was possible to exercise hostilities.” Martianus Capella, Book 1: “But it was possible for the gods to know beforehand.” Koenigius calls this an elegant and uncommon usage.

247. Concerning the leaven, or bread, of the Pharisees, the disciples were saying among themselves: “The Lord has spoken because we have not yet brought bread,” so that, when they bought it, they might beware of the Pharisees’ tricks. Jesus, however, rebuked them because they were concentrating their minds on bread and therefore understood neither his words nor remembered that shortly before he had filled five thousand people with five loaves, etc. They therefore ought not to have been so concerned about bread.

249. *Cophinus*, a large wicker vessel, seems to have been much used among the Jews. Juvenal, *Satires* 3.14: “whose equipment is a basket and hay”; and 6.542: “having abandoned basket and hay.” Omeisius observes that in the first miracle Matthew and Mark call the containers *cophini* (“baskets”), whereas in this second miracle they call them *sportae* (“baskets” or “hampers”).

253. *Compleo* (“I fill”) with a genitive. See the textual note at verse 90 of this book. Cicero and Lucretius used this verb with a genitive.

254. Matthew, in the passage cited: “Why do you not understand that I did not speak to you about bread when I said: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees?”

[Col. 0236C] 255. *Sec uti*, “having followed” or “having attained”: a simple verb used for a compound.

257. CHAPTER X. After Peter’s confession that Christ was the Son of God, Jesus calls him blessed. When Peter then says that Christ ought not to allow his members to be subjected to tortures, he sternly rebukes him, saying: “Get behind me, Satan.” Matthew 16:13 and following; Mark 8:27; Luke 9:18; John 6:69. As elsewhere he often says *terrae per terga* (“upon the back of the earth”), so here he says *per terga profundi* (“upon the back of the deep,” that is, the sea). Compare the commentary on Prudentius, preface to Book 2 *Against Symmachus*, verse 43: “across the swelling back of the strait.” Juvencus understands Christ to have reached the region of Caesarea Philippi by way of the Jordan and Lake Semechon, and in the characteristic idiom of the Hebrews calls any somewhat larger body of water “sea” or “deep.”

262. Why does Juvencus say, “to have heard more frequently … that he was John the Baptist”? Matthew says: “But they said: Some John the Baptist, others Elijah,” etc. Yet in some copies of the Itala version one reads: “But they said: John the Baptist, others Elijah,” etc. The Tridentine Evangelistary: “But they said: John the Baptist, others Elijah,” etc. Mark and Luke express the matter similarly, and therefore seem to indicate that the more common opinion had gained currency: that Christ was John the Baptist. For among the Jews the doctrine of metempsychosis was prevalent. *Firmare* (“to affirm”) is used here for *affirmare*: a simple verb for a compound, as *verto* is used for *everto*. Hirtius, Palladius, and Tacitus, among others, give *firmo* the same meaning.

Alas, how little faith, with dulled understanding, decays!

[245] “You say, being turned away, that taking the loaves into the boat

263 would not have been possible for you, and that I should order you

to beware of harmful grain; yet I thought you would remember and know

that five loaves had filled five thousand of the people

with food, and that such great baskets had collected

[250] the superfluous fragments into a heap of provisions;

and that seven loaves could easily have filled

four thousand diners, and that baskets were brought back.

[Col. 0236A] You saw them again filled with the remains.

264 But I warn you always to beware of the leavens of those men.”

[255] At last the disciples, having followed the life-giving words,

understand the teaching referred to by the name of leaven.

Then, when they had reached the fluid deep upon its back,

the lands that flourish with the famous name of Philippaeus,

he gathers an assembly of the disciples who followed him,

[260] and asks whom the report of the peoples supposed him to be.

They answer that there were then many sayings among the people:

that they had more frequently heard, and many affirmed,

[Col. 0237A] [Note: [Col. 0237B]]

264. Ald, *Pars trepidat memori servans oracula mente* (“Part trembles, keeping the prophecies in a remembering mind”). Our manuscripts, with Hadam., Poelm., and others, *Pars memorat volucris famae sibi cognita verba* (“Part recounts words known to it from fleeting rumor”). Torn. joined both verses, first *Pars memorat*, then *Pars trepidat*. Badius omitted *Pars memorat*, with the approval of Omeisius and Schoettgenius. Reuschius thinks both verses belong to Juvencus.

265. In Rom., *verum* (“truly”), an error for *iterum* (“again”); the meter requires the latter. Reg. and Ott. have *praepete curru* (“on a swift chariot”), which is preferable. The printed editions, with Rom., *praepete cursu* (“with swift course”).

268. Ott., *Jeremiam dixere alii apparuisse prophetam* (“others said that Jeremiah the prophet had appeared”). Reg., Rom., with the printed editions, *Jeremiam dixere alii: pars esse prophetam* (“others said Jeremiah; some said that he was a prophet”). Ott.’s reading could be defended by contracting the third and fourth vowels of *apparuisse* through synaeresis. But the common reading is confirmed by Matthew 16:14: “But they said: Some John the Baptist, others Elijah, still others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.”

269. In Aldus, *Tu Christus* (“You are Christ”) is an error, also copied in the Basel edition, although Aldus himself had already corrected it under the errata. Reg., *cunctos affatus* (“addressing all”); others, *cunctis arridens* (“smiling upon all”).

273. The manuscripts, with several printed editions, have *respondit* (“he answered”). Hadam. and Poelm., *respondet* (“he answers”). In Reg. it may have been correctly changed to *forti* (“to the brave man”).

[Col. 0238B] 276. Ott., *poterint* (“they will have been able”); perhaps the scribe intended *poterunt* (“they will be able”), which would not be inappropriate instead of *poterit* (“he will be able”).

279. Reg., *Hac mole* (“with this mass”), aptly corrected to *Hacin mole* (“on this mass”).

281. Omeisius rejects *inferni* (“of hell”), because *infernum* used substantively for the prison of the damned is not quite correct. Fabricius and Sabatierius printed *Inferni*: this word occurs substantively in the manuscripts of the old Latin version, Corb. 2 and Germ. 2, and in Hilary on this passage. According to Cellarius, it should be observed that with *infernus* it is safer to use the neuter substantive *infernum* than the masculine *infernus*, although ancient Christians often used the latter as well.

282. Reg., Rom., *robur habebit* (“it will have strength”), though in Rom. the first hand has *robor*. The others have *robore habebit* (“it will have strength in its strength”). *Robur habebit* is a probable reading if one punctuates as follows: “This house, not to be overcome by the gates of hell, will possess a prison—an enduring fortress, perpetually secured by strength.”

283. Ald., *permittere* (“to permit”) instead of *committere* (“to entrust”).

284. Ott., *relinquis* (“you leave”); Reg., with many printed editions, more correctly *relinques* (“you will leave”). Rom., with Ald., *quae nexa manebunt* (“which will remain bound”).

[Col. 0238C] 285. Ott., *coeli* (“of heaven”); read *coelo* (“in heaven”) with Reg., Rom., Daventr., and Ald., or *coelis* (“in the heavens”) with Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr. In Rom., *nudata* (“stripped”) is an error for *nodata* (“bound”).

286. Reg., *at* (“but”); other manuscripts and printed editions, *et* (“and”).

287. Ott., *coelesti sede* (“heavenly seat”); the others, *coeli sub sede* (“beneath heaven’s seat”).

[Note: [Col. 0237C]]

263. *Lavit* (“he washed”) is sometimes a present-tense form from *lavo, lavis*, in which case the first syllable is short; sometimes it is the perfect tense from *lavo, lavas*, or even from *lavo, lavis*, in which case it is long. Examples of both usages are common.

266. *Simulata*, “assimilated” or “made similar.” See the note on Book 2, verse 548, and Book 1, verse 394.

267. *Vis flammae* (“the force of flame”) used for *flamma* (“flame”). See the note on Book 1, verse 478, and Gifan’s *Index to Lucretius*, under *Vis morbi* (“force of disease”).

269. *Arridens*, “showing a kindly face.” “It is not recorded that Christ ever laughed,” says Koenigius. But neither can it be inferred from Juvencus that he laughed.

271. *Stabilis Petrus* (“Peter, steadfast”): this indicates the Catholic interpretation of the Lord’s words, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” so that the Church is understood to have been built upon Peter. The Tridentine Evangelistary states the matter more explicitly: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it.” The poet adds *forti Petro* (“to brave Peter”), and speaks more clearly when he turns to the matter itself: “You uphold the name of Peter with worthy strength— / Upon this mass and the strength of this rock I shall place for myself / dwellings destined to remain forever with eternal walls.” Likewise Book 1, verse 458: “And Simon, thoroughly steadfast, worthy of the name Peter.” Omelsius explains: “Upon faith and confession I will place it,” etc. Juvencus clearly refers it to the person of Peter. I demonstrated the truth of this interpretation from the Church’s prayers and liturgical supplications in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn 1 of the Catholic Hymns*, verse 63. The same argument is treated excellently by the eminent Cardinal Gerdil in his work *Refutation of Two Pamphlets Directed Against the Brief Super Soliditate*, in which he refutes the cavils of the innovators with invincible arguments and admirable theological gravity, and utterly dismantles them.

275. Koenigius teaches that this is a rabbinic description of the human being: “flesh and blood.”

277. Above, verse 119: “Which carried across the waters the mighty strength of faith.” Compare the note.

279. *Robur saxi* (“the strength of the rock”) for *saxum* (“rock”), as *robur fidei* (“the strength of faith”) and in Book 1, verse 478, *membrorum robora* (“the strength of the limbs”). Compare the note.

282. *Perpetuo robore* (“with enduring strength”), because the gates of hell will not prevail against it. Gates of oak or other strong timber were considered firm. Ovid, *Amores* 2.1: “The doors yielded to songs; and although the bolt inserted in the doorpost / was oak, the bar was conquered by song.”

285. *Nodata*, “bound into knots.” Virgil, Ovid, and many other ancient writers used this word.

287. *Venient soluta*, “they will come freed” or “they will be free.” This poetic expression is familiar to Propertius, as Scaliger notes, Book 2, elegy 1, verse 2: “Whence may my soft book come to my lips.” Marius Victor, preface to his poem on Genesis: “Nor does the nature of free will, powerful in either direction, / come to us as something to be blamed.”

The righteous John, who washed the people in the river.

265 Part recounts words known to it from fleeting rumor:

[265] “Elijah has come again,” whom, on a swift chariot,

a fiery force of flame once placed among the stars

in a counterfeit quadriga through a heavenly whirlwind.

Others said Jeremiah; some said that he was a prophet.

Then Christ, smiling upon all with a kindly heart,

[270] asks what opinion the disciples hold.

But steadfast Peter says: “You are the Son of the Holy One,

266 Christ, who fills the earth with magnificent light.”

Then the Lord answered brave Peter with these words:

“Peter, you will be blessed; for no human blood,

[275] [Col. 0238A] nor a body, a portion of earth, will ever be able

to reveal such things. The Father’s gifts alone

can grant such mighty strength to faith.

You uphold the name of Peter with worthy strength.

Upon this mass and the strength of this rock I shall place for myself

[280] dwellings destined always to remain with eternal walls.

This house, not to be overcome by the gates of hell,

will possess a prison perpetually secured by enduring strength.

And it is my will to entrust to you the keys of the heavenly kingdom;

and whatever you bind upon earth by your authority

[285] 267 will remain likewise bound beneath heaven’s seat;

and whatever your decision releases again for the earth,

will likewise come released beneath heaven’s seat.

But you disciples, do not tell everyone that Christ is me—

[Col. 0239A] [Note: [Col. 0239B]]

289. Ott., Had., and Poelm. in the text have *quod* (“that”); most have *quo* (“by which”). Rom. has *digna* (“worthy”); correct to *digni* (“worthy,” agreeing with the implied subject).

291. Rom. in the text, Ottob., Hadam., and Poelm., *prona* (“inclined”); this is indicated by the joining of letters in Reg. Ald., Bas., and Rom. in the margin as an alternative reading have *plena* (“full”), which Koenigius preferred. Badius explains *prona* as “impassioned” or “eager.”

293. There is no doubt that *lucifluum* (“light-flowing”) should be read, not *luctifluum* (“grief-flowing”); the former seems to have been written by the first hand in Reg., and was printed by Hadam. and Poelm., as also by Reuschius. So Book 4, verse 119: “a witness with light-flowing speech of holy salvation.” Fabricius printed this verse in the following corrupted form: “But when the third sun shall restore a light-flowing rising.”

296. Rom., Reg. by the second hand, Ald., and Poelm., *perculsus* (“struck”); Ott., *percussus* (“struck”), which perhaps was in Reg. by the first hand. Torn. has the apparent error *perpulsus*. Rom., Ott., and Hadam. have *corde* (“in the heart”), which I think was also in Reg. by the first hand. Reg. now has *corda* (“hearts”), with the gloss *per corda* (“through the hearts”). Ald., Fabr., Torn., Daventr., and Bas. have *corda*. Reuschius preferred *perculsus corda* (“striking hearts”). Ott. has *pavore* (“with fear”), while the alternative reading has *dolore* (“with grief”), which the others give us.

298. Rom., *nefas est* (“it is impious”); read, to avoid corrupting the meter, *nec fas est* (“nor is it permitted”).

300. The manuscripts, with the finest printed editions, have *Christus ad haec: Procul hinc, inquit, procul effuge, daemon* (“Christ at this said: Away from here, he says; flee far away, demon”). In Rom. the text has *inquam* (“I say”), with *inquit* (“he says”) in the margin. Hadam. and Poelm., *Christus ad haec inquit: Procul, o, procul effuge, daemon* (“Christ at this says: Away, oh, flee far away, demon”).

301. The manuscripts and most printed editions have *Nil divina tibi* (“You have nothing divine”), but Reg. has *Non* instead of *Nil*. Ald. and Bas., *Nil divina tuam* (“You have nothing divine of yours”). Poelm. in the text, *Nil divina tibi*; as an alternative reading, *Nil tua divinam* (“You have nothing of your divine [power]”). Reuschius defends *Nil divina tibi*, a syntax that occurs elsewhere in Juvencus.

[Col. 0240B] 302. Reg., Ott., *tremescis* (“you tremble”); Rom., with others, *tremiscis* (“you tremble”).

303. Rom., Ald., Bas., *At siquis* (“But if anyone”); others, *Sed siquis* (“But if anyone”), which is harsher, but must be retained.

304. The printed editions, *Abneget hic sese* (“let this man deny himself”). Our manuscripts Rom., Reg., and Ott., *Abneget ipse sibi* (“let he himself deny himself”). I retain this, although *Se neget ipse sibi* (“let him himself deny himself”) might perhaps be better. Matthew 16 in the Itala version from manuscript Colb.: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself to himself”; likewise other ancient manuscripts and the Fathers: “let him deny himself to himself,” “let him deny his very self to himself,” “let him deny himself to himself.” The Tridentine Evangelistary: “Let him deny himself.” In Juvencus, *corpusque, animamque* (“both body and soul”) stands for “himself,” and is the accusative governed by the verb *abneget* (“let him deny”) and by the present participle *recusans* (“refusing”), as a similar construction occurs at verse 425. See also Book 1, verses 65 and 341; Book 2, verses 238 and 752; Book 3, verses 79 and 139.

[Col. 0240C] 307. Torn., *locis* (“places”); emend to *lucis* (“light”).

308. Reg., Rom., Ottob., with many printed editions, *proficient* (“they will advance”). Hadam. and Poelm. in the text, *proficiunt* (“they advance”). Poelm. as an alternative reading, Daventr., *Commoda sed quid erunt* (“But what will the advantages be?”).

309. Ott., Rom., and Ald., *subeant* (“let them undergo” or “let them enter”), instead of *pariant* (“let them produce”) in Reg. and others. Reuschius, if *subeant* is read, wishes it to be explained as “let them cause their possessors to undergo.” Ott., Rom., *lucis vitaeque perennis* (“of everlasting light and life”); the others, *vitae lucisque perennis* (“of everlasting life and light”).

310. In Rom. *queant* (“they may be able”) seems to have been made from *queunt* (“they are able”); all the others have *queunt*.

313. The manuscripts and several printed editions have *hominum* (“of men”); in Reg., by the first hand, there was *hominem* (“a man”), erroneously. Hadam. and Poelm., *homini* (“for a man”).

314. Ott.: *isthinc* instead of *isthic*. Rom., Reg.: *sub lumine lucis* (“under the light of light”). Ott.: *sub limine lucis* (“under the threshold of light”), though perhaps *sub lumine* was written by the first hand. Printed editions: *sub nomine lucis* (“under the name of light”); Fabricius, however, has *sub limine lucis*. Matthew 16:28 reads: “There are some of those standing here who will not taste death,” etc. Therefore the true reading seems to be *sub limine lucis*, as in Book II, line 654: “and vigorous at the thresholds of light.” This may be understood of life’s very end, as in Apuleius, Book XI of the *Metamorphoses*, near the middle: “already standing at the threshold of the light that had itself been brought to an end, their lifetime having passed.” Some explain Matthew’s text as referring to the rise of the Gospel, others to the glory of the Ascension; likewise some to John the Evangelist, others to the eleven apostles; some to the Transfiguration, which followed shortly afterward.

[Note: [Col. 0239C]]

292. The sacred text has: “To suffer many things from the elders, and scribes, and chief priests.” At Book I, line 39, I observed that Juvencus calls priests *vates* (“prophets” or “seers”).

297. Matthew: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” The Arabic version: “Far be it from you, Lord, that this should happen to you,” to which Juvencus corresponds. The Tridentine Gospel Book: “Be gracious, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” The preposition *a* is usually expressed, as in “let such things be far from your limbs,” but is sometimes omitted when it is already contained in the verb *absum* (“I am absent,” “I am far away”).

298. “Nor is it right to believe so much.” Virgil, Book III of the *Georgics*, line 391: “If it is worthy to be believed.”

300. See Prudentius, Hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 137: “Far away, O far away, from those who wander,” etc.

303. CHAPTER XI. That each person ought to take up his own cross and follow the Lord; also, that some will not die until they see the Son of Man. Matthew 16:24 and following; Mark 8:39; Luke 9:23, etc.

305. “His own,” “his,” as the ancients more frequently said. For *proprius* means belonging to someone alone, particular. Sextus Rufus, Ammianus Marcellinus, and others of the same period used *proprius* for *suus* (“his own”); good poets also did so, including Horace, Lucretius, and Ovid.

310. Matthew: “Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?”

311. *Sub nomine* (“under the name”) instead of *in nomine* (“in the name”).

312. *Fremo* (“I roar”) and *fremitus* (“roaring”) are sometimes used of applause and joy. Virgil, Book VIII, line 717: “They roared along the roads with joy, games, and applause”; and Book V, line 148: “Then the whole grove resounded with the applause and roaring of men and their eager supporters.”

Spare them, so that only those worthy may know such things.

[290] Now the light will come, pressing upon me with swift course,

when raging fury in the walls of Jerusalem

shall sate the distinguished prophets with our blood.

But when the third sun shall restore the light-bearing dawn,

life, likewise crowned with the rays of salvation,

[295] shall rise for me and grant its gifts to all the lands.

Then Peter, deeply stricken in heart with grief, said:

“May these terrible monsters be far, O Christ, from your holy limbs. Nor is it right to believe so much,

nor can so harsh a fate befall you.”

[300] [Col. 0239B] Christ answered: “Away from here, away, flee, demon!

[Col. 0240A] No divine wisdom touches your mind;

you savor earthly things and tremble with soft-hearted fear.

But if any one of you follows our footsteps,

let him deny himself, refusing both body and soul,

[305] and rejoice to add his own cross to our company;

for glory will redeem the life he has lost.

For the possession of light, if preserved on earth, perishes.

269 But what will mortal gains of the world accomplish,

if they bring loss of life and everlasting light?

[310] Or what worthy exchange can be offered for the soul?

The Son of Man will come under the name of the Father,

and heavenly ministers, amid accompanying acclamation, will surround him,

and he will render to human lives their due deserts.

I speak the truth: I shall find certain persons standing here at the threshold of light

[315] [Col. 0241A] [Note: [Col. 0241B]]

317. Most manuscripts have *converso* (“turned”); Ott., on the authority of the first hand, and Fabr., have *convexo* (“vaulted”), which pleased Reuschius more, as it came from the Helmstedt manuscript. In Rom. the error *connexo* (“joined”) also indicates *convexo*. See above, line 224.

320. Reg. and Ott.: *perventum secreti*; as at line 257 of this passage: “from there, when they had reached the clear.” Rom., together with the printed editions: *perventum secreti est*. In Ott., and apparently in Reg., *secreti in montis* was written, but *in* was later deleted.

321. In Ottob., if I am not mistaken, the first hand wrote *facie*, the second *faciem*: the latter is the true reading, by the customary Greek construction.

[Col. 0241C] 322. Rom.: *vestis niveo*; the others: *vestisque nivis*.

324. Ott.: *Moseique*; Rom.: *Moysique*; others: *Mosique*.

326. The manuscripts and most printed editions have *An isthic* (“whether there”); Torn., Poelm., and Hadam. have *Anne isthic*, perhaps introduced so that *an* would not be lengthened. But that *an*, and similar monosyllables considered short, can sometimes be lengthened was shown in Book II, line 517.

327. Reg.: *trino tamen hic tentoria vobis*, and the glossator indicates *trino apparatu*. Ott., Daventr., Ald., Bas., and Westh. in the text: *trina tamen hic tentoria vobis*, with *a* lengthened according to the caesural arrangement. Hadam., Poelm., Fabr., Westh. in the margin, and Torn.: *trina attamen hic tentoria vobis*. Rom.: *tamen hic vobis tentoria trina*.

328. Reg. has *frondes*, correctly emended to *frondis*. In Ott. there is erroneously *diverso paratu*, an error that also stood in Reg. but was corrected there to *diversa paratu*. Ott. likewise seems to have *fronde faciam* instead of *frondis faciam*.

329. In Ottob. *sub nocte*, and in Rom. *receptant*, should be corrected to *sub noctem* and *receptent*.

331. Reg. has *vestiebat*, perhaps the form also originally written in Ott. Most printed editions, together with Ott.’s second hand, and Rom., have *vestibat*. Daventr. and Poelm., according to the first hand, have *condebat*. *Vestibat* is sound: Virgil has, “Then youth first clothed my cheeks with its flower.”

333. Ald., Bas., and Westh. in the text: *Vivens hic meus est* (“This living one is mine”). Other editions, and Westh. in the margin together with our manuscripts: *Unicus hic meus est* (“This is my only-begotten one”). Ald., Bas., Poelm. according to the first hand, and Torn. have *voluptas* (“delight”); our manuscripts, together with other editions, have *voluntas* (“will”), and the gloss in Reg. says: “in whom I was well pleased.” Although *voluptas* may seem more distinctive, we should follow the authority of the manuscript copies, especially since what is said—“in whom I was well pleased”—pertains to *voluntas*. In the first half-line the manuscript reading is undoubtedly preferable, for *Unicus* expresses what the Gospel says: “This is my beloved Son,” or “most beloved,” as in the old version from the Colbert manuscript, or “dearest,” as in Corb.
