I. The Tridentine Gospel Book: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I was well pleased.”

337. Rom.: *ni*; Reg., Ott., with some printed editions: *nisi*. Poelm. according to the first hand, Ald., Fabr., Bas., and Torn.: *quam*. I consider this manner of expression good Latin: “Nor did they dare earlier, unless the right hand had strengthened [them],” etc. The examples are certainly not altogether alike, but neither are they very different: Caesar, Book I of the *Gallic War*, chapter 31: “That his commands could no longer be maintained unless there were some assistance in Caesar.” Others punctuate it differently. Horace, Book I of the *Satires*, line 79: “We should never have crept out, unless the neighboring villa of Trevicus had received us.”

[Note: [Col. 0241C]]

316. CHAPTER XII. Jesus’ transfiguration on the mountain. Matthew 17:1 and following; Mark 9:1; Luke 9:28.

317. “Twice three lights of days,” that is, six days.

323. *Assistere*, “to be present,” in the same way as in Book I, line 617: “and the crowds gladly attend the prayers of joy.”

325. Matthew: “Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make here three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Juvencus expands this, but why does he say, “Look, whether it would rather be fitting for us,” etc.? Perhaps he read it interrogatively: “Lord, is it good for us to be here?”

328. *Paratu*, “equipment,” “preparation.” Valerius Flaccus, Book II, line 652: “with the royal preparation of the table.”

330. *Praefulgidus* (“very bright”) is placed among Latin words by Forcellini solely on Juvencus’ authority. Omeisius attributes the word also to Julius Firmicus. Latin writers more usually say *praefulgens* (“shining brightly”).

331. “He clothed the mountain with light”: an elegant metaphor. Virgil, Book VI, line 640: “Here the ampler ether covers the fields and clothes them with purple light, and the sun and its stars know their own.” Add Lucretius, Book II, line 142: “clothing everything by pouring over it his own light.”

332. Book I, line 396: “Then the voice sent by God ran through the long void.”

333. *Unicus*: “only-begotten,” and therefore intensely and uniquely beloved.

336. *Prono*, referring to those who had fallen forward upon their face.

338. “Soothing, he strengthened their hearts”: the same accusative is governed by two verbs, as we have often seen.

when I shall take possession of heaven’s shining kingdoms.

When he had spoken these things and allowed twice three days’ lights

to pass across the earth beneath the vaulted sky,

he then ordered Peter to climb with him up the steep mountain,

and the two sons of Zebedee by the pathless ways.

[320] 270 When they had reached the summit of the secluded mountain,

Christ immediately changed his face with flashing radiance,

and his garment gleamed with the whiteness of snow.

The companions looked and saw the holy Elijah and Moses standing in their midst. Then Peter said:

[325] “Look, whether it would be better for us to depart far away

[Col. 0242A] or to behold there a spectacle of such great magnitude.

Nevertheless, if you command, I will make here three tents

for you, different leafy structures in their equipment,

one for each of you, to shelter you beneath their coverings at night.”

[330] While he was saying these things, a cloud very bright with light

271 surrounded the mountain, clothing it before their eyes,

and a clear voice ran forth from the midst of the light:

“This is my only-begotten Son, my sole will;

grasp his righteousness with a righteous heart.”

[335] The disciples pressed the earth with their trembling bodies.

Nor did they dare to lift their faces from their prostrate fall

until the holy right hand of Christ,

soothing them, had strengthened their hearts with gentle words:

[Col. 0243A] [Note: [Col. 0243A]]

340. In an old manuscript of Ott., after the line “Rise immediately,” this line appears: “Nor may the vision present be disclosed to anyone of you”; all other verses are omitted. Ald. and Bas. also printed this form. Other manuscripts insert another line between “Rise” and “Nor may anyone,” containing the same meaning: “Nor may this vision be disclosed to anyone of you.” Manuscripts and editions vary regarding the insertion of this verse. Reg. and Rom.: *Horomatis hujus expertes facite cunctos* (“Make everyone without this vision”). Reg. has a gloss: *Horomatis*—“of an oracle, or vision”; Rom. writes *Horromatis*. As thus explained, the verse is harsh and lawless, and therefore unworthy of Juvencus. Others consequently revised it in different ways. Poelm., according to the first hand: *Oramatisque hujusce expertes reddite cunctos* (“Make everyone without this vision”). Torn.: *Horamatis hujus expertes vos reddite cunctos* (“Make you all without this vision”); *vos* should be omitted for the meter. Fabricius and Davent., Poelm. in the text, Hadam., and others have *Gloriae et hujusce expertes vos reddite cunctos* (“Make you all without this glory as well”). Bede, *Retractationes on the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 9, lines 11–12: “For behold, he is praying; and he saw a man named Ananias,” and says: “In Greek it is written thus: ‘And he saw in a vision a man,’ that is, *ἐν ὁράματι*—‘in a vision’; and the presbyter Juvencus also placed this word in his Gospel poem, saying: ‘Make everyone without this vision.’” Labbe, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he discusses Juvencus, observes that this reading is absent from the Vulgate version—namely, from most printed editions of Juvencus—because an ignorant scribe or rash corrector, not understanding the word *horamatis*, preferred to turn it into *gloriam* rather than remain stuck in the mud. Schoettgenius likewise thinks that Juvencus retained the word *horamatis* from the Greek text. By contrast, Omeisius and Joachim Kuhn, in letters sent to Koenig, reject this verse as spurious; Kuhn asserts that it does not occur in his manuscript. But Kuhn’s claim that the edition of Antonio de Nebrija—the first to publish Juvencus with his own explanations—received this verse from the margin into the text is entirely false, as I showed in the *Prolegomena*, no. 71, since no edition of Juvencus with Nebrija’s explanations ever existed. The authority of Bede certainly adds considerable weight to the verse “Make everyone without this vision.” Nevertheless, I judge it to be spurious and to have entered some manuscripts before Bede’s time. Since the word *horama* was unknown to the good authors of Latin and appears frequently used by monks in the later age, it is reasonable to conjecture that some glossator explained Juvencus’ verse, “Nor may the present vision be disclosed to anyone of you,” in this way: “Make everyone without this vision”; or, if he did not wish to compose a verse, “Make everyone [without it].” As time passed, this verse entered the text together with the genuine one; and when the word *horama* later became less familiar, some rewrote it more clearly as “Make everyone without this glory as well.” From this alteration it also follows that explicit mention of the vision is absent from both verses. *Horama*, or rather *orama* without aspiration, is pronounced with various quantities by writers of the lowest period. Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, chapter 26: “By night he rightly saw the heavenly vision.” Gualdo, a monk of Corbie, *Life of Saint Anscharius*, chapter 16: “The avenging punishment of evil was the mark of this vision.” Some wrote *oroma*. Du Cange supplies many examples of the use of this word among medieval and late writers, from the passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, the *Life of Saint Willebrord*, Saint Gerard, Rodulfus Tortarius, Uguccio, Olbertus, abbot of Gembloux, Fulcuin, Fridegodus, and Ermenricus. Regarding the verse that truly belongs to Juvencus, it should be noted that Matthew 17:9—“Tell the vision to no one”—is wonderfully explained by it. The same word “vision,” or “what was seen,” occurs in other ancient versions of Holy Scripture, but *orama* occurs in none of them.

343. The manuscripts and most printed editions have *solumque vident* (“and they see only him”) and require *voce*. Hadam. and Poelm. in the text have *solidumque vident* (“and they see the solid one”). Poelmann according to the first hand and Westh. in the text: *solumque videntes voce requirunt* (“and, seeing only him, they ask aloud”). Westh. in the margin: *solidumque videntes voce requirunt*. Reuschius conjectures *solitumque vident* (“and they see the familiar one”), that is, in the customary appearance or accustomed form. But the sacred text suggests something else, Matthew 17:8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.” This had been said shortly before, but Juvencus appropriately repeats it here.

344. Rom.: *sanctio*; read *factio*, as this word occurs often elsewhere.

347. Ott.: *certe*; others: *certo*.

348. Westh. in the text: *coelo* (“heaven”); in the margin: *saeclo* (“age,” “world”). Reuschius would restore *coelo* with Badius if the manuscripts supported this reading, since it comes closer to the Greek text.

[Note: [Col. 0243C]]

339. *Abjectum*, from the effect: the one who had cast them down.

[Col. 0243D] 340. *Vobis* (“for you”) instead of *a vobis* (“by you”): a phrase very familiar to Juvencus.

341. *Huc* (“here”), meaning into Galilee, as Schoettgenius explains from Mark 16:7: “For he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him.” It is better, however, to interpret *huc* as “here,” into the world, into the lands, as these are distinguished from the realms below.

342. The same accusative, *tropaea* (“trophies”), is governed by the two verbs *reportet* and *referens*, as I recently observed.

344. Matthew: “And the disciples questioned him, saying: Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Mark: “And they questioned him, saying: Why then do the Pharisees and scribes say that Elijah must come first?” This was the tradition of the elders, which Juvencus calls “the writings of the ancients,” just as at line 136 of this passage he says “the precepts of the ancients.” Trypho explains this Jewish tradition in his *Dialogue with Justin Martyr* as follows: “For if Christ has been born and exists somewhere, he is unknown, and does not even know himself, nor is he endowed with any power, until Elijah comes, anoints him, and makes him manifest to all.” They also thought that Elijah would restore everything to a better condition before Christ. Hence, when the disciples saw Elijah immediately vanish, they asked why the scribes, according to the tradition of the elders, taught that the Messiah’s coming would follow Elijah’s coming.

346. “The light of Christ”: Christ manifested in the flesh, who is the true light of the world. Book IV, final line: “Through the Lord Christ of light.”

347. Before the Lord’s second coming Elijah will restore all things; to this pertains the prophecy of Malachi 4:5: “Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes.” Reuschius takes *saeclo* to mean the condition of this life, or human beings living in the world.

349. *Renascens* (“being born again”): Omeisius takes it either as equivalent to the simple *nascens* (“being born”), or as acknowledging seeds of metempsychosis; certainly no reason compels us to attribute that doctrine to Juvencus. He expresses nothing other than that John came in the power of Elijah, according to Luke 1:17, concerning John the Baptist: “And he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.”

Rise, and courageously trample down the cast-off fear,

[340] nor may the present vision be disclosed to anyone of you,

272 until the splendid Son of Man brings back here

273 trophies from death’s abode into the light.”

They rise and see only him, and ask aloud

[Col. 0244A] why the faction of the scribes, in the writings of the ancients,

[345] teaches that Elijah must first return from heaven

to the lands, and that afterward the light of Christ must arise.

Christ answered: “At the appointed time the righteous Elijah

will certainly come, soon restoring to the age its due.

But if anyone believes it, he had already come, being born again.”

351. The manuscripts and editions vary, but *demersit* (“drove down,” “submerged”) is better than *dimersit*. I conjectured *Demisit letho* (“he sent him down to death”), as at line 489, *letho demittere* (“to send down to death”). Yet Horace, Book III, Ode 16, wrote *demersa excidio* (“submerged in destruction”).

352. Ott.: *Inque hominis*; retain *En hominis* (“behold, of man”). Ald. and Bas., together with most printed editions, have *laniantibus*; retain *laniatibus* (“with tortures”). Westh. in the text has *instat* (“presses upon”); in the margin *instar* (“in the likeness of”), though I do not know with what meaning.

356. Reg.: *sobolis* instead of *soboles*, as in other ancient manuscripts *famis* instead of *fames*, and similar forms.

357. Rom.: *natum*, above *nato*; read *nati*.

358. Rom. and the manuscripts, with Torn., have *Proturbes*, as in Livy and Virgil *proturbare hostem* (“to drive back an enemy”). Aldus, with other editions, has *Perturbes* (“disturb”).

359. Rom.: *Nam lunae cursus natum*; others: *Nam cursus lunae*.

360. Rom.: *protrahit* (“draws forth”); the others: *proicit* (“casts forth”); Reg. and Ott. write *proicit*.

364. Rom., Hadam., and Poelm. in the text: *corde* (“heart”); Ottob., Reg. by the second hand, Ald., Torn., and Bas.: *corda* (“hearts”); and the gloss in Reg.: “through hearts.”

[Col. 0245C] 366. Rom.: *An etiam patiar* (“shall I also suffer?”); the others better have *En etiam* (“behold, even”).

367. Ott.: *praeferre* (“to prefer”), perhaps the form also originally present in Reg. Others: *perferre* (“to endure”).

368. Rom.: *pondere magno* (“with great weight”); the others: *pondere multo* (“with much weight”).

369. Reg.: *mentisque sinu* (“in the bosom of the mind”), with a gloss, “that is, from the heart,” and a later gloss on *convulsa*: “that is, cast out.”

373. All our manuscripts, with Daventr., Ald., and Bas., have *labat* (“is unsteady”). Hadam., Torn., Poelm., and Fabr. have *titubat* (“totters”). Elsewhere *labat* also occurs on the authority of some manuscripts with the first syllable lengthened, as in Book II, line 437. The genuine reading therefore seems to be *labat*, not *titubat*, although *titubat*, or even *lapsat*, is metrically closer.

375. Rom.: *Jam si* (“now if”); Torn.: *Sed si* (“but if”); others: *Nam si* (“for if”). Ott. and Rom.: *certa foret* (“were certain”); the others: *tanta foret* (“were so great”). Reuschius prefers *certa*, because *titubare* or *labare*—to be unstable, wavering—preceded. Hadam. and Poelm. according to the first hand have *nobis* (“for us”), less suitably instead of *vobis* (“for you”).

376. Ald., Bas., and Poelmann according to the first hand: *Quae minimi posset granum praestare sinapis* (“which could produce the smallest grain of mustard”). Reg., Rom., and Ott., with most editions: *Instar quae minimi posset praestare sinapis* (“which could equal the smallest mustard seed”). Rom. has *Instar quod*; Ottob. *possit*; Reg. has the gloss *praestare*—“namely, to provide this for you.” The common reading can be understood thus: “If you had faith so great that it could equal the smallest mustard seed,” that is, excel or even be of use; for *praestare* is sometimes simply used for “to benefit,” as I explained in the note to Dracontius, *On God*, Book II, line 607, and line 64 of the *Satisfactio*. Koenigius explains it better: “which could produce the likeness—the equivalent—of the smallest mustard seed”; for *instar* occurs in both nominative and accusative. Instead of *sinapis*, perhaps *sinapi* should be read: for *sinapi* is an indeclinable neuter, whereas when *sinapis, sinapis* is declined it is feminine, and *minimae* would therefore be required. Yet many admit the declinable neuter *sinape, sinapis* from Petronius and Apicius, and some also from Columella. See Forcellini under *sinapi*.

377. In Ott. the first hand has *hic*, the second *hinc*, together with the others. Our manuscripts, with Ald., Torn., and Bas., have *possetis* (“you could”); Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr. have *poteritis* (“you will be able”), a form also found in Juvencus with the third syllable lengthened.

[Note: [Col. 0245C]]

350. Matthew: “But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did in his case whatever they wished. So also the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands.” The comparison must therefore be referred, as it were, to the second killing, etc.

353. CHAPTER XIII. That the lunatic boy was healed, and that one who has faith as great as a mustard seed can move a mountain from its place. Matthew 17:14 and following; Mark 9:6; Luke 9:36.

355. Luke says: “A man from the crowd cried out.” Juvencus calls him an elder, perhaps because he was both a man and a father. Again at line 358: “and restore the consolations of life to the old man.” Here too the same accusative, *Deum* (“God”), is joined to the two verbs *veneratus* and *adorat* (“having revered” and “worships”).

356. Book I, line 312: “both light and salvation for the lands.”

359. Book I, line 482: “For the madness of the mind accompanied the moon’s course.”

363. *In solidum*, used adverbially for “solidly,” “fully,” “entirely,” “truly.” Apuleius used it adverbially in Book V of the *Metamorphoses*. Virgil, Book II of the *Georgics*, line 78: “Or again the knotless trunks are cut, and a path is split deeply through the whole,” where “wood” or “timber” is understood. In forensic usage *in solidum* means “wholly” or “entirely.” Omeisius explains: “They could not satisfy me fully.”

368. Matthew: “And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon went out from him.” The Tridentine Gospel Book: “And Jesus reproved him, and the demon went out from him.” Hilary, on this passage: “After he had rebuked him and reproved the demon, the boy became well.”

369. “The convulsive poisons of the mind of the dreadful demon”: two genitives are governed by the same noun in this common construction, as Reuschius also observed at Book I, line 193. See also Book II, lines 313 and 436.

370. “Of the dreadful demon”: elsewhere the demon is called “black,” as in Book II, line 439.

371. *Illis* (“for them”) is used for *ipsis* (“for themselves”), as Omeisius observed.

374. Pliny the Younger, Macrobius, Ulpian, and Papinian take *lubricum* (“slippery thing,” “unstable matter”) as a substantive, to omit the ancient Christian writers.

378. Reg.: *Hincque alias sedes*; read *Inque alias*.

379. Torn., Poelm. according to the first hand, and Fabr.: *Nam genus hoc morbi dumtaxat vota, precesque* (“For this kind of illness [is driven away] only by vows and prayers”). Ott., with Ald. and most printed editions: *Nam genus hoc morbi precibus sine fine, fideque* (“For this kind of illness [is driven away] by prayers without end and by faith”). The true reading appears in Rom. and Reg.: *Nam genus hoc morbi precibus sine fine, fidesque* (“For this kind of illness [is driven away] by prayers without end, and faith”), explained by the gloss in Reg.: “And faith together with prayers, and many fasts, ward it off.”

381. Fabr.: *Capharnitum* instead of *Capharnaum*. The manuscripts have *pervenerat oras* (“he had reached the shores”); some editions likewise. Aldus, with Torn., Bas., and Poelm. according to the first hand: *pervenit ad oras* (“he reached the shores”). But *pervenio* is also found with an accusative without a preposition. Ovid, Book III of the *Metamorphoses*, line 462: “You report words that do not reach our ears.”

383. The manuscripts and most printed editions have *solitum* (“customary,” “usual”). Ott. also has *solitum* in the margin; the word in the text has been erased. Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr. have *solidum* (“solidus”). These editors understand a whole gold coin of proper weight, which in the later period was called a *solidus*, whose value was not the same in every age. The Gospel mentions a didrachma, not a solidus; according to Calmet in the *Biblical Dictionary*, the didrachma corresponded to ten solidi and two denarii. It is therefore preferable to read *solitum*, namely, the customary tribute.

385. Ott.: *rependere* (“pay back”); others: *dependere* (“pay”), which better suits the meter. Otherwise *re-* in compounds is sometimes lengthened.

386. Ald., Bas., and Poelmann according to the first hand: *propriosve* (“their own or”); others: *propriosne* (“their own?”). Westh. in the text has *sive*; in the margin, correctly, *sibi*. Rom. in the text has *jussere* (“they ordered”); in the margin *misere*, or the unclear error *missere*. It should not be changed from *jussere*.

387. Poelm. according to the first hand: *Petrus his* (“Peter to these”); [read] *alienos* (“foreigners”). *His* is absent from most copies and is not necessary.

390. The manuscripts, with Ald. and others: *En maris* (“behold, of the sea”). Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr.: *Et maris* (“and of the sea”). Rom. in the margin has *undosum* instead of *undisoni*, namely, “surging high.” Ott.: *rupes quae prodit in aequa* (“a rock that projects into the level waters”), but the same old hand changed it to *in altum* (“into the deep”). Poelm. in the text: *in altum*; according to the first hand: *in aequor* (“into the open sea”).

394. Ott.: *pandatur* (“may be opened”); above, *pandantur* (“may be opened,” plural).

395. Ald., Poelm. according to the first hand, Torn., and Bas.: *invento* (“with what has been found”), namely, “pay the tribute with whatever you find there.” Most, together with the manuscripts, have *inventum*.

397. Reg.: *In coelis regno*; read *In coeli regno* (“in the kingdom of heaven”). Bas., against the meter, has *meritisque*, apparently from Aldus, who printed it thus; but Aldus noticed the error in the errata and corrected it.

399. Reg.: *Praecepit et placido*, which conflicts with the meter.

400. Reg. and Ott. preserve this order: first *Quisque cupit*, then *En hujus*. Rom., with the editions, has *En hujus* first and *Quisque cupit* second. Aldus printed *Quisque cupit celsam coeli conscendere sedem* (“Whoever desires to climb the lofty seat of heaven”); in the errata he replaced it with *Qui cupit excelsam coeli conscendere sedem* (“He who desires to climb the exalted seat of heaven”). But the genuine reading is *Quisque cupit*, for Juvencus and his contemporaries often use *quisque* for *quicumque* (“whoever”), as I showed in the commentary on Prudentius, Hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 216, and in the note to Dracontius, Book II, line 719.

401. Reg. and Rom. in the margin: *En hujus pueri similem se fingere certet* (“Let him strive to form himself like this boy”). Ald., Daventr., Torn., Hadam., and Bas.: *En hujus similem pueri se reddere certet* (“Let him strive to make himself like this boy”). Rom. in the text: *Istius en pueri similem se moribus aptet* (“Behold, let him adapt himself in character to this boy”), which Ott. seems to have intended, where it has *sermonibus* (“in speech”) instead of *se moribus*. Ott. according to the first hand indicates *Istius en pueri similem se fingere certet*. Fabricius printed this, but changed *fingere* to *reddere*. Omeisius did not dislike the reading found in some of his manuscripts: *pueri similem se moribus aptet*, namely, in spirit, such as boys are accustomed to be, most simple. In our reading *fingere* means “to form”; failure to understand this produced the variation in the manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0247D]]

378. *Transvolvere*. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, Hymn, line 29: “until the revolving ages have rolled onward.”

380. “Of sturdy breast,” as in Book I, line 407: “but at the same time the fasts of a firm heart woven together.”

381. CHAPTER XIV. That Peter found a coin in a fish’s mouth with which to pay the tribute. Matthew 17:23. Badius notes that *Capharnaum*, with the penultimate syllable lengthened, is used like *Menelaus*.

386. The order is: “Tell me, the kings whose sons they ordered to pay tribute to them: foreigners or their own?” The meaning is clear.

389. Matthew: “But so that we may not scandalize them.” Ambrose, on Psalm 48: “So that we may not cause them offense … cast a hook,” etc. Juvencus uses the same sense: “But so that I may harm no one.”

390. *Undisoni* (“roaring with waves”): Propertius, Statius, Valerius Flaccus, and Dracontius used this word. Juvencus expands Matthew’s words, who says only: “Go to the sea and cast a hook; and take the fish that first comes up, and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for you.”

394. Why does he say “the inner recesses of the belly,” when the matter concerns only the mouth? The Vulgate says: “And when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater.” Juvencus understands that the mouth is to be opened so that the stater may be drawn out from the inner recesses of the belly. This perhaps is suggested by the Old Latin version in the Tridentine Gospel Book: “Bring the first fish that comes up, open its mouth, and, finding a stater in it, take it,” etc.

395. *Dissolvere* (“to discharge,” “pay off”) belongs to a debt, as in “to discharge money,” “to pay a debt,” and similar expressions.

396. CHAPTER XV. That whoever wishes to ascend into heaven must be humble, as a child is, and that not even one little child is to be deceived, while whoever deceives one will suffer deserved punishments. Matthew 18:1 and following; Mark 9:33; Luke 9:46; 17:2.

402. “The snares of error”: see the note at this passage, line 12, *Saeclis* (“for the ages”) instead of “for this world.” “Woe to the world because of scandals,” etc. It is certain that *poni solet* means “is accustomed to be placed” for “is determined,” “has been decided.” Here it means “it is necessary.” It should be observed that Juvencus transposes the sayings: in Matthew, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” etc., occurs first; Juvencus reports it later, at line 404.

[Col. 0248A] He will roll the whole mass into other realms.

For this kind of illness prayers without end and faith,

[380] together with many fasts of a sturdy heart, drive it away.”

From there, walking from Capernaum, he reached the shores.

Those concerned with the tribute came to Peter,

demanding that the customary payment be made in Christ’s name.

277 But he, turning to Peter, spoke as follows:

[385] “Tell me: the kings whose sons they ordered to pay

tribute to them—foreigners or their own?”

Peter answered: “It is certain that foreigners pay.”

“Do you see,” said Christ, “that a king’s son does not pay?

But so that I may harm no one, receive our command:

[390] Behold, a rock of the roaring sea that projects into the deep.

Let a hook be climbed down for you, Simon, and let it be cast

into the depths, joined by a cord of bristles.

The fish that first catches upon its curved point—

let the inner recesses of its opened belly be disclosed.

278 Afterward the disciples asked who was greatest

in the high kingdom of heaven, and on account of what merits.

Then Christ ordered a child to stand in the midst of the assembly

and spoke as teacher in calm discourse:

[400] “Whoever desires to climb the lofty seat of heaven,

let him strive to form himself like this child.

It is certain that the snares of error grow throughout the world.

405. Reg.: *collo*; read *colla* (“necks”).

410. Ott.: *Et siquis* (“and if anyone”); Ald. and Bas.: *Sed siquas* (“but if any”); Reg., with the others: *Sed siquis* (“but if anyone”); in Reg. it is mistakenly written *Set*. Ald. has *tondant*; most have *tondent*; Rom. mistakenly has *tondet*. Sabatier printed: “But if any shepherd, to whom the pastures are entrusted, shearing a hundred bleating sheep,” which, I think, comes from his own conjecture.

416. Ald.: *Quod pro*, followed obscurely by *postea quod nulla* or *quam nulla*. Others have *Quam* instead of *cunctarum numero quod*. Ald., Bas., and Poelm. according to the first hand have *recessit*; the others *resedit*, which Reuschius accepts. Sheep rarely, or never, withdraw from the flock. Reg. punctuates: “in number, of which none remained—of these, the little ones,” with a gloss on *parvis*: “from the little ones.” This punctuation is not very satisfactory.

418. Ott.: *concrescere* (“grow together”); others: *increscere* (“increase”), as at line 402, instead of *crescere*.

419. Reg. and Ott.: *proprium*, which is preferable to *proprio* in Rom. and the printed editions. The verb *proprium* answers to *tuum* (“your own”). Matthew 18:15: “But if your brother sins against you … you have gained your brother”; and line 21: “If my brother sins against me.”

[Col. 0250B] 420. Rom.: *secretis* (“secret places”), perhaps reflecting Reg. *secretim* (“secretly”); although this adverb *secretim* itself was used by Tertullian and Ammianus. I said something about the adverb *secreto* in the note to line 205 of this book.

423. Reg., second hand: *contemnit* (“despises”); *contemnet* (“will despise”) seems to have stood there earlier. Ottob., Reg., Rom., Daventr., and Ald. have *relinquens* (“leaving”); other editions have *reluctans* (“resisting”). I retain *relinquens*, so that the same accusative serves both the verb *contemnet* and the present participle *relinquens*, as in the similar phrase at line 304 of this passage: “let him deny himself, refusing both body and soul.”

424. Reg., Rom., and Ott. manuscripts: *Tunc alius monitor pariter* (“Then another adviser likewise”); Ott. has *Tum*, which does not suit the meter, and *alios* apparently stood there, producing *alius*. Fabr.: *Tunc alius pariter monitor*; most printed editions: *Tunc aliis pariter monitor*. Torn.: *frequentes*; emend to *frequentet* (“let him frequent”).

425. Rom.: *discutiat* (“let him disperse”); Ott.: *dicutiet*, but perhaps *discutiet* was intended. Reg.: *descutiet*. The editions have *decutiet* (“will cut down”), a word that seems preferable amid the divergent manuscript readings, since it also occurs in this book at line 193.

[Col. 0250C] 426. Westh. in the text: *Tunc ad consilium* (“then to the counsel”); in the margin, more correctly: *Tunc ad concilium* (“then to the assembly”). Rom. in the text has *concilium*; in the margin, *judicium* (“judgment”).

[Note: [Col. 0249C]]

403. *Generabitur* (“will be generated”): Quintilian, Book VII, chapter 3: “Words that generate litigation.”

404. *Parvis* (“little ones”), meaning children. See the note to Dracontius, Book II, line 313.

405. “With a millstone.” Thus Prudentius, *On Saint Quirinus*, hymn 7 of the *Peristephanon*, lines 21 ff.:

> From the summit of the lofty bridge—  
> The bishop of the holy people—  
> He is cast headlong into the river,  
> Carrying, suspended by a noose,  
> The huge stone of a mill.

And Lactantius, chapter 15 *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “The household servants, with millstones fastened around their necks, were sunk into the sea.” Luke calls it a “millstone” (*lapis molaris*); Matthew and Mark call it an “ass-millstone” (*mola asinaria*), because the upper stone of a mill was called ὄνος (*onos*) in Greek, that is, “ass.” Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 10: “one pair of ass-mills and one pair of hand-mills”; elsewhere, “two.” As regards the meaning, Juvencus says: “If he should seize, bind, etc., he should cast himself, etc.” Matthew says: “It is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be sunk into the depths of the sea.” Mark: “It is better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.” The meaning is: whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble will suffer greater punishment than if an ass-millstone were hung around his neck, and so forth. Juvencus seems to interpret it thus: you ought rather to choose to be sunk into the depths of the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble. Mark supports this interpretation, for he continues [Col. 0250C]: “And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna.” Luke states it more plainly: “It is more useful for him if a millstone is placed around his neck and he is thrown into the sea, than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.” In the Tridentine Gospel Book this is reported as follows: “It is better that a millstone be placed around his neck and that he be thrown into the sea, than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.”

406. “He should cast himself”: see book I, line 424.

409. “High-throned,” as in book I, line 32. “The stars above”: the preposition has been placed after the word it governs. Virgil, book XI, line 509: “When this spirit is above all things, it is everything.”

411. “Bleating” in place of “sheep” is poetic. Omeisius takes “a hundred” as an indefinite number. The same number is given in the Gospel.

415. “Lamb”: that is, a sheep.

416. An ablative with the particles *quam pro* is elegantly placed after a comparative. Livy, book X, chapter 14: “The slaughter was smaller than was proportionate to so great a victory.”

419. CHAPTER XVI. How one ought to correct the faults of others. Matthew XVIII, 15 ff.; Luke XVII, 3. The early Christians addressed one another as “brothers” and “sisters.” Consult the commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 2, line 73.

423. “But if, being alone, he should despise your words,” that is, if he should despise your words when you rebuke him alone and privately.

424. “Another admonisher”: Matthew says, “Take with you one or two more,” which Juvencus explains in the following verse.

427. “Of the people,” that is, of the multitude.

Yet nevertheless woe to him through whom error will be brought forth.

But whoever deceives one of these little ones,

[405] If he has any sense, let him bind his neck with a millstone,

279 and hurl himself headlong into the waves of the sea.

And let no one, in arrogance, despise these little ones.

Their guardians, in the heavenly seat, behold

The face of the high-throned Father, above the stars.

[410] But if some shepherd, entrusted with pastures where a hundred sheep feed,

Should, through ignorance, lose one of them when it has strayed apart,

He leaves the others and searches for the tracks

Of the one through all the forests;

And if he can find it after great labor,

[415] Then greater joy arises over the lamb that has been found

[Col. 0250A] 280 than over the number of all the others, because none of them has strayed:

Thus the Father does not permit anyone of these little ones to perish,

And rejoices that his kingdoms are increased by his own.

If you see your own brother stained by sin,

[420] Then immediately rebuke him privately, alone, in secret words.

If he praises your words and accepts your guidance,

You will win back your brother’s failing mind.

But if, when you are alone, he should despise your words and leave them,

Then let another admonisher likewise repeat the holy commands.

[425] But if he should throw off the restraints of the two teachers,

281 then let the offenses be reported to a full council,

So that at least the defeated party may be healed by the weight of the people.

[Col. 0251A]

[Note: [Col. 0251B]

429. Ottobonianus and Romanus in the margin: “different”; “divided” is better. Ottobonianus and Reginensis, first hand: “changed.” Romanus, together with the printed editions, correctly has “punished,” or “fined.”

433. Basileensis, incorrectly: “Then Peter asks what he should permit for his brother.”

434. All our manuscripts: “Or if it were permitted to endure seven lapses of men”; and the gloss in Reginensis: “to endure—to tolerate.” The printed editions: “Or to forgive seven lapses of a man.” It is indeed unusual for *an* to be used with *quaero* and similar verbs, but it is nevertheless found employed by good writers. Livy, book XXXI, chapter 9: “The consul was ordered to refer to the college of pontiffs whether a vow involving an uncertain sum of money could properly be undertaken”; and book XXXIX, chapter 50: “After receiving the cup, they say that he said nothing else except to ask whether Lycortas had escaped unharmed . . . and whether the cavalry had escaped.” Juvencus’s reading should therefore be restored from the manuscript copies, all the more because he uses the same phrase here, line 593: “Then Christ asks whether they could drink the cup.”

[Col. 0252B] 437. All our manuscripts: “of the lord”; and the gloss in Reginensis: “for the lord.” The printed editions have “to the lord,” not incorrectly; but it is preferable to retain the reading of the manuscripts.

444. Romanus, Aldine, and Basileensis: “to pay in full”; the others, “to dissolve,” as above, line 395, “dissolve.”

447. Basileensis: “at the very boundary,” less satisfactorily and perhaps incorrectly.

448. Hadamarensis and Poelmannus in the text, Fabricius in the margin: “stronger.” The manuscripts and most printed editions: “stronger.”

450. Reginensis: “immersed in the darkness of prison”; the others: “and immersed in the darkness of prison.” Romanus, incorrectly: “and emerged from prison.”]

[Note: [Col. 0251C]

429. Juvencus takes this as referring to the excommunicated person, as Koenigius explains.

431. *Duum* for *duorum*. Priscian, book VII, teaches that *duum* is used only with neuters, and *duorum* with masculines. Among the ancients, however, *duorum* is also found with neuters, and *duum* with masculines. Compare Charisius, book I, and Cicero, *On Oratory*, chapter 46.

433. CHAPTER XVII. Forgiveness is to be granted to the sinner seventy-seven times. Matthew XVIII, 21 ff.; Luke XVII, 4.

436. “Tenfold”: tenfold, containing the number seven ten times within itself, and therefore seventy-seven times, as it is read in the Gospel. Among writers older than Juvencus, *decuplatus* is not found. Koenigius cites from Augustine the phrase *numerus decuplatus*. Livy, book XXXIX, chapter 44, wrote: “So that they might value those things also at ten times as much as they were worth.” This reading, approved by Manutius and Schefferus but questioned by Gruterus and Gronovius, is supported here by Juvencus. Others read in Livy *decem tanto*, and still others differently. “Above,” as has been said elsewhere, means “in addition” or “besides.” “Let them be given,” that is, “let them be forgiven”; on this see the note to book II, line 81. Sabatierius joins the words as *superdonentur*. On the word *vulnus*, “injury,” “adversity,” and so forth, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, line 695, and *Peristephanon*, hymn 9, line 7. It is also used for a crime or offense, as Arntzenius proves in his note on Sedulius, book IV, line 77.

437. CHAPTER XVIII. The parable: “To what is the kingdom of heaven like?” Matthew XVIII, 23 ff.

441. “To be brought before the court”: a forensic expression.

442. “He adores”: the sacred text has, “He prayed to him.” The older versions have either this or “He begged him.” The Tridentine Gospel Book: “And he entreated his lord, saying.” In the Cambridge manuscript I find Juvencus’s wording: “But that servant, falling down, adored him, saying.”

446. “Beyond the deserts owed”: beyond, or outside, what was deserved. *Trans* often governs an accusative of place. The author of the *Declamations* transmitted under Quintilian’s name, declamation 6, chapter 10: “The penalty is exacted only beyond the final parricide,” that is, beyond a man’s life, or after the man has ceased to exist. Koenigius interprets *trans meritum* as “gratuitously,” “beyond,” or “above what was deserved.”

448. Matthew: “And, taking hold of him, he was choking him,” because he was compelling him to pay. Hence *constringit*, which also means “to choke” or “to throttle,” as I said in the note on book II, line 752. Metaphorically, however, these expressions are used as in Spanish *Me sofoca*, “He suffocates me,” or *No me deja respirar*, “He does not let me breathe.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IX: “They eagerly attack Philebus and his other companions, and, tightening their grip around his neck . . . repeatedly silence them with pressing speech,” and so forth. Both meanings suit that passage. More can be read about the verb *suggillo* in Mazochius, volume I of the *Biblical Miscellany*, chapter XXVII, on Genesis, verses 38–39. In the Tridentine Gospel Book this passage appears as follows: “And, taking hold of him, he was choking him, saying: Pay me what you owe.”

449. *Abigo* with a dative. Silius, book VIII, line 124: “While I drive these things from my mind.” Reuschius says: “He expressed a difficult matter by a difficult and unusual word.”

452. “He heaped words upon him,” as in Horace, book I of the *Satires*, line 11, *ingerere convicia*, “to heap insults,” and in Livy, book II, chapter 45, *ingerere probra*, “to heap reproaches.”

453. *Dicta* sometimes means “insults.” Plautus, *Pseudolus* I.3.125: “Now I shall assail you with my words, shameless man.” “And he stirs up anger,” that is, sharpens it, raises it, and provokes anger against himself.

454. In former times debtors were handed over by creditors not only to prison but also to torture.]

But if, savage, he should despise the faces of many,

let him be to you as one punished by exclusion from the community.

[430] For whenever we are gathered in council,

our presence will always come,

and it is necessary that I stand in the midst of the two,

or if the gathering consists of three in our name.

Then Peter asks how many offenses he should forgive a brother,

or whether it were permitted to endure seven lapses of men.

[435] Christ continues: Not merely seven offenses,

but let wounds be forgiven the brother seventy-seven times.

282 For the kingdom of the Lord of the heavenly court

is like a wealthy man who ordered an account

to be rendered to him of the money,

and commanded that a servant who owed many talents,

[440] [Col. 0251B] together with wife, children,

and all his possessions, be brought forward

and presented for sale.

[Col. 0252A] Then the servant, prostrate on the ground, adores his master,

and promises that, if he had any time available,

he would repay the master the entire sum of money.

[445] The master was moved by pity for the weeping servant,

and forgave the servant all the debts beyond what was deserved.

But as soon as he went out,

he found a fellow servant at the very threshold and seized him;

then, stronger, he pressed him to repay the debt

283 and, savage, drove him away from his pleas,

[450] and, having plunged him into the darkness of prison, oppressed him with punishments.

When the master begins to learn these things

from the words of the servants,

he brought the servant before him and heaped upon him

the most righteous reproaches, grieving,

[Col. 0252B] and, stirring up anger, thrust the savage man

into tortures by severe commands, reviewing everything.

[455] [Col. 0253A]

[Note: [Col. 0253A]

455. Aldine, Basileensis, and Reuschius: *quae* in place of *dum*. Most have: “while he paid the fitting penalties through his bonds.” Fabricius altered it, writing: “while he paid the fitting penalties through his bonds,” which pleased Reuschius less. It is better, for one says *luere peccata*, “to pay for sins,” rather than *luere poenas*, “to pay penalties.”]

[Col. 0253B] 458. Romanus incorrectly has *volentis*; this error entered Aldus’s text and was copied from there into the Basileensis edition. Aldus corrected the error in his *Errata*, but introduced a new one by writing *durae punire voletis* instead of *dure*.

459. Reginensis: “the fields of Galilee”; Ottobonianus: “the fields of Galilee,” but it seems originally to have read “the fields of Galilee.” Romanus, Aldine, Daventriense, Tornacensis, and Basileensis: “the rural lands of Galilee,” a word that occurs in the following verse. Reuschius printed “the fields of Galilee,” with hiatus. Omeisius attributes to Barthius the reading “the fields of Galilee,” which is better. Hadamarensis, Fabricius, and Poelmannus: “the fields of Galilee.” Reuschius, together with the Cambridge manuscript, retains *relinquit*; others have *reliquit*.

460. Reuschius advises that *petit* be written instead of *petiit* if *reliquit* is written in the preceding verse. But he is not entirely consistent, for in the preceding verse he writes *relinquit*, and says that there is no objection in the fact that *dedit* precedes, which he claims can be supported by a thousand examples. Why, then, could *petit* not be written in the present tense, even though *reliquit* in the past tense preceded it? Romanus has *silentis*, perhaps because the copyist intended *silenti*, namely, “in silent procession.” I certainly do not see, nor do the lexicographers indicate, which writer older than Juvencus used the adverb *silenter*.

461. The manuscripts: *perrumpit*; Aldine, Fabricius, Reuschius, and Poelmannus in place of the preceding reading: *prorumpit*. Hadamarensis and Poelmannus in the text: *prorupit*. Reginensis: *amoenos*, but the gloss indicates that it is to be joined with *agmine*, and thus should be read *amoeno*.

462. Ottobonianus: *aegros*, but this has been corrected to *aegris*; this should likewise be read later with *salutem*. Romanus and Aldus: “to grant health to the sick.” Reginensis, Hadamarensis, and Poelmannus: “to grant the sick health.”

463. Romanus, Daventriense, Reuschius, and Westhusius in the margin: *perstat*; Reginensis, Ottobonianus, and the other printed editions: *praestat*.

465. Tornacensis: *retectum*; correct to *rejectum*.

466. In Ottobonianus and Reginensis it seems originally to have read: “Whatever such thing may be, if it touches”; later corrected to: “Whatever it may be that touches the heart of the injured.” In Ottobonianus, *tanget* was made from *tangit*. Romanus: “Whatever it may be, it touches the things of the injured.” Hadamarensis, Daventriense, and Poelmannus: “Whatever it may be, it will touch what belongs to the injured.” Aldus and Basileensis: “If anything occurs, let it touch what belongs to the injured.” The Gospel agrees better with “Whatever it may be.” I would readily admit the first reading of Ottobonianus and Reginensis; but the second is clearer.

470. Reginensis, Romanus, and Ottobonianus, first hand: *animas*. The printed editions: *animos*. Romanus in the text: *inolescere*; in the margin: *increscere*.

472. Reginensis and Ottobonianus: *hominum*, which Aldus printed. Romanus, together with most printed editions: *homini*.

473. Reginensis and Ottobonianus: “Moses commanded.” Aldus and the other printed editions: “Moses commanded.” Romanus: “Moses commanded” [ablative]. It could be written *Moseus praecepit*. In place of *praecepit*, *permisit* would be suitable, for Scripture uses this verb in Matthew XIX, 7 ff.: “They say to him: Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that she be dismissed? He says to them: Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so.” In the Tridentine Gospel Book: “They say to him: Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that she be dismissed? He says to them: Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to send away your wives; for from the beginning it was not so.” The author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, homily 32, noted the distinction between the two verbs: “He rightly said, ‘Because Moses permitted this,’ not ‘commanded it.’” Nevertheless, I retain the verb *praecepit*, which Tertullian also used in book IV *Against Marcion*: “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded that a bill of divorce be given; but from the beginning it was not so.” Moreover, Mark relates the matter in other words: “But he answered and said to them: What did Moses command you? They said: Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be written and the wife to be dismissed. Jesus, answering, said to them: Because of the hardness of your hearts he wrote this commandment for you.” Moses therefore commanded that a writ of separation be written if a husband wished to repudiate his wife; he did not, however, command the repudiation itself.

474. The manuscripts and most printed editions: *discidium*; some printed editions: *dissidium*. See book I, line 568.

475. Romanus, Aldine, and Basileensis: *possent*; the others: *possint*. Romanus, together with many printed editions: *flamma*. Reginensis and Ottobonianus: *flammae*; and the gloss in Reginensis: “of the flame—the anger of both, husband and wife.” Another gloss in Reginensis: “the points—the writ of divorce.” Westhusius in the text: *flammae*; in the margin: *flammas*, which seems to be an error for *flamma*. The passage is obscure, if any passage is. I conjectured *sub judice flammei*. For there was a yellow or saffron-colored veil, called a *flammeum*, which newly married women wore as a sign of an indissoluble marriage. The judge of the *flammeum*, therefore, would be the judge who investigated the legal dissolution of a marriage.]

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

459. CHAPTER XIX. A wife is not to be dismissed except on account of fornication. Infants likewise are not to be kept away from the blessing. Matthew XIX, 1 ff.; Mark X, 1, etc.; Luke XVIII, 15.

460. *Silenter*: Koenigius collects similar adverbs omitted by the lexicographers, such as *urgenter* from Cyprian, *proficienter* from Augustine, and *accidenter* and *consentienter* from Boethius.

461. Poets call a perpetual river “a stream” (*agmen*); Christian writers imitate them, including Juvencus, Cyprian, Victor, and the author of *On the Praises of the Lord*, as Barthius observes, book XXXV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 16, p. 1617.

463. *Perstat* for *pergit*, “continues” or “persists,” with an infinitive, is customary in Silius and others.

465. In *rejectum* the first syllable is lengthened, as in Virgil and others; this often occurs in similar compounds.

466. “The hearts of the husband,” that is, “the husband.” Persius, satire 6, line 10: “Ennius’s heart commands this.” So Martial and others.

470. *Inolescere*: to grow into, grow up, coalesce, be joined, or adhere; in Virgil, Columella, Silius, and Prudentius. In the following verse *concrescere* has the same meaning.

475. Juvencus implies that divorce was permitted to the Jews only in the political and civil forum, not in the forum of conscience. Moses therefore did not approve this abuse, but rather confined it within definite limits so that it would not roam more freely. He established that a bill of divorce had necessarily to be written by those who repudiated their wives, so that the matter could be examined before a judge. To this relates what Juvencus says in book I, line 567: “The ancients command that whoever breaks a marriage write the separation, the deadly words of the law.” The law of divorce in Deuteronomy XXIV, 1 ff., was as follows: “If a man takes a wife and does not find favor in his eyes because of some shameful thing, he writes a bill of divorce, gives it into her hand, and sends her away from his house. And when she has gone out and married another husband, and he too hates her and gives her a bill of divorce . . . or certainly if he has died, the former husband may not take her again as his wife,” and so forth. In interpreting this law the Jews disagreed among themselves. Some held that divorce was permitted only because of some grave offense against moral propriety. Others maintained that even a lighter and milder cause was sufficient, or even that the wife appeared less pleasing to her husband. Christ taught that the law was to be understood as referring to the cause of fornication, and at the same time, according to Juvencus’s interpretation, showed that this cause did not suffice for the complete dissolution of marriage in the forum of conscience. The matter is different with divorce, or separation of bed.]

The debts, while he was paying the fitting penalties in chains.

Thus the Father will deal with you, who possesses

the heights of heaven, if with savage heart

you wish harshly to punish the sins of your brothers who pray.

and to bestow the gifts of the exalted Father.

Therefore, what God commands to grow together by his own word,

285 it is unlawful for men to separate through shameful license.
