[475.] by their own written characters before the judge of ‘flammae’ [a corrupt or uncertain reading].”

[Col. 0255A]

[Note: [Col. 0255A]

476. Ottobonianus: *exsolvit*, from which *exsolvet* was produced.

481. Aldine and Basileensis, with an interrogation mark: *perosis?* Elsewhere the mark is absent.

483. Poelmannus: *alia*, incorrectly, for *talia*. Most have *lectae*; Poelmannus, in the margin, together with Ottobonianus, first hand: *laetae*. Romanus: *lectis*, which is also indicated by Reginensis, where *lecti* occurs, but the gloss “perfect men” indicates *lectis*. Romanus and Reginensis punctuate it: “such gifts are among the chosen.” — “The bodies of virtue are cut off in a threefold manner”: this punctuation is inept.

484. This verse is corruptly read in Romanus: “Your husband is cut off in a threefold body through love.” Reginensis: “The bodies of virtue are cut off in a threefold body through love.” Read, with the others: “Of virtue. The bodies are cut off in a threefold manner.”

485. Koenigius conjectures *geniali lege*, “by the law of marriage.”

486. Poelmannus, in the margin: “the airs of light”; the common reading: “the regions of light.”

488. Romanus, Aldine, and Tornacensis: *atque alios*; most have *ast alios*. Aldine, Tornacensis, and Basileensis: *ipsis sibi*. The manuscripts and other printed editions: *ipsos sibi*.

491. Westhusius in the text: *laetisque Deus*; in the margin: *laetique Deus*. Neither can be tolerated.

492. Romanus, Aldine, and Basileensis: *gaudens quos*; the others: *quos gaudens*.

493. The manuscripts and most printed editions: *laetis*; some printed editions: *laeti*. Reginensis, Tornacensis, Fabricius, and Poelmannus in the text: *ferebant*; Romanus, Ottobonianus, and others: *ferebat*. If one reads *laeti certatim hinc inde ferebant*, understand that gender and number have been changed.

494. Sabatierius printed *sectantem* and, in the margin, added *sectantum*, which is found only in our manuscripts and printed editions. See book II, line 564. Romanus has *prohiberent*, not incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0255C]

476. Book I, line 570: “For the laws of chaste modesty,” and so forth. The meaning is: he who dismisses his wife without a bill of divorce and takes another will be publicly judged an adulterer.

[Col. 0255D] 479. The meaning is: this law of perpetual marriage weighs upon the male part and presses it with an unequal burden of servitude. Matthew says: “His disciples say to him: If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” *Nubere* properly refers to a woman, but Christians also used it of a man. The Greek is γαμῆσαι, “to take a wife.” Jerome, letter to Amandus, volume IV: “If this is so, it is not expedient for a man to take a wife.” Augustine, on Psalm 103: “If such is the case with a wife, it is not expedient to marry.” But why should this law be called unequal for the man and the woman? For just as a man is not permitted to withdraw from marriage, neither is a wife. It should be noted that women were not permitted to repudiate their husbands, as Josephus testifies, *Antiquities*, book XV, chapter 11: “Salome sends a bill of divorce to her husband, contrary to the lawful custom of the country.” For our law grants this right only to husbands; women, even when dismissed, are not permitted to marry unless the former husband consents. Since, therefore, the law of divorce was given for men, the more the permission to repudiate is restrained, the heavier the bond of marriage is for men. Christ therefore left the condition of wives as it was, insofar as freedom to repudiate is concerned; [Col. 0256C] but he made the condition of men more difficult. The Jews thought that in this matter more should be granted to the man, who is the head of the woman, than to the woman, who ought to be subject to the man; and therefore they were distressed that divorce and polygamy were forbidden to them. Other peoples also permitted divorce to men but not to wives. Hence Medea complained in Euripides, line 230:

> Of all creatures endowed with understanding,  
> We women are the most wretched kind.  
> First, with great expenditure of money,  
> We are compelled to buy a husband—  
> That is, to buy the master of our bodies.  
> Then comes what is more grievous and dangerous:  
> Once the die has been cast with uncertain outcome,  
> Whether one marries a good man or a bad,  
> Divorce is dishonorable for us,  
> Nor is it permitted us to separate.

Under Christian law, separation of bed is permitted to wife and husband alike for definite reasons. Cornelius a Lapide shows from the sayings of the ancients that, because of women’s foolishnesses, the burden of marriage is heavier for men than for women.

481. *Perosis*: “worthy of hatred.” *Perosus* is one who hates; here, however, it is taken passively, as more than once in Tertullian.

482. “Under a weight,” that is, “beneath a weight.” Omeisius cites Virgil, book VI, line 465: “And do not withdraw yourself from our sight,” and Ennius: “To carve out prey from a hungry lion.” But these passages belong to another matter.

484. Cellarius restored the verb *truncare* to the language of the golden age against the opinion of some.

487. “The iron force of men,” that is, men by the sword, or a line of steel, or a knife.

489. “Inclined,” namely, toward sexual desire.

490. Ovid, book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, line 243: “Of a mind receptive to instruction.” Matthew’s words are: “He who can receive it, let him receive it.” Juvencus explains them: “He who can accept it, let him accept it.” Mazochius, on this passage, takes *capere* as “to swallow” or “digest,” which is said of difficult matters that cannot be digested, or cannot easily be believed.]

286 For he who rashly releases the laws of a chaste marriage bed

and joins another wife to the chambers of the former,

will undergo the crime of adultery before the witness of the people.

The disciples report: This law presses upon men

[480] and weighs down their portion with an unequal burden of servitude,

so that it would have been better to have been without marriage, hateful as it is.

287 The Lord replied: Not all will submit their shoulders

to so great a burden; such gifts of virtue are for the chosen.

Bodies are rendered eunuchs in a threefold manner,

[485] bodies that take no delight in the generative law of marriage-beds.

[Col. 0256A] For we find that some are born such

into the regions of light; the iron force of men

makes many eunuchs; but others are known

to remove from themselves, for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven,

the love inclined in their hearts.

[490] Whoever is capable, let him embrace by lofty virtue

the gift that God wishes to reveal to the few and chosen.

Having said these things, he receives the children

whom their parents’ delighted care bore from every side,

[495] with joyful prayers, in eager rivalry,

and rebukes the crowd of followers because it was preventing them.

[Col. 0257A]

[Note: [Col. 0257B]

496. Fabricius: *hinc*; the others: *his*.

497. This verse is absent from Tornacensis. Gallandius supposed that it was missing from the editions preceding Reuschius’s edition; but it is present in Aldine, Fabricius, Hadamarensis, Poelmannus, Daventriense, and others. Of our manuscripts, Ottobonianus and Reginensis have *redditque humeris*; Romanus, together with the printed editions, *redditque ulnis*. I consider the true reading to be *redditque humeris portare*, “and gives them back to be carried on the shoulders,” for *humerus* properly means the upper arm, or the bone extending from the shoulder blade to the elbow. Moreover, in the more common sense, children can be carried on the shoulders.

498. Reginensis: *jura*; *rura*, “fields,” is better.

499. Ottobonianus, Romanus, and Basileensis: “And the shining possession of things stood apart in wealth.” Tornacensis: “And both wealth and the possession of things stood.” Reginensis: “And the shining possession of things stood in wealth.” Hadamarensis, Fabricius, and Poelmannus: “And the possession of things stood in wealth.” Aldine and Reuschius: “And the possession of things stood in wealth,” with the final syllable of *gaza* lengthened because of the following *st* of the next word. Bede, *On the Art of Meter*, says that Juvencus shortened the first syllable in *gaza*: [Col. 0257C] he had seen a manuscript in which this verse read, as in Ottobonianus and Romanus, “And the shining possession of things stood apart in wealth.” But since Juvencus lengthens the first syllable in *gaza* shortly afterward, and since the verb *distabat* does not fit this passage well, I incline to the view that this reading is corrupt. Bede’s words are, in the chapter “On Common Syllables”: “The eighth mode occurs when a consonant *z*, a Greek double consonant, follows a shortened vowel in the same part of speech. It is long in this passage of Juvencus: ‘Difficult it is on earth to loosen those fixed in rich wealth.’ It is short in this passage of the same author: ‘And the shining possession of things stood apart in wealth.’” In the preceding chapter, “On the Syllable,” he had said: “For whenever *z* follows a short vowel in the same part of speech, it may lengthen it, if the poet so wishes, as in *GAZA*.” But because the manuscripts and printed books disagree among themselves, I embrace Aldus’s reading, “And wealth stood,” which copyists may have altered because it seemed absurd to them that the final syllable in *gaza* should be lengthened.

503. Our manuscripts: “Here the author.” The printed editions: “For this the author.”

504. Romanus: “Then at last”; read “Now at last.” Basileensis and Tornacensis: “Are they held by what the law commands?” and Tornacensis has an interrogation mark. Retain: “Are they held by what the law commands?” Other copies omit the question mark, but it is correctly supplied from the Gospel text.

507. Reginensis, Romanus, and Ottobonianus, first hand: *liget*, which Aldus and Basileensis printed. Other printed editions: *leget*. Romanus, incorrectly: “A mind not right,” for “A mind, or a right hand.” The same Romanus has *loquaris* for *loqueris*.

510. Reginensis: *isthic*; Romanus: *ista haec*; Ottobonianus: *cuncta haec*, but it seems originally to have read *cuncta isthaec*, which would conflict with the meter. In Reginensis *cuncta* also seems to have been erased. The printed editions have *ista haec* or *isthaec*. “All these things” comes closer to Matthew’s words, for Matthew XIX, 20 has: “I have kept all these things.” The Tridentine Gospel Book: “I have observed all these things from my youth.”

514. Romanus, incorrectly: *praetendere*, for *prendere*. Poelmannus, in the margin: *pro celsis*; the common reading is *praecelsis*. Juvencus does indeed use such forms as *praestupidus* and *praepulcher*. Our manuscripts, together with Aldine and Daventriense: *fastigia vitae*. Hadamarensis, Fabricius, and Poelmannus: *vestigia vitae*. The former is more pleasing, from Matthew XIX, 21: “If you wish to be perfect,” and so forth.

516. In Fabricius there is an error: *Distrahe*, “sell,” and “the wretched.”]

[Note: [Col. 0257C]

495. *Mereri*: Koenigius wishes to establish that ecclesiastical writers used this verb for “to obtain,” without any proper reference to merit. This does sometimes occur; nevertheless, merit is often truly attributed to the works of the righteous.

498. CHAPTER XX. It is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. Matthew XIX, 16 ff.; Mark X, 17; Luke XVIII, 18.

505. “Thefts of marriage beds”: see line 170 above, with its note.

506. “You will assail”: compare the note on Dracontius, book III, line 319, *invasor thalami*, “invader of the marriage chamber.”

508. Juvencus elegantly translated the commandment concerning the honoring of parents in this way, as Cellarius says in *Ecclesiastical and Poetic Latin*, in the later discussion, where he observes with Valla that *genitor* and *genitrix* are more common among poets than among orators.

509. Only ecclesiastical writers use *proximus* as a substantive, in imitation of the sacred Greek idiom, as Cellarius notes in the later discussion of ecclesiastical Latin. Forcellinus, however, observes that *proximus* is used in the same sense by Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 9, and by Quintilian, declamation 259. Matthew says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” which Juvencus does not express very clearly in this verse.

516. *Distrahe*: “sell.” See the note on Dracontius, line 510, book II.

519. A noteworthy phrase: *veniunt per aures*, “they come through the ears,” for *veniunt ad aures*, “they come to the ears.”

522. He interprets the Gospel as referring to the rich, who are fastened to the earth and to riches.

523. The gloss in Reginensis: *leves*—“willing,” perhaps *volantes*, “flying.”

524. So Sedulius, book IV, line 9:

> For just as a camel cannot pass through the opening of a needle,  
> Unable, because of the great bulk of its limbs,  
> To enter the narrow path leading to the threshold  
> Of the heavenly kingdom, so the rich man, swelling  
> With abundant prosperity, cannot approach it.

Some take the Gospel proverb as referring to a ship’s rope, for there is a Talmudic proverb: “The departure of the soul from the body is difficult, like a rope through a narrow opening.” But since a ship’s rope, or cable, is called *kamilos* (κάμιλος) by Suidas, with *iota*, whereas the camel is *kamelos* (καμήλος), with long *e*, and since there is also a Talmudic proverb, “There is no elephant that can enter through the eye of a needle,” it is reasonable, with most ancient and recent interpreters, to explain the Gospel proverb as referring to the animal camel. Two dissertations on this proverb exist, one by Johann Philipp Pfeiffer and the other by Johann Sommer. The Tridentine Gospel Book presents the passage to us as follows: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the cavity of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdoms of heaven.” An older hand corrected *cavernam*. Properly speaking, *caverna* is a hollow place, though it is sometimes used for “opening.”]

288 He declares that such children deserve

the palms of the heavenly court.

He lays holy hands upon them in order,

and gives them back to be carried on their parents’ shoulders.

But behold, from the crowd there approaches a young man

whose fields, house, and wealth stood as a splendid possession of things.

[500] He approaches and, humbly, openly adores Christ:

“O good teacher, tell me now what deeds we should follow,

so that I may be permitted to grasp eternal life.”

Then Jesus, the author of life, replies to him:

289 “Now at last you ask what things are enjoined by the ancient law?”

[505] You shall not take a man’s life,

you shall not commit the adulteries of marriage-beds,

nor shall a guilty mind or hand obtain profit from another’s property;

you shall not give false testimony.

Let your father and mother be exalted in your honor,

and let your neighbor yield to you in pure love.

[510] [Col. 0258A] Then he said: I believe that I have always observed

all these things with continual care;

but lest something should perhaps be lacking,

let me now be instructed by the present word.

Then Christ says: Now, if you seek to grasp

the heights of life through lofty merits,

[515] sell everything that you alone possess

under your own control,

and confidently distribute it to the wretched needy.

290 Then a treasure will be stored up for you in the citadel of heaven,

and, steadfast in virtue, you will follow our footsteps.

When these words came through the young man’s ears,

[520] he lowered his face and, sorrowful, withdrew into his house.

Then the one and only Hope of life speaks thus to the disciples:

It is difficult for those fastened to the earth by rich wealth

to be torn away and to enter the kingdoms of heaven unburdened.

For sooner will the thin limbs of a deformed camel

[525] be able to pass through the opening of a needle,

[Col. 0259A] [Note: [Col. 0259B]

526. Hadamarensis, incorrectly: “Than the rich man can.” Aldine and others: “Than the rich man is able.” The manuscripts and Poelmannus in the text: “Than a rich man can.” Westhusius in the text: “Than a rich man is able”; in the margin: “Than the rich man can.”

529. Reginensis: *Humanum*; correct to *Humano*. Romanus, Reginensis, Ottobonianus, first hand, Tornacensis, Aldine, and Basileensis: *possit*; the others: *posset*. Romanus: *quae possit*; the rest: *possit quae*.

532. It might be preferable to read *aethram*.

533. Romanus: *capesset*; Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Daventriense, Tornacensis, Aldine, and Basileensis: *capessat*. Hadamarensis and Poelmannus: *capessit*.

534. Ottobonianus: *monitus*, correctly emended to *munitus*. Romanus in the text and Aldine: *inquit*; Romanus in the margin, together with the others: *infit*.

535. Poelmannus in the margin, Fabricius, and Aldine: *nostra olim*. The others, together with the manuscripts: *nostrorum*. Romanus: *relinquimus*; correct to *reliquimus*.

[Col. 0260B] 538. The manuscripts: *respondit*; the printed editions: *respondet*.

541. Helmstediensis: *quam*; the others: *quem*, with the same meaning through synesis, or a change of gender, as if *Filius hominis* had preceded. Romanus and Ottobonianus, first hand: *cingit*; *cinget* is better, as in Ottobonianus, second hand, and others.

543. Tornacensis, corruptly: “lofty on the summit”; Reginensis: “on the lofty summit.” In Ottobonianus, *ex sublime vertice* was changed into *sublimi in vertice*.

545. Romanus and Aldine: *Sic*; the others: *Hic*. Ottobonianus: *linquit* for *linquet*.

552. Romanus: “Wherever he proceeded,” which seems more correct than “Here, where he proceeded” in the others. Nevertheless, the latter can be retained with suitable punctuation. In Basileensis, *gressus* for *progressus*; and in Tornacensis, *solus* for *solis*, an error.]

[Note: [Col. 0259C]

532. *Praepandit*: Juvencus delights in compounds formed with the preposition *prae*, as I said in the note on line 514 above. Otherwise, *praepando* is a verb used by Cicero, Lucretius, and Pliny. *Aethra* is an accusative formed by syncopation from *aether, aetheris, aethera*, in the Greek manner. In book IV, line 68, he similarly wrote *in aethra*, as we read from our manuscripts.]

How a rich man may be able to see the heavenly kingdoms.

533. Quintilian, book III, chapter 8: “Our people call it *possibile*; although the designation may seem harsh, it is the only one.” The ancient jurists frequently used that word. Pomponius the jurist is cited for the same word. I pass over the Christian writers Lactantius, Prudentius, Sedulius, and others. The noun *possibilitas* is a harsher form, but it can nevertheless be found in Ammianus, Palladius, Martianus Capella, and Arnobius. “What lofty virtue he may attain,” repeated from verse 490, “Let him attain by lofty virtue.”

534. CHAPTER XXI. Jesus promises that whoever has abandoned all his possessions for God’s sake will receive a hundredfold, and that the first will become last. Matthew XIX, 27, etc.; Mark X, 31; Luke XIII, 30. Peter, fortified by the ramparts of faith, as at verse 274, “But steadfast Peter.”

537. “What, then, remains for our souls?” that is, “What will there be for us?” as Matthew says.

544. *Tractare*, besides other meanings, also signifies “to exercise” or “to administer.”

546. Servius, on verse 763 of book II of the *Aeneid*, asserts that *gaza* occurs only in the singular. Yet Lucretius, Horace twice, Seneca the tragedian three times, and others used *gazas* in the plural. He calls all the affections brothers, sisters, father, mother, or children. Apuleius, book II *On the Dogmas of Plato*: “Deprived of his dearest affections.” Capitolinus, in *Antoninus Philosophus*, chapter 24: “He was not sufficiently disturbed by Cassius’s defection, nor did he rage against his affections”; and in *Maximinus*, chapter 23: “The soldiers whose affections were on Mount Alban.” Jerome, book III on Matthew, chapter X: “Therefore those who for the faith of Christ and the preaching of the Gospel have despised all their affections, as well as the riches and pleasures of the world, will receive a hundredfold,” etc. Koenigius and Schoettgenius cite many others.

547. *Centuplicata*: a word used by Fulgentius the Mythographer, Prudentius, and similar writers. Pliny, book VI, chapter 23, used *centuplicato* as an adverb.

548. Reuschius remarks on the obscurity in Juvencus; but Matthew’s words are no clearer: “But many who are first will be last, and those who are last will be first.”

550. CHAPTER XXII. The parable of the laborers hired for the vineyard. Matthew XX, 1, etc.

551. *Coronant*, “they crown,” that is, “they surround.” Lucretius, book IX, verse 335: “The myrtle groves crown the pool.” Virgil, book IX, verse 380: “They crown the entrance with a guard.” Perhaps in Juvencus *coronant* means “they fill,” as in book II, verse 143: “And they crown the waves.” A *vinetum* differs from a *vinea* in that it contains several vineyards, as the whole differs from a part. Below, verse 712: “A hedge, densely gathered round the many acres of a gleaming vineyard, confines [him].”

*As a rich man may see the heavenly kingdoms,*

Thus astonished, and struck dumb, his companions kept silent,

Pondering what such great power there might be within the human heart—

Power able to embrace such a life.

[530] He regards the glory of the righteous’ eternal life

And says: “These things may perhaps seem harsh to man,

But God readily opens before his chosen ones in heaven

A possible path which lofty virtue may attain.”

Then Peter, fortified by the ramparts of faith, said:

[535] “We have all abandoned all our possessions,

And our only hope now is to follow your commands.

What remains for our souls? Tell us, Christ, we pray.”

In such words Jesus answered Peter:

[Col. 0260A] “All you who preserve my way,

Believing in me within the deepest recesses of your minds,

When the Son of Man shall sit enthroned on high—

[540] The Majesty whom exalted honor will surround—

There, twelvefold, the beautiful power of heaven

Will establish for you seats upon a lofty summit,

And you will also be permitted to administer judgment over men.

[545] Whoever for our name’s sake abandons his own goods, his kindred, and his household’s

Treasures, and all affections,

Will thereafter receive a hundredfold, and everlasting life;

The reward of the first will be surpassed by the last,

And those who came last will scarcely receive the rewards of the first.”

[550] As an attentive master of the fields, whose rich lands

Are widely crowned by sweet vineyards,

When, having advanced with the sun’s first light,

[Col. 0261A] he had hired the strongest young men, having agreed

To pay a fixed wage for one day’s labor,

[555] And then ordered his vineyards to be cultivated with care—

He himself, going out when the third hour had arrived,

Found other men and ordered them to add themselves to the work,

Promising worthy rewards in proportion to their labor;

And they, no less gladly, followed his instructions.

[560] But when thereafter the sixth hour of daylight had passed,

He went on to hire other young men in the same way.

And when thereafter the ninth hour had been completed in the sun’s course,

He likewise ordered other hired men to go to work.

Only the final portion of the declining daylight remained:

[565] Going out, he saw young men and asked the reason

Why, with idle hands, they were sluggish in their slow idleness.

They said that no employer had given them

Any instructions. The master immediately ordered these men also

[Col. 0262A] to begin work in the fields. But as soon as evening had risen,

[570] He ordered everyone to receive the honor of his wage,

And for all to carry away an equal payment in coins.

Then the group of men whose hands had taken up the labor

At first light and had endured a full day through their work,

Indignant, spoke to themselves with such a murmur:

[575] “It is unjust that he should pay these men the same coin as us,

Whom he hired for the work only at the late hour.”

Then the master of the fields spoke with a composed heart:

“Your portion of the wage is returned to you intact,

And the rights of the agreement are faithfully preserved.

[580] It is permitted me to grant these men from what is mine

As much as the final portion of the work has gathered for them in the field.

For holy favor has called many men,

And from among them it is right to set apart a very small portion.”

[Col. 0263A]

### Notes

553. “The strength of young men,” that is, “strong young men.” See the note on book I, verse 478.

555. *Polire*, “to cultivate” or “to refine,” a verb proper to agricultural matters. Nonius, chapter 2, no. 339: “*Politiones*, diligent cultivation of fields, just as we call everything *polita* that has been cultivated and brought to a state of polish.” Ennius, *Satires*, book III: “The broad fields which African soil bears, cultivated.” The same author, *Annals*, book VIII: “The smith fashioned the rakes for the purpose of cultivating the field”; elsewhere, “the smith fashioned them.” Hence *politor agri* in Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 5.

560. *Transfluxerat*: Claudian, *Epistles* 4, verse 5, “The days have flowed past.” Pliny uses the same verb properly for “to pass by flowing.”

562. *Acta est*: Virgil, book III of the *Aeneid*, verse 512: “Nor had night, having completed its hours, yet entered beneath the middle of the heavens.”

564. Prudentius, *Hymns*, *Cathemerinon* 8, verse 11: “A fourth portion of light remains on the sloping axis.”

569. At the rising of evening, *vesper*, or *Hesperus*, is the star Venus, which in the morning is called *Lucifer*. Horace, book II of the *Odes*, ode 9, verse 10: “Nor do your loves depart when evening rises.” Virgil, book I of the *Georgics*, verse 251: “There late-red evening kindles its lights.”

573. *Sustulerat*, from *suffero*. A full day, an entire day, one from which no part was lacking. Columella speaks of *justae operae*, “a full day’s labor.”

575. *Quaerere*, “to acquire” or “to make profit.” Cicero, *Paradoxes* VI, chapter 2: “Those who honorably seek profit by conducting trade.” Hence *quaestus*, “gain.”

578. *Illibata*, “intact” or “whole.” Cicero, *For Sextus*, chapter 43: “That he may pour their ancestral and untouched riches into the deepest whirlpool of his lusts.”

580. *Tantum*, “as much,” that is, “as much as you have.”

581. *Extima*, “outermost,” or “last.” The best writers use the word in this way. *Glomerare* is a verb used elsewhere by Juvencus. See the notes on book II, verses 579 and 723.

582. *Dignatio* is generally a favorable estimation, in which someone rejoices because of the opinion of others. Sometimes it is active: an opinion by which someone judges another worthy of honor. Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 24: “He loved his remaining sisters neither with such desire nor with such esteem.” Justin, near the end of book XXVIII: “He lived in the king’s highest esteem.” Some less accurately read *dignitate*, “dignity.” In Juvencus, *dignatio sancta* is God’s holy goodness, by which he deigns to call human beings to heaven.

### Notes on the preceding passage

553. In the Roman manuscript, *pacis*; correct to *pactus*, “having agreed.”

554. In the Roman manuscript, *laborum*, incorrectly, instead of *laborem*, “labor.”

555. Aldus has *poliri*, “to be cultivated.”

556. In the Hadamar manuscript, *venerit*, “had arrived,” instead of *venerat*, “had arrived.” Poelmann indicates both readings, *venerat* and *venerit*.

557. Our manuscripts, together with the Cambridge manuscript cited by Reuschius, read: “and ordered them to increase their labor.” Tornacensis and Poelmann’s earlier edition: “and ordered them to grow in their work.” Hadamar, Poelmann’s text, Aldus, and Daventria read: “to the work, whom he ordered to go.” Aldus, Daventria, and Poelmann’s earlier edition: “to the work, for whom he ordered them to go.” Reuschius did not object to *adolescere*, “to grow,” in the Paris manuscript, with the same meaning as *accrescere*, “to increase.”

558. The Regius manuscript reads, “Promising rewards for meritorious work,” which could be retained; but it is better, with the others, to read, “For the merits of their labors,” as in Dracontius, book I, verse 12: “For the merits of their character.”

564. The Ottobonian manuscript has *labentes*, “sliding”; corrected to *labentis*, “declining.”

566. The Regius manuscript has *torpere*, “to be numb”; correct to *torperent*, “they were numb.”

567. The Regius, Ottobonian, and Tornacensis manuscripts read: “They say that the employer’s instructions had been given to them—none for himself, the master.” The Roman manuscript, against the metrical rule, reads: “They say that the employer’s instructions had not been given—nothing for themselves: the master.” Poelmann’s text, Hadamar, Aldus, and Daventria read: “The employer says that he had given them nothing.” Poelmann’s earlier edition: “They say that the employer’s instructions had been given—nothing for themselves, the master.” Fabricius: “The employer says that he had given him nothing—his orders.” The master also observes in his commentary that *reddunt* is used for “they answer,” and that this passage was corrupt in earlier editions.

568. Most have *sibi Dominus*, “the master for himself.” Aldus and Basel have *jussa*, “orders.” “The master for his own.”

573. The Regius manuscript has *aequis*, “equal,” which is not so good as *aequum*, “a full [day].”

575. The Regius and the first hand of the Ottobonian manuscript have *similem nos quaerere*, “that we should seek an equal [payment].” The Ottobonian manuscript above and the printed editions have *similem ut nos quaerere*, “that we should seek one equal to us.” The Roman manuscript, less satisfactorily, reads: “It is unjust that we should seek, together with these men, a similar coin”; perhaps the scribe omitted *est* after *injustum*. One may conjecture: “It is unjust that we should seek a similar coin for these men.” Matthew says: “You have made them equal to us.”

576. The Regius, Roman, and Ottobonian manuscripts have *operis*, “of the work.” The Regius has *seri*, “late,” but it seems to have originally read *sero*, “late.” The Roman manuscript and other codices cited by Reuschius have *conjunxerat*, “had joined”; retain *conduxerat*, “had hired.” The temporal expression is used for what the householder had done at that hour, as Reuschius explains.

579. The Regius and Ottobonian manuscripts have *pactis*, “agreements”; but in the Regius, the gloss *promissionis meae* indicates *pacti*, “of my agreement,” which the sense also requires.

581. The Roman manuscript has *Extrema quos*; read *Extima quos*, “those whom the outermost portion.”

583. The Roman manuscript has *Quis per minimam*. In the Regius it was, I think, *Ecquis*, “is there anyone?”; it now reads *e quis*, with the gloss *ex quibus*, “from whom.” Tornacensis, Poelmann, Hadamar, and Daventria divide the phrase as *per minimam*. Aldus and Basel read *per nimiam*, “through the excessive [amount].” The Regius and Ottobonian have *perminimam*, which Fabricius printed; in his commentary he adds that this is an unusual compound. The true reading is *E queis perminimam*, “from whom it is right to set apart a very small portion,” and it agrees with the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” Although examples of the compound *perminimam* may perhaps not occur in the earlier Juvencus, similar compounds are common, such as *permirus*, “very wonderful.”

### Notes on the following passage

584. CHAPTER XXIII. Jesus foretells his passion to the disciples. Matthew XX, 17, etc.; Mark X, 31; Luke XVIII, 31.

587. *Ultima* is used as a noun, as in *ultima pati*, “to suffer the final things,” *ultima experiri*, “to experience the final things,” *ultima expectare*, “to await the final things,” and so forth. Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, chapter 40: “They were bringing Constantius, his father, to the end of life.” Calpurnius, *Eclogues* 3, verse 91: “Lycidas has the end of affairs.” In this sense Juvencus says *ultima mortis*, “the end of death.” Horace, book I, *Epistles* 16, final verse: “Death is the final boundary of things.” Consult Burmann’s note on Calpurnius.

590. CHAPTER XXIV. The request of Zebedee’s wife for her sons. Matthew XX, 20; Mark X, 32.

593. *Calix*, “cup,” used for torments, death, or passion, is an ecclesiastical word taken from the sacred Scriptures. It occurs in book IV, verse 491. I ask whether the use of *si* in place of *an* is rare, as I said in the textual notes on verse 434 of this passage. This usage follows the Greeks, among whom εἰ (“if”) frequently takes the place of an interrogative particle.

597. *Considere*, “to sit down,” from *consido, considis*.

600. “For such words,” as at verse 416 of this passage, *pro numero*, “in proportion.” The sense is that the disciples were more strongly moved than they ought to have been by these words. From the Gospel, however, it is to be understood that the disciples were moved not by Christ’s words but by the words of the mother of Zebedee’s sons on behalf of her sons.

602. *Ditionis* is properly used for power or jurisdiction. *Potestas*, “power,” is used metonymically for magistracy, as in Salvian and others.

604. “Over subject cities”: understand “in subject cities.” One may properly say *exercere odium, iram in aliquo* or *in aliquem*, “to exercise hatred or anger against someone.” Matthew’s Vulgate has *potestatem exercent in eos*, “they exercise authority over them.” The Old Latin in most manuscript copies, and Jerome in his letter to Damasus, volume IV, page 159, has *potestatem exercent in eis*, “they exercise authority in them.”

This he said, and climbed again toward Jerusalem,

And addressed his companions privately:

[585] “We enter once more the regions of Jerusalem,

And approach its savage walls, knowing what awaits us.

The Son of Man will be betrayed to the final extremity of death,

Bearing in his flesh the mockery of scribes and nobles;

Fastened to the cross, he will rise after the third light.”

[590] Then Zebedee’s wife, bowing low, asked

That, with Christ enthroned in the lofty citadel of heaven,

Her fortunate sons might sit at his right and left.

Then Christ asks whether they could drink the cup

[Col. 0264A] which the Father’s command urged him to drink.

[595] They answered that they could together. Then Christ said:

“It is permitted you to drink my cup,

But to sit with me in equal honor upon lofty seats—

My power will not grant this as a gift to anyone.

The Father reserves these exalted gifts for certain persons.”

[600] Thereafter he soothed all the disciples,

Moved by such words, with the honor of this speech:

“Among faithless nations, exalted authority

Sets over them whomever rules them,

And they exercise savage anger in subject cities.

[605] But you are far removed from this: a gentler moderation

Lays smooth the plains of life in harmonious peace.

The great man grows through acts of service,

And no one can be first, alone, unless he serves everyone.

The Son of Man is thus your servant; he alone bears

[610] Holy gifts through his own service,

And gives his life for many with precious blood.

But you wish to rise above those of lesser means,

And thus, having fallen from the heights, you seize the lowly.

If someone calls you to a banquet and sets out a feast,

[615] Let every sensible person avoid placing his limbs at the highest ends of the couch.

Perhaps another of noble rank will come;

He will be forced shamefully to yield his distinguished place,

Which the swelling of his inflated heart had assigned to the highest position.

But if he is content to take a modest place at the banquet,

[620] And afterward a lower-ranking guest enters,

He will modestly move to the better couches.”

[Col. 0267A]

### Notes

606. Reuschius explains the whole passage approximately as follows: “A lofty power of appointment”—that is, God—“places over the faithless nations whomever among them, or from those very unbelieving peoples, he wishes to rule those faithless nations or to rule the subject cities; and these princes exercise fierce anger against those cities, the anger of my Father. But you are ministers not of anger but of clemency. Gentle moderation is benign government. ‘A gentler plain of life in harmonious peace’ means a life conducted peacefully, gentler than any other. ‘Lays smooth’ means spreads out, fills up, for you who are my disciples, here—that is, in this speech and in this life—with the peace which the world cannot give.”

608. *Quisquam unus*, “any one person,” that is, “anyone at all.”

611. *Ponit animam*, “he expends, gives, or lays down his life.” This is an ecclesiastical expression. Augustine, *On John* 121: “As the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to lay down his life for many.”

612. I composed a separate dissertation on these verses in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 5. Since I recently saw a copy of the still-unpublished Tridentine Gospel Book, I think it worthwhile to confirm again the reading of the Old Latin version followed by Juvencus, in the words copied from that Gospel Book: “As the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many. For you seek to rise from a low position and to be made lower from a higher one. When you enter, having been invited to dinner, do not recline in the more prominent places, lest someone more honored than you arrive, and the one who invited you to dinner, approaching, say to you: ‘Move down,’ and you be put to shame. But if you recline in a lower place, and someone more humble than you arrives, then the one who invited you to dinner will say to you: ‘Move higher.’ Then you will have glory before those reclining at table. And when Jesus was leaving Jericho,” etc.

614. CHAPTER XXV. One should recline in the lowest place. Matthew XX in the Old Latin, and Luke XIV, 7, etc. *Vocat*, “he calls,” and *convivia ponens*, “setting out a feast,” are terms proper to banquets. See the notes on book I, verse 795, and book III, verse 80.

615. *Cornua*, “the horns,” are often said of the extremities of anything, such as the wings of a battle line or fleet. Livy, book XXV, chapter 3, near the end: “And by chance Casca was sitting first at the wing.” Apollinaris Sidonius, book I, letter 11, or the last letter, describes a banquet as follows: “On the following day Augustus ordered us to attend his banquet during the circus games. The ordinary consul Severinus sat first at the left-hand wing … Next to him was Magnus, formerly prefect and recently consul … with Camillus, his brother’s son, reclining behind him. Next to him was Poeonius. And next to him Athenius. Gratianensis followed him, a man who had to be kept apart from every disgrace; he had stood behind Severinus in honor but ahead of him in favor. I was the last to recline, at the point where the emperor’s purple-clad left side extended along the right edge.” Sirmond illustrates this passage, from which I gather the following: In a *sigma*, or semicircular couch—that is, a half-round dining couch—there were two extremities resembling horns. These were regarded as the first reclining places. The most honored place on the couch was the right horn, the next the left. This may seem novel and more remote from our custom, since the third, fourth, and remaining places followed in order the person who occupied the first place at the left horn. G. Fabricius thought Juvencus had innovatively used *cornua summa*, “the highest horns,” for the first reclining place. See his *Commentary on Christian Poets*, under *cornua*. Consult also Petrus Chacon, *On the Roman Dining Room*, with the appendix of Fulvius Ursinus; Jerome Mercurialis’s dissertation *On the Origin of Reclining at Dinner*; and many others cited by Fabricius, *Ancient Bibliography*, chapter 19, no. 3.

618. “The swelling of an inflated heart”: pride. Prudentius and other Christian writers speak in the same way. *Per summa*, “at the highest places,” as at verse 615, “At the highest horns.”

619. *Mediocria*, “moderate places,” namely lower places. *Mediocris* often means “small” or “inferior.”

620. From this verse I conclude that Juvencus took the parable from the Old Latin version of Matthew, not from Luke, chapter XIV. For, as we have seen, the Tridentine Gospel Book expresses it under Matthew as follows: “But if you recline in a lower place, and someone more humble than you arrives, then the one who invited you to dinner will say to you: ‘Move higher.’” Luke says only: “But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you: ‘Friend, move higher.’” The Tridentine Gospel Book has it somewhat differently: “Recline in the lowest place, so that when the one who invited you and him comes, he may say to you …”

621. *Pudens*, “modest” or “bashful”: he will move to the more honorable place of the couch and bed because he modestly chose the lower place. It is characteristic of a good man to blush with shame when glory is bestowed upon him as though against his will.

Then he ascended the mountain heights nearest Jerusalem,

Where blue-green-leaved olive trees gleam in ordered rows.

[624] Christ then ordered chosen disciples to set out,

Pointing out the dwelling places of a village opposite them,

And from there to lead away an ass, likewise found

Accompanied by her young; or, if anyone should ask

Why the beasts were being dragged away so suddenly,

To say that the Lord wished to make use of them.

[630] The disciples promptly fulfill his commands.

They bring the gentle colt and spread over it

[Col. 0268A] A soft covering of cloth, offering it a seat.

Then there flowed forth the prophetic voice of an ancient seer:

“Behold, your gentle king comes to you, seated upon the backs

[635] Of the leading ass and the colt that follows.”

Then the people all spread their garments along the roads,

And wherever Christ’s path lay, they crown it with interlaced foliage.

Others then strip the nearby palm trees of their green leaves,

And all together proclaim: ‘From David’s lineage sprung,

[640] Hosanna in the highest! May joyful glory attend the trophies!’”

[Col. 0269A]

### Notes

622. CHAPTER XXVI. With Christ seated upon the colt of an ass, the people spread their garments along the road by which he traveled. Matthew XXI, 1 and following; Mark XI, 1; Luke IX, 29; John XXII, 15.

623. “In rows” is skillfully said of the arrangement of trees. Cicero, *For Caecina*, chapter 8: “They mark off the farthest part of that estate with olive trees in a straight row.” Compare Passeratius’s note. Virgil, book II of the *Georgics*, verse 276: “If the ground is sloping toward the hillocks and the hills rise steeply, give attention to the rows.” *Lucent*, “they shine,” that is, “they are conspicuous, they gleam.” Well-cultivated fields, and the trees themselves, are said to shine. Pliny, book XVII, chapter 4: “The soil in which tall trees shine is not necessarily fertile.” Hence *shining fields*, *gleaming fields*, and *shining earth and grass*; and Juvencus below, verse 712, “the gleaming vineyard.” *Glaucicomans*, “blue-green-haired,” is a word coined by Juvencus, as in book IV, verse 201, *flammicomans*, “flame-haired.”

624. *Lectis discipulorum*, “of the chosen disciples,” that is, “from among the disciples”; or it is a positive used for a superlative, as though *lectissimis discipulorum*, “the most chosen of the disciples,” as in this passage, verse 293, *eximios vatum*, “the most eminent of the prophets.” Virgil, book IX, verse 47: “Turnus, who, flying ahead, had passed before the slow-moving army, accompanied by twenty chosen horsemen, suddenly appeared before the city.”

625. *Obvia*, “opposite,” that is, “situated across from or facing them.” This is the proper meaning of the word. Matthew says: “Go into the village that is opposite you.”

627. *Vel si*, “and if”; *vel* is sometimes used for *et* by reputable authors.

632. Matthew says: “And they brought the ass and the colt, and placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them.” The Old Latin version in the Colbertine manuscript reads: “And they brought the ass and its colt, and placed their garments upon them, and Jesus sat upon it.” Most other manuscripts, together with the Tridentine Gospel Book, read: “And they placed the garments upon it, and he sat upon it.” This reading was followed by the author of the *Incomplete Commentary on Matthew* and by Arnobius the African in his *Annotations on the Gospels*. The other Evangelists explicitly state that Jesus sat upon the colt of the ass. Later, when Juvencus renders Isaiah’s prophecy, he says: “Seated upon their backs, they bear him—the ass and the following colt.” A probable interpretation is that Jesus first used the ass, with the colt following; then, after entering the city, he sat upon the colt, with the ass following. Ancient and more recent interpreters assign several reasons for this mystery. In monuments of the ancient Christians the image of the Savior seated upon an ass or she-ass often appears. It is preserved in this form, engraved on a very ancient silver-soldered spoon, in the possession of the distinguished Giovenazzi, who prudently conjectured that such a spoon had once been used to distribute the sacred communion to the ancient people according to the old custom. Thus the faithful approaching so great a mystery could recall Matthew’s words: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, seated upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.”

635. *Praemitis*: Juvencus likes to form such words in this way, as has been noted more than once.

636. *Stratas*, “roads,” as stated elsewhere.

637. On this triumph of the Savior, the ancient custom of covering roads with flowers, and the children’s acclamation “Hosanna,” Martinus Roa should be consulted, *Singularia*, book II, chapter 13.

638. Judaea abounded in palm trees. Horace, book II, *Epistles* 2, verse 184: “He would prefer to be anointed with the rich palms of Herod.” Pliny, book V, chapter 14: “Jericho planted with palms.” On the word *viror*, “greenery,” see book II, verse 818.

### Notes on the following passage

641. Aldus and Poelmann’s earlier edition have *Sic tunc*; the others *Sic adeo*, “thus indeed.”

642. In the Roman manuscript, *Ingresso primo occurrit*; others, *Ingresso occurrit primo*. Tornacensis has *lumine*; read *limine*, “threshold.”

644. Basel has *jam*, “already,” instead of *tam*, “so.” The Regius, in the text, together with others, has *gressu visuque*, “with step and sight”; above, in an old hand, *visuque et voce*, “with sight and voice.”

646. All our manuscripts, the Dijon manuscript, and another manuscript of P. Pithou collated by Juretus have *tecta clamore*, “the roofs covered with shouting”; the printed editions have *tecta canore*, “the roofs covered with song.” The first syllable of *clamor* is long, and Juvencus also lengthens it in book II, verse 410, and book IV, verses 590 and 702. Therefore *canore* should be retained, a word used by Virgil, Lucretius, Ovid, and other poets especially. See the note on verse 648.

647. On the word *Hosanna*, or *Osanna*, see the variant readings on verse 640. Aldus and Basel have *create*, “created,” instead of *creato*, “sprung.”

648. The Regius, Ottobonian, and Roman manuscripts read: “All ask him what the cause of the shouting is.” I shall read, with the printed editions, “what the cause of the song is,” in accordance with verse 646, “the roofs covered with song,” and book IV, verse 392: “He stood still, filling the hollow rocks with opposing song.” Juretus, in book IV of Paulinus of Petricordia’s *Life of Saint Martin*, verse 172, using the manuscript of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, reads *clamoris* and *clamore* in these passages, supported by the Cambridge manuscript and by the authority of other poets, who shorten the first syllable of that word. Paulinus of Petricordia, in the cited passage: “The blows of the strikers resounded, the words of the shouters.” Tertullian, *On Jonah and Nineveh*, verse 42: “Meanwhile a double nautical shout attempts everything.” Most printed editions have: “Then everyone asks”; Hadamar has *praecontantur*, which is not good Latin. Poelmann’s earlier edition and Barthius’s manuscript have: “All ask him.” Others write *percunctor*, others *perconctor*. The active verb *percuncto* and the passive *percunctor* are not very common; nevertheless I have no doubt that the word is Juvencus’s, since *percunctata* again occurs in the passive at verse 679. Naevius, Gellius, and Apuleius use the same verb.

649. The Roman manuscript, together with the printed editions, has *tantam*, “so great”; the Regius *tantum*, “so great” in the neuter; the Ottobonian *tanta*. The last pleases me above all, because it was altered by ignorant scribes who did not know that the final syllable of *tanta* could be lengthened at the metrical caesura, especially in accordance with the practice of poets of the later age.

650. The Roman and Ottobonian manuscripts, together with Hadamar and Poelmann’s text, read: “Of the law, he says, you …” The Regius, with Aldus and Tornacensis, has: “Of the holy law, you …”

651. The Regius, together with Tornacensis and Poelmann’s earlier edition, has *Creditis*, “you believe.” The Roman and Ottobonian manuscripts, with Aldus, have *Creditur*, “it is believed.” The Roman manuscript, with Aldus and others, punctuates: “to come—the nursing infants, and with tongues.” But Scripture distinguishes the phrase differently: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children.”

652. Reg. has *lactantum*; Rom., Ott., and the printed editions have *lactentum*. The old versions in Sabatier all have *lactantium*, which is likewise read in the Tridentine Gospel Book; this confirms *lactantum* in Reg. Yet many ancient Fathers, together with the Vulgate, present *lactentum*, and for one who sucks milk *lactens* is a more precise word than *lactans*, since some have questioned the latter. Some, in Reusch, have *justis*: retain *justi*, namely, “of Christ.”

655. Poelm., in place of the second reading, has *Stare extendentem*. The correct reading is *Stratae, tendentem*. I do not know whether Aldus intended *Strate tendentem*. Elsewhere too *strata, stratae* occurs in Juvencus for “road,” as shortly before, verse 636.

656. Rom. above *corda* indicates *corde*, which I have not admitted. Reusch conjectures *voluptas* for *voluntas*, that is, “desire.”

658. Reg., Ott., Daventr., and Ald. have *sterilis frondis concreverat umbrae*. Rom. likewise has this, but *sterili*; Had., Poelm. in the text, and Fabr. have *sterili frondis concreverat umbra*. In Reg. the gloss is *UMBRAE*—“in the shade.”

660. Reg. and Ott. have *arbos*; Rom. has *arbor*.

663. Omeisius suspects *Nunc ligni stirpem*; Reusch *Nunc lignum istius*, namely, “of the tree.” Otherwise *arborem* must be supplied: “Now you have been astonished that, by our authority, this tree of wood has ceased to draw earthly juices into growth.” I had thought the reading might be: *Nunc ligni istius nostro stupuistis honore—Desisse vires terrenos ducere succos* (“Now you have been astonished by our honor at this tree’s having ceased to draw earthly juices into growth”), which seems excellent if the final syllable of *desisse* is lengthened by the caesura.

[Note: [Col. 0269D]]

644. *Quos*: a synesis, or alteration of number and gender, as though not “the weak common people” had preceded, but “weak men from the common people.”

647. *Creato*: “created,” “begotten.” This is the proper meaning of the word, although not everything that is begotten can also be called created.

653. CHAPTER XXVII. Christ cursed the fig tree because it was barren, and it immediately withered. Matthew 21:17 ff.; Mark 11:13.

654. In the margin, *stratae*. The sacred text has “beside the road”; the Cambridge manuscript, “above the road.” Properly, a *margo* is the outer edge of anything: the bank of a river, the boundary of a field, the edge of a road or book, and so forth.

655. Book II, verse 146: “When the spreading shade of the fig tree sheltered you.”

657. *Facultas*: “no capacity or power of producing fruit had grown beneath the shade of the barren foliage.”

658. *Pomum* means any fruit. See the note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 186.

661. On the old age and death of trees, see the note on Book II, verse 749, and Gruner’s note on Sedulius, Book I, verse 13.

662. *Stupidis*: “those who were greatly astonished,” as in the following verse, *stupuistis*.

Thus Christ enters the walls of Jerusalem.

As he entered, the feeble common people came to meet him, first beneath the threshold of the temple,

302 lame in their legs and eyes, striving with one another.

When the astonished party of priests recognized that these people had suddenly become vigorous in step and sight,

[645] and saw the temple boys filling the roofs with song—

“Hosanna to the one created from David’s illustrious stock”—

they all ask him what cause makes this unaged crowd raise such songs amid such great rejoicing.

[650] To this Christ replies: “Do you believe that you hold the writings of the Law,

which say that praise rises from the mouths of infants

303 and that the praise of the Just One rises from the tongues of sucklings?”

[Col. 0270A] Having said this, he leaves the ungrateful city with its inhabitants,

and makes for Bethany. On his return, he sees at the roadside

[655] a fig tree extending its spreading shade.

There, perhaps, an appetite seeking food stirs his heart;

he touches the branches of the tree, but beneath the shade of its barren foliage

no capacity for fruit had formed.

To it Christ says: “May you never again have abundance for producing fruit.”

[660] At once the tree withers.

The disciples marvel at the tree’s swift death.

But Christ, standing beside the astonished men, speaks as follows:

“Now you have been astonished, by our authority, that this tree

[Col. 0271A] [Note: [Col. 0271B]]

665. Reg. has *iterum iterumque*: restore *iterumque iterumque*.

666. Reg. has *animae* instead of *animi*. Daventr., together with the Reg. manuscripts, has *consistit*. Ald. and Bas., with Rom., have *consistat*. Had., Fabr., and Poelm. have *consistet*.

667. Westh. in the text has *mutans*; in the margin, *nutans*, which alone should be approved.

670. Ald. has *verbis*; others have *verbo*. Ald. and Bas. have *profundis*: *profundi* is better, namely, “of the sea.”

673. Rom. has *Credendum*: read *Credentum*, and perhaps it would be preferable to punctuate: “*poscet—Credentum semper digna virtute tenebit*.” Shortly before: “*Credentum verbo*.”

676. Poelm., in place of the second reading, has *Mirantes rogitant, qua virtute efficis ista*; in the text, together with the manuscripts and other printed editions, *Collecti inquirunt, virtus quae tanta dedisset*.

678. Ald. has *nobis si*.

679. Rom. has *Praecunctata*: read *Percunctata* or *Percontata*, according to what was said at verse 648. The manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *solvat*; Had. and Poelm. have *solvet*.

[Col. 0271C] 680. Torn. has *Joannis* instead of *Joannes*.

681. Reg., Ott., and Rom. have *Sordentis*; the printed editions have *Sordentes*.

682. Reg., Ott., Ald., and Bas. have *An hominis*. Rom. has *An Joannis*. Hadam., Fabr., and Poelm. have *Anne hominis*. *An hominis* is sound: I have explained at Book II, verse 517, that *an* can be lengthened. Here, however, there is a special reason, because of the aspiration of the following word, which sometimes has the power of lengthening the preceding word’s short syllable.

683. Ott. has *ludens* instead of *claudens*, and perhaps the first hand had *laudens* or *claudens*. In manuscripts *ludens* and *claudens*, or equivalently *cludens*, are easily confused with one another. Nor would *ludens* displease me here. Yet *claudens* is much preferable. Thus in Book IV, verse 8: “Why are you now trying,” he said, “to shut me in with words?”

685. Reg. and Ott., by the first hand, and Torn. have *suspiciebat*; Rom., with most printed editions, has *suscipiebat*. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXVI, chapter 7, column 1265, also corrected *suscipiebat* to *suspiciebat*. He says that this word is corrupted in the *Tree of Life* by Cyprian, or another Christian poet: “They walk about amid the soft grass— / They receive the fruits hanging from the lofty tree.” One should read *Suspiciunt*. See Book III, verse 51, where the same verse occurs.

687. Reg., contrary to metrical usage, has *sublimem si dixissent esse*. Ott., by the first hand, has *Rursus sublimem dixissent esse prophetam*, which seems genuine: the particle *si* is not necessary. In Ott., as in the printed editions, *si* is inserted above the line between *dixissent* and *esse*. The particle *si* is often elegantly omitted, not only by poets but also by others. Virgil, Book VI, verse 31: “You would have had your share in so great a work, Icarus, if grief had allowed it.” Ovid, *Fasti* VI, verse 113: “Some young man might have spoken loving words to her— / She immediately returned such replies.” Cicero, *Philippics* XIII, chapter 11: “If you withdraw, everyone will pursue you; if you remain, you will stick fast.”

689. Torn. and Poelm., in place of the second reading, have *igitur* instead of *tamen*.

[Note: [Col. 0271C]]

665. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 436: “I shall proclaim it, and repeating it again and again, I shall warn you.”

666. *Animi in arce*: as though “on the citadel, summit, or peak of the mind.” Statius, *Silvae* II.2, verse 131: “From the lofty citadel of your mind / You look down upon those who wander and laugh at human joys.”

668. *Arboris substantia*: “the tree.” See the note on Book I, verses 416 and 631.

669. *Celsa montis*. On the substantive use of *celsa*, I have spoken in the note on Dracontius, Book II, verse 3.

674. CHAPTER XXVIII. Jesus was asked by what authority he did these things, and replied: “It will be easy to tell you what you ask, if first you answer what we shall ask you about John’s baptism.” Matthew 21:23 ff.; Mark 11:21; Luke 20:2; John 14:13; 16:23.

675. The order is: “Immediately the leaders, or elders of the people, gathered together and asked what great power had produced these miracles,” or “what power had produced such great miracles.”

680. Above, verse 263: “The just John, who washed the peoples in the river.” Compare the note.

683. *Ancipiti*: “pressing in both directions.” See the note on Book II, verse 233.

684. *Captantum*: “of those wishing to seize or ensnare.” See the note on this passage, verse 134. Sometimes *captare* indicates an attempt to seize, while *capere* indicates success.

688. An admission that they had killed the prophet would have proved the elders’ guilt. But what guilt did the elders bear for John’s having been killed by Herod? It is sufficiently clear from the Evangelists here that the scribes and Pharisees did not believe John. For Luke says: “But they reasoned among themselves, saying: ‘If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From men, all the people will stone us.’ For they are convinced that John was a prophet.” It is therefore probable that they procured John’s death by whatever means they could. From this Lamy confirms his own view that John had been imprisoned twice: first by the scribes and Pharisees, then by Herod, after the scribes and Pharisees had released him because they feared the people.

691. *Responsa superba*: “proud answers,” because they themselves are proud and either do not answer or answer arrogantly.

692. CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the man who, having sons, ordered them to go into the vineyard. Also, that publicans and prostitutes would believe in Christ, while the Jews would remain obstinate. Matthew 21:28 ff.

304 “Having ceased to draw earthly juices into growth.”

[665] “But in truthful words I shall warn you again and again:

For if certain faith shall stand firm in the citadel of the mind,

and shall not lie trembling, wavering amid doubtful vices,

the substance of this tree shall yield to you.

Nor only that of this tree: even the lofty heights of a mountain

[670] may, at the word of believers, be torn up and hidden

together with the deep waters, the forests, the rocks, and the wild beasts.

And whatever the faith of believers shall ask with a steadfast breast,

it shall always obtain by worthy power.”

When he had said this, he entered the temple walls.

[675] Immediately the leaders of the people, gathered together, inquire

what great power had produced these miracles.

Christ says to them: “For you who ask, it is now easy

305 to tell everything, if your answer first resolves for us

[Col. 0272A] in a few words the question we in turn have asked.

[680] Recently John, who washed away the stains of the impure people

in a pure stream: did divine power,

or rather human deceit, seem to you to be at work?”

Thus he spoke, closing the minds of the leaders who sought to ensnare him

with the two-edged weight of his words. For the people’s great reverence

[685] honored John as a prophet,

and they could not call his life deceitful.

If they should again say that he was a lofty prophet,

306 the admission that they had killed him would draw guilt upon them.

Yet the deceitful faction replied that they did not know.

[690] Then Christ said: “It is not unjust to close my voice

when the proud answers of the leaders are closed to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0273A]]

695. Rom. has *retonde*; Helmst. has *reconde*; others have *retunde*. Reusch prefers *retunde* instead of *tonde*. The word is attributed to Plautus, and *retonsus* is used by Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 17, of a grain field. A vine is *tondetur* when it is pruned. Columella, Book IV, chapter 21: “Let the vine be pruned back to a thumb.” Pliny, Book XV, chapter 1: “Olive trees are pruned, as are vines.” Thus also *tonsus ilex*, “a pruned holm oak,” *tonsus myrtus*, “a pruned myrtle,” and similar expressions. In common and Vulgate usage *retunde* has the same sense; and, as far as trenches are concerned, one may say that a vine is *retundi* when it is laid down. Columella, Book IV, chapter 4: “After a trench has been made in the prepared ground, the whole vine is laid down from approximately the middle of the furrow.” To press vineyards with trenches means to dig and prepare the soil, or to turn it over.

698. All our manuscripts, together with Torn., have: *Exsequitur, damnansque sibi responsa coercet*, namely, “he corrects the answers in himself.” Most printed editions have: *Exsequitur, durae damnans responsa loquelae*. I conjectured: *Exsequitur, damnatque suae responsa loquelae*.

702. Poelm., in place of the second reading, and Fabr. have *uter potius*; in the text, together with the others, *quis potius*. Rom. corruptly has *genitoris gloriamque sequatur*.

[Col. 0273C] 703. Reg. has *Olli conlaudant responsum posterioris*; Ott. likewise, but *responsa* is metrically impossible. Rom. similarly has *Illi collaudant responsa posterioris*. Poelm. in the text, Daventr., Ald., and Hadam. have *Illi collaudant nati responsa prioris*. Poelm. in the text, Daventr., Ald., and Hadam. also have *Itti collaudant nati responsa prioris*. Poelm., in place of the divergent reading, has *Olli non laudant responsum posterioris*. Juvencus’ reading should be restored from our manuscripts: *Illi collaudant responsum posterioris*. The ancient scribes, or the first editors of Juvencus, who knew only the Vulgate version of Scripture, corrupted this verse. The words in the Vulgate are Matthew 21:31: “Which of the two did the father’s will? They say to him, ‘The first.’” The ancient version agrees, as found in the Colbert manuscript and Saint-Germain 2; but in Corbie 1 and 2, Saint-Germain 1, the Clermont manuscript, Cambridge, and the manuscript of Saint Andrew of Avignon, instead of “They say to him, ‘The first,’” one finds “They say to him, ‘The last.’” The same reading occurs in the Vercelli manuscript published by Irici and in the Verona manuscript printed by Blanchini. Birchius, in his work *The Four Gospels*, and elsewhere, cites in support of this reading the celebrated Greek Vatican manuscript 1209, the best of all existing manuscripts, Vind. Lamb. 31, and the Syriac Jerusalem version. Wetstein, in the Greek New Testament, records the same reading from the ancient Cambridge Greek manuscript and two more recent ones, as well as from the Coptic, Armenian, Saxon, and Arabic versions, and also from Damascus, Pseudo-Athanasius against Arius, Victorinus, and Hippolytus on Genesis. The Tridentine Gospel Book, often praised by me, now joins these witnesses.

Thomas Mareschallus observed that the Anglo-Saxon version reads: “Then they said to him: ‘The last.’” I omit the Arabic versions in some copies and the Egyptian version, in which the answers of the two sons are reversed; consequently, it is not surprising that the answer of the latter is praised. Among most Latin manuscripts, in which verses 29 and 30 follow consistently without any disturbance of the verses, the reading is “They say to him, ‘The last,’” not “The first.” Sabatier adds Saint Augustine, Book V of the *Locutions*, volume 3, part 1, column 368, and more clearly Hilary, in his *Commentary*, column 716.

Saint Jerome also recognized this reading, although he says that in other copies, which he himself calls genuine, the passage was read differently, *Commentary on Matthew*, volume IV, column 101: “When it is said, ‘Which of the two did the father’s will?’ and they say to him, ‘The last,’ it should be known that in the genuine copies *the last* is not found, but *the first*, so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. But if we wish to read *the last*, the interpretation is clear: we may say that the Jews indeed understand the truth but evade it and refuse to say what they think, just as they knew that John’s baptism was from heaven but refused to say so.”

Sabatier cited Juvencus in support of the Vulgate reading because he had not seen Juvencus’ manuscript copies; from these, however, it is clear that Juvencus read: “They say to him: ‘The last.’” Reusch retained the Vulgate reading in Juvencus, although, as he says, he had no doubt that the verse presented by us was genuinely Juvencus’ own. He interprets it as follows: They praised the answer and words of the latter, but not his deed; by that very fact, however, they approved the deed of the former.

Christian Friedrich Matthaeus states in the Greek and Latin New Testament that in some of his manuscripts the sons’ answers are reversed, and that this transposition arose from the commentaries of interpreters who understood this passage as referring to the Israelite people and the Gentiles. Once this was assumed, the question arose which of the two had been called first.

705. Ott. and Reg. have *comprendere possunt*; Rom., together with the printed editions, has *comprendere certum est*.

707. Ott. and Reg. have *quisquam*; others have *quemquam*, so that this verse corresponds to verse 705. In Ott. *quemquam* may perhaps have stood originally.

[Note: [Col. 0273D]]

694. Virgil, *Eclogue* 2, verse 70: “Your leafy vine on the elm is half-pruned.”

695. *Premens vineta retonde*: the same accusative belongs with both verbs.

696. The bonds of rustic labor are not “filthy” if *sordidus* is understood as “infamous, disgraceful, foul.” In another sense, fields are called filthy, as are plows, the filthy leisure of the countryside, and the filthy roofs of farmhouses and cottages, because no cultivation of cleanliness is practiced in the country. *Vincla laboris* (“bonds of labor”) seems to have been taken from Horace, Book I, *Epistle* 7, verse 67: “To excuse labor and mercenary bonds.”

700. A noteworthy expression: *Jubebat ad vineta dependere jussa sui laboris*—“he ordered them to go down to the vineyards, summoned to their appointed labor”; that is, he ordered them to go into the vineyard to work. *Dependere* can also mean “to expend,” as in *dependere operam*, “to expend effort.” Perhaps this is what *dependere jussa laboris* means here.

701. *Repensat* is a frequentative from *rependo*, with nearly the same meaning. It does not make deeds correspond to words or make them equal.

706. *Quaestus* is frequently used of the profession of prostitution. Plautus, *Poenulus* V.3.20: “And they would make a disgraceful profit from their bodies.”

708. *Non est vestrum*: “It is not yours.” Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* III.2: “It is not mine to lie.”

For the father of two sons spoke these words into the ears of the elder: “A large portion of the vineyard lies half-pruned for me.”

But go on, and now with strong force,

[695] pressing the vineyards, now with trenches, now with the pruning hook, prune them back.

Then the young man says that he is unwilling to endure such bonds of labor.

After all his father’s orders, however, he carries them out,

307 condemning and restraining his own answer.

To another son, born afterward, he gave the same command:

[700] ‘Go down to the vineyards and perform the labor assigned to you.’

The young man agreed, but did not make his deeds answer his words.

Tell me, which of the two is more likely to follow his father’s command?”

They praise the answer of the latter.

308 Christ continues: “Now pay closer attention to the true words.

[705] It is already more certain that those who seek the kingdom of heaven

from the filth of their bodily vices

will enter it rather than any one of you.

For John, the Just One, had come before you;

but believing is not yours.”

[Col. 0275A] [Note: [Col. 0275B]]

710. Reg. and Ott. write *Auserunt*. Reg. has *animae* instead of *animi*.

713. Rom. has *coheret*: read *coercet*. Some join *circumdensa ta* into one word, but *circum* seems rather to be used adverbially.

718. Most write *quis*; some write *queis*.

720. Reg. has *verbere servos*. Rom. and Ott., together with the printed editions, have *verbere saevo*.

721. Reg., Ottob., Hadam., Poelm., and Fabr. have *proterrent*. This may explain the error in Rom., *prosternit*, unless one should read *prosternunt*, which is nevertheless less preferable, since the following verse has the same verb. Ald. and Bas. have *diverberat*. *Proterrent* is used for “drive away,” “expel.” Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* 3.1: “You drove him away from here”—namely, his son.

723. Fabr. incorrectly has *dominos* instead of *dominus*.

724. Rom., Ott., Ald., and Bas. have *rursus*; others have *rursum*. Ott. has *Praecepit*, correctly emended to *Praecipit*.

726. Reg. has *demittere*, perhaps better than *dimittere*. Arntzenius, in his note on Sedulius V, 393, scarcely recognizes any difference between these words.

730. Rom. has *Progeniem exstinctam*; others have *Progenie exstincta*.

731. Our manuscripts have *Cedere credentum*; the printed editions have *Cedere credentes*. This is a figure of synesis: *credentes* as though not “their mind” had preceded, but “they who had a mind polluted,” and so forth.

735. Rom. has *refertur*; the others, more suitably, have *feretur*, for this is demanded by the meaning of the Gospel.

736. Reg., Rom., Torn., and Ald. have *Ad placidam gentem, possit quae reddere fructus*. Ott., together with other printed editions, has *Ad gentem, dignos possit quae reddere fructus*.

737. Rom., Hadam., Fabr., and Poelm. in the text have *At rex*. Reg., Ott., Ald., Torn., and Bas. have *Ut rex*. The latter is preferable. Although *sic*, or something similar explaining the second part of the comparison, is not added afterward, it is already understood that the kingdom of heaven is here compared with the king who made a wedding feast for his son. Compare verse 712 of this passage, where “thus a certain rich man” introduces the parable of the vineyard in a similar manner.

738. The construction of this and the following verse is obscure. I considered: “He orders the leaders to frequent the joyful banquet, summoning servants,” and so forth; or: “He ordered the leaders, frequenting the joyful banquet, the summoned servants,” or *famulis*. In the Vulgate text the tenses vary: “He ordered the leaders to frequent the banquet, and ordered the summoned servants to celebrate together.” Schoettgenius says that *Praecipit concelebrare*, not *Praecepit*, should be repeated.

[Note: [Col. 0275C]]

710. *Sordes animi*: “faults, crimes, sins, greed.” Here the expression is rightly applied to impurities of both body and mind.

712. CHAPTER XXX. The parable of the vineyard workers who kill those sent to them to demand the rent of the leased land. Matthew 21:33 ff.; Mark 12:1; Luke 20:9. On *nitentis vineti*, see the note on verse 623 of this passage.

713. Above, verse 550: “To whom sweet vineyards crown the fields far and wide with rich crops.”

717. *Fructus tempore certo*: “fruit at the appointed time,” namely, at its proper season, or harvest. Ovid, *Remedia amoris* 189: “At the appointed seasons the farmer gathers the ripe grape.”

[Col. 0275D] 718. *Actores*: a word especially proper for slaves who administer money and the revenues of an estate. See the *Digest*, Book XXXIII, title 7, law 20, where Scaevola clearly distinguishes an *actor* from a *vilicus*, although he also counts the *actor* among the duties of an equipped estate. In the earliest centuries of the Church many Christian writers had practiced in the courts, either administering or defending the law. In Prudentius, Dracontius, and Juvencus I have often observed words and phrases drawn from an intimate knowledge of legal matters.

719. The meaning and order are: “to whom a portion of the land was to be given, with a fixed payment of the cultivators preserved or excepted,” that is, “the payment owed to the cultivators.” Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 148 ff., proves that in managing the master’s property the slave *actor* claimed the leading role, and that Juvencus was right to understand the *actores* as slaves sent by the master of the household to the farming tenants to collect the vineyard’s produce.

721. *Lapidum telis*: “with missiles of stones.” Nonius, chapter 6, no. 5: “Authority has taught that stones too can be called missiles, and everything that is thrown.” Sisenna, *Histories* IV: “He distributed hand-sized stones, because the whole field required missiles of this kind.” Gaius, final book of the *Digest*, title 16, “On the Meaning of Words,” law 233: “In common usage a missile is called what is sent from a bow. But now everything sent by hand is meant.” It follows that stone, wood, and iron are all included under this name.

727. A son is called a part of his father. *Vis digna pudoris* is used for “modesty,” or “the virtue of modesty.” Compare the note on Book I, verse 420.

728. *Venerandam* is passive, as in Book II, verse 281. See the variant reading there.

732. *Septa*: “fences.” Varro, *On Agriculture* I.14: “Now I shall speak of fences, which are made for protecting the estate or its divisions.”

737. CHAPTER XXXI. The parable of those who were invited but disdain coming to the wedding. Matthew 22:1 ff.; Luke 14:16. On *thalamorum vincula nectens*, “binding the bonds of the bridal chamber,” concerning the bonds of marriage, compare the note on Book II, verse 278.

For the hearts of prostitutes had rather drunk in a firm faith

[710] and laid aside the shameful filth of the mind.

But you never repent of such great crimes.

“Thus a certain rich man, whose many acres were enclosed

by a densely packed hedge of a flourishing vineyard,

309 built in the middle a tower, a winepress, and vats,

[715] and appointed cultivators, leasing out the fruit to be harvested,

establishing the law that the imposed rent should be paid.

Then he went far away, but at the appointed season

sent household agents to collect the fruit, to whom a portion

of the land would be given, with the cultivators’ fixed rent preserved.

[720] Behold, the fury of the tenants drives some of these away

with savage blows, while others they terrify everywhere

with missiles of stones.

[Col. 0275B] Finally, they strike many down with a deadly wound.

Then the master of the land orders more slaves to come

[Col. 0276A] and again demands the agreed payments.

[725] But the bold injustice rises greater against more of them.

At last the master resolves to send his son,

because the tenants’ sense of shame would require that his offspring, a part of himself, be held in honor in their hearts.

But against him their minds, already stained with blood,

[730] believing that after the master’s son had been killed

the estate would pass to them, strike him down

with a cruel wound, cut him down, and throw his corpse outside the fences.

After this the master will come and exact punishment

for such great crimes. But from you the seat of the shining kingdom,

[735] once entrusted to you, will be transferred

to a people able to produce worthy fruits.

[Col. 0276B] “As a king who, binding the bridal bonds for his son,

ordered the leaders to attend the joyful banquet,
