739. Reg. and Rom. have *Accitos famulis*, with a gloss in Reg.: *accitos—vocatos a famulis* (“summoned—called by the servants”). This reading is preferable, because the corresponding manner of expression is familiar in Juvencus and the sense proceeds more clearly. The common reading is *Accitos famulos*; in Ott., *Accitos* has become *Accitis*.

740. This and the following verse were missing in Reg., but have been added.

743. Koenigius conjectured *convivia lauta*, since *convivia laeta* has already occurred.

744. Our manuscripts and Poelmann, in place of the second reading, have *opibus*; most printed editions have *dapibus*, which better suits the sense.

746. Ald. has *merces*, which is preferable.

747. Ott., together with the others, has *vocarent*; but the second hand has *vocarant*.

751. Reg. and Ott. have *et fusi*. Punctuation would then have to be: “and, avenging the poured-out blood of the servants—then he says to the slaves.” *Effusi*, with Rom. and the printed editions, is nevertheless better.

[Col. 0277C] 753. Our manuscripts have *opibus*; the printed editions have *dapibus*. Here I would more willingly accept *opibus*. Ott. and Ald. have *instruximus, illi—Contempsere*. Most other manuscripts and printed editions have *instruximus illis—Contempsere*.

754. Reg. has *proceris* instead of *proceres*.

756. Ottob. has *glomeraverat*; above, *glomeraverit* is correct.

758. Rom., Torn., Ald., and Bas. have *compita lata*, as in Book IV, verse 206, *per compita lata viarum*; other manuscripts and printed editions have *compita cuncta*.

760. Rom., Ott. by the first hand, Fabr., Had., and Poelm. in the text have *Complentur mensae mixtae sine nomine plebis*. Reg. and Ott. by the second hand have the same, but *plebes* instead of *plebis*, perhaps with this sense: “The mixed peoples were gathered without distinction.” Ald., Bas., and Poelm., in place of the divergent reading, have *Complentur mensae mixta sine nomine plebe*. This reading displeases Fabricius, who states in his commentary that the verb *compleo* here governs the genitive *plebis*. See what we noted in the variant reading at verse 90 of this book and in the note at verse 253.

761. Ott. has *Huc justi, injustique simul venere* and, in place of the divergent reading, *cubuere*. Rom., Ald., and Bas. have *Sic justi*. Reg., Had., and Poelm. have *Hic justi*. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *cubuere*.

762. Rom. has *Et rex*; others have *At rex*.

763. Rom., Reg., and Ott. by the first hand have *vidit*; correctly, Ott. by the second hand has *videt*.

764. Reg. has *Laetitiis* instead of *Laetitiae*. Ott. by the second hand, Had., Poelm. in the text, Westhem. in the margin, and Fabr. have *quae dissona*. Reg., Rom., and, apparently, Ott. by part of the first hand, together with Ald. and Westh. in the text, have *longe*; in Ott. by the first hand there was *lingua* instead, perhaps the divergent reading or a correction of *longe*. Ald. has *dissona valde*.

767. Ott. has *puro*; above, *puri*, together with the others, is correct.

768. In Ottob. *praecepit* has rightly been corrected to *praecipit*.

[Note: [Col. 0277C]]

739. *Votum de nuptiis*: a solemn expression for a wedding, as I noted on Book II, verse 368.

740. *Adire*. Sedulius, in the prologue, verse 5: “Approach the solemnities of the table.” Arntzenius discusses this more fully there.

744. *Diversa*: “opposite,” or “entirely different.”

747. *Vocarent*, and at verse 757 *vocantes*, and at verse 761 *vocati*, and so forth: a word proper to banquets. As noted in Book I, verse 795, Mazochius, *Spicilegium*, volume III, on Luke 14:12, observes from Cicero, Phaedrus, and Lactantius that *revocare* is used of those who return the invitation to a meal.

752. *Festa jugalia*: “nuptial celebrations.” Catullus, poem 64, *On the Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*, verse 302: “To celebrate the wedding torches.” Poets frequently use the expression in this sense.

753. *Praelargus* had previously been used by Persius. *Instruere* is regularly used of banquets, as I said in the note on Book II, verse 53.

756. *Glomeraverit*: a word familiar to Juvencus. See the note on Book II, verse 579.

760. Book I, verse 485: “Mixed crowds follow.” Sedulius imitates Juvencus in Book IV, verse 2: “The nameless common crowd—mixed together,” and so forth.

[Col. 0278C] 763. *Vestis amictu*: a hendiadys.

764. *Dissona*: “discordant,” “incongruous.” Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius*, verse 249: “A barbarism discordant with the rites.”

765. *Sermonis pondere*: as in Book II, verse 483. Cicero, *For Ligarius*, chapter 7: “Yet he could not bear the weight of the words themselves.”

[Col. 0278D] 769. Book IV, verse 395: “With hands and feet bound together.”

770. Mazochius interprets “the outer darkness” in relation to the brightness of lamps that shone upon those dining at night, so that those expelled would necessarily remain in darkness. Mazochius gives another explanation in the note on Book I, verse 797, and Juvencus favors that interpretation in both passages. The interpretation he adopts here, however, is not peculiar to him but common to Maldonado and others. Mazochius had the habit of claiming certain interpretations as his own, as though they had been overlooked by others, while ignoring or concealing the fact that he knew them to be readily found in the most celebrated commentators. Yet Mazochius was not a man who needed to adorn himself with another’s feathers.

771. *Vasti*: “great,” “immense.” Many others use the word in the same way.

311 “Those summoned by servants to celebrate together the honor of the royal vow—

to bind him hand and foot and, with his whole body,

[770] [Col. 0278B] hurl him immediately into the deep outer darkness.

Verse 3. Ott. has *veridicum*, from which *veredicum* was incorrectly produced.

4. Rom. and Ott. have *metuis, Domini vestigia servans*. Poelm., in place of the divergent reading, has *tueris, Domini vestigia servans*. Most printed editions, together with Reg., have *metuens Domini vestigia servas*.

[Col. 0279B] 6. Reg. has, not improperly, *semper ex lege*.

9. The printed editions, together with Reg. and Ott., have *Fallacis mentis*. I had thought of *Pellacis mentis*, since *fallacia* occurs afterward. But in Rom. the reading seems genuinely to be *Fallaces? mentis prodit fallacia*: namely, “Why, deceitful ones, do you test …” In Aldus there is *perdit* instead of *prodit*.

10. Reg. and Ott. have *Inspicite in nummum*. Ald., Fab., Hadam., and Poelm. have *Aspicite en nummum*. Daventr. punctuates: *Aspicite: en nummum*. The reading in Juvencus’ own hand may have been *Aspicite nummum* or *Inspicite nummum*, with the syllable lengthened by the caesura. Indeed, Cant. reads *Inspicite nummum*, as does Reusch, although he printed *Aspicite en nummum*, where *en* seems superfluous. Rom. has *sculpti nusmismatis*: read *sculptique numismatis* or *nomismatis*. In place of *aera*, I would willingly read *ora*, if the manuscripts allowed it. Most write *numismatis*, but Ald. and Bas. write *nomismatis*, which also appears in the Ott. manuscript. I have retained this spelling and defended it in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 2 of the *Peristephanon*, verses 50 and 96, where I discussed this word and the object itself.

[Col. 0280] 11. Rom. has *facile est ubi*; Ald. *facile est ibi*; Fabr. *proprium est ibi*; most have *promptum est ibi*. Reusch says that the word *proprium* should be retained in these three verses, 11–13. Such repetitions are frequent in Juvencus, Homer, and others, and possess elegance.

[Col. 0280B] 12. Rom., Fabr., Had., and Poelm. in the text have *proprium*. Reg. and Ott., together with most printed editions, have *propria*, that is, “particular” or even “one’s own,” since Juvencus often uses *proprius* in this sense.

13. Fabr., Poelm., and Had. have *servetis*. The manuscripts, together with Ald., Daventr., Torn., Bas., and others, have *servemus*.

14. Reg., Ottob., and Torn. have *Post Saducaei hinc inde latratibus urgent*. Rom. likewise has this, and Poelm. in place of the divergent reading; Rom. spells the name *Saducei*, while Poelm. has *Sadducaei*. Ald. and Bas. have *Inde Saducaei tali cinxere latratu*. The same reading occurs in Hadam., Poelm. in the text, Fabr., and Daventr.; but Hadam. begins *Inde Sadducaei*, which cannot be sustained; Poelm. and Fabr. have *Post Sadducaei*; Daventr. has *Inde Saducei*. In the Vulgate and most other ancient versions the name is written *Sadducaei*, but *Saducaei* or *Saducei* is better, since they were so called from Sadoc, their founder. Reusch prefers *Inde Saducaei tali cinxere latratu*. In Book III, verse 221: “Behold the deceitful Pharisees and Sadducees.” But perhaps Juvencus now pronounces this proper name with a different syllable quantity. *Cingere* is a word proper to hunters, and *latratus* is ordinarily used for an inarticulate sound or shameless outcry.

[Note: [Col. 0279C]]

Verse 1. CHAPTER I. Christ is asked whether it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar. Matthew 22:15 ff.; Mark 12:13; Luke 20:20.

5. Book III, verse 395: “Release the tribute.” Eustathius Swartius, *Analecta* II.15, insists that here and in innumerable other places one should write *disolve*, not *dissolve*, just as *dinumerare* and *diluere*. He has not yet persuaded most others of this opinion.

7. “The innermost places of the heart.” See Book I, verse 541, Damasus, *Carmina*, poem I, last Roman edition: “Having deposited their filth, they cleanse the innermost places of the heart”; and poem 13: “Virtue held the innermost places of the heart.” The first verse is read more correctly in the epigram attributed to St. Jerome: “With the impurities laid aside,” etc. Or one should read, “With these things—the admonitions—having been set down,” for Damasus’s poem is preceded by: “Now lend kindly ears to the admonitions of Damasus.” In Jerome’s epigram, however, it is preceded by: “Whoever thirsts, let him come; whoever desires to draw the waters—he will find springs that preserve sweet honey.” It will therefore be preferable to read here: “With their impurities laid aside, these cleanse the recesses of the heart,” namely, the springs.

8. Matthew says: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?” Above, verse 2: “He begins to test.” *Concludere verbis* means “to seize with words,” “to constrain,” and, as it were, “to drive into a corner.” Book III, verse 683: “Closing him in with the weight of an equivocal argument.” Terence, *Hecyra* IV, 4, 80: “My father now hems me in, wretched as I am, with so many circumstances.”

14. **CHAPTER II. Concerning the woman who married seven brothers.** Matthew 22:23 and following; Mark 12:19; Luke 20:28.

The tribute owed under Caesar’s ever-pressing law?”

But he, looking into the innermost places of their savage hearts,

[Col. 0280A] said: “Why are you now trying to entrap me with words,

**Note: [Col. 0281A]**

15. The *Reg.* manuscript has *Moysea*; *Rom.* has *Moyseia*, less correctly; Poelman’s copy of the first edition has *Mosen*; in the text, together with the Ottobonian manuscript and most printed editions: “Mosea, who established the precepts of the laws, commanded.” If *Mosea* is understood as an adjective agreeing with *praecepta*, this interpretation must be rejected. For the Sadducees said, Matthew 22:24: “Teacher, Moses said.”

16. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and *Bas.* have *connubium*; others have *conjugium*.

17. The *Reg.* manuscript reads *pigneribus*.

18. *Rom.* incorrectly has *cujus* for *hujus*, and *sociabere* for *sociabile*.

21. Our manuscripts have *corpora*; but immediately afterward the first manuscript has *vincula*, and the gloss in *Reg.* has *mox … ut*. The printed editions read: “But the eldest by birth, once the marriage-bond had been taken up.”

23. *Reg.* and Poelman’s first edition have *thalami sine fructibus isdem*; *Ald.*, Poelman’s text, *Daventr.*, *Had.*, and *Fabr.* have *thalami sine fructibus aeque*. I recover the true reading from *Ott.* and *Rom.*: *thalamis sine fructibus isdem*, that is, “he fell in those same chambers without offspring.”

25. Poelman’s first edition and Westphal’s text have: “And so that all the tears of the one wife might have groaned together.” Poelman’s text, together with the others, has: “And the wives groaned all the tears of one man,” with *gemere malum suum* and similar expressions. Westphal’s margin has *unius cunctos* without *et*. Either form can be used, with or without *et*.

27. *Rom.* has *sub lumine vitae*; *Ott.* has *sub limina vitae*; *Reg.*, together with the printed editions, has *sub lumina vitae*. Gallandius, with Koenigius and the better manuscripts of Omeisius, preferred *limina vitae*, which also occurs at verse 443. But many read *lumina vitae* at that verse as well, and Juvencus likewise wrote *lumina vitae* at verses 735 and 757. [The letters] h, l.

28. *Reg.* has *cujus conjugio*; others, *cujus connubiis*.

29. Some have *ollis*; others, *illis*.

30. Most manuscripts and printed editions read: “The hard mind resists the laws and commands of the Lord”; *Ott.* has *repugnat* for *resistit*. Poelman’s first edition has: “Ignorant of virtues, the discolored mind wanders from the laws.” *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and *Torn.* join these two verses, first *Legibus*, then *Nescia*. After *Legibus et jussis*, *Rom.* adds: “By the laws and virtue of God the discolored mind wanders.” Koenigius comments on *decolor* in the omitted verse beginning *Nescia*, explaining it as “ugly” or “foul.” Eusthatius Swartius, *Analecta* II, 15, advised reading *gens decolor* for *mens decolor* in the same verse. Reuschius omitted it, following the Helmstedt and Cambridge manuscripts. If one reads *gens decolor* with Swartius, the meaning will be “an abominable people,” for *decolor* is sometimes used as an insult, as in Book II, verse 685, according to the reading of certain manuscripts: “But another discolored one will come,” which is understood of the Antichrist.

31. *Rom.* has *Namque secunda*, which is perhaps better than *sequenda*, that is, “about to follow,” as Omeisius interprets it. Swartius, in the passage cited, restored *Namque secuta dehinc*. He entirely rejects *Namque secunda* in the others, since there can be no restoration that could be called prior. But Wassius, in Havercamp’s edition of Sallust, chapter 100 of the *Bellum Jugurthinum*, directs that *secunda* be read instead of *sequenda* on the basis of the parchment manuscripts of Corpus Christi College.

**Note: [Col. 0281C]**

15. *Posuit praecepta*: “he established” or “ordained.” Thus *leges ponere* means “to enact laws” in Horace and others.

16. *Conjugium relinquet*: “he will leave his wife.” Propertius, Book III, Elegy 11, verse 18: “The pious crowd stands with its wives’ hair arranged.” … “And they struggle over death, which one will follow while alive”—*conjugium*, that is, “the husband.” Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 65: “The marriage of the emperor which she had sought through acts of devotion,” that is, “the emperor’s wife.” A surviving spouse is said to be *relinqui* or *destitui*. Book I, verse 251: “Whom, in the flower of youth, the untimely death of her husband left a widow.”

17. *Pignora* is frequently said of children. *Pignora* are common to both spouses. Propertius IV, Elegy 11, verse 69: “Now I entrust to you our common pledges, our children.”

18. *Sociabile vinclum*: “the marriage bond.” He frequently uses this expression to signify marriage. *Sociabile* is a word used by Livy, Seneca, and others.

19. *Lapsi*: Matthew says: “And let him raise up offspring for his brother.” In the old Italian version from the Colbert manuscript: “the offspring of his brother”; and in Deuteronomy 25:5: “And he shall raise up the offspring of his brother,” which comes closer to Juvencus. *Labi*, meaning “to fail” or “to die,” is used by Virgil. *Generis lapsi* means “of an extinguished lineage.”

21. *Corpora germana septem*: “seven brothers’ bodies,” instead of “seven brothers.” This is noted frequently, as in Book II, verse 731: “With me the sister-bodies sit.” *Major primus*: Matthew says, “And the first,” etc. Mark and Luke likewise. Badius, who reads *major natu* with the printed editions, restores it thus: “In more idiomatic Latin he would have said *maximus natu*, for he is speaking of many.” But other good Latin authors also say *major natu* when speaking of more than two. Here too the syntax should be noted: *major primus*, as though seven brothers, rather than seven bodies, had preceded.

22. *Praeceleri*: Pliny and Statius also used this form before Juvencus. A weapon is attributed to death; hence “the point” and “sting of death,” as in the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*: “You, having conquered the sting of death, opened the kingdom of heaven to believers.” First Corinthians 15:55: “Where is your sting, O death?” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 54: “Where is your sting, O death?”

23. *Alius*, as at verse 173, “and another, unaware.” The best authors sometimes use *alius* for *alter*. The distinction between *alius* and *alter* is that *alius* is said of many, *alter* of two only. But, as I have said, *alius* is sometimes used for *alter*, and conversely *alter* for *alius*.

24. *Jacuere*: “they died.” For *jacere* is sometimes used to mean “to die.”

25. *Maritae*: “wives.” Horace, *Epodes* VIII, verse 13: “Nor let her be a wife who walks about burdened with rounder berries.” Ovid, *Fasti* II, verse 139: “You seize her; he orders the chaste wives to remain so under his leadership”; and *Heroides* 4, verse 134, concerning Juno: “And the married sister makes every law permissible with her brother.” There are many similar examples in ancient inscriptions.

Moses, who established the precepts of the laws, commanded:

316 “If someone, overtaken by premature death, leaves a wife,

With the common pledges of children not yet produced,

His brother must again receive this bond of union,

So that no portion of the extinguished lineage may perish.

[20] In our territory there were seven brothers’ bodies;

But the first, the eldest, soon took up the marriage bond

And fell beneath death’s swiftest point.

Then another brother fell in those same chambers without offspring,

[Col. 0282A] 317 and all the brothers died in succession.

[25] And the wives together mourned all the griefs of one [wife];

Afterward the severity of icy death carried off the woman herself.

If, then, they all come beneath the light of life,

To which husband’s marriage will the woman be restored when she rises?”

Christ said to them: “You are subject to a grievous error;

[30] The hard mind resists the laws and commands of the Lord.

For the joyful restoration of life that is to follow

Knows neither marriage chambers nor the empty joys of earth:

33. In *Reg.* and *Ott.*, *juncta* seems to have been written instead of *justa* by the first hand. Wassius, in the passage cited, reads *juxta* from the same manuscript, that is, “equally.”

35. *Ald.* and Poelman’s first edition have *poscit*; others, *mavult*.

36. Our manuscripts, together with *Ald.* and Poelman, have *Qui terram proni*; in *Ott.* the letters *ro* have been erased in *proni*. *Torn.* and other printed editions have *Qui tetram proni*. I considered *Qui in terram proni* or *Qui proni in terram*, or *Qui terrae proni*, with *terrae* in the dative. It will always remain doubtful what *proni* means, unless we understand it in the sense in which *prona dies* is said of a day that is near sunset. Omeisius explains *terram proni* as “devoted to earthly pleasures.”

38. The printed editions and most manuscripts have *quae sint firmissima legis*; *Hadam.* and Poelman have *quae sit firmissima legis*. Fabricius followed this, but added a verse that does not appear elsewhere and must rightly be removed: “which is the strongest rule of the law that embraces everything else.” One might conjecture *quae sit firmissima legum* or *quae vis firmissima legis*, as at verse 41: “this is the strongest virtue of the law.” Matthew 22:36 has: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?”

39. *Rom.* has *indeficiens*; others more correctly have *indefessus*. *Ott.* has *nullis* for *nulli*.

41. *Ald.*, together with *Reg.* and *Rom.*, has *ista haec*; others, *isthaec*. *Reg.* and *Rom.* have *fortissima*; most have *firmissima*.

45. *Ott.* writes *subolis* for *soboles*.

[Col. 0284B] 47. *Rom.*, first hand, together with others, has *Davidis germine*; the second hand has *Davidis de germine*, which is not unreasonable, with the first two syllables of *Davidis* shortened. Yet Juvencus normally lengthens both, and would more likely have said *David de germine*.

50. *Rom.* and *Ald.* have *proprium*; others, *proprio*. *Ottob.* has *aequum dicere*; the others, *aequum est dicere*.

53. Poelman’s first edition has *Aspice nunc scribas*; in the text, together with the others, correctly, *Aspicite scribas*. The final syllable of *Aspicite* must be lengthened, as many maintain; certainly it may be, because of the following word beginning with *sc*. In the same Poelman edition there is the error *sublime* for *sublimi*.

54. *Reg.* has *quodcumque*; others, *quaecumque*.

56. *Rom.* has *Obrupta*; others, *Abrupta*.

57. *Reg.* has *contigere*; correct to *contingere*. Swartius, in the passage cited, restored *saltem uno prendere nolint*, because he did not know the true reading *contingere* and had read somewhere *saltem comprendere nolint*.

61. *Rom.* has *Quod*, less well, instead of *Sed*. *Bas.* incorrectly has *nos* for *vos*.

62. *Reg.* and *Ott.* punctuate: “Yet aspire to it: for you have one master.” I do not know, however, whether this comes from the first hand. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIX, 5, column 976, says that these verses should be punctuated in this way, since they are commonly mishandled. The printed editions, together with *Rom.*, punctuate: “Aspire; yet for you there is one master.” See the variant reading at verse 130 below, where a similar expression is observed.

**Note: [Col. 0283C]**

34. *Justa sublimis virtus*: two epithets attributed to one noun. See the commentary on Prudentius, verse 169, Book I *Against Symmachus*. Or understand it as “lofty in the court of the kingdom.”

35. The gloss of the *Reg.* manuscript has *illorum … mortuorum*: “of those … of the dead,” as the following verse explains.

[Col. 0283D] 38. **CHAPTER III. That there are two commandments on which everything depends, and whose son Christ is.** Matthew 22:35 and following; Mark 12:28; Luke 10:25.

40. *Devotio cordis*, “devotion of heart,” as in Book I, verse 442: “so that the righteous man, devoted, may worship the Lord of heaven.” Compare the note.

43. *Ad jus fraternum*: the sacred text has: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

46. Book I, verse 230: “Whom all the oracles of the prophets promise to be Christ.”

51. **CHAPTER IV. What the Pharisees say should be done, but not what they do. Hence the scribes and Pharisees are reproved.** Matthew 22:46 and 23:1 and following; Luke 11:46.

[Col. 0284C] 52. Compare Book II, verse 759: “But he, with the crowd of believers brought near.”

56. Matthew: “For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders.” Badius explains *abrupta … gravia* as “heavy things broken off, as though from a mountain.” Barthius, on Claudian, page 1366, says that Juvencus aptly calls it *abruptum pondus*, because by its burden it drives the bearer into a precipitous descent.

59. Among the ancients there were frequent greetings by which prominent men were honored. Pliny, Book VII, Letter 3: “Greet someone briefly, so that it may be more pleasant for you to be greeted.” Several writers have discussed the greetings of the ancients; Fabricius gives their names and works in *Bibliographia antiquaria*, chapter 22.

61. *Nominis arcem*: “the summit,” as in Book III, verse 666, *animi arce*, “the summit of the spirit.”

318 But the lofty, righteous power of the kingdom will establish them as equals

To the lowly ministers of the Father in the court of heaven.

[35] Nor does God prefer to set himself as lord over those

Who, bent toward the earth, have deserved to receive death,

But rather over those who can grasp the light of life.

Look: others ask which commandments of the law are strongest.

He, tireless, denied a response to no one:

[40] Let devotion of heart love the exalted Lord of heaven;

This is the strongest virtue of the law.

A similar command is this: let the innermost places of the just mind

Be held by great love for the fraternal right.

For everything depends upon these twin commandments.

[45] 319 “But whose offspring does it seem that Christ will be,

[Col. 0283B] Whom all the prophets promise for the ages?”

They answer that he will be born from David’s line.

[Col. 0284A] Christ continues: “Why is it written by divine inspiration

That David calls him both Lord and God,

[50] When it is not right for a son to call his own father

By that title?”

Thus spoke the Savior; all stood silent in astonishment.

But he, having summoned the crowd of believers, declared:

“Look at the scribes, proud in their exalted seat.

Whatever they teach, it is right to grasp with the obedience

[55] Of the heart; reject the stains of their lives.

For they impose upon your shoulders burdens

That they themselves do not wish even to touch with a finger.

They rise to the first couch at dinner, and in proud arrogance,

And are lifted up by the empty honor of those who greet them,

[60] 320 And they wish to bear the exalted name of ‘teacher.’

[Col. 0284B] But you—I would not have you aspire

To the summit of the lofty name: you have one master.”

[Col. 0285A] [Note: [Col. 0285B]**

64. In *Reg.* these two verses—“You the same”—and one additional verse were missing, but they have been inserted between the lines.

65. *Reg.* has *qui culmine*; *qui in vertice*; *Ott.*, together with the printed editions, *qui in culmine*.

67. In some copies of Koenigius: *ad infima coeno*.

68. *Reg.*, together with the printed editions, has *claram conscendet liber in aethram*. *Ottob.* and *Rom.* have *clarum conscendet liber in aethra*, which seems to me the true reading. The Greek accusative *aether*, *aetheris*, is *aethera*, and by contraction *aethra*; from this some think that *aethra*, *aethrae*, was formed. See Book III, verse 532, with its note.

69. *Rom.* has *lacrymabilis ejus*; others, *lacrymabilis aevi*.

71. Poelman’s first edition has *callis clausus*; in the text, together with the others, *itiner clausum*.

74. *Rom.* and *Ott.* have *splendere*; in *Ott.* the variant, or correction, *splendore* appears, which the sense itself requires.

75. *Rom.* has *his*; others, *queis* or *quis*. Most have *sordida bustis*. *Hadam.*, *Fabr.*, and Poelman, together with *Ott.* by the first hand, have *turpia bustis*. *Rom.* has *sordida busti*, but *busti* for *bustis* seems to be an error.

76. *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and *Bas.* have *hic vox*. In *Rom.*, *celatur* appears for *velatur*. Omeisius and Reuschius, following Swartius’s conjecture, read: “Thus the night is veiled,” that is, obscure vices are covered with a certain brilliance of falsehood.

77. Swartius, in the passage cited, restored: “And by the merits of the sanctuary the foul hearts are concealed,” that is, “by the virtues of the sanctuary’s threshold itself, hearts covered with vices are hidden.” For *merita* sometimes means “virtues.” *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and *Rom.* have *sordida lucra*; the others, *sordida corda*; *Ott.* has, in its first edition, *turpia corda*. In the Tridentine Gospel Book I find: “So you also outwardly appear to people as righteous, but inwardly you are full of robbery and iniquity.” Thus, I think, it should be read: “So the heart is veiled beneath the appearance of a righteous life, and in the sanctuaries of the mind sordid gains are concealed.”

[Col. 0286B] 78. *Reg.* has *O Solymi, o Solymi*.

79. *Ott.*, *Rom.*, *Ald.*, and *Bas.* have *necatis*; *Reg.*, with *Daventr.* and others, has *necastis*, which is the usual form.

82. Some write *obice*, others *objice*; this variation occurs elsewhere as well. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIX, 14, column 958, praises this verse of Juvencus and says that some are ridiculous in this word, claiming that it must always be written with a single *i*, although whenever poets place it with a long syllable it must be marked with two; as evidence, he notes that when they wish it shortened, they customarily remove the other *i*, as in *adicit*, *obicit*, and other words of this kind. Hence he thinks that *objex*, when lengthened, should likewise be written with *j* in the nominative, and I readily agree with him. In *Rom.*, *circumplexa* is incorrectly written *circomplexa*, which *Bas.* reproduced. Koenigius reads it as one word, *circumcomplexa*; Reuschius says that *circum* is used adverbially.

84. All manuscripts and printed editions have *vastata*. But Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 19, column 744, says: “There is an error in Juvencus, a most devout author, when in the Savior’s discourse he says *vastata templa*.” He therefore asserts that *vastanda* should be written. For when the temple was abandoned by the Lord, it had not yet been laid waste; rather, such devastation was foretold for it by him, so that no stone would remain joined to another. Koenigius and Reuschius followed Barthius’s emendation. Yet, with all manuscripts and printed editions opposed to it, I am not yet persuaded to write *vastanda* for *vastata*. Juvencus presents the Savior as predicting the temple’s future devastation, but narrating it as though it were present: “It is abandoned,” etc. Matthew 23:38 says: “Behold, your house will be left desolate.” Some Greek copies agree with Juvencus in the present tense: Ἰδοὺ ἀφίεται, “Behold, it is left”; and Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 36, has: “Behold, your house is left desolate.” The old version from the second Corbie manuscript, cited by Sabatier, supports this: “Behold, your house is left to you,” without the following word “desolate.”

[Note: [Col. 0285D]**

64. The gloss in *Reg.* has *eadem … lex*, or *charitas*: “the same … law,” or “charity.” *Eadem potestas*, “the same authority,” is better.

66. *Levabit*: “will raise up,” “lift,” “exalt.” A raised neck is a sign of pride; a lowered one, of a humble or abject spirit.

67. “He will be plunged into the mire of the abyss down to the lowest place.” Consult the note on Book III, verse 587: “To the farthest limits of death.”

68. On the ecclesiastical meaning of *humilis*, see the commentary on Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*, verse 199.

69. Below, verse 127: “Now the pregnant women must be mourned,” etc. Reuschius observes that the two genitives *aevi* and *plebis* are governed by a single noun.

70. *Pharisaeae plebis*: “of the Pharisaic crowd,” that is, “the gathering of the faction.” Elsewhere the disciples are called *plebs credentum*, “the crowd of believers.”

72. *Ardua lucis*, “the heights of light,” as in Book III, verse 669, *celsa montis*, “the heights of the mountain,” and here, verse 115, *sublimia lucis*, “the lofty things of light.”

74. *Tectis splendore sepulcris*: “covered with the splendor of tombs.” The sacred text says: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people.” Some think that among the Hebrews white coverings were customarily spread over tombs, from which the Gospel calls them “whitewashed tombs.” I discussed this matter in the note on Prudentius, *Hymns*, 10, *Cathemerinon*, verse 45.

75. The Gospel text reads: “Inside, however, they are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity.” The Tridentine Gospel Book has *immunditia* for *spurcitia*. Properly, a *bustum* is a place where the dead are burned; sometimes it means the burning itself or the burned body. Statius, Book XII, verse 247: “And I think that the poor tomb lies among the pyres.” Juvencus uses the word more broadly for any dead body.

76. The gloss in *Reg.* has: “the word … of hypocrites.”

82. Fabricius, in his commentary on Hericus, cited by Barthius in the passage mentioned, says that *objice pennarum* is used in the sense of “covering” or “protection,” and is a novel expression, in the manner of: “The proud ranks would not dare despise the protector of so great a name.”

83. From Virgil, *Eclogues* 2, verse 44: “And he will do it, since our gifts are contemptible to you.”

Authority imposed for ever by heaven’s law

Joined you together in equal brotherly love.

[65] There is also one Father, who reigns at the summit of heaven.

If anyone among you raises his lofty neck,

He will fall and be plunged into the abyss, into the lowest mire.

But the humble man, set free, will ascend into the bright ether.

The scribes must always be mourned, and the blind deceit

[70] Of the Pharisaic crowd, lamentable in every age.

For because the way is closed to you, and entry is rightly denied,

You do not allow anyone to penetrate through the heights of light,

And you drag everyone into fellowship with the savage flame.

[Col. 0286A] I call you like tombs covered with outward splendor,

[75] Whose face is bright, but whose interior is foul with corpses?

Thus the voice is veiled beneath the image of a righteous life,

And in the sanctuaries of the mind sordid gains are concealed.

O Solymi, Solymi, who have so often slain with the sword

The prophets sent to bring you life,

[80] How I wished to protect your nation and people,

As a mother bird is accustomed, beneath her soft body,

To cherish her young, enclosing them within the shelter of her wings!

322 But heavenly gifts are always contemptible to you.

Now this house is abandoned, laid waste by ruins,

[85] [Col. 0287A]

**Note: [Col. 0287A]**

85. *Reg.*, *Ott.*, and *Rom.* have: “Nor is it any longer permitted for us to behold your face.” The printed editions have: “Nor is it any longer permitted for you to behold our face.”

90. Poelman’s first edition has *Quam mox*; in the text, together with the others, *Quod mox*. To Reuschius, Barthius’s manuscript reading *dejecta* rather than *disjecta* seems more suitable.

93. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 90, column 745, observes that the parchment manuscripts of Cologne prefer *discingeret* for the commonly written *distingueret*, namely, “would release” or “would disengage”; he thinks this should be restored. He adds that there are no authors more corrupt than these Christian poets, who were everywhere in everyone’s hands. Yet he had forgotten this emendation when, in *Adversaria* LIII, 11, he cited this word of Juvencus to prove that *distinguere* means “to teach” or “to interpret.” From this passage of Juvencus he also thinks that the following passage of William the Breton, Book 5, should be understood in this way: “He also promises with kindly mind that he will endure whatever the court of the Franks shall say to them concerning these matters, which the nobles of the kingdom ought to distinguish and settle.” That is, it ought to end the dispute between them—or rather teach them the law, so that they may lay aside hatred in their hearts. Add that *distinguere* properly means “to mark a distinction” and “to explain a matter distinctly”; this meaning is especially appropriate here. Lucan, Book V, verse 399: “The consul marks out the years in the monthly records.”

[Col. 0287C] 94. *Reg.*, *Ott.* have *quo*. *Ottob.*, in the first edition, *Rom.*, together with the printed editions, have *quem*.

95. *Reg.*, *Rom.*, and *Ott.* have *Ejus et adventus*. *Ald.*, *Bas.*, and *Torn.* have *Ejus ut adventus*. *Hadam.*, *Fabr.*, and Poelman have *Cujus et adventus*. Our manuscripts and the printed editions have *consumeret*. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 19, column 745, following the Cologne parchment manuscripts, prefers *Ejus ut adventus terrae confuneret orbem*, because the order of Latin requires this and rejects the other form. For who would speak as follows: “I wish to know what end your promises demand, so that you might consume the world by your coming”? One should say *ut consumas*. Barthius adds that *confunero* should not be dismissed as a word. Indeed, from this emendation of Barthius, Forcellini restored *confunero* among Latin words, and the sense then proceeds clearly. But Barthius himself repeatedly observes elsewhere that changes of tense were familiar to writers of the late period.

96. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *respondit*; some have *respondet*.

97. *Rom.* incorrectly has *capto* for *falso*.

98. *Reg.* has *errorum* for *errantum*, which may have been written by the first hand.

100. *Ott.* writes *robure* for *robore*.

101. *Ott.*, *Rom.*, together with most printed editions, have: “Lest the mind, disturbed by the tumult it has received, lie helpless.” *Reg.* and *Torn.* have: “Lest the mind, disturbed by the tumults begun, lie helpless,” which seems more appropriate.

104. *Reg.* and *Ott.* have *nec morbi tunc*; *Rom.*, with the printed editions, *nec tunc morbi*. *Rom.* has *tractus*; others, *tractum*.

106. *Hadam.*, Poelman, and Fabricius have *Fissa*; others, together with our manuscripts, *Fixa*, as Poelman’s first edition also indicates: *Fissa* is from *findo*, *fixa* from *figo*. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 19, says that *Fissa etiam solido per inania pondere tellus* is read everywhere, and, with the Cologne parchment manuscripts, prefers *Fissa etiam solido per flamina pondere*. In this reading he detected an excellent sense; in the common version he could not understand how the earth could be split through empty spaces by a solid weight. Schoettgenius follows Barthius. But if *Fixa* is read, as many had read even before Barthius, the sense becomes clear. For *pondere*, *Ald.* and *Rom.* have *pondera*, but this makes no sense. Others correctly have *solido per inania pondere*, and the gloss in *Reg.* explains *inania* as “places.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, verse 506: “And through the empty spaces, carried by the swift wind, he placed them in the sky.”

[Note: [Col. 0287C]**

86. **CHAPTER V. Concerning the structure of the temple, whose overthrow is foretold.** Matthew 24:1 and following; Mark 13:1; Luke 21:5.

89. Perhaps from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 499: “While he marvels and remains fixed, his gaze clinging to one thing.” The author of the account of Bebianus’s baptism, in Fabricius, *Poetae Christiani*, column 782: “And, staring stupidly at heaven, he said.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 19, observes that Juvencus’s *obtutus stupidus* means a gaze rendered stupefied by wonder, in which sense many Latin authors have spoken without inelegance. See the same Barthius, *Adversaria* XLVI, 16.

97. **CHAPTER VI. The signs that will occur on the day of judgment are foretold.** Matthew 24:4 and following; Luke 21:12 and 20; Mark 13:14. *Observare dolum*: “to guard against deceit,” that is, “so that you may beware.” Juvencus often uses *observare* for “to beware.”

98. *Laqueis errantum*: Juvencus commonly calls scandals “the snares of error.” See the note on Book III, verse 12.

99. *Bellorum incendia*: a fine metaphor also used by others. Cicero, *Pro Marcello*, chapter 9: “the conflagration of civil war.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 570: “virtues and men, and the conflagrations of so great a war.” Arator, apparently from Juvencus, Book I, verse 25, or verse 1 of Preface 2: “Seeing the conflagrations of wars around the walls washed by waves.”

103. *Obvia*: “opposed.” See the note on Book III, verse 625. Lucan, at the beginning of Book I: “Standards opposed to hostile standards,” that is, equal eagles and spears threatening spears. A similar thought occurs in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 628: “Shore opposed to shore, wave to wave—I pray that arms clash with arms, and even our descendants fight.”

104. Matthew: “There will be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in various places.” In some manuscripts of the old version: “There will be famines and earthquakes in various places.” In the Tridentine Gospel Book: “There will be famines and earthquakes in each place.” Juvencus imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 137: “Suddenly, when a wasting disease had corrupted their limbs, through the corrupted course of the sky there came a pitiable plague upon trees and crops, and a pestilential year.”

105. Grammarians should not reject *pestes* in the plural, since it is found in Cicero, Virgil, and Columella.

Nor is it any longer permitted for you to see our face.

He leaves the temple, and, as the disciples observed

Its lofty walls, he taught them in this speech:

“These marvels of its works seem worthy to you,

Viewed with astonished eyes; but learn from truthful words

[90] That soon all these things will lie scattered everywhere,

Thrown down upon the ground.”

323 Saying this, he reached the summit of Olivet.

After the disciples had seen him alone, they asked

That he explain to them the time of the age to come,

The end toward which his promises were tending,

[95] And when his coming would consume the world.

Christ answered the questioners with these words:

[Col. 0288A] “Beware of deceit, lest credulity, deceived by a false name,

Be driven headlong into the snares of those who err.

The conflagrations of wars will spread through all the lands.

[100] 324 But stand firm with the mighty strength of your heart.

Do not let your mind lie helpless, disturbed by the tumults begun.

For the first conflicts will not soon bring an end;

Nation will bear arms against nation, and king against king,

And then diseases will not cease to corrupt the air,

[105] Nor will pestilences spare the bodies by casting them down.

The earth, fixed by solid weight amid empty space, will tremble,

Shaken by motion through the various places.

325 These things will remain as small beginnings and trials.

Many of you will be betrayed and handed over to death.

[110] And because of my name, nations must inflict upon you

Tortures, savage punishments, and hatreds.

For envy will fill the earth, everything will be full of errors,

And false prophets will arise through the people’s corruption.

Meanwhile, if anyone can preserve a breast protected from harm

[115] To the end, he will approach the heights of light,

Crowned with the eternal wreaths of life.

The proclamation of the kingdom of heaven will spread throughout

All the boundaries of the earth; every nation will have

[Col. 0290A] A witness to holy salvation through the light-giving word;

[120] And then there will be an end, bringing the running ages to completion.

Then the grievous desolation of the earth will come,

326 Which Daniel’s commands declare in a most truthful voice.

Only the worthy reader will be able to understand these things.

Let those in Judaea flee far away and seek the mountains,

[125] And let no one return to the houses to take anything along.”

What might flight take along with it—clothing or anything movable.

Now mothers with the burden of the womb must be pitied, and those who will nourish their wretched infants with sweet milk.

Pray now that your flight may not come in the winter’s bitter cold,

[130] [Col. 0291A]  
[Note: [Col. 0291A]

130. In the Roman manuscript one word is missing: “Let flight come, yet not on Sabbaths or feast days.” The Reg. and Ott. manuscripts read: “Let your flight come, yet not on Sabbaths or feast days”; and in Reg. it is indicated that *poscite* (“pray”) should be understood with *tamen* (“yet”). Hadam. and Poelm. report the same reading in the text, but with *ne* instead of *neu*. Ald., Torn., Bas., and Fabr. have: “Let your flight come, or else not on Sabbaths or feast days.” Since our manuscripts have *tamen*, I shall retain it and, with Reuschius, punctuate as follows: “Let your flight come, yet not on Sabbaths or feast days”—that is, “Pray nevertheless that your flight may not come in the winter’s cold.” This punctuation is also suggested by the gloss in Reg.; and a similar transposition of *tamen* is found at verses 61 ff. of this book: “But I would not have you strive for the citadel of the exalted name—yet strive: you have one teacher,” etc.

131. Ald. incorrectly has *turbae* (“of the crowd”) instead of *turbet* (“may disturb”).

133. Westh. in the text, and Ald., have *nec postea norunt* (“nor do they know afterward”). The manuscripts, together with most printed editions and Westh. in the margin, have *nec postera norunt* (“nor did later generations know”).

134. Ald., Bas., and Rom. have *Et nisi*; others have *Et ni*.

139. For *fingent* (“they will devise”), Barthius’s codex has *fient* (“they will be made”), as Koenigius reports.

140. Rom. has *justos capient miracula lectos*; others have *lectos capient miracula justos*.

141. Ald., Bas., and Torn. have: “Behold, the ages foretold teach you as they hasten”—that is, either “behold, the foretold ages teach you as they hasten,” or “behold, the ages foretold teach you as they hasten.” The manuscripts, with several printed editions, read: “Behold, the foretold ages lie open before you as they hasten”; but some printed editions punctuate it incorrectly: “Behold, the foretold ages lie open; the ages hasten before you.” Reuschius chose *docent* (“teach”), because *vobis* (“to you”) should be construed with *instantia* (“as they hasten”).

142. Ald., Daventr., Bas., and Fabr. have *Desertum* (“the desert”). Rom., incorrectly, has *Disertus* (“eloquent”). Most have *Desertis*. I would prefer *Desertum* or *Deserto*, since that word is more characteristic of Sacred Scripture and Christian poets. In the ablative, *deserto* or *desertis* is a rarer construction. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 19, after noting that Juvencus uses the verb “to traverse” absolutely, added that the reading *Deserti* in a manuscript should not be despised—presumably the Cologne manuscript—on the supposition that it should be connected with *penetralibus* (“the inner chambers”), a view with which I entirely disagree. The syntax would be complicated, and the Gospel clearly distinguishes the desert from the inner chambers. Matthew 24:26: “If therefore they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner chambers,’ do not believe.” The ancient versions agree, though instead of *penetralibus* some have “in bedrooms,” “in the bedroom,” or “in the lodging”; and the Tridentine Gospel Book has: “Behold, he is in the desert; do not go out; behold, he is in the storehouses; do not believe”—for *promptuariis* it writes *promtuariis*. Hilary, commenting on this passage of Matthew, says: “Now they say that he is in the deserts, so that they may corrupt people through error; now they assert that he is in the inner chambers”—which makes me less reluctant to retain *Desertis*.

143. Ott. has *Occultisve* instead of *Occultisque*, and corruptly has *penetrabilibus* instead of *penetralibus*.

145. Ottob. and the first hand of Reg., less correctly, have *fulgor* (“brightness”) instead of *fulgur* (“lightning”).

146. Rom. has *Ut cerni*; read *Et cerni* (“and to be seen”). Reuschius states that the words *Et cerni facile est cunctis* (“and it is easily seen by all”) can be inserted appropriately and meaningfully as a parenthesis.

147. Ald. and Bas. have: “To fly beneath the setting orb sooner than speech.” The common reading of the manuscripts and editions is: “As far as beneath the setting orb of the declining heaven.” Reuschius placed a comma between *coeli* and *vergentis* for clarity. The heaven is said to bend *in orbem* (“into a sphere”) through the deception of the eyes, as though heaven itself touched the earth. Some glossator, troubled by the two prepositions *sub* and *in*, did not think of this optical illusion and substituted another verse.

149. Our manuscripts, together with Torn. and Poelm., instead of the printed reading have: “The sun will hide its glowing rays in dark shadows.” Ald., Had., Fabr., and Poelm. in the text have: “The glowing sun will hide its rays in dark shadows.” When ancient poets mention the sun, they commonly place its name at the end of the verse; Juvencus also observed this, book III, verse 1, and book IV, verse 587. Koenigius noted this after Barthius, in his notes on Claudian, page 206.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D]

132. Matthew has: “For then there will be great tribulation.” The Tridentine Gospel Book has: “For then there will be great distress.” Hilary, on this passage: “A severe affliction will press upon them, intolerable to all.” Translate *pondus*, where it signifies a burden, as applied to calamities. Seneca, *Hercules Oetaeus*, verse 230: “The weight of evil drove away his strength—the disaster that he bore with an even mind.”

135. Manilius, Quintilian, and later writers such as Vegetius, Lactantius, and Orosius used the verb *breviare* (“to shorten”); Orosius also used *breviator*. See Cellarius, *Post. cur. Latin. cad.*

136. *Superarent*: “might outlast,” “might remain,” “might survive.” Virgil, *Aeneid* II.642: “Enough and more of the destruction we have seen, and we have survived the captured city.”

139. *Monstra potentia*: “powerful marvels,” effective for leading people astray. Ovid, *Amores* III, elegy 11, verse 31: “Cease wasting the flatteries and words once powerful.”

144. *Vanissima* is a highly appropriate epithet, indicating fickleness and instability of mind. Omeisius explains it thus.

146. The syntax is: “And it is easy for all to see,” that is, “by all.” Juvencus frequently joins a dative with passive verbs where an ablative would be expected. Observe the interpretation followed by Julian of Toledo, *Prognosticon* III.5, from Chrysostom, *Homily I on the Cross and the Robber*: “Just as, when lightning flashes, we do not need to inquire whether a flash has occurred, so, when the revelation of his presence shines forth, we do not need to ask whether Christ has come.” The same wording occurs in a very ancient manuscript that I have more than once cited in my notes on Dracontius. The printed editions differ slightly.

148. *Clarebunt*: “will shine forth,” “will be manifest.” See Becole’s note on book II, verse 776. Shortly afterward, book IV, verse 154, *clareat* has another sense: “may appear illustrious.”

150. Dracontius, book I, verse 120, calls light “the grace of the sun.” Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn II, verse 5: “Alas, how swiftly the day rolled on, hastening its fleeting grace!” Matthew says only: “And the moon will not give its light.” Lactantius, book VII, chapter 16: “The moon, covered with blood, will pursue extraordinary courses.”]

327 Yet pray that your flight may not come on festal Sabbaths.

Let anxious alarm disturb you in headlong flight.

For the fiercest burdens will then come upon all the earth.

No earlier age, nor any later one, has known such an evil.

And unless the exalted Father, in pity, should wish to cut short the time

[135] and shorten the number of days,

no bodies of trembling life would afterward survive.

But for the sake of the chosen righteous, mercy will come.

Those who deceive in Christ’s name, and false prophets,

will rise up on earth and devise powerful marvels,

[140] [Col. 0292A]  
which perhaps will seize even the chosen righteous.

Behold, the foretold ages lie open before you as they hasten.

328 If anyone says that Christ is traversing the deserts,

and has been hidden far away in secret chambers,

let utterly vain credulity be far from you.

[145] For just as lightning traverses the open sky,

and is easily seen by all, from the regions of the east

to beneath the setting orb of the declining heaven,

so the lights of Christ will shine forth at his swift coming.

329 The sun will hide its glowing rays in dark shadows,

[150] the moon’s grace of light will lose its course,

[Col. 0293A]  
[Note: [Col. 0293A]

151. Rom. has *Ignicomae ruent*; correct to *Ignicomaeque ruent*.

153. Reg. has *qui*; read *queis*, or *quis* in the same sense.

154. Reg. has *deflectio jugis*. Ott. has *deflectio vulgi* instead of the printed reading, or, as though by correction, *deflectio lucis*, with Daventr. Rom., together with most printed editions, has *defectio lucis*. I restore *defletio jugis* from Matthew 24:30: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.” *Defletio* comes from *defleo* (“to mourn”), and Forcellinus has restored this word from Juvencus, verse 121 of this book. Yet here *defletio* is more clearly the correct reading than in the cited verse 121. Barthius’s codex, as Koenigius reports, likewise prefers *defletio*.

155. Daventr., Ald., Bas., and Poelmann. have instead: “He will press upon them when he comes in a fire-colored cloud”; Daventr. has *quoniam* (“since”) instead of *quando* (“when”). Our manuscripts, together with other printed editions, read: “He will press upon them; then he will come in fire-colored clouds”; in Torn. *igni coloris*. Several scribes altered and corrupted this verse because they did not know that *ignicolorus* (“fire-colored”) is correct, not merely *ignicolor*. Compare *unicolorus*, *versicolorus*, *decolorus*, and *tripectorus*; see the commentary on Prudentius’s *Hamartigenia*, verse 819. Ott. and the printed editions have *cum* (“with”) instead of *tunc* (“then”). I adopt *tunc* with the manuscripts Rom. and Reg., because it agrees better with the sense of the Gospel. Tichonius also expressed this in rule 1, from manuscript B. M. Rem., cited by Sabatierius: “All the tribes of the earth will mourn, and then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven.”

159. Our manuscripts Reg. and Ott., and Rom. with Torn., have *Nec praeteribit enim* (“For it will not pass away”), which is more Latin than *Praeteriet nec enim* in most printed editions, though it does not fit the meter. I therefore prefer *Praeteriet*, all the more because the Cambridge manuscript reads: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away”; the old Tridentine Gospel Book: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away”; and Saint Hilary, in Psalm 123: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” The Gothic Missal, Fourth Sunday of Advent, has: “For this generation will not pass away.” Likewise Wisdom 1:8: “Nor will the judgment that reproves it pass away,” and Ecclesiasticus 39:37: “His word will not pass away.” Juvencus therefore followed the reading of the ancient versions of Sacred Scripture, and indeed the authority of several older writers who occasionally used, in the future of compounds of *eo*, forms in *-iet* instead of *-ibit*, such as *inietur*, *transiet*, *redies*, and similar forms. Although the reading is generally doubtful, since Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 13, spoke in this way, and some examples of this type appear in ancient inscriptions, it must nevertheless be acknowledged that the usage rests on good authorities. See Tibullus, book I, elegy 4, with the notes.

163. Our manuscripts have: “What will that day be?” The editions have: “What day will that be?” I have shown elsewhere that monosyllables said to be short seem to me common, and I see no reason why *quis* could not be lengthened. In the Ott. manuscript, however, another reading seems formerly to have stood where *Quis erit ille dies* now appears. Juvencus may have written, in his usual manner, *nesciri est omnibus aequum*, that is, “it is right that it be unknown to all.” The following verse confirms this conjecture.

164. The manuscripts have *Ni soli rerum*; Rom. incorrectly has *Hi soli*. Most printed editions have *Ni solum*. Fabricius, however, printed *Ni soli*. Reg. has *fecit* instead of *torquet*, which I prefer with the others, following Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.93: “He who turns the stars of the universe.”

166. Our manuscripts and some printed editions have *munera* (“gifts”); other editions have *munia* (“duties”).

167. Rom. has *fractu*; correct to *tractu*.

168. Reg. and Ottob. have *subitus*. The editions, together with Rom., have *subitas*, which also stood in Ottob. in the first hand, as I think. Reuschius cites *subitus* from Barthius but does not approve it. Thus: *subitus, flammas volitans*—“suddenly, flying like flames.”

169. Rom. has *ne*; read *nec*.

170. Reg., Rom., and perhaps Ottob. in the first hand have *laeta*. The editions, with Ott. in the second hand, have *lata*. *Laeta* is better, as in book I, verse 194, *pascua laeta*; book II, verse 425, again *pascua laeta*; and ibid., verse 428, *laetae segetes*.

171. Ott. has: “The twin plowmen will cut furrows with the lowered plowshare.” Rom. and Reg. have: “Two will cut furrows beneath the lowered plow.” The editions have: “Two will cut furrows beneath lowered plows”; Ald. and Bas. have *lucis* instead of *sulcis*. I prefer the reading of Ott. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I.45: “Then let the bull begin for me beneath the lowered plow to groan, and the plowshare, worn by the furrow, to shine.” With a different syntax, *Eclogue* 4.32: “Towns that they may gird with walls, towns that may command the earth to cut furrows.”]

[Note: [Col. 0293D]

151. Read again the note on book III, verse 1, where the sun is called *ignicomus* (“fire-haired”).

152. Matthew: “And the powers of heaven will be shaken.”

154. Above, verse 148: “The lights of Christ will shine forth.”

156. The order is: “The Son of Man, powerful in majesty, will come through the stars,” etc.

157. A trumpet is attributed both a hiss and a blast. Lucan, book I, verse 431: “The hissing trumpets sharpened their sounds on curved bronze.” I discussed the blast at book II, verse 400. Juvencus includes both in this verse and expresses the harshness of the sound in highly suitable words.

158. *Quadrifido*: this is a poetic word, used by Virgil, Valerius Flaccus, and Claudian.

160. Matthew: “Until all these things take place.” Barthius, book XXII, chapter 19, brings here Horace’s line: “We and our possessions are owed to death.”

161. Perhaps the sense is “over these things,” “besides these things”; or *super* means “in addition,” or one should write *supersolventur* (“will be dissolved above”). On the phrase *solvi in ignes* (“to be dissolved into flames”), consult the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 443.

166. *Diversa sibi tractantes* (“engaging in different things for themselves”): *sibi* seems superfluous. Matthew: “For as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage,” etc. Perhaps Juvencus means that people then were doing something else, or other things, as the Latins say. Omeisius explains it as “things contrary to one another.”]

The stars with fiery hair will fall, and will abandon the sky.

Likewise every power of the heavenly sky, shaken,

will give signs, by which the Son of Man may shine at the summit of heaven:

unceasing mourning will overwhelm tribes of every kind,

[155] and then he will come in fire-colored clouds,

330 the Son of Man, born powerful in majesty, through the stars.

Then the trumpet, hissing with terrifying blast,

will gather the summoned righteous from the four quarters of the world.

For the present generation will not pass away,

[160] until the end that follows closes all things assigned to it.

This earth and the heaven above will be dissolved into flames,

[Col. 0294A] but my words will never be dissolved from their appointed order.

What will that day be? It is right that it be unknown to all,

except to the Lord of the universe, who turns the stars.

[165] 331 As once the raging waters overwhelmed the lands,

and, carrying off all who were engaged in various occupations,

the violence of the Flood suddenly swept them away,

so our coming will suddenly descend from the ether, rolling flames;

yet it will not press upon all under one condition.

[170] For when two men will be cutting the joyful fields

with the lowered plowshare in furrows,

[Col. 0295A] [Note: [Col. 0295B]

172. Ald. and Bas. have *aratro*; Westh. in the text has *arato*, and in the margin *arator*, with most others.

178. Reg., in the first hand, has *descendit* instead of *descendet*. Our manuscripts have *in oras*; the editions have *in horas*, which is preferable and should be retained.

179. Our manuscripts have: “If a house watchman knew that the thief’s appointed time was approaching.” Rom. has *Si scirent* (“if they knew”). Torn. has “if he knew that the thief’s appointed time, if it were approaching,” where the second *si* is superfluous, and the final syllable of *furis* is correctly lengthened by the caesura. Most editions have: “If he knew the thief’s announced time was approaching”; Westh. likewise, but in the text *Per monitum*, and in the margin *Praemonitum*.

180. Rom. has *Quisquis*; correct to *Quisque*, meaning “each one,” as it occurs several times already. In the same Rom. *Obviam* is also an error instead of *obvia*.

182. Ald. incorrectly has *assistere*.

189. Ald., Fabr., and Poelm. have *cumulabit* instead of the printed reading. Poelm. in the text, with the manuscripts and other editions, has *redimibit*, written for *redimiet*. Thus Virgil, book X, verse 538: “For whom the sacred fillet bound his temples”; and Ausonius, epigram 94: “A Punic girdle bound her swelling breasts.”

190. Reg. and Rom. have *qui sordida luxuriatus*; Ott. has *qui sordide luxoriatus*, later corrected to *sordida luxuriatus*. The editions have *qui obscene luxuriatus*. *Sordida* should be restored from the manuscripts. The gloss in Reg. is “he held filthy banquets,” so that *sordida* would agree with *convivia* in verse 193. Yet this construction would be too complicated. *Sordida* is therefore used adverbially for *sordide*, just as Virgil uses *apprima* for *apprime*, *sera* for *sero* in *Georgics* IV.122, and *crebra* for *crebro* in *Georgics* III.500. Compare *torva tuens*, *acerba sonans*, *multa gemens*. Some write *apprime* even when its final syllable is shortened, just as *inferne* in Lucretius and *superne* in Lucretius and Horace are shortened. On this basis it would not be inelegant to write, with the first hand of Ott., *qui sordide luxuriatus*, with the final syllable of *sordide* shortened. This reading commended itself to Schoettgenius in the Cambridge manuscript, because it is customary among good poets to shorten adverbs ending in *-e*. Compare verses 194 and 547 of this book.

191. Rom. has: “He despises his master and exhausts the servants”; Reg.: “he will despise … exhausting”; Ott.: “he despises … may exhaust,” instead of the various reading *contemnit … fatigat*, which is found in the editions.

192. The manuscripts have *segnique*; but Reg. perhaps had *segnisque*, which the editions prefer. Reuschius restored *segnique* by a metonymy of effect.

193. Poelm., Ald., and other editions, together with our manuscripts, have *concelebrabat*. Ott. has *concelebrari* instead of the printed reading. Hadam. has *concelebrando*. Westh. prints *concelebrabat* but gives *concelebrando* in the margin. The sense seems to require *concelebrabit* (“he will celebrate together”), especially since *contemnet* (“he will despise”) follows.

194. Reg., Fabr., and Ott. in the second hand have: “The Lord will come, and will find the servant raging heedlessly”; with the gloss in Reg. that *incauta* is an adverb. Torn. corruptly has *incavia* instead of *incauta*. Rom. and Ott. in the first hand have *incaute*. Poelm. and Hadam. have: “The Lord will come suddenly, and the raging servant.” Ald. has: “The Lord will come, foolishly raging as a servant”; Daventr. likewise, though it is unclear whether the form is *stolidum*, *stolide*, or *stolido*. The true reading is to be sought in the manuscripts, and *incauta* is used instead of *incaute*, unless one wishes to restore *incaute*. What I said concerning *sordida* and *sordide* at verse 190 may be said of both these forms.]

[Note: [Col. 0295C]

173. *Ignarusque alius*: when two are being discussed, *alter* is usually used instead of *alius*. See verse 23 of this book.

177. *Nescius*, passively, means “unknown” or “unrecognized.” Tacitus, *Annals* I.59: “To other nations, because they were ignorant of Roman rule, punishments were unfamiliar, and tribute unknown.” Plautus, *Captivi* II.2.15: “If I have not known something, I shall hand it over to you as something unknown.”

180. *Obvia*, as at verse 103, *obvia signa* (“weapons brought out to meet him”). On public watchmen of cities and private guards of houses, see Pignorius, *On Slaves*, page 145 and following, where he carefully discusses the whole subject.

182. *Assistite*: “be present,” “stand ready.” See the note on book I, verse 617.

186. *Per longa*: “for a long time.” Silius, book II, verse 465: “Hunger concealed for a long time”; and book XII, verse 294: “The heavy outcomes of his people, which Rome had been accustomed to hear for a long time.” Again, book XV, verse 787: “Like a rabid sea-monster flung for a long time into the barren deep for feeding.”

187. *Pater ipse*: emphatic, as in Virgil’s phrase: “the father himself of the flock.”

190. *Luxurio* and *luxurior* are common verbs for those who spend excessively and extravagantly on food and dress. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, page 161, confirms this with examples, noting that among the ancients slave stewards sometimes stumbled into the snares of prostitutes, with no small loss to their masters’ property.

192. *Indulgens*: “indulging freely,” “devoting himself without restraint.” Thus one is said to indulge in sleep, wine, dances, and so forth.

193. Koenigius observes that this verse has a certain solemnity. Sidonius attempts to imitate it: “He commanded innumerable legions.” Rutilius, in his *Itinerary*: “with Bellerophontic anxieties.” A distich of four words is attributed to Bolislaus Lobkowizius: “The Constantinopolitans were thrown into confusion by innumerable anxieties.”

195. *Cladibus abdet*: because he will thrust him into the underworld and, as it were, hide him there. Thus Tacitus, *Annals* II.85: “And she was hidden away on the island of Seriphos.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 771: “Hide the deniers of Christ; no one begrudges you—hide them; use your lot, to hold the blasphemers through perpetual night.” There he addresses death.

197. CHAPTER VII. On the ten virgins. Matthew 25:1 and following. The term “girl” is often applied to virgins; sometimes also to non-virgins, and to all females of an age at which they can bear children.]

One farmer will be taken away with his body suddenly seized,

while another, unknowing, will be left in the vast field.

Even among two reclining on one bed of straw,

[175] differing judgment will befall them by different destinies.

For one, left behind, will seek his companion along the roads.

Therefore let the servants keep watch, because they do not know

332 at what hour the Lord’s sudden coming will descend.

If each house-guard knew that the thief’s appointed time was approaching,

[180] he would keep watch and bring out weapons to meet him,

lest anyone break into the house.

But remain ever ready, with attentive minds.

For the Son of Man will return here suddenly and unexpectedly,

keeping his rewards for the righteous.

[185] That servant will be faithful whom the master of the house himself,

when setting out for a long journey, wished to entrust with all

the house and the servants: wise and exceedingly blessed

is the one whom the Lord, when he comes, will find carrying out his commands.

He will crown that servant with greater honor.

[190] But that unhappy man who, having indulged in filthy luxury,

333 despises his delaying master and exhausts the servants

with beatings, and, indulging in sluggish drunkenness,

was celebrating the banquets of the luxurious—

the master will come and cast the raging servant headlong

[195] into the deserved calamities of punishment.

Perpetual weeping and gnashing will remain for him.

The heavenly kingdoms may be compared with maidens,

[Col. 0297A] [Note: [Col. 0297A]

198. Ald. has *pars est quarum*.

199. Westh. in the text has *prae stupido*; in the margin, *praestupido*. Badius, with Ald., has *prae studio*, because they devoted themselves to slothfulness and vices; for they were not naturally foolish.

200. The manuscripts, with Ald., have *illae*; other editions have *illi*, which Gallandius says should be preferred from the Greek. But *illae* is better, and Reuschius also retained it. Matthew 25:1: “They went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.” Instead of “the bridegroom and the bride,” Juvencus says *votis sponsalibus* (“with bridal vows”), as in verse 208, “and thereafter hasten to meet him with joyful vow.” The ancient versions likewise read “the bridegroom and the bride.” The Greek copies vary: most have only “the bridegroom,” but others add “and the bride.” Certainly in Juvencus, since the word *sponsi* (“of the bridegroom”) has not preceded, *illi* cannot be understood of the bridegroom; therefore *illae* must be read.

205. Reg. has *tum per membra*; but this may have entered the text from a gloss, since the following verse in Reg. reads *Solvuntur cunctae*, and accordingly the explanation is *per in membra*.

206. Reg. has *Solvuntur cunctae*, but the original reading was *Solventur*. Ott. has *Solvuntur comptae* instead of *cunctae*. Rom. has *Solvuntur cunctae*. The editions have *Solvuntur cunctis*, which is less pleasing than *Solvuntur cunctae*, though I do not deny that *solvuntur membra sopore* (“the limbs are released by sleep”) is correct. Reg. has *per competa latae*. Ott. has *per competa lata*, but earlier it had *per compita laeta*. Rom., together with the editions, has *per compita lata*. See book III, verse 758.

208. Fabr. has *Incoepit*; other editions, with the manuscripts, have *Exoritur*. Reg. has *cooccurrere*, which seems to have stood in the first hand of Ott. instead of *occurrere*. I find *cooccurrere* nowhere else, but it could nevertheless be admitted by analogy.

209. Reg. writes *choriscis*, but the gloss has *splendidis*.

210. Reg. and Rom. have: “The virgins hasten to rise and the lights with torches.” Ott. likewise, but this codex seems in its first hand to have had *properantum* or *properatum*, the more correct reading. The gloss in Reg. on *surgere* is “it was fitting.” But that does not agree well with the Gospel’s words, “Then they arose,” etc. I therefore read *Surgere virginibus properatum* (“the virgins were hastened to rise”) instead of “the virgins hastened to rise.” Juvencus often uses this construction, adding a dative to a passive verb where an ablative would be expected. The editions have: “Then they hasten to rise, and [to carry] torches with bright light.” From this reading, and from the manuscripts Reg., Ott., and Rom., one may conjecture: “Then they hasten to rise, and [to carry] torches with bright light,” with *coeperunt* (“they began”) supplied, or with *surgere* used for *surrexerunt* (“they arose”), a figure also known to historians. *Properatim* is an old adverb, used by Caecilius, Pomponius, and Sisenna. Juvencus formed *mensatim* in a similar way in book III, verse 214.

213. Ott. has the erroneous *jestare* instead of *gestare*.]

[Note: [Col. 0297C]

198. *Sapientior*: “wise,” a comparative used in place of a positive.

199. *Praestupido*: see similar forms in the Index of Words; Juvencus has newly formed this word with the preposition *prae*.

200. For *votis de conjugio* (“with bridal vows”), see book III, verse 739.

201. *Flammicomantum*: a new word, as in book III, verse 623, *glaucicomantis*. Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 775, has *flammicomos ignes* (“flame-haired fires”), and *Apotheosis* 495 has *puerorum flammicomantum* (“of flame-haired boys”), on the authority of certain copies. But in the note on that passage I showed that *puerorum flavicomantum* (“of blond-haired boys”) should be read. Wolfius, together with others, observes in his philological notes on the New Testament that weddings were formerly customarily celebrated at night. Martinus Roa, book II, chapter 21 and following, discusses several questions in this parable as explained from ancient custom: Did the virgins go out together to meet the bridegroom and the bride? From where did the virgins come, and where were the bridegroom and bride going? Why ten, and neither more nor fewer? Why lamps, and not rather torches or firebrands? When the cry arose that the bridegroom was coming, what does this mean? Did he come to the bride’s house or to his own? Alone, or together with the bride? Where was the wedding celebrated, at her house or his? But what interests us more is to ask why Juvencus uses *taedae* (“torches”) for *lampades* (“lamps”), when the sacred text names lamps, and Juvencus himself shortly afterward mentions olive oil, with which the lights would receive fuel or the flames be maintained. This question is resolved from the Rabbinic Lexicon of Henry Otho, where the custom of escorting the bride is explained thus: In the land of Ishmael it was customary to lead the bride from her father’s house to the bridegroom’s house before her introduction into the bridal chamber, and to carry before her about ten wooden staffs, each having at its top a small vessel like a dish, in which there was a strip of cloth with oil and pitch. From these, when lit, they carried a torch before her. Otho cites the book *Aruch* and Rabbi Solomon in *Kelim*. Lamy presents the form of such lamps, depicted from ancient monuments; he further adds that the wise virgins received oil in their own vessels, distinct from the lamps. For, he says, these lamps were not lanterns like ours, into which oil is poured for many hours. Yet this is not sufficiently clear from Otho’s words. He places at the top of the wooden staff a small vessel like a dish, in which there was a strip of cloth with oil and pitch; these, I think, could suffice for a suitable period without the need for other vessels. Once this is understood, it becomes clear that Juvencus aptly and in accordance with ancient custom called the wooden staffs *taedae*. A *taeda* is a tree bearing pitch, and torches made from a *taeda*, or carrying a torch made from a *taeda*, were those that burned after being kindled with pitch. In connection with weddings, *taeda* is an extremely common word, so much so that it is also used for “wedding.” These torches are also called *lampades*, though less often. Statius used the expression for the first wedding in *Silvae* IV.8.59: “with the first torch.”]

334 Twice five virgins, of whom one part was wiser,

while the other part was utterly foolish in its stubborn heart.

[200] All of them went out to meet the bridal pair,

girded with the adornment of flame-haired torches.

335 But that wiser group carefully took along olive oil,

so that the flames might receive fuel.

The foolish, however, had no such prudence.

[205] And while the bridegroom delayed, their limbs were released by sleep

as they lay along the broad crossroads.

[Col. 0298A] In the middle of the night a great cry began

to grow louder, and then summoned them to meet him with joyful eagerness

and to adorn the roads with flashing torches.

[210] The virgins hastened to rise and furnish the torches with lights,

336 and to strengthen the flames with rich olive oil.

Then the foolish asked that a portion of the oil be given to them,

which they saw that the wise women were carrying with them.

But since the wise company fears equally for all—
