215. Ott. has *parvae* instead of *clarae*. Reg. has *nutrimenta*, which also stood in Rom., but was correctly emended there to *nutrimina*.

217. Rom. and Ott. have: “While the foolish continue, and buy liquid olive oil.” Reg. in the second hand has: “While the foolish continue, so that they may buy liquid olive oil.” Reg. in the first hand, Torn., Poelm. in the text, and Hadam. have: “Then the foolish continue, so that they may buy liquid oil.” Ald. has the same, but had printed *mercantur*, which he corrected in the Errata to *mercentur*. The error *mercantur* remains in Bas. and Daventr.

218. I suspected *omina* (“omens”) instead of *omnia* (“all things”).

219. Reg. has: “And only the wise portion accompanies the bridegroom.” Most have: “And only the wise company accompanies the bride.” Fabricius observes that *comitari* here is used with a dative in the Greek manner. Juvencus uses it similarly in book II, verse 695: “Unwavering faith will accompany these words.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V.36: “The other things that accompany this life.” It is also possible that Juvencus uses *comitor* passively, as Ovid does, *Tristia* III, elegy 7, verse 47: “Yet I myself accompany and enjoy my own talent.” Nor should *factio* be changed to *portio*: although *factio* is usually taken negatively, for a mob or conspiracy of evildoers, and Juvencus often uses *factio* in that sense, it was originally an honorable word, as Festus noted; hence the factions of physicians, nobles, actors, and so forth. In this sense Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 1: “Another faction—the Empiric school, so called from its experience—arose in Sicily.”

220. Torn. has *At veniunt*; others have *Adveniunt*. The manuscripts, with Poelm. in the text, have *brutae*. Ald., Fabr., and Poelm., instead of the printed reading, and Bas., have *fatuae*. The genuine reading seems to be *brutae*, for, as Festus says, the ancients called something heavy *brutum*. Hence stupid animals are called *bruta*. Dull and foolish people are likewise called *bruti* by Pacuvius, Seneca, Apuleius, and others. It is well known that the family of the Bruti derived its name from this, because Lucius Junius pretended to be a fool. In Rom. the reading is *sero post tempora segnes* (“late, sluggish after the times”).]

[Note: [Col. 0299C]

215. *Nutrimentum* is more usual, but *nutrimen* was also used by Ovid. On the matter itself, Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 13: “Those lamps, dripping with rich oil, we feed with oil, or with dry torches … The living flame burns strongly, whether the hollow vessel supplies its sap through a thirsty cloth, or whether the pine bears its pitchy nourishment.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I.179: “He received the fire in leaves and gave dry fuel around it.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.352: “When the earth will no longer give food and rich nourishment to the flame, its strength having been consumed through long ages, and nourishment for its devouring nature will be lacking,” etc.

218. *Omnia pompae*, as in book II, verse 554, *omnia patris*. “All things of the father.” The reading “joyful procession” is correct, for there was also a sad or funeral procession, about which book II, verse 401 says: “They were celebrating the final rites of the last procession.”

221. The wedding feast was celebrated at the bridegroom’s house, as is well known.

222. *Nequicquam*: “in vain.” *Ingeminant* is a poetic expression; *pulsare* is supplied as its object. I think *ingrata* is used adverbially: “they repeatedly ask unpleasantly or annoyingly,” that is, “they ask that they may be allowed,” etc. See the variant reading at verse 190 of this book.

224. *Cognoscere*: “to recognize,” “to acknowledge,” “to recognize again.” In Sacred Scripture, *cognoscere* also means “to approve,” while *nescire* means “to reject.”

226. *Certior* means “certain,” or it may refer to what has been said. The Evangelist says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

227. CHAPTER VIII. The talents given to the servants for employment. Matthew 25:14 and following; Luke 19:12. The order is: “As it happened to one who was about to go into a distant country, entrusting [talents] to servants,” etc. That is, after he had departed or set out, it happened that he went into a far country.]

228. Below, verse 249: “That the money, put to work, might bring us profit.” In Cicero, *tractare pecuniam* means to manage or administer money, *Divination against Verres*, chapter 10: “For you were quaestor: you managed the public money.”

“Lest bright, rich nourishment be lacking to the flame,

if an equal portion is given to all from a little.”

Then the foolish women proceed and buy clear oil.

While they go on, all the joyful procession passes by,

and only the prudent party accompanies the bridegroom.

[220] 337 The dull-witted arrive late, sluggish after the appointed time,

and vainly repeat their knocking at the bridegroom’s doors and the closed threshold,

importuning it, unwelcome, with prayers,

that the wretched women may be allowed to enter the joyful threshold.

No one of the bridegroom’s companions wished to recognize them,

[225] [Col. 0300A] nor did the bridegroom himself. Watch in fear,

for the hour of his coming is not more certain to you.

For just as one who happens to set out for distant lands,

entrusting talents to be managed by his servants,

gave five to one, another received two to keep,

[230] and a third undertook the charge of managing one talent,

because differing capacities deserve differing trusts.

338 But those to whom a larger sum of money had been entrusted

strove to increase it by double gains.

But he to whom the charge of one talent had been entrusted,

[235] burying the money in the ground, hid it without profit.

238. Regius has *heros, potiora credere*, with the gloss *heros*—“that master.” Read *herus*, for the first syllable of *heros* is long. The final syllable of *potiora* can be lengthened because of the two consonants of the following word. But the truer reading is *potioraque credere*.

239. Tornesius has *resedit*; others, *refodit*, a word used by Columella and Pliny.

240. Fabricius has *Reddidit et domino*; the rest, *Et reddit domino*.

[Col. 0301C] 242. Tornesius has *meteres* for *meteret*.

244. Aldus, Daventer, and Basle have *Malui, quo semper salvum tibi*. Romanus: *Malui, quo salvum semper tibi*; Regius: *Malui, quod salvum semper tibi*; Ottobonianus: *Malui, quod salvum tibi semper*; Hadamarius, Poelmann, and Fabricius: *Malui, uti semper salvum tibi*. One should retain *Malui, quod*, or *quo* from the manuscripts, making a spondee in *Malui* by synaeresis. Koenigius also wished this, though Reuschius did not follow him. Romanus, Aldus, Basle, and Tornesius have *possim*; others, *possem*.

250. Aldus and Basle, with Regius and Ottobonianus, have *portio nostri*, and the gloss in Regius, *nostri*—“of the talent.” Hadamarius, Poelmann, and Fabricius: *portio nostra*. Romanus: *portio vestri*. Perhaps *portio nummi*.

252. Our manuscripts: *Quem duplis cumulasse lucris*. Most printed editions: *Quem cumulasse duplis lucris*. The first syllable of *lucris* is common.

[Col. 0302B] 254. Romanus, Regius, Aldus, and Basle: *Quis res*, with the gloss in Regius, *Quis*—“by whom.”

257. Some have *Et* for *At* or *Ast*. Read *demersus* with Regius, Tornesius, and Romanus, rather than *dimersus* with the others.

258. Ottobonianus has *Perpetuo* for *Perpetuos*.

259. Romanus and Ottobonianus: *patriisque*. Regius, with the printed editions: *patrisque*.

262. Aldus and Poelmann, instead of the common reading, have *justosque dehinc*; Fabricius, [Col. 0302C] *justosque omni*; most, *justosque omnes*.

264. Ottobonianus has *despectos*, from which *dispectos* arose.

266. Our manuscripts, with Aldus, Tornesius, and Basle, have *dextri permittens mollia prati*, with the gloss in Regius, “pleasant pastures.” This reading fits the following verse best. Poelmann in the text, Hadamarius, and Fabricius: *dextrae permittens mollia parti*. Poelmann in the alternative reading and Daventer: *dextrae permittens mollia partis*.

267. Romanus: *Et leves hircus dumos tondere capellis*, which is corrupt.

270. Regius, incorrectly, has *aequa* for *aequaeva*. Rogerius, Ottobonianus, and Romanus: *mundi . . . nitentis*, with the gloss in Regius, “new.” The printed editions: *mundo . . . nitenti*. Either construction may be used. Just as *aequalis* is sometimes joined with the genitive, so also is *aequaevus*.

274. Aldus and Fabricius: *Hospitiumque domus*; others, *Hospitioque domus.]

239. “Faithful”: Matthew has it thus: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many.”

247. I am certain that “wickedness” here is used in the sense of “sloth.” See what I discussed concerning this word in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 46.

253. He explains Matthew’s words: “For to everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.”

254. “Share” first signifies the money that is contributed so that profit may be made from it. It is also taken to mean an estate.

255. Juvencus gives the word “substance” various meanings. Here it means resources, property, or possessions—a sufficiently established meaning of the word.

259. CHAPTER IX. That on the day of judgment the good will be placed on the right, but the wicked on the left. Matthew 25:31, etc.

260. The alliteration in *sede sedebit* (“he will sit in his seat”) should be noted. This sort of cacophony often occurs in Juvencus, though it is not so harsh that two syllables are repeated in both words. He frequently joins a verb ending in *-re* to another that also begins with *re-*.

262. Concerning the stain of the wicked, Virgil, *Aeneid* II.97: “This was the first stain of evil for me.”

266. “Wool-bearing” means sheep.

270. Matthew: “Possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” The Italian version in some manuscripts has “from the beginning of the world,” in others “from the origin of the world.” The meaning is the same. By “the shining world,” Juvencus understands the origin, or beginning, of the world. Things that are new commonly shine.

274. “Called” means called by me to hospitality. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.302: “So that the citadels of new Carthage might open to the Teucrians in hospitality.”]

Now the present master had arrived; then the first and the second

showed that each had doubled what had been entrusted to him.

Their master praises them and promises to entrust them with greater things

because of such great faithfulness. But that third man dug up

[240] and returned the talent to his master with these words:

Because I knew that my master was severe,

that he would reap crops grown from another’s seed,

I was afraid, and I preferred to entrust your silver to the earth,

so that I might always be able to return it to you safe.

[245] 339 Then the Lord, answering the servant, spoke these words:

If you dared to say that you did not know my ways,

I could perhaps grant pardon for such great wickedness.

Yet you ought rather to have understood this:

[Col. 0301B] that the money, put to work, should bring us profit.

[250] Therefore let the share of our slothful servant be taken away,

and henceforth let the greater possession be given to the prudent man,

whom I found to have increased my five talents with double profit.

For it is certain that greater things are deserved by those

whose richer resources abound from their accumulated share.

[255] [Col. 0302A] But from him whose small substance lies within a slothful heart,

that very little will rightly be taken away altogether.

But let the wicked servant, plunged into the deepest darkness,

continually utter lamentations with the gnashing of punishment.

Behold, the Son of Man will come, accompanied by the ministers of his Father,

[260] and will sit as judge upon a lofty throne.

340 Then all the nations from the various regions of the world

will come together, and he will separate all the righteous

from the stain of the wicked, and gladly place them on the right;

but he will leave the evil, despised, on the left,

[265] as a shepherd distinguishes the pasture of mixed flocks,

allowing the wool-bearing sheep the soft meadow on the right,

but the shaggy goats to crop the thorny bushes on the left.

Then the king, turning toward those on the right, will say:

Let the holy come here; let them now receive the gifts

[270] [Col. 0302B] owed them long ago, gifts of the Father,

which were prepared for the righteous from the beginning of the shining world.

For once, when weakened by hunger, this people refreshed me kindly,

and often relieved my thirst with drink,

and often the house opened its hospitality to me when I was called,

[275] and, naked, I received the most welcome covering of clothing.

[Col. 0303A] [Note: [Col. 0303B]

276. Westphal, in the text together with Aldus, has “in the punishments of prison”; in the margin, together with the others, “of prison and punishments.”

281. Our manuscripts, together with Tornesius, have *dicet* (“will say”). Aldus and the other printed editions have *dicit* (“says”).

286. Regius, Westphal in the margin, Ottobonianus in the second hand, Romanus, Poelmann, and others have “in the dreadful depths of the abyss.” Aldus, Basle, and Westphal in the text have “dreadful.” Ottobonianus in the second hand and Tornesius have “of the dreadful.” Regius and Ottobonianus have “in the depths.” Romanus, together with the printed editions, has “of the depth.”

287. Aldus and Basle have “and his companions, and him himself”; the others have “his companions, him himself,” namely the demon himself.

289. Our manuscripts, together with Aldus, Daventer, and Basle, have “the small pity of bread for the hungry,” to which Barth’s codex offers the reading “small fragments of bread.” From this Koenigius cleverly conjectured: “Nor, in the punishments of hunger, did small morsels of bread [comfort] me.” Poelman and the other printed editions have “small fragments of bread for me.” I do not indeed find the word *miseramen* among the ancient writers, but I consider it genuine in Juvencus in the sense of *miseratio* (“pity”); Christian poets, like Lucretius, delighted in such formations as *peccamen*, *augmen*, *lateramen*, *momen*, *vocamen*, *glomeramen*, and *duramen*. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.1042. Yet since Juvencus elsewhere says “fragments of grain” and “fragments of bread,” the conjecture is not a bad one: “Nor, in punishment, the smallest fragments of bread.” The copyists may easily have been deterred by the word *parvissima* (“smallest”), which Varro used, and Lucretius used more than once.

290. Regius, Ottobonianus, Daventer, Aldus, Fabricius, Hadamarius, and Poelmann have “or a foreigner to me.” Romanus, corruptly, has “or, for a little while, a foreigner to me in houses.” Westphal likewise printed “or a foreigner to me”; but, as can be gathered from his notes, Badius had read or suspected “or, for a foreigner, a shelter,” etc. Gallandius printed “or a foreigner to me,” but approved “or shelter for a foreigner,” which had occurred to Koenigius and pleased Reuschius. He asserts nothing more certain than Koenigius’s conjecture, but does not depart from the common reading. Badius interprets the common reading *peregrina* as “coverings furnished to me, a foreigner”; this interpretation is not displeasing. Yet “or shelter for a foreigner” would be preferable, if the manuscript codices allowed it.

292. Poelmann has *aut* (“or”) in the text and *numquam* (“never”) in the following verse, instead of *haud* (“not”) and *umquam* (“ever”) in the following verse. Our manuscripts have *aut* and *umquam* in the next verse. The printed editions vary. The sense is understood to be the same. Romanus has, incorrectly, *coeptae* instead of *septo*.

294. Regius and Ottobonianus in the first hand have *respondit* (“he answered”). Others have *respondet* (“he answers”), which may perhaps be used for *respondebit* (“he will answer”), from *respondeo*.

295. Ottobonianus and Poelmann, instead of the common reading, have “not indeed ours”; most have “never ours.” Regius writes *aut* (“or”). Reuschius retains “not indeed,” which he considers far more significant than “never.”

298. Ottobonianus has *morboque* (“and by illness”); the others have *morbove* (“or by illness”).

300. The manuscripts have “The Lord will say these matters.” In Ottobonianus in the first hand there was *dicit* (“says”). The printed editions have “The Lord will say these matters.”

301. Reuschius, together with Omesíus, has “in prosperous circumstances,” that is, flourishing circumstances. Others have “in straitened circumstances,” namely those of others.

303. Hadamarius and Poelmann in the text, and Aldus, have *dedit* (“gave”). Our manuscripts, together with Tornesius and Fabricius, more suitably have *dabit* (“will give”). Reuschius prefers *dedit*.

304. Ottobonianus has *poenae* (“of punishment”), above *poena* (“punishment”). Fabricius read “eternal punishment of the wretched,” and observed in the commentary that *miserum* is here a grieving particle placed in parentheses. But our manuscripts, together with the other printed editions, have “the eternal punishment of the wretched,” which is even more pleasing.]

[Note: [Col. 0303D]

276. “Punishments” occurs again in verse 280: “of prison or punishments.” Here *poena* (“punishment”) is used for evil, since punishment is not properly inflicted upon the righteous.

278. Again in verse 295: “No one of ours remembers having visited you.”

279. “In dominion”: in power, authority, and something like tyranny. “Noted” means observed, saw, or perceived.

282. “Labors”: calamities and hardships. Compare the variant readings at book III, verse 28.

283. “To place” is used for “to have placed,” as Badius explains—a tense used in place of another according to the practice of declining Latin.

286. Greek poets called the dwellings below of the condemned *barathrum*, that is, a deep chasm. Latin poets, especially Christian poets, transferred the word into Latin, as Barthius proves with examples from Juvencus and others, *Adversaria* XXXV, chapter 8, column 1646.

288. “Having suffered thirst,” like “having suffered hunger.”

291. “Slender” means a portion, that is, a small portion. *Gracilis* can also sometimes denote something small. See book I, verse 524.

296. “To stir up labor” means, namely, to be tormented and vexed by painful toil. Reuschius explains it as “to struggle with labors.” Thus one says, “labors endured are pleasant.”

297. *Hospitus* is an adjective used by poets. “In exhausted circumstances” means in afflicted circumstances. Pliny, book II, chapter 7: “Vespasian Augustus, coming to the aid of exhausted circumstances.” Virgil, book XI, verse 335: “Take counsel for the common good, and aid those in exhausted circumstances.”

299. “Troubled”: afflicted by anxious cares.

302. “The humble”: the least. The Vulgate has: “To one of these least.” The old Italian version has: “To one of these least,” or “to one of those least,” or “to one of these least ones.”

304. Book II, verse 663: “And by grave judgment make the wicked wretches rise.” *Fodere* also means to prick, stimulate, pierce through, and here to vex or torment.]

341 I received comfort from these men in prison and punishments.

Then the blessed answered the Lord in these words:

None of our number remembers seeing you naked

or, when you were oppressed by harsh hunger, observing you,

[280] or remembers seeing you bound in prison or punishments.

The judge, answering them, will then say these words:

Whatever one has done for these humble brothers of mine,

showing pity for their sufferings, it is certain that he has placed a sweet fruit before me.

but you, unjust ones, depart to the righteous flames,
[285] and torment your wicked minds with punishments forever—
punishments which the Father prepared amid the pools of the dreadful deep abyss
for the companions of the dreadful demon and for the demon himself.

For once, when I suffered thirst, no cups were given me,
[Col. 0303B] nor, in hunger’s punishment, the scant consolations of a little bread,
[290] 342 nor were the coverings of shelter or clothing given me, a stranger, even briefly,
[Col. 0304A] a small share from your great abundance.

Nor did your visitation ever afford me comfort
when I was shut within prison’s enclosing barriers or lay ill.

Then the condemned faction answers these words:

[295] “No one of our number, indeed, remembers seeing you,

or enduring the painful labor of thirst or savage hunger,

or wandering as a stranger through the towns in exhausted circumstances,

or sunk in prison punishments or weighed down by illness,

so that fitting pity might be shown to you in your distress.”

[300] To these things the Lord of all will say: “When your proud

343 savagery swelled beneath your proud heart amid others’ straitened circumstances,

and you trampled the least of the humble, you despised me in them.”

When he has spoken these words, he will give each his rewards according to his merits.

The wicked wretches will be tormented by eternal punishment,

[305] and the salvation granted to the righteous will remain forever.

[Col. 0305A] [Note: [Col. 0305A]

308. Romanus, Tornesius, Aldus, and Basle have *percurrere* (“to run through”); Regius, Ottobonianus, and the other printed editions have *praecurrere* (“to run ahead”).

311. Romanus has, incorrectly, *fratrem* (“the brother”), *domumque* (“and the house”).

312. Our manuscript codices have *amplexus* (“having embraced”); the printed editions have *complexus* (“having embraced”).

313. All our manuscripts have “A messenger arriving reports him lying in extremity.” Reuschius’s codices support this reading, which he calls not inappropriate, though he follows another. The printed editions have “A messenger arriving reports him lying in the death-struggle.” Aldus and Basle have “reports him in the death-struggle.” Fabricius also read “in the death-struggle,” and noted in the commentary that *agon* here signifies the struggle of a man’s final breath, when he is already giving up his soul. Hence *agonizare* (“to struggle”) for “to be at the point of death,” a word that Cellarius rejected as belonging to uncertain Latin. Cellarius is also little inclined to accept *agon* for the struggle of death, although he concedes that Juvencus used the word. Since this word in fact does not appear in our manuscripts, it is highly suspect. I therefore restore “reports him lying in extremity,” where *extrema* is either used adverbially for *extremum* (“at the end”), as in verse 190, *sordida* for *sordide*, or rather is joined with “the grievous extremities of illness,” namely, “lying through the grievous extremities of illness.” Juvencus, as do many others, often uses *jacere* of the sick.

314. In Ottobonianus in the first hand there was *juvenum* instead of *juvenem*.

315. Our manuscripts have *tenentem* (“holding”); the printed editions have *tenere* (“to hold”). I prefer *tenentem*. Romanus has, incorrectly, *somnia* (“dreams”) instead of *summa* (“highest point”).

316. Romanus has “Lazarus had”; read “Lazarus here had.”

317. Romanus in the second hand, Regius, and apparently Ottobonianus in the first hand have *percussus* (“struck”); the printed editions have *perculsus* (“deeply shaken”). In Romanus in the first hand there was *percursus*.

318. Regius, Romanus together with Aldus, Tornesius, and Basle have *ista haec* (“these things”); Ottobonianus and the other printed editions have *isthaec*. Reuschius thinks that Juvencus sometimes, in the Greek manner, wrote two words together in this way, *ista haec*.

319. Romanus and Basle have *justus* (“the righteous man”); most others have *justis* (“for the righteous”), a phrase familiar to Juvencus, who sets a dative with a passive verb where an ablative would be expected.]

306. CHAPTER X. That Lazarus was raised when he already stank. John 11:1, etc. Juvencus says: “While he speaks such things”; but one must understand: “While Jesus was occupied with these or similar matters and conversations.” The poet adds, plausibly and in accordance with ancient custom, that the women tore their loosened hair, since grieving women used to tear their hair.

307. “Sister,” that is, “sisters”—the singular used for the plural. The words of the Gospel are: “Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying.” Or Juvencus, attributing to Mary Magdalene chiefly what both sisters did, proceeds to say in verse 310: “For she had been a woman,” etc. “Of just concern” is taken from Cicero: “jurists say ‘most just grief,’” as Reuschius observed.

308. It is not at all certain that a young man was sent. Nevertheless, here we may understand a servant, with Pignorius, *On Slaves*, page 127.

309. “Friend”: Virgil, *Aeneid* I.490: “His spoils, his chariot, and the very body of his friend he saw.” Servius comments there: “Of his friend” is stronger than if he had said “of Hector.”

310. Juvencus’s interpretation should be noted: he holds that Mary, Lazarus’s sister, was the same woman who was a sinner in the city, of whom Luke 7:36, etc., speaks. Juvencus says that Mary, Lazarus’s sister, was accepted by Christ for her gracious acts of devotion; therefore Christ embraced Lazarus and his deserving household with love because of her service. He explains the passage, as you see, by John 11:2 of this chapter: “Now Mary was she who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick.” This deed had therefore occurred earlier, and can be none other than what Luke relates in the cited passage: “And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment. And standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head … You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.” Again the same Mary anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair in the house of Simon the leper, when she also poured the alabaster jar of ointment upon his head; but John 12:1, etc., clearly teaches that this occurred after Lazarus’s resurrection. Those who wish to distinguish Mary, Lazarus’s sister, from the sinful woman assert that John mentioned the anointing of Jesus’ feet before Lazarus’s resurrection by anticipation, and that he speaks of no other anointing than the one he records in chapter 12 after Lazarus’s resurrection. Juvencus, on the contrary—and, as it seems to me, rightly—holds that the anointing which John recounts in chapter 11 truly occurred before Lazarus’s resurrection. In the Tridentine Gospel Book this is explained so clearly that it should not be called into doubt: “Now this was Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick.” For my part, it is enough to disclose Juvencus’s understanding. Many discuss the question itself. Three distinct women—namely, the sinful woman, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the sister of Lazarus—are recognized by Faber Stapulensis, Jodocus Clichtoveus, Lonnet, Casaubon, Estius, Launoy, Bulengerus, Turrianus, Zegerus, Salmeron, Mauconduit, Anquetin, Tillemont, Baillet, and Calmet. A single Mary—Mary Magdalene, the sinful woman, and Lazarus’s sister—is defended by John Fischer, bishop of Rochester, Balthazar Sorius, Laurentius Surius, Jacobus, bishop of Vienne, Marcus Grandivallus, Baronius, Jansenius of Ghent, Maldonatus, Natalis Alexander, Lamy, Mauduit, Pezron, Trevet, and Sollerius. Compare Zachariae’s *Bibliotheca selecta* in the supplement to Natalis Alexander.

Valerius Flaccus, book VI, verse 374: “Then he strikes Lycaon near the boundary of the breast.” In Juvencus it is rather from *confinium*, *confinii*, which is more commonly used. Quintilian, *Declamation* 8, chapter 19: “He would suspend his soul, balanced by painful distress, on the boundary between death and life.” Ammianus, book 17: “Between the boundaries of life and death.”

322. After this verse Omesíus had read somewhere: “He said this, and all follow with Christ leading the way,” which occurs after verse 333. Omesíus, however, thought that this verse might be an interpolation, such as the following verse in Virgil: “Begin with me, my flute, the Maenalian verses.”

323. Our manuscripts have *aiunt* (“they say”). The printed editions vary: some have *aiunt*, others *reddunt* (“they reply”). Ottobonianus in the second hand has *somnum* instead of *somno*.

329. Regius and Ottobonianus have “far away, because he saw everything.” Romanus has “far away through everything.” Aldus and Basle have “far away, who sees everything.” Poelmann, Fabricius, and Hadamarius have “far away, also everything.” I read: “You see that, though absent, I behold everything from afar,” with *quod* understood as “because” or “since,” unless one also wishes to read *armant* (“they arm”) in the preceding verse instead of *armat* (“he arms”), in this sense: “Because you see that, though absent, I behold everything from afar, it arms your faith more strongly.” John 11:14: “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.” And in the ancient version, from the Colbert manuscript: “So that you may believe, because I was not there.” Reuschius retained “also from afar,” but added that the reading of his codices, “because from afar,” is not unsuitable, in this order: “because you see me, absent, seeing from afar.”

330. Ottobonianus and Romanus write *Didimus*; Regius *Dydimus*; the others generally *Didymus*. The manuscripts, together with Tornesius, Aldus, and Basle, distinguish the words: “But let us hurry, he said. Didymus then spoke these words.” Poelmann and Hadamarius have: “But let us hurry, said Didymus, while he spoke these words.” Poelmann, instead of the common reading, has “then spoke these words.” I follow the punctuation of the manuscript codices, or punctuate more clearly: “But let us hurry, he said. Didymus then spoke these words.” Thus John 11:15–16: “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but let us go to him. Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: Let us also go, so that we may die with him.”

333. Regius has *cuncta* (“everything”). Ottobonianus and the others have *cuncti* (“all”), but the verse was added at the bottom of the page.

335. Aldus and Basle have *mersisque* (“and having plunged”), while Ottobonianus in the first hand has *mersusque* (“and having plunged”), and similarly in the following verse *Germanus* (“brother”). Ottobonianus in the second hand, together with the other manuscripts and printed editions, has *mersasque … Germanas* (“and having plunged the sisters”). Badius and Koenigius suspect that the reading should be *de more* (“from custom”) rather than *de morte* (“from death”). Here, indeed, there is a custom in some places whereby funeral mourning is intensified by keeping the windows of the house almost completely closed.

341. The manuscripts have “your present power for us.” Poelmann in the text, Hadamarius, and Fabricius have “your present power for us.” Poelmann, instead of the common reading, and Aldus and Basle have “if you, Christ, had been present here.”

342. Regius has “If you had been present, and had snatched your brother from bitter death.” Poelmann in the text, Hadamarius, Romanus, and Ottobonianus have the same, with variations in word order. Fabricius has: “If you had been present, no brother would have yielded to bitter death.” Poelmann instead of the common reading, Aldus, and Basle have: “She cries out: No brother would have yielded to bitter death.” One might conjecture: “If you had been present! This would have snatched your brother from bitter death.”]

322. “Young man” is used for “man,” as in book II, verse 419, and elsewhere. Potamius, in his treatise on Lazarus in the appendix to the works of Saint Zenobius, calls Lazarus, whom he had described as forty years old, also a young man. The Ballerinii say in a note, on the authority of Varro, that youth extends from the age of thirty to forty. Isidore, *Etymologies* XI.2, asserts that youth ends at the fiftieth year. “To rise again” means to be resurrected. Prudentius, *On the Resurrection*, at the end of the *Apotheosis*, verse 1063: “I know that my body rises again in Christ.” Juvencus again, verse 457: “May they grant me to rise again into new wines.”

324. “They follow” means “they follow after” or “they overtake,” as elsewhere. It is a simple verb used for a compound.

327. “He fell into death.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.32, said “to fall into illness.” Otherwise *cadere* is ordinarily used simply to mean “to die.”

329. The Gospel text is: “And I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but let us go to him.” Juvencus’s interpretation is this: “Your faith will be stronger because you will understand that, even while absent, I knew that Lazarus had died.” Others explain it thus: “I rejoice that I was not there, because then I would not have refused help to the sisters who asked, and Lazarus would not have died. But your faith will be increased more by Lazarus’s resurrection than if I had driven illness away from him.” Saint Augustine, Bede, and others adhere to Juvencus’s interpretation. The second interpretation seems more common; it is stated more clearly in the Tridentine Gospel Book: “Lazarus has died, and I rejoice for your sake that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Menochius says that the Vulgate’s words, “because I was not there,” should be joined with “I rejoice”: namely, “I rejoice that I was not present when he died, so that, once he had died, an opportunity for performing a miracle might present itself.”

331. “Let us go,” etc. He explains John’s words: “Let us also die with him.” The old version, as well as the Tridentine Gospel Book and Augustine in this passage, has: “And let us die with him.” The relative “with him” may refer either to Christ or to Lazarus. In either case, however, the meaning is: “Let us go, prepared to undergo the death that the Jews threaten Christ and his disciples.”

355. The manuscripts have *ista haec* (“these things”). The printed editions vary between *ista* and *isthaec*. Fabricius, with a question mark, has: “Do you believe these things with a pure heart, Martha?” Poelmann and Hadamarius have: “If you believe these things with a pure heart, Martha.” Romanus, together with Aldus, has: “If you believe these things, say with a pure heart, Martha.” Aldus places the question mark after “Martha.” Reuschius does likewise, printing: “Do you believe these things with a pure heart, Martha?” Observe that *si* (“if”) is used for *num* (“whether”), as in book II, verse 412; some think that the reading is *si credunt* (“if they believe”).

The printed editions have “about to advise her sister as she hastens.” Regius and Ottobonianus in the first hand have “about to move as she hastens,” and Regius’s gloss has “about to call.” In Ottobonianus, *motura* appears to have been corrected to *matura* (“hastening”). Romanus has, corruptly, “Martha hastening her sister.” The reading *motura* (“about to move”) seems more genuine, since verse 362 has “she warned.” It is therefore used for “about to rouse” or “about to call.” Aldus, incorrectly, has “and Martha, about to advise her sister as she hastens.”

400. Daventr. reads *Si tantum*. Rom., together with most printed editions, reads *Qui tantum*. Reg. and Ott., together with several manuscripts of Reuschius, read *Qui tanti*; and the gloss in Reg. explains *tanti* as “many.” This is the sound reading and interpretation. John 11:45: “Then many of the Jews who had come to Mary and Martha, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him.” Although most copies of the Old Latin version, including the Tridentine Gospel Book, and the Greek text do not name Martha at this point, the manuscript of St. Martin and one Greek manuscript cited by Sabatier have “Mary and Martha,” as Juvencus also reads it. *Tanti* for *multi*, or *tot* (“so many”), just as *quanti* for *quot* (“how many”), is not contrary to Latin usage, as can be confirmed by examples from Plautus, Lucan, Valerius Flaccus, Statius, Dracontius, and others. The Spanish and Italian languages derived *tantos*, *tanti* for *tot* from *tanti*.

401. Reg. reads *honore*, with the gloss “through” or “because of.” Others read *honorem*. *Tantae virtutis* (“of such great virtue”) would not be inappropriate.

409. Matthew says: “They were saying: Not during the feast, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people.” *Populi raperent furorem* (“the peoples might seize fury”) is a figurative construction: for fury seizes peoples, or peoples are carried away by fury. Horace, *Epode* 7, verse 13: “Is it blind fury, or does a stronger force carry us away?” Badius explains Juvencus thus: “Lest the peoples should turn the agitation of their minds toward arms.”

When he had said this, he immediately stood at the very entrance of the tomb,

filling the hollow rocks with a song directed toward the opposite side:

[Col. 0311B] 351 “Lazarus, receive the one returning to his limbs from sleep,

[Col. 0312A] behold the soul, and you yourself come forth from the tomb.”

[395] Without delay, with hands and feet suddenly bound together,

he comes forth from the tomb; a woven cloth covers his face,

and a slender band binds his entire body.

Then he ordered him to be unbound and sent him rejoicing back to his home.

When the Jews saw the venerable deed,

[400] those who had followed Mary and Martha in such great numbers,

some, believing, followed the honor of the holy power;

but others returned to the city and reported all the miracles

to the proud leaders, the Pharisees.

352 Therefore a more weighty body of scribes and people is summoned to the council,

[405] now the more distinguished group, where the splendid halls

of the high chief-priest Caiaphas shine.

There it pleased them to cast Christ down to death;

but to avoid the days of Passover, lest among the numerous people

[Col. 0312B] the discordant peoples should seize a fury leading to war.

[410] He was at the house of Simon, whom the dreadful leprosy

[Col. 0313A] [Note: [Col. 0313B]]

411. Rom. reads *defugerat*. Reg., together with the printed editions, reads *diffugerat*. Rom. and Reg. read *ecce jacenti*; and the gloss in Reg. explains *jacenti* as “reclining.” Fabr. reads *ecce cubanti*. Most printed editions read *en recubanti*. Reuschius expressly rejected the reading *ecce jacenti* found in his manuscripts as well, but unjustly. *Jacere* is suitably said of those reclining at table. Silius, Book XI, verses 343 and following:

> You are deceived by believing that he is unarmed among the tables . . .  
> When such a disaster has occurred, will the hands of his companions,  
> and of those lying nearby, grow numb?

412. Reg., Rom., and Torn. read *sanctumque alabastro*. Most printed editions read *frangensque alabastrum*.

413. Reg. and others read *fragrantis*, but Reg. writes *flagrantis*, and this word is written in the same way in many ancient manuscripts. Poelm. and others read *fragrantia*.

414. Ald. and Bas. read *perfundit*; others read *perfudit*.

416. Reg. and Ott. read *corpus*; Ott., instead of *d. s.*, together with others, reads *corpora*.

418. The manuscripts, together with Ald., read *justam*, as at verse 421, a reading worthy of much praise. Most printed editions read *justo*.

[Col. 0313C] 424. Our manuscripts, together with Torn., read *Judas, et ad proceres*. Most printed editions read *Judas, qui ad proceres*. I would willingly read *Juda, atque ad proceres*, for Christian poets such as Prudentius and Dracontius like to place *Juda* in the nominative.

427. Ald., Fabr., Bas., and Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, and Westhem. in the text, read *Argenti ter dena illi mox pollicebantur*, but the metrical rule rejects this. Accordingly, some have emended it to *mox pollicitantur*. Our manuscripts, together with the manuscript of Barthius and others of Reuschius, and with the printed editions of Had., Poelm. in the text, and Westh. in the margin, present the spondaic verse:

> They immediately set out thirty weights of silver for him.

This is the true writing and corresponds to the Greek text and the Vulgate; but because the structure of this verse was not understood by copyists, they corrupted it freely. Bede, *On the Art of Meter*, chapter on the joining and separation of syllables, also reads *ter dena argenti*. In this I disagree with him, however, because he thinks that it sounds like *denarigenti*, so that in the fifth place a dactyl, rather than a spondee, may at least be perceived by the sound. See note 207 of our dissertation on hymns.

428. Our manuscripts read: *Pondera: his Judas*, in which *h* has the force of a consonant. Or read: *Pondera: iis*, namely, “with those weights,” or “with the thirty pieces of silver.” Here too I would restore *Juda*, with the final syllable shortened before the following *sc* of the word. The printed editions read: *Pondera: dehinc Judas*. In Aldus, *Pondere* is perhaps an error for *pondera*.

430. Rom., Poelm. in the text, Hadam., and Fabr. read:

> The disciples ask where they should celebrate the Passover supper.

Reg. has the same, but reads *rogitant* (“ask”) instead of *quaerunt*. Ott. and Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, read: “The disciples ask Christ where they should celebrate the Passover.” Ald., Daventr., and Bas. read: “The disciples ask Christ where they should celebrate the Passover.” In Ottob. the *a* may perhaps have been erased, or one may read: “The disciples ask Christ where they should celebrate the Passover.” Concerning the word *quaesunt*, see the variant reading at Book I, verse 284.

431. Ott. reads *Velit*, correctly emended to *vellet*.

[Note: [Col. 0313C]]

411. This is not established by the Gospel. He is indeed called Simon the Leper, but the Evangelists do not explain how he acquired this surname. Most of the ancients think that he had formerly been a leper but was healed by Christ. Others believe that it was a family name, as among the Romans there were the Claudii and so forth.

412. *Alabastrum* was the name of a certain kind of ointment-box, resembling a pear and without handles. Such vessels were usually made of onyx marble, which was therefore called *alabastrites*. Perhaps Mary Magdalene’s ointment vessel was of glass, which could more easily be broken. Yet vessels made of alabaster stone are also not difficult to break.

413. Matthew says “an alabaster vessel of precious ointment”; Mark, “an alabaster vessel of precious ointment of spikenard”; John, “a pound of precious ointment of genuine nard”; and in the Tridentine Gospel Book, “a pound of genuine ointment,” with *nard* and *precious* omitted. Juvencus names olive oil because olive oil is commonly understood in place of ointment. Catullus, poem 6, verse 8: “Fragrant with garlands and Syrian olive oil.” Propertius, Book III, elegy 15, verse 31: “A light scent will flow from the fragrant olive oil.”

415. “The bodies of the needy poor,” in place of “the miserable poor,” as in Book II, verse 731, *germana corpora*, and so forth.

418. *Puellam* (“the girl”): likewise Arator concerning the Samaritan woman, Book I, verse 942:

> As the girl sits above the mouth of the well, she seeks cups of water

and in the same work, verse 1113, concerning Mary Magdalene:

> Whom the first girl proves to have returned from the darkness.

See the note on verse 197 of this work.

422. *Funeris officium* (“the service of burial”) is appropriately said of funeral rites.

423. CHAPTER XII. Judas asks the price in order to betray Jesus; while dining, Jesus foretells that he will be betrayed by one of his disciples. Thereupon he institutes the sacrament of his body and blood, and foretells that Peter will deny him three times before the cock crows. Matthew 26:14; Mark 14:10; Luke 22:3; John 18.

[Col. 0314D] 426. *Monstrare* (“to show”) is used for “to deliver” or “to point out.” Tacitus, Book IV of the *Histories*, chapter 1: “The worst of slaves voluntarily betrayed their rich masters; others were pointed out by their friends.”

428. *Pondera* (“weights”) is a generic term for a specific object. “He submitted himself to crime” is an elegant metaphor: he yielded and bound himself to a grave crime, which settled deeply, even into his inmost heart.

429. Matthew: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread.” Luke: “The day of Unleavened Bread arrived.” The Gothic-Hispanic, or Isidorian, Missal, Thursday of Holy Week, in the Vercelli and Verona manuscripts, reads “the day of Passover.” Juvencus understands this in such a way that he counts the first day of Passover from the evening of Thursday. Others understand it differently. See below, verse 600.

431. Matthew: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him.” In the old version, manuscript of Clermont: “Go into the city to So-and-so and say to him,” namely, from the Greek *πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα* (“to a certain person”). This is just as when someone says in Spanish *a fulano*, or among others *a N.*, which signifies a name and is taken from ancient books. The ancients used the pronoun *ille* (“that one”), as the Spaniards use *el tal* (“such-and-such a person”). See Mazochius on 1 Samuel 21:2. Someone might suspect that Christ’s name was stated but that the Evangelists suppressed it. Juvencus seems to think otherwise; and from Mark and Luke it is more readily concluded that Christ omitted the man’s name.

His power had put it to flight. Behold, a woman approaches him as he reclines, breaking an alabaster vessel in which were precious ointments of widely fragrant olive oil, and pours them over Christ’s head. The disciples rebuke her, saying that the bodies of wretched needy people could be helped by the price of the ointment. The Lord forbids these words and approves the deed: “Cease to hinder a deserving girl in her service. There will always be time to help the poor, but it will not always be granted to you to see me. She renders a service for my burial, highly worthy of praise, and such deeds will fill the world.” Then one of the disciples, Judas, madly withdraws and runs to the leaders with these words: “What reward may I hope for, if I can betray to you and point out the master whom you have long sought?” They immediately set out thirty weights of silver; with these Judas submitted himself to deep crime. And now the day of Passover had advanced from its first dawn. The disciples ask where he would wish to take the Passover meal; but he orders them to seek for himself a certain unnamed man, who was to receive the Lord’s final commands.

355 As soon as evening came, the twelve reclining together,

the master, with divine voice, addressed them:

[435] “Behold, the time presses on when one of you,

with a criminal heart, will plot to hand Christ over to death.”

Immediately they all ask who, with such an attempt,

could have taken such madness into his heart.

Then he says: “The one who is now dining with me at the feast.

[440] But the Son of Man will undergo the punishment

once appointed for him. Miserable throughout the ages is he

who has betrayed the righteous; how much happier he would be

if he had never touched the threshold of life upon earth!”

356 And Judas, weighed down heavily by a conscience aware of guilt,

[445] says: “Surely such a suspicion touches Judas?”

The Lord replied: “I see you saying such things.”

When he had said this, he began to break the bread for himself with his hands,

and then, having divided it, he gives it, after praying in holiness;

he taught the disciples that he had given them his own body.

[450] [Col. 0317A] [Note: [Col. 0317B]]

451. Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, reads *Magnis sanctificat verbis*; in the text, together with most others, *Gratis sanctificat verbis*. Ald. and Bas. read *Sanctificat gratis verbis*. Badius explains *magnis* as “with words possessing great efficacy.”

453. Reg. reads *redemit*; Ott. likewise in correction, where previously it seems to have read *redimet*. Rom., together with most printed editions, reads *remittet*, which Gallandius prefers from Matthew 26:28: “For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” Gallandius refutes Reuschius, who had asserted that *redemit* clearly agrees with the words of the Gospel. *Remittet* indeed agrees more closely, but *redemit* is by no means foreign to the passage; it was printed by Daventr. and Poelm. instead of *d. s.* Reuschius showed that the whole reading agrees exactly with the Evangelist:

> This blood has redeemed the sins of the people;  
> Drink this, my blood.

I shall now discuss it. He was not concerned about the word *redemit* itself.

454. Reg. and Ott. read *Hoc potate meum*; Rom., together with the printed editions, reads *Hunc potate meum*, a reading defended by Reuschius. Poelmann., instead of *d. s.*, reads *Hoc potate merum*. I think the true reading is *Hoc potate meum*: for in the Greek text of Matthew and Mark it is read in such a way that one may say, “This is my blood”; and Jansenius, chapter 131 of the *Concordance*, accordingly thinks that it should have been translated in this way. In the Old Latin version, in the Cambridge manuscript cited by Sabatier, it is similarly read: “For this is my blood.” Many theologians, whom Suarez cites and follows in volume XVIII of *On the Sacraments*, question 78, disputation 58, article 1, section 7, think that the words of consecration, “This is my body,” convey this meaning: “This, which is contained under these appearances, is my body.” In a similar way they explain the words “This is my blood,” or, following the Greek text, “This is my blood.” Ald. and Rom. read *jam veris*; most read *nam veris*, or *nam verbis*; manuscripts and printed editions vary. But *veris* is better.

455. Reg., Ott., and Rom. read *Posthaec*, or *Post haec*, which Aldus printed. Others read *Posthac*.

[Col. 0317D] 456. Rom. reads *munera*; correct to *munere*.

[Col. 0318B] 457. Ottob., Rom., Ald., and Bas. read *concedant*. Reg., together with others, reads *concedent*.

458. Reg. and Ott. write *ymno*.

460. The manuscripts, together with most printed editions, read *tum*. Poelm. in the text, together with some others, reads *dum*.

465. Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, and Ald. and Bas. read *Hinc cum*. The manuscripts, together with other printed editions, read *Post ubi*.

467. Reg. reads *vadens*. Ott., Rom., and the printed editions read *volitans*.

468. For *Respondit*, which all our manuscripts have, Sabatier printed *Respondet*; but in the apparatus he notes *Respondit*. The manuscripts, together with most printed editions, read:

> all, if it is permissible to believe,  
> whom your commandments, as they stumble, might be able to deny

Rom. reads *Qui tua*. Ald. and Bas. read:

> All (if it is permissible to believe),  
> whom your commandments, as they falter, might be able to deny

Torn. reads *Quod tua*. In Aldus, the sense may be: “Chance will change all who, if it is permissible to believe this, could deny your falling commandments, but it will never change my heart.” In the others, the punctuation should be: “Chance will change all, if it is permissible to believe that I can deny your commandments as they falter, but it will not change my heart.” Others punctuate it in other ways, but with no satisfactory sense. I think it should be restored from the Gospel as follows:

> All of them, if it is permissible to believe it,  
> whom your commandments, as they falter, may be able to deny—  
> but chance will never change my heart.

The words of Matthew 26:33 are: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.”

469. Ald. reads *Qui*; others *Quod*. The manuscripts read *possunt*; among the printed editions, some read *possint*, others *possunt*.

470. Fabr. reads *non ullus*; others *non umquam*.

471. Rom. in the text reads *sidera*; since this is good, I do not know why *pectora* is assigned in the margin as though it were a different reading.

472. Rom., Ald., and Bas. read *Inducit*, which Reuschius accepts: for, as he says, what follows is *incubat*. Others read *inducet*.

473. The manuscripts read *trinis*; the printed editions partly *trinis*, partly *ternis*. I would prefer *trina pavidis*, or *trina pavidus*.

[Note: [Col. 0317D]]

456. Matthew says: “Until that day,” and so forth. Sicl., Book I, verse 522: “I speak the truth, until the destruction of heaven, earth, and sea comes,” and so forth. That is, never.

457. “To rise again,” as above at verse 322, *consurgere rursus* (“to rise again”); and at verse 347, “They will certainly rise into the rewards of life.”

463. *Casibus* means “ruins,” “danger,” or “adverse circumstances.” Peter replied: “But adversity will never change my heart.”

466. *Genitalibus* means “ancestral” or “paternal.” Prudentius uses it in nearly this sense in *Hymn* 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 167: “To be consecrated in the ancestral dwelling”; and in Ammianus, Book XXVII, chapter 5, or 11: “ancestral land.”

472. Horace, Book I of the *Satires*, verse 9: “Night was already preparing to bring shadows upon the earth and scatter the stars across the sky.” Virgil, Book I of the *Aeneid*, verse 93: “Black night settles upon the sea.”

473. “It will hear” is a most elegant metonymy, says Reuschius, unless one prefers, with Aristotle and Quintilian, to call this manner of speaking a metaphor. Similar expressions are “the conscious stars” and many others of this kind.

357 From this the Lord takes the cup, filled with wine,

and sanctifies it with words of thanksgiving, then gives it to drink,

and taught them that he had distributed his blood.

And he says: “This is the blood that has redeemed the sins of the people;

drink this, my blood. For believe the true words:

[455] after this I shall never again taste the liquor of the vine,

until the better gifts of the Father’s kingdom of life

allow me to rise again into new wine.”

Then, after singing a hymn in holy harmony,

they all climb the heights of the Mount of Olives.

[460] 358 Then Christ draws these words from his heart:

“All of you, during the time of this present night,

will be miserably scattered far away, with the shepherd abandoned in terror.

[Col. 0318A] For thus it is written: when the shepherd has fallen,

all the sheep will take flight across the fields in different directions.

[465] But after life restores to me the new honors of heaven,

I shall go before you, and, flying gladly through the ancestral fields,

I shall teach your choirs throughout the fields of Galilee.”

Peter replied: “All, if it is permissible to believe that, as they falter, they can deny your commands;

[470] but adversity will never change my heart.”

Then he says: “This night, which will bring the bright stars

upon the earth and now, pressing down the light, settles upon the waters,

359 will hear you say three times, trembling,

that you deny Christ, most courageous Peter.”

[475] [Col. 0319A] [Note: [Col. 0319B]]

475. Our manuscripts and most printed editions read *alitibus*. Reuschius, I do not know why, prefers *altilibus*, which Badius and Schoettgenius refer to domestic birds, among which are roosters and hens. Prudentius, *Hymn* 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 1: “The bird, herald of day,” and so forth. Propertius, Book I, elegy 16, verse 46: “And it resounds among the morning birds.” Juvencus again at verse 584: “The bird follows with its song,” and so forth. *Alitibus* should therefore be retained.

476. Rom. reads *Et Petrus*; others *At Petrus*.

477. Ott. reads *audita*; but perhaps it originally read *oblita*, which the others prefer: namely, that the voice forgets and denies its master. Juvencus more than once attached the same accusative to both a verb and a participle.

479. Reg. reads *Sunt Geste mania rura*. Ott. reads *sunt Gessemaneia rura*, but perhaps it had previously been written *Gessemaneida*. Rom. reads *Getzemaneida*. Most printed editions read *Gethsemaneida*, because, as Omeisius says, poets frequently form patronymics in place of possessives. In the Vulgate, the name of this village on the Mount of Olives is *Geth-semani* or *Gethsemani*. In manuscripts of the Old Latin version it appears as *Getsamani*, *Gessamani*, or *Gethsamani*. It may therefore be read as *Gethsemaneia*, or, with Ott., *Getsemaneia*, or *Gethsemanica*. For *Gethsemanida* is feminine.

480. Our manuscripts read *vitae, lucisque repertor* (“creator of life and light”); some printed editions likewise; others read *lucis, vitaeque repertor* (“creator of light and life”).

482. Ott. reads *resedere*, from which *residere* arose.

483. Reg. reads *Ipse*, which perhaps was also the first reading in Ott. Most editions read *Ille*.

484. Rom. reads *Zebedeoque simul noctis per devia tendit*. Following the Gospel, read *Zebedeique simul natis*, as the other manuscripts express it.

485. The manuscript of Barthius apud Omeisius reads *ore profatur*, as Virgil frequently speaks.

486. All our manuscripts read *Tristitiam volvens*. The printed editions read *Tristitia nunc volvens*, which will seem better to many; but I would not readily alter the reading of the manuscript copies. If one wishes to change it, I would write *Tristia jam volvens*, which comes closer to *tristitiam*.

489. Rom. reads *paululum*; correct to *paulum*. In Ott., *procedens* was correctly produced from *procidens*.

490. Reg. reads *profatur*; others, more suitably, *precatur*.

491. Fabr. reads *calicis pertranseat*; the others *calicis me transeat*.

492. Rom. reads *tracta*; emend to *tractu*.

493. Reg. incorrectly reads *Tua sed jam veniat*. Ott. reads *Jam tua sed veniat*. The printed editions read *Sed tua jam veniat*. In Rom. I find the reading that seems preferable:

> But rather let what has been decreed for you come to pass  
> than our will, which has been appointed for you as the decision in such great matters.

495. Poelmann., instead of *d. s.*, Torn., Ald., and Bas. read *anhelus*; the manuscripts, together with other printed editions, *anhelis*.

496. Reg. reads *Prostratis*; others *Prostratos*. Badius takes *terrae* adverbially, like *humi*, or as a dative, as in Virgil, Book V, verse 48: “We committed them to the earth.” Most read *terra*.

497. Reg. and Rom. read *non est mihi ponere virtus*, with the gloss in Reg. “virtue—for you.” Ott., together with the printed editions, reads *non est tibi ponere virtus*. The former reading expresses the meaning of the Gospel more suitably, Matthew 26:40: “So, were you not able to keep watch with me for one hour?” It should also be noted that Juvencus uses *mihi* with the same meaning as *mecum*. Some ancient versions read *potuisti*, but other ancient versions, the Vulgate, and the Greek text have *potuistis*.

501. Rom. reads *sed labat debile corpus*. Reg., Ottob., Torn., Daventr., Ald., and Bas. read *sed corpus debile labat*. Fabric., Hadam., and Poelm. read *sed corpus debile lapsat*; Westh. in the text *debile labat*, in the margin *debile lapsat*. *Lapsat* observes the rule of meter better than *labat*. See Book II, verse 437.

[Note: [Col. 0319D]]

475. Prudentius, *Hymn* I of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 13:

> That voice with which the birds resound,  
> standing beneath the very roof.

Virgil, Book VIII, verse 456: “And the morning songs of birds beneath the roof.”

476. *Sumere mortem* (“to take death”): see the variant reading at Book II, verse 193.

479. CHAPTER XIII. Jesus withdraws to the village of Gethsemane and prays to the Father in the garden. Matthew 26:36; Mark 14:42; Luke 22:40; John 18:1.

487. *Morte tenus* means “unto death.” Consult the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 43.

[Col. 0320D] 492. The number changes from *me* and shortly afterward *nobis*. Concerning this change, see the note on Dracontius, *Elegy*, or *Satisfactio*, verses 19 and 299.

493. *Adveniat* means “may it come,” “may it happen,” or “may it be done.”

495. CHAPTER XIV. Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss. Matthew 26:40 and following; Mark 14:43; Luke 22:27; John 18:9.

498. *Tantis sub casibus*: Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*, verse 560: “Son of the goddess, can you lead sleep through such a disaster?”

500. *Lubricum* is used as a noun by many suitable authors, according to Cellarius and the lexicographers.

And before the roofs of the houses resound with birds.

But Peter: “I would rather undergo a harsh death

than let this voice, forgetful of its master, deny him.”

All persist in promising such strength of heart.

The fields of the Hebrew name are Gethsemane.

[480] The creator of life and light proceeds thither,

whom the disciples soon follow, while Judas flees.

There he ordered the remaining servants to stay behind.

But he himself, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee,

360 proceeds with them into the remote places.

[485] Then, sorrowful with deep anguish, he speaks in these words:

“My heart, turning over grief, troubles my breast

[Col. 0319B] unto death; but now keep sluggish sleep away from you,

[Col. 0320A] and together spend the anxious night in watchfulness.”

He said this, and moving a little farther forward, presses his body

[490] upon the earth; thrown down, he prays in these words:

“If it is permitted, Father, may this cup pass me by,

the violence of suffering pressing upon us with mighty force.

But nevertheless let your will come to pass rather than ours—

your will, which has been decreed as the decision in such great matters.”

[495] Then he returns to the disciples, but sleep had dissolved them all,

laid out upon the earth in their exhausted limbs.

Then he says to Peter: “Have you not the strength to keep watch with me

361 for one hour amid such great dangers?”

But keep watch, I beg you, lest temptation, seizing you,

[500] [Col. 0320B] hurl you headlong through the slippery paths of savage death.

The spirit is vigorous, but the weak body falters.”

[Col. 0321A] [Note: [Col. 0321B]]

504. Reg., Ottob., read *potestas*; Rom., together with the printed editions, *facultas*.

505. The manuscripts, together with Torn., read *proveniat*; Had. and Poelm. in the text *praeveniat*; Ald., Bas., and Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, *perveniat*. This discrepancy arises because in manuscript writing *pro*, *prae*, and *per* are often written in very similar combinations of letters.

507. Reg., Ottobon., and Daventr. read *rursus idem*. Rom., together with most printed editions, *isdem* or *iisdem*. *Idem*, namely Christ, as the gloss in Reg. explains, is preferable. Fabricius, as I think, printed *rursus per idem* by conjecture.

508. Ald. reads *fessos nexo*. In Reg. there is an error, *longuore*.

510. Rom. reads *Jam venit*; others *Nam venit*. Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, reads *ille*; in the text, together with the others, *ecce*. Rom., Reg., Ottob. in the second hand, Fabr., read *dedat*. Ott. in the first hand reads *dedit*. Most printed editions read *tradet*. Perhaps it should be restored from the manuscripts as *dedet*, or *dedit* in the present tense of *dedo, dedis*. *Dedat* is also good, with the same meaning as *dedet*. Compare the variant reading at verse 442 of this work.

511. Ott. and Reg. in the first hand read *imponit*. Reg. in the second hand, Rom., and the printed editions read *imponet*.

512. Ald. reads *Hoc dicto*; Bas. *Quo dicto*. The manuscripts, together with other printed editions, read *Cum dicto*, a reading I have shown to be sound at Book II, verse 597, *Cum dicto*, and so forth, as Aldus also reads it there. In Rom., *misero* is an error for *numero*, and perhaps *caterva* in Torn. is also an error for *catervae*.

513. Ald. and Bas. read *Advenit, et procerum*. The conjunction *et* is superfluous.

515. Reg. reads *sequebatur*; others *sequebantur*.

[Col. 0322B] 516. The manuscripts read *Oscula nam pepigit sese contingere Christi*. The printed editions agree; but Poelmann., instead of *d. s.*, cites *Dulcia nam Christi tacturum se oscula pactus*. Reuschius explains *pepigit* as “he made an agreement,” as one makes peace or forms an alliance. *Oscula* means “the mouth.” He adds that these two words, being misunderstood, gave occasion for alteration. But the same interpretation applies to Poelmann’s different reading.

518. The manuscripts and many printed editions read *Ille ubi dissimulans blanda cum voce salutat*. Ald., Bas., and Poelm., instead of *d. s.*, read *Hic ubi dixisset simulata voce salutem*, against Reuschius.

519. Reg. and Ott. in the first hand read *venerabilis*. Ott. in the second hand, Rom., and the printed editions read *miserabilis*, namely, “miserable Judas,” as above at verse 517, “by which he might easily deceive the unknown miserable crowd,” and concerning Judas himself at verse 441, “Miserable throughout the ages is he.” Nevertheless, I prefer *justi venerabilis* (“the venerable [mouth] of the righteous”).

523. Reg. writes *macera*; Rom. and Ott. *machera*.

[Col. 0322C] 524. Ald. and Bas. read *famulo, et sublatus*; the manuscripts, together with other printed editions, *famulo sublatus*, which yields the better sense.

525. The manuscripts and many printed editions read *et excussam*; Poelmann. in the text, together with others, *et excisam*; instead of *d. s.*, *ei caesam*.

527. The manuscripts read *confidet*; many printed editions likewise, others *confidit*. Similar variation is found in the ancient versions. Rom. in the margin reads *judice* instead of *vindice*.

528. Rom. in the margin reads *Nunc* instead of *Hunc*. Retain *Hunc*.

529. Reg. reads *possem*; Ott. and Fabr. *possim*; Rom. *possum*, which most printed editions prefer.

[Note: [Col. 0321C]]

505. May it come about, ensue, take place. Tacitus, *Histories* II.16: “With futile assistance, even had it succeeded.”

507. Book III, verse 85, likewise passive: “With the Father having been entreated.”

509. He joins and explains Matthew’s words: “Sleep now and rest … Rise, let us go.”

[Col. 0321D] 511. Below, verse 545: “By which they could inflict death upon innocent Christ.”

512. The number of the throng, the multitude.

514. Pignorius, *De Servis*, p. 120 ff., counts among military slaves the *caculi*, *calones*, *clavatores*, and *galearii*, who were accustomed to be armed with clubs and wooden nails for guarding their masters; Juvencus confirms this also in the present verse.

516. “To touch with kisses,” that is, “to touch the face.” Shortly afterward, verse 519: “He touched with his lips the face of the venerable just man.”

520. *Totum* means “everything.” Wopkensius gives many examples in his notes on Sedulius III.113: “You who can accomplish everything.”

521. “To have come for a purpose,” that is, “for the sake of coming”; *paratu*, “preparation” or “equipment,” as elsewhere.

523. **CHAPTER XV.** Peter cuts off the servant’s ear. Matthew XXVI.51 ff.; Mark XIV.47; Luke XXII.49; John XVIII.10. Book I, verse 247, similarly: “And the mother’s life with a flashing sword.”

524. *Vatis*, “of the prophet,” that is, “of the priest.” Badius says that Caiaphas is called a prophet because of the prophecy: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people.” “Raised to anger”: finely expressed.

525. “At the time”: because he removed one ear. Sometimes *tempus* in the singular also signifies both times.

526. *Noster* is used emphatically. Terence, *Adelphoe* 5.8: “He is good; he is one of us.”

527. “He trusts in the avenging sword.” Koenigius proves that *confidit* with the ablative is Latin usage, that *ferrum* means “sword,” and that *vindex* is correctly used adjectivally.

529. Badius notes that *an* is lengthened irregularly, although in his view it should be shortened. I have shown elsewhere that this opinion rests on a weak foundation. See the variant readings at verse 517 of Book II. “The heavenly armies”: this is how angels are called in sacred Scripture. See the note on Dracontius II.475.

[Col. 0322C] 531. Poelmann, in place of the second reading, has *dedita*; in the text, together with others, *debita*. Reuschius says that *dedita* is not an unsuitable word, but that *debita* should be read from Matthew: “Because thus it must happen.”

532. Aldine, Basel, Tornacensis, Fabrice, and Poelmann read and punctuate, in place of the second reading:

“But you, with drawn sword, why do you seize me—  
with clubs and swords you rush together? Behold, I came to meet you,”

or *Occurro*. The manuscripts, together with other editions, have:

“But you, who with drawn sword seize me—  
with clubs and swords you rush together; behold, I came to meet you,”

or *Occurri*. The Roman edition has: “But you who seize me with drawn sword,” etc. The first reading is clearer and more straightforward, but the second seems more authentic.

534. Fabrice has *Occurro*; the Reginensis, and, from correction, the Ottobonianus, *Occurri*. The Roman, the first hand of the Ottobonianus, and most editions have *Occurram*.

536. Aldine and most editions have *Insonuit*. Poelmann, in place of the second reading, and Tornacensis have *In solum*, which Reuschius also printed, contrary to Gallandius, who thought it had been introduced without manuscript authority. All our manuscripts, however, read this way; and in the Reginensis there is a gloss: *in solum*—“against me, when I was alone.” The Roman and the first hand of the Ottobonianus have *latrantibus*, corrected to *latratibus*, as most read. I much prefer *latrantibus*, namely, “with so many barking all around,” which Koenigius also approved, citing Augustine’s Letter 136: “The heretics barking all around.” It is better, however, to take *circum* adverbially. It should nevertheless be noted that *latratus* occurs here at verse 14. Many Latin writers used *tanti* for *tot*; Juvencus did so here at verse 400. Many editions have *audax*, but the manuscripts, together with other editions, give *ausus*, which must in every respect be retained in our text.

538. The Roman, Ottobonian, and Reginensis manuscripts above have *Caiphea* or *Cayphea*; the Reginensis in the text has *Caipha*; the editions have *Caiphaea*. The Roman, Ottobonian, and some editions have *astiterat*; the Reginensis and other editions have *steterat*.

539. Westhem has *Cum venere*; in the margin, *Convenere*. Reuschius prefers *Cum venere*, because he thinks the sense requires it. I have judged otherwise.

[Col. 0324B] 540. Some editions punctuate the words awkwardly: “following the tracks, alone—secretly sad he sat,” etc.

546. The first hand of the Ottobonianus has *nullo*; the second hand correctly has *nullus*. The Reginensis has *visus super esse*, which may likewise have been the first hand’s reading in the Ottobonianus. Others have *visus satis esse*.

547. The Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Tornacensis, and Aldine have *Ultima prosiliunt*. The Roman, corruptly, has *Ultimi prosiliunt*. Basel has *Ultimo prosiliunt*, which could be defended if *ultima* were shortened, as in *postremo*. Fabrice, Hadamarius, Poelmann, and others, to avoid this difficulty, read *Tandem prosiliunt*. But the reading of the ancient manuscripts, *Ultima prosiliunt*, should not be abandoned, where *ultima* is used adverbially, as in the similar passage discussed above at verse 190. The Reginensis glosses: *ultima*—“an adverb, finally.” Reuschius likewise accepts this Graecism, while noting that *ultimo* and *ultime* are also correctly used. For the ancients sometimes pronounced adverbs ending in *-o* and *-e* with only a brief difference. The Reginensis and Ottobonianus have *dicere Jesum*; the Roman, with the editions, *dicere Christum*.

548. The first hand of the Ottobonianus and Westhem in the text have *possit*; the common reading is *posset*.

[Col. 0324C] 549. Aldine, Basel, Westhem in the text, and the second hand of the Roman have *ternis*. Most manuscripts and editions have *trinis*.

555. The Roman has *Edicasque palam*; better is *Ut fateare palam*. The second hand of the Ottobonianus, with the editions, has *si fas te credere Christum*. The Reginensis has *si fas est te credere Christum*, contrary to the meter; this also seems to have been the first hand’s reading in the Ottobonianus. The Roman has *si fas est credere Christum*.

557. The Roman, Reginensis, Aldine, and Tornacensis have *Ista haec*; the Ottobonianus and others have *Isthaec*. The manuscripts and editions punctuate as follows: “These words alone proceed from your breast—true, nevertheless …” But, following Reuschius, I think it should be punctuated: “These words alone proceed from your breast—true: nevertheless he will come,” etc.; or, with the Reginensis: “True in your case: he will come,” etc. “True: nevertheless he will come” agrees more closely with the words of the Gospel. Matthew XXVI.64: “Jesus says to him: You have said it; nevertheless I tell you,” etc. In some ancient versions, however, we read: “You have said it; truly I tell you.” The Savior’s words, “You have said it,” contain a reply by which he acknowledges that what the high priest was asking was true—namely, that he was the Christ, the Son of God. Accordingly, the adjective *vera* should be joined with *verba*, especially since *sola* indicates that this alone was truly said by the high priest.

[Col. 0321B]

He withdrew again to the citadel of the secluded mountain,

and prayed to the Father: “Most merciful ruler of all things,

since it is not possible for this cup to pass,

[505] may your will now come about from our lot.”

Again he found the disciples weighed down beneath sleep

and again, having entreated the Father, addressed

those bound by the weary languor of repose:

“Now you may sleep and revisit your companions.

[510] For behold, he has come who will betray my body

to every deed, which the plot will impose upon my stained limbs.”

At these words Judas arrived, accompanied by a multitude,

at the command of the rulers and the savage people.

[Col. 0321B] Some followed with drawn swords, others trusting

[515] in the weight of closed clubs, the promised signs

of the raging Judas.

For he had agreed to touch Christ with kisses,

so that the pitiable crowd might easily seize the unknown man.

When Judas, concealing his intent, greeted him in a gentle voice,

he touched with his lips the face of the venerable just man.

[520] Immediately Christ said: “You may complete everything,

whatever reason has brought you here with this preparation.”

The crowd laid hands upon him and seized Christ.

Then one of the disciples, with flashing sword,

rushed upon the servant of the prophet, raised to anger,

[525] and at that moment tore away his ear by the violence of the wound.

Christ said to him: “Put away the sword, our man.

For whoever in his fury trusts in an avenging sword,

a just vengeance of a like sword will await him.

Can I not summon the heavenly host

and lead the Father’s countless companies into battle?

But the Scripture appointed for my deeds must be fulfilled.

But you who seize me with drawn sword,

rush together with clubs and swords. Behold, I came to meet you,

I who always sat teaching with you in the midst of the Temple court,

and no one dared such acts against me while so many barked all around.”

The disciples scattered, fleeing and leaving Christ behind.

Now the Savior stood in Caiaphas’s hall;

all the scribes and summoned rulers assembled.

But Peter, alone keeping at a distance,

sat secretly sorrowful among the attendant crowd,

awaiting the final issue amid so great a turmoil.

Behold, the priests zealously seek false witnesses

and wish to fabricate charges

by which they might inflict death upon innocent Christ.

But none seemed sufficient for so great a fury.

At last witnesses came forward, who had heard Christ say

that he alone could overthrow the Temple

and restore it, once overthrown, in three days.

The chief priest, burning with rage, persists

in pressing the silent man, and speaks thus:

“Why do you dare make no answer now to charges so grave,

convicted before the rulers’ true witnesses?

Yet I shall adjure you by the realms of highest Thunderer,

that you plainly confess whether you profess yourself to be Christ.”

Then he addresses the proud man in these words:

“These alone are words that proceed from your breast—true words;

nevertheless the majesty of the Son of Man

will come to be seen by you through the air, when it sits at the right hand of holy Power beneath fiery clouds.”

[Col. 0322C] **CHAPTER XVI.** He is condemned, blasphemed, and beaten in Caiaphas’s house. Matthew XXVI.57 ff.; Mark XIV.50 ff.; Luke XXII.54; John XVIII.24.

540. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.711: “And from far away the wife should preserve the tracks.”

541. *Ministra* is adjectival; see the note on Dracontius III.642.

542. *Turbine*: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.614: “Stunned by so great a whirlwind of misfortunes.” This noun is frequently used in this transferred sense.

544. *Incumbunt* with the infinitive. Virgil, *Georgics* IV.249: “They apply themselves to repairing the ruins of their fallen race.” *Contexere*, “to weave together,” “to fabricate.” Cicero, *Pro Deiotaro* 6: “How cleverly the charge is woven together!”

[Col. 0324D] 545. Compare verse 511 above.

551. *Insisto* for *persto*, “I persist,” “I continue,” is frequently used with the infinitive.

553. “Before true witnesses”: Reuschius explains this as follows: since Christ was not accusing them of falsehood, he is asked whether, by remaining silent, he acknowledges their testimony to be true.

554. Matthew says: “I adjure you by the living God.” To swear by heaven, however, is a true oath. Thus Juvencus, Book I.574: “Nor is it permitted for a man to swear by high heaven—for it is the dwelling of the Lord.”

555. *Si fas*, that is, *an fas*, “whether it is lawful,” after the manner of the Greeks, as in Book II.412: *Si credunt* for *an credunt*, as many read.

[Col. 0325C]

And can I not summon the heavenly host

and lead the Father’s countless companies into battle?

But the Scripture appointed for my deeds must be fulfilled.

But you who seize me with drawn sword,

rush together with clubs and swords. Behold, I came to meet you,

I who always sat teaching with you in the midst of the Temple court,

and no one dared such acts against me while so many barked all around.

The disciples scattered, fleeing and leaving Christ behind.

Now the Savior stood in Caiaphas’s hall;

all the scribes and summoned rulers assembled.

But Peter, alone keeping at a distance,

sat secretly sorrowful among the attendant crowd,

awaiting the final issue amid so great a turmoil.

Behold, the priests zealously seek false witnesses

and wish to fabricate charges

by which they might inflict death upon innocent Christ.

But none seemed sufficient for so great a fury.

At last witnesses came forward, who had heard Christ say

that he alone could overthrow the Temple

and restore it, once overthrown, in three days.

The chief priest, burning with rage, persists

in pressing the silent man, and speaks thus:

“Why do you dare make no answer now to charges so grave,

convicted before the rulers’ true witnesses?

Yet I shall adjure you by the realms of highest Thunderer,

that you plainly confess whether you profess yourself to be Christ.”

Then he addresses the proud man in these words:
