“These alone are words that proceed from your breast—true words;

nevertheless the majesty of the Son of Man

will come to be seen by you through the air, when it sits at the right hand of holy Power beneath fiery clouds.”

558. The Reginensis and apparently the first hand of the Ottobonianus have *Vera tuo veniet vobis*. The Roman and the second hand of the Ottobonianus, with the editions, have *Vera tamen veniet vobis*.

559. The Reginensis, Ottobonianus, Tornacensis, and Roman have:

“The majesty of the Son of Man, with the right hand of holy  
Power, sits beneath fiery clouds.”

In the Roman, *proles* appears for *prolis*. Poelmann, in place of the second reading, has:

“The majesty of the Son of Man, while the right hand of holy  
Power sits beneath fiery clouds.”

Poelmann in the text, Fabrice, and Hadamarius have:

“Majesty—the Son of Man’s power—to the heights,  
when he shall sit at the right through fiery clouds.”

Aldine, Daventria, Reusch, and Basel likewise have *hominis proles* for *proles hominis*. The manuscript reading should be retained: *assidet* is the future of *assido, assidis*, and *ignicoloris* comes from *ignicolorus*, a word Juvencus uses here at verse 155. *Dextera* is not a substantive but must be taken adjectivally—namely, “when the majesty of the Son of Man sits at the right hand of holy Power.” Thus he renders the words: “sitting at the right hand of the Power of God.”

[Col. 0325C] 560. See verse 155 above.

563. “Of one who fights against God,” that is, resists and opposes him. This is a poetic use of *pugnare* with the dative, but it was employed by many writers and is therefore elegant.

564. Book II.697: “A generation polluted by evils seeks.” In this book IV.615: “The people inflamed by evil”; Book I.535: “Lest anyone dare to rise in anger.”

568. *Colaphi* are blows delivered with the fist; *alapae* are blows struck with the open hand against the cheek. Juvencus explains both, as Sedulius does in Book V.96: “Nor did the accursed crowd cease to strike the head everywhere with blows, to beat it with the palms, or to spit in the face.”

570. “You will prophesy”: I discussed this verb in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn 13, verse 101.

571. **CHAPTER XVII.** Peter denies Christ three times. Matthew XXVI.69; Mark XIV.66; Luke XXII.55; John XVIII.25. Juvencus gives a plausible reason why the maid recognized Peter as Jesus’ disciple: “sad, because she had seen him.” Matthew says: “Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard,” namely outside the place where Christ was being questioned, but in the courtyard and therefore inside the palace; hence Juvencus says, “sad, because she had seen him inside.” Above, verse 541: “Secretly sad, he sat among the serving people.”

574. Above, verse 394: “And you yourself, come forth outside from the tomb.”

575. Mark says after the first denial: “And he went out before the courtyard, and the cock crowed.” Juvencus interprets this as “first beneath the threshold.” Peter had therefore withdrawn from the courtyard and was again questioned in the vestibule. Matthew narrates: “As he was going out through the doorway, another maid saw him,” etc.

581. “With accursed words”: Matthew says, “He began to curse and swear”; Mark, “He began to anathematize and swear.” The Itala version of Matthew has: “Then he began to devote himself and swear that he did not know the man.” The same expression occurs in the old version of Mark. From this Juvencus took “swearing all things with accursed words”; Peter was devoting himself to curses and invoking every evil upon himself if what he asserted was not true. Properly, *devotus* means “assailed by curses and imprecations”; the word frequently occurs in this sense among ancient writers. Catullus, poem 63, verse 135: “Forgetful, you carry home through accursed perjuries.” In Juvencus, *devotis verbis* seems to mean “with words by which Peter devoted himself.”

[Col. 0325C]

“True: nevertheless the majesty of the Son of Man

will come to be seen by you through the air, when it sits at the right hand of holy

Power beneath fiery clouds.”

At these words the priest tears the garment from his breast and, raging and blind at heart, cries out: “You have heard the foul words of one who fights against God. Let religion, polluted by evils, rise in anger; and now let all of you disclose your judgment.”

All cry out and strive to condemn him to death.

367. Then shameless spittle covers Christ’s holy face; open-hand blows upon his cheeks and frequent fist-blows upon his head assail him, while all strive to mock him with their words.

[570] “Christ, prophesy: whose hand has struck you?”

A woman, seeing Peter sorrowful within, said: “Were you too, young man, added as a companion to this man whom the rulers’ mocking judgment condemns?”

He denies it and tries to make his way outside under cover.

[575] But another woman, seeing him go out beneath the first threshold, addressed the servants in a similar voice. Again she said that, swearing, he denied knowing him.

368. Then many questioning bystanders came up and said that they recognized him by the sound of his voice, because all his words rang with a Galilean speech.

[580] And Peter, swearing every word with self-imprecations, affirmed in denial that he did not know who that man might be.

[Col. 0327A] 585. The Roman has *Circumstant verba tristem praesagia Christi*. The second hand of the Reginensis has *Circumstant tristem vera praesagia*, though perhaps *verbis* stood in place of *vera*. The Ottobonianus has *tristem muneri praesagia*, a different reading, or a correction; beside it *verbis* is supplied for *muneri*, which is certainly inept. The editions have *Circumstant tristem verbis praesagia Christi*. I prefer *tristem vera praesagia*, lengthening the final syllable of *vera* both because of the caesura and because of the two consonants in the following word. Alternatively, *veri* may be read for *vera*.

586. Most editions have: “And thereafter, going out, he poured forth bitter laments.” The Roman, Ottobonianus, Reginensis in its first hand, and Tornacensis have: “And thereafter, going out, his bitter laments were present.” Strictly speaking, prosody forbids shortening the final syllable of plural *ploratus*, but similar examples occur among later poets, so this reading could be defended. Nevertheless, I prefer the correction made by the old hand of the Reginensis: “And thereafter the bitter lament had Peter as he went out,” with the gloss “going out—Peter.”

587. Our manuscripts have *jam luci*, though the Reginensis may have had *lucis*. Among the editions, some have *jam luci*, others *jam coeli*, from which someone might conjecture *jam coelo*. But *jam luci concedunt* is satisfactory, since *concedunt* is used for “depart.” Sabatier’s *lucis* is less good.

Hearing this cry, a bird follows it with song,

beating its wings beneath the roof’s ridge;

Christ’s true predictions encompass sorrowful Simon.

As he went out, bitter weeping seized him.

369. The stars now yield to daylight, and the swift sun

advances, filling the earth with trembling rays.

[Col. 0327C] 588. The manuscripts, Aldine, and Basel have *trepidantibus*. Tornacensis, Daventria, Reusch, Poelmann, and others have *crepitantibus*. It is preferable to read *trepidantibus*, that is, “trembling.” Some prefer *vibrantibus*. Barthius, Book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 1, defends *crepitantibus*. For although no one has ever heard the sun crackle, nevertheless, since it is the most excellent fire, the poet may rightly attribute to it what belongs properly to blossoming flame.

591. The Roman has *celsus*; *celsum* is better. The Reginensis has *stetit*; others, *stans*. But if in the following verse one reads “Having heard such words,” etc., *stetit* must be restored here in place of *stans*. Sabatier published *dominum stantem*.

[Col. 0328A] 592. The Reginensis, Poelmann in the text, Fabrice, and Hadamarius have: “Pilate pressed him, having heard such words.” Tornacensis likewise has this, but with *orsit*, apparently an error for *ursit*, as in Sabatier’s *arsit*. Reuschius confirms that the verse is clear if *exceptum* is understood as “heard.” This also avoids the more frequent designation “Christ” or “Jesus.” The Roman, Ottobonianus, Aldine, and Basel have: “Jesus received such words from Pilate.” Daventria combines both readings: “standing before the tribunal—Pilate pressed him, having heard such words—Jesus received such words from Pilate: ‘You are king,’” etc. Badius does the same. Reuschius’s manuscripts agree with ours. The sense is that Jesus heard such words from Pilate.

593. Our manuscripts, Aldine, Basel, and Poelmann in place of the second reading have *quod dicitur*. Tornacensis has this and punctuates: “the nation (as it is called) stands?” In the Reginensis there is a gloss: *quod*—“said.” Other editions have *qui dicitur*.

594. The Reginensis and Ottobonianus have *Respondit Jesus*, which does not sound like Juvencus; for elsewhere he often pronounces the trisyllabic name *Iesus*.

596. Our manuscripts have *scelerata facundia*; Tornacensis, *scelerosa facundia*. Most editions have *mendax facundia*, which accords with metrical rules. *Scelerata* or *scelerosa facundia* cannot easily be defended according to prosodic rules. But since the reading rests upon manuscript authority, one may infer from it that “the holy man is pressed by the eloquence of crimes,” namely *scelerum* for *sceleratorum*. See the variant readings at verse 644 here and the note on Dracontius II.421: “Amid so many throngs of crimes, one pious and innocent man.” In the Roman, *perstat* is an error for *pressat*.

598. Fabrice has *quaerit, quaenam sit causa*. The Roman, corruptly, has *Pilatus quae tum sit causa tacendi*. The Aldine has *quaerit quae tum sit*.

601. Perhaps: “One condemned to death.”

603. The Reginensis has *infessus*; read *infensus*.

[Col. 0327C] 583. On the clapping of birds, see the note on Dracontius I.257. Above, verse 475, the cock is also placed on the roofs of houses. Consult the learned and elegant work of Francesco Cancellieri, *De Secretariis Basilicae Vaticanae*, Book II, chapter 14, where he discusses why ancient Christians placed roosters on bell towers. Montfaucon, in *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum Manuscriptorum*, column 196, lists among the manuscripts of the Vatican Library a work entitled: “Why a rooster is usually placed above the house of the Lord, that is, the Holy Church.”

587. **CHAPTER XVIII.** Jesus is led bound to Pilate, accused before him, and questioned by him whether he was king of the Jews. Then, when Pilate tells the Jews that at that time they were accustomed to release one of the condemned, they cry out whether they want Jesus or Barabbas released: “Barabbas,” and “Let Christ be crucified.” Matthew XXVII.1 ff.; Mark XV.1; Luke XXIII.1; John XVIII.28.

589. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.57: “Behold, meanwhile, with his hands bound behind his back.”

590. “To the lap,” that is, to the tribunal, to Pilate sitting there. Badius says: “to the middle of his embrace,” or “to full authority.”

593. *Astas*, “you stand”; this is a judicial term. Horace, *Satires* I.9.38: “May I perish if I can stand, or know civil law.” *Astas* may also simply be understood as “you are,” like *exstas* in Dracontius more than once, as the Index shows.

594. *Vestris* for “your.” See the note on verse 492 above.

600. Matthew: “On the solemn day,” etc. Many infer from this that Christ was crucified on the very day of the Jewish Passover; Juvencus favors this view, as I said at verse 429 above. Others begin Passover at the evening of the sixth day, or on the day on which the Savior suffered death. Compare Calmet’s dissertation on this subject.

602. “Of notorious name,” that is, infamous. Matthew: “They then had a notorious prisoner,” etc. “A notorious robber” and “a notorious bandit” are quite common expressions.

The stars now yield to daylight, and the swift sun advances,

filling the earth with trembling rays.

Already they were dragging Christ, bound behind his back,

from the council to the governor’s tribunal amid a great uproar.

Meanwhile the Lord, standing before the lofty tribunal,

received these words from Pilate:

“Are you, as it is said, king of the Jewish nation?”

Christ replied: “I hear these things from your words.”

370. Then a terrible accusation of the just man arose,

roared out, and the holy man was pressed by the eloquence of crimes.

Jesus did not deign to answer anything.

Pilate asks what was then the reason for his silence.

He persists still more and maintains wondrous silence.

But perhaps on the solemn day the laws customarily commanded

one condemned to death to be released.

There was also in chains a robber of notorious name,

whom the people, hostile to Christ, wished to release alive.

[Col. 0329C] 609. The term “law” means custom, as at verses 600, 611, and 625.

610. “With ambition poured out”: with zeal poured out for seeking votes in favor of Barabbas and against Christ.

612. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.177: “And he inflames his spirit with words and heaps up his anger.” The use of *incendere* for “to stir up” or “to provoke violently” is common. *Accendones* were those who incited gladiators to fight. Salmasius restored this word in Tertullian, *De Pallio*, final chapter, where others read *cerdones*.

620. *Increpitans*, “shouting,” as in Book I.402.

622. *Maneo* is elegantly used of things that threaten, especially in adverse circumstances; it is often construed with the accusative and sometimes with the dative. *Genti* means the Israelite people, as noted at Book II.120.

627. **CHAPTER XIX.** Judas, moved by repentance, returns the money and hangs himself from a fig tree; with the money for which Christ was sold, a field is purchased in which the bodies of the condemned are buried. Matthew XXVII.3 ff. Juvencus postpones the whole account of Judas returning the thirty pieces of silver. Matthew arranges the matter as follows: “And having bound him, they led him away and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor. Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing,” etc. “But Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him,” etc. Most therefore establish a harmony by supposing that Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver before Pilate condemned Jesus to death. Lamyus, indeed, thinks that Jesus was not led directly from Caiaphas’s house to Pilate, but first to the Temple, where the seat of the Sanhedrin was; at that time Judas, moved by repentance, met the chief priests and elders, and for this reason is said to have thrown the silver into the Temple. This conflicts with the Evangelists’ words more than the harmony constructed by Juvencus. For after Matthew had narrated that Jesus was led to Pilate, before subsequently weaving together the sequence of the entire Passion, he anticipated Judas’s repentance. This may have occurred only when Christ had already been condemned to death by Pilate but had not yet undergone it.

[Col. 0329A]

It was burning; but Pilate’s wife, terrified by dreadful visions in sleep,

held her husband back with commands and prayers,

asking that the just man be spared punishment.

Then the judge again tries to discover the rulers’ mind

and, at the people’s command, sends word to ask

whom they wished to release from the impending punishment.

[610] But the rulers, with ambition poured out, were asking the people

to demand the robber according to custom and kill Christ.

But after the rulers’ judgment inflamed the crowd,

and it demanded that the robber’s life rather be granted to it,

the governor asked the people what they wanted for Jesus.

[615] The people, inflamed by evil, stirred savage riots

and again and again demanded the punishment of the cross

for the one who desired the name of king, who had confessed himself

an enemy of Caesar, and who had condemned himself with his own mouth.

At last, overcome by force and rejecting the bloody office,

he cries out that he keeps his heart free from this blood

and, before them, washes his hands of the crime,

so that the stain alone might remain upon the nation.

372. They cry out all the more: “Upon us, upon us, let this blood fall,

and upon our race let this crime and guilt rebound.”

[625] Pilate releases Barabbas to the people in accordance with custom,

and delivers Jesus, bound, to the punishment of the cross.

But the traitor Judas, after seeing such things,

having received the price of his crime, that he had sealed the mad deed,

unhappy, condemning his actions with anguished complaints,

then threw the silver into the Temple, detesting it.

[Col. 0331A] 631. The Roman inserts another verse after this one: “And to consume just punishments with bonds and nooses,” etc.—“Formless,” etc.; it is superfluous.

635. The Aldine and Basel have *Sed dare*. Others have *Quod dare*. The Roman and Aldine have *cum* for *dum*. The Reginensis and Ottobonianus have *detraheretur*. The more suitable word is that found in the Roman and the editions, *distraheretur*. Thus Dracontius, on the same subject, Book II.510: “The seller and buyer are stained by blood torn apart.”

636. The Aldine has *agri*; the others, *agrum*.

638. The Reginensis has *Haec condam cooperta*. The Ottobonianus has *Haec quondam comperta*. The Roman, with the editions, has *Haec quondam cooperta*. Poelmann, in place of the second reading, has *cadens*; in the text, with most witnesses, *canens*.

643. The Aldine has *Traditur injustis justus*; others, *Traditus est trucibus justus*. Fabrice has *Traditus at trucibus*. Reuschius considers this the true reading because the sense requires the particle *ast* or *at*, which is frequent in Juvencus. In this passage it is certainly superfluous.

644. Our manuscripts have *Militibus scelerata ludibria corpore praebet*; but the Ottobonianus has *praebent*, which may perhaps have been the first hand’s reading in the Reginensis. The editions have *Militibus scelerata opprobria corpore praebet*; Fabrice has *Innocuas* for *Militibus*; the same Fabrice, Poelmann, and Westhem in the margin have *perfert* for *praebet*. The consistent reading of the manuscripts, *ludibria*, confirms that this is the true reading, especially since the first hand of the Ottobonianus had *lidibria*, corrected by an old hand to *ludibria*. But should we believe that Juvencus shortened the first syllable of *ludibria*? I do not think so, since shortly afterward, at verse 651, he makes the first syllable of *ludibria* long. I shall therefore read: “He bears upon his body, for the soldiers, the mockeries of wicked men”—that is, *sceleratorum ludibria*, as I noted at verse 596. Ignorance of this meaning led the scribes first to write *scelerata* for *scelerum*, and then, to accommodate the meter, to introduce *opprobria* for *ludibria*.

[Col. 0331B] The supplied source ends here, incomplete.

632. Some have handed down that Judas hanged himself from an elder tree, others from a sycamore, most from a fig tree, which, they say, was shown in the Valley of Jehoshaphat even in our own times. Juvencus seems to be the author of this opinion, although some say that he spoke poetically, putting one species of tree for the genus. On the contrary, Bede, *On the Holy Places*, ch. 4: “On leaving David’s Gate, one comes upon a spring running southward through the valley, at the midpoint of which, on the west, Judas is said to have hanged himself. For there stands there a great and very ancient fig tree, in reference to which Juvencus says: ‘He seized a hideous death,’ etc.” From Juvencus and Bede, Baronius, *Annals*, A.D. 34, no. 76, proves that tradition from the ancients held that the tree upon which Judas hanged himself with a noose was a fig tree. He confirms that the fig tree could still have survived in Bede’s time from Tacitus, *Annals*, XIII, at the end, who tells something similar about the fig tree which had sheltered the infancy of Romulus and Remus. On the manner of Judas’s death, see the notes on Dracontius, book II, v. 564, and Theophilus Raynaudus, vol. IX. Juvencus calls hanging a hideous death, after Virgil, book XII, v. 603: “And from the high beam he ties the knot of hideous death.” Similarly Tacitus, *Annals*, VI.49: “Papinius chose a sudden and hideous end, throwing his body headlong.” Homer calls this sort of death impure, *Odyssey* X.464. Mazochius adduces much else, vol. I of the *Spicilegium Bibliorum*, ch. IX on Genesis 4; he thinks this popular belief arose from the command given to Noah’s sons and descendants: “Except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood.” St. Leo, sermon 52, or 3, *On the Passion*, ch. 3, perhaps imitates Juvencus when he says of Judas: “You would have delayed the hanging of hideous death.” Other things worthy of notice may be adduced from Casaubon’s *Exercises against Baronius*.

635. St. Bruno of Asti likewise presses the Jews on this point, on Matthew, vol. II of the latest Roman edition of his works, p. 129: “I say: If it was not lawful to put them into the corban, because they were the price of blood, neither was it lawful to take them from the corban so that they might become the price of blood.” The Vulgate writes *corbonam*; the Greek text and the Old Latin, *corbanan*.

[Col. 0332B] 636. Badius here adduces Virgil, *Aeneid* I.371: “And, having purchased the ground, they called it Byrsa from the hide.”

638. Perhaps Juvencus had read manuscripts in which the prophet’s name was not expressly given. For now, in most manuscripts, Jeremiah is named here as the prophet. Jerome, on this passage of Matthew, thinks that the testimony [Col. 0332C] was taken from Zechariah, not Jeremiah. Augustine, book VII, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, ch. 2, argues thus: “If anyone is troubled because this testimony is not found in the Scripture of Jeremiah the prophet, and therefore thinks that something must be detracted from the Evangelist’s credibility, let him first know that not all manuscripts of the Gospels have ‘spoken through Jeremiah,’ but only ‘through the prophet.’ We might therefore say that those manuscripts which do not have Jeremiah’s name are rather to be believed: for this was spoken through the prophet, namely Zechariah.” Nevertheless, this defense does not please Augustine, who maintains that the testimony is found in Jeremiah, not in words but in substance.

640. The sacred text has thirty pieces of silver, namely shekels, which, by some calculations, amounted to 32 solidi and six denarii. The Hebrew mina was worth 60 shekels, or pieces of silver; the greater Attic mina contained 100 drachmas and the lesser 75 drachmas. Two drachmas were approximately equal to half a shekel. Juvencus therefore used one kind of coin for another, or [Col. 0332D] one species for another, as above, at 427 ff., “thrice ten weights of silver,” genus for species.

642. Again, because it was first the price of blood and afterward the price of the field.

643. CHAPTER XX. Jesus is mocked by the soldiers, clothed in a scarlet cloak, and crowned with thorns. Matthew 27:27 ff.; Mark 15:16; John 19 ff.

645. Matthew says: “They put a scarlet cloak around him”; Mark: “And they clothe him in purple”; John: “And they put a purple garment around him.” A slight distinction is noted between scarlet and purple; scarlet is sometimes also confused with purple because of its affinity with it. Purple [Col. 0333C] was made from the juice of a small fish, and its red was darker and more intense than scarlet, which was made from the grain of the kermes shrub, or from the little worms adhering to it. Sometimes purple was added over scarlet to make it more pleasing. From these facts the Evangelists are readily reconciled. Some think that Christ was clothed in a purple garment and additionally wrapped in a scarlet cloak; for the *chlamys* was a round military cloak in which soldiers were in some sense wrapped. Juvencus favors this interpretation. It is certain that emperors were customarily clothed indiscriminately in scarlet and purple. The soldiers, however, wished to reproach Jesus for having aspired to kingship. Juvencus confirms the Old Latin version of the Vercelli manuscript in Matthew: “And they clothed him in a purple tunic and put a scarlet cloak around him.” The manuscript of St. Gatianus at Tours and Origen have much the same reading, as Iricius observes in his notes on the Vercelli manuscript. Sedulius, book V, v. 164, is added: “And when the Holy One, given over to cruel soldiers for punishment, went away—he is clothed in a worthless cloak under the covering of red scarlet, so that the whole appearance might be an image of bloody death.” Here others read *sublegmine* as one word.

373 Having begun to inflict his punishments upon himself by the noose,

He seized an ugly death from the top of the fig tree.

Then the priests, saying that it was the price of blood,

Believed it unlawful now to store it in the temple’s sanctuary,

[635] Although they thought it had previously been lawful to give it, while the blood-price was being distributed,

They bought a field in the name properly belonging to

Blood, marking impious crimes by a dreadful deed.

[Col. 0332A] 374 These true words of the prophet, once concealed, he sang,

And disclosed the outcome of events in the order of time:

[640] The godless set out thirty minas of silver,

Establishing this as the price of the precious body,

Which soon afterward was transferred again to the potter’s little field.

The righteous man was handed over to savage men and criminal servants,

To soldiers: he bears the mockery of crimes in his body,

[645] 375 And they clothed him in a purple tunic and a reddened cloak.

[Col. 0333A] **Notes**

646. In the Regius manuscript *Induerunt* (“they clothed”) seems to have stood, from which *Induunt* (“they clothe”) now remains. Torn., Bas., and Rom. likewise have *Induunt*, which Aldus had also printed but corrected in the Errata to *Induerunt*. For *Induunt* cannot stand metrically. Ott., Poelm. in the text, Daventr., Fabr., and Hadam. have *Inducunt*. I consider the genuine reading to be *Induerunt*, with the third syllable shortened, as poets sometimes do in similar perfect forms.

648. Rom. and Ald.: “they greet him as lord and king.” Reg., Ott., and Fabr.: “as king and lord.” Hadam. and Poelm.: “as king, or lord.”

649. Reg. has *Jude agentis*, corrected to *Jude aegentis*, perhaps so that it might be understood as “of the Jewish nation.” Rom., Reg. in a second hand, Ald., Torn., and Bas. have *faciemque lavere* (“and they washed his face”); hence Daventr. has *faciemque lavare*. Ort., Reg. in the first hand, Fabr., Hadam., and Poelm. have *faciem lavere*. The latter should be retained, for in the perfect *lavere* the first syllable is long. *Lavit*, when its first syllable is shortened, is the present tense of *lavo, lavis*.

652. Rom. has *propere*; read *propriae*. Rom., Ott., Reg. in the first hand, Ald., Bas., and Torn. have *ducebant*, which is elegant. Reg. in the second hand, with some printed editions, has *ducebat*.

653. Reg. has *trahebat*. Rom., Ott., and most printed editions have *trahebant*.

654. Poelm. has *coepere*; correct to *cepere*.

655. Ott. has “of the Cyrenaean nation, and to bring the wood.” Rom. has “born a Cyrenaean,” etc.; Reg. has “born a Cyrinaean,” etc., with a gloss explaining “from his homeland.” Daventr. and Westhem. print this in the text. Fabr. has *Cyrene*; Hadam. and Poelm., *Cyrenae*; Ald. and Bas., *Cyrena genitum*. Torn. likewise has *Cyrena genitum*, but instead of “and to bring the wood” reads “and to carry the wood.” Reuschius reads “to carry the wood, born at Cyrene.” The words of the ancient versions are “a man of Cyrene,” as it is also read in the Vulgate, or *Cyrineum*, *Quirinaeum*, or *Cyrinaeum*.

656. Our manuscripts have *jussis suffigere saevis* (“to fasten with savage commands”), but in Ott. the earlier reading was *figere*. The printed editions have partly this reading and partly *duris suffigere clavis* (“to fasten with hard nails”), following Aldus. Barthius, according to Koenigius, preferred *gumphis suffigere saevis*. *Gum­phus*, or *gomphus*, is a Greek word denoting a nail.

658. Rom. has *Ast postquam perventum est*; read *At postquam ventum est*. Reg. writes *Gulgotha*; Ott. and Poelm. *Golgotha*; Ott., in the first hand, and Rom., with others, also have *Golgotha*, a spelling found in the ancient versions as well.

659. Reg. in the first hand, Ott. in the first hand, and Rom. have *felle vinum* (“wine with gall”), which is acceptable, the final syllable of *felle* being lengthened because of the caesura. All printed editions, together with Reg. and Ott. in the second hand, have *felli*, which is also sound.

660. Poelm. has *tractare* in the margin; in the text, with the others, *tractata*.

662. Most witnesses have *insultans hominum furor* (“the insulting fury of men”). Torn. has *hominem* instead of *hominum*. Ald. and Poelm., in the margin, and Bas. have *immanis plebis furor* (“the monstrous fury of the crowd”). Rom. has *insultans hominum omnia*; *furor* is absent. Ald., Bas., Torn., and Daventr. have *omnia possit*; Fabr., Hadam., and Poelmann., *omnia posset*; Rom., *omnia poscet*; Reg. and Ottob., *omnia poscit*, although in both it may originally have been *omnia posset* or *poscet*. I think the verses have been transposed here; I would arrange them as follows:

> But nevertheless the insulting fury of men demands everything.  
> Yet he refuses the drink offered at the first taste.  
> And now the body fastened to the cross hung upon the tree,  
> And, by lot, one soldier’s possession preserved  
> The texture of the untouched tunic,  
> So that what had been foretold long ago might be fulfilled.  
> And the inscription, etc.

Recall Matthew 27:34–35: “And they gave him wine mixed with gall. And when he had tasted it, he would not drink. But after they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.’” Perhaps, while retaining the rest of the verse-order I have proposed, one should read after *Ut satis*: *Nec tamen insultans hominum furor omnia poscit*, or *posset*, because they left the tunic intact, casting a lot over it.

They clothed him and encircled his head with bloody thorns,

And, in place of a scepter, a reed accompanied his right hand.

Then, kneeling, they hailed him as king and lord

Of the Jewish nation; they washed his face with spittle,

[650] And madly played wicked games with wounds upon his holy head.

When the mad soldier had completed these mockeries,

376 They led him, clothed in the covering of his own garment,

And dragged the holy and righteous man to the punishment of the cross.

But as they went out, behold, they seized a certain Simon,

[655] [Col. 0334A] Born at Cyrene, and ordered him to carry the wood,

By which the unchanging order of the age pressed insistently

To fasten the Lord of light by savage commands.

But after they had come to the place called Golgotha,

They gave Christ cups of wine mixed with gall.

[660] But at the first taste he refused what had been offered,

So that what had been foretold by such words might be fulfilled,

Yet the insulting fury of men could not demand everything.

[Col. 0335A] **Notes**

663. Poelm., in the margin, has *Cruci affixum* (“fastened to the cross”). Most manuscripts and printed editions have *crucifixum* (“crucified”), but *cruci fixum* must be written as separate words, so that the final syllable of *cruci* may be lengthened; in the compound *crucifixum* it would have to be shortened according to the rules of prosody.

664. Poelm. in the text, Daventr., Ald., and others have *Intactamque dedit tunicam*. Our manuscripts, and Poelm. in the margin, have *Intactaeque dedit tunicae*. The sense of our reading is: “By lot, among all, the possession of one soldier gave the texture of the untouched tunic”—that is, preserved the tunic’s woven fabric. Thus it was not divided. Reuschius prefers the former reading with this explanation: “So that one soldier might possess the intact texture, therefore it happened that the possession sought by several, though it had to and could fall to one alone, gave, or assigned, the untouched tunic by lot among all,” that is, granted an equal right to each.

665. *Textum*, a substantive meaning “cloth” or “woven garment,” occurs frequently among the poets. John says: “The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout”—that is, made by approximately the same process by which knitted stockings are now produced. See Braunius, book I, chapter 16, *On the Garments of the Hebrew Priests*, no. 14.

666. Matthew has: “And they placed above his head the written charge against him.” *Titulus* (“title”) and *causa* (“charge”) are used interchangeably in this matter. Compare Hanke’s discussion of the title of the cross and Samuel Reyher’s dissertation on the titles of crucified Jesus and on the hour of the crucifixion.

667. Most witnesses have *plebis, gestisque*. Reuschius has *gentis, plebisque*, so that, after Juvencus had said “king of the Jewish nation,” he might, in accordance with the impious Jews’ thinking, correct himself: he was not king of the nation but of the crowd. I do not believe that thought occurred to Juvencus.

668. Reg. and Ott. have *poenae pariter*; Rom. has *pariter poenae*. The printed editions vary in the same way.

669. Rom. has *duos*; correct to *duo*.

672. The manuscripts have *trino*; several printed editions likewise; Ald. and others have *terno*.

[Col. 0336B] 673. Reg. has *sobolis venerando*; Rom. *soboles veneranda*; Ott., with the printed editions, *proles veneranda*.

676. Ott.: “But the Pharisees and the scribes together, and the mad faction.” The others have the reading printed in the text.

678. Hadam. and Poelmann. have *aeterna*. The manuscripts, with most printed editions, have *aeternae*, as does the gloss in Reg.: *aeternae—why this?* The passage is certainly obscure. Perhaps Juvencus hints that the Pharisees did this in order to increase the punishment. Aldus punctuates: “They shake them madly, to the eternal bonds of punishment—Was he not once accustomed to preserve others from cruel bonds of illnesses?”

680. Ald., Poelm., and Hadam.: “From the bonds of illnesses? Why does he not free himself from the bonds?” Rom. and Fabr. likewise, but with *poenis* (“punishments”) instead of *vinclis*. Ott.: “From the bonds of illnesses? Why does he conquer his own punishments?” and earlier had *cor* instead of *cur*. Reg.: “From the bonds of illnesses? Instead of freeing himself from punishments,” and *poenas* seems to have stood. I understand *pro* as *proh!* (“alas!”).

681. Torn. has *et regem*; read *en regem* (“behold the king”).

682. Reg., Ottob., Daventr., Torn., Ald., and Bas. have *Debuimus*. Rom., with some printed editions, has *Debemus*.

683. The manuscripts, with Torn., have *poterimus credere signis* (“we shall be able to believe the signs”). Poelm., Fabr., and Hadam. have *poterimus credere verbis* (“we shall be able to believe the words”). Ald., Bas., and Daventr. have *valeamus credere verbis* (“let us be able to believe the words”), which Fabricius also testifies is found in the Rouen manuscript. Fabricius notes that in *poterimus* the penultimate syllable is long. *Signis* is preferable to *verbis*, for this is what the Jews said in Matthew 27:42: “If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him.”

685. Ald.: “Why does he not want his own offspring?”

686. Rom. has *dextera*; emend to *dextra*.

647. Ambrose, book X on Luke: “The reed too is either grasped in his hand, according to Matthew, or strikes his head, according to Mark.” Clearly both things occurred, and both are expressed by Juvencus, for he later adds: “They played impious games with blows upon his head.”

651. **CHAPTER XXI.** Jesus is judged by Pilate and sentenced to be crucified. Simon of Cyrene is ordered to carry the wood of the cross. Jesus is also given gall and vinegar to drink; he is fastened to the cross between two thieves; a lot is cast over his garment; he is blasphemed. The sun is darkened and the earth is shaken. Then follows the Lord’s cry to the Father, his death, and other events that occurred at his death. Matthew 27:31 ff.; Mark 15:20; Luke 23:26; John 19:16.

657. *Urgeo* with an infinitive: see the note on verse 446 of book III of Dracontius.

658. Tertullian lengthened the middle syllable in *Golgotha*; Juvencus, Cyprian, and others more correctly shorten it.

660. *Tractata*: “handled,” “touched.” Horace, book II, letter 1, verse 235: “The handled inks remove their mark and stain.”

662. Accept Schoettgenius’s interpretation: Christ tasted the vinegar first so that Scripture might be fulfilled; then he merely tasted it with his lips, so as not to do everything that would satisfy the fury of the crowd. On this matter, however, I suspend my judgment.

377 And now the body, fastened to the cross, hung upon the tree,

The possession of one soldier preserved the texture of the untouched tunic by lot among all.

[665] And they placed the written title of the charge and of his merit,

Because he had been king of the Jewish crowd and nation.

378 It happened that two thieves bore together

The fellowship of punishment, one on either side; but the blind

[670] Madness of the raging crowd insults Christ, fastened to the cross:

“This is he who alone could destroy the temple;

This is he who could restore the light in a threefold course.

But now let the revered offspring of the Thunderer descend,

[Col. 0336A] And free his body and soul from the punishment of the cross.”

[675] The leaders of the foolish crowd follow up these words;

And the Pharisees, the scribes, and the mad faction

Mock him, shaking their heads and tongues with insane words

Toward the eternal bonds of punishment.

“Was he not once accustomed to preserve others from the savage

[680] Bonds of illness? Alas, he cannot free himself from punishment.

Behold the king whom we were bound to believe

The king of our nation: let him free his body from the wooden cross;

Then we shall rightly be able to believe the holy signs.”

379 “He trusts in God the Father: why does the revered power

[685] Not wish to release its own offspring from punishment?”

No less do they reproach him, groaning on the right and left.

[Col. 0337A] **Notes**

688. Aldus had printed, with others, *cursus lucis* (“the course of light”); in the Errata he corrected it to *cursu lucis* (“in the course of light”), namely, “the sun had ascended the middle of the heavens in the course of light,” etc. Westhem. has *conscenderat* in the text, which is preferred by the manuscripts and printed editions; in the margin, *transiverat*.

689. Daventr. has “when suddenly he fled from their eyes.” Bas. has “when suddenly she fled from their eyes”; Aldus likewise printed that reading but corrected it in the Errata to “when suddenly he fled from their eyes.” Reg., Ott., and Rom. have “when suddenly he fled from their eyes.” Most printed editions have “when suddenly he fled out of their eyes.” The reading of our manuscripts is sound, although *fugit* is in the perfect tense.

691. Reg. and Ott. have *conscenderat*; Aldus and some printed editions likewise. Poelm. and others have *transiverat*, to which the erroneous *transierat* in Rom. corresponds.

693. Rom., Bas., and Ald. have *At*; others have *Et*.

694. Rom. has “but the ignorant crowds think they call him Elijah”; correct to “but the ignorant crowd thinks they call him Elijah.” Torn. likewise has the error *plebs* for *plebes*. *Plebes* is properly used as a singular nominative even by the best Latin authors—Cicero, Sallust, Hirtius, Livy, Phaedrus, Lucan, Florus, Statius, Pliny, Claudian, and others. The singular nominative *plebis* is also read in ancient inscriptions. See no. 51 of the Prolegomena, where I reported from Reuschius that in a certain manuscript *turba*, or some similar word, had been incompetently written for *plebes*.

696. In Ott., *spongo* was changed into *spungo*, as it was also read in Barthius’s manuscript. The letters *u* and *o* are easily interchanged. The more common spelling is *spongo*. In Greek it is written σπόγγος (*spongos*), but in Latin it is usually called *spongia*. I would readily believe that Juvencus wrote *spongia*, with its final two syllables contracted by synaeresis; for the Vulgate and the Itala use the word *spongia*.

697. Rom. has *portare*; correct to *potare* (“to drink”).

700. Ald.: *qui sede*.

701. Rom. has *e miserum*; Ott. *et miserum*, instead of *et misero* in the others. Ald. and Poelm., in the margin, have *crucifixum*; the others, with the manuscripts, have *confixum*.

703. Ald. printed *Aethereis* in the text and *Aetheriis* in the Errata. Either spelling is possible. Most printed editions, with our manuscripts, have *Aethereis*. Rom. has *Aethereisque*, where the conjunction *-que* is superfluous.

704. Rom. has *Finduntur* instead of *Scinduntur*, which is the more correct reading.

705. Reg. has *derupta*. Rom. and Ott. have *disrupta*; the printed editions have partly this form and partly *dirupta*. Tertullian has *dirupta* in *Against the Jews*, chapter 13: “And the monuments were torn open.”

706. Rom. has *excussa*; read *concussa*, unless one prefers to read “the whole earth was shaken by its weight.”

708. The manuscripts, with most printed editions, have *monumenta*; some printed editions have *monimenta*.

709. The manuscripts have *justaeque animae*, as do Ald., Bas., and Reuschius; Gallandius approved this, although he himself printed *vivaeque animae* with most printed editions. The reading *justaeque animae* is supported by the Gospel: “And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose . . . and appeared to many.”

710. Rom. has, erroneously, “and at the command of the people feed.” Barthius, in his note on Paulinus of Périgueux, p. 187, using his manuscript, corrected it to “and having appeared everywhere to the people,” which Schoettgenius considered excellent. Reuschius retained “and having been seen, they suffered the people”; thus Latin authors say *pati contactum* (“to undergo contact”). Our manuscripts have *latae*, but Ott., in the margin, *lata*. The printed editions vary between *latae* and *late*.

711. See whether the conjecture “thus all signs terrify the world” is correct.

714. Rom. has *dextre Dei*; correct to *dixere Dei*.

692. *Consternata*: disturbed, perturbed, confused. Ovidius uses the same word of the horses of the sun in book II of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 314.

694. *Plebes*: some think these were Roman soldiers who did not know the Hebrew language.

698. *Cachinno* and *cachinnor* mean “I laugh immoderately.” Here the word means “to mock.” Apuleius uses it in a similar sense in book III of the *Metamorphoses*: “He laughs at my destruction.”

699. Koenigius observes that *ne* is used for *num*. Matthew has: “Let us see whether Elijah will come,” etc.

703. The soul is called a companion of the heavenly ears because it is spiritual, and nothing among things known to us can better be compared with it than the ear, which is also called spirit. Compare the Prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 15.

704. There were two veils in the temple: one separating the sanctuary, or Holy of Holies, from the holy place; the other hanging at the very entrance of the holy place. The Evangelists merely say that the temple veil was torn, which most interpret not of the veil hanging before the innermost sanctuary but of the outer veil. Juvencus, poetically, as I think, used the plural *velamina* (“veils”) for *velamen* (“veil”).

705. Barthius, book XXXV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 10, observes that among poets *carbasus* may denote any veil or any thin woven fabric. *Carbasus*, and in the plural *carbasa*, is a type of extremely fine linen, first discovered, Pliny says, in Hispania Tarraconensis, book XIX, chapter 1. Hence it is commonly used for a garment or veil of fine linen. Harduinus, in his note on the cited passage of Pliny, says that the fabric called *toile batiste* in French may properly be called *carbasum* in Latin.

707. *Suo de corpore*: the rocks, torn away from the mountain itself, leap apart, or break and leap apart from the mountain as a whole. Petronius Arbiter, poem on the civil war: “The broken peaks thundered, the mountain ridges falling.”

The thieves, guilty men, were fastened to crosses by lot.

The sun had already climbed the middle of the heavens in its course of light,

When suddenly it fled from their eyes and was clothed in dark shadows;

The sun concealed the trembling day in night.

But when the disturbed sun had climbed to the ninth hour,

The startled lights returned to their own world.

And Christ called upon the Father in a loud voice

According to the custom of the Hebrew language; but the ignorant crowd

[695] 380 Thinks that he is calling upon Elijah. Then one man, rushing forward,

Forced a foul sponge, fastened to a reed,

To place the sour drink pressed against his lips.

The rest of the frenzied crowd laughed aloud with such words:

“Let us see whether Elijah, perhaps sent down from heaven,

[700] Will come, he who rests in his lofty seat,

And free the wretched king fastened to the stake.”

Then the Lord’s cry, sent forth with great exertion,

Joined his soul, as its companion, to the heavenly air.

At once the holy temple’s veils were torn,

[705] 381 And the linen fabrics, ripped apart, gaped open in two directions.

The trembling earth was shaken by the whole weight,

And the rocks, torn from their own body, leapt apart.

Then the monuments of ancient men stood open, their barriers removed,

And righteous souls returned through their limbs;

[710] And, having been seen, they passed through the broad walls of the city

And wandered about: thus all things terrify the world.

The hearts of the soldiers were first shaken with fear—

Those who had guarded the bodies handed over to savage punishment—

And they called him the offspring of God and confessed Christ.

[715] **Notes**

715. Rom. has *Et speculis* instead of *E speculis*.

717. Rom. has *Jamque decedenti*; Reg. and Ott. *Jamque decidenti*; neither fits the meter. Ott. in the second hand and Poelm. in the margin have *Jam decedenti*; other printed editions have *Jamque recedenti*.

720. Torn. has *ab Arimathea*; others *ab Arimathia*; Aldus writes *Abarimathia*. The Vulgate has *Arimathaea*; other ancient versions have *Arimathia* or *Arimathaea*.

721. The manuscripts, with Torn., have *praebebat Iesu*. In Ott. in the first hand, *praebeat* stood, which cannot be accepted either by sense or meter as a form used by Juvencus. Most printed editions have *praestabat Iesu*.

724. Ott. has *praeses, et corpus*, which is preferable, the final syllable of *praeses* being shortened because of the caesura. Reg. and Rom., with the printed editions, have *praeses, sed*.

726. Ald. and Bas. have *Concludunt limen*; the other printed editions, with the manuscripts, *Limen concludunt*.

733. Ald., Torn., and Bas. write the word in Greek as πλάνος. But this is entirely unnecessary: it is written *planus* in Latin by Cicero, Gellius, Petronius, Horace, Pliny, Capitolinus, Arnobius, and others. Nor was there any need for Sabatier to transpose the words as follows: “Now it is fitting to remember: since that impostor used always to promise to the common people.” For *planus*, meaning “rogue” or “swindler,” has a short first syllable. Horace, book I, letter 17: “Nor does the swindler, once mocked in the streets, care to rise on his broken leg.” Augustine, sermon 44, volume V, column 217, uses the same word in this very matter: “Lord, we have heard that that impostor—that is, that swindler—said to his disciples that he would be killed and would rise again.” Since the word can suitably be taken from Greek, I do not see why Fabricius, in his commentary on this verse, asserts that it was derived from the insolence of a certain *Planus*. I know that some once held this view. But I want a reason, not an authority.

735. Reuschius advises reading *lumina vitae* (“lights of life”), not *limina* (“thresholds”), since darkness and light are plainly opposed here. I find *lumina* elsewhere as well: again at verse 757, *lumina vitae*, and at verse 762, *luminis oras*.

736. Reg., Rom., Daventr., Ald., and Bas. have *Cum trino solis*; Ottob. *Cum solis trino*; other printed editions *Cum terno solis*.

737. Rom. has *Sed protinus*; correct to *Sed petimus*.

739. Reg. has *replens*, which perhaps also stood in Ott., where *recens* now appears, together with Rom. and the printed editions. The true reading is: “And the last error will be worse than the first.”

741. Our manuscripts, with Daventr., Ald., and Bas., have *Servare, ut vultis*. Poelm., Had., Fabr., and Torn. have *Servate, ut vultis*, which I prefer. Thus the Gospel reads: “Pilate said to them: You have a guard; go, guard it as you know”; and the ancient versions have “You have guards” or “You have soldiers.” Juvencus says *Servate, ut vultis* (“Guard it as you wish”), not *Servate, ut scitis* (“Guard it as you know”), although the latter would also fit the meter, because he expressed the matter itself. Augustine, sermon 44, volume V: “Pilate said to them: You have soldiers; go, guard it as you wish.”

742. In Reg. and Ott. in the first hand, *saxisque* seems to have stood; now it has *saxique*, as in Rom. and the printed editions.

743. Rom. has *limite*; emend to *milite*.

715. **CHAPTER XXII.** The Lord’s body is placed in the tomb. Matthew 27:57 ff.; Mark 15:42; Luke 23:50; John 19:38. A *specula* is an elevated place from which we look out upon something. The same idea is gracefully repeated at verse 727: “From the watchtowers the women preserve and observe everything.” Older women of any kind were commonly called *matres*, and the word was a title of honor. In Plautus, *Rudens* I.5, the women Ampelisca and Palaestra greet the female priest in this way: “We bid you be well, mother.” The priestess replies: “Greetings, girls.” The same usage occurred with the word *father*. Among Christians both titles are given, as marks of honor, to religious men and women.

717. *Vesper*, *hesperus*, *vesperus*: see the note on book III, verse 569.

718. *Justior* used for *justissimus*: compare the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 12, *Cath.* verse 77.

719. *Extremum munus* (“the final service”), as in book II, verse 20: “The last rites are owed to the dead father.”

723. *Vis horrida poenae* (“the dreadful force of punishment”): concerning this phrase, see book I, verse 420.

724. Ulpianus, book I of the *Digest*, “On Punished Corpses”: “The bodies of those against whom punishment is inflicted are not buried unless a request has been made and permission granted.”

725. *Componitur*: see the note on verse 378 of this book.

726. Perhaps by *volumina petrae* (“rolling masses of rock”) he means the rocks, as later at verse 742: “They roll the enormous weights of stone.” Arator, book I, verse 573, uses *volumina* of night: “When the angel came, he drove away the shadowy volumes of night, and suddenly the stars shone in the clear sky.” In two manuscripts I find *atra* instead of *astra*.

728. **CHAPTER XXIII.** The tomb is guarded by armed soldiers. Matthew 27:62.

732. *Erroris laqueos* (“the snares of error”), as in book III, verse 12.

736. *Remeare*, that is, “to be about to return”: a tense used for another tense, as explained elsewhere.

739. *Consurgat*, “may arise.” Thus one says that discord arises, rumor arises, pain arises, a judgment arises in the mind, and anger arises in someone.

743. Matthew says: “After sealing the stone.”

The women watched such great miracles from the watchtowers,

382 All of them who were accustomed to offer service to Christ.

Evening had already begun to succeed the setting sun,

And Joseph alone among the leaders, then more righteous,

Dared to ask for Christ’s body for the final rite.

[720] This man bore the name Joseph of Arimathea,

He who had once lent his ears to Jesus’ words.

He then asks Pilate that the limbs,

Which the dreadful force of punishment had recently deprived of life,

Be surrendered to him. The governor granted it, and they covered the body

[725] With shining linen cloth; it was placed in a new stone cave.

They closed the entrance with the enormous rolling mass of stone.

The women kept watch from the watchtowers and observed everything.

Now daylight was filling the lands with radiant light,

[Col. 0339B] 383 The daylight that, according to the ancient law, always commanded rest:

[730] [Col. 0340A] But the savage fury of the leaders observed no rest.

They came together and jointly burdened the judge’s ears:

“The most just punishment has removed the snares of error.

Now it is fitting to remember, since that impostor used always,

Boasting, to promise the common people

[735] That he would return from the darkness of death to the lights of life

With the sun’s threefold course of return.

But we ask that the soldier guard the new tomb,

Lest a savage audacity to steal the body arise among the disciples

And fresh madness disturb the people.”

[740] To this Pilate said: “A guard is permitted.

Guard the body buried in the earth as you wish.”

384 They came together and rolled the enormous weights of stone,

[Col. 0340B] And guarded the entrance with seals and the stone with a soldier.

[Col. 0341A] **Notes**

744. Rom. has erroneously *qui* instead of *jam*. Heinsius, *Sacred Exercises*, chapter 10, on Mark 16:2, cites this verse as: “The stars of night already yielding to the nearby sun.” But *venturo* (“about to come”) is correct.

745. Sabatier has *tumulo* instead of *tumuli* in the margin; the others have *tumuli*. In Reg. *matres* is absent. Rom. has *septem*; read *septum*.

751. This is the final verse in Rom., immediately followed by “Juvencus ends.” Perhaps the scribe encountered an older codex from which a leaf was missing and assumed that nothing was lacking.

752. Reg. has *fosa*; read *fusa*.

758. Ald. has *sancta*; correct to *sancto*.

760. The Paris manuscript, cited by Omelsius, reads *isthinc* instead of *isthic*, less correctly.

764. Torn. has *persuaderat*; read, with the others, *perfuderat*.

765. Reg. and Ott.: “Joy, astonishment to the stunned, and twofold fear.” The gloss in Reg. explains: “Burning joy poured over the stunned women’s minds, and astonishment poured over their minds with twofold fear.” Ott. in the second hand and Torn. have: “Joy stunned them, and astonishment with twofold fear,” that is, “joy and astonishment poured over minds stunned by twofold fear.” Daventr. and Ald. have: “Joy to the stunned, with sluggish and twofold fear.” Fabr., Had., and Poelm. have: “Joy, sluggishness to the stunned, and twofold favor,” which Reuschius adopted, explaining *favore* as “a voice announcing grace and every good thing.” Juvencus is explaining the Gospel’s words, “with fear and great joy.” Therefore joy and fear, rather than favor, should be mentioned. If *stupor* (“astonishment”) is retained from the manuscripts, I would punctuate as follows: “After these words and sights, burning joy had poured over their minds—joy that stunned them, and astonishment with twofold fear”; that is, burning astonishment poured over minds stunned by joy and twofold fear. Or *attonitis* may be understood in this sense: astonishment had poured over the minds of the women, stunned by joy and twofold fear. Instead of *ardens stupor* (“burning astonishment”), I would prefer *ingens stupor* (“great astonishment”), or something similar.

766. Our manuscripts, with Torn., Ald., and Bas., have *celerantes* (“hastening”); Fabr., Poelm., and Had. have *celebrantes* (“celebrating”).

768. The manuscripts have *iteris medio*; the printed editions have either *iteris* or *viae*.

769. Reg. has *salvare*; read *salvere*.

770. Reg. has *illae, genibus*, without *et*.

771. Ald. has *pavide*; the others *pavidae*.

773. Fabr. has *et isthaec*; the others *et ista*.

774. Some have *hinc*; others *haec*. Juvencus divides *isthaec* into *ista haec*, as elsewhere. *Hinc* has no useful sense. Ald. and Bas. have *referre*; the other printed editions, with the manuscripts, correctly have *referte*.

775. The manuscripts, together with most printed editions: “If concern for seeing us (*nostri conspectus*) exists.” Fabricius, Hadam, and Poelmann in the text: “If concern for our appearance (*noster conspectus*) exists.” Someone might conjecture *ite volantes* (“go, flying”); but *volentes* (“willingly”) is more elegant. Reuschius thought otherwise and adopted this conjecture of Schoettgenius. Schoettgenius adduces much evidence to prove that *volare* can mean “to go quickly,” and accordingly also corrects the same phrase in Statius, *Thebaid* IV.692, and in Josephus Iscanus V.91: *Ite volantes*, instead of *Ite volentes*.

[Col. 0342D] 776. Aldine and Basel editions: *discurrite*; others, together with the manuscripts, *transcurrite*, although in the Regius manuscript it is corruptly *transcurrit*.

782. The Ottobonian manuscript: *redimet*; emended to *redimit*.

[Note: [Col. 0341D]

744. CHAPTER XXIV. Christ rises from the dead on the third day. Matthew 28:1 ff.; Mark 16:1; Luke 24:1; John 20:1.

745. “The enclosure of the tomb”: for tombs were customarily constructed so that they were enclosed by a barrier. Maldonatus, in his commentary on Matthew 8, shows from the form of ancient tombs that they were either cut into rocks or vaulted with stone or brickwork, like wine-cellars today; from this it may be inferred that demoniacs could easily have lived in tombs.

751. *Discluserat*: this very verb occurs in Book III, verse 162.

753. “He addresses the mothers”: so Cicero, *On the Universe*, chapter 11: “Then that God, who generated all things, speaks to them.”

759. “The seat of the tomb”: as in verse 371 of this passage, “the seat of the mound.”

767. “First, afterward”: for the women first left the tomb, and then, after seeing the disciples, reported what had happened.

777. CHAPTER XXV. The guards are bribed with money so that they may conceal the Resurrection. Matthew 28:11 ff. “The hearts of the guards,” that is, the guards themselves, as in Book III, verse 153: “the breasts of the scribes.”

780. “Devoted”: Virgil, *Aeneid* I.716: “devoted to the coming destruction.”

783. “Defended by darkness”: Dracontius, Book III, verse 276, *munita tenebris*, “fortified by darkness.”]

The stars already begin to yield to the approaching sun,

[745] Then the mothers hasten together to see the enclosure

Of the tomb. But immediately a trembling shakes all the earth,

And a messenger, descending from the open sky,

Comes down and rolls the stone from the entrance of the tomb.

His face shines like the flame of lightning,

[750] And the garments of his clothing gleam like snow.

Terror had shut off every sense of the soldiers,

And they fell together like corpses poured out in death.

But he addresses the mothers with this voice:

“Let no fear now, shaking your hearts, weary you;

[755] For your faith is clear: you are seeking the holy body

Which criminal madness fixed upon the wood of the cross.

[385] Christ has risen, and, having conquered death,

[Col. 0341B] Has received the eternal lights of life with his holy body.

Now you may see that no limbs lie there

[760] In the seat of the tomb, which had been buried there.

Moreover, tell the disciples with swift and hurrying return

That Christ has come back to the regions of light

And goes joyfully before them into the land of Galilee.”

[Col. 0342A] When he had spoken these words, an ardent

[765] Joy and astonishment, together with alternating fear,

Had filled the hearts of the women, who stood amazed.

Finally, hastening their joy with headlong speed,

They report these things to the disciples and leave the tomb.

Behold, midway along the road, radiant Jesus appears

And gently commands the faithful mothers to greet him.

[770] They run to him, clasp his knees and feet,

[386] And, frightened, worship Jesus, conqueror of death.

Then he strengthens their hearts with these instructions:

“Let every fear of doubt depart from your minds,

And quickly report these commands to our brothers.

[775] If concern for seeing us exists, go willingly

And hasten across the land to Galilee.”

[Col. 0342B] Meanwhile the frightened hearts of the guards of the tomb

Send out from their number a party to report

Such great miracles to the Jews. But the mad hand,

[780] Already wholly devoted to insane fury,

Lavishes great rewards upon the soldiers in rivalry

And buys the report with silver: that, after the entrance had been broken,

The boldness of the disciples had secretly carried off the body,

Shielded by darkness.

[785] [Col. 0343A] [Note: [Col. 0343A]

786. The Regius, Ottobonian, Daventrian, Tornesian, Aldine, and Basel editions: “a crowd running together”; Fabricius, Hadamian, and Poelmannian in the text: “a crowd rushing about.”

787. Aldine and Basel editions: *esse*; others: *ecce*.

788. Most printed editions: *sanctus chorus*, “the holy choir.” Fabricius: *sancte*. [Col. 0343B] In the Regius and Ottobonian manuscripts, the first hand seems to have written *sanctum* instead of *sanctorum*, or perhaps *sanctum nempe illum*; in the Ottobonian, the second hand has *sancte*; in the Regius, *sanctus*.

790. Regius: *pars credebat eorum*, “part of them believed”; *dubitabat*, “doubted,” is better, following the Gospel.

796. Reuschius suspects *ablatos homines*, that is, “men taken away,” meaning withdrawn from the filth of the world. I would rather read *adductos* or *adjunctos*, “brought” or “joined.” Reuschius explains the common reading, lest it imply rebaptism, as referring to the washing away of uncleanness and to baptism, or the washing of fire and Spirit.

798. Aldine, Basel, and Poelmann editions: instead of *d. s.*, *vivant*, “may they live”; other printed editions, together with the manuscripts: *currant*, “may they flow.” The Tornesian manuscript has *spiramine*, evidently meaning “may the life-giving breath of the Spirit flow with inspiration”; most others have *spiramina*, “breaths.” Reuschius does not strongly reject *vivant spiramine*, if washed persons are intended. But the Gospel has a different meaning.

[Col. 0344A] 801. The Regius manuscript: *nostra praesentia*, which I consider correct, with the final syllable of *nostra* lengthened either because of the caesura or, more likely, because of the two consonants beginning the following word. The printed editions, together with the Ottobonian manuscript: *nostri praesentia*. The Gospel’s words are: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation [Col. 0344B] of the age.”

803. Barthius had written in his manuscript: “This closing line is not in my manuscript.” Nevertheless, I have no doubt that it belongs to Juvencus. It appears in all printed editions and in the remaining handwritten codices seen by Omeisius.

804. Aldine edition: *Coepit*; read *Cepit*. Regius and Ottobonian: *in tantum lucet*; but in the Ottobonian, by the first hand, *in tantam*, corruptly. Printed editions: *in tantum luxit*.

805. Westphal in the text: *gratia legis*; in the margin, together with others: *gloria legis*.

806. Aldine and Basel editions: *tulerit*; others: *caperet*.

808. Ottobonian: *Quem*; corrected to *Quam*.

809. Regius, Ottobonian, Aldine, Tornesian, Westphalian, Basel, Daventrian, Fabrician, Hadamian, and Poelmannian editions in the text: *gratia digna merenti*. Poelmann, in place of *d. s.*: *gloria digna*. The Cantabrigian manuscript: *gratia diva*, which Reuschius thinks comes from a glossator.]

[Note: [Col. 0343C]

785. CHAPTER XXVI. Jesus appears to the disciples in Galilee, commanding them to preach the Gospel and to baptize believers in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Matthew 28:16 ff.; Mark 16:15.

797. *Sub* is used instead of *in*, as noted elsewhere.

798. *Vivifici*: a word used by Ammianus and Apuleius, and especially by many Christian writers in liturgical books.

799. Matthew says: “Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father,” etc.; “teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Reuschius observes that Christ commanded that those who had first been instructed in God’s commandments should then be washed in the sacred bath of the new covenant. Richard Simonius made the same observation concerning Juvencus in *Critical Historical Commentary on the New Testament*, chapter 23, as though Juvencus had reversed the order. But Matthew mentions instruction both before and after baptism.

801. *Deerit*: poets commonly use this as a disyllable.

802. *Consumens*, “consuming,” for *consummans*, “bringing to completion.” “Until the consummation [Col. 0343D] of the age.”

803. CHAPTER XXVII, or EPILOGUE. Juvencus boasts that Christ favored him so that he might complete this work. Hence he praises the emperor Constantine.

804. *In tantum*: I discussed this phrase in the commentary on Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, verse 153, and in the note on Dracontius II.659. Juvencus had asked in Book I, verse 34, that the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with him.

807. He imitates Virgil at the end of Book IV of the *Georgics*, but adorns Constantine with a greater eulogy, attributing to him the peace of the world and the advancement of the Christian religion. At Mérida in Spain there was an outstanding inscription concerning Constantine, reported by Baronius under the year 312, number 86, [Col. 0344C] from Aldus, after the scholium in his commentary on Caesar. This inscription not only refutes the slander of Zosimus, who relates that Constantine continually harassed the people with new taxes, but also wonderfully confirms that he deserved extremely well of the Christian religion through every kind of service and benefaction. I am pleased to reproduce the inscription here, although I think it was not copied faithfully.

**IMP. CAES. FLAVIVS CONSTANTIN. AVG. PACIS ET IVSTITIAE CVLT. PVB. QVIETIS FVND. RELIGIONIS ET FIDEI AVCTOR REMISSO VBIQVE TRIBVTO FINITIM. PROVINC. ITER. RESTAVR. FEC CXIIII.**

“Emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine Augustus, worshipper of peace and justice, founder of public tranquility, author of religion and faith, having remitted tribute everywhere, restored the roads of the neighboring provinces; he caused [this] to be made, 114.”

Baronius says that the title “author of religion and [Col. 0344D] faith” is excessively extravagant; but he correctly explains that Constantine is so called because he was a wondrous enlightener and propagator of Christian piety. The same Constantine is called *Fundator quietis*, “founder of tranquility,” at Rome on his triumphal arch.

808. “Of the open earth”: that is, “of the exposed, unobstructed earth.”

809. Those who do not wish Constantine’s baptism to have been delayed until his death may draw some support from this passage. Certainly scarcely anything greater could have been said about a perfect Christian. Not many years ago Matthaeus Aimerichius, distinguished for the great and long-standing reputation of his learning, published, after his *New Historical and Critical Lexicon*, a dissertation on the two baptisms of Constantine the Great, one Roman and the other Nicomedian. The opposite view is the paradox of the learned woman Gabriela Carola Patinia in her letter on the phoenix, where she denies that Constantine was devoted to the Christian religion; this opinion has rightly been rejected by others. Juvencus seems to imply that Constantine refused the title of Pontifex Maximus. Jacobus Gothofredus supports this opinion at length in his letter to Andreas Rivetus, *On the Prohibition of Communion between Christians and Gentiles*, and Pagius defends it in his commentary on Baronius’s *Annals*, under the year 312, among others.]

Now the anxious crowd of his followers had climbed

The Galilean mountains, meeting Christ’s commands.

387 Behold, the venerable offspring of the Thunderer is seen by his own.

The entire holy choir falls prostrate and worships him,

Yet faith was not equally established in all

[790] Their hearts, for some of them doubted.

Then radiant Jesus addresses his disciples:

“My Father has subjected all things to me in heaven and on earth.

The Father has deigned to send me to you as the light.

Now I have determined to send you in the same way to all nations;

[795] It is your task to join all nations to me.

Go on, and wash people in cleansing waters

[Col. 0344A] Under the holy name of the Father and the Son.

Let the life-giving breaths of the Spirit likewise flow.

Then, after they have been washed, teach them and impress upon them our commands,

[800] So that they may be able to lead an unending life.

Nor will our presence ever be lacking to you,

[388] Until the end, consuming the ages, dissolves them.”

These are the powers of faith and holy fear

That my mind has received; and to such an extent Christ’s grace

[805] Has shone upon me that the divine glory of the law might gladly take

The earthly ornaments of my language in my verses.

This peace of Christ, this peace of the age, which the ruler

Of the open earth, Constantine, cherishes, has granted me this;

and fitting grace attends one deserving it,

[810] [Col. 0345A] [Note: [Col. 0345A]

810. The Ottobonian, Hadamian, and Poelmannian manuscripts have *numinis*, “of the divine power,” which may indeed have been the original; in the Regius manuscript, where *nominis* now stands, as also in the Aldine, Daventrian, Westphalian, Tornesian, Fabrician, Basel, and other witnesses. In fact, *nominis* is more pleasing, so that the following verse may answer it correctly: “Who alone of kings recoils from having the burden of the sacred name imposed upon him.” Whether one understands this as Constantine’s refusal of the supreme pontificate or his unwillingness to be called a god, as earlier emperors customarily were, the reading proceeds correctly: “Who alone of kings recoils from having the burden of the sacred name imposed upon him.” Reuschius printed *sacri sub nominis*; but since he does not notice the variant reading, one must suppose that *sub* has fallen out in place of *sibi*.

811. Regius and Ottobonian: *qui justis*; in the Ottobonian, by the second hand, together with the printed editions: *quo justis*.

813. Regius, Ottobonian, Tornesian, Aldine, Basel, Daventrian, Fabrician: *Per dominum lucis Christum*, “through Christ, lord of light.” Hadam and Poelmann in the text: *Per Dominum nostrum Christum*, “through our Lord Christ.” The former reading is more authentic. So also in Book IV, verse 656: “whom you ordered to be fastened to the cruel cross as lord of light.” Christ is often called the author, discoverer, and lord of light. See Wopkensius’s note on Sedulius III.114. After this final verse the Regius and Ottobonian manuscripts have: “It ends,” etc., as I explained in the *Prolegomena*, numbers 48–49. In a codex of the Laurentian Medicean Library the final verse, “through Christ, lord of light,” is lacking, as I observed in number 45 of the *Prolegomena*.]

[Note: [Col. 0346B]

812. He changes the epithets: “divine life” and “eternal ages” would seem more fitting.]

389 Who alone among kings recoils from having the burden

Of the sacred name imposed upon him, by which he may receive,

Deserving of his righteous deeds, eternal life

[Col. 0346A] In the divine ages,

[813] Through Christ, the Lord of light, who reigns forever.

# APPENDIX. WORKS ATTRIBUTED TO JUVENCUS

[Col. 0345A]

## BOOK ON GENESIS (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0345C] CHAPTER I

[Note: [Col. 0345C]

I discussed this poem in the *Prolegomena*, number 16 ff. Andreas Rivinus published the first four chapters from old editions under this title: “The Genesis of Caecilius Cyprianus, or rather of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus.” I append Martene’s notes, adding or inserting a few of my own.

Verse 1. The printed editions read *creavit*, “created,” a word used by the Vulgate, which was unknown to Juvencus. MARTENE. — The Old Latin version has *fecit*, “made.”

2. In the Vulgate edition we read: “Now the earth was empty and void.” But the ancient Italian version cited by Augustine has: “Now the earth was invisible and unformed.” MART. — Rivinus conjecturally reads *Jamque* instead of *Namque*. Others in Sabatier, together with Augustine, read the same.

5. Pamelius read this verse somewhat differently, in the following form: “While he ordered these things to be separated from the heavenly hinge, he speaks.” MART. Before Pamelius, Morelius and Fabricius had read it in this way.

[Col. 0346C] 6. The printed editions: *claro et*, “and bright,” for which Morelius reads *clare*. MART. — Fabricius reads: “Let there be light, and brightly they shone.” Junius, in Rivinus: “Let there be light; brightly they shone.”

7. Fabricius: “When the Lord of the first…” Morelius likewise.

[Col. 0346D] 9. Printed editions: *verentia*. MART. — Read *verrentia*. Thus Fabricius, following Morelius: “sweeping shores.”

13. Rivinus conjecturally restores *gramina*, “grasses,” instead of *germina*, “shoots.”

15. Martene makes no note; but Fabricius has “The fourth day,” which fits the meter.

16. Printed editions: *fingit*, “shapes.” MART. — *Pingit*, “paints,” is much better.

19. Printed editions: “But the fifth,” omitting *die*, “day,” which is less satisfactory. MART. — The older editors altered the text to accommodate the meter. They understand “But the fifth…”

20. Pamelius reads this verse as follows: “And suspend various birds’ feathers in the air.” MART. — Fabricius agrees with Pamelius, but has *corpore*, “body,” instead of *aere*, “air.”

21. Printed editions: “The sixth [day], very cold…” MART.

22. Fabricius: “And herds of four-footed creatures.”]

In the beginning the Lord established heaven and earth:

For the earth was shapeless and hidden beneath the waves,

And the boundless God moved above the vast waters;

While chaos and black darkness obscured everything.

[5] While he separates these things from the heavenly hinge, he speaks:

“Let there be light,” and everything shone in a joyful world.

When God had completed the works of the first day,

He created the bright axis amid newly forming clouds.

The boundless sea receives the wandering shores,

[10] Sweeping up rivers of many kinds with powerful currents.

On the third day the golden light uncovered the face of the lands.

The dry region was then called by the name “earth.”

[Col. 0346C] Flowering shoots rise in the windy fields,

And branches laden with fruit bend down together.

[15] On the fourth day the moon is born with the sun’s lamp,

And he paints the stars, shining with trembling light.

He gave these elements their distinctions within the ordered world,

To teach the times that must change through their various risings.

On the fifth day the flowing rivers receive fish,

[20] And birds suspend their various bodies upon their feathers.

On the sixth day the Father makes the cold serpents glide in coils,

And spreads whole herds of four-footed animals across the fields.

He commanded all things everywhere to grow in abundant

Seed, to wander, and to feed upon the immense earth.

[Col. 0347A] [Note: [Col. 0347C]
