When the divine power had established these things by command,

Looking out and seeing that a ruler was needed for worldly affairs,

He says: “Let us make man exactly according to our likeness,

One who may rule throughout the whole world.”

And although he could have fashioned him by a single word,

[30] He nevertheless deigned to form him with his holy hand,

And breathes into his unreasoning breast from his divine breast.

## CHAPTER II

When he saw him formed in an image seemingly like his own,

He measures out the ground, turning over painful thoughts.

Immediately he bathes his eyes in refreshing sleep,

[35] So that a woman might be more gently formed from the removed rib,

And the mixed substance might strengthen the two joined limbs.

A name is also given her, called “life”: Eve.

[Col. 0347B] Therefore children customarily leave their parents

And cling to their wives, establishing their own homes.

[40] On the seventh day God, the creator, rested from his works,

Establishing the sacred joys of the age to come.

Immediately, after the living creatures had been displayed in their order,

Adam, endowed with the skillful prudence granted to him,

Gives each one individually its enduring name.

[45] God addresses him, and also deigns to join Eve to him:

“Grow through abundant offspring in the times to come,

So that heaven and the earth, filled with your seed, may be yours,

And, as my heirs, gather the various fruits

Which the groves and the fields produce from their fertile soil.”

[50] When he had explained these things, a joyful paradise

Was established as a court, and looked upon the light of the first sun.

Amid these things a tree with lethal fruits grows,

Producing the joined flavor of life and death.

In the middle of the dwelling a river flows in a pure stream,

[55] From which it waters the distinguished trees with liquid currents

And divides its channels into four from its overflowing spring.

Pison, rich in golden waters, rolls along,

And grinds conspicuous gems from its roaring depths;

Its name is green beryl, the other is blazing carbuncle,

[60] And with its clear shallows it laps the land of Evila.

Beyond it Gihon flows along and enriches the Ethiopians.

The third is the Tigris, joined to the lovely Euphrates,

Cutting through Assyria in a swift, dividing stream.

Here Adam was placed as guardian with his faithful wife;

[65] And the Thunderer, the creator, addresses him in these words:

“Do not together hesitate to pluck the permitted fruits

Which the untouched grove has produced on its leafy branches,

Taking care lest some harmful evil be found there,

Which grows green from a twofold juice, separated for different purposes.”

[70] Meanwhile deep night continued to hold them in blindness,

And the clothing had not covered their newly formed limbs.

## CHAPTER III

Among these dwellings and gardens with gentle fruits,

The foaming serpent, surpassing the animals in cunning,

Crept silently with its cold coils.

[75] Turning livid lies with its biting cunning,

It tests the tender heart within the woman’s breast:

“Tell me, why do you fear the blessed shoots of the apple?

Did God not sanctify all fruits that were born?

Yet if you desire to pluck the honeyed food,

[80] The golden world will return upon its starry hinge.”

She refuses and fears to touch the forbidden branches;

Yet her heart is overcome by weak understanding.

As soon as she had bitten the ripe fruit with her snowy teeth,

The cloudless sky flashed upon her, unstained by any cloud.

[85] Then that flavor, planting temptation in her honeyed jaws,

Drove her to bring the gift to her unaccustomed husband.

As soon as he had taken it, when the night was removed,

Their shining eyes flashed forth, clear beneath the radiant world.

Therefore, when each saw the other’s naked body,

[90] They shade the parts they saw with fig leaves.

[Col. 0348C] Perhaps, beneath the setting light of the Lord’s sun,

They recognize the sound and, trembling, turn toward hidden places.

Then the Lord of heaven addresses sorrowful Adam:

“Tell me, where do you now dwell?” The suppliant answered:

[95] “O Lord, when you speak, I tremble in my fearful heart.

Great one, naked and chilled by fear, I am exhausted before you.”

Then the Lord: “Who gave you the harmful fruits?”

The woman recounted these things, saying that her eyes had suddenly been

The Vulgate has: “You shall eat the earth.” Other ancient versions have: “The earth shall be your food,” or “You shall eat the earth.” This confirms *Mandere*. Suffused with shining day; and the clear sky,

[100] the sun, and the stars of heaven had shone upon her.

Immediately the wrath of God terrifies Eve in her confusion,

While the Most High seeks the author of the forbidden deed.

At this she reveals: “I accepted what the serpent,

Deceiving me by guile and gentle entreaty, persuaded me to accept.

[105] For, weaving his words together with viperous poisons,

He told me that these fruits were sweeter than all others.”

At once the Almighty condemns the deeds of the dragon,

Commanding the hated creature to live detested by all,

Soon to creep forth with its breast spread upon the ground,

[110] And to chew only earth, in a war destined to endure

Through all the ages, between human beings

And the serpent itself, gliding on its head,

So that, cast down, it might crawl behind the feet of men

And strike at their heels while it presses close in its sliding attack.

[Col. 0349B] The woman, miserably deceived by deceitful persuasions,

[115] Is commanded, under harsh penalty, to bring forth children

And to endure, through the zeal of her husband, her servitude.

“But you, whose judgment seemed true to your wife,

Who yielded, overcome, to the cruel dragon—

You shall mourn your wretched labor through long ages.

[120] For instead of wheat-bearing shoots a thistle

And whitethorn with many sharp spines shall rise for you.

So that, when your entrails are weary and your heart sorrowful,

The necessities of sustenance may bring you many anxious sighs,

Until, at the setting time of approaching death,

[125] You return the body you bear to the earth as you lie down.”

After these deeds, the Lord gives the trembling ones the burdens of life,

And drives them, cast out, far from the sacred gardens.

[Col. 0350A] He stations them opposite [the garden] and shuts them out by fire placed in the midst,

Within which a Cherub revolves with exceedingly swift heat,

While the fiery summit boils and rolls its flames.

[130] But the Lord, lest their limbs stiffen from sluggish cold,

Sews together skins torn from the entrails of animals,

Covering their naked limbs with warm clothing.

## CHAPTER IV

When faithful Adam now recognized himself as a husband

[135] Through marriage, he displays to his wife

The name of the beloved mother in two offspring from her seed.

Immediately the father gives them different names:

“This one here is called Cain; joined to him is Abel,

Who carefully tended many harmless two-toothed sheep.

[140] But the other turned the earth with a curved plow.”

When they continually brought their gifts to the Thunderer,

They offered unlike fruits, as their judgment prompted.

[Col. 0350B] The first offered what had grown from the rich soil;

But the other devotes himself to a gentle lamb,

[145] Bringing sincere entrails and snowy fat in his hand.

At once the Lord, observing the pious vows, is pleased.

Because of this Cain burns with icy anger.

God deigns to address him and says:

“Tell me: if you live rightly and perceive what is harmful,

[150] Can you remain pure after contracting guilt?

Stop destroying your brother with mortal hatred,

Who will offer you his neck as one subject to you as master.”

Yet he was not broken by these words, but led his brother into the fields,

And when he saw him caught in the deserted grass,

[155] Gnashing his teeth, he crushed his innocent throat with both hands.

When the Lord observed this deed from high heaven,

He asks where Abel is dwelling in the lands.

He denies that he has been appointed his brother’s keeper.

God says to him: “Does not the voice of his blood,

[160] Sent to me, sound and rise to the lofty heavens?

Know, then, what will remain for you because of so great a crime.

For now the earth, moistened with your brother’s blood,

Cursed because of you, will refuse the seeds

Entrusted to it, and will not produce fruit among its exhausted herbs.

[165] Numb, striking your limbs with great trembling,

As though joined to a funeral, you will always utter sighs.”

Terrified, he groans and asks death from the divine power.

But this is not granted by the hostile Thunderer.

For he is made known by a mark burned upon him,

[170] So that no one may strike the guilty man with a sword,

Lest sevenfold punishments provide a greater funeral.

Immediately, like one lost, he leaves the Lord’s presence.

Facing the dwellings, in the grassy land of Naid,

And from the children whom his faithful mother had borne,

[175] He founded the lofty first city by name.

Enoch begets Naid, and then Malech,

From whom Matusalamus, gradually born beneath the heavens,

Came forth and extended the span of his long life.

But Amalech, dreadful, who strikes Cain with the sword,

[180] Suffers far heavier things when the guilty man has been slain.

For crimes exact the deserved penalty seventyfold.

Groaning, he reproaches himself unbidden for his deed before his wives,

Of whom the first was Ada and the other Sella.

The first bears Aelus, who pastured flocks in the fields,

[185] Feeding sheep happily upon grassy meadows.

[Col. 0351C] Then Jobalus follows, who discovered musical plectra

And strings harmonious with varied murmuring.

Next Sella bears Tobellus, whose custom it was

To pour out streams of bronze and to shape iron

[190] Subdued upon the anvil in various forms within the hissing furnace.

Noema followed him, born from the same father.

Meanwhile Adam, vigorous and not weakened by his advancing years,

Begot Seth after the death of gentle Abel.

Seth then begot Enoch, to whom the Lord granted

[195] A pure heart; when he asked this of him,

God assented to his prayer and accepted the gifts of his peaceful mind.

## CHAPTER V

When Adam had completed nine hundred

Thirty years, he rested, overcome by death.

Then long-lived Enoch lived nine hundred five years,

[200] While Cainan, equaling him, was only five years longer.

Thirty years younger than this man, he dies.

Then old Mahalaleel, and Jared after him, lived

Three [hundred years], shortened by a long span.

[205] Enoch, whose care it was to serve the Almighty

And to join his mind to God, younger than these,

When three hundred years had been completed, if you add five,

And six times ten, covered by sudden darkness,

[Col. 0352B] Is hidden away and removed by the greatly merciful Lord,

[210] And lives a fortunate life in peaceful time.

But Methuselah extends his years to nine hundred cycles,

With seventy years and one more year added.

Lamech, born from this father, begot Noah,

And spoke these things while, in the manner of prophets,

[215] He foresaw the future and sent his thoughts into the coming age:

“He will grant us secure relief in life

And remove the harsh burden, restoring peace,

Which has been driven away by evil deeds and our guilt,

And by the sorrowful right hands whose labor has furrowed

[220] The earth, which refuses fruit because the Lord has spoken a curse.”

He lived seven hundred years,

With seven added, and seventy placed above them, as the total requires.

From this father Noah, noble in his righteous deeds,

Was born, destined to give seed to an innocent age,

[225] And he begot three sons, Seth, Ham, and Japheth,

Accustomed without number to beat softened iron

And readily to forge sparkling masses.

## CHAPTER VI

This prophet had already lived six hundred years

When the Lord, wearied by the world’s wicked crimes

[230] And by the manifold guilt of human beings under the long light of day,

235. Here Juvencus refers to those words of the Italian version: “But when the angels of God saw the daughters of men, that they were good and beautiful, they took wives for themselves.” Here St. Augustine asks how angels could have intercourse with the daughters of men; he replies that some Latin and Greek manuscripts read not “angels” but “sons of God,” and that in Scripture both the righteous and angels are called “angels” and “sons of God.” It is therefore credible that righteous men, overcome by desire, sinned with women. Thus in St. Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, question 3, MART. — St. Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, chapter 23, reads, “because they were good, they took,” etc. He explains “good” as meaning “beautiful.”

265. The diphthong *ae* is shortened so frequently in this poem that this seems attributable not to the copyist but to the author. Nothing of the kind, however, can be found in Juvencus’s work [Col. 0354D].

267. I think it should be rewritten as *de germine mundo* (“from clean stock”), from Genesis 7:2: “Take seven and seven of all clean animals,” etc.

285. Namely, the wives of the sons.

305. Here Augustine asks why the raven did not return, while the dove did—whether the raven may have died. He replies that many conjecture that the raven could perch upon a corpse, whereas the dove naturally avoids it. MART.

317. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 206: “Seen from afar to open the mountains and roll forth smoke.” But I do not know what smoke this author could mean after the Flood, unless perhaps exhaled vapors.

He, in his compassion, restrained the long life’s excesses of sin,

and imposed a limit of sixty years,

which no one could surpass under any law.

Meanwhile earthly pleasure beguiles the saints

[235] and holds captive those making their way from the heavenly citadel:

while they behold women’s faces laughing in beautiful bodies

and cling too closely to pleasing embraces,

they begot giants with savage bulk.

At last the Lord is compelled to be angered by their crimes,

while he conceives a long wrath

and grieves that man, created by his heavenly hand,

[240] has been formed. Moved in his holy heart, he declares:

“It is right for me to destroy the sins of the guilty world,

to envelop the whole earth in watery waves,

and to plunge the human race into vast floods,

[Col. 0353B] together with every kind of beast that happily

crops the grasses through the fields while wandering over high hills.

Let one destruction overwhelm serpents,

birds, and wild beasts alike,

so that my anger may grow mild once their deceit is erased.”

[250] Noah therefore receives the great commands of God,

ordered to join together the ark with double chambers,

so that it may contain nests where birds can preserve their offspring.

And lest the timbers burst apart through splitting cracks,

he coats the ark with thick, rich bitumen.

[255] It was itself three hundred cubits long,

fifty cubits wide across its breadth.

As for the height at which the roof’s summit rises,

it is lifted thirty cubits toward heaven,

built with squared planks, which no waters could carry away,

[260] bearing doors at its center with an easy hinge.

[Col. 0353C] **CHAPTER VII**

When God had looked down from the stars upon these things completed,

he addressed the prophet, whom he was sending onto the waters:

“Climb quickly into the boat amid the swelling floods,

you and your sons and your daughters,

because I have seen that your heart is righteous toward me

[265] and that your will, long known to me,
has merited greater things than those now present.

Shut in with yourself the tame animals of every kind,

seven pairs; but of the unclean herd

allow two to remain with you.

Bring food for all of them,

[270] and your accustomed provisions, lest, when cultivation has ceased,

you too should suffer distress amid the vast floods,

carrying no provisions beforehand across the greenish waters,

and hunger should overcome you in the salt sea.

For when the sun’s bright lights have appeared in heaven

on the seventh day,

[275] I am preparing to pour out all the clouds

from the heavenly axis and to unloose every spring

with a greater rush,

so that Ocean may boil more violently with waves,

receiving all things more abundantly in its foaming waters

and smearing everything with its spreading flood.

For forty days and nights together

[280] I shall fill the dripping clouds with perpetual hail,

so that everything alive may be submerged in the swelling waters.”

When these things had been said, the Lord’s commands were carried out.

The old man, hastening to obey,

who, noble through his long life, had reached six hundred years,

entrusted himself to the waters

[285] and received together his sons and their wives,

although he was confined in a small hidden chamber.

Meanwhile the clouds released all their rains,

and the abyss poured its brimming springs into the waters.

For forty days everything now lay flooded;

[290] birds no longer suspended their bodies on light wings,

nor did any wild beast escape the marble cliffs of the high hills.

Everything was buried beneath the sea; death was common to all.

Meanwhile the ark, floating suspended across the swelling sea,

securely protected the enclosed prophet,

[295] preserving the seeds for the generations to come.

**CHAPTER VIII**

Safe from the wreck, Noah’s ark soon saw the air grow clearer,

as the black clouds began to contract their rains.

The sea diminished as it receded,

and after the boat had floated on a gentle breeze,

[300] the old man sent out a raven with a black breast.

While it was carried on light wings by the flying wind,

it did not return, disappointing the hopes of the righteous prophet.

After it he sent a white dove across the waters.

Exhausted by flight over the watery plain,

[305] finding nowhere any ground, it returned to the kindly prophet.

When the sun’s returning light had shone for the seventh time,

he sent out the bird with beating wings.

Having found a grove, it brought back in its beak

branches of a rich olive tree,

when evening was already rising among the stars

[310] and was preceding the night with trembling fire.

Then, after seven days had properly passed,

the bird was sent once more over the sea.

It descended on swift flight

and never returned to its companion ark.

The prophet had by then passed six hundred and one years,

[315] in the first month that had followed,

and on the first day of the month,

when the free earth seemed from afar to open its mountains

and roll forth smoke,

over which the sea had surged to a depth of fifteen cubits.

When the month had passed, then, as the third part was cut away,

324. This verse lacks one metrical foot, and its meaning is incomplete [Col. 0355D].

325. Through the copyist’s negligence, an entire chapter of Genesis has been omitted here. What follows does not concern Noah but Nimrod, who founded Babylon, Erech, Arcad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. MART.

328. In the Vulgate it is not Acalla but Calneh. MART. — It would be sound to read: “Here he establishes Babylon and Oricham.” Dominicus Schram, in his *Analysis of the Works of the Fathers*, read: “Here Nimrod establishes Babylon. Then Asshur.” But this author is of no use to us here: he changes words at will, omits verses, inserts certain material, and does not always observe the meter.

331. The Septuagint interpreters read this passage of Genesis as follows: “And Rehoboth the city, and Calah, and Resen, which is between Nineveh and Calah.” The Old Version, however, reads: “And Rehoboth the city, and Calah, and Dasem between Nineveh and Calah.” MART. — Sabatier read it thus from St. Augustine: “And Rehoboth the city, and Calah. And Dasem between Nineveh and Calah.”

[Col. 0356C] 339. I would read *nova* (“new”).

346. *Quis* for *queis*, or *quibus*, as we observed above. MART.

353. Juvencus seems here to have suffered a lapse of memory, attributing Milcah, or Melcia, as Lot’s wife, although she had married Nahor. The old Italian version that he used reads: “And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai; the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, daughter of Haran.” MART.

354. *Odescit* is a new word, or, as I rather think, a corrupt one. I was considering “Sarra enriches Abram as his wife,” or “Abram is enriched”.

356. Perhaps: “he sent from the herd.”

361. Perhaps: “Leave behind your accustomed things.”

366. This verse is obscure and one foot too long.

370. The verse could read: “And ascending the mountain.” For *Bethel* he seems to put *fractas undas*; accordingly, *fractas* should perhaps be corrected to *qui respicit undas*.

375. Perhaps *aret* (“is dry”) instead of *ardet* (“burns”).

It reads: “They treated Abram well for her sake [Sarai], and he had sheep, oxen, male and female donkeys, servants, maidservants, female donkeys, and camels.” Here, however, only those things seem to have been left to him that he had brought from his homeland. MART.]

so that the light should remain, the earth, now entirely free from the flood,

became visible and joyfully displayed its own greenery.

Therefore, when the ark came to rest on the wave-washed mountains,

which in the ancient language bear the name Ararat,

the old man opened the barriers; then follows the corrupt, incomplete fragment: “new seeds of the earth, and, rejoicing, to raise the holy God before him.”

**CHAPTER X**

Such as lofty necks and immense heads, after the manner of heroes, would raise high into the air.

Here he establishes Babylon, Oricham, and Archata Acalla,

as well as Asshur among the rugged passes of Sennacherib;

then he founded Nineveh, remarkable for its buildings.

And Rehoboth, Calah, and Dasemata,

whose mountain passes mark them out

and which rise at the middle boundary.

[Col. 0355B] **CHAPTER XI**

While they eagerly strive and give names to their walls,

they come into a plain called Shinar.

They undertake to raise hollow towers toward the stars,

but they do not make mortar with which joined stones are bound.

Instead, clay bricks are baked in a furnace,

so that the walls might shine with immense buildings

before migration divided the peoples into new nations.

[340] Bitumen served instead of mortar.

Drawn out with soft fleece,

it binds the rocks with its slow-setting body.

For among all peoples there was one harmonious language,

and they spoke through similar expressions and civic words.

At last the Lord descended and saw the walls,

[345] commanding different voices to burst forth swiftly

and the various sounds in which each nation speaks.

[Col. 0355C] Immediately the inhabited world was filled with its settled peoples,

and the divided place was soon called Confusion.

After them came Abram, who believed deeply in the Lord,

[350] born to one called Terah by his ancient name.

Lot too was joined to him, a brother of joined blood.

When they had grown strong in the ripening years of youth,

they entered into marriage.

Lot rejoiced in the union with Melcia,

and Abram *odescit* [reading uncertain] with his wife Sarra;

[355] [Col. 0356A] nevertheless she passed into old age without offspring.

Terah carefully sent them away from the Chaldean herd,

while the fields of Canaan pleased them with their leafy hills.

**CHAPTER XII**

But God, who knew the understanding of his chosen Abraham,

commands him to seek a dwelling in another region:

“Come, hasten; remove yourself from your ancestral lands,

from your kinsmen’s houses, and leave your accustomed thresholds.

For I shall now make you the head of an immense nation.

Moreover, I shall add this:

whoever wounds you with malicious words

shall bear sorrow, accursed by the Lord’s mouth;

[365] but whoever recounts your blessings with kindly speech

shall seek joy and shall be greater in skill.”

The dwelling places are changed, and the camp is set at Shechem,

which the Lord had promised to the prophet for a long age.

There he hastily raises sacred altars.

[370] And climbing the mountain that rejects the broken waves,

he looks out upon the sun’s red, swelling lights.

Here too, after blocks have been laid,

an altar is founded,

and God is entreated.

Then the prophet travels alone through the fields,

which the land, divided among its settlers, holds.

[375] While this land burns continually for thirsty veins,

it brings upon him the hunger of fasting,

to which anxiety is attached.

In this fear he seeks the fertile fields of the Nile.

And because Sarai shone with conspicuous beauty,

he orders her to say that she is not bound to him in marriage,

[380] but is his sister,

lest the jealousy of an unrestrained crowd,

driven to monstrous deeds,

should produce danger for her husband

and bring him the sorrow of a rival.

The crowd of Canopus admires her as she arrives.

Sarai, desired by all, is examined from every side.

[385] When she has been praised by the nobles and handed over to the king,

the prophet is received with sweet entreaties and words.

Yet the King of heaven did not wish him to be imposed upon her.

For, assailed by many great terrors,

he drove away the king, guilty of the wrongful attempt,

[390] and rebukes the nobleman, asking why he had called her his sister

rather than his wife

and had deceived him by false cunning.

Then he orders him to lead away the joyful wife,

together with the herds and everything he had brought from his native land.

Juvencus adds a young bull. MART. — Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book II, chapter 8, reads *vitulum trimum* (“a three-year-old calf”) instead of *vaccam triennem* (“a three-year-old heifer”).]

For God had bestowed on his servant,

who always spoke of concord,

great wealth and everything of the highest value.

**CHAPTER XIII**

Lot too received whatever he had brought there,

and at last they were brought back to their ancestral regions.

While they wandered there among herds meeting one another,

the shepherds of the flocks drove one another into conflict,

because the small pastures were too narrow for both.

[400] But the father, wishing to settle their unruly quarrels,

offered his brother whatever fields he wished to choose.

He willingly complied, asking for the banks of the Jordan,

a river that once, swelling with waters in the manner of the Nile,

destroys the fertile fields with its overflowing stream.

The old man received the fields of Canaan by lot as he arrived

and settled his herds among the green fields.

[Col. 0357B] But it was not permitted to establish permanent dwellings.

For the father, ordered to survey the land while guarding it,

[410] [the land] which the flaming sun, returning from the heights,

sees on both sides,

and which the two Bears continually look down upon,

received it as promised to a race that such a father would beget.

Whoever wishes to comprehend the number of that race

will sooner count the throngs of stars

or the grains of sand

[415] which the sea sometimes uncovers along its uncertain shore.

He also went toward the oak grove called Mamre in the ancient name

and dedicated a lofty altar to God forever.

**CHAPTER XIV**

No sooner had concord caused the divided brothers

to settle their desired kingdoms across the fields

than kings from the numerous threefold people rose up

[420] and, fierce with a great army, devastated Sodom.

Three battle lines, supported by twice two leaders,

brandished iron through the clouds as far as the Salt Valley.

Five tyrants took flight, abandoning the battle,

and hid among the leafy mountains,

[425] concealing whatever could survive death.

They are truly called Ariac, Hadachar, and Godullagomor.

Amraphel too rejoiced in these beautiful weapons.

Amid these events, while many things occur through the hazards of war,

Lot too was captured with his entire household and family.

[430] When a messenger reported this with sorrowful voice,

the prophet rose up.

From the great multitude of his servants,

he added three hundred and eighteen attendants

and himself summoned them to war;

they drew their swords again.

[435] [Col. 0357D] At midnight he attacked those who feared nothing,

putting the victors to flight

and killing many enemies.

He also recovered his brother, rescued from such danger,

and dragged the spoils with him in a broad procession.

He was received with the joyful praise of the nobles of Sodom

[440] [Col. 0358A] and of the priest of God, Melchizedek,

renowned for his holy conduct,

who presented bread and wine.

He asked the victor to be willing to return the captives,

while retaining the rest according to the merits of the war.

But victorious virtue, content with its own restraint,

accepted its brother as the desired whole reward.

Soon God, illuminating the prophet’s calmed heart,

[445] commanded him to empty his breast of all fear,

since he was safe beneath the protection of the invincible right hand.

**CHAPTER XV**

He, rejoicing in the permission granted him, said:

“What do your gifts promise me in return for so great a favor?

For advancing old age shakes my weakened body,

and I am not granted a child to leave behind after death.

[Col. 0358B] Since I have no offspring from a noble marriage,

a base-born heir will be created for me by my slave.”

The Lord confirms the prophet while saying these things:

“Do not fear. Trusting in me, you will not have a slave as heir.

For if anyone could know the numberless stars

or traverse all the sands of the sea,

[460] he alone could count, by calculation, the offspring

that is to be granted you throughout the whole expanse of the earth.

A son will be born from your seed, who will look upon what is yours
and will also be born as the son of the eternal King.

For I am the Lord, creator of the heavens,

and I brought you back safely from the Chaldean people by my aid.”

[465] The old man believed these things

and did not measure the Lord’s words as lacking anything,

but with sincere understanding of heart,

supported by faith, he asked as he prayed with gentle beginnings

what signs of God he should bear in his mind

and what he should follow in his heart,

for so great a gift, by which he might beget a child

[470] with his lifeless body, his limbs already chilled by age.

Instructed, he prepares a three-year-old heifer,

joining to it a young bull with fierce brow,

then a ram and a shaggy she-goat,

and paired doves joined with a matching turtledove.

[475] Soon he splits the bodies of the animals into two parts,

leaving the birds whole and unharmed in the flesh.

He arranges everything and sets it upon sacred altars,

and, alert in mind and ear, keeps watch nearby.

But behold, at the first hours of dark night,

the holy prophet’s pure heart is terrified,

and black shadows rush down in confused light.

[480] Stunned by these things, he receives the Lord’s assurances,

while he foresees the new seeds of a future nation,

which will be established through varied misfortunes

under a harsh king of Egypt, whose name was Pharaoh.

For, subjected to the Lord for four hundred years,

It will serve and then be recalled once more to fertile lands;

and, with the roles reversed,

what once trembled as a slave will rule kingdoms,

restraining nations with strong power.

[490] But you, when the appointed limit of life has been measured,

will be committed to the tomb after completing your life.

For the people, torn away from the hostile land,

will come here, to be given the homes of their ancient fathers.

For the peoples among whom the inhabitant now rejoices

in the Nile lands,

[495] and whom the swift Euphrates flows before through the Syrian regions,

will possess the Genaeans and Genezeans,

the Chalmoneans, the Hittites, and the allied Perizzites,

and the Raffanites, whose hand clings to the Jebusites.

They will drive the Canaanites from the dwelling they love.

[500] They will also drive out the Amorite, expelled by the friendly Gergesite,

who will yield his half-dead fields to those who come.

[Col. 0359B] When God had promised these holy words to the prophet,

under the setting sun he gave a clear sign with lightning.

For a flame seemed to boil as in a surging furnace,

and it appeared to lick the flesh of the slaughtered animals.

**CHAPTER XVI**

Meanwhile Sarai, long sterile and wearied by the years,

had also abandoned the hope of becoming a mother.

Since her chilled womb could not bring forth a child,

she began to encourage her husband toward a second joy

[510] and compelled him to recognize union with a slave,

so that at least he might become a father through an inferior pledge.

At once the Egyptian Hagar is brought into the marriage chamber,

and, fertile from her womb, gives birth to the illegitimate Ishmael.

When she looked down upon her mistress with servile cunning,

she was afflicted with harsh blows and fled, wounded.

[515] While she concealed herself in a remote place beside a nearby spring,

a messenger descended from heaven’s ethereal summit.

He first sent her back to her masters’ house,

and even enriched her with a generous gift.

Because she had seen the holy one shining with conspicuous light,
[520] she gave the spring a corresponding name.

**CHAPTER XVII**

Abraham the prophet had now completed ninety-nine years

when he recognized that he was about to become a father

through the great gift of the child to be given.

For him the covenants of the most high God were an accord: he was to be the father and future leader of countless nations,
[525] receiving peaceful dwellings through great stretches of time.

He also emerges greater through a solid name,

as an added letter brings him distinction:

and Sarai, who had been so called,

is commanded to be called Sarra.

[530] [Col. 0359D] Ishmael too, enriched in answer to prayer,

generates and rules twelve peoples as their prince.

After these events, when the eighth day had arrived,

the old man removes the foreskins of the males with iron,

joining to them likewise all those separated from the common people.

Then the time of the promised gift arrives.

He breaks into trembling laughter,

[535] while silently turning the great promises over in his mind,

believing that God can create whatever has never existed

and generate strength from limbs that have not been broken.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

The sun was already climbing the middle of the blazing sky,

and the magnificent old man was seeking shade from the heat,

when suddenly he saw three young men approaching together.

Attentive to all, he honors one above the others

and entreats him not to leave his servant as he hastily passes by,

[545] but to grant peaceful shelter beneath his oak

and to wash his two feet in the cool water,

and to accept the loaves set upon the welcoming table.

His request is granted, and he quickly carries out the venerable commands.

Sarai herself, hurrying, appears.

She measures out and brings three portions of meal,

which she had ordered to be roasted in the heat of baked ashes.

Then a calf, bending its swollen horns beneath its brow,

[550] is tied up, its hide unmarked by any blemish,

and dishes of curdled milk are brought.

While he feeds the God placed beneath a threefold image,

he tastes sweet joys with holy words.

“What is Sarai doing now?” he asks,

for at that time she was hidden within the house,

[560] and he repeats the words that true light had begun.

“Rejoice: before the full year has passed,

she will be a mother,” he declares.

The woman laughed at such words from a distance,

joyfully, although she despaired of bearing a child in her aged body.

He asks what had caused that laughter.

She denies that she had laughed easily,

[565] shaken within herself while she feared

and turned the guilt over silently in her heart.

The young men, equally radiant and handsome,

rise and look upon Sodom, lying beneath the whole light.

Then the Lord, unwilling to let the prophet remain ignorant of anything,

explains why he is setting out toward the grave cities:

“I have been roused by the excessive outcry of Sodom

[570] and neighboring Gomorrah,

and I have come to investigate the truth.

So that what the guilty crowd has wrought,

what the dreadful voice laments,

may cause the two towns together to burn

beneath the heavenly lightning.”

[Col. 0360D] Here the frightened prophet asked in humble speech:

“What number of righteous people will preserve the guilty walls?”

Beginning with the highest total, fifty,

he learns that the people overwhelmed by vices

could escape ruin through five men.

**CHAPTER XIX**

At once two men come to Sodom,

the Born One and the Other,

when evening was already beginning to send down its fire.

There Lot was sitting before the doors according to custom.

When he had examined the men, distinguished by their similar bodies,

he bowed and led them to his accustomed threshold,

[585] although they preferred to lodge in the middle of the street,

where white unleavened bread from fine meal would feed them.

Then they compose their limbs in sleep.

Behold, the whole raging crowd of Gomorrah rushes forth,

surrounding Lot’s house with savage uproar

and demanding the men,

quarrelling with swollen mouth.

[590] Remembering peace, he tries to calm the raging crowd,

and even eagerly offers his daughters,

so that perverse desire might boil instead in permitted lust,

separating shameful acts from their like sex.

But his words move them not at all.

The doors are broken by iron,

[595] and while they gather and tear away the strong barriers,

the enclosed lights groan beneath dark shadows.

After these events, he is ordered to take his dear ones far away,

but he invites his sons-in-law,

who refuse with minds dulled by disbelief.

Nevertheless, whatever his gentle mind could continually request,

he led out his daughters, following their dear mother.

As he went forward and climbed the heights of the opposite hill,

[600] considering with himself what would happen next,

the woman looked back at the cities behind her,

stiffened,

and took on the appearance of salt instead of a body.

He entered safely beneath the roof of lofty Segor.

[Col. 0361C] Soon thunder, hurling lightning from the terrifying sky,

and sulphurous flames fell in foul-smelling whirlwinds.

They licked the walls and lofty roofs alike.

When everything had been torn away in swift destruction into ashes,

[610] Abraham watched from afar the flame,

its gleaming summit rising,

while in his remembering heart he pondered

that he must never join falsehood to the Lord’s words.

Lot too, settled safely in his dwelling,

provided consolation to his tender daughters with affection,

[615] who could not bear children without husbands.

When they perceived that the means of producing offspring had been taken away,

and that their motherly dignity was gone,

with only their father left,

they prepare a meal and bring wine to their father,

so that he, unaware, might not recognize the forbidden act of his daughters.

[620] Before long the burden grows within their female bodies,

and the vital seed swells equally in both.

The first gives birth to a boy,

whom in the language of his father she calls Moab;

the other names hers Ammon with a different utterance.

He is the father of the Ammonites;

the other, the ancestor of the Moabites.

**CHAPTER XX**

Meanwhile Abraham leaves the dwellings he had occupied

and travels with his wife to the land of Gerar.

There Abimelech, desiring union with Sarai,

because the distinguished prophet had said that she was his sister,

lest her beauty should bring about deceit,

[630] while he guarded against the anger of rival husbands,

nevertheless could not prevail,

struck by powerful terrors that afflict the mind

whenever perverse desire is present.

For God tormented the tyrant by sending an executioner,

and the frightened king, scarcely restored to his senses,

questioned the prophet about why Sarai had been called his sister,

[635] as though no marital bonds joined her to her husband,

although she was united to the prophet.

He explains the reasons and clears himself of the charge:

he had lied about nothing,

for Sarai had been born from his brother’s stock,

and the branch joining them was of the same blood.

When this had been established,

the ruler gave a thousand talents

and servants, along with gentle sheep and cattle.

He also gave fields stretching broadly across the countryside,

provided that these gifts might lessen the guilt he had incurred.

For the king’s household, paying the penalty for its transgression,

[645] when he had been terrified by a dreadful vision in sleep,

had been afflicted by an assault of sickness throughout,

and had long shaken offspring from the women’s wombs.

But when the peaceful prophet prayed before God on behalf of the king,

the restored fertility gladly returned to everyone

and filled the fruitful wombs.

**CHAPTER XXI**

He too, in the final period of life,

becomes a father, contrary to his former hopes,

and, recalling the solace of joyful laughter,

calls the child Isaac.

He fulfills the command of the exalted deity,

removing the covering from the boy’s penis on the eighth day,

and seeing him already take steady steps.

Amid kinsmen of his own stock,
the father feasts at rich tables
and rejoices.

For grace becomes greater when hopes had been despaired of.

Now, while the boy plays beside the child of the household,

he drove his mother to swell with burning anger.

[Col. 0362D] Yet the old man, unwillingly obeying the Lord’s greatest commands,

drove both of them away together.

But after the woman had been removed from her master’s dwelling,

she wandered through remote places,

returning into the wilderness.

She had by then consumed all the bread and wine,

and, sighing from her exhausted breast over her weakened child,

came to a well, which she then called “Vision,”

and which, through mournful lament, expressed her grief in the wilderness.

When God was moved by the afflicted woman’s tears across the heavens,

[670] he strengthened her trembling heart

and announced great kingdoms prepared for her son,

whose future calamity would then cause her to groan.

At once she rises, drawing water from the well’s flowing depths,

and rejoices together with her glad son.

The pious commands of God advance:

the boy, still small, begins to draw a bow

[675] and to hurl winged arrows.

Meanwhile the prophet, lest Abimelech the ruler

should secretly prepare some danger,

establishes a treaty of peace.

Since conflicts had arisen over the wells,

the restored quiet made their lives secure.

[680] They swear an oath, and the concord of the desired peace remains.

Then, while the old man plows the earth with his curved plow,

he filled his household with abundant harvests.

After humbly praying through vows to the exalted God,

he settled peacefully in the fields of the Philistines.

**CHAPTER XXII**

In these events he is tested by the commands of the heavenly name:

his only son is to fall by the sword at the altar.

No sooner had he climbed—climbed—the summit of the swelling hill—

leading a pack animal with his servants and his son walking beside him—

than, on the third day,

when the brighter sun shone from the middle of the sky

[690] and drew all the shadows together,

the old man dismissed the boys

and took his son,

so that, carrying the wood for the flames around his neck,

he might climb the heights of the opposite hill with him.

Now, when the altar itself had been set up amid rising flames,

the son was bound, his hands twisted behind his back.

While the father hastened to cleave his son with a knife,

he attentively saw from afar a white lamb,

which would more suitably complete the sacrifice with its shed blood.

**CHAPTER XXIII**

After these events Sarai dies in her aged body.

When the sons of Heth offered a place for her tomb,

the prophet negotiated,

being prepared to set the price.

The wealthy man gave Ephron four hundred *sestertia*,

glad to entrust his companion to a double tomb.

Earlier generations had told that the place was called Mamre.

**CHAPTER XXIV**

At once he orders one of his servants,

whom life and faith had made distinguished,

to speak with the words he had formulated,

and to swear an oath while placing his right hand beneath his thigh.

He binds him by oath that no woman from the Canaanite people

[710] should be joined to his son,

since a wife should rather be brought from his parents’ stock;

and if she should perhaps resist,

one sent from heaven is to be sent,

who may easily soften her anger.

The servant eagerly places gifts upon laden camels

and seeks Assyria,

already seeing the roofs of Nahor.

While silently turning the Lord’s commands over in his mind,

he sees the remarkable Rebecca approaching from the spring.

She is not slow to offer the man cool water

and invites him into the house.

He asks whose daughter she is.

The young man is received as a guest

and soon brings out the gifts.

When everything has been completed,

she goes to the husband whom she is to marry.

[720] Isaac, having already traversed the journey,

now sees her nearby.

When Rebecca sees Isaac,

she lowers herself from the high back [of the camel]

and covers her bowed head with a thin veil.

They are joined in silence

and rejoice with the Lord as their author.

**CHAPTER XXV**

But after the old man had passed beyond one hundred years,

seventy more,

and had distributed gifts to everyone,

he died,

granted a place in the double tomb.

Meanwhile his son, having obtained his ancestral dwelling,

lived beside the well that had been called Vision.

He had now spent forty years there,

and had enriched the ancestral house with the wife already mentioned.

She, though she shone with a distinguished star of *pomae* [reading uncertain],

had long known no maternal joys,

being childless.

But when she sought the Lord with sanctified speech,

asking that his wife, once pregnant, might produce a rightful heir,

she was heard:

the pregnant Rebecca swelled with twins.

She, long wondering at the burden of her swelling womb,

[Col. 0364C] Humbly she consulted the answers of the heavenly Thunderer, and recognized that two peoples were growing in her womb, destined to come forth into the light of life with unequal merits.

[740] For the one who holds the first beginnings of the merited light is driven, subject to commands, to serve the lesser. Thus, when the children were born by an easy delivery, the elder emerged into the air with a crimson body, covered all over with tightly packed black bristles; [745] his father called him Esau, a name pleasing to him.

Born afterward, holding the heels of his brother in his tightly clasped hands, Jacob came forth, endowed with remarkable intelligence. The elder scoured the empty fields in pursuit of game, while he filled the rocks with the tremor of his harsh-sounding horn. [750] But the other, preserving the practices of a gentle heart, rejoiced to live unharmed in his ancestral lands.

[Col. 0364D] The father caressed the elder with tender affection.

[Col. 0365A] [Note: [Col. 0365D]

But his mother cherished the other with all her heart. When he had dissolved the lentils in water, he compelled his brother, as he took the prepared meal with a smile, to yield to him the first honours.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Meanwhile, destructive famine, the first of evils, compelled the seer to leave his ancestral lands. He sought the Philistine countryside and soon crossed Gargara, which Abimelech then held under his own authority.

[760] As he proceeded, he saw the Lord in a brilliant light, warning him in words not to approach the kingdoms of Canopus, but to remain in the land—the field—which the Lord had granted.

“For although you may seem to dwell among unknown peoples, [765] nevertheless you, destined to endure in the boundless world, will rejoice that nations multiply from your seed, and that they receive the greatest covenants of my word.”

Immediately, living in Gerar with his wife as his companion, he explained instead that she was his sister, recounting the deeds of his father, [770] lest the Philistine crowd, stirred by light desire, seize the marriage by force of arms.

But the king, while surveying the open spaces through a broad window, saw the seer playing with his fair wife. Observing their marital union, he restrained everyone under a law, [775] so that no one should attempt to carry off the prophet’s companion.

Now, when the man who had once fled famine from his ancestral lands scattered seed over the softened earth, he harvested a hundredfold crop from the joyful soil. Nor meanwhile did he grow less wealthy in peaceful circumstances, among varied flocks and fertile land.

[780] At once, while wretched jealousy tormented their hearts, they disturbed the well-watered wells and filled them with embankments, so that their owner would leave the fields and depart far away.

Therefore, avoiding the dangers of swollen strife, [785] he withdrew and remained for a long time in the valley of Gerar. When the well was released with anxious effort, he found cold waters springing from a gushing source.

Having been met with deceit, he left the shepherds to their anger and marked the untried places with the name of Quarrel. From there he advanced, and again, after earth had been dug out from the depth, brought cold streams into the light.

[790] Since he had been driven away by bitter contention, he addressed the embittered hearts with words appropriate to their deserts. After golden peace had broken the grim disputes, he took care to record the name “Abundance” for the land.

[Col. 0365D] While intelligently changing the new pastures with swift steps, he came to the hills called Juratio. There, in a clear light, he saw the Lord when the stars were turning through the middle of their courses, [800] and, admonished by him, drove gloomy impulses from his heart, with the unconquered God protecting him through wars and enemies.

After sleep he gathered his chilled limbs, and, reverently, soon prayed to the Lord at an altar he had built. Meanwhile the kings Abimelech and Ozas arrived, with Phicol accompanying them and carrying a sword, [805] so that, wishing to join himself to the peaceful seer, he might bind treaties of harmony by clasping hands.

He was received peacefully, and, satisfied at the same table, brought back the desired peace once the danger had been set aside.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[810] Meanwhile discord arose between the brothers. Their father, already greatly advanced in long age, bearing in his peaceful mind the day lost with the sun, his eyes buried in darkness, and remembering that death was near, [815] urged the elder son—whom affection alone allowed him to see—to take his quiver and swift arrows, and bring him wild meat in the customary manner, intending soon to receive the gifts of his native tongue.

Rebecca, seeing this, made it known to her beloved Jacob and urged him to bring two readily available young goats, [820] and, in place of his wandering brother, to slaughter them for his father.

And lest he expose the deception with his smooth body, she covered him with skins that made him appear hairy, and, concealing his breast and limbs beneath his brother’s garment, presented him with food obtained as though by hunting.

[825] Yet she did not entirely conceal her prophetic thoughts. For while the old man’s right hand examined the whole youth, he recognized Esau by the bristles, but Jacob by the voice.

When his hunger had been satisfied and the table removed, he instructed him to come nearer and sit beside him. [830] When Jacob approached with bowed head beneath his father’s right hand, he received the bright words of the holy-speaking parent, while he tasted sweet kisses with pressed lips.

For, after the desired union of a long life, the elder brother was ordered to serve the younger.

Meanwhile Esau, driven by long wanderings, carried the captured entrails to his father, who was already satisfied. [835] Although he had pleased him greatly by his service and conduct, he could not take the gifts that had been intercepted.

Then came anger, tears, and a scheme sought for harm. Rebecca, seeing this revealed in her brother’s heart, [840] advised Jacob to visit his kinsmen at Carras and seek Laban, his mother’s brother, until the passage of long time should disperse the anger he had conceived.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The seer’s counsel was joined to his mother’s advice. [845] While they quietly instructed him, they prayed together for their son:

“Do not seek marriage, young man, from the race of Canaan, but remember your dear father’s words and adhere to them.

“There is a place among the Assyrians, enclosed by two rivers. There lives Bethuel, the father of my mother and our friend, [850] and Laban, your maternal uncle, who holds rich estates throughout the fields and cherishes daughters in the years of maidenhood.

“Seek your wife there, I advise you, from the stock that derives its noble lineage from our blood.”

The young man, rejoicing to obey his father’s instructions, left his homeland. Wearied by much labor, he lowered his eyes into sweet sleep. [855] When he had spread stones over his freezing bed, he placed a very hard rock beneath his tired head.

While his limbs were refreshed by secure slumber, [860] he fearlessly saw, with the full light of his mind, a ladder fixed through the clear heavens beyond the clouds. Down its steps a lofty throng was rushing, while another group was climbing from the earth toward the heavenly citadels.

As bodies rolled in precipitous descent, the Almighty watched the falling ones with bowed face. [865] Then, standing above them, he said:

“I am the great king of Olympus, long your Lord and your father’s Lord. Cast off fear: the land to which you have committed your limbs shall be a sure abode for you and for all your descendants under your guidance. [870] Now go forward mindful of this, and do not abandon the task you have begun. Under my guidance you shall return again to the cities you left.”

A great terror broke his sleep and shook all his bones, drenching his limbs with a moist flood.

[Col. 0367C] Then he said in remembrance:

“Here is the great house of the Thunderer, [875] and the gate that opens heaven on its two hinges.”

Soon he anointed the stone that had been placed beneath his head. Calling the place the House of the Lord, and using the stone as a marker, he promised that he would give a tenth of his produce.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Now hastening along the journey he had begun, wherever the path led, he reached a well that alone, in the vast wastelands, had always bathed the gentle flock with flowing waters.

[880] Three groups of shepherds were drawing thin streams in the hot sun and relieving the heat. After greeting them, the seer asked about each matter and saw that all whom he sought were safe.

Meanwhile Rachel, advancing with a snowy appearance, was driving her father’s familiar ewes toward the drinking place. [885] When the young man saw her promptly by the light of brotherly recognition, he joined her to his chaste embrace and kindred heart, rolling away the stone that covered the mouth of the well, and at the same time revealing that he was of her brother’s blood.

Laban, seeing him from afar with joyful perception, ran up and welcomed the young man in the customary household. He did not allow his kinsman, the seer, to serve without compensation, [890] but, in return for the man’s labor, promised his daughter to him in marriage.

Thus, when he had completed seven years of service, he asked that his betrothed be joined to him in the marriage bond. Without delay Leah was given to him by a deceitful substitution, her eyes weak, though she had been the first born.

But Jacob, grieving at the contrived fraud, addressed reproaches to his father-in-law, frustrated of the promised maiden. [895] Again, in payment for the other, Jacob endured the obligations of long service, receiving Rachel, his due reward now that the fraud had been put aside.

But God, the greatest ruler of the heavenly court, compensated for the loss of beauty with abundant offspring. Leah first bore Reuben, then Simeon; the third, Levi, was born with an excellent heart.

[900] He possessed the sacred altars of our Lord. Then Judah followed, soon to become the founder of a tribe.

## CHAPTER XXX

But it is proper now to speak of the other children whom Bilhah bore, illustrious offspring. After these, Issachar was born as the fifth child. A sixth descendant followed, receiving the name Zebulun.

[915] Dinah too was born, a girl suited to her brothers. At last God granted Rachel a delayed gift: she brought tender Joseph into the heavenly light.

When both sets of children had been born to the wives, he asked to leave his father-in-law, together with what he had earned. When they wished to pay him his due wages, they laid aside their intentions and asked what he wanted as his compensation.

[920] Wanting nothing foreign, and declaring that he wished to enrich himself solely through the gifts of the Lord, he departed, content merely to have received both wives.

Striving to secure for himself a lasting advantage, he resolved to cut rods from the trunks of trees. The first was myrtle (*myrtea*; the transmitted reading is uncertain), the second was taken from storax. [925] The third was plucked from a walnut-tree, so that the wool, smeared with the sap of the rods, might gradually assume diverse colours.

For, hastening to set the bleating flock before the pools, he marked it with the varied distinction of the coloured sap, because his father-in-law had said that this variegated offspring, which he had sought for many years, would be his wages.

[930] Since Jacob surpassed him in wealth produced without purchase, he aroused the envy of those who grieved with hostile resentment.

## CHAPTER XXXI

While his harsh father-in-law sheared the fleeces, freedom was granted to the man, so that he might carry away all the advantages, as well as the household idols baked in a heated furnace, which the Syrian believed to be gods in his ancestral Carras.

[935] Yet cautious Rachel concealed these things in wrappings, lest her father punish the offence when it was discovered.

Having departed, he climbed the hill beyond the crossed river, which the natives call Galat in their ancestral language. On the third day, the news of the son-in-law’s departure, and likewise that of his daughters, reached his father-in-law.

Immediately he sought help from his kinsmen. Nangus, long sought—now on the sixth day—was forbidden by the holy fear of the Lord to do harm. [940] Mildly he demanded his gods, which he believed to be divine, and grieved because, though sought everywhere, they could not be found.

After certain peace had returned when the complaints were laid aside, a high heap was built from growing stones, so that the place might remain a witness by the fortification constructed there, and so that the boundary set up might distinguish the lands.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[955] Behold, in the middle of the road the seer saw lofty camps, which God, the ruling leader, directs under the guidance of the starry heavens. He gave the place a name, declaring: “Here God fulfills [his promise].”

Meanwhile he ordered chosen young men to go ahead, burdened with gifts, instructing them to offer them to his brother so that he might grant a peaceful return and agree to the request for peace.

He willingly gave his assent. Accompanied by his allies and a large company, he came peacefully to meet his brother. Though a crowd of four hundred men caused alarm, their appearance, more than their weapons, inflicted fear upon the attendants.

[965] He therefore arranged the flocks in separate groups, placing first those which he hoped his brother would deem worthy to accept as gifts. At the same time, bending his neck, he prayed to the Lord:

“O God, hope and substance of the immense kingdom, you who alone are always the God of my father and grandfather, [970] whose commands bring me back from exile, you who have granted great benefits to your enriched servant, you commanded me to cross the slow-moving river with a staff and immediately to cross your Jordan on foot.

“And now you see me dwelling in divided camps, [975] so that I may avoid various dangers under a twofold protection.

“Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils, and, being peaceful, strike the brother’s darts from their unbroken iron as soon as possible, lest he swiftly pierce my heart with a hard weapon.”

After he had arranged his companions and sought sleep, he struggled during the night to overcome God.

[980] He was astonished at the female part of the body when it was seized. When he had long wished to loosen the bonds of his limbs, the Lord, who had struck the seer in vigorous combat, sent him away after granting the requested gifts.

With his name changed, Jacob ceased to be Jacob and, as everyone says, was called “Seeing the Lord” (*Dominum Cernens*). [985] He even dared to learn the Lord’s name, which it is the right of the Thunderer alone to know.

He himself called the place by the name “Vision of the Lord,” because there he had been allowed to see the lofty face of the Lord. When the Lord withdrew after night had been driven away, he went forth, supporting his steps with a long staff.

[990] From this event Judea remembers avoiding the eating of the sinew that strengthened the bound thigh with its rigid protection.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[995] Now, seeing his brother surrounded by a troop and a flock, he greeted his lord with bowed neck and prostrate posture. When they met, they joined their breasts in much weeping, and soon, in varied speech, he asked more fully who had come with him and what company followed.

He explained of what father the wives had been born, and by what recompense the several flocks had been acquired. [1000] At once the daughters-in-law, sinking on bent knees, brought their tender children to their kinsman’s kisses.

But while the elder reverently declined the gifts he had offered, the gentle man caressed the pledges of the harmonious seer. Then, gladly accompanied by his brother, he hurried back, so that through conversation they might gradually recount their deeds to one another.

[1005] But because the pregnant women moved slowly in their advancing company, the seer halted to manage the flocks and servants. He placed small huts beneath a leafy roof and chose to call them, by a fixed name, “Tabernacles.”

He came to Shechem, which lies in the region of Canaan, purchased neighboring fields at a price, and, hastening to build altars, prayed to God.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[1015] There the wicked Correus violated Dinah, whom he had loved, and robbed the tender virgin of her maidenhood. Wishing to be joined to her as a wife, he removed the foreskin and brought great gifts to the seer as payment for the abducted bride.

He was killed, together with the whole population, overwhelmed by the attack. Jacob grieved over these deeds of his sons, speaking of the broken treaty with the allied people.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Immediately the Almighty warned the seer to depart and establish a secure home at Bethel. He hastened to obey God and urged his children [1025] to crush the shrines of the gods, strengthened with rigid metal, and to put on white garments beneath a covering of snow-white cloth.

He hid the gods beneath the terebinth in a cave. He saw the great Lord utter his customary words to him, declaring that he would make the seer mighty in the rich lands which the Lord had promised to Abraham.

[1030] He gave the place a name and consecrated the stone, reverently pouring clear olive oil over it. He raised a dwelling beneath the roof of the tower of Eder.

Meanwhile Rachel, exhausted by grievous pain, became a mother in death and brought Benjamin forth from her womb. For, besides the familiar offspring born of lawful mothers, [1035] thereafter, on the third day, when the wounds burned more fiercely, she bore offspring with Balla substituted as mother [the transmitted wording is corrupt].

He gladly recognized distinguished Dan from the associated stock of Balla, followed by Naphtali. Soon afterwards Zilpah bore others, Gad and Asher.

[1040] Asher also possessed this distinction: he knew that he would be absent when such a large family saw his father’s face. Thus, born to an already aged mother, he could rejoice in twelve grandsons.

When at last the patriarch’s life had lasted twice ninety years and been prolonged through a long age, [1045] he was released, and radiant departed from his weary body, to see the holy abodes granted by wisdom.

There, reclining through the ages in starry splendour, he securely invites the righteous to snowy joys.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Now it is pleasing to tell how the brothers divided their established dwellings. Since they could not contain within the narrow boundaries of the land the many settlers who were increasing with their flocks, [1050] the elder received the Syrian mountain beyond the fields of Canaan and took possession of rich, pleasant pastures.

Jacob, following after him, did not abandon the kingdoms of Canaan, so that his pious mind might always rejoice in the ancestral custom.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

There Joseph undertook remarkable deeds, shining among his brothers in a distinction as great as the moon’s brightness among the stars of heaven.

When he had reached seventeen years, he tended the flocks in the grassy pasture, proceeding as the youngest among all those whom his father had begotten from noble marriages or from a slave concubine.

[1060] And because he flourished conspicuously in the brotherly company, he stirred his brothers’ feelings with the cold of envy.

His father, embracing him from among the whole stock of his children, cherished the tender boy among the strong bodies of his brothers. And so that he might be more conspicuous than all the others, [1065] he covered him with a flowing garment of variegated color.

When he had already served the Lord from his tender years, he once saw, with his eyes lulled by peaceful sleep, himself binding sheaves together with his brothers while they were threshing grain in the middle of the fields.

[1070] Then his own sheaf rose upright with a lofty cone, while those of his brothers fell beside it with bowed necks.

After the young man revealed this in peaceful speech, he stirred their trembling hearts with frightened tumult, speaking of a king and lord and producing a terrifying murmur. [1075] They showed that only a secret deed was lacking for the crime.

To break their hearts still more with twofold sorrow, he disclosed the dreams he had seen to his learned-speaking father, with all those bound to him by the line of blood gathered around.

For he seemed to see the rosy sun, and the moon joined with trembling light, [1080] and ten stars rising together with them, all bending their necks before him as though before a lord.

When his father had learned this in indirect speech, he soon confessed before his frightened brothers that the vision was worthy of reverence.

At once the young men went out and sought their father’s flocks through the blooming grassy valleys. [1085] Joseph was sent to them, and wandered through silent thickets until, directed by one of the young men, he found the retreat where the brothers were grazing the flock amid changed grass.

When they recognized him from afar by his varied garment, they devised an evil plan with discordant voices. All agreed to destroy the brother they hated and to report, once he had been killed, that wild beasts had devoured him.

[1090] While they muttered together in a swift whisper, they said: “Let us see whether the dreams can drive away death.”

The gentler Reuben rejected this proposal and advised the brothers, though they were growling, to hide their hardened iron weapons, remembering that it would be better to throw him into a stagnant pool.

[1095] Immediately Joseph was stripped, and naked he was wrapped in reeds.

Meanwhile a Syrian merchant was driving Ishmaelite camels, heavily laden with Sabaean goods, while he hurried to bring the harvests of Arabia to Canopus.

Then Judah said that it was better to sell Joseph for money; the preceding transmitted phrase is corrupt. His father was kept ignorant, and, seeing the garment stained with blood, believed—without any contrivance—that he had been killed.

[1100] Reuben tore his clothing with hooked hands and wrapped himself in a dark garment of mourning.

[Col. 0373A] [Note: [Col. 0373D]

1131. Perhaps *Nec spes* (“nor hope”).

1133. Saint Augustine, *Questions on Genesis* 130, calls him Putefret; the Vulgate version has Putiphar. MART.

1139. Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.423: “You alone knew the man’s tender approaches and his opportunities.”

1144. From Juvenal, *Satire* 6.285.
