The father, afflicted by grief, searched for the lost son. The eunuch of Pharaoh had long since taken him in and used to load the tyrant’s golden tables with dishes and rejoice in the noise of the great kitchen.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Meanwhile Tamar gave birth, while the joys of guilt pleased her, and her womb was filled with twin offspring. Of these, the first boy deserved the light of life: he thrust out his hand first, and the skillful woman tied it with a crimson thread; then it was hidden again in the womb.

[1120] The other was born immediately instead, although by lot he held the earlier position. Since he had once been separated by a boundary, he received the name Zarah; the other was called Pharez.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Faithful guardianship of the Lord watched over Joseph, not allowing him to live subject to a harsh law. For his former master, so called, entrusted everything to his servant, and not in vain: the gracious Lord from above increased everything that the young man managed.

[1125] Yet the gentle man did not win the love of Petaphra. Because his eyes shone in a remarkable face, the mistress, grievously wounded, solicited intercourse with her servant.

But the young man avoided the shameful act and refused to profane the consecrated bed with excessive guilt. The woman, ruined by forbidden flames, explored tender approaches in vain and sought opportunities.

[1130] Once, when she found the house empty and herself alone, she pressed upon him and forced him to lie down beside her. He sprang up eagerly, slipped his garment from his body, and escaped from between the woman’s arms.

The woman cried out and drew strength from the accusation, shouting that the young man, trusting in his beauty while burning with youthful age, had violated her most cherished honor and attempted to climb into his master’s bed.

[1135] She even addressed her husband in a sorrowful voice and demanded that the innocent accused be subjected to the punishment she desired.

The husband, believing her as though she spoke truth, shut Joseph in prison, where the king’s punishment already confined his ministers. The prison keeper soon treated him kindly, and, seeing that he was innocent, entrusted the prisoners to him.

## CHAPTER XL

There, as it happened, two men whom the grim tyrant, moved by anger, had confined in the lofty palace trembled under the punishment they feared in their anxious hearts. [1140] While they stole sleep amid troubled cares, they saw dreams announcing future events.

When he had examined them in their grief with clear insight, Joseph asked the reasons and compelled them to reveal what was hidden.

Immediately the man who regularly served wine to the tyrant explained what he had seen during the night’s sleep:

[Col. 0374A] “I saw a vine flourishing with green shoots. As it crept along, it hung from its own branches, and among the curling tendrils there were three shoots.

[1145] “A yellow grape cluster hung from the nectar-like vine. Then the king’s cup, from which he pours gentle drinks, foamed with the new wine that his right hand had pressed, and the master held it in his ready palm.”

The young man accurately disclosed everything that was hidden: the three shoots were three days, after which the man would be restored and regain the favor he had lost, mixing for the king the drink he had seen.

[1150] “For such services,” he said, “do this one thing for me: when confidence in your speech has been restored to you, remove the punishment imposed upon us, though we have committed no crime.

“I am called a Hebrew. Sold into exile because of my brothers’ crime, I went into noble servitude.”

After this, the chief of the bakers began to tell what he had seen:

[1155] “I seemed to carry three baskets on my head, filled with royal delicacies and sumptuous preparation, while countless birds snatched them away with their claws.”

After he had spoken these things, which were indeed true but harsh, Joseph declared that he would soon be put to death by a hard sword, that his head would be severed and fixed upon a high stake, [1160] and that birds would immediately tear it apart with curved beaks.

The former was restored to his position; the latter was killed, his body reduced to a trunk.

## CHAPTER XLI

Meanwhile, after two years had passed and the stars were again turning their courses toward the East, the ruler of the Nile saw these dreams.

For he seemed, while gazing at a lovely river, to see seven sleek cows [1165] grazing the green grass along the bank. He saw others, made ugly by emaciation, approaching on their feet, scarcely clinging to their own bones—strange to say—and devouring the splendid cows with open mouths.

The dreams were joined together, not discordant in their corresponding meanings. Behold, he saw seven ears of grain growing from a fertile stalk, and beside them others, thin and devoid of grain-seed, [1170] horrifically appearing to consume the full ears as though pregnant.

The troubled man could not contain this vision in his mind. Trembling, he ordered all who possessed knowledge to appear and asked what interpretation lay concealed in the signs.

When the Egyptian augur, consulted, remained silent—the same man who had recently been released from prison and served wine—the young man spoke. Joseph revealed that he had returned to his former position and that his companion had been killed.

[1175] Men were quickly sent to bring the seer, stripped of all guilt, from the shameful prison, and, cutting his unkempt cheeks and hair nourished by confinement, to restore his former appearance.

Thus, when the upright man was consulted, he gave this answer: the cows signified years, and the light ears signified seven cycles.

[1180] He explained that the events were signs of what was to come: for seven years the earth would be sufficiently fertile, and at the same time would produce dreadful famine, during which the land, dry in its thirsty veins, would consume the pale grasses in its dusty furrows.

For the dreams are joined by corresponding visions; God commands that the certainty of their meaning stand firm.

[1185] “Rather, while the time is present and the care of healing is still possible, choose from among all the nobles one who knows these matters in advance. Once judges have been appointed, let him govern all Egypt from his high position and collect a fifth from every harvest.

“Thus the abundance first granted by the fertile lands may be held in reserve for the barren years, when the crops have been consumed.”

[1190] The nobles received the seer’s judgment with applause. At last the ruler too, his heart calmed, exalted Joseph, who had declared the truth, to high honor. He ordered him to carry authority throughout all the cities.

Then he crowned the seer’s finger with a shining ring, wrapped him in linen beneath a saffron-colored cloak, and placed a flexible golden collar around his neck. [1195] Thus the new ruler stood higher than the chariot.

A herald’s loud proclamation increased the awe surrounding the judge. He was also given a wife named Asenath, whom the seer Petaphres had begotten from a noble line. [1200] By her he immediately became the father of twin pledges: the elder was called Manasseh, the younger Ephraim.

By the lofty counsel of Egypt’s noble seer, he kept the granaries full with all that the lean time could scarcely consume, so that, when need required, he might bring forth the hidden grain for all who asked.

[1205] Later, when dreadful famine had spread throughout the whole world and compelled the frightened people to regard whatever could be eaten as food, the population cried out and demanded provisions from the king.

He ordered Joseph, the nobleman, to give grain to the grieving people, and he filled them all with rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XLII

Meanwhile Jacob, having already mourned the death of his son, sent ten young men from his numerous offspring to obtain grain from a distant land at a price. [1210] But he did not allow Benjamin, the youngest of all, to go, lest, being weak, he should be unable to bear the hard labor.

When they reached the walls of the land of Pharos, they humbly sought the ground and greeted the brother whom they saw sitting in a lofty position, marveling at his high rank. Yet they did not recognize him, since they had not seen him for a long time.

[1215] When the seer saw them, remembering everything, he rebuked them and frightened the trembling men with many words, claiming that they had come to spy out what supply of grain existed and what stout men ruled the lands.

They pleaded ignorance of deceit and confessed that they had once been twelve brothers under one father, that the youngest remained at home to preserve their father’s labors, [1220] and that another had long since perished in a celebrated death.

They said that they were avoiding dreadful famine and, despising the land of Canaan, which nourished seed with scanty fertility, were seeking goods for sale and grain obtained by bidding.

The seer spoke, swearing by the name of the ruler, that the young men were to be confined in harsh custody until they produced the brother whom their gentle father had kept at home.

[1225] They were kept together under guard for three days; afterwards they were released, leaving one behind to be held.

Nevertheless, breaking their hearts with hidden grief, they recalled how justly their dangers had arisen, because they had once, without peace or permission, handed over their innocent brother and were now paying the punishment of their deed before a judge.

[1230] Reuben intensified these words by recounting the truth and the immense crime committed against his will. The seer was moved by this, recognizing their brotherly quarrels; turning away, he wept silently and bitterly.

Meanwhile Simeon, the middle member of the brothers’ group, was taken and kept as a faithful hostage for all those who returned.

Then the young men take up the grain they had requested,

and the mules, burdened with the immense weight, are driven onward.

Already halfway along the road, as he loosens the cords of a sack,

one of them shows his brothers the coins he has found.

[1290] They all do the same, once the payment has been discovered;

astonished, they praise the high ruler with the utmost rivalry.

And now, as they approach the threshold of their ancestral home,

their father rejoices at their return and asks after the one.

Recognizing everything, he takes up the coins and gifts,

[1295] but bitterly laments that another son is now absent.

When their provisions were then consumed and the grain brought in,

they were compelled once more to procure food at a price;

but no one was willing to set out again for Memphis,

unless their father ordered the youngest brother to go with them.

[1300] When he, lamenting deeply, was unwilling to send him anywhere,

Reuben, with loyal words, demands his brother,

entrusting two pledges to his father and feeling secure.

Judah follows, declaring that he too cannot return,

as he bears witness to the words of the stern Joseph.

### CHAPTER XLIII

[1305] When the aged father, now more yielding, had heard this,

he gives up the young man, bathing his face in a flood of tears.

They depart, carrying with them lightly scented frankincense,

incense and drops combined with terebinth,

and honey amid fragrant vapors,

[1310] as well as the double payment, lest any mistake should occur—

the coins that had been placed in their closed sacks.

When Joseph saw them in his splendid hall,

[Note: [Col. 0377D]

1317. Perhaps *imposta* (“imposed,” “laid upon”).

1318. One may conjecture: “having been exempt from theft in all things.”

1340. Perhaps *succo* (“juice,” “sap”). MART.

1342. This is corrupt, as are several other passages. The reference seems to be to the younger brother according to the sacred text.

1351. Perhaps: “They reproach him with theft.”

1353. Schramus reads, “They uncover the sought-for cup.” It would seem better to read, “and they uncover the sought-for cup,” or, if one wishes to observe the meter, “they uncover what was sought and the cup.”

1364. Clearly the land of Gessen. For the Italian version reads: “And you shall dwell in the land of Gessen of Arabia.” MART. Ambrose, *On Joseph*, chapter 12: “Gessen of Arabia.” Most of the Greek witnesses likewise have this. Sabatier observes from Jerome that “of Arabia” is absent from the Hebrew volumes.

1380. In the Vulgate edition only seventy souls are said to have entered Egypt with Jacob; but the Septuagint translators, and the Italian version—which Juvencus follows here—count seventy-five. Saint Stephen agrees with them, Acts 7:14. MART. *Denos* should be corrected to *denas*, and instead of *ut farmula* I read *ut formula*. As for the number of souls who entered Egypt, Ambrose counts seventy in one place and seventy-five in another. In fact, if Joseph’s great-grandchildren are counted by anticipation, the number will be seventy-five; otherwise, seventy.]

He orders them to celebrate joyful banquets with him.

Yet they come murmuring, and in trembling guilt

[1315] suppose that they have been summoned with some contrivance,

because, having previously counted the money and given it to the prophet,

they had been unable to return it after it was placed among their baggage;

nevertheless, they say that they will declare in every respect that they are innocent of theft,

nor have they ever been accustomed to live with concealed treasure.

[1320] The minister restrains them from saying such things,

and declares that he himself knows he has been defrauded of no money,

but that, if any advantages or profit had been given to the men,

they should attribute them neither to themselves, nor to the prophet, nor to the king.

Simeon comes forward to meet them all and presents himself,

[1325] while he supplies the men with water and provides fodder for the mules.

The prophet enters, escorted by a large body of soldiers,

and at his appearance the brothers bring forth their pious gifts.

When he had addressed them all in calm speech,

he asks whether their father was strong and well.

[1330] After they say that he is safe and living in good health,

Joseph assures the prophet that he remains joined to God

as a reward for his life and always persists in what is right.

And as though Benjamin were not known to him,

he questions the young men and promptly inquires,

[1335] asking God in praise of the boy to grant him every blessing.

He can restrain neither his sighs nor his tears,

but, moved by tender affection, he withdraws into his chambers,

anxious, and seeks relief for his excessive grief.

Afterward, when he had reclined at table, the servants set out the meal.

[1340] He eats, and with easy cheerfulness delights to encourage their hearts;

he is glad to distribute the divided dishes to each man,

and offers to one brother a larger portion.

### CHAPTER XLIV

And when their love of eating had been satisfied,

just as before they had loaded the mules with their burden,

[1345] the talent given by Joseph’s accustomed order is concealed,

and the gleaming cup is hidden among your belongings,

Benjamin, more precious than any workmanship.

They have already begun their journey and are not many miles away,

when suddenly a royal troop surrounds the unsuspecting men,

[1350] seizes them, and demands the shining cup,

reproaching the one whom they entangle in a charge with becoming a slave.

They consent, and all together open their own burdens,

uncovering both what was sought and the cup, and leaving their brother behind.

They seek Joseph and, recounting what has happened,

[1355] immediately unfold the commands of their dear father.

### CHAPTER XLV

Moved by their prayers, the prophet orders everyone else to withdraw

and tells the brothers that he is their brother.

They stand frozen, stiff with fear, and in silent guilt,

condemning themselves, hold back their voices in terror.

[1360] Soon he encourages the accused and calls them closer,

requiring them to report what words they might bring

that would please their father—what had happened, what was happening,

and what was said to be about to happen:

urging them to move their people, and offering the neighboring hills

[1365] of the Arabs to those who were arriving with their gathered flocks,

so that, since the land would immediately be dry for five years,

they might feed all their kinsmen on the stored grain.

The king learns of these orders with a joyful heart,

and asks Joseph to take charge of his dear ones;

[Col. 0378B] he orders him to give the grain freely to his brothers.

[1370] Wagons, grain, cups, and bread are given to the men,

and the mules labor beneath the great burdens they carry.

Five robes are given to Benjamin, and five to his father,

and three hundred coins marked by the stamped die.

But the other young men receive, as a second reward,

[1375] two cloaks of snowy cloth.

When the father learns of this, taking the gifts that have been given,

he breathes again and hastens to leave his native land.

### CHAPTER XLVI

He seeks Egypt, which is joined to the fields of Arabia,

leading from his homeland five young men,

[1380] seventy-five in number, as the formula of Genesis prescribed.

And while the company hastens forward with rapid effort,

Judah runs ahead and outstrips the column of his brothers.

He informs Joseph that their father is standing not far away.

Joseph eagerly mounts his chariot and goes out to meet him,

[1385] welcoming the long-desired company when he sees his father.

### CHAPTER XLVII

He quickly returns and goes out to the king’s court,

reporting that the shepherds are approaching, so that the company of his dear ones

may dwell on separate lands in fertile pasture.

The Memphis ruler himself also presses the prophet,

[1390] and orders him to settle his brothers in rich fields.

After this, the long-lived old man slowly explains,

at the tyrant’s request, how many years he possesses,

what his household is, and why he has come to Canopus;

and he honors the exceptional ruler with abundant praise.

[1395] Meanwhile Joseph also sends gifts worthy of his own people

and gives the great ruler a talent,

by which the palace had been enriched through the sale of grain.

[Col. 0379A] When the bronze coins of the merchants had already run out,

the Memphis crowd, competing with one another, brought forward their flocks

[1400] and, with Joseph fixing the price, the needy bought grain.

Stripped even of these things, they surrender themselves and their estates,

on the condition that the seed would afterward make the harvests green.

Only the priests’ property was not taken away,

because it pleased the ruler not to sell them grain for payment.

[1405] From that time a fifth-part payment of the grain is imposed on the people;

this arrangement remains preserved under fixed law.

Meanwhile, reflecting on the completed span of his life,

Jacob adjures his son, turning his thoughts toward what was to come,

to lay his remains in the tombs of his ancestors.

[1410] He agrees to the request, placing his right hand beneath his thigh,

and touches the tip of his staff, making his promise.

### CHAPTER XLVIII

The old man gently caresses his grandsons on either side with his words,

while gradually bestowing kisses upon them.

But wondrously, the right hand consecrates Manasseh,

[1415] while Ephraim, the younger by birth, is touched by the left.

The old man’s prophetic mind compels the elder to serve the younger,

and the first hope yields its place to the second.

Although Joseph wishes to guide the hands back to their proper position,

he nevertheless cannot turn aside the pious words.

[1420] But after the prophet has confirmed the destined blessings for the boys,

he gives Shechem, the sword, and darts to his son,

so that he may rise in honor above them all.

### CHAPTER XLIX

Then he calls his sons and gives rewards to them all,

establishing two and six tribes in accordance with their names.

[1425] When everything has been declared, now blind in both eyes,

he assigns to his pledges and to the descendants of his sons

what will remain for a long time and what had previously been denied them,

granting it for a long age.

The prophet died, leaving only his earthly body behind.

### CHAPTER L

And he gave his eyes to mourning for seventy days,

while the company honored the tomb of the deceased.

The sons too mourned for seven days

with abundant tears, while Joseph restored peace

to his innocent brothers and abandoned his former anger.

After he himself had lived through a hundred years,

[1435] and ten more, having completed the appointed span of death,

he tells his brothers what order would come in the future,

by which they might return and leave the Nile,

provided that they carried back his arranged ashes and bones

and took them with them to be buried in the ancient tombs.

[1440] Thus at last, after the bright years of his long life,

[1441] he died, sought God, and left his body behind.

# On the Praises of the Lord  
*(C, G, S)*

[Note: [Col. 0379D]

In the prolegomena, number 18, I explained why this poem, published under Constantine, may be placed among Juvencus’s doubtful or spurious poems. Barthius calls the poem elegant, learned, polished, and highly erudite, and in *Adversaria* book 35, chapter 9, declares it worthy even of Paulinus. That it is earlier than Paulinus is evident from the very period in which it was written.

Verse 7. “With sluggish procession”: so Juvencus, book 3, verse 461: “The green Jordan bursts through with lovely procession.”

8. I think one should read: “Slow Arar, and Diuvix scarcely unfolds its sluggish stream for a long time.” For I do not understand what “Diuvix” means. The Saône is now meant, a river of Celtic Gaul, concerning which Caesar writes, *Gallic War* book 1, chapter 12: “There is a river called the Arar, which flows through the territories of the Aedui and Sequani into the Rhône with such incredible gentleness that the direction in which it flows cannot be judged by the eyes.” John Michael Brutus maintains in his *Scholia* that one should read “with incredible lightness.” For, he says, nothing seems less suited to the Arar than slowness; yet with excessive lightness it can sometimes happen that vision is deceived. This opinion is refuted not only by Caesar’s words but also by the authority of many ancient writers, who call the Arar slow and sluggish. Pliny, book 3, chapter 4: “The sluggish Arar.” Silius, book 15, verse 504: “The Arar, most sluggish of streams, creeps through their fields.” Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*, verse 53: “Slow Arar”; and book 2 *Against Rufinus*, verse 111: “Whom the swift Rhône surrounds, and those whom the slower Arar surrounds.” To these may be added the author of this poem, who indicates the same thing in the preceding verse by “with sluggish procession.” Barthius is therefore wrong, *Adversaria* book 21, chapter 17, to take “sluggish” simply as “flowing.”]

Who complains that the reward of virtue comes late?

Who thinks that God’s promises proceed with a slow step?

Who measures the judge’s urn by human limits

and thinks that what the ages owe is slow,

[5] although they must hasten the day when he will repay merits?

Noble glory bears witness through an immense deed.

For where the slow Arar glides past the banks

with sluggish procession, and Diuvix slowly unfolds its stream.

[Note: [Col. 0381C]

9. Consider whether one should write: “Where the Aeduan youth of Rome is born from brothers.” The Aedui—whom the more learned write as *Hedui* or *Edui*—had been called by the Roman Senate “brothers” and “kinsmen.” Caesar, *Gallic War* book 1, chapter 33: “Especially because he saw the Aedui, repeatedly called by the Senate brothers and kinsmen, held in slavery and under the power of the Germans.” And afterward: “If they had not done this, the fraternal name of the Roman people would have been far removed from them,” that is, from the Aedui. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* 1.16, elsewhere numbered 19: “The Aedui, our brothers, are fighting.”

12. This formula frequently occurs in the funerary inscriptions of the ancients: “A survivor contrary to his wish.”

13. “To the pious grief of the surviving spouse.”

17. Barthius, *Adversaria* book 26, chapter 10, thinks this verse should be expelled with pitchforks, without which the entire sense coheres admirably. Perhaps it should be transposed in this manner: “After receiving God’s commands, he would raise the common tomb— / and, joining them, would establish eternal covenants.” I restore *uniens* as a disyllable through synaeresis; for *veniens* cannot be retained.

19. Barthius, in the cited place, judges that one should read “After God’s commands,” that is, after the summons, or, as Jerome likes to say, “the falling asleep.” Thus we frequently read in the formulas of Christian wills: “When the Lord shall have commanded concerning me.” This too was transferred from the style of the holy Fathers. Add verse 14 of this poem: “But the earlier page of the decree read the wife first.”

23. *Constringant* is much better than *constringat*: namely, “let the hands bind the repeated bonds to the trunk.” One may observe how this was customarily done in ancient images of the buried Lazarus. Recall the note on verse 395 of book 4 of Juvencus’s *Evangelical History*.

25. The sense is: “lest an unsightly flowing apart should occur among the dismembered limbs with which the functions of life are completed.” *Fluitatio* is a new word, but exceedingly well suited to express the matter. Forcellini omitted it and did not even place it among barbarous words. Julian of Toledo treats this subject in *Prognosticum* book 1, chapter 18, reasoning from Saint Augustine as follows: “Nevertheless, the bodies of the dead, especially those of the righteous and faithful, are not to be despised or cast away; for the Holy Spirit used them as organs and vessels for every good and holy work.” This is how the oldest manuscript of Julian, which I use, reads.

26. This verse and the next do not seem to belong here and may perhaps be corrupt. Certainly without them the sense proceeds well.

33. Instead of *venturae* I read *venturi*, or *venturam*.

37. I think this passage contains an error in *Rectorque regentis*.

39. This passage is explained in the note to Dracontius, book 2, verse 343.

50. Barthius, *Adversaria* book 35, chapter 9, gives several words ending in *-escere* that are not found in ordinary usage, among them *curvescere*, from this passage. Forcellini relegated *curvesco* to the barbarous vocabulary.

51. *Reditus*: returns, fruits, proceeds. This noun is written from *redeo* with the first syllable shortened. Therefore *redditus* can scarcely be tolerated in poets who lengthen the first syllable freely, as in *relligio* and *reppulit*.

53. Is the sacred baptism being discussed? I think so.

56. Have the elements been increased?

58. “The world,” “the heavens”: Barthius confirms this meaning from Manilius and other ancient writers, *Adversaria* book 35, chapter 16.

59. Consider whether *dextera pinxit* (“painted with his right hand”) would be better.

61. Barthius, book 24, chapter 5, says that this elegance was transferred from Greek into Latin: namely, that barbarians of savage character were called fierce and inhospitable. He cites this verse itself along with others by other authors.

62. Accept Barthius’s interpretation, book 46, chapter 16: “So that the seas should not be wholly inhospitable to human pursuits, and so that the sailor might know that a constant—that is, frequent, repeated, almost perpetual—harbor was everywhere available for his labors, the Best and Greatest Creator fixed islands in the sea.”]

Where the Aeduan offspring, brethren, springs forth by the Rhine,

[10] I remember a marriage of the highest piety and faithfulness;

yet divine law increased the worth of their love:

and both had vowed that one should precede the other in death,

and entrust the care of the tomb to the pious survivor.

But the earlier page of the decree read the wife first.

[15] Then the anxious husband, with generous speech, orders that stones,

hospitable after death, be hollowed out for the body:

so that the surviving spouse might receive the one who came,

joining them in eternal covenants,

so that those whom the same marriage-bed had held alive

[20] might, after receiving God’s commands, raise a common tomb.

The wife, foreseeing her husband’s wishes, perceived them,

and assigned great miracles to chaste times.

For when the arms of the dead limbs are joined,

and the hands, binding repeated bonds, embrace the trunk,

[Col. 0381B] lest an unsightly flowing apart should occur

[25] among the dismembered limbs with which the functions of life are completed—

wondrous beyond words!—when life’s course had been completed,

the husband, destined to be joined to his wife, looked toward the prepared place.

After the gate of death had been opened by the man’s death,

and the unwelcome light had uncovered the dreadful dwelling,

[30] the woman was discovered extending her left palm,

inviting her companion with the gesture of living love.

Who gave affection to the tomb? Who loosened the bonds?

From where does the buried woman see the shadow of her future husband?

You bring these things about, Christ God; your signs are set in motion,

[35] and you gradually teach the sleeping limbs to rise again—

you whom the holy prophets foretold as coming,

the incorruptible offspring of God, and ruler of the ruler.

Without you the Father undertakes nothing great or mighty;

at your command the sea was fixed within its appointed shores,

[40] nor is it permitted to run across the lands in an immeasurable flood;

level shores enclose the mountain-bearing waves.

You endowed the stable earth with varied gifts

for our use, generous in fatherly compassion.

With you as guide, mortals entrust their seeds to the furrows,

[45] and a new offspring emerges from the dry turf.

You command the vines to pour forth fertile nectar;

from the trees you draw juices pleasing at human banquets

and medicinal for health;

you bring forth sweet honey.

You command every kind of living creature to serve humanity,

[50] and moreover you make the groves bend beneath heavy fruit,

and cause new returns to arise from no seed.

You make various rivers useful to our labor

and renew the age blessed by sacred springs.

Under your guidance, the seas opened to sail-bearing prows,

[55] and the sailor traversed harbors divided by straits.

After the elements had been formed by waxen figures,

lest the heavenly machine begin to languish in an unformed appearance,

you marked the world with varied gifts;

and whatever shines in heaven, your right hand fashioned.

[60] With these signs you were pleased to weave the Lord’s palace.

And lest the seas be inhospitable to lands everywhere,

and lest the lively sailor fail to count a constant harbor,

a sufficient number of islands is fixed in the swelling sea.

[Note: [Col. 0383C]

68. I suspect *quoquam* (“anyone”) should be read in place of *quidquam* (“anything”).

71. Perhaps *grandius* (“greater”).

77. Dracontius has similar wording, *Satisfactio*, verse 247, and others whom I cited there.

82. Compare the note to Dracontius, book 3, verse 27.

86. See the note to Dracontius, book 3, verse 552: “Not even if I had an iron voice.”

94. More on this in the note to Dracontius, book 2, verse 690.

96. Clearly *a limite vitae praescripto vobis* means “from the limit of life prescribed for you,” rather than “from you.” Or read *a nobis* (“from us”).

97. Barthius, book 25, chapter 7, asserts that *tueor* is used passively by Boethius and by the author of this poem, although he was not certain of this because the book was not at hand. If he is referring to this passage, *tueri* here is taken actively, for *intueri*. The sense is: “so that our faces might endure you watching over them; the Father clothed you, etc.”

102. I would read *delicta* (“offenses”) instead of *directa* (“straight things”).

104. I would prefer something else instead of *dubias* (“uncertain”).

105. Clearly so that something might make your distinguished birth illustrious.

107. This verse and the next are obscure and perhaps corrupt. The perpetual virginity of the Mother of God seems to be indicated, and the point is clear if one reads *ut procul* in the following verse.

112. *Missa Deo* means “sent to God,” instead of “sent by God”; Juvencus has many such expressions.

115. “So that nothing might remain unattempted,” from Virgil, book 8, verse 205, which others also imitated.

118. As in the case of Lazarus’s corpse.

120. Perhaps he refers to Christ’s words, “It is finished,” which concern the cup of the Passion.

126. “The secrets of heaven,” as in Juvencus, book 1, verse 210: “the secrets of heaven.”

127. I correct *succedere* (“to follow”) to *succendere* (“to set fire to”).

130. One should note this author’s peculiar opinion: lest those who had died long before should be bound by Christ’s new commands or judged by them, Christ ordered the deadly places of the infernal prison to be freed and left empty for us—that is, for those who would exist after Christ—after countless people had been drawn out from them, with only those retained whom an impious life had stained. He therefore divided the places of punishment, leaving one part to those so retained and reserving another for those who would not believe in Christ, or who would pretend to believe because they would not maintain faith through good works.

134. He calls the dead “shades,” using a phrase borrowed from the pagans, though other Christian poets also used it.]

Yet it does not fear the mad waves surrounding it,

[65] and, resting upon a small circle amid the straits, it resists,

confident under your guidance, whose venerable covenant,

joined by an equal law, balances the highest and the lowest,

and does not allow those things placed within it to cross their boundaries.

And lest the earth lie too flat or bare,

[70] you ordered hills suitable for vines to rise high,

and groves to spread broad canopies.

Then, lest a vast horror prevail through sluggish forests,

you add countless offspring to the lofty woodlands,

so that the grove might have an inhabitant and the seeker might not lack prey.

[75] Then you caused many birds and a thousand swarms of voices

to resound through the light with mortal harmony and song.

Thus you were pleased to weave the year with varied forms,

and, through joyful alternation, to add fruit for mortals;

so that the unending day might not burn the world too fiercely,

[80] nor the short day snatch away the proper fire from things being born;

and lest toil continually shake everything with unceasing effort,

the dewy night grants rest to the weary cares of humankind.

And so that human well-being might lead a secure life,

healing grasses rise spontaneously from the turf.

[85] The Father himself sows these, rich through a command rather than a plow.

If I were not enclosed in a wall of iron,

if I had an iron voice and a thousand tongues with which to sing,

I could not recount all the gifts of your compassion.

But that Father of yours, established in a hidden place,

[90] not easily accessible to anyone’s sight and revered by all,

sent you, Lord, to the earth as master of life.

And whoever venerates the Son with fitting honor

should offer his vows to both and pray for everlasting life.

You, steadfast in chastity and righteousness, and easy to bend the laws

[95] after sin, if reckless folly has driven someone

from the boundary of life prescribed by you.

So that our faces might be able to gaze upon you,

the Father clothed you in a human appearance and in perishable limbs.

For who would dare raise fragile eyes

[100] if he wished to set you before trembling lands

as you are when you twist lightning bolts in your mighty right hand

and command the fearful to dread the punishment plainly before them,

or when, appeased, you divide rains among thirsty fields

and draw uncertain ears of grain along the furrows?

[105] Yet, lest nothing make your distinguished birth illustrious,

you were conceived by a virgin. It is not enough for her to be chaste,

nor may one who is married unite a brother to the Lord,

lest any foul contamination be far removed from the womb.

Then, when blessed maturity had ripened with the passing of time,

[110] you undertake to preserve minds unwilling to learn in your father’s teachings,

and offer a straight path to those who are slipping.

And so that the commands sent by God might be thoroughly manifest,

you remove authority from death; with disease released,

you order the desperate to take up the duties of life,

restore daylight to the blind, and, so that nothing might remain unattempted

[115] by which faithless error might perish completely,

you reveal consciousness to the tombs and order

limbs long buried to rise again into the upper air;

the beloved corpses recognize their own name.

[120] But after the suitable follower had absorbed the law,

so that the heavenly spirit might strip itself of its mortal dwelling,

you, intent upon the law by which you would teach all things

to be endured for the supreme God, and rightly to assume everlasting life

through contempt of death,

[125] having fulfilled the Father’s commands, returned

to the secrets of the highest heaven, where the bright ether

forbids sluggish clouds to rise into its own sky.

And so that the certain multitude of the perishing might be known,

those who shut out God’s commands from their pitiable ears,

[130] and so that the new laws might not bind the long-dead,

you command the deadly places of the infernal prison

to be free for us, and countless people to emerge from the darkness,

with only those shut in whom an impious life has marked.

And you divide the places of punishment among the shades to come,

[135] those who do not believe in you or who pretend that they believe.

Holy God, venerable pledge of the supreme God,

at whose name, driven forth by violent death

[Note: [Col. 0385A]

137. These six verses are obscure, and something seems to be missing from the sense. I think the subject is those who rose with Christ and those who, by contrast, were left in eternal punishments—or rather those possessed by a demon, who is driven from human hearts by Christ’s grace and sometimes also occupies the bodies of the righteous, from which he departs when ordered to do so in Christ’s name. See Paulinus, *Natale* 11 of Saint Felix, verses 230 and following.

143. Juvencus composed a similar eulogy of Constantine at the end of book 4 of his *Evangelical History*.

145. “The law established for you,” that is, “established by you.”

from their own breasts and having gained alien breasts,

When the maker of the stars was suffering the bitter punishment of death

on the cross, the world and the stars cried out

that they could not endure the sufferings of the Creator:

black night took away the fiery light of the sun;

[5] the earth trembled, cliffs and rocks split apart.

And why say more? All created things mourned.

When Christ, King of heaven, entered the realms of Phlegethon,

the royal prince Pluto looked out from his royal hall,

as soon as he sensed Christ approaching his own threshold:

[10] “Companions,” he cried, “now is the time to take up weapons,

since this man, his limbs drenched in gore, is drawing near,

about to plunder our riches, our shades, and our souls.

Climb eagerly onto the roofs and drive the enemy away from the threshold

with weapons cast before him, and with many bars and interlocking fastenings.

[15] Meanwhile we shall defend this royal hall with weapons,

with frequent barricades and hard levers.”

Having formed their ranks, they rush to the highest battlements

and fill roofs and walls with dreadful cries.

But behold, Christ broke through the dreadful silences

[20] and shone forth in starlike radiance and brilliant light.

“Ho, leaders of the shades, lift up the gates,

and the bars of the gates; remove the great bolts.

Why, wretches, do you dare to take up arms against the Thunderer?

I am your king here; it is useless to resist a king.”

[25] When he had said this, sudden terror seized them all;

they flee in companies and fill the air with howls.

There is no delay: the doors fall with a crash from their loosened hinges,

and the gate, collapsing, produces a great ruin;

the shaken halls admit Christ.

[30] Charon himself is the first to be stunned and hides in the marsh,

and Cerberus is stunned, closing his three mouths.

The Gorgons and Harpies tremble;

Megaera herself is terrified,

and Tisiphone and Alecto are struck by the grievous light,

the avenging Dirae, the Furies, and the sister Parcae.

[35] And why say more? Groans, torments, and pains fall silent.

As soon as Christ enters, everything around him trembles.

But the holy souls and the spirits of the righteous rejoice.

Adam first of all, joyful, raised his palms toward the stars

and prayed to the Lord with devoted voice:

[40] “O holy Redeemer, you have come, awaited by the wretched;

grant rest and an end to our woes, and carry the redeemed to the stars.

Thus father Abraham, the boy Isaac, and Jacob

come forth eagerly, handsome Joseph beside them,

and holy Moses, and Aaron renowned for his life,

[45] and Joshua the unconquered, the remaining kings and leaders,

and Judas Maccabaeus, avenger of his homeland and lineage;

then other fathers, famous beyond the heavens.

That radiant chorus reverently worships Christ.

Before the others, the royal prophet, the most famous offspring

[50] of Jesse’s line, was touching the lyre with an ivory plectrum,

and all the prophets, praying with one voice in harmony,

fashioned sweet melody in a concordant song.

Before the others, the young man who had recently baptized Christ in the waters,

Having said this, he enters the realm of dreadful Dis

through the broken mass of the gates; and immediately he drags him out,

[65] restraining him with chains and an obscure prison.

That dreadful thunderer struggles in vain with his limbs,
