Brought the fathers whom he had snatched from prison into Elysium.

[70] From there he returns, risen from the tomb,

where a watchful soldier guarded the sealed tomb itself with futile zeal.

The soldiers had been so stunned by terror that they dared neither oppose him

with words nor rise against him with weapons.

But, having entered Jerusalem amid great terrors,

[75] they say that Christ had risen with great strength.

Meanwhile the restorer of life showed himself risen again

to his friends and disciples, and after forty days

returned to the heavenly kingdoms.

We await him soon to come again from on high,

[80] as judge to grant all a just reward with an even balance.

Therefore our king Christ reigns over all things.

And just as the great-hearted Greek nobles and Latin kings

once erected trophies of war,

so Christ erected the celebrated victorious signs

[85] of his battle, signs destined to remain through eternal ages.

He himself set up the cross of the tree, the venerable wood,

from whose branches, with their necks broken, his bound enemies hang

with bulging eyes.

Before all the others, the Stygian Pluto hangs from the trunk,

[90] with his bows battered, his arrows, nooses, and snares.

From another part of the trunk hangs an image of Death,
Pale, blind, savage, speechless, numb with cold,

with her teeth knocked out, displaying a hideous mouth

with mutilated nostrils and a throat gaping wide.

[95] On another branch hangs the gate of shattered Hell,

with worn doorposts, hinges, and bolts.

[Col. 0388B] On another branch hang God’s wrath and the mind wickedly conscious of itself,

all of them cleansed by Christ’s rosy blood.

On another branch hangs the bond of the first father,

[100] torn apart in wretched ways and wholly destroyed.

At last the foul-flowing world hangs from the mighty trunk,

full of dissensions and much guilt,

while the varied pomp and cruel deeds of tyrants also hang there.

Christ swallowed up these fierce enemies of humankind,

[105] so that they can no longer condemn the faithful.

They have indeed been granted power to tempt us, but victory is ours.

That too is through Christ, whose victory is ours,

[108] with the Father, who reigns eternally with the Holy Spirit.

## P. Optatianus Porphyrius

*(From the edition printed at Nuremberg in 1692 by Ch. Arnold, from the excellent manuscript of Paulus Velserus.)*

[Col. 0387]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the illustrious and noble Henry Rantzau, the Danish king’s governor in the Cimbrian Chersonese.

I believe that Ulysses loved Ithaca, which, after hardships endured through so many years by land and sea, he persisted in returning to, because it was his homeland. Yet that affair was mere sport and trifling compared with what this Porphyrius undertook from longing for his country. I mean these poems: works of most wretched endurance, of audacity almost beyond belief, and certainly, so far as is known, without precedent. Since by them the exile obtained his return, he seems to have paid penalties enough and more than enough, and no longer to owe even his enemies any further satisfaction of their hostility.

For no cross is ever to be compared with this cross, before which a sensible man might cry out loudly, “Exile!”—as Philoxenus once cried for the quarries rather than be compelled to lend his ears to Dionysius’ verses: “O delay! O punishment!” Let whoever looks in from the threshold repeat it.

It seemed unworthy, however, that the work of so wickedly arduous a labor should remain hidden longer, and that the product of so many wakeful nights should perish through posterity’s neglect. Therefore, trusting to a single manuscript, and that one corrupt in many places, we nevertheless prepared an edition. We removed such blemishes as could safely be removed; other diseased sores, which rejected treatment, we did not touch.

Concerning the author, we have prefixed whatever we have observed from Jerome and others. Jerome clearly had both this poet and this book in view; whether passages of Fulgentius also belong to him remains uncertain. Moreover, Poem VI makes it seem that he was punished with exile either unjustly or for a slight reason; for he addresses Constantine as follows:

> Look upon me, greatest Ruler, afflicted by exile’s punishment  
> for a false charge. As for the other charges  
> now brought against me, overcome them with merciful pardon,  
> venerable divinity; and, surpassing fate by your accustomed  
> gracious nod, holy Caesar, serenely pity your poet.

Poem XX shows that he wrote the book before the killing of Caesar Crispus, which fell in A.D. 324, Constantine’s nineteenth year, although Jerome records that he was recalled from exile only in Constantine’s twenty-third year. But everyone sees that many matters in Jerome’s *Chronicle* have been wrongly transposed. He mentions Crispus thus:

> Crispus, a better descendant …

Many further praises of him and of his brother Constantine follow.

Why Bede regarded him as so pagan that he declined to touch him on that account, I do not quite know. Fables are interwoven; but proofs of Christian piety also occur in many places—above all, the letter Chi, mocked by Julian in the *Misopogon*, and the Constantinian cross, repeatedly reproduced in exactly the form described by Eusebius. These should surely have prevented the charge of impiety, even without Poem IX and many other passages of the same sort.

For the rest, judgment belongs chiefly to the reader. Yet I too would venture to pronounce, in words almost Ausonian, that here is something to marvel at—which no person so unfair as to deny—but far more that calls for pity and ought not to be imitated. Upon this latter point I earnestly implore every child of the Muses, for the hope of his studies.

The present and certain plague of talent is the wish to imitate such productions: things that, under an appearance of correctness and through difficulty’s own seduction, may charm the unwary, but not those who have ever conceived in their mind poetry’s genuine beauty.

Furthermore, when Porphyrius sought a patron who both could and would defend an undertaking of unaccustomed boldness, while Constantine Augustus and the Caesars Crispus and Constantine were far from him, he thought he should place himself under your patronage, illustrious sir. He understood that your virtue, humanity, and learning gave him sufficient protection on both counts.

It is now your part not to neglect a suppliant, since you know how highly Plato thought persons of this kind ought to be valued. Besides, nature has so formed you, and constant practice in doing good to all has so confirmed you, that no one has ever implored your aid in vain; to those who perform Apollo’s sacred rites, you have always freely stretched out helping hands.

Farewell.

[Col. 0389]

## Testimonies concerning P. Optatianus Porphyrius

[Col. 0389A] St Jerome, *Chronicle*, Constantine the Great’s twenty-third year:

> Porphyrius, having sent Constantine a distinguished volume, is released from exile.

Fulgentius, Book XI of the *Mythologies*, on Venus:

> They also paint her floating upon the sea, because every desire for worldly things suffers shipwreck. Hence Porphyrius in an epigram:
>
> > Naked, needy, Venus’ shipwrecked man upon the sea.

Fulgentius, *On the Exposition of Virgilian Content*:

> Whoever is raised up into pride is struck down twice over. Hence Porphyrius says in an epigram:
>
> > Fortune, that treacherous thing, Quintus, raised  
> > that great eyebrow on your forehead—but only a little.  
> >
> > For, lest I believe otherwise, I take you too, Quintus, for a well:  
> > the higher you are, the more you are looked down upon.

[Col. 0389B] Bede, *On the Art of Meter*:

> Besides, there are many other meters, which anyone wishing to do so may find demonstrated by simple examples in books of centimetrical poems. Some occur also in that distinguished volume of the poet Porphyrius, sent to Constantine Augustus, by which he deserved release from exile. Since they were pagan, we did not wish to touch them.

[Col. 0390A] Rabanus Maurus, *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, preface:

> I do not remember putting points in the verses anywhere, except where *quae* was a pronoun, *-que* a conjunction, or *-us* the final syllable of a word. Porphyrius did the same; from his model I learned to scatter letters.

John Cuspinian, *Life of Constantine*:

> When Porphyrius sent Constantine a distinguished volume, he was released from exile.

Subscription to the poem published at Vienna for the arrival of Emperor Maximilian I:

> John Stabius composed this in imitation of Publilius Optatianus Porphyrius, recently discovered by himself.

[Col. 0390B] Lilius Gregorius Giraldus, *History of Poets*, Dialogue 4:

> In Constantine’s age there is said to have been a Latin poet named Porphyrius, who wrote poems on various subjects. Among them he gave a book to Caesar Constantine himself; by this gift he, though relegated, was recalled from exile, as Jerome and Bede note in their chronicles. Fulgentius also mentions him and quotes his epigrams, including this little verse:
>
> [Col. 0391A]
>
> > Naked, needy, Venus’ shipwrecked man upon a plank.
>
> Rabanus also cites him in the preface to his miraculous poems, saying that Porphyrius was accustomed to mark his verses with certain points; he therefore promises to compose verses after his example.

[Col. 0392A] Among the fragments of Petronius Arbiter, beside “Trust the ship to the winds,” etc., someone has noted:

> Unless it belongs rather to the poet Porphyrius, sent into exile under Constantine, whose works I see are for the most part attributed, even by critics, to our Petronius.

[Col. 0391]

## Porphyrius’ Epistle to Constantine

To the lord Constantine, greatest, pious, unconquered, venerable, ever Augustus.

[Col. 0391B] **Variants and notes**

“Greatest unconquered”: Pithoeus’ edition among *Ancient Epigrams and Little Poems*, Lyons, 1596, p. 379, omits *greatest*.

“By your tireless clemency”: Pithoeus has *infatigabilis*.

“It had been sufficient”: Pithoeus has *suffecerit*.

“I had bound”: Pithoeus has *illigaveram*.

“That greater sincerity of devotion than the smallness of my talent supplied for me”: Pithoeus has “that formerly supplied for me.”

“For Helicon’s”: Pithoeus has “for Heliconian,” which Barthius prefers, col. 1107.

“Of Apollo’s lyre”: Pithoeus has “Apollo’s lyre.”

Lemma *tui mihi nominis* (“of your name to me”): Pithoeus prints the corrupt fragment *tui mini . . . . nom.* (“of your … name,” incomplete); Barthius read *tui divini nominis* (“of your divine name”).

Lemma *cum sua veneratione praefatio* (“with its own veneration, a preface”): Pithoeus prints the corrupt fragment *cum sua venerabili .. .. praelatio* (“with its own venerable … a prefacing/setting-forth,” incomplete).

“To dare, and to accomplish”: Pithoeus omits ET (“and”).

“The noble Mantuan, chief of the Roman Muses”: Pithoeus has “to us,” wrongly.

“Of nectar, fruitful, [he raises] his sails”: Pithoeus reads “fruitful of nectar,” wrongly omitting VELA (“sails”).

“He exults in poems”: Pithoeus has “he exults in the poem.”

Lemma *tenui pauper ingenio* (“poor in slender talent”): Pithoeus reads *tenuis pauper ingenii* (“slender, poor in talent”), with different case agreement.

“An immense burden has been placed on me”: Pithoeus omits *mihi*.

“You devote yourself so fully to the Muses familiar to you”: Pithoeus has “you praise these things from the Muses familiar to you.”

“Among which you are always unconquered and foremost”: Pithoeus has “among which you are both always unconquered and foremost.”

Lemma *cum exili sermone* (“with feeble speech”): Pithoeus reads the incomplete *cujus exili serm.* (“whose feeble speech …”).

“So that not even very small things can be worthily reported”: Pithoeus has a reading that removes the negation.

Lemma *ne facundissimis quidem possit impleri?* (“could it not be fulfilled even by the most eloquent?”): Pithoeus reads *ne a facund. q. p. impleri* (“not by the eloquent … to be fulfilled,” abbreviated) and has no question mark.

“Now indeed”: omitted by Pithoeus.

“Wherever my mind goes in poetry”: Pithoeus reads “wherever my mind goes, in a poem.”

“I have dared to bind”: Pithoeus adds “in verses.”

“Farewell”: absent from Pithoeus. Barthius added:

> “One ought not for that reason doubt this letter’s genuineness, because many men in Constantine’s age wrote better Latin. Other persons too may be noted as having spoken thus, or even worse—for example, the *Chorography* published by Jacobus Gothofredus, the *Jerusalem Itinerary* published by Petrus Pithoeus, and other little works. We know that many more such compositions survive in inscribed books; in place of all we might cite the commentaries on the Psalms by a certain Arnobius, certainly not later than the works here set down, which bear the title, etc.”

I confess, Lord Constantine, greatest and unconquered, distinguished no less by piety than by courage, that the greedy and over-ambitious wishes of my small self have been surpassed by the condescension of your tireless clemency. It would indeed have been more than sufficient had the poem which I bound in the tighter chains of the Muses—wherein devotion’s sincere zeal supplied more than my talent’s smallness—reached your victorious hands, most august emperor, to be read by your eyes.

In it, instead of Helicon’s summit-grove [marginal reading: *Per Heliconis*, “through/of Helicon,” and likewise thereafter], instead of a draught from the Castalian spring, instead of Apollo’s lyre, the Muses’ harmonious choirs, and the other things which poets customarily invoke when composing a poem, the eternal felicity of your name, and its manifold preface joined with due veneration, sang encouragement to me to dare [marginal reading: *Audiendum*, “to be heard”], and gave both ability and accomplishment to my talent.

The noble Mantuan, high priest of the Roman Muse, serene light of poets and fountain of pure nectar, fruitfully raises his sails into poetry [margin: *Exultat*, “he exults”] and boasts greatly; again and again he glories in Maecenas’ testimony.

What am I to do, poor in slender talent, and of very little merit until now? By heaven’s gracious judgment, an immense burden has been laid on me through the testimony of that emperor who, amid the virtues of war and peace, triumphs and laurels, enactments of laws and legal rights, devotes himself so fully to Muses familiar to him [margin: *Laude vacas*, “you devote yourself to praise”] that, amid all the insignia of divine majesty in which he is ever unconquered and foremost, the noble splendor of this pursuit also shines in him.

Surely I shall dare to give thanks, although with my feeble speech they cannot be worthily repaid even in the smallest degree [marginal fragment: *Cujus ex illius sermone permin.*, “of whom, from that speech, very slight …,” incomplete; *Possit*, “may be able,” singular, is also marked beside the plural *possint*], and though you, pious emperor, have done such things that even the most eloquent could not repay them in answer to your benefits.

For if, as the wise have held, judgments must be weighed rather than counted, greatest emperor, then, having obtained such a testimony through the heavenly condescension of your piety, I may now safely climb Parnassus’ ridges, dare to lead forth the Muses from the very sanctuaries of the Aonian height, and go secure wherever my mind leads in poetry. Protected by the divine authority of your judgments, and too ready to trust my own flatteries, I shall contend that I have pleased the whole world, since I could please the emperor of the whole world.

Finally, most august lord, forgive my boldness at my prayer, and graciously receive what I have now dared to bind. The clemency of your authority kindled the fuel of my audacity.

Farewell.

[Col. 0393]

## Constantine’s Epistle to Porphyrius

The unconquered Constantine, greatest Augustus.

[Col. 0393A] **Variants and notes**

“Greatest Augustus”: Pithoeus has “Augustus greatest.”

“Were considered in”: Pithoeus has “were expected.”

“And Greek”: Pithoeus omits *et*.

“Eloquence had fallen silent”: Pithoeus has “had become worthless.”

“All glory rested”: Pithoeus has a future-perfect form.

“To draw this judgment from it”: Pithoeus has “to say.”

“Later age produced to please”: Pithoeus omits the infinitive “to please.”

“Does not exclude from favor”: Pithoeus uses the past tense.

Lemma *flexere* (“they bent”): Pithoeus reads *flexerunt* (“they bent”), an alternate verbal ending.

Lemma *cothurnis et prope quotid.* (“with buskins and almost everyday …”): Pithoeus reads *cothurnos* (“buskins,” accusative); another witness has the abbreviated *prope cotid.* (“almost everyday …”).

“Human feelings expressed in words”: Pithoeus has “feelings attracted by words.”

Lemma *locutus est quidam, inaeq.* (“a certain man spoke, unequal …,” abbreviated): Pithoeus reads *locutus est: quibusdam inaequali* (“he spoke: to/for certain persons, unequal …”), likewise fragmentary.

“Elegy was sung in an unequal foot”: Pithoeus has “elegiac poems were sung.”

Lemma *inseruit pro aequ. modulaminis . . .* (“serves … according to the equality of modulation …,” abbreviated): Pithoeus reads *inseruit. Pro qualitate modulaminis ad singulos q.* (“serves. According to the quality of modulation, to each …”), also incomplete.

Lemma *at non circa sing.* (“yet not around each individual …,” abbreviated): Pithoeus continues *ad singulos q.* (“to each …”), an incomplete reading joined to the preceding variant.

“The favor of emperors toward talents”: Pithoeus has “the favor of ages.”

“To water”: Pithoeus has *rigare*.

Lemma *quasi clivosi* (“as though from a steep [slope]”): Pithoeus reads the fragment *quam si cliv.* (“than if a slope …”).

“Tempered”: Pithoeus has a future-perfect form.

“No less kindly”: Pithoeus has “not otherwise well.”

“Was available to orators”: Pithoeus has “to speeches.”

Lemma *ut hoc genere dict.* (“so that those about to speak in this genre …,” abbreviated): Pithoeus reads *ut in hoc g. d.* (“so that in this genre those about to speak …”), also abbreviated.

“Parnassus’ ridges”: Pithoeus has “Parnassus’ sacred places.”

“Also fashions a new lyre for itself”: Pithoeus has “new laws.”

Lemma *qui modis quibusdam arctis innexi litterarum, distinctionibus versuum* (“those bound by certain constrained arrangements of letters and divisions of verses”): Pithoeus reads *ut nodis quibusdam artis innexi citra interventum vitii inculpatum carmen effunderent. Tibi nominum difficultate proposita, numero litterarum, distinctionibus versuum* (“so that, bound by certain knots of art, they might pour forth a faultless poem without the intrusion of error. For you, with the difficulty of words proposed, by the number of letters and divisions of verses”).

“Secretly run through the middle body of the design”: Pithoeus adds *operis*; perhaps the transmitted wording is corrupt.

“The perception of the eyes”: Pithoeus has “the perceptions of the eyes.”

“Maintained this aim”: Pithoeus has an infinitive.

“Hesitation in the poem”: Pithoeus has “hesitating poems.”

“Should not introduce”: Pithoeus has “should not separate.”

“Of your dedication”: Pithoeus has “of your dictation.”

Lemma *comprobata est* (“has been approved”): Pithoeus has the incomplete *comprobata . . .* (“approved …”).

Lemma *si tu cum videas* (“if, when you see …”): Pithoeus reads *tu cum tibi videas* (“when you see for yourself …”).

Lemma *auribus non perisse, et prov.* (“has not perished in [my] ears, and the outcome …,” abbreviated): Pithoeus reads *auribus . . . ., non petis, sed prov.* (“to the ears …, you do not seek, but the outcome …”), corrupt and incomplete.

If only weight and dignity were considered in poetry, Greek eloquence after the Chian or Maeonian poet, and Latin eloquence after the rustic Mantuan, would have fallen silent. Nor would those be wrongly blamed who, choosing subjects according to their talents, had labored in vain, since all glory rested with the first founders of eloquence, dearest brother.

But because this practice has always lain open to view, and no one has been denied the right to draw from it what can delight even those produced by a later age, those who, abandoning weightier sounds, bent toward lighter modes are not wholly shut out from favor’s reward.

One poet bound human feelings in buskins and in language almost everyday and moral; another spoke in comedies; elegy was sung in unequal meter; delightful love of the lyre, through its half-speaking strings, serves many fingers in accordance with its measured modulation.

Yet the glory of desired praise has not overflowed around every individual. [Margin: *An circa*, “whether/about,” a possible alternative at *at non circa*.] Some talents lacked emperors’ favor, which customarily waters and nourishes minds devoted to learning, as a stream drawn from the brow of a steep hillside tempers parched fields with bubbling channels.

In my age, writers and speakers are attended by a favor no less kindly than a gentle breeze. Finally, I do not deny deserved recognition even to studies. Orators have had a free course; but a law fixed by meters confined those who spoke in verse within set bounds. Thus practice reasonably discovered that those who were to speak in this kind should seek Helicon’s or Parnassus’ ridges, since mortal ability’s resources failed and divine aids seemed necessary.

I am pleased [margin: *Grata*, “pleasing” or “pleasing things,” beside *gratum*] that your ready talent for study has gone so far that, while preserving ancient practice in writing verse, it has fashioned a new lyre for itself. Few have achieved this [margin: *Ut*, “so that/as”]: men bound by intricate arrangements of letters and divisions of verses, which secretly run through the middle body of the design [margin: *Oculis*, “for/to the eyes,” beside *occulte*, “secretly”] so that the eye delights in interspersed pigments of color [margin: *Oculorum*, “of the eyes,” beside *colorum*, “of colors”]. Yet they maintained this aim: that manifold observance of the rule should not produce renewed hesitation in the poem.

Therefore this gift of your dedication pleased me. The exercise of your mind and your natural facility have been approved. Since you see that the favor for your work which you sought from my ears has not perished, you ought to rejoice in the success of the present time and seek praise deserved by the exercise of your talent.

[Col. 0395]

## Panegyric of P. Optatianus Porphyrius Addressed to Constantine Augustus

### I

[Col. 0395] **Variants and notes**

Verse 3, “about to approach in purple”: Pithoeus, p. 347, has “wholly shining in purple.”

Verse 10, “because your appearance is now too hideous”: Pithoeus has “because your neatness is too great.”

Verse 11, “what attire”: Pithoeus has “this attire.”

[Col. 0396] Verse 17, “shining within”: the same in Pithoeus. Barthius nevertheless read *imbibit* (“takes in”) for *intus*, in brackets; he took this to mean the book-roll knobs called *umbilici* by Ausonius, *Professors* XXVI. See Barthius, *Adversaria* XXII.18.

You who were once adorned with a beautiful little book,

Thalia, carry the poem into Augustus’ hands.

About to approach, shining in purple,

written in glittering silver and gold letters,

marking the spoken words by a painted border,

well adorned by the scribe’s hand and deservedly gleaming,

fitted for your gracious lord’s sacred eyes—

now pale, overcast with dark color,

scarcely distinguishing poems with poor vermilion,

you make for the roof of the venerable palace

with trembling step,

because your appearance is now too hideous.

Such attire befits the poet’s present fate;

the place from which you come scarcely provided even this.

Yet you may go humbly and entreat the lord:

this squalor and these stains suit the wretched.

When his clemency grants pardon

and restores the poet’s son and home,

you too will go with combed locks,

shining in purple dress,

resplendent within,

as once, proud of your written pages.

### II

[Col. 0395]

**Variants and notes**

This poem is absent from Pithoeus’ edition.

Beside line 1 the margin has *Stendicata* (apparently “extended,” against the irregular STEMDICATA); beside line 4, *Quos litant* (“whom they propitiate”); beside line 10, *Coacta spicula* (“pointed implements brought together”); and beside line 16, *Ut hora quadrae* (“so that the hour of the square …,” an irregular reading beside *ut ora quadrae*, “so that the edge of the square”). Verse 10’s *spiculum* is identified by Barthius as a stonecutter’s tool. Verse 15’s *normata ubique* means “everywhere brought to rule,” according to Barthius.

You see how the altar, extended in Pythian fashion,

has been skillfully polished by the poet’s musical art;

so the beautiful, most sacred company, worthy of Phoebus,

is fitted to these temples where choruses of poets sacrifice,

adorned with so many garlands and flowers of the Camena,

to be placed in the Heliconian groves of poems.

No craftsman carefully polished me out of hard material;

I was not cut from the rock of gleaming Mount Alba,

nor from the gleaming summit of Luna or Paros [the printed form for the latter is *Paride*];

I was not hewn with a hard tool or forced with a pointed implement,

to confine the first projecting angles

and then extend the second more broadly,

and carefully draw each of those [angles] underneath,

step by tiny step along recurving lines,

with a rule everywhere applied,

so that the edge of the square might stand within a rigid boundary,

or so that from there a line, carried down to the bottom and back,

might be extended more broadly in ordered art.

Instead, meters fashion me from the measures of the Camenae,

with only the number of feet never changed,

which the learned rule preserves while obeying its precepts:

the elements of the poems increase and decrease.

Phoebus, as I humbly offer these images of meters,

may you be joyfully present among the temples and sacred choruses.

### III

[Col. 0397] **Variants and notes**

Verse 2, *Auguste*: Pithoeus, p. 378, has *Augusti*.

Verse 3, *imperium*: Pithoeus has *imperii*.

Verse 7, *ni liquerit ille*: Pithoeus has *ne linqueret illi*.

Verse 9, *nobis te*: Pithoeus has *nobis tu*.

Verse 10, “glory, O pious light”: Pithoeus has “glory and light.”

Verse 13, “they give to the Father”: Pithoeus has “they give to the fatherland.”

Last verse, *vatis*: Pithoeus has *vates*.

**Lemma concerning the poem**

“It consists of syllables; it is called Torpalian or Stymphalian”: absent from Pithoeus.

*Torpalius*: Barthius reads *Ropalicus*.

“It consists of parts of speech”: Pithoeus omits *constat* (“consists”).

[Col. 0398] “They change their order in turn”: Pithoeus reverses the word order.

“Ninth, and in the direct direction …”: Pithoeus omits *et*.

“It is heroic”: Pithoeus omits *est*.

“Tenth, in the direct direction a pentameter, and equally reciprocal”: Pithoeus gives, “The tenth is a direct pentameter and, in reverse, with no letter or syllable removed, becomes the same pentameter.”

“Eleventh, in the direct direction a hexameter, and, in reverse, with no letter or syllable removed, becomes the same pentameter”: Pithoeus has only the beginning.

“Thirteenth, a pentameter, becomes heroic and heroic pentameter”: Pithoeus has, “And the thirteenth is a pentameter; they are recurrent.”

*Sotadic*: Pithoeus has *Sotadics*.

Nourishing glory of the world, pious supreme ruler of the universe,

Augustus, governing peoples with unconquered virtue,

Constantine, ruling the empire with justice,

pacifier of unbridled nations through governance,

whom the divine emperor Constantius begot,

spreading golden ages among the Romans through his son;

alas, hastening too swiftly to heaven, had he not left

eternal aid—unconquered, just, and pious—

to us: you, nourishing father of the fatherland, greatest Caesar,

glory of Ausonia, O pious light of the Romulids [margin: *O lux o pia*, “O light, O pious [light]”].

Then it pleases the gods above to distribute these gifts

thus, throughout perpetual ages, for the world’s joy:

[The gods] give the stars to your father, and your father’s

empire to you, holy one;

you have been given as the golden light of great Rome.

These things the lofty Muse of a country poet sings to you.

In this poem the first verse consists of two-syllable parts of speech; the second, of three-syllable parts; the third, of four-syllable parts; and the fourth, of five-syllable parts. The fifth consists of parts of one, two, three, four, and five syllables, and is called Torpalian or Stymphalian. The sixth consists of five parts of speech: while the last remains in place, the other four change their order in turn. The seventh consists solely of all eight parts of speech, having no part twice and none omitted. The eighth is declined through all cases. The ninth is heroic both directly and in reverse. The tenth is a pentameter directly and likewise in reverse. The eleventh is a hexameter directly and, reversed without the removal of a letter or syllable, becomes the same pentameter. The twelfth is heroic. The thirteenth is a pentameter and becomes heroic and heroic pentameter. The fourteenth and fifteenth are heroic directly and Sotadic when reversed.

### IV

*(In this and the following poems, letters printed in vermilion in the Welser edition are represented by larger type.)*

[Col. 0399] **Note**

This poem is absent from Pithoeus.

**Marginal apparatus**

The margin records *Trophaea* (“trophies,” a spelling variant of TROPAEA); *Clarae* (“of the illustrious [feminine]”) beside CLARII; *Verso* (“turned”) beside VERSET (“may turn”); *Laus mea fista* (“my praise …,” with *fista* irregular) beside LAUS MEA FICTA (“my fashioned praise”); *Flumina* (“rivers”) beside FLUMINE (“with a river”); and the irregular division *Vince-siam* beside VINCENS IAM (“conquering now”).

The heavenly signs will be revealed in vermilion to the reader,

Constantine, glory of the world, golden light of the age.

Who could sing your trophies, mingled with wondrous piety?

Exulting supreme leader, my page [sings] with new vows.

rivaling the Clarian father’s Calliope—the margin has *Clarae* in place of CLARII—

My mind, now steeped in such a liquid, composed [it];

may Helicon pour forth versifying waves into joys,

and may it draw a new divine inspiration from a merciful heart. The margin’s *Verso* may instead require “from a changed heart.”

For I shall speak in measured song of the great-souled leader’s

scepters. In *garzae nobis dat Graecia dona*, the word division or the form GARZAE is indeterminate: “Greece gives us gifts of treasure” is possible but not secure.

and you secure the ages with an allied Blemmyan frontier [dividing the continuous letters as *saeclaque Blemmyico sociali limite firmas*].

Romulean light, flourishing and worthy of new vows,

*Voto scripta cano Θali Mars cardine tecto*: “I sing things written by the vow … Mars at the covered pivot.” The theta and surrounding division are indeterminate.

Now encompass the whole Mysian citizenry in wars;

*ut pateat Rubicon parili petit aethera iure*: “so that the Rubicon may lie open; it seeks heaven by equal right” [syntax uncertain].

*Nunc felix proprios pacis me scrupea visus*: the printed sequence is not securely segmentable; its recoverable terms are “now,” “happy,” “one’s own,” “of peace,” “me,” “rocky/rough,” and “sights/aspects.”

Now the Muse, exulting in the signs, urges [me] to mark

joys; glad Phoebus now marks trackless things through me.

*Retito quoque texta novo cane laurea plectro*: “Sing also the woven laurels with a new plectrum”; RETITO remains indeterminate.

Applauding happy ages painted by art in signs,

thus, Pythian one, gathering the poet’s ardor under a faithful leader,

now, safe, may I indeed, supremely bold, despise [the storms].

Now may I successfully break the Sigean sea with my oar.

*Carbasa noctigerum totum si scrupeo tendo*: “If I stretch my sails across the whole night-bearing, rough [expanse]” [segmentation uncertain].

Carrying platforms, may I be seen to weave a ship.

Illustrious hope, joined to your vow, enters upon the Muses.

May it not break the mind, weary through its winding course, with a gaping [wound].

My fashioned praise, standing upon a metrical foot, [stands] beneath the great weight of instruction. The margin instead reads *Laus mea fista*.

I shall openly declare the most joyful signs with a sacred stream. The margin has plural *Flumina*.

With a good mind may [the subject] disdain a contest with the highest things [syntax uncertain].

After the fruit, clemency will restore Mars to the vows. The printed reading is MARTEM (“Mars/war”).

Thus for us golden ages grow, LEECTO QUO [the first word is irregular; if *lecto quo* is intended, “with/by whom or what chosen”].

Soon, victorious now, you will renew twice twenty years for Latium [dividing VINCENS IAMBIS as *vincens iam bis*; the margin has the irregular *Vince-siam*].

Poems which the page may fashion, painted from a wondrous name,

happy as it marks the vow with varied flower,

remembering the distinguished destinies of the Augustan offspring,

shall be prepared as worthy under you as judge, or as pious witness;

the fortunate deeds of descendants will be joined to their titles.

In this poem the reading begins from the monogram of Jesus, so that obscurity may be lifted from the mind. Two verses are in Greek and begin from the left side of the monogram. One uses the remaining parts of the same sign and ends at its central letter N:

> Τὴν ναῦν ἀεὶ, κόσμον κέ δε ἄρμενον εἰνοικίζειν.
>
> “Always to house/furnish the ship, and the ordered world …” [the transmitted Greek is irregular and its exact construction is indeterminate].

The other descends from there toward the ship’s hull and ends by completing the shape of a rudder:

> Οὔροις τεινόμενον σῆς ἀρετῆς ἀνέμοις.
>
> “Stretched by favoring winds, by the winds of your excellence.”

The verses beginning from the prow, beak, oars, or beneath the prow, and ending at the stern’s extreme point, cross the woven figure; others enclose the vows. They are:

> Now, safe, let the sailor utterly despise the storms.
>
> Now, safe, let him utterly despise the black storms.
>
> Safe, let him despise what is heaped up with the highest trophies.
>
> With evil expelled from his mind, let him utterly despise the storms.
>
> With good hope, let Rome utterly despise the storms.
>
> Happy Rome flourishes forever through your vows.

### V

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0401] **Variants and notes**

Verse 1, *fragrarem*: Pithoeus, p. 351, has *flagrarem*.

Verse 9, *laetus*: Pithoeus has *saetus*, wrongly.

Verse 20, *devia vota*: Pithoeus has *devia voto*.

[Col. 0402] Verse 26, *tanto cui munere*: Pithoeus has *tanto cur munere*.

Verse 30, *cito perferat*: Pithoeus has *cata perferat*.

Verse 32, *reddere detur*: Pithoeus has *reddere retur*.

**Lemma concerning the poem**

“By such a poem”: Pithoeus has *tuli si carmine*, wrongly.

“Penultimate”: Pithoeus has “almost last.”

“To its own last letter” (*ad ultimam sui*): Pithoeus has *ad ult. sic* (“to the last … thus”).

“Penultimate”: Pithoeus has “almost last.”

“Likewise to the eighteenth”: Pithoeus has “again from the eighteenth.”

“Orthogonal”: Pithoeus has “octagonal.”

“And decreasing”: Pithoeus has “or decreasing.”

**Marginal apparatus**

Beside line 1 the margin has the irregular *Fraglarem* against FRAGRAREM (“I would breathe fragrance”); beside line 13, *Solutis* (“released”); beside line 21, the irregular *Fraete* against FRETAE (“relying”); and beside line 26, *Cur munere* (“why, by a duty”) against CUI MUNERE (“for whom, by a duty”).

I would yearn to fashion faces through the Muses’ divine power [reading Pithoeus’ *flagrarem*, “I would burn/yearn”; the printed *fragrarem* means “I would breathe fragrance,” and the margin has the irregular *Fraglarem*],

nourishing father of the world, [fashioning] completed duties in verse.

Vows too, if reason does not reject them in Phoebus’ order,

sing deeds which the gracious Aonian divinity

grants the poet by lot to enjoy as gifts of song from this work,

raising [him] and urging the poet’s mouth to sound.

You inspire the poet’s mind; you are always his joy.

In you, holy one, whom you summon, the learned Camenae live [word division uncertain].

Favoring what has been uttered, you, joyful, [grant] favorable vows,

so that they may be ratified; hear them, gentle ruler of Olympus.

Serene piety preserves preeminent times;

now golden ages flourish throughout your victorious world.

Constantine, with these bonds released by law upon the pole,

about to speak in meters, [the poet] moves the Muses in a great company.

But my [Muse], while Phoebus scarcely weaves poems in painted signs—

Calliope rejoices in measures, if she brings your vows to completion.

May the Delian assist the beginnings, so that the Muse, woven beneath an equal path,

may mark golden ages with verse.

But they seize my mind, devoted to you, for joy,

and urge [me] to speak boldly through untrodden vows:

the Aonian Muses, relying … and to defend their words … [ET QUANTIS remains syntactically uncertain; the margin has *Fraete* in place of FRETAE]—

bound to you by laws and by the poet’s entire mind and fidelity.

The poet invokes what is yours, illustrious prince: such great

wars they sing, and new poems from the Pegasean draught;

they exercise the bond and now wish to sound duly.

The distinguished imperial command, for whom it is given to discharge so great a duty—the margin instead reads *Cur munere*—

also delights [the poet] as he speaks lofty things in verse over crags:

the mind’s wondrous work, to weave a poem in meters,

scarcely enclosed within a narrow boundary through its varied courses.

May the knotty design of the art carry the eye swiftly through this.

Yet a mind that has dared so much swells with heat,

and it is not granted thus to render a poem worthy of the vows.

Singing under such a rule, which our page alone [observes],

it will complete from Helicon the gift of love:

a musical texture painted with varied elements.

This poem has thirty-five letters in every verse. The first verse runs by a winding course from its first letter to its last:

> May the Muse be able to fashion faces in such a poem.

By a similar winding course, through the descending acrostic from the second letter to the penultimate:

> Augustus, while the law of meter and verse remains.

Likewise the final verse runs from its first letter to its own last:

> Painted with varied elements in a musical texture.

Again, by an equal winding course through the descending telestich from the second letter to the penultimate:

> The page will burn to surpass Apelles’ wax paintings.

Likewise, beginning at the eighteenth letter of the first verse and descending directly through the middle:

> Great things will be sought if the poet’s Camena is joyful.

Likewise, from the eighteenth letter of the acrostic directly through the middle:

> May the beginning assist, marking golden ages with verse.

On this page are four hexagons containing equal numbers of letters, and eight right-angled figures likewise containing equal numbers, increasing and decreasing by one letter at a time.

[Col. 0401]

**Variants and notes**

Verse 3, *nobis da gaudia*: Pithoeus, p. 349, has *nobis ad gaudia*.

Verse 9, *maesto sic saltem*: Pithoeus has *moestos hic saltem*.

Verse 11, *annuit*: Pithoeus has *adnuit*.

Verse 16, *ad laterum*: Pithoeus has *ad lat.*.

Verse 22, *aeternae, vires et*: Pithoeus has *aeterna, cui res et*.

Verse 26, *et summi laus, grata*: Pithoeus has *et summi ius, grata*.

Verse 29, *dextra salutis*: Pithoeus has *dextra maritis*.

**Lemma concerning the poem**

“Of thirty” (*tricenarum*): Pithoeus spells it *trigenarum*.

“The final letter of the first verse, S, is shared with the telestich; the final letter of the acrostic, S, is shared with the final verse”: Pithoeus instead reads, “with the first letter of the acrostic, that is, S, with the last letter of the telestich, is shared, that is, S is shared with the last verse”—a confused formulation.

“Eighteenth”: Pithoeus reverses the order.

“Descending downward through the middle to the final verse”: omitted by Pithoeus.

“The eighteenth S is the head of the middle verse running directly”: Pithoeus reads *octava decima in capitalium medium versum. q. m. v.* (“the eighteenth into the middle verse of capitals …”; the continuation remains abbreviated).

“These parts”: Pithoeus reverses the words.

“Closed”: Pithoeus has “enclosed.”

“Make writing”: Pithoeus has “written.”

[Col. 0404] “May you arrange”: Pithoeus has “you arrange.”

**Additional marginal apparatus**

Beside line 14 the margin reads *Sit nota prim. usui* (“Let the first … sign be for use,” with *prim.* abbreviated).

Holy Caesar, serenely pity your poet.

Almighty Augustus, making all mortal things joyful

by your nurturing divinity, grant us joy.

Constantine, may your fruitful name, through this poem,

lead forth the Muses under your leadership; for sad care rejects

noble deeds, and now the crimes assigned by the Fates lie still.

Then a more confident voice will sound you more worthily as lord.

The ruler of virtues could scarcely compose these things in verse,

or now at least speak thus to the sorrowing poet:

Calliope, knowing, scarcely nodded assent to me in my fear,

daring to proclaim the prayer and the poet’s fates [dividing PAVITANTICONSCIA as *pavitanti conscia*].

May [the poem] enclose its sad portions within a marked boundary;

by equal law may the poem be harmonious through all its middle.

Let its first [letter] be known, and let its outermost part be of that same kind [dividing PARSEXTIMA as *pars extima*; the margin has *Sit nota prim. usui*]—

as, meeting the first letters of the middle, is more suitably placed there

at the ends of the sides; and may the portion dividing the beginnings

be able to become the head from the middle and return through the verse.

Holy Caesar, serenely pity your poet.

Nurturing salvation of the world, glory of Rome, illustrious in fame,

better in conduct through piety, a father, a victor in warfare [the precise construction of *re melior* is uncertain],

gentler toward pardon, soothing the harshness of laws,

justice, powers of eternity, and glory of the age [AETERNAE does not agree with IUSTITIA as printed],

hope granted full of good things, and happy abundance in affairs,

outstanding pillar of the ancients through courage and fidelity,

great father of Rome, avenger with arms in civil strife,

and welcome praise of the highest God, a mind illustrious from above,

salvation sent to earthly affairs through you, peace, best leader,

and rest secure from wars: all things are sacred through you.

A most faithful right hand grants rights to its own husbands alone,

and the social yoke grants partnerships in life.

The preceding two lines translate the printed SOLIS IURA SUIS FIDISSIMA DEXTRA MARITIS / ET SOCIALE IUGUM PRAEBET CONSORTIA VITAE. The apparatus instead takes DEXTRA SALUTIS (“right hand of salvation”) as its lemma and assigns DEXTRA MARITIS (“right hand … to husbands”) to Pithoeus; the grid itself prints the latter.

Look upon me, greatest Ruler, afflicted by exile’s punishment

because of a false charge; for as to the other matters in the case

now brought against me, venerable divine power, overcome them with merciful pardon,

and, surpassing fate by your customary gracious nod,

holy Caesar, serenely pity your poet.

In this poem all verses contain thirty-five letters. The first letter of the first verse, S, is shared with the acrostic; the last letter of the first verse, likewise S, is shared with the telestich. The last letter of the acrostic, S, is shared with the final verse. The middle letter of the first verse—the eighteenth, S—is the head of the middle verse descending through the middle to the final verse. The middle letter of the acrostic—the eighteenth, S—is the head of the middle verse running directly across. These middle verses may either proceed directly or turn from the center while sounding the same.

The verse sounded through all these parts is:

> Holy Caesar, serenely pity your poet.

Four squares enclosed by the same verse contain sixteen letters on every side. In the centers of these squares, eight letters written directly in vermilion form the verse:

> Thus may you arrange golden ages throughout the whole world.

Constantine, father of the world, glory, consul,

behold: you will grant so many things opened anew by your labor [dividing TOTAPERTA as *tot aperta*].

You will rule among countless peoples, soon dear to the eastern nations;

The good art of justice, close to the gods’ glory [margin: *Justitiae et dijuum*, “of justice and of the gods,” with irregular *dijuum*],

receives from heaven the gifts of the generous good and flows there [syntax uncertain].

*Vota quod optarint pietatis cana subibit*: “The venerable/white [thing] of piety will approach the vows they desired” [subject and segmentation uncertain].

The holy earth returns Ceres and the fallen Bacchic things.

Greatest one, light of justice, concord as an omen,

the whole wounded [world] now desires and implores you as peacemaker.

May you swiftly lift weary affairs through peace; join what belongs to your serene [rule],

the prayers of your world; join willing peoples to yourself.

In this poem there are thirty-five letters. The acrostic joined to the telestich forms the verse:

> Sure salvation of affairs, unconquered offspring of the Thunderer.

In it, the second letter of the ninth verse indicates—

Likewise, beginning with the second letter of the tenth verse, the rubric ascends and descends twice to the penultimate letter of that same verse and contains this verse:

## VIII

[Col. 0403]

[Note: [Col. 0403]

Verse 4, “You, the poet.” See Valesius on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 169.

5, “torn away from the pole.” Pithoeus, p. 362, has “divided from the pole.”

I shall now sing the mighty deeds of the leader, prevailing throughout the whole world,
by which joyful Rome, under so great a prince of her own,
again holds the headship of the world, illustrious. O divine power,
prompt your poet and his song. A part [of the empire], torn by bloody
dominions, exhausted and sundered from the pole, was groaning;
it mourned its sceptres and Ausonia’s lost laws.
If there was any confidence in the Roman name and its great glory,
distinguished by the titles of rulers, nevertheless they seek liberty,
and the sorrowful commonwealth trembles at the world’s enormous wound.
Then Hyperion first, gleaming with rays of light,
scatters the ruddy stars at his rising.
Then your name, greatly venerable to all,
O greatest subduer of warriors, sole light of the world,
is desired in unceasing prayers: men long
to serve it, memorable to utter, marvellous to speak.
So great is the glory which you possess, righteous Augustus.
Behold: now under your covenant the whole world,
after so many slaughters by which it had been wearied,
at last trembles at no commotion;
the Romans obey your pious commands, illustrious father.

In this poem the acrostic contains:

**Most mighty Emperor;**

the fourteenth letters:

**Most merciful Ruler;**

the final letters:

**Constantine unconquered.**

## IX

[Col. 0405]

[Note: [Col. 0405]

This poem is absent from Pithoeus.]

O you who crush Tartarean jaws beneath your sacred foot,
and who put down the fiery shrines once raised against you,
you reign in the heavenly realms of everlasting light.
Your power, eternal God, is with all things, O Christ.
When the Father, issuing from the mass obscured by sluggish
filth, emerged after the covering of darkness had been removed,
before the birth of men, holy and divine Thunderer,
you were the hidden power which the Father’s mind contained:
the wise solace and inward God of God.
As offspring of the beginnings, belonging to no bloodstained destroyer—
because death was reigning—the joy born from life’s mouth poured forth;
with punishment broken, [you brought] perpetual marrow-bearing life [reading uncertain].
After men had been driven away, it pleased [you], from a dark nativity,
then [to restore] the prostrate paths of life; yet once
the fates had foretold you through the prophets’ warning.
For error long continued after your eloquent rising,
until the Creator restored the sum of things by his counsel:
you, Christ, the wisdom of the mighty Father,
manifested by the Word, drove man out of death’s bonds.
Soon you deigned [to take up] man, who is the one salvation,
in the lowest state, according to nature’s right order,
so that, when it had been struck, you yourself might aid the fallen one by bending down.
No body drawn by earthly weight [was yours];
rather, a most exalted Virgin, pregnant in her womb from seed—
not through sluggish intercourse, but joined with heaven—
[bore you], God in body, countenance, deed, destiny, and both natures.
Inviting humankind by commands and examples,
an equal Lord, because you bear the burdensome fall,
in human action you imitated the declared divine things.
You yourself advance under the name of man and among the profane;
greatest one, destined to be punished chiefly by the Jews after many
acts of dutiful service, you allowed death and revealed saving light.
Soon, after human crimes had been cut away, night hung open;
but the Father receives the Son into his dwelling and carries him up.
He gives the eternal sign of salvation to the sacred fabric of the universe.

O almighty Father—and you, O Son, the united distinction [of the Godhead]—
Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one:
favour these prayers.

**ON THE DEVICE ATTACHED TO THE POEM**

“Descending straight downward.” Pithoeus has: “descending in a different order, in a straight sequence.”

“This verse of all the verses.” Pithoeus has: “this Greek verse from the letters of all the verses.”

The Muses dare to combine discordant words;
the mind delights in advancing the noble language through good things.
It is pleased to renew the gifts of the Greeks,
and in turn to sing in Latin verse what chance has supplied.
Now let another texture lead Greek works into poems,
so that the sequence may bind letter to sound in a double utterance.
Now, Muses, let fruitful strains fashion the fairest work;
let the lyre sound illustrious songs of Phoebus from a teachable mouth.
I shall sing the hope of things, the justice
and highest salvation: you, lord, good gifts of God, great father,
greatest ruler of the Roman and Greek world.
All things strive in their minds toward quiet;
let them behold a thousand hostile triumphs,
all things filled with blessings, yours, O Constantine.
Let the Quirites believe nothing dearer to themselves
than you, the beloved great ornament of the world.
The preserved people of Tyre, always under your avenging protection,
rejoice in you as lord, dearer to the world than peace.
Africa, preserved, enjoys peace in your times;
now she calls herself fortunate, now safe beneath
the citadel of your divinity, which venerable Carthage bears.
By right she declares that such great light, illustrious in destiny,
is bestowed upon the world: your noble name, lord,
is hope and kindly adornment. Every region from the northern
bounds, dreadful beneath the north wind, loves peace
and the well-tested laws; with faithful arms it serves you ever well.
Whatever deeds your valour performs, and whatever savage peoples
it drives back and slays, it has you as its dear debtor.
Your victorious fortune receives these things; hence strong men,
with you as leader, raise the standards of unconquered cohorts.
Everywhere, accompanied by the dutiful divine power of the highest God,
they present you to all as avenger, together with law and faith.
They look to you, kindly one, and all things answer their prayers.
Wherever the greatest Saviour makes affairs peaceful,
you will grant joys and bestow rest, victorious in the world.
Bid the vows of twenty years proceed according to the merits of your courage;
the age has grown, with a double hope assured by Caesar.
And you, holy father, after a thousand trophies,
O light of Ausonia, will arrange your descendants’ sceptres.

In this poem the acrostic contains:

**To our lord Constantine, perpetual Augustus.**

The tenth letters of all the verses, and the nineteenth and twenty-eighth letters, descending straight downward, contain three Greek verses. In the tenth letters of all the verses is this verse:

**May Christ apportion to you, O king, and to your children [the reward].**

In the nineteenth is this:

**The honourable prize is to rule by piety and the excellence of virtue.**

In the twenty-eighth is this verse:

**To govern by good order and reign over the Ausonians.**

But when these are read downward in Greek in this sequence, the same letters, arranged otherwise for readers of the Latin verses, render their service in the function of Latin letters: thus they convey their meanings both in Greek and in Latin.

I have indeed sung a few things, perhaps trifles; with these I shall also join
your playful commands, pleasant Muse.
This song has enclosed itself, applauding in Phoebus’ fortunate name;
Calliope, divided among new cares, has bound herself in chains.
By bends she first establishes a rule at variance with itself;
then another art sounds, curving above Pythoia.
So she will act whenever excitement has strengthened her:
the mind, unconquered and not idle but wounded,
may fill varied forms of weightier metre.
At last excitement scarcely permits us to meditate;
may it rightly wish, when set in the middle of the line,
to fashion the image and secretly prepare it in trembling speech,
to speak without fear, binding all things from their origin,
and to compose; but now, returning, Bassus, bring forth the poem.
The obedient Muse commands this and leads me to the Castalian spring,
to weave verses in order through names.

In this poem, from the first letter of the first verse, a descending rubric to the eighth letter of the eighth verse, and then an ascending winding course to the penultimate letter of that same eighth verse, contains:

**Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius played these things.**

Likewise, from the first letter of the last verse to the eighth of the ninth, ascending and descending by a winding course to the penultimate letter of the ninth verse, it contains a heroic verse which, when reversed, becomes Sotadic:

**Composing every kind of metre for you, excellent Bassus.**

Likewise, from the first letter of verse six to the third of verse eight are the three letters **Hic**; from the thirteenth of verse eight to the fifteenth of verse six, **Ver**; then to the seventeenth of verse eight, **Su**; then from the twenty-seventh of verse eight to the twenty-ninth of verse six, **Sua**; then to the thirty-first of verse eight, **Ri**; then from the thirty-first of verse nine to the twenty-ninth of verse eleven, **Oco**; then from the twenty-seventh of verse nine, **Lo**; then from the seventeenth of verse nine to the fifteenth of verse eleven, **Red**; then from the thirteenth of verse nine, **Is**; and from the thirteenth of verse nine to the first of verse eleven, **Par**. These form the hendecasyllable:

**This verse is unlike in varied colour.**

## XII

[Col. 0409]

[Note: [Col. 0409]

This poem is absent from Pithoeus.

Comelinus published it from Velser’s edition at the end of Joseph Scaliger’s notes on Theocritus, p. 29, 1596 octavo edition.]

Hanging from the leafy summit of a lofty oak,
the pipe bears witness to Fauns frequently celebrating the temples of the place.
Fashioned from unequal reeds, compacted from as many pipes,
it delights the woods with Pan’s sweet-sounding melody.
It first taught the choirs of Naiads and Dryads,
the secret rites of Bacchus, his orgies, and shouting Satyrs,
and taught thiasoi their songs in Tempe through music.
Attis first bound together varied sounds in harmony,
Attis, gentle and loving, O great Cybele, your darling.
The god of Ida kindled in me, with tender lips,
the loves of the Idaean mother; he breathed songs
into my happy mind. The Muse, judge of beauty,
raised a high memorial in Ida;
she joined Melian [uncertain: *Mela*] as a votary near her husband.
At the rising of the sun he sings and invites [her].

This is a pipe of fifteen hexameter verses, decreasing one letter at a time from the first verse to the last.

[Col. 0411]

Blessed prince, now beneath the peaceful sky,
with the world favouring just peoples serenely,
victorious, granting a saving divinity through triumph,
ruling the fortunate ages with enduring love,
the author of salvation, rising, will go in peace.
With heavenly right hand favouring the prayers of lords,
he rejoices to enter upon the ruler’s peaceful omen.
Virtue, radiant in strength, offers serenity.
The holy behold remote things of the world from above.
Ruling all beneath the world, he grants saving divinity.
By the favourable nod you will conquer the gods above everywhere.
Alone, blessed, ruling through every age.

Now beneath the peaceful sky, blessed prince,
with the world favouring just peoples serenely,
you victoriously grant saving divinity through triumph;
you rule the fortunate ages with enduring love.
The author of salvation, rising, goes in peace.
With heavenly right hand favouring the prayers of lords,
he rejoices to enter upon the ruler’s peaceful omen.
Radiant virtue prevails with tranquil force;
the holy behold remote things of the world from above.
He rules all beneath the world and grants saving divinity.
By the favourable nod you will conquer the gods above everywhere,
alone, blessed, ruling through every age.

## XIV

[Col. 0411]

[Note: [Col. 0411]

This poem is not in Pithoeus.]

I groaned deeply, pitying my Greek friend,
to whom my grieving mind desires to tell everything it has suffered,
so that he alone, reading these hidden matters, may rouse himself to anger.
From every side the afflicted and guilty man is held in chains;
but the wife, avoiding the many men whom foul disputes
will have wished to make witnesses, [acts] lest a fair woman [harm] the Greek.
Soon, with blunt weapons, the wicked woman may in no way weaken the swan’s dear ones [uncertain];
seeing that Helen had laid them aside—she whose favour, through two
adulteries, [brought] greater threats or gifts, all willingly [uncertain]—
the Muse sounds among Greeks. Wife of Phrixus, trust the singer.
## XV

[Col. 0411]

[Note: [Col. 0413]

Verse 1, “starry.” Pithoeus, p. 353, has “of the stars.”

12, “having been turned.” Pithoeus has “turning.”

15, “sits.” Pithoeus has “sat.” Barthius reads “gave.”

17, “asks.” Pithoeus has “may ask.”

**ON THE DEVICE ATTACHED TO THE POEM**

“Likewise, of three letters.” Pithoeus has “in the third [letters], which are CAE.”]

Victorious, endowed with starry virtues, you will go,
restoring the Persian frontier to Latium with your sons.
Now, prince, after receiving the joyful East,
faithful India dedicates harmonious divine service to you.
Now Parthians, Medes, and every people alike,
dedicated to Augustus and his sons, rejoice.
Holy Constantine, the great Muse favours you
and paints your twenty years in an ample poem.
You, once a famous commander in arms,
will give faith through piety; soon greater glory and honour
will be yours, if you can preserve so many peoples after victory.
Kindly Virtue declares that you must spare those already subdued.
India, Arabia, and rich Media bring offerings;
the Ethiopians rise, famous where the swift Nile flows.
Titan sits at the boundary of the Ethiopians; all things are joyful.
Under good Constantine, leisure now plays throughout the age.
The fortunate Muse asks to report things worthy of you:
rewards for the merits of your virtues, or to sound words of praise.
Why do you compose wandering Pierian verses beneath a valley
shaded by the holm oak? Why do you gather songs beneath the laurel?
The whole Castalian region answers in a clear voice;
from his own spring Phoebus brings forth songs for you.
O poet worthy of God, or if, boldly undertaking
a greater work and weaving it, your mind drinks in the whole mass,
hope will paint the poem; let the Muse thus fashion what she has begun
and complete the ten-year celebration varied in depicted verse.
With a favourable voice, within the fixed boundary of the metre,
leisure granted golden ages of peace to the Caesars,
indulgent to the sons in honour of their father’s piety.
God is rightly gentle, but [grants] strength for Christ’s mighty deeds [text uncertain; Pithoeus reads “Crispi”].
You will be an unquestioned match for guarding the Rhine and Rhône;
in the farther region they prepare harsh laws for the Franks.
Now, holy boy, you will be so great a hope for peace.
Constantine, grant the ages serene gifts sent from heaven;
highest one, receive the tricennial seasons with a pious vow.

In this poem every verse has thirty-five letters, and in the middle of the page is written **AVG. XX. CAES. X.** In the lines of the three letters **AVG** runs this verse:

**When such writing pleases, the Muses dare their wandering ways;**

in the two following letters, **XX**:

**To mark in varied modes the devotions of the mind;**

likewise, in the three letters **CAE**:

**The joys which my Phoebe, painting, speaks to the Muses.**

In the two letters in fourth position, **S. X**:

**Highest Father, grant in pious voice that thirty years be told.**

## XVI

[Col. 0413]

[Note: [Col. 0413]

Verse 5, “justice into the lands.” This verse is absent from Pithoeus, p. 367.

7, “Italian.” Pithoeus wrongly has “Italy.”

10, “unconquered.” Pithoeus has “unconquered one.”

11, “and you, suppliant.” Pithoeus very badly has *supplex*, contrary to metre. Porphyrius, in imitation of the ancients, shortens a syllable made long by position by omitting one of its consonants, as they did in *omitto* for *ommitto* or *obmitto*; *disertus* for *dissertus*; *mamilla* from *mamma*; and *ofella* from *offa*. Damasus used this likewise in his hymn to Agatha: *Pro misero suplica Damaso*. This is the reading of the old editions; those who did not understand it substituted *rogita*. Martius Milesius Sarazanus, editor of Damasus’s works, did not notice it either. So too Galterus, *Alexandreid* I.280 and VIII.7; William the Breton I.197, 428, 799; VI.64; VII.587; IX.121, 326; XI.523, etc. Our Optatianus uses it again in this poem, verse 25.

16, “serene.” Pithoeus has “serenely.”

18, “may you conquer through love.” Pithoeus has “that he may conquer through love.” Perhaps read “may you conquer through love.” So below in verse 24 of this poem; Tertullian, *Against Marcion* II.186; Hilary, *Genesis* 2, 95, 184. See Weitz; likewise Pithoeus, *Ancient Epigrams*, p. 109.

23, “the desired things of the world.” Pithoeus has “desired things for the world.”

24, “a happier age.” Pithoeus has “the happiness of the age.” Velser’s manuscript had this too, as the marginal note shows. See the remarks above on verse 18.

25, “behold, suppliants.” Pithoeus has *supplices*, which neither metre nor Optatianus’s design permits. See above, verse 11 of this poem.

[Col. 0416A] 27, “to yield to you.” Pithoeus has “to yield to himself.”

29, “give good answers.” Pithoeus has “give a good answer.”

32, “the sorrowful divisions of the world.” See Valesius on Eusebius, p. 169.

Third from last, “willing.” Pithoeus has “of the willing.” See Nicolaus Heinsius’s preface to his latest edition of Virgil.

Next to last, “happier for me.” Pithoeus has “gentle happiness.”

**ON THE DEVICE ATTACHED TO THE POEM**

“In which the monogram of Christ.” Pithoeus has “in which [is] Christ’s.”

“The descending rubric.” Pithoeus has “the descending slippery [line].”

“Through which,” etc. Pithoeus has “through which, from the first letter of the first verse.”

“From the letter of the last verse to the final [letter of the first].” Pithoeus has “from the last verse to the final [letter].”

“To the middle.” Pithoeus omits *to*.

“Rubric.” Pithoeus has “slippery [line].”

“The letter-shape contains writing.” Pithoeus has “the letter-shape contains, written along the winding line, ‘Restorer.’”]

Holy adornment of the world, highest salvation of all things,
pious light of the earth: through you alone the princes of the age
are granted boundless joy in blessings. The golden age has come;
the highest God has been appeased, and tyrants have been overthrown.
Justice is sent into the lands, and the bright glory of truth.
You, as leader, restore grateful faith and renewed laws;
the whole world, struck by the great weight of tyrants,
has laid aside the harsh business of war by Italian law.
The sceptre will grant peoples what a pious world desires.
Unconquered Augustus, you will traverse the world’s bounds;
the city of Syene, surrounded by all her leaders,
prays to you and seeks light for her joys.
The deceptive Parthian, treacherous in his promises,
has laid aside his quiver; throughout the red eastern shore
the warrior has abandoned the contest of war.
The Mede and Arab soon rejoice to praise the serene ruler.
The reading is uncertain: “ORIS LUSTRAT VIDAT VERIS SANCTE TROPAEIS.” The margin gives “ORBI,” while noting traces that “ORIS” had first been written. A secure continuous translation is not recoverable.
Great one, happy in your title, may you conquer through love;
may you restore a golden age that endures for ever in the world.
The Indian and Aurora’s soldier, whom the Nile’s river touches,
will come bearing fruitful harvests from fertile soil.
A noble race, praying and seeking pious laws,
All the Ethiopians obey, and the desired things of the world [obey or are granted].
A happier age has given us joyful times.
Behold, the suppliant Persians do not want royal laws for themselves;
they prefer you as lord and continually adore you with their whole prayer.
They desire all their shores and kingdoms to yield to you.
Pious, just, truly mindful, illustrious amid joys,
give favourable answers, always the gentlest ruler of the world,
and mercifully impart your divine power, with your name added.
May those whom you protect, kindly one, be happier alike;
and, yoking them after restoration, [join] the sorrowful divisions of the world.
Join equal worlds; let Rome give laws willingly—or to willing peoples.
With you as mild prince over the peoples, in a happier age,
let all things rejoice and flourish amid golden prosperity.

[Col. 0413] This page has thirty-five letters [in each line]. In it the monogram of Christ is depicted in rubric; a line running from the first letter of the first verse to the final letter of the last contains:

**Safe through the aid and perpetual nod of the highest God.**

From the first letter of the last verse to the last letter of the first, ascending diagonally, is written:

**He pacified the whole world when the tyrants had been slain.**

From the middle letter of the first verse to the middle of the last, descending directly, a rubric contains:

**Constantine, pious and eternal emperor.**

The bend forming a Greek letter contains:

**Restorer of the world.**

## XVII

[Col. 0415]

[Golden light of the world, receive things depicted in novel elegiacs:
the pious signs of the merciful God and an enduring vow.
Highest one, favour us; the whole people duly asks you for joys
and believes them deserved when it keeps the commands in reverence.
Glory, approved under the law of Augustus and of faith in Christ,
has now advanced through the bright and gentle age,
increasing its assemblies and adorning everything with serene
gifts, while furnishing your sons so that golden vows
may now be owed to the first years of their virtues.
A noble age begot them in such a lineage;
for them is distinction from their great-grandfather and awareness of true descent.
Nurturing Rome flows for the prince of the unconquered soldier [the transmitted FLUIT is difficult].
These are the gentlest gifts of one who loves the leisure of peace.
This ancestral merit, the world later brought forth after its vows [uncertain],
burst forth and taught equals not to know how to break
the best laws of faith beneath the cares of unjust Mars.
Faith, harmed by none, hence binds the fates in perpetual thread.
The threads—or destinies—choose these things for you, following peaceful piety;
and illustrious fame now brings forth achievements for Constantine.
Increased by pious stock, accumulated through an enduring vow,
it passes to your holy seats for the mind’s joy,
dwelling happily in the heavenly hinge of the world.
Now [shall I sing] the resources of ancestral courage, lest in the labour of war—
or shall I sing of the merits of a just and serene mind,
and celebrate pious gifts and fruitful hearts for the renowned one?
Thus they rightly flourish in God with a mind whose joys are chaste.
Claudius, unconquered in war, brought forth great distinctions
of virtues, won from the Gothic soldier.
His son Constantius, mighty in age, completed everything in peace,
increased by righteous gifts.
This lineage, sprung from stronger faith and greater merits:
you offer gifts to your world and surpass what came before.
Through your sons you also conquer great renown;
by deeds, God’s law, and enduring commands, these things will come to pass.
May the ages of the pious sceptre be serene with you, Constantine.

## XVIII

[Col. 0417]

[Note: [Col. 0417] This poem is absent from Pithoeus.]

I. III. VII. XII. It is a marvellous work, to arrange and set out such verses;
and so, asked only a little, you invite ivy.
Soon you will draw away whichever fixed pieces I offer;
you yourself teach us how, fortunate in threefold form,
not falsely granting a famous gift to bold endeavour.
Now let equal minds strengthen Clio’s songs,
which can be composed; I shall set down the woven rules,
the things that wander and the things whose bonds run in gentle courses.
You will grant these powers; I shall in turn gather rewards.

XI. With great boldness you will run joyfully toward opposites.

IV. The Aonian spring gleams with a new vein;
it is huge, and you sound with an embrace extending through the whole sky.
You are to consider and plant modes,
that effort may enter upon a difficult task;
do not cast a book aside and consume its glory.
Let wise men see that our sharpness grows by use;
let them discern, with eager study of good paths,
how to lead the mind’s solid, dense, living force.

VIII. What I behold hidden in the restricted rules of verse,

IX. you, kindly judge of character, display through every practice,
with the ruler’s cultivated studies set forth.
You renew your own Ciceros, rich in happy acquisitions;
you contemplate prosperous acts and give joys.
Nothing public comes first, nor anything private, whose care
does not confess the thought of a Sidonian patron in its inmost place.
May you know what is possible there; I strive to invoke his help.

V. The creator gathers hidden things into a noble store.

XIII. Poverty burns with twin new vows of joy;
the rich goddess binds golden covenants with Apollinean lyres.
The learned man knows the praises which so great a ruler sings;
let them be anticipated among blessings; be immediately upright.
Stand with the holy, swift in faith, and hasten into the open.
By merciful nod Augustus grants you these blessed gifts;
he praises, grants, and, as consul, completes your rewards.
Then, when your names are marked by festive acclaim,
you will be most abundant and prudent in every kind of business.
From degenerate hope a greater burden now threatens;
receive this service joyfully, noble man, as a vow.

II. VI. X. XIV.

[Col. 0417]

I. The Muses draw mixed poems apart through winding courses.
II. Or [draw] latticed spaces into contrary bends.
III. We prepare to arrange the sequence more sharply.
IV. The love of poetry rejoices that dense material is exacted.
V. May learned [verse] be able to come together within the boundary of things.
VI. Economy, when not refused, protects the work.
VII. Beautiful, holy in cultivation. [Fragment.]
VIII. A Muse finely depicted in metres. [Fragment.]
IX. May you flow gently, so that briefly in this [form]. [Fragment.]
X. The work must [proceed] through a company in narrow spaces. [Fragment.]
XI. I dare [things] full— [Fragment.]
XII. —to produce forms.
XIII. I shall mark depicted things— [Fragment.]
XIV. —as laws for the Muses.

## XIX

[Col. 0419]

[Note: [Col. 0419] This poem is absent from Pithoeus.]

Kindly one, the age shall raise your laurels to the stars.  
Consul, may you mark the calendar records with your light, without limit.  
Serene once Mars has been cast aside, you possess the duties of the Greeks,  
and you ensure that the sceptres of the Mede return for assessment.  
The fierce [Getae?] in the field—a renowned man, as he loses his sight [syntax uncertain].  
He wishes [something] for the troop; fortunate in his own curved, close-quarter blow [CURVO … ICTV; the intervening syntax is corrupt].  
“The Armenian’s leader” [?]; light to bear—sun, and you also, spears [undivided and corrupt].  
Thus too the victor reports the Franks as arisen—“Dacia” [?].  
By your law, the shorn [one?]; the Rhine [?] springs up for you, an exile.  
Let ranks of missiles advance—those who, amid the din, [undertake] wars.  
To conquer—the Latins, the Sarmatian, under flourishing command [syntax uncertain].  
The king—to you, that the Getae can [do something]; an avenger from the frontier once seen.

Virtue increased by God more openly adorns the Muses.  
The Roman people alone gives its vows far and wide in familiar signs.

[Note: [Col. 0419] *Tropheis*, “with trophies,” a spelling variant of TROPAEIS.]

Holy Clio mingles her vows with your trophies.  
The beauty of painted figures is seen and increases through song.  
May strength attend the twenty-year celebrations; through *Thilen* [?], may grace prevail.  
Such a torch bears the lyre’s gifts from its own signs.  
The poet carries what was begun in an equal rhythm, Delian one.  
With purple light, the venerable leader will be like the sun.  
So that by the laws of Janus you may, forefather, hold a tribunal throughout the world.  
You shall possess distinguished titles through love of piety.  
The summit rejoices that so many seas are transformed by the gift of peace.  
India wishes to reach Latium in the club-bearer’s ship.  
The Nile-born reaper hands over his own camp—or host.

Kindly one, the age shall raise your laurels to the stars.

Castalian maidens, give the palm of virtues to your lord:
Constantine rightly holds the trophy of wars.
With avenging right hand he happily restores the world,
and by counsel urges Rome to renew everything.
Since savage Rome can bind chains of servitude to you in war,
virtue does not arm the mild against an enemy;
thus in great contest it has taught men to spare.
What merciful Piety bestows after the corrupt *piamina* sequence is uncertain.
Now, wholly teachable, Helicon’s Muses send me
palms woven together for a gentle age.
Join songs of virtues to metres, all of you;
sing that a happy fruit may be worthy of the prince.
Let the page, weaving grateful offspring, give
songs powerful through the title of vows.
Grant me, Phoebus, Pierian and Castalian
springs; let my mind wander through your groves,
seek lofty summits, and desire to compose a verse with you.
Now, under so great a prince, the Muse rejoices;
she bears gifts of praise, resounding in distinguished branches.
Boldly she sings triumphs commanded by victorious valour,
and commands so many noble palms to be returned as recompense.
The Aonian valley, watered by its flowing stream, nourishes them.
Holy Saviour of the world, blazing in illustrious arms,
Crispus, better than your ancestors, in this second song,
Clio, the sounding Muse, tells the beauties of your youth;
you are your father’s noble glory and the hope of the city. Caesar, receive these songs of my mind.
You, conqueror, always grant the most welcome bonds of peace;
be forgiving, and unite the peoples who pray to you.
Make the Roman world rejoice, with virtues increased.
Constantine too is the praise of the world and glory of the age,
Roman light, merciful and illustrious brother.
Holy father and highest ruler, restore Caesar’s name and adornment,
the true nobility of his ancestors, memorable in fame;
may solemn celebrations increase tenfold for Augustus and his sons.

In this poem there are thirty-seven letters throughout every part, and the figure of a palm is written. Because the first two branches of the palm appeared too short and could not complete a verse, a line has been added directly and diagonally:

**Castalian maidens, conclude the palm in a teachable verse.**

Keeping the same initial letter shared, and also keeping shared the final **M** of the first verse, the second branch, descending and ascending diagonally, makes the verse:

**Constantine, favour us; now summon Phoebus into song.**

Through the third branch, likewise descending and ascending diagonally, runs:

**The mind calls, daring to impose new laws upon metres.**

Through the fourth branch, likewise descending and ascending diagonally, runs:

**Along an equal boundary, [the palm’s] branches grow on every side.**

Through the middle trunk, descending from the middle letter of the first verse to the middle of the last, runs:

**May the woven verse be rendered in the Muses’ song.**

[Note: [Col. 0423] Inclitssachra. Corrupt printed marginal reading; meaning indeterminate.]

[Note: [Col. 0423] Trophy.]

In this poem there are thirty-five letters in every part. From the first letter of the first verse to the last letter of the final verse, a red diagonal line descends and bears the inscription:

> Constantine, greatest and unconquered emperor.

Likewise, from the first letter of the final verse, a red diagonal line ascends to the last letter of the first verse and bears:

> Most provident guardian of eternal peace.

From the seventh letter of the first verse to the seventh letter from the end of the same verse, ascending in a winding path, is written:

> You rule as father; may you rule as grandfather.

Likewise, from the seventh letter of the final verse to the seventh from the end of the same verse, the same words are written. From the thirteenth letter of the first verse to the thirteenth from the end of that verse is written:

> Pious and fortunate.

By the same method the same words are written in the final verse. From the seventh letter of the acrostic to the seventh from the end of the acrostic is written:

> Restorer of the golden age.

The same is likewise written from the seventh letter of the telestich to the seventh from the end of that same telestich. From the thirteenth letter of the acrostic to the thirteenth from the end of it is written:

> Great in all things.

The telestich likewise bears this inscription from its thirteenth letter to the thirteenth letter from the end.
