### XXII

> Boldly imitating martial deeds in melodious measures,  
> the Muse wove an image of battle-lines in song.  
> And now she drives a column upright beneath the summit;  
> the exact construction of QVINO SVBLIMINE / MVSIGENO SPATIVM is constrained, but the space is separated by a sevenfold boundary.  
> Now, rereading the same thing in verse, so that it may proceed with each movement,  
> she sends companies into winding paths by more than one rule,  
> rejoicing that discordant things are combined in diverse song,  
> welcome to minds through flexible art and continuous metre.  
> The beginning again joins the end, setting boundary against boundary,  
> placing it before the beginnings with no distinction of metre.  
> Indeed, the learned middle portions also perform their function,  
> through exchanges in reversed verses; for from a single end,  
> although the courses are ambiguous, it encloses the deviations.  
> Displaying its art, it offers rugged material to be bound,  
> Sarmaticas usum strages: the constrained phrase is textually uncertain, but refers to Sarmatian slaughter or slaughters as material for the design.  
> I pray that you favour vows composed beneath an assured design,  
> and permit a poet acquainted with the deeds to tell of things so great.  
> Now, Augustus, though the field has so often,  
> after war, lain wet with hostile gore and packed throughout,  
> with bodies strewn on the ground and submerged in the swollen river,  
> let the victorious host marvel at the fierce battle-line.  
> Rejoicing in Phoebean song, I shall attempt to tell very many things:  
> to recall the heavenly deeds at the Margus—BONI/MARGENSIS remains uncertain.  
> To relate assaults and wars: shattered amid ruins,  
> the conquered nation lies fallen through harsh Mars.  
> Neighbouring Bononia, present as witness of the great deeds,  
> sees the vows fulfilled and the battle-lines cut down.  
> Concerning yokes imposed on captives, let the other spoils be recounted.  
> For the victor we undertake great battles with the plectrum.  
> Nor is it enough to speak, unless fulfilment completes the vow.  
> Whatever the Muse prepares to sound beneath her rule,  
> entwined in rugged measures and perfected by the Camenae,  
> wishes again to sound with mine; a witness marks the trophies,  
> depicted in metres, together with the sacred offering  
> of a devoted mind, so that the storms may be appeased amid the fates.

[Note: [Col. 0425] Whatever she prepares beneath the rule.]

[Note: [Col. 0425] Trophies.]

In this poem every verse has thirty-five letters. Across the page run two verses written in red, each composed of five parts of speech. Each part has seven letters. While the final part remains fixed, the other four change places among themselves: the first may become the fourth and the fourth again the first; the second may become the third and the third the second. With the final part remaining fixed, the verse can be made reciprocal in many ways, not merely changing itself but attaining the same principle of variation together with the other verse. The order of the parts that one wishes to change is retained, so that one may alter whichever part of the sentence one wishes in the order of its components.

The two verses are:

> Rejoicing in discordant song, the Muse is bound by a thread.  
> I shall attempt great songs with Phoebean plectrum.

The same verse runs upward and downward through varied windings. In this same poem there are four six-letter squares at the corners, two triangles, two larger halved orthogonal figures, one hexagon in the middle, and scalene figures at the four corners. All have an equal number of letters and increase or decrease in a corresponding order: that is, all alike—triangles with triangles, orthogonal figures with orthogonal figures, squares with squares, and scalene figures with scalene figures.

### XXIII

> Great Augustus, exemplar, gentle clemency,  
> victor of the Ausonians: the Muses sing your mightiest deeds;  
> from the Castalian spring they sing your highest gifts.  
> Phoebus, grant me now the fullness of favour for my vows;  
> grant me a mind and devout thoughts, illustrious, serene ruler,  
> powerful in command and fortunate in sons for martial deeds,  
> to proclaim beneath a pictured poem an empire perpetual through the ages.  
> I pray you: yourself aid me as I dare, glory of poets,  
> to utter a song, although the Muse's resources now  
> cannot be so great without being aided beneath a rule.  
> VERSOALIVDLIMOALIVDQVOPAGINAINOMNES is corrupt and must not be translated as coherent prose;  
> the page is marked into measures so that it may distinguish the seeds of speech.  
> The divine power delights in willing it—the nurturing light and joys of the world;  
> they institute it, and music follows its cares in accordance with the vow.  
> It longs to unfold your virtues and character,  
> holy one; confidence in you has grown in our mind.  
> For, rejoicing with you as its devout leader beneath the marked design,  
> it hastens to the yokes with the Muses, where ever-leafy  
> shelters sing the arts, as do streams known to poets.  
> As victor, whether by the uncertain paths of peace you subdue untamed kings,  
> or lay them low in war, or gently establish treaties by a nod,  
> you make them yours and cause the fields of your people to be cultivated.  
> Through you the more abundant, nurturing presence of God looked upon  
> the world, soon restoring a golden age to human affairs;  
> and God revealed the times of the just ruler.  
> By a heavenly nod, clemency belongs with the peaceful and just.  
> Through you and your people all things are gentle, victor.  
> NATOSRESPOPVLI is constrained and indeterminate; the affairs or offspring of the people flourish for the mind's rejoicing.  
> Through your Caesars, victory throughout the whole world,  
> a fortunate companion by right, flourishes forever through the ages.  
> You will erect captive trophies as memorials of achievements so great.  
> Victor over Sarmatia so often, behold, receive them, illustrious  
> leader; everywhere the fulfilment of your vows is fortunate.  
> Your Romulean youth rejoices, now master of obligations discharged.

[Note: [Col. 0427] Ispe juva: corrupt spelling of ipse juva, 'aid [me] yourself.']

[Note: [Col. 0427] Virtutes ove tuas: corrupt marginal reading, probably associated with virtutesque tuas.]

[Note: [Col. 0427] Caesarnbus: corrupt marginal reading, evidently associated with Caesaribusque tuis.]

[Note: [Col. 0427] Trophies.]

In this poem there are thirty-five letters in every part. From the first letter of the first verse a red line descends to the central square, and from the square ascends diagonally to the final letter of the first verse, making the verse:

> Ausonian pillar, nourishing light, and glory of Rome.

Again, from the thirteenth letter of the acrostic, which is V, ascending diagonally to a point near the middle of the first verse, and thence descending diagonally to the thirteenth letter of the telestich, which is I, it makes:

> Exemplar of virtues, gentle clemency of the world.

The final parts of speech serve these two verses alternately, each in turn. Then, from the fourteenth letter of the acrostic, nine letters descend straight; facing them, in the middle of the poem, are another nine in the same order; beyond the middle of the poem another nine in the same order; and in the telestich likewise another nine. They make the verse:

> Parent of justice, happy hope, peace of the world.

Again, from the twenty-third letter of the acrostic, descending diagonally to the final verse, then proceeding a little in a straight line and ascending diagonally to the twenty-third letter of the telestich, it makes:

> A heavenly gift sent to us through the ages.

The letters from the final letter of the acrostic, from the first letter of the final verse ascending diagonally to the central square, then proceeding a little in a straight line and descending diagonally to the final letter of the final verse, make:

> And through you the presence of God the Ruler flourishes.

In this poem are four hexagons equal in number, eight equilateral triangles measured by letters, and one central square, equal in number of letters on every side.

### XXIV

> After the martial labours  
> and the Caesars' everlasting  
> virtues, while throughout the world  
> so many laurels grow green,  
> and the ruler's trophies  
> amid fortunate triumphs,  
> August through the ages in due order,  
> every generation exults.  
> The cities flourish with pleasing  
> and decorative foliage;  
> the squares grow green throughout.  
> This order, splendid in its dress,  
> together with the purple robes of office,  
> in an auspicious shower of prayers  
> brings gifts with rejoicing.  
> Now the nurturing summit of the world  
> bestows gifts and crowns,  
> bearing things that flash with gold  
> for Victory in her triumphs.  
> And now in theatres  
> and choral dances vows are rendered.  
> My lot, unequal to such  
> solemnities, scarcely permitted  
> me, removed from them, to sound these things:  
> so many vows from Phoebus's spring,  
> adorned by verse alone.

### XXV

> O Clio, if you would measure it with a divided boundary,  
> flowing by its single rule from a single source,  
> while the Aonian heroic verse remains in force,  
> may it grant the one who dares a fortunate weaving of metre.  
> May it enlarge its beginnings, extending from a distant end,  
> in a short course and by a slight movement of increase,  
> until the final line, at the furthest point, forms the whole summit  
> and closes it with an ascent accumulated beneath a continuous boundary.  
> Within one space, counting the elements of the preceding verse,  
> it compels them to be read according to the rule of equality.  
> Small elements with long ones contain much discordant material;  
> under an almost equal boundary and by the same metrical proportions,  
> the Muses prepare a thread equal to half the number.  
> This form will be especially suitable for varied kinds of song;  
> through its measures it rises step by step, fertile in melodious sounds.  
> Enlarged by hollow bronze and by rounded, lengthening reeds,  
> for it, with the keys set beneath the squares in due order,  
> the craftsman's hand closes and opens the measures,  
> testing whether the air-passages harmonize properly in gentle TUMIS—the printed final word is indeterminate, perhaps corrupt.  
> Beneath them concealed water, driven by hastening winds, rushes broadly.  
> Those winds, through frequent alternations, youthful labour, not discordant with itself,  
> here and there sets in motion; struggling, it animates and increases them.  
> It supplies a composition fitted to numbers and proper for songs.  
> And whatever vibration, set trembling, can answer the slightest motion,  
> it makes follow the opened keys, or properly close gentle melodies.  
> And now it can encompass in metre and rhythms whatever exists anywhere.

In this poem a form of an organ is depicted in twenty-six verses. Its entire upper part is written in heroic metre. Its first verse has twenty-five letters; thereafter the verses proceed in order, increasing by one letter at a time, until they reach fifty, the number possessed by the final verse. That verse doubles the first verse in number of letters while remaining in the same metre. Then, written in red through the middle, is the verse:

> Under Augustus victorious, it is pleasing to render established vows.

These letters mark, as it were, the rule of the organ.

### XXVI

> Arduous songs the fortunate Muses compose;  
> Discordant bonds they connect in varied metres;  
> Fashioning rugged things, poets twist hearts;  
> From every side, the individual things will stand among confused words.

These four verses are all composed by the same method: while the final part of speech remains fixed, you can vary all the other parts of the verses merely by changing their positions, either directly or reciprocally. The first parts may interchange with the first or fourth; the second with the second or third. If desired, with no part of speech added, you can make seventy-two verses from these four, so that none is identical with another.

## Dedicatory Letter

Faustinus Arevalus to the most eminent and most reverend prince and lord, Lord Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana y Butrón, presbyter-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, archbishop of Toledo, primate of the Spains, grand chancellor of Castile, decorated with the Grand Cross of the distinguished Spanish Royal Order of Charles III, etc.

Although I understand very well, most eminent prince, that you are such a man that you might almost by right demand from me an account of whatever my studies may be, of whatever quality, and that all I possess is owed to you, yet—to speak freely—I should scarcely even now have induced myself to send you, a man of such dignity and burdened by so many cares and duties, this second specimen of my labours upon Christian poets, unless I had been so richly loaded by your frequent and great favours bestowed in the name of studies of this kind that I readily believe you will receive my Sedulius, which I now offer with reverent and submissive heart, with a kind and gracious countenance.

And, to pass over other things here, permit me to mention just one. I would not have it thought that I say this in praise of any learning or talent of my own, for I know how slight these are; rather, it is a proclamation of your singular and incredible favour and beneficence toward cultivators of Christian literature. Permit me, I say, to mention this one thing: that you wished my portrait also, painted from life by the exceptionally celebrated painter Bonaventura Salesa, to be placed among the portraits of men distinguished for learning which are seen in the public library of your archiepiscopal residence.

What a splendid honour—one to which, to speak truly, I should never have aspired even in a dream! What extraordinary favour and goodwill, as I said, toward students of Christian literature! Behold, then, most gracious prince, this new undertaking of mine in those studies which you so greatly love, cultivate, and advance.

Although, in order to join Sedulius to Juvencus as his imitator and disciple in setting forth the most holy Gospels in verse, I am now publishing Sedulius rather than one of the ancient Spanish Fathers, I have nevertheless not departed so far from that former plan that I have not gladly taken the opportunity, from Vatican documents, to elucidate in the appendices the Roman council held under Pope Damasus for establishing the canon of the divine Scriptures.

Nor, if God grants life and strength, shall I cease to undertake greater works for the honour of the Spanish Church. I am especially encouraged by your example: amid the countless cares of your very extensive diocese and the other affairs which, in a special capacity, the excellent and most prudent King Charles IV entrusted to you and which you discharge with singular wisdom, you add sacred studies and labours in the literary arena, where you have long won immortal glory for your name through many distinguished published works, and where you have recently increased it wonderfully by issuing for public use and benefit the third volume of the Fathers of Toledo.

Indeed, neither your immense generosity in relieving human distress nor the new great expenditure and resources supplied for advancing the war undertaken for country and religion deterred you from providing in this respect also for the public good. For you are thoroughly convinced that, just as arms are necessary for defeating impious men who have taken up arms against every divine and human right, so, for utterly rooting out the seeds of impiety—which, throughout the world, I do not say have been sown, but flourish insolently—the teachings of the evangelical law, expounded especially from the mouths of the ancient teachers, must everywhere not merely be offered but also impressed upon people.

You acted most wisely in joining Roderic Ximenius, a thirteenth-century writer, to the other earlier Fathers of Toledo. In that man, equally distinguished for holiness of life and learning, one may admire, among his other virtues, his religious obedience toward the Roman Apostolic See. I gather from the letters which you arranged to be sent to our Most Holy Lord Pius VI, supreme pontiff—letters that are at once testimonies and pledges of your own veneration for that same first See of Peter—that you have in some measure set him before yourself as an example to imitate.

What courage, then, will you give me, most eminent prince, if you continue to protect me and my little commentaries! I shall not detain you further; I shall merely repeat, in petition, words from Sedulius’s dedicatory letter of the Paschal Work to Macedonius:

> Favour me first, that others may favour me, and let the verdict of authority already approved continually be poured into the minds of all.

[Col. 0435]

## Prolegomena to Coelius Sedulius

### Chapter I. The Life and Deeds of Coelius Sedulius

[Col. 0435A]

#### 1

As I look upon the various vicissitudes of human affairs, and long and deeply consider the calamitous times into which we have now fallen, it has seemed especially useful, for checking the attempts of wicked men, to disseminate everywhere, as far as may be possible, the writings of the ancient Fathers and to make their reading more frequent. Cellarius, though a heterodox man, prefaced his edition of Sedulius in approximately these words:

> We have indeed fallen upon times in which low things are mixed with high, sacred things with profane, or the latter are preferred to the former. For how many are there who, if they do not deny the most august mysteries, nevertheless think coldly of them, as though they were idle questions and contributed less fruit to human morals and duty? This pernicious opinion has arisen from other causes, but especially from neglected knowledge of the Church’s earlier times. How much more illustrious and ardent was the faith of our forefathers! How divinely and distinctly, near the end of the first book, did Sedulius from the mouth of the Saviour restrain, pierce, and overthrow both Sabellius and Arius! What if Cellarius had lived to see our times, in which many seek to overthrow all religion and the worship of God no longer by hidden tunnels, but openly and no less shamelessly?

#### 2

As to neglected knowledge of the Church’s earlier times, it is plain that certain impious men have held nothing more important than declaring war on every approved writer, and indeed upon the Latin language itself. In this way they hoped both that their own eloquence, very far indeed from the vigorous eloquence of the ancients, would find greater approval, and that their errors could be refuted with greater difficulty. Something similar is reported by Quintilian concerning Seneca the philosopher, Book X, chapter 1:

> At that time he was almost the only author in the hands of young men. I certainly was not trying wholly to drive him out, but I did not allow him to be preferred to better writers, whom he never ceased to attack, since, conscious that he belonged to a different kind of style, he distrusted his ability to please those whom they pleased.

#### 3

Indeed, certain enemies of the most holy religion and of the Latin language have already succeeded in making many mortals, abandoning the study of antiquity, love exclusively a painted style of expression: mere pieces of patchwork, so to speak, and sand without lime, as Caesar Caligula not inaptly said of Seneca’s writings (in Suetonius, chapter 53). In that manner of discourse, clipped and frequently obscure periods, like oracles, about matters otherwise altogether commonplace are so heaped up that you may mix and interchange them without any connection of the meanings being lost. For they are no more connected with one another than the numbers drawn at random from an urn in the game called Lotto.

Yet there is another thing which pleases corrupted minds in those impious writers: rash wit, often foolish but deeply embedded in depraved minds, since sharp sayings are uttered against good morals, against lawful authority, or against Divinity itself. What great evil follows from this, why need one explain? Not without reason do pious men complain that, just as Latin is commonly called the language of learned men, so French, in which so many wicked books have appeared, has become the language of the impious. Others add that what the aged Marcus Cicero said of the Romans of his own time and of Syrian slaves for sale (*On the Orator*, Book II), with one word or adverb lightly altered, may now be repeated:

> Our people are like Syrian slaves: the better each knows Greek, the more worthless he is.

[Col. 0436A]

#### 4

This evil can in great part be met if the doctrine of the other Fathers and of the Christian poets is firmly retained and carefully explained. Many do not dare approach these poets, as though they spoke some other language, unless an explanation is supplied. Thus we now add Sedulius to Prudentius, Dracontius, and Juvencus. And Sedulius is rightly added now as companion to Juvencus, recently published by us. Of the two, in the titles of Isidore’s library, we read:

> Both alike in language, both flourishing in verse,  
> They bring abundant draughts from the evangelical spring.

Concerning Sedulius, therefore, in accordance with our established method and plan, we shall first discuss those matters which seem chiefly relevant for knowing his life and writings.

#### 5

Vatican Palatine manuscript no. 242, which I described in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 79, and in a note, briefly sets forth Sedulius’s life, as it does the lives of other poets:

> He was a pagan layman, but learned philosophy in Italy; then, converted to the Lord and baptized by the presbyter Macedonius, he came to Arcadia, where he composed this book.

This seems to be a preface by someone to Sedulius’s Paschal poem, which is absent from that manuscript. Yet these statements, preserved in this form in a manuscript about the twelfth century, can be accepted only where they are confirmed by older evidence. Let us therefore turn to other manuscripts.

[Col. 0436D]

#### 6

The Vatican manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, which I chose to call Reg. 1, after Asterius’s epigram on Sedulius and certain other words on Sedulius’s metrical prologue, to be cited below at no. 66, continues as follows:

> Jerome says in his catalogue of writers: Sedulius the versifier, at first a layman, learned philosophy in Italy; afterward he taught heroic metre in Achaea, together with other kinds of metre, with Macedonius advising. He wrote his books in the time of Valentinian and Theodosius.

Mabillon, *Analecta veterum*, vol. I, p. 363, offers a similar annotation from a manuscript of the library of Corbie:

> Jerome in the catalogue: Sedulius, etc.

For *metrum* read *metrorum*, and For metrum read metrorum, and Mabillon supplies generibus: metrorum (generibus) heroicum, etc. There follows: “Afterward he wrote in the time.” The error in Jerome’s name is immediately detected: Jerome does not mention Sedulius in his catalogue of writers, nor could he have mentioned him, because he was considerably earlier in date.

[Col. 0437A]

#### 7

The scribe, therefore—the author or copyist of that annotation—substituted Jerome for Gennadius. This same confusion is observed elsewhere and, I think, arose because Gennadius continued Saint Jerome’s catalogue of writers, and the two catalogues were often bound together in one volume. Notker the Stammerer even imagined Gennadius to have been bishop of Toledo, presumably because he found Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, continuing a catalogue of distinguished writers of this sort in some manuscript of Gennadius. Notker’s words are in chapter 7, *On the Interpretation of Holy Scripture*:

> If you wish to know ancient authors, read the book of blessed Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, from Saint Peter down to himself, and that of Gennadius, bishop of Toledo, from Ambrose down to Gennadius himself.

He says almost the same thing in chapter 11.

[Col. 0437B]

#### 8

Sirmond reports, in his note on Ennodius, Book I, Letter 24, that he learned from complete copies of Gennadius that Sedulius died while the younger Theodosius and Valentinian were ruling. Sirmond does not quote Gennadius’s words from those complete copies; but, as I suppose, he read there that Sedulius died while the younger Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning. The statement that Sedulius dedicated his work to the younger Theodosius seems, however, to have been added by Sirmond out of his preconceived opinion; another place will later be available for discussing that matter.

In the commonly published books of Gennadius we read nothing concerning Sedulius; nor does Isidore seem to have found anything in Gennadius, though he lists Sedulius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and is accustomed to list only those whom Gennadius omitted. Perhaps even then many copies of Gennadius were incomplete; but it would have been most desirable had Sirmond not withheld from us the complete copy of Gennadius. Others think that the copies of Gennadius called complete are instead interpolated.

[Col. 0437D]

#### 9

The Palatine manuscript cited at no. 5 must be corrected from Gennadius, or whoever the author may have been: it states that Sedulius came to Arcadia. For one must read, “he came to Achaea.” Though Arcadia is part of Achaea, the name Achaea is nevertheless to be preferred.

The Ottobonian manuscript no. 35, which I call Ott. 1, agrees. After Sedulius’s elegy *Cantemus*, it states:

> Here begins the art of the poet Sedulius, who, first a layman, learned philosophy in Italy; afterward, with Macedonius advising, taught heroic metre together with other kinds of metre in Achaea. He wrote his books in the time of the emperors the younger Theodosius, son of Arcadius, and Valentinian, son of Constantius. Peace …

The remaining words are lacking because the leaf, torn at this point, fails. On its reverse is written, “Here begins a gloss upon Sedulius’s prose,” and a few lines of glosses follow.

Georgius, in his notes on Baronius under the year 494, reports the words of this manuscript, which among the Ottobonian manuscripts he identifies as no. 553, formerly no. 1396 in the library of the Queen of Sweden. He punctuates and reads:

> He taught. In Achaea he wrote his books in the time of the emperors, the younger Theodosius, son of Arcadius, and Valentinian. Peace of Constantius.

But the manuscript is written as I transcribed it; I shall return to the matter. It has *Archadii* and, incorrectly, *Valetiani* or *Valentiani* for *Valentiniani*.

Mabillon, in the cited place of the *Analecta*, transcribes from an old manuscript of the monastery of Lérins the same words found in Ott. 1:

> Here begins the art, etc.

But he gives *consulante* for *consulente*, omits *in* after *scripsit*, and omits the final word *pax*.

10. Two other codices differ somewhat from these: one is the Almeloveenian codex, which Arntzenius cites; the other is the British codex, which Cellarius, following Usserius, *On the Beginnings of the British Church*, chapter 16, says is five hundred years old. The Almeloveenian codex reads as follows:

> Sedulius, a versifier, first a layman, learned philosophy in Italy; afterward, with others, he learned heroic meter while Macedonius was in exile; in Achaea he wrote his books during the time of Valentinus and Theodosius.

The British codex is more accurate; it reports:

> Sedulius, a versifier, first a layman, learned philosophy in Italy; afterward, together with other associates, he learned heroic meter, with Macedonius as adviser. In Achaea he composed his books during the time of Theodosius and Valentinian.

To these I add [6] a certain paper codex of mine, which at the end of Sedulius has the following:

> Sedulius the poet, during the consulship of Theodosius and Valentinian, learned philosophy in Italy. Then, converted to the Catholic faith and baptized by the presbyter Macedonius, he departed for Achaea and composed this book in verse against error and in commendation of the Christian faith.

In place of *Valentiniano*, within the sequence of letters, one may read *Valentino*.

11. These few details concerning the life of Sedulius can be gathered from ancient codices, and there are no other older records from which we may add more. But so that the things commonly said about him may be explained more precisely, we must first discuss his native country.

Most people assert that Sedulius was a Scot. Cellarius, however, maintains that in that period Ireland was called Scotland, and that the name was transferred from that smaller island to the larger one, or rather to the part of the British island facing the north. From this he argues that Sedulius was Irish.

Usserius had held this same opinion in *On the Beginnings of the British Church*, chapter 16:

> Sedulius himself does not allow us to doubt about his native country, since at the beginning of his letters, as we have learned from Trithemius, he calls himself “Scot-born” (*Scotigena*), and the annotations on the Pauline Epistles attributed to our Sedulius, published from a venerably ancient Fulda exemplar, bear this title: “The Collectanea of Sedulius the Scot of Ireland on all the Epistles of Paul.”

Dempster, in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scots*, when discussing Sedulius, asserts that the expression “Scot of Ireland” was not used in Sedulius’s age, but only later, to distinguish the forest-dwelling or mountain Scots from those living in the interior. Usserius, however, contends that the Irish themselves were called “Scots of Ireland,” a usage that appears to have been current already in the time of Orosius. Dempster’s distinction between the peoples of Scotland belongs to a later period, as may be inferred from Ferrari’s *Geographical Dictionary*.

12. Arntzenius, together with Barthis, Dempster, the author of the notes on Gyraldus, Borrichius, Vossius, and others, considers Sedulius’s homeland to have been the part of the larger British island now called Scotland. Certainly, when most people simply call Sedulius a Scot, they seem to mean this, although they do not clearly distinguish one Scotland from the other.

I shall readily adopt this opinion, as if it were supported by a common and prevailing tradition; but I should like it to be confirmable by stronger arguments. [Col. 0439B] Barthius’s interpretation of verse 20 of Book I may perhaps be brought into the discussion, where he explains the words *Ridiculove Getae* as referring to a certain ridiculous god of the ancient Scots, whose genealogy Asser describes. From this someone might conjecture that Sedulius wished to criticize the superstition of his own people. But Barthius’s explanation, as well as Asser’s and those of others, will be rejected by us in its proper place.

I find no plausible writer older than Trithemius who assigned Scotland as Sedulius’s homeland. Trithemius, however, reports several things unknown to others:

> Sedulius, a presbyter, a Scot by nation, from early childhood a disciple of Hildebert, archbishop of the Scots, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, left Scotland out of a love of learning, came to France, then traveled through Italy and Asia, and finally, after leaving the borders of Achaea, shone forth in the city of Rome, distinguished by marvelous learning.

13. Trithemius does not possess such authority that we ought to believe him without another guide. Moreover, the fact that Trithemius says the beginning of Sedulius’s letters to various persons is “Sedulius the Scot-born,” and attributes to our Sedulius the *Collectanea* on Paul’s Epistles, whose author is identified as “Sedulius the Scot of Ireland,” makes the matter much more uncertain.

For critical scholars agree that these works do not belong to our Sedulius the poet, but to another, younger Sedulius, of whom I shall speak later. Someone might therefore suspect that Trithemius and others called the poet Sedulius a Scot by nation because they thought that works belonging to the younger Sedulius were his—works that bear the name “Sedulius the Scot.”

Indeed Labbe, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume II, openly asserts that later authors, confused by the similarity of names, merged three Seduliuses into one: Sedulius the poet of the fourth century, Sedulius the bishop of the eighth century, and Sedulius the interpreter of sacred Scripture of the ninth century.

14. But should we exploit this conjecture to declare that Sedulius the poet may be counted among our Spaniards? Certainly not. The love of truth leads us to regard as fictitious the account in the *Chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter*, under the year 428, no. 1:

> Isicius, a Palestinian monk, succeeds Foetadius, bishop of Toledo; he keeps his friend Sedulius, bishop of Oretum, at Toledo for the sake of preaching. Distinguished by the gift of God in poetry and oratory, Sedulius composes many books.

The similarly fictitious Haubertus gives approximately the same account in his *Chronicle*, under the year 428.

Cellarius seems to doubt the reliability of such chronicles. Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, Book III, chapter 5, no. 115, rejects it outright:

> I am inclined to believe, he says, that by assigning him an episcopal office in Spain the author also wished to indicate that he was Spanish by birth. But Sedulius’s having been born among us is no less false than his having been a bishop anywhere.

In refuting the false chronicles that were disseminated throughout Spain during the preceding century, Nicolás Antonio sometimes went further than was reasonable. Sedulius was not Spanish; indeed, it is not established that this was heard of before the fabrication of Pseudo-Dexter. But the fact that he was a bishop somewhere is supported by more weighty authority, as I shall explain later.

Damianus a Goes and Sebastian Münster derived Sedulius’s Spanish birth from the spurious chronicles in their descriptions of Spain; without making any distinction, as Usserius observes, they placed Sedulius the poet among the Spaniards. Bivarius, however, the commentator on Pseudo-Dexter, doubts whether there were two poet-Seduliuses.

15. The forename *Coelius*, or *Caelius*, is usually added to Sedulius. Arntzenius says that the better-quality codices recognize it. I readily believe that the forename *Caelius* is found in many manuscripts, since the oldest editions also display it. Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, confirms that among later authors Sedulius’s forename appears as *C.*, *Coelius*, or *Coecilius*. Hence “Gaius Coecilius Sedulius” was perhaps invented in the *Dictionary of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Dempster, in his *Ecclesiastical History of Scotland*, gives “Gaius” or “Coecilius.”

My duty, however, is to state that no such forename appears in the codices I have seen, except in the Vatican codex of the Queen of Sweden, no. 333, which I call Reg. 1, where the order is reversed and we find “Sedulius Coelius,” and in another codex of the Queen, no. 29, which I shall call Reg. 5, where he is named “Coelius, or Celius Sedulius.” This codex is extremely recent and can scarcely be regarded as a manuscript, for I believe that it was copied from Aldus’s edition and is certainly later than it.

In a certain codex of Barthius, Liberius’s acrostic is said to be on “Coelius Sedulius,” as I shall report in the Appendix. Among the ancient Romans, *Caelius* was a nomen, not a forename, as in M. Coelius Rufus and L. Coelius Antipater; but under the emperors great confusion was introduced into names and forenames.

[Col. 0440D] 16. The name Sedulius occurs in Cicero, *Pro domo sua*, chapter 30; in Gruter’s inscriptions, page 4, no. 7, “P. Sedulius Julianus”; and page 181, no. 9, “Q. Sedulius”; in Muratori, page 1213, “Sedulia Laeta”; and on page 125, no. 4, the following inscription is found, apparently with little correction:

> Q. SEDVLIVS. FIL  
> SEDVLI, MAIOR  
> DIS. MARIS. AC  
> AVG. ARCVM  
> STATVAS. IDEM  
> M. D. D

The abbreviated text reads approximately: “Quintus Sedulius, son of Sedulius, the elder, … of the gods of the sea and of Augustus, [dedicated] an arch and statues; likewise M.D.D.” The abbreviated middle portion and final letters are uncertain.

Among Christians, several persons appear to have borne this name. In Bernard Pez’s *Introductory Dissertation* to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, pages 5 and following, there is described a manuscript necrology of the Abbey of St. Peter at Salzburg, begun under Arn, the first archbishop of Salzburg, and continued by contemporaries down to the twelfth century. In the list of bishops and abbots of various places, a bishop Sedolius is designated; this is how the name is written.

Moreover, in the year 721, at the first Roman council under Gregory II, Sedulius, bishop of Britain, appears. Hepidannus, a monk of St. Gall, discusses another Sedulius of the ninth century in his *Annals*, edited by Duchesne in volume III of the *History of France*, page 473. Under the year 818, “Sedulius the Scot” is regarded as illustrious.

There was also a Henry Sedulius of the Order of Friars Minor, a writer of the seventeenth century, not very well known, although he composed a work on the celebrated *Book of Conformities of St. Francis*. Samuel Hundius wished to remain concealed under the name Sedulius Numa in his work *The Bull of Innocent X against Five Propositions*, and so forth.

Concerning Sedulius who took part in the Roman council under Gregory II, Labbe reports the following subscription:

> I, Sedulius, bishop of Britain, of the race of the Scots, have subscribed this decree promulgated by us.

In Vatican codex 1342 there is a collection of canons, which someone noted at the beginning of the codex to be the same as that commonly called the Cresconian collection by Baronius in his *Annals*. But the Ballerini brothers, who discuss the collections of canons with great learning in their edition of the works of St. Leo, rightly observe that this collection differs from the one called Cresconian by Baronius.

On page 191 of this codex are the *Titles of the Decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger*, that is, Gregory II. At the beginning, among the bishops, are listed Sinderedus, archbishop [Col. 0441C] of Spain; Sedulius, bishop of Britain; and Fergustus, bishop of Scotland. In the subscriptions, however, we read:

> Sinderedus, archbishop of the region of Spain, have subscribed this decree, etc.;  
> Sedulius, bishop of the race of the Britons, have subscribed this decree, etc.;  
> Fergustus, bishop of the race of the Goths, have subscribed this decree, etc.

In place of “Goths,” “Scots” should apparently be read. In another codex, Vatican 1341, the participants in this council also include Sinderedus, archbishop of Spain, and Sedulius, bishop of Britain.

Sinderedus—thus he is called in the catalogues of the bishops of Toledo—fled to Rome after the Saracens occupied Spain and he had abandoned his see of Toledo. For what reason Sedulius came to Rome is unknown to me.

17. Trithemius, as we have seen, relates that the poet Sedulius was from early childhood a disciple of Hildebert, bishop of the Scots. Baronius, however, refutes this under the year 429, no. 4. He observes that the first bishop of Scotland was Palladius, sent by Pope Celestine. He confirms this from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Theodosius and Valentinian, and from his work *Against the Collator*, at the end, where, praising Celestine, he says:

> Having appointed a bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian island Christian.

He calls Britain the Roman island and Scotland the barbarian island, because although many people in Scotland had embraced the faith of Christ long before, most of that nation nevertheless worshiped idols and lived according to the customs of barbarians.

How, then, could Sedulius, who flourished at this very time, have had Hildebert, archbishop of the Scots, as his teacher from early childhood?

18. Although it is not established under whose instruction Sedulius advanced from early childhood, there is nevertheless no reason to believe that he was a pagan layman who, after learning philosophy, turned to God and received the sacrament of Baptism from Macedonius, as is narrated in the Vatican codex mentioned under no. 5 and in my paper codex, no. 10.

I believe this even less because I see more clearly where the error arose. Sedulius says in his dedicatory epistle to Macedonius:

> While occupied with secular studies, I was applying the force of my restless intellect—which divine providence generated in me—not to the benefit of the soul but to the vanity of life; and the skill of literary training was serving the diversions of unproductive work rather than its author. At last the merciful Creator of all things looked with greater clemency upon the structure belonging to him and grieved that the senses of worldly wisdom had remained foolish in me for so long, etc.

These words, and other similar ones that follow, do not prove that Sedulius was at that time devoted to pagan superstition—for that would have had to be declared in stronger terms—but merely indicate that his mind was devoted to profane disciplines and paid too little attention to divine matters.

19. Accordingly, when he adds later, addressing Macedonius, “I knew that I had made some progress in learning, whether through you, most blessed father, or through others whom heavenly grace likewise enlightens,” this does not indicate that Sedulius had been cleansed by Baptism from Macedonius, but rather that he had received from him knowledge of sacred literature.

And when Sedulius subsequently gives reasons for dedicating his work to Macedonius above all others, he would not have failed to state clearly, had it been true, that he had been baptized by him—especially since he says of others to that same Macedonius: “You have made others sheep within the enclosures of your flock.”

20. Trithemius reports that Sedulius, out of a love of learning, came to France, then traveled through Italy, Asia, and Achaea, and finally became famous at Rome. Xystus of Siena expands and embellishes this account in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca sancta*, where he says of Coelius Sedulius:

> Like another Apollonius of Tyana, seeking fleeing wisdom throughout the entire world, he traveled through Britain, Spain, Gaul, Italy, Greece, and Asia with an extraordinary eagerness to learn. At last, illustrious in divine and human learning, he flourished at Rome under the emperor Theodosius, excellent in verse and prose.

That Sedulius came to France is not recorded elsewhere; [12] but if we say that Scotland was Sedulius’s native land, it is plausible that this happened in that way. Most codices confirm that he learned philosophy in Italy, but it is not known under what teacher or in what region of Italy.

Asia is mentioned by Trithemius, but not likewise by the others. In Achaea—and, if one is willing to believe the account given in Palatine codex no. 5, in Arcadia—Sedulius lived after learning philosophy in Italy.

21. What Sedulius did in Achaea is explained in more than one way by the manuscript codices. One reports:

> He taught heroic meter in Achaea together with others, with Macedonius as adviser.

Another:

> Together with other kinds of meter, he taught heroic meter, etc.

Another:

> Together with other associates, he learned heroic meter, with Macedonius as adviser. In Achaea he composed his books, etc.

What, then, should be retained? I am certainly at a loss. The word *consulente* (“as adviser”) leads me all the more to believe that Sedulius taught others heroic meter, together with other kinds of meter, on Macedonius’s advice. This agrees with the fact that he is called a rhetorician in many places. See the note on the title of the epistle to Macedonius, and in these *Prolegomena*, nos. 25 and 90, as well as the note on verse 60 of Book I.

Yet it also seems probable that he learned heroic meter, together with other associates or fellow students, while Macedonius advised or taught him. Something nevertheless stands in the way of this interpretation: in his dedicatory epistle Sedulius not only does not acknowledge himself to have been Macedonius’s pupil in studies of this kind, but rather suggests that Macedonius was accustomed to devote himself not to these humble disciplines but to loftier pursuits.

The sense also becomes somewhat different according to the punctuation. For if a full stop is placed after *docuit* (“he taught”) or *didicit* (“he learned”), it will be understood that Sedulius composed his books in Achaea. If the sentence continues and a full stop is placed after *Achaia*, it will signify that he taught in Achaea.

In Ottobonian codex 1 and others, no full stop is placed either after *didicit* or after *Achaia*, but everything proceeds without any punctuation at all. In Reg. 1, however, the text is clearly punctuated as *docuit in Achaia* (“he taught in Achaea”), followed by *libros suos scripsit tempore* (“he wrote his books during the time of…”).

22. But whichever way the period is punctuated, it can sufficiently be inferred that Sedulius stayed in Achaea when he composed all or most of his sacred poems. The Palatine codex, no. 5, mentioned above, expressly says:

> He came to Arcadia, where he composed this book.

Sedulius the presbyter also appears to have been made a presbyter in the same church in which Macedonius was presbyter and Bishop Ursinus, and in which Laurentius, Gallicanus, Ursinus or Ursicinus, and a certain Felix—who is not called a presbyter—also served.

In the same church or province there appears to have flourished Syncletice, a virgin minister or deaconess, whom Sedulius praises in his epistle to Macedonius, commending her because, in addition to her other virtues, she had eagerly drunk in the Scriptures of ecclesiastical doctrine.

She therefore does not seem to be different from the Syncletice to whom Eustathius dedicated his Latin translation of St. Basil’s *Hexaemeron*. This translation appears among the appendices to volume I of Basil’s works, edited by Julian Garnier of the congregation of St. Maur. The dedication begins as follows:

> Eustathius sends greetings in Christ to Syncletice, his sister, the deaconess.  
> The devout and studious mind of your sisterhood, desiring to know the fullness of the heavenly Scriptures, investigated through frequent readings all the ecclesiastical libraries and their founders; at last it came to the *Hexaemeron*, etc.

But neither can we add more about this Syncletice from Eustathius, nor does Bollandus, who mentions on January 5 the Syncletice praised by Sedulius in the preface to the *Life of St. Apollinaris*, produce anything else except what Sedulius himself relates in his epistle to Macedonius. Some have thought that Eustathius flourished shortly after the age of Constantine.

Nor have I been able to learn anything else about this Macedonius, whom, as we shall observe in the various readings to the title of Sedulius’s dedicatory epistle, it is incorrect to call an abbot. At the urging of this same Macedonius, Sedulius turned the *Paschal Poem* into prose, as can be inferred from the dedicatory epistle.

It is also reported that the epigram of Asterius, who collected Sedulius’s poems after his death, was dedicated to Macedonius, to whom Sedulius had dedicated his work. I shall show in its proper place that this is not entirely certain.

23. Concerning the time when Sedulius wrote his books, we have the following evidence from manuscript codices. One gives:

> He wrote his books during the time of Valentinian and Theodosius.

Another:

> During the time of the emperors, the younger Theodosius, son of Arcadius, and Valentinian, son of Constantius.

Another:

> During the time of Valentinus and Theodosius.

Another:

> During the time of Theodosius and Valentinian.

In these passages *Valentini* is an error for *Valentiniani*.

Dominicus Georgius read the Ottobonian codex 1 differently, as I said under no. 9; but the parchment has the text as I transcribed it, with a full stop clearly placed after *Constantii* before the word *pax*, which begins another period.

There is therefore no doubt that Sedulius flourished during the time of the younger Theodosius and Valentinian. Sigebertus consequently went far astray when he says of Sedulius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> He flourished during the time of Constans and Constantius, the sons of Constantine.

Nor should Heinsius be followed, in his letter to Reinesius 176, volume V of Burmann’s *Sylloge*, page 198, who, together with others, refers Sedulius’s age back to Theodosius the Great on the basis of the dedication to Theodosius, *Romulidum ductor*, etc.; it will be demonstrated below that this dedication does not belong to Sedulius.

Dempster, moreover, is seriously mistaken when he says that, according to some, Sedulius lived under Theodosius the Elder in the year 430, and that this is the more probable opinion. Perhaps he intended to indicate a different year in place of 430. Some assign the year 378 as the year in which Sedulius flourished; others assign 381.

24. Since Valentinian, the son of Constantius, began to reign in the year 424, and the younger Theodosius died in the year 450, it follows that we should say that Sedulius composed his books between the years 424 and 450.

Trithemius indicates the year in which Sedulius flourished as follows:

> He flourished under Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 430.

Justus Fontaninus, *On the Antiquities of Horta*, Book II, chapter 3, believes that Sedulius’s poem was published by him around the year 434. Georgius, however, suspects that this occurred in the year 420, arguing from the name Constantius, which appears in the Ottobonian codex.

Constantius married Placidia, the sister of Honorius, in the year 417; in 421 he was proclaimed Augustus, and died in that same year. But, as I have already noted, Constantius is mentioned in the Ottobonian codex so that Valentinian may be identified as his son and distinguished from the two Valentinians who preceded him, one called the Elder and the other the Younger.

The opinion of Usserius is much more deserving of rejection: he places Sedulius as late as the year 494, or at least after 470. He derives his argument from Asterius’s dedication to Macedonius, whom he wrongly believes to be the same person to whom Sedulius wrote, as I shall demonstrate later.

Xystus of Siena asserts that Sedulius died in the very year 450; other recent writers state that he lived in 449 or 450. But no definite year can be established.

25. Some doubt whether Sedulius published his poems or merely kept them within private walls. This controversy will be better explained when we discuss Asterius, who is said to have collected and published Sedulius’s poems.

It must also be investigated on what basis Trithemius asserts that Sedulius, after finally leaving the borders of Achaea, shone forth in the city of Rome, distinguished by marvelous learning. Most scholars strongly doubt this.

I nevertheless find that it may be confirmed by the authority of Paschasius Radbertus, in the book *On the Birth of the Virgin*, once attributed to St. Ildephonsus. But the most eminent Cardinal Francisco Lorenzana, a devoted student and distinguished patron of sacred literature, in his highly learned and elegant edition of the Toledan Fathers, restored the work to its author Radbertus and rejected, among other doubtful or spurious works, those attributed to Ildephonsus.

Radbertus therefore says, volume I of the *Toledan Fathers*, page 314:

> Hence Sedulius, rhetor of the Roman Church, says in his paschal work…

Add the words to be cited from Usserius below, no. 180 and following.

The account of Sedulius’s wealth rests on a weaker foundation. Guilielmus Eysengrein mentions it in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, under the year 412:

> Since he had learned everything that seemed necessary for a fully accomplished theologian, he shone no less through the inner gifts of his soul than through his external riches of wealth, etc.

26. The matter of Sedulius’s episcopate is different. Nicolás Antonio, cited under no. 14, altogether denies it. To me, on the contrary, it seems certain that Sedulius was eventually appointed bishop somewhere.

For, leaving aside the fact that Sigebertus calls him a bishop, as does an ancient author who copied the Decree of Gelasius, which we shall produce under no. 152, there are two extremely ancient poems in praise of Sedulius, composed by Belisarius and Liberius, which we shall discuss in the appendices.

In both there is an acrostic, or anacrostic: the name “Sedulius the bishop” (*Sedulius antistes*) is formed from the first letters of the verses and likewise from their final letters. The anonymous author of Melk, a contemporary of Sigebertus, also calls Sedulius by this name in *On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Belisarius and Liberius therefore believed Sedulius to have been a bishop. Christian writers, however, scarcely ever called a presbyter *antistes* (“bishop” or “overseer”); rather, they wished this name to be proper to a bishop, as can be seen in the Justinian Code, Book I, title 3, laws 18, 22, and 25, and often elsewhere.

Labbeus, whom Nicolás Antonio appears to have followed in denying Sedulius’s episcopate, responds that Sidonius and other ancient writers recognize presbyters as *antistites ordine in secundo*, “overseers in the second order,” that is, presbyters, in his work on Claudianus Mamercus.

Even if some presbyters were occasionally called this by others as a mark of honor, it cannot be denied that the word, when used without qualification to indicate an ecclesiastical order, signifies a bishop. Sidonius does not call Mamercus simply an *antistes*, but an *antistes ordine in secundo*. From this some have fabricated the claim that he was a chorepiscopus, or vicar general of his bishop.

Moreover, Sedulius’s episcopate is confirmed by Urbinate codex 584, formerly 828, in which he is repeatedly called “the distinguished bishop Sedulius,” as will be evident from the various readings at the beginning and end of the books. See no. 89.

27. Albinus, or Alcuin, also plainly calls Sedulius a bishop in *Offices for the Week*, Saturday, where, in the alphabetical hymn of Sedulius, *A solis ortus*, he gives the title: “Hymn of B., Bishop Sedulius.”

Labbeus says that this title is in a more recent hand; to me, on the contrary, it appears to be in Albinus’s own hand.

These codices, therefore, in which Sedulius is called a bishop agree with the poems of Liberius and Belisarius and with the old inscription of Sedulius’s prose work from the Pithoean codex:

> Here begins the preface of Sedulius the bishop in prose to the *Paschal Poem*.

Perhaps Sedulius was already a bishop when he rendered the *Paschal Poem* into prose, although he composed it while still a presbyter. This may explain why he is commonly called a presbyter in the *Paschal Poem*. Then, once the *Paschal Poem* was in everyone’s hands, the designation “presbyter” adhered to Sedulius, while the other designation, “bishop,” which was less evident, was omitted.

In the appendix to Margarini de la Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, he is called in the index “Coelius Sedulius the Scot, presbyter or bishop.” Mabillonius, volume I of the *Ancient Analecta*, page 363, infers from the acrostic verses on Sedulius that he was an *antistes*, or bishop; but he entirely treats *antistes* and “bishop” as equivalent, as is clear from the index and from the authority of Sigebertus cited in support of this opinion.

Nicolás Antonio objects with reference to Asterius’s verse about Sedulius:

> “Through whom the righteous Sedulius speaks such things”—

for Asterius would scarcely have called Sedulius “just” if he had wished to praise him as a bishop.

But this conjecture should have little force. In Asterius’s epigram Sedulius is not called a presbyter either. Asterius may have been unaware that Sedulius was a bishop, or he may have remained silent about this dignity as a known fact that was not necessary for explaining the subject of his epigram.

The arguments of the hypercritical Basnage should move us still less. In volume III of his *Political Annals*, under the year 434, he denies even that Sedulius was a presbyter because he calls Macedonius “father” and says that he himself, supported by no privilege of ancient learning, was occupied with secular studies.

These statements prove only that Sedulius spoke modestly: he called the presbyter Macedonius his father because Macedonius was his teacher in ecclesiastical disciplines, and he called several others fathers; he also acknowledged that, while he was a layman, he had devoted himself chiefly to secular studies.

Grunerus explained that when Sedulius called Macedonius “father” in the dedicatory epistle, Sedulius was not yet a presbyter.

28. In what place Sedulius exercised the office of bishop is entirely unknown, for the claim that he was bishop of Oretum has been rejected by us under no. 14. Until a clearer light appears, I am inclined to conjecture that Sedulius was raised to an episcopal see in Achaea, where he had been a presbyter and composed his books, and that he finally died there.

Someone may also doubt whether religious honor was ever paid to Sedulius anywhere. Asterius calls him “just,” and Alcuin calls him “blessed,” as we have just seen. The copyist of the codex of the Laurentian Library at Florence likewise calls him this, as will be reported under no. 86, and so does our Reg. 2 codex, as you will read in the notes on the title of the *Paschal Poem*.

Mabillonius, *Ancient Analecta*, Paris, 1723, page 548, cites from a Vatican codex then approximately five hundred years old a work bearing the following title:

> Revelation shown to the venerable man Ildefonsus, bishop of Spain (in the year 845).

In this work Sedulius is praised as follows:

> The holy Sedulius declares wondrously, saying: “Not because he who is the highest Father is…” [18]

See Book I, verse 319.

I have been unable to discover anything elsewhere about the author of this work or about this Spanish bishop Ildefonsus, except that one may conjecture that he was Adefonsus, bishop of Salamanca, whose epitaph, composed by Peter of Poitiers, is found in volume XXII of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Nicolás Antonio does not mention him in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*.

The work deals with the loaves offered in the Church and with the signs that ought to be present in the consecrated host. It begins:

> In the year 845 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ… there appeared to me in a vision, etc.

I saw the Vatican codex itself, no. 1341. After a collection of councils written approximately in the tenth century, a more recent hand has written the *Revelation of Ildefonsus* at the end of the volume. It incorrectly reads *hoc et filius est* instead of *et filius hoc est* (“and this is the Son”).

As for Sedulius, such praises as “just,” “blessed,” and even “holy” may confirm the uprightness of his life, but they cannot establish that divine honors were ever shown to him, since his name is found in no martyrology among the saints, nor is his memory celebrated with religious worship in any liturgical books.

The Bollandists, under February 12, list C. Coelius Sedulius among those passed over. Colgan mentions him on that day, but only under the title “Venerable.” He is indeed called this in the Gelasian Decree, as he is called “venerable” by Hincmar in *On the Non-Trine Deity*.

Dempster, Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History of Scotland*, and David Camerarius, Book III of *Scottish Piety*, call him a saint on February 20. Camerarius says that others place his feast day on June 13.

The Bollandists found the name Sedulius in no calendar. Dempster, in the place cited, reports that Johann Gropper, volume I of *On the Altar of the Sacrament*, page 360, proves from the translation of Christophorus Cassianus of Trabach that Sedulius was numbered among the saints.

## CHAPTER II. The Works of Sedulius Are Catalogued

29. Trithemius compiled Sedulius’s catalogue of works as follows:

1. To Macedonius the Abbot, a distinguished work following the sequence of the entire Gospel, which he entitled *The Paschal Poem*, in verse, four books: “Whoever—Paschal banquets …”;
2. On all the Epistles of Paul, in prose, fourteen books: “Before the apostolic words…”;
3. On the Miracles of Christ, one book: “From the pivot of the sun’s rising…”;
4. To the Emperor Theodosius, one book: “Illustrious leader of the Romulids…”;
5. On the larger volume of Priscian, one book;
6. On the second edition of Donatus, one book;
7. An exhortation to the faithful, one book: “Let us sing, companions, to the Lord…”;
8. Several letters to various persons, one book: “Sedulius the Scot-born…”;
9. On the Miracles of Christ, in prose, two books.

30. Trithemius adds that Sedulius published several other works that had not come to his knowledge. We shall examine these individually.

Sedulius’s most celebrated work is the *Paschal Poem*. In the various readings to the dedicatory epistle I observe that Macedonius, to whom this poem was dedicated, is called a presbyter in the manuscripts, not an abbot, as Trithemius calls him.

Trithemius likewise recognizes the metrical prologue, “Whatever Paschal Feasts.” Yet he does not seem to attach to this poem the epigram addressed to Theodosius, “Leader of the descendants of Romulus,” which he presents as a separate and distinct book.

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, asserts that the epistle prefixed to Macedonius was added after Sedulius’s death by Turcius Rufius Asterius. But he is certainly mistaken, perhaps misled by Asterius’s epigram, “Receive, sacred one,” etc.

### 31.

There is great controversy concerning the number of books of the *Paschal Poem*, which Trithemius says were four. Parrhasius published Sedulius’s entire poem without any division into books. The second Vatican codex, which I shall describe under no. 65, divides the whole poem into only [Col. 0448C] two books. The Anonymous of Melk, chapter 35, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, following Bernard Pez’s *Bibliotheca Benedictino-Mauriana*, adopted this arrangement:

> Sedulius, bishop, composed for Macedonius, his presbyter and teacher, two books in heroic meter, namely, one on the Old Testament and one on the New Testament; and he prefixed to them a lengthy prose prologue.

Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 20, distinguishes only three books as follows:

> Sedulius the presbyter published three books composed in dactylic heroic meter. The first of them most clearly celebrates the signs and mighty deeds of the Old Testament; the remaining books resound with the mysteries, or miracles, of Christ’s deeds.

Some suspect that an error entered the manuscript copies of Isidore; such errors readily occur in numerals, so that III may have been written instead of IV or V [Col. 0448D]. Moreover, copyists easily expressed numbers by letters: if they found *III libri*, they themselves would write *tres libri*. Perhaps Isidore, like the Anonymous of Melk, divided the *Paschal Poem* into two books and added a third—namely, the elegy and hymn, in which Christ’s life is also expounded.

Jonas of Orléans, book II of *On the Cult of Images*, calls the third book of the poem what we call the fifth. Yet from two manuscript copies of Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men* that I have seen, I conclude that the conjecture of certain scholars concerning an error in the numbers in Saint Isidore’s book is not without foundation. In the paper codex Vat. Reg. 349, a miscellany, p. 107, there is a copy of Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men* already prepared for publication, as is evident from the end, where one reads: [Col. 0449A]

> If it seems good to the Reverend Father, Master of the Sacred Palace, let it be printed. M. Antonius, Archbishop of Wasina, vicegerent.  
>   
> [The final words are unclear.]

In this book Sedulius’s notice is composed twice, namely in chapters 11 and 21. Chapter 21 agrees with the published notice, but chapter 11 differs considerably and reads as follows:

> Sedulius the presbyter, thoroughly trained to perfection in the study of grammatical learning, published five little books in heroic meter on divine marvels. In the first he set forth the mighty deeds of the Old Testament; in the others, as he himself records, he arranged the miracles of the four Gospels. He gave this work the title *Paschal Poem*.

In another codex, Vat. Reginae 551, formerly Petavianus no. 211, a parchment folio manuscript dating approximately from the thirteenth century, the books *On Illustrious Men* by Saint Jerome, an anonymous author, Gennadius, and Isidore follow other works. In chapter 7 of Isidore’s book [Col. 0449B] one reads clearly:

> Sedulius the presbyter published four books in dactylic heroic meter, etc.,

as in the printed editions. Isidore’s intention concerning the number of books in the *Paschal Poem* is therefore uncertain; and the notice of Sedulius in chapter 11 of Vat. Reg. 349 comes much closer to the truth.

### 32.

In note 93 to Sedulius’s dedicatory letter, among the variant readings, I shall observe that most codices of his letter read: “Four little books of divine marvels,” although in some places one also finds: “Three little books of divine marvels.” Funck, *On the Decline of the Latin Language*, chapter 3, section 21, understood this as though Sedulius had at that time written only four books, extending to the Passion, etc., and had later added a fifth on the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension. I find this less convincing [Col. 0449C]; for Sedulius’s words, “extending to the Passion, etc.,” must be understood as intending to include the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension as well.

The poem itself is divided in more than one way in our codices. Reg. 1 and Ottob. 1 assign the first book to the Old Testament; they call the second book the first of the New Testament, and proceed in this way through the final book, which is called the fourth book of the New Testament, although it is the fifth book of the poem. The same arrangement is found in a codex of excellent quality in the Turin library, and I do not believe that any older one survives. Although Mansi, in his note to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*, says that this codex has only four books, the matter is otherwise. The Canterbury codex mentioned by Grunerus likewise has five books. Usserius, too, testifies [Col. 0449D] that manuscript copies divide the *Paschal Poem* into five books.

From the variant readings noted at the end of each book, and from Sedulius’s own prose, it can be inferred that the division of the entire poem into five books is extremely ancient and, it seems, originated with Sedulius himself. Barthius and Poelmannus hold the same opinion.

Since Sedulius appears to have placed the first book, on the Old Testament, as an introduction to the following four, he perhaps therefore said in his letter to Macedonius, “four books of divine marvels.” For he adds: “Gathering together the sayings of the four evangelists, I arranged them.” Aldus and other early editors followed this arrangement to some extent; and in the prose it is stated more distinctly at the end of the title of chapter 22:

> The chapters of the Old Testament are concluded. The chapters of the first book of the New Testament begin.

Juretus noted that this was written by an old copyist in red minium letters [Col. 0450A].

### 33.

Grunerus and Arntzenius divide the poem into five books because they found it divided in that way in most editions. They nevertheless believe that the poem’s genuine division is into four books. In support of this opinion they cite the manuscripts of Arntzenius and Almeloveen, four manuscripts mentioned by Fabricius—namely, the Chemnitz, Ghent, and two Liège codices—and many old editions, such as the two old editions. In these, however, the first and second books are combined into a single book, as in Aldus; thus the first book serves almost as an introduction to the work. In most manuscripts, on the other hand, the four books are arranged so that the fourth book is attached [Col. 0450B] to the third, and what remains of the fifth becomes the fourth.

Georgius Cassander likewise divided the *Paschal Poem* into four books.

### 34.

Trithemius says that the title of the poem is *Paschal Poem*. Sedulius himself says so in his letter to Macedonius:

> With the Lord’s favor, I have given this work the name *Paschal Poem*, because Christ, sacrificed, is our Passover.

And in another letter to Macedonius, prefixed to the prose, he similarly calls the poem *Paschal Poem*, while he calls the prose itself *Paschal Work*. This should be noted against Gyraldus, Nebrissensis, and others, who assign the title *Paschal Work* to the poem.

Thus, says Sedulius, the earlier books, because they were arranged in verse, received the name *PASCHAL POEM*; the following books, however, rendered in prose, without any variation of poetic rhythm, are designated by the title *PASCHAL WORK* [Col. 0450C]. Nevertheless, Hincmarus, in his work *On the Non-Trinal Deity*, calls the same poem sometimes *Paschal Work* and sometimes *Paschal Poem*.

Since Sedulius presented the subject of the work in these words—“Four little books, therefore, of divine marvels, which I have gathered together from many sources into a small compass,” etc.—some have entitled the books *Divine Marvels*. Arntzenius suspects that Asterius was the first to do this. Nebrissensis asserts that in nearly all ancient codices the title is *Work of Divine Marvels*, whereas in the decree of Gelasius it is *Paschal Work*. He does not think this contradictory, since both may be genuine titles prefixed by the author, just as there are two titles in the *Dialogues* of Plato and Cicero.

I shall discuss the decree of Gelasius below, under no. 153. Our older codices of Sedulius entirely ignore the title *Divine Marvels*; accordingly, I am inclined to believe that this title is more recent than Asterius. See the variant readings at verse 1.17 of book I, and Prolegomena no. 50, where, on the basis of a certain manuscript, this poem is called the *Paschal Song*. Alva was misled by the title of *Paschal Poem* and *Paschal Work* when he asserted in *Militia Conceptionis* that Sedulius was commonly called “Paschal.”

### 35.

Some place after Sedulius’s metrical prologue a dedication to the Emperor Augustus Theodosius, consisting of fifteen hexameter verses and beginning, “Leader of the Romulids” (*Romulidum ductor*), etc. Trithemius mentions this in fourth place as a distinct book of Sedulius.

The *Index of Expurgated Books* by Joannes M. Brasichellensis, whom I mentioned in my notes on other Christian poets, p. 260, lists Sedulius’s edition in Margarino de la Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, 1589. Nothing deserving censure is observed there in Sedulius; but it is noted that Sedulius wrote under Theodosius I and dedicated his *Paschal Poem* to that emperor. This is said to be manifestly clear from the poem printed by Margarino in the chronological index of authors at the end of volume I, in the fifth century. This is the epigram addressed to Theodosius, “Leader of the Romulids,” etc. Heinsius, whom I cited above, likewise believed that this poem was by Sedulius and was addressed to Theodosius the Elder.

### 36.

Cellarius asserts that Trithemius assigns Sedulius to the period of Theodosius the Elder when he attributes this dedication to Sedulius; for the words “and may you hand it on to the younger Arcadius” indicate Theodosius I [Col. 0451B]. Yet Trithemius expressly says that Sedulius flourished in the year 430 under Theodosius, which Gerhard Johannes Vossius, *On Latin Poets*, correctly understands as Theodosius the Younger. It cannot be understood otherwise, since the definite year 430 is specified.

It may therefore be uncertain which Theodosius is meant by this dedication. From the opening verses it is clear that the emperor of the East is being praised:

> Leader of the Romulids, second light of the bright sun,  
> You who hold the realms of the East—or, as it seems it should be corrected,  
> “You who hold the eastern realms.”

Both Theodosiuses were emperors of the East; but since Theodosius the Great had a son, Arcadius, the poem should rather be understood of him [Col. 0451C].

There is nevertheless room for doubt concerning the meaning of the words, “Hope of the world and glory of your brother.” Who is this brother of Theodosius the Great? Labbeus, with Usserius, understands it as Valentinian II, whose sister Galla Theodosius had as his wife. I would not object if someone understood it as Gratian, who can be called Theodosius’s brother because Theodosius took him into partnership with himself in the imperial government.

It must therefore be inferred from the chronology that the dedication to Theodosius was written in the year 380 or shortly afterward. Fabricius, under “Falconia” in his *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*, believes that the dedication should be addressed not to Theodosius but to Honorius, Arcadius’s brother. This conjecture is completely refuted by verse 2; Honorius held the empire not of the East but of the West [Col. 0451D]. Moreover, the poem is commended to the emperor so that he may hand it over to Arcadius as his son, who was still of a younger age.

Norisius, *Cenotaphia Pisana*, dissertation 4, chapter 2, section 1, suspects that one should read, “And may you hand these things on to the younger Arcadia, for her own offspring.” For Arcadia, the sister of Theodosius the Younger, survived until the year 444; and although she married no one, perhaps the poet was predicting royal nuptials and future offspring. Norisius, however, assigns little weight to this conjecture, which he considers closer to fiction.

### 37.

Once these points have been established, Sedulius, who wrote his books about the year 430, cannot be called the author of this dedication. Other considerations support this conclusion: the dedication is entirely absent from Sedulius’s prose, in which the metrical prologue was converted into a prose discourse [Col. 0452A]; in his dedicatory letter to Macedonius Sedulius says nothing about dedicating the *Paschal Poem* also to Theodosius; and this dedication is found in none of the manuscript copies of the *Paschal Poem* seen by Cellarius and Arntzenius. It is also absent from our manuscripts.

I nevertheless see it cited from a very old codex of the Turin library in the catalogue of that library’s manuscript codices. After the letter to Macedonius, the catalogue’s author notes:

> There follows a preface to Augustus Theodosius, which Fabricius and Cave deny to Sedulius.

But, as I shall explain more fully later, the authors of that catalogue were not very accurate in describing that celebrated codex. I have received reliable information that the epigram “Leader of the Romulids” is absent from it as well.

In the Angelica Library I saw a manuscript dating approximately from the tenth century in which, after Fulgentius the mythographer, several miscellaneous verses occur. Among these, in sixth place, there is the rubric:

> Verses to be written at the head of Sedulius:

namely, “Leader of the Romulids,” etc. From this, however, we can in no way infer that the verses truly belong to Sedulius.

### 38.

Georgius Fabricius, who also published the same epigram in *Commentaries on Christian Poetry*, p. 25, as a dedication of the *Paschal Poem* to Augustus Theodosius the Younger, believed the little preface [25] to be by another poet, who wished to commend Sedulius’s poem to the emperor and his son.

Someone might think that it was the work of a copyist, on the basis of the words, “To be written by the servant whom you ordered.” But once it has been demonstrated above that the poem is dedicated to Theodosius the Great, and that Sedulius alone composed his books around the year 430, this entire conjecture concerning another poet who wished to dedicate Sedulius’s *Paschal Work* by means of this poem collapses.

### 39.

Nor is the subject of the *Paschal Poem* of the kind described by the dedication to Theodosius:

> Here he will set forth for you the beginning of the world,  
> The form of the heavens, and the human being created from clay.

Arntzenius thinks that what is contained in verse 61 and a few following verses of book I is sufficient for the dedication to mention the beginning of the world, the form of the heavens, and the human being created from clay, even though the poem does not expressly treat that subject there.

But, apart from the fact that the creation of the human being from clay is not even mentioned individually in those verses of book I [Col. 0452D], the word “he will set forth” indicates a subject that is treated expressly in the work.

### 40.

Arntzenius considers the argument drawn from the words of the dedication stronger:

> Deign to recognize Maro,  
> Transformed for the better by divine meaning.

For these words indicate a Virgilian cento. Although Sedulius imitated Virgil, he does not everywhere copy Virgil’s words in such a way that he can be said to have transformed him for the better through divine meaning.

This argument led some scholars to attribute to Sedulius the Virgilian cento on the Incarnation, which Martenius published from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Corbie, and to say that the dedication of this cento is the aforementioned poem addressed to Augustus Theodosius [Col. 0453A].

We shall return to that Virgilian cento later. For now, it is enough to observe that, if the dedication is referred to Theodosius I—as we have shown it must be—it cannot be called the work of Sedulius, who devoted himself to sacred poetry long after Theodosius I. Therefore, if the dedication belongs to the poem on the Incarnation, the author of that poem must be a poet other than Sedulius and older than him.

### 41.

There remains for consideration the opinion of Johann Albert Fabricius, who in both his *Bibliotheca vetus* and his later *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis* believes these dedicatory verses to be by Proba Faltonia, prefixed by her to her own Virgilian cento and addressed to Augustus Honorius.

Fontaninus, *On the Antiquity of Hortus*, book II, chapters 1 and 2, maintains the same opinion. He argues that Proba was Hortana, not Roman, and that her cento was dedicated to Honorius after the year 393, but composed by Proba at the command of Arcadius the Younger.

Yet, as is clear from the verses themselves, the cento was composed at the command of the emperor to whom it appears to be dedicated. I explained in no. 36 why this sort of dedication should not be referred to Honorius. Otherwise, the subject indicated in the dedicatory verses is consistent with Proba Faltonia’s cento.

Arntzenius therefore inclines to the view that these verses should be attributed to Proba Faltonia, to whose cento they were prefixed.
