I myself see that in a certain codex of the Florentine Laurentian Library, no. 86, which also contains Sedulius, these verses precede Proba’s cento. Proba’s cento was also published in duodecimo, Rome, 1588, edited by Julius Roscius from Vatican codices and one Hortan codex, with this dedication prefixed.

The argument is not yet sufficiently secure, however; for in verse 7 the author says, “To be written by the servant whom you ordered,” something a woman would not have said of herself. Someone may propose reading *famulae*, “female servant.” I would not object if there were other evidence persuading us that these verses were composed by Proba. Indeed, Fontaninus, *On the Antiquity of Hortus*, book II, chapter 2, reads plainly *famulae*, apparently following his own conjecture or that of Julius Roscius.

In Roscius the title is:

> To Honorius, son of Theodosius Augustus the Great and brother of Augustus Arcadius.

The style seems different to me from the style of Proba’s prologue. Three times in this dedication, in “Leader of the Romulids,” the force of a consonant is assigned to aspiration; I have not encountered this license even once in Proba’s verses. Roscius does read those three verses differently, as I shall explain in the notes; but I believe that he handled this little poem too freely in attempting to correct it.

### 42.

In the *Index of Expurgated Books* of Brasichellensis, p. 263, there is listed a Virgilian cento by Proba, who there is called not *Falconia*, as by others—especially Fontaninus, *On the Antiquity of Hortus*, book II, chapter 1—but *Falconia* [27], as she is named in ancient inscriptions.

Several other details are added concerning her; but what is relevant to our subject is that she seems to have written the Virgilian cento for her husband, as appears from the end of the poem:

> Maintain this observance of sacred rites, which your companions maintain;  
> Maintain it yourself,  
> O sweet husband; and, if they deserve it by their devotion,  
> May our grandchildren remain in this chaste religion.

[Col. 0454A] This makes it more difficult to believe that she intended the same poem to be dedicated to an emperor.

Someone might nevertheless suppose—as I suggested earlier—that this poem was the work of some servant or copyist whom the emperor ordered to transcribe a Virgilian cento, whether Proba’s or another poet’s. This fits the words, “To be written by the servant whom you ordered,” more closely.

### 43.

In second place Trithemius lists fourteen books on the Epistles of Paul in prose and gives the opening as “Before the apostolic words.” Cellarius observes that this opening is now absent from the printed editions.

This is Sedulius Scotus the Irishman’s *Collectaneum* on all fourteen Epistles of Paul, which appears in volume VI of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 494. There it is noted:

> This Sedulius seems to be different from the preceding one.

The preceding works were the *Paschal Poem*, the elegy, the hymns, and the prose of our Sedulius.

Grunerus clearly distinguished Sedulius the Irishman of the eighth century from the poet Sedulius of the fifth century. Labbeus more accurately calls the author of these annotations Sedulius Scotus the Irishman, who, according to Hepidannus, flourished in the ninth century. Ceillierius is mistaken when he asserts that Hepidannus himself attributes the *Collectaneum* to Sedulius.

Sedulius’s *Annotations on All the Epistles of Saint Paul* were published at Basel by Heinrich Petri in 1527 and 1538. They also appear in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1624, volume I, p. 849.

Calmet, in the *Bibliotheca sacra* before the *Biblical Dictionary*, judges this Sedulius as follows:

> Sedulius Scotus, or the Irishman, composed his work from Origen, Saint Jerome, or rather Pelagius—whose errors he nevertheless removed—from Saint Ambrose, or Hilary the Deacon, [Col. 0454C] and Saint Augustine.

Labbeus adds Eusebius, Rufinus, Gennadius of Constantinople, John Chrysostom, and even Saint Gregory the Great, as Benedictus Justinianus, S.J., rightly observes in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 6:5.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXVI, chapter 12, gives the title from a manuscript:

> Here begins the *Collectaneum* of Sedulius Scotus the Irishman on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul.

[28] Thus, in a later age, *hymnarius*, *cubiculus*, and *balneus* are found in certain writers. In the first edition of the *Collectaneum*, Basel, 1527, folio, and in the second, 1538, octavo, the neuter form *Collectaneum* is prefixed to each epistle.

The same Sedulius appears to have written the *Collectaneum* on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, which will be discussed below, under no. 56 and following. Barthius calls the author of the *Collectaneum* the younger Sedulius in his note on Claudian, *Fourth Consulship of Honorius*, verse 261.

### 44.

In third place Trithemius lists one book *On the Miracles of Christ*, beginning, “From the rising point of the sun.” This is the alphabetical hymn to which we assign a place among Sedulius’s works after the elegy “Let us sing, companions.”

Bede praises it under Sedulius’s name in *On the Art of Meter*, and Alcuin entitles it:

> On the Nativity, Baptism, Miracles, Betrayal, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

Olaus Borrichius writes of Sedulius in *On Latin Poetry*:

> He also left two hymns still familiar to the Church: one on the Nativity of Christ, and another on his Epiphany.

But in reality it is one and the same hymn, containing the life of Christ. From it we sing the first seven stanzas at Lauds on the Nativity of the Lord, and four others at Vespers on the Epiphany, omitting the rest.

Parrhasius omitted this hymn, together with Sedulius’s elegy, from his edition, perhaps because he did not find these poems in his codices or did not believe them to belong to Sedulius. Some doubt the elegy; but there is scarcely any reason to doubt this hymn, as will be clear from the variant readings.

Some call this hymn an acrostic, but improperly, since no name is formed from the initial letters of the verses. See the variant readings at the hymn’s title.

### 45.

Trithemius lists in fourth place one book addressed to the Emperor Theodosius. This is nothing other than the dedication to Theodosius, about which enough, and more than enough, has been said above.

As for Trithemius’s listing, in fifth place, of one book “on Priscian in a larger volume,” and, in sixth place, of one book “on the second edition of Donatus,” we can scarcely discover from any other source what these works were. The second edition of Donatus is the one that treats the eight parts of speech.

In his letter to Macedonius, Sedulius admits that he was once occupied with secular studies and with the diversions of literary skill, serving a fruitless work rather than God the author. By this we may understand any profane works.

In cod. Vatic. Ottob. 1, after Sedulius’s elegy “Let us sing, companions,” there is this note:

> Here begins the art of Sedulius, who at first was a layman, etc.,

as was explained under no. 9. Perhaps the “art of Sedulius” indicated here, though not preserved in the manuscript, is one of the books on Priscian and Donatus.

Labbeus, in his *Historical Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume II, p. 329, gives these exact words from an old codex of Pithou, which perhaps is not distinct from our Vat. Ottob. 1. On p. 338, from the Thuana Library, the same Labbeus lists a manuscript *Little Commentary on the Art of Eutychius*, and, from the manuscripts of Goldastus, *On the Governance of Princes* and an exposition of Priscian’s art. He attributes these to Sedulius Scotus, who flourished in the year 818.

Oudinus agrees with Labbeus in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the ninth century and the year 820. He lists these manuscript codices: in the Leiden library, among the manuscripts purchased from the heirs of Isaac Vossius, cod. Latin. 21, no. 3, “Sedulius on Priscian”; and in the Norfolk Library in London, cod. 43, “Sedulius the bishop’s exposition of the first edition of Donatus.” See no. 88.

### 46.

In seventh place Trithemius mentions one book, *An Exhortation to the Faithful*. This is the elegy that follows the *Paschal Poem* in the editions. It is usually entitled *A Comparison of the Old and New Testament*, and was printed separately in the *Biblical Manual*, Frankfurt, 1610.

Barthius, Cuspinianus, Leyserus, and several editions listed in the catalogue of the Leiden University Library, p. 30, deny this elegiac poem to Sedulius and attribute it to Asterius. G. Fabricius, in his *Commentaries*, p. 25, asserts that it is attributed to Asterius in ancient codices, and on p. 136 says that in another codex it appears under the name of Claudianus Mamertus.

Arntzenius cites the Canterbury codex, among others, and old editions in support of Sedulius as author. In his own Arntzenian codex he found Asterius’s epigram improperly transposed at the end of the *Paschal Poem*, whereas in the Almeloveen codex and other manuscripts it is placed before the poem [Col. 0456A].

After the epigram comes:

> Here begin his poems,

which must be understood as referring to Sedulius, not Asterius. Although Asterius’s epigram immediately precedes it, this happened through an error. Add that Asterius himself speaks of Sedulius’s verses.

Panvinius, in his *Consular Fasti*, held that this epigram was addressed and sent by Sedulius to Turcius. Nebrissensis says in his notes on this elegy:

> There are those who say that this little work was not published by Sedulius but was found among his writings; that is sufficient for it to be considered Sedulius’s.

Indeed, Aldus, immediately after the *Paschal Poem* and directly before the elegy, writes:

> This little work was not published by Sedulius the author, but by Turcius Rufus Asterius, a man of consular rank and a former ordinary consul, as well as a patrician, who found it among Sedulius’s writings.

The word “little work” can be applied not to the preceding *Paschal Poem* [Col. 0456B] but to the elegy that follows immediately. Yet from the variant readings at the end of the *Paschal Poem* and the beginning of the elegy it is perfectly clear that the elegy is genuinely Sedulius’s work.

Aldus’s note was mistakenly applied by him to the elegy, although it belongs either to the *Paschal Poem* or to the collection of Sedulius’s poems, as will be demonstrated when Asterius is discussed.

### 47.

In eighth place Trithemius lists one book of “Several Letters to Various Persons,” and Arntzenius says that a book of several letters to various persons is in circulation. According to Trithemius, the beginning of this book is “Sedulius the Scot”; from this it may be understood that it belongs to the younger Sedulius. I have been unable to discover anything else about this work.

### 48.

In ninth and last place Trithemius mentions two books of *The Miracles of Christ in Prose* [Col. 0456C]. Perhaps Trithemius made an error in the numbers and II was printed instead of V. Certainly Sedulius’s prose version of the *Paschal Work*, or *On the Miracles of Christ*, as Trithemius calls it, is divided not into two but into five books, approximately in the same way as the *Paschal Poem*, as I observed under no. 32.

Here Sigebertus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, must be corrected. He says that the prose was written first and that the *Paschal Poem* came afterward:

> Sedulius the bishop wrote for Macedonius the presbyter books on the miracles of the Old and New Testaments, which he later recast under the law of meter and entitled *Paschal Poem*. For he rendered all the works of the Lord in dactylic verse.

The order was in fact the reverse, as can be understood from Sedulius’s own letter to Macedonius prefixed to the prose:

> My revered lord, you instructed me to transfer into rhetorical speech the text of the *Paschal Poem*, which I had simply carried out as an act of pure devotion and offered to you to read.

Franciscus Juretus first published Sedulius’s prose from Pithou’s manuscript [31]. It was reprinted in the appendix to Margarino’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, 1624, with Juretus’s notes. It was also published in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1618, volume V, part I, together with other works of Sedulius, and again in the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Most editors of Sedulius’s poems, however, omit it.

I nevertheless thought it appropriate to append it to the *Paschal Poem*, since it can be extremely useful for explaining the poem and, in certain places, for establishing its correct text. Critical scholars do not wish the reading derived from the prose, or apparently closer to it, to be preferred everywhere. The places in which it should be preferred will be explained more suitably when the opportunity arises.

Bede mentions the *Paschal Work* in book V, chapter 19, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*:

> Adhelm also wrote an excellent book *On Virginity*, which, in imitation of Sedulius, he composed in a twofold form: in hexameter verse and in prose.

The Anonymous of Melk repeats this same statement in chapter 30, as does Sigebertus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 66. Bede further reports that, following Sedulius’s example, he first composed the life of Saint Cuthbert in heroic meter and afterward in plain prose.

Paschasius Ratbertus quotes words from Sedulius’s *Paschal Work* in *On the Birth of the Virgin*, among the doubtful works of Saint Ildefonsus, volume I of the *Toledan Fathers*, pp. 314 [Col. 0457B] and following.

### 49.

Besides the works that Trithemius attributes to Sedulius, Montfaucon, in *Italian Diary*, chapter 21, and in the *Bibliotheca of Manuscript Libraries*, reports from the Neapolitan library of D. Valletta a parchment manuscript of Sedulius the Christian poet, *On the Deeds of the Prophets*. You will find a similar title from the same Montfaucon under no. 89.

Arntzenius doubts whether this poem should be assigned to the class of spurious works or whether the *Paschal Poem* lies hidden under that title. In the first book of the *Paschal Poem* certain deeds of the prophets are indeed narrated; perhaps these were copied separately and acquired a distinct title.

Although I find the entire *Paschal Poem* entitled in the Ottobonian codex, which I shall discuss under no. 76:

> On the Deeds of the Prophets and the Entire Course of Christ the Savior,

and therefore believe that other codices listed under the same title in catalogues also contain the same *Paschal Poem*.

Thus many, misled by the variety of titles, attribute to Sedulius, besides the *Paschal Poem*, one book *On the Signs and Mighty Deeds*, which is book I of the *Paschal Poem*; likewise four books *On the Deeds and Miracles of Christ*, which are the four books of the *Paschal Poem* on the New Testament [32].

### 50.

In the catalogue of the Uffenbach Library, p. 224, there is listed a quarto paper volume written in the fifteenth century, containing “Sedulius the poet, *On the Pre-eminence of the Sixth Day*, and the *Paschal Song*.” Arntzenius mentions this codex, as does Grunerus, who gives the title as *On the Pre-eminence of the Sixth Day*.

Arntzenius does not dare determine with certainty whether the verses cited under Sedulius’s name by Le Moine, *Sacred Variants*, volume III, p. 639, were drawn from poems of Sedulius contained in such manuscripts:

> The Jewish odor is washed away by sacred baptism,  
> And a new offspring, restored, rises from the waters.

But the same Arntzenius reasonably suspects that Sedulius was named in place of another poet by a hurried pen; for these verses belong to Fortunatus.

### 51.

G. Fabricius often cites Prudentius’s *Dittochaeum*, which some less appropriately call the *Enchiridion* and others the *Diptychon*, under Sedulius’s name in his *Commentaries on Christian Poetry*, and Sichardus suspected that it was a work of Sedulius.

The true author is Prudentius. On this matter I shall not repeat the many things I said in my writings on Prudentius and in my commentary on the *Dittochaeum*.

### 52.

Arntzenius, citing Fabricius’s commentary mentioned above, p. 23, observes that Nebrissensis produces an epigram under Sedulius’s name in which one reads:

> … and briefly touches upon  
> Your triumphs, O Christ.

He adds that this is found among the acrostic verses of Liberius.

But Nebrissensis does not attribute these verses to Sedulius. Rather, he quotes them from an epigram that is found written under his name—Sedulius’s, that is. He speaks in such a way as to indicate that the name Sedulius is read in the first and last letters of the epigram.

Another genuine epigram of Sedulius, “This of yours, perpetual…,” will be produced by us after the alphabetical hymn.

### 53.

The very learned Franciscus Antonius Zacharias, in his *Select Library of Ecclesiastical History*, as a supplement to Natalis Alexander’s *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, section 1, no. 5, praises our Sedulius as the author of the hymn “The six lustres now completed,” or, as we now sing it following the correction of Urban VIII, “The six lustres he has now completed.”

But perhaps through an error the name Sedulius slipped into his text in place of Fortunatus, who is the author of the hymn “Sing, tongue, the battle of glorious combat,” or, as it now appears in the breviaries, “the victor’s laurel of combat.” “The six lustres he has now completed” is part of this hymn.

Others say that the author was Claudianus Mamertus, as I explained more fully in my dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, no. 185, in the note.

There might be greater difficulty concerning the hymn “The royal banners forward go,” which Angelus Rocca lists among the hymns of Saint Ambrose in his *Theological and Scriptural Index*. He adds:

> Some attribute this hymn to Theodulf, others to Fortunatus, and still others to Sedulius.

I likewise believe that this hymn belongs to Fortunatus; I discussed it in the cited work, no. 189.

### 54.

Martenius, volume IX of the *Collection*, columns 126 and following, publishes a poem on the Incarnation from the same ancient Corbie codex from which he transcribed the poem on Genesis under the name of Juvencus; we have listed the latter among the spurious poems of Juvencus in the appendices.

Martenius attributes the poem on the Incarnation, which was reprinted in volume VI of Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*, to Sedulius because it is attached to book I of the *Paschal Work*—by this I mean the *Paschal Poem*—as though it were part of the same work, with no intervening distinction, division, or title. He adds that, when he had read it with particular care, he noticed the same style in the earlier and later composition.

Permit me to use Gallandi’s words from his dissertation on Sedulius, appended to volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*:

> I would rather that the indefatigable Benedictine editors had employed a weightier body of arguments by which to prove Sedulius the author of this poem.

One is immediately led to wonder how Martenius detected the same style in the poem on the Incarnation and in the *Paschal Poem*. The poem on the Incarnation is composed as a cento woven from Virgilian verses, as Martenius himself observes by indicating the passages; but the *Paschal Poem* flows in Sedulius’s own style, although Sedulius occasionally uses Virgilian half-lines or one or another complete verse [Col. 0459A].

As for the poem on the Incarnation having been attached to book I of the *Paschal Poem* as part of the same work, this certainly occurred through the carelessness or ignorance of a copyist. No one could be so blind as not to see that the poem on the Incarnation cannot in any way belong to the *Paschal Poem*.

### 55.

Some, together with Martenius, derive an argument from the epigram to Theodosius—which, as explained earlier, is prefixed to the *Paschal Poem* in certain editions—in order to assign the poem on the Incarnation to Sedulius.

It is indeed true that the words of the epigram fit the poem on the Incarnation better:

> … Deign to recognize Maro [Virgil] …

Recognize the change for the better by divine perception. [Col. 0459B] But this epigram too has not Sedulius as its author, as has already been proved, nor can it suit the poem on the Incarnation. For the subject of that poem is only the Incarnation; whereas the epigram touches on several other matters that would have been set forth in the poem: the creation of the world and of man, the life, miracles, death, and ascension of Jesus Christ.

In the Gelasian Decree we read, among other things: “An apocryphal cento on Christ, composed of Virgilian verses.” Blanchinus, in the *Prolegomena to Anastasius*, volume IV, reading from Vatican Palatine codex 493, reads *Centoneni* (perhaps *Centonem*): “An apocryphal cento on Christ, composed of Virgilian verses.” This chapter had been omitted in an old Florentine manuscript. In the Jura manuscript it is reported as follows: “Centos on Christ, composed of Virgilian verses, apocryphal.” In Vatican codex 3791, which I collated, I found: “A cento on Christ, composed of Virgilian verses, apocryphal.”

Nevertheless, among many people the title *Centimetrum* prevailed, from *cento* and *metrum*; for what Bede’s commentator on the *Art of Meter* says in the Vatican manuscript—“A *centimetrum* is so called because it is a book containing a hundred meters”—perhaps should be understood of Servius’s *Centimetrum*. Most people, following Saint Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, take it to refer to the Virgilian cento of Proba Faltonia. In the Brasichellian Expurgatory Index it is conjectured that Proba’s poem is not the cento listed by Gelasius among the apocrypha. Why, then, may we not conjecture that the poem on the Incarnation published by Martenius is the *Centometrum* or *Centimetrum* rejected by Gelasius among the apocryphal writings? [Col. 0459D]

Certainly Gelasius says that the subject of the cento is Christ; and this agrees perfectly with the cento published by Martenius. Proba’s cento, however, has a wider scope, as is clear even from its title, “For the Testimony of the Old and New Testament” [35]. As for the authority claimed by the Brasichellian Index among Catholics, one may consult Papebrochius, in his reply to the presentation of errors published by Sebastian of Saint Paul, part II, article 3, page 20. For heretics raise wondrous but empty tragedies among themselves about this work, which is exceedingly rare among them and not very common even among us, as may be gathered from the *Observations on Literary Matters*, Halle-Magdeburg, 1700, volume III, and the following volumes.

### 56

Labbe, in *New Library of Manuscripts, or Specimens of Ancient Readings*, part I, page 23, says that in a manuscript of excellent quality he saw Sedulius’s *Collection on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, excerpted from various Fathers and divided into 355 chapters or sections. In *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he likewise affirms that this *Collection* of Sedulius on Matthew exists in the library of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, written on exceedingly fine parchment in a most elegant hand, more than seven hundred or eight hundred years old. It cites not only Saint Eucherius, Saint Leo, Arnobius the Younger, Faustus of Riez, Saint Gregory, Saint Isidore, Arculfus, and the Venerable Bede, but also the poet Sedulius himself. Thus, on the words “And lead us not into temptation,” the author of the *Collection* says:

“Here Sedulius describes this most excellently in verse, saying:

[Col. 0460B]

Not because the Lord, creator of light and life,

leads us into the snares of the tempter, etc.”

Labbe believes that the same Sedulius was the author both of the *Collection on the Epistles of Paul* and of that on the Gospel of Matthew, and that he flourished in the ninth century under Charlemagne and his son Louis the Pious. For this method of explaining the sacred books has entirely the character of the ninth century, to which Hepidannus assigns a third Sedulius.

### 57

He nevertheless notes that Aubertinus, on page 911 of his *Deceptions concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, believed the author of the *Collection on Paul* to have been Sedulius the bishop who took part in the Roman council of the year 721. But since the *Collection on Matthew* sometimes draws its words from the Venerable Bede, who died in 735, it is far more probable that the author of this *Collection*, and consequently of the other one on Paul as well—for the same author is considered responsible for both—was the third Sedulius, who flourished in the ninth century [36], whether he was a priest or a bishop; for we have no certain information about him.

Bayle, in his *Dictionary*, reproaches Dupin for asserting that Bede is praised in the *Collection on the Epistles of Paul*. This, however, was not reported by Labbe of that *Collection*, but of the other one on Matthew.

Mabillon, volume I of the *Ancient Analects*, page 364, says that those who believe Sedulius, the author of the *Paschal Poem*, to be the same as Sedulius the Scot, or Irishman, a priest and likewise a poet known to have flourished in the eighth century, are far from the truth. But the controversy chiefly concerns the works of the Seduliuses, since most scholars distinguish two or more Seduliuses.

The Sedulius known to have flourished in the eighth century was a bishop. Mabillon affirms that he was also a poet, but does not prove it; nor does he seem to have kept before his eyes what Labbe and other critical scholars had observed about the Seduliuses. For among the poetic works he places first, as unpublished, two very well-known acrostic epigrams concerning Sedulius, although they had been published long before and very often.

Perhaps Mabillon attributed to the eighth-century bishop Sedulius the work *On the Government of Princes*, composed partly in connected verse and partly in prose; I shall return to it below, at number 61. It is much more uncertain that this same Sedulius, who flourished in the eighth century, was the author of some work on the sacred canon of the Mass, which Dempster attributes to him.

### 58

A work different from the *Collections* mentioned thus far, but which seems to have the same Sedulius as its author, is preserved in Vatican codex 242, formerly 1556. This codex contains Prudentius’s *Psychomachia* and a satirical narrative about Grimoard, bishop of Toledo—I mean Bernard—and Pope Urban II.

At the beginning of the volume are Sedulius Scotus’s explanations of the four Evangelists. It begins: “The book of the generation. Moses wrote the book of the generation of heaven and earth. Matthew, however,” etc. On the verso of page 9 one reads: “In the time of the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius he flourished”—a statement made about the poet Sedulius, which some incompetent antiquarian transferred to Sedulius the interpreter of Holy Scripture. On the same page and the following pages, Saint Jerome’s prefaces to Damasus and Eusebius are explained.

Page 38: “Here begins a little explanation by the same Sedulius Scotus of the difference between summaries, chapters, and canons. Here begins the summary according to Matthew. The birth of Christ. The Magi come with gifts [37],” and the rest. “One must investigate the difference between a summary, a chapter, and a canon. For by these three, as by certain keys, all the mysteries of the Gospel volume are unlocked. Once summaries, chapters, and canons had been removed, everything was confused and ambiguous,” etc.

### 59

It will not be unwelcome to transcribe the explanation that follows:

“A summary is a brief and concise exposition of the events narrated in the text of the Gospel. A chapter is any statement or narrative in the Gospels. A canon is a heading by which the agreement of the Evangelists is recognized.”

Then, on page 41: “Here begins a little exposition by the same Sedulius Scotus of the subject according to Matthew.” Thus, on page 49, according to Mark; on page 56, according to Luke. The little exposition according to John is missing.

The volume is in duodecimo or sextodecimo format. At the beginning it is noted: “This codex belongs to the monastery of Blessed Mary Magdalene in Franchenthaell” (the word is not sufficiently clear), situated between Speyer and Worms, belonging to the Canons Regular. Pennottus discusses this now-suppressed monastery in *History of the Canons Regular*, book II, chapter 39, drawing on Trithemius’s *Hirsau History*, which reports that it was founded around the year 1135.

### 60

I should not omit the observation that, in the margin of the verso of page 34, in the same old script—which seems to belong approximately to the tenth century—Saint Isidore is named in the following passage: “Matthew, the apostle and evangelist, who also took the surname Levi from his own tribe,” etc.

These very words are Isidore’s, in *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 76. I wished to record this so that this Sedulius the Scot may be added to Braulio, Ildefonsus, Bede, Fulbert of Chartres, Ascaricus, a Spanish bishop of the eleventh century, and others cited in the old Spanish *Bibliotheca* by Nicolás Antonio and his exceedingly learned editor Francisco Pérez Bayer. All of them attribute the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* to Isidore, against certain more recent scholars—Baronius, Natalis Alexander, Cajetanus Censius, and others—who deny this for almost no other reason than that they once resolved to deny everything that seemed in any way favorable to the preaching and arrival of Saint James in Spain.

For Isidore plainly says of Saint James the Greater, in chapter 71 of this book: “He preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions [38], and at the setting of the world he poured in the light of preaching.”

I could add more from other Vatican manuscripts in the same sense, but it is preferable to reserve these matters for another time.

### 61

As is clear from Labbe, number 45, Goldast possessed a manuscript work of Sedulius entitled *On the Government of Princes*. Schoettgen, who edited volume six of Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, reports that Fabricius mentions a work by Sedulius, *On Christian Rulers and the Appropriate Rules by Which the Commonwealth Should Be Properly Governed*, published at Leipzig in 1669 in octavo—perhaps in the few manuscript sheets that Fabricius left prepared for the sixth volume.

Schoettgen adds that Freher, in his notes on Peter of Andlau’s *On the Roman Empire*, II, 16, writes that in 1612 he was preparing this unpublished book for the press. Nicholas of Cusa quotes eight distichs from the same little book in the preface to book III of *On Catholic Concordance*. I do not find that anyone else saw the book or spoke about it. It is certainly not an unworthy work to reprint for the purpose of overturning the novelties of our own age.

It exists in Vatican Palatine codex 591, a paper manuscript in quarto. Preceding it are the *Ecclesiastical Rules*—that is, the Canons of the Apostles—Ambrose’s *Pastoral Care*, Augustine’s *On Pastors and Sheep*, then Sedulius, and finally certain poems on virtues and vices, together with other works formerly existing in the Basilica of Saint Peter at Rome.

On page 99 of this volume, in red letters, appears: “Here begins the preface to the following work.” Its beginning is:

“Every ministry, which stands forth above the three-branched orb,

must be governed by art; there are very many gifts of art.

The Lord, creator of all, creates the lands, sea, stars, and heavens

by art,” etc.

There are twenty-five hexameter verses. Then: “The preface is complete.”

“With you, Christ the King, are beginning and end;

be the Alpha of your servant’s work, O God, and its Omega.”

It was written *si Deus* (“if God”). Next follows: “Here begin the chapters of the same book.” This index contains twenty chapters.

After the index, in red letters: “Here begins the book of Sedulius, *On Christian Rulers and the Appropriate Rules by Which the Commonwealth Should Be Properly Governed*.” Its beginning is: “After the royal scepter.”

At the end of a chapter: “How immeasurable a palm of glory will he possess if a ruler beloved of God [39] adorns the holy Church, which is the spiritual tabernacle of the living God? But let us conclude these matters, which we have expressed briefly in prose style, with the sweetness of several verses.”

Elegiac verses follow, and thus, after the remaining chapters, the point of each chapter is concluded in various meters.

In chapter 8 mention is made of a certain man to whom it had been revealed that King Theoderic appeared bound between Pope John, whom he had killed in prison, and the patrician Symmachus, whom he had slaughtered with the sword, and that they had cast him into the fire.

In chapter 9 he praises the piety of Charlemagne and Louis. I understand this to mean Louis the Pious, the son of Charlemagne, who began to reign in 814. Accordingly, Sedulius, the author of this work, did not flourish before the eleventh century; and he seems to be the very person praised by Hepidannus, and perhaps Sedulius Scotus, whose hand Montfaucon records as having written a Greek Psalter, *Greek Paleography* III, 7, page 236.

Dempster asserts that Sedulius, a Greek bishop, was venerated in Ireland; the Bollandists, under 13 June, do not accept this.

In chapter 15 he mentions Saint Germanus of Auxerre, bishop, who had been sent to Britain with Blessed Lupus, bishop of Troyes, to eradicate the Pelagian heresy.

After chapter 19 there is an epilogue, which is designated as chapter 20; but a later hand erased the number 20. The entire prologue is written in prose and is addressed to a certain king.

End: “Sedulius’s *On the Government of Princes* is complete.”

## CHAPTER III  
### The Manuscripts of Sedulius Are Catalogued

[Col. 0463B]

### 62

Since there are many works of which our Sedulius is by no means the author, although they bear the name of Sedulius, as is clearly established in the preceding chapter, we shall here chiefly enumerate those manuscripts that contain Sedulius’s poems and his *Paschal Work*, or *Prose*. We shall briefly indicate some that contain doubtful works; for manuscripts in which Holy Scripture is expounded have been sufficiently discussed above, at numbers 43, 56, and following.

The most distinguished manuscript of Sedulius is preserved in the library of the Royal Athenaeum of Turin [40]. A catalogue of the manuscripts of that library has been published; its authors are Joseph Pasinus, Antonio Rivautella, and Francesco Berta. In volume II of the catalogue, page 244, manuscript 766 is described: a parchment codex of square format, consisting of thirty-six leaves, whose script is said also to belong to the sixth century. Mansius, who examined the codex itself, does not disagree, in his notes to Fabricius’s *Library*.

Sedulius’s works are listed in the following order. First comes a letter of Sedulius to Macedon—read “Macedonius”—which is mutilated; it begins: “Since you are free from the loftier Scriptures, you should also willingly devote yourself to the humbler ones. The eagle does not always fly aloft above the clouds,” etc.

At the end of the letter: “Here ends Sedulius’s letter to Macedoneo Pbi, successfully.”

After the letter follows the preface to Theodosius, “leader of the Romulids,” etc., which, as we have said, is not by Sedulius. Book I begins, “When his own,” etc. The catalogue says nothing about the metrical prologue, *Paschales*, and so forth. The poem is divided into five books, as we shall note in most of the best manuscripts.

After the third book of the poem, which is the second of the New Testament, this subscription of the corrector is found: “I, Abundantius, have successfully collated this book.”

The elegy *Cantemus* follows the *Paschal Poem*. The catalogue makes no mention of the alphabetic hymn *A solis ortus*. When I wished for a fuller and more exact description of the codex, my wishes were most generously answered by Count Galeanus Napione of Cocconato, renowned for his distinguished published works and most deserving in every branch of learning.

On the first page of the codex, in an ancient hand—but one more recent than the first script—appears: “Book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio.” This shows that the book once belonged to the monastery of Bobbio; see number 94.

Although in the specimen of the script displayed in the manuscript catalogue the letters are majuscule, or Roman, as we now call them, it is clear from specimens of various passages sent to me that three kinds of letters are found, such as many maintain existed among the ancient Romans: one kind of majuscule especially proper to inscriptions; another used commonly, much like our own; and another cursive and smaller, of the same or scarcely different form.

At the beginning of the poem, therefore, the codex appears to have been written in square majuscule letters. Later the same scribe changed the form, but [41] sometimes returned to majuscule letters, especially when writing verses in red letters, as occasionally happens.

After the letter to Macedonius is finished, the poem immediately begins, “Although the Gentiles [have] their own ...” The dedication to Theodosius, “leader of the Romulids,” is entirely absent; consequently the authors of the catalogue were mistaken in attributing it to the codex.

The metrical prologue *Paschales* is also absent. But on the final leaf of the codex—which it is not clear was added to the volume—the verses are written partly in red and partly in black letters, by a very ancient hand different from that which wrote the poem. Most of the letters have disappeared; but as far as can be gathered, the metrical prologue was written incorrectly.

The alphabetic hymn *A solis ortus*, Sedulius’s epigram, and the acrostic verses of Liberius and Belisarius are likewise missing from this old exemplar.

The headings of the contents are not written in the margins everywhere, but they are found in some places, sometimes apparently indicated in a more recent hand. Asterius is mentioned on the final leaf of the volume, as I shall say elsewhere.

The learned describer of the codex observed that *e* often occurs for *i*, as *explecit* for *explicit*, *ordenavit* for *ordinavit*, and *alet* for *alit*. In the specimen of the script sent to me, I observe that *k* is sometimes written for *c*, as in *kanant* and *paskae*, and *o* for *u*, as in *Sedolius* for *Sedulius*. This bears on the ending of the letter, *Macedoneo*: in my opinion it was written in this form for *Macedonium*, and perhaps the line above the *o* disappeared.

These and other observations I have made lead me to conjecture that the codex is not older than the eighth century. Others may assign it a greater antiquity if they wish; nor will they lack similar examples from other manuscripts with which to defend their opinion.

Gallandius, volume IX of the *Library*, in his dissertation on Sedulius, concludes from the collation of the codex made by the authors of the catalogue that it is less corrected, and that its authority is considerably impaired by the dedication to Theodosius prefixed to the poem. But as regards the dedication, I have already noted that the authors of the catalogue falsely attributed it to the codex.

I have been entirely unable to determine the age of Abundantius, who collated the codex. For I do not think he was the Abundantius to whom an epigram by Ennodius is extant, the latter having flourished at the beginning of the sixth century.

### 63

In the Vatican Library, besides the Palatine codex, which contains a little about Sedulius, as I said at number 5, and two others that exhibit [42] the works of another Sedulius, as I explained at numbers 58 and 61, I collated eleven other codices, which I shall now describe.

Two belong to the old Vatican Library and are simply called Vatican manuscripts; six belong to the library of Queen Christina of Sweden and were transferred to the Vatican; two are Vatican Ottobonian manuscripts; and one is a Vatican Urbinian manuscript.

### 64

Vatican codex 1665, a parchment manuscript in small folio, contains Arator and Sedulius. There are some glosses, mostly faded; numerous abbreviations of letters; not a few errors; and some corrections by an old hand. The diphthongs *ae* and *oe* occur. The letters *l*, *b*, *f*, *p*, and similar letters extend farther than usual, especially in the first and last lines; this suggests that the codex is not very old.

I would be inclined to assign it approximately to the eleventh century; Montfaucon, however, in his *Library of Manuscripts*, page 126, assigns it to the ninth.

Immediately after Arator, Sedulius’s metrical prologue begins, as will be explained more fully in the variant readings, and after the metrical prologue comes book I of the *Paschal Poem*.

At the end: “Here ends Sedulius’s book; here begins his poem: *Cantemus*, etc.” After the untitled elegy comes Sedulius’s epigram *Haec tua*, and immediately afterward, likewise without a title, the hymn *A solis ortus*. When this is finished, the letter to Macedonius begins, but proceeds only as far as the words “But concerning daily mercy.” The rest is missing, one or more leaves having been torn away.

In the apparatus of variant readings this is my first Vatican manuscript, or Vat. 1.

### 65

The other Vatican codex, number 3178, is a fifteenth-century paper manuscript. It contains Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, the metrical prologue, *Paschales*, and the poem divided into two books.

At the end of the poem is a note also transcribed in other codices: “This work Sedulius among the little papers,” etc.; more will be said about it below.

After the note, without any title, comes the elegy *Cantemus*. It is followed by a poem of the poet Raphael Zovenzonius, *O custos hominum*, and the hymn *Virginis partu*. Aldus published this hymn, along with other poems by Zovenzonius, after Sedulius and the other Christian poets.

The codex seems to have been copied from a good exemplar, but it has been stained by not a few errors caused by the copyist’s carelessness. In the apparatus of variant readings this codex is Vat. 2.

### 66

The Vatican codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, number 333, is a parchment manuscript in quarto. It is the very one I used in editing Juvencus. I displayed a specimen of its script in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, number 48, page 24 [43].

For me, this is the most beautiful of the Sedulian codices.

After Juvencus, the letter to Macedonius begins; it is followed by the metrical prologue, *Paschales*, and then the poem divided into five books. The arrangement is such that, once the first book of the Old Testament is finished, the next is called the first book of the New Testament, and the remaining books follow in order as the second, third, and fourth.

After the poem begins Arator’s letter—or rather the title of the letter, since much is missing from this codex. This is clear from a note added in the margin, which instructs us to look in this volume for Sedulius’s elegy after Arator. But the whole of Arator is missing, as are Sedulius’s elegy and hymn, which, I think, followed the elegy.

Only one leaf remains, on which, in smaller script, is written the note already mentioned: “This work Sedulius,” etc. It is followed by Asterius’s epigram *Sume, sacer*.

After this epigram there is another note explaining the metrical prologue, expressed in a similar manner in Ottobonian I, number 75, which I shall describe:

“Sedulius, in the letter prefixed to the priest Macedonius, invites readers to the sixteen-verse prologue that follows. He compares the poverty of his slender talent with the lowliness of vegetables. From his poem, concerning the individual miracles of both Testaments, these chapter headings have been written in advance.”

There follow lists of twenty-five titles, joined to the chapters that follow—perhaps a word is missing here.

“Jerome, in the catalogue of writers,” etc.

The codex continues as stated at number 6, but the twenty-five titles are not actually given.

The acrostic verses of Liberius and Belisarius are added to the note without any written title. Although all these materials have been placed here, there is no doubt that they chiefly belong at the beginning of the book. For scribes often added at the end of a work things they had perhaps found in other codices but had been unable to insert appropriately in their proper places.

In the apparatus of variant readings this codex will be designated Reg. 1, that is, the first Vatican codex of Queen Christina of Sweden.

### 67

In the same library, Queen Christina’s codex 300, a parchment manuscript in folio, exhibits Arator and Sedulius, together with some verses after Sedulius.

It contains glosses, chapter titles marked in red, the diphthongs *ae* and *e*, and the spellings *dampnare*, *adgredior*, *istoricum*, *clodum*, *sollempnia*, *inradiat*, and *ymnus*.

The order in this codex is: the letter to Macedonius; the metrical prologue; the *Paschal Poem* [44], divided into five books in the same manner as in Reg. 1; the elegy; the hymn *A solis ortus*; and the acrostic verses of Liberius and Belisarius, without any inscription.

Montfaucon, *Library of Manuscripts*, page 52, column 2, lists among Queen Christina’s manuscripts codex 1687, “the poems of Arator”—read *Aratoris*—“and Sedulius,” which perhaps is not different from ours.

This codex is Reg. 2 in the apparatus of variant readings.

### 68

The third manuscript of the queen’s library that we use is number 166, formerly 1594, a parchment manuscript in octavo. After some letters of Sidonius and various other materials, it offers, in a rather old script perhaps belonging to the tenth century, the letter to Macedonius with glosses and, at the end of the letter, the note: “This work Sedulius,” etc.

The beginning of Prudentius’s *Psychomachia* follows, together with several verses from the end of Sedulius’s book V. Then come the elegy *Cantemus* and the beginning of the hymn *A solis ortus*.

When cited, this codex will be called Reg. 3.

### 69

Also belonging to the queen’s library is parchment codex 1560, in quarto, which contains several works: Cato the Philosopher—Dionysius—Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius without its beginning; after the letter several leaves are missing; and Sedulius’s poem begins at verse 121 of book I, “Lot in Sodom,” and ends at the final verse of book II, “the wolf’s jaws.”

The materials relating to Sedulius are written in a very ancient script and may be assigned to the eighth century. The other materials are more recent, such as the work that follows, *The Art of Phocas*, and another anonymous work afterward, whose first title is *On the Voice*.

A note has been added in the margin by a hand that I believe to be that of the most learned Lorenzo Zacagni, formerly prefect of the Vatican Library: “Perhaps this is by Servius Maurus Honoratus, whose commentaries on only the second art of Donatus have been published.”

It does indeed seem to be a commentary on Donatus, but its author is certainly much later than Servius: for he praises Sedulius, Fortunatus, and Bede.

It begins: “When Donatus is about to speak of grammatical arrangement, he rightly begins with the voice.”

When discussing syllables and asking which may be shortened or lengthened, he chiefly follows Bede, or rather copies him. Accordingly, the lacuna can easily be supplied when, discussing the first syllable in *gaza*, he says: “Long in this verse of Juvencus: ‘Difficile in terris ad [lacuna].’ Short in this verse of the same author: ‘Et gaza distabat rerum possessio fulgens.’ Read: ‘Difficile est terris adfixos vivere gazis’ (‘It is hard for those fixed to earthly treasures to live’).”

The author adds, to prove that the first syllable in *gaza* is common [45], this badly Latinized verse: “Lay up the treasure of heaven; empty the bags of treasures.”

I said in my notes on Juvencus, book III, verse 499, that Bede had come upon a corrupt copy of Juvencus in which “And the possession of treasure stood apart” was read instead of “And the treasure stood apart.”

In any event, the script in which this commentary on Donatus is written seems no more recent than the tenth century.

The same volume contains several satires of Persius; commentaries on Donatus; commentaries on Bede, *On Meters*; Remigius on Dionysius Cato; the life of Persius by Remigius; and a commentary on Persius.

In the apparatus of variant readings we shall designate this codex by the siglum Reg. 4.

### 70

Another manuscript of the queen’s library, number 29, is a paper codex in folio, written at the beginning of the sixteenth century. I shall describe it somewhat more carefully, since it may shed some light on what Fabricius reports in his *Library of the Middle and Lower Ages* about Peter Aurorarius, or of Riga.

At the beginning appears this title:

“The most elegant work of Peter Aurorarius, an outstanding doctor of theology, newly discovered, explaining in verse the hidden mysteries of the Old and New Testament.”

He was born in the province called Saxony, and this book is said to have been composed by Peter of Saxony.

It is preceded by an elegiac epigram in praise of sacred poems, or concerning the sacred subject:

“Let the golden poems of Maeon’s bard yield,” etc.

Then several verses from Juvencus’s prologue are copied, without the author’s name, “And if so long,” etc., through the end of the prologue, expressing the same thought.

Next come certain verses that appear to be hexameters and pentameters but are actually without meter, in praise of Christ.

A prose preface to the Pentateuch follows: “The frequent requests of my companions,” etc., as in Fabricius, but with some variation in the readings.

Then: “Here begins the book of the histories of the Bible called *Aurora*.”

After the Pentateuch: “Here end the five books of Moses. Here begins the book of Joshua the king.”

“After Moses, Joshua rules over the Hebrew people.”

After Joshua: “Here ends the book of Joshua, king of Israel. Here begins the book of Judges.”

“After Joshua, let a narrative be made of the Judges.”

When the book of Judges is finished: “Here begins the book of Ruth.”

“To Ruth Peter’s style hastens, so that her deeds—

a brief speech may depict in delicate verse.”

Then: “Here ends the book of Ruth. Here begins the prologue to the books of Kings.”

“Here end the books of Kings. Here begins the book of Tobit.”

“Here ends the book of Tobit [46]. Here begins the book of the prophet Daniel.”

“Here begins the book of Judith the woman. Here begins the book of Esther the queen.”

“Here begins the first book of Maccabees. Here end the books of Maccabees and of illustrious men.”

### 71

In the same volume there follow figures of the Incarnation of the Son of God. Each is expressed in epigrams composed with such artistry that one letter is entirely absent from each: the first lacks *a*, the second *b*, and so forth.

In the Spanish language we have five stories among those commonly called novels, composed so that the first contains no *a*, the second no *e*, the third no *i*, the fourth no *o*, and the fifth no *u*. This may be offered as an argument demonstrating the abundance and variety of the language.

Barthius observes a somewhat similar and curious diligence in *Adversaria*, book XLVI, chapter 22, in the eclogue of the monk Hucbald to the emperor Charles the Bald, all of whose words begin with the letter *c*, as in: “Sing, Muses, clear-sounding songs for Charles the Bald.”

Returning to the Vatican codex, there follows an epigram entitled “The Names of the Ancient Fathers,” and another, “The Names of the Fathers of the New Testament.”

Immediately afterward: “Here begins the prologue on the Evangelists”:

“After the old law, breathe again, Peter: the new law shines forth.

Make verses new concerning its newness.”

The Gospel narrative is told from the four Evangelists.

At the end:

“Here Jesus speaks of the end, and Matthew brings

the book to its end, as Peter himself brings his to an end.”

Two epigrams are added, one on Saint Anne and one on her three daughters. Some discussion follows concerning them, including the reasons why the Mother of God was betrothed and concerning the final judgment of the Son of God.

Gerson, in his sermon on the Nativity of the Mother of God, quotes and approves one of these epigrams about Saint Anne, beginning “Anna married three times.” Learned men, however, reject that account.

### 72

In the aforementioned Vatican codex there follows a “Salutation to the divine Theotokos”: “Hail, holy mother,” etc. These are verses of Sedulius, book II, verses 63 and following.

Then comes the prayer *Salve Regina* in elegiac verse, followed by the prayer of the illustrious prince, blessed Casimir, king of Poland, “Every day say to Mary,” etc. Pez says, in his dissertation on church hymns, number 141, that it is older than Saint Casimir.

Other praises of the Mother of God, written in prose [47], are added. These are followed by a metrical book *On the Concord of the New and Old Testament*, in leonine hexameters, with glosses.

There are also elegiac verses:

“There will always be, as they were, the joys of eternal life,” etc.

Prosper’s epigram 78 has: “There will always be, as they are, the joys of eternal life.”

Next comes the *Garland of the Virgin Mary*, in elegant verse, by the venerable Peter of Riga, professor of sacred theology. The verses are elegiac. The second book is entitled *On the Evangelists*, the third *On the Prophets*, and the fourth *On Paradise*.

There follow elegiac verses to Pope Sixtus; some of his bulls concerning the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God; an elegiac poem by John of Florence to Peter Tiven in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary; other poems by Jerome of Padua—Vida—and Philip Beroaldus; the *Paeans* of Francesco Petrarch; a poem under the name of Ausonius, “Almighty One, whom I worship in my mind”; other anonymous poems; and the *Physiologus* of Theobald, bishop, describing the natures of twelve animals in varied verse.

These works have been listed somewhat more fully so that the poems of Peter of Riga—most of them unpublished—might be identified. I discussed the attempted collection of these poems by some scholars in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, number 20.

### 73

Accordingly, on page 275 of this volume there is a work of Sedulius under the following title: “Book I of the Divine Miracles of Caelius Sedulius the Priest.” It begins: “Although the Gentiles [have] their own ...,” etc.

The letter to Macedonius and the metrical prologue *Paschales* are missing. The poem is divided into four books.

At the end is a note concerning Asterius, the collector of Sedulius’s poems: *Cantemus*, *A solis*, and *Haec tua*, arranged in this order, somewhat differently from Aldus’s edition, in which the epigram *Haec tua* precedes the hymn *A solis ortus*.

Otherwise, I judge that Sedulius’s poems in this codex were copied from Aldus’s edition, with which they agree almost everywhere.

The entire codex was copied at Kraków Castle by Matthias, son of Adam Sculterus, a mansionary of Kraków Cathedral.

This codex will be designated Reg. 5, that is, the fifth manuscript of the queen.

### 74

In Queen Christina’s Alexandrian codex, number 1360 or 2078, a ninth-century parchment manuscript, which I discussed in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, number 78, after some verses of Theodulf of Orléans [48], the poems of Alcimus Avitus, Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*, and the *Orthography* of Caprus and Agroetius, on page 79, there are verses of Belisarius the scholastic.

Thus are entitled two acrostics of Liberius and Belisarius concerning Sedulius, which I shall append, collated with this codex, which I shall now call Reg. 6.

Seven verses follow in this codex under the corrupt title: “Avienus V. C. Adamus Cos alegro.” This is the beginning of Rufus Festus Avienus’s poem *To His Friends, On the Field*, which is extant in Burmann’s *Anthology* and elsewhere.

### 75

In the Vatican Ottobonian Library there are two Sedulian codices. One is number 35, which I discussed in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, number 49; a specimen of its script has been engraved on copper.

This codex approaches the age of Reg. 1.

Sedulius is prefixed to Juvencus in the following order: the letter to Macedonius; the note “This work Sedulius,” etc.; Asterius’s epigram *Sume, sacer*; another note concerning the metrical prologue, “Sedulius, in the letter,” etc., as was explained from Reg. 1 at number 63; the hymn *A solis ortus cardine*; the metrical prologue *Paschales*; the *Paschal Poem* in five books, distributed in the same manner as in Reg. 1; Belisarius’s acrostic on Sedulius, “Sedulius of Christ,” etc., without any inscription and with the other acrostic of Liberius omitted; the untitled elegy *Cantemus*; and finally the note “Here begins the art,” etc., which was reported at number 9.

I call this codex Ott. 1.

[Col. 0470A] **76.** The other Ottobonian codex, number 36, is a parchment quarto, most elegantly written, adorned with many gold and variegated letters and with illustrations. The title of this codex is distinctive: *Here begins Sedulius’s book on the Acts of the Prophets and on the entire course of Christ the Savior*; compare, if you please, above, no. 49. The letter to Macedonius is lacking. After the metrical prologue, *Paschales*, the poem is divided into five books, but in a different manner from the other codices in which five books are likewise numbered, as will be clear from the various readings. To the *Paschal Poem* are added the elegy *Cantemus* and the hymn *A solis ortus*, without titles, together with the acrostic verses of Liberius and Belisarius. The following corrupt, or even barbarous, verses follow without a heading:

[Col. 0470B]

> How, fixed to the lofty wood, Christ now—

> Sedulius sang, should encompass the whole world,

> 49 or should show that he hangs for the whole world,

> With these verses, Christ, in his mercy, bringing salvation to the world:

> “Four wounds then,” etc.

Six verses of Sedulius follow, from Book V, verse 190. They are also commended in another ancient manuscript and by Bede, as I shall report in no. 170. Immediately afterward: *The End*. Antonius Sinibaldus of Florence, *the shield of King Ferdinand* [or: “Ferdinand the king’s *testudo*”], wrote this under the year of the Lord 1473, on 15 March, at Naples. The codex appears to have been copied from a good exemplar, but it teems with many errors through the copyist’s ignorance and carelessness. Certain peculiar features occur in its rubrics or titles; these will be indicated in their proper places. I shall call this codex Ott. 2.

[Col. 0470C] **77.** There is only one Urbinas codex of Sedulius in the Vatican Library, number 584, formerly 828. It is a parchment quarto, written in a polished script and copied with many gold letters and elegant titles, but by some negligent fifteenth-century copyist; for frequent errors occur in it. After the metrical prologue *Paschales*, the poem follows, divided into four books. For the third and fourth books have been made into one, as in many editions. After the poem comes the elegy *Cantemus*, which is called *Paracterium*, and “the elegiac poem of the distinguished bishop Sedulius”—an honorific description with which Sedulius is presented five times or more in this codex. Other items are missing, such as the letter to Macedonius, the hymn *A solis ortus*, Sedulius’s epigram, Asterius’s [epigram], and so forth. After the elegy the copyist merely noted, “I have completed this work,” etc., etc., and added nothing more, either concerning his own name or the year in which [Col. 0470D] the work was completed. In the same volume follow Bede’s *Martyrology*, Bede’s verses on the Kalends, and poems by various authors concerning the year, the months, and so forth. The siglum for this codex in the various readings is Urb.

**78.** The Library of the Roman College supplied us with a codex which we collated and described when editing Juvencus, in the *Prolegomena*, no. 50. The script in which Sedulius was written appears to be older, and as many errors do not occur in Sedulius as in Juvencus. The title is: *Here begins the book of the poet Sedulius*. Immediately follows the metrical prologue, without the letter to Macedonius. Titles are frequently distinguished throughout the poem, but the books are not; nor are the titles themselves marked toward the end of the poem, [Col. 0471A] although a blank space was left there. 50 After the *Paschal Poem* comes the elegy *Cantemus*, without a heading; after the elegy: *The End. This book belongs to St. George Major*, etc. The hymn *A solis ortus* and all the other items usually found in the other codices are missing. In the notes to Juvencus I called this codex Rom., and I shall call it so here as well.

**79.** In the Angelica Library at Rome there is a paper manuscript which I described in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 76. After an elegy on the Resurrection under the name of Lactantius comes the metrical prologue, *Sedulius’s Paschales*, without any title; then the *Paschal Poem*, divided into four books as in other recent codices; and finally the elegy *Cantemus*, without a heading. Only after the last verse of the [Col. 0471B] *Paschal Poem* does one read: *The book of Sedulius is completed*. The sections of the *Paschal Poem*, however, are distinguished by their own titles. The name of the Cistercian monk who copied it appears to have been Antonius Lemos. It is also obscurely indicated that the codex belonged to the monastery of Clairvaux at Milan, of the Cistercian order; for the letters have now almost faded away in many places. I saw and examined this codex, which I shall call Angelicus, or Ang. I spoke in no. 37 of another, older codex of the Angelica Library, which shows us only the poem beginning *Romulidum ductor*, etc.

**80.** I possess another paper codex of Sedulius, which I acquired not many years ago; it was written at the beginning of the fifteenth century. At the beginning of this volume are Ovid’s *Remedy for Love*, with glosses, and Homer’s *Batrachomyomachia* rendered in Latin verse, beginning: *Of frogs and mice together the cruel wars*. Sedulius follows, but the beginning is lacking up to verse 45 of Book I, *Labruscam*. Titles written in red are added in the margin. The *Paschal Poem* is divided into four books, as in other more recent codices, in which the third and fourth books are made into a single book. The elegy follows the *Paschal Poem*; it is called the distich epigram of that same Sedulius. Next comes the hymn of the same poet, *A solis ortus cardine*, and at the end the note *Sedulius the poet*, reported above at no. 10. Other sacred and secular miscellanies are appended, including pieces by Statius, Calpurnius, Propertius, and Claudian, who is called Conopeus, a citizen of Florence. Sedulius’s poems are not very carefully corrected because of the copyist’s negligence, but nevertheless many noteworthy various readings occur, [Col. 0471D] 51 and are not easily found elsewhere. I therefore mean this codex whenever I call a codex “mine.”

There is an older parchment octavo, apparently of the thirteenth century, preserved in the excellent library of the House of Albani at Rome, which I was also permitted to use. Its simple title is *Sedulius*. Under this title are copied the metrical prologue *Paschales* and Book I, with divisions and indications of the subjects. At the end of Book I is the rubric:

> The first book of the Old Testament is completed. The book of the New Testament begins, concerning the expulsion of man from Paradise.

The poem is divided into four books; the fourth begins with the verse *Jam placidas*, etc., and continues to the end. Then:

> The fourth book is happily completed, amen.

There begin certain poems of the same author: namely, the elegy *Cantemus*, after which comes:

> The hymn of Sedulius the presbyter begins,

namely, *A solis ortus*. I shall call this codex Albanianus, or Alb.

[Col. 0472A] **81.** I shall now report the manuscript codices which Arntzenius used in his edition of Sedulius. First he praises a codex belonging to his father, which the latter calls, in connection with Pliny’s *Panegyric* 25.5 and 49.8, ancient and “parchment of laudable antiquity.” This parchment codex, in a small format, contained Sedulius’s *Paschal Poem*, Asterius’s epigram, and Sedulius’s hymn, or elegy, *Cantemus*. The remainder was lacking.

From Petrus Burmannus the Younger, Arntzenius received the Almeloveenian codex, of large format, which Cellarius had previously used and which was highly commendable for its antiquity and certain very elegant scholia. In it, however, everything from verse 197 of Book I, *Cum spirante*, to verse 13 of Book IV, *Ni genitor*, was missing. The same Burmannus added Georg Fabricius’s edition, in the margin of which Carolus Andreas Dukerus had written various readings from the edition of Parrhasius and from Pulmannus’s, or Poelmannus’s, papers. This edition of Fabricius is mentioned in the catalogue of the Dukerian Library, quarto, no. 571. The various readings in Poelmannus’s papers appear to Arntzenius to have been taken from a manuscript; for Poelmannus himself sometimes indicates this, as at Book V, verse 276. Daumius himself also wished to publish the Christian poets and had Poelmannus’s hand in the codices of Sedulius, Arator, and others, as he testifies in his letter to Heinsius, no. 220, volume V of Burmannus’s *Sylloge*. Fabricius too, in his *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 24, mentions codices collated by Poelmannus, but their [Col. 0472C] readings differ from those found in the papers. For in the papers Sedulius’s poem is divided into five books, whereas in the codices of which Fabricius speaks only four are numbered. Arntzenius had not seen Poelmannus’s edition, which I shall review at no. 109. Poelmannus, therefore, after publishing Sedulius with various readings as well, collated other copies, both published and unpublished, and noted readings that differed from his edition; he often also expressed his own judgment about them.

**82.** Burmannus also sent Arntzenius certain excerpts from four codices of the Leiden Batavian Library, extracted by Nicolaus Heinsius and copied by another person from Heinsius’s papers onto the margin of the Fabrician edition. The first codex came from the Vulcanius chest, the other [Col. 0472D] three from the Nansius chest; but they were distinguished from one another by the letters A, B, C, and D. These excerpts contained only the letter to Macedonius and Asterius’s epigram. In Codex C the following was written by a later hand:

> Argument of Sedulius’s book:
>
> Sedulius disdains chaff and chooses suitable  
> things for the Gospel, through the diligence of metre.

As I think, *eligit altas* (“chooses lofty things”) would not be a bad reading.

Arntzenius also received from Petrus Burmannus the Younger, as a gift, Cellarius’s edition of Sedulius, which the uncle of Petrus Burmannus the Younger had used. Its margin contained various readings not only from Aldus and the Edinburgh edition, but also from a manuscript in the Leiden Batavian Library, [Col. 0473A] which is found before the works of Virgil and, to distinguish it from the other four just mentioned, is designated by the letter E. There was also an unpublished letter from P. Burmannus to Gisb. Cuperus, dated 28 July 1704, containing many elegant conjectures of Burmannus. Petrus Burmannus the Younger had himself written certain additional matters in his copy of the Cellarian edition.

**83.** Grunerus, who had published Sedulius somewhat earlier, had himself seen no codices or manuscript copies, but he nevertheless used the Tornesian edition of 1565, with the manuscript notes of Ericus Benzelius, taken from a Canterbury manuscript, the Nansius codex, and the Vulcanius codex. Of these latter two, however, he used them only for the first book, and not even for that book in its entirety. Arntzenius also profited from these same two codices, collated by Nicolaus Heinsius, and appropriately praises them.

53 **84.** In preparing his edition of Sedulius, which he produced at the beginning of this century, Cellarius used a manuscript codex of Sedulius, exceedingly ancient, from the Pauline Library of the Leipzig Academy; a book of Sedulius from the library of Christian Daumius, which Gaspar Barthius had collated with a written codex; another collated by Ericus Benzelius at Cambridge with ancient parchment; and yet another, which Nicolaus Heinsius had checked against an ancient codex through the first three books. Cellarius also mentions parchment manuscripts of excellent quality, which Theodorus Janssonius van Almeloveen sent him; Arntzenius used these as well. Cappusotus, who prepared the edition of Sedulius to be reviewed at no. 95, collated several manuscript copies, but they were partly mutilated and partly covered with errors.

**85.** Several other learned men who illuminated particular passages of Sedulius praise manuscript codices. Barthius, for example, often brings forward at least two codices, one older than the other, to correct corrupt verses. G. Fabricius’s four manuscript codices are discussed at no. 33. Wassius refers to manuscripts in his edition of Sallust, concerning which see the notes on Book II, verses 29 and 116. Davisius mentions certain manuscript codices, as I shall say in connection with Book I, verse 103.

**86.** Bandinius, in the *Catalogue of the Laurentian Library at Florence*, vol. III, pp. 722 ff., lists a fifteenth-century parchment codex containing Prudentius, Juvencus, and other Christian poets. Number 8 of that volume is Faltonia Proba’s *Cento*, mutilated [Col. 0473D] at the end, but preceded at the beginning by the epigram:

> Leader of Romulus, second light of the bright sun,

which some offer as Sedulius’s dedication to Theodosius, but read *Romulidum* instead of *Romulei*. In this codex, however, there is a prologue to Proba’s *Cento*. After the verse *Fit sonus: ingenti concussa est pondere tellus* (“A sound arises: the earth is shaken by a mighty weight”), although other verses are added in other copies, this one has written:

> Proba’s *Cento* from the poems of P. Virgil is completed.

For that is what they called Proba, *Centona*, from the title of her poem, *Cento*.

Number 9, page 231:

> Of Sedulius the Catholic poet, four books in heroic verse on the individual miracles of both Testaments, addressed to the presbyter Macedonius.

This is the title Bandinius gives. The order of the works is recorded as follows: the letter to Macedonius; the hymn *A solis ortus*; the note “This work is by Sedulius,” as elsewhere. Then:

> To God and our Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the human race, be infinite praise: he has permitted me, his sinful servant, to complete by writing the evangelical teaching which blessed Sedulius arranged in verse. He lives and reigns with God the Father, etc.

Some information about the author of the poem and the occasion on which he composed it is appended. It begins, “At the head of each book,” and ends, “the things contained in the books are made manifest.” Next comes the metrical preface *Paschales* and the *Paschal Poem*, contained in four books, as in similar codices of the recent period. After the *Paschal Poem*, without a title, comes the elegy *Cantemus*. I also mentioned this codex in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius and Juvencus*. Bandinius calls it exceptionally handsome, [Col. 0474B] with the initials of the books in gold, and apparently copied from a very ancient exemplar. It is useful to observe here that in the fifteenth century, when good letters began to be restored, the ancient Christian poets were held in great honor and were eagerly and elegantly copied from very ancient codices. Ambrosius of Camaldoli is famous among those who labored to preserve and illuminate ancient monuments. In Book II, letter 14, volume III of the *Collectanea* of Martène, he wrote as follows to Michael, a monk who copied and corrected ancient codices:

> Our cardinal wishes Prudentius and Sedulius to be copied for him in the most ornate and finest script; he still desires Juvencus.

**87.** In the Florentine Library of Santa Croce, Bandinius, volume IV, p. 178, describes codex 11, containing certain poems of Sedulius, Statius, and Claudian. The poems of our Sedulius are arranged in this order, without definite titles: first, the metrical preface *Paschales*; second, the *Paschal Poem*; third, the elegy *Cantemus*; fourth, the epigram *Haec tua*; fifth, the hymn *A solis ortus*; sixth, *The Book of Sedulius*, or rather a fragment of a letter written in a fading script to the presbyter Macedonius. Thus says Bandinius. But, as may be gathered from the words of the letter which he quotes, apart from the heading of the letter to Macedonius, nothing else belongs to Sedulius; for what follows concerns later times and was improperly added by some completely ignorant copyist. It reads as follows:

> Sedulius sends greetings in the Lord to my holy lord, my father Macedonius the presbyter. The consuls of Genoa send friendship and greetings in Christ to the consuls of Tortona, and likewise to all the people, great and small. We ask—and in asking, we earnestly beseech you—that you come together with us as soon as you can.

**88.** Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, lists, on p. 672, among the Latin manuscripts of Isaac Vossius, *Sedulius Scotus on Priscian*; and among the same manuscripts, on p. 681, *Sedulius the Bishop on the First Edition of Donatus*. I discussed these works above, at no. 45, on the basis of Oudinus. Ceillier praises a manuscript in the Leiden Batavian Library, *An Explanation by Bishop Sedulius on the First Edition of Donatus*. I do not think it differs from the one which Oudinus, in the place cited, locates in London. But, as was observed at the cited no. 45, these are certainly not works of the earlier Sedulius; this should be perfectly clear to anyone in the case of the commentary on Priscian. For Priscian is not as ancient as many commonly think. He flourished in the sixth century, as is clear from Cassiodorus, *On Orthography*. This is confirmed by the anonymous author of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, who, in chapter 18, places this highly skilled grammarian Priscian among Christian writers.

Sedulius’s explanation of Donatus is variously called an explanation of the first *ars*, or edition, of Donatus, and by others an explanation of the second edition of Donatus. Perhaps this Sedulius wrote on both editions. Montfaucon, in the same work, p. 417, lists from the library of the Benedictine monastery at Florence *Sedulius’s sacred poem*; in a parchment codex, p. 483, from the library of St. John in the Garden at Padua, *Sedulius with glosses*; [Col. 0475B] p. 632, from the King of England’s library, *The Paschal Work* (by which I understand the poem); p. 671, from the library of St. Benedict at Cambridge, *Sedulius*; p. 673, from the library of York Cathedral, *Sedulius, on the Old and New Testament*; p. 685, from the manuscripts of Edward Bernard, *Sedulius*; p. 686, in London, at the Jacobean buildings, *Sedulius’s Paschal Work*. As I think, and as I recently indicated, by the name “Paschal Work” Montfaucon does not mean Sedulius’s prose, but the *Paschal Poem* itself; many people speak in this way.

**89.** He continues on p. 1084, from the Coislinian Library at Saint-Germain, *Sedulius’s Paschal Work*; on p. 1089, in the same place, *Sedulius, on the Acts of the Prophets*. This is the very *Paschal Poem*, as I said at no. 49, where the same title is produced from the library of D. Valletta. [Col. 0475C] From the same Saint-Germain library, on p. 1136: *The Paschal Poem of Sedulius the Bishop*, etc.; *Belisarius Scholasticus’s panegyric of Sedulius and Liberius*. I would correct this to: *The panegyric of Sedulius by Belisarius Scholasticus and Liberius*. From the library of Murbach, p. 1176: *Sedulius’s Paschal Poem, and other works of the same author*. *The verses of Belezarius Scholasticus*: title, *Sedulius the Bishop*, on a parchment folio. These are the acrostic verses of Belisarius, whose name is expressed in more than one way in the manuscripts.

**90.** In the cited work of Montfaucon, p. 1180, from the library of the monastery of Moyenmoutier in the Vosges: *The poems of Sedulius*, a tenth-century codex; p. 1203, from the library of the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Vendôme: *Sedulius*, twice; p. 1222, from the library of St. Albinius of Angers: *Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, a sacred work on the Old and New Testament, two hymns*; p. 1245, from the library of St. Peter of Chartres: *Here begins the art of Sedulius, the Christian poet*. This is a certain copyist’s note, also observed by us in Ottobonianus 1; concerning it, compare nos. 9 and 45. From the library of the monastery of Lyre, p. 1258: *Sedulius’s Paschal Poem*; from the monastery of St. Peter at Préaux, p. 1266: several copies, apparently, of Sedulius; p. 1270, from the monastery of Saint-Evroult at Ouche: *The works of Sedulius the rhetor*. Our ancient poet Sedulius is called a rhetor by Ratbert and others, as I said at no. 21. From the library of St. Victor at Paris, p. 1375: *Sedulius*; in the same place, from the library of Laon: *Ancient glosses on Virgil and Sedulius*. Thus far the manuscript codices listed from Montfaucon.

**91.** In the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, no. 2506, among the codices of Thomas Bodley: *Five books of Sedulius*—by which I understand the *Paschal Poem* distributed into five books. Labbe, in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, supplement 4, from the library of Charles de Montchal, codex 84, reports:

1. The poems of Sedulius, whose preface differs greatly from the published one;
2. The verses of Liberatus Scholasticus in praise of Sedulius;
3. The verses of Silvius on the names of the Savior;
4. The verses of St. Columbanus;
5. Verses on the Day of Judgment;
6. Arator’s two books on the Acts of the Apostles, together with two letters of his in elegiac verse.

Labbe does not explain what the beginning is of the preface that differs so greatly from the published one. The verses [Col. 0476B] of Silvius on the names of the Savior, which exist in that codex, are also indicated by Montfaucon in the *Library of Manuscripts*, p. 126, codex 553 of the Vatican Library. He reports the first verse:

> Hope, reason, way, life, salvation, wisdom, judge;

and the last:

> Word, man, net, stone, house—Christ is all things, Jesus.

These verses are attributed to St. Damasus. In most editions, among his poems, the first verse is written corruptly, as also in Merenda.

**92.** Antonius Sanderus, in the *Library of Belgian Manuscript Codices*, reports from the library of the Augustinian canons regular at St. Martin’s Valley in Leuven: *The poems and hymns of Sedulius Scotus*. Fabricius, in the *Old Latin Library*, mentions a manuscript of Sedulius at Nuremberg, in the possession of Gottfried Thomasius.

[Col. 0476C] **93.** The catalogue of the manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris indicates the following. Codex 242: *Sedulius’s Paschal Work*, with interlinear glosses of the twelfth or thirteenth century. Codex 7558: *Sedulius’s elegiac poem on the Incarnation of Christ*, ninth century.
