Codex 8092: *The Paschal Poem of Coelius Sedulius in four books*. Also, *The poem of the same author on the miracles of the New Testament in four books*, with the acrostic poems of Liberatus Scholasticus and Silo in praise of Sedulius appended, tenth century. Perhaps these are two copies of the same work. The reason, however, why only four books are counted in many places is, I think, the work’s own division into Book I of the Old Testament and four books of the New Testament. The name Silo appears to have been substituted for Belisarius.

In the same place, codex 8093: *The Paschal Poem of Coelius Sedulius in four books. A comparison of the Old and New Testaments in elegiac verse, by the same author.* [Col. 0476D] Codex 8094: *The Paschal Poem of Coelius Sedulius*, with glosses frequently written between the lines, eleventh century. Codex 8313: *The Paschal Poem of Coelius Sedulius. A comparison of the Old and New Testaments, by the same author*, thirteenth century. Codex 8314: *The Paschal Poem of Coelius Sedulius the presbyter*, thirteenth century. *The Comparison*, etc. *A hymn containing the whole life of Christ*, apparently fifteenth century. Codex 8315: *The Paschal Poem, the Comparison*, etc., by the same author. Codex 8316: *The Paschal Poem, the Comparison*, etc. Codex 8317: *The Paschal Poem with scholia, the Comparison, the Hymn*. Codex 8310: *Sedulius’s hymn on the Life of Christ*. These items indeed belong to our poet; for Sedulius’s little commentary on the *Art* of the grammarian Eutyches, in codex 7830, is believed to belong to another Sedulius, as I said at no. 45.

[Col. 0477A] **94.** Muratori, volume III of the *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 818, transcribes a catalogue of the library of the monastery of Bobbio, written approximately in the tenth century. Among the books of the old library the author lists:

> Four books of the poet Claudian, and in one of these a certain portion of Sedulius and other little works.

Later he lists four books of Sedulius, perhaps four copies. I think one of these was the Turin codex described at no. 62. Among the books which Dungal, the foremost of the Scots, offered to the most blessed Columbanus—that is, to the monastery of Bobbio—was *Sedulius on Orthography*. Among the books of the presbyter Theodore was one book of Sedulius, Juvencus, Prosper, Prudentius, and other versifiers.

In the various readings to Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, before the *Paschal Poem*, the manuscript codices Blandin., Scotti, Roseweydi, and [Col. 0477B] Bollandi are indicated; that letter is illuminated by them in the passage dealing with Syncletica. In the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, among the books which Abbot Wando acquired in the eighth century, are listed “four books containing an exposition of the Four Gospels, published by Sedulius, a most learned man, for the presbyter Macedonius.”

**CHAPTER IV. Editions of Sedulius, his interpreters, and authors of conjectures concerning him**

**95.** **Edition I**, without indication of year, Paris, quarto, from the Ascensian press, edited by Nicolaus Cappusotus. Thus Fabricius in the *Old Latin Library*. I saw it in the Corsini Library under this title:

> *The five books of Coelius Sedulius the presbyter, On Divine Miracles, together with a hymn and an elegiac poem by the same author.*

Jehan Petit. They are sold in Paris, on the road to St. James, under the Silver Lion, and on Mount St. Hilary, under the Mirror.

Nicolaus Cappusotus dedicates the preface to Jean Guillard, a Parisian youth of great promise. At the end:

> On the fifth day before the Kalends of March, from the Ascensian press at Paris.

After the *Paschal Poem* come Sedulius’s epigram, then the hymn and the elegy. Cappusotus had resolved to interpret Sedulius. “I cannot help wondering,” he says, “that so religious and so delightful a writer has not previously been more widely read in the schools of Paris.” He also produces Sedulius’s panegyric from the Gelasian Decree in Gratian, which is repeated in other editions.

59 **96.** An edition in quarto, without year or consul, says Arntzenius, who used it and reports only this from the title:

> *The four books of the Paschal Poem of Sedulius, the most Christian poet. Two worthwhile hymns by the same author.*

A distich for the reader:

> If sacred reading leads you, buy for yourself  
> These sweet poems of Sedulius, the divine singer.

The testimony of Gelasius followed. Arntzenius calls it *Ancient 1*.

**97.** **Edition III.** Arntzenius also saw another edition without indication of year, at the end of which the following was read:

> This work was printed with a happy outcome by the industrious Georg Richolff, at the expense of Laurentius Bornman, in letters of bronze, in the distinguished city of Münster, the most noble metropolis of Westphalia.

Certain epigrams of Martial had been added to this edition. At their end was written:

> The first book of selected epigrams of Valerius Martial, that most charming poet, with the very familiar exposition of Hermannus Busch, happily ends, printed in the most renowned university of Cologne in the year 1509.

From this Arntzenius infers that Sedulius too was printed in the same year, 1509. But, as it appears, these two works had been bound together in one volume, and consequently the definite year of the Sedulius edition cannot be established. Some annotations had been written in the margin by a man who was by no means unlearned, but the letters were so carelessly written that Arntzenius was able to extract little from them. He calls this edition the Münster edition.

**98.** **Edition IV**, 1499, Leipzig, by Jacob Thanner, quarto, from Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, [Col. 0478B] with the notes of Mansi.

**99.** **Edition V**, 1499, Paris, folio, with Juvencus and others, as I explained more fully in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 53. See also Maittaire, *Annales Typographici*, p. 362.

**100.** **Edition VI**, 1501, Milan, edited by Janus Parrhasius. Arntzenius searched for this edition in vain for a long time, since it is extremely rare in the Netherlands. It is not readily encountered at Rome either, but it exists in the possession of the distinguished Bishop Reggio, one of the few equitable and learned judges of more recondite sacred learning. This collection of Christian poets owes him a great deal, both because he is prefect of the Vatican Library and because he is equipped with select books and exceptional philological expertise.

The title is:

> *The Paschal Poem of Sedulius. The poems of Aurelius Prudentius.*

60 The decree of Gelasius concerning Sedulius follows. Then comes Parrhasius’s dedication, or preface, to Michael Riccius of Naples, royal governor of Insubria. This is lacking in the copy before me, and scarcely anything can be read except certain words from the end:

> Meanwhile accept the poem of our Sedulius and that of the most eloquent man Prudentius—would that all his writings existed, or at least that those which are found had not been corrupted by the neglect of the ages. Certainly I would not have undertaken so much labor in correcting them, and those devoted to the study of divine things would lack nothing in this field. But I preferred to have these works, whatever they may be, read rather than perish completely. Please regard them favorably, and love your Janus, who honors you. Farewell, glory of our land. Milan, the Ides of June, 1501.

Parrhasius thought that Prudentius and Sedulius had not previously been published, but he was mistaken. After the preface:

> *The Paschal Poem of Sedulius, the Christian poet.*

Sedulius’s metrical prologue follows, and then the *Paschal Poem*, without any title or division into books. At the end:

> *The Paschal Poem of Sedulius is completed.*

Several hymns of Prudentius are added, as I explained in the commentary on *Peristephanon* hymn 2, verse 1, where, on the basis of letters from the most learned Jacobus Morellus, I noted that this edition exists in the library of St. Mark’s at Venice. I made further observations about this edition in the same place; it is also preserved in the Corsini Library at Rome. I shall present Parrhasius’s observations on Sedulius and Prudentius at no. 189 and following. Arntzenius reports various readings from Parrhasius because he found them written by a learned hand in Georg Fabricius’s edition of the Christian poets.

**101.** **Edition VII**, 1501, published in 1502, Venice, at the press of Aldus, with other Christian poets. I described it in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 60. In the second volume of Christian poets, Aldus gave Sedulius first place under this title:

> *The first book of the Divine Miracles of Coelius Sedulius the presbyter. When the Gentiles with their own…*

The letter to Macedonius and the metrical prologue are missing. The sections are distinguished here and there by their own titles. The first book continues uninterrupted up to the verse *Ora lupi*, which in other editions is the end of the second book. After the *Paschal Poem* comes the elegy *Cantemus*, with the heading *This little work*, etc., concerning which elsewhere; then Sedulius’s epigram, beginning *Haec tua*; and finally 61 C. Sedulius the presbyter’s hymn on Christ, briefly covering the period from the Incarnation to the Ascension. Bayle was unaware of the earlier editions and stated in his dictionary that this was the first edition of Sedulius’s poems.

**102.** **Edition VIII**, 1504, Leipzig, quarto. Grunerus noted its various readings.

**103.** **Edition IX**, 1509. Arntzenius collected its various readings, written in the margin of the Tornesian edition of Sedulius from 1566. The place of publication is unknown. A learned hand had noted only this at the prologue, verse 4:

> Nowhere does a diphthong or accent appear in our edition of 1509.

Salmasius discussed the antiquity of its orthography in his letter to Sarravius, no. 183. Arntzenius calls this edition *Ancient 2*. Perhaps it is not different from the one said in Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle and Lower Ages* to have been produced in Leipzig in 1509 by Jacob Thanner, quarto.

**Edition X**, 1509, Cologne, from Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle Ages*.

**Edition XI**, 1512, Lyon, with the commentaries of Nebrissensis, quarto, from Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle Ages*. Perhaps *Lucronium* should be read instead of *Lugdunum*. See the following note.

**104.** **Edition XII**, 1515, quarto, Zaragoza, with Nebrissensis’s paraphrase. Majansius describes this in *A Specimen of His Library*, p. 27. On the title page Sedulius is depicted explaining a volume, with this title:

> *The Paschal Work of Coelius Sedulius the presbyter*;

and somewhat lower:

> *Sedulius’s Paschal Work, with the commentary of Antonius Nebrissensis*.

At the end of the work:

> *Sedulius’s Paschal Work, together with the remaining little works that exist, written in verse, is completed. Finished at Zaragoza through the labor and expense of Georgius Coci, on 8 September, in the year of Christian salvation 1515, after the first impression, which Antonius Nebrissensis corrected, punctuated, divided by punctuation, and supplied with a paraphrase in the more obscure passages* [sic].

Thus another edition had preceded it, perhaps at Alcalá in 1514, which may have been attached by error in the Library of Nicolás Antonio under the year 1524, or at Lucronium or Lyon, according to what was said in the preceding note. Dempster says that he had not seen Sedulius’s Life, which Gesner and Simler report to have been composed by Nebrissensis. But, in my opinion, Nebrissensis wrote only a brief preface to the poems.

[Col. 0480A] 62 **Edition XIII**, 1516, Turin, at the press of Joannes Angelus and Bernardinus de Silva, under the direction of Joannes Brema. The distinguished Zacharias praises it in his excellent work *Storia Polemica delle proibizioni de’ libri* (*Polemical History of the Prohibitions of Books*), under the year 496, no. 10, p. 51.

**105.** **Edition XIV**, 1524, Alcalá, quarto, with Nebrissensis’s paraphrase, as Nicolás Antonio reports in the *New Spanish Library*, under the entry Antonius Lebrixa, or Nebrixa, in Latin Nebrissensis. He says that Nebrissensis published:

> *A Paraphrase on Sedulius’s Poem concerning the Miracles of Christ*. Alcalá, 1524, quarto,

unless the numbers contain an error—1524 instead of 1514—as I just said. Nicolás Antonio’s *Old and New Library* was reprinted a few years ago at Madrid in very elegant type. In the *Old Library*, the distinguished Franciscus Perez Bayer added his own notes—not as many as the scope of the work warranted, but nevertheless learned and well chosen. In the *New Library* there appear only the posthumous additions of Nicolás Antonio himself. Would that the supplement to the *New Library*, mentioned in the preface to this Madrid edition, had appeared at the same time, or were now finally brought to light. Since the learned men Thomas Antonius Sánchez, Joannes Antonius Pellicer, and Raphael Casalbon devoted much effort and labor to enlarging and correcting the *New Library*, it is greatly to be desired that at least their corrections should be made public.

**106.** **Edition XV**, 1528. Fabricius assigns to this year an edition of Sedulius at Basel in octavo, revised by Theodorus Poelmannus, in the *Old Library*, when he discusses Sedulius; he implies that it was reprinted in 1534 and 1537, and at Cagliari in 1573. He is speaking of an edition of Sedulius together with Juvencus, Arator, and two hymns of Venantius Fortunatus restored to their original integrity by G. Cassander. Yet when Fabricius himself lists the editions of Juvencus, he reports only an edition revised by Poelmannus at Basel without indication of year, preceded by Hadamarius’s letter, which was later reprinted at Cagliari. Compare no. 109. Ceillier likewise mentions a Basel edition of Sedulius from 1528, but, as may be conjectured, on the basis of Fabricius.

**107.** **Edition XVI**, 1534, Basel, octavo, as I recently said on the authority of Fabricius. Ceillier agrees.

108. Seventeenth edition, in the year 1537, in octavo: *The Evangelical Histories of Juvencus the Spaniard and Sedulius the Scots-born [63], priests and most Christian poets, rendered with exactness in heroic verse, now brought forth more polished and much more carefully corrected through the collation of several ancient books*. Cologne, at the press of Eucharius (Cervicornus). Edited by Reinhard Lorich of Hadamar. I also discussed this edition in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 69. After Juvencus comes Sedulius, with his letter to Macedonius and metrical prologue. As in Aldus, the poem is divided into four books. Then follows: “Here begins the hymn of the same author,” etc. This is the elegy *Cantemus*. Finally, Sedulius’ poem, or alphabetic hymn, *A solis ortus*.

109. Eighteenth edition, in the same year, 1537, in octavo: *The Four Books of Juvencus the Spaniard’s Evangelical History. The Four Books of Coelius Sedulius’ Divine Miracles, or Paschal Poem, together with several hymns. The Two Books of Arator on the Acts of the Apostles. Two hymns of Venantius Honorius Fortunatus restored to their integrity by G. Cassander. All revised by Theodorus Poelmannus of Kranenburg*. Basel, without a definite indication of the year, preceded by Hadamar’s letter, from the Cologne edition of the same year, 1537.

In the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, nos. 70 and 75, I conjectured that this edition should be assigned to the year 1551, and I still hold the same view, although Fabricius lists the Basel edition of Sedulius and Juvencus with Arator, etc., under the year 1537. Fabricius, indeed, seems more accurate when, among the editions of Juvencus, he says that this Basel edition of Poelmannus is without a date [Col. 0481B]; yet he is mistaken in asserting that it contains four hymns of Fortunatus restored to their integrity by G. Cassander. In his eulogy of Sedulius he correctly mentions only two.

Poelmannus places Sedulius after Juvencus: he first prints the letter to Macedonius, then the metrical preface. The *Paschal Poem* is divided into four books, in such a way, namely, that the third consists of the third and fourth books of our edition. After the poem comes “The elegy of Coelius Sedulius, *Cantemus*,” etc. After the elegy, “The hymn of Coelius Sedulius, *A solis*,” etc. After the hymn comes the epigram on the four Evangelists, “Matthew instituted,” etc., which in our edition of Juvencus was placed, from a very ancient exemplar, as Juvencus’ first preface. In Poelmannus’ codex the author’s name was not written. After the epigram come acrostic verses on Sedulius: “Sedulius [Col. 0481C] of the Lord,” and “Sedulius of Christ,” with the authors’ name omitted. At the end of the volume, after the various readings added to Juvencus, several others on Sedulius are included; these also appear to have been placed in their proper locations in the margins of the poems.

110. Nineteenth edition, in the year 1538. Gruner collated the Cologne edition of Sedulius from this year, in octavo.

111. Twentieth edition, in the same year, 1536, at Antwerp, at the press of the Widow of Martin Caesar, in octavo, according to Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

112. Twenty-first edition, in the year 1541, in octavo: *The Paschal Work, or Five Books of Divine Miracles, of Coelius Sedulius, a priest both most devout and most learned, with the most lucid commentaries of Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis. We have also added the Evangelical History of Juvencus the Spaniard, a priest, on the same subject, together with commentaries on it. Everything collated with and corrected against the most ancient exemplars*. Basel, 1541. I also mentioned this edition in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 71.

The printer is Westhemerus, who also added a preface. I have seen Nebrissensis’ commentaries only in this edition; Arntzenius and other recent editors of Sedulius entirely lacked them. After Nebrissensis’ preface, the letter to Macedonius is omitted, and Sedulius’ metrical prologue begins: “The Paschal [Poem] of Sedulius.” Then comes the poem divided into five books; thereafter: “Here begins the hymn of the same author,” etc. This is the elegy *Cantemus*. Finally: “The iambic dimeter hymn of Sedulius the priest,” etc. Nebrissensis’ commentaries are placed among the verses.

[Col. 0482A] Twenty-second edition, in the year 1545. Basel, in octavo, with Juvencus and Arator, collated with the Rottendorf codex and other manuscript codices, according to Fabricius and Reusch in their catalogue of Juvencus’ editions. Perhaps this is a different edition from the Basel Sedulius of the same year with Nebrissensis’ commentary, which is listed in Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Sedulius.”

113. Twenty-third edition, in the year 1548. Basel, in octavo, with Juvencus and Arator, according to Fabricius among the editions of Sedulius. I fear that in so many Basel editions there may be some fraud on the part of booksellers, who often reprint the first title-page of books so that the edition may appear new. Perhaps the date 1548 is also an error for 1545.

114. Twenty-fourth edition, in the year 1551. Basel, in octavo, edited by Poelmannus, as I stated under the year 1537, according to the catalogue of the [Col. 0482B] royal library of Paris. In the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 75, I doubted, and I still doubt, whether this was Poelmannus’ first edition or a reprint.

115. Twenty-fifth edition, in the same year, 1551. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLIX, chapter 5, cites a Lyon edition of this year, which presents Arator, Sedulius, and Juvencus as completely renewed according to the reading of the manuscripts.

116. Twenty-sixth edition, in the year 1553. Lyon, with Juvencus, in duodecimo, which Arntzenius collated and calls the first Tornaesian edition. It also contains Arator. I mentioned it in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 76.

117. Twenty-seventh edition, in the year 1554. Basel, as Ceillier reports.

[Col. 0482C] 118. Twenty-eighth edition, in the year 1564, with other Christian poets, edited by Georg Fabricius, as I explained at greater length in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius, Juvencus,* and *Dracontius*. Arntzenius confirms what I said about Fabricius in the place cited:

> “He allowed himself, in one or two places, what he ought not to have allowed,”

as Daumius judges, in Heinsius’ letter 223, volume V of Burmann’s *Sylloge*. He did the same in Sedulius, usually transposing words whenever the laws of meter seemed to suffer some damage; these transpositions, although by no means based on the manuscripts, were nevertheless sometimes eagerly adopted by later editors. I have often observed this in the transposed word *JUGIS*, . . . although in certain instances Fabricius certainly had predecessors whom he followed.

119. Twenty-ninth edition, in the year 1566, with Juvencus and Arator, in duodecimo or sextodecimo, which Arntzenius calls the second Tornaesian edition. I too used it, from the extremely rich library of the excellent prince, the most eminent Cardinal Valenti Gonzaga. See the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 78.

120. Thirtieth edition, in the year 1568. Leipzig, as Ceillier reports, who states that it is in octavo, with other Christian poets, prepared by G. Fabricius. I think this is nothing other than what Fabricius mentions in *Bibliotheca Latina*, book IV, chapter 2, among the editions of Prudentius:

> “The exposition of Georg Fabricius on the three *Paeans* of Prudentius, Sedulius, and Fortunatus, on the Life and Death of Christ, and on three other hymns of Prudentius, and on the Roman martyr.”

Leipzig, 1568, in octavo. A hundred marked adages are appended.

In Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca medii aevi* [Col. 0483A], among the editions of Sedulius, a Basel edition in quarto, from the year 1566, in G. Fabricius’ *Christian Poets*, is listed; but this is not different from the edition that I assigned to the year 1564.

121. Thirty-first edition, in the year 1573, at Cagliari, reprinted from Poelmannus’ edition, as I explained more fully in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 80.

122. Thirty-second edition, 1575. Paris, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, by Margarin de la Bigne, volume VIII, where the *Paschal Poem*, the elegy, and the hymn are found. Sedulius appeared with some variation in other *Bibliothecae Patrum*. For in the second edition, Paris 1589, and in the appendix to Margarin’s *Bibliotheca*, Paris 1624, the *Paschal Poem*, elegy, and alphabetic hymn are attributed to Sedulius; nevertheless the elegy is printed again under this title:

> “The *Collation of the Old and New Testament* of Turcius Rufius Asterius, a man of consular rank,”

until now attributed to Sedulius.

It is noted that Asterius was consul with Flavius Praesidius. On the authority of Cuspinianus and Aldus, it is added that this poem was published by Asterius and inscribed to Sedulius; on that of Panvinius, that it was inscribed and sent to Turcius; and that manuscript codices exist which say that it is by Claudianus Mamertus. The elegy is printed in the same way, and this very point is noted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Cologne, 1618; yet in that *Bibliotheca* the elegy is not listed among Sedulius’ works.

“Cn. Spinianus” for “Cuspinianus,” and “Panninius” for “Panvinius,” are errors repeated in these *Bibliothecae*. The entire account is false, as is clear from nos. 46 and 162. To Sedulius these *Bibliothecae* add acrostic verses by Liberius and Belisarius about him; and in the Cologne *Bibliotheca* of 1618, the *Paschal Poem* is preceded by a preface to the emperor Theodosius, *Romulidum ductor*, which we have denied to be by Sedulius.

After Belisarius’ acrostic comes Sedulius’ *Paschal Work*, or prose; then the *Collection on the Epistles of Paul*, which belongs to another Sedulius. Sedulius was likewise printed in other *Bibliothecae Patrum*, especially in the Lyon edition of 1677.

123. Thirty-third edition, in the year 1588, Lyon, in duodecimo or sextodecimo; see no. 82 of the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*. Joannes Albertus Fabricius possessed this edition, collated by Nicolaus Heinsius with manuscripts. Arntzenius calls it the third Tornaesian edition and observes that nearly the same readings are preserved in this third Tornaesian edition and in the Lyon *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*.

67. 124. Thirty-fourth edition, in the year 1603, in the *Corpus of Latin Poets*, Lyon, in quarto. To this I refer the other editions of the *Corpus* and the *Chorus of Latin Poets* reviewed in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 83. Nor are the other works dissimilar which contain more of Sedulius, such as the *Flores Poetarum* and Albert Eyb’s *Margarita Poetica*. I add Hieronymus Freyer’s *Fasciculus of Latin Poems*, in which selected poems of Ausonius, Prudentius, Claudian, Sedulius, Boethius, and Columbanus are included, besides other ancient and recent poets. Halle in Saxony, 1713.

125. Thirty-fifth edition, in the year 1610. Sedulius’ *Collation of the Old and New Testament*, or the elegy *Cantemus*, etc., in the *Biblical Manual*, Frankfurt 1610, p. 13. I described this *Manual* in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 113. Sedulius’ elegy was published with the hymn in the Venerable Thomasius’ *Hymnary*; the hymn also appeared in Alcuin’s *Offices for the Ferias*, and at Leipzig in 1522, in octavo, by Petrus Mosellanus, after the book *Cathemerinon*, according to Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, under “Sedulius.”

Thirty-sixth edition, in the year 1701, Edinburgh, in octavo, which is regarded as accurate and is listed in Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca medii aevi* on the authority of Georg Mackenzie’s *On the Learned Scots*, volume I, p. 346. This, in my opinion, is the edition Arntzenius calls the Scottish and Edinburgh edition.

126. Thirty-seventh edition, in the year 1704, in octavo, edited by Cellarius. *The Books of Divine Miracles of Coelius Sedulius, the Most Elegant of the Ancient Christian Poets, Called the Paschal Poem, and Two Hymns*. Christoph Cellarius revised it from manuscript codices and illustrated it with notes. Halle in Magdeburg, at the expense of the Orphanotrophium. This edition is accurate and adapted for use in schools.

127. Thirty-eighth edition, in the year 1739, a Cellarian edition reprinted in Germany, according to Arntzenius, who says that it was disgraced by errors more shamefully than the earlier edition.

128. Thirty-ninth edition, in the year 1747, in octavo. *The Five Books of Coelius Sedulius’ Divine Miracles, or Paschal Poem. Also Two Hymns, Revised According to the Authority of Manuscript Codices and Ancient Editions, with Various Readings, Observations, and Necessary Indices Added*, by Joannes Fridericus Gruner. Leipzig, at the press of Joannes Wendlerus.

Gruner is diligent and comprehensive in recording the variant readings, and occasionally appends brief and learned notes. Arntzenius, with a more acrid pen, reproaches Gruner [Col. 0484C] for his treatment of Vonck’s conjectures; he also points out several typographical errors in the transcription of the poem, though certainly not many.

129. Fortieth edition, in the year 1761, in octavo. *The Five Books of Coelius Sedulius’ Paschal Poem and Two Hymns, with the Notes of Caspar Barthius, Christoph Cellarius, Cornelius Valerius Vonck, Joannes Fridericus Gruner, and Others; to Which Are Added the More Correct Adversaria of Thomas Wopkensis, for the Most Part Still Unpublished*, edited by Henricus Joannes Arntzenius, I. F., who added a specimen of notes and observations. Leeuwarden, at the press of H. A. de Chalmot.

Sedulius owes much to Arntzenius, who collected the choicest materials from others and added much from his own resources, being learned beyond his age, but [Col. 0484D] in such a way that, even if he himself did not repeatedly boast of it, one could easily recognize that he was still too young. The specimen of observations that he added, arranged in thirteen chapters, has nothing to do with Sedulius except for one or two chapters.

130. Forty-first edition, in the year 1773, edited and prepared by Gallandius in volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 533. *The Five Books of the Paschal Poem of Sedulius the Priest and Two Hymns, from the Edition of Christoph Cellarius, Now Revised Again and Collated with a Manuscript Codex of the Royal Library of Turin, and Enlarged by the Poem On the Incarnation of the Word.* There were also added the five books of the *Paschal Work*, first published and annotated through the efforts of Franciscus Juretus, now revised and corrected again. [Col. 0485A] Gallandius used Cellarius’ selected notes and added some of his own.

131. I shall now add a few remarks about Sedulius’ commentators and about others who wrote observations or conjectures on his poems. Glosses occur everywhere in manuscript codices, and in some they are more extensive; from them the true reading is sometimes recovered, while at other times an obscure meaning is explained. We have used such ancient glosses whenever it seemed appropriate.

After the restoration of letters, the first to consider the elucidation of Sedulius was Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis. He published brief notes adapted to the use of the School, though they could also assist theologians. It is less surprising that he sometimes went astray than that he was the very first to bring so many excellent interpretations [Col. 0485B] into the light.

69 132. To Nebrissensis we add two other Spaniards. One of them, Bartholomaeus Morlanes, wrote commentaries and notes on several poets, specifically on Prudentius, Alcimus Avitus, Marius Victor, Juvencus, Sedulius, and Arator, as I related in a note in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 259. Later Nicolaus Antonius’ *Bibliotheca Hispana* was reprinted at Madrid, and in its posthumous additions mention is made of Bartholomaeus Morlanes; it is indicated that his manuscript commentaries still exist at Zaragoza.

An older commentator than Morlanes, and a contemporary of Nebrissensis himself, was Joannes Soprarius. Nicolaus Antonius praises his commentaries on Sedulius the poet in the *Bibliotheca Nova Hispanica*, citing an epigram by Lucius Marineus Siculus [Col. 0485C], book II of the *Carmina*, from which I select these few couplets:

> If anyone, with me as judge, compares outstanding poets,  
> Great is Sedulius’ glory, great his honor.  
> Read these holy poems, believe me, master:  
> They will make your disciples learned and holy.  
> For if any poems contain hidden meanings,  
> Sobrarius will render them all in prose.

Marineus calls him Sobrarius, not Soprarius, in his poems, which were published after the letters at Valladolid in the year 1514.

133. Georg Fabricius also explains several passages of Sedulius in his *Commentaries on the Christian Poets*, together with the other authors. Barthius very often, especially in his *Adversaria*, emends and explains Sedulius’ verses from manuscripts and from his own conjectures. Thus he says in *Adversaria*, book LIV, chapter 7:

> “I confess that in the ancient Christian poets I love the very simplicity both of diction and of thought; and the purer it is, the more deservedly pleasing it is. For that swelling style and the painted display of affected eloquence do not allow the mind to rejoice in the pure sweetness of things infused into the rhythms. I wish, as a repayment, that those blessed souls should receive this from me: that their writings, through my efforts, may be read in a more corrected form. Let Sedulius enter the discussion—or rather return to it—whose fourth book, etc.”

And after much else:

> “We have also charged our Sedulius with this here. At one time we wrote complete notes on him, as we also indicated in that earlier edition of Claudian; but I fear that they may slip into other hands, and that this author, dear to us nevertheless, must be commended to posterity by us with these few and slender remarks, if he cannot be explained in most of his more difficult passages [Col. 0486A]. Yet the fair-minded reader will find even this here.”

Certainly Barthius brought great illumination to almost all ancient writers, but at times he wants to force them, through his subtle conjectures, to speak as perplexedly and obscurely as he himself does. For the most part, it is easier to understand the works of the authors whom he attempts to elucidate than his own commentaries.

134. Daumius had resolved to publish a more carefully corrected corpus of Christian poets, among whom Sedulius had his place. On this subject, see Heinsius’ letters 87 and 92 in Burmann’s *Sylloge*. Arntzenius says that Daumius could have made an outstanding contribution concerning the poets of the later period, although Withof, in his dissertation *On the True Author of the Distichs of Cato*, p. 561, seems to regard him as a man of greater diligence and learning than judgment.

Arntzenius likewise suspects that Joannes Albertus Fabricius intended to secure some distinction for Sedulius when he planned to publish part of the Christian poets, as Reimarus reports in his *Life*, p. 209.

135. Cornelius Valerius Vonck published two books of *Latin Readings* at Utrecht in 1745, in octavo; in book I, chapter 6, he endeavors to purify Sedulius through conjectures, which Arntzenius inserted into his notes. I willingly accept Gruner’s judgment of Vonck and declare it true:

> “Vonck,” he says, “is too inclined to innovation and more concerned with correcting the writings of the ancients than with understanding them.”

The critical observations of Thomas Wopkensis on Sedulius are found in the *Miscellaneous Critical Observations on Ancient and Recent Authors*, volume IV. [Col. 0486C] Later he sent Arntzenius his *Adversaria* of corrected observations, so that they might serve a new edition of Sedulius. Wopkensis, as Arntzenius admits, applied a correcting hand based solely on conjecture rather than assisted by the authority of manuscripts.

Gruner’s judgment of Wopkensis’ emendations is perfectly fair: many things, he says, are expressed admirably and with the greatest judgment, while some should be abandoned. It would be tedious, and indeed unnecessary, to enumerate the many others who corrected or elucidated particular passages of Sedulius.

71 CHAPTER V. On Asterius, who collected Sedulius’ poems; and on Liberius and Belisarius, who adorned Sedulius with acrostic verses.

136. In many manuscript codices of Sedulius it is noted that Asterius collected and published Sedulius’ scattered poems [Col. 0486D]; but since this is explained differently by different writers, the very words of the codices must be brought under examination.

Our most ancient Vatican codex, Reg. 1, reads as follows:

> “Sedulius left this work scattered on separate sheets; it was collected, united, and published with every elegance by Turcius Rufius Asterius, a distinguished man, former ordinary consul, and patrician.”

In the codex one reads *in certa*, but this is plainly an error for *in certas*. Although this note is separated from the work in this codex, as I stated in no. 66, it nevertheless seems to have been taken from another codex in which it preceded the metrical prologue. Immediately after the note Asterius’ epigram is copied:

> “Receive, sacred in merits,” etc.,

but it is not stated who this “sacred in merits” person is.

Reg. 3, immediately after the letter to Macedonius, reads as follows [Col. 0487A]:

> “Sedulius left this work scattered among the sheets. It was collected, united, and published with every elegance by Turcius Rufius Asterius Quintus, a most distinguished man, former ordinary consul, and patrician.”

The *Paschal Poem* apparently followed; only its final portion is found in this codex.

The Ottobonian codex I gives the same note after the letter to Macedonius and before the explanation of the metrical prologue, although after this explanation the metrical prologue itself does not immediately follow, but rather the hymn *A solis ortus*, as I explained in no. 75. It differs from Reg. 1 in reading *inter chartulas* instead of *in certas chartulas*, and later *devulgatum*; it also reads “by Turtio Ruffo Asterius Quintus, vicarious consul in ordinary,” etc.

The words *Quinto vicario*, which are also found in several other codices, were inserted by ignorant scribes [Col. 0487B] in place of *V. C.*, that is, *viro clarissimo*, “a most distinguished man,” as many have observed. This codex likewise does not identify the person whom Asterius addresses when he says, “Receive, sacred in merits.” In Vatican codex 2, which is fairly recent, the same note is placed at the end of the *Paschal Poem*. It also differs from Reg. 1 in the following readings: *inter chartulas . . . et adunatum, atque omni elegantia d. e. a Turcio Rufio Asterio Quinto V. C. exconsule ordinario, atque patricio*.

137. Sirmondus, in his notes on Ennodius, book I, letter 24, produces from a Reims codex Asterius’ epigram, “Receive, sacred in merits,” etc., which he says was addressed to the same Macedonius to whom Sedulius dedicated the *Paschal Poem*. He observes that after Sedulius’ letter to Macedonius there is this note:

> “This work,” etc.,

as in Reg. 1, though with the following differences: *inter chartulas d. r. q. r. adornatumque, a. a. o. e. d. e. a Turcio Rufio Asterio V. C. consule ordinario*, etc. The epigram follows: “Receive, sacred.”

Labbeus, in *Bibliotheca Nova of Manuscripts*, part I, p. 23, testifies that he saw a copy of the *Paschal Work*—by which I mean the *Paschal Poem*—mutilated at the beginning, at whose end there was the same note:

> “This work of Sedulius, scattered among the sheets, was collected, united, and published with every elegance by Turtio Rufio Asterius, former ordinary consul and patrician.”

Then came Asterius’ verses, “Receive, sacred in merits,” etc.

Bandinius found the same note in the Laurentian Library codex that I reviewed in no. 86:

> “This work of Sedulius, scattered among the sheets, which was collected and united, and published with every elegance by Tertius Rufius Austerius, a most distinguished man, former ordinary consul, and patrician.”

Usserius reports nearly the same words from the Thorney manuscript, placed at the beginning of the *Paschal Poem* [Col. 0487D]:

> “This work of Sedulius, scattered among the sheets, was collected and united, and published with every elegance by Turcius Rufinus Asterius Quintus, ordinary consul and patrician.”

138. Barthius found Asterius’ epigram in very ancient parchment manuscripts, prefixed to the *Paschal Work* under this heading:

> “The Paschal Work, which was collected, united, and published with every elegance by Turcius Russius Asterius Quintus, former ordinary consul and patrician. First book of the Paschal Poem.”

A fragment of Sedulius’ letter to Macedonius follows. The Almeloveen codex reads:

> “This work of Sedulius, scattered among the sheets, was collected and united, and published with every elegance by Turcius Rufus Asterius Quintus, a most distinguished man, ordinary consul and patrician.”

The Arntzenian codex, however, reads:

> “This work of Sedulius, scattered among the sheets, was collected, adorned, and composed and published with every elegance by Turcius Rufus Asterius, a most distinguished man, former ordinary consul and patrician.”

Wilthemius also found in the codex of St. Albins the words “former ordinary consul and patrician,” the rest being as in the Reims codex cited by Sirmondus. Labbeus confirms this in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he observes that in the manuscript of St. Albins the note and Asterius’ epigram are appended to the *Paschal Poem*, whereas in the Reims manuscript they are inserted between the letter to Macedonius and Sedulius’ metrical preface.

In a very ancient Turin codex another hand wrote, partly in red letters—most of which have faded—and partly in black, apparently copying from another codex, a note about Asterius. From it Count Galeanus Napione was able to transcribe only the following:

> “Here begins the work of Robaeus, that is, your … amen … book … first … four … Sedulius left [it] among his sheets, and they were collected and united by Tuscius Rufus Asterius, a most distinguished man, former ordinary consul and patrician, the editor of the books above written.”

I shall suggest in the commentary on the metrical prologue that *Bobio* should perhaps be read instead of *Robeo*. Other portions may perhaps be explained in something like the following manner:

> “Here begins the Sacred Work, that is, the first book of the Old Testament. The other four books of the New Testament Sedulius …”

The distinguished Franciscus Antonius Zacharias, *On the Prohibition of Books*, under the year 496, no. 10, simply denies that a notice concerning Asterius as Sedulius’ corrector exists in the Turin codex. Either the note sent to me escaped him, or he means only that no such note was written by the first hand.

139. Once these matters have been set out, we must ask why in recent editions of Sedulius Asterius’ epigram appears under this heading:

> “The epigram of Turcius Rufius Asterius, who collected and published Sedulius’ poems after his death, addressed to the same Macedonius to whom Sedulius had dedicated his work.”

In no manuscript codex is the name of the person to whom the epigram is addressed expressly given. For what Sirmondus says—that the epigram was directed to the same Macedonius to whom the *Paschal Poem* was dedicated—he apparently did not take from the codex; rather, he inferred it from the fact that he found in his manuscript the note mentioned after Sedulius’ letter to Macedonius. He produces no title for the epigram from the codex.

But the manuscript codices do not all place the note in the same location: some put it at the beginning of the poem, others at the end, and others elsewhere, as we have seen. Even if the fixed position of that inscription, or note, had been after the letter to Macedonius [Col. 0488D], this would still not be certain evidence that Asterius dedicated the edition of Sedulius to Macedonius in that epigram. Indeed, as Labbeus observes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, even if Macedonius were mentioned in that note in some manuscript, it could not nevertheless be certainly inferred that he was the same Macedonius whom Sedulius and Asterius addressed.

It may also have happened—as commonly happens—that some copyist, having read Asterius’ epigram after the letter to Macedonius, invented the heading that now stands there, thinking that Asterius’ epigram had been dedicated to the same person to whom Sedulius’ letter was addressed.

[Col. 0489A] 140. Let us nevertheless retain the note prefixed to Asterius’ epigram. In transcribing it, the manuscript codices differ among themselves. I think that the wording given by Reg. 1 is more accurate:

> “Sedulius left this work scattered on separate sheets,”

in place of the reading found in the others, “scattered among the sheets.” Sedulius therefore composed the *Paschal Poem* not as a work contained in a single volume, but scattered on separate sheets. For the reading found elsewhere, “scattered among the sheets,” would suggest that the poem had been hidden among several other sheets of Sedulius, which I consider less likely.

Our Reg. 1 codex continues:

> “It was collected, united, and published with every elegance.”

Others read *adornatum* (“adorned”) in place of *adunatum* (“united”); but *adunatum* seems preferable. Since the poem had been scattered on separate sheets, Asterius collected and united it, and so forth.

Even if one prefers to read *adornavit*, this word, as well as those that follow, must be understood as referring to the adornment and elegance of the codex or volume, not as implying that Asterius thought himself entitled to alter anything in Sedulius’ words. In the epigram he says only of himself:

> “Through whose effort and care it was published for the peoples.”

The *Paschal Poem*, therefore, collected from many sheets and reduced to a single body, and elegantly transcribed, was published, or disseminated, to the people by Asterius. It also seems to have been Asterius’ care that the poem should be published in corrected form.

141. The ancient exemplars do not agree sufficiently in giving his names. The following seem preferable: *Turcius Rufius Asterius*. In place of *Turcius*, some have *Turtius* or *Tertius*; in place of *Rufius*, others have *Ruffus* or *Rufus* or *Russius*.

In Sedulius’ manuscript codices, as in the epigram itself, the name *Asterius* is consistently found, except in the Medicean Library codex, whose title gives *Austerius*. In other documents we find at various times *Austerius*, *Astorius*, *Aterius*, *Austurius*, *Asturius*, *Astyrius*, and *Hasterius*, unless we suppose these to be different family names, as some wish.

The name of the Turcii was once famous, as is clear from ancient inscriptions and other monuments. Sometimes *Turgius* is written instead, through the error by which C is often changed into G. Some authors have *Turcicus* and *Curtius Rufus Apronianus*, because certain inscriptions were badly copied.

Panuinius, book III of the *Fasti*, under the year 494, names “Turcius Secundus Asterius”; but he inserted the name *Secundus* by mistake. Norisius discusses the Turcia Aproniana Asteria family in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, dissertation 4, and Muratorius in dissertation 1 on the poems of Paulinus.

The cognomen *Rufus* is found in many Roman families. Quintilian writes of it as follows, book I, chapter 4, section 7:

> “He will investigate the origins of names, such as those which, from bodily appearance, produced the names Cicero, Rufus, and Longus.”

For this reason it seems contrary to orthography to write *Ruffus*. From personal names, praenomina, and cognomina, numerous gentile names were derived, such as the Decimii, Sextii, Tullii, and Quinctii. It is therefore preferable, with many codices, to retain the name *Rufius* rather than *Rufi*, found in others. In the inscription of the Medicean Virgil codex, which will be produced shortly in no. 145, these three names are clearly given: *Turcius Rufius Apronianus*.

[Col. 0490A] 142. Many Asteriuses occur among pagans, Christians, saints, bishops, and every other class of distinguished men. But the Asterius whom we must seek is the one who lived after Sedulius, who was consul, and whose name was Turcius Rufius Asterius.

There were two consuls named Asterius in the fifth century: one in the year 449 with Protogenes, the other in the year 494 with Praesidius. The former Asterius was the one who collected Sedulius’ poems, according to Sirmondus in his notes on Ennodius, book I, letter 24; Cellarius, p. 10 of his edition; and Arntzenius, chapter 10 of his *Specimen of Observations*, who supports this opinion with many arguments.

Sirmondus’ reasoning seems to have been the following: Asterius, who published Sedulius’ poems after collecting them into a single body, sent or directed them to the same Macedonius to whom Sedulius had dedicated the poem [Col. 0490B]. Moreover, Asterius who was consul with Protogenes in 449 is closer in time to Sedulius, who flourished around the year 430, than is Asterius who was consul with Praesidius in 494.

143. Arntzenius advances this same argument, because Asterius appears to have been joined by a bond of friendship to Sedulius and Macedonius. He was certainly a friend of the latter, as the words of Asterius’ epigram prove: “and your Asterius,” etc.

It is impossible, or scarcely possible, for Macedonius, whom Sedulius calls the father and teacher of many, to have lived until the year 494, when the other Asterius was consul.

Moreover, it must be held that the Asterius who corrected Virgil’s codex and composed an epigram about this correction is the same Asterius who adorned his edition of Sedulius with a similar epigram, especially because in the epigram on the corrected Virgil codex he says:

> “And, living on, sends his own Asterius into future ages,”

a verse that reveals the author of the epigram prefixed to Sedulius:

> “And bid me always remember your Asterius.”

That Asterius who revised the Medicean Virgil codex was the earlier Asterius, consul in 449, is proved by Arntzenius on the authority of Heinsius, in his letter to Papebrochius, no. 495, volume II of Burmann’s *Sylloge*, and in his letters to Reinesius, volume V, pp. 191 and 197, as well as by Reinesius’ letter to Heinsius, volume V, letter 178.

Finally, in most manuscript codices Asterius, Sedulius’ editor, is called a former consul. The second Asterius, however, was consul in the year 494, the year in which the decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received and not to be received was issued; there Sedulius and his work are commended in a distinguished eulogy.

144. These are, broadly speaking, arguments of no little weight in favor of Sirmondus’ opinion. Nevertheless, I prefer the opposing view, which was also held by Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca Latina*, Fontaninus in *On Antiquities*, Hortus, book II, chapter 3, Norisius in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, dissertation 4, Pagius in his notes on Baronius under the year 494, and others.

In the notes on Baronius under the year 449 in the Lucca edition, the consul Asterius of that year is called simply Asterius, without any other name, on the authority of Relandus and Marcellinus. In the *Fasti* of Idacius and Victor, and in an epistle of Pope Leo to Flavianus preserved in ancient codices of the Church of Verona, he is called *Asturius*; in Prosper’s Vatican manuscript, *Astyrius*; in certain recent compilers of the *Fasti*, [Col. 0491A] *Flavius Asturius*; and in others, *Turcicus Secundus Asterius*. In the Greek *Fasti* of Heraclius he is called *Astyrius*; Sidonius, letter 6 of book VIII, calls him *Asterius*. In the *Codex Justinianus*, book V, title 17, *On Divorce*, law 8, the subscription reads:

> “Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Protogenes and Asterius.”

Others have *Astori* or *Astorio*, as in Ferretus, *Lapidary Museum*, 3, 14:

> “Octavius dedicates this altar to Asterius, who deserved it.”

For *Asterio*, some read *Astorio*.

Nothing else concerning the praenomen *Flavius* is produced from ancient monuments except the Leodium diptych, on the ivory cover of a Gospel book:

> “Fl. Astyrius, a most distinguished and illustrious man, count and master of both soldiers, ordinary consul.”

[Col. 0491B] Wilthemius illustrated this diptych; Norisius and Sirmondus discuss it, the latter writing *Asturius*, while Pagius, together with Wilthemius and Norisius, has *Astyrius*.

145. These authors, however, disagree among themselves. For in the same Leodiense diptych Norisius and Pagius recognize Asterius as the colleague of Protogenes in the consulship of 449, and therefore attach to him the praenomen *Flavius*. Wilthemius understands this same Asterius to be the consul of 449, but considers him to have been Flavius Turcius Rufius Asterius, who possessed these four names. Sirmondus thinks that the reference is to Asterius, consul with Praesidius in 494. He adds that Asturius, the colleague of Praesidius, appears to have been different from the Asturius to whom Ennodius sent Letter 24 of Book I.

It is difficult to settle this question except by conjecture. This seems to me highly probable: the Flavius Asterius praised in the diptych was different [Col. 0491C] from Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius, who corrected the Virgil manuscript. For since the latter set out these four names of his distinctly, he would not have omitted the name *Flavius*—which alone is read together with the name *Asterius* in the diptych—if he himself had been called by that name. It may also be added that *Flavius* appears rather to be the name of the Flavian *gens*; accordingly, there were two Asterii of different *gentes*: Flavius Asterius and Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius.

Norisius conjectures with sufficient prudence that the consul Asterius, or rather Asturius, of 449 was that Asturius whom Idacius mentions under the year 443: “Merobaudes, his son-in-law, is sent into Spain as successor to Asturius, master of both services.” Asterius, or Astyrius, praised in the Leodiense diptych, had already been master of both services when he was consul, and [Col. 0491D] for that reason is called “former master of both services.”

*[78]*

146. Asterius, who punctuated and corrected the Virgil manuscript, assigns himself several other titles, but not the title “master of both services.” Nor does it seem likely that the titles of Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius would have been omitted from the Leodiense diptych, especially the title “former prefect of the city” and that of patrician, which were highly distinguished, if that Asterius were truly being described in the diptych.

Here is the subscription preserved in the very ancient Medicean manuscript of Virgil:

> TURCIUS RUFIUS APRONIANUS ASTERIUS, V. C. AND ILL., FORMER COUNT OF THE DOMESTICS, FORMER PROTECTOR, FORMER COUNT OF THE PRIVATE LARGESSES, FORMER PREFECT OF THE CITY, PATRICIAN [Col. 0492A] AND ORDINARY CONSUL, READ AND PUNCTUATED THE CODEX OF HIS BROTHER MACARIUS, V. C.—NOT TRUSTING IN MY OWN ABILITY, BUT IN THAT OF HIM TO WHOM I AM DEVOTED IN ALL THINGS, ACCORDING TO HIS JUDGMENT—ON THE ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY, AT ROME. OF PUBLIUS VERGILIUS MARO.

“Read and punctuated”: while correcting it and accepting the welcome service of a friend, I applied myself diligently to the work.

> THE BOOK OF THE BUCOLICS ENDS

> At the time when we yoked winged horses to the Circus, and raised an improvised stage upon the Euripus,
>
> so that Rome might joyfully behold games, chariots, and the varied contest of beasts all together.
>
> For I won three cries of *sophos* (“bravo”); three ranks of the crowd [Col. 0492B] resounded with my applause through the tiers.
>
> The loss of money ran toward the acquisition of fame. For such losses produce the fruit of praise.
>
> Thus the spectacles preserve so many spent treasures, and of the three festival days one day remains.
>
> And his living fame transmits Asterius to the ages, who so generously bestows wealth upon the purple robes.

> HERE BEGINS, WITH GOOD FORTUNE, BOOK I OF THE GEORGICS

> Whoever you are who read, read again happily, and kindly spare any point at which your mind, not wholly unoccupied, may have passed by.

At “Toward the acquisition of fame” a variant reading is noted, namely “toward the price.” Above, *benigne* is marked as corrected to *benignus*. These verses are presented for the most part in a corrupt form by Mabillonius, *De re diplomatica*, Norisius, and others. An asterisk marks the beginning of a new line.

147. Norisius discusses this manuscript exceptionally well, as well as its antiquity and excellence, in the place cited. He observes that [Col. 0492C], according to Holstenius’s opinion, it appears to have been written around the time of Valens or Theodosius, and later given by Macarius, a man of senatorial rank, to his friend Asterius. For this reason Asterius calls Macarius first his “brother,” then his “friend.”

This manuscript once belonged to Cardinal Rodulphus Carpensis; afterward it belonged to Cardinal de Monte, who later became Julius III, as may be gathered from a letter of Cosimo I, grand duke of Etruria, addressed to him in 1567, cited by Biscionius, *Catalogus Codicum Orientalium Bibliothecae Mediceo-Laurentianae*, preface, p. 39, and by Bandini, vol. II of the catalogue of the same library, p. 282 and following. Many assert that the same manuscript belonged to Achilles Statius, whose epigram is read at the beginning, and to the Vatican Library. They nevertheless seem to have been misled by an error.

The epigram of Achilles Statius does indeed indicate that the manuscript did not then belong to him, but to Cardinal Rodulphus Pius. Moreover [Col. 0492D], Cosimo I’s letter of 1567 could not have been addressed to Cardinal de Monte, who later became Julius III, as Biscionius asserts, since Julius III had died long before; indeed, Cardinal Rodulphus survived him, and in that letter is said already to have died.

Nor is that letter—perhaps written to another Cardinal de Monte—at all an effective argument against Manutius, who had used this manuscript and, in that very period, under the word *aethereus* in his *Orthographia*, reported that Rodulphus had bequeathed the manuscript to the Vatican Library: “And I think,” he adds, “that it was stolen by someone.”

The entire manuscript was printed at Florence [Col. 0493A], with types reproducing forms of the letters extremely similar to those of the manuscript and with exactly the same punctuation and corrections that Asterius had added. Peter Francis Foggini reviewed the edition and promised in his preface a separate work in which he intended to discuss the manuscript, Asterius, and so forth. The specimen of the script presented by Foggini differs considerably from that which Mabillonius published on plate 6 of *De re diplomatica*.

148. Once the distinction has been established between Flavius Asterius, the consul praised in the Leodiense diptych, and Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius, the consul and corrector of the Virgil manuscript, it is easy to show that the editor of Sedulius was not Flavius Asterius but Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius. This follows both from the similar style of the epigram prefixed to the Virgil manuscript and that prefixed to Sedulius’s poem, and from the three names of Sedulius’s editor, “Turcius Rufius Asterius.” For the name *Apronianus* [Col. 0493B] is proper to the Turcia Rufia family.

Furthermore, the titles of honor with which the editor of Sedulius and the corrector of the Virgil manuscript are adorned agree more closely with one another, since both were patricians, while neither is called master of both services.

149. The question is not yet resolved, however. It remains to investigate whether Flavius Asterius or Turcius Rufius Asterius was consul in 449. Norisius and Pagius reply without hesitation that Flavius Asterius was consul in 449 and Turcius Rufius Asterius in 494. I wish, however, that they would confirm this by some ancient monument. For the ancient consular fasti give only the bare name *Asterius* in both years. The fact that the Asterius who was consul in 449 [Col. 0493C] is called *Astyrius* and *Asturius* in some sources is not weighty enough to force us to maintain that Flavius Asterius—or Astyrius or Asturius—was consul in 449 and that Turcius Rufius Asterius was consul in 494.

If, however, we say that Turcius Rufius Asterius, who published Sedulius’s poems, held the consulship in 449, the arguments brought forward by Sirmondus and Arntzenius in no. 142 and following press us toward that conclusion. Norisius also felt their force, and therefore says that it is probable that Sedulius completed both his writing and his life around the year 494, or a few years earlier.

As for Sirmondus’s statement that in complete manuscript copies of Gennadius one reads that Sedulius died during the lifetime of Theodosius the Younger, Norisius believes that this was not written by Gennadius’s hand but added by someone else, just as he says that several other sections were appended to Gennadius. We have nevertheless shown from many manuscript copies [Col. 0493D], in no. 23 and following, that Sedulius’s age cannot be postponed so long.

150. Usserius, Pearsonius, Norisius, and Pagius explain another argument, drawn from the decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received or rejected, by denying that such a decree was issued under the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, that is, in 494, as the title in the collection of the councils indicates.

Learned men have held various and mutually conflicting opinions about this decree. In Labbe’s *Collection of the Councils*, vol. IV, col. 1260, the heading reads:

> The First Roman Council, at which, under Gelasius, in the year of the Lord 494, during the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, the sacred and authoritative books were distinguished from the apocryphal.

In the margin, from a very ancient manuscript [Col. 0494A]:

> Notice of the sacred Scriptures, or canonical books, with a description or annotation of Pope Gelasius.

After the books of the Old and New Testaments have been listed:

> Decree of Pope Gelasius, enacted with seventy bishops, concerning the apocryphal Scriptures.

Pearsonius, in his *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, believes that this decree was composed after the fifth synod, held in 553. Perhaps related to this is the fact that Damianus Grana, in the preface to Proba’s *Cento*, Rome, 1588, calls it the decree of Pelagius. It is more likely, however, that Grana inadvertently wrote “Pelagius” instead of “Gelasius.”

Baluzius saw a manuscript of the collection of Dionysius Exiguus in which this decree was attributed to Damasus. Cardinal Baronius, under the year 69, no. 4 [Col. 0494B], reports that the Cresconian Collection contains a Roman council under Damasus in which the apocryphal books are discussed. He should rather have said “the sacred Scriptures.” For the Roman Council under Damasus, which I have transcribed from a Vatican manuscript, gives a canon of the books of the Old and New Testaments but says nothing at all about apocryphal books. I therefore believe that the canon of Damasus was inserted into the decree concerning apocryphal books.

Baluzius testifies that the same decree is attributed to Hormisdas in the very ancient Urgell manuscript. Peter Francis Chiffletius published the decree itself from a manuscript of the Jura, under the following heading:

> Here begins the decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas.

In Vatican Manuscript 1341, perhaps of the tenth century, there is a Hispanic collection of canons such as the Ballerinii describe in their dissertation on collections of canons. The index of the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs [Col. 0494C] lists only genuine letters. After the letters of Saint Gregory the Great to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, it notes:

> Decrees of the Roman See concerning books to be received and not received.

Nothing else is added, nor are these decrees inserted in the body of the collection. But a decree concerning books to be received and not received is certainly indicated. In these ancient Hispanic collections it was the last item among the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, as appears not only from the index of this collection but also from the indexes of other fuller collections in which the old index was retained.

The opinion of certain heretics should therefore be dismissed with contempt: they suppose that the decree concerning apocryphal books was fabricated and number it among the wares of Isidore Mercator. Indeed [Col. 0494D], the canon of the sacred Scriptures that chiefly troubles them was composed under Damasus, as I have said; from it Gelasius—or another pontiff—constructed the first part of the decree concerning apocryphal books, or concerning books to be received and not received. The learned Zacharias deals very diligently with this controversy in his excellent work *On the Prohibition of Books*, under the years 379 and 496.

151. The opinion of Pagius and others is that Gelasius was the author of the decree, but that Hormisdas arranged for it to be promulgated more widely.

In *Lives of the Pontiffs*, chapter 51, Luitprandus says the following about Gelasius and his decree:

> He likewise praises the history of Orosius, and the work of Sedulius and Juvencus.

Pope Nicholas I, Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, Hariulfus, monk of Saint-Riquier, in the *Chronicle of Centula* preserved by Duchesne, Gratianus, Burchardus of Worms, many manuscript copies, and all printed editions praise Gelasius as the author of the decree [Col. 0495A].

In the *Chronicle of Fontanelles*, vol. III of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 240, among the books donated to the monastery of Flavigny under Louis the Pious by Abbot Angesisus, the *Decrees of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received and not received* are listed.

Pearsonius read a very ancient manuscript brought into England by Lanfranc from the monastery of Bec, in which this title appeared:

> Decrees of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received and not received, written by him with seventy most learned bishops.

The manuscript of Justellus in Labbe’s *Collection of the Councils* agrees completely with this in the margin of the decree.

I myself found a similar heading in Vatican Manuscript 3791, a small parchment volume dating approximately from the tenth century. The manuscript begins:

> Here begin the chapters of the decretal letters of the Apostolic Church of the holy Roman See.

After Felix’s letter to Zeno, bishop of Seville, one reads [Col. 0495B]:

> In the name of Christ begin the decrees concerning books to be received and not received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops at the Apostolic See of the city of Rome.

In another Vatican manuscript, Reg. 6018, approximately of the tenth century, I found the same decree under this heading:

> Here begins the confirmation of the Lord Pope Gelasius concerning the books of the Old and New Testament: namely, the five books of Moses, etc.

Other similar corruptions occur.

Another manuscript is Vatican Reg. 199. After an expanded book of Isidore’s *On the Deaths of the Fathers*, it contains an anonymous work on numbers. The author, on the occasion of the number two, discusses the two ways in which all Scripture is to be understood and inserts the entire decree of Gelasius, freely transcribed by him. He prefaces it as follows:

> Therefore [Col. 0495C], the order of the divine books that the Catholic Church ought to write, read, and receive, according to the tradition of holy men and orthodox Fathers—that is, of Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops at the Apostolic See of the city of Rome—and according to the tradition of Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

The *Decretal of Gelasius concerning books to be received*, and so forth, is also praised at the beginning of Vatican Manuscript Reg. 551.

Joseph Blanchinus, in the *Prolegomena* to vol. IV of Anastasius, *Opusculum* 3, gives the title from a very ancient Florentine manuscript:

> Here begins the decree concerning books to be received and rejected, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops at the Apostolic See in the city of Rome.

From Vatican Palatine Manuscript 493, fol. 101 [Col. 0495D], formerly collated by Justus Fontaninus and later more carefully by Blanchinus himself, he gives:

> Here begins the decretal [a corrupt form, *decretalem*, for *decretale*] of Saint Gelasius, pope of the city of Rome.

Blanchinus carefully recorded the variant readings from these two manuscripts and from Chiffletius’s manuscript of the Jura, which is often called *Furensis* in the *Prolegomena*, in my opinion through a typographical error.

I also saw Vatican Palatine Manuscript 493. Before the Decree of Gelasius it contains an old Gallican Missal, called by the Venerable Thomasius, whose antiquity Mabillonius and Thomasius greatly exaggerate. Lesleus, however, in the preface to the *Gothic Missal*, no. 290, conjectures [Col. 0496A] that it does not date beyond the time of Charles the Bald.

The script of the Gelasian Decree [Col. 0496A] appears more recent than the majuscule script in which the missal is written, and Blanchinus says that it belongs approximately to the ninth century. To me the entire book appears to have been written in the tenth or eleventh century, when certain wealthy abbots used great expense and luxury to have manuscripts, especially sacred ones, written in imitation of earlier examples.

Finally, Jacobus Petitus, in his notes to the *Penitential of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury*, observes that the same decree is attributed to Gelasius by Theodore and in other manuscript copies, which he lists.

152. Let us therefore assume that Gelasius published the decree concerning books to be received and not received, and let us explain in another way, if possible, the difficulty arising from its words about Sedulius.

In Labbe’s collection of the councils, the decree says the following about Sedulius:

> Likewise [Col. 0496B], we place before—or prefer—with distinguished praise the Paschal Work of the venerable man Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verses.

Gratianus has the same reading in distinction 15, except that he has *proferimus* (“we bring forward”) instead of *praeferimus* (“we prefer”). The variant reading *preferimus* is also noted.

The Florentine manuscript used by Blanchinus and the Jurensis manuscript used by Chiffletius have *praeferimus*. Vatican Manuscript 1341 has the same reading, although in an abbreviation of the letters that could easily be misread by the unwary as *proferimus*. Vatican Reg. 6018 clearly has *preferimus*.

The author of the work on numbers in Vatican Reg. 199, with a few alterations, writes:

> Likewise, we place before—or prefer—with distinguished praise the Paschal Work of the venerable bishop Sedulius, which he composed in theoretical verses—read “which,” not “whom.”

In the Vatican Palatine manuscript used by Blanchinus, the main text has *referimus* (“we report”); in a second revision, *praeferimus*. In the same manuscript [Col. 0496C], the main text has *Sedulii*, corrected in the second revision to *Sydulii*; the main text has *erroicis*, corrected in the second revision to *eruditis*, which Blanchinus adopted in place of *heroicis*.

Pagius reports the final words as *insigni laude praeferimus* (“we prefer with distinguished praise”). This is indeed how they are read in Vatican Manuscript 1341, but, as I think, with the same sense—not so that the work is said to be distinguished, but that it is distinguished by praise, or by distinguished praise.

There is another difference in Vatican Manuscript 1341: *descripserit* (“he may have composed”) instead of *descripsit* (“he composed”), as all the others give it. We could not omit this, for perhaps a different interpretation of the decree may be derived from it, as I shall now explain.

153. It has already been observed in no. 34 [Col. 0496D] that Sedulius wanted his poem to be called *Paschal Poem*, while the prose version, or interpretation, published later was called *Paschal Work*. Juretus, the first of all to publish Sedulius’s prose, weighing Gelasius’s words—which name the *Paschal Work* and the heroic verses in which it was composed—concludes that Gelasius seems to have intended to include both works.

Gelasius’s statement is certainly somewhat obscure, and therefore the passage may invite conjecture as to whether we should read: “the Paschal Work, and which he composed in heroic verses.” Since, however, in the letter to Macedonius prefixed to the *Paschal Work*, or prose version, Sedulius says that he had previously arranged the same work in verse, someone may reasonably doubt whether, if we retain the reading of Vatican Manuscript 1341—“which he may have composed in heroic verses”—Gelasius intended to praise the *Paschal Work*, which he had learned from the preface to have been composed in verse, although he had not seen the poem itself [Col. 0497A].

154. In this way the difficulty raised by many concerning the date at which Gelasius’s decree appeared could easily be resolved. For the decree is said to have been issued under the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius; yet Turcius Rufius Asterius did not collect and publish Sedulius’s poem until after his consulship. Although some manuscripts call him “ordinary consul,” most explicitly call him “former ordinary consul.”

No one doubts that the *Paschal Work*, or Sedulius’s prose, was published without the assistance and care of Asterius. Gelasius could therefore commend the *Paschal Work*, even though the *Paschal Poem* had not yet been published for the general public.

Nevertheless, I consider it more probable [Col. 0497B] that Gelasius praised either both works or, above all, the *Paschal Poem* with that distinguished commendation of his. For when he joins Juvencus to Sedulius, he immediately adds:

> Likewise, we do not disdain the laborious work of Juvencus, but admire it.

By this he indicates that Juvencus’s poem is no less laborious and no less worthy of praise.

155. Pagius therefore concludes, with others, that Gelasius’s decree was issued after Asterius’s consulship. He testifies that he saw a manuscript written in very ancient script in the Royal Library at Paris, and another in the Parisian Library of Saint Victor, from which the chronological note “under the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius”—which Baronius and the collectors of the councils attached to Gelasius’s decree—was absent.

The two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript mentioned above likewise lack such a chronological note, nor do I see it produced from any of the designated ancient manuscripts.

Pagius therefore argues that the first Roman synod under Gelasius was held in 495, on the third day before the Ides of March, at which Misenus was reconciled with the Church; and that the second synod was held either in the autumn of the same year or, more probably, in the following year, at which the apocryphal books were discussed.

Fifty-five bishops attended the first, and seventy-two—or, as most others have it, seventy—the second. In the collections of the councils these synods are presented in the opposite order.

156. From these considerations an adequate reason emerges for Gelasius’s having honored Sedulius with so splendid a eulogy. Perhaps he wished to do a favor to the recent editor of Sedulius, Asterius, a patrician and man of consular rank.

It also occurs to me [Col. 0497D] to wonder whether Asterius may have dedicated his new edition of Sedulius to Gelasius. For Asterius seems to have written his epigram at Rome; and whom else should we conjecture him to have addressed as a priest, except the supreme pontiff Gelasius?

Most manuscripts have in the first verse:

> Take, holy one, in virtue, the words of the truthful poet.

Sirmondus produced *veracia* (“truthful things”) from his manuscript, and Cellarius has *pater* (“father”) from the Cantabrigian manuscript instead of *sacer* (“holy”). In Vatican Reg. 1, *Summe* (“supreme”) is read instead of *Sume* (“take”).

It would not be absurd to reform the whole verse as follows:

> O most high priest, rich in merits, receive the utterances of a true poet.

Or:

> Supreme father, etc.

I nevertheless think it more likely that *sacer* is being used substantivally to mean “priest.” Thus, in the elegiac poem of Ermoldus Nigellus [Col. 0498A] for the emperor Louis, in Muratorius, vol. II, part II, col. 3:

> This priest, looking upon it, etc.

Parrhasius, whose words I shall present in no. 190, noticed something similar in Prudentius, although others take *sacer* in Prudentius’s verse adjectivally, as I said in my note on *Peristephanon*, hymn, verse 2.

But even if the verse is retained as it appears in most manuscripts, the conjecture remains probable that Asterius presented Sedulius’s poems to Gelasius.

157. Fontaninus, *De Antiquitate Hortensi*, book II, chapter 3, believes that Sedulius published his poem around the year 434, and that Asterius later published it, revised and corrected from the author’s papers, just as, while still consul, he had done with Virgil’s writings.

Cellarius had already noted Sedulius’s own words [Col. 0498B] in the letter to Macedonius prefixed to the prose version:

> I have simply offered you for reading the text of the Paschal Poem, which, in the service of pure devotion, I have completed and presented to you.

“What need, then, was there for a collector of papers?” Cellarius asks.

Grunerus replies that the words of the manuscript copies—“he left it dispersed”—should not be given too much weight. Sedulius offered the complete poem to Macedonius for reading, but did not publish it publicly. It was therefore Asterius’s care to bring the *Paschal Poem* into public circulation.

Arntzenius observes that Sedulius’s poem was not merely collected but also embellished by Asterius, as the heading of the epigram indicates. When Sedulius had offered the poem to Macedonius, and the latter had wished it to be transferred into plain prose, Sedulius began to suspect that the poem itself had not pleased Macedonius; he therefore neglected the poem, whose parts consequently lay scattered in different places. Asterius accordingly collected and published the rejected and neglected papers.

158. Arntzenius reasons in this way [Col. 0498C] because Sedulius, addressing Macedonius in the letter prefixed to the prose version, says of the *Paschal Poem*:

> Whether you wished it to be repeated because it pleased you, or because it offended you and, as I rather suspect, you judged that it should be expressed in a freer style, I seem to waver in uncertain judgment.

These words nevertheless do not seem sufficient to make us believe that the poem was not actually published by Sedulius. Rather, Sedulius implies that he released the poem publicly when he offered it to Macedonius; and because the earlier books bore the title *Paschal Poem*, he therefore entitled the prose version *Paschal Work*.

Why, then [Col. 0498D], should we not maintain that the *Paschal Poem* was published by Sedulius but dispersed among separate papers? The inscription of Asterius’s epigram proves nothing else:

> Sedulius left this work dispersed among separate papers, etc.,

as we showed in no. 136.

From this it may be inferred that it is not necessary to postpone the decree concerning apocryphal books until after 494, or after Asterius’s consulship. Although Asterius declares in the epigram that Sedulius’s words were published to the people through his own assistance and care, this must be understood as referring to a more elegant edition of all the parts of the poem, which had previously been scattered among separate papers.

Perhaps the fact that Sedulius’s poem had initially been so dispersed [Col. 0499A] is the reason for the great discrepancy in the division and numbering of the books, as is clear from no. 31 and following. See note 12 on the dedication of the prose version.

159. It is certainly established that in former times many learned and noble men brought new light to the works of ancient writers, which were already being worn out in the hands of the general public, by issuing, reviewing, and correcting new copies.

Asterius himself, of whom we are speaking, punctuated and corrected Virgil’s manuscript, as we have seen. It is clear from no. 62 that a certain Abundantius collated an extremely ancient manuscript of Sedulius, preserved in the Turin Library.

Rusticus the deacon collated and corrected copies [Col. 0499B] of the Council of Chalcedon in the sixth century. His words are reported by Labbe from manuscripts, vol. IV of the *Councils*, col. 309, after the first action:

> Rusticus, by the grace of God deacon of the holy Roman Church, have collated, annotated, and punctuated. Thanks be to God.

Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, book XII, under the year 721, p. 154, no. 56, mentions a commentary of Ambrose on Luke, written at the command of Leutcharius, or Leodegarius, abbot, in the year 752, which Ratbertus later corrected with his own hand.

In manuscript copies of Terence this subscription often occurs:

> Calliopius revised this.
