Barthius proves at length, *Adversaria*, book VI, chapter 20, that this Calliopius was Alcuin, the teacher of Charlemagne.

From the manuscript papers of the learned Giovenazzi, in his commentary on Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 909, I produced the subscriptions of Nicomachus Dexter, who corrected a manuscript of Livy from the exemplar of his father Clementianus; of another Nicomachus, who at Henna also corrected a manuscript of Livy from that of Victorianus, a man of senatorial rank; and of Victorianus, who likewise corrected a copy of Livy for his patrons, the Symmachi.

It is evident from the Putean manuscripts that Celsus Constantinus [Col. 0499C], a man of senatorial rank, corrected Caesar’s commentaries.

In the Vatican Library there is a manuscript of Terence written in the age of Charlemagne by Hrodgarius and revised by Calliopius Scholasticus. Paulus of Constantinople corrected a manuscript copy of Lucan in the same manner.

For this ancient practice, see Walchius, *Dissertation on the Ancient Roman Art of Criticism*, no. 26; Philibert de La Marne, letter to Heinsius 595, vol. V of Burmann’s *Sylloge*; and Fontaninus, *Vindiciae diplomaticae antiquae*, book I, chapter 3. Fontaninus believes that Calliopius, the corrector of Terence, was called *Scholasticus* because of his ecclesiastical rank. He nevertheless exaggerates greatly when he says that in the fifth century it was customary for the literary works of distinguished men not to be published by scribes until they had first been reviewed and corrected by men holding office.

It should also be noted that such subscriptions of correctors [Col. 0499D] are often not autograph. For when scribes copied a manuscript exemplar, they faithfully reproduced everything they found in it, including the subscriptions of the original correctors.

Moreover, I fear that the fraud of scribes sometimes entered into the matter: they may have fabricated the subscription of some distinguished and ancient man in order to increase the value of the manuscript by means of its antiquity and correction.

To this point the words of Phaedrus, book V, fable 1, are relevant [Col. 0500A]:

> As certain craftsmen do in our own age,
>
> who find a greater price for their works
>
> if they have inscribed Praxiteles upon their new marble,
>
> and Myron upon their worn silver.

160. I recently found what seems to me a sufficiently clear example of this fraud. In Vatican Alexandrian Manuscript 1598 there is a catalogue of the books of the library, or Archive, of the Vatican Basilica, written around the year 1620. On page 16 of that catalogue it says:

> Satires of Persius Flaccus, written 1,200 years ago and corrected at Barcelona by Flavius Julius Trebatius, of the Sabine name, in the year of Christ 416.

The author of the catalogue proves this because the following subscription is read on folio 63 of the manuscript:

> Flavius Julius Trebatius, of the Sabine name, as a protector of the domestics, attempted to correct this without my exemplar, and annotated it at Barcelona, under the consuls, our lords, Arcadius and Honorius, Qs.

In the same manuscript [Col. 0500B] there follow verses of Priscian on “is” and “is not,” a sermon on the words “Son of man, stand upon your feet,” and so forth, and the precepts of rhetorical art collected by Julius Severianus.

These must have been written in a different and more recent script; for they cannot possess the antiquity attributed to Persius’s satires.

Indeed, if the subscription were genuine, this manuscript would surpass in antiquity the celebrated Medicean manuscript of Virgil corrected by Asterius in 494. For Trebatius’s correction belongs not to 416, as the author of the catalogue says, but to 402, when Arcadius V and Honorius V were consuls. This is what, as I interpret it, the notation at the end, *Qs*, intends.

Petrus Relandus, *On the Consular Fasti*, observed [Col. 0500C] that the consulship of Arcadius and Honorius was designated in this way in certain manuscripts of Persius and Nonius—namely, at the end of the manuscript of Persius:

> Flavius Julius N. N. Sabinus, protector of the domestics, attempted to correct this without an exemplar and annotated it at Barcelona, under the consuls, our lords Arcadius and Honorius, five times consuls.

And at the end of Nonius Marcellus:

> Junius Tryphon Sabinus, protector of the domestics: I read [Q.?] with our lords Arcadius and Honorius, five times consuls, correcting it as best I could without a teacher, in [a year uncertain in the printed text], at the age of thirty and in the fourth year of my military service, in the city of Toulouse.

The same corrector of Persius’s manuscript and of Nonius’s seems to be indicated.

I am entirely convinced that the subscription of the manuscript of the Vatican Basilica is spurious. Perhaps the author did not write *ut*, or *Vi*, as Relandus more clearly has it, but *v. c.*, meaning “a man of senatorial rank.”

Apart from the other indications of forgery [Col. 0500D], the word *Barcellonae* arose much later. Writers of that period, such as Ausonius, Prudentius, and others, said *Barcino*, or *Barcinon*, *Barcinonis*. Nor will one readily find *antigraphum* meaning “example” or “exemplar” among writers of that century; and the notation *Qs* cannot be found for *V* or *Quintum* in ancient monuments.

The reading *quinquies* (“five times”), as Relandus reports it, is even less acceptable.

I could discuss here the manuscript of Saint Hilary belonging to the same Vatican Basilica, but I reserve a fuller treatment of it for chapter 7.

161. To return to Asterius, it must be concluded that the *Paschal Poem* was issued in such a way by Sedulius that Sedulius’s name became much more illustrious through Asterius, the compiler of the sheets and portions of the poem, who took care to have the entire work copied elegantly, ornately, and correctly, and perhaps added the elegy and hymn. Thus, whether Asterius had already completed a new edition of Sedulius’s poem, or was then engaged in that undertaking, it is quite likely that Pope Gelasius was thereby moved to mention Sedulius among a few others and to exalt him with lavish praise.

This passage prompts me to dispel a charming little tale into which heterodox writers readily wander whenever an opportunity is given or seized. They relate that Gelasius’s passage was at some time corrupted by copyists, who substituted: “We rank above others the *Paschal Work*, which he composed in heretical verses instead of heroic ones.” This error allegedly led Paul II to a mortal hatred of poets and imposed the same view upon ninety and more other professors of law; indeed, some of them add that, by a decree of Gelasius thus corrupted, poets were ordered to be expelled from the Catholic Church, since many believed that all poets were heretics.

But who could fail to see that it could not have entered any sane person’s mind to infer from Gelasius’s decree—by which Sedulius’s poem is adorned with outstanding praise—that all poets were heretics? In no variant readings do I find that Gelasius’s words were mistakenly written in this form: “We rank above others the *Paschal Work*, which he composed in heretical verses.” Let us nevertheless suppose that this error entered the text somewhere. Do you seriously think that anyone could simultaneously believe that the *Paschal Work* had been composed in verses for heretics and that it deserved to be preferred with outstanding praise?

The point is so obvious that Bayle himself—who certainly had no desire to plead the cause of the Roman pontiffs—nevertheless suspected that this little tale had been invented by Italian devotees of humane letters in order to mock those who seemed insufficiently favorable toward the poets of that age. I am not unaware that Platina and other learned writers, whom Paul II had attacked for just reasons, treated him so badly that they pretended he regarded all learned men and all students of more refined learning as heretics. But this slander was splendidly refuted both by Raynaldus in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* and by the most eminent Cardinal Quirinus in his *Life of Paul II*.

The heterodox consider the tale they bring forward to be sufficiently supported by Pierius Valerianus’s *Oration in Defense of Priests’ Beards*. But first I shall ask why heretics everywhere mention Paul II, when Valerianus tells the story about Hadrian VI. It is well established that Hadrian VI, who was extremely devoted to stricter discipline, showed little favor toward the poets who at that time in Rome affected a foolish imitation of paganism and lived too freely. Hence the poets’ insults against him, especially after his death; hence Pierius Valerianus, in his *Oration in Defense of Priests’ Beards*, published at Rome in 1531, writes after Gelasius’s words about Sedulius:

“Yet up to that time the standard copies read *heretical verses* instead of *heroic verses*. This gave certain good professors of law grounds for suspecting that all poems were heretical and that poets were by no means to be counted among the pious, even when they treated sacred subjects. We have seen that this was so firmly impressed upon Hadrian IV, the supreme pontiff, that for this reason he pursued no class of men with greater hatred than poets, judging that the name signified nothing other than impiety. And even now some bishops—though not bad men—led astray by the delusion arising from that corrupt reading (I read: “reading”), and by the error concerning the other matter of having the beard shaved, consider no one worthy of the priesthood who either grows a beard or composes verses. Such is the power of once absorbing a false opinion.”

These statements may have been exaggerated and invented by some jester to provoke laughter; certainly no one ought to believe them. It is therefore all the more astonishing that Funck, in chapter 3 of *On the Old Age of the Latin Language*, although citing Bayle as his sole authority, should nevertheless reheat the same stale dish as established history and reconcile writers who tell different stories in such a way as to attribute to both pontiffs, Paul II and Hadrian VI, so absurd an error.

162. Another question concerning Asterius, already treated to some extent above in sections 46 and 122, must now be dispatched briefly: whether he was the author of the elegy, “Let us sing, companions,” and so forth. Norisius argues that, because in Vatican Codex 1165 a note is written after the *Paschal Poem* indicating that the poem was edited by Asterius, and because the elegy immediately follows, it is uncertain whether that elegy had an author, and that Labbeus ought not to have so confidently denied the elegy to Turcius Rufius Asterius. He seems, in my opinion, to be speaking of the recent Vatican Codex 3178, which I described in section 65.

Yet although, as I have already noted, some codices place that note after the *Paschal Poem*, it can in no way be inferred that Asterius was the author of the elegy. The note identifies Asterius as the compiler and editor of the poem, not its author. In Vatican Reginensis Codex 5, which is also recent and appears to have been adapted to Aldus’s edition, the same note is presented as follows:

“Turtius Rufus Asterius Quintus found the following poems among the writings of Caelius Sedulius.”

The elegy, hymn, and epigram of Sedulius then follow. I would readily believe that the elegy too was collected by Asterius and published by him together with the *Paschal Poem* in a more elegant form, as Labbeus and Goldastus state in their notes on the poems of Saint Columbanus. From the note, however—“This work, Sedulius …”—whether it is placed before or after the *Paschal Poem*, this cannot be demonstrated with certainty. For the work mentioned in the note must be understood either exclusively or principally as the *Paschal Poem*. This is indicated by the second verse of Asterius’s epigram:

“What were composed without the fault of fiction.”

This alludes to Sedulius’s first verse after the metrical prologue:

“When the pagan poets devote themselves to their own fictions.”

There is therefore no reason to deprive Sedulius of the elegy, which many very ancient codices assign to him, as is clear from chapter 3 and from the variant readings of the elegy’s title; so too do Bede more than once in *On the Art of Meter*, the author of the manuscript commentary on Bede’s *Art of Meter* in the Vatican Library, an anonymous tenth-century author, Osbern, John of Tynemouth in the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, William of Malmesbury in *On the Lives of the Pontiffs*, book I, and others.

163. Enough has now been said about Asterius. Concerning the two other ancient poets who praised Sedulius in acrostic verses, I must speak more briefly than the subject deserves. Nothing presents itself on which we can firmly base our conclusions. Their sufficient antiquity is clearly demonstrated by the ancient codices of Sedulius in which the acrostic verses are found.

Dempster, in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scots*, asserts without indicating any foundation, even a slight one, that Liberius and Belisarius lived in the year 440. Nevertheless, it will not be unreasonable to conjecture that those poets who, as though competing with one another, commended Sedulius in similar poems lived at the same time and were contemporaries either of Sedulius himself or of his editor Asterius.

In the index of books to be expurgated by John Maria Brasichellensis, page 256, it is prescribed that the title “Saint” should be deleted before Liberius and Belisarius. Some, however, still call them “Saint Liberius” and “Saint Belisarius,” understanding the abbreviation “D.” to represent the praenomen *Decimus*. Labbeus found *Liberatus* for *Liberius* in one manuscript, and Usserius found the same in another; Barthius, however, found *Libertus*. Mabillon, in volume I of the *Analecta*, calls Belisarius, on the basis of his manuscript, “Bellesarius the schoolmaster,” or Belisarius; others have *Belaesarius* or *Bellaesarius*, and others *Belezarius*. Indeed, I noted in section 93 that in a certain royal Parisian codex he is called Silo, since the catalogue of that library lists the verses of Liberatus together with those in that codex, and in Codex 8094: “The acrostic verses of Bellesarius in praise of Sedulius.”

Some codices omit the names of these poets; others attribute both epigrams to Belisarius, so that it may be questioned whether the two have a single author, Decimus Liberius Belisarius.

The famous general Belisarius, who lived not far from Asterius’s time, after Pope Silverius had been sent into exile and Belisarius had returned to his senses, took care to have a church built at Rome. The following inscription is found there:

> This church the patrician Vilisarius, friend of the city,  
> Founded to obtain forgiveness for his fault.  
> You who set foot in this holy building,  
> Pray often to God that He may have mercy on him.  
> This is the gate of the temple, defended by the mighty Lord.

In the manuscript notes of Joseph Blanchini on Roman inscriptions, preserved by the right reverend bishop Reggio, I find it recorded that Gruter, page 1562, no. 10, relocated this inscription to the church of the Crucifers in the Campus Martius and that it no longer exists. But Baronius, who reports it under the year 538, no. 10, observes that it could be seen on the wall of the church of the Crucifers between the Pincian Hill and the Quirinal. That church is called Saint Mary in Trivio, and the inscription can still be seen on its exterior wall opposite the De Comitibus residence.

From the style and orthography of the inscription it may be inferred that it was written and installed around the ninth century. If this inscription was truly written by Belisarius or by one of his contemporaries, it may be used as evidence confirming the antiquity of Leonine verses.

Baronius and others read *misereatur*—“may he have mercy”—in verse 4; but the stone reads *miseretur*—“he has mercy.” Cajetanus Marinius, in his extremely rich collection of ancient Christian inscriptions, which learned men have long desired, likewise reads it from a similar inscription that he himself saw and that is preserved in the private residence of Monsieur de Balneo.

The name of Belisarius is written differently on a stone lying to the left of those leaving through the Porta Pinciana:

> Give an obol to Belisarius.

This inscription seems to belong to a later period, since the story itself—that Belisarius had had his eyes torn out and used to beg alms with these words—is reported by many as a fable. Thus, in his notes on Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 561, no. 4, John Tzetzes, the Greek poet, reports these very words in his iambics:

> Holding a wooden cup, he cried out to the people in the stadium:  
> “Give an obol to Belisarius, the emperor.”

Many relate that this little tale is still current at Constantinople.

## CHAPTER VI. Eulogies of Sedulius and the Judgments of Learned Men Concerning Him

164. We have already brought forward several testimonies of the ancients concerning Sedulius: namely, from the manuscript codices of Sedulius in section 5 and following; in section 76, from the decree of Gelasius in section 152; from a certain Eldefonsus, or Ildefonsus, who flourished in the ninth century, in section 28; from Isidore in section 31; from Sigebert in section 48; from Trithemius in section 12; from Alcuin in section 27; from Luitprand in section 151; from the anonymous writer of Melk in section 31; from Sedulius the Younger in section 56; from Xystus of Siena in section 24; and from Eysengrein in section 25.

I gave a lively judgment of Sedulius and of the other Christian poets in the prolegomena to Juvencus, section 112. We present the epigram of Asterius and the acrostic verses of Belisarius and Liberius in the appendices.

165. Cassiodorus, book XXVII of *On Divine and Secular Literature*:

> It is indeed, as I think, a necessary work, but exceedingly difficult in view of its magnitude, to wish to comprise in two books the exceedingly abundant sources of divine and human literature.

Here we must understand Sedulius’s verses beginning, “I ask for great things,” and so forth. They are verses 349–350 of book I, which in some editions of Cassiodorus are corrupted.

The same Cassiodorus, in his exposition of Psalm 113, verse 12:

> To these must also be added, if I may put it so, those verses of Sedulius, the poet of truth: “Wooden one, you ask for wood,” and so forth.

These are from book I of Sedulius, verse 268. Moreover, in the exposition of Psalm 36, at the conclusion, he cites verse 325 of book I, “Both equal in error,” and in the same exposition, at the conclusion, verse 349 of book I, “I ask for great things.”

166. Venantius Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 9:

> What Ambrose thunders, and Jerome flashes forth,  
> Or what Augustine waters from his flowing spring,  
> The sweet Sedulius produces, and the keen Orosius publishes;  
> A line born for Caesar is his own rule.

The same author, again, in the *Life of Saint Martin*, book I, verse 15:

> For Juvencus, first distinguishing the poem  
> In a teachable order, sings with the art of meter  
> A work of majesty.  
> From this source too Sedulius’s conspicuous language shone forth.

167. Isidore, in verses that many confirm were once affixed in his library:

> Read through the studious poem of eloquent Avitus;  
> Behold, Juvencus is here, and Sedulius too.  
> Both equal in language, both flourishing in verse,  
> They bring abundant cups from the evangelical spring.  
> Therefore cease to insert yourself among pagan poets:  
> While you can possess such good things, what need have you of Callirrhoe?”

I said something about these verses in the prolegomena to Juvencus, section 92. But, to add something now, I have scarcely any remaining doubt that they are Isidore’s, on the basis of ancient manuscripts. For in Vatican Reginensis Codex 215, dating from the end of the ninth century, I saw the following verse produced under Isidore’s name among other verses cited for testing syllabic quantity:

> You too our library brings forth for your books.

This is Jerome’s eulogy in the verses of the *Library of Isidore*, but it is more correctly transmitted in this Vatican codex. It is likewise found in Vatican Reginensis Codex 425 under an uncertain author, and in another Reginensis Codex, no. 571, under Augustine’s name.

The same Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 4, cites the final verse of the metrical prologue:

> Arretine vessels are called such from Arretium, a municipality of Italy, where they are made; they are red, too [perhaps “also”]. Of these Sedulius says:

> “Because a red earthenware vessel serves the vegetable set before it.”

168. In the splendid edition of the Toletan Fathers, prepared through the scholarship and at the expense of the most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, sermon 5, *On the Assumption of Blessed Mary*, is placed among the doubtful sermons of Saint Ildefonsus. This sermon is found among the works of Abbot Odilo. There, on page 363, we read:

> Concerning the Lord’s burial, however, some say that the Mother of God was even more concerned than those holy women. If I am not mistaken, that view seems to be supported by the good Sedulius, the evangelical poet, eloquent orator, and Catholic writer.

Compare Sedulius, book V, verses 322 and 361. Some also attribute to Ildefonsus the short work *On the Birth of the Virgin*, although the very learned editor correctly observes that it should be attributed to Paschasius Radbertus. In this work, volume I of the *Toletan Fathers*, page 314, we find the following concerning Sedulius:

> If the woman giving birth were exposed to such and similar torments, she would unquestionably not be a virgin, because virgin integrity would have been violated. Hence Sedulius, the rhetorician of the Roman Church, says in his *Paschal Work*: “For the infant …” And again the same author says: “Truly of divine generation …” Nothing, therefore, could be said more openly or more clearly by those holy teachers concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, and so forth.

These words are taken from book II of the *Paschal Work*, or prose version.

169. Some writers report that Sedulius was praised by Arator. Cellarius believes that this derives from Aldus’s account in the *Life of Arator*:

> Arator is said to have turned to writing the Acts of the Apostles in verse because he had seen that Juvencus and Sedulius had done the same thing in the Gospel.

This may be seen in the Arator who is bound in the library at Venice, both in the church called Saint George Major and in the garden of the ever-Virgin Mother of God. In the Vatican Library there is Palatine Codex 1717, in a large folio, dating approximately from the eleventh century. At its beginning I find the following written:

> Arator was a subdeacon of the holy Roman Church of God. Observing that Juvencus and Sedulius had written their books in verse, he resolved to write the Acts of the Apostles in verse.

170. Bede, commentary on Luke, chapter 49, on the words “They crucified him,” and so forth:

> How the Lord was placed upon the cross, and what royal type is contained in the position of that most sacred body, Sedulius beautifully expressed in verse in his *Paschal Poem*, so that no one might be unaware of it, and so forth.

He quotes verse 188 and the following seven verses of book V. In our Ottobonian Codex 2, these verses are separately listed beginning with “The four wounds”; they are preceded by four other verses beginning “How affixed,” and so forth, as I explained in section 76.

Usserius produced the same four verses, “How affixed,” and so forth, from an ancient Thorney manuscript without any difference in reading. Sedulius’s verses on the Cross, beginning at verse 184, “He himself was the peace of the cross,” are also cited by Dungal and by Jonah of Orléans to support the veneration of sacred images, as I shall explain at that passage.

Again, Bede, in question 28 on the Books of Kings, after reporting from John, Bishop of Constantinople, that the Greeks had imagined a chariot, horses, and rays of the sun from Elijah’s ascent, added:

> For the sun is called *helios* in Greek, as Sedulius too demonstrated when he sang of Elijah’s ascent, saying, and so forth.

He cites verse 184 and the following three verses of book I.

From the same Bede we recite in the Roman breviary, at the Dedication of Saint Mary of the Snows:

> Truly blessed is the mother who, as someone says,  
> “Gave birth, a woman in travail, to the king,” and so forth.

These are Sedulius’s verses from book II, verse 63 and following. Here it is appropriate to observe that Sedulius’s words are often used in liturgical offices. Besides the hymns taken from Sedulius in the Mozarabic and Roman breviaries, as I shall say in the variant readings on Sedulius’s hymn, words from that same hymn are repeated at the second nocturn’s responsories for the Lord’s Circumcision: “House of a chaste heart,” and so forth. They also occur in the entrance chant of the votive Mass of the Mother of God:

> Hail, holy mother, who, a woman in travail, gave birth to the king,  
> Who rules heaven and earth.

These are from book II, verse 63. Sedulius is also praised in the rubric of the missals.

Nebrissensis likewise noted that the following was read about Sedulius in the nocturnal lessons for the Feast of All Saints:

> The outstanding versifier considers that God’s wisdom knows and can do all things, saying: “You who count the stars,” and so forth.

These are verses 66 and following of book I. This is no longer read in the Roman breviary, but it was formerly read, as is clear from the Roman breviary called the Camera breviary, printed at Venice in folio by the Giunta press in 1550, where, at the Vigil of All Saints, the following is quoted from a sermon of Rabanus:

> And that outstanding versifier, Sedulius, says that God’s wisdom can do and know all things, and so forth.

Finally, Bede very often confirms his rules in his book *On the Art of Meter* by the example and authority of Sedulius, sometimes leaving his name unmentioned and sometimes expressing it, as I shall note in the notes and variant readings.

An ancient writer, whoever he was, illustrated Bede with a commentary in a Vatican manuscript that I call Reg. 4, as I said in section 69. He too, in the same way as Bede, produces Sedulius’s verses as examples.

171. From the same Bede, in section 48, I observed that Aldhelm, in imitation of Sedulius, composed his book *On Virginity* in prose and verse. Aldhelm, however, first composed the prose and then the poem, whereas Sedulius did the opposite.

In Aldhelm’s poem, printed by Canisius in volume V, part 2, of the *Ancient Readings*, page 837, Sedulius’s name being suppressed, his verses are quoted:

> Thus, when God changes them, the hearts of wild beasts are changed,  
> Although the hearts of foolish men grow numb.  
> As once the poet expressed it in cola and comma:  
> “The fierce lions learned to guard their prey.”

This poet is Sedulius, as is noted in the margin of Vatican Palatine Codex 2078, a manuscript of Aldhelm. In that codex Sedulius’s verse is also corrected to “And the fierce lions learned,” for that is how Sedulius writes it in book I, verse 219.

In the prose work Aldhelm writes:

> As the poet says of the prophet:  
> “And the fierce lions learned to guard their prey.”

Canisius’s marginal note beside the half-line “He expressed it in cola and comma” refers to chapter 28 of the prose work, where Aldhelm says:

> He skilfully impressed it through cola and commas in the honeyed epigrams of his verses.”

We must therefore ask what Aldhelm’s phrase “He expressed it in cola and comma,” or “He impressed it through cola and commas,” means.

I infer from Aldhelm himself that these words signify that the verses were composed with a certain pleasing artistry. At the beginning of the poem he says:

> I do not ask the rural Muses for verses and commas,

and shortly afterward:

> Let the cola proceed with feet, and the commas in threes;  
> Let the dactyl run on, except at the end of the meter;  
> Let the spondee’s fifth syllable disdain its portion;  
> Thus let the final letter of the trochee conclude the verse,  
> Whose final foot continually delights in being held by a gentle cadence.  
> Thus let the epigrams of the meter hasten in three feet.

The first verse in the common editions has *commoda*—“conveniences”—instead of *commata*, or *comata*; both spellings are found. You will search in vain for the true meaning among the lexicographers.

The grammarian Sergius, who in Vatican Palatine Codex 1578 is called *Serregius*—unless the copyist intended to write *Servius Regius*—concludes as follows in his commentary on the first edition of Donatus, the one dealing with letters and related matters:

> Cola and comata are understood to be the individual parts of the same discourse.

But we must remember that in prose, *cola* and *comata* are the same and signify one thing, whereas in verse they signify something else and are distinct. When two feet are free, it is called a *colon*, as in Horace, “He terrified cities.” It is a *comma* when, after two feet or after three, a syllable follows that concludes a part of the sentence, as in the first verse of the *Aeneid*: “Arms and the man I sing.” Likewise: “Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy …”

The Vatican codex gives the passage in this form; but in Putsch’s edition among the ancient grammarians, the correct common reading is: “Likewise, ‘Arms and the man I sing of Troy …’” For in that form a syllable follows after three feet.

To return to Aldhelm: he also praises Sedulius in chapters 2 and 10 of the prose work, as I shall explain in connection with verses 13 and 179 of book I.

172. I shall add to Aldhelm another imitator of Sedulius, although a less learned one, from Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 25. Speaking of Chilperic, king of the Franks, Gregory says:

> The same king wrote other books in verse, as though following Sedulius; but those little verses conform in no way whatever to the rules of meter.

And again, book VI, chapter 46:

> He also composed two books as though meditating upon Sedulius; their feeble little verses cannot stand on any feet. Since he did not understand the matter, he put short syllables where long ones belonged and made long syllables stand for short ones.

Ruinart gives no variant reading for *meditatus*, “meditating upon”; but others have *imitatus*, “imitating.”

Chilperic’s foolishness has been common in every age, so that Horace rightly complains of it in book II, letter 1, verse 115:

> What belongs to physicians—  
> Physicians promise; smiths practice the crafts of smiths.  
> Learned and unlearned alike compose poems everywhere.

173. At least versifiers of this sort might imitate Jannitius, who very modestly titled a work composed by him in meter and prose—perhaps in order to blunt the boastfulness of others in magnifying their titles—as follows:

> *The Library of the Convent of Saints John and Paul of the Order of Preachers, Recently Opened at Venice, by Brother Jacopo Maria Jannitius, Professor of No Science Whatever and Entirely Unversed in Poetry.*

174. Sedulius also entered into the controversy between Hincmar and Gottschalk over whether one may speak of a triune deity. Gottschalk, in his memorandum to Hincmar, writes:

> As your faithful poet Sedulius says: “This threefold faith,” and so forth.

Hincmar, in his work *On the Non-Trine Deity*, explains Sedulius’s words and repeatedly calls him venerable.

175. Theodulf of Orléans, book IV, poem 1, verse 11:

> There was a fitting concern for the distinguished Fathers of former times;  
> See, below, the names of those men written here:  
> Radiant Sedulius, Paulinus, Arator, Avitus,  
> And Fortunatus—and you, thundering Juvencus.

I discussed in the prolegomena to Juvencus, section 100, whether *radiant* is an epithet of Sedulius or the proper name of another Christian poet. To me it seems more likely to be an epithet. Thus Petrarch, *Eclogue* 10:

> One was the radiant Arator of the divine field.

176. In the same place, section 101, I cited the testimony of Notker Balbulus, chapter 7 of *On the Interpreters of Sacred Scripture*, from Pez’s *Anecdotal Treasury*, volume IX:

> I know that you have already committed to memory Juvencus and Sedulus the orator, and the hymns of Ambrose.

I pointed out that the passage is corrupt in Pez and that it should read: “Juvencus and Sedulius, Arator,” and so forth. In volume V of Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, Notker Balbulus’s book was reprinted, and there the reading is: “Juvencus and Sedulius the Orator.”

Indeed, in some ancient codices Sedulius is called a rhetorician. Nevertheless, I do not abandon my first conjecture. Balbulus was writing to Solomon, the third bishop of Constance, whose verses appear in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, volume I, and from the prologue it is sufficiently clear that Solomon had read Sedulius thoroughly. See the variant readings on book I, verse 298.

177. Among Alcuin’s works there is a book *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, whose author is believed to be Fortunatus Amalarius. Whoever he may be, he says:

> We believe in the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and we have received—or perhaps, “we receive”—the verses of Sedulius: “Not because he who is supreme,” book I, verse 319.

In Alcuin’s *Homiliary*, compiled and published from various authors at Cologne in 1569, the anonymous author of the sermon for the feast of Saint Luke has the following:

> Concerning him the priest Sedulius speaks beautifully:  
> “Luke holds the priest’s laws upon his flourishing lips.”

This is corrupt in place of “upon the flourishing lips of Juvencus,” as I shall say in connection with book I, verse 357.

In the same work, however, Paulinus’s verses on Luke are more correctly transmitted, *Nativity of Saint Felix*, book IX, verses 424 and following:

> Twice a physician …  
> He strengthens the limbs and now, in sick minds—  
> He composed twin books of medicines for life.

For this Muratorius reads:

> He treated earthly things by earthly means, and now, for sick minds,
>
> He composed the medicines of life in a twofold book.”

178. Placidus Lactantius, or Lutatius, the scholiast on Statius, *Thebaid*, book VIII, verse 287, cites verses 200 and following of Sedulius, as I shall also say concerning the scholiast on Lucan. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XI, chapter 2, column 514, observes that Sedulius is praised by the scholiast on Horace, *Epode* 17, or perhaps verse 13, “The dread storm.”

179. Asser of Menevia wrote at the beginning of the *Life of King Alfred*:

> For a long time the pagans worshiped Geta as a god; the poet Sedulius mentions him in his metrical *Paschal Poem*, saying: “When the pagan poets,” and so forth.

Matthew of Westminster repeats nearly the same words in the *Flores Historiarum* under the year 758, page 142, where he presents the entire genealogy of Geta, and Simeon of Durham in *On the Deeds of the Kings of England* under the year 848, where he calls Sedulius an outstanding poet. Compare the variant readings on book I, verse 19, “Or the ridiculous Getae.”

180. Usserius, *On the Origins of the British Church*, chapter 16, transcribes the following words from John of Tynemouth’s *Life of Saint Dunstan*:

> Singing that poem of the wise senator Sedulius:  
> “Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing his honor.”

This is the first verse of Sedulius’s elegy, adapted by John of Tynemouth to his own subject with some difference. Tynemouth flourished in the fourteenth century.

Osbern reports it in the same way in chapter 8 of the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, printed among the Bollandists under 19 May. He wrote in the eleventh century. Another earlier author, Blessed B., a contemporary and eyewitness, writes somewhat differently in chapter 6 of the same collection:

> He saw … bands of virgins circling in the choir—or perhaps *circling*—singing this hymn of the poet Sedulius as they moved: “Let us sing, companions, to the Lord,” and so forth.

William of Malmesbury, *On the Lives of the English Pontiffs*, book I, page 203:

> And to sing and repeat in measured melody that Sedulian verse:  
> “Let us sing to the Lord, companions,” and so forth.

William Thorne reports the same thing in chapter 2 of his *Chronicle*, without naming Sedulius. Gervase, a monk of Canterbury, *Images Concerning the Disagreement among Monks*, page 1326:

> Singing and saying the verse of Sedulius:  
> “Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing his honors.”

Others give *honor* in the singular. This vision of Saint Dunstan was famous among writers on English affairs.

181. Aedilwaldus, in his poem to Winfrith:

> As with honey-flowing  
> Heroic verses  
> The once-renowned poet,  
> A native of the city of Rome,  
> With the shrill pen of his style  
> Carefully composing,  
> Inserts into sacred writings  
> The eloquent Sedulius.

Thus Usserius reports it in the cited passage. In the second verse, *Heroicorum* may perhaps be the correct reading.

182. From Ralph of Dunston, Usserius likewise cites this couplet:

> Sedulius rises and, with diligent elegance, sings  
> The texture of the old and the new Scriptures.

183. Honorius of Autun, book III, chapter 7, repeats almost the same words about Sedulius that we cited above from Isidore.

184. In the prolegomena to Juvencus, section 104, I transcribed several verses from Petrarch’s *Eclogue* 10 in praise of the Christian poets. The following two celebrate Prudentius and Sedulius:

> With Prudentius here as companion, and with another Sedulius there at the plough,
>
> They competed to tear up the clods with the rigid rake.

An eulogy of Arator had preceded this.

185. Gerson, sermon 3, *On the Conception of the Mother of God*, or whoever the author may be:

> Then the seventh virgin arose, namely true poetry, saying that she possessed countless poetic arts. For Sedulius, in book I of the *Paschal Poem*, speaks poetically of Mary as follows: “Behold, as if …” See book II, verse 28; for the author of this sermon seems to have made one work out of the first and second books, as others also did.

186. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book X, chapter 9:

> Among Christian poets no one preserved the Virgilian phrase more gracefully, insofar as this could be done despite the different subject matter and the changes of the age, than Sedulius. He was among most of them a man of excellent talent, although he too has blemishes—not so much his own as those of his age. This was also the judgment of the ancients, as is evident from some old epigram. Here he reproduces not merely the poet’s phrase, but Virgil’s very abundant figures and ornaments of expression.

187. Olaus Borrichius judges Sedulius as follows in *On Latin Poetry*:

> His diction is easy, ingenious, rhythmical, clear, and sufficiently polished, if one excepts certain prosodic faults; above all, it commends Christian piety.

188. Walchius, *Critical History of the Latin Language*, chapter 10, no. 7:

> Nor is it unworthy that Christian antiquities should not be unknown in Christian schools. Under this heading subjects and periods can be distributed in such a way that Aurelius Prudentius is not excluded from them, and that the books, especially the *Daily Matters* (*καθημερινῶν*) and *On Crowns* (*περὶ στεφάνων*), which explain the fortunes of the ancient Church, may be admitted among them. Let Sedulius, an imitator of the ancients, who so skillfully and devoutly adapted the words of Publius Maro and the sweetness of weaving verse from secular to sacred subject matter, be read privately. It is truly disgraceful that Christian poets should be so neglected that their very name is unknown to school-age students.

The danger that some fear from this for the study of good Latin and poetry is sufficiently removed if suitable notes are added indicating the usage of the best writers. Cellarius already expressly advised that the study of poetry be assisted in this way in his preface, where he continues:

> Finally, benevolent reader, I should also like to warn you not to judge Sedulius’s poems from his letter to Macedonius, which is prefixed to them and immediately presents itself to the reader. It is customary for most writers of that age to be more pleasing in verse than in prose, as is clear in Sidonius, Paulinus of Nola, Alcimus Avitus, and Prosper of Aquitaine. If you ask the reason, I shall explain it. In prose they wrote from their own ingenuity; poems they composed only from reading and imitating the ancients. Therefore do not be surprised that Sedulius’s letter is somewhat rough, while the *Paschal Poem* is so smooth, gentle, and pleasing that it approaches the praise and elegance of the ancient poets.

Grunerus observes in his preface that Sedulius’s learning is evident from his letter to Macedonius. He agrees, however, with Mosheim, *Institutes of Christian History and Antiquities*, that the learning of the fifth century was limited.

189. In his edition of Sedulius and of certain poems of Prudentius, Parrhasius made several observations about both poets. Since these characteristics are common to most Christian poets, it is not inappropriate to add them here:

> “To begin with Sedulius: he uses words neither wholly elevated with poetic figures nor yet vulgar, but preserves a kind of middle diction, so that the words retain their proper place. Yet he displays a thorough knowledge of sacred matters. For he says *factura* (‘created thing’), *factor* (‘Creator’), *deitas* (‘divinity’), *testamenta legis* (‘testaments of the Law’), and *coeli* (‘heavens’), although Lucretius too did not abstain from the last expression; also *ficulnea* (‘fig tree’), and, more unusually, *duodecim millia legiones* (‘twelve thousand legions’), from Jerome’s phrase, ‘Twelve thousand from the tribe of Manasseh were sealed.’ Prudentius is more Latin in this respect, saying *milia multa notarum* (‘many thousands of marks’), not *multae notae* (‘many marks’).
>
> “He also introduces several foreign expressions, though they had already been accepted by Christian authors: *patriarcha* (‘patriarch’), *synagoga* (‘synagogue’), *pharisaei* (‘Pharisees’), and, instead of *fortunatae insulae* (‘Fortunate Isles’), *paradisus* (‘paradise’); *gehenna*, meaning ‘burning’; and finally *manzeres*, that is, those conceived through adultery and sexual violation.
>
> “In some matters he follows analogy, as when he says *urbem libertatis opem*, that is, ‘a city fruitful in freedom,’ since its opposite is *inops*, ‘poor’ or ‘needy.’ In other matters, neglecting proportion, he follows common usage and takes from the ordinary people *praesumptor* (‘presumer’) and *traditor* (‘betrayer’). By the same principle he pronounced *Mariam* with the accent on the penultimate syllable, although Claudian always, and he himself sometimes, shortens it.
>
> “He likewise uses *populatio* for an unorganized multitude: ‘A multitude was present’ (*Fiebat populatio praesens*), although some prefer to read, ‘The people present were weeping’ (*Flebat populus quoque praesens*). He also substitutes a derivative for its primitive, as in *Memphitis in oris* (‘on the Memphite shores’) instead of *Memphitidi*, from which it is derived. Tibullus has:

> *Pubes miratur Osirim—*  
> *Barbara Memphitem plangere docta bovem.*  
>
> “The youth marvel at Osiris—  
> the barbarian woman, skilled in lamenting the Memphite ox.”

> “He similarly uses *tempus* for *tempore*, as anyone can easily recognize for himself. He brings certain obsolete words back into use, such as *peniculum* (‘brush’) for Terence’s and Plautus’s *spongia* (‘sponge’); *praesepe* (‘manger’) in the Latin case-form from the ancient declension; and *deterta capillis* (‘wiped from the hair’), which he had read in Ennius: *Terta nitet galea* (‘The helmet gleams, wiped clean’).
>
> “He coined a few expressions, such as *pompare*, which he contrived, rather inflatedly, to the discredit of the ancient poets; and *simplat*: ‘What is simple, let him make triple; what is capable of being tripled, let him make simple’ (*Quod simplex, triplicet, quodque est triplicabile, simplet*). This is how it should be written, not *simplex*.
>
> “At times he departs from the prescribed metrical quantities. For you will often find in him the letter *h* functioning with the force of a vowel. He makes the first syllable of *Ioannes* short, although it is marked by the Greek omega [in the relevant tradition]. This is defended by the example of Maro, who changed the same letter into *o* and shortened it in *Orion*.
>
> “In him *regulus*, a name of dignity, is an anapest or a tribrach, although *rex*, from which it is derived, lengthens all its oblique cases. But this is to be understood of words that alter the quantity of their primitive and contract the quantity they receive, such as *dicax*, *lucerna*, *stabilis*, and several others. He also made an anapest of *Darius*, although its middle syllable is long because of the Greek diphthong. Ovidius has:

> *Utque necatorum Daraei fraude secundi*  
>
> “Unless, as I believe more nearly correct, he pronounced it as a disyllable; for many such contractions are found, as when he rather frequently says *aiscipulum* for *discipulorum* and *vestigis* for *vestigiis*.
>
> “He made *suave* a trisyllable, as Horace did *suetus* and Papinius *suasit*. But he acted far too boldly when, in the following verse, he contracted *-us* in the plural accusative of the fourth declension:

> *Non ratio, primosque necans vagitus, et audens.*  
>
> “But where you read in all copies, including ours, ‘It is written upon the title: This is the king of the Jews’ (*Scribitur in titulis super: Hic est rex Judaeorum*), I should judge it necessary to correct the text to: ‘It is written upon the title: This is the king of the Jews’ (*Scribitur in titulis: Hic est rex Judaeorum*), so that the verse may be reciprocal and spondaic, in imitation of Maro and others, and so that he may not, by this unprecedented example, shorten one and another syllable in *Judaeo*.”

190. “Prudentius,” Parrhasius continues, “although more carefully worked in his diction and less licentious, nevertheless claims the same poetic indulgence in *idolo* (‘idol’) and *paraclito* (‘Paraclete’), in which respect he found Apollinaris as a model. What of the fact that he pronounced the dative of the relative pronoun *cui* as a disyllable and three times in the same poem changed its final consonant into a vowel?

> *Caesaraugustam vocitamus urbem,*  
> *Res cui tanta est.*  
>
> “We call the city Caesaraugusta—  
> a matter for which it is so great.

> “And again:

> *Sanguinem Justi, cui Pastor haeret.*  
>
> “The blood of Justus, to whom the Shepherd clings.”

> “A little later:

> *Morsque Vincenti, cui sanguis hinc est.*  
>
> “And the death of Vincent, to whom this blood comes from here.”

> “This may be forgiven, but it cannot be approved, just as neither can the following: *Malorum tetrius omnium est* (‘It is more dreadful than all evils’).
>
> “He also frequently substitutes an anapest and a proceleusmatic for a spondee, on the basis of the quantity of the syllables; these are equal to and compatible with it. In *Nola*, whose first syllable Virgil lengthened—if Gellius has transmitted the truth—Prudentius shortens it:

> *Jamque Nolanus adest.*  
>
> “Some, however, write *Ianicolanus*, confusing the order of the places.
>
> “He too attempted to restore grace to words that had fallen into disuse. For *volupe*, meaning ‘it is pleasing,’ he borrowed from Ennius and Plautus; *ninguidos* from Lucretius, who calls what others call *nix* (‘snow’) *ninque*; and he says *pultet* for *pulset* (‘may he strike’) and *altar* by analogy:

> *Altar tepescit ore, saxum pectore.*  
>
> “The altar grows warm in the mouth, the stone in the breast.

> “Nor does he reject certain foreign words: *Messias* (‘Messiah’), *Nazarenus* (‘Nazarene’), *Levitas* (‘Levite’), *charaxat*, which is Greek *χάραξεν*, meaning ‘he pierces the body with the sharpened and slender points of reeds and stakes,’ a kind of punishment that the Spaniards still retain; *crypta* (‘crypt’); *colymbus*, that is, a basin or vessel into which flowing water is received; and *tumba* (‘tomb’) instead of *tumulus*.
>
> “Nor did he wish it to appear that he had wasted his labor in reading related writers. From them he took most of his expressions: *ecclesia* (‘church’), *evangelista* (‘evangelist’), *factor* (‘Creator’), *passio* (‘passion’), *animabus* (‘souls’), from which the ancients abstained; *psalmi* (‘psalms’); *martyres* (‘martyrs’), which he also interprets in Latin as *testes* (‘witnesses’), just as *angeli* are ‘messengers’; and other expressions that you will observe for yourself.
>
> “He also has certain expressions of his own: *cohaerant*, meaning ‘they attach’ or ‘they devote themselves’; *ab aere*, with an aspiration inserted to avoid hiatus; *artisis*, for the articular disease:

> *Nodosa torquet quos podagra, et artisis.*  
>
> “The gout and arthritis torment those afflicted with knots.

> “He uses *anulla*, a diminutive of *anus* (‘old woman’); *prosperante* for *favente* (‘favoring’); *prosperare* for ‘to be present’; and *sacrum*, where others use *sacerdotem* (‘priest’):

> *Vidimus, o Christi Valleriane sacer.*  
>
> “We have seen you, O Valerian, sacred to Christ.

> “In this name he doubled the liquid, as elsewhere in *Valleriis* and *relligione*. He also says *sacrare* for *sacrificare* (‘to sacrifice’) and *sacrantem* for *sacrificantem* (‘sacrificing’).
>
> “Some hold that *esto* in his works is not a verb or a particle of affirmation but an adverb of exhortation, serving neither number nor person:

> *Esto, precor, fortes, et vincite viribus annos.*  
>
> “‘Come, I beg you, be strong and conquer the years by your strength.’

> “We, however, think that *este* should be read.
>
> “You will also encounter some rather obscure expressions: *fornix*, meaning ‘brothel’; *solum* for the sole of the foot; *terrigenae*, that is, ‘men born from the earth,’ whom God is said to have fashioned from clay; and *virginal*, the membrane in women’s genitalia that guards modesty. Solinus uses the same word.
>
> “He says *lancinant* (‘they tear apart’ or ‘they lacerate’). Hence the Greek *lancinatores*, ‘butchers.’ He used *cautis* in the nominative singular, as P. Victor does *aedis*; *camurus* for *curvus* (‘curved’); *hyalus* for *vitrum* (‘glass’); and *sudus* for the clear serenity of the sky.
>
> “Following Virgil, he also says *aedituus* for one entrusted with the care of a temple; and *mera calce* for ‘with a bare foot,’ since the ancients called everything pure *merum*.
>
> “Six hundred other examples remain, which it is not now the time or purpose to enumerate. For his knowledge of things and words is so great that I would maintain that it equals that of any other writer among us.”

191. Thus far Parrhasius on Sedulius and Prudentius. Although his observations ought not to be approved in every respect, as is evident throughout from the Prolegomena to Prudentius and from the notes to him and to the other Christian poets, it nevertheless seemed worthwhile to transcribe them, so that a fair judgment might be formed when reading the sacred poets.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On Correctors and Corruptors of Manuscript Books. A Digression on the Codex of St. Hilary Preserved in the Archive of the Vatican Basilica

192. It was demonstrated above, in no. 159, that many learned men formerly existed, especially in the fifth century, who corrected and punctuated the books of ancient authors so that they might be made public in a more accurate form. The copyists themselves were sometimes compelled to compare what they had written with ancient exemplars and correct it against them.

In Vatican Codex Regina Sueciae 2034, a paper manuscript in folio, there is a chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea continued by Jerome and Prosper. It is preceded by Prosper’s adjuration:

> “I adjure you, whoever shall copy these books, by our Lord Jesus Christ and his glorious coming, at which he will come to judge the living and the dead, that you compare what you have written and carefully correct it against the exemplars from which you have copied it; and that you likewise copy this form of adjuration and transfer it into the codex that you shall copy.”

Matthew Palmerius imitated this adjuration of Prosper—or rather, perhaps, of someone else—at the end of the preface to his own Chronicle, which has not yet been published in full, as it is found in this same codex:

> “I therefore ask whoever shall at some time copy this book to copy it carefully, preserving the same order, and to compare what he has copied with the exemplars and correct it.”

See also Ducange, in the preface to his *Glossarium*, no. 6, and Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VI, chapter 21, who quotes similar words from Aponius’s preface to his commentary on the *Song of Songs*.

But the method of correction was not everywhere one and the same. Often words were entirely erased, so that what had been written could not be understood at all, or only with difficulty. This occurred when the words were plainly erroneous or when the corrector judged them to be so. Sometimes the word requiring correction was marked only by a little line placed above it, so that the reader would understand that the first hand’s writing was false and the second hand’s true. Sometimes, while leaving the word in the codex untouched, the corrector wrote a variant reading obtained by comparing other codices. At other times he added his own conjectures. There were also special signs for readily indicating such corrections, which Isidore explains in *Etymologies*, book I, chapter 20.

193. When codices corrected in this way came into the hands of others for copying, it often happened that one copyist adopted one reading and another a different reading. Since each copyist also introduced new errors of his own, there arose that abundance of variant readings which modern critical editors commonly collect when publishing the works of ancient authors.

I have found a rich harvest of such variants among the other Christian poets, but especially in Sedulius—perhaps because this celebrated poet found not only Asterius as an editor and corrector of his poems but also Abundantius as a collator.

194. We may add corruptors to the correctors of manuscripts, for it often happened that those who intended to correct actually corrupted. Although there can be no doubt that many people deliberately adulterated manuscript copies, either to confirm their own error or to weaken contrary authority, yet, in my view, this more often occurred through ignorance or preconceived opinion.

Walchius, in chapter 7 of his *Critical History of the Latin Language*, says:

> “Books are commonly corrupted by THEIR OWN AUTHORS, when, through a slip of the hand, they can easily write something other than what they think; by SCRIBES, who hear incorrectly, do not always understand orthography and ancient letters, and write what they think rather than what they hear; by THE DICTATOR, who sometimes does not understand the writing, sometimes reads the document without sufficiently careful attention, sometimes pronounces it incorrectly, and sometimes inserts glosses written in the margin of the book into the author’s own discourse; by COPYISTS and CRITICS, when they prefer elegant and polished writing to a corrected reading, and when they are either wholly absent from the task of correcting books or perform it in such a way that they corrupt more than they heal; and by AGE, which produces in books written on parchment or paper gaps of several words or of several letters.”

My concern now is with copyists and critics. One of them would come upon a passage that he did not understand, or that contradicted the opinion he himself considered true. Although he ought to have left the words untouched, he assumed that they were not the author’s but had been incorrectly written by the copyist; so he erased them and substituted others.

I have noticed that many verses in Juvencus were adulterated so as to conform to our Vulgate, which he himself could not have had before his eyes. In the works of other Fathers likewise, some took upon themselves the same liberty, reforming the words of sacred Scripture quoted from the Itala according to the model of our Vulgate. There is no need to revive the complaints of Latinius concerning this matter.

195. In Sedulius there are countless passages that are plainly shown to have been falsified, as the variant readings demonstrate. Sometimes this is evident for the sole reason that the verse, as composed by the poet, seemed to proceed less correctly, as in book IV, verse 8:

> *Clarifica, dixit, nomen tuum, magnaque coelo.*  
>
> “He said, ‘Glorify your name, and [make it] great in heaven.’”

When words are somewhat similar to one another, although they signify different things, the interchange of words is especially frequent. Thus, in book I, verse 3, I shall show that *mella* (‘honey’) was wrongly written by the copyists for *mala* (‘evils’); and in the same book, verse 247, *homo pronus adoret* (‘let the prone man adore’) was written for *homo plenus adoret* (‘let the full man adore’).

The copyists followed what appeared clearer to them, not what was truer. This will seem less surprising if we observe that in monasteries young men, generally not fully trained in the sciences, were assigned to the task of copying, and that they hurried improperly so as to reach the end of the book as quickly as possible.

In Vatican Codex Reg. 254, which contains the books of Isidore’s *Sentences* and *Soliloquies*, together with excerpts from the Fathers and other works, the copyist wrote childishly:

> *Explicit, expliceat: ludere scriptor eat.*  
>
> “It ends; may it be unfolded: let the scribe go play.”

There is also great disagreement among codices in the interchange of *adopto*, *adoro*, *adorno*, and *adapto*, as I note in book III, verse 294, and in the elegy, verse 31. Yet these passages were often rewritten differently by collators or readers according to each person’s differing opinion in theological matters, rather than according to what the author intended.

196. An opportunity now presents itself for me to expand upon what I promised above in no. 160: to discuss at greater length the ancient and celebrated codex of St. Hilary preserved in the Archive of the Vatican Basilica, which I myself inspected, and in which the word *adoratur* now appears, although it seems previously to have been *adoptatur*.

The matter had been related to me as though it were absolutely certain that the codex had been corrupted at the beginning of this century. I had also read in the life of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, written by the distinguished Antonio Francesco Vezzosi and prefixed to Thomasius’s theological institutions, that several censors had been appointed on 15 December 1707 to inspect the codex, among them the venerable Thomasius.

All of them, Vezzosius adds in no. 57, examined the codex most carefully and acknowledged, or confessed, that the corrupter of the word *ADOPTATUR* was not merely recent but VERY RECENT. They describe the matter, and so forth.

This account is written out more fully in the codex itself and described in detail in the *Vindications of the Ancient Codices Confirmed*, published at Paris in 1715. When I first saw the codex and inspected the passage, I was greatly surprised that the appointed censors could have judged the corrupter to be not merely recent but most recent. For it seemed to me, on the contrary, that the correction was indeed later than the codex’s original script, but nevertheless ancient and made many centuries before our time, and that it was not unlike other corrections observable in the same codex.

I therefore read the judgment of the censors written—or rather added—in the same codex. I was then even more surprised, since I found nothing about a most recent corrupter and nothing that contradicted my view of the correction as ancient.

197. These are the words of the censors, also quoted by Constantius in the *Vindications of the Ancient Codices Confirmed*:

> “In the original script of the first hand, ADO is still read; and in the space between the two erased letters, in place of those letters, another hand, in darker and more recent ink, different from that in which the codex was written, has superimposed the aforesaid letter R. This letter is followed by the two syllables of the first hand, namely ATUR; of these, the first letter A is partly covered with the same more recent ink and reshaped, as is most clearly apparent.”

From this nothing else may be inferred except that the letter R is later than the original script of the codex and than the handwriting of a certain scholar who says, in a subscription, that he collated the codex in the fourteenth year of King Trasamundus, that is, in the year of salvation 510.

Nor did the censors, when asked by the Reverend Father Guillelmus Laparre, Procurator General of the Maurists, to give their judgment, indicate the slightest suspicion of a very recent corruption of the codex.

How, then, could that rumor and fable have arisen concerning the very recent adulteration of the codex of the Vatican Basilica? Certainly from nowhere other than the *Diary of the Learned Men of Italy*, published at Venice in 1716, volume XXIII, article 13, where Constantius’s book, *The Vindications of the Ancient Codices Confirmed*, is announced.

There I read the following about the appointed censors:

> “They discovered that it had RECENTLY, and VERY RECENTLY, been adulterated and retouched with NEW AND MOST MODERN ink.”

It is fortunate, however, that no witness is cited except the very document we have quoted, by which the slander is completely disproved. It is unbelievable how ineptly the author of that article fabricated his falsehoods. To pass over everything else, he mentions the first *Vindications of the Manuscript Codices*, published by Constantius in 1706; then he reports that Father Tellier had noticed the Vatican Basilica codex during Holy Week of 1707 in order to oblige Germonius. When others had detected this, censors were appointed to deliver their judgment on the codex, and an authentic document was sent to the Maurists in Paris.

198. He continues:

> “Father Coustant, in his abundance of charity and moderation toward his opponent, was content merely to show in handwriting the document received from Rome, without printing it in his first Vindications.”

But how could he publish in the first *Vindications*, issued in 1706, a document drawn up in 1707?

In 1716 Germonius published from Paris a letter to the editors of the Venetian *Diary*. It was also inserted in the *Trevultine Memoirs* and appeared in Italian. In it he vigorously rebuts the slander directed not so much against himself as against Tellierius, a man of outstanding seriousness who had guided the conscience of King Louis XIV and had become still more illustrious through his writings and approved character.

He states that Tellierius inspected the codex of St. Hilary in the presence of the Most Eminent Gozzadini, then prefect of the Archive of the Vatican Basilica, and Zaccagnius, prefect of the Vatican Library. He observes that Tellierius was the first of all to notice and to report, in a letter addressed to Germonius on 19 April 1707, the correction of the word *adoratur* from *adoptatur*.

199. He adds that no reason can be devised why Tellierius would have corrupted the codex except so that Germonius might obtain some advantage from it. But Germonius could obtain no advantage from a passage that Tellierius demonstrated to be corrupt and that Germonius himself was the first to publish in print as corrupt.

Finally, from the very document produced by Constantius, he clearly proves that it is slanderous to claim that the censors declared the corrupter of the codex to be most recent.

Nevertheless, many people still tell this story. In a copy of Constantius’s *Vindications Confirmed* preserved in the Casanatense Library, a not very recent hand has written in the margin of part III, chapter 5, beside the words *virum doctissimum reperio*:

> “That is, Father Le Tellier, the Jesuit, who is thought to have falsified this passage.”

To make clear how false this is, I shall return to the matter from its beginning and add several observations of my own.

Felix of Urgel supported his heresy—that Christ was the adoptive Son of God—by this passage from book II, chapter 27 of St. Hilary’s *On the Trinity*, along with other testimonies of the Fathers:

> *Aliud intelligitur, aliud videtur, aliud oculis, aliud animo conspicitur. Parit Virgo, partus a Deo est: infans vagit, laudantes angeli audiuntur: panni sordent, Deus adoratur. Ita potestatis dignitas non amittitur, dum carnis humilitas adoptatur.*  
>
> “One thing is understood, another is seen; one thing is perceived by the eyes, another by the mind. The Virgin gives birth; the birth is from God. The infant cries; the angels who praise are heard. The swaddling clothes are soiled; God is adored. Thus the dignity of power is not lost while the lowliness of the flesh is adopted.”

200. The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt charged Elipandus and Felix with deceitfully abusing corrupted testimonies of the Fathers:

> “It is time for us to come to the examination of the meaning of your little book, in which we find testimonies of the holy Fathers placed in various passages, but corrupted by the poison of wicked treachery, and the teeth of your error inserted among the most beautiful flowers of the Catholic faith. You have suppressed the names of the books and the numbers of the chapters, so that your error might be investigated with greater difficulty; and from this alone it is clear that you have erred deliberately.”

And later:

> “We find—and, as we stated above, we find with absolute certainty—that you have infected their most holy writings with the poison of heretical perversity and have INSERTED words that we nowhere read in their books.”

201. At that time Alcuin, an outstanding defender of Catholic doctrine, was active against Felix. In book VI he attacks him as follows:

> “Moreover, through the wickedness of your cunning you suppress certain things that seem to condemn your heresy. But you do not fear to alter other things with the trickery customary to you, as you appear to have done in the books of blessed Hilary. There that outstanding and Catholic teacher says, ‘The dignity of power is not lost’; but you, in the utmost perversity, say ADOPTATUR, where blessed Hilary says ADORATUR.”

We therefore cannot agree with Constantius, who claims that Alcuin sufficiently indicates that he had never seen a codex in which *adoptatur* was read. On the contrary, Alcuin ought not to have reproached Felix so openly and plainly unless he was certain from the codices that Hilary had written *adoratur*, since Felix could very easily have refuted him.

Thus, when Alcuin replies to Elipandus, who cites certain words from the Gothic office, Alcuin—because he had not seen the codices themselves—merely conjectures either that those words were not found in the codices or that such liturgical codices were corrupt, as I shall explain later.

202. From what the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt and Alcuin report against Felix, the only certain conclusion is that Felix quoted the words of the Fathers, and specifically of Hilary, differently from the way they stood in manuscript copies; it cannot be concluded that he himself corrupted the codices.

But when Alcuin pressed him concerning the passage of St. Hilary, it is most probable that Felix attempted to substitute *adoptatur* in some codex in which *adoratur* was read.

Isidore says of heretics in book III, chapter 12 of the *Sentences*:

> “Sometimes they insert their blasphemies into the books of our writers by concealed deceit and corrupt the true doctrine by adulterating it: either by adding what is impious or by removing what is pious.”

This is what Constantius refused to believe when Hincmarus related it concerning Felix, although so many details have been added that confirm the account.

203. Hincmarus, in his work *On the Non-Trinal Deity*, testifies as follows against the monk Gottschalk:

> “Felix, once bishop of the city of Urgel, unhappy in name and deed, in the book of blessed Hilary, where that same saint had said, ‘The lowliness of the flesh is ADORED,’ during the time of the emperor Charlemagne adulterated every copy that he could seize, changing it everywhere to ‘The lowliness of the flesh is ADOPTED,’ so that, since he could not support his opinion by truth, he might support it by falsehood.”

204. Hincmarus relates the same matter again and produces the gravest witnesses in the preface to his treatise *On Predestination*:

> “As we learned from the report of those who were present at the council [of Aachen], how the lord Charles, of blessed memory, proved Felix, the unhappy bishop of the city of Urgel, to be a heretic by synodal decree, and discovered him condemned, indeed found him convicted anew, because, after corrupting by bribes a younger librarian of the palace of Aachen, he scraped the book of blessed Hilary and, where it was written that in the Son of God ‘the lowliness of the flesh is ADORED,’ inserted: ‘the lowliness of the flesh is ADOPTED.’”

205. Hincmarus therefore asserts and confirms, with no one at that time or afterward contradicting him, that Hilary’s passage had been corrupted. He relates this of the heretic Felix, whose frauds and perjuries are known from other sources.

When Felix was disseminating his heresy, he was convicted at the Council of Regensburg in 792 and abjured his error; and again in the same year at the Roman council under Pope Hadrian:

> “He made an orthodox written confession while in chains, anathematizing and affirming, among other things, that the Son of God was in no way adoptive, as he had said, but that ‘I confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be the proper and true Son of God.’ Therefore, placing this same orthodox written confession upon the sacred mysteries of God in our patriarchate, he swore that he would hold and confess it thus. And again, placing that same orthodox written confession upon the body of blessed Peter the Apostle, he likewise swore there, and so forth.”

This is related in the Roman council under Pope Leo III, held in the year of Christ 799, act 2.

206. From this council itself it is clear that when Felix had returned home, he again defended his heresy, disregarding all his sworn confessions. He was condemned again at the Council of Frankfurt in 794. When Alcuin sent him a letter urging him to return to the right path, Felix replied with an entire book and taught things even worse than before.

Alcuin consequently took the occasion to write seven books against Felix. Leidradus—also called Laidradus or Laidracus—archbishop of Lyons, was sent to Urgel, Felix’s own see, to recall him from error. Felix obtained permission from Leidradus to approach Charlemagne; and thus, when a synod had been assembled in the palace at Aachen, Alcuin disputed with Felix and compelled him to renounce his heresy, although shortly before, in the same year 799, the Felician heresy had also been proscribed at Rome by Pope Leo III.

207. At the Council of Aachen there survives Felix’s confession of the Catholic faith, composed after he had already been deposed from the episcopate. He says that he returned to the Church with all his heart, not through any pretense or veil of falsehood, as formerly—“God knows”—but, as I have said, through true belief of heart and profession of mouth.

Yet this same Felix, sent into exile at Lyons, carefully and deceitfully restored, as far as he could, the whole perversity of his doctrine, as Agobard relates at the beginning of the book he wrote against Felix after Felix’s death.

Constantius presses Germonius with the objection that Albinus made no mention of this crime after the Council of Aachen. Germonius replies that Albinus did not wish to revive the memory of the corrupted codices, lest it prove offensive both to others and to Felix, who had sung a recantation and, by shaping his conduct to an outward appearance of virtue, had drawn many people into admiration of himself.

But in my view Albinus, although he spared Felix’s name, nevertheless indicated the matter clearly enough in book II against Elipandus. Speaking of the prayers of the Gothic office, he says:

> “And it appears that by certain corruptors *adoptivi* [‘adoptive’] has been put in place of *assumpti* [‘assumed’] with reference to the man … And perhaps in the older copies *assumpti hominis* [‘of the assumed man’] was written there, but was later corrupted … It must therefore be judged all the more seriously that certain younger men, bound by the chains of this new unbelief, corrupt the sayings of the holy teachers to their own destruction and stain the name of their fathers with the worst obstinacy … And this appears likely to be true because we have recognized that you either interpret the Catholic opinions of the most approved and universally accepted teachers of the Church of Christ in a perverse sense or alter them with treacherous audacity, as we have proved in certain passages, when several little writings of your error reached us through Felix, formerly yours but now our fellow soldier.”

208. Everything therefore leads us to believe that Hincmarus’s account is true. Indeed, in the German codex of Hilary, formerly Corbeiensis and once belonging to Aachen, Constantius found traces of Felician corruption—namely *adoptatur* in an erased passage. He even suspects that this is the codex which Hincmarus complains was corrupted by the younger librarian who had been bribed.

Although in the *Vindications* Constantius asserts that the alteration in the Germanus codex occurred either through a copyist’s mistake—the copyist first wrote *adoratur* and immediately corrected himself—or through an erasure caused by parchment that had not been smoothed evenly, he had expressed his own view more openly in a note on the passage of St. Hilary, book II, chapter 27:

> “We possess a Corbeiensis book written more than 800 years ago, displaying these final syllables, PTATUR, in an erased place. Although perhaps written in bad faith, ADOPTATUR has nevertheless been written correctly.”

He speaks according to his own opinion.

209. The German codex, which, by Constantius’s own admission, was present in the library at Aachen during the time of Charlemagne, therefore lends credibility to Hincmarus’s account.

But there is also another codex written long before the time of Charlemagne, namely the Veronensis, in which the first reading is clearly *adoratur*, although someone attempted to change it to *adoptatur*. Let us hear Maffei in his preface to Hilary:

> “First, then, let it be accepted as certain that in this book *ADORATUR* is written, with no trace of scraping and no suspicion of an overwriting. Yet because after that word the verse is resumed from the beginning, *ADOPTATUR* was added in the vacant space that remained, either by the same hand or by one only slightly later.
>
> “No insult was directed against the earlier word, but lines placed above it and an R written in the upper margin indicate, according to the customary practice, that the added word should be substituted for the earlier one. In other codices, however, more certain testimony must still be REQUIRED …
>
> “In the word *ADOPTATUR* the shape of the letters and precisely the same color of ink are found; yet it is now apparent that someone formerly used a light knife and attempted to remove and erase the letters and the lines written above them.
>
> “All these things lead me to the following conjectures: first, the copyist clearly and without hesitation wrote *ADORATUR*. Then, either by the copyist himself after subsequently examining other copies or by someone else, *ADOPTATUR* was added, together with an indication that *ADORATUR* should be deleted. Someone else then came along who did not approve the second reading and attempted to remove the word *ADOPTATUR*, as the cloudy traces of scraping sufficiently testify.”

Thus Maffei judges prudently.

210. In favor of the reading *adoptatur*, Constantius cites two ancient codices, the Colbertinus and the Carnutensis, which he says are approximately a thousand years old and earlier than the time of Charlemagne.

Germonius, on the other hand, strongly doubts whether these codices are so ancient that it can be determined with certainty that they were copied before the Felician heresy, even if they do indeed claim an age of approximately a thousand years. Nor are the arguments brought forward by Constantius of such a character that they ought to be accepted in so fallible a method of judgment.

211. If we consider the ancient editions, they chiefly prefer the reading *adoratur*: for example, the edition of Badius Ascensius, Paris 1510; the two Basel editions that followed, one of 1523, revised by Erasmus, and the other of 1535; and the edition of Ludovicus Miraeus, which Constantius considered more carefully corrected than all those published before and after it.

This edition is rare. When Constantius had already despaired of finding it, he discovered it in the large Carmelite convent. It is also held in the Roman College under the following title:

> *The Works of D. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, formerly corrected by Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam with no small labor, now once again revised with the most vigilant care against exemplars of marvelous antiquity. Paris, from the workshop of Carolus Guillard, under the Golden Sun.*

Ludovicus Miraeus supplies the preface.

Nevertheless, Constantius cites several other editions in favor of *adoptatur*: those of Martinus Lipsius, 1544; Grineus, 1570; Gillotius, 1572; and the Paris editions of 1605, 1631, and 1652.

Constantius had observed in his preface that Gillotius left Hilary’s text untouched; that the reprinted edition of 1570 was more corrupt than the earlier one; and that, because of the multitude of errors, the Basel editions seemed plainly preferable to the Paris edition of 1605, which was later reprinted.

In fact, in the Paris editions of 1572 and 1605 I find an error in this very passage:

> *Ita potestatis dignitas non admittitur*  
>
> “Thus the dignity of power is not admitted”

Correct *admittitur* to *amittitur*:

> “Thus the dignity of power is not lost, while the lowliness of the flesh is adopted.”

212. Influenced by these considerations and by the two codices, the Corbeiensis and the Carnutensis, which he believed to have been written before Felix, Constantius preferred the reading *adoptatur* in his edition of St. Hilary.

Although Constantius had indicated that no codex of St. Hilary could be found older than the codex of the Vatican Basilica, and although he inserted in their proper places the various readings of this codex that had been sent to him from Rome, at this passage he did not even mention the codex of the Vatican Basilica in support of the reading *adoptatur*.

213.
