Germonius, who had not approved Constantius’s preference for the reading *adoptatur*, wanted to ascertain what reading was found in the codex of the Vatican basilica; thus, having been informed first of all by Tellier, he publicized the corruption of that codex, in which [Col. 0521C] *adoratur* is now read, but in which previously, as it seems, *adoptatur* was read. From this it is entirely clear that there is no ground for suspecting any fraud either in Germonius or in Tellier. No one had said a word in this controversy about the reading of this codex when Germonius wrote, in part II, chapter 9 of *On Corrupt Codices*: “Since, however, I consider it a religious obligation to omit nothing that can contribute to elucidating the truth, I shall not conceal a matter which seems to have escaped Constantius: namely, that *ADOPTATUR* was originally written in that codex. For so I learned from a most learned man who, at my request, carefully examined that book.”

214. Let us now demonstrate this point more clearly. Constantius writes as follows about the codex of the Vatican basilica in the preface to his edition of Hilary, no. 2: [Col. 0521D] “None seems likely to be found more ancient than the one preserved in the archive of the Vatican Church. . . . Yet it must not be denied that an ancient codex contains ancient errors. . . . For that reason, we have attributed nothing rashly to the antiquity of this codex, granting it only such veneration as led us carefully to record ALMOST ALL the readings in which it differs from the others. Our brothers residing in Rome transcribed these readings for us, after they had been collected by Giovanni Battista Bandini, canon of the Vatican basilica, while he was preparing a new edition of Hilary; and, carefully checking several things themselves, they commended the diligence of the aforementioned Canon.”

In the same way, in the *Second Vindication*, part III, chapter 5, Constantius reports the following while speaking of the same codex: “But our good faith compelled us to remain silent about the passage now under dispute, [Col. 0522A] since we lacked the edition of Ludovicus Miraeus which our brothers had used at Rome for collating it with the codex, and consequently it was not established what was read in that codex. Nor did I then think that we needed the authority of this codex to confirm a reading which we had always regarded as sufficiently certain on other grounds. Moved by our silence, the disputant—and, as may be suspected, believing that the codex favored him—urged a most learned man to examine it carefully.”

215. Therefore, since the edition collated with the codex of the Vatican basilica presents *adoratur*, and since Bandini and Maurini did not record any variant reading for this passage, it must consequently be held that the diligent men whom Constantius describes found *adoratur* written in that codex. Even if they noticed that the letter *r* had been written in a more spacious erased place by a second hand, they nevertheless did not think it necessary to mention this, because they believed it to be a true correction of an error, as many such corrections occur in that codex.

Indeed, Constantius, who also cites Miraeus’s edition of Hilary in his first book, may seem somewhat negligent in failing to consult it for this passage of the second book. But what if he had consulted it? He would have read there the word *adoratur*, contrary to his own position; and since, among the various readings sent from Rome, he had recorded no discrepancy at this passage, he would have had to conclude that *adoratur* was read in the codex of the Vatican basilica.

216. But that the same word *adoratur* had existed in that codex much earlier is clear from the collation carried out by the most diligent scholar, Latinius Latinius. His various readings and observations on the Paris edition of Saint Hilary, printed under the Golden Sun in 1544—that is, Ludovicus Miraeus’s edition—are preserved in his *Sacred and Profane Library*, pp. 38 ff.

At the beginning there is this annotation: “On 22 January 1561, I collected from the codex of the basilica of Saint Peter, written in almost majuscule letters and of astonishing antiquity, the various readings marked with the letter P.” He then records with the greatest accuracy the variants for the twelve books *On the Trinity*, the book *Against Constantius*, the two books *To Constantius*, the book *Against the Arians or Auxentius*, the letter of Auxentius, and the book *On the Synods*. In this last book, at the words “Truly of the Holy Spirit, and not simply by these names,” he immediately adds this warning: “Thus far extends the exemplar of the basilica of Saint [Col. 0522D] Peter, in which several quires are missing.”

217. To make clear how carefully and diligently Latinius worked through the codex and illustrated Hilary, I shall record a few of both his variant readings and his conjectures.

Book I, or chapter 1, *On the Trinity*, in Miraeus’s edition: “That the one without the other”; in the codex of the Vatican basilica: “What else without the other.” Constantius reads as Miraeus does, but observes no discrepancy in the wording.

In the same place, Miraeus has: “happy with luxuriant pastures as they wander”; in the codex of the Vatican basilica: “pastures luxuriantly as they wander.” Constantius prints “happy with luxuriant pastures as they roam,” and merely notes, from the Colbertine and Germanic manuscripts, *vacantibus* instead of *evagantibus*.

Again, Miraeus has “from the pastures”; the codex of the Vatican basilica has “from feeding.” Constantius prints “from the pastures” and records no variant.

Again, Miraeus has “the most complete use of human life will be considered”; the codex of the Vatican basilica has “the complete use of human life would exist.” Constantius agrees entirely with Miraeus but does not indicate the divergent reading.

218. I have drawn these examples from number 1 of book I, which comprises only thirty-two short lines. Latinius continues in the same manner. In chapter II of that same book, where Miraeus’s edition has “for an inept and brutish life,” he records nothing from the codex of the Vatican basilica but proposes his own conjecture, *inertis* for *inepte*. Constantius prints “of an inept and brutish [life].”

In the same chapter, Miraeus has “because of which indeed”; the codex of the Vatican basilica has “to which.” Latinius notes that *to* should be removed. Conversely, the word *munus* is absent from the codex, and Latinius judges that it should be added.

What more is needed? Latinius had recorded at least twenty-six corrections or variant readings by chapter 10, where Constantius first names the codex of the Vatican basilica, at the words “from the will of bodies.” There he notes: “The most ancient codex of the Vatican basilica, along with most other manuscripts, has VOLUPTATE”—a variant also recorded by Latinius in his edition.

219. When this great man, endowed with such keen intelligence, had reached chapter 27 of book II *On the Trinity*, and in his own edition read “the humility of the flesh is adored,” with *humanity* in the margin instead of *humility*, he recorded nothing. Retaining in the text what had been received from the codex, he printed “the humility of the flesh is adored,” and inserted none of his own conjectures, as he did elsewhere.

He could, however, have observed that the word *adoratur* had been written by a later hand either from *adoptatur*, or from *adornatur*, or from *adaptatur*: for in the letter *o* there is also some trace of a later hand and more recent ink. But however that word may have been written by the first hand, Latinius judged that it was an error properly corrected by the second hand through *adoratur*.

The corrector certainly did not wish to pretend that *adoratur* had been written by the first hand. For although the inserted letter *r* bears the appearance of antiquity, as is evident from its form, it differs very greatly from the form of the same letter *r* written by the first hand in the same word *adoratur* and elsewhere.

220. Someone might perhaps think that Latinius had fallen asleep while reviewing this chapter XXVII of book II, or had been less diligent than elsewhere. Certainly not. Rather, one should admire the man’s consistent diligence everywhere.

Miraeus reads in this chapter *Emmanuel*, that is, “God with us”; for in Latinius’s *Sacred Library* it is incorrectly printed *Deus*, “God,” as is clear from the context and from Miraeus’s own edition. Constantius likewise has “Emmanuel, that is, God with us,” as Maffeius also printed it. But Latinius, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, notes *Emmanuehel*, that is, “God with us.”

In the same place Miraeus has: “The Spirit proclaims through the prophet; the angel is a witness.” Constantius likewise prints this without any variant reading. Latinius, however, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, has: “The Holy Spirit proclaims through the prophet; the Angel has testified.”

Miraeus has: “A new light of the star from heaven is brought forth for the Magi.” Constantius likewise prints this, adding the note: “The old books consistently write *ECFERTUR* or *HECFERTUR*.” But Latinius, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, observes: “A new light of the star from heaven rises for the Magi.”

Miraeus and Constantius have: “Then, glory to God in heaven, and peace.” Latinius, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, has: “Glory to God in the highest, then peace.”

Miraeus and Constantius have: “And after that hidden operation of his empty knowledge.” Latinius, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, has: “And after those things, in the hidden operation of his empty knowledge.”

Miraeus has *desuper veniens*, “coming from above”; Latinius, from the codex of the Vatican basilica, has *superveniens*, “coming upon.” Constantius printed the latter as well, adding the note that the common editions have *desuper veniens*.

221. All these observations by Latinius concern chapter XXVII of book I; and not far from the word *superveniens* occur the words “the humility is adored” in Miraeus’s edition. Latinius passed over them as agreeing with the codex, without recording any variant reading.

It must nevertheless be mentioned that shortly before this, Miraeus reads “and the Angel himself announcing,” whereas Constantius has “and the angel announcing,” with the note: “Thus the manuscripts; in the common editions *id ipsum* is added here.” Latinius, however, did not recognize in the codex of the Vatican basilica a reading different from Miraeus’s *et ipsum angelus*.

Although Latinius’s *Sacred Library* should in itself be sufficient to establish that he appended no variant from the codex of the basilica of Saint Peter at the word *adoratur*, I arranged for the exemplar of Miraeus’s edition itself—on whose margin he had entered the readings of the aforementioned codex—to be examined by a trustworthy friend. I learned from him that Latinius had written nothing at this passage beside the word *adoratur*.

That exemplar is preserved in the library of the Chapter of Canons of Viterbo, together with other books that had belonged to Latinius, on whose margins he had entered many observations, either on the authority of manuscript codices or by conjecture. I also examined these books while I was at Viterbo.

After investigating and recording these matters, I happened by chance upon a Paris edition of Hilary, printed by Sebastian Nivellius in 1572, in the library of the Roman College, though it had been placed out of its proper order and location. I discovered that it had been collated with the celebrated codex of the Vatican Basilica by the supreme critic M. Antonius Muretus with the utmost accuracy, with variant readings added in the margin.

The codex is called “of Saint Peter,” and that it is the very codex under dispute is entirely evident from the place where it begins, where it ends, and from the various readings. [Col. 0524D] Although part of the first leaf was deliberately cut away at the beginning of the first page—on which, as I believe, was written “From the books of Muretus: Library of the Secret Collection of the Roman College,” as can be seen in Muretus’s other books preserved in the more private library of the Roman College—the hand of the variant readings is wholly Muretus’s. This will be clear to anyone comparing it with Muretus’s hand in other books collated by him in the same manner, and with his other autographs preserved in that library.

In this edition, therefore, *adoptatur* is printed; at this passage Muretus notes: “s. e. it became *ADORATUR*.” I understand this to mean: “This is how it stood; it became *ADORATUR*,” or “the erased writing became [*ADORATUR*],” and so forth. Certainly Muretus affirms that even then *adoratur* could be seen as the resulting reading. He also observes other similar corrections made by an ancient hand.

It would certainly have been desirable for Constantius to have had before his eyes these various readings of Muretus, together with the notes that he intersperses. For the readings sent from Rome by his associates are exceedingly rare and do not sufficiently conform to the exemplar. Thus, in book IX, chapter 63, he notes: “Only in Mart. and Bas. Vat.: *CONSUMMABUNTUR*,” whereas Muretus, at the words in chapter LIX of the same book, “of the future will to be set in motion,” observes instead that in the old codex of Saint Peter a quire is missing up to the words “they are mine” in chapter 73.

Moreover, since the writing of the codex is more recent at the beginning, near the end of book I *On the Trinity*, at the words “It is the signification of birth,” Muretus adds this note: “Here the ancient writing begins.” In the book *On the Synods Against the Arians*, at the words “and truly certain of the Son, truly of the Son,” he notes: “Thus far the codex of Saint Peter. The rest must be collated with the Vatican codices”—which he in fact did, adding the differing readings from the Vatican codex to the margin in the same manner.

222. A further question then arose concerning the antiquity of the codex preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica. First, I observe that the codex of Saint Hilary does not seem to have been brought to the archive of the basilica of Saint Peter before the fifteenth century. For Ambrosius Camaldulensis, who searched everywhere with the greatest care for ancient codices, especially those of the Fathers, examined first the library of the Pontiff and then the library of Saint Peter at Rome. Of the latter he reports in the Martenian collection, *Script.*, vol. II, col. 545, letter 16:

“I wished to see the library of Saint Peter, hoping to find something new. For I had heard that it contained many volumes; but I found absolutely nothing worth remembering. I encountered scarcely a few things from well-known subjects, worthless, etc.”

Mabillonius, in *De re diplomatica*, p. 356, says in his discussion of the second period of Roman script that the codex in question was written toward the end of the fourth century or at the beginning of the fifth. But, as is clear from the context itself, he meant toward the end of the fifth century or at the beginning of the sixth; and he corrected it accordingly in the *Supplement to De re diplomatica*, pp. 78–79.

At the end of the book *Against Constantius* there is an inscription by a certain scholar who collated the codex in the fourteenth year of King Trasamundus. That year, as Mabillonius observes on the authority of Holstenius, corresponds to the year 510.

223. In the Alexandrian codex of the Vatican Library, no. 1598, a paper manuscript in octavo, there is at the beginning a catalogue of the library of the Vatican basilica, apparently compiled at the beginning of the seventeenth century. The codex of Saint Hilary preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica is described in this catalogue, folio 4 verso, as follows:

“Saint Hilary’s book, written in the most ancient character more than eleven hundred years ago.” On folio 288 is recorded: “I collated this in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, established at Putrasulis, in the fourteenth year of King Transamundus.”

In the margin of this catalogue appears, in the same hand, the note “Around the year of Our Lord 500”; and beside the word *Putrasulis* another note in the same hand reads: “A place in Africa, in the province of Numidia, between Tunis and the fortress of Goletta, today commonly called PUTRACCIO.”

The description of the codex continues: “It contains the twelve books *On the Trinity Against the Arians*; the book *Against the Emperor Constantius*, folio 276; the same author’s two books *To the Emperor Constantius*, folio 288; the book *Against Auxentius of Milan*, folio 294; the book *On the Synods Against the Arians*, folio 300.”

“In this volume there are eighteen folios written in a different and not equally ancient hand, and after folio 192 eight folios are missing. At the end of the book twenty-four folios are missing, on which the book *On the Synods* was contained.”

“On folio 33 are inserted these poems in praise of Saints Maurus and Benedict: ‘You who desire to be blessed, come here joyfully; seek the aid of Father Benedict,’ etc.” The complete hymn is transcribed, whose ending is: “May Christ grant us to follow [him] thereby.”

By chance I came across the author of this hymn. John Mezler, in *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, while praising Ekkehard the Elder, who died in 966, reports: “He wrote sequences: ‘You who desire to be blessed,’ etc.”

224. Mabillonius, in *De re diplomatica*, also presents the inscription of the year in which Hilary’s codex was collated, appended by an unknown person to Hilary’s books *On the Trinity*—though he should rather have said “to the book *Against Constantius*.” He observes that the person who arranged the catalogue of the Vatican church read “I collated,” etc., as *Putzalis*, and explained it as referring to the town of Putrazzio.

Although he had not seen the codex, Mabillonius himself argues from the form of the characters transmitted to him that the reading should be *Kasulis* rather than *Putzalis*, and understands it as Casula, a city in the province of Byzacena.

225. Since everyone agrees on the fourteenth year of the king—whom most assert is called Trasamundus, while others say Transamundus in the codex—in which the codex was collated, there seems to be no remaining doubt that its age should be placed around the year 500.

But can we be certain of the truth of this inscription? I said above, in no. 159, and demonstrated with the clearest example in no. 160, that such subscriptions were often added by ignorant scribes or introduced through fraud in order to increase the value of codices. The example was another codex of the same Vatican basilica, said to have been corrected at the beginning of the fifth century.

Mabillonius himself, though highly experienced in this matter, was once deceived by a similar forged inscription. He attributed a document written in the year 564 to the earliest period of Roman script, believing it to be the will of Gaius Julius Caesar; later, by chance, he himself discovered the fraud.

226. I certainly do not deny that the inscription should be accepted as true unless there are grounds for doubt. But in our case there are grounds for doubt, and not slight ones.

The character of the codex shown in Mabillonius’s specimen gives no certain indication of such great antiquity that it can be assigned to the sixth century. Thus think not only Germonius but also Maffeius, in the preface to his edition of Saint Hilary. Nor did the codex itself appear otherwise to me when I examined it.

The specimen provided by Mabillonius—and, following Mabillonius, by the two Maurist authors of the *Diplomatic Treatise* in French, vol. III—seems to display greater antiquity than the actual exemplar of the Vatican basilica. Those two Maurists understand this to be the codex they call “the Vatican manuscript” on p. 263.

Certainly Hilary’s text is not divided into two columns, as are all codices that we know with certainty to have reached such antiquity; the same is true of the two Veronese codices of Hilary whose specimen Maffeius presents in the preface to Saint Hilary’s works.

The form of all the characters suggests a later age. The words are separated from one another by a suitable interval, which is considered a most certain indication that the codices are not very ancient. If you examine the codex carefully according to the rules that Trombellius has handed down to us in *The Art of Recognizing the Age of Codices*, you will conclude without hesitation that the codex was written in the eighth or ninth century.

227. Germonius brings forward many arguments for the falsity of the subscription itself. For although at the end of other books of Hilary one reads, in a sufficiently clear hand, “I collated,” or “I collated in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” the words added at the end of the book *Against Constantius*—“established at Kasulis in the fourteenth year of King Trasamundus”—appear to be of a different form and a later age, as is evident in the specimen of the Mabillonian plate.

This is also indicated by the fact that they are read and explained differently by different scholars, whereas the earlier words of the subscription are immediately understood by everyone.

Moreover, Maffeius approves neither *Putzalis*, as Holstenius read it, nor *Kasulis*, as Mabillonius read it; he thinks that a different name was written in place of *Trasamundus* or *Transamundus*.

Furthermore, in this subscription certain letters extend so far beyond the line that I know of nothing similar in codices of the sixth or seventh century.

Nothing certain, therefore, remains from which the age of the codex can be fixed in the sixth century, although it cannot be denied that the codex is of venerable antiquity and deserves to be highly valued.

228. Some may perhaps ask which reading of Hilary is ultimately genuine: “the humility of the flesh is adopted” or “the humility of the flesh is adored.”

Maffeius concludes from his own codex that *ADORATUR* was indeed once readily read; nevertheless, he concludes that this reading too was questioned in antiquity, and long before Felix of Urgell.

The interchange of these words in codices is so easy that, whether Hilary wrote *adoratur* or *adoptatur*, it is highly probable that both readings existed in codices even before Felix. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the Veronese codex, which alone indisputably predates Felix’s time.

We may therefore conjecture that Felix really found *adoptatur* in some codex, and seized upon that word because he thought it favored his heresy. Alcuin, by contrast, read *adoratur* in Hilary, believing that the sense also required it.

But Felix—either because the codex in which he had read *adoptatur* was not available to him, or because he wished that word to be absent and another, *adoptatur*, to be substituted in the other codices in which *adoratur* was read—arranged for the Aachen codices to be corrupted, as Hincmar testifies.

229. After the Felician heresy, the same word was changed in the codices, either because some codices copied from those corrupted by Felix preferred *adoptatur*, and certain Catholics, judging the word spurious, changed it to *adoratur*, or because the same question always remained: whether, according to Hilary’s meaning, it was preferable to read *adoratur* or *adoptatur*.

Even if someone wishes to pretend that the word *adoptatur* could to some extent be drawn into support of Felix’s heresy, everyone agrees that Hilary’s thought is very far from that heresy, as is evident from innumerable passages of his works. This is the true method of interpreting the more obscure expressions that sometimes occur in the Fathers.

For this reason Agobard, who attacked the Felician heresy after Felix’s death, having obtained a copy of Hilary in which *adoptatur* was read, explained that word from what preceded and followed it as meaning “is assumed.” He did not accuse the codex of being falsified, either because he did not know of the matter or because he did not wish to offend Felix’s friends, whom he complains were still alive.

Certainly he did not touch upon those charges that had been proved against Felix at the Council of Frankfurt.

230. The ancient scholastic theologians, with Saint Thomas, seem to have recognized no reading other than *adoptatur*, and they reply that Saint Hilary had spoken improperly.

Saint Thomas proposes the argument as follows in part III, question 23, article 4: “It seems that Christ, insofar as he is man, is the adopted Son of God. For Hilary says, speaking of Christ: ‘The dignity of power is not lost, while the humanity of the flesh is adopted.’”

He responds: “To the first, therefore, it must be said that, just as sonship does not properly belong to a nature, so neither does adoption. Therefore, when it is said that the humanity of the flesh is adopted, the expression is improper, and adoption there means the union of human nature with the person of the Son.”

It should be noted that Saint Thomas read *humanitas*, “humanity,” where most read *humilitas*, “humility.”

231. Gabriel Vasquez, a very acute theologian, having noticed that *adoratur* was read in some codices, judged this reading greatly preferable. In volume I, on part III, question 23, disputation 89, chapter XV, he writes:

“Although in some recently printed codices that word is *ADOPTATUR*, in others it is read *ADORATUR*. Through the carelessness of scribes, some error could easily have crept in. I am persuaded that this is the genuine reading, because of the excellent sense given by the word *ADORATUR*, whereas the word *ADOPTATUR* can scarcely express any good sense.”

Cardinal de Lugo, *On the Incarnation*, disputation 31, section 1, and others approve Vasquez’s judgment.

232. The most learned Petavius is in a certain sense opposed to these men. In book VII *On the Incarnation*, chapter 4, he thinks that *adoratur* fits less well with what precedes than *adoptatur*, and that the sentence seems less suitable if the word *adoratur*, which had occurred in the preceding period, is repeated.

His teaching that *adoratur* should not be restored in place of *adoptatur* without suitable authority from ancient codices, and that Hincmarus’s claim concerning Hilary’s genuine reading should not be accepted rashly, can certainly be admitted without difficulty. But the central question is whether the codices written before Felix favor one reading more than the other, and whether faith can be denied to Hincmarus when he recounts the same event repeatedly, supported by Alcuin’s testimony and by the traces of fraud that remain in the Aachen codex.

[Col. 0529A] 233. Maffeius, in the preface to Saint Hilary’s works, considers *adoptatur* preferable, because it better accords with rhetorical elegance by avoiding repetition of the same word, as Petavius also maintained; and because Hilary seeks something remarkable from oppositions.

But it is by no means established that Hilary was concerned with oppositions at this passage, nor is it difficult to find several words repeated in this way in his writings.

While engaged on another matter, I encountered an example in book I, chapter 35: “It is the signification of birth; it is the sole profession of birth. But where there is the name of creation, there the cause of that same creation is prior.”

In the Paris edition of 1572 one indeed reads *professio sit*, “let it be the profession”; but the codex of Saint Peter, which from this passage transmits an ancient reading, has *professio est*, “it is the profession,” as Muretus observes. Constantius and Maffeius likewise read it without any variation in the text.

234. If I must disclose my own opinion, I shall gladly embrace the judgment of Francisco Suárez, than whom no one is accustomed to weigh arguments on both sides more diligently. In part III, question 23, disputation 48, section 4, he writes:

“To Hilary, Saint Thomas and the Scholastics generally reply that he IMPROPERLY called the grace of the union of the flesh ADOPTION. . . . Others conjecture that Hilary’s text is corrupt, and that where *ADOPTATUR* is read, *ADORATUR* should be read. . . . For this fits the argument extremely well: he shows that Christ’s majesty was not diminished amid his cries, etc., since he is adored precisely in those circumstances.

“This reading is found in the Paris edition of 1544, Miraeus’s edition under the Golden Sun. According to this reading, the clause ‘while the humility of the flesh is adored’ is not to be taken causally. . . . Therefore, that clause cannot give the cause, but rather a sign, so that the sense is: ‘while [it] is adored,’ that is, ‘since [it] is adored.’

“The only apparent difficulty in this reading is that, in common usage and according to Latin propriety, the clause does not seem to have that meaning. Nevertheless, the reading and the response are probable.

“But the other reading, found in the more recent codices, is not to be despised. It is clearly ancient and common, as is evident from Saint Thomas and the Scholastics. And it can yield a sufficiently genuine sense. Hilary teaches in that passage that the majesty of the Word was not diminished through the assumption of our nature. . . . Hence he concludes that, through the humility of the flesh joined to the Word, the majesty and power of the Word were not lost.”

235. Suárez adds, in order to make the doctrine of Saint Thomas more coherent, that the grace of the union is sometimes called “adoption” by way of translation and metaphor:

“In this metaphor, taken in that sense, there is no error; but we must avoid it, both because, as we have shown, it is not truly and properly adoption, and also because that metaphor is extremely rare and can provide an occasion for error.”

These statements are true if the matter concerns the jurists’ meaning, or the theological meaning, of the word *adoptare*. Otherwise, among the ancient Latins *adopto* sometimes simply meant “I assume,” and sometimes “I assume as a son”; the distinction was inferred from the argument and from the matter itself.

236. Although Saint Hilary very often uses the word *assumo* in this matter, he writes the following on Psalm [Col. 0530A] CXXVII:

“To each one, the inheritance of the Church from the Father was betrothed through the adoption of the body which he was to assume from the Virgin.”

Constantius restored this reading from the manuscripts, whereas the printed editions had *per adeptionem corporis*, “through the taking possession of the body.” Constantius’s reading *per adoptionem* is confirmed not only by Maffeius from the Veronese codex, but also by Muretus from the Vatican codex, with which, as we have said, the Paris edition of 1572 was carefully collated.

## CHAPTER VIII. What has been accomplished in this new edition of Sedulius

237. Since many features are shared by Sedulius with the sacred poets whom I have already discussed—Prudentius, Dracontius, and Juvencus—it seemed appropriate sometimes merely to indicate them, and more often to omit them altogether.

The principal work and labor of this edition, therefore, is to draw out and establish the true text from the manuscripts. If anything needs to be added from variant readings, it will be enclosed in the same annotations. Since I have decided to print Sedulius’s prose alongside the poem, it would be inelegant to append notes or a commentary on the variant readings, especially since the prose itself makes many notes unnecessary.

238. It is appropriate to publish the prose together with the poem in the place of an interpretation. From it not only is the poet’s meaning more clearly perceived, but the true reading is also very often confirmed.

Would that we possessed other ancient exemplars from which we could correct the prose itself in many passages! For Gallandius truly declared in his dissertation on Sedulius, prefixed to volume IX of the *Library of the Fathers*:

“When we first approached its [the prose’s] reading, Cicero’s remark came to mind: ‘As for the Latin books, I do not know where to turn: they are both written and sold in such a corrupt state.’”

Another difficulty also arises: Gallandius did not see the exemplar of the prose published by Juretus in 1585, nor was I able to obtain it. Gallandius collated the Paris *Library of the Fathers* of 1624 and the Lyons edition; I had other, earlier ones in hand, as I shall soon explain.

I have come to suspect that, since it is impossible to deny the prose to Sedulius in opposition to the authority of Bede and other writers of approximately the same period, it was interpolated by someone and in certain passages adjusted to a corrupt wording of the poem. Since the prose sometimes ranges more freely, it is often necessary to derive the true reading of the poem from the manuscript exemplars alone.

To make it easy to understand the sigla by which old editions and manuscript codices are indicated in the notes, I append their list.

- **Alb.** Codex of the Albanian Library. See no. 80.
- **Ald.** Aldus’s edition, discussed at no. 101.
- **Alm.** Almeloveen’s codex. See no. 81.
- **Ang.** Codex of the Angelica Library, no. 79.
- **Arntz.** Arntzenius’s codex, no. 81.
- **Barth.** Barthius’s codices, nos. 85, 133.
- **Burm.** The codices and conjectures of Peter II Burmannus, no. 82.
- **Cant.** The Canterbury codex, no. 83 and following.
- **Capp.** Cappusoti’s edition, no. 95.
- **Cell.** Cellarius’s edition, no. 126.
- **Cod. a. b. c. d. e.** Five codices from which Arntzenius obtained variant readings, no. 82.
- **Col.** The Cologne edition, no. 110.
- **Edimb.** The Edinburgh edition, nos. 82, 125.
- **Fabr.** Georg Fabricius’s edition, no. 118.
- **Gall.** Gallandius’s edition, no. 130.
- **Grun.** Grunerus’s edition, no. 128.
- **Had.** Hadamarius’s edition, no. 108.
- **Lips. cod.** The Leipzig codex, no. 84.
- **Lips. ed.** The Leipzig edition, no. 102.
- **Mab.** Mabillonius’s codex, no. 163.
- **Meus.** My own transcribed codex, no. 80.
- **Mon.** The Monastery edition, no. 97.
- **Nans.** Nansius’s codex, no. 82.
- **Nebr.** The Nebrissensis edition, nos. 103, 111.
- **Ott. 1.** Vatican Ottobonian codex 1. See no. 75.
- **Ott. 2.** Ottobonian codex 2. See no. 76.
- **Palat.** Vatican Palatine codex, nos. 5 and 63.
- **Parrh.** Parrhasius’s edition, no. 100.
- **Poelm. ed.** Poelmannus’s edition, nos. 106, 109.
- **Poelm. schedae.** Poelmannus’s manuscript notes, no. 81.
- **Reg. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.** Six Vatican codices of the Queen of Sweden. See nos. 66–74.
- **Rom.** Codex of the library of the Roman College, no. 78.
- **Scota.** This is the same edition as the Edinburgh edition mentioned above.
- **Taur.** Codex of the Turin Library, no. 62.
- **Torn. 1, 2, 3.** Three editions of Tornaesius, nos. 116, 119, 123.
- **Vat. 1, 2.** Two codices of the old Vatican Library, nos. 64, 65.
- **Vet. 1, 2.** Two old editions used by Arntzenius, nos. 96, 103.
- **Urb.** Vatican Urbino codex, no. 77.
- **Wonck.** Conjectures of Cornelius Valerius Vonckius, no. 135.
- **Wopk.** Observations of Thomas Wopkenius, no. 135.

239. After various readings have been examined here and there, together with occasional brief critical and philological notes, it sometimes becomes necessary to explain certain theological controversies. I generally do this without ambition or ostentation, merely to confirm Catholic doctrines by the authority of ancient Christian poets, or to place some particular opinions of theirs in a favorable light.

Although nothing is more important to me than to follow the celebrated positions of the most approved doctors, I do not dare to present as certain my own opinions, from which some serious theologians dissent. I call them only more probable or more generally accepted—“a ploughshare a ploughshare, a mattock a mattock.”

I should like those who at some point subject my notes to examination to bear this in mind, especially when they bring the matter before the public, which certainly has no interest in hearing such more subtle theological questions.

If it pleases you, let us offer an example from the Roman ecclesiastical newspaper of this year, 1793, no. 19, in which it is announced that Dracontius was edited by me at Rome in 1791.

### 240

The author of the article on Dracontius carefully describes the entire edition and the subject matter of the poems, and commends my labor with the choicest praise. There was, however, one point that he thought worthy of comment. Here are his words:

> At verse 484 of Book I of *De Deo*, the distinguished author says that there is a considerable question concerning the knowledge of supernatural mysteries [Col. 0532A] with which Adam was endowed: namely, whether it was true supernatural faith, as is more probable. Permit us, too, to state our own view. Once Adam is granted knowledge of supernatural mysteries, as he says, it seems to us that the consequence of supernatural knowledge necessarily follows; otherwise we would have to recognize in nature alone a power proportionate to knowing what surpasses the knowledge of nature. Here the discussion concerns certain knowledge, not conjectural knowledge.

### 241

What judgment, I ask, will those form about this whole matter who do not know Latin and cannot compare my words with the Italian words of the *Diario*? And what judgment will be formed by those who do know Latin, but have either no knowledge of theology at all or have touched upon it only superficially, as most people now do?

I shall therefore deal with the author of the *Diario* himself, who is not only a theologian but also a most distinguished professor of theology. I asserted that the more probable opinion is the one which holds that the knowledge [Col. 0532B] of the mysteries of faith with which Adam was endowed was true supernatural faith. What, then, can you rightly object? Do you not know that this is precisely what is at issue, and that certain eminent doctors deny that such knowledge was true supernatural faith? Yet nothing is more familiar among theologians who write about the work of the six days—especially in Suárez, Book III, chapter 18, where he discusses at length the knowledge of supernatural things which man possessed before the Fall.

### 242

First, he denies that this knowledge was the beatific vision; then he takes it as certain that it was supernatural knowledge; and finally he asks whether it was true supernatural faith, as most maintain with Saint Thomas, or something more perfect than supernatural faith, intermediate between the beatific vision and supernatural faith, [Col. 0532C] as Hugh of Saint Victor, Alexander of Hales, Saint Bonaventure, Gabriel, 133 and others hold. He follows Saint Thomas’s opinion, which I too called the more probable one.

You reply: “Once Adam is granted knowledge of supernatural mysteries, supernatural knowledge seems necessarily to follow from this.” But do you not see that, by this manner of arguing, the middle term—as the schools call it—is being changed? The question concerns true faith, not supernatural knowledge, which is rather presumed to have been granted to Adam. Supernatural knowledge, moreover, may be either the beatific vision, faith, or—according to the probable opinion of some—a knowledge intermediate between the vision of God and faith.

### 243

There is no advantage in adding more; but I fear that, if I pass over in silence the argument advanced by this highly praised theologian, my silence may seem to indicate that I approve it. [Col. 0532D]

“Otherwise,” he says, “we would have to recognize in nature alone a power proportionate to knowing what surpasses the knowledge of nature.”

If he means nothing more than asserting that, apart from divine revelation, supernatural mysteries cannot be known, I readily agree. But if he thinks—as his words suggest—that no certain natural knowledge of supernatural mysteries can exist even after revelation, it is plainly false: a heretic assents with certain natural knowledge to many supernatural mysteries.

### 244

There are indeed many who exaggerate excessively the weakness or incapacity of fallen human nature, just as there once were those who, with Pelagius, exaggerated its powers in the opposite direction. [Col. 0533A]

But, apart from the fact that the matter here concerns Adam’s unfallen nature before original sin, even with respect to fallen nature we must uphold the doctrine handed down to us by the holy Fathers [Col. 0534A] and sanctioned by the Council of Trent in its decrees and canons. The Council explicitly declares in Session 6, chapter 1, in the decree on justification, that in human beings after Adam’s sin free will was by no means extinguished, although its powers were weakened and it was inclined. And in canon 5:

> If anyone says that the free will of man, after Adam’s sin, was lost and extinguished, or that it is a matter existing only in name—indeed, a name without a reality—or finally a fiction introduced into the Church by Satan, let him be anathema.

If, then, free will was by no means lost and extinguished after Adam’s sin, by what right shall we deny every natural good to fallen human nature? [Col. 0533B]

Nor is it fitting to abuse the venerable name of Augustine 134 against the Catholic position, or to allege—as I remember having heard from someone—that the Council’s doctrine concerning justification was incomplete. For even if you wished to imagine that something was lacking in the decree and canons concerning justification, you must nevertheless admit that they contain nothing contrary to the Catholic faith.

This, at any rate, I confidently profess concerning Saint Augustine: his doctrine of justification agrees most perfectly with the doctrine of the Council of Trent. If, however, some slightly obscure expression should perhaps be found in his works, I prefer to interpret it with his true disciple, Saint Thomas, rather than borrow an interpretation from the Lutherans or Calvinists.

Those who, in controversies of this kind, show little concern for the unanimous consensus of the Catholic Church, and who boast grandly of some glorious title that they arrogate to themselves, [Col. 0534B] flattering themselves about it with greater confidence than security, should remember that satirical line of the poet:

> “Now it is enough to have said: ‘I compose wondrous poems.’”

[Col. 0533]

## COELIUS SEDULIUS’S PASCHAL POEM, DISTRIBUTED IN FIVE BOOKS, TO WHICH THERE UNDERLIES AND CONTINUALLY RESPONDS THE PASCHAL WORK WRITTEN IN PROSE. (C)

### Dedication of the *Paschal Poem* to Macedonius

To the holy lord and most blessed father Macedonius, presbyter: Coelius Sedulius sends greetings in Christ.

[Note: In Codex Reg. 1 the title is: “Here begins the Prologue of the presbyter Sedulius to Macedonius. To the holy lord and most blessed father Macedonius, presbyter: Coelius Sedulius sends greetings in Christ.” Ottob. 1 has: “To my lord and most blessed father Macedonius, presbyter: Sedulius sends greetings in Christ.” Vat. 1 agrees with Ottob. 1 but adds *holy* after *my lord*. Vat. 2 agrees with Vat. 1 but omits *my* and adds: “To the holy lord and venerable father Macedonius: Sedulius sends his fullest greetings in Christ.” Reg. 3 has only: “To my lord, father Macedonius, presbyter.” Reg. 2 reads: “Here begins the letter of the eminent poet Sedulius to the presbyter Macedonius.” The others, like Vat. 1. The manuscript of Barthius agrees entirely with Vat. 1, except that it writes *presbyt.* The manuscript of Nansius B reads: “To the venerable Macedonius, *presbo*: Sedulius sends greetings in Christ.” The word *holy* is also absent from the manuscript of Almeloveen, although it was frequently and elegantly used by ancient Christians. In a certain manuscript cited by Usserius and Labbe in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, this letter is called “the apologetic prologue of Sedulius the rhetorician.” It is omitted in some editions; most editions include it. Poelmann has the form of Vat. 1, but without *my*. Aldus: “To the holy and venerable father, etc.” Fabricius: “To the holy and most blessed father Macedonius, abbot: Coelius Sedulius, etc.” Perhaps he is called an abbot here because the name *father* is customarily applied to monks. In former times, however, it was commonly applied to bishops and presbyters as well. Nevertheless, Trithemius himself calls this Macedonius an abbot in *Prolegomena*, no. 29. The word *lord* was commonly applied to bishops, holy men, and others, especially in letters.]

[Col. 0533B] **135** Before you, venerable father, judge me, once I have completed the volume of our work, and perhaps [Col. 0534B] rebuke me with customary severity [Note: Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, in the first hand, have *rite* (“properly”). So do many printed editions. Most of our witnesses, together with Barthius’s manuscript, Poelmann’s papers, Almeloveen’s copies, codices A and B, those cited by Arntzenius, the first old edition, and Monast., have *ritu* (“in the manner”). Vatt. 1 and 2; Ottobon. 1, in a second hand; Reg. 1, in the first hand; Reg. 2 and 3, perhaps together with some printed editions, have *forsan* (“perhaps”). The remaining witnesses have *forsitan* (“perhaps”). Fabr. has *rite forsitan, severeque* (“perhaps properly and severely”).], as one who, supported by no advantage of ancient learning [Note: Vet. 1 has *prorogativa*. Retain *praerogativa*, which is used for a certain special privilege and is so called according to Roman custom. The *praerogativa* was the tribe that was asked to cast its vote first.], have ventured in a small skiff as a novice across so immense a sea of paschal majesty [Col. 0535A], one that even the most experienced men must fear, **136** let me clear myself before you concerning the reasons for this undertaking [Note: Wopkensius and Grunerus rightly reject Cellarius, who thought the sense required *liceat expurgem* (“may I excuse myself”). For *expurgem* here means “let me clear myself,” or it is used for *expurgabo* (“I shall clear myself”). Grunerus also criticizes Wopkensius, who conjectured *exponam* or *expromam*, because the phrase *expurgare facti causas* seemed unusual to him. Certainly such forms of expression are sufficiently frequent among writers of those times. A gloss in Vaticanus 1 has *exponam*. In Reg. 1 the gloss is *utinam excusem* (“would that I might excuse myself”), an optative future used for the indicative future.], so that, when you have recognized that I was not presumptuous but devoted, you may receive me into the harbor of your heart with gentle tranquility: a harbor in which, with God as pilot [Note: Reg. 1 has “with the Lord as pilot”; the others, “with God as pilot.”], you will rejoice that I have suffered no shipwreck.

While occupied, therefore, with secular studies [Note: Vet. 1 and Mon. have “therefore occupied with secular studies”; the others, “occupied with secular studies.” Secular studies are profane studies, a frequent meaning among ecclesiastical writers.], I was devoting the force of an impatient intellect [Note: Codex B has *patientis* (“patient”); the others, more appropriately, *impatientis* (“impatient”), whose gloss in Reg. 1 is *ardentis* (“ardent”).], which divine providence had generated in me [Note: Most manuscripts and editions have *quod* (“which”); Cellarius printed *quam* (“which”), claiming that this was found in Almeloveen. Arntzenius also found *quod* in Almeloveen and acknowledged in his Addenda that this reading is more reliable.], not to the usefulness of the soul but to an empty life, and making the skill of literary learning [Note: Ott. 1, Reg. 1 and 3, and Almeloveen have *litterariae*; Vatt. 1 and 2, Reg. 2, and the Leipzig manuscript have *litteratoriae*; codex A also has *litteratoriae* but omits *disciplinae*; codex B has *litteralis*. Tertullian used *litteratorius*; Coelius Aurelianus and Diomedes used *litteralis*, but *litterarius* is more Latin, and should be restored on the authority of the good manuscripts, although most printed editions have *litteratoriae*. Arntzenius also preferred *litterariae*. Among medieval and late writers, *litteratoria ars* meant grammar.], serve the amusements of unproductive labor rather than its author [Note: Most of our manuscripts have *auctori serviret* (“serve its author”); others have *auctori deserviret*. Aldus and Vat. 2 have “serve God, its author.” Codex B and Poelmann’s papers have *auctori serviret*, which Cellarius printed; *Deo* (“God”) is a gloss in Reg. 2.].

At last God, merciful creator of all things [Note: Codex A has “merciful God, creator of all things”; the others, “merciful God, creator of all things.” Arntzenius, following Poelmann’s papers, omits *Deus*, thinking that the word arose from a gloss. It is also absent from Reg. 1. Yet there is no reason to abandon the reading common everywhere else. It appears in four of our manuscripts.], looked with greater clemency upon the work of his own authority [Note: Ottobon. 1, Reg. 1 and 3, and other manuscripts and editions have *fabricam sui juris*; Vatt. 1 and 2 and Reg. 2, together with Aldus, have *sui fabricam juris*.], and grieved that foolish perceptions of worldly wisdom had so long been retained in me, then seasoned the foolish intellect of mortal prudence with heavenly salt.

[Col. 0535B] **137**

And as soon as the inner darkness abandoned the eyes of my heart [Note: Some printed editions have *mox ut*; the others have *moxque ut*. The expression “eyes of the heart” is elegant, like Cicero, Quintilian, and others’ “eyes of the mind.” *Dumosi ruris* (“of the bushy countryside”) is like Virgil’s *dumosa arva* and *dumosa rupes*. Ott. 1 has *deserit* (“abandons”); retain *deseruit* (“abandoned”), with all the others.], I retraced my wandering footsteps through the thorns of the bushy countryside onto the grass of the flower-filled turf [Note: Vatt. 1 and 2, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers have *floridi* (“verdant”); the others, together with Reg. 1, 2, and 3 and Ott. 1, have *florei* (“flower-filled”).], and, with all the effort of a better judgment, dedicated to God the cultivation of an enlightened heart [Note: Codex B and all our manuscripts have *dicavi* (“I dedicated”); Poelmann, Arntzenius, and others have *dedicavi*.], not taking up the burden of so great a task in reliance on my own strength, but embracing the burden of Christ—which is exceedingly light—with humble and submissive devotion. I judged, namely, that I would not be free from the guilt of silence [Note: Poelmann’s papers have *sancti arbitratus silentii*, which I do not understand unless *tanti* (“so great”) is to be read for *sancti*. Yet even *tanti* is not necessary.], if I denied to truth the service of an eager mind that I had offered to vanity, since divine matters may be asserted reverently [Note: Vat. 1 has *divina opera* (“divine works”)], and human matters may be treated honorably [Note: Aldus has *possunt* (“can”); Poelmann’s papers have *possent* (“could”); most have *possint* (“may”).].

Again I was distressed by another storm of an agitated mind [Note: Almeloveen, Vet. 1, Mon., and other printed editions have *rursus alia* for *alia rursus*.], and that consideration often stirred my labored breathing [Note: Codex B has, not improperly, *procella turbatus* (“disturbed by a storm”). The epithet *aegros anhelitus* (“labored breathing”) is taken from Virgil, Book IX, line 814; Virgil, however, has the singular *aeger anhelitus*.]—the consideration through which I knew that I had made some progress in learning, whether through you, most blessed father, or through others whom heavenly grace likewise enlightens [Note: Vatt. 1 and 2 have *illuminat* (“illuminates”); Ottobon. 1 and Reg. 1, 2, and 3 have *illustrat* (“enlightens”). Poelmann’s copy has *illustrarat* (“had enlightened”); other editions have *illustrat*. Barthius found *illuminat* in his manuscript, which Grunerus and Arntzenius consider a gloss.], although you yourselves, who show everything [Note: Barthius’s manuscript has “although you yourselves, showing me everything,” which Barthius considers more emphatic. In Reg. 1 there is a gloss *vos* (“you”) above *ipsi* (“yourselves”), and *mihi* (“to me”) above *monstrantes* (“showing”).], may believe that some little spark can shine in me: but the torpor of a dull heart [Note: Some write *obtunsi*; most have *obtusi*. On this orthographic variation I have also spoken in the note on Juvencus. *Obtusi* is the more common spelling.] scarcely sends forth a faint spark through its veins, like **138** flint [Note: Reg. 1 has *tamquam silicis vena* (“as a vein of flint”), but this was previously different. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *silicis vena*. The common reading is *tamquam silicis per venas* (“as through the veins of flint”). Vaticanus 1 has *tamquam silicis per venam*; Vat. 2 and Aldus, *tamquam per venas silicis*. Virgil, Book VI, line 7: “Hidden in the veins of flint.”].

[Col. 0536B] And even that small nourishment of fuel [Note: Almeloveen has *et ad ipsum*; the others, *et id ipsum*. The phrase imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* I.175. Others likewise use *nutrimentum* and *alimentum ignis*.] which the oil of the heavenly gift was able to preserve in me [Note: Vet. 1, Monast., and Fabr. have *permanare* (“flow through”); the manuscripts and other editions have *permanere* (“remain”).], I considered it wrong, through the tenacious muteness of silence, to share it with no one, lest, while I tried more carefully to guard the quantity entrusted to me of the one talent [Note: Aldus, Vatt. 1 and 2, and Poelmann’s papers have “while I tried to guard the entrusted quantity”; Ott. 1 has “the quantity entrusted to me”; most manuscripts and editions have “the entrusted quantity.”], I should not be free from the guilt of buried money. For he does not wash the stain of envy from himself who refuses to confer upon another what, once he has given it, he does not lose [Note: Almeloveen, Vet. 1, Monast., Poelmann, and our manuscripts have *amittit* (“does not lose”); Arntzenius, with other editions, printed *amittet* (“will not lose”).]. The same word is used in a not dissimilar sense by Curtius, Book VII, chapter 8.

Amid the various turns of anxious hesitation [Note: Reg. 2 has “amid these various turns of anxious...”], I nevertheless undertook to lay the foundation of this work, prompted especially for this reason [Note: Fabr. has *hoc maxime*; the manuscripts and most editions have *ob hoc maxime*, which Grunerus approves and Barthius does not reject, although the preposition *ob* is sometimes omitted by the best writers.], that, while inviting others by exhortations of truth to the fruit of a good harvest, if I should ever be attacked, perhaps assailed by the faults of human weakness [Note: Vat. 1 has *humanae infirmitatis* (“of human frailty”) rather than *infirmitatis humanae*. Almeloveen, Vet. 1, Monast., and Fabr. have *vitiis necessitate forsitan lacessitus* (“perhaps provoked by faults under compulsion”). Barthius thinks that *necessitate forsitan* are glosses added by someone wishing to remove blame from the holy man, but added without his intention. They are absent from his manuscript. Certainly *necessitate* occurs in none of our manuscripts, nor in Poelmann’s papers, nor in Aldus. Reg. 1 and 3 retain *forsitan*; Reg. 2, Ott. 1, and Vatt. 1 and 2 have *forsan*; the editions vary likewise.], I might fear, warned by the words of my own argument, and, having forbidden theft, be afraid of appearing a thief [Note: Barthius conjectured *me tuear* (“I defend myself”); Cellarius inserted the conjecture into Sedulius’s text. Grunerus and Arntzenius restored the old reading on the basis of the sense and the words that follow. Sedulius means that he wishes to be warned and to fear because of the words of his own argument, lest, while forbidding theft, he appear to be a thief. Cato says in his distichs: “It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault reproves him.” Cicero used the same reasoning to dissuade Quintus Caecilius from prosecuting Verres in the *Divination against Verres*.],

[Col. 0537D] **139** and, having shown the path of firm ground, be afraid to pursue the dangerous tracks of a more precipitous slippery way [Col. 0537B], and, armed with the shield of the Lord’s protection, easily repel and disdain the missiles of hostile attack [Note: The phrase “with the shield of the Lord’s protection” is familiar among ecclesiastical writers from the sacred Scriptures, where shield and wall are used for defense and protection.].

But why I wished to compose these things in metrical form [Note: Poelmann has *hac*; Vat. 1, *hoc*; the others, *haec ratione*.], I shall not delay briefly to explain [Note: Ott. 1 and Reg. 1 have “I shall not briefly delay to explain.” Ott. 1, codex B, and Poelmann’s papers have the same order.]. Rarely, best father, as your knowledge also recognizes through constant reading [Note: Most manuscripts have *vestra* (“your” plural); some editions, including old ones, have *tua* (“your” singular), as do Poelmann’s papers and Grunerus, since Sedulius usually uses the singular number in this letter. Arntzenius disagrees, observing that Sedulius likes to use the plural in the prose letter to Macedonius, as do other writers. Barthius’s manuscript and Reg. 1 have *cognovit* (“has recognized”), which Barthius considers more suitable and Cellarius approves. Grunerus and Arntzenius restored *cognoscit* (“recognizes”). They also restore *pietatis* (“of piety”) with some editions, since *pietas*, that is, kindness and clemency, suits the passage very well. Yet all our manuscripts, together with Barthius’s manuscript and Poelmann’s papers, have *potestatis* (“of power”); Vat. 2, in abbreviation, may be read as either *potestatis* or *pietatis*. This would be an appropriate place for Sedulius to have remembered Juvencus, the first Christian poet, as I observed in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus*, no. 91. Aldus’s inference that Juvencus was not read by Sedulius does not seem probable to me. See the notes on Book I, verses 38 and 188.], has anyone adapted the gifts of divine power to the style of this kind of rhythm; and there are many whom the discipline of secular studies attracts more through poetic delights and the pleasures of verse. Whatever they read of rhetorical eloquence [Note: All our manuscripts, together with many editions, have *hi quidquid* (“these people, whatever...”); Poelmann has *hi quoque quidquid* (“these people also, whatever...”); elsewhere appears *hi quaeque rhetoricae*, which the notes of Poelmann regard as less correct. Aldus has *perlegent* for *perlegunt*. The words *haud diligunt* (“do not love”) are absent from codex B.], they grasp less attentively, because they do not love it; but whatever they see sweetened by the charm of verse [Note: Poelmann’s papers have *viderint versuum*; so do Vatt. 1 and 2 and Reg. 2.], they receive with such eagerness of heart that, by repeating it frequently, they establish and store it in their deep memory.

[Col. 0538D] **140**

I therefore judge that the character of such people is not to be rejected [Note: Vat. 1 has *supra* (“above”) for *eorum* (“their”). Reg. 2 has “I judge that they are not to be rejected”; Reg. 1, “I judge that they ought not to be rejected”; most have “I judge that they are not to be rejected.” Aldus has *existimo* (“I think”), but Arntzenius supports *aestimo* with many examples, since other writers also use it for *existimo*. Manuscripts vary in other authors as well.], but to be treated according to their established habit or nature, so that each may be more willingly won for God by his own natural inclination [Note: Ott. 1, Reg. 1 and 2, and Poelmann have “so that each may by his own natural inclination be willingly won for God.” Reg. 3 has *magis suo* (“more by his own”). Vat. 2 has “so that each may be won for God more by his own inclination”; Poelmann’s papers, Aldus, and Vat. 1 have the same, though Vat. 1 mistakenly has *quis quos* for *quisque*. Codex B and Almeloveen have “so that each may by his own inclination be won for God.” *Voluntarius* (“willing”) may be a gloss on *suo ingenio* (“by his own inclination”), but Wopkensius, citing examples, shows that it may perhaps be a pleonasm like others. I do not see why Arntzenius restores it, although he thinks such a pleonasm can be defended; it scarcely fits this passage. Virgil, *Georgics* II.10: “For some come of their own accord, with no human compelling.” Cicero, *On Ends* II.10: “When he had returned to Carthage of his own will, compelled by no force.” Lactantius V.20: “We do not seek that anyone should worship God unwillingly, whether he wishes it or not.” Other writers use the expression similarly; Arntzenius cannot easily offer any reason for distinguishing them.].

Nor does it matter by what occasion anyone is instructed in the faith [Note: Almeloveen, Poelmann, Reg. 2 and 3, and Vatt. 1 and 2 have “nor does it matter by what occasion anyone is instructed.” Ott. 1 has “nor does it matter by whatever occasion anyone...” Reg. 1 has “by what occasion anyone...”], provided that, having entered the way of freedom [Note: Vat. 1, together with some editions, has *libertatis viam* (“the way of freedom”); the others, *viam libertatis*.], he does not return to the snares of wicked servitude in which he had previously been entangled [Note: Vatt. 1 and 2 and Reg. 1, in the first hand, have *ante* (“before”); Poelmann’s papers and codex B have “before he had been entangled”; the others have “in which he had previously been entangled.”].

These, distinguished father, are the reasons for our work—not useless, as you have learned, but beneficial. If they do not displease you on reasonable grounds [Note: Vat. 1 and 2, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers have *displicent tibi* (“displease you”); the others omit *tibi*.], may they be granted the favor of your kindness, so that, laying aside for a little while the loftier Scriptures [Note: Some have *a scripturis*; most have *ab scripturis*. There are many examples of this kind of spelling. Some write *impartias*, others *impertias*. For *super nubes* (“above the clouds”), Almeloveen and some editions have *supra nubes*; Poelmann’s papers have *per nubes* (“through the clouds”). From the Turin manuscript, in the *Prolegomena*, no. 62, one may also observe *quoque te* (“you also”) and *supra nubes elata* (“raised above the clouds”). For *terram* (“earth”), Vatt. 1 and 2, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers have *terras* (“lands”).], you may willingly bestow yourself also upon humbler things. An eagle does not always soar above the clouds; at times it also descends to earth on more relaxed wings.

[Col. 0539C] **141** Often a warrior delights and plays with the weapons with which he is accustomed to fight [Note: Cellarius printed *saepe etiam belliger* (“often even a warrior”), inserting *etiam* from the preceding “but also with more relaxed wings,” a customary scribal error. *Etiam* is absent from all our manuscripts. Almeloveen, Vet. 1, and Mon. nevertheless support Cellarius. In place of *delectatur et ludere* (“delights and plays”), some editions have *delectatur etiam ludere* (“delights also to play”); Arntzenius praises Aldus for this reading, though Aldus actually has *delectatur et ludere*. Arntzenius conjectured *delectatur et etiam ludere*, for which the phrase may perhaps have some example; nevertheless, *et ludere* should not be changed, since *et* here means *etiam*. Vossius suspects *assuetus est laedere* (“is accustomed to wound”) and *delectatur et ludere* (“delights to play”) as a wordplay, as in Martial I.5 [elsewhere I.7]: “While the boar plays, the boar knows how to wound.” Arntzenius rightly disagrees and illustrates Sedulius with similar passages. Cicero, *On the Orator* II.20: “But let them see whether they are going to take up arms for play or for fighting.” Ovid, *Tristia* IV.1.72: “As a young man I avoided the harsh contests of warfare; I moved my weapons only with a hand about to play.” All our manuscripts read *dimicare* (“fight”). Arator imitates this passage of Sedulius in his prologue to Florianus: “The soldier accustomed to place the cuirass upon his limbs,” and so forth.].

Or perhaps, to draw you away into hidden places from the burden of reading poetry [Note: Poelmann’s papers, Vatt. 1 and 2, Reg. 2 and 3, and Ottobon. 1 in the first hand have *an* (“or perhaps”); the editions have *at* (“but”); Reg. 1 has *at*, with a gloss above *an*: “speaking interrogatively or playfully.” Other codices have *forsan* or *forsitan*. Vat. 1 has *ut ab te sine hac* (“so that from you without this...”); codex A has *perlegenda* less correctly. Codex A has *alloquens* (“addressing”); codex B, *alloquaris* (“you may address”) instead of *alloqueris*.], you address me with such words of gentle speech [Col. 0540A], saying: “Why,” you say [Note: Grunerus, with some editions, preferred *inquies* (“you will say”), and Arntzenius approved. Yet although that manner of speaking may perhaps be more elegant, all our manuscripts, other witnesses, and the best editions must be followed: *alloqueris. Cur, inquiens* (“you address me. ‘Why,’ you say”). Reg. 1 has *in quies*, but the same hand changed it to *inquiens*; the gloss in Reg. 2 and 3 is *dicens* (“saying”).], as a kindly friend whom I embrace with the grace of pure affection, do you strive more earnestly [Note: Poelmann’s papers have *profundius niteris* (“you strive more deeply”). Vatt. 1 and 2, Aldus, Reg. 1, 2, and 3, and Ott. 1 have *et fidi propositi sedulitate sectaris* (“and pursue with the diligence of faithful purpose”). In Ott. 1 it seems originally to have been *fidei*; Reg. 1 has a gloss *fidelissimae devotionis* (“of most faithful devotion”), while the text had *et fidei proposita*. Most editions have *fide propositi sedulitate amicos sectaris* (“you pursue friends with the diligence of a faithful purpose”). Codex A has *fida propositi*. Grunerus rightly judged that *amicos* should be deleted, especially since Almeloveen and Poelmann’s papers, apart from our manuscripts, support its omission. Codex B and Ott. 1 in the first hand have *offendas* (“you offend”) instead of *offendis*.] to honor me above the rest and pursue me with the diligence of a faithful purpose, while you offend others as though they were neglected—although they are not inferior in learning [Note: Vat. 2 and Aldus have *cum non sint impares* (“although they are not inferior”); Vat. 1 has *cum sint non impares*; Reg. 1, 2, and 3 and Ott. 1 have *cum sint doctrina non impares* (“although they are not inferior in learning”), as do most editions.], and ordinarily join with me in the fellowship of religious faith—when you choose or single out me alone, above all, as the one to whom you entrust the words of your devotion?

You have Ursinus, a bishop [Note: Many old editions have *Habes autem* (“you have moreover”); some manuscripts likewise, including Ott. 1 and Reg. 1; others omit *autem*, including Vatt. 1 and 2.], full of priestly reverence, who, from the apprenticeship of his earliest age [Note: Most of our manuscripts have *qui ab aetatis suae primaevae* (“who from the earliest period of his age”). Ott. 1 and Vat. 2, with many editions, omit *suae*; the author uses a similar expression in the declamation on Sallust, chapter 4: “But, by Hercules, having slipped through the apprenticeship of youth, he corrected himself.” Some editions have *qui ab aetatis suae primaevo* (“who from the first period of his age”). Vet. 1 and Mon. have *qui dum ab aetatis primaevae*; codex B has *qui dum ab aetatis tirocinio*, omitting *primaevae*. Vatt. 1 and 2, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers have *deserens dum vixit* (“not abandoning while he lived”).], never abandoned the camp of the eternal King, lived piously among **142** barbarians and peacefully amid wars [Col. 0540C].

[Col. 0540D] He received the testimony of already blessed merit through the sacrament of evangelical teaching [Note: Vatt. 1 and 2, Reg. 1 and 3, and Ottobon. 1 have *meriti evangelicae sacramento doctrinae* (“by the sacrament of evangelical teaching of blessed merit”). The Leipzig manuscript and Aldus likewise have this. The gloss in Reg. 2 is *sacramento—statuto, confirmatione, sacratissimo fonte* (“sacrament—ordinance, confirmation, most holy font”). Cellarius printed *testimonium beati jam meriti, et evangelicae sacramentum doctrinae* (“the testimony of one already blessed in merit, and the sacrament of evangelical teaching”), following a second old reading in Reg. 1 and Almeloveen’s manuscript, where a gloss explains *sacramentum* as *mysterium* (“mystery”). Wopkensius preferred the reading of our manuscripts, but for *beati jam meriti* conjectured *beatitatem meriti* (“the blessedness of merit”). Nothing need be changed, however, since *meritum beatum* (“blessed merit”) is used for *meritum beatitatis* (“the merit of blessedness”), through an improper use of adjectives familiar to Sedulius and other poets. Thus Sedulius speaks of “fasting bites,” “shipwrecked arms,” and so forth. Grunerus preferred *per evangelicae sacramentum doctrinae*. Yet although that is the sense, it is not necessary to change the words.].

For we read: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God.” [Note: Most manuscripts and editions have *ipsi filii* (“they themselves are sons”); others omit *ipsi*.]

You have Laurentius, a presbyter of difficult comparison, who loved the substance of his patrimony [Note: Vatt. 1 and 2, Reg. 2, Aldus, Poelmann’s papers, and Fabr. have *sic erogavit* (“thus distributed”); Reg. 1 and 3 and Ott. 1 have *sic amavit* (“loved thus”), as most printed editions do. *Census* is correctly used for patrimony, possessions, and riches.], in such a way that, distributing all of it to churches and the needy, he lost nothing by the outpouring of so great a fortune: ever-watchful in wisdom, gentle in mildness, so that he might preserve the serpent’s cunning [Note: Codex B has *astutia* instead of *astutiam*. Wopkensius conjectures “and not lose the simplicity of the dove.” Sedulius’s actual words are preferable. Vet. 1 has *amittit* (“does not lose”) instead of *amittat* (“may not lose”). Almeloveen and Poelmann’s papers have *non amittat animum* (“may not lose the spirit”).] together with the law, and not lose the spirit of the simple dove.

You also have my Gallicanus, likewise a presbyter [Note: Reg. 2 has *habes meum quoque*; Ott. 1 and others, *habes quoque meum*; codex B omits *quoque*. Reg. 2 and most editions have *Gallicanum*; the other manuscripts, together with Almeloveen, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers, have *Gallianum* or *Galianum*.], not educated in secular books [Note: Wopkensius suspects *in litteris saecularibus* (“in secular literature”), but says that nothing should be changed. Compare Daniel 1: “In every book and wisdom.” The Leipzig manuscript has *placida benignitate* (“with calm kindness”).], but exceedingly gentle in tranquil goodness, teaching the rule of Catholic discipline by deeds rather than displaying it in speech [Note: Reg. 3 has *dictis* (“words”) instead of *sermone* (“speech”); others have *sermone*. Some printed editions omit both, incorrectly. The opposition of these two terms—things and speech, deeds and words, reality and name—is elegant and frequent.].

What should I say also of the presbyter Ursicinus’s many years of **143** patience [Note: Reg. 1 and 2, Vatt. 1 and 2, and Aldus have *Ursicini dicam quoque*; Almeloveen, *Ursicini quoque dicam*; Reg. 3 and Ott. 1, *Ursini quoque dicam*. Poelmann’s papers prefer *Ursici*. Arntzenius prints “What shall I say also of the presbyter Ursinus?” In Ott. 1, *Ursicini* was corrected from *Ursini* by a second hand. In Ottobon. 1 and Reg. 1, *patientiam* (“patience”) was written by the same hand in place of an earlier variant. Vatt. 1 and 2, Reg. 2 and 3, codex B, Almeloveen, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers have *sapientiam* (“wisdom”) instead of *patientiam*; Peter Burmann approves this, and others have already observed that these words are sometimes confused in manuscripts.], and of his youthful old age, never failing in the service of Christ [Note: Codex B has *famulatum* (“service”) instead of *famulatu*. Vat. 2 and Poelmann’s papers have *deficientem* (“failing”); the others, *deficiendo* (“by not failing”).]? What, too, should I say of Felix, truly happy, an enemy of this age, for whom the world has been crucified?

There are also very many other memorable men [Note: Vet. 1 and Monast. have *venerabiles* (“venerable”) instead of *memorabiles*. Ott. 1 has *esse constat* (“are known to be”). Shortly afterward Jerome is called a “cultivator of the heavenly library,” in the sense in which *bibliotheca* was used by Jerome himself and other Christian writers for the sacred books. See Ducange.],

[Col. 0542A] whom it is clear to be suitable for undertaking this office. Nor should you be ashamed to imitate the examples of Jerome, interpreter of the divine law and cultivator of the heavenly library [Note: Arntzenius says that the words *te pudeat* (“let you be ashamed”) are absent from codex B and the editions of Aldus, Vet. 1, and Mon. But, as I think, only *te* is absent; for Aldus certainly has *pudeat* without *te*, and it is likewise absent from Reg. 1, 2, 3, and 4, which begin here, and from Vatt. 1 and 2. Almeloveen’s manuscript has *pudeat te*. Aldus and Vat. 2 omit *quoque* (“also”). Poelmann’s papers have *subnixas fama* (“supported by reputation”).], and to transmit the lessons of my own argument also to noble women, supported by the reputation of distinguished character, in whose minds assiduity in sacred reading has established a sober dwelling of wisdom [Note: Reg. 1 has *sapientiae*, but a second hand changed it to *sapienti*, with a gloss *Christo* (“Christ”). Observe *instantia* in the sense of assiduity and perseverance, as in Pliny, Solinus, Apuleius, and similar writers.].

Who would not wish and strive to please the outstanding judgment of Syncletice [Note: Vat. 1 and 2 have *Sincleticis*; Reg. 1 and 2, and apparently Ott. 1, *Sincliticis*. The same form appears in the Blandin manuscript cited by Bollandus on 5 January, where the preface to the Life of Saint Apollinaris also mentions this Syncletice, whom Sedulius celebrates. He himself reads *Syncletices*. Reg. 3 has *Syngleticis*; Reg. 4, *Syngleticae*; codex B, *Sincleticae*; Aldus has *Syncletices*, not *Sincletices* as Arntzenius attributes to him; Vet. 1 and Monast., *Sindeticae*; other editions, *Sindeticis*. This variation partly arises because *cl* and *d* are easily confused in manuscripts, and partly because the long Greek epsilon is sometimes rendered in Latin by *i*. Cellarius derives the name from the Greek word for senate, which the following context confirms; Poelmann’s papers derive it from “covenant.” Cellarius’s opinion is more probable. Cassian, *Conferences* VII.10, reports Saint Basil’s judgment about a certain senator who became a monk: “You have lost a senator and have not made a monk.” Saint Syncletice is traditionally said to have founded the first monastery of virgins in the fourth century. A certain Syncletice is mentioned in an inscription cited by Vignoli, p. 333. Vat. 2, together with some editions, has *ac Dei ministrae* or *et Dei ministrae* (“and servant of God”); Reg. 1–4, Vat. 1, Ottobon. 1, and codex B have *ac ministrae* (“and servant”); other witnesses have *et ministrae*, omitting *Dei*. A gloss in Reg. 1 explains *ministrae* as *diaconissae* (“deaconesses”). Compare the *Prolegomena*, no. 22. Ziegler discusses deaconesses and widows. Arntzenius printed *et ministrae Dei*. Vet. 1 has *glorias* (“glories”) instead of *gloriam*. Aldus and some other editions have *athleta* (“athlete”) instead of *allecta* (“enrolled”). Reg. 3 has *alleta*; in Reg. 1 another reading formerly stood, now *allecta*, as also in the Blandin manuscript and Bollandus, who regards *athleta* in a manuscript cited by Scottus as an error. Ott. 1 now seems to have *anthleta*, though something else formerly stood there. Poelmann’s papers alone support *athleta*. Yet *allecta* should be preferred with most witnesses: Livy, Pliny, Suetonius, and ancient inscriptions use the word in a similar sense. Those who were enrolled in the Senate were properly called *allecti* when, because the number of senators was insufficient, men from the equestrian order were admitted to the Senate. Seneca, *Agamemnon* 812, says *allegi coelo* (“to be enrolled in heaven”) for “to be counted among the gods.”], a sacred virgin and servant of God? By humility she advanced the nobility of her proud **144** lineage to glory, so that she deserved to be enrolled in the senate of the heavenly homeland [Col. 0542D].

Truly worthy is the temple in which the Lord may dwell [Note: Some editions have *habitat* (“dwells”); so Ott. 1 and Reg. 3, whereas the other manuscripts and our editions have *habitet* (“may dwell”), as Wopkensius also conjectured—], disciplined by fasts, refreshed by prayers [Note: Cellarius, with Almeloveen’s and the Leipzig manuscripts, has *refectum* (“refreshed”), that is, strengthened. Ott. 1 and others have *refertum* (“filled”). Reg. 1 in the first hand, 3, and 4 have *refectum*. A gloss in Ott. 1 has *completum* (“completed”).], and utterly clean through purity.

[Col. 0543A] She also drank in the Scriptures of ecclesiastical doctrine with such thirst that, if the liberty of her sex [Note: Wopkensius suspects *ut nisi sexui licentia defuisset* (“if liberty had not been lacking to her sex”), for he does not understand what *sexus licentia* means. But it can be explained quite adequately as “if the liberty of the male sex had not been lacking”; for the following words add, “although her spirit is manly.”], had not been lacking, she could also have taught [Note: All our manuscripts, including Vat. 1, where the rest of this preface is missing, have *posset etiam edocere* (“she could also teach”); Reg. 4 has *posset etiam et edocere*, which seems to be a variant in Reg. 1; codex B has *potuisset etiam docere* (“she could also have taught”). Aldus agrees with our manuscripts. Poelmann has *posset et edocere*. Arntzenius has *posset et docere*, noting no variant in *docere*. Bollandus likewise reads this and reports from Scottus’s manuscript *potuisset* for *posset*. Almeloveen has *licet in membris* (“although in her limbs”); Aldus, Poelmann, our manuscripts, and codex B likewise. Arntzenius has *cum in membris* (“although in her limbs”), which gives a clearer sense. Reg. 1, in a different hand, has *licet et in membris*; a gloss in Reg. 3 explains *licet* as *quamvis* (“although”). Bollandus has *licet et in membris*, while from the manuscripts of Scottus and Rosweydus he reports *quam et in membris*, which seems sharper.], although in a female body her spirit is manly.

But I shall be silent about the distribution of her daily mercy, which she practices so that it remains unspoken, and gives so that it remains hidden. Yet her poor attire indicates [Note: Arntzenius notes that Poelmann’s papers advise reading *indicat* (“indicates”), not *judicat* (“judges”); he adds that he does not see on what grounds. I too do not see what he means. Aldus and all our manuscripts have *indicat*, and Arntzenius himself printed *indicat*. Poelmann has *judicat* in the text and *indicat* in the margin.
