Ott. 1 has *habitus ejus pauper* (“her appearance is poor”); the other manuscripts, together with Aldus, *ejus habitus pauper*. Poelmann and Arntzenius have *ejus pauper habitus*. Poelmann’s papers and his edition’s margin have *refulgeat* (“may shine forth”) instead of *proficiat* (“may prosper”).], that her rich estate prospers.

And so that the greatness of such wisdom, shining with a double **145** lamp, might shine more brightly [Note: Poelmann’s papers note that *et ut magnitudo* is correctly read and that *ut* should not be deleted. Our manuscripts and editions indeed have *et ut*. A manuscript of Bollandus lacked *gemina lampade* (“with a double lamp”). Ott. 1, Reg. 1, 2, and 3, codex B, Almeloveen, Vat. 2, and Aldus have *germanam* (“a sister”); others, together with Reg. 4, have *et germanam*. Sometimes *et* has been omitted by scribes because the preceding word ends with the same letters; sometimes it has been repeated from the preceding word. Although here it could mean *etiam* (“also”), I nevertheless think it better omitted. Reg. 2 has *amittere, quo vocatur* (“to lose what she is called”); the others have *quod* (“that which”).], she has a sister, rightly named Perpetua, unequal in years but equal in deeds, young in age yet venerable in goodness, who, nourished by the dignity of her name, lives in such a way that she cannot lose what she is called. Illustrious through marital power, more illustrious through divine religion, she holds the palm close to virginity [Note: Vat. 2, Reg. 2 and 4, and Aldus have *virginitati* (“to virginity”); Ott. 1, Reg. 2 in the second hand, Reg. 3, and Almeloveen have *virginitatis* (“of virginity”), which Poelmann printed, though his papers appear to reject it. Ott. 1, Aldus, codex B, Almeloveen, and other manuscripts have *manens pudica* (“remaining chaste”). Barthius’s manuscript has *manens perpudica* (“remaining exceedingly chaste”). Poelmann’s edition and others have *permanens pudica* (“continuing chaste”), but Poelmann’s papers restore *manens pudica*. Arntzenius also preferred it because the simple verb is more usual in this expression. *Nuptae* (“of a married woman”) is absent from codex B. The elegance of *conjugii foedere* (“by the bond of marriage”) is familiar and supported by similar examples from Arntzenius.] in marriage...

Remaining chaste under the bond of marriage. The other qualities, apart from the conspicuous adornments appropriate to a married woman, which we have already mentioned in connection with her sister, we find likewise in this woman’s character. To these I shall once more make a fitting reply:

> “I beg you, my lord, my father, do not cast away the one whom you profess to love; do not maliciously frighten the one whom you are accustomed to cherish.”

For indeed I avoid none of all these people, nor do I distrust the merits or instruction of any of them; rather, I see them all in you. Some you have driven toward better things through the exchanges of constant disputation; some you have filled with a longing for holy conduct through the maturity of your gentle teaching; to some you have become an example leading to salvation; others you have made [146] sheep within the enclosures of your flock; others you have nourished; you have become all things to all, so that you might make all safe.

[Note: In Vat. 2 and Ald., and in Poelmannus’s papers, the reading here is *ad hoc ego*; so Ott., book 1, though obscurely, *hoc*. Reg. 1, 2, Poelm., and Vet. 1 read *ad haec ego*. Reg. 4 has the erroneous *ad hac ego*. Reg. 3 has *ego ad haec*: Arntzenius printed this reading, noting its elegance, since the pronoun *ego* is placed first when these words give the impression of belonging to somewhat more elevated speech. There are indeed many examples of this sort, but there are no fewer in which it is placed afterward. Reg. 3 adds *ergo*, namely, *ego ad haec ergo congrua*; it is absent from the others. Codex B has *perfungatur*; retain *perfungar*. Poelmannus’s papers judge that *domine mi* should be deleted; Alm. has *mi domine*; Reg. 2 omits *mi*. Vat. 2 and Ald., together with Poelmannus’s papers, read *ne, quaeso, pater*; and in Vat. 2 it seems to have been *ne quaeso te, pater*. Most have *ne quaeso, domine, mi pater*. Reg. 2, Vat. 2, and Ald. read *diligere profiteris*; other manuscripts of ours have *diligere te profiteris*. Barthius found *deteras* in his manuscript, which he seems to approve, since Tacitus and Horace used the expression in this way. Nevertheless, *deterreas* is sound: that is, “you should drive away from yourself through fear,” as Wopk­ensius explains, adducing several similar examples. *Institutione* occurs in Poelmannus’s papers instead of *instructione*, and *consolationibus* instead of *collationibus*. Vat. 2 reads *factus ad salutem* without *es*.]

[Note: Reg. 2 has *alios intra septa gregis tui accipiens oves*. Reg. 3 has *alios accipiens intra septa gregis tui oves*. Reg. 1 and 4 have *alios intra septa tui gregis accipiens oves*. Ott. 1, Vat. 2, and Ald. have *alios intra septa gregis tui oves* without *accipiens*. In Ott. 1, however, the words from *quibusdam* through *enutristi* are absent from the text and added in the margin. *Accipiens*, which occurs in many printed editions, was also absent from Barthius’s manuscript; he judges that it is better absent than present. Codex B has the worse reading *aspiciens*. Gruner’s edition has *inter septa*, not *intra septa*. Poelmannus’s papers and codex B have *tui gregis*, not *gregis tui*. This signifies fellowship or close association. Compare Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book VI, letter 1: “And I wish that you had restored yourself to your old flock.”]

[Note: Vat. 2 and Reg. 2 have *alios in fide enutristi*. Reg. 1, 3, and Ottob. 1 have *alios enutristi*. Reg. 4 has *alios nutristi*. Poelmannus has *alios salvos enutristi*; some other printed editions have *alios salvos enutrivisti*. In Poelmannus’s papers, variant readings are recorded as *enutrivisti* in one place and *implesti* in another, but they preferred *alios in fide enutristi*. Arntzenius states that *in fide* is absent from codex B and Aldus; but as far as Aldus is concerned, my edition of Aldus reads *alios in fide enutristi*.]

[Note: Reg. 4 has *cesset nunc, obsecro*. Alm. has *plurium*; above, *plurimorum*. Alm. has lost words; like Ott. 1 and codex B, it reads *longae deinceps*. Most have *nec pigeat te*. Reg. 1 has *nec pigeat sine te*, which is also absent from codex B and Reg. 4; but Reg. 1 adds *supra*. Reg. 2 and 3 have *ne pigeat te*. Reg. 4 has *nec pepigeat*, perhaps for *nec te pigeat*. For *adhuc fluctuanti*, with the order reversed, Vat. 2, codex B, Ald., Vet. 1, Mon., and Poelmannus’s papers have *fluctuanti adhuc*. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, and some printed editions have *commodare*; others, with Ald., Vet. 1, Vat. 2, Mon., and Poelmannus, have *accommodare*.]

Let there be an end, I beg you, to the waste of so many words; let the long windings of apology cease from now on, and do not hesitate, after I have traversed the dangers of so great a whirlpool, still to lend the anchor of your authority to this page that continues to struggle in the waves.

[Note: Ott. 1 has *Igitur mirabilium divinorum tres libellos*—“therefore three books of divine wonders”—but *tres* has been written above the line. St. Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, also lists three. Our other manuscripts—Vat. 2 and Reg. 1, 2, and 3—have *Quatuor igitur mirabilium divinorum libellos*, “therefore four little books of divine wonders.” Reg. 4 has *Quatuor mirabilium igitur divinorum*. Codex Alm. likewise counts four. In Poelmannus’s papers, *quinque* is substituted for *quatuor*. Other editions have four. This variation in the letter may have arisen from the numerals, as often happens, or from the way the books were divided by the judgment of copyists, or from the very variation among the exemplars of this letter. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 31 and following.]

Therefore I commend to your defense the four little books of *Divine Wonders*, in which, gathering together a few matters from many sources, I have arranged the sayings of the four evangelists up to the passion, resurrection, and ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, against all rivals, to your defense.

[Note: Some printed editions have *Huic autem carmini*—“to this poem”; the true reading is *operi*—“to this work.” In Barthius’s manuscript there was a gloss explaining it as “to the present poem.” Sedulius more than once calls his poem *opus*, and others speak in the same way. Otherwise, Sedulius intended the name of the poem, as distinguished from prose, to be *Paschal Poem*, while the name of the prose work was *Paschal Work*. All our manuscripts, together with Ald., Mon., Vet. 1, and Poelmannus’s papers, have *favente Domino*—“with the Lord’s favor”; other printed editions have *favente Deo*—“with God’s favor.” Codex B has *Huic autem, favente Deo*, without *operi*. Ott. 1, together with Ald. and our other manuscripts, has *Paschalis Carminis nomen imposui*—“I gave it the name of Paschal Poem.” The Barthius manuscript has *Paschalis Carminis novum nomen ideo imposui*—“for this reason I gave it the new name of Paschal Poem.” Arntzenius considers *novum* superfluous and not sufficiently appropriate. Some printed editions have *Paschalis Carminis ideo nomen imposui*.]

With the Lord’s favor, I have given this work the name *Paschal Poem*, because Christ was sacrificed as our Passover. To him be honor and glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Vat. 2 and Reg. 1 give, as a secondary reading or gloss, *cui est honor*—“to whom belongs honor”; Reg. 4 and Ald. have the same, while our other manuscripts and the printed editions have *cui honor*, without *est*. Reg. 4 has *honor, gloriaque cum Patre*—“honor and glory with the Father.” Ott. 1, Vat. 2, Ald., and other printed editions have *et Spiritu sancto*—“and the Holy Spirit.” Reg. 1 has *et cum Spiritu sancto in saecula saeculorum. Amen*—“and with the Holy Spirit throughout the ages of ages. Amen.” Other manuscripts and printed editions have *et sancto Spiritu*—“and the Holy Spirit.” In Lipsius, the words *cum Patre et Spiritu sancto*—“with the Father and the Holy Spirit”—are absent. The same codex has *in saecula*, not *per omnia saecula*—“throughout all ages”—as others do. Arntzenius says that *omnia* seems superfluous, but in support of the received reading he cites Sedulius himself at the end of the prose dedicatory letter, Prudentius, *Hymns*, *Cathemerinon* 9, final verse, and the manuscript *Life of Saint Odilia*. Nothing is more common in our liturgical books. In Vat. 2, *amen* is absent. Reg. 4 has *amen*. Here ends Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius. The old Turin manuscript is substantially the same, as I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 62.]

## Dedication of the Paschal Work TO MACEDONIUS

To the holy and most blessed father Macedonius, presbyter, Sedulius sends greetings in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0545C] The first person to publish the *Paschal Work* in print was Franciscus Juretus, who also supplied notes to it. These notes were reprinted in certain editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, especially in Gallandi’s *Bibliotheca*. Gallandi had not seen the first edition of the *Paschal Work*, prepared by Juretus at Paris in 1585. When he noticed that, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, especially the Paris edition of 1644, Sedulius’s work was everywhere teeming with such gross errors that one could scarcely at times grasp the author’s meaning, he compared the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1644 with the Lyon edition and appended his own notes, attempting by them to remove some errors and shed light upon the work. I too was unable to consult the first edition of the *Paschal Work*. I nevertheless collated the editions of Margarini de la Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum* (Paris, 1589), the Ducaean supplement to that *Bibliotheca* (Paris, 1624), the Cologne edition of 1618, the Paris edition of 1644, the Lyon edition, and Gallandi’s edition. The oldest of all these editions is certainly the Paris edition of 1589, which I shall chiefly follow. The Paris edition of 1624 is faulty, but the other Paris edition, that of 1644, is still more faulty. From the notes of Juretus and Gallandi, however, I have omitted nothing that I judged relevant to illuminating these books of Sedulius. Wopkens’s judgment concerning the prose is as follows: “Yet I do not assign such weight to this prose that I have often condemned my emendations to the sponge on its authority, since I am firmly convinced that it does not always adhere sufficiently exactly to the poem’s meaning, and at times has even been conformed to a corrupt text.” Arntzenius reports this in his preface, although he maintains that only a few passages remain in the poem itself concerning which it would be more difficult to determine from the prose what is correct. See *Prolegomena*, no. 238.]

[Col. 0545]

[Col. 0545C] 148 You commanded, my revered lord, that I should transfer into rhetorical discourse the text of the *Paschal Poem*, which I had simply executed and presented to you for reading as an act of pure devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Gallandius printed *me potius transferre* (“that I should rather transfer”), perhaps from the corrupt reading of the Paris edition of 1644, *me potuit transferre* (“was able to transfer me”). The word *potius* seems superfluous to me: it occurs shortly afterward and is omitted here in the other editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.]

Whether you wished it repeated because it pleased you, or because it offended you—so, rather, I suppose, you judged that it ought to be set forth in a freer style—I seem to waver in uncertain judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] It would be clearer to read: “Whether it pleased you,” etc. But Juretus retained the reading of the old codex, because it is characteristic of this author to alter the true and rounded order of words: for he was stronger in poetry than in prose. Perhaps Sedulius wrote: “Whether you wished it repeated because it pleased you,” etc.]

Nevertheless, not resisting your holy commands, I undertook the task imposed upon me. I committed my rain-soaked sails once more to the labor of the swelling sea, although the ship had still been shaken by stormy rains, after traversing the courses of renewed danger. I ranged in a long circuit around the vast Cyclades, which earlier, in precipitous fear, I had passed more swiftly, so that I might now inspect with more diligent labor those harbors and shores which, while passing by before, I had merely surveyed.

For many things had certainly been handed over which, because of the narrow constraints of metrical necessity, had by no means seemed capable of being inserted in the earlier commentary; later, the loosening of the tongue was better able to attain them.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Juretus emended it thus: in the old codex it read, “For many things had delayed.”]

Hence we shall give our detractors an opening, and some will say that the fidelity of the translation has been corrupted, because there are plainly things in the discourse that are not found in the poem. Yet if anyone makes this objection, he does so—indeed—without understanding, so that he understands nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Gallandius, with all the other editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, printed *faciunt nec intelligendo* (“they do so without understanding”); I do not know whether Juretus’s edition also has this. But *nae* is certainly the true reading: Sedulius repeats Terence’s words from the prologue to the *Andria*, to which he returns below, “Nor unequal,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Juretus corrected this to *Nam si* (“For if”); the old codex had *Nam sicut* (“For just as”).]

For if they seem to have mastered secular literature or to have been instructed in the divine books, they ought to review the examples of the ancients, lest they unjustly attempt to tear apart similar works. Let them recognize that Hermogenianus, that most learned lawgiver, produced three editions of his work. Let them recognize that Origen, most skilled in divine law, likewise adapted nearly everything he discussed in three editions. None of these men is assailed by the injustice of a biting tongue; rather, they gain an increase of praise because, through the fruits of richer talent, they instructed posterity with greater diligence in what must be known of the truth.

[Col. 0548A] For it is one thing to alter what has been composed and another to restore what is complete. For although the immense expanses of divine law are full—words are always being added and lacking, like the sea, which does not altogether perceive the increase of rivers—they cannot be bounded by any understanding or explained by any tongues. So, too, our books do not altogether differ from one another. But what was lacking in the first has been added in the second. They seem not unequal in subject or arrangement, but different in style and discourse.

Let those who seek to criticize the works of others bring forth their own. It is easier for everyone to judge than to create, and to observe dangers from a fortified camp with a secure face.

Yet I believe, excellent Father, that there will be no reproach—however shameless—if I deserve to obtain the favorable judgment of your heart.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Gallandius conjectures *obloquum*; I prefer *obloquium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Gallandius supplies *dextrum (tui) pectoris*—“the favorable judgment of your heart.”]

Favor me first,

[Col. 0548B] so that others may favor me, and so that an opinion of enduring authority, once approved, may continually pour itself into the minds of all.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Perhaps: “Favor first.”]

You will make it pleasing to have escaped the dangers, when you begin to reveal the calmer serenity. I am now sailing once more upon the sea, though I am already sailing in harbor.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] The passage seems defective and mutilated; Juretus indicated this with an asterisk.]

At last, after the waves, may I be permitted to tread upon the sands—we who have touched the mountains from the sea. Let us touch the mountains from the rock, and let us strengthen our infirm steps, set down in a naval station, amid the waters rushing upon us.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Gallandius restored the corrupt passage as follows: “At last, after the waves, may we be permitted to tread upon the sands, we who have touched the mountains from the sea.” I prefer the lighter alteration: “may we be permitted to tread upon the sands.” “We have touched the mountains from the sea”: let us touch the mountains from the rock. Most printed editions give *non* (“not”) rather than *nos* (“we”).]

Therefore the earlier books, because they were arranged in verse, received the name *Paschal Poem*. The following books, rendered in prose without any variation of rhythm, are designated by the title *Paschal Work*.

At your request, I supplicantly present and offer both works to the Lord Jesus Christ, who does not reject the prayers of the humble; the transmitted reading is *et grego* [meaning uncertain], and I offer them to him,

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Juretus testifies that the old codex clearly has *et grego*, which he defends instead of *et congrego*. In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* I find *et rogo* (“and I pray”); I would prefer *erogo* (“I offer”) or *congrego* (“I gather”), a verb Sedulius uses at the end of the preceding letter. These details sufficiently suggest that both the *Poem* and the *Paschal Work* were published during Sedulius’s lifetime, as I maintained in the *Prolegomena*, no. 158.]

to whom belong might, honor, and glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Metrical Prologue. TO THE READER

[Note: [Col. 0549A]

Here begins the preface of Sedulius the bishop, in prose, to the reader of the *Paschal Poem*.

Whoever you are, a guest invited to the paschal banquets, and not disdaining to recline upon our couches, lay aside the hauteur of your raised brow if you come as a dear friend; and do not here seek the work of an elaborate author. Rather, gladly accepting the modest ceremonies of a little table, be content to partake, and satisfy yourself in spirit more readily than with food. Or if you are captivated by the great abundance of rich things and, as a connoisseur, await sumptuous delicacies, you ought to be satisfied at the banquets of noble teachers, whose manifold preparations cannot be enumerated. There you will surely find whatever the wave of the sea supplies for eating, whatever the fruitfulness of the earth provides, whatever winged creature sustains itself in the clouds by the poise of its body.

[Col. 0552A] Even in those very dishes, richly adorned with precious variety, their honey glows yellow with its nectar and wax, and the honeycomb placed in golden baskets plays a visual counterpart to the metal.

[Col. 0552D] Juretus notes concerning this passage: “I have reproduced it from the traces of the worn writing of the old exemplar. From this it may be inferred that even what preceded concerning the honey could not be read with sufficient clarity.”]

But we have plucked from the seeds of a poor garden a cheap vegetable, which we see served in a red earthen dish more for its being desired than for its splendor.]

[Col. 0549A]

[Note: [Col. 0549B]

1. In codex Reg. 1, after the preface, or letter to Macedonius, is added: “The preface ends. The second begins.” In Ott. 1, after the hymn concerning Christ: “Here begins the prologue of Sedulius: *Paschales*, etc.” The Taurinensis codex has, on its final folio, outside its proper place and in a different hand: “To Robeo. Preface of the sacred work on the books of the New and Old Testament.” Should *Robeo* be read as *Bobeo* or *Bobio*? For it was a book of the monastery of Bobbio. Vat. 1, after Arator’s poem, has: “Here begins the metrical prologue of Sedulius, the Catholic poet, of the *P. F. Paschali*”—perhaps it originally read *Paschalis*—“*Carminis*.” Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, reports the abbreviation in codex 1665 as: “For the paschal feast. *Paschales*, etc.” But he omits *carminis*; and in other codices the letters *P. F.* generally indicate a preface. Reg. 2: “The preface of the *Paschal Poem* of the blessed poet Sedulius.” The Urbinas codex: “Here happily begins the prologue of the excellent bishop Sedulius concerning the history of both Testaments: *Paschales*, etc.” The preface to Macedonius is absent. Ott. 2: “Here begins Sedulius’s book on the deeds of the prophets and the entire course of Christ the Savior: *Paschales*, etc.” The letter to Macedonius is also missing, as in the Roman codex, which reads: “Here begins the book of the poet Sedulius: *Paschales*, etc.”

2. In Reg. 1, *choris* has become *thoris*; some write it this way, but incorrectly, instead of *toris*. *Accumbere*, *discumbere*, and *recumbere* are common words for banquets. Hence *accubitus* and *accubito*, a verb formed by Sedulius, which Braulio also used in the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, chapter 24, and Suger in *Louis VI*: “as though reclined upon couches.”

3. Burmannus conjectured *si me cognoscis* (“if you recognize me”). Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 287: “Learn to lay aside your hauteur.”

4. Printed editions have *Nec quaeras* (“Nor seek”); so also the prose and Reg. 1, according to a different reading. But in the context *Ne quaeras* (“Do not seek”) is retained by the other manuscripts. These same manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *opus hic codicis artificis* (“the work here of an artistic book”); Rom. corruptly has *conditis artificis*. Alb., with the order reversed against the meter, has *artificis codicis*. Poelm. writes *opes* (“riches”) in the margin, and in Ott. 1, from the first hand, *opes* seems to have been written. The law of meter resists this, and Nebrissensis does not sufficiently accommodate it when he reformulates the line as: “Do not seek here the riches of an artistic book.” Arntzenius did not know who had published the verse in this form, although he observed that Savarone cited it thus. But, as I said, the adverb *hic* cannot be shortened. It would be better to read: “Here do not seek the riches of an artistic book.” Otherwise the verse proceeds correctly: “Do not seek here the work of an artistic book.” Grunerus explains it: “Do not seek in this book the work of an artist”; Arntzenius agrees with him. But far better is Arntzenius’s own interpretation, which Nebrissensis also adopted: “Do not seek here the work of an artistic book,” that is, “an artistic codex,” or one made by an artisan’s hand. In Ott. 1 there is a gloss on *artificis*: “that is, artificial.” The adjective *artifex* is sometimes used in this way by good writers. Someone might suspect that, by “an artistic book,” Sedulius meant some culinary handbook, such as the books bearing the title of Apicius. For my part, I understand the verses of Martin of Braga in no other way; their title places them in a refectory:

“Here banquets are not adorned with golden supports;  
nor has Assyrian purple furnished you with a dining couch;  
nor through the many recesses of a shining sideboard  
will polished dishes be set forth by the art of a book.”

Sedulius’s meaning seems to be the same. Vonckius, with an entirely dictatorial tone—as Grunerus says—and with those formulas which Menckenius and the annotators of the work *On the Charlatanry of Scholars* criticize in such critics, says: “I would dare swear that this reading never came from our poet; it must immediately be replaced with: ‘Do not seek here the work of an onyx artisan.’” Or, if the quantity of the first syllable in *onychis* offends anyone because it has been neglected, he orders it replaced with: “of a noble artisan.” Vonckius’s reasoning is that Sedulius maintains a continuous metaphor drawn from a banquet, and therefore there seems to be no place for a book. But this argument is far too weak to undermine the reading found in all manuscripts and printed editions.

5. A modest table is an ordinary—or rather a small and inexpensive—one. “To approach banquets,” “a feast,” and similar expressions are customary phrases. In the Taurinensis codex this couplet is corrupt:

“But content with a modest table, approach the solemnities;  
and more willingly feed the mind than satisfy the body.”

6. Some printed editions, with Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers, have *libenti animo* (“with a willing spirit”). All our manuscripts, together with other and most printed editions, have *libens animo* (“willingly in spirit”). Reg. 1 and 2, Vat. 1, Ott. 2, Rom., and Urb. have *satiare* (“to satisfy”); Vat. 2 has *saturare* (“to fill”). This also seems to have been the reading in Vat. 1, where *saturari* (“to be filled”) is now found, a reading that cannot stand. Grunerus, with many printed editions, has *satiare*; Arntzenius, from the prose verb *saturavit* and because Sedulius elsewhere uses the verb *saturo*, namely in book III, verse 266, printed *saturare*.

7. In Reg. 1, *Aut* (“or”) occurs instead of *At* (“but”). In the Taurinensis codex *Aut* still remains, as in the prose.

8. *Deliciosus* is a word used by Rutilius, Martianus Capella, and Arator.

9. Vonckius, carried away—as Grunerus says—by a marvelous desire for innovation, wishes *doctorum* (“of teachers”) to be rewritten as *dominorum* (“of masters”), because a banquet of teachers is inappropriate. All copies, including the prose, resist this, and the banquet metaphor should not be so continuous that Sedulius entirely forgets the learning which he compares to a banquet. Arntzenius adds that *doctus* (“learned”) is said of someone skilled in his art, including a cook. That is true; but, as I said, Sedulius is referring rather to learning and literary expertise.]

151 Whoever you are, a guest seeking paschal banquets,

Who have deigned to recline upon our couches,

Lay aside your hauteur if you recognize yourself as a friend,

152 Do not seek here the work of an artistic book.

[5] [Col. 0550A] But, content with the modest rites of a table,

Feed your mind more willingly than satisfy it with food.

But if you are captivated by the sweetness of great things,

153 And, as a connoisseur, love sumptuous riches more,

Feed upon the splendid banquets of noble teachers,

[10] [Col. 0551A]

[Note: [Col. 0551B]

10. Nic. Heinsius ordered the reading: “Whose manifold riches are counted.” Wopkensius restores *nec* (“not”), rather than *non*, and explains that Commodianus speaks in this way in *Instructions* 16: “There are besides other demons in the shrines, / which are not counted.” The meaning of the prose is clear: namely, that their riches cannot even be counted. Herm. Cannegieter’s other conjecture, *vel numerantur* (“or are counted”), or *aut et numerantur*, must therefore be rejected. Parrhasius, together with Reg. 2, punctuates it: “Whose manifold riches are not counted”—that is, they are manifold and cannot be counted. An indication of great riches is precisely that they are not counted; for, as the common saying goes, “It is the poor man who counts his livestock.” Horace, book I, letter 6:

“The house is poor where many things do not remain—  
things that deceive the master and benefit thieves.”

11. Nic. Heinsius again conjectures *mittit* (“sends forth”) for *nutrit* (“nourishes”), with Wopkensius likewise dissenting; he observes that *nutrit* is harmonious with the following verb *creat* (“creates”). Most punctuate: “There you will find whatever the sea nourishes, for eating”; Burmannus, not inelegantly: “There you will find whatever the sea nourishes—for eating.”

13. The old Taurinensis codex has: *Terea gemmatis flavescunt mella canistris*. *Terea* is corrupt. Poelmann and some other printed editions have *Caetera*; the true reading is *Cerea*, on the evidence of the manuscripts and the sense. The prose confirms this. For *flavescunt*, Arntzenius reads *flavescent* (“will glow yellow”), which coheres properly with *invenies* (“you will find”). But *collucent* follows in the present tense, unless one takes it as a future indicative from *colluco*. For many verbs of the second conjugation are also used in the third, especially by poets. Bartholomaeus cites *florescunt*, less aptly. Although so many critics have examined this prologue and shifted many words into their place, it is remarkable that no one has questioned *mella* in this verse. Nebrissensis indeed gave grounds for suspicion: “How honey can be placed in baskets at a dinner I do not see, unless you prefer to read *catinis* [‘dishes’].” Yet all copies have *canistris*, which is also defended by the acrostic of Belisarius, verse 6, in the Appendix. In manuscript Reg. 2 there was this gloss above *cerea*: *favum* (“honeycomb”), and above *mella*: *licentia poetica dicit* (“he says this by poetic license”). All the manuscripts I have seen and the printed editions read *mella canistris*; Aldhelm also cites it in chapter 2 of his prose treatise *On Virginity*, when speaking of the bees’ art of making honey: “The distinguished poet, relying on metrical eloquence, is believed to have sung the achievement of this art in a catalectic verse when he said: ‘Waxen apples glow yellow in gem-studded baskets’; and below, in a brachycatalectic verse, or colophon: ‘And golden vessels shine with their own honeycombs.’” But Sedulius is not singing here of the bees’ craft, but of dessert courses. I therefore scarcely doubt that the genuine reading is *mala canistris* (“apples in baskets”): both Nebrissensis’s reasoning, a better depiction of the dessert course, and passages from other authors imitated by Sedulius recommend it. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.672: “And, when the first tables had been slightly moved aside, they make room for the second. Here are nuts, here figs mingled with wrinkled dates, plums, and fragrant apples in open baskets, and grapes gathered from purple vines; in the middle is a white honeycomb.” The proverb “from the egg to the apples” is widely known. Certainly Sedulius had no reason to mention honey being served in baskets when he speaks of honeycomb shining in golden vessels, in accordance with the ancient custom of serving honey at banquets—as Iamblichus testifies concerning the Pythagoreans, *Life of Pythagoras* 21.97: “For lunch there was bread and honey, or honeycomb.” Although Sedulius in book II, verse 268, joins the two—“Honeycombs and sweet honey abound”—as though they were synonymous expressions, that would be less appropriate here, where he seems to have wished to describe two different things. Nor should *catinis* be read, as Nebrissensis conjectured, but *canistris*: besides Ovid, Cicero also recommends it, *Letters to Atticus* VI.1, about the middle: “You are not accustomed to feed on vegetables from platters and very splendid baskets; what am I to suppose that you will serve in earthenware vessels?” I think Sedulius also had this in view. See also Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 4, verse 15: “Bearing precious gifts in baskets.” *Cerea mala* (“waxen apples”) are so called either because of their waxen colour, to which *flavescunt* refers, or because they are soft. This too seems drawn from Virgil, *Eclogues* 2.59: “I shall add waxen plums.” The very formation of the letters leads us to suppose that *mella* was made from *mala* by ignorant scribes, especially because in the Middle Ages an apple was called *melum*, from Greek μῆλον, “apple”; this word also passed into Italian. Compare Du Cange.

14. Nebrissensis doubts whether honeycombs are called *suis* (“their own”) as being of their own colour, or because they were customarily placed in golden vessels. But *suis* merely indicates that the honeycombs were then contained in golden vessels.

15. A poor garden is a scanty, not an abundant, one, as elsewhere a poor field or poor table. Virgil, *Eclogues* 7.34: “You are keeper of a poor garden.”

16. Reg. 1 has *oppositum*; above it is a variant reading or correction, *appositum*, which alone must be retained. For *appono*, like the simple *pono*, is frequent in descriptions of banquets. See Cicero’s words quoted just above, and the note on Juvencus, book III, verse 80. In Urb. there is the plain error *testum* for *testa*. Isidore cites this verse, as I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 167; Bede also cites it in *On Metrical Art*, but corruptly has *Rubrae* for *Rubra* in the copy I use.]

Whose manifold riches cannot be counted.

[Note: [Col. 0551B] See note 11 above concerning *nutrit*. See note 13 above concerning *cerea* and *mala*.]

There you will find whatever the sea nourishes for eating,

Whatever the earth creates, whatever flies toward the stars.

Waxen honey glows yellow in gem-studded baskets,

[Col. 0552A] 154 And golden vessels shine with their own honeycombs.

[15] But we have plucked a small thing from a poor garden,

A vegetable which, placed in a red earthen dish, serves as food.

## BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0553A]

Since the industrious practice of pagan poets commends the fabulous trifles of noble verse with a pomp of words, and commits to the papyrus of the Nile’s swirling stream, ploughed by the reed-pen, whether the clamours of buskined tragedy, the comic obscenity of the ridiculous Geta, or, in any metres of poetic art, the wicked deeds of ancient times and certain shameful matters shaped by narrative art: why should I, exercising the songs of Davidic melody on the ten-stringed psaltery amid the choirs of blessed doctrine and reverently giving voice to spiritual utterances, keep silent in a subdued voice about Christ’s wondrous and saving powers, when I ought to take up the work of truth and not pass over in silence the gifts of heavenly grace by the instrument of faithful speech?

[Col. 0555D] I think the reading should be: “and by the instrument of faithful speech.”]

For no duty of the human heart and understanding serves anyone more justly than the omnipotent Lord, who established understanding and founded hearts, so that matter devoted to its Creator may never abandon its own author—a structure that it is fitting neither to withdraw from his jurisdiction nor to let perish.

[Col. 0556D] Some read “established, and hearts”; others omit the conjunction *and*.]

To him, under perpetual dominion in the heavenly citadels, belong with the Father one power, equal splendor’s brightness, a shared and undivided loftiness of majesty, equal honor, the same might, a common exaltation, a kingdom without temporal limit, an origin always remaining through unbroken eternity, fellowship of the scepter, shared glory, and equal majesty.

This is the road directing us toward the dwelling of salvation; this is the path that opens with firm steps toward the paschal gifts. Here we lay the foundations of our work. Turn all your sick minds here, therefore, and apply this medicine to deadly diseases—you whose minds the vain intention of harmful disputation creeps through, and whose reason the incurable discipline of Attic doctrine wounds with the poison of Cecropian teaching—so that, when you drink in the vital airs blazing with the breath of divine law and fragrant with pleasing sweetness, you may thereafter abandon the filth of Athenian foulness with a purer understanding.

Why, Theseus, do you still wander through the labyrinthine twists of dark errors, traversing caves made dim by blind perplexities, while your footprints perish in the tangled exit? Why do you still prefer the wild vine to the good vine? Why do you set the *saliunca* (a lowly aromatic herb) before bright rose gardens? What benefit is there in trusting with empty worship in stone images and bronze figures, and in venerating profane shrines and metallic objects, except to condemn your souls to servitude?

Spare yourselves, I beg you—spare yourselves now—from the filthy clods of sandy dust and from enjoying the naked dryness of barren fields, where the farmland, never knowing how to repay the labor of the sweating farmer with a fruitful reward from its pregnant depths, yields nothing.

Nor should you tear from grassy plots the poisonous nourishment of deadly sap, the sprouts of bloodshed, which, ever friendly to Tartarean foods, do not know how to serve life but only death. Rather, enter through the clear waters of the pure spring into the pleasant meadows of flowering growth and the lovely approaches of the blessed dwelling, where fruitfulness, quickened by divine waters, nourishes a crop of life-giving seeds; with the harshness of thorns torn away, it grows, so that through the manifold abundance of an immense harvest it may now be God’s harvest, await the hope of the reward to come, and store the greatest fruit in hundredfold heaps within the barns.

[Col. 0559D] Juretus read and punctuated it thus; in the old codex he found: “And the growing immense abundance of the harvest of manifold God.”]

Almighty God of undivided and eternal divinity, who by your holy command hold the whole world together, who made firm the structure of heaven by the work of your fingers, and established the fabric by your mighty word,

[Col. 0559D] This may be understood as “by the operation of the mighty word,” or read as “by your mighty word.” Gallandius conjectures: “You fashioned the structure by the power of your mighty word,” because the author seems to allude to the Apostle’s words in Hebrews 1:3, “sustaining all things by the word of his power.” Compare Psalm 8:4 and Job 38:11.]

who prevent the swift madness of the raging sea from overwhelming the boundary of earthly proximity by forbidding it, through established limits, to pass beyond its appointed bounds; who, bringing the sight of the radiant sun and the horned face of the moon into contact with day and night, distribute the alternations of both lights by the balance of sacred regulation; who alone gather and alone know the number, powers, signs, functions, places, courses, and seasons of the stars; who gave life through diverse movements to the inert limbs of the raw earth by means of living bodies; who, after condemning the human being who ate the fruits of the trees through forbidden presumption to death, restore him through the sacrament of better food;

[Col. 0560D] Some have the less suitable reading *resuscitans* (“restoring”). Shortly afterward Gallandius wishes *multiplicas* (“you multiply”) to be restored, or rather *multiplicare statuisti* (“you determined to multiply”).]

and preserve him from the pleasurable deceit of the serpent’s bite by the drink of immaculate blood; who, after the name of the human race had been completely submerged and buried by the sudden flood of the rising Deluge, except for those whom the guardian had protected in the ark, restored it to multiplication from one offspring, so that, by the mystical manifestation of your power, you might reveal for cleansing through the one baptism of the whole world what the sins of the flesh had slain, guarded by the faithful protection of wood;

grant me in your mercy that road, now show me in supplication that path which directs a few footsteps by a narrow way toward the walls of the city of salvation—namely, Jerusalem, the Lord’s city, bearing our Pasch in the passion of Christ—so that, through the hospitality of bodily grace shining upon this path, we may deserve to reach that homeland of spiritual glory.

And may your word, Lord, be a lamp for my feet,

[Col. 0561D] From Psalm 118:105.]

whose radiance may lead me along the straight path to those places of flowering grass; where the good shepherd keeps his shining sheepfold; where every flock, clad in white, follows the lamb of the virgin, purest in the snowy brilliance of his appearance.

The way is not difficult if you deign to offer yourself as guide. Everything lies subject to your power. All nature bows to your commands and, at the dominant command, passes into contrary forms and shapes.

If you wish the annual crops to turn yellow amid icy seasons, sluggish winter will produce a reaper nimble with sickles.

If, in the season of the spring quarter, when the earth shines clad in its first mantle of flowers, you command the vine to bring forth for the wine-maker, swollen with new wine, then, not rejecting the nectar-bearing inward parts of the fruitful grape, it will gladly drive away the injury of the drunken pressing.

[Col. 0561D] Juretus observes that the old codex wrongly has *nam nec repudians*. The whole period is certainly obscure. [Col. 0562D] A little earlier the printed editions have *plagae temporis* (“the season’s region”), and shortly afterward *fidei judicium* (“the judgment of faith”), followed soon by *corde permittimus* (“we permit in the heart”).]

And the changes of all seasons, through altered fruits, will not refuse to serve the Creator.

For ancient faith reveals the evidence of divine wonders, and the ancient origin of the fathers bears witness to them. The immortal signs of heavenly powers, which must not be erased by the ages as time grows old, endure from times long past.

Of these, out of fear in a trembling mind, we scarcely permit ourselves to touch upon even a few in bold narration, with our minds and feeble heart, as one entering a forest of great density strives to reach some branches with the very tips of his fingers.

For even if the human body supplied a hundred mouths at once, and an iron voice did not cease to cry out through a hundred movements of the tongue, who could explain all the things whose number could be matched neither by the densest stars of heaven nor by the thirsty sand of the sea?

From this confused material, called chaos, the Word fashioned the clear appearance of things and brought it forth.

[Col. 0563A] Enoch, most pleasing and beloved of God, attained living glory. Transgressing the limits of human nature through countless courses of years, by being born he fulfilled the earth’s due, but brought about a miracle for death, from which he was taken away.

Sarah’s limbs, already weakened by old age, were withering, and the blood extinguished in her aged body had condemned its veins to the sterility of hopeless offspring. Yet, when her marriage to an old man had been made fruitful, she suddenly stretched out the lap of her chilled womb; and, with her womb swollen by a new birth, the trembling mother lifted to the breasts of milk her child, born late and begotten in belated happiness, as the hope of a future nation and people. The father offered him as a gift to God, whose promise he had received in his despair.

[Col. 0563] Some incorrectly have *promisso* (“by the promise”); shortly before, many printed editions have *sanguinis exstinctus* (“the blood of the bloodline extinguished”), which I likewise consider an error rather than the sound reading.]

The boy stood beneath the knife, and a ram became the burnt offering. O undefiled mind of the holy patriarch! He rejected what was human and looked toward what was divine: while denying life to his son, he acquired it. Abraham drew the sword in order to strike, and the Lord changed the sacrifice so that he would not strike the son. Clearly, a great mystery was being enacted in this matter, so that for the life of the human race Christ, the gentle Lamb, might willingly offer himself as a victim.

Lot was fleeing from perishing Sodom. His wife, through the boldness of careless presumption, looked back at what she had escaped and, transformed into a statue of salt, remained—not for wisdom but for punishment.

For no one who has once despised the dangers of the world and then turns back toward them in precipitous desire will enjoy the pleasant joy of salvation. Nor is that plowman worthy to rejoice in the coming fertility of his crops who, confusing the furrow intended to be formed by the plow’s straight course through a backward turning of his face, has scattered the order of his former labor.

[Col. 0565D] Perhaps *retrorsum* (“backward”). Others have *firmandi* (“of strengthening”).]

Once the bush was wrapped in harmless fires, and seemed to burn without burning. Its wood supplied no fuel to the flames, nor, seized by the fire of the surrounding heat, did it suffer the losses of consumed strength. Thus the touch of divine kindling was tempered, so that while the flame caressed the fevered branches, radiance—not destruction—was seen among the leaves.

The pliable nature of a gentle staff was changed into an unkind and unmanageable serpent. With it, exercising the movements of a viper in such sinuous coils and brandishing a three-forked tongue, it swallowed the twin serpents of hostile deceit, and then, through a rigid reversal of its transformation, resumed the staff’s proper form.

Through the depths lying amid the sea’s waves, as the waters rolled back to either side and were suspended by a divinely constructed watery barrier, the pedestrian multitude crossed. The sea stood everywhere like a wall, and the land, stripped of the covering of its kindred waters, remained bare, until the people, walking through the sea where no sea was present, traveled with foreign footsteps along a watery road of dry ground.

Nature changed its path, ordered for a little while to relax its constancy. A countless multitude crossed the slippery fields of salt and, without knowing it, bore the mystery of an unformed baptism: it had crossed through the life-giving passages of the waters under Christ’s leadership.

Thus, finally, the prophet sang, signifying this:

“The voice of the Lord is over many waters.”

[Col. 0567D] Psalm 28:3.]

Who would doubt that the voice is called the Word? Who would deny that Christ is the Word? He, the author of both the Old and the New Testament, by his coming opened the immense abyss of the first law,

[Col. 0567D] Some read *immensum*; retain *immensam*. A little earlier it would be preferable to read *quis dubitet* (“who would doubt?”), for *quis abneget* (“who would deny?”) follows. Below I have restored *familiari semper ardore* (“with the ever-familiar heat”) for *ardoris* (“of heat”).]

so that, through more recent teaching—as though the innermost and deepest masses of water had been pushed aside—the succeeding age might walk without fear of danger along the level path of freedom, already secure.

What shall I say of the innumerable multitudes of that same people who, in the deserts, amid vast stretches of land condemned to complete barrenness of sustenance, obtained angelic foods and bread of heavenly grace? There a nectarous cloud of heavenly majesty, watering the people, poured out dishes from rains and abundant foods from showers.

Again, the thirsting army was languishing across fields scorched by violent heat, where, with springs denied by the ever-familiar heat, the earth lay exhausted; where the nature of water, withdrawing the hope of drinking and thereby of living alike, had failed.

Then, from the stunned rock’s interior, torpor imprisoned within it suddenly overflowed into foaming liquid from the surging stone, and the veins of the dry and fasting marble vomited forth abundant drink for everyone.

Thus, through these three things, Christ was already announcing the great mysteries of his own mystery: Christ was in the sea, Christ in the bread, Christ in the rock.

The she-ass, a lowly and foolish beast, terrified by the sight of angelic power, addresses its rider in words, and the inarticulate clamor of its braying tongue is expressed through the utterances of human speech.

At the sun’s position at the summit in mid-heaven, restraining the swift courses of its panting flame, it fixed the light against Gibeon, prolonging the evening through the extraordinary delay of the day. Nor did the moon, moving according to its own laws, cross the threshold of its sluggish station or carry out the order of its customary course, until the sword of the victorious army utterly cut down the hostile force through the intervention of heavenly aid. At last the very stars, serving Virtue, were already showing—through the mystery of a similar name—that Jesus the Lord would come, with the name preceding him.

Ravens supplied Elijah with his daily meals contrary to the order of nature; and the bird, subjected to the greed of its voracious beak—which readily provides easy prey for its hollow throat—carried untouched food to his fasting bites.

[In an old manuscript there was *feracis* (“fruitful”) in place of *voracis* (“voracious”); but the scribe himself corrected it.]

Now he who was good and faithful toward Elijah, though once evil and faithless toward Noah, washed away on earth the guilt contracted in the inundation of the waters. But Elijah, after displaying many miracles to the earth and transferring to his friend, as a worthy successor, the gift of his own power through the Spirit, as though it were an inherited generosity, was snatched away by fiery horses and chariots through those expanses of clear serenity. There, where the lighter road of the pure pathway preserves no furrows made by burning wheels sinking their tracks into the heavenly field, he sought the right-hand regions of the greater space in such a way that, resplendent on the axle of heavenly triumph, he scorned the boundary of human limitation, relying on his long-continued vitality.

How well, suitably, and deservedly did majesty smile upon the brightness or name of Elijah through the corresponding designation of the shining path! If, in Greek, one letter could be changed by a shift of accent, the sun itself would seem to be expressly indicated.

In the case of Hezekiah, the most righteous king, when he had reached the final limits of life, the Lord in his mercy—or by his right—added fifteen years to his life and, closing the already opened gates of death, recalled life, languishing at its setting, back to its beginning at the rising.

Jonah, tossed about on the waves of the sea by the anxious trembling of the ship, and hidden in the belly of the devouring whale, did not experience the waters while he remained in the sea. He had entered, of course, a life-giving tomb so that he would not die; and, safely held under the gentlest guardianship within the voracious belly, he seemed to have been deposited there, not seized as prey, and preserved more healthfully by an enemy’s protection. He came to land by vomiting, not by a ship.

To this event, in a contrary variation, the sailor’s ferocity supplied a parallel: the beast provided the vessel.

[An old manuscript had *nauta veritatem praebuit* (“the sailor supplied truth”). Juretus corrected it to *feritatem* (“ferocity”) and observed that in ancient manuscripts *v* is often written for *f* because of their affinity. On this basis he emends, in the *Panegyricus* delivered to Maximian—or rather, as Gallandius notes, in the *Panegyricus* delivered to Constantius Chlorus by Eumenius, chapter 9—*viros attonita feritate trepidantes* (“men trembling with stunned ferocity”) in place of *veritate* (“truth”); and in Eumenius’ speech *For the Schools*, chapter 19, *feritate Francorum* (“the ferocity of the Franks”) in place of *veritate*; and in Arnobius, book VI, chapter 9, *instincta feritate naturae* (“impelled by the ferocity of nature”). Isidore likewise attests the ferocity of the Franks in book IX, chapter 2 of the *Etymologies*, and suggests that they were named from it.]

When, with God breathing from heaven, the single intention of the hearts of the three youths utterly despised and rejected the sacred things of Babylon and accepted the harsh outcome of death under the cruelty of a tyrannical law, whose fury, kindled by the fire of Achaemenian madness, overcame the heat of its own furnace, they were handed over, bound, into the midst of the pyre. The fire did not dare to touch the youths who, burning so fervently in their hearts, overcame the punishment borne by the image of suffering.

[Some printed editions erroneously have *cadentes* (“falling”) in place of *candentes* (“glowing”). Above, perhaps *truduntur* (“they are thrust”) should be read, together with *et vicerunt imaginem poena deferente supplicium* (“and they overcame the image that bore the punishment”). Some have *deferiente* in place of *deferente*.]

O how great is the salvation of believers, when the youths, glowing with faith more brightly than the flames, caused the force of the extinguished furnace to grow cold!

The author, therefore, did not escape a punishment worthy of such a wicked judgment. For he who, carried away by foolish madness, had despised the rights of human compassion, lived like a beast through the forests, followed the wild companionship of animals, and exchanged the luxurious nourishment of a courtly banquet for hay as food and a river as drink. Under the appearance of this deformity, shaggy and wandering through forests and mountains, he was seen for seven years.

Nor, later, while the ruling Darius imitated that former madness, was Daniel, the supreme glory of the Hebrews, treated with less severity. He was shut in with beasts goaded by fasting, and his innocent body was assigned to be devoured by their savage bites. Yet the beast became gentle and peaceful: lest hunger should tear the holy limbs with a maddened tooth, it began already to love its hunger. Softening the terrifying expression of its face and submitting its rage, while a gentler anger came to rest in its savage jaws, it taught the lions, forgetful of their innate ferocity, to spare their prey.

Tell me, O stubborn Nature, where after such things are your laws? Who so often withdrew your rights from you? Who commanded the man carried away to learn of the underworld; who granted fecund old age to a barren mother; who compelled a sheep to come willingly to the altar; who transformed a woman’s likeness into an image of salt; who showed that branches blazing with fire did not burn; who changed a shrub into a serpent; who opened pedestrian passage through the waves of the sea; who poured down nectar-like manna in rain-filled clouds; who brought forth waters from the arid entrails of a rock; who permitted the mouth of a mute four-footed creature to speak human words; who suspended the elements in their fixed courses for a long station; who fed a human being through the services of birds; who led him into heaven on the axle of a flashing cavalry; who granted three lustra to a dying king; who gave the shipwrecked man a harbor in the womb of a savage predator; who washed the children’s limbs with starry dew in the furnace; who made a wandering king a guest at table among beasts and cattle in thorny pastures; who taught lions to spare their prey and not to love plunder?

[Some have *Qui* (“who”) and others *Quis* (“who”).]

Indeed, the foundations of the work of the Creator of all things—whose entire creation, whether known or hidden, stands fashioned by the mechanisms of his word—lie subject to him; and creation follows the command of the one who orders it, wherever the divine judgment by its nod has drawn the law of nature.

Woe to the wretched who, bent toward empty cults, devote the foolish service of their perverse hearts to images carved by themselves, and, abandoning their own Maker, venerate the likenesses made by their hands! What madness is this, what such insanity plays upon the mind, that a human being sound in all his limbs should worship a shameful bird, a most obscene ox, a twisted dragon, and a half-human dog? Some, blinded by clouded minds, wish the sun to be regarded as the progenitor of all things because, flooding the regions of the earth and the expanses of clear serenity with its light, it never ceases to traverse the zones of heaven and the fiery stars with swift movement. Yet from its very unstable motion, by which the wandering fire carries out its rapid courses, it is clear that the sun is an instrument, not a master. For, while the fixed order of its administration is preserved, it rises at one time and at another, as the hours incline toward sunset, bends toward its setting and divides its alternations with the night. Nor is it always present everywhere; and no one saw the beginnings of the world at its birth, unless the provident Creator had ordained it to radiate at the beginning of the third light, after a second day had passed without the sun.

So too many lavish useless vows upon the moon, which they observe always increasing and diminishing at the appointed times of the months. So too they do not cease to sacrifice to the stars, which, when the night has withdrawn, are driven away by the faces of the morning light. One is a worshiper of waters, another of flames. Yet things whose forms are naturally opposed do not dare to make each other enemies, lest, through a nearer discord, either the hotter fire dry up the weaker waters or the unequal pyre suddenly die, extinguished by the great floods.

Another, setting up altars at the roots of trees, placing food before them, never ceases to pray tearfully to branches and logs that they protect his children, houses, fields, marriage, servants, and wealth.

O wooden object, why do you entreat wood? You waste your efforts by crying out to the deaf; you await answers from the mute, though you will hear nothing.

Those objects support the stability of houses only in this way: when cut down by axes, they support the hanging roofs of buildings, or, placed upon hearths and set alight, serve in the preparation of food.

Some are even more foolishly devoted to vegetables; by watering their transplanted gods in gardens, they convince themselves that they are true worshipers of deities.

But I am now ashamed to say more about such people, lest, while we chastise the numerous errors of folly on the page of holy religion, a harsh bramble should scorch the lilies, soft with excessive beauty, or a purple thistle and prickly hawthorn, armed with spines, should rise among the violets of the flowering field. It is therefore enough now to rebuke those whose monstrous objects of worship we have ridiculed for their human errors—or rather, whose actions we have lamented with compassion.

Now it is pleasing to proceed along the course already begun, to climb the lofty mountain with firm step, and to reach, with the effort of all our strength, the city that is the author of our freedom. It is itself the peaceful house of peace, itself the secure dwelling of salvation, itself the perpetual service of freedom.

For if, concerning the city of an earthly mortal dwelling, founded by a mortal builder, the poet of secular literature sang:

> What was the great reason for you to see Rome?  
> Freedom.

How much more shall we believe that the laws of perpetual freedom exist in the city of the heavenly kingdoms, which God the Lord established as its builder! Concerning this city the prophet of spiritual songs says:

> The Lord builds Jerusalem,

and in the following psalm likewise explains:

> Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion,  
> for he has strengthened the bars of your gates;  
> he has blessed your children within you;  
> he has established peace within your borders, etc.

[Psalm 146, verse 2, and the following psalm, verses 12 and following. More is added here to the poem.]

Let us also hear the Creator of all things himself in his Gospels, in whose holy utterance he declared this city to belong to him:

> But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.  
> (Matthew 5:34 and following)

It is as though he were saying, “It is mine,” while he more openly concealed the expression of this fact, so that by the humility of his speech he might reveal the summit of his majesty. For while teaching, he admonished them in these words:

> Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.  
> (Matthew 11:29)

This is the place where the royal hall shines with golden roofs; where the one who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and the door is soon opened to the one who knocks. Here is that precious stone, rejected by the builders, shining as the head of the corner. Its burden is felt to be exceedingly light; its yoke is proved to be exceedingly gentle.

Therefore, through selected miracles of the Old Testament, we have recounted what the Father, in fellowship with the Son and with the Holy Spirit established with him, accomplished. Likewise, through selected miracles of the New Testament, we shall recount what the Son, in fellowship with the Father and with the Holy Spirit established with him, accomplished, so that the one power of the Godhead, always conspicuous through inseparable strength and simple majesty, may be threefold, and through threefold majesty may be simple.

This is the true faith and firm belief. The wretched Arius refused to possess this salvation. While, through the winding turns of a crooked path, he tried to divert the straight road, he fell into a foul pit and followed the darkness of the darkening Tartarus. As empty and senseless in understanding as he was, he expired with his belly also empty, his entrails poured out, at the moment of his just punishment.

Madman! He thought that the rights of the Father’s divinity—which cannot be made equal to anything by any example of similarity—could be reckoned by mortal degrees. Among human beings born according to the law of the flesh, the son is inferior to the father, because the father himself, who now precedes his son, was shortly before a son, and it is not uncertain that the one who is now a son can become a father. Thus, through the whole succession of descendants, a new offspring proceeds, and the ancestors of grandfathers are counted in vast old age.

[Some have *cum pater fieri* (“when he can become a father”), others *compater fieri* (“become a fellow-father”). The syntax is involved both in the poem and in the prose, which is often more obscure than the poem; the meaning is sufficiently clear in itself.]

The Lord, who is the Word, Power, Wisdom, and the whole common possession of the Father, is Christ: light arisen from light, born alone from the One alone. He is in no respect less than the Father, nor is there anything by which he might grow, since he is exalted above all things. Because he is begotten, not created, he bears the name “Beginning” as the summit. For, according to John, when the Jews asked him who he was, he said that he was the Beginning.

What, then, is “Beginning” except the lofty summit above which nothing at all is found, always remaining in the Father, in whom the Father always remains? He is the head of all things, the one God of undivided majesty—not because this Son is believed to be the one who is the Father, but because the Son is believed to be what the Father is, as he himself spoke through the evangelical teaching, saying:

> I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.  
> (John 10:38)

Then he added accordingly:

> I and the Father are one.  
> (Ibid., 10:30)

Let Arius hear the word “one”; let Sabellius recognize the word “are”: one fleeing from the Trinity, the other dissenting from unity. Both are equal in error, although they hold different opinions.

How the authors of pagan doctrines, whose teachings contradict one another, try to oppose one another with their words! They extend their arms with bare shoulders, displaying them, and are prepared not to transmit any teaching but only to contend in lengthy disputation. Their wisdom lies uncultivated, because before the Lord the fragile discipline of worldly wisdom is vain.

One speaks more; the other is more silent. One argues while walking; the other pronounces while standing. One is always shedding tears; the other never ceases to laugh. Thus, in all of them, equal madness appears under different forms.

Meanwhile, as we lighten by words the burden of the journey’s labor, and hope and faith accompany my difficult progress, we reach more gently the summit of the highest citadel, difficulty laid aside.

Behold, the standards of the holy cross already shine! Behold, the camp of the great King displays its most holy, flashing light, and with a breath from heaven the trumpet of the Lord’s station cries out. Access to his gate lies open to the soldiers; let the one who serves as a soldier enter without fear.

The gate of eternity invites you—the gate that is Christ, namely, the Father’s voice. You will rejoice in the golden reward of everlasting life, because you bravely handle the heavenly weapons of the Lord and, with honor fixed upon your forehead, display the mysteries of the faithful sign.

Behold, I carry your honor and heavenly weapons, O good King, the smallest part of your army, consecrated to you. Grant that I may receive my own dwelling here; grant that within the walls of this city I may be deemed worthy of a small habitation. As your perpetual inhabitant and your servant, established in a small corner of the holy dwelling among the citizens of the blessed order, may I deserve to be enrolled last in the book of life as one of the city’s inhabitants.

I certainly ask for great things, but your greatness supplies the means to grant great things; the one who entertains doubtful hope of such great mercy offends you all the more.

Christ, grant my prayers. In haste to give life to the dying world, you sought earthly things from heaven and deigned to assume human form, taking upon yourself what was alien while not abandoning what was your own.

Matthew first undertook this task and set forth humanity in general. Mark, like a wondrous lion, roared out through the wilderness with a cry. Luke took his likeness from the beginning of priestly worship, in the form of a young bull. John, with the force of a flying eagle, penetrated heaven through the majesty of the Word.

These four leaders and heralds, singing you alone, are dispersed like a corresponding number of seasons throughout the broad expanse of the whole world.

[As I said, Juretus and Gallandius read *unate* (“united”), while other printed editions have *unita*. I divide the words as they are divided in the poem: *una te* (“you alone”).]

Thus, too, the twelvefold summit of the honor of the apostolic height, ever shining, imitates the hours and the months in its numbers, so that, when all things are gathered together, the whole year may serve you.

Therefore, recalling here the ancient beginnings of former death, I rejoice to hasten toward new life, so that we who sowed tears in Adam may reap joy in Christ and may deserve to utter the Davidic song:

[Shortly before, I restored *metamus* (“let us reap”) in place of *metemus*. At times, by the slight change of a single letter, I have made the meaning of the prose—otherwise certain—clearer, as on page 178, where I read *imitatur* (“imitates”) for *imitatus* (“imitated”), and *deputatur* (“is assigned”) for *deputatus* (“assigned”). Sometimes I leave the same words as they are, although they could easily be reshaped to fit the text of the poem, as on page 193, where *gaudebitis quia* (“you will rejoice because”) can be restored from the poem as *gaudebitis qui* (“you will rejoice, you who”). More often, however, the prose is so corrupted that without the help of other manuscripts it is useless to attempt a cure.]

> Those who sow in tears  
> shall reap in joy.  
> Going, they went and wept,  
> carrying their seeds.  
> But coming, they shall come in exultation,  
> carrying their sheaves.  
> (Psalm 123:5–6)

[Col. 0553]

### Note 17

Here again new inscriptions appear in many copies:

- Reg. I: “The metrical prologue ends. The same sacred work on the Old Testament begins.”
- Ott. I: “The Paschal poem of both Testaments begins. The first book of Sedulius begins.”
- Vat. I: “The sacred work on the Old Testament begins: the first book of Sedulius on the individual miracles of both Testaments.”
- Reg. 2: “The sacred work from the Old Testament begins. The poet urges himself to write.”
- Urb.: “The preface of the same, arguing against the pagans.”
- Ott. 2: “On the inventions of the poets.”
- Rom.: “The preface arguing against the pagans.”

The Laurentian Library manuscript, exhibited by Bandini, has *pigmenta* (“pigments”) in place of *figmenta* (“inventions”); but *figmenta* should be retained. The same error occurs in Bede, *On the Art of Meter*: *Cum tua*. Petrus Paulus Justus, in *Specimen*, observation 21, thinks that one should read:

> Thus the pagan poets strove to display their invented fictions,

because he found this wording in the old author of the *Life of Blessed Adalberon*, among Pez’s *Writers of Austrian Affairs*, volume II, page 6. But he did not notice that this author adapts Sedulius’ words, altering them somewhat for his own purpose: thus he has *sic* (“thus”) for *cum* (“when”), and *studuerunt* (“they strove”) for *studeant* (“they may strive”), which the sense in Sedulius requires.

### Note 18

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book II, chapter 2, quotes from William Brito, an imitator of Sedulius:

> If each poet was permitted to inflate his own pagan falsehoods  
> with a resounding roar—

Concerning the verb *pompare* (“to inflate, parade”), see the judgment of Parrhasius in number 189 of the *Prolegomena*. *Pompatus* is a verb used by Tertullian. Writers of the later period used not only *pompare* but also *pompizare*. See Ducange and Colvenerius’ note on Balderic’s *Chronicle of Cambrai*.

In the prologue to the *Life of Blessed Adalberon*, according to the edition of John, Abbot of Ljubljana, one reads *grandisonis ornare modis* (“to adorn with resounding modes”); but in the *Writers of Austrian Affairs* the reading has been restored from the manuscript as *pompare*. The author of that Life continues:

> and to shade and enclose his beautiful falsehoods, of little benefit to posterity, with beautiful riddling figures, in a tragic roar and with masterly style.

These words are taken from the following verses of Sedulius; hence the earlier edition was less accurately written, with *et ritu magnifico* (“and with magnificent style”) instead of *et ritu magistro* (“and with masterly style”). It should also be noted that the author of the Life seems to explain the words *Niliacis biblis* in verse 22 through “beautiful riddling figures.”

### Note 19

Our manuscripts have *Ridiculove Getae*. Rom. and Ang. write *Ridiculo vegete*, which arose because in very ancient parchment manuscripts words were not separated and diphthongs were sometimes absent. Thus foolish scribes made *Ridiculo vegete* from *Ridiculovegete*. Some have tried to defend this reading, as though it referred to *vegete*, which they say Palladius uses for a wine cask.

Grunerus seems to attribute to Vonckius the instruction that *Ridiculove scaeva* should be read instead of *Ridiculove Getae*. But if Grunerus believed this, he was mistaken: Vonckius wanted *Scaeva* restored for *Saeva* in the following verse.

Parrhasius, Nebrissensis—who observed that *Ridiculo veteri* should not be read—Fabricius, and others correctly printed *Ridiculove Getae* and interpreted it as referring to comedy, from the name of Geta, a slave. Barthius does not approve this interpretation. He himself thinks that Geta was the name of some ridiculous god among the most ancient Britons, about whom writers on English affairs speak, especially Asser in his Life of Alfred, who flourished at the end of the ninth century. Asser gives the genealogy of Geta and brings forward these very verses of Sedulius for that purpose.

I have presented Asser’s words in the *Prolegomena*, number 179, where I added other similar testimonies. Ethelred, or Aetred, abbot of Rievaulx, perhaps has the same matter in view, although he does not name Sedulius, in *On the Genealogy of the Kings of England*:

> Geta, who himself was considered to possess such wisdom and virtue that he was worshiped by the pagans as a god.

Yet Asser first calls him *Geada*, from which he derives the name *Geta*.

Gronovius, in *Observations on Ecclesiastes*, chapter 2, rejects Barthius and the other eminent men who had embraced this view. He observes that all comic characters are ridiculous and that Geta in particular was introduced as a comic figure by Menander. Ovid, book III of *The Art of Love*, verse 331, writes:

> Let Sappho also be known—for what woman was more wanton than she?—  
> or the woman whose father is mocked by the clever art of Geta.

Sedulius clearly explains himself in the prose: *Ridiculi Getae comica foeditate* (“with the comic ugliness of ridiculous Geta”). Since a tragic roar has preceded, it follows that the ridiculous roar of Geta should be understood as referring to comedy.

Grunerus thought that Parrhasius had corrected the reading to *Ridiculove Geta*, but this is false. For Parrhasius, along with the manuscripts and other editions, reads *Ridiculove Getae*, except that he writes *Gete*, since in his edition diphthongs are sometimes omitted.

Nor is it clear whether Gronovius wished *Ridiculove Geta* to be read, as Grunerus and Arntzenius affirm; they retained this reading. I find it unconvincing. Sedulius does not say *pompare ridiculo Geta* (“to parade in ridiculous Geta”), but rather *pompare ridiculo boatu Getae* (“to parade with the ridiculous roar of Geta”), or *renovare contagia tragico boatu* (“to renew the contagions with a tragic roar”), or *ridiculo boatu Getae* (“with the ridiculous roar of Geta”), or by any comparable art of singing. This is how I understand the meaning and syntax.

### Note 20

Vonckius ordered *Scaeva* to be read in place of *Saeva*, and Burmannus also approved this. In some manuscripts *scaevus* is consistently written for *saevus*. See the variant readings on Juvencus, book I, verse 287, where I noted a similar variation.

Arntzenius, if anything were to be changed, would prefer *sacra*, that is, “dreadful.” Asser, in the passage cited, has *renovant* (“they renew”), and in the following verse *canunt* (“they sing”); both are incorrect.

### Note 21

Here too the old books vary in spelling: *monimenta*, and more correctly *monumenta*. Arntzenius has *canunt*; read *canant*. Note the phrase *monumenta scelerum* (“memorials of crimes”), like *monumenta furoris* (“memorials of fury”) and *monumenta clementiae* (“memorials of mercy”).

### Note 22

Urb. has *juliacis*; retain *niliacis*, since the Nile abounded in papyrus. Fulgentius, book I of the *Mythologies*, preface, page 12, writes:

> and whatever one wishes to inscribe on Nile papyrus.

Reg. 1 incorrectly has *tradunt* (“they hand down”) in place of *tradant* (“let them hand down”), as it also has *canant*, *renovent*, and *studeant*. Munckerus, in his note on Fulgentius at the passage cited, offers *miracula chartis* (“miracles on sheets of paper”). But *mendacia* (“falsehoods”) should be retained on the authority of the manuscripts, printed editions, prose, and the author’s meaning.

*Biblis* is likewise defended by the manuscripts and printed editions, except that Vulcanius’ manuscript has *libris* (“books”). But Sedulius intended *biblis* on the authority of Lucan, book III, verse 222:

> Memphis had not yet learned to weave papyrus from the river.

In Greek, *biblos* or *byblos* means papyrus, from which paper was made; by the same word a book was signified, whence *biblia* and *bibliotheca*.

### 155

When the pagan poets strive to parade their inventions  
in loud-sounding measures and with a tragic roar,  
or with the ridiculous roar of Geta, or by any art of singing,

### 156

and renew the savage contagions of unspeakable deeds  
and sing memorials of crimes, and with masterly style  
hand down very many falsehoods on Nile papyrus—

### Note 23

We retain the common spelling *davidicis* (“Davidic”); otherwise all our manuscripts, except the recent Urbinate, write *daviticis*, which is also found in many old editions.

Arntzenius has *Cur ego daviticas assuetis vocibus odas* (“Why should I, accustomed to familiar voices, [sing] Davidic odes”), which, as Arntzenius says, could be defended if *assuetis* were changed to *assuetus*. Indeed, the meaning would also proceed well with *assuetis* if *vererer* (“I should fear”) or *verebor* (“I shall fear”) were read afterward:

> Why should I, accustomed to familiar voices, fear to resound Davidic odes of ten strings and to stand with the holy choir, etc.?

Aldhelmus expressed himself similarly:

> Modulating Davidic odes in holy song.

Nevertheless, the received reading should not be rejected.

### Note 24

Vulc. has *resonare darem* (“I would give back a sound”); correct this to *decem* (“ten”), for the passage concerns a ten-stringed musical instrument, which is mentioned more than once in the Psalms.

See Calmet, dissertation on the musical instruments of the Hebrews, in the second volume of the commentary on the Psalms.

Vat. 1 and 2, Reg. 1 and 2, Ott. 1, Ang., and Asserus have *verenter* (“reverently”), which is relevant to the error in Alb., Ott. 2, and Urb., where *verentur* (“they fear”) appears. Parrhasius, Cappusotus, Aldus, and other printed editions likewise have *verenter*, a reading also retained by Arntzenius.

As for this wording, I shall say nothing about whether the verb means *assuetus* (“accustomed”). Nebrissensis notes here that it means *verebor*, that is, “I shall fear with a certain profound reverence.” Yet in the text of the verses in the Nebrissian edition that I use, *verenter* is printed, and the note itself implies this reading.

Poelman, with some printed editions, has *vererer* (“I should fear”), namely: “Why should I, being accustomed, fear to resound, etc.?”

### Note 25
