In Nebrissensis’ note, *placitis* appears in place of *placidis*, but perhaps this is an error, since the explanation “not turbulent” supports *placidis* (“peaceful”).

### Note 27

Some printed editions have *domumque* (“and the house”), an error perhaps arising from the abbreviation by which manuscripts write *dominumque* (“and the Lord”). Arntzenius offers some similar examples to prove that the verse correctly ends with a participle, contrary to Servius—or whoever it was who mixed many foolish things into Servius’ works.

### Note 28

Our manuscripts have *delectet* (“may delight”); in one, however, it seems doubtful whether the reading is *delecter* (“may I delight”). Other manuscripts, Poelman’s sheets, and several editions support *delectet*. Wopkensius, with Parrhasius, Fabricius, Vulcanius, and Lipsius, prefers *delecter*, as in the letter to Macedonius, *delectatur et ludere* (“he delights in playing”). Poelman has *delectat* (“delights”) in the text and *delecter* in the margin. Col. has *delectat*; Alb. likewise.

### Note 30

Cant. and Poelman’s sheets incorrectly have *servare* (“to preserve”) in place of *servire* (“to serve”). Rom. has *cui jure perennis* (“to whom by perpetual right”). We have already discussed the expression *factura* (“the work made”) for *opere facto* (“the work accomplished”) in the note on Prudentius and Dracontius.

### Note 31

Reg. 1 has *aetheris* (“of heaven”), with a gloss above it, or a correction to *aethereis* (“heavenly”), which is correct.

### Note 34

All our manuscripts, along with most printed editions, have *sceptrum juge*, with the first syllable of *juge* shortened, as often occurs in Sedulius. Fabricius, to avoid this metrical fault, often corrupted the old reading.

### Note 37

Sedulius seems to have borrowed this from Juvencus, book I, verse 27:

> For my song will be the life-giving deeds of Christ.

### Note 38

Ott. 2 has *laetis* (“joyful”); read *laesis* (“wounded”).

### Note 39

Hermann Cannegieter conjectured:

> To whom deadly evil, to whom the teaching of poison creeps in—

### Note 40

In place of *Cecropii*, most of our manuscripts and others, with Parrhasius, have *cecropei*, but Grunerus warned that they should not be followed.

All our manuscripts have *serpit* (“creeps”), as do Cant., Arntzenius, Lipsius, and Almeloveen; in the latter a gloss has *invadit* (“invades”), as do most ancient editions. Barthius’ manuscript has *cepit* (“seized”), which Cellarius and Arntzenius adopted. Some printed editions have *sepit*. The Turin manuscript has:

> Attic doctrine of Cecropian poison creeps in.

Cannegieter suspects *inserpit* (“creeps into”), as I mentioned recently. Johann Conrad Schwartius read *carpsit* (“gnawed”), from which Wopkensius preferred:

> Attic doctrine gnaws with Cecropian poisons.

But since the verb *serpit* occurs not only in nearly all the manuscripts but also in the prose, it must certainly be retained. Although this verb *serpo* is frequently constructed with a preposition, as in “to creep across the earth,” “into a tree,” or, in a special construction, “to creep along the ground,” nothing prevents it from being used with an accusative without a preposition, either because the preposition *per* (“through”) is understood—as poets sometimes omit it—or because the accusative functions as the person affected.

For *serpo* is used passively by Solinus, chapter 32, or 35:

> When the earth is crawled over by no serpent.

Why, then, could one not say:

> When no serpent crawls over the earth?

### 157

Why should I, accustomed to Davidic songs,  
fear to make the odes of ten strings resound,  
to stand reverently with the holy choir,  
and to sing heavenly things in peaceful words,  
while I remain silent about the shining miracles  
of Christ the Savior?

Since I can speak openly and delight to confess with all my senses and with my whole heart  
the thundering Lord, who gave both senses and hearts,  
to whom alone it is fitting that his work should serve,

### 158

to whom by perpetual right there is, in the heavenly citadels,  
one power with the Father, equal splendor,  
a common summit, a shared height,  
equal honor, the same power, a kingdom without time,  
the everlasting Beginning, an unchanging scepter,  
shared glory, similar majesty—  
for this is the way of salvation,  
this leads firm steps to the Paschal gifts.

This will be my song: turn your minds here, everyone.  
Apply this aid steadfastly to wounded hearts—  
you whom deadly evil, whom the doctrine  
of Attic Cecropian poison, devoted to empty cares, creeps through.

### Note 42

Most and the better manuscripts and editions have *paedorem* (“stench”); others have *fetorem* (“stench”), which has more the character of a gloss. Cellarius takes *Athenaei* to mean “Attic”; “Athenian” is clearer, as many others used *Athenaeus* for “Athenian.” The Athenian *pagus* is the superstition of the pagan Athenians. Christians called pagans *ethnici*, from the rural districts (*pagi*) in which idolatry persisted longer. Christian poets therefore used *pagus* for vain superstition, as Prudentius and others do. Iscanus appears to imitate Sedulius in book I of *The Trojan War*, verse 30:

> Indeed, may the feigned licence of the Cecropian *pagus* [not …]

and in book III, verse 454:

> Cease, fatal licence of the Cecropian *pagus*,  
> to beget incestuous gods.

### Note 43

In place of *Quid* (“what”), Arntzenius has *Qui* (“who”); *Quid* is better. Most of our manuscripts write *laberintheo*; Poelman, *labirynthaeo*; Arntzenius, *laborintheo*, with the foolish gloss, also found in other manuscripts, as though it meant “labour within.” Others have *labyrinthaeo*. The correct spelling is *labyrintheo*. Most of our manuscripts have *Theside*; Aldus, *Tesidae*; manuscript E, *Thessidae*. Retain *Thesidae*: this is how Virgil calls the Athenians.

### Note 44

Of our manuscripts, some have *Daedalii*, others, with the editions, *Daedalei*. In place of *tecti*, Col. has *tectis*, perhaps *Daedaleis lustratis limina tectis* (“thresholds surveyed in Daedalian buildings”). But Arntzenius observes that the expression *limina tecti* for “thresholds of a house” is familiar to poets. Virgil and Ovid likewise called the labyrinth a *tectum* (“building”).

### Note 45

For *placidis*, Burmannus preferred *placitis* in the margin. For *quid*, Arntzenius has *qui*, as at verse 43.

### Note 46

Parrhasius incorrectly has *saluincam* for *saliuncam*. Compare Virgil, *Eclogues* 5.16:

> As much as the pliant willow yields to the pale olive,  
> as much as the lowly *saliunca* yields to scarlet roses.

### Note 47

Reg. 1 now has *fana* (“shrines”), but it seems formerly to have had *vana* (“empty things”), which was also Wopkensius’s conjecture. Yet he recognized the clearer sense in *fana*, the term by which the Fathers commonly call temples of idols. “To worship temples [and] shrines” is a legitimate and customary expression. Compare the variant readings, or scholium, on verse 242 of this work, *Heu miseri*. Aldus and Nebrissensis have *profani*, namely, “O profane men.” In my manuscript, which begins at verse 45, *Labruscam placidis*, *profani* seems more likely to be written than *profanis*. Nebrissensis recognized the other, common reading, *quid fana profanis … proderit?* (“what benefit will shrines bring to profane men?”). That is, what benefit is it for stones, bronze, and shrines to be worshipped by profane people? I have often noted in the annotations that Juvencus was accustomed to this sort of dative in place of an ablative with passive verbs.

### Note 48

Rom. has *multis*, corrected to *mutis*. Burmannus wished *nudis* to be read, so that bare metals—that is, metals which are nothing but metals—might be understood. He also conjectured *donare*. Retain *mutis damnare*: mute images are meant. Similarly Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 210:

> He poured forth and sought riches for himself from the blind rock.

And in *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, verse 68 and following:

> You command that gods be worshipped—  
> hewn by the craftsman’s hand,  
> reheated in hollow furnaces and bellows—  
> things that lack voice and movement,  
> motionless, blind, tongueless.

In *damnare*, Cellarius and Arntzenius think there is an allusion to those condemned to the mines, to whom idol-worshippers are like. Nebrissensis more aptly thinks the phrase taken from Virgil, *Eclogues* 5.80, *Damnabis tu quoque votis* (“you too will bind [them] by vows”). *Damno* often means “to bind” or “to make liable.” Gods were therefore said to bind people, and make them bound by a vow, when they granted what was sought in a vow and made people liable to render what they had promised. Sedulius therefore says that those gods did not bind people to themselves, since they were stones and bronze, but that people themselves bound themselves to mute metals.

### Note 50

Rom. has *casas* (“cottages”); in the margin is a correction, or an alternative reading, *plagas* (“regions”).

### Note 52

Aldus incorrectly has *velatis* for *vellatis*. Arntzenius has *mortiferi … succi* (“deadly juices”). Some printed editions have *mortiferis … fucis* (“deadly dyes”). But poison is everywhere attributed to *succus* (“juice”), and this scribal confusion of *succus* and *fucus* is common, perhaps arising because many write *sucus*, not *succus*. *Toxica livida* (“livid poisons”) is said because that epithet is commonly attributed to poison.

### Note 53

Reg. 1, Arntzenius, manuscript E, with other manuscripts and editions, have *Tartareo damnata cibo* (“condemned to Tartarean food”). Ott. 1 and 2, Vat. 1 and 2, Reg. 5, my manuscript in the text, Ang., together with Parrhasius, Aldus, and Sedulius’s prose, have *Tartareis damnata cibis* (“condemned to Tartarean foods”), which seems more poetic to Arntzenius. Most manuscripts write *virecta* for *vireta*. A similar variation occurs in other writers as well; I prefer *viretum* to *virectum*. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.679:

> They came to the joyous places and pleasant green groves  
> of the blessed woods, the abodes of the fortunate.

See the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 679.

57. My manuscript has *adeptis*: read *ademptis*.

58. Vat. I has *Et messis*: read *Ut*. Thus, approximately, St. Ignatius the Martyr: “I am Christ’s grain; I am ground by the teeth of beasts, so that I may be found pure bread.”

60. For the title, Ott. 1 has: “Here begins the supplication of Sedulius the rhetorician.” *Oration.* Reg. 1: “Invocation.” Rom.: “Invocation of the poet.” Ang.: “Invocation of Sedulius.” Similar inscriptions occur in other manuscripts and printed editions; they were not composed by the author but arbitrarily devised by copyists, and it would be superfluous to list them all. Parrhasius has no such chapter titles. The poem of Dracontius begins almost in the same way, Book II: “Almighty eternal God.”

61. *Ades* instead of *es*: a compound verb used in place of the simple one, as elsewhere.

62. This sentence has been explained with similar examples in the note on Dracontius, Book II, verse 343. Some have *undisonam … procellam*.

64. Barthius, in *Adversaria* XXV, chapter 15, cites *ad lunam* instead of *et lunam*, apparently through a typographical error. Perhaps, however, he intended *at lunam*, which is elegant but contrary to the manuscripts.

65. For *metiris*, Cant. has *concedis*. Wopkensius explains *Inque diem ac noctem* as “by day and by night”; the prose interpretation is clearer.

66. Taken from Sacred Scripture. Barthius says that these verses are sketched from Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 170.

68. Gallandius, from the Turin manuscript, supplies as a variant reading: “You who formed the diverse earth into new bodies.” It is also recorded in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Turin, from which, I think, Gallandius drew his variants.

72. Some printed editions have *ab unque*; the manuscripts and better editions, with Parrhasius, have *ab angue*. The prose version supports this.

73. For *praeter quos*, see what I said about this phrase in the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 430.

74. My manuscript has *gravida*; a marginal correction or variant reading gives *rapida*. Ott. 2, together with certain printed editions, has *rabida* instead of *rapida*. Copyists often write *rapidus* for *rabidus*, and conversely, so that it is frequently uncertain which reading is preferable. Here *rapida* is the more common and preferable reading, since the flood’s speed is being indicated.

76. In the Poelman papers it was noted that some read *Quos carnis*, others *Hos carnis*. Rom. originally had *Quod*, corrected to *Quos*; the others have *Quod*. Most manuscripts and editions have *praesule ligno*. Poelman’s margin has *praeside*, which some printed editions report. Nebrissensis conjectured *praestite* or *praeside* instead of *praesule*. Arntzenius disliked *praeside*, though I do not know why he considered it erroneous. The meaning is the same, and one may equally say *praestite*, *praeside*, or *praesule ligno*—that is, “through the aid, protection, or power of the wood of the cross.” Cellarius is absurd in interpreting it as “the ark leaping over the waters.” Such heterodox people so recoil from the Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration of the Holy Cross. Wopkensius, while defending the correct interpretation against Cellarius, was likewise carried away by this preconceived opinion and conjectured that the reading should be *praesule signo*, that is, “by a preceding symbol” or “through this portent.” He nevertheless rejected this conjecture after observing that other Fathers also compared the wood of the flood-ark with the cross, for example Augustine, *City of God* XV.26, and Alcimus Avitus, Book IV, verse 300.

77. My manuscript has *revocari*, not implausibly, instead of *renovari*. In Rom. the error is *renovare*.

78. The Turin manuscript erroneously has *Toto* instead of *Totum*.

heap the greatest yield of a hundredfold into the barns.

[60] Almighty, eternal God, the world’s only hope,  
you who are the maker of heaven and the creator of the universe,  
who prevent the shorelines of the neighboring earth  
from being submerged by the sea’s resounding storms as its waves rise,  
who fill the sun with rays and the moon with horns,

[65] 162 and measure out to day and night their respective light,  
who number the stars—whose names,  
signs, powers, courses, places, and seasons you alone know,  
who formed the various earth into different new bodies,  
[Col. 0560A]  
and gave living limbs to the torpid soil,

[70] who restore fallen humanity, ruined by the sweetness of the forbidden fruit,  
with better food and the draught of consecrated blood, and drive away  
the venom infused by the serpent,  
who once again create the human race—apart from those whom the ark had enclosed—  
after it had been buried beneath the rushing mass of the foaming flood,

[75] from a single stock, so that the mystical power  
might show that what the sins of the flesh destroy  
can be renewed through the flowing waters by this presiding wood;

163 for you wash the whole world clean in a single baptism.

[Col. 0561A] [Note: [Col. 0561C]

80. Some printed editions have *Augusto*: correct it to *Angusto*, in accordance with the Savior’s own words.

82. Ald. has *quo servat*; others *qua*.

83. Ottob. 1 has *quo vellere*; so also Reg. 1 in its first hand, but corrected to *qua*.

84. Burmannus conjectured *agnus ovat*. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 in their first hands have *oves*, corrected to *ovis*, with a gloss in Reg. 1: “of Mary.” The same gloss occurs in Reg. 2, and *ovis* is written in the other manuscripts and editions, as also in the prose version. But perhaps the true reading is *oves, grexque*, with this punctuation: “The Virgin’s Lamb, the sheep, and every shining flock enter.” For at God’s judgment the sheep will be placed on the right, the kids on the left. In manuscript copies, *i* frequently occurs in place of *e*. Fortunatus is relevant here, Book II, poem 4: “On the cross the Virgin’s Lamb restored the sheep.” Indeed, even if *ovis* is read, the same punctuation and meaning can be maintained. In Rom. *que* is absent after *grex*.

87. My manuscript has *nominante*: read *dominante*.

88. *Arere* means “to ripen,” as in *arentes aristae*. *Pruinis* is used for “winter,” as commonly by other poets.

89. Urb. and Rom. have *producit*; others *producet*, with a gloss in Reg.: *dabit*. So later *calcabit* and *parebunt*.

91. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.29: “Autumn stood there, filthy with trampled grapes.”

93. Ott. 2 has *Judicio est*; these readings are easily exchanged. Here *Indicio* must unquestionably be retained. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.296, has *cana fides*; thus *cana jura* and similar expressions mean “ancient” or “old.”

95. The Poelman papers have *exstant* instead of *constant*.

96. Burmannus preferred *volatu* or *meatu* to *relatu*, because “to touch upon” is properly attributed to birds. This is certainly an inept basis for conjecture. Sedulius may perhaps be imitating Claudian, *Rape of Proserpine*, at the beginning: “To disclose Juno’s bridal chambers in daring song,” and so forth. Even pagans considered it audacious to attempt to explain divine matters.

97. The same Burmannus suspects *Vix alis committo meis*, led by the same reasoning. Reg. 1 and Urb. have *potentem* instead of *patentem*. Rom. has *sonantem* instead of *pro d. s.*

98. Instead of *aliquos*, Parrhasius has *paucos*; the reading in manuscript E appears to be either this or *parcos*. Burmannus conjectures *patulos*, an epithet often applied to branches. My manuscript has *nitor paucos*. Corippus, *Panegyric on Anastasius*, at the beginning, expressed the same idea: “As I strive to touch the lofty branches, gazing upon the immense forest of your praises, just man,” and so forth. Barthius observed that this was sketched from Theocritus, *Idylls* I, verse 22. The author of the old *Life of St. Theobald*, which I saw at the end of a very ancient manuscript, Vat. Regina Sueciae 571, clearly imitates Sedulius: “I call as witness its inhabitant, the Holy Spirit, that I have passed over many things I knew and, from the great forest, scarcely touched upon a few branches.”

Open for me the path leading to the saving city,  
which runs for me along a narrow road,

[80] and grant that the lamp of your word may shine upon my feet,  
so that the path of life may lead me from the countryside to the folds,  
where the good shepherd guards his beautiful sheepfold,  
where the Virgin’s Lamb, first in white fleece,  
and every shining flock enter.

[85] 164 With you as guide, the road is not difficult; all nature  
is subject to your commands, and, with its customary order released,  
at your commanding will it passes into contrary forms.

If you should command the crops to wither amid winter frosts,  
[Col. 0562A]  
winter will produce a reaper; if you should wish must  
to run beneath the springtime sun over flowering fields,

[90] the vintner, filthy, will tread on pressed grapes,  
and all seasons will obey divine commands.

Ancient faith is the proof, and the hoary origin  
of our forefathers is a witness that cannot be destroyed by any age;  
[95] the signs of your powers remain constant through all times.  
From these I scarcely dare, in bold narration,  
165 to touch upon a few things with my mind, as I enter  
the open forest and strive to reach a few branches.

[Col. 0563A] [Note: [Col. 0563B]

99. Vat. I has *sonet*, apparently a gloss above *clamet*. The law of the meter requires *clamet*. Virgil and other poets say that an iron voice and a hundred mouths are insufficient to explain certain matters. Compare the note on Dracontius, Book III, verse 552, and the learned Martin de Roa, *Singularia* II.3. Add the author of the *Life of St. Dunstan*, chapter 5.

103. The title in Reg. 1 is “Exposition on Enoch.” Ott. 1: “On Enoch.” Rom. likewise. In Ott. 2: “The poet’s invocation or prayer ends. Book One begins. On Enoch’s passage.” The Cant. manuscript: “Here begins the book of the Old Testament.” The Leipzig edition: “Book I, containing several histories of the Old Law.” For *ab usque chao*, Leipzig and other manuscripts cited by Davisius in his note on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.33, have *ad usque chaos*. Davisius nevertheless retains the reading common to our manuscripts and editions. Rom. has *ab usque chaos*. Yet *chao* is correct, as in Prudentius, *Hymns* 12, verse 40: “older than heaven and chaos.” A gloss in some manuscripts of Sedulius says *absque morte* (“without death”), but the poet’s meaning is rather “from the beginning of the world,” or “from chaos,” which preceded the world. See Prudentius, *Hymns* 12.40. In the prose version the beginning of the chapter has been misplaced.

105. Lucretius, Book VII, verse 532: “From that point the slaughter lost all measure.”

106. Some manuscripts and editions punctuate: “The earth brought forth what was begotten: but …” Several others: “The earth brought forth: what was begotten, but …”

107. The inscription in Reg. 1 is “On Sarah.” Rom.: “On Sarah.” Ott. 1: “On Abraham and Sarah.” Many write *Sarra* and *Sarrae* with double *r*; others do not. Arntzenius suspected *arida* instead of *saucia*, and thought Sedulius had Ovid, *Tristia* III, elegy 14, verses 33 ff., before his eyes: “Misfortunes broke my talent; and before that / its spring was barren and its stream small. / But whatever it had been, with no one exercising it, it withdrew, / and after long neglect it perished, having become dry.” Nothing, however, should be changed, for Sedulius more truly imitates Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 514: “wounded by the long-standing condition of the entrails.” On the verb *marcebant*, compare the note on Dracontius, *Satisfactio*, verse 228.

108. Arntz. has *sinu*: retain *situ*, in accordance with the passage from Apuleius just cited.

109. Lucan, Book II, verse 339: “While blood remained, while maternal strength, I fulfilled / your commands, Cato.”

110. Urb. corruptly has *Cum se more viri*. My manuscript, with Aldus, punctuates: *sanguis—Cum seniore viro*. Better: *sanguis—Cum, seniore viro, gelidi*. Here *vir* means “husband,” as frequently elsewhere.

112. The Turin manuscript has *Algentis*, through a different spelling, instead of *Algentes*.

113. From Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.764: “Whom your wife Lavinia, in your old age, / will bring forth for you in the woods.”

114. Poelman adds a new title here: “The ram is sacrificed instead of Isaac.” Some manuscripts are nearly the same. In Urb. the corrupt reading is *ac sacrat ipsum*. This manuscript frequently has corrupt readings; it is enough to have noted this once. Vonckius instructs us to read *istam* instead of *ipsam*. Grunerus argues that *istam* cannot occur here, whereas *ipsam* can. Wopkensius likewise prefers *ipsam*, namely “the very one” at whose altar Isaac would otherwise have been sacrificed. Thus Prudentius, *Hymns* 12, verse 131: “Before that altar,” and *Peristephanon* IV, verse 39: “He will extend it to the altar.” Arntzenius observes that *ipsa* and *ista* are frequently confused by copyists; his conjecture is *ipse*, that is, “of his own accord,” instead of *ipsam*, if Vonckius’ suspicion regarding the following verse is accepted. He nevertheless admits that *ipsam* has emphatic force, as in many other passages. Some printed editions have *ac* instead of *at*.

115. Vonckius thinks that *mactatur* should be read as *mox statur*, that is, “he is immediately halted”; Arntzenius says that this conjecture is to some extent supported by Chrysologus, sermon 2: “The son was being sacrificed unknowingly; the son was being halted unawares.” Petrus Faber made the same correction in sermon 3.8. I find the received reading in Isidore, *Etymologies* XII.1.9, concerning the ram: “This animal was first sacrificed upon altars by the Gentiles. It is called *aries* because it was placed upon altars. Hence the saying: ‘The ram is sacrificed at the altar.’”

116. Dracontius writes nearly the same about the same Abraham, Book III, verse 102: “And pious though unyielding,” and so forth.

119. All the manuscripts I have seen, together with Parrhasius, Aldus, Poelman’s papers, and the manuscripts seen by Cellarius and Arntzenius, have *sanguine Christi*. Poelman, together with other printed editions, has *sanguine fuso*, which Cellarius accepted, asserting that *Christi* in the manuscripts was a gloss. Arntzenius holds the same view and adds that the gloss may have arisen because someone wrote *Christus* above the word *agnus* in the following verse. Certainly, if *Christi* is retained, it is difficult to extract a satisfactory sense; therefore, until something clearer appears, I follow the printed reading. In my manuscript the gloss above *agnus* is *caro Christi* (“the flesh of Christ”). Thus the word *Christi* could easily have been substituted for the final word of this verse.]

For even if an iron voice, moving a hundred mouths, should cry out,  
[100] and the human breast should breathe forth a hundred sounds,  
who could explain all the things whose number is matched  
neither by the bright stars of heaven nor by the sand that drinks up water?

From the beginning of chaos, Enoch, the first through his living merits,  
has already reached many centuries of innumerable years,  
[105] 166 while nature, exceeding the limit that the right of creation had set,  
marvels that the earth brought forth one who was born, yet taken away by death.

The wounded entrails of aged Sarah were already withering,  
consumed by long-standing decay, and denied offspring;  
[Col. 0564A]  
her cold blood, dying in an aged body,

[110] had grown old. Yet, with an older husband, the cold depths  
of her womb swelled for a new birth, and the trembling mother,  
her icy bosom burdened, brought forth  
the late-born child and held him to her breasts, the hope of a mighty nation.

The father offered him to God for sacrifice, but a sacred ram  
[115] 167 was sacrificed at the altar instead of the boy.

O holy mind of the righteous man! Having set piety aside,  
yet possessing even greater piety, he disregarded the wounds of his son;  
embracing God’s commands, he teaches by the aid of the symbolic blood  
the future things: that through blood shed

[Col. 0565A] [Note: [Col. 0565B]

120. Reg. 1 and 2, Vatt. 1 and 2, Urb., Alb., Ott. 1, Cant., Alm., Arntz., and Leipzig, together with Aldus, have *occumberet*. Parrhasius has *procumberet*. This seems to have been the reading in Ang., but it was corrected by the same hand to *occumberet*. Ott. 2 has *succumberet*, which many editors accepted, including Cellarius and Arntzenius, though Arntzenius admits that *occumberet* appears more suitable. In this reading the final syllable of *pius* is lengthened by the caesura. Cellarius and Arntzenius call this a hiatus, though I do not know on what grounds: a hiatus occurs when several vowels come together and none is elided, so that they must be pronounced with the lips parted and the mouth open. Poets of this period commonly lengthen a short vowel by the caesura, as we have observed in Prudentius, Dracontius, and Juvencus.

121. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 give the title “On Lot.” Reg. 1 and Ott. 2 have *Sodomis*; Ott. 1 likewise, but it was changed from there to *Sodomi*. Grunerus does not object to *Sodomis* in the Cant. manuscript. Thus Prudentius, *Hymns against Symmachus*, verse 725: “Lot fleeing from burning Sodom.” The editions, with most manuscripts, have *Sodomae*; so also Reg. 4, which begins again here. Bede quotes these verses in *On the Art of Meter*, where *Loth Sedomis* is printed corruptly.

123. Vat. 1 has *suam est*. Many manuscripts, with most editions, clearly have *quia*; others ambiguously have *quia* or *quod*. Parrhasius printed *quod*.

125. Our manuscripts—Reg. 1, 2, 4, and 5, Urb., Ang., Vatt. 1 and 2, Ott. 1 and 2, my manuscript, Alb., and others—together with Parrhasius and Aldus, have *Aspiciens*. Most editions, including the older ones, have *Respiciens*. Arntzenius considers this pleonastic “looking back again” to be by Sedulius’ own hand and collects many similar examples, which we have also noted in Dracontius and Juvencus. Nevertheless, he retained *Aspiciens* when he saw that all the manuscripts agreed on it. It is more likely that *Respiciens* came from the hand of some copyist or editor who had the words of the Vulgate in mind, whereas Sedulius usually follows another ancient version.

126. In Bede, *On the Art of Meter*, *multum* is an error for *vultum*.

127. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 title this “On the bush.” Rom. has “On the blazing bush,” rather than “the burning bush.” My manuscript: “The Lord in the form of fire over the bush.” See Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 55.

128. Arntzenius rightly condemns Barthius, who, in *Rape of Proserpine* I.166, reads *Non audens ardere*. My manuscript has *ardore*; *ardere* is better. In Ott. 2 the reading appears to be *vincta*. Leipzig has *victa*; the others *juncta*. These readings are easily confused in manuscripts because of the similar formation of the letters.

129. My manuscript has *videns* incorrectly instead of *vivens*; Leipzig’s *virens* is no better. Arntzenius thought the latter could be defended because Palladius, Book XIV, *On Grafting*, verse 39, says: “For whatever tree is green with foreign leaves.” But he did not observe that the first syllable of *virens* is short, as is clear from Palladius’ own verse; in Sedulius’ verse it would have to be long, as it is in *vivens*. Latin authors say *cespes vivus*, “living turf,” *radix viva*, “living root,” and *vivens frutex*, “living shrub,” when these are still growing and living their vegetative life, as philosophers call it. Conversely, they are said to be dying, as I noted in Juvencus, Book II, verse 749.

130. Leipzig has *amicti*: retain *amici*. Perhaps Sedulius is imitating Virgil, *Aeneid* I.180: “and snatched a flame from the firebrand.” Nebrissensis’ note is not sufficiently clear: “The firebrand is an enemy to fire, but here it was a friend.” Perhaps he means that a firebrand is normally consumed by fire, but that here it was not consumed.

[Col. 0566D] 131. Weitzius, in his notes on Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 56, or 124, cites *blanditiae* instead of *blanditae*, perhaps through a typographical error. On the verb *lambo* (“to lick”), when it is applied to flame, see the note on Dracontius I.660.

132. Reg. 1: “On the rod changed into a dragon.” Ott. 1 similarly, but *conversa*. Rom.: “On the rod that the Lord gave Moses.” My manuscript: “Moses’ wondrous rod.” Reg. 4 has *draconum* incorrectly instead of *draconem*. Bede, *On the Art of Meter*, praises the elegance of this verse because the adjectives are placed before the substantive nouns.

133. The Basel edition with Nebrissensis’ commentary has *Per flexus*, but Nebrissensis explains it there and reads *Per flexos*. In Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, the first hand also seems to have written *Per flexus*. The imitation of Virgil is evident in *linguisque trisulcis*, from *Aeneid* II.475.]

while the pious Lamb would die for the human race.

168. When Lot fled from Sodom’s chaos, and his wife looked back,  
she remained astonished, changed into a pillar of salt,  
turned into her own punishment: for no one who looks back  
and avoids the guilty dangers of the despised world

[125] will be saved, nor should a plowman, while performing worthy work,  
turn his face behind him.

[Col. 0566A] Once, blazing amid harmless fires,  
the bush appeared to burn without burning; nor did material joined  
to the heat supply fuel, nor did the living shrub, scorched,

[130] 169 feel the damage, but the leafy flames  
licked the branches in the warmth of their friendly firebrand.

A gentle rod was animated into a fierce dragon,  
curving itself through winding coils, and with three-forked tongues

[Col. 0567A] [Note: [Col. 0567C]

134. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.381: “and swelling with a blue neck.” The adjective *squameus* (“scaly”) is commonly applied to a serpent.

135. In my manuscript there is clearly the error *reddit* instead of *redit*; likewise *vigoris*. Perhaps someone intended *viroris*, but *rigoris* is sound.

136. Reg. 1: “On the Red Sea and the Israelite people.” Ott. 1: “On the Red Sea and the crowd.” Rom.: “Where the Israelite people went through the sea on dry feet.” My manuscript: “The Red Sea yields to God’s people.” In Althelmus and others one finds *caerula ponti* (“the sea’s blue waters”); similar expressions are *aversa castrorum* (“the reversed sides of camps”), *recta montium* (“the straight sides of mountains”), *flexa collium* (“the curves of hills”), *porrecta camporum* (“the stretches of fields”), *acerba fluctuum* (“the sharpness of waves”), and *convexa vallium* (“the hollows of valleys”).

138. Cant., Parrhasius, Reg. 2, and Reg. 5 have *at turba*; others *ac turba*; Reg. 1 *et turba*.

139. Observe the tautology, familiar also to other poets: *pelagus*, *mare*, *profundum*, *marmora*—“sea,” “sea,” “deep,” “waters.”

140. It is elegant that astonishment is attributed to the sea. For *marmora* meaning “sea,” see Dracontius I.578.

141. Burmannus conjectures *natura vices*. All have *viam*, but in Ott. 1 something else seems originally to have stood instead of *viam*.

142. Cellarius, Aldus, and the Heinsius and Almeloveen manuscripts have *incedens*. All our manuscripts and others have *ingrediens*, which comes closer to the Vulgate version of Exodus and to Sedulius’ prose. Rom. has *rude baptisma*; read *rude jam baptisma*.

143. The reading should be noted: *lectio* means Sacred Scripture or doctrine, as in Paulinus, *Life of St. Martin* IV.181, Julius Firmicus, and others. Hence *lectiones* in the church offices, and *lectionarius* and *lectionarium*. Orientius calls his sacred poems *lectio* in these beautiful iambics at the end: “If spiritual reading offends anyone, / let him despise reading; / let him not alter the form of the reading; / I denounce the serpent, the teacher of falsehood, / so that he may neither add nor subtract a letter.” He appears to rebuke corruptors of manuscripts.

144. The Poelman papers and Parrhasius have *denuo* instead of *denique*. Reg. 1 and 4, Ott. 1, Ang., Rom., my manuscript, Vat. 1 and 2, Parrhasius, Aldus, and most editions have *verbum est*. Cellarius has this with the manuscripts. Arntz., Almel., Cant., and some of our manuscripts have *verbum* without *est*, though it is understood.

145. Reg. 5 and Aldus have *at est* instead of *adest*. Some printed editions have *quod* instead of *qui*.

146. Reg. 2 and 5, Alb., Vat. 2, Ott. 2, Aldus, and Parrhasius have *gerens*. Other manuscripts, with many editions, have *regens*; my manuscript has *ferens*. Nebrissensis reads and explains *gerens*. Cellarius and Arntzenius printed *regens*, the reading of the best manuscripts.

147. Reg. 3 has *incederat*; correct it to *incederet*.

148. Reg. 1: “On manna.” Ott. 1: “Where they received heavenly bread.” Rom.: “On the manna given from heaven.” My manuscript: “God’s people are fed with manna in the desert.”

150. Most of our manuscripts have *aeria*, some *aerea*. Poelman’s margin has *aetherea*; other editions and the Poelman papers have *aetheria*.

151. Torn. 1 and Edinburgh have *In plumis* instead of *In pluviis*, so that quails may be understood. Burmannus noted that these words are likewise confused in Tibullus, Book I, elegy 2, verse 79. The common reading, however, is far better. My manuscript has, not implausibly, *dapes, in nubibus escas* (“food, provisions in the clouds”).

152. Reg. 1: “On the water produced from the rock.” Ott. 1: “Where he brought water from the rock.” Rom.: “On Moses, when water flowed from the rock.” For *in exustis*, my manuscript incorrectly has *inexhaustis*.

153. Arntzenius, in the *Miscellanies* which he published in 1765, after preparing Sedulius’ edition with the notes of various scholars, chapter 17, corrects by conjecture *quia terra* to *qua terra*. I find this entirely unconvincing.]

swelling with scaly necks, swallowed the hostile serpents,  
[135] and its own stiffness returned to the branches.

The blue waters of the divided sea opened a passage,  
rolled back into two sides, and the exposed land,  
stripped of its kindred waters, was entered by the crowd on foot.

170 The people entered the sea of the withdrawn deep, across the deep,  
[140] and the dry waters marveled at foreign feet.

Nature changed its course, and the people, entering  
through the middle of the sea, already bore a rough baptism;  
Christ was their leader. For Scripture cries out:  
“The voice of the Lord is over the waters”; the voice is the Word,

[Col. 0568A]  
[145] the Word is Christ, who, governing the two harmonious  
Testaments of the law, opened the ancient abyss,  
171 so that the following doctrine might proceed over level fields.

Why should I recount the countless multitudes who received  
heavenly bread and angelic food,

[150] and, fed with the sweetness of the heavenly nectar,  
had provisions in the rains and food in the showers?

Again, when the army was thirsty in scorched fields,  
where the places had long been excessively dry, where the earth, denied

[Col. 0569A] [Note: [Col. 0569C]

155. *Metallum*, that is, “rock.” *Metallum* is used of marble by Silius and Statius, and of gems by Pliny the Younger. Nebrissensis explains it as “stone,” or rather “a vein of stone.” See Cerda, *Adversaria* 101.

156. The most ancient Turin manuscript has: “It drew up the waters, and liquid flowed from the barren rock.” In ancient manuscripts aspiration is often omitted and often added; thus *Ausit* stands for *Hausit*. Although *manavit* is contrary to the meter, it is retained in many manuscript copies. My manuscript, Ang., Alb., Reg. 1, 2, 4, and 5, Ott. 1, Vatt. 1 and 2, Cant., and manuscript E have *manavit*, which is the basis for Arntzenius’ *manabat*. In Ott. 1 *cucurrit* appears above it as a gloss; in Reg. 2 the glosses are *eduxit, cucurrit, fluxit*; in Vat. 1, in a second hand, *cucurrit*. Urb., Ott. 2, and recent manuscripts of Rom. have *cucurrit*. Aldus printed *manavit*; Parrhasius has *salivit*, which, as is observed in the Poelman papers, scarcely conforms to grammatical rules, since although *salii* and *salui* occur in the perfect, *salivi* is rare. Most editions have *cucurrit*, and Grunerus asserts that *manavit* is a gloss. Arntzenius agrees, demonstrating with similar examples that *currere* can properly be said of water, and adducing from Antonius, *Against the Gentiles*, verse 15—or rather from Paulinus, final poem—a similar passage: “Manna ran to them from heaven, and a spring from the rock.” I would not find it difficult to believe that *manavit* is the true reading, since Eugenius of Toledo and other Christian poets shortened the first syllable of this verb.

157. Rom. has *vomuere*; read *vomuerunt*.

158. Vonckius conjectures *His jugiter* instead of *His igitur*. Although it is true that Sedulius sometimes shortens the first syllable of *jugis* licentiously, there is no reason for alteration here. Parrhasius and the Poelman papers have *His igitur sacrata tribus*, which I consider less correct.

159. This verse occurs in Bede, *On the Art of Meter*.

160. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1: “On the she-ass that spoke.” Rom.: “To Balaam, on the speaking of the she-ass.” My manuscript: “The little she-ass speaks to Balaam.”

161. My manuscript has *rudendi*; retain *rudenti*.

162. *Edere* is used of uttering words, as of uttering a voice, sounds, or a cry. The word *pecualis* is also used by Venantius Fortunatus, *Life of St. Martin* II.146.

163. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1: “On Joshua.” Rom.: “On Joshua, concerning the halting of the sun.”

165. Wopkensius suspects *Invalidus* or *Insolidus*, the latter word being used by Ovid. He interprets it as “unaccustomed to restrain,” although it had already learned—read *dedidicisset*—to restrain or govern the day. Arntzenius more suitably explains the received reading: in accordance with its own order, the sun is not accustomed to extend the day for a longer period. My manuscript has *retinere* instead of *frenare*, perhaps from some gloss. Arntzenius thinks that *frenare*, as well as *anhelantem*, alludes to the ancient belief that horses belonged to the sun. But Sedulius is usually very far removed not only from myths but also from mythological names; *frenare* can be understood metaphorically as “to restrain.” The meaning is: “The sun, unaccustomed to restrain the day.”

166. My manuscript has *plena*: read *pigra*. Vat. 1 has *arvis*, corrected by a second hand to *armis*, correctly.

167. Aldus has *Fervidus in gentem*, unless this is a typographical error for *ingentem*. *Fervidus gladius* (“the blazing sword”) is elegant. Lucan, Book VII.502: “Then the sword stands cold; then the guilty iron grows hot with blood.”

168. Some have *jam tum*; most *jam tunc*. Sedulius imitates Claudian, *Third Consulship of Honorius*, verse 98: “For whom the sky wages war, / and the conspiring winds come to the trumpet-calls”; and *The Gothic War*, verse 49: “Or should we complain that the clear sky has conspired?”

169. In Reg. 1 the reading may originally have been *promisso*; it is now *praemisso*. Rom. clearly has *promisso*; my manuscript is uncertain. Compare Prudentius, *Hymns* XII, verse 173.

170. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1: “On Elijah.” My manuscript: “Elijah is fed while the raven ministers.” Rom.: “On Elijah, fed by ravens.”

171. Parrhasius and the Poelman papers have *Reddentes* instead of *Praebentes*. Arntz. manuscript has *rapinae* instead of *rapinis*, not inelegantly, since poets sometimes use the singular for the plural.

173. “With hungry bites,” says Nebrissensis, “or the ravens”—that is, either because the ravens were hungry or because Elijah was hungry.

174. My manuscript has *Tunc bonus*. Cellarius conjectured *ante ea*. Thus *postea* has sometimes been found by copyists instead of *post ea*. Here, however, *antea* is not bad. Reg. 1 has *ante*, perhaps before *Noemo*. Some have *Noae*, others *Noe* without the diphthong. The raven was faithless because it went out and did not return. Nebrissensis’ appeal to the Hebrew reading, “It went out and returned,” is pointless.]

lying without water, when the hope of drinking  
[155] and living had been taken away, drew sudden water  
from the parched rock, and liquid flowed from the barren stone,  
172 while the dry waters vomited forth a new drink.

Thus the sacred Trinity, bestowing gifts through these three things:  
Christ was bread, Christ was rock, Christ was in the waters.

[160] Shaken by angelic threats, the little she-ass addressed  
her rider in words, and, with braying tongue,  
the animal uttered human speech.

The sun stood still at Gibeon and fixed its panting light  
at the summit of mid-heaven, prolonging the evening,

[165] unaccustomed to restrain the day; nor did the moon proceed  
slowly along its own course, until, with weapons ravaging,  
a blazing sword destroyed the enormous enemy,  
while the heavens conspired. Even then the stars saw  
that they were serving the one who was to come,

Jesus, whose name had been sent before him.

[170] Once, ravens as ministers fed Elijah,  
providing food beyond the customary manner; and the bird,  
devoted to plunder, filling its hollow throat  
with its greedy beak, delivered food untouched  
to one whose bites were hungry.

Now the good raven of Elijah, once faithless to Noah,

[175] [Col. 0571A] [Note: [Col. 0571C]

177. My manuscript has *Plurima dedit*: read *Plura dedit*.

179. A similar verse occurs in Juvencus, Book II, verse 548. Aldhelmus, chapter 10 of *Prose on Virginity*, cites Sedulius’ verse: “As the poet says in heroic hexameter, ‘Golden …’” Virgil used *aurea sidera* (“golden stars”).

180. Most manuscripts have *aerios* or *aereos*; others *aetherios* or *aethereos*. The editions likewise vary. The prose version, however, seems to require *aethereos*.

181. Reg. 1 has *Siderium*; others *Sidereum*.

182. Parrhasius has *Exteriora*, less well; Vet. 1 and Mon. have *Deteriora*, very badly. Glosses in Reg. 1 and Alm. explain *Dexteriora* as “better” or “heavenly places.”

184. Instead of *bene*, Alardus, in his note on Valerius Flaccus III.211, cites *vel*, apparently through a scribal or typographical error; nevertheless this reading occurs in Bede, *Book of Questions on Kings* 28, where he quotes these verses. A “lightning-bright sky” is a luminous sky, shining as though with lightning.

185. Most of our manuscripts, and the better ones, together with Nic. Heinsius’ manuscript and most editions, including Parrhasius, have *meritoque et nomine*. Arntzenius praises Aldus for the same reading; but Aldus gives me *merito qui, et nomine*, which appears to be the true reading and occurs in Alm. and Reg. 5, and ambiguously in Ott. 2. In manuscripts *que* and *qui* are often written in similar forms, so one is easily substituted for the other. Arntz. has *meritoque qui*. Alardus, in the passage cited, reports *merito qui nomine*. Nic. Heinsius and Meursius, in their note on Theocritus, *Idylls* XXVI, p. 150, approve *merito qui, et nomine*. Recent editors follow them. Bede has the erroneous *fulgent* instead of *fulgens*. The prose version cannot establish the reading of this verse, for here, unless it is corrupt, it is certainly obscure.

186. Parrhasius has *Aethere dignus erat*; some printed editions likewise, but all the manuscripts, including the most ancient Turin manuscript, have *Hac ope dignus erat*, namely, worthy of the fiery chariots by which he was to be carried into the stars. Bede agrees.

187. Beda, in the passage cited, has *mutatur*; others *mutetur*. Some accuse Sedulius here of having been ignorant of the true Hebrew meaning of Elijah’s name. But Sedulius could have known it and nevertheless alluded to a meaning drawn from the Greek language, since the fiery chariot was being mentioned. Nor should it seem surprising if Sedulius was not skilled in Hebrew. Nebrissensis explains *per accentum* by saying that the acute accent is transferred from the penultimate to the antepenultimate syllable. In Greek, “sun” is ἥλιος (*hēlios*); among the Septuagint it is written Ἠλιοὺ (*Ēliou*, “Eliu”), and elsewhere Ἠλίας (*Ēlias*).

188. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1: “On Hezekiah.” My manuscript: “Fifteen years are added to Hezekiah’s life.” Rom.: “On King Hezekiah, for fifteen years.” This verse seems to have been taken from Juvencus III.564: “The final portion of his waning light remained.”

189. Rom. adds *addit*: correct it to *addidit*.

190. Parrhasius printed *lumina*; Arntz. in a second hand, Urb., and Rom. in its first hand have the same, corrected to *limina*, as the prose version also reads. Vat. 2 has *patefacta limina* incorrectly.

192. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1: “On Jonah.” Rom.: “On Jonah shipwrecked.” My manuscript: “Jonah in the whale’s belly.” Urb. and Rom. have *quippe* instead of *puppe*, noted in Rom. as a variant reading.

194. *Fera* is not commonly used of fish, but it occurs in Manilius V.189 and 192.

195. Leipzig, Arntz. in a second hand, Aldus, Parrhasius, and our manuscripts Ang., Alb., Vatt. 1 and 2, Ott. 2, Reg. 5, Urb., Rom., my manuscript, and apparently Ott. 1 in its first hand have *Depositus*. Alm., Reg. 1, 2, and 4, Ott. in a second hand, and Arntz. in its first hand have *Depositum*, which is the more correct reading. Grunerus observes that the same word is used of Jonah by St. Maximus, *Summer Homily* I, on Easter: “When the fish vomited him forth unharmed, he was deposited and on the third day restored to the earth.” The term passed from the books of jurists into other authors, among whom Cicero, Juvenal, and others also use it.]

How fittingly the lightning-bright path of heaven, shining before him,

[185] [Col. 0572A] is suited to Elijah, who shines both in merit and in name,
175 He was worthy of this aid: for if, in the language of the Greeks, a single letter is changed through the accent, the word means “sun.”

Having pitied the final moments of the setting light,

God once added three times five years to the king,

[190] exercising his right, and, closing the opened gates of Death,

turned life from its setting into its rising.

Jonah, falling from the ship, swallowed and devoured by the whale,

did not feel the waters in the deep; he had a living tomb,

so that he might not die, safe within the beast’s belly,

[195] deposited, not prey, and across the vast sea

[Col. 0573A]

[Note: [Col. 0573B]

197. Reg. 1, Ott. 1: “Concerning the three boys.” Rom.: “Concerning King Nebuchadnezzar and the three men.” Meus: “The three boys are delivered from the furnace.” — Instead of *Cum spirante*, Urb. has the erroneous *Conspirante*. Reg. 4 has *Cum inspirante*, which is perhaps the genuine reading. Although verses of this kind are considered somewhat inelegant, in which the first word is a monosyllable to be pronounced with elision, examples are nevertheless not lacking among the best poets. *Inspirare*, “to infuse the divine Spirit,” is an ecclesiastical term, but one deriving its origin from good Latin authors, as I showed in Book II of Dracontius, verse 15: “You, God, breathe inspiration.” But whether *spirare* is found anywhere with the same meaning, I do not know. All the printed editions, however, together with most manuscripts, give *Cum spirante Deo*, “When God breathed upon them.”

198. Most manuscripts and printed editions have the harsh reading *durumque*; the prose version also supports it. Reg. 5, Ott. 2, the Poelman papers, Lips., Parrh., Ald., and Ott. 1 in its first hand have *dirumque*, “dreadful.”

200. Some printed editions incorrectly have *accenderet* instead of *accenderat*. In the Scholiast on Statius, *Thebaid* VIII, verse 287, this verse is read as follows: “Whose Achaemenian rage his anger had kindled,” but the text is corrupt. It must certainly be written *Achaemeniam*, that is, “Persian,” from Achaemenes, the grandfather of Cyrus; Horace, Valerius Flaccus, Sidonius, [Col. 0573D] and others used this epithet. The Scholiast on Statius is Placidus Lactantius, or Lutatius, whose words are: “Achaemenian itself is Chaldaean, so called from a certain most cruel king, concerning whom Sedulius says: ‘Whose Achaemenian …’ For his anger could be appeased only by human blood.” Some write *Achemeniam* less correctly. Burmannus noted that this verse is also quoted by the Scholiast on Lucan II, 49. It is also scanned long by the Scholiast on Horace’s *Epode* XIII, at the words “Now also Achaemenian.”

201. Meus has *traduntur*, “are handed over”; the others have the better *truduntur*, “are thrust.”

202. Ott. 1, 2, Urb., Ang., Alb., Vatt. 1, 2, Reg. 2, 5, Rom., Meus, Parrh., Ald., Lips., Cantabr., Tornaes 1, 2, 3, and the Poelman papers have *urente*, “burning.” Poelman in the text, Fabr., and other printed editions have *ardente*, “blazing,” which Arntzenius considers not inelegant and which Burmannus supports. Reg. 1, 4, Arntzenius, the old editions 1 and 2, and Mon. have *audente*, “daring,” supported by the prose version; Grunerus and Arntzenius retained it. In Reg. 1 the gloss on *audente* is *urente*; in Arntzenius it is *laedente*, “harming.” In Ott. 1, *audente* was made from *urente* by the same old hand. Nor is it surprising, as Grunerus says, that *audere* should be used of a pyre, since Drepanius in his hymn of the three boys attributes forgetfulness to the fire: “And, forgetting its power, the fire did not harm the holy men.” The old Turin codex has only *tantumque ardore*, “and only with such heat,” which Cellarius accepted with Lips.; the prose version does not disagree. But the common reading is *tantoque*, “and with so great a heat.”

203. The gloss in Reg. 1 is *imagineae*, because the fire appeared to burn but did not consume. Nebrissensis interprets it as “an imaginary punishment,” that is, one proposed for those who would not worship the image of King Nebuchadnezzar. Better, with the gloss, *imaginea poena* is taken as “imaginary,” because it was not truly a punishment. Fortunatus uses this same word, *imagineus*, in Book II of *The Life of Martin*, verse 276. A similar thought is explained by St. Leo in his sermon for the feast of St. Laurence: “The love of Christ could not be overcome by flame, and the fire that burned outside was weaker than the one that kindled within.” The Fathers commonly attribute ardor both to love and to faith, which Sedulius explicitly names.

204. Parrh., with Vat. 1, omits *O* after *animi*.

206. Reg. 1: “Concerning Nebuchadnezzar.” Rom. and Meus: “The fury of Nebuchadnezzar.” Ottobon. 1 omits this title.

210. Ott. 1, Vatt. 1, 2, Urb., Rom., Ang., Alb., Parrh., Ald., and Reg. 1 have *pro d. s.*; Reg. 2 has *lustrans*, “traversing,” and in the following verse *errans*, “wandering.” The printed editions also vary.

211. Reg. 4 has *lustrat*: “All bristling with woods, he wanders in the mountains.”

212. Reg. 1, Ott. 1: “Concerning Daniel.” Meus: “Daniel is delivered from the lions’ den.” Rom.: “Concerning Daniel guarded from the lions.” Parrh. and Edimb., with the Cantabr. manuscript, have *feruerunt*, “they boiled,” which Grunerus adopted because *fervere* is often used of hatred and anger, while *furuerunt* appears to be a gloss. But since all our manuscripts, together with most printed editions, retain *furuerunt*, it is preferable to retain it, although some grammarians deny a past tense from *furo*. The prose version supports it, and the past tense *furui* is attributed to Servius, and also by Harduinus to Pliny. Arntzenius further shows that *furor* is attributed to more intense anger, and therefore that *feruerunt* could be a gloss for the past tense *furuerunt*. In *Darius*, the ancients lengthened the first and second syllables; Sedulius, Sidonius, and others shorten both, although in Sedulius synaeresis may occur, or the word may be read *Dari*.

176 He came to unknown lands with an unfriendly oarsman.

When, with God breathing inspiration, three men united in mind rejected

the Babylonian sacred rites and underwent

the harsh destruction imposed by the savage Chaldaean tyrant’s law,

[200] whose Achaemenian rage had inflamed his anger

177 more than his own furnace; they were thrust into the midst of the flames,

while the pyre, daring nothing, and their hearts glowing

with such heat, overcame the fires of an imaginary punishment

with the fire of their spirit. O how great is the glory of believers!

[205] [Col. 0574A] The flame of the furnace was extinguished by the flame

of burning faith.

But soon a fitting vengeance struck the merciless king.

For when, foolishly, he withdrew from human piety,

he became a companion of beasts among the pasture grasses,

changing royal banquets for fodder after grazing.

[210] Bending forward, he drank from the stream, and, traversing seven seasons,

178 all bristling with woods, he wandered through the mountains.

Nor were the commands of the tyrant Darius any less frenzied.

[Col. 0575A]

[Note: [Col. 0575C]

213. This verse, *Ecce*, is absent from Vat. 2, Alb., Ang., Reg. 4, 5, Urb., Meo, Rom., Ald., Parrh., Arntzenius, Lips., the Heinsian manuscript, and Cant. It was added by a later hand in Vat. 1, written at the bottom of the page in Ott. 1, and placed in the margin of Reg. 2. In Reg. 1 the verse *Ecce* appears first, followed by *Nec minus*, but a transposition mark is present. The same Reg. has *Ecce etenim*, although something else may perhaps originally have stood instead of *etenim*. Ott. 2, Codex E, and another manuscript cited by Burmannus have *Ecce aliud*, which Burmannus remarks was taken from Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “Behold another, greater thing.” Others give *Ecce etenim*.

219. In the commonly printed poem of Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, this verse is inserted and reads *Edidicere*; but in the manuscript I found *Et didicere*, “and they learned.” Nebrissensis quotes from Martial I, epigram 105, concerning the lion and the hare: “And the prey is safer in its mouth.” Martial himself, I, epigram 7, says: “And the hare, safe, plays in the great mouth.”

220. Reg. 1: “Recapitulation of all the punishments.” Ott. 1: “Recapitulation of all the miracles.” Rom.: “A question against nature.” Meus: “Epilogue of the foregoing.” Arator clearly imitates Sedulius, Book I, verse 890, elsewhere 825: “Tell me, where are they, O nature, your worldly wisdom and laws?”

221. The printed editions have *Quis toties*, or *totiens*. Codex E, with Reg. 1 in its first hand, has *Qui toties*. The manuscripts also vary between *toties* and *totiens*. The printed editions have *qui tartara*; from our manuscripts, Vat. 1 in its first hand, Reg. 4, and Meus have *quis tartara*; others agree with the printed editions.

222. It could be *sterilique marito*. Cellarius and Arntzenius interpret *tartara* as the tomb or the condition of the dead. But why not the realms of the underworld, to which we believe Christ’s soul descended in order to free the souls of the holy fathers? I know that some heretics deny this very thing, but Petavius refutes them splendidly in Book XIII of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 15. See Book V, verse 428.

223. Ott. 2 has *anum Saram, praecepit*. In the other manuscripts *Saram* is a gloss written above *anum*.

227. Burmannus thinks the punctuation should be: *mirabile! nimbis*. But this place does not seem suitable for an interjection.

228. Reg. 5 and Vat. 2, contrary to the meter, have *pluit, qui saxo*. Aldus printed this as well, generally following these two manuscripts. Most manuscripts and printed editions have: “It rained; from the rock it brought forth streams from below.” Poelman less correctly has *producit*, and Parrh. *ab uno*. Arntzenius suspected *ab icto*, since the rock was struck; but from the Arntzenius manuscript he restored *saxi latices produxit ab imo*, as in this book, verse 302, *ima profundi*, and similar expressions, especially among poets. In the Addenda, however, he acknowledged that *imum saxum*, “the bottom of the rock,” *imum pulmonem*, “the bottom of the lung,” and *imum profundum*, “the lowest depth,” are also common. Understand that it rained manna.

229. All thirteen of our manuscripts, together with Parrh., Ald., the Heinsian codices, Lips., Arntzenius, and Cant., consistently read *plano*, “plain”; not a few printed editions have *pleno*, “full.” The Poelman papers and Arntzenius supported *plano*, whose gloss in Reg. 1 is *articulato, recto, vel apto*, “articulate, correct, or suitable.” Burmannus preferred *pleno*, as in Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 348, *plena voce*, “with a full voice,” and adds Lucan VI, verse 622.

230. Some printed editions have *Suspensus*: read *Suspensis*. Reg. 4 and Meus have *abstulit*; in Reg. 4 it was changed by a later hand to *distulit*.

231. Reg. 5, Ott. 2, Meus, and Alb. have *Per volucremque hominem*. Vat. 2 and Ald. have *Per volucremque hominem*, and Vat. 2 adds the error *pisci* for *pasci*. Other manuscripts, with Parrh. and most printed editions, have: “He allowed man to be fed by flying creatures, and by flashing horses he carried him upward.” Urb. and Rom. have: “He gave him, that man, to the flashing ones.”

232. Perhaps from Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, verse 145: “His eyes already weighed down by death,” where some less correctly have *jam in morte*, “already in death.”

234. Urb. has *Naufrago*; Ott. 1 in its first hand has the same, but above it correctly *Naufragio*, as do the rest of our codices and many printed editions. The Lipsian and Heinsian codices likewise have *Naufragio*. Poelman, the old editions 1 and 2, Mon., Fabr., and other printed editions, together with the Arntzenius manuscript, have *Navifrago*. But *Naufragio* is preferable, understood as standing for *naufrago*, just as *conjugium* is sometimes used for *conjuge*, *matrimonia* for *conjugibus*, *servitia* for *servis*, *ministeria* for *ministris*, *officium* for *officialibus*, *philosophia* for *philosophis*, and many similar expressions.]

Behold, for fury’s crime added crime to crime,

and Daniel, the glory of the Hebrews, was decreed, though innocent,

[215] to be food for the fasting beasts; but the wild creature, made gentle

toward the just man lest it harm his holy limbs,

began to love hunger; its rage softened and laid aside its fury,

and anger fell silent in the savage jaws,

and the fierce lions learned to spare their prey.

[220] 179 Tell me, O nature, where are your laws after such events?

Who so often imposed laws upon you? Who commanded the underworld

not to know the man who had been transported, and made

the old woman fertile for her husband, and commanded the sacred beast

to come of its own accord to the altar,

[Col. 0576A] and transformed feminine limbs

[225] into images of salt; he caused branches touched by fire

not to burn; he changed a shrub into a serpent;

he dried a path across the sea; wondrously for the clouds

he rained manna, and from the rock he brought forth streams from below;

he compelled a four-footed creature to speak in plain language;

[230] 180 he delayed the swift hours, with the elements suspended;

he allowed man to be fed by flying creatures, and on flashing horses

carried him into heaven; when the man was already weighed down by death,

he added three periods of five years; in the mouth of a pirate,

he established aid for the shipwrecked in the mouth of a devourer; in the blazing furnace

[235] [Col. 0577A]

[Note: [Col. 0577B]

235. Reg. 1 has *de rore*, “of dew,” which is not objectionable; above it is the gloss, or variant reading, *sub rore*, “beneath the dew.” Dew is mentioned in Daniel III, 50, as in “as though it were a wind of dew,” and so forth.

236. Poelman has *victusque*; correct it to *rictusque*, for which Ott. 2 and Meus erroneously have *ritusque*.

237. The Poelman papers and some printed editions have *Instigante* instead of *Instimulante*.

239. All thirteen of our manuscripts consistently read *machina sermo est*, and in Reg. 1 the gloss is *Cum ipse dixit, et facta sunt*, “When he himself spoke, and they were made.” The Heinsian manuscripts, Lips., Cantabr. in its second hand, the Poelman papers, Parrh., Ald., and the ancient Turin library codex agree. The prose version supports it. Therefore Davisius, Wopkensius, and Burmannus should not be followed when, together with a certain manuscript, an undated and unidentified quarto edition, and other inferior printed editions, they prefer *machina serva est*. Although *machina sermo est* may seem harsh, Sedulius certainly intended to say that all created things exist solely through God’s word. The alternative *serva est* is not sufficiently clear and can be explained only through the tautology “Every work of his serves him.”

241. Davisius, in reference to Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 2, distinguished the construction thus: *quocumque trahit sententia, nutu*, “wherever his will draws, by a nod,” and joined *nutu* with *jubentis*, “of the one who commands.” Wopkensius, under that punctuation, preferred to refer *nutu* to *sequiturque*, and explains it as “at the slightest indication of the divine will,” which elsewhere is expressed as occurring in the blink of an eye or in an instant. Wopkensius likewise conjectures: *Imperii, quocumque trahit sententia, nutum, vel sequiturque jubentis — Imperii, quocumque trahit, patientia nutum*. These conjectures are sufficiently inept, especially in a matter clear in itself. Burmannus approved Davisius’s punctuation, but prefers another reading in the prose version. Of our manuscripts, Reg. 1, Meus, and Vat. 2 obscurely have *quocumque trahit sententia nutu*; in Reg. 1, however, it seems originally to have been *quemcumque trahit sententia nutum*. Ott. 1, Vat. 1, Reg. 2, 5, Urb., Rom., Alb., and apparently Ang. have *quacumque trahit sententia nutu*. Reg. 4 and Ott. 2 have *quaecumque trahit sententia nutu*. Parrh. and Ald. agree with Ott. 1.

242. Reg. 1: “Concerning various worshipers.” Ott. 1: “Concerning various heresies.” Meus: “Against the pagans.” Rom.: “Concerning the poet’s criticism of those who worshiped idols.” Ott. 1 in its first hand, Reg. 2 in its second hand, Reg. 5, Ang., Alb., Vat. 1, 2, Ott. 2, Rom., Meus, Cant., Arntzenius in its first hand, and Ald. have *fana*, “shrines.” Other manuscripts, with Parrh., the Poelman papers, Ott. 1 above the same old hand, and others, have *vana*, “empty things,” which the prose version confirms. Urb. has *ana*, with the first letter missing.

243. Meus and Ald. have *scalpunt*, which is certainly better if we follow the grammarians, for some doubt whether *sculpo* is Latin. But most have *sculpunt*, and the verb is also found in other authors, although the manuscripts generally vary. Some printed editions have *simulacra deorum*, “images of the gods.”

244. Reg. 5, Vat. 1, Meus, and Ald. have *ea, quae*; others have *et quae*.

245. Ott. 1 has *animas* instead of *animos*. Ott. 2 has *dementia fallit*. Arntzenius took *dementia cepit* from Virgil, *Aeneid* V, verse 465: “What great madness seized his mind?” From the prose version Arntzenius conjectured *quae tanta animis dementia ludit?*, “what great madness plays upon minds?”

246. Ott. 2 has *Et volucrem*; read *Ut*, “that.” Rom. and Arntzenius have *torvumque*; retain *tortumque*, “twisted,” which is a frequent epithet of a dragon or serpent. A bull is called *turpis* from Virgil, *Georgics* III, verse 52: “The form of a bull, whose head is misshapen.” The ibis, Apis, Anubis, the Egyptian gods, and Aesculapius are mocked under the name of the dragon. The ibis is a bird, Apis a bull, and Anubis half-man, half-dog. The stories are well known.

247. Arntzenius printed, with most editions and manuscripts, *homo pronus adoret*, “let the man bow down and worship.” But Sedulius’ own reading must be restored, an acute and elegant one: *homo plenus adoret*, “let the complete man worship,” alluding to the half-man dog. In Reg. 1 this reading is clear, although another hand attempted to write *pronus* above it. The gloss is also clear that this was the original reading, not *semis*, but *plenus sensu*, “complete in understanding,” or “made in the image of God.” In Ott. 1 and Reg. 2 *pronus* is now read, but it seems originally to have been *plenus*, as the gloss in Reg. 2 plainly indicates, namely *totus*, “whole.” Grunerus therefore correctly printed *plenus*, following the Cantabr. manuscript and the prose version, where the word is *integer*, “complete.” Wopkensius and Arntzenius disagree for the inept reason that Sedulius elsewhere, and other authors too, use the phrase *pronus adorat*, “bows down and worships.” They should rather have concluded that inept scribes, misled by this more common phrase, corrupted the verse. In Reg. 4 this verse is placed after verse 272.]

He preserved the pious beneath the dew; he fed the king through the pastures

like a shaggy beast, and commanded the lions’ jaws,

when hunger urged them, to forget their fury.

Indeed, every work of the Creator—for whatever things are seen

or whatever things lie hidden, and the structure of the universe is his word—

[240] 181 serves him, and follows the command of the one who orders it,

wherever his will draws it with a nod.

[Col. 0578A] Wretched are those who worship empty things, who with a perverse heart

carve sacred images for themselves, and flee their Maker,

fearing the things they themselves have made.

[245] What madness is this? What great insanity plays upon minds?

182 That a suppliant, complete man should worship a bird,

a misshapen bull, a twisted dragon,

and a half-man dog?

[Col. 0579A]

[Note: [Col. 0579C]

248. Vat. 1 has *actu*; in the margin it is correctly changed to *acti*.

251. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 in their first hand have *constat* instead of *constet*.

252. Vat. 1 has *decursibus*, corrected above to *discursibus*. Vet. 1 erroneously has *discordibus*.

253. Meus has *Officio non esse Deum*; the true reading is *Officium, non esse Deum*, namely, “not to be God, but a servant, an official.” In this sense *officium* is sometimes used, as I noted in the variant readings at verse 234. The thought itself is explained fully and elegantly by Prudentius, Book II against Symmachus, verses 309 and following.

254. As elsewhere in compounds of this kind, the codices vary here: some have *dimissus*, “sent down”; most have *demissus*, which is preferable. Meus has *demersus in oras*, “sunk toward the shores,” not inelegantly; instead of *oras*, some printed editions and manuscripts have *horas*, “hours.” In the prose version too one writes *horis vergentibus*, “as the hours decline”; but in both places the aspiration should be omitted. In Reg. 1, although *horas* is written with aspiration, the gloss *fines*, “boundaries,” is added, suggesting *oras*.

255. Urb. has *ubique* without *est*. Compare the note on Dracontius II, 10: “Having shared turns with his brother.”

256. Meus has *Hoc lumen*; correct it to *Nec*, “nor.”

257. Reg. 4 has *Cum genitum sine sole diem*; this seems also to have been the reading in Vat. 1. Ang. has *Cum geminam*. The remaining manuscripts and all printed editions have *Cum geminum*, concerning which our Nebrissensis noted that there were not two but three days. In fact, God made the sun and moon on the fourth day, as Genesis chapter 1 relates. But perhaps Sedulius counts two days after the first; for *genitum sine sole diem*, “a day brought forth without the sun,” is not satisfactory.

258. Codex E has *qui*; Parrh. has *quia*; *quam* is better.

260. Meus has *latices*, “streams.” Cannegieterus wanted *lapidem*, “stone.” But from what follows it is clear that the subject is water and fire, both of which the pagans worshiped. Vossius, *On Idolatry* II, reports that the Egyptians, Scythians, and Persians worshiped water. The worship of the household hearth among the Romans is well known. For *sed jungere*, the Poelman papers have *hi jungere*; it is preferable to retain *sed*.

261. Meus has *Nec audent … nec lite*. I reject both. After this verse Meus contained another, unknown to everyone else: “Let the humid power scatter the dry deity into the air.” In the margin it was marked *vacat*, “to be omitted.”

263. *Moriantur*, “may they die,” is an elegant expression used by others as well for *exstinguantur*, “may they be extinguished.” Thus *vivus* is used of fire, and *vivere* for “to burn,” and *ardere* for “to be aflame.”

264. Reg. 4 has *ponitur*; read *ponit*. The madness of the pagans, who even worshiped trees, is attacked by Prudentius, Book II against Symmachus, verse 1009; this superstition also seems in some way to have been revived in our own time.

266. Reg. 5 has *charam domum*; the meter requires *charamque domum*.

267. In Ott. 1 and Vat. 1, *censusque* was corrected to *censumque*. In Reg. 2 it also seems originally to have been *censusque*. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *censusque*; most have *censumque*. Nebrissensis interprets *conjugii fidem* as “a faithful spouse.” It has already been noted elsewhere that *conjugium* is sometimes used for *conjuge*.

268. Wopkensius had conjectured *Lignea signa rogas*, “you ask wooden images”; but from the prose version he understood that the common reading is correct and also more elegant. Nebrissensis explains *rogas* as “you ask,” that is, “you ought to ask.” The matter is clear without this interpretation.

270. Cannegieterus was dissatisfied with this passage and read *regant, sic caesa*. Change nothing. Meus’ reading is not bad if *scissa* is read instead of *caesa*. Wopkensius conjectured *axis* instead of *actis*, but later rightly rejected it, and accepted *actis* for *adactis*, “struck, driven in.” Wopkensius illustrates the phrase *regere jura*, “to govern laws,” from Rutilius, *Itinerary* I, 157: “If I have not displeased, I would govern with the laws of Quirinus,” where Sitzmannus has further material.]

Let them support the lofty roofs of a hanging house,
or, placed beneath hearths, serve in preparing banquets.

But others, driven by blinded minds, assert that the sun

is the father of things, because it is rightly seen

[250] to pour bright lights over the serene earth

and to traverse the entire sky, although it is clear that from those

motions, that the unstable fire, in its swift courses,

is a servant, not a god, and that it, in a fixed order,
now rises and now descends toward the western regions,

[255] 183 shares his turns with night, and is not always everywhere,

nor was he the abiding light at the world’s beginning,

when the new universe had a double day without the sun.

So too they bring vows to the moon, which they see waxing

[Col. 0580A] and waning, and sacrifice to the stars, which are driven away by light.

[260] This man worships water, that one the household hearth; but they do not dare

to join hostile powers in sacred rites, lest in a neighboring conflict

either a stronger pyre dry up the little waves,

or the thin fires die before powerful springs.

Another places altars at the roots of trees,

[265] 184 establishes banquets, and tearfully prays to the branches

that they govern his children, his dear home, his beloved fields,

his marriage bond, his servants, and his wealth.

“You ask wood, O man; you seem to shout to deaf things,

you seek answers from the mute—things which in this way

[270] govern the laws of households, if cut down by axe blows.”

[Col. 0581A]

[Note: [Col. 0581B]

271. Some manuscripts have *sustentent*, and immediately afterward *famulentur*; others have *sustentant … famulantur*; others *sustentent … famulantur*. The printed editions vary in much the same way. The common reading favors the subjunctive; but the indicative may also be retained. The subjunctive should not, however, occur in one verb and the indicative in the other.

272. Poelman has *Aut subjecta foci*; the Poelman papers note that *focis* should be read. Reg. 4 has *Aut subjuncta focis*, which may perhaps be the genuine reading. Nebrissensis noted here *subjecta*, indeed *superinjecta*, “cast over.” *Aut injecta focis*, “or cast upon the hearths,” would not be bad; that is what appears in the prose version. I discussed the verb *famulentur* at the preceding verse.

273. Juvenal mocks this mad superstition in Satire XV, verse 10.

274. Reg. 4 has *viridique hac arte*; I retain *verique*.

276. Reg. 4 has *pudent*; read *pudet*. Ott. 2 has *longum est*.

277. *Urere*, “to burn,” is used for “to dry up, to consume moisture” by Virgil, Pliny, and others.

278. Urb. and Meus have *ne per*.

279. Vat. 1 has *ex spinis*, correctly changed to *et spinis*, from Virgil, *Eclogue* 5, verse 39, from whom Sedulius borrows this verse. The author of the poem *On Genesis*, included among the spurious or doubtful poems of Juvencus, also borrowed it; at verse 121 I noted that the same verse occurs in Proba’s *Centon*. Reg. 4 has *paliurus acutus*; but Virgil and Columella, Book X of *On Gardening*, verse 22, have *acutis*: “and may it bear the paliurus with sharp thorns.”

280. For *addita*, Wopkensius and Burmannus wanted to restore *edita*, that is, “produced.” The meaning is the same: through human error, worship was offered to false deities. Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII, chapter 11, states that the fictions of pagan poets played a major role in promoting the worship of the gods: “Poets also contributed to their praises and, composing songs, raised them to heaven.” And below: “But all this was fabricated by the poets so that they might adorn their gods,” and so forth. He first says in chapter 10: “Pagans are so called from the villages of the Athenians, where they arose,” and in chapter 11 confirms that Cecrops was the first of all to devise images. This makes Sedulius’ verses concerning Cecropian poison and the Attic village, verses 40 and following, easier to understand here.

281. Most of our manuscripts and printed editions have *aut tales potius*; others have *aut potius tales*.

282. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 display no title. Poelman has “He attacks the heresy of Arius and Sabellius.” The Poelman papers and the Lipsian edition have *placet*; *juvat*, “it pleases,” is more poetic and is also adopted by the prose version. Reg. 4 erroneously has *juvet ire*, and Arntzenius *per almum*.

283. Curtius, Quintilian, and others say *firmare gradum*, “to steady one’s step,” as Virgil says *firmare vestigia*, “to steady one’s footsteps.” Rom. has *ad urbem*, “toward the city.”

284. Reg. 1, 2, 4, Ott. 1, Rom., Parrh., the old editions 1 and 2, Mon., and Poelman have *Libertatis opem*. Vatt. 1, 2, Ott. 2, Reg. 5, Meus, Ang., Alb., and Ald. have *Libertatis ope*. Grunerus preferred the latter, punctuating: “Let us hasten into the city—radiant with the aid of freedom, where the royal palace gleams …” Grunerus thought Fabricius had changed *ope* into *opem*, but the manuscripts and the oldest editions prove this false. Wopkensius attempted *properemus in urbem; Ubertas ubi opum*, but from the prose version he understood that *Libertatis opem* came from Sedulius’ own hand; this is what the prose version says: “to the city, the author of our freedom.” Burmannus also supports this reading, [Col. 0582D] and explains *opem* as a thing that accomplishes something, aid, and so forth. Thus Iscanus, *On the Trojan War* II, verse 261: “This shine of steel, this hostile gold, he wrested as an aid to beauty.” Parrhasius says that Sedulius followed the analogy of *Libertatis opem*, that is, “fruitful freedom,” since its opposite is *inops*, “destitute.” Compare, if desired, the note on Dracontius III, verse 415: “Nor did iron chains restrain the aid of freedom.”

285. In Vat. 1, *ex tholis* was changed to *thoris*; restore *tholis*. Ott. 1 has *potenti*, correctly changed by the second hand to *petenti*.

286. Parrh. and the Poelman papers have *Quaerentem*, which can stand. But the manuscripts and most printed editions give *Quaerenti*, and in Vat. 1 it is clear that this was corrected from *Quaerentis*.]

the help of freedom, where the royal hall shines radiant with golden domes,
where worthy things are given to the petitioner, certain hope awaits the seeker,
and, with the barriers removed, accessible thresholds open to the knocking heart.

This is that rejected stone which the Corner

187 carries upon its summit and presents miracles to our eyes,

[290] whose burden is light, whose yoke is pleasant to bear.

Through the miracles of the ancient law, arranged beforehand,

we have recounted what the Father accomplished through the joined agency

[Col. 0584A] of the holy Spirit, by the shared power of the Son.

of the holy Spirit, by the shared power of the Father.

makes what is simple threefold, and makes what is threefold simple.
