299. Poelman gives the title: “He attacks the heresy of Arius and Sabellius.” — This verse is absent from Ott. 1, but was inserted by a second hand. Paulinus, *Life of St. Martin* I: “Nevertheless, he held faith in his mouth, or salvation in his heart.”

300. Arntzenius has *cuncta per avia*, “all things through byways,” less well.

301. Rom. has *Flectere iter nisus*, “having attempted to bend the path,” which is not bad. Vet. 1 has *Flectere visus iter*, perhaps a typographical error. Reg. 1, Vat. 1, Rom., Arntzenius, and Ald. have *dilapsus*, which Arntzenius condemns. Most have *delapsus*; but such interchange is frequent in compounds with the preposition *de*. Reg. 1 in its second hand has *delapsus*.

304. A shameful kind of death, by which Arius is known from the ecclesiastical histories to have perished.

305. Reg. 4 has *quia non*; Virgil, whom Sedulius imitates, has *qua non*.

306. Reg. 1, 2, 4, 5, Rom., Alb., Vat. 1, and others have *similavit*. Ott. 1 has the same, but seems originally to have had *simulavit*, which appears in many manuscripts and printed editions. Some insist that *similare* is not Latin and that wherever the verb occurs it should be changed to *simulare*. But it cannot be denied that *similo* was frequent among later writers. In this passage, however, *simulavit* seems correct, from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 585: “Madman, who had imitated the clouds and the inimitable lightning with bronze, and the running of hoofed horses.” Compare the variant readings at Juvencus I, verse 394.

308. Meus has *parenti*, “for the parent,” which is not bad instead of *parentis*.

309. Arntzenius notes that some printed editions have *filius nunc est*. The meter requires *filius est nunc*.

311. Poelman and Fab. have *In nova*; Rom. has *Id nova*; correct to *It nova*. Virgil’s words are in *Georgics* IV, verse 208: “And the grandfathers of grandfathers are counted.”

313. Arntzenius has *Est totum*, which he thinks can be defended if *sapientia* is punctuated: “Christ is … everything shared by the Father.” Vat. 1 has *Et totum est commune Patris*. Nevertheless, the common reading should be retained. This explanation of the Trinity may be compared with Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 278, and *Hymn* 10 of the *Peristephanon*, verses 316 and following.

314. The Poelman papers have *qui nec minor est Patre quidquam*. The manuscripts and printed editions have *cui nec minus est Patre quidquam*, but in Ott. 1 in its first hand it was *minor est*. Perhaps one should read *qui nec minor est Patre quidquam*, that is, “who is in no respect less than the Father.” For *nequidquam* is not rarely used for “nothing” or “not,” as in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, chapter 31: “To separate the soul from the body is nothing other than learning to die,” whether one reads, with others, *nec quidquam* or *nihil quidquam*. The common reading is defended by the prose version.

315. Poelman punctuates very badly: *habet genitus: non quippe creatus*, “he has been begotten: certainly not created.”

316. This verse was missing from Codex E, but was added in the margin.

### 319

The Father is the same as the Son, not the same person as the Son, because the masculine *idem* indicates a person, whereas the neuter indicates nature. See the note on Dracontius, Book II, line 105. Orientius, *Poem on the Trinity*: “Not the same, but wholly the same.” Thus he distinguishes the masculine and neuter *idem* by the differing quantity of their syllables.

### 320

Ott. 1: “But since we are what”—*quod* is obscure; *sumus* is certainly an error for *summus*. Poelmann’s manuscripts preferred *summis* without any justification, as Arntzenius suggests. Instead of *et filius*, Arntzenius has *quia filius*; he maintains that prose does not reject this, but he is mistaken, for in prose *quia* is read only once, as in the verse, whereas in the reading he himself indicates—for he speaks ambiguously—*quia* would occur twice. This verse and the preceding one are quoted in a certain *Revelation* of Ildefonsus, bishop of Hispania, in the ninth century, as I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 28, but corruptly: *hoc et filius est* instead of *et filius hoc est*. There is also an error in the edition of Bede that I use, where it reads *quidquid* instead of *quod*; the commentator on his book *On Metres*, however, has *quod*. See also the testimony of Amalarius in the *Prolegomena*, no. 177.]

This is the true faith; this salvation he scorned to possess,

[300] Unhappy Arius, who, trying to bend the straight path

Through crooked byways, fell headlong into a black pit,

And, sunk in the depths of gloomy darkness, sought its bottom:

So empty of understanding that, when the time came for rightful punishment,

After his entrails had been poured out, he remained empty in the belly.

[305] Madman, who imitated the laws of the everlasting Father—

Laws not to be imitated—through the ranks of perishable honors!

For among human beings the son is held by the carnal law

To be younger than his father, since the father himself was once

A son before his parent; presently he who is now a son

[310] Will be a father. Thus, through every generation of descendants,

A new offspring proceeds, and grandfathers are numbered among ancestors.

[Col. 0586A] But the Lord—Word, Power, Wisdom, Christ—

And wholly shared with the Father, Light from Light,

Alone from the One, who is in no respect less than the Father,

[315] Nor, being begotten, not created, does he possess anything by which he might increase,

He himself is the Beginning. For just as he is held to be glorious

While remaining in the Father, so the glorious Father also remains in him,

And the one God is everywhere the head of all things.

Not because the Father is what is supreme and this is also the Son,

[320] But because the Son is what the supreme Father is.

[Col. 0587A] [Note: [Col. 0587B]

321. Vet. 1 has *agit*, ineptly, instead of *ait*; the two are often interchanged in manuscripts as well. All our manuscripts, together with the codices of Heinsius, Lipsius, and Arntzenius, and the editions of Parrhasius, Aldus, and others, admit a hiatus in *Ego in Patre, et Pater in me est*. To avoid the hiatus, some printed editions, together with Cappusotus and Poelmann, have *docens: Et ego in Patre*; others have *docens: Ego et in Patre*. That this did not come from Sedulius’s hand is sufficiently evident in itself. Recent editors admit the hiatus here, although they refused to admit it at verse 290. Bede also reads it as we have printed it, but thinks that Sedulius sinned against the rule of grammatical arrangement in order to retain the Redeemer’s words. He scans it thus: *Sic ait—ipse do—cens e—gin Pa*, and consequently admits a trochee in the third position. The anonymous commentator on Bede in a Vatican manuscript seems to hold the same opinion. They think that Sedulius did not wish to admit the hiatus. I think very differently, as I shall say again at the end of the *Elegy*, where I shall explain Bede’s opinion more fully.]

### 322

The Taurine codex has *sumus*. If *Arrius* is retained, Arntzenius was troubled by this verse and proposed either *Ego, atque Pater sumus unum*—with *Arrius unum* involving a hiatus between *unum* and *Arrius—or *Ego, Pater atque unum sumus*. *Arrius unum*. But what purpose would such a transposition of words serve? What inconvenience is there if the final syllable of *Pater* is lengthened by the metrical caesura?

### 323

Reg. 4 has *summusque Sabellius*; Parrhasius and Poelmann’s manuscripts have *simulque Sabellius*. Read *SUMUSque Sabellius*: of those two words, *unum sumus*, Arius denied *unum*, while Sabellius denied *sumus*—that is, Arius denied unity of essence, Sabellius the Trinity of persons. Reg. 5 and Aldus have *sumus Sabellius* without the conjunction *-que*, which can be tolerated. It is better, however, to shorten the first syllable of *Sabellius*, as in Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, line 178, and elsewhere.

### 324

Arntz. has *Ille fidem*; the others have *Iste*. In manuscripts *iste* and *ille* are frequently confused. In this verse *iste* and *hic* mean “the one” and “the other.” Most manuscripts and the oldest printed editions have *ternam*; more recent ones have *trinam*. Gothescalcus adduces in his memorandum, among the works of Hincmarus, p. 417, the possibility that one may speak of a “threefold divinity,” and reads *Iste fidem ternam*. Hincmarus, p. 503, distinguishes between *ternus* and *trinus*, because *ternus* derives from *ter* (“three times”), whereas *trinus* derives from *tria* or *tres* (“three”), and observes that Sedulius wished to use not *trinam* but *ternam*. In reality, however, the meaning of both words is the same, as is clear from Juvencus’s word-index. I have also said more about this phrase, *trina deitas*, in the *Hymnodia Hispanica* and in my commentary on Prudentius. Add Florus the Deacon of Lyon, in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. I, poem 6: “By night and by day, proclaiming the threefold divine power with hymns.” Florus flourished in the same century as Hincmarus. In Arntzenius’s codex, *non* had been deleted, although prose and sense require it.

### 325

Arntz. has *quamvis*; others have *quamquam*. Reg. 1 and 4, and my manuscript, have *sequentes* in place of *d. s.*; Vet. 1 and 2, Mon., and Taur. likewise have *sequentes*, which prose confirms. Others have *sequantur*. Cassiodorus likewise reads it in his exposition of Psalm VIII, at the end. In Rom. *sequatur* is an error.

### 328

Reg. 1 has *Ostentant*, which is preferable, although the others favor *Ostendunt*. *Ostentant* conveys more, namely, “they display them in order to terrify and threaten.” Arms are said to be *exserta*, as are exposed shoulders, upper arms, and so forth. See Cerda’s note on Tertullian, *De Pallio*, chapter 3, near the end, where he cites both our Sedulius and several others.

### 330

*Jacet* is used for “is despised,” as elsewhere.

### 331

In my manuscript *ille stat* conflicts with the metre; correct it to *hic stat*.

### 332

Ott. 1, Reg. 5, and Aldus have *cachinnos*; the others have *cachinnum*. The former reading is supported by Persius, whom Sedulius imitates, *Satires* 3.87: “With his nose wrinkled in laughter.” The plural is also required by *fletus* (“weeping”), which is placed on the other side. He means Heraclitus and Democritus, of whom the latter loved laughter and the former weeping.

### 334

Poelmann’s manuscripts: “He exhorts the soldiers of Christ”; in most copies the title is absent. *Viam sermone levamus* (“we lighten the way with conversation”) comes from Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.309: “As he entered, he lightened the way with varied conversation.”

### 335

Reg. 4: *comitentur*.]

Thus he himself says, teaching: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

Again: “I and the Father are one.” Arius must know that *one*

Is to be read, while Sabellius must admit that *we are*.

This one holds a threefold faith, but the other does not embrace a unity.

[325] Both are equally mistaken, although they follow different doctrines;

Accustomed in this way to produce various sects,

The men attack their own statements, displaying their arms

With bare shoulders, untrained in conveying anything.

[Col. 0588A] But only clever at fighting,

[330] Their foolish wisdom lies prostrate, because the world’s wisdom is vain before God.

One speaks excessively, the other is silent; one walks, the other stands;

Meanwhile, as we properly lighten the way with conversation,

[335] And hope and faith accompany my steps on the difficult ascent,

337. Vet. 1 has *ducis* instead of *crucis*, needlessly: Sedulius is praising the sign, or standard, of the cross, and perhaps has in mind the military standards of Christians, which from the time of Constantine were adorned with the sign of the cross. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.464 ff.: “You must willingly recognize, O queen, my standards, / On which the image of the cross shines forth, set with gems, / Or is displayed on long poles in solid gold,” and so forth.

338. In Poelmann there is the error *turba* for *tuba*. My manuscript has *cantat* instead of *clamat*; but if this were to be changed, *clangit* would better be restored, since that is proper to a trumpet. Paulinus, *Life of St. Martin* II.423, and Drepanius, *Hymn to St. Michael the Archangel*, likewise speak of “holy camps”; Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 16, speaks of “heavenly camps.”

339. My manuscript has *intrat*; I retain *intret*.

340. Urb. and Rom., in the first hand, have *quae janua est Christus*; Alb. has *quae janua Christus est*, against the metre, with *est* taken from a gloss. Ott. 2, Parrhasius, and apparently my manuscript have it with an interrogation: *quae janua? Christus* (“What gate? Christ”). This reading seems elegant and is approved by Burmannus, but the interrogation is absent from the prose, and the context itself requires it to be absent from the poem.

341. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s manuscripts have *gaudia*; the others have *praemia*, which prose supports. The same reading is found in an ancient author of the *Life of St. Gerard*, quoted by Baronius under the year 939, no. 4, who borrows from Sedulius: “That he may attain the golden rewards of everlasting life,” adapting it to his own subject. Dracontius calls them “the gifts of everlasting life” in Book II, line 569, and “the gifts of eternal life” in Book III, line 455. Tertullian likewise has, *On the Judgment of the Lord*, near the end: “Thus you too shall receive the heavenly gifts of life”; and Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, line 295: “The golden gifts of the righteous.” In liturgical prayers *praemia vitae aeternae* (“the rewards of eternal life”) is common.

342. Paulinus, *Life of St. Martin* I.271: “With all the strength of prayer”; and II.182: “He prays with the full strength of faith.” Wopkensius attributes similar expressions to Quintilian’s *Declamations*: “with all speed”; to Ammianus: “with all swiftness”; to Optatus, this very expression and, besides, “with all importunity” and “with complete confidence”; and to Minucius, “in complete silence.”

[Col. 0590B] 343. In Vat. 2 and Rom. *alterutrum decus* is lacking.

345. Reg. 2 and 5, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ang., Poelmann’s manuscripts, [Col. 0590C] Rom., Ott. 1 and 2, Urb., Arntz., the Leipzig codices, and Barthius with Parrhasius and Aldus have *Hic propriae sedis*, so that it connects with *domum*. Cant. with our Reg. 1 and 4 and many printed editions has *Hic proprias sedes*, which Grunerus, Wopkensius, and Arntzenius preferred. My manuscript has a reading that ought to be preferred: *Hic propriae sedes, cujus tu moenibus urbis / Exiguam concede domum* (“Here are my proper abodes; within the walls of whose city grant me a little house”). The more common reading, *Hic propriae sedis*, can also be referred to this, for *sedis* appears to have been written for *sedes* according to the ancient manner of writing. *Hujus* is also found instead of *cujus*. Sedulius imitates Virgil, as often elsewhere, *Aeneid* III.167: “These are our proper abodes; from here Dardanus arose.” Perhaps Sedulius wrote *Hae propriae sedes*. He means that heaven is the proper abode of human beings, because they derive their origin from there—that is, from God—and must return there. It can also be explained as *Hic propriae sedes*, namely, “for you,” since heaven is God’s dwelling. Juvencus, Book I, line 574: “It is not permitted for a human being to swear by high heaven, / Which is the Lord’s dwelling.” In favor of the other reading, *Hic proprias sedes*, stands Virgil, *Aeneid* III.85: “Give us a proper home, O Thymbraean; give walls to the weary, / And a people, and a city that will endure.” Add the prose.

347. Poelmann’s manuscripts have *alboque beari / Ordine, et extremus*, ineptly.

348. Dempsterus, in Rosinus, Book I, chapter 17, cites *Ordinis externus*. There he explains what it means to be enrolled in the register of the blessed order. My manuscript corruptly has *cinis* instead of *civis*. Sedulius seems to have wished to explain a passage of Prudentius that is otherwise difficult, *Hamartigenia* 953: “I do not seek a home / In the blessed region.”

351. In the Heinsian codex the title is *Prologue to the Four Gospels*. Ott. 2 has *fave coeptis* (“favor my undertaking”), which is appropriate to *mundum*.

353. Cant. has *sumere carnem* (“to assume flesh”); the others have *sumere formam* (“to assume form”), a phrase sufficiently common not only among Christian but also among pagan poets.]

At last, more gently, we have reached the highest citadel.

Behold, the consecrated standards of the cross flash forth:

Behold, the holy camps of the King gleam; the lordly trumpet sounds;

The gate stands open to his soldiers; let him who serves enter:

[340] The eternal gate calls you—the gate that is Christ.

You shall receive the golden rewards of everlasting life,

Weapons with which the Lord’s battles are waged with all strength,

And honor fixed upon your brow. I bear honor and arms,

And remain the final member of your army, good King.

[345] Grant me here my proper dwelling-place, within the walls of this city

[Col. 0590A] Grant me a little house, so that, as your inhabitant,

And be enrolled forever as the last citizen of the blessed order.

I ask for great things indeed—but you know how to grant great things.

[350] Whoever grows lukewarm in hope offends you all the more.

Christ, favor my prayers: when the world lay dead in death,

From heaven, deigning to assume human form,

354. Reg. 2 above, Reg. 4, and some printed editions have *nosses*; most have *posses*; Reg. 2, in the first hand, has *possis*. *Posse* and *nosse* are often interchanged, and sometimes it makes little difference which one is chosen, since the same meaning results.

355. In Cantabr. the heading reads: “The work on the Old Testament ends; the work on the four evangelists begins. Prologue.” Alb. has “Invocation of the New Testament.” Ott. 1 has “On the Four Evangelists.” Ott. 2 has “Sedulius’s Invocation in the Second Book.” Instead of *agens*, Reg. 1 has *aiens*, with a gloss reading *scribens*, although *agens* seems to have been written first. Aldus printed *aiens*, and in his list of corrections changed it to *ait*, as it is also read in Reg. 5. Observe the phrase *implere hominem*, that is, “to fulfill the role of a human being,” just as one says *implere amicum, Deum, judicem*, “to fulfill the role of a friend, God, or judge,” and *complere duces*, “to complete the leaders.” In the prose it is *expedivit*.

357. Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Vat. 1 and 2, Ott. 1 and 2, Urb., Rom., and my manuscript have *sacerdotii*. The Cantabrian and Arntzenian codices and the editions of Parrhasius, Aldus, and others likewise have *sacerdotii*. The Leipzig edition has *sacerdotum*. Most printed editions, together with Ang., Reg. 4, Alb., and apparently Ott. 1, have *sacerdotis*, although where *sacerdotii* now stands in Ott. 1 the same old hand is visible, and something else appears to have been erased. An ancient homily, which I mentioned in the *Prolegomena*, no. 177, also has *sacerdotis*, and corruptly *ore virenti* instead of *ore juvenci*. It is highly probable that *sacerdotii* came from Sedulius: Parrhasius observed that he makes much use of such contractions, and in such genitives he had better models to imitate, such as Virgil’s *auxili*, and so forth. Although *sacerdotii* has four syllables, it should nevertheless be written this way rather than *sacerdoti*, so that all ambiguity may be removed.

359. Juretus reads *unate voce* in the prose and insists that it should likewise be read together in the poem, drawing the manuscript copies into support of this view. But nothing compels us to acknowledge so unusual a word as *unas, unatis*. Therefore, both in prose and in verse, the words must be separated as *una te*, namely: “singing of you, Christ, with one voice.”

362. Urb. and Rom. have *imitatur, et horas*. Arator, Book I, line 164: “The twelve signs of the choir shine forth”; and line 348: “The crown of the Church was growing.”

364. Urb. corruptly has *Hic igitur ne terris recolens*. For *exordia mortis*, the old Taurine codex has *exordia mundi*, which is nevertheless less satisfactory.

366. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *nam qui deflemus in Adam*; Ang. and Vet. 1 have *nam quod*; in Reg. 2 there seems originally to have been *nam quos*, but it became *nam qui*, with *nos* written above as a gloss. Poelmann’s manuscripts admit *nos* into the text instead of *nam*, and this is how it appears in Poelmann’s own edition. Urb. has, incorrectly, *nam qui deflevimus Adam*; Rom. and Alb., against the metre, have *nam qui deflevimus in Adam*.

367. Arator, Book I, line 419, seems to imitate Sedulius: “Give the seeds of the Word,” and so forth: “May that hand gather sheaves, since you make them fruitful.”

368. Rom. has the less elegant *Christo nostros* instead of *nostros Christo*. The oldest codex of the Turin library: “The first book of the Old Testament ends. The first book of the New Testament begins. Perpetual life to the reader.” Reg. 1: “The book of the Old Testament ends. The first book in the New Testament begins.” Ott. 1: “The first book of Sedulius’s Old Testament ends. The first book of the New Testament begins.” Vat. 1: “The work on the Old Testament ends. The work on the New Testament begins.” In some codices a division is indicated between the first and second books, but without any title. Aldus continues the first book as far as the verse “The Lord deigned to be present at his first wedding chamber”; with this verse others begin the third book.]

Thus, bearing what belongs to another, so that you could not abandon what is yours.

[355] In doing this Matthew generally fulfills the role of a human being.

195 Mark, as a lion’s voice thunders in the wilderness,

Luke holds the laws of the priest in the mouth of a young bull.

Flying in the manner of an eagle, John seeks the stars by his word.

These four leaders, singing of you with one voice,

[360] Like four seasons, are spread throughout the wide world.

Thus, too, the apostolic honor of twelve

[Col. 0592A] Shines forth in its number, imitating the months and the hours,

So that the entire year may serve you in all things.

Therefore, recalling here the beginnings of ancient death,

[365] I shall hasten toward new life, sowing tears,

And reap lasting joys; for all of us who mourn in Adam,

196 By scattering seeds, shall soon rejoice,

[368] Carrying our sheaves when Christ comes.

## BOOK TWO

[Note: [Col. 0593B]

That most wicked serpent had driven the first man from his flower-bearing paradise by deceitful arts, and by the allurements of a pleasant taste had made him taste the death hidden beneath it, which soon became bitter. Nor had the transgressor of the commandment alone received the sentence of divine indignation at the cost of life; the human race, proceeding from him, had also been subjected to the condition of a long death. Alas, cruel and guilty wife! Or was that treacherous dragon, the murderer, more so? But you too, wife, were cruel and guilty. Alas! There had been only two immortals. After their offspring began to increase, then it perished, and, bringing forth calamity, the race inherited ruin from its seed. What benefit, in that age, was there in a numerous day and a long span? What benefit was it to exceed nine hundred years of a prosperous life, and, with the tenth generation of descendants growing old, already to see the foreign blood of one’s own race, when the final fate of the human condition, seized by the last courses of an irreversible hour, though late, nevertheless did not turn aside from death, and life, existing briefly through a long succession of time[[Col. 0593] Gallandius has *vita … cum clauderetur*; others have *vitae … qui clauderetur*.], lamented that nothing is lasting if it is closed by an end? Nor did any hope promise that a remedy for this evil would come. But the sepulchral destiny deserved by the first earth-born man would everywhere swallow the nations even of the last offspring with its greedy throat, [Col. 0595B] unless that merciful Creator and Maker of all things, whose characteristic is to pour forgiveness into sins rather than to threaten punishment, had deigned to raise again, through the same Stone, the structure of his work, weakened from its very foundation, on a firmer basis. So that the image which had been made living in the likeness of God might not, through death, be regarded as unlike him, and so that he might bestow the gift of forgiving indulgence and prevent the apples[[Col. 0595D] In an old codex there was *acerva*, arising from the similarity of the letters *b* and *v*, which easily change into one another, as Juretus observes. He also notes that this is taken from Jeremiah 31:30 and Ezekiel 18:2, and is repeated in *Decretum*, distinction 30, where *uvam* is read instead of the *pomum* used here by Sedulius. Perhaps one should read *pomis … obstupescere*.] which the fathers had devoured while unripe from stupefying the teeth of their children, the most gentle and appeased one would grant that, from the place where sins had contracted death, there the boundless mercy of life might nourish them. And just as a sweet and very tender rose grows from a thorny mound, not harming its mother, which it eclipses by the grace of its loveliness, so Mary, coming with sacred light from the stock of guilty Eve, a virgin following the ruin brought by the first virgin, might wash it away; so that human nature, formerly polluted by vices and subjected to the condition of harsh death, might, with Christ born through a human being, allow a human being also to be reborn through Christ, casting off the foulness of the original stain through the renewal of the body's old age.

After the prophetic voice had often foretold these things, and the angel Gabriel had already announced them to Mary, who was present, faithful conception inspired by the Word remained in the womb of the believing girl, and the heavenly offspring lay hidden under the law of birth, though by its own will it granted all things permission to be born. The virgin’s womb swelled, and her untouched body marveled at the fertility of its entrails. A great salvation for the world was promised by the mystery of a female birth without a man: she, stained by no blemish of sin, nourished the child within her stretched belly, soon to become the mother of her own begetter.

Meanwhile the ninth month had passed, and the light of the tenth was shining. In the virgin birth the manifest promise of spiritual grace became clear, and[[Col. 0597D] John 1:14. Ratbertus, who, as I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 168, praises Sedulius, reads it thus: “For the infant was small … little, but withdrawing from the Godhead … which was not … of generation … conceived in the wombs …”] the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—that is, he dwelt in a human being, whose flesh he deigned to put on. A little and yet immense infant, small in limbs, exalted in divinity, flowing forth through the pure chastity of a hospitable temple, did not injure the body as he departed, since he had not injured it when he entered. Truly this is the secret of divine generation: the virgin’s childbirth is presented as its witness. As guardian of his mother’s modesty, he entered through closed wombs and was both conceived and created. What brightness of new light then filled every region of the world! What joy there was in heaven! What radiance flashed forth when Christ, shining with starlike splendor, came forth from Mary’s womb like a bridegroom coming from his marriage chamber (Psalm 18:6)! His divine appearance seemed so preeminent[[Col. 0598D] The editions add *poenitere* in the margin as a variant reading.] that the psalm of David itself declares him in this way: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men. Grace is poured upon your lips,” and so forth (Psalm 44:3). He rightly defined him as beautiful beyond the sons of men, because although he assumed the appearance of a human incarnation and often called himself “the son of man” in evangelical preaching, original sin had nonetheless defiled us, whereas he did not possess it: by the purity of his birth he cleansed us. O merciful and readily accessible compassion that brings salvation! So that the yoke of enduring servitude might not oppress us on account of sin, the Lord assumed the limbs of a servant. Let us hear the voice of Paul the Apostle saying: “He emptied himself and assumed the form of a servant,” and so forth (Philippians 2:7); he who clothes all things from the beginning of the world allowed his limbs, as they were born, to be wrapped in swaddling clothes. And he for whom heaven is too small, for whom earth fails and the wave of the sea does not suffice, remained entire in a child’s body: God lying in a little manger. Hail, excellent mother, consecrated by the birth of so great a King, who rules continually over things above and below in such a way that his authority, power, and name know neither a beginning nor an end; you are shown, through the conspicuous honor of your blessed womb, to be both mother and virgin. No woman is found anywhere equal to you, who either preceded or followed your glory in the same way[[Col. 0599D] Gallandius prudently conjectured and restored *sequatur* for *reperisset signatur*, since sense and metre require it.]; alone pleasing uniquely to Christ, you are incomparable as an example. Then[[Col. 0600D] Gallandius begins chapter 4 here.] through the eloquence of the angelic message the shepherds, first among those keeping watch over their flock by night, recognized the Lord who had been born, so that the Shepherd of the world might shine among shepherds and the Lamb born among flocks might appear. Therefore, as the evangelical message testifies, it declares: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke XI, 13–14). The faithful assertion of the Evangelist shows whose kingdom was being discussed here, when the multitude of the heavenly army praises God in Christ: although his creation was human in accordance with his mother’s condition, the one communion of his divinity demonstrates that the Father is recognized in the Son. They were saying, therefore: “Glory to God in the highest.” Certainly God’s glory remained in the highest, from which Christ, when he came, did not depart. “And on earth peace to people of good will.” We must understand that “earth” here means human beings, from whom we come, formed by the Lord our Maker, who rebuking Adam said: [Col. 0600B] “Because you are earth, you shall go into earth” (Genesis 3:19). Then our earth deserved peace after that savage war in which it fell, when Christ assumed the earth of our flesh. For if in this passage we suppose that “earth” means fields and mountains, what peace can a mass that has been changed and made sluggish possess—or what battles? Thus that peace descended especially upon human beings whom he found capable of good will, so that wherever he saw the searcher of things and hearts to find a sincere purpose, there he might delight to establish the dwelling place of his habitation. For peace, and the principle of better judgment, is not to favor the flesh's struggle against the spirit, but continually to preserve both in harmonious purity under the spirit's rule. Nor should we distrust the weakness of the flesh so much that we seem to despair of heavenly aid. For almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who is acknowledged as mediator between God and human beings, wishing to offer us an excuse based on bodily weakness, sought only the devotion of our will and reserved the perfection of good work for his own majesty. For apostolic teaching explains it in this way, saying: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good,” because, plainly, willing the good is ours, while completing it belongs to God, who pours his peace into people of good will. Then the divine message continues, saying:

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.’ When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ was to be born. They said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judah. For so it is written through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you will go forth a leader who will govern my people Israel.”’ Then Herod, having secretly summoned the Magi, learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child. And when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him’”[[Col. 0601D] Matthew 2:1 ff.].

The birth of Christ, harmonizing appropriately with the authority of the Scriptures[[Col. 0601D] Some place a full stop after *concordans*, taking the subject to be the divine message mentioned at the end of the preceding chapter. A little farther on I have restored *corde persequeris* instead of *prosequeris*.], shone forth from the East, fulfilling what the prayer of Zechariah indicates[[Col. 0601C] Luke 1:78.]: “The Rising One from on high has visited us.” The psalm of David likewise contains something similar[[Col. 0602D] Psalm 18:6.]: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun,” and so forth. By “sun” he means the East, since day always rises from that region. What, then, Herod, are you plotting more cunningly? Why are you madly raging? You confess Christ with your tongue, but persecute him in your heart, and disguise your dark mind, condemned to the obscurity of a cloudy gloom, beneath the serenity of a cheerful face. You order Christ to be sought, not in the worship that you pretend to offer him, but to be killed by the frauds that you devise. You are greatly mistaken and deceived. Believing that he will succeed you, you think he will occupy the royal throne first; yet he neither succeeds nor gives way at all, but, eternal, possesses the throne of his majesty; you read the law and neglect it, while threatening your kingdoms to the King of kings. This guilt lacks words; this treachery lacks excuse. You are trying to extinguish the one whom you had promised to worship. Perhaps you would commit a lesser crime if you sought nothing concerning Christ, so that, by persecuting him merely as an unknown human being, you might appear only a murderer, not also a sacrilegious person offending God[[Col. 0602D] I find *videris* in Gallandius and in other editions of the Fathers, but I think *videreris* should be read.]. Had you not read him warning in David’s song: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104:15)? Why, then, must one obey the divine command, so that neither his Christ nor his prophet may suffer anything from wicked malice[[Col. 0602D] Some have *propheta*, which makes no sense. For *sustineam*, *sustineant* seems to require restoration.], since it is a great sacrilege to treat with insult those consecrated by spiritual anointing? What name will this crime bear, that you seek by your schemes to kill the Lord Christ himself, from whom Christians are named, and the prophet himself, from whom true prophecy descends? Should you not have followed David, who served the Lord’s commands and, when compelled to kill Saul, who had entered the cave where he was hiding[[Col. 0603D] Perhaps *cum ira cogeretur* (“when he was compelled by anger”). Some copies have only *cum cogeretur*. Others have above, incorrectly, *a quo christiani* instead of *a quo Christi*. Some have *in qua latebat*.], answered in this way[[Col. 0603D] First Book of Kings 24:7.]: “Far be this entirely from me; may it not happen to me from the Lord, if I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, for he is the Lord’s anointed”? And he indeed spared an enemy who wished to destroy him. But you lie in wait for the Lord, who was born for the salvation of the world. If, forgetful of the ancient examples, you were moved by none of them, you ought at least on account of this parricidal attempt to lay down your weapons, lest you overthrow the power of the scepter that you wield, since you are acknowledged as an anointed man while persecuting the author of anointing. Yet so that your bloody treachery may not withdraw from the fullness of such a crime, under the honor of the heavenly cross, but with the guilt of your earthly race below[[Col. 0603D] The older editions of the *Library of the Fathers* have *Nec tamen*; *Ne tamen*, with Gallandius, is better. *Infero* is opposed to *aethereo*.], another Herod will later see what you vainly rage to accomplish.

Following the Gospel, therefore, he says this passage:

“When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was. Seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. Falling down, they adored him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

What does it mean that the star they had seen went before them, except that, as they gazed upon the guidance of the little star, they might find the substance of the full light? They adored him because they had truly come to adore him—something Herod, who falsely claimed that he would do so, did not deserve to obtain. For the Lord is not granted to false worshipers to adore him, just as our Lord himself said to the Samaritan woman:

“You adore what you do not know; we adore what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will adore the Father in spirit and in truth. For the Father also seeks such worshipers of him.”

Although the words of the Lord’s teaching are clear and explicit—that none but truth adores the Lord—we must nevertheless examine more carefully the force of the statement: “The hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will adore the Father in spirit and in truth.” I therefore judge, according to the meaning that God grants to my littleness, that by the indication of the present time, in which he openly revealed himself to the world, he said that the Father was to be adored in him. For he made this clear in what follows, saying:

“The Father has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

After saying “in spirit,” he magnificently added “and in truth,” because truth follows those who bear the Spirit of God, while deceit accompanies what is alien. The mystery is also disclosed in the person of the Magi. Through them—Gentiles and foreigners entering into him—our Lord Jesus Christ showed the grace of the future law, namely, that he had already prepared access for all the nations coming to him. For he is known to have spoken this both through his prophets and through himself.

Although he had often foretold this through the prophets, he explained it nevertheless through David’s testimony:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

He called them an inheritance because they were destined to be acquired for the Lord through the grace of the New Testament.

Through himself, in the Gospel, he promised this as a good shepherd:

“I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these also I must bring, and they will hear my voice. And there will be one fold and one shepherd.”

Nor should we think that the devotion represented by the gifts was without divine direction. For through the particular forms of the offerings, each possessing its own proper meaning, Christ’s power was revealed. Gold, if we investigate carefully what is signified by the gift, plainly represents so splendid a substance, radiating the opulence of metallic brilliance, as is fittingly remembered to have been brought to a king. Yet in this king we acknowledge a twofold substance: for Christ reigns especially in heaven, and, having been born in the flesh, is king of the Jews.

The gift of frankincense, because it was formerly used in religious libations and was suitable for incense, is given to Christ as God. Myrrh, which is appropriate for burying bodies, signifies his human nature, destined to die according to the law of burial through the flesh.

The offering of the threefold quantity itself also proclaimed, through its number, the worship of catholic doctrine. For the almighty God, who beholds past and future and always remains—who has always remained and will always remain—established, throughout the course of those times, the foundation of all things in the power of the Three within the one Godhead, although all present things always stand before his eyes. He has taken on neither the old age of antiquity nor the growth of youth. Yet what always is does not cease to be the same.

For when Moses diligently sought the exalted name of his power, so that he might announce it to the people of Israel, God declared it from the flame of the burning bush:

“I am who I am.”

And he said:

“Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Likewise, in the Gospel, he said to the Jews who placed Abraham before him in antiquity:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

Observe the distinction between the two substances, discerning God and man. He said of Abraham, “before he came to be”; concerning himself he did not say, “I was,” but “I am,” because existence belongs to divinity, not having-been, for it abides always in eternity: it arises neither from beginnings nor is it brought to an end by limits. Time is from God; God is not from time.

The text of the reading proceeds:

“Having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way.”

We too, therefore, must imitate the faithful deeds of the Magi. Just as they believed the dream, so let us now believe the clearest manifestations, so that, having been found worthy to adore Christ shining before us through the sign of the Cross, and having offered him threefold gifts of praise from the treasures of our heart, we may no longer return to the ruler of this world, the deceiver who had previously led us astray. Leaving behind the former path, let us proceed along the hidden tracks of him who directs our steps toward the heavenly homeland by confession.

After this, the deeds are related in order:

“Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became exceedingly angry; and he sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the Magi.”

Thus the impious king, deceived by the Magi whom he had believed he would deceive, publicly displayed the concealed impulses of his sudden anger. If indeed it is appropriate to call him a king who neither retained piety nor restrained the passions of his own mind. Rather, he was a most savage and bloodthirsty lion: if perhaps a tender lamb could be snatched away from him, he directed his beastly violence against the entire flock of little ones; he chewed, tore, plucked apart, and destroyed the most delicate sheep, while the wretched mothers stood at a distance, calling for their offspring, already lost in vain, and with repeated bleatings stirred the empty air.

Thus Herod, provoked by the removal of Christ, did not cease, through his bloodstained tyranny, to slaughter the crowds of little ones. By what crime, I ask, does an innocent multitude succumb to death? Why are those who have scarcely just been born already deemed worthy of punishment? It is madness, not reason, in the bloodstained king: hostile to their first cries, and attempting to perpetrate an unspeakable crime, he slaughtered thousands of the infant age and deprived so many mothers at once of their children in a single grief.

One pitiable woman, tearing her dishevelled hair, wounded her bare head through the shameful disfigurement of the loss of her hair. Another furrowed her cheeks, wet with showers of tears, with the violence of her fingernails. Another unhappy mother beat her bloodstained breast with hard blows; no longer truly a mother, she fell upon the cold corpse of her only child and poured out, together with her blood, the milk from her severed breasts.

No one can set forth all the varied and manifold images of that calamity. Amid different kinds of lamentation, the grief was one and the same. What was your feeling, what the intention of your mind—not now a tyrant, but a butcher? What growls did you belch forth in your fury when, looking down from the summit of your citadel upon the wounds of innocent infants, you saw the vast sea of tears gathered into a flood?

Yet among the infants who were certainly killed, not lost, although Christ was absent, he could not be absent. He is always present amid the dangers of the saints and, in a pious movement, feels in himself the punishments inflicted upon other bodies for his sake.

When he had advanced in age and was carrying twelve years—having drawn from the flesh the measure of that number, passing through temporal life according to human reckoning—he revealed himself in wisdom to be older than the elders and in teaching to be the teacher of teachers, demonstrating, as the manifest interpreter of his law, how great he was within.

Nor, after a long delay of time—for what delay can there be in times which flee in winged course, not yet arriving and already departing, as the Evangelist indicates?—was Jesus himself, as it were, already about thirty years old, as was thought, the son of Joseph. Both words—“about” and “was thought”—preserved most admirably the truth of his divinity. For just as he appeared to be about thirty years old although he is eternal, so he was thought to be Joseph’s son although he was begotten from a virgin.

Then he came to the banks of the Jordan to baptize, seeking what he had come to grant: he came to be washed, although he was the one who came to wash. When John the Baptist saw him—the one whom he had sensed while he was hidden in his mother’s womb, already conscious of the coming Christ—he exercised the office of prophecy. Although he could not speak, he began to proclaim, as though emerging from the temporal silence of his mute father, and said:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

When he says “takes away,” he shows that the one who takes them away does not possess them—he took them away not in order to carry them himself, but in order to destroy them himself. Just as we suddenly see the radiance of the rising day poured into the darkness of nocturnal blindness, yet the light does not lose the grace of its splendor through contact with the gloom that it strikes down, so the Lord Jesus Christ, taking upon himself the offenses of the human race, did not retain them but drove them away.

For just as fire purifies metals by consuming their impurities, so the good craftsman cleansed us from our original contagion by his flame. Then the spotless one entered the waters and washed in himself our filth, possessing nothing of his own that required washing. Finally, purifying the very waters by the majesty of his sacred body, he blessed the liquid of the stream, which had received the honor of the Lord’s baptism.

The waves perceived the dread presence of the Godhead. The sea withdrew from the shore; the river turned back toward its source. Concerning these things the prophet sings and signifies:

“The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back.”

What does it mean, “Sea, why did you flee,” and “Jordan, why did you turn back”? The text of the Gospel reading proceeds as follows:

“After he had been baptized, Jesus immediately came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’”

Let us consider more attentively how great a mystery is revealed in this passage. After the Lord had been baptized and had come up from the water, the heavens were immediately opened. How were the heavens immediately opened to Christ, for whom the dwelling above the stars is open and to whom heaven is never seen to be closed? But I judge—so far as his mercy deigns to breathe upon my understanding—that the heavens were opened at that time, when the Lord, baptized, ascended from the water, in order that, through his merciful example, he might teach that the kingdom of heaven is opened to the human being, whose likeness he assumed, when that person has deserved to be drenched with the consecration of spiritual water.

That the Spirit of God descended upon him in the form of a dove shows, through a bird without the bitterness of gall, how great are his goodness, gentleness, and simplicity. And so that no one might fail to understand that God had appeared bodily, the voice of the Father affirmed it, saying:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

This splendid expression of love contains the full firmness of catholic doctrine and declares that the Father and the Son possess one and the same power. For the love that exists in God does not depart from the spirit of likeness and equality. He who, by the law of his commandment, said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” taught that no separation ought to exist between the one who loves and the one who is loved.

Moreover, in the following words that he added—“in whom I am well pleased”—he is understood to have explained the common power of the one Godhead. For “I am well pleased” is stronger than “I am pleased”: “I am well pleased” is a word of mutual accord and perceives two persons adhering to one another. The heavenly voice expressed this for the purpose of showing that the Father is well pleased in the Son and the Son in the Father.

And when the fellowship of the paternal voice, the baptism of the Son, and the descending Spirit had been gathered together, the Trinity shone forth in one God; one who has enumerated the Trinity does not deserve to be worthy of him.

Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. The tempter approached him and said:

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

He was therefore tempted by the devil, who is always the enemy of faith. No one questions an evident matter except one who, full of deceitful ingenuity, does not believe an established truth—like the devil himself, who, after recognizing from the glory of the Father’s utterance that Jesus was the Son of God, and having been terrified by his unique power while he ate nothing for forty days and forty nights, nevertheless attempted to tempt him.

Moses and Elijah likewise endured a fast of the same number of days and nights. But the devil knew that they had done this, although supported by assistance not their own, through their own merit. He saw that Jesus was acting by his own power. He suddenly seized the utterly vain hope of a foolish temptation because the Lord was hungry.

He did not dare to attack the divinity unless he saw that humanity was mingled with it. Immediately reviving his ancient stratagems concerning food, the wicked one raised his customary deceit. Showing him stones as his preferred food, the serpent said:

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

As though he could not do this—he who, continually exercising such an action, brings forth from the rocky entrails of the earth a harvest pregnant with nourishing food, and from the fecundity of stones grants an abundant supply of bread as grain multiplies densely in the ears of corn.

But the singular Wisdom preferred to disregard the glory of a wondrous deed, lest he grant the tempter’s request. For God receives believers but excludes those who tempt him. The people of Israel are read to have offended God especially for this reason: forgetting his benefits, they dared to tempt him, asking for food in desperation. Moses did not remain silent about their unbelief in his books. David likewise recalled and briefly explained it:

“They tempted God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls. And they spoke wickedly against God and said: ‘Can God indeed prepare a table in the wilderness?’” and so forth.

For what can be difficult to him who, because of the immense possibility of all things, is called almighty?

The Lord answered Satan and said:

“It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’”

A very fitting and appropriate answer was given to the enemy. When he asked whether he was the Son of God, he answered as a human being, so that the tempter might be defeated through the very one whom he appeared to have attacked.

When he heard this, broken and weakened, he nevertheless did not lay down the weapons of his audacity.

“And the devil took him and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time. And he said to him: ‘I will give you all this power and their glory, because it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you will worship before me, all these things will be yours.’”

What wonder if the wretched creature spoke perversely? He took the image of the twisted serpent so that he might not walk on straight paths. He supposed that Christ could be touched by desire for a fragile and fleeting kingdom, although Christ had come rather to bestow one strong and eternal.

Or would he deem it worthwhile to acquire worldly riches who had come to teach that they should perish? Would he worship the monster cast down from heaven, for whom heaven is a throne, the earth a footstool, the whole world an act of service, whom no one dares to behold, and whom all the powers above the stars praise with bowed voices?

But again the Lord confounded him with such a reply, saying:

“It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

Here too he is seen to answer from a human persona, disdaining to subjugate the weak rebel by the greater power of his divinity. Although that viperous spite, cast down by the clash of this word, had still not laid aside its disposition toward insolence, it nevertheless raised its wounded head a third time, trusting in the triple vibration of its forked tongue against the victorious hand of the Trinity.

“Then the devil took him into the holy city, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’”

O how much blindness and darkness always rule in his blackened breast! His mind, obscured by the darkness of its own malignity, does not know how to preserve its undetected deceit. Behold: by saying, “If you are the Son of God,” he shows that he does not know this. When he asks again, saying, “He has commanded his angels concerning you,” he confesses that this is the one whom he sees; but, by the ambiguous variation of his speech, he is found to be both a pretender and a dissembler, and is proved a liar by his own arts.

The heart of the wicked is not only a house of deceit but also of stupidity. For what could be found more foolish than that he should believe that the one who is seen upon the level earth to have descended from the highest citadel of heaven would fear a precipitous leap from the lofty heights of the temple and the summit of its exalted pinnacle?

David cries out concerning him and says:

“He descended, and he inclined the heavens,”

containing at once the lowest things and not abandoning the highest.

Therefore the divine voice struck down the failing audacity of the tempter, saying:

“It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

Here he already reveals that he is himself the Lord and God, and forbids the tempter to undertake such attempts any further. Through his own examples, the gracious teacher admonishes us that the spirit, the artificer of ancient wickedness, is undoubtedly subject to human virtues wherever God has been infused into the simplicity of a pure heart.

For the instruction of the reading says:

“Then the devil left him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.”

It seems to me that, in the departure of the fleeing devil and in the ministry that appropriately followed from the angels, an image of paschal glory was being declared through preceding signs. For just as, after the temptations had been conquered and the devil driven away, the angels ministered to the Savior, so, after the insults of the Jews and the punishments of the blessed Passion had been despised, and after the devil’s deceit and death itself had been trampled down, Christ rose from the underworld, was carried up to the stars, and, in his accustomed majestic rule, is adored by the angels in heaven.

After this he summoned and joined to himself certain disciples from among the fishermen, who would thereafter fish for human souls. These souls, pursuing the slippery joy of the world, had wandered through pleasurable falls along uncertain paths, like swimmers upon the fluctuating ways of the tossing sea. He brought such men into the fellowship of eternal life—men whom neither birth from a noble lineage could inflate with earthly nobility nor the brilliance of learned eloquence exalt through the glory of vain chatter. Instead, the holy discipline of a simple life made them conspicuous through a humility that was exceedingly noble and rendered them already near to heaven.

For almighty God chose rather the foolish and weak things of the world, rejecting what appear to be wisdom and strength. As the outstanding teacher, the apostle Paul, says:

“What is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.”

And again he immediately said:

“God chose what is foolish in the world in order to confound the wise; and God chose what is weak in the world in order to confound the strong; and God chose what is ignoble in the world and despised, and what does not exist, as though it did not exist, in order to destroy what does exist.”

Editorial references and textual notes:

- [Col. 0603C–D] John, ch. IV, vv. 22 ff.
- [Col. 0604A–D] Perhaps read *quid sit* (“what it is”) for *qui sit* (“who it is”). John, ch. V, vv. 22–23. Gallandius reads *sicut honorificant patrem* (“just as they honour the Father”); the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum* (1589) and other editions read *sicut honorificavit patrem* (“just as he honoured the Father”). The Gospel reads *honorificant* (“they honour”).
- [Col. 0604C–D] There is an error in many copies of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, which have *et prophetas* (“and the prophets”) without *per* (“through”).
- [Col. 0605B–D] Psalm II, vv. 7–8. Gallandius has *dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam. Haereditatem dixit*, etc. (“I will give you the nations as your inheritance. He said ‘inheritance,’” etc.). Older editions of the Fathers have *Dabo tibi gentes. Haereditatem dixit*, etc. (“I will give you the nations. He said ‘inheritance,’” etc.), which proceeds less satisfactorily.
- [Col. 0606B–D] An old codex reads *sollite*; Juretus restored *sollicite* (or *solicite*), “diligently.” From Exodus, ch. III, v. 14, and shortly afterwards John, ch. VIII, v. 58.
- [Col. 0609B–0610D] The older editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* err in reading *gelidum corruens cadavere*; perhaps the author wrote *gelido corruens cadavere* (“falling upon the cold corpse”). A little later, *semper incertus* is an error in certain printed editions. I have also restored *insontium vulnera* (“wounds of the innocent”), where I found *sontium* (“of the guilty”).
- [Col. 0611A–0612D] Luke, ch. III, v. 23; then John, ch. I, v. 29; and below, Matthew, ch. III, etc. Shortly afterwards *baptizaturus* (“to baptize”) occurs for *baptizandus* (“to be baptized”): many writers of the later age spoke thus, including Isidore and Julian of Toledo, in whose editions similar words now appear altered.
- [Col. 0617A–D] The serpent’s rather proper food: from Genesis, addressed to the serpent, “You shall eat earth.” See the note on the poem *Genesis*, which I published after Juvencus, v. 110. In many copies of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, *amitteret* (“should lose”) is corrupt for *admitteret* (“should admit”). Shortly afterwards occur words from Psalm LXXVII, vv. 18–19.
- [Col. 0618B–D] I would think that *An ille*, etc. (“Or would he?”) should be read with a question mark.
- [Col. 0619B–C] Psalm XVII, v. 10. The Vulgate reads, “He inclined the heavens and descended.” Just before this, it would be preferable to read *videretur* (“might seem”) for *videtur* (“is seen”).
- [Col. 0621A–B] From the corruption *contiavit*, Juretus rightly restored *conciliavit* (“he joined” or “he brought into fellowship”).

Quin etiam, desiring in his mercy to bring swift salvation, the Savior also established the manner of prayer and appointed the petitions. The most compassionate Judge wishes to be asked briefly, so that he may the sooner grant the petitioner’s request. Thus he taught us to pray to the Father—his Father by nature, but ours by grace—bestowing his own title upon human beings, so that what he alone possesses in a distinguished manner he might generously grant to all:

**Our Father, who art in heaven.**

Since we dare to call the everlasting ruler of heaven by the name “Father,” we must first observe that the house of so great a gift has been assigned not separately to individuals, but communally to everyone. For, as though set apart from the others and secretly dwelling in more secluded places, no one should beseech the Lord in the words of this prayer by saying “My Father,” but “Our Father,” because this expression properly belongs to Christ alone, whose Father God truly is.

Although this is recorded throughout all the Gospels, nevertheless, in the Gospel of John the Lord Jesus clearly taught, in the chapter concerning his own right, that this power was uniquely his and distinct from the common crowd, when he encouraged his disciples by saying: “I am going to my Father and your Father.” By saying “my,” he appropriately claimed this special glory for himself; by saying “your,” he revealed that grace was generally shared by all.

Let us offer here some comparison, so that we may grasp divine matters through human examples. Let us suppose, then, some nobleman who has an only son and several servants. Can the condition of the servants’ affection toward him be equal to that of his son merely because he is called the head of the household, when the son himself is evidently lord of them all? We therefore use this prayer; Christ does not, because in this prayer of supplication we ask even him for something—him who, together with the Father, is one Lord, coeternal.

Thus, when we say “Our Father,” we confess that we all exist as brothers in him. We must not scorn the affection belonging to this name by banishing mutual love, nor follow the memorials of original hatred, by which Cain, shedder of his brother’s blood, became the originator of the stain of fratricide. Rather, burning with the fire of a gentle spirit, let us lay aside the wickedness of our carnal antiquity and rejoice that we have been clothed with the new man. Otherwise, when earthly deeds begin to degenerate from heavenly ones, we may appear unworthy of so great a Father, who, with Christ as our guide, received us as those born through holy adoption.

**Hallowed be thy name.**

What sanctification can be imagined by which the Lord may be sanctified, when he sanctifies all things, except that we prepare for his entrance a pious, gentle, peaceful, and chaste heart? In this way, delighted by such a dwelling, he may increase his sanctification within us, just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself recalled that he had been glorified in his disciples, although he always shone with the clear light of divinity.

For in the Gospel according to John, while he was pleading with the Father on behalf of his disciples, among the various words he uttered he said: “And I have been glorified in them”—that is, “because he found his glory in them.”

Wherever, therefore, he finds signs of his own sanctification, he says that he sanctifies himself there. For that boundless and most gentle piety declares that whatever it produces in its servants is conferred upon itself. A similar meaning is also shown when he commands himself to be blessed, although he himself rather blesses all things. Indeed, the universal hymn of the three youths singing in the furnace calls upon every creature, in its order, to bless the Lord.

**Thy kingdom come.**

We ask that the kingdom of the ruler may come—of him who never ceases to reign—so that he may punish the false prince of this world for his presumed tyranny, and that he alone, who alone truly is, may display his dominion, neither bound by death nor destined to be consumed by time.

For that day of light knows no time: it is an unbroken day without night. There the strongest soldier, having adored Christ, will rejoice, after emerging victorious from the various battles of the world, adorned with the perpetual distinction of a crown that will decorate his blessed head.

**Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.**

Here too the meaning seems to belong to the preceding thought: we ought to ask with unceasing prayers, day and night, that the will of him who nowhere wishes wickedness to exist may fill heaven and earth. Thus, when the devil has been cast down from heaven, the earth may not suffer him as an enemy; nor may the fierce serpent attack the earthly substance of our body, formed as it is from clay, as food for his voracity, or, once he has entangled us in his most evil persuasions, clasp and encircle us in scaly coils until, intoxicating us with deadly poisons, he consumes our wretched life by his licking.

Therefore let us continually beseech the Lord to protect equally both soul and flesh within us: for with one part we are heaven, while with the other we are the seed of earth.

**Give us this day our daily bread.**

For those who ask for the nourishment of daily bread, a threefold meaning of interpretation is disclosed, although all the Scriptures ought to be understood in this way. According to the literal sense, therefore, we seem to ask specifically for bread from the grain-bearing seed, in order that we may eat it; morally, we ask the Lord as servants that we may deserve to obtain our daily ration, since we know that the pattern of both kinds of reasoning proceeds from spiritual discipline.

For this reason we are commanded to ask every day for food to sustain life, lest, by storing anything up for tomorrow, we appear to doubt divine providence. Yet this is proved so difficult and arduous that only a few, and very rare, men can observe such a rule. The Lord himself, faithful in all things, who sustained the children of Israel after leading them out of Egypt through many years of wilderness desolation, feeding them daily while they rested only on the Sabbath, promised in the Gospel sayings that he would do the same for us if our faith did not fail. Addressing his disciples, he said among other teachings: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself.”

But if we wish to understand more fully, in the spiritual sense, the things of which we are speaking, we shall perceive that this bread is the divine word. If the mind fasts even briefly from its substantial teaching, it will suffer the deprivation of great hunger. There is indeed no small difference between spiritual and bodily banquets. We are commanded to eat the latter sparingly, but never to refuse the former. In the one case abstinence is healthy; in the other, appetite becomes life-giving.

Thus David, practicing meditation on the Lord’s law day and night, declares himself to cling to blessedness in these words:

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.”

This meditation surely satisfies and delights, like the rich sweetness of honey. Although it quickly fills the belly of the one who eats, it is nevertheless never found to offend nature with its nectarous sweetness.

Let us hear also what the same prophet says:

“How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!”

He precisely defined the words of the law as something to be understood when he said that they are sweet to the palate, not to the ears; that they are supplied like honey and the honeycomb to the mouth, not to the hearing. Even the deaf, whose hearing offers no assistance, are likewise filled through the service of the mouth when they read the heavenly commandments.

The Apostle also, in the letter he used for the Corinthians, made clear that spiritual food is teaching, saying: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

Who could doubt, or alone hesitate, that all these things are represented spiritually? No fool could suppose that those people were infants or that they had received nourishment of milk from the Apostle. Rather, as beginners in absorbing the words of the law and gradually being imbued with divine teachings, they ought to be understood as drinking beginnings that were like milk for infants. For just as good teaching is nourishing food, so evil teaching is harmful.

Therefore the Lord warned his disciples spiritually to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He knew that men of an acid doctrine could corrupt the abundance of all sweetness by a slight touch, since, as the same Apostle Paul says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.”

For even if we believe that this bread is more particularly the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, nevertheless it does not depart in any way from spiritual understanding, especially because such a banquet, and such a prayer, is divinely handed down to no Gentiles and no Jews, but only to Christians.

**And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.**

If we carefully weigh the vows of our petition, it becomes clear that the pardon either to be granted or to be denied us is determined by our own examples. We are commanded to hope from the Lord for that which we are seen to have forgiven a fellow servant. For the same law of condition binds us all equally, so that, just as we do not wish to be debtors, neither should we desire to have debtors.

In the persons of others we are either released or bound. If it is thought uncertain what debtors are meant here, the weak material for an excuse must be set aside: whether your brother has been liable to you through fault, or money, or anything else, release it. For it is not merely the frequent presumption of offenses, but also the dishonorable handling of financial amounts, that shows many people to be entangled in numerous bonds before the Lord.

Whoever, in proportion to the measure of his means, has been inhuman toward a needy person denies to God what belongs to him and renounces him whose infinite mercy so protects the straits of the wretched that whatever benevolent stewardship gives to the poor, he testifies to have benefited himself.

We are also debtors because, having received divine benefits, we make promises in our vows, until we discharge them with faithful intention. Thus we ought to understand that what has been said about monetary debts also applies to the various other kinds of sins by which we are held bound under eternal judgment.

We know why offenses have been compared with a monetary debt: “For the love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10), and without that vicious seed scarcely any crimes are generated in evil.

Here one man commits murder in order to seize from an innocent person what he desired. Another, enticed by the reward he has received, becomes a swearer of false testimony. Some are driven into the prostitution of adulterous intercourse by the shameful purchase of sexual commerce. Others stain themselves by theft; others deny a deposit entrusted to them. There are many more things like these, with which the ever-present hunger for gold is always allied.

Yet no crime is easily committed in which the agency of money does not lend its assistance. Therefore, having obtained the gift of divine mercy and received the impunity of heavenly forgiveness, let us not deny one another what we have received. Otherwise, though released from greater debts, if we do not cancel the smaller ones, we shall again become entangled in the greatest bonds.

Then that merciful giver, the Lord who does not demand the debt, who released for us ten thousand talents, if he perceives that for the sake of a hundred denarii we are strangling a fellow servant, will command that everything be exacted by delivering us to savage torturers. Cast into prison custody, we shall not be allowed to leave until we pay everything, down to the last farthing, that has been lost through our offenses.

**And lead us not into temptation.**

This does not mean that the Lord, who is the way of light and the path of peace, leads anyone into the snares of temptation. Rather, when he abandons those who reject the divine commandments, he permits them to enter. For all who pursue the contagions of the slippery world, caught in seductive nets and seeking the luxuries of alluring destruction, are abandoned by the Lord, who loves pure virtue, and proceed wherever pleasurable temptation has dragged them.

Therefore let us strive to draw our foot back from this, rather choosing to tread down the narrow path, which, by a slender track unknown to many, secretly climbs toward the difficult gate of the heavenly kingdoms.

**But deliver us from evil.**

When we ask to be delivered from evil, we confess that the one whom we ask to deliver us is good. Nor is it without reason that the deliverer must be pursued, while the one who slaughters must be avoided. In the one case, the tree of life is recognized through good fruits; in the other, through evil acts, the root of the ancient transgression.

The Gospel reading has made clear that “fruits” are to be understood as works. There the Lord, opening up the minds of different people, commanded that each person be recognized from his own fruits—that is, from his deeds—saying: “You will know them by their fruits.”

Indeed, just as heaven is separated from earth, fire from water, light from darkness, peace from wars, and life from tombs, so, through an equally great distance of separation, good things are distinguished from evil.

For there are always two choices at the service of the judgment of our deliberation, by which we may either hold the right-hand path or the left. We are not ignorant or uncertain that the right-hand path belongs to the righteous, rejoicing in the bosom of the patriarch Abraham, while the left is assigned to the deep punishments of the ungodly. Hence no one can cross from one side to the other through that vast chaos and the immense danger of the precipitous mass.

This, then, is the freedom we desire: that, if we are worthy to be counted sheep and lambs of the supreme Shepherd, we may deserve to escape the savage bites of wolves and already enjoy a secure life through the sweetest pastures of Christ, in the most delightful beauty of abundant flowers.

**Editorial notes on the preceding exposition**

[Col. 0623D] In the old codex there was an error, *Nam quasvise semotus*, which Juretus corrected. Shortly afterwards words from John, chapter 20, verse 17 are cited. One *in* seems superfluous in the phrase “in that … in chapter.”

[Col. 0624D] In most Libraries of the Fathers the reading is: “that I found his glory in them.” Gallandius has: “that because I found my glory in them.” It seems necessary to restore: “that because he found his glory in them.” The sequence of the following sentence confirms this reading.

[Col. 0625D] In the old codex Juretus found *hujus* in place of *mundi* in “the prince”; he suspects that the author wrote *hujus mundi proprincipem* (“the fore-prince of this world”). This is not pleasing. Shortly afterwards the old codex retained the corrupt reading *nec morte constium*, for which Gallandius conjectures *nec morte constrictum* (“not bound by death”); this is indeed the reading in certain Libraries of the Fathers, and I would not readily alter it. I likewise retain below *adorato Christo* (“Christ having been adored”) from the Libraries of the Fathers, whereas Juretus and Gallandius, with the old codex, read *odorato Christo* (“Christ having been perfumed”). Juretus rightly corrected the error *praelia victor* to *praelio victor*.

[Col. 0627D] In some printed editions *mortaliter* is erroneous for *moraliter*. Shortly afterwards the old codex had *Quod tamen illaboriosum probatur*; Juretus corrected it.

[Col. 0628D] I willingly accept Gallandius’s conjecture *illas numquam* (“never the former”), in place of *illas namque*, which all printed editions give with the contrary sense. Juretus corrected the old book’s error *beatitudinis his verbis* to *beatitudini se his verbis*. The words of Psalm 1:1 ff. and, again, Psalm 118:103 are cited.

[Col. 0629D] Below the old codex read *Quis dubitet que solus ambigat*; Juretus restored the passage. The mention of leaven which follows occurs in Matthew 16:6 and in 1 Corinthians 5:6.

[Col. 0629D; 0630D] All printed editions read *generantur in malo* (“are generated in evil”). Gallandius inserted *generantur in mundo* (“are generated in the world”) into the text from his own conjecture. I do not think it necessary to abandon the old reading. Below, *quadrantis amissa* seems to require *admissa*, that is, “committed,” or “sins.” Some prefer *amissa*, that is, “squandered.”

[Col. 0631D] In many Libraries of the Fathers the text has *subdit* (“brings under”); but, with Gallandius, *subit* (“goes up”) seems the reading required.

[Col. 0631D; 0632D] In the old codex there was *arborem vitae* (“the tree of life”); in certain Libraries of the Fathers, *arbores vitae* (“trees of life”). Gallandius prints *arbor vitae* (“a tree is of life”). Perhaps it would be preferable to rewrite *arbor est vitae* (“the tree is of life”). Juretus says that the word *actus* seems suspect. Gallandius restores, or says it should be understood, as “through evil [lacuna] acts.” The syntax is indeed intricate, but perhaps this is characteristic of Sedulius’s style.
