[Col. 0632D] Juretus seems to have retained the old codex’s reading *nullus adulterum*, which is plainly corrupt. Others report *nullus ad alterum*, which can be tolerated; others *nullus ad ulterum*, which has no sense.

[Col. 0632D] Juretus wished it noted that this was the reading in the old codex.

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593A] **Note:**

1. Reg. 2: “Here begins Book I, concerning the expulsion of the first-created man from Paradise.” Vat. 2: “The second book of Sedulius the presbyter.” Meus: “Here happily begins Sedulius’s second book on the history of the Lord.” Ms. of Nic. Heinsius: “The first book of Sedulius on the New Testament.” Cant.: “The first book on the New Testament.” Ott. 2: “On the New Testament.” Arntz.: “Here begins the second book.” Ott. 1, as the title of the first chapter: “Concerning Adam.” Rom.: “That Adam was expelled from Paradise.” Urb.: “Concerning the fall of the first-created man through the dragon.”

   This first verse and the following six are reproduced in the *Pisaurian Collection of Poets*, vol. VI, p. 282, among the minor poems of uncertain authorship, taken from the Maurist *Tractatus diplomaticus*, vol. III, part II, section 4, chapter 2, article 1. The Pisaurian compiler evidently did not know that they belonged to Sedulius.

2. Some printed editions have *blandisque*; the manuscripts and most editions have *blandique*, supported by the prose. Poelm., with certain printed editions, has *soporis*; other printed editions, together with most manuscripts and the prose, have *saporis*, whose gloss in Reg. 1 is “of that fruit.”

3. Parrh. has *laeto misero*; the others, *lethum misero*. Reg. 1, instead of *d. s.*, or by correction, and Vatt. 1, 2, Ottob. 2, Urb., Ald., Rom., Alb., Reg. 5, and Ang. have *portarat*. Reg. 2, apparently by the first hand, Reg. 4, Poelm., and others have *portabat*. Meus has *portavit*. Reg. 2 by the second hand, Parrh., and perhaps Reg. 1 by the first hand have *potabat*. Ott. 1 has *potabat* in the margin and *portat* in the text, but it seems originally to have been *deportat*; this same *deportat* is another reading in Reg. 1.

   The genuine reading seems to me to be *potarat*, although I find no example of the active meaning of *potare*—“to give someone water or wine to drink”—or metaphorically, *lethum*, “death,” for “to offer something to be drunk or tasted.” Compare Book IV, verse 180: “About to taste the bitter death after a short time.” If *potarat* is less pleasing, certainly *portarat* is much better than *portabat*.

4. Ott. 2 has *sumpserat*: read *senserat*.

7. Parrh. punctuates: “You, harmful wife, or rather that treacherous dragon?” In Virgil, whom Sedulius is imitating, the punctuation could likewise be: “Cruel mother, or rather that wicked boy?” Most people place a comma after *magis*.

12. Reg. 4 reads erroneously: “To see, no longer the father.”

13. The printed editions, together with most manuscripts, have *senum*. Ott. 1 has *senes*, which could be explained as: “What good was it that old men should see the tenth generation of grandchildren,” and so forth. Burmann conjectured *senem*, I think with the same meaning. The best copies have *spectare*, that is, “to see.” Some printed editions, with Ang., have *exspectare*, a word frequently confused by scribes with *spectare*; nevertheless, *exspecto* is sometimes used for *specto* or *aspecto*. See Book I of Dracontius, verse 356.

14. Parrh. has *convicta*; it should be read with *victa*. Nebrissensis interprets it: “which is finally overcome by the multitude of years.”

15. Reg. 4 has *inseparabilis horae*, an error against meter and sense arising because many manuscripts write *inreparabilis*. Virgil, Book X, verse 467: “Each has his appointed day; brief and irretrievable time is given to all.”

17. Reg. 1, Vatic. 2, Ald. have *nihil esse*; most have *nil esse*, which amounts to the same thing. Taur.: “A brief life is nothing long, with an end of sorrow.” Our manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *cum fine doleret*. Fabr. and some other printed editions have *doceret*, contrary to the prose.

197 The most savage serpent had driven the first-born man

from the flower-bearing seat, and with the allurements

of pleasant flavor had made that wretched man drink bitter death.

Nor had the presumptuous man alone felt the deserved anger,

[5] lying under the mortal law; rather, from him the entire human race

had likewise fallen. Alas! harmful wife,

198 harmful wife, were you more harmful, or that treacherous dragon?

That treacherous dragon was harmful, but you too were a harmful wife.

Alas! the two had been eternal. After the origin

[10] began to grow, it perished and took destruction from its seed.

What benefit was there in the long succession of days, what in that time,

to see more than nine hundred years happily,

and behold the tenth generation of descendants from old men,

and now not know one’s own race, when, overcome by the final

[15] courses and when the irretrievable destiny of the last hour,

though late, was to come, and a short life would grieve

through a long age that it was nothing for long?

Nor would hope bring returning help, nor would the tomb of the first earthborn man swallow his descendants in its blind throat:

[Col. 0595A] **Note:**

19. Wopkens, although he approves *caeca*, nevertheless suspects *saeva*.

20. Ottob. 1: *Ne pius*; read *Ni pius*. Cant. incorrectly has *prius* for *pius*. In Ott. 1, *culpis* seems to have been written instead of *culpas*. Although *ignosco* is more frequently found with the dative, it is also correct with the accusative, especially when *Reddere difficilis*, namely “difficult to repay,” follows.

21. *Reddere culpas*, “to repay offenses,” meaning “to punish” or “to exact vengeance,” is a phrase taken from sacred writings and also used by Augustine, Paulinus of Petricordia, and similar authors.

23. Parrh. observed in the additions that in one place *vernale* was written instead of *veniale*, namely “servile work,” or “a servant,” who was performing his own work. The connection of letters by which *veniale* is written in some manuscripts may have given rise to this reading. In Reg. 1 the gloss is *veniale — recuperabile*, “pardonable—recoverable.” Others interpret it as “worthy of pardon.” It may also be understood adverbially. See the note on Dracontius, *Satisfactio*, verse 121: “For you threaten that the offenses of enemies are pardonable.”

25. Meus has *mandare*; correct to *mandere*. The syntax is obscure and must be explained from the prose. From that prose it seems that the past tense should be read: *Quae mansere*, “which remained,” or, as some prefer, *mansere*, or *manduere*, which can stand through synaeresis.

26. *Donare* for *condonare*, “to pardon” or “to remit,” is elegant; but it is usually joined with an accusative, such as “injuries,” whereas here the construction is “so that piety might give,” and so forth.

28. Reg. 1, Burmann’s manuscript, and some printed editions have *Et velut in spinis*. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *Et veluti e spinis*. Most have *Et velut e spinis*. Ottob. 1 has *Ut velut spinis*; the *e* is missing, and *Ut* is not satisfactory. The Alb. manuscript has *Et velut ex spinis*.

   In Gerson’s sermon 3, *On the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God*—or whoever the author of that sermon may be—the reading is: “Behold, as from thorns the noble rose”; but *nobilis* cannot stand metrically. In those verses the author of the sermon proves that the Blessed Virgin was conceived without the stain of original sin. Sedulius is imitating Virgil, *Eclogues* 5.39.

29. A certain manuscript cited by Wassey in the index to Sallustius has *honorem*, “honor,” which cannot be approved. Wopkens conjectures: “Nothing harmful, having a mother whom he obscures by honor.” But the common reading is clearer; its gloss in Reg. 1 is: “and the mother—her thorny shoot.” In the cited sermon of Gerson, the text is: “Nothing that harms, having—or that obscures—honor,” which I do not approve.

30. In Ott. 1 the title here is “Concerning Eve”; in Reg. 1, “Concerning holy Mary.” The Arntz. manuscript has *pia* instead of *sacra*. Sedulius sometimes lengthens and sometimes shortens the first syllable of *Maria*, as at verse 49 below: “What was that radiance of Mary?”

31. In the cited passage of Gerson, read *piaret* for *piat*.

32. Parrh. and the Poelm. sheets have *Et quoniam*.

34. Ottob. 1, Vat. 1, and Urb. have *Possit*; the others have *Posset*. In Reg. 2, *Poscet* was corrected to *Posset*. Reg. 1 has *maculas* instead of *maculam*. Arntz. has *culpae* instead of *carnis*; but *carnis* is preferable, for the subject is the old man, as Paul calls him in Ephesians 4:22. *Macula*, “stain,” is often used by Cicero and others for disgrace, infamy, or shame.

[Col. 0596D] 35. Rom., as title: “Where Mary received the Holy Spirit.” Meus: “The Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin.” Vat. 1: “The Angel to Mary.” Urb. has *praedixere*, contrary to the meter. Our manuscripts, together with Ald., Parrh., and other printed editions, have *dixere*, which Arntzenius also restored, although he found *cecinere* in some printed editions. Both verbs are suitably used of oracles; but *cecinit* occurs in the following verse.

36. Taur. has the corrupt reading *propheta* instead of *properata*, as Bede also reads in *De metris*.

37. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *dictum est comitata*, which comes from a gloss.

199 Unless that pious sower, ready to forgive offenses

but difficult to repay them, had restored his work,

lest what had been made should perish,

and, taking pity, had renewed the image that stood alive,

like to God, though it would become unlike him in death,

and had forbidden the bitter fruits

[25] which the fathers would eat, while the teeth of their children shuddered,

and, always appeased toward his own, had granted

that, from the place where guilt had given death,

piety might give salvation.

And just as a soft rose rises from sharp thorns,

[Col. 0596A] 200 having nothing that harms and obscuring its mother with honor,

[30] so Mary, coming sacredly from Eve’s stock,

a new pious virgin, might atone for the crime of the ancient virgin:

so that, since the earlier nature lay corrupted

under the dominion of death, when Christ was born

man might be restored and lay aside the stain of the old flesh.

[35] After the prophets had foretold these things to the elders,

the angel sang to the untouched Mary of what had been hastened,

and faith accompanied the declaration, as well as the womb of the maiden—

[Col. 0597A] **Note:**

38. Parrh. has *complevit* instead of *mox implet*, contrary to the Poelm. sheets.

39. Reg. 1 has *Nascendo*; the second hand has *Nascendi*. Cellarius, with the sole manuscript of Heinsius, has *plenos*. Gruner and Arntzenius restored *tensos*, which the Taurin. manuscript and our copies confirm, except Vat. 1, where *plenos* occurs. Both phrases are poetic. The prose supports *tensos*.

40. Burmann’s conjecture is *clauditque suum*. I, on the contrary, if I had found *clauditque*, would have conjectured *gaudetque*: so much more pleasing is this reading than the other.

41. Rom.: “The Nativity of the Lord.” Poelm.: “Christ is born of the Virgin.” Arntzenius notes that in Vet. 1 and Mon. *decem* is pointless, but does not distinguish whether *decem* is used for *novem*, “nine,” or for *decimi*, “of the tenth.” Either alternative must be rejected. The same Arntzenius, together with the Poelm. sheets, has *de lumine*; the recent Ott. 2 also has this. All our other copies, with Parrh., Ald., Edimb., and the Arntz. manuscript, have *de limine*. In the prose I likewise prefer *limen* to *lumen*. Nebrissensis explains it as “in the beginning” and notes that one preposition is used for another, namely *de* for *in*.

43. Ott. 1 hesitantly has “The Word became flesh”; Reg. 5 and Aldus have it clearly. The punctuation should then be: “The Word completed the promised work, having become flesh—wishing to dwell among us.”

47. Ottob. 2 has *clausam ingrediens, clausamque relinquens*, “entering closed and leaving closed,” which also occurred to Burmann. But the common reading, with the manuscripts’ gloss *clausa — viscera*, “closed—womb,” is sound. In Ang. *clausam ingrediens* seems to occur; afterward *et clausa relinquens* is clear. Ratbertus extracted this clear testimony to the untouched virginity of the Mother of God before and during childbirth from the prose, as I stated in note 168 of the *Prolegomena*.

48. In Reg. 1 the reading seems originally to have been, as in the others, *gratia*; but an old hand also wrote *gaudia*, “joys,” which certainly need not be displeasing and is supported by the prose.

50. Vat. 1 by the first hand, Cant., and Torn. 2 have *decore*. In Vat. 1 this became *decoro*, as in our other manuscripts and most printed editions, supported by the Poelm. sheets. Some printed editions have *decora*, which is less satisfactory.

[Col. 0598D] 51. Urb. has *ovas*; read *ovans*.

52. Reg. 1 has, above *filiis*, another reading or correction, *Prae natis*, which most other manuscripts and printed editions reproduce. In Ott. 1, above *natis*, *filiis* appears as a gloss. In the Leipzig edition *Prae filiis* was printed, with two syllables contracted into one.

53. Parrh. has *In labris*.

55. Urb. and Ott. 2, with Parrh., have *damnante*; the others have *dominante*.

56. Vat. 1 has *primaque*.

58. Ott. 1 has *Obvisis*; above it, *Obsitus*. *Obsitus pannis* occurs in Terence; although many understand this as “soiled with rags,” *obsitus* properly means “covered” or “wrapped.”

59. Some printed editions have *Quem procellosi*, contrary to the meter.

60. Cant. and Torn. 2 and 3 have *speciosaque*; *spatiosaque* better fits the meaning. These words are frequently changed one into the other.

201 Soon he filled the heavenly burden, and the creator of all things

was subject to the law of birth; the unwedded Virgin marvels

[40] at her swollen womb and rejoices that she will give birth to her own parent.

And now, after nine months had passed, from the threshold of the tenth month

the sacred day shone forth, when the Word, made flesh,

the Word, made flesh, fulfilled the promised work;

wishing to dwell among us, then the greatest Infant,

[45] preserving undefiled the inner chamber of his own temple,

emptied the unharmed passage; childbirth stands forth as witness

to the Virgin: entering while it was closed, and leaving it closed.

202 What new light for the world, what grace for the whole heaven!

[Col. 0598A] What was that radiance of Mary when Christ came forth

from her womb in new splendor? Just as the bridegroom himself,

triumphant, handsome in form, comes from the bridal chamber,

beautiful beyond the sons of men, whose radiant countenance

[50] diffused a gentler grace upon his lovely lips.

O easy mercy! Lest the yoke of servitude should hold us

under dominant sin, the supreme Lord took on servile

limbs, and he who from the beginning of the world

clothes all things that are born with gifts of his own,

203 wore coverings of tiny rags:

nor could the unmoving wave of the stormy deep,

[60] nor all the soil of the lands, nor the broad expanses of the wide—

[Col. 0599A] **Note:**

61. Vet. 1 and 2: *puerile*, “childlike.”

62. *Praesepe* is ablative, just as Plautus, Lucretius, and Ovid more than once used *mare* in the same case. *Praesepe* may also derive from *praesepis*, feminine genitive, if *angusta* is read. Compare Book IV, verse 301.

63. Rom.: “Here he praises the Lord’s mother.” Meus: “The Salutation.” Poelm.: “A Greeting to the Virgin Mother.” These seven verses are distinguished in red lettering in the Urb. manuscript. See *Prolegomena*, no. 170.

64. All our manuscripts, together with most other manuscripts and printed editions, have *tenet*. Parrh., Lips., the Poelm. sheets, and the Poelm. edition in the margin have *regit*, which may perhaps be a gloss somewhere, since in Rom. the gloss on *tenet* is *gubernat*, “rules.” Arntzenius shows from Justin and Mela that *tenere* can be understood in this sense. Bede, in Alcuin’s *Homiliary*, Cologne 1569, in the commemoration of the Blessed Virgin, gives these six verses and the more recent reading *regit*.

65. Reg. 1 has *Nomen*, but corrected to *Numen*. In the Lips. manuscript Cellarius suggests *Numine* or *Nomine*. Urb. and Rom. have *Numen aeterno*, omitting *et*. Meus has *Numen ab aeterno*. The true reading is *Numen, et aeterno*. Wopkens would prefer *jure* for *gyro*, with which I cannot agree: there is a fine opposition between *in gyro* and *manet*. For the ages revolve in perpetual circuit and motion, whereas God, and his nod—that is, his divine will—and his dominion remain unchanged. Nebrissensis thinks that *aeterno* refers to the archetypal world, or is used for “always.” But the verb *gyro* rather indicates the perpetual motion by which created things are moved. From the prose, however, no certain interpretation of this passage can be extracted.

68. Parrhasius’s reading is plausible: *Nec primam, aut similem visa es, nec habere sequentem*. *Primam* could be understood as “the earlier one.” All the others disagree. Reg. 1 has *Nec primam visa es similem*; the rest, as also the liturgical books, have *Nec primam similem visa es*. Saint Bernard, in sermon 4 *On the Assumption*, transposes the verses to fit his sermon: “In this one thing she has neither been seen to have an equal before nor a successor—possessing a mother’s joys together with the honor of virginity.”

70. Ottob. 1: “Where he shone forth to the shepherds.” Meus: “Announced to the shepherds.” Ottob. 1 by correction, Ott. 2, Alb., Reg. 2, 4, 5, Rom., Meus, Vatt. 1 and 2, Urb., Ald., Parrh., the Cant. manuscripts, and Arntz. have *creator*. Reg. 1 has *creatus*, which may also have been in Ott. 1; there the gloss is *secundum humanitatem*, “according to his humanity,” and in most printed editions it is retained instead of *natus*, “born,” since *creari* has this meaning, which the prose confirms.

71. All our manuscripts, together with the oldest printed editions, the manuscript of Heinsius, and the Poelm. sheets, have *Enituit*. Cellarius, with other printed editions, preferred *Emicuit*, from a similar passage in Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 9, verse 27: “The one long promised shines forth.” Arntzenius retains this because those who emerge suddenly and unexpectedly are said to *emicate*, like lightning. But here the common reading of the old copies, *Enituit*, seems more genuine and more appropriate, especially if attention is paid to the expression *Enituit pastoribus*, “he shone forth to the shepherds,” because the Lamb, who is the shepherd, shone forth to the flocks. The prose confirms this with *claresceret*, “might become bright.” Vat. 1 has *qui pastor erat*, “who was a shepherd”; Vat. 2 ambiguously has *qui* or *quia*.

The court of heaven cannot contain him, full

though he remained in a child’s body; God rested in a narrow manger.

Hail, holy mother, woman who bore the King,

who holds heaven and earth throughout the ages, whose

[65] divine will, embracing all things in an eternal circuit,

and whose dominion remains without end; you who possess

a mother’s joys together with the honor of virginity,

[Col. 0600A] 204 have neither been seen to have an equal before nor a successor,

you alone, a woman without example, pleased Christ.

[70] Then, first to the shepherds who had known nothing, he who had been born

205 shone forth, because he was a shepherd, and the Lamb

shone upon the flocks; and the angelic assembly sang of the wonders.

[Col. 0601A] **Note:**

73. Rom.: “When the star appeared to the Magi.” Meus: “He is signified to the Magi.”

74. Meus has *summumque tyrannum*, “and the supreme tyrant,” which I do not follow. Bede, *On Meter*, also retains the common reading *saevumque*, “and the savage tyrant.”

77. Alb. has *Per genitum*; read *Progenitum*. Reg. 4: *ducem, ac coelitus*; Urb.: *ducem, haec coelitus*. The others have *ducem, hoc*. Bede, *On Meter*, in the chapter on synaloepha, approves this hiatus because of the aspiration of the word *hoc*, which has the force of a consonant; he praises this verse of Sedulius together with another by Juvencus, Book I, verse 61: “You must remember to call him John by name,” as I noted on that passage of Juvencus.

78. Urb. has *Haec stellam*.

79. Meus has *succedere terrae*, which gives no sense.

81. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, Alb., Parrh., Vet. 1 and 2, Monast., the three Tornæsian editions, and other editions read *habens* (“having”). Reg. 2 and 5, Urb., Ott. 2, Meus, Rom., Ang., Vatt. 1 and 2, Cant., read *alens* (“nourishing”), with a gloss in Reg. 2, *nutriens* (“nourishing”). In Ott. 1, *alens* seems to have arisen from *habens*, with the gloss *tegens* (“concealing”); and in Reg. 1 someone tried to change the *b* in *habens* into *l*, so that it now reads *halens*. More recent editors—Cellarius, [Col. 0602D] Grunerus, and Arntzenius—condemn *habens*, as though it were a scribal error. Expressions such as *alere vulnus* (“to nourish a wound”), *alere sitim* (“to nourish thirst”), *alere sententiam* (“to nourish an opinion”), *alere amorem* (“to nourish love”), *alere curas* (“to nourish cares”), and *alere malum* (“to nourish evil”) certainly occur frequently. Nevertheless, *habens* seems to me to come from Sedulius’s own hand: it means nothing other than that Herod concealed the clouds of his mind beneath a serene expression, which is better expressed by *habens* than by *alens*. Our two oldest manuscripts support *habens*. The prose version allows either reading.

82. Ott. 2 wrongly divides *Sicut ad orandum* (“As though for worship”). For *tractat* Burmannus conjectured *tractet*. In Rom., *tradat* seems to have arisen from *tractat*. Meus, with the others, has *tractat*, but for *d. s.* has *tecta*, perhaps so that the sense would be “whom, under cover of deceit, he orders to be killed”—a rather awkward meaning. *Tractare* means “to turn over in the mind, to resolve.”]

While such events were taking place on Bethlehem’s shores,

the Magi from the East arrived, and with alarming words

[75] disturbed the savage tyrant with momentous news:

that recently, for the Jewish peoples, from the eastern quarter,

a ruler born had shone forth; that the stars proclaimed this from heaven,

that a new star radiated this. The savage ruler of the court

boils with anxiety, thinking that this man might succeed

[80] [Col. 0602A] 206 him soon, who had been first; then, with a tranquil face,

having clouds in his mind, he secretly orders him to be sought everywhere,

as though for worship, whom he is planning to kill by deceit.

Why do you rage, Herod? In your speech you confess Christ,

[Col. 0603A] [Note: [Col. 0603C]

84. Arntzenius thought that all editions except Lips. read *Et sensu*. He himself, together with the prose version, reads *Sed sensu*. Parrhasius had also printed this. Ott. 1, Reg. 2, Ang. have *Sed sensu*. Rom. has *Sensu* without *Et* or *Sed*, contrary to the meter. Other manuscripts have *Et sensu*, which yields the same meaning.

85. Most write *Neglegis*, from which Ott. 1 has *Nec legis* (“and you do not read”). Although that reading may seem clever, the true reading is *Negligis* (“you neglect”), as is sufficiently clear from the preface to Dionysius Cato’s *Distichs*, book I: “Read my precepts, therefore, in such a way that you understand them.” For to read and not understand is to neglect. Some, however, pursue a point even here and take *nec legere est* (“not to read”) for *negligere est* (“to neglect”). The Poelman sheets have *damna* (“losses”) for *regna* (“kingdoms”). Others, along with the prose version, retain *tua regna* (“your kingdoms”), whose gloss in Reg. 1 is *potestatem* (“power”), and explain *ad minaris—tollere* as “you threaten to take away.” Nebrissensis explains it more clearly: “By the power of the kingdom you threaten that you will rage against him.”

86. Reg. 4, Rom., and some editions have *Nec, tamen* (“nor, nevertheless”); Urb. has *Nec tantum* (“not only”); the *Bibliotheca Lugdunensis Patrum* has *Et tamen* (“and nevertheless”): correct to *Ne tamen* (“lest, however”). Ott. 1, Reg. 2, 4, and 5, Urb., Rom., Ang., Meus, Vatt. 1 and 2, and Ald. have *numina* (“divinities”). Reg. 1 has *nomina* (“names”), perhaps as a gloss above *numina*, or rather as a different reading; the latter is more likely. In Reg. 2, the gloss above *numina* is *potestates* (“powers”), but something else seems previously to have stood in place of *numina*. Some printed editions have *munia* (“duties”). Meus has *nomina* for *d. s.*, or by correction; Parrhasius also has *nomina*, which the Poelman sheets and recent editors rightly approve. For another king of the same name—that is, another Herod—saw Christ killed, whereas this Herod, the Infanticide, wished to perpetrate the deed. In Rom., someone seems to have wished to correct *facto* (“by the deed”) to *fato* (“by fate”); this is not an inept conjecture.

87. Reg. 4 and Edimb. have *Patrando* (“by perpetrating”); *Patrandum* (“to be perpetrated”) is more suitable.

88. Many printed editions have *Herodesque*, where the conjunction *-que* is entirely superfluous. Some printed editions have *Et Herodes*, suffering from the same defect and additionally violating the meter. Reg. 4 and Cant. have *videbis* (“you will see”); the sense requires *videbit* (“he will see”).

89. Rom.: “When the Magi came to worship the Lord.” Meus: “The Magi follow the star.”

90. The first syllable of *Magi* is correctly shortened; in the dedication to Theodosius, which I have denied to Sedulius, it is improperly lengthened.]

207 yet in your mind you desire to murder him; and, though reading the law,

[85] you neglect it, and threaten the King of kings with your kingdom.

Yet, lest your names lack a mad deed,

another Herod will see carried out—under the honour of the cross, but through the crime of the Gentiles—

[Col. 0604A] what you are plotting.

208 Therefore, the Magi, keeping their eyes fixed

[90] on the highest heaven, followed the shining royal star,

[Col. 0605A] [Note: [Col. 0605D]

91. *Tenere viam*, as *tenere iter* and *tenere cursum*, means “to proceed” or “to travel.”

93. Urb. has *salutis* (“of salvation”); correct to *solutis* (“having been released”).

94. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *possint* (“they may be able”), but in Reg. 1 it was subsequently changed to *possent* (“they might be able”).

96. Some printed editions, with Fabr., have *sepulto* (“for the buried one”). The manuscripts have *sepulcro* (“for the tomb”), as in Rusticus, *On the Benefits of Christ*: ““Bearing proofs in symbolic form, you give gifts to the king—riches; you give incense to God, and myrrh to the tomb,” where perhaps *Per species* (“by forms”) should be read instead of *Per speciem*. St Leo, Sermon II on the Epiphany, likewise spoke of the mystical forms of the gifts.

97. Vat. 2 has *trina* (“threefold”), rightly emended to *per tria* (“through three”), to satisfy the meter. Reg. 4, Urb., and Meus omit *est* (“is”) in *vitae sine est*. Some place a full stop after *est*.

98. Reg. 4 has *Tunc numerum* (“then the number”). Urb. has *fides est Tempora* (“faith is the times”).

101. Cellarius explains the threefold virtue as the three divisions of time; but Christian poets commonly use this expression to signify the Trinity of persons in one essence. See the scholia on book I, verse 324.

105. The Poelman sheets noted that *Si cupimus* (“if we desire”) should not be changed to *Sic cupimus* (“thus we desire”); neither we in our copies nor Arntzenius in his found that reading. This verse and the following ones down to verse 163 were missing from my codex; evidently a single leaf had been torn away.]

They kept the desired road which, by the law yet to come,

led the worshiping nations to the sacred cradle.

And when their treasures had been released for religious purposes,

the very forms of the gifts, so that they might display Christ,

[95] poured forth golden gifts for the newborn king,

gave incense to God, and offered myrrh to the tomb.

But why three gifts? Because faith, which has confessed this number,

is life's greatest hope, and the highest God,

[Col. 0606A] who sees all times—present, past, and future—

[100] is always present, always has been, and always will remain

210 in the threefold virtue of his being. Then, warned from heaven

in sleep to disregard the tyrant’s commands,

changing their route, they went by paths off the road

and returned to their own country. Thus may we too,

[105] if we desire at last to reach our holy homeland,

[Col. 0607A] [Note: [Col. 0607B]

106. Vet. 1 and 2 and Mon. have *jam nos* (“now us”); the sense requires *jam non* (“now no longer”).

107. Rom.: “When Herod saw that he had been deceived by the Magi.”

109. Ottob. 2 has *qui propriam non regit iram* (“who does not govern his own anger”); read *propriam qui*.

111. The construction would proceed more clearly as follows: “Like a roaring lion, which, when it slips from his mouth, etc.” Yet similar examples are not lacking elsewhere. The prose version is equally involved; perhaps *sicut leo* (“like a lion”) should be read.

112. Virgil, book XII, verse 6: “Then at last the lion takes up arms”; and book IX, verse 340: “He chews and drags—the tender flock.”

113. Most punctuate *fetae—Nequidquam* (“the mothers—In vain”); Arntzenius does likewise, though from the prose version he thinks it should be punctuated *vocant sua pignora fetae—Nequidquam, et vacuas implent*, namely, “the mothers call their offspring in vain.” This punctuation seems more convenient. The prose version had *stantes eminus* (“standing at a distance”).

114. Arntzenius writes *Nec quidquam* (“and nothing”), but *Nequidquam* or *Nequicquam* (“in vain”) is better. Reg. 4 and Rom., in the first hand, have *ballantibus* (“bellowing”); retain *balatibus* (“bleatings”). In Rom., *aures* (“ears”) seems to have been corrected from *auras* (“breezes”), but it must certainly be rejected.

116. Vassius, commenting on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 84, reports *coelicolas* (“heaven-dwellers”) from a manuscript of the public library at Cambridge, while he himself conjectures *lacteolas* (“milky”). Thus Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* XII, verse 119: “He scatters the milky brain”; and in *Dittochaeon*, verse 115: “The cradles smoke with the milky blood of the little ones,” whom Hartmannus of St Gall imitates, as I observed in my note on that passage. In Sedulius, however, the common reading is more correct. Nor does the repetition in *sternere collisas* (“to lay low the shattered ones”) present an obstacle, as Wopkensius shows by an example from Avienus, fable XI, verse 7: “Lest the threshing-floor should crush the shattered shell”; and from Paulinus, book IV, verse 183. In some editions *pravorum* (“wicked”) is an error for *parvorum* (“little ones”). *Parvi* and *parvuli* (“little ones”) are customarily used for children, as I once noted.

117. Rom., Barthius with his manuscript, Wopkensius, the Leipzig edition, and *Immerita*, a reading also retained by Nebrissensis with the explanation that the infants deserved nothing of the sort. Most manuscripts and editions have *Immerito* (“undeservedly”), and the gloss in Reg. indicates that it is an adverb modifying *collisas*. Arntzenius, with the Arntzenius manuscript and the Poelman sheets, restored [Col. 0608B] *Immerita*. *Immeritas* (“undeserving ones,” feminine plural) would not be bad, as in Virgil, *gentem immeritam* (“an undeserving people”), and elsewhere.

118. The very ancient Turin codex has: “Since thus the crowd perishes: scarcely had they been able to be born.” But in that form there is no sense. Perhaps it should be restored as follows: “For what simple crime—why does the crowd perish? Scarcely had they been able to be born—have they already deserved to die?”

120. Barthius thinks that one should read: “No reason to perpetrate the crime,” with the other words omitted, which he considers interpolated. Cellarius conjectured: “No reason, and at the first cries of the enemy he dares.” Wonckius preferred: “and, savage, he dares at the first cries,” or *ferus* (“savage”) instead of *ferox* (“fierce”). Yet he does not claim that this reading is correct; rather, he says that one should write: “forbidding the first cries, and daring—to perpetrate an uncounted crime.” For he considers “to kill the first cries” an extremely unusual expression. Arntzenius’s conjecture is: “denying the first cries, and daring,” or “at the first cries he denies and dares.” In reality these scholars wasted their efforts in harassing this passage; nor did we perform any great service by reporting their suspicions. The reading of all the copies is sound: the ending *-us* in *vagitus* (“cries”) is shortened by Sedulius, as is his custom, contrary to the rule of prosody—something Parrhasius says he did with excessive boldness. In Alb., *que* is missing from *primos negans vagitus*. *Vagitus* is used for “those who cry,” as Wopkensius noted from Prudentius, *Peristephanon* X, verse 743: “The Father commanded the years to be capable of every virtue; he excluded no day, granting triumphs to their very cries.” Thus in the same Prudentius *gemitus* (“groans”) means “those who groan,” *cursus* (“runs”) means “those who run,” *vota* (“prayers”) means “those who pray,” and *culpa* (“guilt”) means “the guilty one”; in Statius, *lacrimae* (“tears”) means “those who weep”; in Paulinus, in the poem *On the Life of St Martin*, *enses* (“swords”) means “armed men”; in Sedulius, *naufragium* (“shipwreck”) means “the shipwrecked person”; and there are countless other examples everywhere.

121. Most manuscripts and editions have *Innumerum* (“countless”); Rom. has *In numerum* (“into a number”). Wopkensius confirms that the latter should be read by reference to Lucan’s verses, which Sedulius imitates, book II, verse 108: “For what crime could the little ones have deserved slaughter? Yet it is enough now to be able to die. The force of madness itself draws him on, and he seemed to have sought a slow-moving culprit. A great part perishes into a number.” That is, they perish indiscriminately, as though merely to produce a very large number; Wopkensius made observations on this construction in his note on Tacitus, *Annals* XV.71. *Puerilia millia* means “thousands of children,” as in Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* XII, verse 148: “To remove the child as a pledge.”]

We have come to Christ; let us no longer return to evil.

Therefore, when the impious king discovered that he had been deceived,

he gives free rein to his anger—if that man may rightly be called a king—

who lacks compassion, who does not govern his own anger,

[110] and, mourning the deed snatched from him, like a roaring lion,

211 whose tender lamb suddenly slips from his mouth,

he turns all his weapons against the flock, chews and drags

the tender animal, while the frightened mothers call their offspring

[Col. 0608A] in vain and fill the empty air with their bleating.

[115] In no other way, once deprived of Christ, does savage Herod cease

to lay low the shattered ranks of the little ones in a massacre,

undeserving of such treatment. For what simple crime

does the crowd perish? Why have those who had scarcely been able to be born

already deserved to die? It is madness in a bloodstained king,

[120] 212 not reason; killing the first cries, and daring

to perpetrate an uncounted crime, he slaughters thousands of children,

[Col. 0609A] [Note: [Col. 0609C]

122. Reg. 1 has *Millia tum, luctumque dedit* (“then thousands, and he gave mourning”), but this was corrected to *Millia, plangoremque dedit* (“thousands, and he gave lamentation”).

123. Reg. 2 and Rom. have *rumpit* (“tears apart”); others have *rupit* (“tore apart”). In the following verse the manuscripts vary between *tempora secuit* (“cut their temples”) and *ferit* (“strikes”).

125. From Ovid, *Ars amatoria* II.93: “But the unhappy father, now no longer a father, cries, ‘Icarus!’”

126. Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 614, uses *innupto ubere* (“with an unmarried breast”). Thus also *orba ubera* (“bereaved breasts”).

127. Arntz. in the first hand, Fabr., and some printed editions have *nunc* (“now”) for *tunc* (“then”), as these words are easily confused. The sense requires *tunc*, as does the passage of Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.408 ff., which Sedulius expresses. Prudentius imitates Virgil more freely, as I noted on *Peristephanon* V, verse 421: “What sense did such things then give you, Datianus, as you listened?” In the Roman Breviary, for the feast of the Seven Sorrows of the Blessed Virgin Mary, third nocturn, first responsory, similarly: “What sense was then yours, Virgin, while you saw such things?”

128. The Poelman sheets and the Leipzig edition have *gemitus* (“groans”), the word Virgil uses of Dido in the passage cited. *Fremitus* (“roarings”) is preferable, with the prose version and most copies, so that the vigorous spirit of the man—or rather, of the king—kindled by anger may be expressed.

129. Arntzenius attempted: “and you might see the vast ether mingled before your eyes with such lamentations.” With a lighter change one could have written: “and you might see the vast expanse mingled before your eyes with such lamentations,” taking *aethra* as a contracted Greek accusative for *aethera*, a form Juvencus uses more than once, as I noted on book II, verse 532. A similar ancient inscription in Gruterus, page 1164, no. 4, reads: “And may he send his poured-out prayers to the heavens,” as it is also found in Vatican Palatine codex no. 833, from which Gruterus drew most of his Christian inscriptions. Nevertheless, the reading of the manuscripts and editions is correct, as Arntzenius himself acknowledged from the prose version, where *pelagus* (“sea”) occurs instead of *aequor* (“surface”). Alb. had *aether* (“ether”), but the same hand corrected it to *aequor*. Cellarius explained *aequor* in his index as “through tumult,” which Wopkensius and Arntzenius rightly reject. If the prose version did not stand in the way, *aequor* could be explained as “plain” or “open expanse.” Wopkensius says that Sedulius retained Virgil’s word because he thought *aequor* could refer to the waters of the Jordan or other waters which mothers fleeing with their infants might attempt to cross. Herod himself was not present; nevertheless, the words “you might look forth” and “you might see before your eyes” can reasonably be understood of the eyes of the mind. The prose version’s interpretation should be retained: namely, that the sea is understood as gathered together by the flood of tears. Spanish likewise calls abundant weeping “a sea of tears.”

130. Ott. 1 has *clamoribus* (“with cries”), from which *plangoribus* (“with lamentations”) arose.

131. Vat. 2 and Reg. 5 have *Exstinctis tamen* (“although they had been extinguished”), without the conjunction *que*, contrary to the rule of the penthemimeral caesura. Aldus followed these codices, as he often does; unless, as I think, Reg. 5 follows Aldus. Urb. has *Exstinctisque tantum* (“and only when they had been extinguished”); retain *tamen*. The meaning is: “And yet, although the infants had been extinguished, etc.”

132. Wopkensius thinks *quae* (“which”) much more elegant; but *qui* (“who”), which is received by everyone and retained by the prose version, is no less elegant.

133. Fabr. and some other printed editions have *Suspicit* (“he looks up to”). These two words are commonly confused with each other. Here the sense requires *Suscipit* (“he takes upon himself”). Nebrissensis explains: “He charges to his account what others suffer in his place. He feels compassion for them.”

134. Rom.: “Where the Lord was seated among the teachers of the law.”

137. Early Christian writers commonly called the more mature wisdom of young men “the old age,” or “old age of the mind, heart, or spirit.”]

gave thousands of children, and one lament, to so many mothers.

One tore her hair with uncovered head,

another cut her cheeks; a third struck her bare breast

[125] with her fists; and the unhappy mother—now no longer a mother—

pressed her bereaved breasts in vain over her cold child.

213 What sense was then yours, butcher, as you saw such things?

What roarings did you utter when you saw from the highest citadel

the wounds boiling everywhere, and saw the vast expanse

[130] [Col. 0610A] mingled before your eyes with such lamentations?

Though absent, while the infants were extinguished,

214 Christ was present, who always takes upon himself

holy dangers and feels punishments in another’s body.

But when he reached twelve years of age,

[135] drawing this span from the flesh and passing through the course of life

on the human side, he seemed older in heart

than the elders, and among the teachers of the law

he sat as a master already honored by experience.

[Col. 0611A] [Note: [Col. 0611B]

139. Rom.: “When Jesus came to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” Ottob. 1: “Where Christ is baptized.”

140. The Arntz. manuscript has *majore senecta* (“with greater old age”), which Arntzenius suspects to be a gloss on *majore juventa* (“with greater youth”). But a gloss would be inappropriate: old age cannot be called “greater youth,” especially since *Sex quasi lustra gerens* (“bearing almost six lustrums”) follows.

141. Reg. 5 has *placidas ad Jordanis undas* (“to the tranquil waves of the Jordan”). Most manuscripts and editions have *placidam Jordanis ad undam* (“to the tranquil wave of the Jordan”); Aldus printed this as well, and I do not see why in the Errata he instructs us to read *placidas ad Jordanis undas*. Shortly afterward Sedulius himself, with all copies agreeing, lengthens the second syllable of *Jordanis*. Some nevertheless shorten it. See the note on Juvencus, book I, verse 383. Six lustrums are thirty years, as in the hymn: “He who has now completed six lustrums,” etc. Arator, *Acts* I.300, elsewhere 246: “Bearing eight lustrums.” Others say that *gerere annos* means “to spend years.”

143. Rom. has *potens vidit* (“the mighty one saw”); *ut* (“when”) is missing. Others make *Joannes* four syllables, shortening the first and lengthening the second. Fortunatus and others also call John *potens* (“mighty”).

144. Reg. 1 has *latens* (“lying hidden”); this may also have been the reading in Reg. 2, where it is now *latet* (“lies hidden”). Ottob. 2, incorrectly, has *nudumque creatus* (“and having been created naked”).

145. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *abstruso* (“hidden”); but *obstruso* (“closed off”) is correct, with the manuscripts and most printed editions. The philosopher Seneca, Statius, and Prosper use *obstrusus* for “hidden, enclosed, concealed.” It could also be written *obtrusus*. Reg. 1, with many printed editions, has *prophetes*, namely, “he himself, John, the prophet,” or “*prophetes* understood,” etc. Reg. 2 now has *prophetae*, but perhaps it had *prophetes*, as indicated by the gloss *propheta, vates* (“prophet, seer”). Most of our manuscripts—Ott. 1 and 2, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ang., Reg. 5, Urb., and Alb., together with Parrh., Ald., the Poelman sheets, and the Leipzig edition—have *prophetae*, while Rom. and the Arntz. manuscript suggest *prophete*. The Leipzig edition has *propheta*. Reg. 4 has *prophetis* (“to the prophets”), a reading that is not unreasonable. In some manuscripts the gloss is *prophetae, Zachariae* (“the prophets, namely Zacharias”), and Nebrissensis explains the passage in this way. If we read *prophetis*, the sense will be that John, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, understood Elizabeth’s speech as prophetic, or as the speech of a prophetess. Even if *prophetae* is retained, the same explanation may be adopted: for *prophetes* and *prophetae* can also be said of a woman. See the verse of Juvencus that I restored, book I, verse 249: “Then behold the prophetess fills a woman’s mind with holy inspiration.” From this it could also be questioned, with the reading *prophetes*, whether John or Elizabeth is designated by that word. The more likely interpretation, however, is that John himself, enclosed in his mother’s womb, perceived this through some hidden prophetic utterance, because he leapt in the womb and was already then a prophet; the prose version is flat on this point.

146. Rom. has *Et muto genitore* (“and with his mute father”), instead of *Ut muto genitore* (“as his mute father”). Monast. has *mutuo*, erroneously. Parrhasius has *fruens* (“enjoying”); Nebrissensis conjectured *silens* (“silent”), which some printed editions followed with Fabricius. Most editions, together with the manuscripts, have *fluens* (“flowing”), whose gloss in some codices is *nascens* (“being born”). This reading also occurs in the very ancient Turin codex and is indicated by the prose version.

147. Rom. and Vet. 1, contrary to meter and sense, have *Post novi* (“after I learned”). Cant., Ald., and a few other printed editions have *tacitura*, which Nebrissensis explains as *tacentia* (“silent things”). Most have *taciturna* (“silent”). In Alb., the words *noni taciturna* are missing. Understand “silent gifts.”

148. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *Partu* (“by birth”). Reg. 2 has *Parto* (“having been born”), with most copies, but this is from correction: *Partu* was the original reading. Reg. 1 has *Edito* (“having been brought forth”), and for *d. s.*, *Parto*; but with *Edito* the verse does not scan, and in Rom. *Edito* is a gloss above *Parto*. Nebrissensis observes that in Greek and ancient Latin copies of the Gospel the reading is *peccatum* (“sin”), not *peccata* (“sins”).

149. Sedulius uses *tollere* both for “to carry” and for “to take away,” namely, “from me” or “for me.” Others interpret it differently. Compare the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 602.

150. Arntzenius reports, from Parrhasius and the Poelman sheets, *dum dicit* (“when he says”).

151. Vet. 2 has *ut ipsa gerat* (“so that she herself may bear”); better is *ut ipse gerat* (“so that he himself may bear”). Parrhasius and the Poelman sheets have *ferat* (“may carry”) for *gerat*. Rom. has *sed ipse* (“but he himself”); read *sed ut ipse* (“but so that he himself”).

152. Some printed editions have *dum lux* (“while light”).

153. Reg. 1, in a later hand, Reg. 4, and apparently Ott. 1, with Vet. 1 and 2, Mon., the three Tornæsian editions, Poelm., and other printed editions, have *et proprium non offuscata serenum* (“and not darkened in its own serenity”), a customary Greek construction. Most of our manuscripts—Reg. 1 in the first hand, Ang., Reg. 2, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ottob. 2, Urb., and Rom., together with Parrh., Ald., the Cambridge codex, and the Poelman sheets—have *et proprio non offuscata sereno* (“and not darkened by its own serenity”). In Ott. 1, after the other words were deleted, only *et propri . . . sereno* is now visible. The verb *offusco* occurs in Tertullian and Orosius.]

Without delay—for what delays can the world,

flying through time, be known to have?—having reached a greater youth,

bearing almost six lustrums, he came to the tranquil waters of the Jordan

215 so that he might receive what he himself had come to give.

When the powerful Baptist John saw him from the river,

him whom, while he still lay hidden in his mother’s womb and was not yet born,

[145] he had perceived, by a hidden prophetic utterance—he who sprang from a mute father,

[Col. 0612A] to whom the gifts of speech,

after the silent breathings of the ninth month,

216 were restored when his child was born—he immediately proclaimed: “Behold

the Lamb of God, who comes to take away the sin of the world.”

[150] When he says “to take away,” he takes away from me what he does not possess:

not so that he himself may bear evils, but so that he himself may destroy harmful things.

As brilliant light is poured into the midst of darkness

and, not darkened by its own serenity,

[Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613C]

154. Arntzenius raises some suspicion as to whether *Discutit* (“shakes off”) should be read. Rom. certainly has *Discutit*; but the verb *decutio* (“shake off”) is frequent among Christian poets. Compare the variant readings on Juvencus, book III, verse 193. Reg. 1 has *expulsas* (“banished”), with the others; above it was apparently corrected to *expulsans* (“banishing”). Martial uses this verb, *expulsare*.

155. Arntz. has *fugando* (“by fleeing”), incorrectly, for *gerendo* (“by bearing”).

156. Rom. has the error *Tersit, et tactu*. Nebrissensis explains *a tactu* (“by touch”), that is, “by contagion.” In the Poelman sheets, *attractu* seems to be attributed to Nebrissensis, unless it is someone else’s reading; certainly it is not found in the edition of Nebrissensis that I use. Cellarius and Arntzenius reject *attactu* in Parrhasius. But *attactu* seems to me a sound reading, and I also find it in Reg. 1, from which *atactu* arose in Reg. 2 and 4, Ott. 1 and 2, Alb., and Urb. Vat. 1 and 2, Reg. 5, and Ang. have *attactu*, but in Vat. 1 *attacta* seems originally to have stood, namely, modifying *delicta* (“sins”). Sedulius took this word from Virgil, book VII, verse 350: “It rolls by contact with nothing.” Varro likewise uses the noun in the ablative; examples outside this case are scarcely to be found. Varro’s words are, book II of *On Agriculture*, chapter 5: “The hide is not rough to the touch.” Juvencus also uses it, book I, verse 776: “Then Christ’s right hand, by touch alone, cleansed the discolored limbs.” In Sedulius, book IV, verse 104, almost everyone has *Attactu patuere fores* (“At the touch the doors opened”), as Arntzenius admits, though there too he inserted *A tactu*.

157. Nebrissensis says that one should read *Tum in vada* (“then into the waters”), or supply the preposition. The latter should be retained, especially since the preposition *in* is already contained in *ingressus* (“having entered”). In *simplex* understand “innocent,” “pure,” or, with the prose version, “undefiled.”

158. Reg. 1 and 4, Ott. 2, and Ang. have *lavit* (“washed”); but in Reg. 1 *lavat* (“washes”) may previously have been written. Either is correct: *lavat* from *lavo, lavas*, or *lavit* from *lavo, lavis*.

160. Rom. has *lymphamque* (“and the water”).

161. Vonckius cites *caerula membris* (“blue over the limbs”), which Arntzenius says is not inelegant. But perhaps he accidentally wrote *caerula* for *flumina* (“rivers”), the reading uniquely supported by the manuscripts and editions. This is why many formerly wished to be baptized in the Jordan, as I explained in my note on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* II, verse 64. See also Gregory of Tours, *Miracles* I.88: “When the holy day of the Epiphany had arrived, and everyone descended into the Jordan to wash both bodily wounds and the scars of the soul,” etc. Georgius Gemnicus, chapter 23 of book II of the *Ephemeris*, in Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume II, speaking of the Jordan, reports: “We drank from it, and abundantly sprinkled our hands, feet, head, and face from it. Moreover, we carried water with us in a vessel all the way to our homeland, without any stench or corruption.” In our own time we know that water has been brought from the Jordan to Portugal for use in holy baptism.

163. In Reg. 1, *Jordanes* originally stood for *Jordanis*. Some have *Jordanus*. For *refluas* (“turning back”), Rom. has *refluens* (“flowing back”), with the gloss *revertens* (“returning”), but this is inferior.

164. Reg. 4 has the distinctive reading *canens, Quidnam est mare, quare fugisti?* (“singing, ‘What is the matter, sea? Why did you flee?’”). But the final syllable of *quare* and the first of *fugisti* are disastrously shortened. Most have: “What is the matter, sea, that you flee?” he says. The Arntzenius manuscript has *quinam est*, which Arntzenius does not consider inept if one supplies *quinam est Deus* (“who is this God?”), namely, the one on whose account you flee. That would be extremely obscure. If *quidnam* needed changing, I would prefer *quianam* (“why”) for *quare*, or *cur*. Thus Virgil, whom Sedulius frequently imitates, book X, verse 6: “Great dwellers in heaven, why has your judgment been turned back?”; and book V, verse 13: “Alas, why have such clouds encircled the heavens?” Some have wrongly read *quidnam* or *quinam*. Virgil took this word from earlier writers, Naevius and Ennius, as Servius and Quintilian note in book VIII, chapter 3, near the middle. Ennius, book VII, in Festus: “Why has the judgment been changed by our words?” In Sedulius, *quianam* is confirmed by *quia* in the following verse. Since *quod* follows, however, nothing should be changed.

165. Cant., Reg. 1, and Ottob. 1, for *d. s.*, and some printed editions have *quia subtrahis* (“because you withdraw”), a reading followed by the recent editors Grunerus and Arntzenius. Ott. 1 in the text, Arntz., Ang., Alb., Ott. 2, Urb., Rom., Meus, Parrh., Ald., and most printed editions have *quid subtrahis* (“what do you withdraw?”). In Vat. 1 and 2 it is uncertain whether *quid* or *quia* should be read. In Reg. 1, first hand, *quid* may perhaps have stood; above *quia* there is now a gloss, or rather the different reading *quid* or *cur* (“why”). The more authentic reading is *quia*, supported by the prose version and by the words of Psalm 113: “What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, why have you turned back?” Similar examples occur in the Vulgate version of Holy Scripture and elsewhere in Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, where *quia* is used for *quod* (“that”) or *cur* (“why”).]

shakes off the expelled shadows from faces unharmed,

[155] so the Savior, by bearing our sins,

wiped them away and by his touch ordered them to vanish far off.

217 Then, entering innocently the channels of the flowing waters,

he washes all the contagions of our life into himself,

while possessing nothing of his own that needs to be removed; and with his holy

[160] [Col. 0614A] body he cleansed the flowing waters, blessed the waters of the deep,

sanctified the rivers with his own limbs.

The elements perceived God: the sea fled, and the Jordan itself

turned its backward-flowing current into waves.

For the prophet, singing, said: “What is the matter, sea, that you flee?

[165] 218 And you, Jordan, why do you withdraw your stream backward?”

[Col. 0615A] [Note: [Col. 0615C]

166. In my codex a heading is added here: “The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove.” Cant., [Col. 0615D] Arntz., the Poelman sheets, Reg. 2 and 5, Vatt. 1 and 2, Urb., Ott. 2, Alb., Rom., Meus, Parrh., Ald., and other printed editions have *fluminei post mystica dona lavacri* (“after the mystical gifts of the river-washing”). Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, with many printed editions, especially recent ones, have *flumineum post mystica dona lavacrum* (“after the mystical gifts of the river-washing”), which pleases me more.

167. Rom., Meus, Ott. 1, Reg. 2, Parrh., and Ald. have *siccas Dominus* (“the Lord [trod] dry [sands]”); Reg. 1 and the others have *Dominus siccas* (“the Lord [trod] dry [sands]”). Arntzenius printed *siccas Dominus* and attributed *Dominus siccas* to Parrhasius and other printed editions, but Parrhasius has the opposite.

169. Vonckius attempted *Christum investivit honore* (“clothed Christ with honor”); Arntzenius calls this an extremely easy conjecture, since nothing is more common in the manuscripts than confusion between *m* and *in*. Wopkensius more rightly thinks that nothing should be changed here.

170. Ang. has *multum incedere* (“to walk greatly”); others have *multumque incedere*. Although Wopkensius admits that *multum* is sometimes constructed with adjectives in the sense of “very,” he would prefer *mitemque incedere* (“to walk gently”), *mitem* (“gentle”), or *humilemque incedere* (“to walk humbly”), or *justumque incedere* (“to walk righteously”). Grunerus and Arntzenius rightly disagree.

171. Vet. 1 and 2 and Mon. have *notoque*, an obvious typographical error and certainly corrupt. The popular belief that a dove lacks bile is false, as those who claim expertise in such matters report.

172. Ott. 2 has *Deus ratione* (“God by reason”); to make the verse scan, one should read *Deus ex ratione* (“God on this ground”), though *Deus hac ratione* (“God on this ground”) would not be bad.

173. Meus has *ubi* (“where”); read *ibi* (“there”).

174. Cant., Reg. 4, and Ott. 1 in a later hand have *honoraverit* (“has honored”). The editions, with most manuscripts, have *numeraverit* (“has counted”). In Ott. 1, *adoraverit* (“has worshiped”) or *oraverit* (“has prayed”) originally stood; above it there is either a gloss or the reading *numeraverit* from a different hand. Arntzenius says that among the ancients *numerare* could mean “to revere” or “to esteem,” citing Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XII.11. I do not accept *numerare* in the sense “to revere,” but I readily admit it in the sense “to reckon” or “to esteem,” when what is counted is placed among similar things, as in “I count it a great benefit,” “I count it among good things,” and the like. But when the subject is the one God, this phrase creates a difficulty: *numerare unum Deum* would mean “to confess one God.” I suspect Sedulius wrote *qui non memoraverit unum* (“who has not named one”). Thus in verse 237 of this book: “We name the Lord of heaven as Father; in him it is already fitting for us to be brothers.” The other reading, *adoraverit* or *honoraverit*, is rejected by the meter. The prose version is either obscure or corrupt; nevertheless, this explanation can be extracted from it: “who has counted not one, but three Gods.”

175. Rom.: “Where the devil tempted the Lord by fasting.” Meus: “About the tempter who approached the Lord after he had fasted.” Ott. 1: “Where he is tempted by the devil.”

176. Some manuscripts and editions have *Jejunium* (“fasting”); Aldus corrected this error in the Errata.]

Therefore, when he came out of the river-born washing after the mystical gifts,

the Lord stepped upon the dry sands.

At once the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit in the form

219 of a dove clothed Christ with honor,

[170] teaching him to walk meekly and gently,

through the bird that lacks bile, while, after the Son had been called,

the Father’s voice proves God to be threefold in this respect:

because there is a Father, a Son, and the Holy Spirit,

and whoever does not reckon God as one remains unworthy.

[175] 220 From there, for fourteen nights and days,

fasting from food and filled with holy inspiration,

[Col. 0617A] [Note: [Col. 0617C]

177. Dracontius I.471: “The treacherous one approaches.”

179. In some manuscripts *lapides* (“stones”), and in some printed editions *repentem* (“repenting”), are errors.

181. All our manuscripts, together with the Leipzig, Heinsius, and Cambridge manuscripts and the very ancient Turin codex, as well as the Poelman sheets, Aldus, and Parrhasius, have *Haec eadem non semper agat, qui* (“as though he who does these same things did not always do so”). Many printed editions have *Haec non semper agat Dominus, qui* (“as though the Lord, who does this, did not always do so”). Meus has *saxa* (“rocks”), incorrectly, for *saxea* (“stony”). Augustine, *Tractate* 24 on John, praises the wondrous and astonishing works of God in a similar manner in every grain of seed.

182. All our codices, together with Aldus, Parrhasius, the Arntzenius manuscripts, Cant., and the Poelman sheets, have *frugiferis* (“fruit-bearing”). Some have *fructiferis* (“fruitful”), a reading Arntzenius preferred. *Frugiferis* is more pleasing; Reg. 5, with *fruiferis*, points to the same word.

183. Rom. has *tunc* (“then”); in the margin there is either a correction or a different reading, *hac* (“this”), which is preferable.

184. Rom. alone has *solum*, corrected from *solo*.

186. *Arma* (“weapons”) means plans with which he might harm, if he could. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.99: “And, conscious, to seek weapons.”

190. Torn. 3 has *tamen* (“nevertheless”) for *tantum* (“only”). These two words are frequently confused in the manuscripts, but here neither the meter nor the sense permits *tamen*. Reg. 5, Vat. 2, and Ald. have *tantum est* (“it is only”) perversely; in the others the substantive verb is absent, an elegant omission.

191. Reg. 1 in the text, Reg. 2 for *d. s.*, Ott. 2, Vat. 2, and Reg. 5 have *fragiles regni affectaret honores* (“he might seek the fragile honors of the kingdom”); Arntz. has *fragiles mundi affectaret honores* (“he might seek the fragile honors of the world”); Reg. 4 has *fragilis regna affectaret honoris* (“he might seek the kingdoms of fragile honor”). The more common reading is *fragilis regni affectaret honores*, supported by the prose version. Most printed editions have it as well. Parrhasius, Aldus, and some others have *fragiles* for *fragilis*.

192. Cellarius, in his Addenda, recommends reading *externa* (“external”) for *aeterna* (“eternal”), unless this too is to be attributed to a typographical error, as Arntzenius observes.

195. Nebrissensis considers *summissa voce* (“with lowered voice”) to be an expression drawn from Psalm 64, verse 2, where the Hebrew text reads: “Silence befits you, God, in Zion,” instead of which our Vulgate has: “Praise befits you.” But in Reg. 1 the gloss is *summissa*, that is, “sent upward” or “raised.” The more accurate gloss is in Ott. 1: *summissa—supplici* (“lowered—supplicating”). The prose version retains the same word, *summissis vocibus* (“with lowered voices”).

197. Meus has *soli et* (“and to the one alone”); others have *et soli*. Some printed editions have *famulari et uni* (“to serve one”), contrary to the meter. Reg. 5, incorrectly, has *famulariter* (“in a servile manner”). The Arntz. manuscript has *famularier illi* (“to serve him”), which Arntzenius adopted in the text, supported by the prose version. But the prose preserves the words of Holy Scripture, while in the poem the poet added *soli uni* (“to the one alone”) to express the point more forcefully; these two words are frequently joined, as it would be easy to demonstrate with examples. From the sense itself it is understood that the one Lord God alone must be served, even without adding *illi* (“him”).]

The tempter approaches with treachery, skilled by his art

in offering deceptive food. “If you are seen to be

the Son of God,” he says, “speak, so that this stone may suddenly

[180] be changed into the substance of bread.” As though he did not always perform

such things, he who gives life to the stony entrails of the earth

with fruit-bearing ears of grain and creates bread from rock.

Thus repulsed first by the words that man does not live by bread alone,

221 [185] but by every word of God, shaken and maddened,

he renews his weapons with viperous poisons.

With the Lord he climbs the mountain and showed him all the wealth

of the kingdoms throughout the world, saying: “All these things,

[Col. 0618A] if I grant them, you shall possess, if you fall down and worship me.”

[190] As perverse as he was, so perverse were his words.

as though he might seek the fragile honours of a kingdom,

222 and might worship prone a monstrous and abominable being—he

who prepares eternal things for peoples,

whose seat is above the heavens, whose footstool is the earth,

[195] and whom every power praises in the heights with lowered voice.

Christ to this replied: Scripture commanded that only the Lord and God

be worshiped, and that service be rendered to him alone.

198. Reg. 4 has *ardet* for *audet*, as do Cant. and several others; and *iniquis* for *iniquus*. The common reading *audet iniquus* is better. By simply using the name “the wicked one,” he also understood the devil above, at verse 106: “Let us not repeat ‘the wicked one.’”

199. Reg. 4 and Ott. 2 have *praestare*: read *perstare*.

200. Arntzenius has incorrectly *considere bello* for *confidere*.

201. Mon. has *Hinc*; others, together with the Prose, have *Tunc*.

202. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *vestigia*, incorrectly.

203. Rom. and Urb. have *tute*, which Parrhasius published and which is also found in Mon. and in Arntzenius’s manuscript. This reading is preferred by the three Arntzenii, the editor of Sedulius, his father in his commentary on Pliny’s *Panegyricus*, and his uncle in his commentary on Cato’s *Distichs*, book I, distich 4. Arntzenius gathers several similar examples at this passage. The reading is certainly not to be condemned, but there is no reason to depart from the received reading, which is more common in the manuscript codices.

204. Meus has *delapsus*, which Parrhasius also published. Other manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *demissus*; but Rom. writes *dimissus*, as regularly happens in this and similar words compounded with the preposition *de*.

206. Reg. 4 has *subjectus*: retain *subvectus*.

208. *Mens*, *pectore*, and *corda* are virtually synonymous words; but poets often expand their expression in this way.

209. Bede’s commentator on the *Art of Meter* cites this verse.

210. Meus has *Culmina et rectae*; Rom., *Culmina erectae*: read, so that the verse scans, *Culmina et erectae*.

212. *Membra poli*, like *membra urbis* in Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.446. See the Commentary.

214. Reg. 1, 2, 4, 5, Ott. 1, Vat. 2, Arntz., Ald., and others have *et non*. Meus has *at non*. Vat. 1, Ott. 2, Ang., Alb., Urb., and Parrh. have *sed non*, which Arntzenius preferred because it was easy, and often happened in manuscripts, for *sed* or *set*—for many scribes wrote it in that form—to become *et*, especially when the preceding word ended in the letter *s*.

215. Meus has *confusus*, but the following word *cuspide* requires *confossus*. Reg. 4 has the error *cospide*.

216. Reg. 4, Vat. 2, Urb., and Meus have *Dominum, Deumque*: the metrical rule requires *Dominumque, Deumque*. For *nequiret*, Reg. 4 has *nequisset*; Parrhasius, *requirit*. Aldus printed *Dominum, Deumque nequiret*; in the *Emendata* he replaced it with *Dominumque, Deumque requiret*. But neither *requirit* nor *requiret* suits this passage, and perhaps both are typographical errors.]

In these encounters also failing, the wicked one dares,

Raising himself three times, to persist in proud spirit,

[200] And three times rolling on the ground, to trust in fragile warfare.

Then the criminal took him into the holy city,

And, setting him above the pinnacles of the lofty temple,

223 “If you assert that you are the son of God the Father,” he said,

“Leap down eagerly from the roof’s summit.

[205] For Scripture teaches that the Thunderer commanded concerning you

That, borne upon angelic arms, you should go more safely,

[Col. 0620A] Lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”

How obscure in its own darkness! It believed that he would recoil in terror and plunge headlong

[210] From the temple’s lofty summits,

And from the pinnacles of the erect wing, although he himself

Seeking what lies below, yet not abandoning what is high.

[215] 224 He had spoken, and, pierced by the point of the powerful word,

Because he could not tempt his own Lord and God,
