219. Ald., together with Vat. 2, has *Angelici et Christo*. The conjunction *et* is better omitted. Arntz. rightly has *pro rite*.

220. Ott. 1 has *Ubi ex piscatoribus fecit discipulos*; Meus, *Quomodo legit sibi discipulos*; Rom., *Ubi Dominus elegit discipulos*. In Reg. 4 this verse, *Protinus*, is missing.

222. Cellarius, together with some printed editions, has *vada caerulea*, which can be defended. But all our manuscripts except Rom., where *vaga* or *vada* has been omitted, prefer *vaga caerula*. Arntz., Parrh., Ald., Vet. 1 and 2, Mon., the Poelm. sheets, and others agree.

223. Vat. 1, Urb., Rom., and Poelm. in the margin have *praecipitis*. Most other manuscripts and printed editions have *praecipites*, from which, through differing spelling practices, *praecipiteis* and *praecipitis* arose. Ott. 2 corruptly has *Caeca quod praecipitis*. Reg. 4 has *tranent*: *tranant* is more correct.

225. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.656, concerning the eloquence of Symmachus: “To play with airy arrows, with the cast wasting away,” where, from Petronius, I have restored *ventosa loquacitas*.

227. Marcklandus, in his commentary on Statius, book V, *Silvae* 3, together with some others, has the form *tacens*. But here the subject is silent or silenced fame, opposed to the windy glory of speaking. Wassius, in his index to Sallust under *rumor*, cites from a manuscript of the public library at Cambridge *fama jacens*, that is, obscure fame. That reading should not indeed be displeasing, but it must nevertheless be preferred to the other. “Silent fame” is obscure fame. Compare what others have noted on Silius XI.777: “That blood of mine—the Dardanian …” For *inflet*, *alat* is elegant, from Virgil V.231, “These successes nourish him,” and Silius XI.555, “No obscure favor nourished their spirits.”

228. Arntz., from a gloss and against the metrical rules, has *vicinos* for *propinquos*.

229. Reg. 4 corruptly has *Namq. elegit infirma potens*; [Col. 0622C] Meus is no better: *Nam sibi stulta potens elegit, et infirma mundi*. Fabricius, together with some printed editions, has *Namque infirma potens*. Parrh., *Nam quia stulta potens*; the Leipzig edition, *Nam quoque stulta potens*. Most printed editions, including the more recent ones, have *Nam quae stulta*. Wopkinsius conjectured *Namque stulta*. Aldus and several others in fact printed it thus. Grunerus praises Wopkinsius’s conjecture; Arntzenius confirms it from Arntzenius’s manuscript, where, in abbreviation, *Namq. stulta* is read. He would nevertheless wish other codices to agree. Yet nearly all our manuscripts—Reg. 1, 2, and 5; Ottobon. 1 and 2; Vat. 1 and 2; Urb.; Rom.; Ang.; and Alb.—unanimously write *Namq. stulta*, which must without any doubt be expanded as *Namque*. Some inept editors, knowing that *que* was short, thought the meter would be corrupted if *Namque stulta* were printed. But since a double consonant follows, *st*, according to the opinion of some, *que* ought to be lengthened; according to everyone, it may be lengthened, as I have discussed more fully in the Prolegomena to Prudentius. Moreover, many consider *que* to possess the common interval of quantity. Indeed, as I have shown more than once in my notes on Dracontius and Juvencus, in my opinion there is no short monosyllable that cannot be lengthened. In Rom. the conjunction *et* after *elegit* is missing.

230. Vat. 1 and 2, Urb., Reg. 5, and Ald. have *confundens*; others, *confringens*, which also seems to have been written by the first hand in Vat. 1. Some manuscripts, in an uncertain ligature of letters, have *perdens* or *prodens*; but *perdens* should be read. Ott. 1 has this, though perhaps *prodens* was written there earlier.

231. Meus has *Tunc etiam celerem*.

232. Vonckius bids us read *indexque benignus*. *Judex* and *index*, *judicium* and *indicium*, are often confused; but since all the manuscripts, no less than the printed editions, display *judexque*, I prefer to change nothing.]

Groaning, he flees the Victor’s face. Then, with the enemy repulsed,

The noble heavenly dwellers stand nearby, and the shining assembly

Of angelic ministers duly serves Christ.

[220] Immediately, therefore, he commands men suitable from among fishermen

To fish for human souls, which, pursuing the slippery

Joys of the world, as though they were the wandering blue waters of the sea,

225 Swim headlong across the dark uncertainties of the deep,

And orders them to be his disciples, and brings such men

[225] [Col. 0622A] Into the life above, whom neither the windy glory

Of speaking nor a bloodline proud of empty nobility

Nourishes, but whom silent renown, and brightness shining in a humble

Mind, make close to heaven though sprung from the people.

For the mighty God chose the foolish and lowest things of the world,

[230] 226 Breaking the strong and destroying the wise.

Moreover, desiring to bestow swift salvation,

He gave the rules of prayer, both judge and gracious benefactor,

[Col. 0623A] [Note: [Col. 0623C]

234. Arntzenius, from Arntzenius’s manuscript, printed *patrem in baptismate nostrum*, because the preposition *in* may have been concealed beneath the preceding letter *m*. But the other witnesses more elegantly omit that preposition. The same Arntzenius attributes *vestrum* to Parrhasius and the Leipzig edition. But Parrhasius clearly has *nostrum*. Arntzenius, together with Cellarius, distinguishes *nostrum*—“By right his own and proper to man,” etc. Cellarius explains that the honor is “his by right and proper to him.” Sedulius intended something else: “Pray to the Father, our Father through baptism—by right his own: and he granted man the honor proper to him.” God is, of course, Christ’s Father by right and by nature, but ours through baptism and adoption. Since it is Christ’s proper honor to call God Father, he granted us this honor, and so forth. The gloss in Ott. 1 is *est jure suum—natura*; and later, after *habere*, *adoptive*.

237. Reg. 1, Ottobon. 1, Rom., and Meus have *Pater noster, qui es in coelis*. Ott. 2 has *Qui Deum coeli*. Ald. and Vat. 2 have *Cui Dominum*; correct to *Qui Dominum*.

238. Reg. 4 has *Jam decet nos esse fratres*, but the words cannot be placed that way metrically. In Nebrissensis’s notes I read *origine mundi*, but in the text of the edition itself it is *origine carnis*. Nebrissensis says that the preposition *in* must be supplied, or *ab*. The meaning is: “It is not fitting for us to handle or pursue hatred such as that which burned against his brother Abel in Cain at the origin of the flesh, or at the beginning of the world; rather, it is fitting for us, aflame with the fire of the Spirit, to erase the memorials of ancient crime, or of fraternal hatred.”

239. Reg. 1 and 4, Vat. 1, Meus, Rom., Ott. 1, Alb., and most printed editions have *tractare*. Reg. 5, Ald., Fabr., Ang., Reg. 2, Parrh. have *gestare*. Ott. 2 and Reg. 2 in the text have *sectari*, which Arntzenius adopted from Arntzenius’s manuscript. The first hand in Ott. 1 likewise has *sectare*. Arntzenius prefers *sectari*, citing similar examples: *sectari bonum, vitia, charitatem*. The prose supports this. Others have *tractare*, together with the older manuscripts, in the sense of mentally considering or even dragging along. Reg. 5 and Ald. have *sed pneumatis igne*, which was inserted by recent editors against the poet’s intention so that the final syllable in the contracted case of the fourth declension would not be shortened. Sedulius claims this liberty for himself more than once.

244. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, and others have *Sanctificetur nomen* [Col. 0624D] *tuum*. Meus has *Sanctificetur ubique Deus*, which has no meaning. Poelm. has *Sanctificatur ubi Dominus* without a question, although a question is necessary. Most of our manuscripts, the printed editions, and the Poelm. sheets have *Sanctificetur ubi Dominus*. Wopkinsius prefers *Sanctificatur*, supported by Cant., Arntz., and many printed editions. In Reg. 1 the gloss is *ubi poterit sanctificari*, which I understand interrogatively.

245. Meus and Reg. 1, in the first writing, have *corpore*; the common reading is *pectore casto*, namely, “with a pure breast.”]

He briefly commands that pardon be sought, so that he may grant it quickly,

Saying thus: “Pray to the Father, our Father through baptism,

[235] By right his own; and he granted man the honor proper to him,

And what he alone possesses, he permitted all to possess.

227 “Him whom we name as the Lord of heaven, our Father,

It is now fitting that we be brothers in him, and not, from the origin of the flesh,

[Col. 0624A] Cherish fraternal hatred, but, aflame with the fire of the Spirit,

[240] Erase the memorials of ancient deceit,

And put on the new man, lest earthly things degenerate

From God above; through Christ as guide, heavenly grace

Made us adopted children born to him.

228 “Where may the Lord be sanctified—he who sanctifies all things by creating them—

[245] unless by a devout heart, unless by a pure breast?”

[Col. 0625A] [Note: [Col. 0625B]

247. Reg. 1, 2, and 5; Vat. 1 and 2; Ang.; Alb.; Ott. 1; Urb.; Rom.; Meus; Ald.; and other editions have *Annuat*, which Arntzenius says is futile. He himself retains *Annuet*, found in the Poelm. edition and several others. Reg. 4 has *Annuit*, which pleased Wopkinsius, as did *Sanctificatur* above. He punctuates: “So that we may deserve to sanctify him by worshiping him—he himself first grants it.” Others place a period after *colendo*. The verb *annuere*, meaning “to grant, bestow, assign,” is used by Virgil, Prudentius, and others.

248. Reg. 4 has *benedicimus*; read *benedicimur*.

249. Reg. 1 and Ottob. 1 give *Adveniat regnum tuum* as the title. Ten of our manuscripts, together with Heinsius, Cambridge, and many printed editions, have *regnum jam*, namely “that kingdom now,” with the *que* in *jamque* lengthened because of the *sc* of the following word, or because it is genuinely common, as has been noted elsewhere. Bede and his commentator on the *Art of Meter* read it in the same way, saying that *que* in this verse is long by position. Other inept scribes corrupted it in various ways. Ottob. 2 has *regnum jam jam nunc*, namely that kingdom now. Parrh. has *regnum coeleste videlicet illud*, “the heavenly kingdom, namely that one.” Meus, Vat. 1 in a later hand, Arntz., apparently, and several printed editions have *regnum jam jam quoque scilicet illud*. Some printed editions have *regnumque tuum jam scilicet illud*. The true reading is also more elegant than the others. *Jam jam* indicates an imminent event, and greater speed is indicated when *que* is added to the second *jam*. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.7: “Since we must think day and night that now, now we must die”; and book XIV of the letters to Atticus, final letter: “Although I myself shall now, now be here.” From Nebrissensis’s notes I infer that he read the passage differently, for he says: “The kingdom is understood. To this he himself responds.” In the edition I use, I do not find *quod* in this verse, to which the note belongs, but *jam jam quoque scilicet*; for Nebrissensis’s notes were reprinted here and often refer to other words not appearing in the text. I therefore think that Nebrissensis’s edition read *Adveniat regnum jam, jam*. “What?”—“Namely, that one.” This is clever, but less true and less elegant.

251. Arntzenius, together with many printed editions, presents *Succedent*, and cites *Succedunt* from Cant., Parrh., Ald., and others, which he considers less correct; this is what he implies when he says “without necessity.” Nearly all our witnesses—Reg. 1, 2, 4, and 5; Ang.; Alb.; Vat. 2; Ott. 2; Meus; and Rom.—have *Succedunt*, which I also infer from the connection of the letters in Vat. 1; Ott. 1 may have *Succedant*. *Succedunt* is sound, and its gloss in Reg. 1 is *subveniunt*, “they assist”: for in God’s eternal kingdom all things are present, and times do not succeed one another.

252. Meus has *Aeternus* in the first writing; read *Continuus*.

[Col. 0626C] 253. Christian writers commonly use “crown” for eternal happiness.

255. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in coelo, et in terra*. The common reading is *Hoc jugibus votis*, with the first syllable of *jugibus* shortened, as elsewhere in Sedulius. Cant. has *precibus* for *jugibus*. Cellarius attributes to Fabricius the change to *Jugibus hoc votis*, but I find it also in Reg. 5; this too should be noted because that codex scarcely ever departs from Aldus, who has *Hoc jugibus votis*. In the Ascensian edition of Cappusoti I likewise find *Jugibus hoc votis*; the Poelm. sheets prefer the same reading, adding, “Not *hoc jugibus*.” Reg. 4 has *noctu*; correct to *nocte* for metrical reasons. Rom. has *precamur*; retain *precemur*.

256. In Reg. 4 this verse is corrupted as follows: *Illius ut fiat in coelo, et in terra voluntas*. Arntzenius’s codex has *Ipsius* for *Illius*. Arntzenius says that *Illius* should be retained because the word carries emphasis when ancient profane writers speak of illustrious men or gods.

257. In Reg. 4 there seems to be *ore* for *esse*, and the latter alone should be retained. Cant. has *hostemque malignum*.

258. Wopkinsius asserts that in *utque* the *que* is superfluous, inserted solely for metrical reasons, as in other passages of Sedulius, namely book III, verse 89; book IV, verse 68; and Avienus, fable 17, verse 13. Perhaps to avoid this difficulty, the scribe of Reg. 5 wrote, and Aldus printed, *ut coelo, sic pellat humo*. I see no reason why Sedulius should not have written this way. Nevertheless, the oldest exemplars oppose it, and Sedulius more than once adds *que* in the sense of “also,” as in our modern expression *hodieque*. For *ne*, Ott. 2 and the first hand of Rom. have *nec*.]

“So that we may deserve to sanctify him by worshiping him,

May he himself first grant it, just as he commands himself to be blessed

By us, by whom all are blessed.

“May that kingdom come now, now indeed that kingdom,

[250] 229 Free from death and without end, to which through all ages

[Col. 0626A] An everlasting crown embracing its noble head,

[255] “With these unceasing prayers, this by night and by day, let us pray:

230 “May the will of him be done in heaven and on earth,

Who nowhere wills wickedness to exist; and may he drive

The harmful enemy from earth just as from heaven, lest he

259. Reg. 1 has *sibi indicet*; corrected by a later hand to *sibi vindicet*. Perhaps the first scribe intended to write *sibi vindicet*, for the codices vary: most of ours write *vendicet*. Cellarius and Arntzenius printed *hydros* in the correct Greek case from Heinsius’s manuscript. All our witnesses, Cant., and most editions have *hydrus*. The serpent feeds on earth; hence one understands what is meant by “as a worthless soil.” See above the note on the Prose corresponding to verse 176 of this book.

[Col. 0627D] 263. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie*. Arntzenius and all our manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *speramus*, but in Reg. 2 it was corrected to *speremus*. Arntzenius alone approves this; but for that reason I do not abandon the common reading. Later, at verse 269, *rogamus* occurs, which Arntzenius does not alter. *Diurnus* is used for “daily,” as in Tacitus, Ambrose, and Prudentius, *Psychomachia* verse 616: “The foods return with the daily sun.”

265. Wopkinsius conjectured *pectore et ore*, but says that the received reading can be explained thus: “While he supplies us with the nourishment of mind and faith, he fills us at the same time in body and mouth.”

266. Torn. 2 has, corruptly, *Non saturat*. Vat. 1 has *Nos satiat*. Arntzenius punctuates: *Nos saturat simul ipse, manens*, perhaps led by Wopkinsius’s opinion just mentioned. I prefer: *Nos saturat, simul ipse manens*.

[Col. 0628D] 267. Vat. 1 and Meus have *namque dei nostris*. Reg. 5 and Ald. have *si faucibus* for *in*, which makes no good sense.

268. Arntzenius has *Favos, et dulcia mella*, less elegantly. *Dulcia* has already occurred.

269. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, and others have: *Et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris*. Arntzenius has *nobis qui*; others, *qui nobis*.]

As a worthless soil, the savage serpent may claim them for himself;

But may the Almighty, who cherishes all things and overflows

With complete compassion, preserve souls and limbs alike:

For we are one part of heaven, the other of earth.

Let us hope for the nourishment of faith in daily bread,

231 So that our mind may never feel hunger for instruction,

[265] [Col. 0628A] Having fasted from its own Christ, who in body and mouth

Fills us, while himself remaining both Word and food.

For the sweet utterances of the Lord cling to our mouths

232 And surpass honeycombs and every kind of honey.

We who ask that all debts be released for us,

[270] [Col. 0629A] [Note: [Col. 0629C]

271. Vet. 1 and 2 and Mon. have *tenent*; correct to *tenet*.

272. Reg. 1 and Ott. 2 have *negemus*; in Reg. 2 it was *negemus*, but the same old hand corrected it to *negamus*, which is the more common reading in our codices. Arntz., Parrh., Aldus, and many printed editions likewise have *negamus*. Others have *negemus*. Either is correct, for the particle *si* is used indiscriminately with the indicative and subjunctive.

275. Urb. has *cum servum*; read *conservum*. For *ullum*, Meus has *illum*, Arntzenius *unum*. Such forms are often confused in manuscripts. *Unum* seems better. Some think that the second syllable of *Denarios* is shortened here, as in similar examples in Martial and Dionysius Cato. Others more plausibly say that the trisyllable is formed by synaeresis. Conrad the monk used the word in the same way in Pezzius’s *Dissertatio Isagogica* to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 3, where it is indicated that the thirty silver coins for which Christ was sold by Judas were minted in the time of the king of Assyria. It begins: “With thirty denarii the Galilean sells God.”

[Col. 0630D] 276. Meus has, not badly, *atque* for *inque*.

278. Vonckius conjectures *levem* for *brevem*, rightly opposed by Wopkinsius, Grunerus, and Arntzenius. *Brevis* is used for “small” or “slight.” See the note on Juvencus, book I, verse 554: “Let the smallest portion of the coin be returned.” Avienus, fable 38: “The feeble crowd will buy you at the same time for a small bronze coin.” And so elsewhere.

279. Reg. 1 and Ottobon. 1 have *Et ne nos inducas in tentationem*. Sedulius the Younger, author of the Commentary on Matthew, cites these verses, as I said in Prolegomena no. 56.]

Let us also release them; for the explicit pledge of our own word,

Which we make, holds us more tightly bound

If we refuse to release another’s bonds:

233 And the merciful Lord will begin by forgiving ten thousand talents,

If he perceives that we have afflicted a fellow servant

[275] For a hundred denarii, and immediately handed him over

[Col. 0630A] To torturers, and, bound in a savage prison,

We are not permitted to depart until we repay everything,

Down to the last small coin.

234 For the Lord, the way of light and path of peace,

[280] [Col. 0631A] [Note: [Col. 0631C]

280. In Ott. 1, *agit* seems to have been made from *agat*; *agit* can nevertheless stand.

284. Ottob. 1 has *Linquet*, corrected in the same manuscript to *Linquit*.

285. Cellarius and Arntzenius printed *Nos hac ergo pedem retro abducamus, et arctum*. Cellarius took *Nos hac* from the Leipzig manuscript, although he says that *Ab hac* conflicts with the meter. To avoid this difficulty, Arntzenius and Meus have *Ex hac*. In place of *retro faciamus*, which Cellarius considered harsh because it was found in the manuscripts, he substituted *retro abducamus* from the Prose. Thus Virgil, book V, verse 428: “They led [the ships] back.” Burmannus, however, defends *retro faciamus*, following Casaubon on Suetonius, *Augustus* chapter 16. Other editions have reworked this verse differently: Poelm., Bas., Fabr., Torn. 3, and the *Bibliotheca Lugdunensis Patrum* have *Jugibus hanc igitur studiis vitemus, et arctum*. It would be better to transpose the words into Sedulius’s customary manner of writing: *Hanc igitur jugibus studiis*, as Arntzenius observes; for Sedulius usually shortens the first syllable of *jugis*. But the true reading is the one which Cellarius and Arntzenius abandon without necessity: *Ab hac ergo pedem retro faciamus*. Thus our manuscripts—Reg. 1, 2, 4, and 5; Ott. 1 and 2; Vat. 1 and 2; Urb.; Rom.; Ang.; Alb.—read it, together with the ancient Taurinensis codex mentioned elsewhere, apparently the oldest; so do Parrh., Aldus, and other printed editions. *Ab* is lengthened because of the aspiration of the following word *hac*, which has the force of a consonant, as I have often noted in Prudentius, Dracontius, and Juvencus. *Retro pedem faciamus* is less usual than *retro pedem feramus*, or *referamus*, which would fit the meter; but the words of the codices, which can be retained, ought not to be changed. One may also question whether Sedulius used a nautical expression: *facere pedem* means to spread a sail so that it catches the wind, with the lower ropes extended, which are called the “foot” of the sail. Perhaps, therefore, in Sedulius *retro facere pedem* means to direct the ship, or its course, in the opposite direction. By this explanation the metaphor varies somewhat in what follows.

287. Perhaps by imitation of Juvencus I.717, elsewhere numbered 683: “Go through the narrow gate, righteous ones, above the stars.”

288. Reg. 1 and Ottobon. 1 have *Libera nos a malo*. Meus has *Si cupiamus*; the metrical rule requires *Si cupimus*. He uses *malum* in the masculine gender for the devil, as in the following verse he uses *bonum* for God.

293. In Reg. 4 there seems to be *malo* for *malis*. Fabr., Cellarius, together with the Leipzig and Heinsius manuscripts, and Arntz., have *cuicumque*, which Wopkinsius and Grunerus condemn. *Quicumque*, meaning “each person,” is indeed better and sufficiently clear. Thus *unusquisque* was inserted from the gloss in Reg. 5 and Aldus. Most of our manuscripts, together with Parrhasius and many other printed editions, have *quicumque*. Arntz. has *necesse* without *est*.

294. Ott. 1 has *Ut*; correct to *Aut*. Meus has *gradiantur*; retain *gradiatur*.

296. Reg. 4 has *Inque tuo sinus paradise*, but perhaps the scribe intended, for metrical reasons, *Inque tuos, paradise, sinus*. The sense requires *Patriarcha*, for the passage concerns Abraham’s bosom.]

Leads us into the snares of the tempter; rather, when he abandons our evils,

He permits us to go; for whoever follows the world’s seductive nets

And loves the luxury and pleasures of alluring destruction,

God, the lover of virtue, abandons such a person,

And he enters wherever temptation leads.

[285] Therefore let us turn our foot back from this, and seek the narrow

235 Path with our heart, where the slender way shows us

How to go through the narrow gate to the heavenly kingdoms.

If we wish to avoid evil, we must approach

And pursue the good: the one liberates, the other slaughters;

[290] [Col. 0632A] This one nourishes, that one kills. For as far as the stars are from the earth,

Fire from water, light from darkness, harmony from wars,

Life from tombs, so far are good things, separated

From evils. Everyone necessarily walks

Either the right-hand or the left-hand path,

[295] 236 The path of the good calls the conspicuous righteous

Into its joys and into your bosom, Patriarch; but the left-hand path

Of evils inflicts punishments and sends them to impious Tartarus.

[Col. 0633A] [Note: [Col. 0633A]

297. Cant., Reg. 4, Ott. 1 and 2, Rom., Urb., and the Leipzig edition have *ducit*. Ott. 1, in its first writing together with the others, has *mittit*, as Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.537: “But the left-hand path of evils inflicts punishments and sends them to impious Tartarus.” Cellarius printed *mittet*, which, I do not know whether by chance, slipped from his hand.

300. After this verse Reg. 1 and 2 and Vat. 1 have: “Book I ends. Book II begins.” Ott. 1: “The first book of Sedulius’s New Testament ends. Book II begins.” Reg. 5: “The second book of divine wonders.” Ott. 2: “The end of the discourse of Jesus. The second book begins: the miracles and deeds of Christ.” Urb.: “The second book of the distinguished Sedulius, bishop, on the history of the New Testament, ends; it treats of the life, virtues, and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ. The third book of the same author begins, concerning the miracles and wondrous signs of the only-begotten Redeemer, our God and Lord, and first, how, invited to a wedding, he wondrously changed six water-jars into mild wine.” In Vat. 2, Rom., and my codex, no division of the book is indicated. The remainder is missing in Reg. 4, and after the verse *Ora lupi* there follows the *Art of the Grammarian Phocas*. The Taurinensis codex has: “The first book of the New Testament ends. The second book begins. Life everlasting to the reader.” Thus in the catalogue of manuscripts; but in the description of the most learned Count Napione I read only: “…er. The first. The second book begins. Life everlasting to the reader.” In Alb.: “The second book of the New Testament ends. The third begins.” These statements must be understood in such a way that the third book of the poem begins, although it is the second book of the New Testament, as explained more fully in the Prolegomena.]

Therefore this alone is the will of God for lambs and sheep:

[Col. 0634A] A good freedom: to escape the grim

[300] Face of the savage wolf and enjoy life through Christ’s pastures.

## BOOK THREE

[Note: [Col. 0633C]

At the beginning, the Lord deigned to attend a wedding and revealed the proofs of his power. There, as the principal guest unveiling divine authority, he did not appear to be fed but to have fed others. For the wine had failed at the solemn celebration, and amid the heaps of dishes gathered for the feast, only the emptied cups languished in utter dryness. The earthly drink had departed, clearly so that the heavenly drink might enter. Christ therefore changed the liquids into the appearance of wine. The waters lost what they had been born as, now lacking water for drinking; and the water, made nobler than what had generated it, changed both its color and its name. Finally, sweet must glowed red in all the cups, and the guests, captivated by delight throughout the pleasant tables, were intoxicated by draughts of liquid nectar. The servants at the spring were astonished at the six water-jars they had filled, now darkened by overflowing wine, and at Christ’s entire vintage suddenly boiling forth—indeed, the cultivator of the vine of power was present, a fruit-bearing vine born beneath the shade of leafy heaven, nourishing clusters that would live forever in the perpetual beauty of a spiritual shoot.

[Col. 0635B] Then some royal official tearfully begged the Lord to relieve the illness of his dying son and prevent the feeble soul, distressed in its bodily dwelling, from slipping away. Then the humanity of divine power, which denies nothing to one who believes and does not delay a gift that does not depart from the company of faith, granted the boy complete health with a word and bestowed it by speech. For he replied: “Go; your son lives.” How commanding is the Lord’s power, how magnificent! He did not declare that the boy would live, but indicated that he already lived. This is the unique quality of divinity: to see as past whatever it had decreed would come.

From there, directing his saving steps through various cities and crossroads, through the countryside, villages, and fortified settlements, he healed all limbs by driving away the defects of disease[[Col. 0635D] Juretus observes that scribes commonly confused the letters *b* and *m* because of their similarity, as in the old codex, which had *mormorum* for *morborum*.].

Suddenly, from the midst of the gathering crowd, a leper covered with varied misery and made still more wretched by an obscene whiteness asked the Lord, saying: “Lord, if you wish, you can cleanse me.” The petitioner’s faith in this word was not small, since he believed that the effect of his cleansing had been established solely by the divine will. For when the Lord touched him with his sacred hand, saying, “I will; be cleansed,” the two-colored disease immediately departed, and, laying aside the horror of the spotted skin, the body was freed from its foreign ugliness. The people saw him suddenly changed by aid[[Col. 0635D] In place of *mutatus*, the old codex had *motatus*. [Col. 0636D] Later I would gladly read *vera magis in specie*, and *suoque minus agnosci visus est in colore*, that is, “he was scarcely, or less, recognized when he returned to his own color.”] and, now displaying a healthy form, he seemed more recognizable in appearance, though less recognizable by his colour.

Peter’s mother-in-law, violently afflicted, was oppressed by panting fever, her entrails seized by fire, and a powerful lamp of heat had settled harshly in her seething marrow. The fate of her trembling soul hung uncertain between death and life, and the arrival of icy death was being overheated by the flame of her limbs. But when the Lord visited the sick woman, wrapped in dangers, with his healing touch, the deadly fire suddenly fled, quenched by a living fountain; and the woman, rising restored, became diligent in service—the very woman who had just been weak became the attendant of her physician.

Moreover, in merciful contact he repeatedly expelled from human limbs the madness of diabolical severity, lest a non-divine spirit, inserted into the work of divinity, rage there; and throughout countless crowds he restored the use of the body as diseases fled, rescuing peoples from the danger of various[[Col. 0637] The old codex incorrectly had *aqua varia*; for this Juretus restored *atque varia*.] afflictions as the peril of illness subsided.

Then, walking along the shores of the sandy path, he boarded the planks of a small boat and, with the disciples accompanying him, began to cross. When the vessel had already been carried far from the shore, driven by the movement of the swelling sail, a merciless storm arose, violently agitating the entire sea with tempests from its depths and lifting the stern, submerged as the wave receded, again upon the swelling waters. Despair of safety had disturbed the grieving disciples, and even the sailors were forced to admit that no remedy lay at all in their own skill; finally, all believed that they were perishing and would be dashed as shipwrecked men against rocky shores, whether clinging to the timbers of the boat or being whirled about by the labor of their arms at the oars. But Christ, the true and watchful pilot[[Col. 0639D] Juretus, Gallandius, and others have *ac profidus*; *ac providus* is better, which is the reading in certain libraries of the Fathers and was also Juretus’s conjecture. The words that follow are from Psalm 120:4. In many libraries of the Fathers one finds *non dormitavit*, “he did not slumber”; but *dormitabit*, “he will not slumber,” must be retained.], supported by a small pillow, rested sleeping in the stern amid the tossing waves, asleep in body but ever-watchful in majesty; as David’s prophecy says: “He will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel.”

And when the disciples cried out with one voice, “Lord, save us; we are perishing,” he rose, awakened, commanded the winds to be still, ordered the sea to be silent, and suddenly the unexpected calm of both the sea’s course and the air became a sign revealing his presence and divinity. What, then, should be thought of that storm? Did the sea raise savage waves against the Lord, or did the winds attempt to stir up a rebellious struggle against their own creator? Far be it that the elements should have attempted something that would inflict injury upon majesty. Rather, so that we may judge all things to be subject to Christ’s powers in humble devotion, the entire sea is believed to have been exceedingly joyful at the Lord’s voyage, since it came in obedience and, rushing forth from the depths of the waves, boiled with a whiter swell. Likewise, the naturally swift force of the light winds had surrounded the stern in which Christ sat, their wings spread with winged delight, like the royal camp of a commander, encircled by an attending company. For no one who enjoys the license of violent power can easily be compelled to obey an imperious lord, as the waves of the sea and the winds, bending before Christ’s divine commands, suddenly laid down their headlong courses, stirred into rapid motion, in languor and torpor.

[Col. 0640C] Meanwhile the Lord of the deep, carried along by the calm, left the boat and proceeded along the shore of the neighboring coast, [Col. 0641A] when suddenly two exceedingly savage men, possessed by a crowd and legion of demons, burst forth from the tombs with a terrifying roar. And for this reason they were bound with links of iron chains. Alas, how grievous is the condition of madness! Whoever endures the violence of raving insanity must also lie beneath punitive bonds. Yet fittingly that most wicked spirit dwelt among tombs and ashes, having nothing in common with life. Then, terrified at the Lord’s coming and driven from the dwelling of the purified mind, fearing to enter again into the human form which he saw Christ bearing, he obtained permission to approach the herd of swine, exceedingly delighted by the obscenity of filth and always wrapped in friendships with stinking mud, as the reward for his own merits. For, black, shaggy, and horrible, he sought to choose a dwelling resembling his own deformity; and, continually launching sad assaults, he invaded and drove the herd of swine, and killed it by hurling it headlong into the waters of the sea. Nor is the devil improperly called the enemy in general, since he is harmful to all: he attacks those whom he hates and destroys those whom he loves.

[Col. 0643B] From there the Lord, again carried by the obedient boat, entered the boundaries of his native soil. The creator of all chose to be born everywhere[[Col. 0643D] Gallandius rightly observes that it seems necessary to read *ubique*, “everywhere,” so that *census* may be clear—*ubique*, that is, “and where.” I therefore adopt this reading, although all printed editions have *ibique*.], and he called the town of that region his homeland. Then four men brought to him, carrying a certain sick man on a bed laid upon their shoulders, one scarcely still a man, already a corpse. His life, devoid of bodily movement, foreshadowed the image of death. Thus his limbs lay inert, their sinews’ bonds loosened, their functions dispersed through the slackened limbs; wounded by disease and estranged through the wasting of putrid decay, they could no longer perform their proper tasks. When the Lord, seeing that the man required the restoration of his strength from the power of heaven, perceived this, he first cured him by absolving him from sins, which are the roots of all evils, [Col. 0644B] so that salvation might enter the man, cleansed and purified after the filth had been driven away, as though into a house prepared for it. Thus he said to the man lying there, then wretched but soon to be happy[[Col. 0643D] In some printed editions I read *effecturo*, in others *affecturo*, and in others, corruptly, *furo*. I scarcely doubt that the true reading is *futuro*, or *affuturo*. Below, in an old manuscript, there was *ex becilli* for *ex imbecilli*.], “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” Without delaying to obey the command, he rose—strong from weakness, confident from despair, destined to live from dying—and, taking up the little bed on which he had lain motionless, now drier than the strength of the very withered wood, he rejoiced to walk at last on his own feet and to have dispensed with another’s footsteps; and, in a grateful exchange of service, he soon carried back on his obedient shoulders the one who had carried him.

Thus, while the Lord was performing these miracles, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, having reached the limits of life, had lost the breath of heavenly light and lay an immobile body, already owed only to burial. Then her father, wounded by the disaster of his wretched child, ran out; the final end had robbed him of the hope of his flourishing lineage. Weeping and groaning, he threw himself at the Lord’s feet. Scarcely able to complete his pleading words, shaken by sobs, he said: “Have mercy on an orphaned father; have mercy on an abandoned old man. I have one daughter—or rather, I had one—who, now failing while not yet established in the years of puberty, seems to have taken from me the names of fatherhood. Bring aid and help; restore the departed soul to limbs already cold—one for whom all power is available, whom nothing can obstruct from exercising all power.” Scarcely had he completed these prayers when the Lord, already surrounded by disciples [Col. 0645C] and crowds, was walking toward the girl’s funeral in order to raise her.

Meanwhile a woman wounded for twelve years by a great flow of blood mingled with the crowds. She had spent much on physicians, accomplishing nothing, and emerged emptied alike of her possessions and her blood. But when faithful confidence began to abound in the secret place of a heart already healed by belief, she thrust herself forcefully into the midst of the crowds, desiring at least to touch the very edge of the Lord’s garment; hiding afterward, she suddenly snatched secret health from the extreme hanging border of its hem. O how much more powerful confidence is in obtaining difficult things than petition! For confidence comes from the heart, whereas prayers are often poured forth by the tongue without the heart; confidence cannot arise without the heart. Behold, now a woman despairing under the punishment of a long illness came to the physician, not pleading, not groaning, not lamenting, but silently took away what she sought. Silence stood upon her mute lips, while her mind cried out to the Lord. Soon a flood of greater faith dried up the streams of her surging blood; and, though all were unaware of the woman’s act of grace, Christ was not unaware of the gift of his own power, from whose fountain flowed what fulfilled the hope of the believing woman. By making the theft public, he rewarded so faithful an act with saving gifts and gave the force of the seizure its due recompense.

[Col. 0647B] Meanwhile they had reached the roof of the pitiable house, where the premature funeral of the virgin lay exposed amid the tears of all. A lamenting assembly and tumult had filled the entire house with the voices of bitter rejoicing. The flute-players lamented[[Col. 0647D] Juretus found *clangebant* in an old manuscript and restored *plangebant*, “they lamented.” Originally the manuscript also had *tubicines*, “trumpeters,” but the scribe later wrote *tibicines*, “flute-players”; Juretus declares the latter more correct, because flutes were customarily used at the funerals of the young. [Col. 0648D] Compare the note on the verses. For *inferis blandientes*, “soothing the dead,” Gallandius’s conjecture *inferiis blandientes*, “soothing the funeral rites,” is not bad. A little later he reports that the text read *defunctam dixerit*, “he called the dead woman”; most libraries of the Fathers have *defunctum dixerit*, “he called the dead man,” which I would certainly not dare condemn.], while flute-players, their lament shaped into melody, sang songs soothing to the dead; and the joyless crowd, running about and crying out with repeated cries of grief, had thrown the unhappy house into confusion. The Lord forbids her to be mourned as one dead, for she is composed in sleep; he forbids her to be lamented as dead, because she will live. To everyone the body seemed extinguished. To Christ alone, who had come to bestow life, it appeared merely filled with sleep. This also contributed to his singular glory: he called the dead woman sleeping, so that, intending to display the marvelous deeds of his power to her parents, he might avoid the affront of human praise by declaring that he was giving less than he was actually giving. Then, softening the motionless corpse and cold body, bound by the rigidity of icy death, with the fire of the spirit, he raised the virgin from Tartarus by the command of his authoritative voice and granted the girl, born once, to live twice. Her parents stood amazed, hesitating to believe in their daughter what they saw; and, moved by the sudden joy of the event, they changed the kind of their lamentation, pouring forth more tears of joy.

After completing the work of renewed light and departing from there, he saw two men wounded by the loss of their sight, entreating him in almost these words: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” They were asking for that mercy by which, removing the darkness of night, he might restore day to all faces. How safe it is to believe, how wholesome it is to trust diligently in God! For they already saw with the heart who, as Christ walked by, felt the path of light. Then their eyes, oppressed by the gloomy blindness of their punishment, like a fire made sluggish by oil poured upon it, flashed at the Lord’s touch; and when the right hand of serenity was applied, [Col. 0650B] their seeing faces shone with their own lamps.

After these men had been dismissed, another was brought forward, weak through illnesses of three kinds. Bereft of speech, deprived of hearing, with his limbs’ functions snatched away into emptiness, he seemed to be filled with nothing but a demon. Reversing the causes of his condition, the Lord immediately healed him: having expelled the demon, he filled him equally with speech and hearing[[Col. 0649D] Juretus observes that *vacuasset* should be read instead of *vacuaret*, “had emptied,” and *replevisset* instead of *repleret*, “had filled”; likewise in Book V, chapter 7, *meruisset* instead of *mereretur*. This alteration of tenses is familiar among writers of the later age.].

Nor did he hesitate to give the twelve disciples an equal measure of power. He commanded them to accomplish everything they saw him accomplish, and, rich in every power, sent them to seek the lost sheep—the house of Israel—because the dignity of this name had not yet been scattered continuously among all the nations. [Col. 0651B] “Go,” he instructed them among his other commands, “preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near; cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received freely; give freely.” It was as though the Lord, anxious with pastoral care, were saying: “As a good shepherd, I entrust the flocks to you, my workers, since you are diligent; for their sustenance I allot fields belonging to my own right. Let no one therefore sell pasture to my lambs and sheep that are subject to my authority.” He first entrusted this principle to apostolic discipline, so that afterward, propagated through their teaching, the doctrine of the following age might flow down to posterity, just as countless streams derived from a single source wander throughout the boundaries of the whole world[[Col. 0651D] In the printed editions *sicut*, or *ut*, is omitted, and the sentence reads without any sense: *doctrina, derivata*, etc. Gallandius has already noticed the error. In some libraries of the Fathers there is the error *lumina*, “lights,” for *flumina*, “streams.”]. Whoever therefore exercises the work of the Godhead—a work he does not claim as his own but has received as one worthy of spiritual tradition—having obtained the grace of a pure gift, should devote himself to the grace of that pure gift, so that he may appear to be a steward rather than a merchant. And, when David’s song of joy has been fulfilled, let him declare this hope of life to come for himself[[Col. 0652D] Juretus retained the reading of the old exemplar. Although the Vulgate now reads in Psalm 70:15, “For I have not known letters; I shall enter into the powers of the Lord,” many ancient authorities, such as Jerome, Augustine, Arnobius in his Commentary, and the Roman Psalter, have *negotiationem*, “business,” instead of *litteraturam*, “letters.” In the libraries of the Fathers there may be an error in *qui*, “who,” for *quia*, “because,” as Gallandius actually printed it. The Apostle’s words are from 1 Corinthians 4:1, 2, and 7. Below, at verse 109, in the prose text *in* appears to be an error for *in antiqua*.]: “I have not known commerce; I shall enter into the power of the Lord.” For no servant can have anything to administer, or anything from which to distribute gifts, without the Lord’s generosity, unless he has received what he is to dispense. Let us hear the apostle Paul saying the same thing: “Let a man regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that one be found faithful.” And again the same teacher admonishes us, saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

Then, after the Lord had entered the synagogue, he saw a cripple, deformed by the paralysis of his body, half-dead in his wounded limbs, neither wholly living nor wholly dying. The ice of sluggish torpor had amputated the use of his withered right hand, leaving it already numb for all practical purposes. [Col. 0654A] Then, by his powerful and commanding aid, the man earned a palm of victory. When the movements of the veins, which should have brought blood’s warmth, had ceased, the Lord restored animation not by technique but by command, saying: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched out his hand, and it was restored to him like the other. Truly this is the singular gift of God, which he continually exercises: he takes nothing away from human well-being and always restores everything.

[Col. 0654B] Behold again that slippery serpent, the Chelhydra, and that harmful renewer of evil, exceedingly rich in the livid poison of gall, who rejoices to grow fat on human corruption. The venom which he had often poured out upon many people seized by alternating illnesses, he gathered together by raging against the whole body of one man: he stole his mind, closed his voice, extinguished his sight, and, fastening three calamities upon him at once, compelled him to become both mute and blind [Col. 0655B] and to rave. To this man the merciful savior of the whole world, our light, the Father’s Word, restored sight when the obscene spirit had been disturbed; he renewed his mouth, and through the Word words advanced, while through the light lights revived.

A woman, too, had come to be healed, bent more by an old disease than by age. Her movements trembled, she panted with groans, her shoulders were curved, her face inclined, and she continually looked downward, her head bowed toward the lowly earth. Raised upright by the Lord’s powers after eighteen years, she lifted her erect limbs and gazed upon heaven and the stars and the burning globe of the sun, remembering that she had once seen them. You who worship idols, consider what difference there is between the God whom you flee and the demon whom you appease—if he can be appeased, since he never ceases to harm. For all whom he possesses are crushed; those whom Christ burdens with the yoke of his sweetest lightness are lifted up.

Then, seeing that the people had followed him into the wilderness, like the typological Moses and true prophet, and were failing from the ancient scarcity of food, he restored the ancient comforts with the greatest increase. For then, in place of the suddenly supplied flesh of many birds, he made the quantity of two fish abound. Then he poured down manna from heaven in abundance: by distributing only five loaves, he permitted food to abound for five thousand men. The movement of the rest of the crowd remained uncounted, since the multitude of women and children had no number. And what you will admire even more, whoever reads these things—if you have not already learned them as familiar—after the hunger of the satisfied people had been expelled, twelve baskets were filled with the mass of fragments that had been gathered up. The abundance was not so great when he gave the food as it was in the leftovers, already rejected, when they were collected.

Meanwhile, as the ocean received the day beneath the deep-blue wave of its seething heat and was beginning to plunge toward evening, while the approach of starry night was being announced through the pallor of the sky, the Master remained on land, and the disciples alone sought the vessel of the sea. The sea raged against the boat exposed to hostile winds. Then, at about the fourth watch of the shadowy night, the Lord walked upon the waves he was treading down; with calm progress he compressed the swollen billows of the foaming deep, and the gentle sea washed the sacred footprints of Christ with a mild flowing. Those in danger marveled at the sudden sight: paths for walkers had opened beneath a pedestrian route across the waters normally traversed by ships. While all wavered, uncertain whether the Lord truly appeared or whether uncertain phantoms of darkness were deceiving eyes overshadowed by fear of danger, Peter, wounded by faith and a friend whom familiar grace always allowed to recognize Christ, asked to go to him. When called, he descended into the sea without trembling. He was not submerged by the grasping force of the receding wave; raised by the help of the Lord’s hand, he would have taken refuge in the safest harbor of the powerful right hand. Cutting a path across the glassy fields of the salt sea, he became a traveler contrary to the sea’s nature. O increase of growing faith! Earlier he had despised the poor man’s nets, the solace of life; now he refused life itself, so that he might come to Christ.

Then the Lord left the ship and walked upon the land of Gennesaret, accompanied by a gathering of disciples. Its inhabitants, receiving his arrival with gratitude, brought together their own people impeded by various illnesses to be healed in the presence of the divine power, so that merely touching the fringe of his garment might cure the most severe diseases. And whoever was permitted to obtain this became immediately possessed of health. How precious was that garment! Or rather, it had no price, since, sold in no commercial exchange, it itself redeemed everyone with the gifts of a small thread.

From there, as he passed through the roads of the region of Tyre and Sidon, a Canaanite woman earnestly begged him on behalf of her daughter, wounded by a disease in which a dark spirit had taken its seat. She asked that she be counted among the dogs, which do not cleverly leave their masters’ tables but feed by licking up the crumbs that have been shaken off and dropped, in the smallness of fallen morsels. Her voice was most humble, but her faith was exalted. Once her daughter was healed, that faith quickly transformed a dog into a sheep and caused one born among the thorns of her people to enter the pastures of Hebrew grass.

Then, ascending the high ridges of a mountain, accompanied by an innumerable people, he restored their former use to thousands of the lame and blind, as well as to the deaf, lepers, those weak in their hands, and everyone sick who had flocked together; he set the organs of their weakened limbs in harmony with their proper nerves and movements.

While by the marvelous working of his power he refreshed the wounded multitude, the third day was passing. In places dry with arid sterility, the exhausted people had not obtained any food. Through the double burden of their labor, their languishing hunger was nourishing its own hardship, if the people, worn out, had to bear the long burden of want along the difficult path by which their steps would return[[Col. 0662D] The old manuscript has the erroneous *exhausus* for *exhaustus*.]. Moved by compassion, the almighty one, who is always the generous bread of the needy, wherever he distributes food and wherever necessity has denied barren crops, satisfied four thousand men with a very few small fish and seven broken loaves, apart from the immense company of women and the swarm of children, comparable to bees. And, so that you may marvel even more at another thing, the food increased while it was being eaten, and the losses produced by the bites of the diners generated more nourishment. Hunger fled in terror from its own leftovers, gathered into seven baskets, when it saw, from the abundance of so many fragments collected, a multiplied harvest overflowing from a small seed.

Although Christ seemed to bear the mortal limbs of a human body from the beginning of his mother’s generation, he could not remain hidden as God. For neither is a city hidden when it has been established upon a mountain, nor is a burning lamp placed under a bushel; rather, raised higher, the substance of its living flame supplies light to everyone. With three disciples as witnesses, whom he had led with him up a lofty mountain, he displayed the appearance of his glory, transfigured; and his countenance radiated like a fiery sun, imitating the whiteness of snow in his garments[[Col. 0663D] Gallandius inserted *ardor*, “heat,” namely, “like the fiery heat of the sun,” so that, as he says, the meaning might be clear. This is indeed how it is read in the poem; yet the old reading can be defended in this sense: “and his fiery appearance shone like that of the sun,” namely, “like the fiery appearance of the sun.” Sedulius likes to speak in similar verbal constructions. A little later Gallandius retained the common reading and therefore connected *illud speciem* with the preceding phrase, but observed that one might read *illius speciem*, “his appearance,” or rather *illud speciei*, “that [appearance] of the likeness”—namely, of both sun and snow. I especially approve and adopt *illud specimen*, “that image.”]. Why, then, did the most prudent Evangelist compare the most brilliant splendor of divine majesty, whose brightness no eye can behold, with the forms of the sun and snow? The reason will teach us more clearly. In this world nothing is brighter than the sun or whiter than snow; therefore he judged that the image of supreme divinity should be compared with them, since nothing greater is shown to have been granted to mortal eyes. For that extraordinary radiance of the Lord surpassed both the sun and the snow to such a degree that anyone’s gaze can easily behold the sun and snow. But when the apostles could not look upon Christ shining with the brightness of his own light, they fell face down upon the earth. O great height of sublime merits, to which it was granted to recognize in this world what the world was not worthy to perceive[[Col. 0664D] The reading *merebat*, “was worthy,” is old and sound, not *merebatur*, “was being worthy.” It is similarly found in *moderat*, *lucraret*, and comparable forms in our author and others, as Juretus indicates. Nonius’s little book *On Contrasting Forms of Words* is relevant here.]! What is more, they recognized with their inward eyes both Elijah and Moses, unknown to bodily sight, so that, as the truth of greater faith became manifest, he might show himself to be the Alpha and Omega, that is, the beginning and the end. To him such prophets appeared to have come together: one still enjoys vigorous old age, while no human course can surpass the other’s final boundary of light. And when the heavenly oracle of starry speech was extended from heaven and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” the Father’s voice taught that Christ was begotten.

But after the Lord had resumed his bodily appearance and again covered his heavenly form with the veil of flesh, openly displaying himself to the people, a certain humble man suddenly approached, kneeling, cast down by grief, and praying in these words: “Lord, I have only one son left—or, if he can be called ‘left,’ he hangs suspended at the boundary between death and life. An exceedingly unclean spirit grievously subdues him and, tearing him apart, frequently tries either to burn him with flames or to drown him in the hostile waters; after exhausting him with many dangers, it contrives his final end. I beg you: drive away the madness of his mind and restore him to me—or to himself—lest the power hostile to the light, blind and wretched, take away his desperately clinging life.” While he was still pouring forth these words with tears and groans, the Lord, already moved by a compassionate heart, healed the boy. [Col. 0667B] Then the furious and turbulent robber, who had long tormented a structure belonging to another’s jurisdiction, about to depart from the dwelling of the perverse house, was inflamed with burning anger. He seized the boy’s limbs and tried to tear them apart, but, forbidden by the Lord and unable to prevail, he flew into the infernal regions, leaving the boy unharmed.

The King, too, who alone is King of kings and is proved to be Lord of rulers, did not disdain to pay the imperial tribute. He ordered Peter, who was fishing in the sea, to raise from the waters a bearer of a golden didrachm[[Col. 0667D] The printed editions have *dragmatis*; I read *didrachmatis*, as Gallandius’s reading from the poem requires.]. Then the swift inhabitant of the waters swallowed the trembling snare of the deceiving hook, hanging from the native seas while the rod lashed them; and the most worthless fish, carrying the rich payment, proved more valuable in the honor of another’s weight than in its own. How much, nevertheless, did Christ wish us to imitate his teaching in this act! Although he could have refused the indignity of this payment—for he had nothing in common with the common people except that he should assist all with saving benefits—he preferred to pay an unnecessary contribution rather than deny anything to one who asked, so that the author and teacher of justice, who said, “Give to everyone who asks”[[Col. 0668D] Gallandius has *Omni petenti te tribue*, “Give to everyone who asks you,” from the Vulgate, Luke 6:30. Other editions of Sedulius omit *te*.], might first fulfill the institutions of his own law.

When the apostles, as was their custom, asked him simply who might be considered the greater in the kingdom of heaven, he, as God and marvelous teacher, answered that the humble person was superior to all and surpassed everyone who had made himself last of all. He set in the midst of them a little child, as an example of spiritual conduct, prescribing that the disposition of a tender and immature age, not its years, should be imitated. For childish years of small stature neither cherish the pomp of the world nor are touched by ambition for honor, nor are they inflated by the swelling of proud arrogance[[Col. 0669D] The old manuscript has *exigui*, masculine, for *exiguae*, feminine, and *qui diligunt* for *quid diligunt*. In many libraries of the Fathers the reading is *non diligunt*, not *deligunt*.]. Therefore the simplicity of life, the nearer it comes to the ground through its humility, comes that much nearer to heaven. For the mind that bends downward is raised up, while the mind that is raised up is bent downward; and the lower movement of the heart, by which it seeks to descend, is exalted. For God raises the humble and poor from the filth and joins them to the company of the powerful. He cast headlong from heavenly dignity into the depths of filthy Tartarus the neck of truly diabolical pride. Thus divine Scripture declares[[Col. 0669D] The first words are from the Epistle of James 4:5. The second are from Psalm 112:7–8; the final words are from Proverbs 10:4 according to the Septuagint, which Sedulius generally follows.]: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud.” And again, remembering the same thing, it says: “Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dungheap, to place him with princes, with the princes of his people.” For all poverty is the companion of humility. Hear Solomon saying: “Poverty humbles a man.” But we report matters far too small and insignificant if, running through the divine deeds one by one, we review them individually; they are not to be explained in words, but are to be recognized in their totality.

[Col. 0633]

[Col. 0633B] [Note: [Col. 0633D]

1. Vaticanus 1: “Where he changed water into wine.” Reginensis 2: “On the miracle of water changed into wine.” Romanus: “Where the Lord, invited to a wedding, changed water into wine.”

4. Cellarius restored *amittere* from the manuscripts, since he had found *dimittere* in the common text. All our manuscripts likewise have *amittere*, as do the editions of Parrhasius and Aldus, except that the latter corruptly has *ammittere*, as it is also read in the Anglicus and Albinus manuscripts.

5. Cantabrigiensis, Fabricius, and several other printed editions have *laesa*, “injured,” instead of *laeta*, “joyful.” This reading should be retained. Nebrissensis notes the following on the word *pallorem*, “pallor”: “This is the color of the finest wine; in the category of white wine they call it yellowish (*gilvum*).” And on *rubuerunt*, “they reddened”: “Some jars were changed into yellow wine, some into red.” But Sedulius asserts that the waters lost their pallor, not that they took on the pallor of wine. Learned men note that in Palestine there were no wines other than red, and no other symbol could have been found more suitable for representing Christ’s blood than red wine.[Col. 0634D]

8. *Lacus* is ordinarily understood as a large vessel in which must is received. Cicero, Ovid, Columella, Nemesius, and others used the word in this sense.

9. In Ottobonianus 1, *verax* has apparently been correctly emended to *ferax*. Most of our manuscripts—Anglicus, Albinus, Reginenses 2 and 5, Vaticani 1 and 2, Meus, Urbanus, Romanus, and Reginensis 1—read *virtute colenda* for the abbreviation *d. script.* Ottobonianus 1, in a second hand, together with Arntzenius, Parrhasius, Aldus, and Poelmann’s papers, has *virtute colona*. Ottobonianus 2 and Reginensis 1, in the first hand, and Ottobonianus 1, in the first hand, have *colona*, which the prose text and most printed editions retain. Nebrissensis explains *virtute colona* as “cultivating by her power.” The prose text supports another reading: it calls the vine *virtutis colona*, “the cultivator of power,” unless *virtute* is to be read.

10. Meus has *fructiferans*. For the abbreviation *d. s.*, *fructificans* is better; it is a word used by Calpurnius and Tertullian. The other form should be relegated to barbarisms.]

First gave proofs of his own power; and, present as a guest,

He came to feed, not to be fed, and wondrously changed

The waters poured out into wine. The liquids rejoiced

[5] To lose their pallor; the joyful water changed its flavor,

[Col. 0634B] Giving forth wine, and throughout all the tables

Sweet cups reddened with must not born of grapes.

Thus Christ filled six jars with this nectar;

238 For he was a fruitful vine, a cultivator by his power,

[10] Making everything bear fruit; beneath whose kindly shade

[Col. 0635A] [Note: [Col. 0635B]

11. Vetus 1, Monacensis, and Poelmann’s papers have *mitis*, “gentle.” In Ottobonianus 1 it is uncertain whether the reading is *mitis* or *vitis*. The true reading is *mitis*. Virgil, Book 1 of the *Georgics*, verse 448: “Alas, the vine will then poorly protect the gentle grapes.” Some printed editions wrongly have *in occiduas*, “into perishing [grapes],” instead of *inocciduas*, “imperishable,” as the glosses explain. Parrhasius, Anglicus, and Poelmann’s papers have *emittit*, “sends forth”; our other manuscripts, together with most printed editions, more correctly have *enutrit*, “nourishes.”

12. Ottobonianus 1: “On the son of the royal official.” Meus: “He frees the boy of the royal official while absent.” All our manuscripts have *Post regulus nato quidam*, except the most recent Reginensis 5, which reads *Regulus hinc nato quidam*. Aldus printed *Post regulus* with the manuscripts, but corrected it in the errata to *Regulus hinc nato*. I believe Fabricius followed Aldus, although Cellarius seems to attribute to Fabricius the transposition of the manuscript words. Cappusotus, Parrhasius, and other old editions, together with the manuscripts of Arntzenius, Cambridge, and Turin—of remarkable antiquity—confirm the reading of our manuscript copies. Nevertheless Cellarius and Arntzenius, concerned about the meter, retained *Regulus hinc nato*. The other reading is more correct, whether Sedulius disregarded the quantity of the syllable in this name, as in certain others, or, following the derivation from *rego*, “I rule,” thought that the first syllable in *regulus* could be short.

13. *Flebilis*, “lamenting,” is used for *flens*, “weeping,” just as *fragilis*, “breakable,” is used for *fractus*, “broken”; *fugitivus*, “fugitive,” for *fugiens* or *fugatus*, “fleeing” or “driven away”; *sanabilis*, “curable,” for *sanatus*, “healed”; *mutabilis*, “changeable,” for *mutatus*, “changed”; *fugax*, “fleeing,” for *fugiens*, “fleeing”; and similarly elsewhere.

15. Vaticanus 2 has *animum*, “mind”; the others have *animam*, “soul.” The same occurs at verse 112, *lapsamque animam*, “the fallen soul.”

16. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *quia nulla*, “because nothing.”

17. Vaticanus 1: “*Velocem est comitata*,” “it accompanied the swift [faith].” *Est* is better omitted.

[Col. 0636B] 21. Meus has *quia cuncta prius quam nota videndo*, “because, seeing all things before they were known,” which is less satisfactory. As Nebrissensis observes, Sedulius seems in the words *prius quam nata*, “before they were born,” to mean that the royal official’s son was not healed immediately. But the Evangelist John, 4:52 and following, reports that he was healed at the very hour when Jesus said, “Your son lives.” Nor does Sedulius mean anything else when he says, “Granting salvation by an easy word.” Therefore the principle of verbal equality must not be brought forward against Sedulius’s clear intention.

23. Romanus: “On the healing of a leper.” Meus: “He cleanses a leper.” Poelmann: “Various illnesses are removed.” I will not omit Nebrissensis’s note: “Every *oppidum* is a city except Rome, which is not an *oppidum*. *Rura* are cultivated lands. *Casas* are huts in the fields. *Vicos* are places not enclosed by a wall, unlike *castella*, which are surrounded by walls.”

26. Poelmann: “A leper is cleansed.” In the others, the heading is placed before verse 23. Reginenses 1 and 2, Vaticani 1 and 2, Romanus, Ottobonianus 2, Anglicus, Cantabrigiensis, Arntzenius, Albinus, the Leipzig edition, Parrhasius, Cellarius, and *mediae*; Reginensis 5, Meus, Aldus, Vetus 1 and 2, Grunerus, and Arntzenius have *medio*. Ottobonianus 1 has *medio*, but it seems corrected to *mediae*. The prose text supports *medio*, but the more excellent manuscripts omit *mediae*. In Urbanus there is the error *media*.

28. Vetus 1 and 2 have *nitens*, “shining”; but *miser*, “wretched,” is defended by the manuscripts and the prose text. Vaticanus 1 has *Deus*, “God,” instead of *Domine*, “Lord,” a reading that should be retained, or at least is supported by the Gospel itself.

29. Cellarius and Grunerus, together with some printed editions, have *purgare*, “to cleanse,” a word certainly suitable to this matter. Nevertheless, Arntzenius, in chapter 9 of the *Specimen Observationum*, proves by many arguments that *mundare*, “to cleanse,” should be preferred, on the basis of the prose text, the manuscript of Arntzenius, and the editions of Parrhasius, Fabricius, Monacensis, and others. Add our manuscripts Romanus, Meus in the first hand, Albinus, Reginenses 1, 2, and 5, Vaticani 1 and 2, Ottoboniani 1 and 2, and Urbanus. Meus has *at*, but *ut* is better.]

The gentle vine nourishes imperishable grapes.

Suffering from fever, and prevent his trembling soul

[15] From slipping from its seat. Then great power,

Which denies nothing to the believer and delays no gifts,

By an easy word: “Your son lives now,” he said;

“Go; he is yours.” How great the authority carried by Christ’s command!

32. Arntzenius: “And in his own color he was scarcely recognized.” Anglicus and Albinus: “And in his own color he was scarcely recognized.” Others: “And in his own color he, scarcely recognized, was more [fully restored].” Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *cognitus*, “known,” instead of *agnitus*, “recognized.” In Reginensis 1 the gloss is: “He is scarcely recognized more in his own than in another’s color.” Vetus 1, Vetus 2, and Monacensis incorrectly punctuate: “And in his own [color], he is scarcely recognized.” The Leipzig edition corruptly has *vir agnitus*, “a recognized man.” Wopkensius, with Cellarius, explains *magis* as “more” or “thereafter,” as in Fortunatus, *On the Benefits of Christ*: “Nor does the creator choose the sinner’s death more readily, when by his own punishments he gave us the weapons of salvation.”

33. Meus: “He frees Peter’s mother-in-law from fever.” Romanus: “On Peter’s mother-in-law.” Barthius, in his commentary on Claudian, page 874, cites *Nam Petri*. Arntzenius attributes *Morte Petri* to Aldus, but Aldus does not have this; he has *More Petri*, which is also found in Vaticanus 2 and Reginensis 5. The sense may be: “Fever, after the manner of a powerful lamp, burned Peter’s mother-in-law with its heat.” Cantabrigiensis and some printed editions have *torquebat*, “tormented,” instead of *torrebat*, “burned.” But *torrebat* is much more appropriate, so that the heat of the fever may be expressed. Compare Juvencus, Book 1, verse 807: “Whose panting mother-in-law lay prostrate under heat and fever.”

34. Arntzenius has *socri*, “of the father-in-law”; read *socrum*, “the mother-in-law.”

36. Monacensis corruptly has *colebat*, “cultivated,” instead of *coquebat*, that is, “cherished” or “prepared.” Silius, Book 1, 430: “And when the shameful evil and the final undertakings of the man were being prepared for Latium.” Livy, Statius, Sidonius, and others use the word in the same way.

38. Meus has *ingens*, “huge,” which is not as good as *igneus*, “fiery.” Reginensis 5 had *erat*, “was”; Aldus, together with the others, printed *abit*, “departs,” but placed *erat* in the errata.

40. Meus: “He frees many from spirits.” Poelmann: “Demons and all diseases are driven away.” Romanus and Meus have *rapidas*, “swift,” a word sometimes interchanged with *rabidas*, “raging,” in the manuscripts. *Rabidas* is more appropriate to this passage.]

### 42

Vonckius confidently asserts that one should read *faedaret honorem* (“he might defile the honor”), because it is absurdly said that someone’s honor is “vexed.” But, apart from the fact that “to vex someone’s reputation” is not a new expression—Aurelius Victor uses it in *Epitome*, chapter 52—here *honos operis Dei* (“the honor of God’s work”) is put for the human being, who is the honor of God’s work. The gloss in Reg. 1 is: “Whom he so vexed that he seemed not to know that man is the image of God.” Cellarius explains it: “That evil breath knew that the man, honorably created, was not devoted to God.” Better, in agreement with the prose version: “That breath which God knew was not divine.”

### 43

Rom., Urb., and Ang. have *noverat* (“he had known”), which conflicts with the meter. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *non esse deum* (“not to be God”). Nebrissensis conjectured *non esse reum* (“not to be guilty”), that is, “deserving blame.” In Westhemer’s edition, with Nebrissensis’ commentary, Sedulius’ words are reported in the notes as: “Whom he marks as not being God.” I think *notat* is an error, since it conflicts with the meter. The common reading is *non esse Dei* (“not to belong to God”).

### 44

Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Vat. 1 and 2, Ang., Alb., Ott. 2, Urb., Meus, and Rom. have *Ut pius*, that is, *utpote pius* (“since he was pious”), for the demon, by contrast, is a savage spirit. Arntzenius adopted this reading from the Arntzenian manuscript, Poelman’s papers, Aldus, and others, against those who had printed *Ut prius* with Parrhasius. The old Turin manuscript likewise confirms *Ut pius*, and the prose version supports it.

### 45

Vat. 1 has *a clade resolvit* (“he released from destruction”).

### 46

Meus has “He commands the storm.” Rom. has: “Where the Lord calmed the sea.”

### 47

In Reg. 2, *cymbae* (“of a small boat”) has become *lymbae*, with the gloss “of a small ship, a skiff.” But *lymbae* means nothing; perhaps the scribe intended to write *limbi*, since someone writes *limbi* for *lembi*. Yet *exiguae cymbae* (“of a small boat”) is required, unless someone prefers *lintris* (“of a skiff”).

### 48

Burmannus conjectured *vehentes* (“carrying”) for *sequentes* (“following”). But Sedulius expressed Matthew’s words, chapter 8, verse 23: “And when he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him.”

### 49

Arntz. has “The disciples balanced the nautical [sails].” Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 35, chapter 10, cites *carbasa vento* (“sails to the wind”). It is indeed more customary to say *carbasa praebere vento* (“to offer the sails to the wind”), and similar expressions; but *ponto* (“on the sea”) is defended by Seneca, *Medea* 318: “To spread the sails upon the vast sea.” What it means to “balance the sails” may be understood from Ovid, *Fasti* 3.585: “The sails fall at first, and are balanced by the uncertain breeze,” that is, they are not stretched tight but flutter loosely.

*The joyful limbs changed their foreign form,*

*and he was scarcely more recognized in his own complexion.*

*Perhaps a fever, gasping, was scorching Peter’s mother-in-law*

*with the heat of a powerful lamp; hanging in uncertain death,*

[35] *wounded life burned amid icy dangers,*

*and immense heat was cooking deadly cold.*

241 *But after the Lord’s hand touched her weary limbs,*

*the fiery heat departed, and, extinguished throughout the marrow,*

*the flame’s violence fell from a spring of hidden water.*

[40] *Indeed, he also drove away the raging fury of black*

*spirits, lest the savage breath tear human beings*

*with an unjust plague and vex the honor of God’s work—*

*whom he knew was not of God; and everywhere, in his mercy, he restored*

*innumerable crowds to health,*

[45] *when their sickness had been driven away, and lifted peoples*

*from diverse destruction.*

242 *From there, making for the sea, he trod the dry seaweed*

*with his feet, and, climbing onto the timbers of a small boat,*

*entered the waters of the sea; and the disciples, following the Lord,*

*balanced their sails upon the tranquil sea.*

[50]

[Note: 50. Vat. 1 has *a terra* (“from the land”).]

### 52

Rom., for *d. s.*, and Arntzenius’ copies of Poelman have *Tunc* (“then”) for *Cum* (“when”). Rom. has the erroneous *subita surgit* (“a sudden [storm] rises”).

### 53

*Vada salsa* (“salty shallows”) comes from Virgil, book 5, verse 158.

### 54

In Monast. *Pertulerat* is an error for *Perculerat* (“fear had struck”).

### 56

In Reg. 1 the reading is *placidum*, as in the others; but the gloss *sereno* (“calm”) points toward *placido*.

### 57

Most of our manuscripts, together with Parrh., Poelman’s papers, and Aldus, have *quia non* (“because he does not”). Some editions, including ancient ones, have *qui non* (“who does not”), as does the prose version. In Vat. 2 it is uncertain whether *qui* or *quia* should be read. Urb. has *quae non* (“which does not”), namely, “majesty.”

### 58

Poelman’s papers instruct one to write *prorsus nec* (“nor altogether”). It is preferable, however, to retain the common reading *neque prorsus* (“and never at all”). In Rom. *dormitat umquam* (“ever slumbers”) is a metrical error.

### 59

Reg. 1, Ott. 1, the oldest Turin manuscript, Cant., and the editions Vat. 1 and 2 have *lacrymantibus* (“weeping”). The manuscripts Alb., Reg. 2 and 5, Vat. 1, Urbin., Ottob. 2, Rom., Ang., and Meus, together with the prose version and most printed editions, have *clamantibus* (“shouting”). Vat. 2 erroneously has *cunctisque clamantibus* (“and all shouting”). In Reg. 2 the gloss likewise reads *clamantibus*, which indicates that something else had stood in the text.

### 60

Parrh. and Poelman’s papers have *Miserere Deus* (“Have mercy, God”), which is not satisfactory: although the prose version has *Domine* (“Lord”), the disciples at that time called Christ “Lord,” certainly, but not “God.” Vat. 1, Ott. 2, and Ang. have *Miserere cito* (“Have mercy quickly”); other witnesses more elegantly have *citus* (“quickly”).

### 63

Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.146: “He spoke, and, quicker than his words, calmed the swelling waters.”

### 68

Some printed editions have *Obsequio servire* (“to serve in obedience”); *fervere* (“to seethe”) has greater force, and also indicates the word’s etymology. See the note on Juvencus’ expression *freta fervida* (“boiling seas”), book 3, verse 127.

### 69

Poelman’s papers have *subitas* (“sudden”); Urb. and Parrh. have *rapidas* (“swift”), which is supported by the prose version. Most witnesses have *avidas* (“eager”), that is, “eager to obey Christ.” Cellarius’ explanation—“The rejoicing winds retreat when Christ commands”—is contrary to the poet’s meaning. The poet says that the rejoicing winds, circling around Christ in obedience alone, exulted in a sense. Wings are attributed to the winds. Juvenal, *Satires* 5.101: “He dries his wet wings in prison.”

### 70

Rom. has: “Where the Lord freed a certain man from a legion of demons.” Meus has: “He drove out the legion of demons which had invaded the herd of pigs from the two men.” *Lege Joanne* (“read John”) is corruptly written for *Legionem* (“the legion”).

*The boat had already been far from the shores, and, driven by the winds,*

*the secure stern was furrowing the middle of the deep,*

*when suddenly a savage storm arose and the sea was turned*

*by tempests; the salty shallows shook the trembling vessel.*

*Fear had struck their minds, and they thought that, shipwrecked,*

[55] *they were already stretching their arms toward the rocks along the shore.*

*But he himself was taking peaceful sleep upon his breast,*

243 *watchful in majesty, who never sleeps through eternity,*

*who rules Israel, nor ever sleeps completely.*

*Therefore, when the calm had been driven away, while all together*

[60] *cried out with one voice, “Have mercy quickly, have mercy—we perish!*

*Come to our aid with your holy help,” he delayed their prayers not at all.*

*The Lord rose and ordered the powerful winds*

*to grow mild, and, quicker than his words, calmed the swelling sea.*

*It was not the fierce, combative boldness of the sea*

[65] *that compelled the swelling waves to rise against the Lord,*

*nor were threatening blasts driving their savage forces;*

*but the sea, leaping joyfully for Christ, compelled the deep*

*to seethe in obedience, and the joy of the winds*

*moved their eager wings with rapid flight.*

[70] *Meanwhile, carried across the tranquil sea, he left the vessel*

[Note: 72. Parrh. has *gemini* (“two”), supported by the prose version, but opposed by the manuscripts and other printed editions.]

### 73

The older codices write *Prosiluere*; others have *Prosiliere*. I discussed this orthographic variation in the note on Juvencus, book 1, verse 119.
