In Ott. 1, *malo* (“evil”) appears above *mala* (“evil things”); in the margin it seems to be a different reading, *male* (“badly”). Urb. has: *quos non male daemone pauco*. Reg. 5 divides it as: *quos non mala, daemone pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox* (“whom not evil things, by a few demons—but a savage legion—was troubling”). Vat. 1 has: *quos non de mala daemone pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox*; but *de* appears to have been erased. In Reg. 1 the gloss is *mala—pestis* (“evil—plague”).

Vonckius conjectured: *quos non ala daemone pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox*, with the first syllable of *ala* shortened, as elsewhere Sedulius disregards quantity. Grunerus rejects this, saying that *mala* does not refer to the legion but is a plural accusative. I think he meant a plural nominative, with the sense: “whom evil things were not troubling by a few demons, but a savage legion was troubling.” Wopkensius is not much pleased by this explanation, and therefore tried: *quos non daemonia pauca—Sed legio vexabat atrox*, lengthening the second syllable of *daemonia*, as Sedulius sometimes does elsewhere; or rather: *quos non malus agmine pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox*, so that *malus* should be understood as “demon.”

I would not readily admit the first conjecture, since elsewhere Sedulius shortens the second syllable of *daemon*. The other is not so inept, but even so the construction is harsher; it would have to proceed in this way: “Whom not a wicked spirit with a small troop, but a savage legion, was troubling.” The meaning certainly is: “Whom not a few demons, but a savage legion of demons, was troubling.”

From Vat. 1 perhaps the sense can be extracted as: *quos non de daemone pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox*, namely, “whom not a legion from a few demons, but a savage—or immense—[force] was troubling.” For *legio* can be taken for any company or crowd of demons, which may be larger or smaller.

But until something better appears, let us retain the first interpretation, taken from Grunerus—or rather from Nebrissensis, who explains: “*Non mala*—repeat from the lower line, ‘were troubling.’ *Pauco daemone*—that is, ‘a few evil demons.’” It may also be understood as: “Whom an evil legion was troubling, not by a few demons but by a savage one,” that is, a numerous force. One may also suspect: *quos non macra daemone pauco—Sed legio vexabat atrox* (“whom not a meager force with few demons, but a savage legion, was troubling”).

### 75

Reg. 1, Ott. 1 in the text, and Poelman in the text have *gestantes* (“carrying”); the more common reading in the manuscripts and editions is *gestabant* (“they were carrying”), which Ott. 1 also has in the margin in the same old hand. Arntzenius printed *gestantes*.

### 76

Reg. 1, Ott. 1, Vat. 2, and Heins.’ manuscript have *dura* (“hard”), as is supported by the prose version *gravis* (“heavy”). Most have *dira* (“dreadful”). The punishment was double, because he endured both the demon and the chains.

### 80

The old Turin codex has *Effigiem reddit* (“he restores the image”). Reg. 1, Meus in the margin, Vulc., Nans., Torn. 1, Bas., Colon, Vet. 1 and 2, Mon., Poelman’s papers, and Poelman’s edition in the text have *reddens* (“restoring”), whose gloss in Reg. 1 is *deserens* (“leaving”). Reg. 2 and 5, Ottob. 1 and 2, Vat. 1 and 2, Urb., Rom., Meus in the text, Alb., Ald., Parrh., and Ang. have *repetens* (“returning” or “reassuming”). In Reg. 2 and Ott. 1 something else seems originally to have stood; after it was erased, the same old hand added *repetens*. In Vat. 1 the text originally read *Effigiem non repetens* (“not returning to the image”), but *non* was later erased.

Poelman’s edition in the margin, Torn. 3, Lips., Fabr., and the *Bibliotheca Lugduno-Batava Patrum* have *fugiens* (“fleeing”). The Cant. manuscript has *linquens* (“leaving”). Cellarius introduced *reverens* (“revering”) by conjecture; but, as Grunerus says, conjectures should be admitted only when absolutely nothing suitable is found in the manuscripts. Grunerus himself therefore chooses *fugiens*. Burmannus prefers *repetens*, or *recolens* (“recalling”), that is, reconsidering in his mind, for Cellarius had found *recolens* somewhere.

Arntzenius thinks *reverens* contrary to Sedulius’ meaning: the demon did not leave out of reverence, but was forced out by the power of Christ’s command. He considers *fugiens* more suitable here, but since it is not found in the manuscripts, he attributes it to the ingenuity of some learned man. He therefore follows the Arntzenian manuscript in retaining *linquens*.

The very oldest reading is certainly *reddens* or *reddit*, and it should not be despised if *reddens* can be explained by the gloss as *deserens*. Yet although *reddo* can mean “restore,” “release,” or “give forth,” it is not easily found with the meaning “leave.” I therefore retain *repetens*, with most manuscripts, though not in the sense Burmannus intended. The meaning is: “He does not dare approach the man, returning to the image which he sees Christ possessing”; or, “He does not dare approach the man and return to the image which …” Shortly afterward the poet says similarly: *petiere pecus* (“they sought the herd”), and so forth.

### 81

Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.26: “A filthy dog would have lived, or a sow friendly to mud.” Wopkensius also observes that *semper—amicum* (“always—friendly”) likewise occurs in Avienus, Symmachus, Arator, and Helpidius, with the hyphenated compounds *graveolens* and *semper-avarus*.

### 84

Edim. has *Porcorum tenuere* (“they held the pigs”). Others have *Porcinum*, as do Bede in *On Metre* and his commentator, who cite this verse without naming the author.

### 85

Arator likewise calls the demon a “guest” in book 2, verse 640: “Let it be polluted by its own guest,” and so forth.

*He had left the boat and was traversing the middle fields with his steps,*

*when, rushing from the burial mounds with a twin shriek,*

*two men leapt forth, whom not an evil demon, few in number,*

245 *but a savage legion was troubling; with bloody bonds*

[75] *they carried cruel chains upon their fettered arms.*

*They were also oppressed by a double punishment. Alas, the dreadful*

*condition of madness! The one who suffers force is more tightly bound.*

*Then, trembling at the Lord’s command, which ordered him to leave,*

*the unhappy spirit did not dare approach the man,*

[80] *returning to the image which he saw Christ possess.*

246 *But the herd, rejoicing in filthy pollution, always friendly*

*to filth and accustomed to live in foul mud,*

*was sought by them according to their merits; and the gloomy phalanxes*

*occupied the herd of swine: black, bristling, dreadful—*

[85] *such a guest was worthy to have such a house.*

[Note: 86. Meus: “He frees a paralytic.” Rom.: “Where the Lord raised a dead man.” But there is an obvious error in this title. Some printed editions, followed by Cellarius, have *pelagi* (“of the sea”). The manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *pelago* (“on the sea”). Thus Lucan, book 2, verse 88: “Carried across the hostile sea into enemy land.”]

### 87

Some printed editions incorrectly have *de corpore* (“from the body”), instead of *corpore* (“in the body”), namely, “in that body alone in which he wished to be born.” Matthew, chapter 9, verse 1, says: “And entering a boat, he crossed over and came to his own city.” Sedulius explains this as the native land, or Bethlehem. Others understand it better as Capernaum, the city in which Jesus frequently stayed.

### 88

Arntz. has *Deus* (“God”), others *Pater* (“the Father”), and the gloss in Reg. 1 is “who had already made it.” Nebrissensis has *Pater ipse* (“the Father himself”), saying: “For he will be called a Nazarene.” But Sedulius is speaking of Bethlehem, not Nazareth. Therefore “the Father dedicated [that land] to himself,” that is, to the Lord, as his homeland, when he said: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah; for from you will come a ruler who will govern my people Israel.” Although the syntax may seem difficult, it is not unusual. It is better, with the gloss, to understand *pater ipse* as “the Father himself, Christ, who had made it,” or, with the prose version, “the creator.”

### 89

“Living corpse” is an opposition of terms; concerning this I wrote in the note on Dracontius, book 1, verse 648: “Carrying living funerals, a living corpse in death.” Chrysologus likewise called the paralytic a “living corpse” in sermon 50.

### 90

Juvenal, *Satires* 1.64: “Let a sixth [part] be carried as a service.”

### 93

Lactantius and Juvencus also used the expression “the functions of the limbs.” *Desertus officiis* means “deserted by its functions”; Propertius, Statius, Tacitus, Phaedrus, and Boethius likewise omit the preposition in comparable expressions.

### 94

Vat. 1, Meus, and Reg. 2 have *dimissis* (“released”); in Reg. 2 it was earlier *demissis* (“lowered”), which the rest of our manuscripts, together with Arntzenius and the finest editions, retain. Arntzenius preferred *dimissis* from the prose version; but the prose should have been compared with the many manuscripts, so that the true reading might be extracted from it here and elsewhere. Otherwise there is frequent confusion in such words as *demitto* and *dimitto*, *demersus* and *dimersus*, *delapsus* and *dilapsus*. As far as the meaning is concerned, it makes little difference which one prefers.

### 95

Arntzenius, with only the Arntzenian manuscript, has *egere* (“to lack”), likewise confirmed by the prose version. I do not see why he maintains that *egere* is more suited to the poetic idiom than *egentem* (“lacking”), which the other manuscripts and editions unanimously support—unless perhaps he favors a view rejected by us elsewhere, namely, that a verse should not properly end with participles of this sort. “The Lord of virtues,” or “the Lord God of virtue,” are ecclesiastical expressions received into liturgical prayers.

### 96

Cant., Arntz., Burmannus’ codex, Poelman’s papers, Parrh., Ald., and Lips., together with our manuscripts Ott. 1, Vat. 1, Reg. 5, Urb., Rom., Alb., and Meus, confirm the reading. Other manuscripts and editions have *mundavit* (“cleansed”), which more recent editors adopt from the prose version and from the similar passage in book 1, verse 57: “The field made joyful is cleansed when the thorns are removed.”

### 97

Fabr. and some other editions have *misero inde jacenti* (“thereupon to the wretched man lying there”).

### 99

Edimb. has *discede* (“depart”), which is also Wopkensius’ conjecture. Grunerus defends *descende* (“go down”), because that verb is commonly used for “to go.” In Reg. 2 the gloss is *ascende, perge, vade* (“go up, proceed, go”).

### 100

Vet. 1 has *confessa*; read *concessa* (“granted”).

### 102

The gloss in Reg. 1 is *Vectorem—grabatum. Grataplacida* (“the carrier—the pallet. Grataplacida”). Here is Nebrissensis’ explanation: “His carrier, or himself, or the pallet. With a pleasing reward, because he had been carried by others for a fee, but not a pleasing one.”

### 103

Meus: “The chief priest asks the Lord for his dead daughter.” Rom.: “Concerning the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue.” The Turin manuscript: “He raises the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue.”

### 104

Nebrissensis cites the verse of Virgil, *Aeneid* 2, word for word at *clauso die*: “Before day, evening will set the heavens with its doors closed”; and at *superas auras*: *Aeneid* 6, “to escape into the upper air.”

*From there the Lord, carried across the sea to other shores,*

*entered the native land, in that body in which*

*he had chosen to be born, and the Father himself had dedicated it to him as his homeland.*

247 *Behold, they were already present, carrying a living man who was now a corpse,*

[90] *four men by the neck, while he lay upon a bed,*

*scarcely a man, whose life remained without use of the body,*

*an image of death; his limbs lay relaxed,*

*deserted by their functions, and through his slack limbs*

*the languid bonds hung down from loosened sinews.*

[95] *When the Lord of virtues saw him lacking strength,*

*he first cleansed him by removing his sins,*

*which produce increases of evils; and to the wretched man lying there*

248 *he said, “Rise, and lift your own pallet onto your shoulders,*

*and go down into your house.” Delaying not at all to obey the command,*

[100] *he whose salvation had been granted, leaving behind at last*

*the footprints of others, rejoiced to walk on his own feet,*

*and with a welcome reward carried back his carrier.*

*Meanwhile, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, when her day had closed,*

*had died and lost the upper air.*

[105] *But the father, whose hope of an adult offspring devouring death*

[Note: 110. Vat. 2, perhaps in a more recent hand, has *necnon* (“and also”), or *nec adhuc* (“nor yet”).]

### 111

Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *mihi patris* (“of a father to me”). An elegant reading would be: “He died—alas! He took from wretched me the name of father.”

### 113

Vonckius was troubled by the reading and proposed *Qui totam* (“who the whole”) or *Qui votum* (“who the vow”); Wopkensius rightly refutes him, proving with many examples that *totum* can mean “everything.” Compare Juvencus, book 4, verse 520: “It will be permitted to complete everything.” Ambrose, Zeno of Verona, and Chrysologus spoke similarly.

“The author, discoverer, and lord of light” is frequently said by sacred poets. In a hymn of Saint Vincent, which I possess copied from a very old Vatican Palatine manuscript, no. 833, and which I believe has not been published, the expression occurs similarly: “But fighting against him, you confessed more insistently the Father, author of light, and his Son, who alone is the true God.” This imitates Prudentius, hymn 5, *Peristephanon*, on Saint Vincent, verses 37 and following: “The Father, author of light, …”

### 116

Meus has *fluorem* (“flow”); retain *cruorem* (“blood”).

### 117

Parrh. has *expendit* (“he expended”); others have *tenuarat* (“had weakened”). In Reg. 1 there was originally another reading, but the same old hand added *tenuarat*. Rom. erroneously has *tenuerat* (“had held”). In Ott. 1 *tenuarat* was changed to *tribuebat* (“was granting”). *Tenuarat* should by no means be displaced for *minuerat* (“had diminished”).

### 120

Ott. 2 has *credenti jam sano pectore* (“when faith was already sound in her believing heart”), which can be accepted.

### 121

Ottob. 2 has *mediisque* (“and in the midst”); the conjunction is superfluous.

### 122

Ottob. 2 and Urb. have *adversi*; read *aversi* (“turned away”), from the Gospel: “She approached from behind.”

### 123

Vat. 1 has *subito* (“suddenly”), perhaps written by the same hand that changed it to *subitam* (“sudden”). Arator, book 2, verse 1209: “From every side they seized sudden salvation.”

### 125

Meus has “He healed.” Rom., in the prose version, has *curavit* (“he cared for” or “he healed”); in the text it has *damnavit* (“blocked”), which the other manuscripts and all editions exhibit. Burmannus conjectured *stagnavit* (“stagnated”), noting that blood is said to stagnate, as Faber observes on Justin, book 37, chapter 11.

Wopkensius rightly explains *damnavit* as “blocked.” Nebrissensis observes that *damno* can mean “I bind” or “I restrain,” citing Marcellus and Servius on Virgil, *Eclogues* 5.80: “You too will bind by your prayers.” In support of his interpretation Wopkensius cites Prudentius, *Peristephanon* 2.479: “Let him condemn the unspeakable thresholds, closing the bronze bolts”; *Hamartigenia* 650: “Father almighty, close my ears”; and *Apotheosis* 752: “Before the doors of the tomb, which enormous stones had blocked with a hard barrier.” Arator likewise has, book 2, verse 195: “Moreover, after a guard had been appointed, they wished to seal the tomb against the twofold crime and to block the path of rising prepared for the Lord.”

In other contexts *damnare* can also mean “to inflict harm,” as the Spanish *dañar*; I demonstrated this in the note on Dracontius, book 2, verse 316, where I also cited this verse of Sedulius. But here the sense truly requires *damnavit* to be explained as “blocked,” “bound,” or “prevented,” so that the veins would not flow out with blood.

### 126

Some printed editions have *cujus in fonte* (“in whose fountain”), less suitably.

*had taken away, fell weeping and groaning before the Lord’s holy feet,*

*scarcely able to utter words of prayer,*

*as sobbing shook him: “Have mercy on a father*

*bereaved, have mercy on an old man,” he said, “whose daughter,*

[110] *his only child, not yet mature beneath maiden years,*

249 *has died and taken from wretched me the name of father.*

*Bring help, and pour the fallen soul back through her limbs,*

*you who can provide everything.” He spoke; and the author*

*of light proceeded toward the funeral of the extinguished girl,*

[115] *moving scarcely at all while the crowd pressed around him.*

*Mixed among the throngs went a woman who had suffered*

*an overflowing discharge of blood,*

*who had depleted great wealth in order to become healthier,*

*and, having exhausted her household without benefiting from treatment,*

*had lost her own strength together with her blood.*

[120] *But when faith began to be present in the believer’s heart,*

*now sound, she pressed through the middle of the crowds,*

*striving to touch even the hem of Christ’s turned-away garment.*

250 *Then, hiding behind him, having stolen sudden salvation,*

*she seized it from the outer edge of his clothing;*

*and bold confidence blocked her open veins.*

*God perceived these things, from whose fountain flowed*

*what hidden power had granted, and he praised the faithful theft*

[Note: 128. Fabr. and some other editions have *sua dona* (“her own gifts”), which can be supported by the prose version. Others have *sua vota* (“her own vows”), that is, the woman’s vows, those things which she had vowed or desired. In Reg. 2 there was another reading, but the same old hand rewrote *vota*. Shortly afterward, at verse 141, the same meaning occurs in *Inopinaque vota parentes—Aspiciunt* (“the parents behold unexpected vows”).]

### 129

Poelman’s edition in the margin, Poelman’s papers, the Leipzig edition, and the reading *limina tecti* (“the thresholds of the house”) are more customary among poets. Wopkensius therefore wished by conjecture to change *culmina tecti* (“the roof’s summit”) to *limina tecti*. But since all the old copies agree on *culmina tecti*, it should be retained; perhaps Sedulius wished to suggest the size of the house. See Barthius on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* 1.205: “These roofs greater than your own in their summits.” Otherwise *culmen tecti* is usually understood as the roof of the house itself; yet, like *tectum* (“roof”), *culmen* (“summit”) is sometimes used for the building itself.

### 130

*Moriens* (“dying”) is used in the special sense of “dead.” The verb *jacere* (“to lie”) is frequently used of those who have already died.

### 131

Vatic. 1 and the Leipzig edition have *Extremam* (“the final [day]”), which Arntzenius considers preferable if we adhere to the grammarians’ rules. Servius, commenting on Virgil, book 10, verse 467, *Stat sua cuique dies* (“Each person’s day stands appointed”), says: “*Dies* means the period of life when used in the feminine gender; when used in the masculine, it truly means a day.” Whatever may be the case with this distinction—which Arntzenius himself admits is not observed strictly by everyone—in the present passage he thinks Sedulius means the final day of life. Thus Horace, *Epistles* 1.4.13: “Believe that every day has dawned for you as your last.”

### 133

Arntzenius conjectures from the prose version *cantu modulante* (“with measured song”), namely, “the flute-players were groaning with song as they played funeral melodies”; nevertheless he thinks that nothing should be changed. Vat. 1, Meus, Rom., Ang., Reg. 5, Urb., Ottob. 1, the recent hand of Parrh., and others have *gemebant* (“were groaning”). In Ott. 1 the first hand had *gemebat* (“was groaning”), which Poelman’s papers prefer, but with the reading *Tibicen* (“the flute-player”), not *Tibicines* (“the flute-players”). Arntz., Cant., Ald., Vet. 1 and 2, Monast., Col., Lips., and many other editions, together with Reg. 1 in a later hand and other manuscripts, have *gerebant* (“were carrying on”). Reg. 1 originally had *gerebat* (“was carrying on”). Fabr., Torn. 3, and the *Bibliotheca Lugdunensis* have *ferebat* (“was carrying”). The prose version has *gemebant*.

### 134

Fabr., Torn. 3, Poelman’s papers, and, I think, Nebrissensis have *Tibicen*, which satisfies both the meter and good sense, as a singular used for several flute-players, like *miles* (“soldier” used collectively), whether one reads *gemebat* or *gemebant* in the preceding verse.

In Ott. 2, *Tubines* was corrected to *Tubicines*, and by a more recent hand to *Tibicines*. In Reg. 1, although the first hand has *gerebat*, the text reads *Tibicines*, with a gloss indicating that the second syllable is long. Ang., Alb., and other manuscripts and editions likewise have the metrical error *Tibicines*. *Tubicines* could be defended by lengthening the first syllable, since three short syllables occur together, as often happens in similar cases.

Juvencus indeed mentions trumpets at the funeral of this girl, book 2, verse 400; and in the Vercelli manuscript of the Old Latin version of Matthew, not *tibicines*, as in the Vulgate, but *tubicines* is read, as I noted in the relevant place and in the Addenda. As for what some say—that the *tibia* was always used at the funerals of people of lesser age—if this is admitted on Servius’ authority, it must be understood of infants. The girl now mentioned was twelve years old, and so there was already occasion for trumpets.

In Reg. 2, *fremens* (“roaring”) seems originally to have stood instead of *frequens* (“abundant”); this may be the sound and genuine reading. Sedulius is imitating Juvencus, who describes the same funeral in book 2, verse 400: “The roar of the grieving people and the blaring of trumpets were celebrating the final rites of the last procession.”

### 136

Reg. 2 has *ne funus* (“lest it be a funeral”), but this was written by a later hand; the reading should be *nec* (“nor”).

### 137

Poelm. has the erroneous *lugere* (“to mourn”).

### 138

Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Ott. 1 and 2, Vat. 2, Urb., Poelman’s papers, Parrh., and Ald. have *gelida* (“icy”), a customary epithet of death. In Vat. 1, and apparently in Vat. 2, *gelida* was changed to *gelidum* (“icy,” neuter), which Poelman’s edition and Vet. 1 and 2 print.

### 141

Ott. 1 has *animas* (“souls”), correctly changed by a later hand to *animis* (“in their minds”). Wopkensius conjectures *parentis* (“of the father”), so that the flute-players and others present would have been astonished at the father’s vows. But from the prose version and Luke’s Gospel, chapter 8, it is clear that the parents were astonished. Therefore the reading in Vat. 1 is correct, where the same first hand changed *parentis* to *parentes*.

*He praised it and attributed her own wishes to the noble theft.*

*They had come to the sorrowful roof of the grieving house,*

251 *where the girl lay dead, having received her final day,*

*and a frightened tumult, howling everything with bitter laments,*

*filled the house; the flute-player groaned funeral melodies,*

*and frequent mourning confused the rooms.*

[135] 252 *“Set aside the pains conceived in your anxious mind.*

*This is sleep,” the Savior said, “and believe that there is no funeral,*

*nor mourn the girl laid down in sleep.”*

*He spoke, and the spirit warmed the corpse, constricted by icy death,*

*with fire; by his word he raised the motionless body*

[140] *and granted the girl born once the privilege of living twice.*

*The parents were astonished in their minds and beheld unexpected vows*

[Note: 142. Our manuscripts unanimously have *plangunt* (“they mourn”). Poelman’s text and other editions have *plaudunt* (“they clap” or “applaud”). Wopkensius says this is correct, meaning “they rejoice”; nor would he dislike *pangunt* (“they compose”), that is, “they sing hymns.” He nevertheless prefers *plangunt*, in the sense in which one is said to weep or shed tears for joy. This was also Nebrissensis’ interpretation and that of the glossator in Reg. 1: “They weep from excessive joy and wonder.” This relates to the earlier contrary mourning: “And frequent mourning confused the rooms.” The prose version supports it, as does a similar passage of Victorinus of Pettau on Christ as God and man, verse 39: “And the commanded corpse leaps before their eyes; mourning becomes joy throughout the company.”]

### 143

Rom.: “Concerning two blind men illuminated by the Lord.” Meus: “The two blind men see.” Urb. has *Unde pedem* (“from where the foot”), Vat. 1 *Inde pedes* (“from there the feet”); the same old hand has *pedem* (“the foot”).

### 144

Meus has *clamore* (“with a shout”), which Fabricius printed; but *clamare* (“to cry out”) should be retained.

### 145

All our manuscripts have *Decute* (“shake off”). Parrhasius and most editions have *Discute* (“dispel”). Cellarius, together with several parchment manuscripts, restored *Decute*. See book 2, verse 154: “It shakes off the expelled shadows from unharmed faces.”

### 146

Vat. 1 has *Et clare* (“and clearly”); others have *Et clarum* (“and clear”). Ott. 2 and the Leipzig edition have *tutum est* (“it is safe”). Meus erroneously has *tuum est* (“it is yours”). In Ott. 1 the reading seems to have been *totum* (“the whole”), changed to *tutum* with the gloss *sanum, firmum* (“sound, secure”). The common reading of all is *tutum* without *est*.

### 147

Parrh. has *Quam sanum sit nosse Deum* (“How sound it is to know God”). Reg. 1 in the text, Reg. 2 and 5, Ott. 1 in a second hand, Ald., and many editions have *Quam sanum est cognosse Deum* (“How sound it is to know God”). Arntz. has the same without *est*. Burmannus’ manuscript and Reg. 1 in the margin, for the first reading, have *Quam clarum est cognosse Deum* (“How clear it is to know God”). Ott. 1 in the first hand has *Quam clarum novisse Deum* (“How clear it is to have known God”). Meus in the text has *Quam sanum novisse Deum*; Meus, for the first reading, erroneously has *Quam clarum est cognoscere Deum*. Rom. has *Quam sanum cognoscere Deum*, corrected to *cognosce Deum* (“know God”). Vat. 1 erroneously has *Quam sanum est cognoscere Deum*. Vat. 2, Urb., and apparently Alb. have *Quam sanum est, cognosce Deum*. This cannot be accepted. For *cognosse*, the prose version has “to trust earnestly in God.”

### 148

The first hand in Arntz. writes *videre* (“to see”) instead of *sensere* (“they perceived”), contrary to the prose version.

### 149

Reg. 1 has *defuso* (“poured out”), changed to *diffuso* (“spread abroad”). Similarly, in Vat. 1 *defuso* was changed to *difuso*. Most other manuscripts have *diffuso*. The editions also vary. Burmannus approved *defuso*. I discussed this orthographic variation in the note on Dracontius, book 3, verse 73.

### 150

Arntz., Poelman’s papers, Parrh., Meus for the first reading, Reg. 2, and Ott. 1 in a second hand have *fulsere* (“shone”); others have *micuere* (“sparkled”), which is entered in Reg. 2 as a gloss or second reading.

### 151

Arntz., Poelman’s papers, and Reg. 2 have *micuerunt* (“sparkled”); in Reg. 2 the gloss or second reading is *radiarunt* (“radiated”), which is the more common reading. Most editions have *radiarunt*, while Parrh. has *micuerunt*. In Ott. 1 a later hand wrote *radiarunt*.

### 152

Rom.: “Concerning a certain sick man.” Poelm.: “A mute demon is driven out.”

### 156

Urb. and Rom. metrically transpose *Deus versis* (“God, with [things] turned”); Meus has *versis Dominus* (“the Lord, with [things] turned”), which is contrary to the sense. In the margin, for the first reading, it correctly has *versis Deus in contraria* (“God, turning [things] into opposites”).

### 158

Rom.: “Where the Lord gave the disciples power over everything.”

### 159

Vat. 1 has *totis virtutibus et simul implens* (“and filling [them] with all virtues and at once”). Vonckius says the sense requires *tot eosque simul* (“so many, and them together”). Wopkensius rightly disagrees; he himself conjectures *totosque simul* (“all of them together”), that is, “everyone,” but retains *totisque* in the sense of “all.” He asserts that this use of *totus* for *omnis*, characteristic of a later age, is sought in vain in Virgil and Cicero. Others cite similar examples from Plautus, Phaedrus, and Hirtius. Wopkensius’ conjecture *totosque* occurs in my codex, but the same hand corrected it to *totisque*. The prose version confirms this reading, and we can explain it as “filling them with complete, universal powers.”

*They look upon them, and, with their songs turned toward joy, mourn.*

253 *Then, turning back his step, behold, he sees two blind men following,*

*crying aloud: “Illustrious Son of David,*

[145] *shake off the nightly shadows from our extinguished faces,*

*and grant us clear day. How safe it is to believe,*

*how sound it is to know God! They already saw in their hearts,*

*those who perceived the path of light; then the blind eyes*

*of the suppliants, like a fire languishing in scattered oil,*

[150] *sparkled beneath the Lord’s hand, and, restored by his tranquil touch,*

*their faces radiated with their own lamps.”*

254 *After these men had been dismissed, another sick man was brought forward,*

*wretched with a manifold illness, deprived of speech,*

*empty of hearing, and filled with a demon alone*

*through his hollow limbs. Immediately, in sacred order,*

[155] *God cured him, turning the causes toward their opposites,*

*emptying him of the demon and restoring his hearing and speech.*

*Meanwhile, he likewise orders his own disciples*

*to be able to do everything, filling them all at once with every power*

[Note: 160. Rom. has *pellite* (“drive away”); Meus has *expellite* (“drive out”); others have *excludite* (“exclude”), which is better, since *depellite* (“drive away”) recurs shortly afterward.]

### 161

Arntz., Ott. 2 together with Monast., Fabr., Lips., Poelm., and other editions have *Sed domui Israel* (“but to the house of Israel”), which Wopkensius defends: namely, “Say to the house of Israel: the kingdom of heaven …”

Nearly all our manuscripts, together with Cappusotus, Parrh., Ald., and others, have *Sed domus Israel* (“but the house of Israel”), which Grunerus defends against Wopkensius. The meaning would be: “Exclude the plagues, but the house of Israel”—for at that time other nations were not yet called by this name, as Paul later called Abraham the father of nations and called the nations Abraham’s seed and children. This interpretation and reading should be retained, being especially confirmed by the Gospel and the prose version. That the final syllable of *domus* is shortened in the genitive is not unprecedented in Sedulius. Wopkensius offers another conjecture, *munere* (“by gift”) for *nomine* (“by name”), but the prose version clearly condemns it.

### 162

Poelm., for the first reading, has *Sanxerat hoc* (“he had sanctioned this”); Rom. has *ducite* (“lead”); read *dicite* (“say”), that is, “preach.”

### 163

There is an error in Reg. 5, *Daemonis* (“of the demon”), and in Poelm., *auferre* (“to remove”).

### 164

Cant., Parrh., Vet. 1, Bas., Torn. 1 and 2 have *Cunctaque* (“and all things”). With most witnesses, read *Functaque* (“and the dead”), that is, “the deceased.” This verb is commonly used as a simple form in place of a compound.

### 165

Juvencus, book 2, verse 442: “And you likewise, freely spend your gifts.”

### 168

Mon. has the erroneous *Cum bonus* (“when good”).

### 169

Urb. has *questus* (“complaints”); read *quae sunt* (“which are”).

### 170

Wopkensius thinks the punctuation should be: *Ac*—as if he were saying, “I … should sell”—*Haec in apostolicas*, and so forth. The prose version suggests a different punctuation.

### 171

The Arntz. manuscript has *ministris* (“ministers”); others, supported by the prose version, have *magistris* (“masters” or “teachers”).

### 172

Cant. has *discurreret* (“might run about”); others more suitably have *decurreret* (“might run down”), although similar words compounded with *de-* and *dis-* are often exchanged and are not always distinguished in meaning.

### 173

Parrhasius omits this verse and the following seven, up to *Exin conspicuam* (“then conspicuous”). In Grunerus’ edition this verse, *Qualiter* (“in what manner”), is missing because of an obvious typographical error, since the next two verses are printed there.

Isidore, *Etymologies* 6.16, uses this same comparison: “Among the other councils, we know that there are four venerable synods which principally encompass the whole faith, like the four Gospels or the same number of rivers of paradise.” Grialius, Isidore’s annotator, says that this passage appears to have been taken by Braulio, who arranged Isidore’s *Etymologies* into books. But the reasons he offers scarcely prove this.

### 174

The Heins. and Arntzenius manuscripts have *irrigui* (“watered”) instead of *ingentes* (“great”). In Vat. 2 this word seems to have been divided into two, *in gentes* (“among the nations”), which is not convincing.

176. These and the following five verses are absent from the manuscripts of Heinsius, Canterbury, Leipzig, Arntzenius, from all our codices, including the Angers and Albani manuscripts, from the very ancient Turin manuscript, Aldus, and the editions Vet. 1, 2, Mon., Lips., and others. The Poelmann edition and others print them; so do the more recent editors Cellarius, Grunerus, and Arntzenius. Their substance is found in the prose; but since the prose sometimes extends into material that is not present in the poem, we may reasonably suspect that these verses are not by Sedulius but by someone else who composed them from the prose. Arntzenius judges from the style that they were sewn onto Sedulius’ fabric by another hand. For my part, I do not see so obvious a difference between these and Sedulius’ verses, nor should I find it difficult to believe that Sedulius himself, after completing the prose, added these verses to the poem as well; and this could have resulted in their being absent from many copies.

177. Wopken’s conjecture, *sub munere puro* (“under a pure gift”) instead of *sub nomine puro* (“under a pure name”), as the printed editions have it, rests on the prose and on the entire context; consequently, we should accept that reading. We ought not retain the more awkward common reading merely because it is found in the printed editions. These words correspond to verse 165, *Sumpsistis gratis, cunctis impendite gratis* (“You received freely; distribute freely to all”).

180. Arntzenius conjectures *Davidicisque* from the prose; certainly this, or—as it is more commonly written in the manuscripts—*Daviticisque*, has more of Sedulius about it. The printed editions have *Davidisque*.

181. *Nescio mercem* means “I do not know merchandise,” as he says shortly before, not “to be regarded as a merchant”; or, “I have not known commerce,” as the prose says.]

Go, he says, and drive away the grievous plagues of disease,

But proclaim the kingdom of heaven to the house of Israel

[255] (for as yet he had not increased all nations by this name);

Take away the demons’ place, drive out leprosy;

And restore to life the corpses withdrawn from life.

[165] You received freely; distribute freely to all.

And as though saying this: “For I, as your ministers,

Commit flocks to you to be preserved; I, finally, the shepherd,

Am good, and generously grant my own fields for their sustenance.

Let no one sell pasture to my sheep, which are mine.

[170] These words the Almighty therefore first proclaimed

To apostolic ears, so that from them, now serving as teachers,

Instruction, flowing onward under his authority,

Might continue through the ages.

As from one spring of paradise four mighty rivers

[175] Are read to flow forth in separate courses,

From which streams are scattered throughout the whole world,

So whoever carries out the work of divinity—which he does not possess from himself,

But receives from the Lord—should accept it as a pure gift

And distribute it as a pure gift, so that he may be regarded

As a distributor, not as a merchant,

[180] And sing, in Davidic fashion, of the life to come:

‘I shall enter into the Lord’s rest, for I do not know merchandise.’”

[Col. 0653A] [Note: [Col. 0653B]

182. Rom. “Where the Lord restored his hand to a certain cripple.” The Arntzenius manuscript and the Leipzig edition write *Exhinc*. Wopkensius more plausibly thinks that the reading should be *Exin continuo* (“then immediately”), or *Exin contiguam* (“then adjoining”). But there is no reason to reject *conspicuam*.

183. Reg. 1, 2, *Meus*, Urb., Rom. have *dimenso*, which has a gloss in Reg. 1, as though it meant “not possessing a measure,” and in Reg. 2, “diminished.” In Ott. 1 it too has been changed from *demerso* into *dimenso*. Grunerus followed this reading, which was also found in Burmann’s manuscript and is confirmed by the prose. Other copies vary extraordinarily. Vat. 1, 2, Reg. 5, Ang., Ald., Poelm. in the text, Lips., Fab., and Cell. have *demisso*, which scarcely yields a suitable sense. Nebrissensis, Barthius, and Poelmann’s sheets have *demesso*, that is, “mutilated,” as Nebrissensis explains it. In the Poelmann edition’s margin, *demessos* is an error for *demesso*. Cappusotus and Parrhasius have *dimerso*, or, as it is better written—and as it appears in Ott. 1 in the first hand—*demerso*. The Arntzenius codex has *demisso*, changed by a second hand into *demso*, which may perhaps be *demenso*. Alb., Vet. 1, 2, Mon., and Ott. 2 have *dimisso*.

184. Arntzenius printed *nec* (“nor”); the prose indeed has this, but our manuscripts, along with most printed editions, do not. One word is commonly used for the other, and in manuscripts they are frequently confused.

185. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *damnaret*. This was also found in the Ottobonian, Roman, and Meus manuscripts, but was corrected to *damnarat*. Vat. 1, despite the meter, has *damnaverat*.

187. Reg. 1, 2, 5, Ott. 1, 2, Ang., Alb., Urb., Meus, Rom., Vat. 2, Cant., Arntz., and Ald. have *et reduci*, with a gloss in Reg. 1, *reverti* (“to return”), indicating that *reduci* derives from *reduco, reducis*; but then the second syllable would have to be lengthened. In Reg. 2 the gloss is *remeabili*, from *redux, reducis*. Vat. 1 has *ac reddit*. Parrhasius has *et reddit*, and Fabr. likewise *reddit*. Torn. 3 and others have *salutem* instead of *saluti*. Arntzenius, with Poelmann’s sheets and other printed editions, has *et reddi divino more saluti*, since he does not understand what *reduci* is meant to signify. Yet this reading, found in nearly all the manuscripts, should be retained. The meaning is: “And, as he always acts, he takes nothing away from the salvation returning in divine fashion, but restores everything.” The prose has the same reading.

188. Ott. 1 has *semper ait* (“he always says”); retain *agit* (“he acts”). Nebrissensis explains *nil tollit* as “he takes nothing as payment,” or “he diminishes nothing.” The latter is preferable.

189. Rom. “Of the blind and mute.” Meus: “A blind, mute demoniac is delivered.” Aldus printed *Ecce iterum* (“Behold, again”).

190. Arntz. and Reg. 1 in the first hand, as well as Ott. 1 in the first hand, have *nigro*, as in Seneca, *Aed.* 358: “and the liver, wasted by black bile, foams.” In Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 the correction indicates *nigri*, which is the common reading; and “black poison” is found everywhere, so that examples are unnecessary.

192. Meus has corruptly *Quique*; other copies more correctly have *Quodque*. Arntzenius, contrary to the rules of prosody, omits *que*. He observes that this often happens in manuscript codices. Rom. has *diffuderat aegros*. The meaning is: “which, infecting several sick people in turn, had dispersed” the disease, and so forth.

194. Cellarius printed *lucemque*, following Fabricius, Poelmann, and several other printed editions. Poelmann’s sheets, Arntz., Parrh., and all our manuscripts more correctly have *lumenque*, for *lumen*, and more often *lumina* in the plural, is used for “eyes.” *Tulit* is often used for *abstulit*, a simple form for a compound.

195. Vonckius conjectured *Saucia membra terens* (“wearing down the wounded limbs”). But how much better is *tenens* (“holding”), that is, “occupying and, as it were, keeping under his control”! You will scarcely find *orbum* used simply for “blind,” or *orbus visus* for “deprived of sight,” among the earlier Latin writers. In Italian, *orbo* means “blind.” Some trace of this meaning appears in Isidore’s glosses. Conversely, they called the blind *orbati* (“deprived”), because, being deprived of their eyes, they were regarded as equal to the sightless, as Barthius observes from the old translator of *Apollonius of Tyre* and from Quintilian, book 57, chapter 6. Fortunatus used the word in the same sense as Sedulius in book 8, poem 25: “He continually illuminates the blind through sacred merits.]

257 Then, entering the conspicuous hall of the synagogue,

He sees a weak man, crippled in his diminished body,

Half-dead in his limbs, not wholly alive, whose

[185] Arid right hand had condemned part of his motionless body;

By command healing him, he orders the cold palm

To grow warm again, and, in divine fashion, restores him to salvation,

As he always acts, taking nothing away and restoring everything.

[Col. 0654A] Behold, again that slippery serpent appears,

Restoring his ancient arts:

[190] He, livid with the black bile of poison,

Delights to grow fat on human gore;

And the venom that he had so often dispersed among different sick people

He poured, once advanced, into the entrails of one man.

He had taken away his voice and his sight, and, holding his limbs

[195] Wounded by a threefold fury, he shook the mute and blind man.

[Col. 0655A] [Note: [Col. 0655B]

196. Poelm. in the margin, Fabr., and several other printed editions have *lux vera* (“true light”). Poelmann’s sheets, together with our manuscripts and the finest editions, have *lux nostra* (“our light”). Rom. has *nostra sermo* (“our word”); the meter requires *nostra* and *sermo*.

197. Meus corruptly has *Moribus* instead of *Sordibus*. The Leipzig edition has, not inelegantly, *expulsis* instead of *exclusis*. Sedulius elsewhere also uses *excludo* for *expello*. St. Damasus, poem 1, in praise of David, writes: “With the seats removed, they cleanse the inner chambers of the heart.” In Vatican codex 84, containing the Psalter from St. Jerome’s version, and in a certain epigram attributed to St. Jerome, the line is better read: “With filth exposed,” and could be read *expulsis* or *exclusis*. In another Psalter of Jerome, Vatican codex 4226, the epigram published under Jerome’s name is attributed to Damasus, and similarly reads “With filth exposed.”

198. Meus corruptly has *Umbraque* (“and shadow”) instead of *per verbum* (“through the word”), and less elegantly has *per lucem lumina* (“through light, eyes”), although *lux nostra* has preceded it.

199. Rom. “Of the bent woman.” Meus: “A curved woman is raised.” Cappusotus has *contacta*; read *contracta*. Urb. absurdly has *morbo contracta venusto* (“bent by a beautiful disease”).

200. Meus and Urb. have *Non senio tremebunda gemens, sed curva caducis vultibus*, which cannot be approved. Arntzenius punctuates *incurva caducis*. Vet. 1 punctuates *incurva, caducis vultibus*, which yields a tolerable sense; but the prose intends something else.

202. Arntz. writes *jugis* instead of *juges*, based on the differing ways of ending such plural forms: *jugeis*, *juges*, and *jugis*. Wopkensis rightly rejects Barthius’ conjecture *reserante Deo* (“with God opening”). Certainly *Domino miserante* (“with the Lord showing mercy”), that is, “by the Lord’s favor,” is sound and more in keeping with ecclesiastical style. Fabricius printed *Quae, miserante Deo, juges*; some printed editions followed him, and Poelmann’s sheets defend the reading because *juges* lengthens the first syllable. But what does that matter, when the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts shows that Sedulius often shortened the first syllable of *jugis*?

203. Meus corruptly has *lavat* instead of *levat*. Cant., Reg. 1, Rom., Meus, Parrh., and Reg. 2 in the first hand have *obscure*; Vat. 1 after correction, Ott. 2, Urb. have *menses*. Reg. 2 after correction, Reg. 5, Ald., Vat. 2 apparently, Vat. 1 in the first hand, Ang., and many printed editions have *messes*, which must be retained exclusively from Luke 13, where this woman is said to have suffered from that disease for eighteen years. *Messis* (“harvest”) is often used for “year,” as are *hiems* (“winter”), *arista* (“ear of grain”), and so forth. Arntz., Ott. 1 in the text, and some editions have *et*; most manuscripts and other editions have *ac*. Alb. has a gloss: *levat annos* (“he raises years”), followed by “then heaven, and finally the stars.”

204. Reg. 2 has *ac*; others more elegantly have *et*.

205. Vet. 1 has *quia nos*; it should be corrected to *quia quos*.

206. *Ima petunt* is from Virgil 8.67.

207. Rom. “Where he rained manna upon God’s people in the desert.” Poelmann more correctly has “Five thousand are fed with five loaves.” This is the principal subject of the passage.

208. Most, and the very oldest of our manuscripts—Reg. 1, 2, 5, Vat. 1, 2, Alb., Ottob. 1, 2, Rom., Ang., Meus, together with Cant., Parrh., and other printed editions—write *Moyses*. More recent copies, with Aldus and others, prefer *Moses*, because, as Grunerus observes, the trisyllabic *Moyses* shortens the first syllable and lengthens the second. Yet although there are examples showing that Christian poets shortened the first syllable of *Moyses* and lengthened the second, it is difficult to establish a rule for these Hebrew proper names by which the verses of Christian poets should be reshaped, since poets of the later age, even pagan poets, often claimed great license in pronouncing all kinds of proper names. I have discussed this matter more fully in my notes on Prudentius. As for *Moyses*, the first syllable ought rather to be long, since it is written in Greek with omega. In any case, nothing prevents *Moyses* as written here from being disyllabic through contraction of two vowels. The trisyllabic *Moyses* occurs in this same book at verse 285.

210. Arntz., Cant., and Poelmann’s sheets, together with our manuscripts Reg. 2, 5, Vat. 2, Vat. 1 after correction, Ottob. 2, Ang., Urb., and Alb., have *multo*. So do Parrh., Ald., and many ancient editions. Other manuscripts and editions have *multa*. Either is correct, since *ales* is of both masculine and feminine gender.

211. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *geminis modo panibus amplum*, and in the following verse *pluit*, “he rained,” followed by *modo piscibus auxit*, “he increased it only with fish,” in an inverted and preposterous order.]

259 Then the Lord of the world, our light and the Father’s Word,

Having expelled the filth, renewed eyes and mouths;

Through the Word, words arise; through the light, eyes arise.

A woman too had come, bent by an ancient disease,

[200] Not by old age, trembling, groaning, bent, with fallen

Features, and looking down toward the ground alone.

She, when the Lord showed mercy, raised her limbs after eighteen

Years, and at last beheld heaven and the stars,

260 Seeing everything upright; for those whom the evil enemy oppresses

Sink to the depths, while those whom Christ nourishes rise unstained.

And when he then saw that the people who had followed him

Into the desert were feeling ancient hunger,

He displayed ancient aid through greater deeds; then with abundant food

[210] He fed the great multitude of men and increased it with only two fish.

[Col. 0657A] [Note: [Col. 0657C]

212. Some printed editions have *nunc* (“now”); read *tunc* (“then”), as in verse 210. See also what I have just said about this verse.

216. Cant., Reg. 1, 5, Urb., Rom., Vat. 1, 2, with Aldus and other editions, have *Quoque magis*. Others have *Quodque*, which may perhaps have been the first hand’s reading in Reg. 1, just as *Quoque* seems formerly to have stood in Reg. 2. Both readings are good. It is taken from Juvenal, satire 6, verse 87: “And the more you may wonder.” Meus corruptly has *replent* instead of *replerunt*.

218. Arntzenius, with Cellarius and the Heinsius manuscript, printed *Redditaque a cunctis*. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *Reddita quae cunctis*. Reg. 1 has, in place of *d. s.*, from the same old hand, *quae redit a cunctis*, which most other manuscripts and editions also present. Arntzenius cites Parrhasius for this reading; but he printed *Reddita quae cunctis*. Our reading is clearly confirmed by the prose when *tollitur* (“is taken away”) is supplied.

219. Rom. “Where the Lord walked upon the sea.” Reg. 1 and Meus in the text have *calidi*, with a gloss in Reg. 1, *ferventis* (“burning”); yet perhaps *gelidi* (“cold”) formerly stood there. Meus in the first hand agrees with the rest. The more learned reading is *calidi*: poets imagined the sea growing warm from the setting sun. Horace, book 1, satire 4, verse 29: “Here he changes his wares from the rising sun to the place where the evening region grows warm.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.63: “Evening, and the shores which grow warm beneath the setting sun.” Tibullus, book 2, elegy 5: “And wherever the risings lie open, and wherever the river washes, with its flowing waters, the sun’s panting horses.” Other ancient writers thought that the sun was extinguished each day in Ocean; consequently the sea had to grow warm again. The sun, or the waning day, is said to be “growing old” for setting, much as the waning moon or waning month is said to grow old when near its end.

224. Meus corruptly has *Turba labrantem jacebant*; it seems to have been corrected from *Turba* to *Perturbata*. Reg. 1, with most copies, has *Torva*, with the gloss *aspera* (“rough”); but *Turba* seems to have stood there previously. In Ottob. 1 *Turba* is clear. Urb. and Vat. 2 have *jactabat*. The common reading proceeds correctly.

225. Arntz. has *ventus* instead of *flatus*.

227. Vat. 2 and Reg. 5 have *glaucique fluentis*, which Aldus printed; but the sense is lacking unless one reads *glaucique fluenti*, namely, “the marbles of the flowing blue sea.” Wassius, in his commentary on Sallust, *Catiline* 21, p. 27, read from the Cambridge public-library codex *siccisque fluentis* (“with dry streams”), which Grunerus and Arntzenius prefer. I do not approve of calling the waters “dry” because the plants were dry; nor did this please Wopkensis, who himself conjectured *raucisque fluentis* (“with hoarse waters”), but more wisely concludes that what is sound should not be altered. Arntzenius cites from Arator, in his letter to Vigilius, instead of *siccisque fluentis*: “For whom there was a dry path amid the waves.” But here too the waves are not called dry; and Sedulius himself in the prose in no way suggests dry waters.

229. Most copies have *calle*. Poelm. in the margin and Meus in the text have *calce*; Meus in the margin has *calle*, which should be retained.

232. Meus has *dextera*; to preserve the verse, *dextra* should be restored.

236. Rom. “Where the Lord healed a certain sick man.” Meus: “The sick are delivered by touching his garment.” Ott. 1 writes *Genezar*, and it seems that *Gennezar* previously stood there; Alb. has *Genessar*. Meus has *Ganezar*, Rom. *Genesaret*. Only the meter permits *Genesar*, and this is the form found in the Vulgate, Matthew 14:34: “They came into the land of Genesar.” Ott. 2 and Ang. have the bad reading *Unde soli*; Urb. has the worse *in soli*. Most refer *soli* to the inhabitants of the soil, that is, the land of Genesar. But in Reg. 1, 2 and Vat. 1, *solum* may perhaps have stood originally; it appears in Vat. 2, Alb., Reg. 5, Aldus, and several other printed editions. The sense would then be: “From there, when the Lord came, the land of Genesar,” that is, “onto the land of Genesar.]

261 Then sufficient manna rained down; instead, he gave abundant food

Of five loaves to five thousand men.

The rest of the crowd remains hidden, enclosed by no number,

[215] The vast legion of little ones, or the vast number of mothers.

And, what may make you wonder even more, they filled twelve baskets

With the fragments that had been taken away; and though the people ate, the food increased,

Yet what returned from all of them was not available for the meal.

And now, while the waning day was being carried away by the warm

[220] Ocean beneath the blue surface of the sea, when night’s pallor

Was approaching and evening was bringing on the star-bearing shadows,

The disciples, while the Master remained alone upon the earth,

Sought the billowing sea; and as the waves swelled,

[Col. 0658A] The rough sea tossed the laboring boat,

[225] For the wind was against them. Then, in the time of dark night,

The Lord walked over the waves that had been trodden down,

And pressed the fields of the vast strait; the blue flowing waters

Lapped the marble-like soles of his sacred feet.

The astonished company marvels that, beneath a pedestrian’s path,

[230] Ways had opened where ships could sail. But Peter, taught

To possess a friendly faith and always to recognize Christ,

Descended into the midst of the waters; his right hand raised him

As he was sinking, and he suffered nothing in so great a whirlpool.

263 That hand became his harbor, and the traveler of the sea

[235] Moved freely across the glassy fields.

From there the inhabitants of Genesar, when the Lord came,

[Col. 0659A] [Note: [Col. 0659C]

238. Rom. has, not inappropriately, *Vix ac tacta*. Ottob. 2 has *morbos sanaret acerbos* (“he might heal bitter diseases”), which comes from a glossator’s hand or from some inept corrector. Arntzenius, with many printed editions, retained *morbis medeatur acerbis*; although he acknowledges that *mederetur* appears in the Arntzenius manuscript, the Cambridge manuscript, Aldus’ edition, the Leipzig edition, and others, as well as in the prose, he disregards it because the most learned men have shown elsewhere at length that scribes often made this kind of error. But the question should be whether the scribes who wrote *mederetur* or those who wrote *medeatur* were in error. In our manuscripts, Ang., Alb., Reg. 1, 2, 5, Vat. 1, 2, Ott. 1, and Rom., I find *mederetur*. The reading is supported by the error in Urb., *mederentur*, and in my codex, *modderetur*, unless one prefers to take the latter as *moderetur*. Parrhasius likewise printed *mederetur*. In Reg. 2 perhaps another reading formerly stood, but now *mederetur* is clear, with the gloss *sanaret* (“he might heal”). Reg. 1 has a similar gloss, *medicaretur*, above *mederetur*. The very ancient Turin codex also supports *mederetur*. This must therefore be regarded as the true reading, confirmed exclusively by the old copies. Someone may object that the second syllable of *mederetur* is long. That is indeed true, and this seems to have been the reason why some editors adopted *medeatur*. Nevertheless, since several verbs of the second conjugation are sometimes transferred to the third, such as *fulgeo*, *ferveo*, and similar verbs, we must hold that Sedulius used the analogy and placed *mederetur* in the third conjugation, shortening the second syllable.

239. Fabricius appears to have been the first to introduce, against the manuscript evidence, a wholly unnecessary transposition: *Senserunt jugem, quotquot tetigere, salutem* (“All who touched it felt enduring salvation”). Others followed Fabricius. But it is established that Sedulius often shortened the first syllable of *jugis*.

240. Vat. 1 has *nunquam est vendita* (“was never sold”); others omit *est*. Why does he say that Christ’s garment was never sold? Perhaps because the soldiers did not wish to tear the seamless tunic and cast lots over it to determine whose it would be, as John 19:25 reports.

242. Rom. “Of the Canaanite woman.” Meus: “The daughter of the Canaanite woman is delivered.”

243. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, and Meus have *atris*; most other manuscripts, with Arntz., Parrh., and Aldus, have *atrox*. But in Reg. 2 *atris* seems formerly to have stood, and its gloss now appears as *cum pessimis affectionibus* (“with the worst afflictions”). Arntzenius considers this preferable. *Ater* would agree well with the prose.

244. Most write *Cananaea*, but the Vulgate reads *Chananaea*.

245. It would seem clearer to read *qui nare sagaci semper odorantes* (“who always smell with an acute nostril”), since an *odorata mensa* would be a “fragrant table.” Fabricius already printed *nare*, but all manuscripts and the best editions prefer *more*. The prose *sagaciter* can readily be drawn toward either reading.

249. Fabricius, and some printed editions with him, have *genitisque*. The sense requires *gentisque*.

250. Cellarius, with the Leipzig codex, has *Ebraici*; most have *Hebraei*, *Ebraei*, or *Hebrei*, according to the differing but plausible spelling. In Ott. 1 *Hebraeo* seems formerly to have stood. Cellarius, with the manuscripts of Barthius and Heinsius, has *germine*. Parrhasius also printed this. Grunerus rightly defends the common reading *gramine*; the prose supports it.

251. Rom. “Where the Lord restored a multitude of sick people to health.” Meus: “He heals various sick people.” Wopkensis would prefer *subiit* (“he undertook” or “he entered”).

255. Wopkensis conjectured *Venerat, his priscum condonat roboris usum* (“he had come; by these he restored their ancient use of strength”), or *confirmat roboris usum* (“he confirms the use of strength”); but he notes that the received reading is confirmed by the prose.

256. Poelm. in the margin has *membris*; in the text he has *nervis*, together with the prose and other witnesses.

257. Rom. “Where the Lord satisfied four thousand men with seven loaves and two fish.” Arntzenius, Vat. 2, Ang., Reg. 5, Aldus, and others have *Cumque medens* (“and while healing”); our better manuscripts, with Parrhasius, have *Dumque medens* (“while healing”).]

They brought their sick, so that merely touching the fringe

Of God’s garment might heal their grievous diseases;

And all who touched it felt enduring salvation.

264 How precious was that garment, which was never sold,

Yet by the gift of a modest thread redeemed everyone!

From there, as he approached the regions of Tyre

And the fields of Sidon, an anxious woman pleaded for her daughter,

Who was tormented by an evil spirit with dark

[245] Stings. She confessed herself equal to dogs, which, with keen instinct,

Always lie beside the threshold of a fragrant table,

Accustomed to lick up the crumbs falling from their masters.

[Col. 0660A] A humble voice, but lofty faith, which, when the daughter was safe,

Made a sheep from a dog, and compelled one born among the thorns

[250] Of the nations to feed upon the grass of the Hebrew field.

Then, climbing the high ridges of the mountain,

With the people following, he restored thousands of blind,

265 Thousands of lame, lepers as well,

Crowds of deaf people, weakened hands,

And whatever infirmity afflicted the common people,

[255] To their limbs’ former use, restoring their organs

And fitting them again to their proper nerves.

While healing, he quieted the tumult of the sick by his power,

[Col. 0661A] [Note: [Col. 0661C]

260. Meus has *Nutrierat geminata fames* (“hunger had nourished”), whereas most have *Nutribat geminanda fames* (“hunger was nourishing as it increased”); but in Reg. 1 *geminando* may perhaps have stood, which is also suggested by the gloss *multiplicando* or *crescendo* (“multiplying” or “increasing”). Nebrissensis explains it as “present and future hunger.” *Nutribat* is Virgilian.

262. Meus and Poelmann’s sheets have *Tunc flexus*; Wopkensis conjectures *Quo flexa pietate* (“by which compassion having bent him”), or *Cum flexus pietate* (“when bent by compassion”); but he retains the common reading in this sense: “Wherefore, or because God, moved by compassion,” using the relative pronoun in a way supported by Hyginus, Livy, and Aurelius Victor. Some printed editions have the error *egentem* (“the needy one”).

264. In Vet. 2 and Mon. *victum locis* lacks *que*. Arntz. has *affert* instead of *infert*.

265. Cant., Ott. 2, Rom., and Alb. have *inorme*, which seems formerly to have stood in Reg. 2 and Vat. 1. The error *inorbe* in Urb. belongs to the same category. Munkerus, in his commentary on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* 1.1, defends this spelling. Most write *enorme*; it makes no difference that the first syllable is shortened, since among poets of the later age *e* is often shortened in compounds. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 8, verse 64, *Corpus enervans*, where some similarly write *inervans*. The Arntzenius codex has *grande* instead of *enorme* or *inorme*, and in Reg. 2 the glossator has written *Vel grande* above *enorme*. Nebrissensis also reads *Pavit grande*. Scribes did this to escape a metrical fault. By this method many other passages in Christian poets were corrupted.

266. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Arntz. have *Sexus, aetatis*, which Aldus, Fabricius, and others printed. The true reading is *Sexus, et aetatis*, despite the fact that the final syllable of *sexus* is shortened in the oblique case; this is familiar in Sedulius. Meus has *illi*; read *illic*.

267. Vet. 1 incorrectly has *vescentem*. Grunerus, from Cant. and the Leipzig edition, has *mireris adauctas*. Arntzenius, with Poelmann’s sheets, adheres to this because the conjunction *et* is wholly idle in the common reading. But all our manuscripts, together with the finest editions, present *et auctas*. In Urb. the error *exhaustas* rather suggests *et auctas* than *adauctas*. Poelmann’s edition has *adauctas* in the margin and *et auctas* in the text. The conjunction *et* is not idle; indeed, it is elegantly used for “also.” To make you wonder even more, learn that the food was also increased.

271. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *Explevit*; retain *Expavit*.

272. Rom. has *medico*; read *modico*. In my codex, twelve verses from Fortunatus’ *Life of Saint Martin* have been inserted after this verse: “For he, distinguishing the poem in teachable order at the beginning,” and so forth. They are written in red ink. Such insertions commonly occur in codices, and perhaps the scribe copied these verses because Sedulius is praised in them after the encomium of Juvencus.

273. Meus: “How the Lord was transfigured in the presence of three disciples.” Rom.: “Of the Lord’s Transfiguration on the mountain.”

274. Reg. 2 has *ab hoc casu*, with a gloss, *ab hoc casu dicitur*, because infants at birth fall toward the earth. Reg. 1 has a similar gloss, *quando cecidit a ventre matris* (“when he fell from his mother’s womb”), but the common reading of the other copies is *ab occasu*. Thus the compound *occasus* (“setting” or “fall”) is used for the simple *casus*. In Reg. 2, *gementem* has correctly been changed to *gerentem*.

276. Arntzenius notes that *sedere* (“to sit”) is not said of elevated places, such as a city established on a mountain, but of depressed and level places; he therefore prefers *jacens* (“lying”), if the manuscripts allowed it. But although *sedere* is sometimes used of things located in a flat and low place, it is often used for “to stand,” “to be,” or “to remain” in any place, whether low or elevated, as could be demonstrated by hundreds of examples from ancient writers.

277. Wopkensis conjectures *spargens latius ignem* (“scattering fire more widely”). But why should *altius* (“more deeply” or “more loftily”) be objectionable? Whether one joins it with *spargens altius* or with *anhelantem altius*, a suitable and Gospel-consistent meaning emerges. The epithet *anhelans* (“panting” or “breathing”) is often applied by poets, and sometimes by others, to fire, as I have shown in my notes on Dracontius. Compare the Index.]

The third day was present, and on the barren turf no food

Had reached so great a people; increasing toil,

[260] Growing hunger intensified their excessive toil, if the wounded crowd,

Hungry, was to return along the immense road for food.

Moved by compassion, God, who is always present as bread to the needy

And brings food to places without crops,

Fed the enormous multitude of men with a few little fish

And seven loaves; moreover, he satisfied four thousand there,

266 Besides the weak of the second sex and age,

Who were eating. To make you wonder even more, learn

That the food was also increased: by eating, the crowd

Nourished the meal, and the food increased beneath their bites.

[Col. 0662A] The fleeing hunger was terrified by its own leftovers,

The tops of seven baskets, when, after a fragment had been taken,

It saw an abundant harvest from a modest seed.

Yet although Christ was in a human body,

267 Bearing mortal limbs from his mother’s birth,

[275] It was not hidden that he was God, because a city seated on a mountain

Is never concealed, nor is a burning lamp placed beneath a bushel;

Rather, it scatters its breathing fire more loftily,

[Col. 0663A] [Note: [Col. 0663B]

278. Vonckius conjectures *lumen alit* (“he nourishes the light”). Wopkensis, however, defends the phrase *lumen agit* for “he emits” or “he pours forth,” citing Victorinus of Pettau, *On Christ God and Man*, verse 111: “Perhaps then the royal light of heaven first emitted its light,” and Drepanius Florus, hymn to Michael the Archangel: “Destroying the enemies, and inwardly emitting light.” Reg. 1 and Meus distinguish *lumen agit radians* (“he emits light, shining”), for they have *testibus amplo* (“to the three witnesses”), and in Reg. 1 the gloss joins *radians* to *lychnus* (“lamp”), though it may also be joined to *lumen*. The printed editions have *agit radians nam*.

280. Reg. 1 and Ottob. 1 have *aetheriam*; others have *aetheream*. The printed editions likewise vary.

284. “Things that were not believed by the world.” Nebrissensis explains: “Either things incredible, or because the world did not know him.” The prose suggests something else.

285. Fabr. has *Heliam, et clarum virtute Moysen* (“Elijah, and Moses, illustrious in virtue”). The Leipzig codex has *Helian, et clarum lumine Mosen* (“Elijah, and Moses illustrious in light”). The Heinsius codex, Arntz., Reg. 2, Ang., Vat. 1, 2, Ott. 2, Alb., Urb., and Rom. have *Heliam, et clarum videre Moysen* (“Elijah, and to see Moses illustrious”), but in Reg. 2 and Vat. 1 something else formerly stood instead of *et clarum*, and the gloss in Vat. 1 suggests that *clarum* is an adverb meaning “clearly.” Ott. 1 has *Heliam et clarumque videre*. Parrhasius has *Heliam clarum Moysenque videri* (“Elijah illustrious and Moses to be seen”)—“Unknown to the eyes, they saw with the light of the heart.” Wopkensis conjectures *Heliam, et clarum, ceu sidera, Mosen* (“Elijah and Moses, bright as stars”), or *Heliam, et claro sub lumine Mosen* (“Elijah and Moses beneath a clear light”); for he observes that Sedulius never made *Moyses* trisyllabic. Burmannus conjectures *Helian, et clarum sidere Mosen* (“Elijah and Moses bright with a star”). Poelmann’s sheets have *Heliam, et clarum denique Mosen* (“Elijah and finally Moses, illustrious”). Most printed editions have *Heliam, et clarum videre Moysen*; some retain Fabricius’ reading, which did not displease Grunerus. To many, the received reading seems inept because the past infinitive *videre* occurs in this verse and *viderunt* immediately in the next. A plausible reading appears in Reg. 1 and my codex, and is indicated in Ottob. 1: *Quid quod et Heliam, clarumque videre Moysem?* The present infinitive *videre* is then connected with *contigit*: “What if it happened to them also to see Elijah and illustrious Moses?” “They saw with the light of the heart those unknown to the eyes.” The prose supports the common reading; nor is the repetition of the past tense inelegant.

287. Parrhasius has *hoc esse*; others *hunc esse*. Urb. has the error *huc esse*.

288. Most have *Principium ac finem, hunc alpha viderier, hunc ω*; Reg. 1 and Vat. 1 have *et* instead of *ac*. Some printed editions, such as Bas., Col., Fabr., and Poelm., have *hunc simul alpha* (“this one at once Alpha”), to avoid a hiatus, contrary to the poet’s intention. Poelmann’s sheets likewise have *finem, sic alpha*. Parrhasius, inelegantly, has *hoc esse per orbem—Alpha Deum verum, et o principium sine fine* (“this throughout the world is Alpha, the true God, and O, the beginning without end”). In Ott. 1, *videri* formerly stood, as did *hunc ω*; these were corrected to *viderier, hunc ω*. In Alb. and Reg. 5, the omega is lacking at the end of the verse. This statement, in which God is called Alpha and Omega, is explained in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 214, note a, and in the commentary on *Cathemerinon* hymn 9, verse 11.

290. In Poelm. there is the error *Altera adhuc*. Vat. 2, Alb., and apparently Reg. 5 have *limite*, which Aldus printed and which appears in the Edinburgh edition. Others have *limine*. Cant., Ott. 2, and Fabr. have *mortis* instead of *vitae*, which most copies present. In Arntz., the first hand gave *mortis*, while the second corrected it to *vitae*. Cellarius retains *limine vitae* and explains it as meaning that Elijah—Cellarius names Enoch, but I think he intended Elijah—is still alive, while Moses was at the threshold of life, that is, about to rise again bodily immediately after Christ’s resurrection. Wopkensis prefers *limine mortis*, or “of death,” meaning that Moses was existing or dwelling in death; thus the dead Moses is set against the living Elijah. Gallandius similarly explains it of Moses dead in the land of Moab, according to Deuteronomy 34:5. Grunerus and Arntzenius defend *limine vitae* and interpret it from the prose as meaning that Moses is in the state of eternal life, since, although he departed from this life, he was immediately transferred into another and thus never withdrew from the threshold of life. Certainly the verse’s meaning is obscure, and the prose is no clearer, for where it reads *finalem luminis metam* (“the final limit of light”), there is grounds for establishing either the reading *limite vitae* or the conjecture *lumine vitae*. Nor do I dislike Burmann’s explanation in his commentary on Valerius Flaccus 1.823, that by *limen vitae* one should understand the threshold by which one departs from life. The meaning would then be that Moses continues to exist even though he has departed from this life. In Dracontius, *limina mortis* (“the thresholds of death”) often occurs, just as in Juvencus one finds *limine lucis*, *vitae*, and *mortis*, as the verbal indexes show.]

He emits light for all; for, shining with abundant radiance

To the three disciples as witnesses, like the fiery heat

[280] Of the sun, transformed into an ethereal form by his splendor,

He surpassed the day in his face, while they gazed upon the garment itself;

The white form of the Lord flashed from his robe, white as snow.

O sublime privilege of the three, to whom it was granted

To see in the world what the world did not believe!

[285] What is more, to see Elijah and illustrious Moses?

Unknown to the eyes, they saw them with the light of the heart,

So that our faith might be greater: that this one throughout the world

Should be seen as the beginning and the end, this one as Alpha, this one as Omega.

269 Around him these prophets shone,

[290] One still living, the other standing at the threshold of life.

[Col. 0665A] [Note: [Col. 0665A]

291. Parrhasius has *hic est*; others *est hic*. Rom. has the error *agens* instead of *aiens*, just as *agit* is frequently found for *ait* in manuscripts.

292. Parrhasius has *verbum genitum* (“begotten Word”). Nebrissensis, having found *verbo genitum* (“begotten by the Word”), restored the reading: “Rather—*verbum genitum*.” But the manuscript reading *verbo genitum* need not be disturbed. Christ is not only the begotten Word but also begotten by the Word. I have explained this patristic expression theologically in my notes on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 2: “Kindly Father of all, begotten Word,” and hymn 11, verse 17: “Although you were born from the Father’s mouth and brought forth by the Word.”

293. Rom.: “When the Lord returns to his former form.” Meus: “He casts out an unclean spirit from a boy.” In Reg. 1, *regressa* has correctly been made from *egressa*.

294. Urb., Rom., Vet. 1, 2, Monast.: *adorandam*. Most manuscripts and printed editions: *adoratam*. Poelm.’s edition, in the margin, and the Leipzig edition: *adornatam*. Poelmann’s sheets have *adoratam*, with the explanation “that is, then by the three disciples”; for *d. s.* they indicate *adornatam* and *adorandam*. In Ott. 1 it now reads *adoratam*, but formerly it was *adornatam*, or perhaps *adoptatam* or *adaptatam*. I frequently find the words *adorno*, *adoro*, *adopto*, and *adapto* interchanged in manuscripts. I discussed this more fully in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 7. Someone might perhaps suspect that *adoptatan* was written by Sedulius himself, and that others, especially after the heresy of the Adoptionists, regarded it as an error and erased it after substituting another word. The prose paraphrase explains it as “heavenly.”

295. Reg. 5 and Ald.: *Atque palam*: read *Seque palam*. Parrhasius, with the order reversed: *populis Dominus*.

296. In Poelm., *humili* is an error; in Ott. 1, something else originally stood in place of *moesto*. Arntzenius transposes the words and reads *vultu dejectus lumina moesto* (“with his eyes cast down in a sorrowful face”). Bede, in *De arte metrica*, and his commentator, without naming the author, quote this verse. *Dejectus lumina* is comparable to Ovid’s *oculos dejecta*, Statius’ *vultum dejectus*, and Virgil’s *vultum demissa*.

297. Ottob. 1: *Procidit*, corrected to *Procedit*. The meter indeed does not allow *Procidit*. Wopkensius conjectured *Prociderat, supplexque*; Arntzenius, *Procumbit, supplexque*. Yet both maintain that nothing should be changed without manuscript support. Matthew 17:14 says: “A man approached him, falling on his knees.” Sedulius explains *accessit ad eum* by *procedit*, and the remainder by *supplexque*, and so forth; more clearly still, in verse 305: “Clasping his knees and rolling upon his knees, he clung to him.” Poelm., Vet. 1, Mon., Bas., Col.: *simplexque*; the manuscripts and better printed editions: *supplexque*, which Poelmann’s sheets rightly prefer.

298. Meus: *filius, ait*, though the meter resists it. Arntz., Alb., Poelmann’s sheets, Ang., Reg. 1, 2, 5, Vatt. 1, 2, Ott. 1, Urb., Rom., together with Parrh. and Ald.: *filius unus*. Nebrissensis notes that the repetition *unus, unus* signifies “only one.” Ottob. 2: *filius, inquit*, which most printed editions retain and Arntzenius preferred. Sedulius seems to imitate Juvencus, book II, verse 298: *Implorat lacrymans*. Compare the note. Wopkensius takes *implorat* as equivalent to *plorat*, unless we prefer to understand “himself” implicitly. The sense here is rather: “Groaning, he implores help.”

300. Vet. 1, 2, Mon.: *quin* for *nisi*. Parrhasius: *Nunc liquidis demergit aquis, nunc ignibus atris*. Poelmann’s sheets perhaps likewise derive this reading from Parrhasius.

301. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s sheets: *Opprimit, et fatigat*. In Ott. 1 it was *fatigat*, but this was corrected to *fatiget*. In Ott. 2, Ang., Alb.: *fatigat*, which can be defended even if *Opprimat* is retained.

302. Cellarius: *Nunc*; most others more correctly: *Hunc*. Wopkensius conjectures *excluso* for *expulso*, because writers of the later period often use *excludo* for *expello*. Yet the common reading is supported not only by the manuscripts but also by the prose paraphrase. Poelm., Col., Bas.: *utrinque*. Meus, Arntz., from a second hand: *utroque*. The true reading is *utrumque*.

303. Parrhasius: *tetra potestas*. Wopkensius suspects *saeva*; but *caeca* is correct, that is, “raging,” deprived of every light of reason, as he himself explains.

305. Ott. 2, Vet. 1, 2, Mon., Poelmann’s sheets: *volutus*. The more common reading, *volutans*, is confirmed by Virgil, *Aeneid* III.607, from whom Sedulius borrowed this entire verse. But Virgil has *genua amplexus* (“clasping his knees”). *Volutans* is equivalent to *se volutans* or *volutatus*, as in *volventia plaustra*, *volventibus annis*, and similar expressions.

306. Ott. 2: *Merebat*. Perhaps the scribe intended to write *Moerebat*, but *Haerebat* is much better.]

With a heavenly sound, saying, “This is my Son,”

the Father’s voice displayed Christ, begotten by the Word.

After the power that had returned through his bodily limbs

270 had clothed the adored form in the veil of flesh,

[295] and the Lord had openly given himself to the peoples, behold, suddenly

a humble man, with eyes cast down in a sorrowful face,

came forward, stretching out his hands and arms,

and groaning implored: “I have one son, one

son, Lord; a dreadful spirit tears him apart in fury,

[300] [Col. 0666A] nor does it leave him unless it overwhelms him in the waters

or crushes him in black fires

271 and wears out his life beneath uncertain death.

Have pity, I beg, on us both, and, having expelled the madness,

restore him to me, or restore him to himself, lest blind power

drive his trembling life away by taking away his light.”

[305] He spoke, and, clasping the Lord’s knees and rolling upon his knees,

he clung to him; and the Lord, already in his loving heart,

[Col. 0667A] had nodded assent to the prayers.

309. Ott. 2, Ang.: *Perversa*; read *Pervasa*, that is, “invaded” or “possessed.” Ammianus likewise uses the participle *pervasus* in this sense. Ottob. 2 is joined by Cant., Mon., Bas., Torn. 1, 2, Edim., the Lyon Library, and the prose paraphrase, as it is now read. Burmann’s manuscript: *Pervasta*; the Leipzig edition: *Provisa*. Since, however, most of our manuscripts and the best printed editions offer the more suitable word *Pervasa*, it should be retained. Indeed, as Arntzenius proves, the same word should be restored in the prose in place of *perversae*. Arntzenius cites *pervasus* and *pervasor* from Cassiodorus, and *pervasio* from Salvian.

310. Meus, Vet. 1, 2, Mon.: *corpore*; retain *carpere* with the others, as both the sense and the prose require.

313. “Where the Lord commanded Peter that tribute should be paid.” Arntz.: *Rex etiam regum solus, Dominus*. Most of our manuscripts, together with Heinsius’ and the Leipzig manuscripts, Parrh., Ald., and other excellent editions: *dominantum*. Rom.: *dominantium*, which was also found in Reg. 1, but was corrected there to *dominantum* according to the better rules of meter. Arntz.’s manuscript, Poelm., Torn. 1, 2, 3, and other common editions: *dominorum*. This seems to have been the reading in Ott. 1, where *dominantum* now appears. Vat. 2, without a conjunction: *Rex etiam solus regum, Dominus dominantum*. The Apostle says, 1 Timothy 6:15: “The only sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords.”

315. Arntzenius’ manuscript writes *Caesarium*.
