316. Vatt. 1, 2, Ang., Alb., Reg. 5, Ott. 2, Rom., Meus, Lips., Poelmann’s sheets, Ald., Parrh., and other editions: *auri*. Reg. 1, Ott. 1, and several editions: *aurei*, which seems also to have been the original reading in Reg. 2, where *auri* now stands. In Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, *aurei* seems to have arisen from *auri*. *Aurei*, a disyllable by contraction, is better; scribes who did not understand this converted it into *auri*. Wopkensius nevertheless does not reject the use of *didrachma auri* for “a golden coin,” just as *numisma argenti* means “a silver coin” and *statua salis* “a statue of salt.” Some write *didragma*, others *didrama*, for *didrachma*.

317. In the Lyon Library, *prudentia* is an inept reading, and in Rom., from the first hand, *pandentia*, for *pendentia*. Instead of *pisce*, read “inhabitant of the sea”; so Pliny, Cicero, and Phaedrus.

318. Reg. 1: *honorante*, correctly emended to *onerante*.

319. Vat. 2 incorrectly has *piscibus*. This verse is absent from Vet. 1, 2, and Mon., but is found in all our copies; nor does the sense proceed without it.

320. Rom.: “Concerning the disciples’ question: who would be greater in the kingdom of heaven.” Meus: “Who is to be greater in the kingdom of heaven.” Arntz.: *suis semper cunctantibus*; read *suis se percunctantibus*, that is, *se* for *eum*, just as elsewhere *suus* is used for *ejus* and *sibi* for *ei*. This manner of speaking should not be adopted rashly, but it should not be condemned. Many write *percontantibus*; the variation concerns orthography. Meus, Rom., Cant., Vatt. 1, 2, Urb., Reg. 5, Parrh., and Ald.: *aulae*. Reg. 1, 2, Alb., Ott. 1, and apparently Ang.: *aula*, though in these three it may earlier have been *aulae*. Most printed editions: *aula*, that is, “in the court” or “palace.”

321. Meus: *Regni coelestis*. Most of our manuscripts: *quis possit major*. Fabr., Poelm., and several editions: *major quis possit*. Arntzenius printed *quis major possit*, which is found in Alb. Arntzenius’ manuscript: *quis posset major*; likewise the prose has *posset* for *possit*. One should note the use of the expression *possit haberi* in the sense of “may be considered” or “ought to be considered.” Similar examples occur elsewhere in Sedulius.

322. Reg. 1: *Tum*; above, in place of *d. s.*, *Ut*.

325. Vat. 1, Rom., Parrh.: *Dimissa*, for *Demissa*, which seems preferable. Cant., Poelmann’s sheets, Ott. 1, Ang., and other manuscripts, as well as several editions: *gerit*. Ott. 1, in place of *d. s.*, Alb., Reg. 1, 2, Lips., Fabr.: *feret*; but in Reg. 2 there was another reading, and the gloss is *gerat*. Parrh.: *geret*. More recent editions prefer *feret*.]

He had nodded assent. Then the raging robber and guilty enemy,

who had long possessed another’s rightful habitation,

forced to depart from the invaded house, was driven into anger,

[310] and, seized by fury, attempted to tear the limbs apart,

272 but labored in vain, since the Lord forbade it,

and fled into dark shadows, while the boy remained alive.

The only King of kings, and Lord of lords,

did not disdain, while Peter was fishing, to pay

[315] the imperial tribute; from the middle of the lake

he orders him to bring up, from the midst of the sea, a hook bearing a golden didrachm.

[Col. 0668A] Soon an inhabitant of the sea bit the hanging threads,

bringing the commanded tribute; and, heavier because of the weight of the metal,

the worthless fish was weighed out at a greater price.

[320] 273 When his disciples were asking among themselves

who could be considered greater in the court

of the heavenly kingdom, he, as God and wondrous teacher,

said: “The humble is higher than all and will go forth more powerful than all,

the one who will be subject to everyone and make himself less,

[325] carrying his head bowed, just as this little one appears to do.”

And he points out the little boy standing there.

327. Meus: *sectamur et*; the sense requires *sectemur ut*.

329. Reg. 1, Cant., Ott. 1: *mundalis*; in Ott. 1, as though a gloss, there is *mortalis*. Ott. 2: *mondalis*. Most manuscripts and editions: *mortalis*, which Grunerus prefers, because although the prose has *mundanae*, *mortalis* is more poetic, and *mundalis* is not found elsewhere. Sedulius again has, book IV, verse 293: *Qui pompae mortalis honor* (“who is the honor of mortal pomp”). I would not object to *mundalis* in Sedulius, or even to *mundialis* as a trisyllable by contraction, a word used by Tertullian, Jerome, Prudentius, and Salvian.

330. *Resupinus* is used by Ovid and Seneca for “proud,” just as others use *supinus*. “Of pure life,” because the boy is said to derive from *purus*, as Nebrissensis says; or, according to Isidore, *Etymologies* XII.2, from purity.

331. Vat. 1: *Quantum est prona*; others omit *est*. This verse of Sedulius can support the conjecture I proposed in my note on Juvencus, book IV, verse 36: *Qui terrae proni* for *Qui terram proni*, as it is read in the manuscripts. See the textual variants. The use of *tantum* and *quantum* for *tam* and *quam* is sufficiently common.

333. Vonckius preferred *Inferiorque gradu quo vult*; the old copies and the prose require *gradus*. All our manuscripts and most others have *quo vult descendere, surgit*. Poelmann’s sheets noted: *Quo*, that is, “to that place” or “in that direction”; otherwise, “when.” The same sheets state that one should read *descendere surgit*, not *descende, resurgit*. Arntzenius had not found this variation in his copies. It nevertheless appears in Poelmann’s own edition, where one reads *quo vult descende, resurgit*, with *cum vult* in the margin. But, in my opinion, *descende, resurgit* is a typographical error; no sense can be extracted from it.

334. Cant., Arntz., Ang., Alb., Reg. 2, 5, Vat. 2, and Ott. 2: *egenum*. Ott. 1 likewise, but corrected to *egentem*, which Reg. 1 and others present. The printed editions vary in the same way.

335. *Tyrannos*, in its ancient meaning, namely “kings.”

336. Meus: *Econtra*, or *E contra*. This expression is defended by the authority of Aurelius Victor, Jerome, Servius, and, as some think, Tacitus; but simply *contra* is more Latin. Therefore *At contra*, the common reading, should be retained.

337. Vat. 1: *Praecipitem e coelo*; others: *Praecipitem coelo*.

338. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s sheets: *Pauca loquar*. Rom., Ang., Alb., and others: *Parva loquar*. The more common and more correct reading is *Parva loquor*, supported by the prose. Wopkensius explains it: “I feel that I am saying very little.” Sidonius, poem 5: *Parva loquor. Quid? quod*, etc. Vat. 1, if read with the others, has *sed*; above, however, it seems to be *nisi*. Writers of the later period used *currere per facta*, *per miracula*, and so forth, for “to recount briefly,” as in Sulpicius Severus, Paulinus of Nola, and Augustine. A similar expression is Cicero, *Verrines* 5, oration 3, chapter 42: “For my speech runs through all the communities that owe the tithes.”

339. Dracontius likewise joins the general and the particular, book II, verse 183: “And you command the particular to be guarded as though it were the general.” After this verse, Reg. 1: “Here ends book two. Book three begins, in Christ.” Reg. 2: “Here ends book II.” Ottob. 1: “Book II ends. Book III begins. The Evangelist’s titles follow, compressed into individual chapters.” This is written corruptly, perhaps to indicate that separate titles are placed before the individual chapters. Vat. 1: “This third book is divided according to persons.” Clearly *Hic liber tertius* is sound; what follows is confused and obscured by letters intermingled with one another. Reg. 5: “End of the second book. The third book, the third book of divine miracles.” Meus: “The second book of the poet Sedulius. Book III begins.” The very old Turin manuscript: “Here ends the second book. The third book begins. I, Abundantius, have successfully collated this book.” In other manuscripts of inferior quality there is no division between books at this point. The same is true of the printed editions: some begin another book at verse 339, *Jam placidas*; others do otherwise. The book that ends is called the second in the manuscripts, and the book that begins is called the third, because the first book of the poem is placed, as it were, outside the sequence and bears the title “Book of the Old Testament.” The second book of the poem is called the first of the New Testament; the same order is then maintained.]

Let us, then, follow the character of tender age,

which he commands us to pursue not in years but in mind,

because the softer age loves nothing of mortal pomp

and does not seek honor,

[330] 274 nor swell with proud arrogance; thus the path of a pure life,

as much inclined toward the earth, so much does it become nearer heaven.

For the mind that bends downward seeks what is high,

and turns toward the heights; the lower step rises

in the direction in which it wishes to descend.

Behold, the Lord raises the humble needy man from the dungheap

[335] and makes him sit among distinguished kings.

But, on the contrary, he commanded the swollen rebel,

rebellious in a defiant spirit, to fall headlong from heaven

beneath Tartarus.

275 I speak briefly if I were to recount God’s deeds one by one,

and review the particular blessing, though it is universal.

## BOOK FOUR

[Note: [Col. 0671B]

Now, when once again crossing the streams of the Jordan and passing along the path of Judaea, the Lord healed everywhere an immense crowd and countless companies of people suffering from every kind of nameless illness, receiving the sick and allowing the healthy to return. Therefore nothing is difficult to offer to the Most High Lord for those who hope in him, since divine power readily supplies the means to level steep things and straighten crooked ones—that is, to bring down the proud to humbler things and show the path to those who have gone astray. [Note: Juretus emends this as *ardua planare, curva dirigere*; for this, he says, an old codex had *curva dirigere*. Perhaps Juretus should read *digerere*; otherwise it is not understood what he emends. An ancient proverb was *curva corrigere* (“to correct crooked things”).] For the magnificent prophet Isaiah is known to have spoken thus when he announced the coming of Christ: “And crooked things shall become straight, and rough places into level ways.” Did he prophesy about rocks, thorns, or the winding bends of crooked roads, when Christ came to save the world, which was constituted not by woods and mountains but by human peoples? This is also what is meant by “the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” which commands that the way of the Lord be prepared and his paths made straight: namely, the way of knowledge and the paths of the will, by which the Lord advances with a straight step toward the dwelling of the heart of the world. For thoughts and wills are the roads of actions, which seem to precede the good or evil outcome of anyone’s conduct. Therefore whatever natural force denies is made easy under divine power. For just as the enormous beast, the camel, cannot pass through the narrow opening of a needle because of the bulk of its body, so the wealthy, swollen rich man cannot enter the heavenly kingdoms through the narrow gate of the slender path—unless the provident governor of all things, who holds everything within the law but is himself not held under the law, whom no face has ever seen but who himself always beholds all things, had comforted his troubled disciples with such consoling words: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” For not every rich man’s inheritance is a burden to him; it is a burden to the one who is a wicked steward of his own abundance. When the Lord says through the prophet, “The gold and silver are mine,” he shows that what belongs to him is not evil if a good steward possesses it. For it makes no difference whether someone gives nothing to good works or pours out a great deal upon evil ones. The person who safely preserves and invests his wealth is the one who hides and stores his treasures in heaven, where neither the bite of destructive moths nor the rough corrosion of rust consumes anything, and where no excavated entrance is opened to thieves for plundering; the one who supplies food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, hospitality to strangers, comforts the sorrowful in prison, tends the sick in body, and, most generous to everyone, is poor and needy only toward himself. No one should doubt that the substance which is proved to have been expended for Christ under the most contemptible appearance of a poor person truly reaches heaven: it is increased by losses, preserved by being scattered, perishes in order to remain, and, though dead, represents life. [Note: In the old codex *vita* stood for *vitam*.]]

Now, while the Lord, surrounded by the accompanying people, had gone out from Jericho, he saw two blind men sitting beside the road, asking that their sight be restored. Thus they confidently asked to obtain the mobility of walking. [Note: This is obscure, whether one reads *confidere* with the old codex or *considere*, which Juretus preferred.] But hostile darkness resisted; nor did that power delay even briefly, which refuses nothing to mercy and is accustomed to bring salvation wherever it perceives faith burning. It awakened their eyes, long compressed in sleep, with a sudden, watchful touch, and, opening beneath the brow the shutters of the hidden windows, immediately drove away the dark night as daylight entered.

From there, walking again through the sacred walls of the temple, he gave sight to the blind and restored movement to the lame. After these memorials of noble deeds, leaving the city of David, he came to the region of Bethany; and, returning on the following day, he proceeded again toward the roofs of that city. Not far from the road stood a fig tree, shaded by a woven covering of leaves. When the Lord, hungry in the flesh, found no fruit at all upon its strong branches, he did not wound the inhuman branches of the tree with a curse but condemned them by command, rebuking it thus: “Never shall fruit grow on you forever.” Immediately the fig tree, deprived of its sap, became barren and withered, stripped of the beauty of its leafy crown. Yet let us not understand this literally, although it is plainly believed to have been fulfilled, because the divine law ought to be understood as corresponding to spiritual causes. For what had the insensible material committed as a sin? Especially since, as the evangelist Mark records, it had no fruit because the season was unsuitable—unless the Lord did this for our instruction and benefit, showing us the way of life through parables of deeds and words. Thus every effort of human conduct that makes no effort to nourish anything pleasing to God will be compared to a useless tree, like a sluggish trunk full of leaves but without a shoot, destined for firewood. So too did that fruitless fig tree stand, which the Lord of the vineyard, who had planted it, ordered to be cut down but allowed a reprieve of one year, so that, if it produced fruit even late, it might remain; otherwise, it would rightly perish. But in accordance with the psalm’s song:

“The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree,

and shall multiply like a cedar that is in Lebanon.”

Meanwhile, someone was brought to him who suffered from an affliction of madness and also from impairment of speech. With the passages of his throat blocked, no voice sounded from the cymbals of his lips; and, proclaiming nothing at all with his mouth, he made his madness known by remaining mute. But that heavenly creator, accustomed to strengthen the weak, drove off from the siege of the throat the threatening one with the constricted breaths of robbers, and, through the open paths of voice, released the tongue from its bonds and restored it to full freedom of speech.

[Note: The old manuscript incorrectly has *anhelantibus*, unless one reads *angustiis anhelantibus*. Juretus would better have restored *anhelitibus*. I think *latronum* is an error for *latronem*, and afterward *homini* should be deleted in favor of *exi de homine*.]

Furthermore, while the Lord was honoring by his humility the banquet of a certain Pharisee who had invited him, a sinful and notorious woman arrived in haste. Wounded by many injuries of sin, she was living an obscene life. Falling down and prostrating herself at his feet, she did not cease washing them with her tears, wiping them with her hair, and moistening them with precious ointment through kisses, until God’s sentence was proclaimed—he who does not regret extending his hand to those who fall, if we regret the slippery path of our ancient ruin—and he released forgiveness in these words: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” O how much it helps wretched and afflicted people to reveal through confession what becomes deadly when hidden! The person who conceals a wound nourishes it and, uncertain because of the pain’s sting, neglects to expose the injury to the physician. Behold, now the woman polluted by the long contagion of disease is cleansed by the affliction of a small groan and washed in the torrent of her own tears; drenched with tears and wiping herself with her hair, she departs clean who had come soiled.

When the Lord also came to a city named Capernaum, in which he was teaching many people of the heavenly synagogue’s assembly, that utterly wicked devil suddenly cried out through the instrument of a human voice: “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Then, terrified and cast down by the Lord’s threatening command—“Be silent, and come out of the man, unclean spirit”—he left the human heart with a great echoing roar, by which he confessed that he had been struck down by divine authority, fleeing into the unseen darkness of the air.

[Col. 0680A] Likewise, the Lord brought saving aid to many who were suffering from different illnesses and afflicted by various calamities. He expelled many demons by a word of his power and did not allow them to speak at all, disdaining to have the faith of his heavenly majesty confirmed by such a common witness. For that ancient infernal serpent, destroyer of life and inventor of death, together with the entire madness of his associated host and the shameful satellite of his condemned army, cast down from the heavenly summit, was astonished to see on earth Christ, whom he had known in that starry citadel, clothed in the humility of flesh; and he groaned all the more resentfully because he saw that the Lord of power loved human beings so greatly.

While the Lord was afterward passing through the region of Tyre and walking along the Sidonian shore, a certain wretched man afflicted by a double calamity was brought to him. Deprived of the functions of both voice and hearing, he could neither produce his own words nor receive those of others. But when the heavenly hand, by its touch, broke open all the inner passages which violent force had closed, the doors suddenly stood open, and the guardians of the veins were immediately released. The man who had seemed mute and deaf now deserved both to speak himself and to hear others speaking.

You too experienced the gifts of the Lord’s power, when Christ spat upon your eyes, compressed by infernal blindness, and immediately wiped away the appearance of simulated death. And while he taught the peoples through sacred ordinances to possess the supports of eternal life, revealing himself more openly as God, he briefly avoided the crowds that had rushed together and came to the lake of the sea. Sitting in Simon’s small boat, he filled the people remaining on the shore with divine pronouncements. At last, bringing his words to an end—he who was never satisfied by desires—he ordered the fishing nets to be lowered into the deep water as the boat moved farther out. After the entire circle of night had passed, they had been unable to draw anything from the depths despite their fruitless labor. Simon gladly obeyed the sacred command. Skilled in enclosing the wandering crowds of waves within a line, he captured the peoples of the watery marble as though enclosed by a wall of protection. So great a multitude of fish filled the stretched nets that both Simon’s boat and the companion vessel standing nearby, occupied by masses of scales, were scarcely rescued from danger. Thus the unexpected happiness of great success often disturbs us too; and when the joy we receive according to our wishes exceeds all measure and limit, we begin to fear it as an intolerable gift. Human beings fear to desire what divine readiness grants.

Renowned and distinguished by such deeds of power, the Lord was hastening with his disciples to enter the city called Nain. Surrounded by the people, he suddenly saw a young man’s corpse being carried out, raised up in the grim service of empty funeral rites. His mother had first been deprived of her husband by hostile fate and now, a widow for the second time, had been bereaved of her son and left to suffer the misery of a double urn. Mercy, which is hostile to grief, did not delay, but immediately supplied life-giving aid. Touching the bier with the hand of redemption [Note: The old codex has *manus* for *manu*. Juretus further observes that Sedulius has used *redemptionis* for *redemptoris*, as is his custom.], the Lord said to the dead man: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And the one who had been dead sat up, began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. Although the young man, deprived of light, had been oppressed in body by sluggish death, and the funeral procession carried him forth extinguished, neither the servant, when the Lord called, could remain silent, nor could the spirit fail to return in the presence of life. Immediately, therefore, the entire gathering, which had been weeping and had a clouded face, was made serene; turning grief into a renewed path, the gathering, turning its course back with grief laid aside, restored the rejoicing mother to her own home in a radiant procession. [Note: Juretus restores *nubila facie* (“with clouded face”), where the old codex corruptly had *nubila facile*.]

Nor was the salvation granted to you, Mary, a small one. While the Lord was healing, it cured the hidden wound of your breast, injured by many blows, which a sevenfold fury, wedged together in a demonic mass, possessed through sevenfold movements of weapons. But the scaly, spotted serpent of error, fleeing the dreadful commands of the Almighty, was driven from your heart and sought the chaos of Tartarus’ inferno, twisting the coils of its seven limbs and vanishing in seven turns.

Then, lest the abundant shoot of the rich harvest should languish because of the failure of a few laborers, he ordered another seventy-two disciples—simple in mind and radiant in purity, conspicuous in number and merit, worthy to be named in the golden balance—to go like innocent and gentle lambs among the harsh minds of human beings, as among ravenous wolves. Having encouraged and addressed them in these words, he said: “Go; behold, I send you as lambs among wolves.” When they returned again in high spirits, reporting that even the demons had been subject to them, he admonished them, saying: “Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you. Rejoice because your names are written in heaven.” This is the rule of divine judgment: to put life before deeds, and not deeds before life. For if the merit of holy discipline has ceased, miracles have no importance, though they are also frequently displayed by the wicked. To such people he—the witness of secrets and judge of deeds, whether requiter of words—foretold in the Evangelist’s utterance: “I do not know you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” [Note: The old codex had *monumenti* for *momenti*. Shortly afterward, some printed editions incorrectly have *doctorum* for *dictorum*.] Under the tyranny of the Egyptian Pharaoh there were once two practitioners of a wicked association. Trusting in Memphite deceptions, they attempted to imitate Moses’ heavenly miracles and, through magnificent tricks, set before human eyes images and forms fashioned from mist.

Meanwhile, having been invited to a meal by a certain ruler of the Pharisees, he came—not so much for the sake of eating as because he hastened to honor that man’s house—and saw a man distended by a deceptive swelling of corpulence. Because water overflowed within him, he seemed to be a transparent wineskin; it was not a womb but an enormous, pregnant skin, giving birth to an enclosed death, while the cavity expanded excessively through the wasting away of his limbs. Thus, with emaciation ruling everywhere, it had gathered the entire dropsy into a distended belly. The Father of the world could not tolerate this sight in his presence, nor did he at that time observe his Sabbaths, hastening to heal the man whom he desired more truly to be his own. For God did not institute man for the Sabbath, as the Lord himself taught in another chapter of the holy Gospel, but created the Sabbath for man. Then, granting the work of salvation, he commanded the watery flood of the entrails to be dried up. Suddenly the diseased wave of bodily marsh withdrew, and the lake of the now glass-like flesh, drained of its watery disease, was suddenly emptied and vanished. [Note: Perhaps the reading was *fuit vacua* (“was empty”).]

As the Lord, making his way to Jerusalem, was passing through Samaria, Galilee, and Jericho, he mercifully entered a certain town. From a distance, ten wretched lepers saw him; they were utterly filthy, made hideous by the spotted indecency of their bodies, and disfigured into grotesque forms by the multicolored punishment scattered across their faces. All together they cried out mournfully with one voice: “Jesus, master, have mercy on us.” Then that singular power, which is never empty of compassion, answered and mercifully said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” At once, as they hurried away, all the wickedness fled from their limbs. Looking at one another, they rejoiced together in mutual purification, since nothing at all of the horrible disfigurement remained in any of them. One of them, as though about to offer a tithe of the gift received above all the others, returned with grateful haste and fell prostrate on his face before the Lord. Great was the man’s faith, and great his prudence: through the effect of a single act he fulfilled a double duty of devotion. His faith lay in believing that he had been cleansed because he had asked; his prudence, in preferring to worship Jesus even though he had been ordered to show himself to the priests. For who, unless Christ the Lord—the high priest of high priests, the priest of priests, the author and creator of the double offering—could be the one whose gifts, offered for us when he was crucified according to the order of Melchizedek, are presented through the kinship of his body: the sweet food of wheat’s seed and the pleasing drink of the lovely vine?

When the son of Timaeus was sitting beside the road, deprived of sight, and had learned that Christ was passing by, he cried out repeatedly and loudly. He did not fall silent even when the crowds ordered him to do so, but asked ever more insistently that the abundance of visible brightness be granted to him. Ordered to come to Christ, he proceeded with another’s hand and, having obtained what he desired, returned without the support of any guide. O virtue of unbroken confidence, which obtains by force what it desires and, gathering repeated prayers from the heart, demands what it seeks as though it were owed! By the manner in which you ask, so you deserve to receive. [Note: Gallandius has *qua quod postulas, sic mereris*; the ancient *Bibliothecae Patrum* have *qua postulas, sic mereris*. The editor would prefer *qua postulans, sic mereris* (“by asking thus, you deserve thus”).] For whatever difficulty in proportion to the matter a harder circumstance may have denied, frequent prayer by the petitioner, with simple and honorable requests, obtains by itself—not because anything is difficult for God, but because the greatness of the matter is humanly despaired of. So it was with the man who, in the silence of night, kept asking a friend for bread, after a long period of refusal: what he could not obtain by right of affection, he justly wrested from him by the aid of persistence. [Note: The old codex incorrectly has *extorsi* for *extorsit*, and shortly afterward *adorem* for *ardorem*, as Juretus notes.]

The Lord, too, while passing through the region of Samaria, had gathered the heat of human thirst on a day burning with heat. The ever-accessible fountain, perpetually watered by eternal streams, desired a small quantity of water with which the bodily matter might be given to drink. Here a woman native to that region, who drew liquid from the depths of a well, hesitated to grant the modest gift of water. Recognizing through prophetic speech that the Lord knew the life of her crimes, whether with many husbands or with a stranger’s husband, she asked him to bestow upon her immortal streams, whose substance would never fail and whose thirst would be abolished. She was wholly ignorant and unaware that no one would enjoy so great a gift unless, submerged in the flood of Jesus Christ and in spiritual waters, the soul—not the body—had been satisfied.

[Col. 0694B] And while the Savior, thundering with his voice, was seated within the sacred walls of the temple, taking pity on the wandering people and turning them toward the straight path by a friendly admonition to life,[^c0067-1] behold, an adulterous woman was dragged headlong before him, disheveled, from the midst of a great crowd, to be overwhelmed by the customary throwing of stones according to the established law. The savage fury of her accusers brought her before the merciful Judge, wishing him to condemn her; he set her free. For when the condition was proposed that the author of the punishment should come forward—whoever had no share in the crime—no one was found, by his own judgment, pure enough to strike the impure woman. Nor did anyone dare to remove the speck from another’s eye, knowing that a beam remained in his own.

Soon, therefore, the whole fire of the swift sedition was extinguished by the uncleanness of conscience, and the accuser was discovered silently confessing himself guilty.[^c0067-2] Then the Lord’s merciful and gentle judgment did not condemn the adulteress after her manifest crime, but, taking pity on her, did not punish her—obviously leaving her to return to punishment if she returned to guilt. For whoever, like a dog,[^c0067-3] desires and licks again the filth that he has vomited, neither seeks to retain the pardon already granted nor to obtain that which is to come: losing the profit of the former pardon, which he acquired in vain, and experiencing the loss of the latter, to which he did not deserve to attain.

[^c0067-1]: The old manuscript incorrectly has *vita* (“life”) instead of *vitae* (“to life”); shortly afterward it has *qui ferret in puram* instead of *qui feriret impurum* (“who should strike the impure woman”).

[^c0067-2]: In the old manuscript there is *confitenda* (“to be confessed”), and, as it seemed to be written, *tacitecte*. Juretus therefore restored *tacitate confitendo* (“by confessing in silence”), because Sedulius delights in expressions of this kind. I retain the reading found in some libraries of the Fathers, *tacite* (“silently”). A little earlier most editions have *immunditie* (“by uncleanness”), but the 1589 Paris Library of the Fathers has *immunditia*; there too it reads *fuit* (“was”) instead of *fugit* (“fled”).

[^c0067-3]: In most libraries of the Fathers, corruptly, *camini ritus* (“the manner of a furnace”) instead of *canino ritu* (“in the manner of a dog”). The sentence is taken from the Second Epistle of Peter, chapter 2, verse 22.

Leaving this place as well, the Lord sees a man blind from birth, who, having fallen from the womb of his wretched mother, still more wretched, came into the light without light. Then that Sower of the human race, Creator and Perfecter of the world,[Col. 0696B] not allowing the workmanship of his mouth to remain less than complete, since material for a mirror was lacking, smeared mud—naturally, the material instrument—over the barriers of his cheeks, supplying from old clay what he had seen to be lacking in the man.[^c0067-4] Yet the man did not receive sight before, instructed by the Lord’s commands, he came to the healing waters of Siloam and, protected by the medicine of his kindred clay, washed his eyes with the water poured over them.[^c0067-5] Immediately, therefore, twin rays shone from his restored face, at last worthy to behold the day that they had previously known not at all.

All who read these things spiritually must therefore attend to what the mystical miracles of this event teach. For we are blind, a most wretched offspring created from the descendants of Eve, walking through the darkness of our native gloom in long wanderings. But after God deigned to assume the likeness of human flesh,[^c0067-6] saving earth was given to us from a virgin; washed by the waters of holy baptism, it opened eyes of brightness to those being reborn.

[^c0067-4]: Some have *luto*, others *lutu*, and Gallandius *lutum*. Juretus’s annotation escaped Gallandius: Juretus, agreeing with the old manuscript, reads *lutu* and says that it should be read instead of *luto*, according to ancient usage, just as *lauru* is used for *lauro* and in several other cases. Nevertheless, *lutum* should be retained with Gallandius, for Sedulius uses the same form in verse. The period is often punctuated incorrectly, namely, *impletam speculari, deficiente materia*. It is much better punctuated *impletam, speculari deficiente materia* (“to remain incomplete, since material for a mirror was lacking”).

[^c0067-5]: In place of *tutus* (“safe”), Gallandius thinks *fotus* (“cherished” or “bathed”) should be read. I restored *lavisset* (“had washed”) instead of *habuisset* (“had possessed”).

[^c0067-6]: The old manuscript has *humani* (“of human”), while Juretus restored *humanae* (“of human flesh”). He also notes that the author, when speaking of Christ’s body, ordinarily says *effigies corporis* (“the likeness of the body”). Sedulius uses *effigiem* for the true body, as is clear from the whole sequence of the discourse, both here and elsewhere.

He had then come gently to Bethany by his accustomed steps. There Lazarus, having met the end appointed by human condition, lay beneath a sepulchral stone, already foul after the course of four days’ light had passed.[^c0067-7] When the Lord came to his tomb, his sisters gathered there and wept with loving grief. The assembled crowd wept, and the Almighty himself wept at the same time—not in his divinity, but in his body—for, in the part in which he was to die, he grieved over the cold, lifeless limbs. For he shed tears as a friend, but displayed the glory of his majesty as God.

Why do you still not believe, Martha? And you, Mary, why do you groan, hesitating in doubtful fear of Christ, wondering whether one man can be raised from the dead—he who will cause the innumerable crowds of the whole world to rise again with renewed animation? Then the Lord, crying out with a wondrous command of his imperious voice, “Lazarus, come forth!”—[Col. 0699A] suddenly the realms of Tartarus lay open, shaken with terror; the innermost chamber of hell trembled; deadly chaos was afraid; the law withdrew from the deep recess of death; and the soul, poured again into its body’s limbs, was seen to stand as a living corpse, the protection of the tomb having been broken.[^c0067-8] After the proper rites, after the burial of the funeral had been completed, as though he had been brought forth and created anew, he himself became both dying and posthumous to himself, and departed as one who had survived.

[^c0067-7]: The old manuscript incorrectly has *quarta* instead of *quartae* (“of the fourth day”), and below *frigentis cortus exanimes*. Juretus conjectured *corpus exanime* (“lifeless body”), but preferred *artus exanimes* (“lifeless limbs”) from the poem: “And the lifeless limbs…”

[^c0067-8]: The sense seems to require *exclamat* (“he cries out”), but all the Vulgate editions report *exclamans* (“crying out”). Shortly afterward Gallandius corrected the text to *et lex profundae mortis abscessit* (“and the law withdrew from the deep [place] of death”); other editions have *ex profundo mortis abscessu* (“from the deep retreat of death”). The printed editions consistently have *et lex profundo mortis abscessu*.

And when the Lord, scorning the perishable grandeur of the world,[^c0067-9] wished to show himself even more exalted by humility, he did not travel borne along in a four-horse chariot with the speed of a team of four horses—vehicles in which the pomp of mortal honor is displayed—but proceeded along a dusty road cut by wheels,[Col. 0700B] nor did he press the lofty back of a neighing horse, conspicuous with trappings and purple, shaking its restless face and chewing the foaming weight of blood-red gold. Rather, the honor of that Lord was sufficiently shown by the slow bearing of a most worthless ass. Its hoof, distinguished beneath its burden not by price but by the merit of so great a rider, was not inferior to that animal which, although it saw Christ in a humble manger, recognized him as Lord. By his favor this beast of burden shone—the one to whom the whole crowd submitted its garments as he walked along the middle of the path.

Tell me now, all peoples who until this time are subject to gentile errors: to what ruler has glory ever been comparable? To whom has a festival ever come, filled with a dense crowd, palms and branches, singing a song in heavenly hymns? To no one but the Lord Jesus Christ, who governs the starry empire with the Father, prince within the eternal Prince.[^c0067-10]

[^c0067-9]: The old manuscript incorrectly has *caduce* (“foolishly”) instead of *caduca* (“perishable”), in *saecularis ambitus caduca contemnens*.

[^c0067-10]: Gallandius’s conjecture readily commends itself to me: from the poem he restored *honor* (“honor”), where the editions had *amor* (“love”) in *qui pompae mortalis amor ostenditur*. Shortly afterward, in some editions, *hastamine* and *hestamine* are errors for *gestamine* (“bearing” or “carrying”).

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671A] **Note: [Col. 0671C]**

1. Vatican 1: “Concerning the rich man who cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.” Regius 1: “Where the Lord heals innumerable throngs of Adam.” **Judaeae* (“of Judea”) should be read instead of *ad Adae*, as the gloss indicates. In Ottobonian 2 the reading is *congressus* (“having approached”); Aldus has *ingressus* (“having entered”); I retain *transgressus* (“having crossed”). My manuscript, incorrectly, has *iste transgressus*.

2. Some have *sectatur iter* (“he follows the road”). Most manuscripts and editions have *mixtum* (“mixed”), and perhaps Sedulius is imitating Juvencus, book 3, verse 760: “The mixed tables of the nameless crowd are filled.” The Leipzig edition has *mestum*, perhaps for *mistum*; many other editions clearly have *moestum* (“sorrowful”). In Regius 1, *moestum* is the first reading, with the gloss *infirmum* (“weak”); *mixtum* is the second reading. The reverse occurs in Regius 2.

[Col. 0671D] 3. Arntzenius has *a morte* (“from death”); others have *a clade* (“from destruction”), as in book 3, verse 45: “He lifted the peoples from destruction.”

8. Cantabrigian, Arntzenius, the Poelmann sheets, Parrhasius, Edinburgh, Rome, Angers, Ottobonian 1 and 2, Vatican 1 and 2, Regius 5, Alb., and Urb.: *Nam quidquid* (“For whatever”). Regius 1 and 2, with many printed editions, especially recent ones: *Et quidquid* (“And whatever”). My manuscript: *Qui quidquid*. Vonckius conjectured: “Whatever nature denies, he provides as judge of himself.” Grunerus defends *Et quidquid*, although he admits that this connection of words is harsher. The clearer reading is the one held by most of our manuscripts, *Nam quidquid*, and it seems closer to prose. The absolute ablative *se judice* (“with himself as judge”), meaning *ipse judex praestat* (“he himself as judge provides”), occurs similarly in Juvencus, Avitus, Arator, and Fortunatus, not to mention ancient inscriptions, such as *Se vivo fecit* (“He made it while alive”). On this subject one may consult, for example, Ignatius Potenza’s learned work published this year, 1793, *Notices Concerning the Sacred Tomb of Saint Augustalis the Martyr*, etc. The tomb of this martyr was recently discovered at Rome with this simple inscription: “Augustalis made it while alive.”

10. Ottobonian 1, Alb., Urb., Rome, Parrhasius, and Burmannus’s manuscript have *pro mole* (“because of the mass”); *prae mole* (“because of the mass”) is better, although the prose has something else.

11. Bentley, in his *Emendations to Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations*, p. 34, substituted *Altilitate* for *Fertilitate*, a new term for “fatness” or “richness.” Arntzenius rightly condemns this alteration. *Fertilitas* means abundance or plenty of things. Arntzenius, Parrhasius, Aldus, Vatican 1 and 2, and Regius 5 have *posset* (“could”); Arntzenius finds this acceptable. In Ottobonian 1, *posset* was made from *possit*; in Regius 1 and 2, *possit* was corrected from *posset*, which is preferable for *poterit* (“will be able”).

15. Poelmann closes the parenthesis at *conspicit* (“he sees”); others close it at *ipse* (“himself”). On the word *impossibilis* (“impossible”), I discussed the matter in my note to Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 833, as also the simple form *possibilis* (“possible”) in Juvencus 2.533.

276. Now, having crossed the peaceful sands of the Jordan,

and following the road through Judea, he receives the nameless

mixed crowd, and, relieving innumerable throngs from destruction,

he takes in the sick and sends them away healthy.

[5] Nothing, therefore, is ever difficult for God to grant

to those who hope greatly in him, for whom it is an easy power

to level what is steep and to turn what is curved into straightness;

[Col. 0672A] 277. for whatever nature denies, he provides as judge of himself.

For just as a camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle

[10] because of the great mass of its limbs, so the rich man,

swollen with abundant wealth, cannot approach the narrow path

that leads to the thresholds of the heavenly kingdom,

unless the Father of creation—who restrains the world by law,

and remains under no law, since for him to will to create is enough,

[15] whom no face sees, but who himself sees everything—

[Col. 0673] **Note: [Col. 0673C]**

16. Most of our manuscripts, with Arntzenius, Aldus, Fabricius, and other editions, have *at alto* (“but he said aloud”); most editions have *et alto* (“and he said aloud”). In some of ours, *et* or *ac* seems originally to have stood in place of *at*. Wopkensius, Burmannus, and Arntzenius rightly prefer *at*, supported by the prose. In Ottobonian 2, *dixisse, sed alto* appears to be an error for *dixisset, et alto*.

22. Burmannus conjectures *Nec male depostum* (“nor badly deposited”), that is, what the miser hides when he ought to use it; or he says that *defodere* (“to bury”) should be understood in a new sense as *effodere* (“to dig out”), since thieves do not usually steal gold buried in the earth’s depths. Arntzenius says it may be explained as *male defossum* (“badly buried”), placed so carelessly that it offers thieves an easy opportunity. He defends the common reading from Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius: “I would not be free from blame for money buried.” But in that letter the subject is money, or the talent, which the servant hid because he was afraid of his master, since he was harsh.

The true basis for defending the received reading is found in Matthew 6:19 and following: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where thieves dig up and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where thieves do not dig up or steal.” Gold, therefore, is *male defossum* (“badly buried”) when the miser, although he ought to use it well, buries it—something that thieves sometimes dig up and steal. The proper meaning of buried gold is gold hidden beneath the earth. Cicero, book 2 of *On the Orator*: “For if I wished to point out to someone gold that had been buried in many places, it ought to be enough to show him the signs and marks of the locations,” etc. After *aurum* (“gold”), Cellarius and other printed editions place a full stop and thereby wrongly break the sense. The intended subject is “the one who…” or “whoever…”

23. Regius 1 has *pro d. s.*; Regius 2, by correction; Vatican 1 and 2, Ottobonian 2, Urb., Alb., Rome, my manuscript, Regius 5, and other manuscripts cited by Arntzenius, together with Parrhasius and Aldus, have *qui ferre* (“who can bear”). In the Poelmann sheets *ferre* was written in, namely, “he wishes.” Arntzenius does not approve this because of the following *largitur* (“he gives”). Regius 1 in the text, Ottobonian 1 by correction, and Angers have *quicumque* (“whoever”); this may perhaps have been written by the first hand in Regius 2, and it is retained in most editions.

27. Vatican 1, wrongly, has *Haec* (“these things”) instead of *Nec* (“nor”). The Poelmann sheets have *Nec dubium* (“nor doubtful”); Ottobonian 2, *Nec dubio*; Regius 1, *Nec dubiae*, but the gloss *dubitanter* (“doubtfully”) calls for *dubie* (“doubtfully”).

31. Rome: “Concerning the two blind men healed by the Lord.” My manuscript: “He heals two blind men.” Wopkensius thinks *Interea* (“meanwhile”) more suitable; it does occur in the prose, but the manuscripts and editions give *Praeterea* (“moreover”). Almeloveen reverses the order to *Dominus geminos* (“the Lord [sees] the pair”). Arntzenius has *geminos cernens* (“seeing the pair”), but the prose opposes this. Parrhasius has *consistere* (“to stand”) instead of *considere* (“to sit”), which the prose confirms.

32. Arntzenius and Parrhasius have *Cum* (“when”); others, *Dum* (“while”). *Iter* means not only the act of going but also a road. *Comitante caterva* (“with a crowd accompanying”) is Virgilian.

33. Wopkensius suspects *exstinctae poscentes lumina frontis* (“asking for the extinguished lights of the face”). Compare book 3, verse 145: “Strike away the nocturnal shadows from extinguished faces.” The prose and the reading of my manuscript and the Leipzig edition, *lumina formae* (“the lights of their form”), favor this conjecture. But the received reading is more poetic: blind people are deformed, as Wopkensius himself notes, and the blind men were asking for this favor, to recover the form extinguished by the loss of their eyes.

34. Cantabrigian has *vacuas* (“empty”), an epithet poets appropriately apply to ears, but here metrical law requires *vagas* (“wandering”), unless, omitting the conjunction *que*, one reads *Flebilibus vacuas*, as indeed it is read in Ottobonian 1.

35. My manuscript corruptly has *Nec cuncta solens* (“not accustomed to all things”); Arntzenius’s manuscript has *Nec cunctis cessans* (“not ceasing for all”), which Arntzenius considers not inappropriate. The construction is harsher, namely, “nor was piety, accustomed to bring salvation to all, delayed.” The Leipzig edition has *conferre* (“to bring”) instead of *inferre*. Sedulius more than once uses *pietas* (“piety”) simply instead of *Deo pio* (“the pious God”) or *divina pietate* (“divine piety”).

36. Wopkensius conjectures *cum* or *Qua* instead of *Quae*. The Munich edition and the prose have *Qua*. Vatican 1 has *Que*, corrected to *Qua* or *Quae*; the others have *Quae*. Regius 1, Alb., Ottobonian 1 and 2, and Angers have *sensit* (“felt”); in Ottobonian 1 it may originally have been *sentit* (“feels”), which is the common reading. The Leipzig edition absurdly has *Quam sentit flagrare saltem* (“which he feels at least to burn”). The Poelmann sheets reject replacing *lumina tangens* (“touching the eyes”) with *munera tangens* (“touching gifts”); I do not know where Poelmann found the latter, nor did Arntzenius know.

“This is impossible for man,” he would have said, “but with God every power is possible”; and at last he would make troublesome wealth yield to many rich men.

For he manages his own riches well, and wishes his treasures

to be stored in heaven, where whatever is possessed

is not consumed by biting rust, nor furrowed by moth,

nor is gold badly buried made the servant of thieves;

whatever person gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty,

shelter to guests, clothing to the naked,

[25] consoles those bound in prison, warms the sick,

279. and, generous to others, remains needy only for himself.

[Col. 0674] That substance undoubtedly reaches heaven,

which, bestowed upon Christ, is given under the form of the poor,

which gains increase through losses, which is scattered in order to exist,

which perishes in order to remain, which, dying, grants life.

[30] Moreover, while the Lord was passing along a certain road,

with a crowd accompanying him, he sees two blind men sitting,

asking for the gifts of a form whose light was extinguished,

and filling the wandering air with mournful voices.

[35] Nor did the accustomed piety delay bringing salvation,

280. which perceived faith burning; soon, touching their eyes—

[Col. 0675A] **Note: [Col. 0675C]**

38. Ecclesiastical writers commonly call the eyes “windows,” as I noted in my commentary on Dracontius, book 3, verse 619.

40. Poelmann: “The blind and lame are healed.” Arntzenius has *limina templi* (“the thresholds of the temple”), a phrase sufficiently familiar to poets, but *moenia* (“walls”) is better for expressing the size of the building. Thus Juvencus, book 3, verse 674: “He enters within the walls of the temple.”

42. Most manuscripts write *daviticam*.

43. Arntzenius has *tandemque* (“and at last”); Parrhasius, *eodemque* (“and by the same [way]”); others, *eademque* (“and the same”). My manuscript has *revertens* (“returning”), not ineptly, instead of *reversus* (“having returned”).

45. Poelmann: “The fig tree withers.” Urbino has *constans* (“standing”) instead of *astans* (“standing nearby”). Rome, against the meter, has *stans* (“standing”).

46. This verse is found in Bede’s *On the Art of Meter* and in his commentary, but the author’s name is not given.

47. Aldus and Parrhasius incorrectly write *exuriens*. Ottobonian 1 has *lustrata stipite*; read *lustrato*, according to the rules of grammar.

48. Most punctuate *pomum—Arboreisque comis: Jam nunc* (“fruit—And with leafy branches: now”). Burmannus says the passage is weakly expressed, whereas it has its proper rhythm if the period ends after *pomum*: “fruit. And with leafy branches, now from your shoot…” Arntzenius follows Burmannus. Parrhasius has *gramine* (“grass”) instead of *germine* (“shoot”), less well. Fabricius and some other editions have *germine vasto* (“from the vast shoot”). *Vestro* (“your”) is better than *tuo* (“your”); in Urbino, *verso* appears to be an error for *vestro*.

50. *Arbor* (“tree”) may be understood with *ficulnea* (“fig-bearing”), for the latter is an adjective in Latin.

53. Vonckius, Wopkensius, and Burmannus conjecture *istis* (“these”) instead of *ustis* (“burned”). Parrhasius had already printed *istis*, and the Poelmann sheets also display it. The constant reading of the manuscripts is *ustis*, that is, “to be burned,” as the prose explains; or “burned,” as the Almeloveen gloss has it; or “dried,” according to the gloss in Regius 1; or “to be burned,” according to Nebrissensis. Bede also reads this verse in this way, and correctly, in his *Collectanea*.

54. Regius 1 has *amoenas—semper habens frondes* (“pleasant—always having leaves”), with the gloss *pulchras* (“beautiful”). Others have *amoenae* (“pleasant”), and some write *amaene*, which can be taken adverbially.

55. Ausonius shortened the first syllable of *Libanus*; Sedulius lengthens it. But what is more characteristic of Sedulius is that he uses *Libana* adjectivally from *Libanus*, the name of the mountain. Bede quoted this very verse of Sedulius in the *Collectanea*, but with the order reversed: “Always having leaves, and like the cedars of Lebanon,” etc. He speaks in the plural because he adapts Sedulius’s words to the righteous, using the plural number.

56. Some have *sidera vertice* (“the stars with its crown”); others, *tanget* (“will touch”) instead of *tangit* (“touches”).

57. My manuscript: “He drives out the mute demon.”

58. Almeloveen, by the first hand; Regius 1 in the text; Ottobonian 1; Vatican 1 by the first hand; and Vatican 2: *atris* (“dark”); Cellarius followed this reading from written manuscripts, as he says. But the reading common to nearly all our manuscripts, and found in Arntzenius and in Almeloveen, which Cellarius used, by correction, is *artis* or *arctis* (“narrow”), which has the same force. The prose and context demand this very reading. Parrhasius, Aldus, and the better editions agree with it. Thus in the following verse: *Angebat* (“was choking”); others have *Urgebat* (“was pressing”).

He commands them to awake, whom deep sleep had weighed down,

and, opening the windows long closed beneath their brows,

when day entered, he made the night depart.

[40] Hence, walking again through the walls of the holy temple,

he gave light to the blind and footsteps to the lame.

After such deeds he had left the city of David,

seeking the region near Bethany; and, returning by the same road,

as day was brightening, he hurried to visit its dwellings.

[45] But behold, standing amid the fields,

there was a leafy fig tree, in whose strong trunk,

after examining the tree, the hungry man found no fruit.

“And now, with your leafy branches, from your shoot

[Col. 0676A] 281. let no fruit be produced for any age to come,” he said.

At once the fig tree, deprived of its own sap,

dried up and remained dead upon its dry branches.

For everyone who nourishes nothing fertile for God

will be made equal to burned wood, like a barren trunk.

But the righteous man will bloom like a palm, pleasant,

[55] always having leaves, and like a cedar of Lebanon;

he comes to be multiplied and touches the stars with his crown.

282. After the speechless madman had been brought to him,

he felt the power of his Lord;

a confined force of evil choked him in his narrow throat,

and through silence had revealed the defect—

[Col. 0677A] **Note: [Col. 0677B]**

60. Some have *Sic* (“thus”), less well, instead of *Sed* (“but”).

61. Arntzenius has *repulit* (“drove out”); Regius 1 has *reppulit*, but according to metrical rules *repulit* should be written. This reading seems sufficiently probable, although the other is much more common. To lengthen the first syllable in *repulit*, it is customary to write *reppulit*; perhaps some copyists, thinking that the first syllable was always prolonged, changed *repulit* to *pepulit*. In place of *daemone* (“demon”), our poet uses *latronem* (“robber”), as Prudentius does in *Hamartigenia*, verse 946: “Lest he see some savage man from a race of robbers.”

62. Ottobonian 1, Almeloveen, Arntzenius, Angers have *vocis* (“of the voice”). *Vocis iter* (“a path for the voice”) occurs in Virgil, book 7, verse 534. Ovid, book 4 of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 69, supports *voci* (“for the voice”): “And you made a path for the voice”; although in some editions of Ovid I also find *Et vocis fecistis iter*. Most editions have *voci*; Fabricius and a few others have *vocis*. Parrhasius, incorrectly, has *patefeci* (“I opened”) instead of *patefecit* (“he opened”).

63. Arntzenius suspects *placidas* (“peaceful”), that is, “such as would enable him to praise God.” *Placida* is often changed into *tacita* (“silent”). I make no alteration.

64. Rome: “Where the woman who was a sinner in the city bathed Christ’s feet with tears.” My manuscript: “He frees Magdalene from sins.” Rome, incorrectly, has *Pharisee*.

65. Burmannus’s manuscript, together with Angers and Alb., writes *impartivit* (“bestowed”); most have *impertivit*, while some use an abbreviation of the letters.

66. Rome has *pluria*, corrected to *plurima*. *Pluria* and *compluria* are indeed found in place of *plura* and *complura*. Nevertheless, here the superlative *plurima* (“very many”) is better.

68. Wopkensius suspects *Irruit* (“he rushed upon”) or *Corripit* (“he seizes”); nevertheless, he acknowledges *Corruit* (“she fell”) to be sound, as in book 3, verse 107: “She fell before his feet.” The same Wopkensius says that the enclitic *-que* in *quaeque* seems to have been inserted solely for metrical reasons; otherwise one might suspect *quas et profusis*, namely, “the feet,” so that *et* (“also”) would be used in both *verbis* and *crine soluto*. Perhaps *sacras plantas* (“sacred feet”) is an accusative in apposition: “And those footprints—the sacred feet—that she waters, she does not cease either to wipe or to lick.” The truer interpretation, however, is derived from the less common meaning of the conjunction *-que* as “also” or “too,” as in *hodieque* (“today also”). For other examples from Pliny, Tacitus, Velleius, and Aurelius Victor, Forcellinus may be consulted. Sedulius uses it again in this book, verse 152: *Discipulosque alios* (“and other disciples”), as I restore it from the manuscripts, instead of *Discipulos quoque alios* (“also other disciples”).

70. My manuscript, Rome, Parrhasius, the Poelmann sheets, Almeloveen, Arntzenius, and Angers have *Tergere nec sacras, nec cessat* (“nor to wipe, nor does she cease [to…]”), which Burmannus preferred because *tergo* (“I wipe”) is more customary among poets than *tergeo*. Tornacensis 3: *Tergere nec cessat, nec sacras lambere plantas* (“nor does she cease to wipe or to lick the sacred feet”). Most manuscripts and editions have *Nec tergere sacras, nec cessat lambere plantas* (“nor does she cease to wipe and lick the sacred feet”), which better satisfies the ear. *Lambere* means “to kiss,” as in Paulinus, poem 35, verse 541: “Kissing the chaste footsteps of the Lord Christ.”

71. Manuscripts vary, as happens in other writers, in the spelling of this word: some have *fraglante*, others *flagrante*, others *fragrante*, which is more usual in this matter. A verse, I do not know by whom, says: “What *flagrat* burns; what *fragrât* gives off an odor,” establishing the different spelling.

72. The Poelmann sheets have *Lata* (“having been borne”), which the prose can support. Ottobonian 1 also has *Lata*, but the order of these verses is wrongly reversed: *Lata* comes first, then *Unguento*. The common reading is *Laeta* (“joyful”), and Nebrissensis explains it as “making the woman joyful.” Compare Juvenal, satire 2, verse 62: “A sad judgment is pronounced.” After this verse, Rome and Ottobonian 2 insert another verse that the others do not know: “Oh, how quickly the distinctions of death perish,” or, as I think it should be read, “of the grave.”

73. Vatican 1 incorrectly has *non* (“not”) instead of *nos* (“us”). Rome has *fecisse* (“to have done”) instead of *quaesisse* (“to have sought”), not without justification. Arntzenius reports *sensisse* (“to have felt”) from a certain manuscript, but this makes no sense.

74. Ottobonian 1 and Rome have *salvabit* (“will save”), an error arising because *b* and *v* were easily exchanged owing to their similar pronunciation.

75. Cantabrigian, Almeloveen, Arntzenius by the first hand, Regius 1 by correction, Regius 2, and Ottobonian 1 and 2 have *mali* (“of evil”). In Vatican 1, *mali* perhaps stood earlier, later changed to *malo* (“evil”), and then another corrector restored *mali*. In Regius 1, *male* (“badly”) stood before correction. Vatican 2, Regius 5, Urbino, Ottobonian 2, Rome, my manuscript, Aldus, and most editions have *malo*. The Poelmann sheets and Arntzenius, by a second correcting hand in a similar manner, display *malo*. Parrhasius, Fabricius, Tornacensis 3, and some other editions, together with Angers and Alb., have *malum* (“evil”). More recent editions prefer *mali*; Wopkensius, however, favors *malo*, since examples of similar transposition occur in Sedulius and others.

But the Creator, accustomed to raise all the weak,

drove the robber from the throat he had occupied,

opened a path for the voice, and, the knot being loosened,

the mute tongue, silent for so long, poured forth words.

Afterward the Lord, seeking the Pharisee’s banquet,

[65] bestowed himself upon the food of his praying friend.

Then the woman, whom an evil reputation and very many sins

283 of her life tormented, fell as a suppliant seeking mercy,

[Col. 0678A] embracing the feet; leaning over, she drenched them

with pouring tears and loosened hair,

[70] nor did she cease to wipe the sacred feet or to lick them,

cherishing them with fragrant ointment, until the joyful sentence

of God—who never regrets extending his hand—

“If we repent that we sought our former ruin,

Go, woman; your faith has saved you from everything,”

[75] he would have said, whatever evil you may seem to have done:

[Col. 0679A] **Note: [Col. 0679C]**

76. Consult the note on Dracontius 1.34: “Thus it was permitted to the guilty to sin with impunity by confessing.”

77. The Poelmann edition has *abscondit* (“he hides”), which the Poelmann sheets rightly condemn. The sense is: “It is a great remedy to confess what harms if it is hidden.” In Regius 1, *abscondit* perhaps stood earlier; now it is *abscondi*. Juvencus, Prudentius, Prosper, and Arator use *vulnera* (“wounds”) for vices and sins. Relevant to the present passage is Severus Sanctus, *On the Death of the Oxen*: “He opens the wound who publicizes evils; he closes it who suppresses it in silence.” In the prose the word *doloris* (“of grief”) had been inserted.

79. Almeloveen has *Impolluta* (“undefiled”); others, *En polluta* (“Behold, polluted”).

80. Rome has *propriosque* (“and her own”); read *propriique* (“and of her own”). Vatican 2, Regius 5, Parrhasius, and Aldus have *lavans se gurgite* (“washing herself in the stream”); it is better to omit *se*, as most have it: *lavans in gurgite* (“washing in the stream”).

81. Edinburgh has *rediit detersa* (“she returned wiped clean”). Parrhasius has *redit, et deterta* (“she returns, and dried”), saying that Sedulius wrote it this way because he had read in Ennius, “The helmet shines, dried.” But this passage belongs to Varro, preserved by Nonius, chapter 2, no. 847. In our manuscripts and nearly all editions this word is written *detersa*, not *deterta*. Alb. corruptly has *redit et detensa* (“she returns and stretched out”).

82. Rome: “Where the Lord entered Capernaum.” My manuscript: “He drives away the demon.” The Poelmann sheets write *Capernaeae*; others have *Capherneae*, *Caphernae*, or *Caphernaeae*.

86. Arntzenius has *nos jam* (“us now”); others, *nos heu* (“alas for us”). Vatican 1 and 2, Ottobonian 2, my manuscript, Parrhasius have *quis sis* (“who you are”); others, *qui sis*. A similar variation occurs on the same matter in Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 419: “Who you are, why you come, by what power you drive us away—we know.”

[Col. 0680C] 87. Parrhasius has *Te sanctum* (“you, the holy one”); the rest, *Et sanctum* (“and the Holy One”). I have already observed in notes on other Christian poets that Christ is, by excellence, simply called “the Holy One.” Huetius provides many testimonies from sacred Scripture in his *Demonstratio Evangelica*, proposition 9, chapter 81, in which Christ is called “holy” and “the Holy One of God.”

88. Arntzenius and the Leipzig edition have *jacet* (“lies”); the others more suitably have *tacet* (“is silent”). The Cambridge edition, Regius 1, and some printed editions have *relinquit* (“he leaves”), which may also have been in Regius 2; it now appears as *reliquit* (“he left”), as in most editions and the prose.

90. My manuscript: “And he heals many sicknesses.” Poelmann: “Christ cures various diseases and commands the demons to be silent.” Most manuscripts, including the very ancient Turin manuscript, and the best editions have *Sic etiam* (“thus also”). Vatican 2, Fabricius, and some other editions have *Hic etiam* (“here also”).

91. Ottobonian 2 has *Fecerat, et clausos* (“he had made, and the closed…”); retain the common reading. The phrase *fecit esse finem* (“he made there to be an end”) instead of simple *fecit* (“he made”) was not unknown among Sedulius’s contemporaries.

92. Regius 1, Ottobonian 1, *pro d. s.*, and Vatican 1 have *supra Daemonas* (“above demons”); most manuscripts have *Daemones* (“demons”). The editions prefer *Daemonas*, in the Greek manner, so that the final syllable may be shortened. Aldus printed *ac tali prohibet se pandere testi* (“and by such a witness he forbids himself to be revealed”). Regius 5 has the same. In Ottobonian 1 and, apparently, Regius 1, *tali* may originally have stood, but in both the clear reading is *testem* (“witness”). Angers has *et* instead of *ac*. In Poelmann there is the error *panderet testem* (“he would reveal a witness”); otherwise someone might suppose the reading to be *ac talem prohibet se panderet*.

96. Rome reverses the order: *quem Christum noverat* (“whom he knew as Christ”).

99. Rome: “Concerning the two blind men.” My manuscript, more truly: “He heals the mute and deaf.” Arntzenius, the Poelmann sheets, Vatican 2, Regius 5, my manuscript, Rome, Urbino, and Aldus have *Cumque* (“and when”); the better manuscripts and editions have *Dumque* (“while”), as does Parrhasius, to whom Arntzenius incorrectly attributes *Sumque*. In Regius 1 it is unclear whether the reading is *iter* (“road”) or *item* (“likewise”); *iter* should be retained. In the prose there was an error, *Dumque tria dehinc* (“and while three thereafter…”).

“Use my peace. It is a great remedy to confess

what harms when hidden; for he nourishes his wounds

who conceals them and fears to expose the sore to the healer.

Behold, she, long polluted, withdrew slightly cleansed

[80] through groaning, washing in the stream of her own tears;

she returns cleansed by her tears and dried by her hair.

Now he had entered the synagogue of the city of Capernaum,

teaching the peoples in due order. When the wicked spirit,

lying hidden beneath a human heart, had seen him,

with insolent outcry the spirit roared, saying:

[85] 285. ‘What have we to do with you, Christ?

Have you come, alas, to destroy us? I know at last who you are,

[Col. 0680A] and I recognize the Holy One of God.’ Saying no more,

silenced by the terrifying command, it left the man,

driven out, and fled away, vanishing into the empty air.

[90] Thus also he brought an end to various diseases

and always forced the expelled demons to remain silent,

and forbade such a witness to reveal itself.

For once that guilty serpent, fierce and a lover of black death,

cast down from the summit of heaven,

[95] 286. with its pomp, its companions, and the whole

host of its wicked army, sees on earth Christ,

whom it had known there, covered by a veil of flesh,

and groans that the Lord of power has become a friend to man.

And while, having crossed the road through Tyre, he again approached Sidon—

[Col. 0681A] **Note: [Col. 0681B]**

100. In Ottobonian 1, *calcarat* perhaps stood earlier; it now has *calcaret*, as do the others.

102. My manuscript, Parrhasius, and the Leipzig edition have *nec* (“and not”) instead of *non* (“not”). *Non* is more elegant and better fits the meter, although these monosyllables, which are considered short, are either actually common in quantity or easily lengthened.

[Col. 0681C] 104. Although Arntzenius agrees that nearly all copies have *Attactu*, he prefers *A tactu*. The old reading *Attactu* should be retained; some write *Atactu* instead, and from this, apparently, Vatican 2 and Alb. have *A tactu*. It should nevertheless be observed that capital letters at the beginnings of verses are sometimes somewhat separated from the initial letter of the following word. My manuscript has *Attactu*, with *Ad tactum* (“at the touch”) in the prose. In the prose the form is *tactu*, because *attactu* is more characteristic of poets. Compare the textual notes on book 2, verse 156.

105. Parrhasius and the Poelmann sheets have *loquentem* (“speaking”).

106. My manuscript: “He heals the blind man.” Parrhasius reverses the order to *sensisti virtutis* (“you felt the power”); the Poelmann sheets, very badly, have *sensisti virentis* (“you felt the green one”).

107. The Arntzenius manuscript, Fabricius, and some other editions have *in cujus* (“in whose”); others, *cujus in*, lengthening the final syllable of *cujus* for the sake of the caesura. Cantabrigian, Arntzenius, most of our manuscripts, Parrhasius, and Aldus have *lumine* (“by the light”), with the gloss *aspectu* (“by sight”) in Regius 2. The prose supports this. Regius 1 and several editions have *lumina* (“the eyes”), which accords better with grammatical rules. Cannegetierus nevertheless holds that the more elegant and ancient a writer is, the more frequently he uses *ab* indiscriminately with either the accusative or ablative case. The Edinburgh editor had thought Sedulius wrote *Procumbens* (“falling down”), etc., in imitation of Lucan 3.713. But Burmannus rightly observed that Lucan is speaking of something else. Perhaps the Edinburgh editor meant to indicate another passage.

108. Most manuscripts agree on *simulatae* (“feigned”); elsewhere this word is written *similo* and *simulatus*, unless one prefers to regard these as two distinct words. Vatican 1 also has *simulatae* here. Weitzius, in his note on Prudentius, p. 567, cites *noctis* (“of night”) instead of *mortis* (“of death”), perhaps by accident. Poets do sometimes use *nox* (“night”) for death.

109. Rome: “Where the Lord, sitting in the stern, taught the crowds.” My manuscript: “He commands Peter to fish.” Arntzenius has *homines* (“men”) instead of *populos* (“peoples”), perhaps from the gloss.

110. Urbino and Rome have *sequentes* (“following”); the others more suitably have *frequentes* (“numerous”).

[Col. 0682B] 112. The better of our manuscripts, together with many editions, have *parvaque sedens Simonis in alno* (“and sitting small in Simon’s alder”), since poets sometimes use *alnus* (“alder”) by synecdoche for a boat. Rome, against the meter and without sense, has *parvo sedens in Simonis alvo* (“sitting small in Simon’s belly”). The Leipzig manuscript, Almeloveen, Vatican 1, Ottobonian 2, Urbino, my manuscript, and Angers have *parvaque sedens in Simonis alno*. Vatican 2, Alb., and Parrhasius have the same, but *alvo* instead of *alno*. Regius 5 has *parva residensque Simonis in alno* (“and sitting in Simon’s small alder”); Aldus gives the same in his *Errata*, with the punctuation: *Stagna petit parva, residensque Simonis in alno* (“he seeks the small waters, sitting in Simon’s alder”). Earlier he had printed *parvaque sedens in Simonis alno*, which Fabricius, Cellarius, and Arntzenius follow. Nebrissensis had read *in Simonis alno*, but corrected it to *residens Simonis in alno* so that the verse would scan. For the varying quantity of *Simonis*, see the note on Dracontius, book 3, verse 230, and on Juvencus, book 1, verse 458, textual variants.

113. Cellarius retained *firmabat* with the manuscripts, as did Fabricius, and praised Poelmann for *formabat*. Wopkens accepted this from Poelmann’s manuscript; Arntzenius did likewise, adding that all the printed editions he had examined preferred *firmabat*. In fact, however, Cellarius, as I think, means Poelmann’s edition, in which *formabat* certainly appears. All our manuscripts, together with Ang., have *firmabat*, and the gloss in Reg. has *docebat* (“he was teaching”): the error *firmabit* in my manuscript belongs to the same category. Parrhasius, Aldus, and the finest printed editions agree. Wopkens, Burmann, and Barthius, however, retain *formabat*, which Arntzenius extensively defends in *Observationes*, chapter 9. The change between *firmabat* and *formabat* is easy and frequent; and Luke’s *docebat* (“he was teaching”) is more aptly expressed by *formabat*. Nevertheless, the manuscript reading *firmabat* should not be abandoned. In prose it is *imbuebat* (“he was instilling”).

115. Rom. has *In pelago*; retain *In pelagus*. Most codices write *ratem*; some *ratim*.

116. Ott. 1, in the first hand, Meus, Rom., Ang., Alb., Ott. 2, Vatt. 1 and 2, and Reg. 2 have *dimitti*; others have *demitti*. This variation occurs very frequently in this verb.

117. Someone conjectured *vano*; but Wopkens rightly proves that *vacuo* may be used for *vano*, and Arntzenius follows him, although this interchange frequently occurs in manuscript codices.]

Traversing the fields, the Lord trod the tranquil sands,

He healed the wretched man shut in by a twofold impediment,

Who gave no voice through his mouth and drew none in through his ear,

And, when the inner chambers had been broken open, by the touch of the starry hand

All the doors lay open; and suddenly, rejoicing,

[105] Speaking, he gained the power both to be heard and to hear those who spoke.

You too experienced the gift of your lordly power,

287 Prostrate, with the eyes into which Christ

Spat, and from which he removed the appearance of feigned death.

Then, teaching the peoples greater heavenly things, he reveals

[110] [Col. 0682A] Himself as God through speech, and, wishing for a little while

To avoid the dense crowds that had rushed together too violently,

Seeks the waters and, sitting in Simon’s little alder-boat,

Instructed from the water the people standing on the shore.

288 And when the speech had already come to an end, he then commands

[115] The boat, driven farther out, to go into the open sea,

And the fishing nets to be lowered into the vast deep—

Nets which, after a whole night of empty labor,

Had been able to enclose nothing.

[Col. 0683A] [Note: [Col. 0683C]

118. Aldus has *Simo paret*; the others, *Simon*. The gloss of the Alm. codex, or of Burmann, is: “He speaks of the *GENTES* among the fish, just as Virgil speaks of the bees.” Virgil also spoke of a “people” of fish, *Georgics* IV, 430: “the watery people of the sea” (*Gens humida ponti*).

119. It is surprising that, among so many conjectures, no one conjectured *Linea clathra jacit* (“the line casts its lattice”); for although Caper denies that *clathra* can correctly be used in Latin in the neuter gender, Nic. Heinsius nevertheless found it in the better books of Propertius, IV, elegy 5, verse 72: “When the deceiving lattice was to be [worked] by my thumb.” Others have *claustra forent*.

122. Vet. 1 has incorrectly: *Nam socio istic quis erat* (“For who was there as a companion?”), and Mon. no better: *Nam socio istic pius erat* (“For he was pious there as a companion”).

123. Ott. 1 has *perpensaque*; others have either clearly *propensa* or *perpensa*, or *propensa* where the connection of the letters is uncertain. In Poelmann’s manuscript notes, *magna* was written beside *propensa*; this is a gloss in Rom. and Reg. 2, while Reg. 1 has *copiosa*. Arntzenius rejects this explanation unless *impensa* is written. With Wopkens, he explains *propensa* as “prosperous,” as in Velleius, II, chapter 69, *prona fortuna* (“favorable fortune”). Thus one says *propensus favor* (“favorable approval”), *propensa munera* (“generous gifts”), and *propensus animus* (“a favorable disposition”), the figurative meaning being derived from scales, the heavier side of which hangs down or sinks. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *timemus* (“we fear”), which prose and sense require; some, following Poelmann and Fabricius, have *tenemus* (“we hold”).

125. Reg. 1: “Of the son of the widow raised from the dead.” Meus: “The boy rises.”

126. Parrh. and Ang. have *Quae fit*; others have *Quae sit* for *quae est*, or *erat dicta* (“which is,” or “was, called”). Some have *Quae sit dicta* (“which is called”). Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes have *Naum*; others *Naym*; most *Naim* or *Nain*. Our Vulgate has *Naim*. Ott. 1 has *velatus* (“veiled”), but perhaps it originally read *vallatus* (“surrounded”), which should be retained with all the others.

127. Reg. 1 has *discipulo* (“to the disciple”); the same hand wrote *discipulum* (“the disciple”), with the gloss *discipulorum* (“of the disciples”). But *discipulo* was not wrong as an adjective, and it also seems to have stood in the first hand of Ott. 1. Dracontius, *Satisfactio*, verse 154: *Cinctus apostolica discipulante manu* (“girt by an apostolic, discipling hand”), as the manuscript codices have it. Sirmondus printed *Cinctus apostolica, discipulaque manu* (“girt by an apostolic and instructing hand”). All our manuscripts, Arntz., Parrh., Aldus, and the prose version have *cum*. Poelmann and other printed editions have *tunc*; Arntzenius cites *dum* from some manuscript.

128. Most of our manuscripts and all the best editions have *efferri* (“to be carried out”), which Meus and Ferri support. Ottob. 1 has *offerri* in the first hand and *efferri* in the later hand. Poelmann and other printed editions have *afferri* (“to be brought”). But *efferri* is the proper funeral term.

129. In Reg. 1, *passum* was changed into *passim*, with the gloss *late* or *ubique* (“widely” or “everywhere”); again, in the margin, *passum* is given in place of *passim*, in agreement with the others.

130. “A sad service” (*Triste ministerium*) is taken from Virgil, VI, 223.

131. Reg. 5 has *una*; correct to *urna*.

132. Urb., Rom., Parrh., Arntzen., and Cant. have *dolori*, which Cellarius preferred. Most manuscript codices and printed editions have *doloris*, which is equally good, or better. Shortly afterward Rom. has *dedit* (“gave”); the others *tulit* (“brought”). The Lyon Bible has *tectoque*; emend to *tactoque*. There is also an error in Reg. 1, *tactuque*.

135. Meus has *residens, loquensque* (“sitting and speaking”); the conjunction *-que* is required for the meter.

136. Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes have *abit, non funere torpens* (“he departs, not numb with death”). Nevertheless, the received reading is more convenient.

137. Most manuscripts and printed editions have *Et licet*; some printed editions have *En licet*, others, with Fabricius, *Ilicet*, as Poelmann’s notes also indicate. Juvencus likewise says *amissae vitae* (“of lost life”), II, 523. Wopkens observes that *discrimina vitae amissae* (“the dangers of lost life”) is used for *vita amissa* (“lost life”), just as other writers use *discrimen* (“danger”) or *periculum* (“risk”) with *mortis*, *sanguinis*, and so forth. He also notes that Avitus and Arator use *discrimen* for loss, distress, or misfortune.]

Simon obeys joyfully and casts the line among the watery peoples;

He throws the net, and so filled its vast open folds

[120] That the overflowing catch disturbed the twin boats,

Their holds piled high with fish.

For a companion boat was there. Often we cannot bear

The greatest joys, and we fear our prayers when they prosper;

289 And what is easy for God, human beings do not even dare to hope for.

[125] Distinguished by such virtues, he went into the city

Called Naim, surrounded by a populous crowd
