And a company of disciples. There, behold, he sees nearby

[Col. 0684A] A young man being carried out, a cold corpse,

Having undergone many funeral rites and an empty burial—

[130] A sad service whose hostile lot had long before

Had twice bereaved the mother through the urn.

Pity, hostile to grief, did not delay,

But brought life-giving aid; and, touching the bier,

290 He said, “Rise, young man”; and the dead man rose at the appointed word,

[135] And, sitting and speaking, came back to life,

Then departed as his mother’s companion. For the servant,

Numb with death, and though he had suffered the dangers

Of lost life, could not remain silent when the Lord called,

Nor die while life was present. Soon, the procession having turned,

140. Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ott. 2, Urb., Rom., Ang., Alb., and Meus, together with Parrh., Aldus, Poelmann’s notes, and the Leipzig manuscript, have *recidivo*. Ott. 1 has *redivivo* in the later hand and *recidivo* in the first. The manuscripts of Arntz. and Burmann, together with most printed editions, have *redivivo*. Nebrissensis seems to adopt *recidivo* (his notes read *reidvo*), with the explanation *remenso* (“having turned back”). Nic. Heinsius found *recidivus* for *redivivus* in several parchments; Burmann noted that Heinsius took particular pleasure in substituting *recidivus* for *redivivus* in Samonicus, *De Medicina*, chapter 50. Cellarius wrongly attributes to Johann Friedrich Gronovius what was reported about Nic. Heinsius. For the distinction between these words, see the note on Dracontius I, verse 558, and II, verse 633. In Sedulius’s prose, *recidivo* is defended. *Redivivus* is indeed the more Latin form, but writers of the later age often followed the usage of their own time rather than what was more strictly Latin. Consult Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII, chapter 6, section 10.

141. Rom. has *renovavit* (“renewed”), correctly emended to *revocavit*, that is, “called back again and again,” as Arntzenius explains; or rather, as I think, “brought back into the house.” In place of *pompa* (“procession”), Cellarius, following Gronovius—or rather Heinsius—printed *turba* (“crowd”), quite inappropriately, as Wopkens and Arntzenius demonstrate; for a procession accompanying a funeral is customarily called a *pompa*. Barthius interprets *pompam candidam* (“white procession”) in Book II, *Adversaria*, chapter 2, because the ancients customarily covered the biers of the dead with linen cloths. I think, however, that the procession is called “white” because it was joyful, whereas a funeral procession is mournful. Thus Ovidius also uses the same word of a festive procession, *Fasti* IV, verse 906: “A white procession blocked the road in the middle.”

142. Rom.: “Of Mary the sinner.” Meus: “Mary is freed from seven spirits.” Reg. 1: “Of Mary Magdalene.” In fact, Mary Magdalene is meant. See the note on Juvencus IV, 310.

143. Poelmann printed incorrectly *Jesum curavit* (“he healed Jesus”) instead of *laesum* (“the injured man”).

144. Poelmann’s notes direct us to read *Quem* instead of *Quam*, against Arntzenius. The common reading is *Quam*, but in Ottob. 1 it may originally have been *Quem*.

145. Urb., Rom., and Meus have *Daemoniaco*; read *Daemonico*, so that the meter may stand. Reg. 1 has *conjuncta* (“joined”), in place of *cuneata* (“formed into a wedge”), with most others. In Ott. 1, the first hand had another reading in place of *cuneata*, which was added by a recent hand. Cellarius cites *connexa* (“connected”) from Lips., whether a codex or an edition; and in Vat. 2 there seems to be *cunctata* (“hesitating”) instead of *cuneata*, which must certainly be retained, from the military *cuneus*, that is, a multitude of infantry drawn up in wedge formation.

146. Ott. 1, Vat. 1, and Burmann’s codex have *Imperio sacri* (“by the command of the holy one”), which may also have stood in Reg. 2. The gloss in Vat. 1 is *secundum imperium* (“according to the command”). Most have *Imperiosa sacri* (“the commanding [words] of the holy one”). In place of *Christi*, Parrh. appears to have *verbi* (“of the word”), apparently from a gloss.

149. This is a verse of Virgil, V, 85.

150. Reg. 1: “Where he sent the seventy-two disciples to preach.” Meus: “He sends the disciples with power.” Rom.: “Where the Lord sends his disciples into the world.” Parrhas., Poelmann’s notes: *gramine* (“grass”); others, better, *germine* (“shoot” or “offspring”).

152. Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Ang., Alb., Vat. 1, Ott. 2, Urb., Meus, Rom., Burmann’s codices, and Arntzenius, together with Aldus, Vet. 1 and 2, and Mon., have *Discipulosque* (“and the disciples”); Ott. 1 seems to have had this reading, but the *-que* has been erased. It is surprising that so many manuscript codices agree in inserting the conjunction *-que*, which certainly does not seem necessary and is therefore omitted in most editions. I think, however, that Sedulius wrote in such a way as to reproduce Luke’s words, X, 1: “After these things the Lord appointed also seventy-two others.” Sedulius used *-que* for *et*, or even added it, as I have already noted at verse 68 of this book, *Mens conscia recti* (“a mind conscious of right”), from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 608.

154. Cellarius thinks that *libra* (“pound” or “balance”) should be understood not as a *stater* or *examen*, but as a weight, so that the passage may refer to the parable of the talent. I would rather believe that the metaphor is taken from a *libra*, or *libella*, a surveying instrument by which the height of seas, springs, rivers, and so forth is tested. Or there may be an allusion to the twelve ounces of a pound, since six times twelve makes seventy-two.

156. Reg. 2 has *Jure* (“by right”), but this has been corrected to *Jura* (“commands”). The edition and Poelmann’s notes, together with some other printed editions, have *timeatis* (“may you fear”). Most of our manuscripts and others have *metuatis* (“may you fear”). The half-line *Jura potestatis* (“the commands of power”) occurs twice in Dracontius, II, 237 and 730.

157. Reg. 1 and 2, Vat. 2, Alb., Rom., Meus have *et scorpionum, atque inimica* (“and of scorpions, and hostile”); Ott. 1 likewise, but apparently originally had *scorpion* and *inimice*. Vat. 1 has *et scorpionum, atque inimice*. Urb. has *et scorpio atque inimica*, perhaps erroneously for *scorpion*. Ott. 2, Ang., Parrhasius, and most printed editions have *et scorpion atque inimica*. Reg. 5 has *et scorpi inimica venena* (“and the hostile poisons of the scorpion”); Aldus corrected this in his *Errata*, while in the text he had printed *et scorpionum inimica venena*. Nebrissensis followed Aldus’s correction, which is also found in Poelmann’s notes, though Arntzenius does not approve it. The Alm. codex has *et scorpion, atque inimicae*. In such disagreement among the ancient copies, I think Sedulius wrote: *Vipereasque minas, et scorpionum, atque inimicae / Omnia virtutis*. The third syllable of *scorpionum* is normally long, but the vowels *i* and *o* can contract into one syllable through synaeresis. *Omnia virtutis inimicae* is used for *omnem virtutem inimicam* (“every hostile power”); I have observed such expressions more than once in Juvencus, as may be gathered from the word *omnia* in the verbal index. Luke’s words are X, 19: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall harm you.” From these words Arntzenius’s punctuation should be corrected. He has:

“Assume, he says, the commands of power; fear no one as an enemy;  
the viper’s threats and the scorpion—tread upon every hostile  
power with faithful understanding.”

But *calcate* (“tread upon”) must be joined with *minas*, and so forth.]

Setting aside fearful grief by a returning path,

The bright procession recalled the happy parent.

291 Nor was your salvation small, Mary, when the Lord was your physician:

He healed your sense, wounded by many blows,

Which savage madness had assailed with seven weapons,

[145] Driven together into a demonic host. But the scaly serpent,

Fleeing the commanding miracles of the holy word,

Departed, driven from your heart, and, flying through the air,

Slipped into the inner recess of hell’s abyss,

Dragging seven enormous coils, seven winding circuits.

[150] [Col. 0686A] And lest the Lord allow the overflowing harvest

To languish under the care of too few cultivators,

292 He numbered other disciples, whose mind was conscious of right,

[155] Bloodstained wolves. “Take up,” he says,

“The commands of power; fear no one as an enemy;

The viper’s threats, and scorpions, and every hostile

[Col. 0687A] [Note: [Col. 0687D]

158. Cant. and Meus have *virtuti*; Rom. *virtute*; read *virtutis*, as I recently said. Rom. has *fidei* (“of faith”) instead of *fideli* (“faithful”); the second syllable in *fidei* would then have to be lengthened, as in Paulinus. It is nevertheless preferable to retain *fideli*.

159. Some printed editions have *feritas famulis* (“savagery toward the servants”).

160. Some printed editions have *quid* (“what”); retain *quod* (“that which”). Compare the note on Juvencus II, 45, *Spiritus ater* (“the dark spirit”), that is, the demon.

161. Torn. 2 has *Subjiciat vobis* (“may he subject to you”); correct to *Subjaceat* (“may it lie beneath you”).

162. Burmann’s manuscript and Reg. 1 in the first hand have *Scribat* (“may he write”). Urb. and Rom. have *Scribit* (“he writes”). Reg. 1, in place of the first reading, has *Scripsit* (“he wrote”), added by a later but ancient hand; most prefer this.

163. *Facta* means deeds worthy of being remembered or miraculous, just as *vita* is sometimes used simply for a good life. Wopkens cites a passage from Severus Sulpicius, chapter 26 of the *Life of Saint Martin*: “For although his deeds could in some fashion be explained in words, no speech will ever explain his inner life.”

165. Meus and several others have *plerique* (“most”); the remaining witnesses, more appropriately, have *plerumque* (“for the most part”).

166. Vet. 1 has *docturus* (“about to teach”); read *dicturus* (“about to say”).

168. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *simulatis* (“you have pretended”); the others more correctly have *simulastis* (“you have pretended”). Vat. 1 has *similastis* in the first hand, corrected to *simulastis* by a second, later hand. Most manuscripts have *Moysi*; Poelmann’s edition *Mosi*, his notes *Mosis*; Aldus *Mosae*, which Nebrissensis retained, namely *Moses, Mosae*, like *Anchises, Anchisae*. Arntzenius rejects *Moysi*, as though it conflicted with the meter. But it can be disyllabic through synaeresis.

169. *Memphitis* is usually joined with a substantive, as in *Memphitis ora*, *aula*, or *terra* (“Memphite shore,” “hall,” or “land”); among earlier Latins the genitive form is *Memphitidis*. Sedulius uses *Memphitis* by itself, in a new fashion, for the Egyptian region: *Memphitis, Memphitis*. Memphis was a city of Egypt.

170. Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes have *falsi* (“of falsehood”); others, in agreement with the prose, *falsa* (“false”).

172. Rom.: “Where the Lord healed a dropsical man.” Meus: “He heals the dropsical man.”

174. Reg. 1 and Rom. have *facilis*, which is not wrong, in place of *facili*.

176. Almost all our manuscripts, together with Arntz., Parrh., Aldus, Fabricius, and others, have *aquae* (“of water”). Ott. 1 has *a que*, but perhaps it originally read *aquis* (“with water”). Meus, Alm., Poelmann’s edition and notes, and many printed editions, especially the more recent ones, have *aquis*. Cant., Ang., the Leipzig manuscript and edition, Vet. 1 and 2, and Mon. have *aqua*. The singular is supported by the prose. Wopkens conjectures *gravidaque* (“and pregnant”), so that the *a* before *-que* would be lengthened, which is not unprecedented. Arntzenius rightly objects, however, that in prose *praegnans* (“pregnant”) refers to *cutis* (“skin”), not to *alvus* (“belly”).

177. Vat. 2 and Vet. 1 have *Inclusa*; retain *Inclusam*. Some manuscript codices write *Inclausam*.

178. Urb. and Rom. have *Arescente sinu* (“as the bosom dried up”), which yields no suitable sense. *Infusa per artus* (“poured through the limbs”) is Virgilian, VI, 726.

179. Most have *perflatum* (“blown through”), and in Reg. 2 and Ott. 1 there is the gloss *valde flatum* (“strongly blown”). In Reg. 1, although it appears to be a single word, the gloss is *fetidum anhelitum* (“foul breath”), which indicates *per flatum* (“through the breath”). My codex has *per flatum*, and in the margin, in place of the first reading, *per flatu*. Urb., Angl., and the Edinburgh edition have *per flatum*.

180. *Spatium uteri* means the size, breadth, or mass of the womb, as elsewhere one finds *spatium corporis*, *lateris*, *plantae*, *rhombi*, and similar expressions.]

205. Vet. 1 and 2 have *vera*; emend to *vero*: Christ is the true priest, as is clear from what follows.

207. *Gemini libaminis* (“of the double offering”), because just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine, so Jesus Christ offered his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine, a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

209. Reg. 1 and 2, Ott. 1, Vat. 2, Ang., Alb., Poelmann’s notes, and Parrh. have *fructus, segetis, et*; others, with most printed editions, *segetis fructus, et*. This was perhaps done by inexperienced scribes so that the final syllable of *segetis* might be lengthened in its position. It is pointless, however, since in *fructus segetis, et* the final syllable of *segetis* can be lengthened by the caesura, and in the other reading *fructus et* the same difficulty remains, since Sedulius also customarily shortens the final syllable of *fructus* when it is plural. The better codices have *fructus segetis, et gaudia vitis* (“the fruits of the harvest and the joys of the vine”), which is also clearer. For why wine is called *gaudia vitis* (“the joys of the vine”), see the note on Dracontius I, 172, *Munera laetitiae* (“gifts of joy”), and so forth.

210. Rom.: “Of the blind son of Timaeus.” Arntz. has *Dum* (“while”); others *Cum* (“when”).

211. The Leipzig edition incorrectly has *praeter iter* (“past the road”); *praeter* indicates motion, whereas *propter* indicates position in a place. Aldus’s *prope iter* (“near the road”) is no better, for it conflicts with the meter.

212. Vat. 1 has *petivit* (“he sought”); the others *petisset* (“he had sought”).

214. *Palpante manu* (“with a groping hand”), that is, he approached with a groping hand; the Spaniards say *a tientas*.

215. Torn. 1 and 2 have *docente* (“teaching”), which Arntzenius says conflicts with the prose; he should also have added that it conflicts with the meter. This error passed from Aldus into other editions, but Aldus substituted *ducente* (“leading”) in his *Errata*. Arntz. has *o quam*; the metrical rule does not permit it. Fabricius and some other editions have *quum* instead of *quam*, incorrectly.

216. Urb., Rom., Meus have *negaret* (“would deny”); this was also in Reg. 1, but was corrected to *negarit* (“has denied”), with the gloss *vetaverit* (“has forbidden”). In Ott. 1 it is uncertain whether *negavit* or *negarit* was written. The common and sound reading is *negarit*. The words *res dura* (“hard circumstance”) recall Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 267: “Hard necessity, and the novelty of kingship, compel me to such things.”

218. Rom.: “Of the man who asked his friend for bread.” Our older codices Reg. 1 and 2, Ott. 1, and Vat. 2 have *Unanimum*; others *Unanimem*. The printed editions vary in the same way.

219. Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes have *inverso ordine clausis foribus* (“with the doors closed in the reverse order”). Poets call night *opaca*, that is, “dark”; hence *opaca silentia noctis* (“the dark silences of night”).

220. Reg. 1 has *Obnexoque*, from which *Obnixoque* was produced, with the gloss *resistente amico* (“while the friend resisted”); it was later corrected to *Obnixeque* (“persistently”). In Ott. 1 something else seems to have stood originally, but the same first hand added *Obnixeque*. Reg. 5 has *confidensque* (“and trusting”), perhaps taken from Aldus; but in Aldus the connection of the letters indicates *confidenterque* (“and confidently”), which sense and meter require. Parrh. incorrectly has *negavit* (“he denied”) instead of *neganti* (“to the one refusing”). Rom. also originally had *negavit*, but a correction was added to *neganti*.

222. Reg. 1: “Of the Samaritan woman.” Rom.: “Where the Lord came to the well.” Meus: “He asks for water, in order to give it.”]

He falls to the ground, worshiping the Lord of power,

[205] And presented his face to the true priest.

After all, who is present as chief of priests and supreme high priest

Except Christ, author of the double offering

According to the order of Melchizedek, to whom gifts are always given—

Gifts that are his own: the fruits of the harvest and the joys of the vine.

[210] When the blind man, the son of Timaeus, sitting beside the road

Along which he had learned that the Lord was passing,

298 Repeatedly cried out, asking for light,

[Col. 0692A] And, though the crowd tried to silence him, did not keep quiet,

He was ordered to approach the Lord with a groping hand,

And received his sight;

[215] And, with no one leading him, he returned. How forcefully

Persistent faith presses on! Whatever hard circumstance denies,

Frequent prayer alone grants to honorable petitions.

Thus that man sought bread from a friendly neighbor,

And, while the doors were closed amid the dark silences of night,

[220] By persistent and confident insistence extracted it from the refusing man

299 With repeated cries and breathless prayers.

As the Lord passed through the Samaritan region,

[Col. 0693A] [Note: [Col. 0693C]

223. Vat. 2 has *Humana*; correct to *Humanam*. Arntzenius has *conceperat*, which is a gloss in Alm. for *collegerat*. Heinsius, in his note on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, verse 446, cites *Immensa* for *Humana*, and in *Aristarchus Sacr.* chapter 20, *contraxerat* for *collegerat*. But such substitutions often escape writers who attend more to the subject itself than to the wording.

224. Vat. 2 has *Fons perennis*; correct, in accordance with the *Lex Pediana*, to *Fonsque perennis*.

225. Almost all our manuscripts, together with Lips. and Aldus’s edition, have *qua corpus erat* (“where the body was”), which the prose confirms. Alm., Vet. 1 and 2, and Mon. have *quia corpus erat* (“because the body was there”). This stood in Reg. 1, but *quia* was changed into *qua*. Parrh. has *qui corpus erat*. The following variants occur in Poelmann’s notes: *Al. quia*, *al. qui*, *al. qua corpus alat*; Arntzenius considers the last not inept. It appears in my codex, whose margin indicates the variant *qua corpus erat*. Its gloss in Reg. 1 is *qua de qua parte* (“where, from which part”). Regarding the word *accola* (“inhabitant”), Nebrissensis notes: “What if you read *incola*?” In fact, *accola* and *incola* differ in that an *accola* is someone who lives beside or around a place, whereas an *incola* lives in a place. But since Sedulius says *accola* not of a city but of a people, *accola* may perhaps be more suitable here than *incola*.

226. Reg. 1 has *haustus* (“a draught”), which appears to have arisen from *haustum*. The sense would then be “a small draught,” as though *parum haustus* (“scarcely drunk”). The common reading *haustum* is not unsuccessful.

228. Wopkens would prefer *parvam* (perhaps *pravam*) instead of *propriam*, or even *culpam* or *noxam* (“fault” or “guilt”) instead of *vitam*, while retaining *propriam* with *tunc*. *Vita* may sometimes be understood absolutely as a way of life, good or bad, determined by the surrounding words.

232. Ott. 2 and Meus have *Praecipiat* (“may he command”); others, better, *Percipiat* (“may he receive”). Ott. 2 has *placidasque animae* (“and the soul’s peaceful [waters]”); the conjunction *-que* is superfluous.

233. Reg. 1: “Of the woman caught in adultery.” Meus: “The woman is acquitted of the charge of adultery.” Cant., Arntz., Urb., Rom., Meus, the Leipzig edition, and Aldus have *Cumque* (“and when”); most have *Dumque* (“while”). Reg. 2 and Ott. 1 have *media residens* (“sitting in the middle”); others *residens media* (“sitting in the middle”). Vat. 1 has *residens medii*. Virgil, from whom Sedulius draws, has *Media testudine templi* (“in the middle of the temple’s vaulted roof”), *Aeneid* I, 509. Servius should be consulted on this passage; Isidore describes him in *Etymologies* XV, 8—not, as Arntzenius says, to pass off as his own what he owes to Servius, but because Isidore’s work itself is a cento.

236. *Ecce trahebatur* (“behold, she was being dragged”) is from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 403. *Magna stipante caterva* (“with a great crowd surrounding her”) is from the same poet, *Aeneid* IV, 509.

238. Poelmann’s notes have *Quum* instead of *Quam*, with a defensible sense if the following verse reads *Condemnare*.

239. Fabricius and some other editions have *Dum damnare parat* (“while he prepares to condemn”); Reg. 1 has *Cum damnare paret*, from which *Condemnare parat* arose, as Ott. 1, Urb., Ang., Rom., and other manuscripts cited by Arntzenius, as well as Poelmann’s notes and Parrhasius’s edition, also show. Again, in Reg. 1 the common reading *Cum damnare parat* is indicated in place of the first reading, with *cum* used for *dum*. Vat. 1 may originally have had *Condemnare*, but now has *Cum damnare parat*. In Reg. 1, *illis* (“those”) was made from these readings, with the gloss *Judex Christus* (“Christ the judge”); again, in place of the first reading, Parrhasius punctuates: *plus liberat omnibus illis. Nam simul* (“he frees more than all those; for at once”). Aldus has the same: *plus liberat, omnibus illis. Nam simul*. But *omnibus illis* must be joined with *turbis* (“crowds”).

240. Meus has *ex*; others *e*.

242. Meus has *fugiens* (“fleeing”); I retain *feriens* (“striking”), which the prose confirms. *Contagia moechae* means “the contagion of the adulteress,” that is, “the contagious adulteress,” as Sedulius employs many similar expressions.

243. Fabricius and a few other editions, in agreement with the prose, have *evellere* (“to pull out”), which Meus suggests in *evelere*. Most have *vellere* (“to pull”), Alm. *pellere* (“to drive away”).

244. Meus, Rom., and Parrh. have *qui in lumine* (“who in the light”); Urb. likewise, but incorrectly has *limine* (“threshold”) instead of *lumine* (“light”). Most omit *in*.

246. *Sententia* (“judgment”) is elegantly used for the judge who delivers it; this can be supported by many examples.]

He had taken on human thirst in the burning heat,

And the ever-flowing spring of water desired a modest draught,

[225] That he might drink, since he had a body. Then a woman of that people,

Standing nearby, had drawn a small draught from the well.

When she hesitated to give the gifts of perishable water,

Recognizing her own life with many husbands,

She prayed that gifts might be granted to her from the inexhaustible stream,

[230] Gifts that would put away everlasting thirst, which no one

Will be worthy to escape unless, immersed in the torrent of Christ the Lord,

300 He receives the peaceful waters of the soul, not of the body.

And while, seated in the middle of his temple’s vault,

He thundered with his ancestral voice and turned the wandering people

[235] Toward the accessible paths with friendly admonitions,

Behold, a woman was dragged forward, with a great crowd surrounding her,

A shameful adulteress, condemned to be stoned for her offense.

The Pharisaic hand, presenting her before the gentle judge,

When it prepares to condemn her, it frees more; for at once,

[240] Among all those crowds there was no accuser

Without a crime of his own who could take up the first missile stone,

Striking the contagion of the obscene adulteress.

301 And no one could pull the small splinter from another’s eye

Who knew that a large beam was present in his own eye.

[245] Thus that attack withdrew, and the merciful judgment

Grants pardon for the offense,

[Col. 0695A] [Note: [Col. 0695C]

247. Meus has *salutem* (“salvation”), which can be explained in some fashion; but the common and correct reading is *solutam* (“released”).

248. *Relambo* (“I lick back”) perhaps has no author earlier than Sedulius. *Canis ore* (“with a dog’s mouth”) refers to the behavior of a dog, as Nebrissensis explains.

250. Cant. has *damna ferens* (“bearing losses”); others *damna tenens* (“holding losses”), though something else stood in place of *tenens* in Reg. 1. Most have *perdens* (“losing”), either written plainly or abbreviated. Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes have *perdit* (“he destroys”). Barthius, against the prose, judges *pendens* (“hanging”) best in his own manuscript. Urb. has the corrupt reading *compendia tenens*.

251. Meus: “He sees the man born blind.” Parrh. has *consistere* (“to stand”); *considere* (“to sit”) is more accurate, from John IX, 8: “Is this not the man who sat and begged?”

252. Reg. 2, Ang., Ott. 1, Meus, Parrh., and many printed editions have *delapsus* (“having slipped down”); other manuscripts, Burmann’s codices, Arntz., and most editions have *dilapsus* (“having departed” or “having slipped away”). Arntzenius defends *delapsus*. It is elegantly said *delabi de ventre parentis* (“to slip down from the parent’s womb”), just as *cadere de matre* (“to fall from the mother”) means “to emerge from the mother’s womb.” *Delapsus* is wrong, because he was born blind.

253. *Sanguinis* means, namely, “of lineage.” Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII, verse 45: “They produce neither a boy of our lineage nor of our blood.”

254. Rom., contrary to the meter, has *mundi quoque orientis* (“also of the world’s rising”).

255. Reg. 1 has *habere* (“to have”); above, *haberi* (“to be held”) is preferable with the others.

256. Meus corruptly has *per clausta*, from which someone might conjecture *per clausa genarum*, that is, “through the closed cheeks.” The Evangelist says, “He smeared clay upon his eyes,” which proves that the received reading is correct. *Natale lutum* (“birth-clay”), as at verse 260, corresponds to *consanguineus limus* (“kindred mud”).

258. Parrh. and Poelmann’s notes recommend *monentis* (“of the one warning”); *jubentis* (“of the one commanding”) is more vigorous and agrees with the prose and with the others.

259. Arntz. has *Siloe*, which the prose supports. The common reading is also good, as in *terra Asia* (“the land of Asia”) and *humus Graecia* (“the soil of Greece”). *Vox accepta* (“the voice received”) means “the voice heard.” At times *auribus accipere* (“to receive with the ears”) is used for “to hear.”

260. Reg. 2 has *Nam cum sanguinei*; but this is a gloss in place of *consanguinei*, namely: “For since the human being was formed from clay,” and so forth. Ott. 1 and Meus have *totus* (“entire”) instead of *fotus* (“cherished” or “nurtured”), perhaps because *fovisset* (“had cherished”) occurs immediately in the following verse. One could read *lotus* (“washed”) here, or rather *lavisset* (“had washed”), as I shall now explain.

261. Arntz. [reads] *lavisset*, which Burmann had conjectured, led by the plausible reasoning that I indicated just above at verse 260 [Col. 0696D]. The Codex Alm. has *gemellis*; read *gemellae*.

262. In place of *merentur*, Arntz. reads *videntur*; others object, and [retain] *merentur* in accordance with the prose.]

Now no longer released under the condition of not sinning.

For whoever licks back his own vomit with a dog’s mouth,

neither seeks the former pardon nor wishes to possess a future one,

[250] holding fast the losses of the former and forfeiting its gains.

Thence, moving onward, he sees one born blind sitting,

who, having fallen disastrously from the pregnant womb of his parent,

302 rushes into the light without light. Then that creator of human blood,

the source also of the world’s rising,

[255] not long permitting the limbs of his own work to remain imperfect,

[Col. 0696A] smearing natal mud through the barriers of the cheeks,

restores the man from the ancient seed.

Yet he does not receive sight before, having heard the voice of the commanding Lord,

he comes to the water of Siloam,

[260] and, anointed with the healing remedy of kindred clay,

has bathed his eyes with pure water; immediately, therefore, twin

303 blades of sight shine forth in his face, and at last they deserve

to behold the unknown day. Learn, all of you,

what the mystical miracles teach our minds.

[265] [Col. 0697A] [Note: [Col. 0697B]

265. Parrh. [reads] *de faecibus* (“from excrement”); Ott. 2, *de fletibus* (“from tears”); Urb., *Meus* [reads] *defectibus* (“from deficiencies”): let us retain, with most witnesses, *de fetibus* (“from offspring”).

266. “To bear darkness,” as “to bear sin,” “salvation,” and so forth.

268. Most of our manuscripts, together with many printed editions, have *ex virgine* (“from a virgin”); Aldus likewise, to whom Arntzenius incorrectly attributes *de*. *Meus*, with Fabr. and other common editions, has *de virgine*. Ott. 2, *ex virgine vobis* (“from a virgin for you”).

269. *Meus* mistakenly has *fetibus* (“offspring”) instead of *fontibus* (“fountains”). Reg. 1, 5, Vatt. 1, 2, Ott. 2, Urb., Rom., Alb., *Meus*, Lips., Alm. have *abluta* (“washed”); so also Parrh., Ald., and other printed editions. In Reg. 2 there is *oblita* (“forgotten”), but earlier it was *abluta*; in Ott. 1, *abluta*, and instead of *d. s.* [*de fonte sacrato*, “from the sacred fountain”], *luta sacratis* (“soiled by the sacred things”), written by a later hand, which perhaps wished to correct the meter to *sed fonte abluta sacrato* (“but washed by the sacred fountain”). Ang. has *ablita*; Vet. 1, 2, Mon., and certain other printed editions have *oblita*, which suits this passage poorly. Let us therefore retain *abluta*, with its second syllable shortened contrary to the practice of the ancients. Thus, in Prudentius, *Hymn.* V *Per.*, verse 362, many read *Mortis lavacris elutam* (“washed by the baths of death”), although in that passage, with the finest manuscripts, I retained *erutam* (“snatched away”). An unknown author on the baptism of Bebianus has: “And now washed clean from deadly filth.”

270. Wopken attempted: *Clausa renascenti reserat spiramina luci* (“It opens closed breaths to the light being reborn”). But he retains the received reading and explains it in the sense of pregnancy: by opening [them], he makes [the passages] bright. This entire passage should be compared with another similar passage in Prudentius, *Apoth.* 692 ff.

271. *Meus* has *Lazarum suscitat* (“raises Lazarus”); Fabr., the Bibl. Lugd., *Bethaniae* alone. Rom. and Torn. 3, contrary to the meter, have *Bethaniae solum*. In Rom. there is everywhere an error, *pro* in place of *ibique* (“and there”), which the other manuscripts, the sense, and the prose require.

274. Arntz. reads *exhalarat odorem* (“had exhaled an odor”); the others, *exhalabat* (“was exhaling”).

275. Parrhasius observes in his *Emendata*, or *Addenda*, that some prefer *populus quoque praesens* (“the people also being present”). In Arntz.’s manuscript, a glossator wrote this instead of the original reading. In Reg. 2 there is now *populatio* (“the populace”), written by an old hand; but another reading seems to have stood there previously. The gloss in the *Cant.* is *populatio*—“a multitude of people”; in Reg. 1, “a crowd of the city.” Nebrissensis explains it as *populus* (“the people”). From this meaning of the word comes the Spanish name *población*. For an assembly of people, a village, and a parish, writers of the late period used *populatio*, as is clear from Ducange’s Glossary. For plundering or devastation, the ancient Latins used *populatio*.

277. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *Exanimosque* (“and lifeless”), not improperly; in both, however, it has been corrected to *Exanimesque* (“and lifeless”).

278. Most printed editions have *lacrymisque* (“and with tears”). Our manuscripts, Arntz., Parrh., and Ald. have *lacrymis* without *-que*. The Burmann manuscript, Reg. 5, Ott. 2, Ald., Parrh., and the Poelman sheets have *implebat* (“was filling”); our better manuscripts have *implevit* (“filled”). The *Cant.* has *lacrymis complevit* (“filled with tears”). Elsewhere this expression is discussed: *implevit amicum* means “fulfilled the role of a friend.”

[Col. 0698C] 280. Reg. 1 has *Meus* obscurely; Parrh., Edimb., and certain other editions have *Christus, dubitatis* (“Christ, do you doubt?”), which gives a clearer sense with the following *possit*. Ott. 1 has *Christo*, but *Christum* is the more established reading; Wopken defends it together with the following *possit* by similar examples, such as Gellius, book VII, chapter 12: “Would anyone doubt that he did the same?” He also cites a passage of Juvencus from book IV, verse 468:

“Peter replied: If it is permitted to believe all—  
which your wavering precepts can deny—  
yet no circumstance will ever change my heart.”

But this passage, as I said then, can be explained so that *cunctos* is the accusative of the verb *mutabit*. Nevertheless I preferred: “All, if it is permitted to believe,” and so forth. But for Sedulius to appear to have written *Christum dubitatis*, apart from the authority of the ancient copies, is also supported by the prose, which retains the same expression.

281. Reg. 2, Urb., Alb., and Rom. have *Posse ab infernis* (“to be able from the infernal regions”); the meter does not allow this unless a hiatus is admitted or one reads *Posse ex infernis* (“to be able out of the infernal regions”). The syntax would then be: “Do you doubt that Christ can raise a man from the infernal regions?” Vat. 1 also originally had *Posse*, but it was corrected to *Possit*. The *Cant.* has *inferni* (“of hell”); although this can be used substantivally in Sedulius, the common reading *infernis* (“from the infernal regions”) is nevertheless preferable. In place of *cavernis* (“caverns”), Parrh. reads *catervis* (“crowds”), which must be rejected.

282. In Reg. 1, the reading apparently corresponding to *dabit* above has a different form. Wopken says that *innumeris … turbis* (“innumerable crowds”) may have been written, but he confirms that the received reading is also good. The Arntz. manuscript has *formas* (“forms”) instead of *turbas* (“crowds”), and, in place of the original reading, *turmas* (“companies”), which is also found in the Poelman sheets, Reg. 5, and Aldus.]

We are the blind offspring of wretched Eve,

bearing the darkness born of a long error.

But when God deigned to assume mortal form,

a saving earth was made for us from a virgin,

which, washed in sacred fountains,

[270] opens the bright breaths of reborn light.

And, returning to Bethany, he entered, and there

304 Lazarus lay buried by the setting lot,

already on the fourth day without light, and shut within a tomb

of marble; he exhaled an odor corrupted by decay.

[275] The sisters wept, the populace present wept,

[Col. 0698A] and the Almighty also wept—but in body, not in divinity—

and he grieved for those lifeless limbs in that part

in which he was to die; and with tears he filled his friend,

God in majesty. Why do you delay believing, Martha?

[280] Or why do you groan, Mary? Do you doubt whether Christ alone

305 can recall a man from the infernal caverns—

he who will cause innumerable crowds to rise after death?

[Col. 0699A] [Note: [Col. 0699B]

285. Cellarius, Grunerus, and Arntzenius understand *Tartara* (“Tartarus”) as referring to the tomb, and consequently deny that Christ descended to the infernal regions. Who could tolerate so forced an interpretation with equanimity? The discussion will return to this matter in the following book.

286. Burm., Arntz., Reg. 1, 2, 5, Ottob. 1, *Meus*, and Ald. have *Extremuit* (“shuddered violently”). Rom., Urb., and the Lipsian edition have *Extimuit* (“was afraid”), which is a gloss in Reg. 1. Others, with Parrh., have *Et tremuit* (“and trembled”). In Vat. 2, the beginning of this verse and the end of the preceding one are missing. The verb *extremisco* is also cited from Minucius Felix, chapter 28, but other readings occur there as well, including *contremiscunt*. That writers of the later period at least used the verb *extremisco* is made sufficiently clear by the Spanish *estremecerse*.

287. Burmann conjectured *primas* (“first”) in place of *proprias* (“its own”). But writers contemporary with Sedulius, and somewhat earlier ones, commonly use *proprius* for *suus*. See above, verse 201, in this passage, and the note on Juvencus, book III, verse 305, where I indicated that ancient poets spoke in this way. Vat. 2 has *repente* (“suddenly”), which seems to have been the reading in Vat. 1, where *repetente* (“returning”) now stands, with *subito* (“suddenly”) as a gloss for *repente*. In Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, *repetente* was made from *repente*. Urb. corruptly has *repete*. *Repente* could be explained and defended in some sense from the active verb *repo* with an accusative; but there is no doubt that *repetente* is the true reading.

289. Fabr. and certain other printed editions have *tandem* (“at last”); the others, together with the prose, have *tamquam* (“as though”). In Reg. 1, *tandem* is written instead of the original reading.

291. *Meus* has *Triumphabat Dominus* (“the Lord was triumphing”). The Poelman sheets have “Christ enters Jerusalem seated upon a she-ass.” Arntz. has *mundi* (“of the world”) instead of *saecli* (“of the age”), apparently from a gloss. Christian writers commonly use *saeclum* and *saeculum* for the world and worldly affairs.

292. Arntzenius attributes *Monstrare* (“to show”) rather than *Monstraret* (“might show”) to the *Cant.* manuscript and to the Aldine, Basel, and other editions. But Aldus, in my copy, has *Monstraret*; nor can the other reading be defended. Rom. has *cursibus* (“with courses”); retain *curribus* (“with chariots”).

293. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *Qui pompae est mortalis* (“which belongs to mortal pomp”); the substantive verb is better omitted, since, I believe, it entered the text from a gloss.

294. *Frementis* (“snorting”): thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 12: *Frementem … fudit equum* (“he poured forth the snorting horse”).

296. The manuscripts Cant., Lips., Ang., Alb., Reg. 1, 2, Vat. 1, Ott. 1, and Urb. have:

*Ora cruentatum mandentia concutit aurum*  
(“He shakes mouths that bite bloodstained gold”),

a reading first rejected by Wopken and later accepted by him in his second considerations. For it is entirely correct to say that a horse shakes mouths that bite bloodstained gold. In Arntz.’s manuscript the second writing was *Ori c. mandenti concutit a.*, which Arntzenius also attributes to Aldus; but in Aldus the reading *Ore* is clear, and the verse does not scan with *Ori*. The reading *Ore … mandenti* is shared by Vat. 2, Reg. 5, Parrhasius, and several older editions, such as Vet. 1, 2, Fabr., Mon., and Lips. Vet. 1 and 2 have *Ore … mandendo*, which Ott. 2 also gives. In place of *concutit*, the Bibl. Lugd. incorrectly has *concoquit* (“cooks”), as one may learn even from Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 134:

“Distinguished by purple and gold,  
the warhorse stands and fiercely bites the foaming reins.”

The received reading is also confirmed by the prose.

298. Why a light hoof, if the little ass is slow? Nebrissensis replies that *levis* is used for *vilis*, “lowly” or “humble.” The prose likewise supports this.

300. Wopken would prefer *Mobilior* (“more agile”); but *Nobilior* (“nobler”) is more suitable, with its gloss in Reg. 1: “Nobler than all horses.” The prose itself supports this. The Lipsian edition, the Poelman sheets, and the same Poelman’s marginal notes have *non vilior illo* (“not inferior to that one”); the others have, more suitably, *non illius impar* (“not unequal to that one”). Beside the word *fasce* (“burden”), Burmann wrote in the margin of his edition an allusion to Virgil, *Georgics* III, 347: *Injusto sub fasce viam cum carpit* (“when he begins the road beneath an unjust burden”). For *fascis* is used for any burden; Nebrissensis also noted this.

301. I discussed the ablative case of *praesepe* (“manger”) at book II, verse 62. Nebrissensis wanted *patula* (“open”) to be read here, so that *praesepe* would derive from *praesepis*, with feminine gender. Cellarius notes that many of the Fathers, through a pious error, transferred the saying about the ox and ass in Isaiah 1:3 to Christ’s manger. But who taught Cellarius that an opinion which he himself admits to be pious and handed down by many Fathers is an error?]

Therefore, when the trumpet of the Lord crying out sounded, saying:

“Lazarus, come forth!” the realms of Tartarus, shaken by great fear,

[285] burst open; the recesses of Erebus were revealed,

the deathly chaos shuddered violently, and the law

of deep death perished; and, as the soul returned to its own marrow,

a living corpse was seen standing before their eyes.

306 And afterward, as though restored to burial honor,

[290] he himself, dying and posthumous, stands forth as his own heir.

And, scorning the fleeting heights of the wandering age,

[Col. 0700A] so that he might properly show himself to be God—not in lofty chariots,

the honor of mortal pomp, nor with swift quadrigas,

which furrowed the dusty road, nor pressing the high back

[295] of a snorting horse, painted with trappings and purple,

shaking mouths that bite bloodstained gold—

rather, the lowly ass’s slow conveyance

was honor enough for its rider, and the light hoof of the beast,

bearing a marvelous distinction beneath so great a rider,

[300] might be nobler beneath the burden, not unequal to him

who recognized Christ, though lying in an open manger.

[Col. 0701A] [Note: [Col. 0701B]

(Among the glass reliefs of the Borgian Museum there is an ancient image in which the Savior’s manger is represented with an ox and an ass. On the left, a horned moon is visible, hanging above the halo of Saint Joseph, who sits below; on the right, a star placed opposite the moon is joined to the child’s head as though by a ray drawn from its center. Beneath it Saint Mary sits, her head surrounded by a halo, while her feet are wrapped in bands in the manner of women who have recently given birth. The learned scholiast, whose discussion my edition has taken care to reproduce, explains this image as follows. EDIT.)

In my commentary on hymn 11 of Prudentius’ *Cathemerinon*, I exhibited an ancient image in glass relief from the Borgian Museum, in which the Savior’s manger is represented with an ox and an ass. I shall present it again, if I may, in order to defend and vindicate this sacred monument of Christian piety against the cavils of certain people. There exists a letter by P. D. Giovanni Andrea Paternò Castello, a Casinensian monk, concerning an ancient gem, printed after Lactantius’ book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* at Venice in 1766. That ancient gem, preserved in the museum of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of the Sands at Catania, is very similar to ours and is made of ancient glass.

The author of the letter, Paternous, argues against the distinguished men Francesco Gori and Francesco Victorius that gems of this sort were employed for superstitious purposes, fabricated by semi-Christians or heretical Gnostics, and should be numbered among the famous Abrasax gems. But what arguments does he offer for so abnormal an opinion? “Very frequently,” he says, “on Abrasax gems the sun, in the form of a certain star, was engraved on one side, and a horned moon on the other, just as is also seen on our gem.” But in the gem whose image I present, who would dare recognize an engraved sun, since the star represented bears no indication whatsoever of the sun?

Moreover, since the Savior’s manger is depicted, it is most fitting that the moon should be placed there to indicate the night when the Savior was born, and the star that led the Magi to the manger. Paternous refuses to believe this; but he can easily be refuted even by the ray of the star directed toward the head of the child Jesus. That ray does not appear in the gem engraved by Paternous, but is clearly visible in ours.

Paternous insists that the Virgin Mother of God is shown in the gem lying on a bed and bound with bands from the waist downward, which is contrary to her perpetual virginity. But, leaving aside the fact that what the Mother of God sits upon does not appear to be a bed but a bench, why could a Christian artist not have represented the Mother of God wrapped in bands in this way, after the manner of other women who had given birth—either because of the secret discipline, as Victorius thinks, or to indicate more clearly the mother of the child lying in the manger?

Paternous is amusing when he argues that such a gem could not have been fashioned by Christians in the earliest centuries of the Church, the period to which it is believed to belong, because at that time the foolish tale—as he calls it—of the ox and ass tied to the Savior’s manger had not yet gained currency. He therefore claims that, according to the school of Basilides, Osiris or Apis is represented by the ox on the gem, and the god Sabaoth by the ass. But he does not explain why Osiris and the god Sabaoth would have been tied to a manger by the Basilidians.

As for his assertion that the story of the ox and ass at the manger of the child Jesus was not mentioned before the author—whoever he may have been—of the book *On the Promises*, who flourished in the fifth century, that is certainly false. The story was remembered not only by Sedulius, who wrote at the beginning of the fifth century, but also by Prudentius, who flourished in the fourth century, in the passage cited above, and by Merobaudes, or Claudianus, from approximately the same period.

As for Sedulius’ apparent attribution of a certain nobility, almost arrogance, to the ass that carried Christ and vaunted itself under so great a rider, this too was indicated by an ancient artist on a spoon, which I mentioned in the note on Juvencus, book III, verse 632.]

302. Ottob. 2 and Urb. have *tantum esse* (“to be so great”).

303. Alm., Ang., and the Poelman edition in the margin have *In solido* (“on solid ground”), with a gloss in Alm.: *in duro* (“on hard ground”). Reg. 1, Alb., and *Meus* refer to the same reading, writing the words together as *Insolido*. In Reg. 1 the original reading is *Insolito* (“unusually”), which is the more common reading and is not unsuitable; but the other seems preferable, and more recent editors favor it.

305. Ott. 2 corruptly has *Talis morte fuit* (“such was death”). In place of *vel*, *Meus* has *omnis* (“every”); Parrh. and the Poelman sheets have *palmis compta juventus* (“youth adorned with palms”), which gives no acceptable sense.

306. Ottob. 1 has *laudes* (“praises”), as Arntzenius printed it. Most of our manuscripts, together with Parrh., Ald., and Poelm., have *laudem* (“praise”).

307. Aldus punctuates: “gave praise to the Lord?—unless together with the Father Christ.” This is not satisfactory, nor did Sedulius intend it in the prose.

308. Ott. 2, *Meus*, and the Arntz. manuscript, outside the context, at the bottom of the page after the verse *Qui regit*, present this additional verse:

“with whom the holy Spirit always reigns together equally.”

It is absent from our better manuscripts—Reg. 1, 2, 5, Ang., Alb., Vatt. 1, 2, Ott. 1, Rom., and Urb.—as well as from the Lipsian, Alm., and Barthian manuscripts, Sedulius’ prose, and the editions of Parrh., Ald., and others. Certain older editions nevertheless include it. Some printed editions have *cum regnat* (“with whom he reigns”) instead of *conregnat* (“reigns together with”). In a very ancient manuscript from Turin, from which the verse “with whom the holy Spirit” is also absent, the book ends with these words:

“Here ends Book III. Here begins Book IV. I, Abundantius, have collated this book.”

Similarly, manuscripts Reg. 1, 2, Vat. 1, and Ott. 2 have: “Here ends Book III. Here begins Book IV.” In Reg. 5: “The fourth book of the divine miracles of Caelius Sedulius begins.” *Meus*: “Book III of the poet Sedulius ends. The fourth begins.” Urb.: “Here ends the third book of the excellent Sedulius, bishop, concerning the miracles and wondrous signs of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Here begins the fourth book of the same author concerning the most devout passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and his resurrection, manifestation, or appearance before the disciples; and first concerning the prayer made by Christ to God the Father before he supped with his disciples.” Vat. 2 and Rom. indicate no division of the books.]

308 Yet he acknowledged that he was God. All the people worshiping

laid soft garments along the solid path.

309 Tell me, Gentile peoples: for what king was there

[305] [Col. 0702A] ever such glory in the world? For what king did a crowd

adorned with palms or ever with leafy branches

meet with praise in heavenly hymns? For none but the Lord with the Father Christ,

the prince who rules the ethereal kingdom in the Prince.

BOOK FIVE. [Note: [Col. 0703A]

Amid these abundant stores of virtues without end, the Passover had already begun to draw near, when the glorious power of Christ wished to lay down mortal flesh, soon to take up again flesh now living forever—not another, but the same—which, filled with the recompense of light, he raised from the infernal regions and lifted to the stars. [Col. 0703: Juretus emended the text thus; in an old manuscript he found *mortalem vel exponere sumptura carnem*. Shortly afterward he restored *vicinia* from *vicina* in the old manuscript.] And, troubled a little by the nearness of death, like a man who feels fear, he cries out to the Father in such words, with the confidence of devout religion, showing that he is the Son of God:

“Father, save me from this hour; but for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

He spoke with surpassing divinity and power: while asking that he himself be glorified, he signified that the Father’s name must be glorified. For “God” is the name that Father and Son alike possess in common, with undivided majesty.

Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” What could be clearer than the testimony fulfilled by the Father’s declaration? What could be more plainly an oracle of heavenly assertion? Yet the faithless Jewish people, which had heard the weight of so great a truth, was in no way moved by signs so manifest to acknowledge the divinity of the Lord Jesus Christ. Some asserted that it had been the sound of thunder; others argued that an angel had spoken to him.

O truly blind people, hardest of heart! Isaiah, prophesying about it, spoke as follows [Col. 0705D: Isaiah, chapter VI, verse 10]:

“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn back, and I heal them.”

For neither thunder nor an angel—a creature—generated Christ, its own creator, to whom, when he cried out confidently to the Father, it would have replied as the Father. Rather, a voice proceeded from the mouth of God, specifically from the Father [Col. 0705D: an old manuscript has *diei* (“of the day”) instead of *Dei* (“of God”); Juretus corrected the error. It also seems that *ille responderet* (“he would reply”) should be restored], who truly knew the Son, answering him, so that in this way at least the excessively unbelieving crowd, struck with remorse, might at last be led to faith in the heavenly one.

Thus, for the Father to answer the Son is for him to echo in harmony with his own voice, because Christ, begotten as the Word, is the Father’s Word; and by a corresponding pattern of speech the Father revealed himself in the Son, and revealed the Son in the Father.

Then, when he was celebrating the sacrament of the communal meal and observing the Paschal feast according to custom, so that he might teach by his own example that humility should rather be loved, he rose, girded himself with a linen cloth, and, as teacher and Lord, bowed down to his disciples, washing the feet of servants. He so laid aside the height of his power that he did not exclude even Judas from the honor of this service, although he knew him to be the author of the unspeakable betrayal.

But you gained nothing from this glory, accursed traitor: you were made to appear clean in your footsteps, while you were polluted in your spirit, like a tomb whitewashed on the outside, which within bristles with the filthy uncleanness of corpses and is filled with it. Nor did the Lord fail to perceive the plots that had been arranged; he identified the man who was to be the head of the coming crime, to whom he would hand bread—the very Bread destined to be handed over to death.

Then David’s saying was revealed, which says [Col. 0707D: Psalm XL, verse 10. Later, Gallandius conjectures that *Judae cor* (“the heart of Judas”) should be read instead of *Judae corda* (“the heart of Judas” in the printed text). But in this author the old reading is free from any suspicion of falsity. In the manuscript there is the error *serviris belli* instead of *servilis belli*, and below *sor melior* instead of *sors melior*.]:

“He who ate my bread has magnified his treachery against me.”

After the Lord Jesus Christ had consecrated the two gifts of life, his body and blood, and had offered spiritual food and drink to his own disciples, so that faithful souls, nourished by heavenly banquets, might no longer feel hunger or thirst,

a moment later the ferocity of the most evil spirit entered the heart of Judas, that wicked dwelling where envy had found a home. Seizing accursed weapons against the Lord, it stirred the madness of servile warfare, having agreed to a great crime for whatever reward.

For guilt does not remain in the price; rather, the crime grows stronger in the deed. With thirty pieces of silver, blind to sacrilege, he committed as great a crime while taking a small payment as he would have committed if he had gained all the kingdoms of the earth at once, the riches of the sea, and the entire ethereal region wandering with the clouds. For the goods of the whole world would not suffice to equal Christ’s blood when poured out—the blood of him who is the father of the entire world, who also permitted this accursed man to be born.

Would that, condemned to the sterile barrenness of his mother, he had never seen his natal day, nor looked upon the pleasant light of heaven, remaining in eternal torpor; and would that it had been a better fate for the wretched man never to know the life given him than to feel it taken away. Or, as soon as he deserved to be born, would that he had also deserved to die, becoming an example of the first psalm, so that he might utterly perish from the whole age, exactly like dust that the wind casts from the face of the earth [Col. 0709D: Psalm I, verse 4. Later, in some libraries of the Fathers, the error *Tunc igitur* occurs instead of *Tune igitur*, and *tunc fallax, tunc traditor* instead of *tune fallax, tune traditor*. Above I restored *aeterno torpore* instead of *tempore*.], and might leave no memory of his name behind, unhappy man.

Then, bold, bloodstained, savage, rebellious; then deceitful, cruel, wicked, venal, and faithless; then traitor, robber, savage betrayer, pitiless and impious—you accompany, as guide and standard-bearer, the horrible battle-line of the enemy, sacrilegiously and violently armed with swords and clubs, as you move it threateningly; with lying kisses you bring harm to the covenant, add honey to poisons, and flatter the Lord with savage betrayal.

Why do you falsely profess to be his companion, and why are you wounded by the greeting of friendly deceit? Never does peace conspire in harmful swords, nor does a wolf offer ferocious kisses to a lamb.

Thus the holy worker, handed over to accursed men, did not abandon his customary mercy. The ear violently cut off from the boy by Peter’s sword he immediately restored and healed, lest the pious man, at any time, be separated from piety [Col. 0711D: the old manuscript has *ne quaeso tempore* (“I beg, at no time”). Juretus restored *ne quo se tempore* (“lest at any time he should”). In many libraries of the Fathers, *suspenderet* is followed immediately by *et protinus*; *et* is superfluous and seems to have been repeated from the preceding word.].

For it was not consistent with reason that human vengeance should assist God, who could have asked his Father to send more than twelve thousand legions of angels to defend him, if he had preferred to exact punishment from the wicked rather than pardon the injury of his own death. He therefore commands that the edge of the naked sword be returned to its sheath, since he had plainly come to lay down his own life for all, not to rescue that of anyone else.

To Peter himself, who confidently promised that he wished to die with the Lord, Jesus replied [Col. 0712D: in the manuscript copy, *iecoys* was written instead of *Jesus*; evidently the scribe intended to use Greek characters], and said:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock will not crow today before you deny me three times.”

He was not then accusing him of unbelief, but revealing the fear of future trembling.

Soon he was led to the house of Caiaphas, who, according to the religious custom of the Jews, was indeed chief of the priests at that time. But because he sat in the seat of pestilence and stood in the way of sinners, he seemed to possess the primacy of crimes. For the council had begun to be violently inflamed and stirred up by false witnesses.

A thousand lies flew against the Lord. Dead amid the empty sparks of the accusers, they came to light without living by the warmth of faith [Col. 0713D: perhaps *viventia apparebant* (“they appeared alive”), and below *protinus resoluta* (“immediately dissolved”)]. Soon all, exhausted by their own fickleness, were spent, like a raging fire racing through the straws of dry stubble, whose weak material does not supply strength to burn the lofty peaks, but which immediately collapses into ashes and loses the flame’s empty victory.

After no path opened for deceit, fraud, yielding to force, turned into fury, and the impatient populace armed itself to raise its hands against the Lord. Alas for me! With what showers of tears obstructed, with what movements of the soul wounded, I shudder to recall the sacrilegious hands of the rabid tumult raised against the Lord!

Finally, the accursed people did not cease striking his head with blows, spitting upon his face, and beating him with blows of the palm. Yet he patiently endured everything, gave himself over to our salvation, and appointed his body to punishment for us. Through those blows we possess the health of our head; those spittings are the baths of our faces; by those slaps we have obtained everlasting freedom.

But the elder, to whom the author of truth had foretold everything, and for whom what Christ had declared would happen could not remain unfulfilled, followed the Lord’s footsteps all the way to the house of the high priest. Although he too was one of his disciples, he was recognized three times, denied him three times, and the cock, herald of the day, crowed. Once the oracle of the divine decree had been fulfilled, Peter’s former understanding also returned. Recalling the memory of his guilt, he chastised the error of his forgetfulness in himself; and as continual groaning accompanied him, sins fled, offenses departed, and the showers of tears poured forth brought sweet pardon through the bitterest weeping.

Therefore, instructed by the apostolic examples, we ought to recognize the power of repentance and its merit, striving with life-giving remedies to drive out the deadly diseases from our souls. If we have been wounded by the harmful poisons of thoughts, by deed, or even by the contagion of shameful speech, let us hasten at once to flee to the most health-giving medicine of repentance, so that, grieving because of guilt, we may not grieve because of punishment; weeping because of the wound, we may not weep because of death.

Nor should we prepare repentance for future errors, but apply it to offenses already committed. For those who sin in reliance upon indulgence scarcely obtain the forgiveness they desire, which many promise themselves in presumptuous security so that they may sin. Thus the remarkable prophet David, when he sought pardon for a past error, indicated before God in the following words that he had sinned through ignorance, so that he might obtain it more easily [Col. 0715D: the old manuscript has *praecisignavit*; Juretus restored *prae se signavit*. The passage is from Psalm XXIV, verse 7. Juretus observes that in the following words the old manuscript has the corrupt *amiserit* instead of *admiserit*, while *juvenalis aetas* is correct in the old form instead of *juvenilis aetas*. Sedulius often speaks in this way.]:

“Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance, O God.”

What, then? Whatever crimes youthful age may have committed—are they to be kept until old age to be forgiven? Far be it that they should remain and grow old in us. But while divine mercy, with patient forbearance, was suspending the gentlest vengeance of judgment, let no hope of impunity blunt any of these [Col. 0716D: Juretus conjectures *indultae* (“of indulgence”) in place of *indutus*, which is the manuscript reading. Some libraries of the Fathers have *indutos*. I would consider *inductos* or *inducta* better. Shortly before, one should apparently correct the text to *ut ita maneant* (“that they may remain so”), or *ut ista maneant* (“that these things may remain so”).].

But, like servants who have long been fugitives, let us at least return late to our Lord, asking from him, even in old age, pardon for the slippery sins of youth. Yet it is fitting for every sinner to do so immediately, lest the beginnings of the disease of the serpent, like the roots of a bitter shoot buried more deeply through the negligence of a careless farmer, later be impossible to uproot completely by any labor.

Finally, that same prophet, lest he appear negligent regarding youthful sins, added ignorance to his plea, so that before the gracious Judge he might more easily deserve to have his error forgiven.

Thus the Apostle Peter also did not deliberately seek to deny Christ, but simply and ignorantly fell into a lapse of forgetfulness. For he had promised with complete devotion that he wished to die with the Lord; he could not bear to appear separated from his companionship under any danger. He had already offered, among other things, a splendid example of his faith: fear of death could not separate him from Christ, toward whom, hastening through the middle of the sea, he had earlier plunged into the swift waves, deterred by no fear of imminent death.

[Col. 0716C] Meanwhile the day, destined to witness a new crime, dawned more mournfully than the shadows of night; once the darkness had been removed, it publicly disclosed the unspeakable counsels of the Hebrew assembly.

Then Judas, the last dragon, a murderer resembling the earlier venomous one—for just as that one, after depriving Adam of life, became the persecutor of the human race, so this one became its persecutor after handing Christ over to death—saw the Lord being led to Pilate’s praetorium. Seeing him bound in chains, although he had loosed the bonds of sins, the wretch stiffened and shuddered.

Returning the money—the funeral payment, namely, for innocent blood—to the savage stewards, and throwing back the price of his crime, he emptied himself of the payment, not of the crime. For what can the fear of death contribute to safety when it is conceived there where no fear can now bring healing, according to the statement of the psalm:

“There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm XIII, 5),

that is, in the very judgment, where the time for correction and the opportunity for an unproductive fear do not exist; or when one is already established in the jaws of hell, what help can confession offer, since we read:

“But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm VI, 6).

For Judas, a public murderer, who killed not merely his own parent—one whom he did not deserve to hear—but the author of the whole world, vainly sought the remedy of repentance. After his audacious betrayal, the punishment of judgment already held him, and, with an axe laid against the roots of the tree that had produced an accursed fruit, it was destined to cut away the useless shoot of evil at its very base [Col. 0717D: perhaps *viamque gutturis* (“the passage of his throat”). The printed editions have *vitamque gutturis* (“the life of his throat”). In place of *vendens*, many libraries of the Fathers have the erroneous *videns* (“seeing”). I would also prefer *omnium redemptorem* (“the redeemer of all”), although in Sedulius this very meaning is expressed by the word *redemptio*. In the old manuscript, Juretus noted *travalibus laqueis* instead of *trabalibus laqueis* and collected many examples to prove that ancient writers called whatever was huge and strong *trabalis*: a *trabalis clavus* (“beam-like nail”), *trabalis hasta* (“massive spear”), *trabale telum* (“massive weapon”), *trabale sceptrum* (“massive scepter”), *trabalis vectis* (“massive lever”), and *trabalis jussio* (“weighty command”). Juretus adds that in his note on Arator, book I, no. 4—“Hated by heaven and earth, he perishes between the two”—he explained why Judas perished between heaven and earth. Below, at verse 145, I would prefer the prose reading *renuerit* (“will have denied”).].

Suddenly seized by madness, he was driven into fury and nevertheless prepared a deadly destruction for himself. Yet he was saner then than when he avenged upon himself the crime of the unspeakable conspiracy: [Col. 0718B] he sold the redemption of all, and, binding his throat with tightened nooses, drove out his wretched soul with massive ropes.

That punishment might seem small for so great a crime, since no magnitude of torment could equal it; nevertheless, the very kind of deadly end, and the death of a corpse hanging aloft, denies the sight of heaven and forbids contact with the earth. Thus, guilty of an unheard-of crime, he was judged unworthy of both elements alike: he could neither enjoy the air for life nor, laid to rest according to the universal custom of humankind, release his departing soul into the earth.

This has another indication of disgrace in the forms of its own abasement. For the traitor and deserter, receiving death upon a lofty height, revealed from how great a summit he had fallen: recently a disciple, now already a condemned man; recently an apostle, now called an apostate.

[Col. 0720B] When, however, the Lord stood undaunted before the governor’s tribunal, like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, and the accusing people could bring no charge worthy of death against him, they angrily shouted, with the aim of stirring up rebellion, that he had called himself a king—though he was plainly a king. Nor should anyone wonder if the crowd, friendly to falsehood, dragged truth into a criminal charge and rejected the heavenly sovereignty and divine power which, ungrateful toward the Creator’s decrees, had once worshiped sacred groves and served in obedience to idols. For there appears to be one and the same madness, an equal insanity, in preferring Baal to the Lord then and Barabbas to Christ now. While the righteous is killed and the wicked preserved, the people, erring in both judgments, changed the path of justice: the author of death was appointed to live, while the author of life was appointed to die.

Therefore, all of you who remain steadfast in the faith to this day, believe now that Christ suffered for the salvation of the world. Scourged with lashes, assailed with insults, he embraces every punishment, so that not even a robber, who deserved to perish by his own deeds, should undergo destruction.

[Col. 0721A] Alas, how grievous is the sharpness of the sickle that cut down the harvest of the Jewish posterity! For, demanding the Lord’s death, they declared that his blood would remain upon themselves and their children, saying furiously and shouting:

[Col. 0721B] “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

They condemned the entire fruit of their offspring, until this stain should be spiritually washed away from them by the water of him whose blood, sprinkled upon them, lethally holds sway. Alas, Pilate, the wickedness of your crime—what a deed you committed! In one judgment, or rather in one prejudgment, you committed so many crimes that, if you recognized them with a mind made wise for healing, you would not wash only your hands, but ought continually to bathe your whole body in the sacred washing of spiritual water.

You scourge the just unjustly; as governor, you examine the king. You, a mortal man, do not tremble to set yourself above the Lord. In what chains of punishment, then, are you now held, since through numerous wounds you fasten the Lord of creation to the cross, and fear offending Caesar more than you fear Caesar’s creator?

[Col. 0722B] When Christ had been handed over to the soldiers for execution and was subject to the sentence of death, even in the very attire that he assumed under the deceptive appearance of royalty, the mysteries of a great sacrament were being enacted. For the fact that he was clothed in a scarlet cloak displayed the bloody appearance of his future death. A crown of thorns encircled his head, because in loving humility he alone bore the thorns of all sins, which had invaded the human race everywhere. For he carried a reed that was truly like the scepter of a worldly kingdom, which, because it is repeatedly shaken, is seen to be fragile, empty, light, and perishable.

Then, stripped of the clothing belonging to others, he was immediately clothed in his own, as though at his death he were about to lay aside the garment of his body, which he knew he would shortly take up again, no longer taking up anything subject to change—[Col. 0723D] in the old manuscript *motabile* appears instead of *mutabile*, and *prae mortem plenam* instead of *post mortem plena*. In some printed editions *majestatis* is mistakenly read, unless one restores *plena cum majestatis suae carne*, which nevertheless does not suit the meter—since after death he would return and rise again in the fullness of the majesty of his flesh.

Nor did this depart from the fellowship of divinity: he took wine mixed with gall, touched it with his lips, and expelled it from his mouth. For it was a wondrous sign that the Lord tasted a bitter death and immediately rejected its dreadful poison by turning his face away.

Thus, nailed high upon the cross, he transformed the wrath of that dreadful punishment through devoted reverence. When peace had ascended the cross after cruelty had been cast aside, he glorified the violent instruments of savage strength in his own limbs, clothed punishment with honor, consecrated suffering to salvation, and, sanctifying the torments in himself, made the sign intended for condemnation sacred through blessedness.

So that no one may wander here in ignorant thought, everyone ought wisely to understand that the form of the cross displays the reason for veneration: it was worthy to bear the Lord in worship. It should be understood as extended through the four regions of the world. For the head of Christ, whose limbs were stretched upon the cross, received the eastern axis. The western boundary smiled upon his feet. The north shone upon his right hand, and the middle region gleamed upon his left. The entire substance of the world, made glad by the Creator’s body, displayed in itself the line of the cross, filled out by straight and oblique boundaries—the line that it is seen to have followed from the beginning of the first light.

And when the soldiers divided his clothing among themselves, they cast lots to determine who should have the tunic, because it had not been sewn but woven throughout from above, and they considered it a sacrilege to violate the appearance of so great a miracle. Let the teachers of the schismatics read this and learn what impiety they practice by tearing apart Catholic concord. If it seemed harsh to the sacrilegious and murderous soldiers to tear Christ’s garment, what sacrilege do those commit who, having disturbed ecclesiastical peace, do not cease to divide the Lord Christ himself through schisms?

The inscription too, written in the meaning of three languages, with Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters—“This is the King of the Jews”—was placed above the Lord and could be read. It does not seem unreasonable to inquire into the meaning of this sacrament as well. For nothing manifested in Christ is outside the great mystery.

Why, then, was this inscription written in three languages, when the account in the Acts of the Apostles testifies that many different nations and peoples were certainly present at Jerusalem? Either one language, through an interpreter, could have sufficed for different peoples; or, if Pilate wished to display this to the eyes of everyone, he could have made the inscription intelligible to the common people by providing it in the commercial languages of the many nations—[Col. 0725C] Juretus notes that an old manuscript mistakenly reads *fulgi* for *vulgi*. But let us understand spiritually that what was not completed through human arrangement was fulfilled in this way.

For the true faith and Catholic confession, which were signified in Christ, proclaim in a particular word one King for all peoples, who rules over every creature—something appropriate both to the secular circumstance and to divine reason. First, whether because of fear of Caesar or because of an admission of his own belief, Pilate defined what kind of king the man who had called himself king was, lest, if he designated him simply by the name of king, he might seem to proclaim him king in general and against Caesar, and thus, by ordering his death as though he were also his own ruler, become sacrilegious—[Col. 0725C] the old manuscript wrongly reads *amissum aquae*. Juretus corrected it to *admissum, qui*; Gallandius thought *admissum, quod* more correct. At the end of the chapter he conjectured *relinquentes honorem* instead of *relinquentes horrorem*. The sentence beginning “For the true faith” is obscure.

Second, because Christ is devoutly called the King of the Jews, and the whole Gentile world, occupied with the worship of idols, begins to be called God’s people among the children of Abraham when it has been deemed worthy to receive the mysteries of Christian doctrine. He is recorded as having promised Abraham that he would make him—as indeed he did—the father of all nations.

Jesus, therefore, was called the King of the Jews not only of those who were present but also of those who were to come: they would abandon the useless bitterness of their natural stock and soon, by the fruitful sweetness of the anointing of holy chrism, be grafted into the olive tree, losing the bitterness of the barren wild olive.

Moreover, the savage and guilty crowd, unsatisfied by any punishment, caused men stained with blood to be crucified on both sides of the Lord under the same sentence, so that the injury inflicted by such persons might make the wounds more bitter, although similarity of sentence does not imply similarity of merit. While the executioners hang a just man among robbers, the punishment appears to be the same for all three, but the cause of two is different. Those men are greatly guilty before the world on account of their crime; in this man, the world itself is guilty, for it was freed from sin by his blood.

Yet, when the Lord stood upon that cross, he did not lose the rights of his power. From the tribunal of the lofty cross, as from a royal throne, he looked upon both as an impartial judge and weighed their merits in the balance of the divine heart. He chose one and abandoned the other, considering not the deeds of the past for which they were paying, but the present differences of their minds.

One of them, whose savage ferocity did not retreat even in the crisis of death, tore at the Lord with cruel insults, accursed in his biting words, like a shaggy goat hostile to the branch of the sweetest vine through the touch of its poisonous teeth. Mocking him, he said: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.”

The other, more modest because he possessed a better hope, spared both his tongue and the punishment of his penalty. He addressed the Lord with words of prayer, turning his eyes downward and directing only the freedom he still possessed toward the earth, because the tight bonds of his wounds prevented his palms from willingly inclining in the service of humility—[Col. 0727D] there was a lacuna here in the old manuscript. It evidently read: “and addresses the Lord with words of prayer.” Most commonly printed editions have: “and addresses the Lord with words of prayer.” Gallandius omitted *ac*, which seems detrimental to the sense—[Col. 0728D] while the stretched bonds of his wounds prevented his palms from inclining in the service of humility.

For after he rebuked his companion, who already deserved to be separated from him, with the reproach of a righteous speech, and acknowledged his own guilt and insolence, he prayed to the Lord in this way:

“Remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

The merciful Lord immediately gathered him back with joy, like a shepherd gathering a wandering sheep from pathless deserts, and addressed him, saying:

“Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

O wondrous and divine promise! He says that he is entering paradise who was hastening to descend to the underworld, so that he might teach that there is no time when the Lord is not present everywhere.

In order to free the robber’s spirit from fear of blessed death, he said not merely—[Col. 0730D] something appears to be missing, as though the text read: “Not merely, he says, ‘I will remember you,’ but ‘today,’ and so forth.” Gallandius makes this conjecture—“Today you will be with me in paradise,” where perpetual spring smiles gently across the fields, delight, nourished by flowing springs and softly spread through beautiful gardens, gladdens everything with pleasing sweetness; and among the blessed leafy branches, with the deceptive snares of fruit no longer present, that infernal serpent groaned that the ancient inhabitant now lived without falling.

Thus the two robbers, advancing along different paths with different movements, entered roads of different kinds and, approaching places far removed from one another, enacted a separation through their deeds. One entered the gates of hell; the other burst into the realms above. One, submerged in deep darkness, penetrated the bars of Gehenna; the other, entering the light of radiant brightness, seized the kingdoms of heaven.

Meanwhile, the whole world was suddenly darkened. Overcome by unexpected blindness and covered with the mournful mass of clouds, it celebrated funeral days as a funeral procession. But the sun, with its rays withdrawn and hidden, lay concealed beneath a dreadful covering and stained the globe with the mourning of an alien night.
