The elements, deprived of the consolation of their father, deserved to assume such a countenance, so that they might grieve at his setting whose rising had made them glad. For just as light shone when the Lord was born, so it departed when he died.

Then a star shone during the day, but now it did not appear even at night. Yet although fugitive light withdrew from heaven and earth, it did not remain longer in this withdrawal. That it should be suspended for those intervals of time was fitting in view of the great mystery. For just as the world’s surface lay oppressed by darkness for three hours, so the Lord’s burial concealed him in the tomb for three days.

Nor did the earth then stand without suffering. It trembled in all its foundations, sensing such things being done, and, believing that the end of the world had already come, nature hung uncertain beneath its limit. It feared that the highest summit, descending to the underworld, might immediately incline the entire mass with it into death, and that the world, following its own creator, might plunge headlong into chaos.

But that immense piety of the Godhead was hastening mercifully to the realms of the dead, in order to restore what had been lost, not to destroy what had been created. And when those who had fastened the Lord to the wood of the cross saw such dangers occurring, they were not at all frightened.

[Col. 0733B] O unheard-of signs, prodigies of so many manifestations of present fear! Moreover, when he asked for a drink in his thirst, one man from the savage crowd fastened a sponge to a reed and offered vinegar to his mouth.

O how fitting that drink was for the wicked mind of the Jews! They followed worse things, or rather, weakened through the guilt of unbelief, and were called *Manzeres*—[Col. 0733D] the old manuscript reads *Mazires* instead of *Manzeres*, and *tangens ista* instead of *ita gens ista*. Above, one might perhaps read “they were not frightened by the signs,” and “from the cups of the tables” instead of “from the peoples”—just as sweet wines, when changed into bitter vinegar, are rejected and cast away by all the diners, so this savage and impious people, which in ancient times had pleased God, is now hateful and utterly accursed.

When, therefore, the blessed Lord had fulfilled everything belonging to his Passion, he himself immediately laid down his soul from his holy body, intending himself to take it up again voluntarily, as he did. For he had indeed died, but he remained alive: his limbs had died, but his divinity had not.

Let us hear what the Evangelist John reports in his person. The Lord said to his disciples:

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life. I will take it up again, and I have authority to take it up again. I received this commandment from my Father.”

Who, then, could doubt—or fail to listen to him—to whom it was permitted to lay down his life when he wished, and who therefore could also take it up again when he desired? He demonstrated this power in many people, and was willing to exercise it all the more in himself.

Behold, at Christ’s coming, the gates of hell are thrown down; the path of the underworld, now exposed behind, lies open; rocks are split; the earth is cleft; tombs are emptied of their bodies; the crowd comes back to life. And, so that faith might not fail among believers, the multitude of those rising is recognized.

Then that wondrous temple as well, filled with ancient reverence, seeing the summit of the greater temple fallen—[Col. 0734D] the old book mistakenly reads *templi cum mina cecidisse*—like a sad and grieving foster-child mourned its own creator.

Immediately, when the veil was torn, it showed its naked breast to all, clearly signifying that its inner and secret things were to be opened to the Gentiles and to the peoples who would faithfully follow: for the law, which had long remained concealed beneath Moses’ veil, shone forth when Christ came to us.

Speak, then, sad and impious death: where is now that savage victory of yours? Where now is your accursed sting, serving you at the tombs? From the first destruction of the human race, you have never been satisfied with funerals, invading humanity and habitually ruling over miserable frailty with perpetual punishment.

Behold, you did not come to Christ in your wickedness; rather, Christ descended willingly to you. He, who could die without being subject to death, created all things and established all things, but did not create you alone in your livid form. For venerable Scripture says: “The Lord did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13).

If you desire to recognize the material of your origin, you were conceived from the serpent as father and begotten from guilt as mother. But now, while indulgence reigns, you are consumed.

Meanwhile, the Lord’s spirit had departed from the body for a time, and Christ’s cold limbs hung upon the wood of the cross. Yet fury, still not abandoning its weapons, supplied the hostile hand with a spear, and by a wicked blow it pierced the Lord’s side, opening a deep and sunken wound through which blood and water flowed together.

O how closely this cause is joined to Catholic doctrine! O how greatly these sacred things accord with the faith of the Trinity! For body, blood, and water are the three gifts of our life. All of us who, under Christ our leader, are reborn in the fountain of water receive and eat his body and blood, and drink, so that we may deserve to be the temple of the Holy Spirit.

For the Apostle Paul speaks in this way, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Let us pray that the Lord may command us to carry an undefiled temple, so that he may make these narrow and frail bodies suitable and capable of housing so great a dweller.

[Col. 0737B] After that sacred place received the treasure of the precious body deposited there—a place that shone nobly while the Lord lay dead and triumphed more nobly when he rose again—the generation devoted to deceit, inventing its customary crime in an impious heart, spread the claim that Christ would be removed by his disciples in the silence of night, so that, as he himself had foretold, it might be announced that he had risen on the third day—[Col. 0737D] all printed editions read *haec*; *hac* seems preferable.

The Jews, therefore, terrified by this suspicion of theft, demand that a very large guard be more carefully assigned, and that the doors and entrance of the tomb be surrounded by a thoroughly reliable watch.

If, after the bitter sufferings of the cross, after the blows of iron and the wounds, after the mortal burial of the body, you have not yet fulfilled your bloody executioners’ duty, and if, after the death of the innocent, you have not satisfied your unjust hatred—[Col. 0737D] most printed editions read *saturatis*; Gallandius reads *saturastis*, which is more suitable. What follows is sufficiently obscure and apparently corrupt—then, since you do not believe that the Lord, who so often by his singular power brought souls out of the underworld, would instead call back his own, carry out councils suited to your worse purpose. Foster in your hearts deceit armed with the nourishment of treachery; seal the barriers of the tomb; place military watches; close the monument with a stone; arrange everything with the malicious plans you are accustomed to make.

Then say: “Who will be able to guard the Lord, for whom everything is opened and nothing is obstructed? He reigns in heaven, commands the seas, and rules the underworld.”

What need, then, have the faithless of watchmen and labor? Why do you strive to discover an end that you do not wish to admit, even when you are shown it?—[Col. 0738D] Juretus restored this passage in this way, since the manuscript exemplar read: “how noble you are also proved to admit losing. Meanwhile … to shine upon the feasts that belong to the Lord.”

[Col. 0739A] Meanwhile that sad day after the Sabbath had begun to shine forth, a blessed day which, because the Lord ruled over it, took its name from his majesty and was called “the Lord’s Day.” For it attained such honor that it was the first to behold the origin of the world’s birth and the power of the risen Christ.

For the Book of Genesis, the manifest witness to events, says that on the seventh day of the Sabbath God rested from his works. It therefore clearly appears that this day is the head of the world: it is counted as the seventh day of the Sabbath, established first in order. The glory of the eternal King, illuminating it also with the trophy of his resurrection, judged that it should retain the primacy granted to all the days in religious observance.

At the visible rising of this light, the virgin mother, faithfully gathered together with the other women, came to the tomb carrying spices as a shared offering. She furrowed her face with tears and shook her breast with groans. Soon they saw that the place of burial was empty, open now without the body, yet overflowing with wondrous power.

For an angel had descended from heaven and, after the tombstone had been rolled away from the entrance, sat upon the astonishing stone. His face was fiery and his clothing white, so that, shining with this double distinction, he might display both terror and joy: terror, threatening the guards with his fiery face; joy, delighting those who sought Christ with the gladness of his snow-white garment.

Thus, strengthened by the angelic revelation, the women rejoiced that the Lord had come back to life after death. The soldiers, terrified by such a vision, could not preserve their lives while placed in this perilous crisis. They immediately abandoned their post and hurried headlong back to the city, reporting the miracles and openly announcing them—[Col. 0739D] in the old manuscript Juretus found *miracula perserentes* and argued that this should be read, as in Paulinus of Périgueux, *Sevit* in Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*, and in our text *miracula plurima terris*, where others have *suevit*. Sedulius’ poem better supports *perferentes*—but, after selling their faith for money, they exchanged it for cowardly falsehood and soon pretended that Christ’s disciples had ambushed them during the night’s rest and carried him away.

Tell us, impious and wicked guard—speak, criminal band—what do you intend to assert? In your eagerness to obtain money, you do not see the pit into which you are falling, and you do not understand how much punishment you deserve, since you prefer to appear negligent rather than truthful.

It is evident that you were fully awake, attentive, and watchful; you never lowered your eyes into sleep except when another colleague properly took your place in relieving the labor. You had secured the place with such vigilance that it appeared impossible for anyone to approach it by deceit.

For if Christ, as you dare to compose in your false report, was snatched from the tomb during the night, while his followers slept, whose linen cloths are there? Whose wrappings lie beside him? Around whose remains does the angelic power sit? Did the man who carried away the blessed body first strip and uncover it, thinking it could be removed more quickly when exposed than when it remained bound as it was?

“Wickedness has lied to itself” (Psalm 26:12).

Yet this matter has a splendid grace in its figurative meaning. For it is established that Christ was taken away spiritually from the Jews, while we carry him with complete devotion of mind and heart.

Mourn, therefore, O Judaea, your priests; mourn your ministers and your people. Abandoned on account of such crimes, you will no longer rejoice with the trumpet, be strengthened by the Anointed One, or enjoy sacrifices.

For with what hope of power will the trumpet sound for you, when you see the king slain? What Anointed One will be given to you any longer, when you have lost the sovereignty of the Anointed One himself? What victim will be struck, when the shepherd himself has been slain as the victim?

[Col. 0742C] Let the synagogue depart, already darkened in its own color. Christ has joined to himself the beautiful Church in snowy splendor.

She grants honor to Mary for glory. Though she is always seen to be a mother, conspicuous in radiance, she is nevertheless always seen to be a virgin. Immediately after the triumph of the resurrection, the Lord showed himself to her, so that this devout mother, kind and destined to proclaim the testimony of such a miracle—she who had been the gate of his birth when he came into the world—might also be its messenger when he departed from the underworld.

Soon afterward he took part in a meal with certain people, like a traveler passing by, and revealed himself to their minds and eyes in the breaking of bread. For by their eyes it became known that he himself is the true bread: faith, implanted and unveiled within them, led them by the brightness of grace to recognition of the Lord.

He also showed himself visibly to the disciples at different times and moments: now appearing unexpectedly while they were eating, now taking food—roasted fish and honeycomb—so that he might demonstrate more clearly that the foods were bodily food, which he proved by eating before their eyes, and that he now possessed the same limbs that he had possessed shortly before, before his death.

Again, when the apostles were afraid to endure the violent cruelty of the people who had often denied the Lord, they remained behind closed and barred doors. He suddenly stood at the doors and gave peace to all in his greeting, granting sudden joy to those in distress and confirming what had been signified by the prophetic voice: “The Lord will not despise a contrite and humbled heart.”

Then he opened his pierced hands and uncovered the wound driven into his side, lest they should believe him to be a phantom if they did not see the marks of the wounds.

But because the equally venerable apostle Thomas, whom they call by the name Didymus, was not there and did not believe what his companions reported, behold, when he afterward was sitting with the brothers, the Lord once again presented himself before the unmoved doors. He had never spiritually departed from them, and, appearing in the midst before them all, did not disdain to accommodate himself to the trembling disciple.

Having shown his palms and side again, he allowed himself to be tested by the touch of the wounds, and was recognized more clearly as the Christ himself, who had received the doubting soul and nourished it with gentle calm.

For whoever practices the tricks of an artificer under the blind appearance of deceit, constructing empty mists and shapes to deceive unsuspecting minds, does not want his deeds to be recognized. He hides beneath the covering of deceptive cloud, mocks miserable eyes with contrived apparitions, and hates vigilant people and friends when he begins to be detected—[Col. 0745D] all printed editions read *et amictos*. Gallandius says that the word seems suspect. Why should it? The correction is clear and certain from the verse: “the simulator hates vigilant friends.” The prose adds *et*, namely, that he also hates vigilant friends. Shortly afterward the old manuscript had *dubitandi* instead of *dubitanti*, and *abigenti* instead of *ambigenti*. Juretus supplied the necessary corrections.

But the true Christ, in all things truthful and exceedingly gentle toward the one who doubted whether he should believe, does not grow angry with the uncertain man. Rather, he readily permits him to insert his fingers into the wounds, knowing that the example of this testing was intended not only for Thomas, who was so blessed, but for the faith of many thereafter.

A few days later, the Lord again showed himself to Peter, who was fishing with his companions by the shore of the sea. Seeing that, after the labor of the entire night, the exhausted men had caught nothing—*perpili* is the old manuscript reading, which Juretus suspects to be corrupt and conjectures as *pervigili* or *perpeti*. In his notes, Gallandius found Juretus’ text corruptly printed as *perti* and thought this might perhaps stand for *pertinaci*. But the Paris Bibliotheca Patrum of 1589 clearly reads *perpeti*. Gallandius preferred *labore perpero*, that is, “with fruitless or unsuccessful labor.” I think the passage should be expanded. Below, “through the waves of the age” also seems corrupt. Soon perhaps one should read “by Catholic reasoning”—he ordered the nets to be cast immediately on the right side into the deep. When they had been plunged into the salt waters of the whirlpool, the noisy nets brought up their folds with the catch, which they joyfully cast at the Lord’s feet.

This kind of miracle should not be understood as an ordinary event but weighed through typological interpretation. Let us believe that the nets signify exceedingly clear and evident commands, by which all who follow the right hand are enclosed and brought low amid the bloody tracks of the world’s waves.

The fish placed upon the coals, together with the bread found by them in the same place, is likewise understood, according to Catholic belief, not to be without meaning. The fish appears to signify the water in which we are certainly washed and reborn; the bread signifies Christ the Savior, whose body we eat for salvation. The fire bears the image of the Holy Spirit, by whom we are consecrated in devotion to the faith. He appeared and shone forth in this same form when, as the Book of Acts testifies, he flooded the blessed apostles with the radiance of his divinity.

Then he invites them to take food with the peaceful words of a solemn command. Gathered together in unity at the Lord’s table by his voice, they receive food of holy blessing and recognize Christ in the full truth of faith.

[Col. 0749A] When they had risen and been suitably filled with a modest meal, the Lord mercifully asked Peter whether he loved him. When Peter immediately answered yes, the Lord, wishing to increase the flocks like a good shepherd, entrusted his sheep and lambs to him as to an exceedingly faithful laborer and proven servant.

He repeated and revisited the question three times, so that the threefold denial might be cleansed by an equal number of professions of love, corresponding to the recent fault.

That he granted Peter in particular the dignity of feeding the flocks, although he is proved to love everyone equally, does not concern the detriment of others but seems connected with reason. For this most gentle animal, because of its natural simplicity, is compared with the just, whom the King of all, when he comes in his majesty, addresses as they stand at his right hand:

“Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” and so forth.

Thus he appropriately entrusts those just people who are to enter the kingdom to the one to whom he had promised that he would give the keys of that same kingdom.

Then, teaching them with blessed instructions and strengthening them through the peaceful tradition of doctrine, he commanded them to spread the precepts of the devout faith throughout all lands and to extend to all nations the one Trinity of sacred baptism, speaking and decreeing as follows:

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you,” and so forth.

When the Divinity had commanded everything to be fulfilled, he soon led them all together out toward Bethany. In the presence of the blessed men who were deemed worthy to behold such a great triumph, he was carried upward through the heavenly regions, ascended to the citadel of celestial dominion, and sat at the right hand of the majesty of the Fatherland, ruling and governing everything according to his own will.

Possessing all heights and depths forever, he descended from heaven to Tartarus and, after Tartarus, returned to heaven.

For this reason he wished to migrate to the stars in the presence of these men—as far as he deigns to disclose it to the understanding of my smallness—in order to show them the road by which they were to follow him. Before his Passion they had said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” He answered them clearly and said:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

The way, because through him one reaches the grace of the Father. The truth, because he grants believers what he promises. The life, because those whom he adopts are not subject to death.

Therefore, gazing with joyful faces upon the Lord exalted above the clouds, treading with his own feet upon the shining courses of the stars after conquering the world, the disciples reverently venerated and worshiped him. With most welcome return to his household, they turned over in their hearts the regions of the aerial path that they had seen with their eyes, and all carried the report to men of every race, so that the nations might believe.

For they are proved to be faithful witnesses and great witnesses to divine power: although they saw the deeds of the Lord Jesus Christ, they wrote down only a small portion of his innumerable acts. For if all the miracles of our Savior could have been attached to pious writings, perhaps even the world itself, as the Evangelist John testifies, would not have contained all the volumes that would have been written.

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703A] **Notes**

1. In *Reg. 2*, where the Lord asks the Father to glorify him by the word. *Ott. 1*: “Christ’s prayer to the Father.” For “miracles,” the Christian poet commonly uses *virtus* and *virtutes*. Paulinus likewise says *opem virtutis* in *The Life of Saint Martin*, Book V, line 215; Dracontius uses *opem libertatis* and *opem sapientiae*.

2. Petrus Burmannus the Younger, in *Anthologia veterum Latinorum epigrammatum*, Book I, p. 87, conjectures *ire dies*. The prose text, however, gives *esse*. In my manuscript the error is *Dominus*.

3. *Vívam*, that is, “immortal,” taken from sacred Scripture.

5. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book LIII, chapter 3, cites *remeans* instead of *relevans*. Barthius’ manuscript has *ducit*, from which Barthius conjectures *ducat*. *Alm.*, *Reg. 5*, Aldus, and Arntz read *vexit*, which more recent editors approve; but our oldest books prefer *duxit*.

Nebrissensis did not sufficiently attend to the meter and sense when he commented as follows: “From the infernal groves, not because there are trees among the dead, but he alluded to the etymology of the word *lucus*, as though it meant ‘deprived of light’: Virgil, Book VI, ‘We dwell in shadowy groves.’” But, as I have said, sense and meter require *lucis* to be the genitive case of *lux, lucis*.

6. The *Codex Burmannianus*, *Reg. 1* above, *Reg. 2*, *Alb.*, *Ang.*, and *Vat. 2* read *istac*; others read *ista*. *Ott. 1* has *ab hora*, which the prose and the words of the Gospel confirm, and which more recent editors follow; most manuscripts and printed editions, however, have *in hora*.

7. *Alm.* and *Reg. 1* have *Salvifica* in the text. In the margin of *Reg. 1*, in place of *d. s.*, appears *Clarifica*, which is the common reading; above *Salvifica* stands the gloss *glorifica*. On the basis of the prose text and the Gospel, *Salvifica* seems preferable.

8. Manuscripts and printed editions vary extraordinarily in this verse [Col. 0703D]. Reg. 5 and Aldus read: “Clarify, he said, your name, and high in heaven,” with hiatus in *tuum*. Cappusotus and Parrhasius: “Clarify your name, he said, and great in heaven.” Cantabrigiensis, Poelman, and Fabricius: “Clarify your name, and very great in heaven.” Some older editions read: “Clarify, he said, your name, and very great in heaven,” by which arrangement the verse becomes one foot too long. Poelman’s sheets: “Clarify your name, he said, and very great in heaven.” Barthius’s manuscript and the Leipzig edition: “Clarify, he said, the name; then great in heaven,” where *que* is redundant (*παρελκόν*), as Barthius notes, something found even in the best writers.

This variation arose from synaeresis, which created difficulty for ignorant scribes in the true reading. That true reading is found in most of our manuscripts—Reg. 1 and 2, Vat. 1 and 2, Ott. 1 and 2, Rom., Meus, Urb., and Ang.—and apparently by correction in Alb.; also in the very oldest manuscript, that of Turin, as well as in Alm. and Lips.: “Clarify, he said, your name, and great in heaven.” Here *tuum* is monosyllabic, by the poetic license that I explained in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius* and occasionally in the notes to Juvencus.

Cellarius, Vonckius, and Wopkensius attribute to Bede the reading “Clarify, he said, the name, whose great [name is] in heaven.” Yet in the edition I use I find: “Clarify, he said, your name, and great in heaven”; and this also appears to have been the reading of Bede’s anonymous commentator in a Vatican manuscript that I have seen. He quotes the Redeemer’s actual words from John 12:28: “Father, clarify your name.”

Bede had said that Sedulius placed the order of secular prosody second, so as to preserve the Redeemer’s words. He thinks that Sedulius inserted into the fourth position of this verse an amphimacer, or cretic, foot, consisting of three syllables—long, short, and long. I cannot accept this, since a spondee can be admitted in the fourth position, with *tuum* contracted by synaeresis. Thus, among Putsch’s grammarians, *cujus* is printed erroneously instead of *tuum* in Bede’s work.

More recent editors have pursued several conjectures, for the most part inept ones, which I can scarcely bring myself even briefly to mention after establishing the true reading from the manuscripts. Wonckius: “Clarify, he said, the name, gracious one, and great in heaven.” Wopkensius: “Clarify, he said, the name, divine and great in heaven”; or “Clarify, he said, the name now, and great in heaven”; or “Clarify, he said, the name, very great in heaven”; or “Clarify, he said, the name, greater”; “and great in heaven.” Arntzenius: “Clarify, he said, your name; and great in heaven.” In his text, however, Arntzenius retained the more common manuscript reading, following Cellarius.

10. Reg. 1, Vatt. 1 and 2, Arntz. in the first hand, and Ottob. 1 read *Clarificemque*; and a gloss in Reg. 1 notes that the future subjunctive is often used for the future indicative. In Ott. 1, the reading may previously have been *Clarificabo*. In Reg. 2 there is *Clarificabo*, though it seems formerly to have been *Clarificemque*; for *clarificabo* is also read as the gloss, and this gloss occurs in Vat. 1 beside the word *Clarificemque*. The second hand in Arntz. gave *Clarificabo*, which some manuscripts, together with Ang., Alb., and nearly all printed editions, adopt. [Col. 0705B] The third hand in the same Arntz. has *Clarificans*, as do Parrhasius and Poelman’s sheets.

I consider *Clarificabo* the more authentic reading. Perhaps *Clarificemque* was written by a scribe who thought the conjunction *-que* necessary. Another may judge that copyists changed *Clarificemque* into *Clarificabo* because the latter is clearer. In Vet. 1 there is the error *Clarificemque* again; more plainly: something is missing.]

### 310

Amid these resources of virtue, the day of Easter

had already begun to draw near, when the Lord in glory

wished to lay down mortal flesh and take up living flesh again—

not another flesh, but once more that same flesh,

[5] which, rich in light, he raised from the realms below

and led to the stars.

[Col. 0704A] And crying aloud in public: “Father, save me from this hour;

yet for this reason I have come to this hour.”

### 311

“Clarify,” he said, “your name;” and a voice resounding

through the clouds came from heaven: “I have clarified it,

[10] and I will clarify it again.” What could be clearer,

with the Father himself bearing witness,

[Col. 0705A] [Note: [Col. 0705C]

11. Most manuscripts have *ac nec*; some printed editions *at nec*. Grunerus preferred *nec* instead of *ne*. All our manuscripts read *agnoscere*, except the recent Reg. 5, which has *cognoscere*. Grunerus and Arntzenius prefer the latter with Cant., Ald., and other printed editions. Grunerus falsely attributes to Barthius the claim that his manuscript had *coelum* instead of *Christum*. Barthius, however, reports and defends from his own manuscript the reading *nec sic agnoscere*. He then explains that *coelum* in the preceding words, “with heaven as witness,” means God, as in Petronius: “No one thinks heaven [to be responsible].” Nebrissensis says that a masculine is used for a neuter, as in *tempus repertor*.

12. Arntz. has *suum*; others, following the prose text, *Deum*. Vat. 1, for *d. s.*, had *pars una*, which is not unacceptable.

13. Most have *crepuisse*; Reg. 1 *increpuisse*, which seems more elegant. Although the singular ablative is *tonitru*, and the dative and ablative plural *tonitribus*, *tonitrus, tonitri* is declined as a masculine noun, or *tonitruum, tonitrui*.

15. The manuscripts Alm., Arntz., Barth., and most of ours, together with Parrhasius and other printed editions, read *Num tonitrus*. Meus, Vat. 2, Cant., and certain editions have *Non tonitrus*, which Grunerus and Arntzenius printed because the sense is smoother and supported by the prose. Ott. 2 has the error *Numen tonitrus*. Rom. may have *retine potuit*. Most manuscripts and editions have *seu angelus*, with hiatus; others *sive angelus*.

16. Vat. 1 and Meus have *generare*; others *generasse*, which may also formerly have stood in Vat. 1.

17. In Reg. 1 the reading was *Auditore sponsa daret*; corrected to *Audito responsa daret*. In my manuscript this passage too is corrupt: *Audito response dato*.

20. Reg. 1: “Concerning the time when he washed the disciples’ feet.” Arntz. and Ott. 2 have *celebrans convivia coenae*, which receives metrical support from the prose. Thus *dapes* is an accusative in apposition. Meus has *celebrans pro munere coenae*; the others *celebrans per munera coenae*.

21. All manuscripts and editions have *ministrum*, except the very ancient Turin manuscript, which has *magistrum*. This can be defended to some extent from John 13:13 ff.: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am. If therefore I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example,” and so forth. In manuscripts *minister* and *magister* are often confused, although in reality they differ greatly. Urb. has the error *ministerium*, but it formerly had another reading.

22. *Exempla* instead of *exemplum*: see the note on Dracontius III.314.

23. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *famulatus*; in Reg. 1, however, the correction is *famulatur*, although the gloss *obediens ipse alterum* still indicates *famulatus*. Vat. 1 has *famulatur*, but formerly had another reading; the gloss *deserviens* argues for *famulatus*. In some other manuscripts it is uncertain whether *famulatur* or *famulatus* should be read. The sense is complete either way; in the editions I find only *famulatur*. Wopkensius willingly explains it as *benigne* and gives similar passages from other authors; in those passages, however, *libens* can equally mean *readily* or *voluntarily*.

24. Vat. 2 has *inclinaret honorem*; this should be corrected to *inclinavit*.

25. *Vestigia* sometimes, as here, means the soles themselves; elsewhere it means footprints impressed upon a place.

26. Ott. 2 has *Nec Judam sprevit*; others *Nec Judam exciperet*, which the tense of the preceding *ut* requires. The prose proceeds in the same way.]

28. Meus has the corrupt reading *vela* instead of *illa*. Urb. has *dabit*; retain *dabat*. In some printed editions *nudis* appears instead of *mundis*, an error.

30. In Reg. 1, Ottob. 1, and perhaps also Reg. 2 the reading was *velamine*, but everywhere it was corrected to *velamina*, which is correct, although the other form could also be defended. Reg. 1 has the gloss *tegumenta*. On such white coverings of tombs, see the note on Juvencus IV.74.

31. Ott. 2 has *internis*, and someone cites this verse in that form. The common reading *interius* is confirmed by the prose. Ott. 2 has *plenum est*; the others omit the substantive verb, as is often done elegantly. In Reg. 2 *ex pleno* was rightly changed to *plenum*.

32. Reg. 1: “Concerning Judas, who, being a thief, betrayed him.” Barthius, *Adversaria* LIII.3, cites *nefandi* instead of *futuri*, against the prose. Urb. has *futurum*, less suitably. Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* I.134: “Nor were the tricks hidden from his brother,” and so forth.

33. Parrhasius and Poelman’s sheets have *Edidit*, which Barthius preferred in the cited passage from his own manuscript. Grunerus and Arntzenius nevertheless contend that *Prodidit* is much better. Ang. has *Protulit*. In manuscripts *prodere* and *edere* are frequently interchanged.

37. Most manuscripts have *Esurient, sitientque*; others *Esuriant, sitiantque*, which the prose supports. The printed editions vary similarly. You may follow whichever you prefer. Vat. 1 has *fidelis*, following the old orthography in which *fideles* is written *fideleïs* and *fidelis*. You see that Sedulius too clearly explains the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist, so that the heretics who call it into question are plainly fools.

39. *Arma* means devices, or the art of causing harm, as elsewhere and in Virgil: “and, knowing guilt, to seek weapons.”

41. Cant. and Ott. 1 in the text, and Reg. 1 as a correction, have *quavis*. Ott. 1, as a correction, together with the others, has *parva*. In the text of Reg. 1, where *parva* now stands, there was formerly another reading. Grunerus prefers *quavis* with the prose; Arntzenius disagrees because Judas carried out this crime not for any random but for a definite small payment. Yet this argument would imply that the prose too should not read *sub qualibet mercede*. I therefore follow Grunerus, because Sedulius expresses Matthew 26:15: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” Arntzenius writes *neque illi* according to grammatical rules; most of our manuscripts and the printed editions have *nec illi*, disregarding such rules, as often elsewhere.

42. Reg. 2 has *sed haerent*, not improperly according to the orthography of Sedulius’s age, when *h* often had consonantal force. Above, however, *sed inhaerent* is written.

43. Meus has *Tantum idem sceleris*; read *Tantumdem sceleris*. In Reg. 1 *numismata* has been corrected from *nomismata*. Most of our manuscripts have *numismata*. I discussed this orthographic variation in the notes to Prudentius and Juvencus.

44. Meus has *Argento*; retain *Argenti*.

46. Arntz. in the first hand and Meus have *aethrem*; Rom. and Ott. 2 *aetherem*, against the meter; Vat. 1 and Alb. *aethra*, which may be the true reading instead of *aethera* by contraction. See the note on Juvencus II.532. Most have *aethram*. This verse is missing from the Ang. manuscript.

47. Meus has *neque jam bona*, less suitably; Vat. 1, against the meter, *neque bona*.

48. Cant. and some printed editions have *magno*; the others more correctly *magni*. Meus, with the order reversed, has *pro fuso*.

50. Reg. 2 as a correction and Parrhasius have *ventre*; others, following the prose, *matre*. Urb. corruptly has *morte*. “How,” asks Nebrissensis, “could he have been condemned if he had not been born?” He answers: because that very nonexistence would not have been the evil which he later brought about. The sense itself is clearer once these subtleties are removed.]

[Col. 0709A] [Note: [Col. 0709B]

52. Aldus has *Auxisset*; correct to *Hauxisset*. Barthius, *Adversaria* LIII.3, cites *fibris* instead of *flabris*. The common reading is *flabris*, to which the error *fabris* in Urb. corresponds.

53. Meus and Parrh. wrongly have *torpere*, and Rom. *corpore* instead of *torpore*. Barthius philosophizes too subtly about this eternal torpor, concluding that it is the ignorance of mortals and the nothingness that has never existed at all. But, as I said concerning Nebrissensis, whoever does not understand Sedulius’s verse and prose will understand such interpretations even less.

54. Arntz. in the second hand and Parrhasius have *nescisse* instead of *nescire*. Most insert *nescire datam, quam perdere vitam*; some *nescire, datam quam perdere vitam*.

55. The Leipzig manuscript, Meus, and Vat. 2 have *homo*; most have *humo*. The latter is understood from the ancient custom by which a newborn infant was placed on the ground, so that the father might lift it into his lap. Yet *homo*, which also occurs in the ancient Turin manuscript, may be the more authentic reading. Sedulius seems to have wished to retain Matthew 26:24: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed; it would have been good for that man if he had not been born.” Poets commonly use *fusus* for “born.” The prose explains it as “as soon as he deserved to be begotten,” which can suit either reading.

57. Ott. 1 has *auctus*, correctly amended to *actus*. The phrase is scriptural: “From the face of the earth.” See the note on Dracontius II.457.

59. Poelman has *Invectio in Judam*; Meus *Apostrophat*. Meus has *ferox Judas, insane*; the others *audax* instead of *Judas*. Bede too, who praises this verse in his *On the Art of Meter*, reads *audax*. In the prose there is no distinction of heading here, just as elsewhere the prose differs from the manuscript copies of the poem, and those copies themselves differ from one another.

61. Critical scholars dispute the word *traditor*, asking whether Tacitus used it for “traitor.” Tertullian and other ancient Christian writers certainly do not avoid it.

[Col. 0710B] 62. Meus has *Primus et horribiles*, namely, “the first and standard-bearer of your companions.” Alb. and Reg. 1 have *horribilis*. Ott. 1 likewise had this, but it was corrected to *horribiles*.

63. Poelman’s sheets have *manum* instead of *aciem*. Meus has *sudibusque minantem*.

64. Alm., Arntz., Parrhasius, Ottob. 1, Alb., and many printed editions have *Commoveas*. This also stood in Reg. 2, but was corrected to *Cum moveas*, or *Cummoveas*, as it is also written in Reg. 1, with the gloss *cum sollicites*. Meus corruptly has *Commoves*; most have *Cum moveas*, which the sense requires. Manuscripts and editions variously have *ori ora*; Reg. 5 and Aldus have *ore ora*, also found in the second hand of Arntz. and in Poelman’s sheets. Grunerus and Arntzenius choose this because it is not Latin to say *ori ora premere*. Certainly *ore ora premere* is more Latin, but I would not readily condemn the other. Vat. 1 has *premes*, corrected to *premis*. Parrhasius has *premens*, because he previously printed *Commoveas*. Rom. had *mellisque*; Poelman has the error *melleque* instead of *mellique*.

65. Most of our manuscripts have *et blanda Dominum*; Arntzenius, reversing the order, printed *et Dominum blanda*, following others.

66. Wopkensius tried to adjust this verse in the following ways: “Why, pretending to be a companion, do you greet him with hostile deceit?”—that is, pretending to be his companion and greeting him; or, “Why do you pretend to be a companion and greet him with a friendly face?”; or, “Why do you pretend to be a companion and greet him with blind deceit?” Yet from the prose Wopkensius himself recognized that the manuscript reading is genuine. Arntz., Reg. 5, and Aldus have *amicum*; others, with the prose, *amica*, that is, “under the appearance of friendship.”

67. Barthius’s manuscript, Cant., and Aldus have *Numquam*; some manuscripts obscurely have *Numquam* or *Numquid*. Barthius, Grunerus, and Arntzenius prefer *Numquam* with the prose. Most, and the best manuscripts, have *Numquid*, which produces the same meaning as a question and is no less elegant. Moreover, one should not cling so closely to the prose as to prefer its reading to another more graceful reading, supported by the finest ancient copies.]

69. Aldus: “Jesus restored the ear of Malchus after it had been cut off.” Barthius takes *operator* as “worker,” never idle; Wopkensius more suitably takes it as “beneficent, generous,” since *operatio* can also mean almsgiving. On this word see the commentary on Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 573.

[Col. 0711C] 70. Some printed editions have *linquit*. *Puero*, that is, “servant,” in its familiar sense.

71. Reg. 1 and Meus have *vocaret*, but in Reg. 1 it was correctly amended to *vacaret*. This phrase also occurs in IV.196. Arator I.862, elsewhere 807: “That he may never be lacking in devotion.” From the prose it seems that *nequa* should mean “at no time.” It may also mean “in no way” or “by no means.”

73. For this expression, *millia legiones*, one may consult Parrhasius’s judgment in the *Prolegomena*, no. 189. Livy nevertheless speaks similarly at times, for example XXXIV.52 near the middle: “fourteen thousand gold coins of Philip,” and XXXIX.5; also Columella V.1.

74. Ott. 2 has *possit* instead of *posset*.

77. *Parci mucrone*: compare Dracontius, *Satisfactio*, verse 157: “He spared him with the sword.”

78. Parrhasius has *nec*; the others more correctly *non*. Meus in the text has *quemquam*; as a correction, *cuiquam*. Vat. 2, in an abbreviation, has *quemqaum* or *quidquam*; only *cuiquam* should be retained. On the expression *ponere animam*, see the note on Juvencus I.611.

79. Aldus: “Jesus foretold to Peter that he would deny him.” Arntzenius attributes to his manuscript Arntz. in the first hand and Torn. 1 the reading *Jam Petro*; the Cantabrigian manuscript and Arntz. in the second hand have *Namque Petro*; in the text he printed *Jamque Petro*. I do not know whether *Jamque* was deliberately supplied or whether it dropped out of the typesetter’s text in place of *Namque*. More and better of our manuscripts have *Namque*; others, with Parrhasius and Aldus, *Jamque*.

80. Barthius takes the words of Isidore’s glossary, *Alliger, gallus*, as a gloss on this passage. Here, however, *aliger* is an epithet appositional to the nominative *gallus*, not a gloss. Perhaps Isidore’s gloss merely indicates that the epithet *aliger* is suitable to a cock.

[Col. 0712C] 82. Reg. 2 and Ott. 1, as well as Meus, against meter and sense, have *praedicando*. In Reg. 2 and Ottob. 1 it was correctly corrected to *praedicendo*.

83. Aldus: “Jesus was led into the house of Caiaphas.” Meus: *Ducitur ad Caipham*. Barthius’s manuscript, Poelman’s sheets, and Parrhasius have *Protinus* or *Protenus*; the others *Continuo*. The prose has *mox*. For *ad tristes*, Reg. 5 and Aldus have *ad vastas*, which Nebrissensis retained to indicate the magnificence of Caiaphas’s house. Sedulius intended something else, as is clear from the best copies.

85. Parrhasius has *hic*; Meus *hac*; read *hoc*.

86. *Pestifera* comes from Psalm 1: “He has not sat in the seat of pestilence.”

87. Parrhasius and Vet. 1 have *Consilium*; retain *Concilium*.

88. Vatt. 2, Reg. 5, Cant., and Aldus have *labellis*. Alm. has *fabellis*. Most of our manuscripts—Ang., Alb., Reg. 1 and 2, Ottob. 1 and 2, Vat. 1, Urb., Rom., Meus—as well as the Leipzig manuscripts, Arntz., Parrhasius, and the oldest other editions, have *favillis*. Nic. Heinsius, in his note on Prudentius, *Hymns* II, *Peristephanon* II.318, conjecturally corrected this to *conflata cavillis*; Cellarius, Grunerus, and Arntzenius adopted the correction. Grunerus did not dislike *fabellis*, unless it was contrary to the meter. It could nevertheless be defended to some extent by the similar example from an epigram attributed to St. Damasus in a manuscript of the Angelica Library: “I have not devised false tales with empty zeal.” In any case, there is no reason to depart from the common manuscript reading *favillis*, since Sedulius himself most clearly confirms it in the prose.]

89. Most have *Et*; some printed editions *Quae*. Barthius, *Adversaria* LIII.3, substituted *At*; Arntzenius preferred *Sed*, if anyone disliked *Et*. Parrhasius, omitting *et*, printed *Depereunt*. Barthius’s manuscript, Cantabr., and Meus have *sua*, which Arntzenius falsely attributes also to Aldus; Aldus, with the others, retains *sui*, which is correct.

90. Barthius’s manuscript, Arntz. in the second hand, Poelman’s sheets, Parrhasius, and Ott. 2 have *vis est cui*; the others *vires cui*, which the prose supports and explains. Barthius attempts in vain to disentangle the former reading.

91. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *victaeque furore*; read *victoque*.

93. Aldus: “Jesus was struck with blows and palms.” Wopkensius says the punctuation should be: “the arms are raised—he arms [them] against the innocent,” that is, the arms are raised, according to the very common use of the infinitive. Then *armat* means that he arms them, namely the men. Arntzenius conjectures: “he raises his arms—and weapons against the innocent.” In the Lyon Library, by what I believe is an error, the reading is *brachia tollit—arma in insontem*. Vet. 1, Parrhasius, and Poelman’s sheets have *hei* instead of *heu*.

94. Vet. 1 and 2 and Mon., against meter and sense, have *Armat insontem*.

95. Arntz., Vet. 1, Ottob. 1, Urb., and Rom. have *rapidum*; in Ottob. 1 it was correctly corrected to *rabidum*. Wopkensius punctuates: “to recall the raging tumult—did sacrilegious hands move?” That is, *memorare tumultum*, “to recall the tumult,” namely the crowd of men moving sacrilegious hands. Or the passage may be punctuated another way: “to recall the tumult—did sacrilegious hands move?” Here *movisse* means *moverunt*. Arntzenius approves only the first punctuation. If the prose did not suggest this very thing, I would think *movisse* should be joined with *quievit*: “the accursed crowd did not cease to move sacrilegious hands,” nor finally did it cease striking his head everywhere, and so forth.

96. Meus has *novisse*; as a correction, *meminisse*. The sense is thus smoother, but the remaining copies oppose it. Reg. 1 has the gloss *passim, leviter*, which does not suit this passage.

98. Someone cites *Vel spuere*, perhaps by accident, not deliberately. Quadrigarius too used *quiesco* with the infinitive, in Gellius IX.12: *Quiescerent pugnare*. Some old parchment manuscripts, however, read *Quiescerent pugnarum*.

99. *Totum* means “everything,” as in other writers of the later age and as we have explained elsewhere in Sedulius.

102. All our manuscripts, Parrhasius, Cappusotus, Aldus, the oldest editions, and the manuscripts Alm. and Arntz. have *Haec sputa per*. Poelman’s sheets rejected this because it is against the meter. Barthius, on Claudian IV, *Consulate of Honorius*, verse 617, cites *Sputa per haec*. More recent editors more readily changed it to *Sputa haec per*. But since the ancient manuscripts agree in the reading *Haec sputa per*, we should follow it. It is no more surprising that Sedulius shortened the first syllable of *sputa* than that he similarly made the first syllable of *jugis* and the second of *elutus* short. Some printed editions wrongly have *lavare* instead of *lavere*.

103. Parrhasius has *plaudit*. Rom. and Urb. have *crevit*, perhaps from some gloss. The true reading is *plausit*, according to the ancient custom by which freedom was conferred upon manumitted slaves through a slap and a clap on the cheeks, as is well known. Consult Isidore, *Etymologies* IX.3. Nebrissensis perhaps has something else in mind when he explains *plausit* as “he smiled upon.”

104. Reg. 1: “Peter’s denial.” Vat. 1 and 2 have *Et*; in Vat. 1 this was corrected to *At*. Vonckius conjectures *At Simon*, applauded by Wopkensius and Arntzenius. But the received, older reading is confirmed by the prose and by all the copies, and it also suits the event itself, since Peter was senior to the other disciples, leaving no room for the contrary conjecture. One who foretells future events is usually called their author. Juvencus I.233: “The Spirit, the author, foretold.” Prudentius, *Hymn* 13, *Peristephanon* verse 9: “That Spirit of God, who had flowed as author into the prophets.”

105. Barthius’s manuscript, Cant., Parrhasius, Poelman’s sheets, many old editions, and the prose have *nequibat*. Reg. 1 and Ott. 1 have *nequibit*; in Reg. 1 this became *nequibat*, and in Ott. 1 *nequivit*. Arntz., with many of our manuscripts, Aldus, and other editions, has *nequivit*.]

119. Meus corruptly has *In casum facti pretii*. In Reg. 1 *Incasum* was correctly made *Incassum*. Reg. 1 has *relinquit*; most have *reliquit*.

120. Fabr. has *Nam quid enim*; our manuscripts, two others cited by Barthius in *Adversaria* LIV.7, and most others have *Quidnam etenim*. Reg. 5, Ottob. 2, and Aldus have *timorem*; retain *timore*.

121. Alm. has *tetra*; the others correctly *tetro*. Meus corruptly has *tretro*.

122. The Leipzig manuscripts, Alm., Poelman’s sheets, Reg. 2 by correction, Ottob. 1 by correction, and many editions have *jam demersa*. Reg. 1 as a correction, Reg. 2 in the first hand, Reg. 1, Vatt. 1 and 2, Urb., Rom., Meus, Cant., Arntz., and obscurely Ang. have *dimersa*. Alb. has *dimissa*. In the text of Reg. 1, *demissa*; most editions likewise have *demissa* or *dimissa*. In the Leipzig edition and the Lyon Library copy, *diversa* may be an error. The verb *demergo* is elegantly used for plunging something deeply and with great force, as many examples establish.

124. Parrhasius has *gramina*, not *gramine*, as Arntzenius imputes to him. Meus corruptly has *gemina*; the true reading is *germina*. Alm. and Parrhasius have *vertit*, which recent editors follow; others *vertat*. In Reg. 2 *vertat* was corrected from *verat*. The prose supports this reading.

125. Barthius’s manuscript, the Leipzig edition, and recent editions have *ut*; others *et*: namely, “let it turn and perish.” Juvenal, *Satire* 10.145: “the barren evil strength of a fig tree.”

126. Barthius seems to have found *conceptus* somewhere instead of *correptus*; he conjectures *trucis correptus monte furoris*. Wopkensius, however, suspects *trucis completus mente furoris*, against the prose. The mind of savage fury is put for fury itself, or for a furious mind.

127. Cantabrigiensis, Reg. 1 in the text, and some editions have *quamquam*, which Grunerus and Arntzenius retain with the prose. Reg. 1 as a correction, together with most other manuscripts and editions, has *tamquam*. The former pleases me more. Rom. wrongly has *esse*. *Morte petere*, “to seek through death,” is an elegant and customary expression for “to kill.”

128. Meus has *percurreret*; the others *praecurreret*, although in some abbreviated manuscripts it could also be read *percurreret*. Urb. has *procurreret*. Barthius attempted *ulcisci nece curreret*; Grunerus *ulcisci praesumeret*. Change nothing.

131. Meus has *in alto*. Wopkensius speculated: *laqueis expelleret altis*, or *laqueo disperderet alto*, or *disperdidit*. The received reading must be retained, since *anima* here means the whole person, as often elsewhere.

[Col. 0718D] 132. Urb., Vat. 2, Ottob. 2, Rom., Meus, Barthius’s manuscript, the Leipzig edition, have *Levior ira*, from which Barthius conjectured *Ira quidem levior*, so that the verse would scan with *levior*. Reg. 1 also seems to have *Levior ira*, but formerly had another reading; above it has the gloss, or correction, *mitior*. The common reading, *Lenior ira quidem*, need not be disturbed. Meus, Parrhasius, Arntz. in the second hand, and many editions have *tantae*; most of our manuscripts, together with Aldus and other printed editions, have *tanto*.]

He left behind in vain the price of the deed, not the deed itself.

[120] For what does it profit to tremble there with fear,

where no fear exists? Or what confession shines in the dark

underworld, when the axe, already buried at the roots

of the accursed tree that produced the deadly fruit,

turns its lethal shoots completely to destruction,

[125] and evil tree-trunks perish in fires they deserve?

### 325

Immediately seized by a mind of savage fury,

[Col. 0718A] he sought his own death as well. Yet he would have been saner then,

if he had hastened to avenge the crime, and the very throat

of the dreadful voice, which had dared to sell the Redeemer

of the whole world, tightening the wretched soul

[130] in knotted jaws, had strangled it with a noose hanging high.

A milder wrath indeed for the crime of so great a fault—

a fault for which no punishment could have been equal among all evils.

### 326

Yet this manner of death, and the lofty corpse,

[135] displayed to the peoples from what height he had fallen,

[Col. 0719A] [Note: [Col. 0719B]

136. Some printed editions have *qui est nunc reus*; most manuscripts and other editions more elegantly omit *est*.

137. Ott. 1 has *descenderat usque*; the later hand, with others, *descendit ad usque*.

138. Vat. 2 has *nunc vir apostata*; read *nunc vilis*.]

139. Aldus: “The Jews brought against Jesus the charge that he had said he was a king.” Arntzenius says that Sedulius was mistaken in calling Pilate a governor (*praeses*). But Sedulius uses the wording of our Vulgate and of several Latin Fathers; whatever the historical situation, it remains to be asked whether, before the time of Claudius, the *praefectus* of Judaea bore the title *praeses*. See Calmet, *Biblical Dictionary*, under “Governor.”

140. Cellarius explains *jugulum* as the place of strangulation in the index. But there are many examples in which *jugulus* or *jugulum* means death, killing, or strangulation, as in Prudentius, Paulinus of Pétra, Saxo Grammaticus, Abbo, and even Manilius IV.128: “And it will yield its fruits for slaughter.”

141. Vat. 1 reads *insonti sanguine* (“innocent blood”); the reading of the others, *insontis*, is better.

142. Barthius’s manuscript, Poelman’s papers, Vet. 1 and 2, Mon. and other printed editions read *comperiens*; all our manuscripts, and others alongside Parrhasius and Aldus, read *reperiens* or *repperiens*, so that the first syllable is understood to be long. My manuscript, Ott. 1 by correction, Vat. 1, and Reg. 1 and 2 in the text read *dixerit*; other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read *dixerat*.

143. Alm. and Urb. read *dicit*, which may perhaps have stood in Ott. 1, where the present reading, as in most copies, is *ducit*. Alb. and Rom. read *duxit*. The gloss in Reg. 1 has *ducit*, “he balances.”

144. The manuscripts Reg. 1, 2, and 5, Vat. 1 and 2, Parrhasius, and Aldus read *impia*. In Reg. 1, in a later hand, there is *perfida*, which seems to be a gloss in Reg. 2; but *perfida* appears in the text of other manuscripts and of most printed editions. The prose version supports it.

145. Aldus, so that the second syllable of *idola* in the following verse would not be shortened, altered this passage to *semper quae idola adamavit*—“which always loved idols”—*Dilexit lucos*—“It loved the groves.” The same reading occurs in Reg. 5, but, I think, from Aldus’s edition. Nebrissensis also, following Aldus, read the second syllable of *idola* as long, although elsewhere he admits that Sedulius shortened it.

146. Poelman’s papers read *Idola erexit*—“It raised up idols”—apparently to accommodate the meter. But I discussed the shortening of the second syllable in *idola* in my notes on Prudentius and Dracontius. The author of the unpublished poem *On Virtues and Vices*, in the Vatican Library, no. 591, in the chapter “On Drunkenness,” writes: “For I, a devourer, once made great idols for the peoples.” The author of the poem may perhaps be Bishop Boniface, mentioned by Sigebertus and Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca medievalis*.

147. In Parrhasius there is an error, *eligere*. Reg. 1 and Ott. 2 have *Bahal* for *Baal*. Some write *Barabbam*, others *Barabam*, and some *Barrabam*; the last does not suit this meter.

149. In Ott. 1 it is uncertain whether *utrumque* or *utramque* is written. The correct reading is *utrumque*, which in Reg. 2 was produced from *utramque*.

150. This verse and the following one are placed in different orders in the manuscripts. Barthius’s manuscript, Alm., and Reg. 2 first have *Auctor lucis erat*, then *Auctor mortis erat*; but in Alm. the verse *Auctor lucis* is absent from the text and added in the margin, while in Reg. 2 the order is reversed, *Auctor erat lucis*, for *Auctor lucis erat*. In my manuscript the verse *Auctor lucis* is entirely absent. In Ott. 1 the verse *Auctor mortis* is placed at the beginning of the page, but in such a way that it precedes the other, *Auctor lucis*. Barthius says that it is better for life to precede and death to follow. The prose version, however, is against this. Poelman’s papers read *sumere lumen*; others, *sumere lucem*.

153. Arntzenius reads *Qui dubitatis*—that is, “Why, or for what reason, do you doubt?” The others, with the same meaning, read *Quid*. My manuscript has *membra* for *terga*. Sedulius seems to imitate Horace, *Epodes* IV.11: “Cut by the triumviral scourges”; Martial and others write similarly.

154. Parrhasius, Poelman’s papers, and Urb. read *subditur*; most have *subditus*, which is better.

155. Ott. 2 incorrectly reads *Sed dignus*. Reg. 1 has *Ne*; above it, *Nec*; Ott. 1 and Reg. 2 have *Nec*, corrected to *Ne*. Urb., Fabr., Ang., Alb., Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Aldus read *Nec*; most of the others, more correctly, *Ne*. Fabr. and some printed editions have *ceu latro*; the others *vel latro*. Above the reading in Reg. 1 is *ut*, while Ott. 1 has *vel*, though it had another reading previously. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, and Aldus read *perire*; the others *periret*; my manuscript has *perisset* for the reading of the later hand.

Once a disciple, now the accused, abandoning the lofty stars,  
he descended as far as the Tartarean abyss;  
then an apostolic man, now become a vile apostate.

But while the patient Lord stood before the governor’s tribunal,

[140] led like a gentlest lamb to the place of slaughter,  
the hostile band, finding nothing worthy of innocent blood,  
brings against him the charge that he had said he was a king,  
and takes the truth, falsely, as a crime.

Nor is it surprising if a faithless people avoids God’s laws,

[145] which always loved the groves and cherished idols,  
for in the same manner, raging,  
they once worshiped Baal and now chose Barabbas;  
with the pious man condemned and the insolent man preserved,  
their judgment, through both, altered the just course.

[150] He was the author of death, who was ordered to receive the light;  
he was the author of light, who was ordered to receive death.  
Believe now that Christ suffered for all—believe it.  
Why do you still doubt? Behold, his back cut by scourges,  
subject to insults, he embraces every punishment,

[155] lest even a robber, deserving to feel death, should perish.

156. Aldus: “Jesus led away to punishment.” My manuscript corruptly has *flax*, and Alb. *felix* for *falx*; in Reg. 1, *fallax* seems to have stood for *falx*. The correct reading is *falx*. Parrhasius has *falx curva*, which Nebrissensis also conjectured. Reg. 1 has *torva*, as do most copies, but perhaps it was originally *turba*. In Ottob. 1 it clearly reads *turba*, though this was altered, and *torva* appears in the margin. The prose version has “the grim edge of the sickle.”

157. Ott. 1 and Urb. read *quod*; read *quot*.

158. Arntzenius: *Crimine*; correct to *Crimina*.

159. Reg. 5 and Aldus read *Nec*; others, more suitably, *Non*. Arntzenius has *solum*; Rom. has *solas*, corrected to *solum*. It is preferable to retain *solas*, with the others and the prose version. Wopkensius thinks *sed corde reloto* or *sed pectore loto* more harmonious. The ancient books and the prose version oppose this; nor is there reason to consider *sed corpore toto* inelegant. Indeed, the preceding words, “not only having washed his hands,” demand it.

160. Reg. 1 in a later hand, Reg. 2, Alb., Vat. 2, my manuscript, Ottob. 1 by correction, manuscripts of Leipzig and Canterbury, Alm., Arntzenius, read *sperare*; other manuscripts and most printed editions read *spectare*, which Poelman’s papers support. Wopkensius substituted *spirare*, a reading not displeasing to Grunerus and Arntzenius. But either *exspectare* or, preferably, *sperare* suits this passage well.

161. Vet. 1 and Mon. incorrectly have *corporis* for *corripis*. Parrhasius has *et sistis*; others, following the prose version, omit *et*.

162. Our manuscripts, together with Ang., Barthius’s manuscript, Alm., Arntzenius, Parrhasius, Aldus, and other old editions, read *Praeponis humana*; Alban. and many later printed editions read *Praeponisque humana*. Arntzenius prefers the latter; I do not know why. Sedulius often gives the consonantal force of *h* so that the preceding short syllable may be lengthened. Arntzenius in his second manuscript and Parrhasius read *qui morte teneris*; read *qua morte*.

163. Ottob. 1 has *crucis*, correctly corrected to *cruci*. Reg. 5, Aldus, Fabr., and some other printed editions have *post vulnera*; most manuscripts, together with other editions, more correctly have *per vulnera*.

164. Aldus: “Jesus led away to punishment.” The heading is repeated. Urb. and Rom. have *ad poenas*. Vat. 2 corruptly has *sensus* for *Sanctus*.

165. Arntzenius, with Fabr. and some other editions, reads *rubri vilem*; our manuscripts, together with Parrhasius, Aldus, and most editions, have *vilem rubri*. In Ott. 1 the reading may perhaps have been *chlamydem rubri sub tegmine cocci*—“a cloak of red beneath a covering of scarlet.” The reading in my manuscript is *Vestitur vilem*. Wopkensius wishes *subtegmine* to be read as one word; most write *sub tegmine*.

166. Arntzenius has *Vestitus*. Vat. 1, Ott. 2, Ang., and Alm. read *speciesque*; others *species* without *-que*. Alm., Ott. 1 and 2, Fabr., and some other editions have *cruenta*; it stood thus in Reg. 1 but was corrected to *cruentae*, as most copies present it and as Poelman’s papers support. I discussed the cloak in which Jesus was dressed in my notes on Juvencus IV.645. Sedulius calls it *vilem* as though it were the characteristic garment of some low-ranking soldier. The First Council of Toledo, in the year 400, canon 8, says: “If anyone after baptism has served as a soldier and has taken up a cloak or belt, etc.” Nebrissensis nevertheless thinks it is called *vilem* because it was used to dishonor Christ, not because it was of little value. But it is likely that the cloak, being used for dishonor, was also actually cheap and of little value.

167. The Lyon Bible reads *circumdabit*, which is corrupt. Someone might conjecture *almum* for *amplum*; but Nebrissensis explains *amplum* as “honorable.” Hence *amplitudo*.

170. Ottob. 1, my manuscript, Reg. 5, Ang., and Vat. 2 seem to read *ut videtur*; Aldus has *quia*, which may also have stood in Reg. 1, where the present reading is *quod*, as in most copies. In Ott. 1 as well, *quod* was originally written. Reg. 1 in a later hand, Vat. 1, and many printed editions have *semper*. Other manuscripts, together with Ang., Barthius’s manuscript, Parrhasius, and Aldus, have *terrae*, which Grunerus and Arntzenius prefer, along with the Canterbury manuscript, Poelman’s papers, and the prose version. Barthius had conjectured *per se*, that is, “by its own nature.” Ott. 1 has *terrae*, but it seems originally to have had *semper*, which the prose version supports.

171. *Leve* is absent from my manuscript. Reg. 5 and Aldus have *mox alienos* without *-que*.

Oh! grim sickle of the fathers, destined to cut the harvest of their descendants;  
oh, Pilate, your crime! If, with watchful mind, you noted  
how many crimes you committed in one judgment,  
you ought not merely to have washed your hands, but your whole body,  
[160] and to have hoped for the sacred washing of forgiveness.

You seize the innocent and set the king before the governor;  
you place human things above God. By what death are you held,  
you who fasten the Lord to the cross through many wounds?

[Col. 0722A] And when the Holy One, handed over to savage soldiers, departed for punishment,

[165] he is clothed in a vile cloak of red beneath a covering of scarlet,  
so that the whole appearance might be an image of bloody death.  
He encircled his broad head with a crown bound with thorns,  
because, in his goodness, he had taken upon himself  
all the thorny growths of our evils;

[170] he fills the hand with a reed, an ever-shifting scepter,  
weak, fragile, empty, light; and soon, *alienos* (“others’/foreign”—fragment).

172. *Habitus*, meaning the body’s outward appearance, especially clothing, is found used in this sense by good authors.

174. The Leipzig manuscript has *nil jam mutabile*; Parrhasius and Poelman’s papers, *nil ut mutabile*; Rom. and Urb., *nil jam ut mobile*. The common reading is *nil jam ut mutabile*. Nebrissensis observes that Sedulius uses *item* for *iterum*. From the prose version’s *motatione* one might suspect *motabile*, “changeable.”

175. In some old books *refulgens* appears for *resurgens*; Barthius and Burmannus rightly condemn this.

176. This verse was absent from Reg. 1 and Ott. 1, but in both it was added at the bottom of the page so that it could be placed here. It is absent from Cant. and from the prose version. In my manuscript the order is first *Humano*, then *Post mortem*, an inverted and disordered arrangement. In Alm. it is corrupted as *Humano patiens mortalem sumere carnem*. Poelman’s papers contained the addition: “that is, taking up again the same immortal [nature], which is indeed the human covering beneath which divinity lies hidden.”

177. Aldus reads *Fel Domino datum*. Arntzenius has *factum* for *gestum*.

178. Reg. 2 has *vino*, correctly corrected to *vinum*. Rom. and Urb. read *datur*; the others, better, *datum*. *Tristis* is commonly used for “bitter.”

179. Vat. 2 and Parrhasius have *labris* for *labiis*.

182. Aldus: “Jesus fastened to the exposed wood.”

183. Nebrissensis’s note on the word *Relligione* is: “Unless this is an error, it means that the cross, formerly a punishment, has now been changed into an honorable object of worship.”

184. Rom. and my manuscript have *violentiaque*; read *violentaque*. Mon. has *robore*; correct to *robora*. Dungalus, in his work against Claudius of Turin on the worship of sacred images, volume XIV of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, p. 206, and Jonas of Orléans, book II on the same subject, volume XIV, p. 182, quote this and the following eleven verses to prove that the cross is to be venerated. Dungalus cites book IV of the *Paschal Poem*, while Jonas cites book III, owing to a different division of the poem, discussed in the *Prolegomena*.

185. My manuscript corruptly has *panem* for *poenam*. Urb. reads *honorem*; retain *honore*.

187. In Jonas at the cited passage: *Ipseque sanctificans*, less well.

188. Cellarius says that *colendam* means “to be cultivated,” not “to be worshiped religiously,” since religious worship is due only to Christ fastened to the cross. What could be more foolish? With what worship, then, is the cross to be honored? The Catholic doctrine concerning the adoration of the cross is so certain and has been so clearly explained by the doctors that heretics ought at last to be ashamed to quibble about it and to cook the same cabbage over a hundred times. For when, together with the Fathers, the Councils, and the Church in the liturgical offices, we say that we venerate, honor, and adore the cross, everyone recognizes that this adoration is relative and secondary. Away, then, with the foolishness of the heterodox, who infer from such signs of veneration that we worship lifeless things with an absolute and primary adoration, the *latria* owed to the Divinity alone.

Orientius also has a similar eulogy of the cross in his poem *On the Trinity*: “But why should the elevated form retain this appearance of the cross? Its character shows in every respect what is to be adored. Because it stands forth as a sign divided into four parts, it makes known the Lord of the world and all the archangels. You yourself rule as many wounds as the cross sees regions of heaven,” and so forth. All the poems of the very devout poet Orientius have been badly corrupted. In the fourth verse there is an obvious error, which I prefer to correct as: “Every corner makes the Lord of the world known.” In the first I would read *cum tamen*, and in the last *Tot regit*.

189. Lipsius, book I *On the Cross*, chapter 10, preferred *patenti* to *potenti*. Some printed editions incorrectly punctuate: *portavit ovans ratione potenti—Quattuor*.

190. My manuscript reads *colligat*, which is also Vonckius’s conjecture and is supported by the prose version; most copies nevertheless have *colligit*.

191. Reg. 2 has *fulgit*, corrected to *fulget*. In Jonas at the cited passage there is the error *Eois*. Christian poets frequently call God the author—that is, the lord and creator—of all things, as Prudentius, Dracontius, Avitus, Fortunatus, and Arator do.

Putting off his clothing, he took up his proper mantle,  
namely, intending to lay aside the coverings of human flesh,  
and intending likewise to take them up again, so that nothing changeable would remain,

[175] rising after death in his own majesty,  
and putting mortal flesh beneath a human covering.

Nor was it without divine governance that he acted thus:  
when wine mixed with gall was given to him,  
he received its bitter taste, touched it with his lips, and removed it from his mouth.

[180] For he was about to taste bitter death for a brief time,  
so that afterward, restored in the flesh, he might disdain it.

[Col. 0724A] Immediately, suspended from the summit of the exposed wood,  
by holy religion transforming the anger of punishment,  
he himself was the peace of the cross, illuminating  
the violent wood with his own limbs;

[185] he clothed the punishment with honor,  
and made the execution a sign more truly of salvation,  
sanctifying the torments themselves in himself and blessing them.

And lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross is to be venerated,  
which carried the Lord in triumph, by its powerful design

[190] it gathers the four wounds of the square world.

The splendid East shines from the summit of the Creator;

192. Cellarius found *flaccae* somewhere for *sacrae*; but *sacrae* is correct. Vat. 1, my manuscript, Jonas, Alb., and Urb. read *labuntur sidera*; correct to *lambuntur*.

193. Rom. has *dextera*; the law of the meter requires *dextra*. In Ott. 1 something else originally stood for *erigit*. Reg. 1 has *leva subrigit*, and in a later hand *leva erigit*; poetic usage requires this, for it must be written with the diphthong, *laeva*.

194. Arntzenius reads *Tonantis*; others, with the prose version, *creantis*, which seems more vigorous to Arntzenius.

195. At this point the prose version inserts material belonging to verses 200 and 201 here. In Vat. 2 there seems to have been *complexus*; this was also the earlier reading in Reg. 1, Ottob. 1, and Rom., but in all three it was corrected to *complexum*. I consider *complexus* more elegant; Christian poets, as I have often noted in Juvencus, are accustomed to attach one accusative to two verbs. Most retain *complexum*.

Cassiodorus, apparently drawing on Sedulius, writes in his commentary on Psalm XXII.18: “The very position of the cross is such that its upper part seeks the heavens, its lower part does not abandon the earth, and its fixed point touches the depths of the underworld; and, as though with arms extended, its breadth reaches toward all the regions of the world.” Lactantius preceded him, *Institutes* IV.26: “Christ extended his hands in his passion and measured out the world.” Jerome, commenting on Mark XV, says: “What is the very shape of the cross if not the square form of the world?” See Cerda, *Adversaria*, chapter 100. Amalarius also cites these verses in *On Ecclesiastical Offices* I.14.

196. Aldus: “The inscription on the cross in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew.” Most of our manuscripts and others read: “And the inscription is written: ‘This is the king of the Jews.’” Arntzenius attributes to Aldus the reading: “The inscription: ‘For this is the king of the Jews.’” Aldus did indeed print this, but corrected it, as in most of our copies. My manuscript reads: “The inscription: ‘Because he is king of the Jews,’” which does not scan well. Alb. is no better: “And the inscription is written above: ‘This is the king of the Jews’”; nor is Parrhasius: “It is written in the inscriptions above: ‘This is the king of the Jews.’”

It should nevertheless be observed that Parrhasius, in his annotations after Sedulius, remarks that this is how it is read in all copies, but that it ought to be corrected to: “It is written in the inscriptions: ‘This is the king of the Jews,’” so that the verse may be reciprocal and spondaic, in imitation of Virgil and others, rather than shortening one or another syllable unusually in *Judaeorum*. Cappusotus followed this view. Vet. 1 and 2 and Mon. have: “And the inscription is written: ‘Jesus, king of the Jews.’” The Lyon Bible and Fabr. have: “The inscription: ‘This king is of the Jews.’” Col. has: “The inscription: ‘This king of the Jews is.’” Poelman’s papers have: “The inscription: ‘This is the king of the Jews.’”

In the commoner manuscript reading, which Bede also adopts in his *On Meters*, the final syllable of *titulus* is lengthened by the force of the following aspiration, or also by the force of the caesura. In the fifth position a spondee is used in place of a dactyl. Sedulius reproduces the words of the inscription found in Luke. Dominicus Maria Mannius published a learned commentary on the archetype of the inscription of the Lord’s cross in volume IX of Gori’s *Literary Symbols*. See also my note on Juvencus IV.666 and on the *Elegies* verse 110, where I shall discuss Bede’s view of the scansion of this verse, which is by no means to be approved, and Benedict XIV, *On Beatification*, IV, part II, appendix 3.

197. Alm. and some of our manuscripts, together with many printed editions, read *Quod*; others, with Barthius’s manuscript, Parrhasius, and Poelman’s papers, more correctly read *Quo*. Parrhasius has *nil*; others *nihil*. My manuscript reads *vacat*; most have *vacet*, but in Reg. 1 *vacat* was made from *vacet*. *Vacet* is more correct, especially with *Quo*.

The sacred feet are touched by the setting star;  
the right hand holds the Bear, the left raises the central axis,  
and all nature lives from the limbs of the Creator,

[195] while Christ, embraced by the cross, governs the whole world everywhere.

[Col. 0726B] The inscription is written: “This is the king of the Jews,”  
from which nothing is empty of divinity; for what was done from heaven  
the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages report this.

199. *Ter* indicates the Holy Trinity, not a threefold kingdom, as Cellarius suspects.

200. Poelman’s papers have *Super tunicam sortiuntur*. Dempsterus, in his notes on Rosinus VIII.8, p. 840, conjectures *in exuvias*, which seems formerly to have stood in Vat. 1; but *in exuviis* is correct.

201. My manuscript has *necaret*; read *vetaret*. These verses were explained above in the prose version.

202. Aldus: “Two thieves crucified beside the Lord.” Parrhasius: *Cum simul*; others *Quin etiam*. Ott. 1, Vat. 1 and 2, Reg. 5, Aldus, Cant., and Poelman’s papers read *insonti*; most have *insontis*, but in Reg. 1 it seems to have been corrected to *insonti*. Using *cruentum* for *sceleratum* is not unprecedented.

203. In Rom. something is missing from *meritum omnibus unum*. Urb. has the similar error *meritumque omnibus*. Barthius cites from an excellent manuscript *meritum non omnibus unum*, printed by Parrhasius and found in his own manuscript by Arntzenius’s later hand. Most have *licet omnibus*, which Grunerus disliked because the particle *quamvis* is repeated in the following verse. Therefore, from the Leipzig edition, he restored *meritum licet omnibus unum—Non faciat*, though the sense is similar. My manuscript and another of Barthius have exactly this reading, and Poelman’s papers recorded that it also appeared in other editions.

Nevertheless, the common reading should be retained and explained with Wopkensius as: “Although one merit, however similar, does not make all alike”—that is, although a judgment, however similar, does not make everyone equal or give them similar merit. Moreover, Latin writers sometimes join *licet* and *quamvis*, as Lucretius and Cicero do.

204. In Reg. 1 *similes* was corrected to *similis*, with the gloss *sententia*, “judgment.” Alb. corruptly has *Nec faciat quamvis simul sententia*. Barthius cites from another excellent manuscript *Hos faciat similes*; from another, *Non faciat, similis tamen est sententia*. Parrhasius has *Hos facit assimiles*. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *Hos faciat similes*. Compare the variant readings at the preceding verse.

206. Arntzenius’s *tribus* is not bad in place of *trium*; then *duobus* could be read, as it is in Urb.

208. Rom. has *salvandus*; the others *salvatus*.

209. Vat. 1 has *Suppliciis tamen*; *-que* is missing for the meter.

211. *Tuens*, that is, “looking upon,” as in Virgil and others.

212. Cant., Ott. 1, Alb., Parrhasius, and Fabr. have *meritum*, and Poelman’s papers prescribe the same spelling. But the common reading *merita*, which also seems originally to have stood in Ott. 1, should be retained; its final *a* is lengthened before the *pr* of the following word, without even considering the caesura, which would produce the same effect. Aldus has *ex agmine*; correct to *examine*.

213. Arntzenius reads *Unus erat*; read, with the others and the prose version, *Unus enim*. In Ott. 2 there seems to be *nec in morte*, but the meter opposes this. Urb. and Rom. have *relinquit*; others *reliquit*. *Relinquit* is not bad, especially if there is an imitation of Virgil, book VI.444: “Cares do not leave them even in death.”

214. Urb. has *loquens* for *movens*.

216. In Reg. 5 and the Lyon Bible, *vitam* for *vitem* is an error. My manuscript has *mordebat*, which has already occurred in the preceding verse; the others have *lacerabat*. Barthius, *Adversaria* LIV, chapter 7, cites *vitem populatur amoenam*. Many writers record that a goat’s bite destroys a vine.

This one faith teaches that the king is to be called one three times.

[200] For his clothing, the lot is cast, so that the sacred garment,  
remaining undefiled, might forbid schism from Christ.

Moreover, on either side of the innocent man they placed bloody men;  
although a judgment, however similar, does not make one merit for all,

[205] while, with the Holy One hanging among executioners, there were thieves,  
the punishment of the three is equal, but the cause of the two is different.

These two are guilty to the world because of their many crimes;  
the world is guilty toward this one, saved by righteous blood.

[Col. 0728A] Yet even amid punishments the ruler of all things  
did not lose the rights of his authority: an impartial judge,  
looking upon both, chose one and rejected the other,  
weighing the merits of each by lofty judgment.

One, whom a savage life did not leave even in death,  
directed criminal insults against the Lord and with words

[215] gnawed at him, and like a bristling goat  
with poisonous mouth tore the lovely vine;

the other, having worshiped Christ with pleading words,  
with wounded eyes cast down bent his gaze, only

219.
