Some manuscripts cited by Barthius, Reg. 1 in a later hand, Rom., and some printed editions have *Libera*; most of ours, together with Alm. and Parrhasius, have *Lumina*, from Virgil, *Aeneid* II.405: “Stretching his burning eyes toward heaven in vain—his eyes, for bonds held back his tender hands.” Compare Prudentius, *Peristephanon* V.235. Cellarius follows *Libera* and attributes *Lumina* to the Canterbury manuscript. Grunerus found *Libera* in the Canterbury manuscript and preferred it because that is the reading in the prose version. But the elegant repetition of Virgil’s word is as appropriate to the verse as its explanation by *libera* is appropriate in the prose version. Unless we also wish to suspect that an error entered the prose and that, as in the poem, *lumina* should be read: “only eyes, free.” The manuscripts and editions also vary between *vincula* and other readings; it is preferable to retain *vincula* with most copies, because of the same Virgilian imitation. Cellarius, with Alm., prefers *vulnera*, since the unfortunate men were fastened to crosses with nails, not bound with ropes; but this is worthless, for Sedulius himself says again at verse 303, “After the bonds of the cross.”

224. Wopkensius conjectures *interque beate—Conspicuos*, or *interque malignus*, namely, “the serpent.” All the ancient copies oppose this; *benigne* is not bad, whether one understands “to dwell kindly” or “gardens kindly conspicuous.”

225. Here again Wopkensius conjectures *decipientibus* for *deficientibus*; the elegant sharpness of this conjecture greatly pleased Arntzenius, namely because in the paradise of heaven the fruits will not deceive as in the earthly paradise. The common reading indicates an unfailing abundance of fruits. In Reg. 1 something else originally stood. For this reason I would regard Wopkensius’s conjecture as correct, since the prose version indicates not the perpetual abundance of fruits but the exclusion of deceptive snares.

226. Nebrissensis had suspected *antiquus serpens* from Revelation XII.9: “That great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil.” Indeed, my manuscript has *antiquus serpens*; it also stood in Rom., but there it was corrected to *antiquum*.

228. Three adjectives are applied to one noun: *varium*, *violentum*, *grande*. The same accusative, *facinus*, belongs to both verbs, *aggressi* and *patrarunt*. Some punctuate: *facinus violentum grande patrarunt*, that is, “they committed great violence” or “something extremely violent.” Others: *Aggressi facinus violentum, grande patrarunt*, namely, “they committed something great, a great deed.” The meaning is clearer as we explain it: “Both took different paths and committed a varied, violent, great crime.” Nor does the prose version oppose this.

230. Cant., Aldus, and some other printed editions read *petens*; others *sequens*, whose gloss is *petens* in Burmannus’s manuscript.

231. Barthius’s manuscript reads *Austulit*.

232. Aldus: “The sun obscured at the full moon, contrary to nature.” Poelman’s papers: *Tenebrae*. Vet. 1 has *horrendi*; correct to *horrendae*.

234. My manuscript has *tenuere diem*; Rom. *traxere diem*; read *texere diem*, which is beautifully expressed.

235. Juvencus IV.149: “The sun will hide its gleaming rays beneath dark shadows.”

236. The manuscripts and editions vary: some have *Dilituit*, most, more correctly, *Delituit*. For *infecit*, Poelman’s papers have *implevit*. Aldus and Reg. 5 have *replevit*. The prose version supports *infecit*.

After this verse Reg. 5, Aldus, and Fabr. add these three:

“Because Delia had the brother opposite to her,  
while he was beneath the earth, that one above was at heaven’s summit;  
the impious ages feared everlasting night.”

Some give *supera ille* for *super ille*. Most printed editions omit these verses, as does Parrhasius, to whom Arntzenius falsely attributes them. All or nearly all our manuscripts ignore them; for Reg. 5, as I have said elsewhere, seems to have been copied from Aldus’s edition. They are also absent from the Augsburg manuscript and from Alban. In Barthius’s manuscript the first two verses were absent, but the third was present; it is taken from Virgil, *Georgics* I.468: “And the impious ages feared everlasting night.” Barthius, *Adversaria* LIV, chapter 7, says that the first two verses are not by Sedulius, indeed that they contradict his meaning, since Sedulius does not attribute this eclipse to natural causes. But whoever wrote these verses, they exclude natural causes from the eclipse: the sun does not fail at the full moon, when the moon is beneath the earth and has the sun opposite it, but when it is placed between the sun and the earth. Therefore the impious ages feared perpetual night all the more because the solar eclipse occurred at the full moon. Nebrissensis, who read these verses, explains *suberat terris* as follows: “Since the moon was then full, namely on the fourteenth day of the month, it was also necessary that the sun should be at the summit of heaven at the sixth hour of the day and the moon at the angle of midnight.” I do not at all think these verses are by Sedulius, not only because they are absent from the manuscripts and the prose version, but also because Sedulius does not usually use mythological names. Arntzenius doubts the third verse, *Impia*, in *Miscellanea*, chapter 16, and suspects that it should be inserted after this verse 236, *Delituit*.

The eyes, for bonds held back his twin palms.

[220] Whom the Lord, like a shepherd, gathers as a sheep wandering  
through deserted fields, and gladly leads with himself  
into your fields, O paradise, where the meadow  
with its everlasting flower caresses him,  
and the delight of the groves is nourished by flowing waters,  
amid gardens kindly conspicuous

[225] for fruits that do not fail. The serpent  
groans that its ancient inhabitant dwells there.

Thus both thieves, taking different paths,  
undertook a varied, violent, great crime.

The one approaches the gates below, the other the gates above;

[230] the one, following the depths, penetrated the bars of Gehenna;  
the other carried off the kingdoms of heaven as his spoil.

Meanwhile dreadful darkness suddenly came,  
and covered the whole heavens, holding the sky  
in blackness and shrouding the day in mournful funeral rites;  
the sun, hiding its gleaming rays in a cloud,

[235] veiled in a gloomy covering, disappeared  
and stained the sorrowful world with mourning.

237. Barthius’s manuscript and Poelman’s papers have *metuerunt*, a reading Barthius defends. The prose version has *meruerunt*, as do most manuscripts; but something else had originally stood in Ott. 1 and Reg. 1. Reg. 2 and Ott. 2 have *merebant* or *moerebant*, though something else was originally in Reg. 2. Perhaps Sedulius intended *moeruerunt*, which would be trisyllabic by synaeresis; this is expressed above by *tristemque* and soon afterward by *Moesta per occasum*. Priscian, book VIII, says that the perfect *moerui* from *moereo, moeres* is not in use, but this should not greatly deter us in Sedulius. For now let us follow Barthius’s manuscript, *metuerunt*, though not his interpretation: he wants it to mean that they feared to see the face of the dying Christ, whereas it more likely means the face, or appearance, of the world, made sorrowful by the eclipse and mourning.

238. Vet. 1 has *laetaque*; correct to *laetata*. In Reg. 1 *laetata* was made from *laeta*.

244. Urb. has *atra sepulcri*, which can be tolerated.

245. Aldus: “That there was a dreadful earthquake at the Lord’s death.” My manuscript: *Terra tremuit*. Poelman’s papers: *Non tellus*; better, *Nec tellus*. The varied use of this phrase without disaster can be observed in Dracontius’s word index.

247. Barthius preferred *obitum* to *modum*; the ancient books oppose him. *Modus supremus* is the ultimate end, or measured limit. The prose version has *termino dubio*.

250. Vat. 1 incorrectly transposes the order, first *Perdita*, then *Sed pietas*. In poetic usage *umbras vagas* means the souls of the dead. Therefore there can be no doubt that Sedulius clearly asserts Christ’s descent into hell. Nebrissensis says that the shades are called *vagas* because poets imagined souls wandering through the underworld. I think more correctly that the souls are called *vagas*, as though “wandering” and straying from their heavenly homeland; this is suggested by the following verse, *Perdita restituens*.

251. Reg. 5, Urb., my manuscript, Rom., Alb., and Aldus have *nec* for *non*. Arntzenius seems to attribute *restituens* to Parrhasius, but this is not consistent, as he says, and is metrically impossible. Parrhasius does exhibit *restituens*, with only a slight difference from the others: *restituens, sed non constantia perdens*, that is, “restoring, but not losing what is constant,” or “what endures.” Cellarius and Wopkensius were mistaken in thinking that Sedulius meant “not losing things that do not consist,” namely crimes, things neither instituted nor created by God. Sedulius is doing something else here: Nature was terrified lest the world perish. Sedulius replies: Christ was hastening to Tartarus, not to destroy the world and the things that endured, but to restore what had been lost.

252. My manuscript has *Aceto potatur*. Aldus: “Vinegar was offered to the thirsty Lord.” Vat. 1 has *timuerunt*; others *metuerunt*, to which the errors in Rom. (*meruerunt*) and in my manuscript (*mutuerunt*) point.

253. Reg. 1 has *qui*; correctly changed to *quin*.

This the elements deserved to behold: his face,  
bereft of his Father’s aid, rejoicing at the rising  
and mourning at the setting. For as the light shone  
[240] at the birth of the Lord, so at his death it withdrew,  
not absent for long, but marking hidden mysteries  
through its own appointed interval; for just as  
the stars of the darkened heaven lay blind for three hours,  
so the Lord endured the closed chambers of the tomb for three days.

[245] Nor was the earth without upheaval: seeing such things,  
it trembled to its foundations, and at the doubtful end  
Nature feared its final limit, lest the highest summit,  
seeking the underworld, should force the whole structure to collapse,  
and the world, following its Creator, should go away through Tartarus.

[250] But boundless piety hastened toward the wandering shades,  
restoring what had been lost, not destroying what endured.

Yet none of those who fastened the Lord to the cross feared  
the signs of so great a danger, nor moreover the draught [fragment].

255. Some write *Penniculo*; others *Peniculo*.

256. Most of our manuscripts write *Manzeribus*. Some have *Mansseribus*, *Manceribus*, *Manseribus*, *Mameribus*, or *Mamseribus*. In the Vulgate, Deuteronomy XXIII.2, *Mamzer* is written, retaining the Hebrew word, which means “illegitimate”: “A Mamzer, that is, one born of a prostitute, shall not enter the assembly of the Lord.” Venantius Fortunatus, book V, poem 4, verse 75, uses *agmina manzera*. Canonists call the children of prostitutes *manzeres*: “A prostitute gave birth to *manzeres*, but an adulteress to bastards. As a crop comes from an ear of grain, so an illegitimate child comes from a mistress. They give natural children, who are special to us.”

258. Most manuscripts and editions have *cum*; Reg. 1 and others *dum*. Ott. 1 has *convertantur*, corrected to *convertuntur*.

259. Arntzenius has *mensa* (“table”) for *mensis* (“months”). Parrhasius has *sic* for *ita*. Reg. 1 has *sic* in a later hand, *ita* originally.

260. Rom., Urb., Ott. 1, and Parrhasius have *exosa*; the others *odiosa*. Perhaps *odiosa* originally stood in Ott. 1 as well.

261. My manuscript has *Exspiravit*. Aldus: “Jesus expired, and many bodies of the saints were raised.” On the epithet *bonus*, by which Christ is distinguished above all others, see Theophilus Raynaudus II, section 1, chapter 3, which he entitled *Christus bonus, bona, bonum*.

262. Urb. and Rom. in their first hand, and some printed editions, have *demisit*; the others, better, *dimisit*.

265. Fabr. has *abeunte*, less appropriately, for *obeunte*.

266. Arntzenius has *patescunt*; others more correctly *fatiscunt* or *fatescunt*; Parrhasius *fathiscunt*. In Ott. 1 it seems originally to have been *dehiscunt*.

267. In Vat. 1 *Divisa* seems to have been corrected to *Divisae*. Someone might conjecture *Divulsa compage*, as in Minucius Felix, chapter 9, *Coelesti compage divisa* (“the heavenly structure divided”), or, as others have attempted to restore it, *divulsa*.

268. Vet. 1 has *abire*; this also stood in Rom., but was correctly corrected to *abiere*.

272. The Leipzig manuscript and some printed editions have *discusso*; read, with the others, *discisso*, or, as some have it, *disciso*. Thus *abscissus* and *abscisus* are frequently interchanged. In this passage, however, *discisso*, from *discindere* (“to tear apart”), is preferable. A fine image, referring to those who, at the funerals of their relatives, bare their breasts, tear their garments, and so forth.

274. Arntzenius’s first hand has *monstrata*; others, *reseranda*. But Ottobonianus 1 had something else, and Reginensis 1 reads *reserenda*, which appears to be an error: the verb is *resero, reseras*, not *resero, reseris*. Here, as elsewhere, the manuscripts and printed editions vary: most have *Moysi*; some, *Mosi*; Aldus, *Mosae*. Nebrissensis explains this either as “the law of Moses” or “the law covered by the veil of Moses,” about which the Apostle speaks in 2 Corinthians 3. The glossator in Reginensis 1 adopts this second interpretation. In the prose version it was *sub Moyse velamine* (“under the veil of Moses”).

When, thirsty, he asked, one man from the impious crowd

[255] Offered him vinegar on a reed, soaked into a sponge.

That liquid suited mamzer peoples rolling headlong into worse things:

For just as sweet wines are turned into dreadful vinegar,

So, cast away from the tables, they lie; thus in former time

[260] The nation accepted by God is now an abominable offspring.

Therefore, when every suffering of the good Christ had been completed,

He himself sent forth the holy soul from his own body,

He himself, intending to take it up again, since he was the same man dead

[Col. 0734A] And alive, with his limbs dying within him,

[265] While God did not die; by whose power the ways of hell opened in reverse, and rocks, their structure split apart, gaped open; the revived bodies of the saints who lay dead went forth from their shattered tombs, animated into their own ashes; and suddenly, with a crash,

[270] Seeing that triumphant temple—the summit of the greater temple—

Had fallen, in the manner of a grieving foster-mother,

He bared his wounded breast by tearing apart the veil,

Teaching that the hidden things within him were now to be revealed

To future peoples, because the law, long covered

[275] By the veil of Moses, lies open when Christ comes to us.

[Note: [Col. 0735C]

276. Meus has “he apostrophizes triumphant death.” Aldus: “With Christ’s side pierced, blood flowed forth together with water.” Arntzenius’s second hand, and a manuscript cited in Poelmann’s papers, together with Fabr. and some printed editions, have *sis*, which can be defended if the following verse is read, “Death, dreadful because of your goads.” But the other reading is truer, from 1 Corinthians 15:55: “Where is your goad, O death?” See the note on Juvencus, book 4, verse 22.

277. Ottobonianus 1 and 2, Urbinas, Vaticanus 2, Reginensis 5, Anglicus, Albinus, Aldus, and others have, with those whom I mentioned above as having *ubi sis*, “Death, dreadful because of your goads.” If one reads *ubi sit*—“Death, dreadful because of your goads”—the meaning is “where victory may be.” But, as I have already noted, the other reading, which is more common and appears to have stood earlier in Ottobonianus 1, should be retained.

278. Most manuscripts and all printed editions have *Instaurata*; but Reginensis 1 and Ottobonianus 2 present another reading, rightly preferable: *Insaturata* (“unsated”). Avienus, in the *Phaenomena* of Aratus, verse 183: “Nor does the unsated one abhor hatreds.” Venantius, in the elegy on the Resurrection: “The insatiable infernal realm, opening its hollow throats.” — “He who always seized becomes your prey, O God.” See Dracontius, book 2, verse 531. The prose version is also clear.

279. Albinus has *Venali*; read *Poenali* (“punitive”).

280. The final syllable in *pervenis* is shortened contrary to the rule, as in Arator’s *advenis* in the preface to *Vigilius*. Orientius likewise, book 2, chapter “On Vain Praise”: “And you do not know that a beam is in your eyes.” Earlier poets always lengthened the final syllable in the second-person present indicative of the fourth conjugation. In accordance with Sedulius’s practice, book 2 of Eugenius of Toledo’s poems, no. 59, the text may be corrected to: “Hence, as you run through them, you find the acts of the apostles,” rather than *invenies* in the edition and *invenire* in the manuscripts.

281. Poelmann has *cum licuit*, with *Cui licuit* written in the margin “with all our manuscripts and others.” The latter should be retained, as Poelmann’s papers indicate. They also had a note stating that some witnesses read *esse* for *mori*.

282. Romanus has *constituit*; the other witnesses, more suitably, *constituens*.

283. In Romanus, *creavit* has rightly been corrected to *crearis*. For God did not form death, which was created from the serpent’s seed and through the mothering agency of guilt. “Serpent’s seed,” namely, the serpent’s—the devil’s—as Nebrissensis explains.

285. Urbinas has *paulo jam*; read *patulo jam*. Above, verse 182: “Immediately suspended from the summit of the open wood.”

286. Reginensis 1 and Monacensis have *pandebant*; but in Reginensis 1, in the corrected hand, *pendebant* has rightly been restored, and the prose version confirms it. In Urbinas the error is *pendebat*. Ottobonianus 1 has *ministrat*: “Pierced through by the spear,” etc.; this is not bad and closely imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.150: “Now torches and stones fly; frenzy supplies the weapons.” It has already been noted by others that *viscera* (“entrails”) can sometimes mean the whole body.

287. Vaticanus 2 erroneously has *Lapide* for *Cuspide*. Cantabrigiensis and the Leipzig edition, with Vaticanus 2, Ottobonianus 2, Meus, and *atque patenti*, correspond to Arntzenius’s second hand, which has *adque*. Parrhasius and some printed editions have *ecce patenti*. Most manuscripts and editions have *eque patenti*. Urbinas corruptly has *latusque patenti*.

288. Lampeus, in his commentary on John, volume 3, pages 627 and 629, explains this passage and cites *unda recurrit*, as Arntzenius observes.

289. The Lyon Bible has *sacro* for *sacrae*.

290. Arntzenius transposes *vitae tria*. Although this can be defended by lengthening the final syllable of *aqua* on account of the caesura, the other reading is truer, in which the syllable is lengthened because of the two consonants beginning the following word.

292. Urbinas and, apparently, Vaticanus 2 have *habemus*; retain *habemur* (“we are regarded as”).

[294] Albinus has *faciet*; the sense requires *faciat*. Meus, instead of *tenues*, gives *mentes*; this is unconvincing. Mansor: an otherwise unattested word.

295. Aldus: “The body of the Lord placed in the tomb.”

297. Arntzenius, Aldus, and some others punctuate: “When the nobler one had arisen, yet a deceitful generation”; the others, with a much better arrangement, punctuate as printed here. Wopkensis conjectured *tamen trepidatio fallax*—“yet fearful agitation”—“pressed beneath its heart (horror!),” which, in the silent night, or more suitably according to the prose sense, would be *tamen generatio fallax*—“yet a deceitful generation”—“was devising wickedness beneath its heart in the silent night.” I believe nothing should be changed.

298. The manuscript, Leipzig edition, and Parrhasius have *Angebat*. Fabr. and some printed editions have *Audebat*. The accepted reading, *Augebat*, proceeds well. Ottobonianus 2 has *nefas, ne nocte*; the others, *nefas, quod nocte*; but in Romanus the latter appears to have been corrected to *quia* for *quod*.

299. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *Dominum*; others, and the prose version, *Christum*.

303. Meus says, “He apostrophizes the Jews.” Parrhasius has *Sed nondum*; the sense requires *Si nondum* (“If you have not yet…”).

305. Nebrissensis read *Carnificis implestis opus*, with the explanation “of the executioner who customarily punishes the condemned.” Westhemer’s edition reads *Carnifices*.

306. Parrhasius has *revocavit ab umbris*, which Poelmann’s papers do not support; the others have *produxit*, though in many abbreviated scripts it could be read as *perduxit*. Albinus has *producit*.

307. Urbinas has *actos*; correct to *aptos*.

308. Perhaps *Conciliis*, on the basis of the prose version.

310. Hermann Cannegieter conjectured: “Who could preserve God? At what hinge of the universe? Everything lies open.” Arntzenius praises the conjecture, but does better by not following it.

311. Arntzenius has *terris habitat*; others, *undis habitat*, supported by the prose version; some have *in aquis*.

312. An imitation of Lucan, book 1: “thundering from the Tarpeian cloud.” Some punctuate *quid, saeve, tumultus—Excubiis* (“what need is there of tumult, savage one—for the guards?”), and Nebrissensis explains *opus tumultus* as “the work of tumultuous men.” Others punctuate *quid, saeve tumultus—Excubiis*, and in Reginensis 1 there is the gloss *o saeve tumultus* (“O savage tumult”). This passage has been troubled by numerous conjectures. Crusius, *Probationes Criticae*, page 170, proposed *quid, saeve, tumultu—Excubiis quid densis opus?* (“What need is there of dense guards amid the tumult, savage one?”). This conjecture fits the meter no better than another of Crusius’s conjectures in Valerius Flaccus, book 1, verse 94: *Moliri hinc puppim jubet, et demetere ferro—Robora*, for *demittere ferro*. Crusius also read *scaeve* for *saeve*, which makes little difference. Burmannus the Younger, who criticized Crusius, tried *quid, saeve tumultu—Excubiis distendis opus*, that is, “you stir up tumult in various places and post guards.” Cellarius, on the basis of the Albinus and Cantabrigiensis manuscripts, proposed *quid, saeve tumultus—Excubiis dependis opus*, that is, “you expend effort,” from Columella, book 4, chapter 22: *Incassum dependitur opera* (“effort is expended in vain”). The same reading occurs in Vaticanus 1 and Ottobonianus 2, and had stood in Ottobonianus 1, where *dependis* was corrected to *deperdis*. Reginensis 2 has *deperdis*, with *dependis* written as the correction. Other manuscripts, together with Arntzenius and Parrhasius and many printed editions, have *deperdis opus*. Meus has *dependis opes*. Anglicus has *dependis opus*. O. Arntzenius, Henry’s uncle, conjectured *quid, saeve, tremendae—Excubiis est gentis opus?* (“What need is there of a trembling people for the guards?”), or *trementis*, because the soldiers fled in fear. Hermann Cannegieter proposed another arrangement: *quid, sedule, multis—Excubiis defendis opus* (“why, diligently, do you defend the work with many guards?”). Arntzenius, the editor of Sedulius, made the fanciful proposal *quid, saeve tumultus—Excubiis dementis opus*: by “savage” he understood Pilate, and by “mad tumult” the guards. But all these conjectures are much more obscure than the text of the ancient copies themselves: *quid, saeve tumultus—Excubiis deperdis opus*, or *quid, saeve tumultus—Excubiis dependis opus*, or, as in my manuscript, *dependis opes*, or as other manuscripts read, *disperdis opus*. The prose version says nothing about tumult: the guards are called treacherous because they failed in their duty, as is explained at verse 366.

314. Virgil, *Eclogue* 9.34: “But I was not credulous toward him.”

And may he make the thin ones capable of so great a burden.

[295] Therefore, when that noble place received the great treasure

Of the body laid down, with the Lord lying there,

Yet nobler when he arose, a deceitful generation

Was increasing wickedness within its heart, so that in the silent night

The disciples might steal Christ and report that he had departed,

[300] When the third day returned, just as he himself had foretold.

Driven by this fear, they ask that stronger protections

Be supplied for the guards and that the place be held under savage siege.

If, after the bonds of the cross, after the wounds of iron,

[Col. 0738A] After death’s demise, bloodied by a great slaughter,

[305] Executioners, having completed your work, you do not believe that he

Who so often brought souls up from the deepest shades

Could call his own back still more readily, arm your deceit

With worse counsels, seal the tomb,

Set guards, and roll a stone against the monument.

[310] Who could guard God, to whom everything is open

At the hinge of the universe? He dwells in the waters, reigns through Tartarus,

And thunders from the cloud of heaven. Why, savage tumult,

[Col. 0739A] Do you squander effort on guards? Why do you strive

To test the faith in which you do not wish to believe?

[Note: [Col. 0739C]

315. Meus: “the dignity of the Lord’s day.” Aldus: “Christ rose from the dead on the third day.” Aldus has *in terra* (“on earth”); the others, together with the prose version, *interea* (“meanwhile”). Nebrissensis suspects *post tertia sabbata* (“after the third Sabbaths”), that is, after three days; but he interprets it as *post tristia sabbata* (“after sorrowful Sabbaths”), that is, after those sorrowful days. The clearer explanation, however, is “after the sorrowful Sabbath,” meaning after that sorrowful Sabbath day.

316. Statius and Claudian use *irradiare* to mean “to illuminate with rays”; Sedulius, together with Ambrose, Prudentius, and Rusticus Helpidius, uses it to mean “to emit rays.”

319. Meus has *ostendit*; in the margin, together with *cum dicat*; this is also found in the edition and Poelmann’s papers. The others have *cum dicit*. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *clarat*; the others, better, *claret*.

320. Vetus 1 and Monacensis have *Nunc orbis*; read *Hunc orbis*. Recently impious and criminal men attempted to abolish the holy Lord’s day, ultimately aiming, by disturbing the order of all things, to overthrow the Christian religion if they could. Concerning them, Psalm 73:8 says: “Their whole kindred said in their heart together: Let us abolish all the feasts of God from the earth.” But, as was stated earlier, Psalm 2:4 says: “He who dwells in heaven will mock them.”

321. Most manuscripts, Parrhasius, Aldus, and other printed editions have *Nunc etiam*, which Wopkensis also favored. Arntzenius, with some printed editions, preferred *Hunc etiam*; he observed that it should follow the king’s punctuation, so that the sense would be smoother. *Nunc* is nevertheless better: it is set against Genesis and refers to the Lord’s resurrection. For *trophaei* or *tropaei*, Meus gives *triumphi*.

323. Odilo, in a sermon attributed by some to Saint Ildefonsus, as I stated in the *Prolegomena*, no. 168, reports, following the opinion of Sedulius and others, that the Mother of God was much more anxious than the other women to go to the tomb. Since this opinion fits the Gospel narrative poorly, most learned writers reject it. See the note on verse 362.

324. Reginensis 1 has *notum*, with the others, but it appears to have been *noctu* (“by night”), which does not agree with this rising of the light. For this reason Arntzenius rejected *noctu* in the Cantabrigiensis manuscript and in some editions. Ottobonianus 1 and 2 have *venere dolentes* (“they came grieving”); but in Ottobonianus 1 it may earlier have been *gementes* (“groaning”).

325. Meus has *virtute vident*; correct to *vacuumque vident*.

327. They were removed by the angel—not because the stone had been rolled away at the moment Christ rose, as Nebrissensis argues against the painters. On this subject one may read the elegant and learned writer Joannes Interian de Ayala of the Order of Mercy, in his distinguished work *Pictor Christianus Eruditus*, book 3, chapter 20.

328. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *vestitus*; Reginensis 1 also has *vestitus*, instead of the received *praeclarus*, which is found everywhere.

330. Arntzenius, with many printed editions, has *igne minaci—Venerat*, “he had come in threatening fire,” and takes *alba* with *forma*, “in white form,” for those seeking Christ; he notes no variation. Most of our manuscripts, however, have *igne minacem—Venerat in formam, Christum quaerentibus, albam*: “he had come in a threatening form of fire to the guards, in a white form to those seeking Christ.” Some retain *minaci* but otherwise have the reading just given. Aldus likewise has this arrangement, but with *minace*, corrected from *minaci*. In Reginensis 1, *minacem* appears to have been made from *minaci*, as the gloss *terribilem* (“terrible”) indicates. Meus punctuates: *igne minaci—Venerat, in formam Christum quaerentibus albam*. The common reading of our manuscripts suggests: “He had come to the guards in a form threatening with fire; he had come to those seeking Christ in a white form.”

334. Meus: *retinens* (“holding fast”).

Meanwhile, after the sorrowful Sabbaths, the blessed day

Had begun to shine forth—the day that draws the summit of its lofty name

From the Lord who rules, and first earned the privilege

Of seeing the world be born and Christ rise again.

For when Genesis speaks of the seventh Sabbath, it makes clear

[320] That this day is the head of the world, which the glory of the king,

[Col. 0740A] Now also granting it the radiance of its own trophy,

Has permitted to retain primacy. At the rising of this light

The virgin mother, and with her the other mothers,

Bearing the gift of an aromatic harvest, came grieving

[325] To the familiar tomb, and now see the place emptied of the body,

Yet full of power. For an angel sent from the stars

Was sitting on the top of the removed stone,

Flaming in appearance, splendid in a snow-white garment.

Bearing terror and joy in a double form,

[330] And arranging all things, he had come to the guards

In a threatening form of fire, and to those seeking Christ

In a white form.

Thus they learned on the angel's testimony that the Lord lived,

Having trampled death; but the soldier, terrified,

Holds his life in a perilous dilemma,

[Note: [Col. 0741C]

335. Romanus and Urbinas have *fuga*; the others, better, *fugax*. Ottobonianus 2 has *testique*; read *testisque*.

336. Many printed editions have *gratis*, but *post data* should follow. Parrhasius and Aldus, together with all our manuscripts and other witnesses, have *gratis*: “after the gifts had been given, he deceives.”

343. In Ottobonianus 1, *exuvias* has been corrected to *excubias*. Reginensis 2 has *exuvias*, but the gloss *vigilias* (“watch”) indicates *excubias*. Reginensis 1, with most witnesses, has *exuvias*, with *excubias* written in the margin instead of it; this appears to have stood in the first hand in the text, since the gloss *vigilias* supports it. Urbinas corruptly has *ad eximias*.

346. Many punctuate *devectare ligatum?*—“to carry away a bound man?” Since delay is contrary to theft, “more cautiously, therefore”; some place a question mark after *contraria*, referring it back to the preceding words. Sedulius refutes the guards’ lie with a very powerful argument and, as Maldonatus says in his commentary on Matthew 28, exposes it subtly and elegantly.

348. Romanus has *Mentita vox*; the others more correctly, *Mentita est vox*. In Reginensis 1 the reading was *sibi*, corrected to *tibi*, then again written in the margin as *sibi*, which is sound. There, something else formerly stood for *vana*. It seems more likely to be superfluous; yet such redundancy is often found in an elegant Hellenism. Since delay, says Sedulius, is contrary to theft, it would have been safer to remove the linens with the Lord than to linger while untying them.

350. Reginensis 1 in the text, Anglicus, Albinus, Vaticanus 1 and 2, Poelmann’s papers, and some editions have *corpore*; Reginensis 1, in the margin, has *pectore*, together with most and the best manuscripts and printed editions, supported by the prose version.

351. Aldus: “Judaea will be wretched, since it killed Christ.” Meus: “He apostrophizes the Jewish people because it has lost its dignity through the pride of its own people.”

352. *Pro talibus ausis* (“for such acts of daring”) comes from Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.535.

353. Urbinas and Romanus have *vel jam*; the others, *non jam*. G. Fabricius, commentary, page 142, takes *unctus* in the fourth declension as meaning *unctio* (“anointing”). Cellarius’s interpretation, “for the king and high priest,” is better, as verse 355 clearly shows.

354. From this verse the manuscript Reginensis 3 begins again.

355. Reginensis 5, Aldus, and Westhemerus in the margin have *occideris*; the others, *amiseris*.

358. Printed editions generally have *pulchro Christus*; all our manuscripts, together with Albinus, Arntzenius, Parrhasius, and Aldus, have *Christus pulchro*. Reginensis 2, Urbinas, Poelmann’s papers, and Parrhasius have *vinxit*; most have *junxit*; some uncertainly have either *junxit* or *vinxit*. These two words are written similarly in manuscripts, especially where the dots over the letter *i* are not added. In *Ecclesiam*, the second syllable is shortened according to the practice of other Christian poets, who more clearly make a dactyl from the first three syllables in the pentameter, as Rabanus does in poem 100: “Holding this altar, he dedicates the church.” In certain verses in honor of Saints James, Matthew, Simon, and Thomas, which I have copied from an old Vatican manuscript, Queen Christina no. 300, we find: “Shepherds for the sheep, and fathers for the churches.”

Fleeing from the deserted post, and bearing witness to fear,

He reports the truth without cost; after the gifts have been given, he deceives,

And, pretending to be composed, says that during the calm sleep

The disciples secretly carried Christ away in a nocturnal theft.

Speak, wicked guard; answer, criminal band: if Christ, as you dare

[340] To say, was secretly brought out from the closed cavern

While the sleeping guards lay unaware, whose garment lies within, and beside whose grave-clothes an angel sits?

Did the one who removed the blessed body think it quicker

[345] To untie what was covered than to carry away what was bound?

[Col. 0741B] Since delay is contrary to theft, it would therefore have been safer

[Col. 0742A] To take away the linens with the Lord.

The lying voice deceived itself; yet this matter

Has an excellent symbolic meaning: it is established that the Jews lost

[350] The one whom we carry in our devoted hearts, Christ.

Mourn the priests destined to perish, mourn the ministers,

And your people, Judaea, for such acts of daring.

No trumpet, no Anointed One, no longer is your accepted victim.

What wars will a trumpet sound for you, with the king slain?

[355] Who will be your Anointed One, you who have lost the true Anointed One?

What victim will be offered, when the shepherd is himself the victim?

Let the synagogue depart, darkened by its own color;

Christ has joined the Church to himself in beautiful love.

[Note: [Col. 0743B]

359. Meus has *perspicuo* for *conspicuo*.

361. Arntzenius has *cujus* for *hujus*. Cantabrigiensis has *manet: Mariae se quippe resurgens*, which is not inept and accords with the prose wording, “after the triumph of the resurrection.”

362. Arntzenius has *pius obtulit*; perhaps a copyist changed it to *pius* so that Jesus would not be said to have appeared first to the Virgin Mother. For Mark 16:9 says: “Rising early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene.” Nevertheless, there is no doubt that Sedulius held the view that the Lord first appeared to the Blessed Virgin, as the entire context proves. Engelbertus, who died in 1331, says this in *On the Grace and Virtues of the Mother of God*, part 2, chapter 2, in Pez’s *Anecdota*, volume 1. Sedulius also writes this in his *Paschal Work*: that he appeared first to his Mother before all others, as was fitting.

The opinion that the Mother of God came to the tomb together with the other women is attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Theophylact, Nicephorus, and others. A much more widely accepted tradition, however, is that Christ first appeared to his most holy Mother. In Vaticanus Recens, paper manuscript 349 of the *Miscellanies*, there is a short work on the three appearances of Our Lord Jesus Christ that are not found in the Gospel. The first was to Mary, his most holy Mother; the second to James son of Alphaeus; the third to Joseph, who buried the Lord. The author proves from Ambrose, book 3 *On Virgins*, from Augustine’s sermon on the Saturday after Easter, and from the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, that the Lord appeared first of all to his Mother: “And thus,” he says, “the Roman Church appears to hold this view, since on the first day of the Resurrection, namely Easter, it celebrates the station at Saint Mary Major.” This is the common opinion of Catholic writers, as Suárez proves in part 3, disputation 49, section 2; he nevertheless rightly denies that the Mother of God went to the tomb with the other women.

364. In the Litany of Loreto the Mother of God is acclaimed as Queen of the Apostles; and indeed she was the first of all to announce Christ. The reign of the Blessed Virgin over the Apostles is vividly represented in an ancient glass vessel, whose drawn image the most eminent Cardinal Borgia kindly communicated to me, as he is accustomed eagerly to promote the studies of all learned men. The glass is in Borgia’s museum at Velletri; I know of no other ancient glass on which the most holy Virgin is clearly depicted. Saint Peter is at her right side and Saint Paul at her left, so that we may understand her to be Queen of the Apostles.

Alexander Borgia, Archbishop of Fermo, has a highly learned homily on this same royal title of the Mother of God among his works, as well as in a booklet printed at Naples in 1792: *On the Kingdom of Mary: Homilies of Monsignor Alessandro Borgia*, etc. Augustine is an authoritative witness to the ancient and frequent practice of painting Peter and Paul together. Refuting heretics—or pagans—who had fabricated a book of Christ on magic addressed to Peter and Paul, he writes in *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book 1, chapter 10:

“Peter and Paul came before them; I believe that they had seen them painted together with him [Christ] in many places.… Thus they deserved to fall completely into error, who sought Christ and his apostles not in the sacred books but on painted walls. Nor is it surprising if, by being deceived by those who painted fictions, they themselves were deceived,” and so forth.

365. Meus: “He was recognized by two disciples.” Aldus: “Christ was recognized by the disciples in the breaking of the bread.” Poelmann’s papers and Parrhasius have *callemque petens* (“seeking the road”); the others, *conviva potens* (“as a powerful guest”); in my manuscript *convivia potens* is an error.

366. Reginensis 2, Albinus, Vaticanus 1, Reginensis 5, and Aldus have *quia*; this was also in Reginensis 1 but was corrected to *qui*, the more common and more accurate reading.

369. Meus: “He appeared to others.” Aldus: “Christ appeared often to the disciples.” Before this verse, some place verse 376, *Cum foribus clausis* (“When the doors were closed”), as Cellarius reports. All our witnesses preserve the usual order. For *proprios*, the Lyon Bible uselessly has *proprior*. Elsewhere Sedulius also uses *proprius* for *suus*, and in book 3, verses 158ff., he says *discipulos proprios*. Romanus and Meus have *diversis*; retain *diversi*. Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *hora* for *horis*.

371. Ottobonianus 2 has *Exemplo*; correct to *Extemplo*. Reginensis 1 in the first hand, Reginensis 2 and 4, Urbinas, Ottobonianus 1 and 2, Vaticanus 1 and 2, and Aldus have *abusti*. Reginensis 1 in the corrected hand, Anglicus, Meus, Albinus, Reginensis 3, and most printed editions have *obusti*. In Romanus, *ambusti* appears to have been made from *abusti*, but the meter rules it out. Arntzenius’s second hand, Parrhasius, and Poelmann’s papers have *adusti*. *Adustus* and *obustus* are more commonly used than *abustus*, but the latter can also be defended from *aburo*. Prudentius uses this verb on the authority of good manuscripts in *Hamartigenia*, verse 785, where others read *amburitur*, *oburitur*, or *exuritur*. Sedulius’s prose editions also vary: some have *adusti*, others *abusti*.

This is Mary, radiant in conspicuous honor:

[360] She, who, always bearing a glorious name, is the mother,

Always remains a virgin. Standing before her eyes,

The Lord openly offered himself first in light, so that the good mother,

[Col. 0744A] Proclaiming the great miracles of old,

Who had once been the way of his coming,

Might now be the herald of his return.

[365] Soon, as a powerful guest, he shone forth to others in the breaking of bread,

Recognized; he who is the true bread is always present

Before eyes made clear by the grace of faith,

So that they can see the living Lord.

Afterward, at different hours of different times,

[370] He openly approached his own disciples while they were eating,

Now presenting his face, now a roasted fish,

And eating honeycomb as food, thereby properly teaching

That corporeal things are food, and that he himself was visible

In the limbs in which he had formerly been. When fear again

[Note: [Col. 0745C]

375. In Reginensis 1 and Ottobonianus 1, *apostolicae* formerly stood instead of *apostaticae*, and this may also have been in my manuscript. But the true reading is *apostaticae*, as the following context makes clear. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have, not badly, *necasset* for *negasset*. The prose version, however, often has *negaverat*, from which it may be inferred that *negasset* is the true reading.

377. All our manuscripts, Anglicus, Albinus, Parrhasius, Aldus, and other printed editions have *Pace salutantis sese intulit* (“he introduced himself with the greeting ‘Peace’”), a reading accepted by Grunerus and Arntzenius. The Leipzig manuscript and the not very recent second hand of Albinus have *salutatis*, which I retained, following Cellarius. Arntzenius has *Pace salutaris*; a second hand has *Pax salutaris*, which is contrary to the meter. Arntzenius and Cantabrigiensis have *obtulit* for *intulit*, quite suitably. Arntzenius did not dislike—and I too do not dislike—*Pace salutatis sese obtulit* (“he presented himself after greeting them with ‘Peace’”). In some printed editions the order is reversed, with *Pace* placed before *Cum foribus*.

378. Reginensis 1, 3, and 5, Vaticanus 1 and 2, Urbinas, Anglicus, Albinus, Romanus, Aldus, and Ottobonianus 1 after correction have *Expediens*, which Nebrissensis interprets as “showing them to be freed.” Other manuscripts, with Parrhasius and most printed editions, have *Expandens* (“displaying”); this appears to be a gloss in Reginensis 1 and was deleted in Ottobonianus 1. Arntzenius has *atque ibi*; most manuscripts and editions have *ast ibi*; some printed editions have *ast ubi*.

380. Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *dubioque*, namely “in his heart”; others, *dubiamque*.

382. Arntzenius’s second hand has *erit*; *erat* (“was”) is correct instead of *fuerat* (“had been”), for the imperfect is sometimes used for the pluperfect. In my manuscript this verse and the following verses up to *Facta redemptoris*, almost at the end of the book, are missing because a leaf has been torn out.

384. Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *Discipulis*; less suitably.

385. Romanus has *patientem*; read *patienter*. Ottobonianus 2, Leipzig, Albinus, Arntzenius’s first hand, and some editions, together with Reginensis 1 and 3, Ottobonianus 1, Anglicus, and Albinus, have *labentis*, which also appears to have been written in Reginensis 2. The correction in Reginensis 3 and Ottobonianus 1 is *labantis*. The rule of the *Pedia* requires *labantis*; but in the manuscripts of other Christian poets as well, *labans* is sometimes changed to *labens*. Here *labantis* better suits the meaning. Vetus 1 and 2 and Monacensis have *labantem*; the Cologne edition, through the error just discussed, has *labentem*.

386. Romanus has *fit*; retain *sit*.

387. The Lyon Bible reverses the order of these verses improperly. Urbinas and Romanus have *Quisquis artificis*; something is missing. Ottobonianus 1, Reginensis 3, and Albinus have *Quisquis enim artificis*, but in Ottobonianus this was corrected to *artifices*, which is correct as an adjective, namely “craftsmen of fraud.” The editions Vetus 1 and 2 should therefore be corrected, since they read *fraudis*; nor should Wopkensis be followed, for he preferred *artifici caecas sub imagine fraudes*, against the ancient books and the prose version. *Artificis fraudis* may be retained if the accusative *figuras* is taken as governed by the verb *instruit*.

388. Romanus has *Instituit et*; the meter rejects this, and the more suitable verb is *Instruit*.

389. Cantabrigiensis has *cognosci*, the same verb found in the prose version and favored by Grunerus; all the others consistently have *agnosci*.

390. Romanus and Urbinas have *redundens*; the same error occurred in other manuscripts, where it appears to have been corrected to *recludens*. Cellarius suspects *recondens*; from the error *redundens*, *refundens* (“pouring back”) might more easily be conjectured. But *recludo* means not only “to open” but also the opposite, “to shut away” or “close”; and in Arntzenius there is the gloss *recludens—claudens* (“reclosing—shutting”). It is well established that there are many such verbs compounded with *re-* that possess two contrary meanings.

391. In Ottobonianus 1, *simulatus* was corrected to *simulator*. This is the genuine reading, although the other would not be contemptible.]

Of the apostate people, which had blindly denied the Lord,

When the faithful crowd was sitting behind closed doors,

He entered, greeting them with “Peace,” and, spreading out

His pierced hands, bares his side. But Thomas was there,

[380] Whose surname was Didymus; he had not been with the brothers,

And carried doubtful faith within his heart.

Until, while they were again sitting together, he came—

He who had never been absent. Then, with the threshold closed,

[Col. 0746A] He stood in the midst, not disdaining to show the open side

To the disciple and to have the wound tested by touch,

[385] And patiently to bear the mind that wavered.

Hence he was recognized all the more, because he is the friend of the doubter.

For whoever, beneath a hidden appearance, constructs

Cunning frauds and wishes to practice empty tricks

Does not wish to be recognized; he does not wish his deeds to be investigated,

[390] So that they may remain hidden beneath a cloud of deceit,

And, by closing everything in mist, the impostor hates anxious friends.

[Note: [Col. 0747C]

392. Aldus: “Christ commanded Peter, while fishing, to cast the nets to the right.”

393. In Reginensis 1, *dimittere* was corrected to *demittere*. Here too, as elsewhere, the manuscripts vary: most have *dimittere*. The difference is slight. Wopkensis preferred *demittere*.

395. Albinus has *traxere*, contrary to the meter. *Fluctivagam* is a word used by Statius.

396. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *quia*; others, *nam*. Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *et non*, which appears also to have been in Reginensis 2 and Ottobonianus 1, but the sense is contrary. In Urbinas the preceding verse is joined to this one at *traxerunt retia dignis*; the rest is missing.

397. Ottobonianus 1 has *in illo*; it was corrected to *in illa*. Psalm 18:9: “The commandment of the Lord is luminous.”

398. Romanus and Aldus, contrary to the meter, have *dextera parte*.

399. Parrhasius and Poelmann’s papers have *apostolicis alma ad vestigia*.

400. Poelmann: “He eats with the disciples.” Reginensis 5 and Aldus have *Nec pisces*; the same appears to be in Vaticanus 2. The others have *Nec piscis*, drawn from the Gospel.

401. Arntzenius, with some printed editions, preferred *ambiget*; all our manuscripts, including Anglicus and Albinus, together with Albinus, Arntzenius, Parrhasius, and Meus, have *ambigat*. Aldus corrected this, although he printed *ambiat* in the text.

403. Printed editions have *sanctus quoque Spiritus*; most of our manuscripts, Reginensis 1 and 3, Vaticanus 1, Ottobonianus 1, and Urbinas, have *sanctusque Spiritus*, which Romanus, Albinus, and Ottobonianus 2 also seem to indicate through their abbreviations. Vaticanus 2 has *panis, et sanctusque Spiritus*, where *que* is redundant, or rather *et* should be read; for Sedulius’s hand has *panis, sanctusque Spiritus*, with *que* lengthened before the *sp* beginning the following word, as Sedulius and others commonly do. Vaticanus 2 and Reginensis 5, which usually agree with Aldus, are recent manuscripts and have *sanctus quoque Spiritus*. Anglicus has the same in its joined letters.

404. Ottobonianus 1 has *Hinc etiam abluimur*. Parrhasius, Poelmann’s papers, Vaticanus 2, Reginensis 5, and Aldus have *hinc pascimur*; others, *hoc pascimur*.

405. Some printed editions transpose the words: *Tunc praeceptor eos epulis*. Arntzenius attributes this also to Parrhasius; but Parrhasius preserves the received reading. In Arntzenius’s manuscript, *salvator* may be a gloss for *praeceptor*.

406. Reginensis 1 has *Alloquis*; read *Alloquiis*.

407. Grunerus and Arntzenius, together with the manuscript Arntz. and many printed editions, have *pietate*; all our manuscripts, with Parrhasius, Aldus, and others, have *bonitate*, which should not be abandoned. In Ottobonianus 1, *notaque Dei bonitate* was written and corrected to *nota Domini bonitate*.

409. Ottobonianus 2 corruptly has *aucta* for *victa*. Urbinas: “After hunger had been conquered, they rose.” Romanus, contrary to the meter: “After hunger had been conquered, they rose.” Albinus, Ottobonianus 2, and Anglicus have *exsurrexere*; Reginensis 3, *adsurrexere*; Albinus, *esurrexere* for *et surrexere*. Ottobonianus 1 had *exsurrexere*; the common reading is *et surrexere*. An imitation of Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.384: “When hunger had been removed by the food and the tables cleared.” Lucan and Valerius Flaccus likewise use *vincere famem* (“to conquer hunger”).]

The Lord likewise, when Peter was fishing across the sea

With his companions and had caught nothing, instructed him

To lower the lines into the waters on the right; soon, when the whirlpool closed,

[395] The hanging nets dragged along their wave-roaming prey,

[Col. 0748A] To be understood by a symbolic path: for the nets are the shining

Commands of God for the worthy, by which everyone remaining on that right side

Is enclosed, and at the same time is carried in apostolic arms

To the feet of the Lord Christ.

[400] Nor were fish, coals, and bread lacking,

Found together in one place for the disciples. Who could doubt

That one faith consists in these things? For the water is the fish,

Christ is present as the bread, and the Holy Spirit as the fire.

From the water we are washed; by this we are fed; from that we are sanctified.

[405] Then the Teacher invites them to a meal,

[Col. 0749A] Addressing them, as is customary, with pious words.

As they approach the table with one accord, they enjoy the Lord’s

Recognized goodness, and they perceived their Christ. When hunger

Had been conquered by the modest provisions, they rose, leaving them behind.

[Note: [Col. 0749C]

410. Aldus has *choris*; correct to *toris*. Reginensis 5 reverses the order, contrary to the meter: *corde se Petrus*.

411. *Nitentes* means “fat,” “well nourished,” or “in good condition”; Virgil, Horace, Phaedrus, and both Plinys use *nitere* in this sense.

412. Reginensis 2 has *operario omni*, but perhaps it was *operari in omni* or *operarier omni*. Ottobonianus 1 also appears to have had *operari*. The true reading is *operario in omni*.

413. Ottobonianus 1 has *bono*, corrected to *bona*. This correction is plainly inept.]

414. Vat. 1, 2, Reg. 3, 5, Rom., Ottob. 2, Ang., Alb., Parrh., Ald., and others: *haec* (“these”) instead of *hoc* (“this”). The Lipsian edition has *trino* and *trina* instead of *terno* and *terna*. Urb. corruptly has *Aeterno* instead of *Haec terno* or *Hoc terno*. Vat. 1 and Ott. 2 have *movens*, which was also found in Ott. 1 but was correctly emended there to *movens*. Vat. 2 erroneously has *terga* instead of *terna* or *trina*.

416. Ald.: “What Christ commanded the apostles when he appeared to them for the last time.” Poelm.: “He commends the preservation of peace.” Vat. 2 and Reg. 3 and 5, with the order reversed against the meter: “Have peace,” he says, “all of you.”

417. Reg. 3 first inserts *Pacem per populus*, then *Pacem ferte*.

418. Ott. 1, with the others, has *sanctis* instead of *sacris*, unless one prefers to take *id* as a gloss.

419. Ald., Fabr., and some other printed editions have *vocate*. The sense requires *vocari*, as *lavari* occurs immediately afterward.

420. Vat. 1 has *et cunctis*. This was also found in Ott. 1 but was properly corrected to *e cunctis*.

[Col. 0750C] 421. Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, verse 97: “I shall wash everyone in the spring.”

422. Ald.: “That Christ ascended into heaven before everyone.” Rom. incorrectly transposes these verses, placing *Bethaniae* first and *Haec ubi* afterward.

425. In Reg. 1 the reading was *Aetherius evectas*, correctly corrected to *Aetherias evectus*; others write *Aethereas*. Fabr. and several other printed editions have *subvectus*; most have the better reading *evectus*. Vet. 1 and Mon. have *sublimus*, which Arntzenius says better reflects the usage of the ancients. Accius, Sallust, and Lucretius spoke in this way. Our manuscripts support *sublimis*. Reg. 1 and 2 have, instead of *in auras*, *in oras*, which seems to have been found in Ottob. 1, where the common reading *in auras* now appears. In the prose version: *per oras*.

426. Reg. 2 and 3, Vatican. 2, Rom., and the Lipsian edition have *Et dextra sedet ipse Patris*, which seems to have been found in Reg. 1, where it now reads *Et dextram sedet ipse Patris*, without suitable syntax. Ott. 1 has *Et dextra sedit*, correctly corrected to *sedet*. The corruption in Urb. derives from this: *Et dextra sed ipse*. Ang., Vat., Ott. 2, Reg. 5, Ald., and several printed editions have *Ad dextram sedet*. Vet. 1 and 2, Mon., Bas., and Col. have *In dextra sedet*. The Poelm. manuscripts, Torn. 1–3, and other editions have *Et dextram subit*. The Poelm. edition in the margin has *Ad dextram subit*. Alb., without sense or meter, has *Et dexteram sedet*. The probable reading is *Et dextra sedet*, clearer in prose as *Ad dextram sedet*. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, Ald., and the Poelm. manuscripts have *mundumque gubernat*; our better books, together with Alm., Heinsius’s manuscript, and the prose version, have *totumque*, that is, “everything,” as has already been noted in Sedulius. In the prose version some have *totumque orbem*.

Rite toris, an corde Petrus se diligat alto,  
The Lord duly probes whether Peter loves him with a deep heart;

Explorat Dominus: Petrus annuit: ergo nitentes  
Peter assents. Therefore the loving shepherd, desirous of increasing

Pastor amans augere greges, operario in omni  
His radiant flocks, entrusts the sheep—and also the lambs—

Parte bono commendat oves, commendat et agnos.  
To every good worker in their several parts.

Hoc terno sermone monens, ut terna negantis  
By this threefold utterance he warns that the fresh fault

[415] 357 Culpa recens parili numero purgata maneret.  
Of the one who denied three times might remain purged by an equal number.

Inde sequenda docens, Pacem omnes, inquit, habete,  
Then he teaches what must be followed: “All of you, have peace,” he says;

[Col. 0750A] Pacem ferte meam, pacem portate quietam,  
“Bring my peace; bear tranquil peace;

Pacem per populos monitis dispergite sanctis,  
Spread peace among the peoples by holy admonitions,

Et mundum vacuate malis: gentesque vocari  
And rid the world of evils. I command that nations

[420] Finibus e cunctis, latus qua tenditur orbis,  
From every region, wherever the broad world extends,

Jussis mando meis, omnesque in fonte lavari.  
Be called, and that all be washed in the fountain.”

Haec ubi dicta pio Dominus sermone peregit,  
When the Lord had completed these words in a devout discourse,

Bethaniae mox arva petit: coramque beatis  
He soon sought the fields of Bethany; and, before the blessed men

Qui tantum meruere viris spectare triumphum,  
Who deserved so great a triumph to behold,

[425] Aethereas evectus abit sublimis in auras.  
He was raised on high and departed sublime into the heavenly breezes.

358 Ad dextram sedet ipse Patris totumque gubernat  
He sits at the right hand of the Father himself and governs all things.

[Col. 0751A]

[Note: 427. Vat. 1 has, not badly, *tenet* (“holds”), with the final syllable lengthened because of the caesura. Cant., Ald., and some other editions have *excelsaque, et ima* (“the heights and the depths”); retain *excelsa, vel ima* (“the heights or the depths”), for *vel* is sometimes used for *et*, especially by writers of the later period.

428. The Poelm. sheets and Parrh. have *Conservando regit, penetrat*. The true manuscript reading is far more elegant: *Tartara post coelum penetrat, post tartara coelum* (“He penetrates Tartarus after heaven, heaven after Tartarus”). Once again Sedulius professes Christ’s descent into the lower regions; for *tartara* may not be interpreted as “the tomb.” See the note on Book I, verse 222, and the dissertation of Liberatus Fassonius, an elegant writer, in which he proves that Jesus Christ descended to the lower regions before he rose from the dead.

429. Reg. 5 and Ald. have *laeti*; the others, better, *laetis*. Vat. 1 rather inelegantly transposes the words: *cernentes, laetis*.

431. Parrhasius printed *Vestigis* and Cellarius accordingly suspects that it should be read contracted, to preserve the meter. Wopkensius retains *Vestigiis*, but makes its second syllable short, as Sedulius elsewhere offends against prosody. The manuscripts and most editions give *Vestigiis*. When this word is so written, there is no metrical fault if the final two vowels are contracted by synaeresis, as the first two are in the disyllables *deerat* and *deinde*. Our excellent manuscripts Reg. 1 and 2, Ott. 1, and Ang. have *veneranter* (“reverently”); the gloss in Reg. 1 is *reverenter*, and that in Reg. 2, “with reverence, with veneration.” Reg. 3 and Rom. have *venerantur* (“they venerate”), corrected to *veneranter*. Vatt. 1 and 2 and Alb., in their letter-abbreviations, suggest *veneranter* rather than *venerantur*. The more recent codices Reg. 5, Urb., and Ottob. 2 have *venerantur*. From other manuscripts Alm. and Cant. have *veneranter*; Barthius’s manuscript has *venerantur*. The editions vary likewise, but the older ones have *venerantur*. The prose supports this reading, and recent editors adhere to it. In Corippus, Book II, verse 35, occurs *famulantur, adorant* (“they serve, they worship”). In Dracontius, Book I, verse 4, I printed: “Let them confess their maker and reverently worship him,” following the authority of Tertullian and of Sedulius here. In a doubtful matter Dracontius’s verse could indeed have been recast as *venerentur, adorent*. Yet the adverb *veneranter*, used by Dracontius and Sedulius, still seems to me genuine.

433. Aldus punctuates: *doceant testes. Nam jure fideles*; I do not approve.

436. Mon. has *voluisse*; correct it to *voluissent*. Instead of *chartis* (“writings”), Arntzenius has *libris* (“books”), perhaps from a gloss; Parrh. has *scriptis*. This hyperbole from the Gospel of Saint John resembles other Hebraisms, or Jewish modes of expression. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XLI, chapter 24: “I join those who prefer to interpret ‘the world would be unable to contain’ not by the number of books but by the weight of mysteries, rather than to hear a HYPERBOLE. But, they say, such things also have been written. I grant it; but what prevents further and loftier things from having been left over? . . . Thus, writing of all Christ’s mysteries, the most learned theologian Prudentius gives us a foundation for this opinion in the *Apotheosis*: ‘From thousands of things I shall unweave only a very few—reviewing them summarily, which the whole world does not contain.’” Nonnus the paraphrast, following the letter, measures the world’s capacity by the extent of the immense structure. Prudentius’s passage, to be sure, is not sufficiently clear for Barthius’s opinion; Sedulius is certainly opposed to it. Theophylact thus summarizes three different interpretations of the final chapter of John: “Do not be surprised that he said the world could not contain the books, if any were written concerning the works of Jesus; rather, receive the saying faithfully, understanding the ineffable power of the Word of God. For as it is easy for us to speak, so it is much easier for him to do whatever he wills. Some think it was said hyperbolically, after the manner of Scripture; for it is Scripture’s custom to employ hyperbole. . . . Others understand by WORLD those who set their minds on worldly things. But the works done by Jesus are divine and full of mysteries, both in the visible and in the invisible creation, and those which are to come are full of mysteries; the worldly human being cannot understand them.”

438. In Ott. 1 this verse was written by a recent hand, another having been erased. It is followed by the epigram in praise of Sedulius, “Sedulius Christi,” etc., not by the other, “Sedulius Domini,” then by the elegy, “Cantemus.” In Reg. 1: “Book IV ends. The book of Arator begins. It is finished.” In another ancient hand: “Ends”; and in the margin: “Seek in this volume ‘Cantemus, socii, Domino,’ after Arator.” But in this codex of Arator there is only this: “To the most holy and blessed father and first of all priests throughout the whole world, Pope Vigilius, Arator the subdeacon.” Only one leaf remains, containing the notice already transcribed in Prolegomena no. 136, “This work [of Sedulius],” etc., and the epigrams of Asterius, Liberius, and Belisarius. In Reg. 2: “Book IV of the heroic Paschal Song ends. The elegiac poem begins, called *Paracterium*, that is, a repercussion, because one verse is echoed by another: the beginning of the first becomes the end of the second. *Paractera* in Greek is called *repercussio* in Latin.” In Vat. 1: “The book of Sedulius ends. His poem begins: ‘Cantemus,’ etc.” Vat. 2: “End.” Then the notice “This work,” etc., discussed in Prolegomena no. 136 and following; immediately follows the elegy, “Cantemus,” etc. Reg. 5 has: “The poem has an end, nor do I seek garlands of laurel—May you, Mary, be the reward of my study.” Read: “The poem has an end.” The notice follows: “Turtius Ruffus Asterius found the following poems among the writings of Coelius Sedulius,” “Cantemus,” etc. There follow the hymn *A solis ortus cardine* and the epigram of Sedulius himself to be given below. Reg. 3 and Ang.: “The book of Sedulius ends,” and, with no other heading, the elegy “Cantemus.” Urb.: “The fourth and final book of the excellent bishop Sedulius, concerning the passion, resurrection, and ascension of the only-begotten Son of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, happily ends. The *paracterum* poem of the same author begins, that is, the repercussive poem, because the middle part of the first verse is the end of the second verse. In which,” etc., as I shall now explain. Ott. and Rom., after the end of the Paschal poem and without any title: “Cantemus.” My codex: “The fourth and final book of Sedulius the poet ends; the distich epigram of the same begins, which our people call repercussive and the Greeks παράντερον [“echoing”]: ‘Cantemus,’ etc.” Parrhasius: “Sedulius’s Paschal Song ends.” Nothing else by Sedulius is added, but certain poems of Prudentius. Heinsius’s manuscript: “Sedulius’s Paschal Song ends; the hymn of the same begins.” Juretus, at the end of the prose: “Sedulius’s prose ends.”]

Jure suo, qui cuncta tenens excelsa, vel ima,  
By his own right, he who holds all things, the heights or the depths,

Tartara post coelum penetrat, post tartara coelum.  
Penetrates Tartarus after heaven, and heaven after Tartarus.

Illi autem laetis cernentes vultibus, altas  
But they, seeing with joyful faces the Lord

[430] Ire super nubes Dominum, tractusque coruscos  
Going high above the clouds and treading the shining paths

Vestigiis calcare suis, veneranter adorant,  
With his own footsteps, worship him reverently;

Sidereasque vias alacri sub corde reportant,  
With eager hearts they bear back the starry paths,

[Col. 0752A] Quas cunctos doceant: testes nam jure fideles  
That they may teach to all; for they were rightly faithful witnesses

Divinae virtutis erant, qui plura videntes,  
Of divine power, and, having seen many things,

Innumerabilium scripserunt pauca bonorum.  
Wrote a few things out of innumerable blessings.

For if they had wished to commit to sacred writings all the deeds

Nam si cuncta sacris voluissent tradere chartis  
Of the Redeemer, not even the whole world would have sufficed

Facta redemptoris, nec totus cingere mundus  
To contain the crowded books through so many volumes.

360 Sufficeret densos per tanta volumina libros.

[Col. 0753]

## COELIUS SEDULIUS’S ELEGY. (C)

[Col. 0753B] [Note: The matters just mentioned should be compared with Prolegomena no. 46, where this title is cited from Trithemius: “An Exhortation to the Faithful,” or “An Exhortatory Book to the Faithful,” and with no. 162. Bede, in *On the Art of Meter*, repeatedly draws examples from this elegy, also citing Sedulius by name. Osbern, an eleventh-century writer, takes several verses from it in his *Life of Saint Dunstan*, in the Bollandists, under 19 May. Reg. 2 explains its subject as follows: “After having described the miracles, the poet urges everyone to sing with him to Christ and to give thanks.” Urb.: “In these repercussive (*paracterial*) poems, the author Sedulius, having described the deeds and sayings of our Savior Christ in heroic verse, summons all the faithful to praise almighty God and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” In the Almel. manuscript the title is “Sedulius’s Hymn.” In Arntzenius’s edition: “The hymn of Coelius Sedulius.”

1. A comparison of the Old and New Testaments, repeated in alternate verses by the figure of *epanalepsis* (ἐπαναλήψεως, “repetition”). By this same device others composed elegies, as in the *Veterum Analecta* of Mabillon, vol. I: Theodulf of Orléans, Paul the Deacon of Aquileia, Eugenius of Toledo, Peter Damian, Godfrey of Vendôme, and the manuscript *Moral Distichs* inserted as Book XIV of Martial in the parchment manuscript of the Roman College.

[Col. 0753D] 1. Vat. 2 and Ottob. 2, with the order reversed: *Cantemus Domino, socii*. The Turin manuscript: *Cantemus, socii, Dominum*. See Prolegomena no. 180. Reg. 5 and Ald. have *honores*, which Nebrissensis explains as “praises”; the others have *cantemus honorem*.

2. Cappusotus: *Christo*; others: *Christi*. In the Turin manuscript the word is in Greek instead of *Christi*, and appears to be *praesonet* instead of *personet*.

3. Vat. 2: *de magna luce*; others: *magna de luce*. The subject is Lucifer’s fall.

4. Arntz., first hand; Alb.; Meus; Vet. 1; Torn. 3: *cum timuit*; others: *cum tumuit*. To this belong Ottob. 1 and Rom., which have *contumuit* instead of *cum tumuit*. This is the genuine reading, since the passage concerns pride, which is usually expressed by swelling, as I have already said concerning other Christian poets. Osbern likewise wrote it this way in the *Life of Saint Dunstan*.

5. Vet. 1 erroneously has *perire minoris*; Rom. first corrected it to *per minores*, that is, “Adam’s descendants.”

6. Osbern, with the order reversed, perhaps to avoid hiatus: *Cuncti salvantur*.

7. Alm., Reg. 3, and some printed editions: *quae*; the others: *qua*; in Ottob. 1 the reading is ambiguous, *quae* or *qua*. Eve is understood.

8. Almel., Reg. 2 and 5, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ott. 1, Ald., Cellarius, Meus, Ang., Alb., and Osbern: *ex qua*. Reg. 3 likewise, but instead of *ex qua*: *Per quam*. Vet. 1 erroneously has *Et quia*. Urb., Ott. 2, Rom., and Goldastus in the *Biblical Manual*: *Et qua*, which Grunerus preferred with most of the common editions, because *qua* without *ex* occurs earlier; *ex* could easily have been changed into *et*. The Mother of God is praised.

11. Meus has *quod* in the first occurrence and in the following verse *Quod ventura*; others more correctly have *quid* in both places. Urb. accepted *amisit*, which I retain.

12. Meus, Reg. 5, and Ald.: *paret*, which is also Wopkensius’s conjecture—namely, what the origin, or the coming people and offspring, acquires. Others have *parent*. The gloss in Arntz. and Reg. 2 explains it as referring first to Enoch, translated into heaven, and afterward to Christ’s ascent into heaven. Cellarius interpreted the first “passing” as Abel and Cain’s going out into the field; Wopkensius more aptly interpreted it as Abel’s death. I should prefer something clearer.

13. Reg. 3: *homines ut perderet*; the sense requires *ne*.

14. The ark is the Church, saved through baptism, or also Christ, the institutor of the sacrament of baptism.

15. Vatican 1: *per nati vulnera*; the others: *pro nati vulnere*; Petrus Burmannus conjectured *funere* instead of *vulnere*. In Rom. I think *cunctos* is a corruption of *cuncto*. The father here is Abraham.

16. Vet. 1, Mon., and Poelm., with the order reversed: *Cum Christum tradis*; all our manuscripts, together with most printed editions: *Cum tradis Christum*. In Reg. 1 *Contradis* was written instead of *Cum tradis*. Cant. and some printed editions have *Cum sumis Christum*, which is less good.]

361 Cantemus, socii, Domino cantemus honorem,  
Let us sing, companions; let us sing honor to the Lord.

Dulcis amor Christi personet ore pio.  
Let the sweet love of Christ resound from a devout mouth.

Primus ad ima ruit magna de luce superbus,  
First the proud one fell from the great light to the depths;

Sic homo, cum tumuit, primus ad ima ruit.  
So man, when he swelled with pride, first fell to the depths.

[5] Unius ob meritum cuncti perire minores,  
Because of the merit of one, all the lesser ones perish;

Salvantur cuncti unius ob meritum.  
Because of the merit of one, all are saved.

Sola fuit mulier, patuit qua janua letho:  
There was one woman alone, through whom the door to death was opened;

362 Et qua vita redit, sola fuit mulier.  
And there was one woman alone through whom life returns.

[Col. 0754B] Frater iniquus erat justum qui perculit olim,  
The wicked brother was the one who once struck down the just man;

[10] Damnator Christi frater iniquus erat.  
The wicked brother was the condemner of Christ.

Transitus ille monet, quid prima amisit origo,  
That passage warns what the first origin lost,

Quid ventura parent, transitus ille monet.  
And what future generations will prepare; that passage warns us.

Arca levatur aquis, homines ne perderet aequor,  
The ark is raised above the waters so that the flood might not destroy mankind;

Ne pereant homines, arca levatur aquis.  
So that mankind may not perish, the ark is raised above the waters.

[15] Sume, pater, populos pro nati vulnere cunctos  
Take all the peoples, Father, in exchange for the wound of your Son;

Cum tradis Christum, sume, pater, populos.  
When you hand Christ over, take the peoples, Father.

[Col. 0755A] [Note: 17. Urb. and Rom.: *sanctis signata*; Alm. and Ott. 1: *dudum signata*; others: *tacitis signata*. Here again Isaac is the subject.

18. Vet. 1 and Mon.: *reserat*, which Arntzenius suspects is a typographical error; but Rom., Ald., and apparently my manuscript also have *reserat*. The true reading, however, is *referat*; I would nevertheless prefer *refert*, since the first syllable of *refert* is usually lengthened.

19. Cellarius and Arntzenius printed *heros*; all our manuscripts, together with Ang. and the ancient editions, have *heres*, with no satisfactory sense. Someone might suppose that, in *praevalet Israel*, the final two syllables of *Israel* are contracted so that the word becomes a spondee. The name Israel itself means “prevailing with God.” But the common reading *heros* seems sound; Prudentius uses *heros* in this way, as do Saint John the Evangelist in *Hymn* 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 114, and Tobias in *Hymn* 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 70. In the Alb. manuscript *heros* seems to have stood, later corrected to *heres*.

20. In Ott. 1 the words seem to have been divided as *Asper agens*; but they must be read *Aspera gens*.

21. A learned hand in Arntz. noted that some copies have *Pepulit* instead of *Reppulit*, an obvious error. Some write *repulit*, thinking that *re* may be lengthened even when the following consonant is not doubled. I follow the more usual practice, according to which *reppulit*, *relligio*, and certain similar words are written with doubled consonants when *re* is lengthened. In *refert* another usage prevails: when the verb is impersonal, its first syllable is always long; when it comes from *refero*, it is short, although it is sometimes lengthened. Many editions have *distractus crimine fratrum*, which can be defended. Dracontius uses the word in a similar context, *Book* II, verse 510: “The seller and buyer are stained by blood in the transaction”; likewise Juvencus, *Book* IV, verse 635. Our manuscripts do not know this reading, and in Alm. *distractus* is a gloss on *venitus*. Cant. with Alm. and Ang. has *venitus*, from *veneo*, whose supine is *venum* and *venitum*, with the penultimate syllable short according to Priscian, *Book* X. The form in ordinary use is *venum*. Recent editors defend *venitus*, whose second syllable Sedulius is supposed to have lengthened freely. Support is provided by the supine *ambitum*, whose second syllable is long, although in *itum* the first syllable is short. In Vat. 2 the reading seems to be *venitus*, and it also appears in Reg. 3, but there it has been corrected to *venditus*, with the gloss *venumdatus*. Ott. 1, Arntz., first hand, and Reg. 3 have *venditus crimine fratrum*, which the meter rejects; still more contrary to the meter is Ott. 2: *famem qui venditus crimine fratrum*. Reg. 2, Vat. 1, Rom., Alb., and Meus have *famem venatus crimine fratrum*, with the gloss *venditus* in Reg. 2; Urb. is related to this, *famem, qui venatus crimine fratrum*. But *venatus* for *venditus* is not Latin, and in Urb. *qui* would also violate the meter. Arntz., second hand, Reg. 5, and Ald. have, in another form, *famem, frater quem vendidit auro*. Both meter and Latinity can be satisfied if the reading is reconstructed from the traces of the manuscripts as *Reppulit ille famem venum actus crimine fratrum*. Everyone sees that Joseph, sold by his brothers, is the subject.

22. Reg. 5 and Ald.: *Venditus ab Juda*. Grunerus, with his manuscripts and editions: *Venditus a Juda*; Fabricius says he does not know where he derived *Venditus est Christus*. But almost all our manuscripts, together with the Poelm. edition in the text, Ang. with Arntzenius’s manuscript, and the editions Vet. 1, Vet. 2, and Mon., have *Venditus est Christus*, for which Alm. has *Venditus est Dominus*. In Arntz., later hand, and in the Poelm. sheets: *Venditus a Juda*.

24. Arntz. has *poenae* instead of *plagae*, less elegantly; it is written *pene*. Pharaoh is the treacherous one here.

25. Arntz., second hand, Reg. 5, and Ald. have *conduxit* instead of *revocavit*. Reg. 2 has *revocavit*, but seems to have originally read *reduxit*, which I would not reject; I find this written in Ang. The subject is the paschal lamb.

26. Ald.: *nos revocat*, which, together with the accepted reading *revocavit* in the preceding verse, is elegant. Others have *nosque refert*, where the conjunction *-que* may be omitted.

27. *Nefas*, that is, the wicked Egyptians together with Pharaoh.

28. Meus and Ang.: *Cum mundi populis*. Cellarius, with Alm.: *Cum populis mundi*, admitting hiatus. Reg. 2 and Ott. 1 likewise have this, but in the latter it became *Nunc populos mundi*. Alb. has the corruption *Nec populis mundi*. Reg. 3 and 5, Vatt. 1 and 2, Ott. 2, Rom., Urb., Ald., and Fabr.: *Nunc mundi populis*. Many common editions: *Nunc populis mundis*. Arntzenius’s manuscript: *Nunc mundi populi*; the Cambridge manuscript: *Nunc populi mundi*, that is, “the Christian peoples,” a reading and interpretation followed by Grunerus and Arntzenius. Wopkensius conjectured *Nunc populos mundans*.

29. Alm. and Meus: *referta*, to which the corruption *referto* in Ott. 2 is related; other manuscripts have *refecta*, which is better.

31. Some printed editions erroneously have *Plebs si* in both verses instead of *Plebs sibi*. Ott. 1 and Rom. have *capit* in both verses; in Ott. 1 it was correctly corrected to *caput*. The Poelm. edition in the margin has *adorat*, and this is preferred by the Poelm. sheets. The others have *adopta*, with the gloss “chooses” in Reg. 2, which better suits this passage: just as the hard-hearted Israelite people adopted the calf’s head for itself, so the hard-hearted Jewish people took Christ away as its head. Otherwise these forms are easily exchanged in manuscripts: *adorat*, *adoptat*, *adornat*, *adaptat*, as has already been shown elsewhere.

32. Ott. 1: *hunc*; correctly corrected to *heu*.

33. Reg. 2 has *initium* in this and the following verse; both were corrected to *indicium*, which must be retained. Ott. 1 originally had *discrimine*, as in Vat. 1, but in Ott. 1 it was changed to *de crimine*, which is the true reading. Meus has *de culmine*.

34. The Poelm. edition: *Quoque* instead of *Quodque*. Rom., Ott. 2, and Urb. have *venit*, which also seems to occur in Meus; but the meter requires *veniat*. John 5:39: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they are the ones that bear witness about me.”

35. Vet. 2: *En lapsus*; the Col. edition has *irriguis* in this and the following verse; Arntz. has *fronte*. Correct to: *En lapis irriguus, et fonte*. The stone struck, which poured out water, is a “watered stone,” as Cellarius rightly explains. Yet he foolishly takes *satiare* as the passive indicative *satiaris*, whereas it is an imperative mood.]

Hostia summa Patris, tacitis signata figuris;  
The highest offering of the Father, marked by silent figures;

Quam referat Christus, hostia summa Patris.  
Which Christ represents, the highest offering of the Father.

Claudicat ecce videns Dominum, dum praevalet, heros,  
Behold, the hero limps as he sees the Lord, while he prevails;

[20] 363 Aspera gens Christum claudicat ecce videns.  
Behold, the harsh people limps as it sees Christ.

Reppulit ille famem, venitus crimine fratrum:  
He drove away hunger, sold through the crime of his brothers;

Venditus est Christus, reppulit ille famem.  
Christ was sold; he drove away hunger.

Perfide, corde peris, dum vastant omnia plagae,
