Treacherous one, you perish in your heart while the plagues ravage everything;

Dum cessant plagae, perfide, corde peris.  
When the plagues cease, treacherous one, you perish in your heart.

[25] Agnus ab hoste sacer revocavit sanguine patres,  
The sacred Lamb recalled the fathers from the enemy by his blood;

[Col. 0756A] Sanguine nosque refert agnus ab hoste sacer.  
By his blood the sacred Lamb also brings us back from the enemy.

364 Obruit unda nefas, populo gradiente per aequor,  
The wave overwhelmed the wickedness as the people crossed the sea;

Nunc mundi populis obruit unda nefas.  
Now the wave overwhelms wickedness for the peoples of the world.

Murmurat impietas, manna veniente refecta,  
Impiety murmurs, though refreshed by the coming manna;

[30] Panis adest Christus, murmurat impietas.  
Christ the bread is present; impiety murmurs.

Plebs sibi dura caput terrae cultoris adoptat,  
The hard-hearted people adopts for itself the head of the cultivator of the earth;

Abstulit, heu! Christum plebs sibi dura caput.  
Alas! The hard-hearted people took Christ away as its head.

Lex dedit indicium veteris de crimine poenae,  
The Law gave a sign of the ancient punishment for sin,

Quodque salus veniat, lex dedit indicium.  
And the Law gave a sign that salvation would come.

[35] En lapis irriguus, satiare, incredule, fonte:  
Behold the watered stone; be satisfied, unbeliever, from the spring.

[Col. 0757A] [Note: 36. Meus and Ang. have, not badly, *Quid Christum reprobas?* Others have *Qui Christum reprobas*, for which Ott. 1 originally had *reprobis*, without sense. Alb. has *Quod Christum reprobas*.

37. Reg. 5, Alb., and Ald. have *priorum*; Reg. 2 has *piorum*; above, *priorum*; the gloss is “Moses and Aaron”; in Vat. 1, *et vota priora*, corrected to *priorum*. The more likely and more common reading is *votumque piorum*, opposed to the rebellious tribe. Cellarius recognizes Korah, Dathan, and Abiram in the rebellious tribe; but these were not consumed by fire—the earth swallowed them. The reference must therefore be to the 250 men who offered incense and were consumed by fire, and likewise to the 14,700 who murmured and perished in the conflagration, as reported in Numbers 16. Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, were also consumed by heavenly fire. But it does not seem appropriate to speak of only these two as a rebellious tribe.

39. *Haeres legis*, unless one prefers *heros* by conjecture, seems to refer to Moses, who did not enter the Promised Land. The gloss in Reg. 2 says: “None of those who departed from Egypt entered the land of promise except Caleb and Joshua.”

40. Ald. has *Christus*; others, *Jesus*.

41. Some common editions have *hostis*, namely, “he destroys the walls of the enemy while he circles them.” The manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have *hostem*. Arntzenius punctuates: “The ark of God destroys the walls while it circles the enemy,” but the distinction indicated by the pentameter is preferable; in fact, the ark circled the walls of Jericho, as is clear from Joshua 6.

42. Cant. has *mundi et destruit*; the conjunction *et* is superfluous.

43. The sign given to Gideon: first, the fleece was wet on the dry threshing floor, then the fleece was dry on the wet threshing floor. Judges 6.

45. A learned hand in the margin of the Mon. edition wanted *amore Dei*, as appears somewhere in the pentameter. Wopkensius seems to have wanted *amore Dei* in both places; certainly either this must be read in both places, or *honore Dei* in both. The manuscripts and most editions prefer *honore Dei*. Some editions have *promisso munere*, without *in*; *in* is also absent from Vatt. 1 and 2, Alb., Urb., Rom., and was absent from Reg. 3, where it was added by a recent hand. Some have *praemisso* instead of *promisso*.

46. Reg. 5 and Ald. have *Effectum*; the others correctly have *Affectum*, which Nebrissensis ordered to be restored by conjecture, because Jephthah placed love for his daughter after religious duty. The subject here is Jephthah.

47. Rom. has *sternes*; correct to *sterns*.

51. Vatican 2 has *regis*; correct to *legis*. In this verse it has *tulit* instead of *attulit*, and in the following verse instead of *abstulit*, as the gloss in Alm. explains.

53. Vat. 2, Rom., Reg. 5, Urb., and Ald. have *nullo temerata pudore*. Ottob. 2, Meus, Reg. 3, Ang., Alb., and Vat. 1 have *nullo temerante pudore*. Reg. 2 and Ott. 1, with most editions, have *nullo temerante pudorem*.

55. The question arises because he was placed as a sign “against which there would be contradiction.” On this question consult the note on Juvencus, Book I, verse 245: “A sign spoken against.”

57. The Cambridge manuscript, Arntz., Alm., Ott. 1, and Reg. 5 have *percepit*. The same reading appears in our other manuscripts, but in abbreviated letters; in some, such as Meus, it seems more likely to be read *praecepit*. This was Peter Burmannus’s conjecture, meaning “he commanded in hope.” Reg. 2 has *accepit*, either as a gloss or, rather, as a variant reading. Most editions, including recent ones, have *mundus haec sentit, et ambit*. Vat. 2 corruptly has *mundus percipit, et ambit*. The meter rules this out, although *ambit* is more naturally connected with *percipit* than with *percepit*. Burmannus thinks that *ambit* stands for *ambiit* or *ambivit*.

59. Reg. 5 has *magnalia coeli*, incorrectly. Rom. has the worse reading *magnalia Dei*; but in it the correction *caeci* has been made.

61. Vet. 1 and 2 have *reducta*; read *deducta*, as in the others. Reg. 1 and 2 originally had another reading. Above, Reg. 1 seems to have *manavit* as a gloss on *cucurrit*; elsewhere in Sedulius some manuscripts incorporate this gloss into the text. The meter rules it out. Ang. corruptly has *succurrit*. The verse alludes to the wood of the forbidden tree, the following verse to the wood of the cross.

63. The gloss in Alm. gives *attulit martyribus* for *tulit* in this verse and *sustinuit* for *martyribus* in the following verse. It is clearer, however, to understand all human beings in the word *servis*.

67. Here too Sedulius repeats that Christ the Lord descended to the regions below.

68. Arntz. and Rom. have *Nec credunt*; the other manuscripts and editions, better, *Nec cernunt*.

69. Bede quotes this verse in *On the Art of Meter*, as does his commentator. The Apostle, Romans 5:12: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death.”

70. In Alm., where this verse was written in the margin, and in Arntz., Reg. 2 and 5, Vat. 1 and 2, Ott. 2, Urb., Rom., Ang., and Meus, the reading is *congemuit*. Ott. 1, Reg. 3, and Alb., together with most editions, have *contremuit*, a word Arntzenius considers more suitable to the subject. *Congemuit* is no less suitable.]

[Col. 0759A] [Note: 74. Cant. and Alm. have *suscepit primum*, with hiatus; Cellarius and Arntzenius followed this, and the glosses indicate that *primum* refers to the Lord. Ott. 1 also originally had *primum*, but it was corrected to *primus*, the common reading of our manuscripts, with the final syllable lengthened because of the caesura. Rom. has the less elegant *Et suscepit primum hic*. Cellarius says that this distich sets Jews and Christians against one another. But it may also be understood to mean that the first to receive Christ were Jews. Since, however, few Jews received Christ and their people are rather opposed to him, I think Cellarius’s interpretation should be retained.

75. Vat. 1 and Reg. 2, instead of *redit*, and Arntz., first hand, have *ridet*, which neither the sense nor the metrical rule permits. The true reading is *redit*. The same should be understood in the pentameter.

79. Rom.: *devicerat*; Meus: *disjunxerat*; the others, better: *devinxerat*. In Nebrissensis’s notes *definxerat* is perhaps an error; in Westhemer’s edition, to which these notes were added, *devinxerat* is printed.

83. Goldastus: *Jam supra astra*, and in the following verse *Jam super astra*; both should be retained.

85. Meus: *ille sedet*, incorrectly repeated from the preceding distich; read *tonat*, which the same manuscript has in the following verse.

86. Meus, Reg. 5, and Ald.: *faciant*; Reg. 2 and 3, Urb., Ott. 2, Alb., Vat. 1 and 2, Rom., Arntz., and Ang.: *faciunt*, a reading neglected by the printed editions but certainly not to be dismissed; in Reg. 3 it was corrected to *facient*. Ott. 1, with most printed editions, has *facient*. Burmannus, commenting on Ovid, *Heroides* 21, verse 26, preferred *faciant* from what he calls the better manuscripts. Either form is possible; Virgil likewise has *Quid domini facient?* in *Eclogue* 3, verse 16.

87. Reg. 2, 3, and 5, Ott. 1, Arntz., Ang., Alm., Fabr., and more recent printed editions: *Christo veniente figura*. I think the shadow is dispelled by the approaching Christ, “by the figure of Christ coming.” Cant. and our other manuscripts, together with most printed editions: *Christi veniente figura*. The gloss in Reg. 2: “shadow—figure,” and immediately afterward: “with Christ coming, figure—presence.”

89. Reg. 2 and 3 and Vat. 1: *docent signa et saecula*; one *et* is missing before *signa* and was added by a second hand in Reg. 3.

90. Vet. 1 and Mon.: *Non sacra*; correct to *Nos sacra*. The New Testament and Christ’s second coming are indicated.

91. Cant., Reg. 2, 3, and 5, Urb., Rom., Ang., Alb., Meus, and Ald.: *vota priorum*. Vat. 1 has *vota priora*, corrected to *vota priorum*. Ott. 1 and 2, Vat. 2, Alm., and most ancient printed editions: *piorum*. More recent editions prefer *priorum*, because this is opposed to *nobis* in the following verse; Nebrissensis likewise took *priorum* from Ald. and explains it by saying that Christ was desired by the holy fathers.

93. Cant., Alm., Arntz., Reg. 2 and 3, Ang., Urb., Alb., Ott. 1 and 2, and Vat. 1 have *tui* in both verses. Vat. 2, Reg. 5, Meus, Rom., and most printed editions have *tua*, which in Reg. 2 is supplied either as an old reading or as a gloss. Reg. 3 has *implevit*, corrected to *complevit*.

95. The manuscripts vary again. Almel., Cant., Alb., Reg. 2, 3, and 5, Urb., Ald., and Ang. have *priorum*, which Nebrissensis retains and explains as “of the prophets.” Vat. 1 has *priorum*, corrected to *piorum*. In Rom. it is uncertain whether the reading is *piorum* or *priorum*. Ott. 1 and 2 and Vat. 2 have *piorum*, which more recent editors follow, because the pious of the Old Testament are opposed to the pious of the New Testament.

96. Ald. and Reg. 5: *Spes cum fine*; others: *in fine*. Meus is corrupt here: *Saepe in fine suis hic quidem Deus est*.

97. All our manuscripts, together with Almel. and Arntz., have *erit* in both verses. Most printed editions have *erat*, which recent editors adopt because, as Cellarius says, it signifies the whole age, that is, the time of the Old Testament. I see no reason for this, and in the pentameter there is no explicit mention of the New Testament. Sedulius therefore says that all who will at some time believe will possess this through the gift of faith, and that this gift will belong to the one who granted them the ability to believe. Vat. 2 has *in toto*; the others omit *in*.

98. Reg. 2: *ut credent*, correctly corrected to *ut credant*. This might suggest the reading *munus erat*; but the sense seems to be: “He who gave them the ability to believe.”

100. Cellarius with Fabr.: *Occidet hic mundus*. Grunerus with Ald. and Reg. 2 and 5: *Concidit hic mundus*, because *concidit* is elegantly repeated from the preceding verse. Arntzenius with his manuscript, Alm., and our Reg. 3, Rom., Meus, Vat. 1 and 2, Urb., and Alb.: *Occidit hic mundus*. Ott. 1 and 2, Reg. 3 instead of the stated reading, and most ancient printed editions: *Occubuit mundus*; Ang. likewise. But, as Grunerus observes, writers use the present for the future when they wish to indicate the certainty of an event. Ovid, *Heroides* 2, verse 20: “I said to myself: If he is well, he has come.”]

101. In Ott. 1, *Gloria*, corrected to *Gratia*, as it is read in the pentameter. In Rom., in both verses of this couplet, despite the meter, *Dei plena est*.

102. Poelm. and certain other editions have *Ascendant*. Ald. with the manuscripts has *Abscedant*, which should be retained—unless one prefers, with Alb., *Discedant*, a word that recurs shortly afterward. In Rom. *Abscedat*, and in Meo *Abscendant*, are written incorrectly. Reg. 2 omits *est* in this verse.

104. Cant. and certain common editions have *Descendant*; the sense requires *Discedant*. It seems certain that Christ is called the dove here. The gloss in Reg. 1 explains Sedulius as referring to the Church. But, as I think, Sedulius expressed Prudentius’s thought in *Cathemerinon* III, verse 166:

> You are for me, Christ, a mighty dove,  
> Whom the bird, nourished by blood, yields to.

I said at that passage that Laureto, in the *Silva allegoriarum*, indicates the Fathers who recognized Christ’s type in the dove carrying an olive branch; and I added several other things about the symbol of the dove. John Baptist Passerius observes in his *Expositio in monumenta sacra eburnea* following Gori’s *Diptycha*, p. 70, that the sacred vessels in which the Eucharist is kept were sometimes called “doves,” because of the outward form of a silver dove. Although there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove, is chiefly signified by this symbol, it is nevertheless also established that some Fathers include “dove” among the names of the Savior. Ennodius, Book I of the poems, no. 9, verse 17:

> Victim, rod, shepherd, mountain, net, dove.

Silvius, in Goldast’s *Manuale biblicum*:

> Virgin, dove, hand, rock, son, Emmanuel, light.

Someone might suspect that *columna* should be read instead of *columba*; but what shall we say about Orientius?

> Often a dove, because it knows no deceit and has no gall.

Perhaps *sine* should be read instead of *ac sine*. As for Silvius, I mentioned him in *Prolegomena*, no. 91, where I noted that Damasus’s verses on the surnames of the Savior are attributed to Silvius in certain manuscript codices. Silvius’s fuller verses exist—or rather, lie concealed in a certain way—in Goldast’s *Manuale biblicum*, a work not generally accessible. They are entitled:

**“Blessed Silvius’s verses on the names of the Savior.”**

I gladly present them here so that they may be compared with the verses of Damasus:

> Almighty, triple power, God, best Father of all things,  
> By whose begetting he was born without seed, without  
> time, without a mother,  
> Born in origin, end, place, or limbs, afterward flesh,  
> Permitting himself to be seen, and called by many a name.  
> Hope, reason, way, life, salvation, wisdom, mind, mountain,  
> Judge, gate, giant, king, gem, prophet, priest,  
> Messiah, Sabaoth, Rabbi, bridegroom, mediator,  
> Virgin, dove, hand, rock, son, Emmanuel, light,  
> Vineyard, shepherd, sheep, peace, root, vine, olive,  
> Fountain, bread, character, lamb, calf, lion, Jesus,  
> Word, man, net, stone, Lord, God, all things, Christ.

Damasus’s verses number only seven, and I found them in no Vatican manuscript. Sarazanius published them as follows:

1. Hope, life, salvation, reason, wisdom, light. The meter is defective.
2. Judge, as in Silvius.
3. Messiah, as in Silvius.
4. Rod, column, hand, rock, son, and Emmanuel.
5. Vineyard, as in Silvius.
6. Fountain, wall, lamb, calf, lion, propitiator.
7. Word, man, net, stone, house, all things, Christ Jesus.

In verse 2 of Silvius, perhaps *datus* should be read for *natus*, and in the penultimate verse *ethos* seems to be an error. In his explanation of the names of Christ, Orientius explains the name of the virgin, the rod, and the dove, but not the column. The Roman Council celebrated under Damasus, which I shall place among the Appendices, lists the names of Christ, as does Isidore, Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2; but in both places the name “dove” and the name “column” are omitted. Both names are likewise absent from the old hymn of Christ’s surnames, which I transcribed from the Veliternian codex in note a to no. 212 of the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*. At that time I and others considered the hymn unpublished; but later I discovered that it exists among the sequences of Notker Balbulus in volume I of Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, and had been printed much earlier in Clichtoveus’s *Elucidatorium*, Book I, beginning *Alma chorus Domini*, etc.

[105] [Col. 0761A] [Note: [Col. 0761D]

105. Arntz. has *signa*; read *digna*.

106. Rom. has *miseris adveniet*; corrected to *miseri adveniet*, which the others provide with hiatus. He again takes *miseros* for *pravos*. In this couplet and the following one, the subject is the Last Judgment, and a comparison is made between the rewards of the just and the punishments of sinners—between the vision of the Judge, from which the wicked will suffer punishment and torment, and that same vision of Christ, from which the good will obtain glory. Therefore the title assigned by some to this elegy, “A Comparison of the Old and New Testaments,” is not entirely appropriate.

107. In Reg. 3, *est* was missing after *malorum* and was added by a recent hand.

108. Meus has *magna*, taken from the following verse; correct to *cuncta*. [Col. 0762B] Reg. 2 has *tui est*, but *est* is absent from the preceding verse.

109. Ott. 1 has *Gloria*, corrected to *Gratia*, but *Gloria* should be retained, as in the following verse. Reg. 2 has *semper tibi sit gloria*; *sit* should be omitted for the verse to scan. In some editions I find *compar* instead of *semper*, which seems to belong to a later period.

110. Most manuscripts and editions have *Cum sancto Spiritu*; Bede likewise reads this in *De metris*. Here I shall explain his particular view concerning the scansion of certain verses of Sedulius:

> The authority of the grammarians’ rule is disregarded, as when Sedulius, in the close of the poem mentioned above, after saying, “Great glory to the Father, glory always to you, O Son,” adds: “With the Holy Spirit, great glory to the Father.” The true scansion of this verse is therefore: *CUM SAN*, a spondee; *CTO SPIRI*, an antibacchius, and not a dactyl. But the poet, wishing to sing aloud the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity, neglected the rule of grammatical arrangement.

The same author says in the Paschal poem:

> Thus he himself teaches: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

For this is scanned as follows: *SIC AIT*, a dactyl; *IPSE DO*, a dactyl; *CENS E*, a trochee; *GIN PA*, a spondee, with the *o* removed by synaloepha. Or if you wish to scan *CENS EGO* and make it a dactyl, you act contrary to Sedulius’s practice, which he observed throughout, so that the second vowel remains free when another vowel follows.

Again, in the same work:

> “Glorify,” he said, “your name, and greatly in heaven.”

Here, to commend the truth of the Lord’s saying more clearly, he set aside the order of secular discipline. Again:

> “The inscription is written: ‘This is the King of the Jews.’”

Let whoever can judge how this should be scanned: whether *JUDAEORUM* is to form two spondees in the fifth and sixth positions, contrary to custom, or whether, with the syllables resolved as shown above, he wished to make a dactyl and a spondee.

Critics will not easily approve all this doctrine of Bede. As for the present verse, Bede often encountered corrupted codices, as I observed in the notes to Juvencus. For that reason, in my note to Dracontius, Book II, verse 54, I suspected that Sedulius wrote *Cum sancto Spirtu*, or *Spritu* by syncope, as poets used many similar forms, concerning which see Salmasius on Trebellius, p. 303. Sedulius very frequently used the word *Spiritus*, and always lengthened its first syllable; and he could certainly have sung aloud the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity by arranging the verse differently, without neglecting the rule of grammatical arrangement.

Having now examined the manuscript codices, I find the following textual variants. In Reg. 2 and 3 and Ott. 1, the word is written by a contraction of letters, from which it should more likely be read *Spirtu* or *Spritu* than *Spiritu*. I think that this gave rise to the form in which scribes, expanding some similar abbreviation, wrote *Spiritu* against the meter and Sedulius’s intention. In Vat. 1 the same abbreviation occurs; above it, clearly, is *Spirtu*, with an old glossator’s hand in the margin: “Or, *Spiritui sancto*.” Reg. 5 has *Spiritui et sancto*. Cappusotus and Ald. have *Spiritui et Nato*. Poelman has *Cum sancto Flatu* (“With the holy Breath”).

Of our manuscripts, only the seven most recent—namely Meus, Ang., [Col. 0763A] Alb., Rom., Urb., Ott. 2, and Vat. 2—clearly exhibit *Cum sancto Spiritu*. Peter Damian, although imitating Sedulius, changed the expression:

> Great glory to the Father, glory to the begotten Son,  
> With the holy Breath, great glory to the Father.

At the end of the elegy, Reg. 2 reads: “It ends. Sedulius’s Ambrosian hymn begins.” Ott. 1: “It ends, amen. The art of the poet Sedulius begins,” as stated in *Prolegomena*, no. 9. Rom.: “It ends. Other works of Sedulius are lacking.” Meus: “The distich epigram of the same poet Sedulius on the Catholic faith ends. The hymn of the same poet begins.” Vat. 1: “The book of Sedulius ends. Immediately thereafter follows an epigram of Sedulius.” Vat. 2: “End. Nothing else belongs to Sedulius.” Reg. 5:

> The poem has reached its end; nor do I seek laurel wreaths.  
> Let you, Mary, be the reward of my study. Amen.

The hymn of Caelius Sedulius the presbyter, proceeding concisely from the Incarnation to the Ascension, follows. Urb.: “End. The *Paracterium*, and the elegiac poem of the excellent Bishop Sedulius, happily end. Thanks be to God. May the name of the Lord be blessed through the book that has been written. I have completed this work. Bede’s Martyrology follows.” In Ott. 2, a hymn follows the elegy.]

370 The Lord will come to give the worthy things to the godly and evils to the wicked,

> Believe now, wretched ones; the Lord will come.

> Your vision, Christ, is torment and punishment for the wicked,

[Col. 0762A] Your vision, Christ, is complete glory for the good.

> Great glory to the Father, glory always to you, O Son,

[110] 371 With the Holy Spirit, great glory to the Father.

[Col. 0763]

**THE HYMN OF CAELIUS SEDULIUS. (C)**

[Col. 0763B] [Note: [Col. 0763B]

Some learned men also call this hymn an acrostic, but foolishly; for no word is formed from the initial letters of the verses. It should therefore be called alphabetic, or abecedarian. Alm. gives the title as “Here begins the hymn of Sedulius.” Ott. 1: “Verses of Sedulius concerning Christ.” Vat. 1, after Sedulius’s epigram, has *Haec tua* and immediately, without a title, *A solis ortus cardine*. In Reg. 3, after the elegiac poem *Cantemus*, there are verses of Liberius and Belisarius in praise of Sedulius, followed by “Sedulius’s Alphabetic Poem.” In Reg. 2, this hymn is called Sedulius’s Ambrosian hymn, as I have just said concerning the end of the *Elegy*, because, since St. Ambrose is regarded—and rightly—as the principal and most distinguished author of hymns, all ecclesiastical hymns began to be called Ambrosian, as I noted in my dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, no. 67.

The first stanza of this hymn is the beginning of the hymn for the Hypapante, or the Purification of St. Mary, and for all its feasts. Venerable Thomasius includes it in his Hymnary from the Mozarabic breviary, on December 18 at Lauds. The same stanza appears in the same breviary on the same day at Vespers, where certain other stanzas from this hymn are also produced; together with St. Ambrose’s hymn *Fit porta Christi pervia*, they form a complete hymn. Vezzosius, in his notes to Thomasius, thought that the entire hymn at Lauds had been attributed to St. Ambrose by St. Ildephonsus. But St. Ildephonsus merely praises, under Ambrose’s name, a stanza taken from his hymn.

2. Bede, in *De metris*, reads *Et usque*. The Mozarabic breviary at Lauds on December 18 likewise has this reading.

4. Alm. has *Mariae Virginis*.

6. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* XI, 45: “He put on a mortal body.” See the note.

7. Reg. 3 incorrectly transposes *Ut carnem carne liberans*.

8. Reg. 2, 3, Ottob. 1, Meus, and Alb. have *quod condidit*; others, together with the printed editions, have *quos condidit*. In Vat. I, *quos* is broken off from *quod*. *Quod* seems more elegant, especially in a poem. Otherwise St. Gregory the Great said in Homily 19 on the Gospels: “Our Creator, who rules those whom he created”; and Alcuin reads *quos* in Sedulius.

[Col. 0764C] 9. Reg. 2, Ottob. 1, Alcuinus, Fabr. and other editions have *Clausae*. Poelm.’s sheets, Reg. 5, Ott. 2, Ald. and other printed editions have *Castae*. Alm., Alb. and Cant., by correction, have *Clausa*; Reg. 3 likewise, although it previously had *Clausae*. Vat. 1 has *Casta*; but neither *Casta* nor *Clausa* satisfies the meter. The Roman Breviary retained *Castae*. Venerable Thomasius presents part of this hymn from a certain monastic breviary at Lauds, in which the reading is *Clausa*; the Mozarabic breviary on December 18 at Vespers likewise has this.

13. Ott. 1 has *corporis*, corrected to *pectoris*.

16. The printed editions, together with Alcuin, have *Verbo concepit filium* (“By the Word she conceived a son”); but the verse does not scan at all in this form. Reg. 2 now has *concepit*, but seems formerly to have had *creavit*, which is good in place of *genuit*, *concepit*. In Ott. 1, Alb. and Reg. 3, *creavit* is clear, although a recent hand in Ott. 1 has written *concepit* above it. When the correctors of the hymns in the Roman Breviary found in the ancient hymn *Verbo concepit filium*, they changed it, to accommodate the meter, to *Concepit alvo filium*. But the meter is equally well served, and the sense expressed by Sedulius is better served, if with these three manuscripts we read *Verbo creavit filium* (“By the Word she created a son”). I think the scribes disliked the word *creavit*, although it is good Latin in place of *genuit*. The Mozarabic breviary on December 18 preserves the old reading *creavit*.

17. Most editions, including recent ones, have *Enixa jam puerpera*. The Mozarabic breviary on December 18 at Vespers, together with all our manuscripts, Alcuin, Ald. and other editions, has *Enixa est puerpera*, with a hiatus, which Sedulius uses elsewhere as well. To avoid it, the correctors of the hymns in the Roman Breviary substituted *Enititur puerpera*.

23. All manuscripts and editions have *Parvoque lacte pastus est* (“And he was fed with little milk”). Alcuin likewise reads this. The correctors of the hymns in the Roman Breviary disliked calling milk “little”; therefore they substituted *Et lacte modico pastus est* (“And he was fed with a small amount of milk”). Although this proceeds correctly in both meter and Latin, it is less suitable for ecclesiastical song, as I showed in the dissertation on ecclesiastical hymns prefixed to the *Hymnodia Hispanica*. The Parisians preferred to have their breviary read *Et indiget lactis cibo* (“And he needs milk for food”). Nevertheless, Sedulius’s verse could have been retained: *Parvoque lacte pastus est*, for “little milk” means a moderate amount of milk, or little milk. Lucan, Book IV, verse 239, uses a similar phrase: “If a little hot blood comes into his mouth.”]

26. Almost all our manuscripts, together with Alcuin and Ald., have *canunt Deo* (“they sing to God”); but in Reg. 2 there was *Deum*, which appears in Meus, Poelman’s sheets, and Alm., although in the latter a second hand seems to have intended *Dominum*. Meter rejects that reading. Several editions have *canunt Deo*, an ecclesiastical phrase drawn from the Vulgate and occurring in Optatus Afer and others. Some editions, especially recent ones, have *canunt Deum*, which is more Latin.

29. All our manuscripts, Alcuin and the old editions have *Hostis Herodes* (“Enemy Herod”), but Ott. 1 has *Hostis Herodis*. [Col. 0765C] The ancient breviaries likewise read *Hostis Herodes*. Erasmus, as far as I know, was the first to think that this verse should be reformed differently, namely: *Herodes hostis impie* (“Wicked enemy Herod”). I quoted his words from the *Colloquy of the Poetic Banquet* in a note to my dissertation on hymns, no. 178. Their substance is this: in the verse *Hostis Herodes impie* there are two errors. First, *Hostis* is placed as a trochee, which is not admitted in an iambic poem; second, *Hero* is a spondee, although it ought to be an iamb.

Fabricius and other editors followed this conjecture. More recent scholars also followed it: Munckerus, in his note to Hyginus, *Fabulae* 233, p. 289, wanted *Herodis hostis* substituted, because otherwise the final syllable is shortened contrary to the rule of prosody. Arntzenius replies that such things must sometimes be admitted in Sedulius. Erasmus, however, had already met this objection: since *Herodes* is a Greek word, its final syllable may be shortened in the vocative. Erasmus adds that the epithet *impie* joins more smoothly with *hostis* than with *Herodes*.

The correctors of the hymns in the Roman Breviary under Urban VIII reformed the verse as follows:

> Cruel Herod, why do you fear  
> That God, the King, should come?

In the first edition, however, in 1629:

> Cruel Herod, why do you fear  
> That he should come to earth?

I myself think that Sedulius wrote *Hostis Herodes impie*. Erasmus’s first objection—that *Hostis* is a trochee, which has no place in an iambic poem—is easily answered: the aspiration in *Herodes* can have the force of a consonant, as it often does in Sedulius and other poets of his period. Thus *Hostis* is a spondee. Indeed, on this basis one could restore the verse, so that its sense would agree better with what follows:

> Herod, wickedly, as an enemy—  
> Why do you fear Christ’s coming?

Erasmus then says that *Hero* is a spondee. That is true if the first syllable in *Herodes* must necessarily be long; but since poets of the later period claimed for themselves the liberty of lengthening or shortening syllables in proper names at will, we may reasonably recognize an iamb in *Hero*. It also often happens that Christian poets shorten or lengthen the same syllable in the same proper name. In verse 20 of Sedulius and in Book II, verse 143, the *o* in *Ioannes* is shortened, although it is written with omega. Likewise, in Book II, verse 49, he shortens the second syllable of *Mariae*, but lengthens the same syllable in Book II, verse 30, and elsewhere. Even in Sedulius’s own name Fortunatus varies its form in our *Prolegomena*, no. 166, making the first two syllables sometimes short and sometimes long.

30. Alb. has *venisse*; correct to *venire*.

31. Reg. 3 has *diripit*; Vat. 1, with most editions, has *arripit*. Fabr., in the *Bibliotheca Lugdunensis*, has *abripit*. Most of our codices, together with Cant., Alm., Arntz., Alcuin and Ald., have *eripit*, which also occurs in the breviaries.

33. Reg. 2, Ott. 1, Alm., Reg. 3 and Alcuin have *qua venerant*; in Ott. 1 the earlier reading was *qui venerant*; Reg. 3 has a different reading, *quam viderant*. Edimb. perhaps has *qua viderant* through a printer’s error. The common reading, also found in the breviaries, is *quam viderant*, which seems to have been taken from Matthew 2:9: “When they had heard the king, they departed; and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them.” Cellarius nevertheless preferred *qua venerant*, that is, “by which road they had come from the East.” I do not approve this.

35. Alcuin incorrectly has *requirunt munere*.

36. Meus has *Diem*; correct to *Deum*. In Reg. 3 the remainder is missing.

37. Vat. 1 has *personant*, made into *personat* afterward. *Personant* would not be wrong, however. It should be observed that in editions everywhere, including recent ones, *Caterva* is written; Aldus printed *Katerva*, which is Sedulius’s spelling. For, so that the alphabetic order may be preserved, this stanza must begin with K. Others who composed similar abecedarian hymns, such as Bede and Amoenus, likewise write *Karus* and *Kastris*, about whom I shall speak later. Isidore, Book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 27, says that the ancients prefixed K whenever A followed; Diomedes restricts this to short A, as in *caterva*.

38. Vat. 1 has *Concisa*; others more correctly have *Collisa*.

40. Meus, Reg. 2 and Alcuin have *victima*, but in Reg. 2 it seems to have been changed to *victimam*. Peter Burmann conjectured *victimas*. Arntzenius says that Sedulius may perhaps have used the singular for the plural. Otherwise *victimam* is properly singular by apposition: “whose thousands the tyrant sacrificed to Christ as a victim, or sacrifice.” Burmann’s conjecture is confirmed by *Carmen Paschale*, Book V, verses 73ff.: “Thousands of angelic legions.”

41. Poelm. incorrectly has *Lavacro*.

44. Alcuin has *obluendo*, which is perhaps an error.

46. Alcuin corruptly gives *Habere secundum Patrem*.

48. Reg. 5, Cant., Ald. and some editions have *Resuscitans*. Most of our manuscripts, together with Alm., Alcuin and many editions, have *Et suscitans*. Arntzenius observes that *Resuscitans* can be retained, because in compounds beginning with a consonant *re* is anceps. This reasoning is foolish: since the first foot in this iambic poem may be either an iamb or a spondee, even if the first syllable in *resuscitans* were necessarily short, the verse would still stand; indeed, it would stand with the foot more proper to it, namely an iamb.]

50. Alcuin has *Aqua*; correct to *Aquae*.

54. Reg. 2, Ott. 1 and 2, Meus, Alcuin, Alb. and Cant. have *Nixus genu* (“kneeling on one knee”), a form followed by Grunerus; others commonly say *nixi genu*, *nixi genibus*. Vat. 1, Reg. 5, Ald. and most editions have *Flexus genu* (“with knee bent”); Tacitus likewise uses this expression in *Annals*, Book XVI, chapter 4. Vet. 1, Mon. and Col. have *Flexo genu*, which is the more usual phrase.

55. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *Credenti ardor*. Although this can to some extent be defended despite the hiatus, the true manuscript reading is *Credentis ardor*.

56. Vatic. 1 and Edimb. have *Exstinguit*, and in Vat. I the earlier reading was *Exstinguat*; most have *Exstinxit*. Sedulius changes tenses throughout this hymn, and other poets do so as well.

57. Vet. 1, Mon., Fabr. and some other editions have *ambulans*, and in the following verse *levatur*. Some other editions have *ambulat*, and in the following verse *levatur*; our manuscripts and Alcuin have *ambulat*, and in the following verse *levatus*, which Arntzenius retained.

58. On the word *levatus*, compare what has just been said. Meus, against the meter, has *dextra*.

61. Cant., with many editions, has *Quarto*. Meus, with others, has *Quarta*. Similar variation occurs in Book III, verse 131. Both are equally good: “on the following day” or “on the following day” with masculine or feminine agreement.

63. Cant., Alm. and our manuscripts Reg. 2, Ott. 1 and 2 and Meus have *Mortisque liber* (“free from death”), a reading adopted by recent editions. It is more elegant because life has just been mentioned. Vat. 1, Reg. 5, Ald. and the old common editions have *Cunctisque liber* (“free from all bonds”), which conveys a reasonable sense: namely, that Lazarus was miraculously freed also from the bonds in which he had been wrapped.

64. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *Factus sibi superstes* (“made a survivor for himself”). Arntzenius adds nothing else, but I think the reading is *Factus sibi superstes est*, which is not inept and appears in the Cologne edition of 1537. Alcuin transposed it against the meter: *Factus est superstes sibi*, which I also find in manuscript Alb. In Vat. 1, *Superstes est sibi* occurs, with *Factus* missing after *est*.

65. Arntzenius apparently cites *Rivum* from his own manuscript instead of *Rivos*. Ott. 1, Alb., Vat. 1, Meus, Alcuin and two manuscripts of Cellarius have *torridi*, which recent editors follow. Reg. 2, Ott. 2, Reg. 5 and the old editions have *horridi*. I prefer *torridi* to *adusti*. In Livy, Book IV, chapter 30, *torridi fontes* means “dried-up springs”; but that meaning is not very suitable here, and there is a similar variation of readings in Livy’s words.

66. Ott. 2 has *ablu[it]*; correct to *obstruit*.

67. Ott. 1 and 2, Alcuin, Alb. and Meus have *Fletus rigantis*. Vet. 1, 2 and Mon. have *Fletus rogantis*. Ald., Reg. 2 and 5 and Poelm. have *Fletu rigante*. Arntzenius and other commonly printed editions have *Fletu rigant*.

[Col. 0768B] 68. Where the preceding verse reads *Fletus*, this verse corresponds with *Clausit*, which Burmann notes is exhibited in the manuscript, and is in fact found in ours. Those who retain *Fletu* read *Arent*. *Fletu rigantis supplicis—Arent fluenta sanguinis* (“By the tears of the suppliant who waters them—the streams of blood dry up”) is more graceful.

69. Vet. 1 and Mon. incorrectly have *solutos*; Alcuin’s edition likewise has *omni languore* against the meter.

80. Reg. 2 and Ott. 1 have *Conjunctus est latronibus*, a reading also retained by Alcuin. The editions, together with other manuscripts, have *Conjungitur*.

81. Most manuscripts and editions have *Xeromyrrham*. Arntzenius found *Xyro myrrham* in his manuscript, which is also read in some editions and in Alcuin. Ott. 2 and Alb. corruptly have *Sero myrrham*. In Reg. 2, *Xero mirram* appears, but something else stood in place of *mirram*. The gloss there says: “The Greeks call *xerum* ‘dry’; hence *xerophagia* [dry-eating] is so called. Myrrh is an aromatic substance with which the bodies of the dead are prepared.”

The letter X must begin this verse so that the alphabetic order may be preserved. In Basil Faber’s *Thesaurus Latinitatis*, enlarged by another hand, it is reported that *Christo myrrham* should be read, and that the error in the manuscripts arose from the abbreviation χρό for *Christo*. I ask you to note that the very learned Francisco Pérez Bayer, whom I now hear has departed this life, in a note to Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, vol. I, Book VI, chapter 9, no. 231, adduces among other arguments for the spuriousness of certain monuments from Granada abbreviations of words that are plainly Spanish, such as Xpo for *Christo*.

But concerning the name of Christ Isidore says in Book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 27: “*Xristus*, because it is Greek, must be written with X; so also *Xrisma*.” The annotator observes that Christians formerly used this spelling so commonly that the shape of the cross was retained in X. For in certain Gothic copies of Isidore, Book I, chapter 4, the following had been added: “The letter X was discovered in the time of Augustus, when the name of Christ became known; it is written with the letter that represents the form of the cross.” Yet X was in use before Augustus. See also Bede, *De arte metrica*, at the beginning.

Gisbert Cuperus defends *Xeromyrrham* as a compound of two Greek words, just as *Xerolibya* is compounded. Nebrissensis interprets *Xeromyrrham* similarly, that is, “dry myrrh,” made from the wood of the myrrh tree. He gives *Xylobalsamum* as an example of a similar compound.

The interpreters, however, are not very concerned to explain the metrical measure of this verse. In *Xeromyrrham*, the first foot, *xero*, is a trochee, which an iambic poem does not admit; the second, *myrrham*, is a spondee, which is not accepted in the second position of an iambic poem. I therefore think that the verse should be restored as:

> For Christ, certain female companions carried ointment after the Sabbath,

or, by the abbreviation once commonly used, χρό *myron*, etc., which even in the most ancient codices appears written as Xp~o. For Greek rho has a shape similar to the Latin p.

It cannot be written *Christo* in Latin, for then the alphabetic order would not be preserved. It is therefore written in the Greek manner, as Christians often did; from this arose the monogram of Christ, consisting of the first two Greek letters of Christ’s name. The form of the first Greek letter of Christ’s name is the same as the form of the Latin letter X. Sedulius therefore respected the abecedarian order by writing Christ’s name with its first character in Greek, just as in verse 2 of the *Elegy* it is written in nearly the same manner in the Turin codex.

I know of two other abecedarian hymns composed in imitation of Sedulius: one by Bede, *Apostolorum gloriam*, and another under the name of the poet Amoenus in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1618, vol. V, part II, p. 982, beginning *Agnoscat omne saeculum*. In both, the stanza that ought to begin with the letter X begins with the name of Christ. Bede has *Christe, precamur, ut quibus* (“Christ, we beg that for those whom…”); Amoenus, *Christus sereno lumine* (“Christ with serene light”). This surely provides remarkable confirmation of our reading.

That poet Amoenus is none other than Venantius Fortunatus, among whose works the same hymn is found. In Isidore’s rhythm on the lament of the penitent, and in two other abecedarian poems by Bede on the Last Judgment, the X-stanza likewise begins with Christ’s name. These two rhythms occur in Bede’s *Collectanea*.

The word *myron* then forms an iamb. In Greek, *myron* means “ointment,” which Sedulius intended to express together with Luke 23:55ff.:

> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed, and saw the tomb and how his body had been placed. Returning, they prepared spices and ointments; and on the Sabbath they kept silence according to the commandment.

And immediately, Luke 24:1:

> On the first day of the week, very early, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.

I do not see how these spices and ointments can be called “dry myrrh.” Myrrh was indeed used in ointments, but for the sake of fragrance and oiliness, in place of oil. In no way, therefore, can an ointment be called “dry myrrh.”

Jerome uses the word *myrum*, or *myron*, in the preface to his book of the Old Testament: “With the most precious myrrh of faith you anoint the head of the reclining Lord.” It often happened that scribes used *i* for *y*; and thus it was easier for writers who did not understand *miron* or *mirum* to substitute *mirrha* or *myrrha*, which gave them a clearer sense. See Galeardus’s note to Gaudentius, Sermon 13, where he proves that Hilary, Cassian and the Vulgate used the word *myron*. Some think that Sedulius should read *Xeromyrum*, meaning “dry ointment,” or ointment suitable for drying bodies.]

82. Reg. 2, Ott. 1, Arntz.’s manuscript and edition, Edimb., Alcuin have *compares*; most editions, together with other manuscripts, have *corpori*; Ott. 2 has *corpora*, apparently corrupt. *Compares* should be restored, for *vehebant corpori* is less satisfactory. *Quaedam compares* means “certain female companions,” or “companions”; *compar* is sometimes used in this sense.

83. Cellarius and Arntzenius, with manuscript Alm. and certain editions, have *Quibus definit*, against the meter, since the first syllable of *definit* is long and ought to be shortened to make an iambic foot. Cant. has *Quibus cecinit*; the metrical law also rejects this. Alcuin, Reg. 2 and 5, Ott. 1 and 2, Ald. and most editions have *Quas allocutus Angelus* (“Whom the Angel addressed”), which is good; *est* is understood. Meus, Alb. and Vat. 1 have *Quas alloquuntur angeli* (“Whom the angels address”).

[Col. 0770A] 84. In Alcuin: *Vivum sepulcrum non tegit* (“The tomb does not cover the living one”).

85. It should be written *Ymmis*, not *Hymnis*, as many editions have; for the law of the abecedarian poem requires Y here. Ancient writers frequently omitted the aspiration *h*, both in other words and especially in *hymnus*. Earlier Latins, however, always prefixed the aspiration to the letter y. Consequently, when explaining the alphabet, they omitted the letter y. I observed this in an unpublished work of St. Isidore entitled *Glosses and the Distinction of Words*, where, after omitting y, he says concerning the letter z that it was admitted because of foreign names, as in *zona*, *zelus*, etc.

Isidore’s work exists in Vatican codex 6018, approximately from the ninth century. After other short works there appears a large, multicolored cross, with this inscription running down both sides:

> In the name of the supreme God begins the book of the glosses of Saint Isidore the bishop on the distinction of words. This banner of the cross shines in heaven; now it saves us through the upright timber.

Then the book begins: “*Acrocius* with C and O, not with Y, as some think.” I believe *Agroicus* should be read, which was the name of one of Plautus’s comedies. From this work of Isidore arose another similar work, circulated among the Latin Grammarians under the name of Agroetius. At least, this is my suspicion.]

86. Meus, contrary to the meter: “Let us all sing,” unless one transposes it to “Let us sing all.” Vet. 1, 2, Mon., Col.: “all singing.” Burmann’s manuscript: “Let us all sing those subjected,” which agrees neither with the meter nor with the sense.

88. Cellarius and Arntzenius, together with Alcuin and Alm.: “Who redeemed those who had been sold”; all our manuscripts, together with most printed editions: “Who, having been sold, redeemed us,” which is much more elegant. Sedulius says that Christ was sold by Judas in verse 22 of the *Elegy*. Burmann’s manuscript has the erroneous reading, “Who redeems those sold.”

92. Alcuin’s edition gives “He who restored himself to the heavens”; emend to “And restored himself to the heavens,” in accordance with the meter. In the Cologne edition, Vet. 1, and Monast., after this verse a doxological stanza is added by an incompetent scribe—whom I do not know why Arntzenius asserts to have been a monk of stupid intelligence—in these words, perhaps taken from another hymn:

> Together with the Holy Spirit,

The same stanza appears in Alcuin’s *Office for the Days of the Week*, after Sedulius’s hymn, and in Reg. 2. There, *sit* is added above *Patri* in verse 1; verse 3 alone reads “and with the Holy Spirit”; after verse 4 *Amen* is appended. Explicit. In the codex of the Laurentian Library at Florence, in the *Prolegomena*, no. 86, examined for the hymn’s conclusion, this couplet is found:

> May he make us persist upon the straight road,  
> So that we may be able to render him worthy service.

In Ott. 1, after the verse “And restored himself to the heavens,” the note “The verse ends” is written. “Sedulius’s prologue begins: *Paschales*, etc.” In Vat. 1, a letter to Macedonius begins after this hymn. In Reg. 5, Sedulius’s epigram “These doctrines of yours” follows. In Ott. 2, after the alphabetical hymn has ended, epigrams in praise of Sedulius are copied under the titles “Sedulius of Christ” and “Sedulius of the Lord,” with the heading “The name of Bishop Sedulius” at the beginning and end of the meter. We place these among the appendices after another epigram of Asterius.]

## EPIGRAM OF COELIUS SEDULIUS. (C, G, S)*

[Note: [Col. 0771A]

This epigram occurs in Vat. 1 and in Aldus immediately after the *Elegy* and before the hymn “From the sun”; in Reg. 5 it follows this hymn, where it is entitled “Sedulius’s epigram.” In the Ascensian edition it is placed between the *Paschal Poem* and the hymn. Barthius also published it from his own manuscript in book X, chapter 9 of the *Adversaria*, and Usserius did so in chapter 16 of the *Antiquities of Britain*. Poelmann found it in an old manuscript; Fabricius transcribed it in the *Corpus of Christian Poets*, p. 662, and it was also printed by the Scottish editor. Heinsius found the same epigram in Nansius’s codex.

Barthius, in the passage cited, says: “This little epigram is certainly not unworthy of Sedulius, especially since his character shines forth from it: he seeks verbal ingenuity in the similar words *te, tua; tete; tibi*—a kind of play which this swan of Christ loves with a certain propriety.” Goldastus, in the *Biblical Manual*, calls it a prayer of Sedulius and describes it after the *Elegy*.

The epigram consists of only four verses, as it appears elsewhere; but in Reg. 5 several more are added, which I judge to have been written by Matthias, son of Adam Sculterus, the sacristan of the church at Kraków. Thus the epigram proceeds continuously:

> The poem has its end; I seek no laurel wreath.  
> May you, Mary, be the reward of my study.  
> Late have I begun to survey the sea of your praises,  
> O serene Virgin, with my inadequate hand,  
> Offering learned men an example worthy of imitation,  
> So that they may strive to add more to my beginnings;  
> And, abandoning false Jupiter and savage Juno,  
> May they begin to celebrate you as the true goddess.  
> Now, where you sit as the great and blessed queen of men,  
> Full of the beauty of your Son at your right hand—  
> He who lives with God the Father throughout all ages  
> And reigns together with the Holy Spirit: amen.

In the verse beginning *Nunc*, the word *Nunc* is obscurely written; and in the verse beginning *Qui cum*, etc., *cuncta* is not sufficiently clear. The first couplet, “The poem has its end,” etc., is found elsewhere in the same codex.

In the pentameter “May they begin to celebrate you as the true goddess,” it will rightly be displeasing that the Virgin Mother of God is called a true goddess. Lamindus Pritanius—or, by his real name, Ludovico Muratorius—in his work *On Regulated Devotion* teaches the faithful that Mary is not God. Benedictus Plazza, in part 2 of the *Vindication of Devotion*, chapter 1, argues against him that such a warning is unnecessary or even insulting, since no believer either thinks or says that Mary is God.

It is nevertheless certain that some have imprudently called the most blessed Virgin Mary a goddess. To pass over the anonymous author of this epigram and the heretic Apollinaris, who also called her a goddess in a poem, the following verse of Justus Lipsius is well known:

> If he had uttered prayers to the goddess of Halle,

as Lipsius, according to Raynaudus, observes in *Marian Nomenclature*, vol. XVII, book II. Raynaudus says that Lipsius was compelled by the demands of the meter to write this, and that his authority—though supreme in refined literature—is not of equal weight in theological matters.

The same Raynaudus denies that Peter Damian used the word *goddess* in his praises of the Mother of God, as others had claimed. He does, however, wonder whether Leo X—or rather Giovanni de’ Medici, in letters written in Leo’s name—called Mary a goddess; for he found nothing of the sort, although some have asserted that the matter stands thus.

Jacobus Balde errs in nearly the same way as Lipsius in *Epode* 15:

> A Virgin, surrounded by the garment of the sun made radiant,  
> Pressed the sun beneath her heels,  
> Her face and shoulders like those of a goddess—such greatness  
> As august majesty can portray.]

3. Nansius’s codex has *cum placeant*; others have *quae placeant*, including Aldus, to whom Arntzenius falsely attributes *placeat*. Our manuscripts, together with Aldus, have *tete favente*, though this conflicts with the meter. In Vat. 1 the earlier reading was *tete fatente*, which is worse; it was subsequently corrected to *favente*, with the gloss *concedente*. Cappusotus, in the Ascensian edition, and Barthius from his own manuscript have *tete fautore*. Fabricius, apparently by conjecture, has *tete formante*. The Scottish editor emended it to *tete faciente*, which Usserius noted in the margin as though it were a variant reading; Burmannus, the nephew of Secundus, approves it on the authority of Heinsius’s note on Ovid, *Epistles* I.39 and *Metamorphoses* VIII.251. This reading is elegant: *facias* precedes it, and it seems to be the true reading, since *faciente* could easily have been altered by scribes into *favente*. Goldastus printed *tete manente*, which agrees neither with the meter nor with the sense.

I now proceed, after presenting Sedulius’s genuine poems, to add the appendices. In the first I shall assign verses falsely attributed by some to Sedulius; in the others I shall gather whatever I have judged likely to contribute to his praise or to the elucidation of his works. To the Virgilian cento in the first appendix I shall append verses of Virgil collected by Martenius and collated once more by me, from which the cento is composed. Why this kind of cento should not be placed among Sedulius’s poems I discussed in the *Prolegomena*, no. 54 and following, against Martenius, who thought he had detected in that centonary poem the same style as in Sedulius’s *Paschal Poem*.]

381. These teachings of yours concerning perpetual life,

Which I have written, O Christ, I ask you to make remain in my heart:

382. So that, seeking what pleases you, with you making it possible,

I may attain the joys of heaven, with you, Christ, as my guide.

## POEM ON THE INCARNATION, A VIRGILIAN CENTO. (C)*

### DEDICATION TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0773A] [Note: [Col. 0773A]

I demonstrated in the *Prolegomena*, no. 42, that this dedication is not by Sedulius but appears to be the work of some copyist who transcribed the Virgilian cento of Proba Falconia at the emperor’s command. These verses occur in Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 25; they are included in some editions of Sedulius after the first metrical prologue and by Arntzenius in his preface to his edition of Sedulius.

1. Bandinius, vol. I of the *Florentine Library*, p. 723, reads from a manuscript *Romulei doctor*, which is less satisfactory.

2. The reading seems to be *Eoi qui regna tenes*, that is, *Eoi* meaning “of the East.” Ovid, *Tristia* IV, elegy 9, verse 22:

> Whatever we say from the rising, it will go toward the setting;  
> And the Eastern star will be witness to the voice of the West.

One might also read *Eoa qui*, with the final syllable of *Eoa* lengthened according to the caesura. If *Eoum* is retained, it will be an appositional case modifying *regna*; or, preferably, one should write, with Labbeus, *Eoum* for *Eorum*, just as *Romulidum* is used for *Romulidarum*. Bede, in *On the Art of Meter*, observes that the first syllable of *Eous* is common, citing Sedulius, book II, verse 74: “The Eastern Magi came,” and book V, verse 191: “The splendid Eastern star shines from the author’s summit.” There are many similar examples. In the very old parchment of the Angelica Library, which I discussed in the *Prolegomena*, no. 37, the reading is *Eoa*, which had been my conjecture. Roscius had the text printed as *Eoi qui regna regis*. Arntzenius has *quia*; the Pisaurian edition of the *Collection of Poets* more correctly has *qui*.

3. Julius Roscius has *dignare, Marone, mutato in melius, divinum agnoscere sensum*—“deign, O Maro, to recognize the divine meaning changed for the better.” Another old copy of the Angelica Library has the same reading as the printed edition.

5. The Angelica manuscript has *jusseras*. Although this plainly conflicts with the meter, it may nevertheless be accepted if we say that the author of these verses lived long after Sedulius; this perhaps is not far from the truth. For some people occasionally assumed the identity of earlier authors and produced verses in their name. In the Roman edition of Proba’s cento, based on Julius Roscius’s recension, one should write *famulae quem jusserat*—“whom he had commanded, his handmaid”—which seems to have been done so that the poem would appear to have been composed in a woman’s name. By the verb *jusserat*, Roscius may perhaps have meant Honorius’s brother, since he thinks this little poem was dedicated to Honorius.

[Col. 0774A] 6. Roscius, apparently by his own conjecture, has *polos* for *poli*.

7. Roscius, for the same reason, altered *Expediet limo Christi hic tibi proferet* to avoid a hiatus or the attribution of consonantal force to the aspirate. He likewise substituted *ortus* for *ortum*.

9. Roscius has *pelagique vias*.

10. The Pisaurian edition has *Hic fluctum*; Arntzenius has *Hic fluctuum*. One should rather write *Hic fluctum*; in such cases poets commonly use syncope. See the example in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 215. *Fluctuum*, or *fluctum*, is the genitive of the noun *jugum*, to which the adjective *famulare*—that is, “servile”—is attached. The Angelica manuscript has *Hic fructum*, which makes no sense; Roscius’s *Hic fractum* is no better.

11. Roscius has *ducis*; others have *crucis*.

14. Dempsterus, at the beginning of book III of his *Ecclesiastical History of the Scots*, thinks this verse should be corrected to *Arcadio ille suo generi, sic haec tua semper*, perhaps to avoid the hiatus between *Arcadio* and *haec*. But the poets of that period used to give the aspirate the force of a consonant when they wished, as happens above in verses 6 and 7. In Fabricius’s *Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, the same verse is read differently, without hiatus: *haec legat ille tuo generi, haec tua semper*, where *tuo* is also inserted for *suo*. The genuine and more common reading is the one we print. I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 36, that Norisius’s conjecture—*Arcadiae: haec illa suo generi*, etc.—was not approved even by the author himself. In the Angelica Library’s codex, *semini* appears instead of *generi*, against the meter. In the Roman edition of Proba’s cento, Roscius apparently composed the text by ingenuity as *haec legat ille suo generi, haec tua semper*.]

Leader of the Romulids, second light of the brilliant sun,

You who hold the Eastern kingdoms under just governance;

Hope of the world and glory of your brother, deign to recognize

Maro, changed for the better, with divine understanding.

[5] The writing which you commanded your servant [to make]: here he will unfold for you

The world’s beginning, the form of heaven, and man created from clay;

Here he will set forth Christ’s birth,

The King’s plots, the Magi’s gifts, the learned disciples,

[Col. 0774A] The dangers of the sea and his passage across the waters;

[10] Here, the servile yoke of the waves, and life restored

By the aid of a single cross; and the return of buried

Death, and likewise the ascent of him who seeks his own kingdoms.

Read these things again, preserve them for a long time, and hand them on to the younger

Arcadius; may he receive these things for his own offspring; may your august line

[15] Receive them and teach them to its descendants.
