In this centonary poem the author or the scribe has made several errors. In verse 11, the first syllable of *matura* is improperly shortened; in verse 20, there are too many syllables; in verse 22, the first syllable of *fides* is lengthened; in verse 25, one might perhaps read *haud tali equidem*; in verse 28, after *jussa Dei*, and in verse 30, *patris sequar haec*. In the *Middle-Ages Fabrician Library*, verse 50 reads *praestigia fraudis* instead of *vestigia*; and verse 54 has *regent* instead of *reges*. Verse 58, *Jam propiore Dei. Nam tempore eodem*, is one foot too short. In verse 73, the final syllable of *diverso* and the first syllable of *sedem* are shortened; in verse 76, the first syllable of *datum* is lengthened. Verse 78 has one syllable too many, and is falsely attributed to Virgil in the note; the first two words, *Concordes animae*, are from book VI, verse 827. There is also a metrical error in *quoque* in verse 87, unless one reads *quae*, and in *exuberat* in verse 93.

For verse 17, note 12 should have cited Virgil’s verse *Quos bonus Aeneas dictis solatur amicis* (“Whom good Aeneas comforts with friendly words”). For verse 32, note 24 should have read, in place of *Aspicit*, Virgil’s *Castraque Dardanidum aspectat* (“And looks upon the camp of the Dardanids”). For verse 52, note 39 originally gave *Eclogue* VI; I restored it to *Eclogue* IV. In note 40 to verse 53, verse 195 was cited instead of 295; I have removed these and other numerical errors. In note 51 to verse 63, *Monstrat iter vobis* (“shows you the way”) are not Virgil’s words, but *Causa fuit* (“was the cause”). In Martenius’s edition, verse 30 reads *patri exsequar* instead of *patris exsequar*.

[Col. 0780B] The author of this poem either did not know or disregarded the rules for the cento laid down by others: he sometimes joins two verses of Virgil just as they stand together in Virgil. See note 84. Ausonius, however, teaches in his letter to Paulinus that this is not permitted. He defines a cento thus: “From various passages and different meanings, a certain structure of verse is consolidated into a single line, so that either two divided portions, or one whole line and the following half-line, come together. For placing two lines together is inept, and three in a single sequence is sheer nonsense.” Ausonius adds other points, which Julius Roscius explains in the discussion he appended to the poems of Laelius and Julius Capilupus. Possevinus may also be consulted, *Select Library*, volume II, book XVII, chapter 24. He observes that Laelius Capilupus's centos were prohibited because of certain expressions foreign to the usage of our religion and some other expressions too licentious for those times; they subsequently appeared again in an expurgated edition, to which Julius Capilupus added his own, being in no way inferior to his uncle Laelius. Possevinus gives as an example Julius's cento to the Blessed Virgin of Loreto. Yet even there an expression foreign to [Col. 0780C] the usage of our religion slipped through, as in verse 4: *Quae nunc aetherios inter dea candida nimbos* (“You who now, a radiant goddess, amid the ethereal clouds”). I discussed this epithet “goddess” in the note on Sedulius's epigram; I would not wish it applied to the Mother of God even in a cento. For these reasons, I think, Gelasius listed among the apocrypha the cento on Christ assembled from Virgilian verses, perhaps following St. Jerome, who says in his letter to Paulinus: “As though it were a great achievement, and not a most vicious manner of speaking, to distort meanings and drag a resisting text to one's own wishes! As though we had not read Homeric and Virgilian centos, and could not in this way call even Virgil a Christian without Christ, because he wrote, ‘Now the Virgin too returns,’ etc. These are childish things, like a mountebank's game: to teach what you do not know.”]

The clear springs will not be lacking for the flocks, nor the grasses;

Nor what the herds will crop during the long days.

Only the chill dew will restore a small amount during the night. [Note: [Col. 0779A] *Georgics* II.200:

> The clear springs . . . will not be lacking.  
> Nor what the herds will crop during the long days;  
> Only the chill dew will restore a small amount during the night.]

These are the things with which it is fitting that you be admonished by my voice. [Note: [Col. 0779A] *Aeneid* III.461:

> These are the things with which it is permitted that I admonish you by my voice.]

[100] Live happily, and keep these things stored in your minds. [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* III.388 and 492:

> Keep it stored in your mind.  
> Live happily, you whose fortune has been fulfilled.]

When he had spoken these words, he soon lifted himself into the air,

Looking toward heaven, and hid his head among the clouds. [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* IV.176–177:

> Soon he lifts himself into the air,  
> He proceeds upon the ground and hides his head among the clouds.]

And thus, departing from the earth, he removed from the minds of his followers

[Col. 0780A] The accumulated stain

And left behind a pure ethereal sense and the fire

[105] Of simple air. [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* VI.746–747.]

From that time onward his honor was celebrated, and joyful descendants [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* VIII.268–269.]

Preserved the day, and every year these pious rites [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* V.59:

> And these rites of mine every year.]

Mothers and men, boys and unmarried girls [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* VI.306–307:

> Mothers and men, bodies released from life,  
> Of great-hearted heroes, boys and unmarried girls.]

Celebrate in songs, and pour offerings upon the altars from bowls. [Note: [Col. 0779B] *Aeneid* XII.174:

> And pour offerings upon the altars from bowls.]

[110] But I, who have sung of the great and wondrous divine power,

These same things shall remain for my people and my race.

[Col. 0779]

## EPIGRAMMATIC POEMS. (C)

### Epigram of Turcius Rufius Asterius, who collected Sedulius’s poems, or Dedication of the Poems

[Col. 0779C]

[Note: [Col. 0779D]

1. A discussion of Asterius as the author of this epigram is found in the *Prolegomena*, nos. 136 and following. In verse 1, recent editors, from the Cambridge manuscript, read *pater meritis* (“father in merits”). Barthius, Sirmondus, Labbeus, our codices, and others have *sacer meritis*, which is also acceptable, with *sacer* used substantively for “priest.” I discussed this meaning in the *Prolegomena*, no. 156, where I also presented other conjectures of mine concerning the verse. Arntzenius retained *pater*, although his own codex also gives *sacer*; he says that Macedonius had already been honored with the title *father* by Sedulius in the dedicatory letter: “Before me, venerable father,” etc. This conjecture is slight, however. Cellarius, with Sirmondus, printed *veracia* (“true things”); all the others have *veracis*, which fits better with the following verse.

2. *Figmenti* (“of fiction”): Asterius refers to Sedulius’s verse I.17, “While the Gentile poets strive after their own fictions.” Paulinus, poem 10 to Ausonius: “The fictions of poets cloud the truth.”

3. In the note to Gyraldus, *On Poets*, the reading is *Quo calet* (“by which it burns”); correct to *Quo caret* (“which lacks”). Arntzenius has *sancti quo*; others have *quo sancti*.

4. Reg. 2 has *justus tot talia* (“the just man says so many such things”); others, more correctly, *justus ait talia* (“the just man says such things”).]

Take, holy one in merits, the words of the truthful poet,

[Col. 0780C] Which have been composed without the fault of fiction.

The fault which gracious faith lacks, and which the grace of holy Christ lacks,

Through which righteous Sedulius speaks such things.

[5] [Col. 0781A] [Note: [Col. 0781A]

5. Withof, in *Preliminary Remarks*, chapter 8, p. 108, shrewdly proposed *juvet te* (“may it help you”) instead of *jubeto* (“command”). The phrase *juvat*, *juvet*, *juvabit meminisse* (“it helps, may it help, it will help to remember”) is extremely common. All the old books oppose this, however, and their reading can be explained as follows: “Command others always to remember your Asterius.” A similar thought occurs in Asterius himself, who says in the epigram in which he reports his correction of Virgil:

> And sends his own Asterius into living time.

6. Arntzenius has *cura haec edita*, a reading Burmannus had conjectured in the margin of his edition. Barthius preferred *cura didita*. The common reading *cura edita* (“care published”) is sound; for Sedulius, like other poets, sometimes permits hiatus, especially in the pentameter after the first two feet.

7. Arntzenius has *Quae*, as is also read in the note to Gyraldus. The true reading is *Quem*, namely Asterius. Codex B. less correctly has *celebrant*. Reg. 2 has *factos*, corruptly. Cellarius, with some others, has *fasti*; most have *fastus*. For *fastus* belongs to the second and fourth declensions, and consequently one is frequently written for the other in manuscripts. Labbeus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 325, printed *fasti*, but cites *fastus* from the manuscript of Saint-Albin. The error in the Thorney codex and in codex B., *factus*, points to *fastus*.]

8. Codex B omits *est* (“is”); Barthius omits it in some places and retains it in others. Among Gruter’s inscriptions, p. 1172, no. 6, there is an epigram of similar meaning:

> Although illustrious as consul from a patrician stock,  
> You adorn your noble insignia with distinction;  
> Yet your merit grows still greater because, through blessed death,  
> You bear your name through the blood shed by a martyr.

One might suspect *nobilitate tua* (“by your nobility”); but in Vatican Palatine Codex 833, from which Gruter drew this and most of the Christian inscriptions, it is read in the same way. Gallandius, in his dissertation on Sedulius in vol. IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, thinks that Asterius is speaking in this distich about Sedulius; but it is plainly about himself, namely, “Asterius, whom,” etc. For the *fasti*, or highest records, which celebrate someone’s name through the ages, are certainly the consular fasti. Rather, the question seems to be whether this same Asterius should be regarded as the author of the epigram included among Gruter’s inscriptions, and who the consul-martyr is whom those verses praise. The same thought, the same style, and the same devotional taste are perceptible in both epigrams. Something similar also appears in the epigram in which Asterius set forth his correction of Virgil: for there too he calls the consulship *trabeae* (“robes”):

> And sends his own Asterius into living ages,  
> He who so well bestows riches won through the robes.

Claudius and others use this word with a similar meaning. Nevertheless, I think that both epigrams—“Take, sacred one” and “Although illustrious from a patrician stock”—had the same author, Asterius; or, if they had different authors, that one drew upon the other. The consul-martyr celebrated in the epigram “Although illustrious from a patrician stock” seems to have been named Florus, as appears from the following two distichs:

> Joined to God, whom you sought with your whole mind,  
> As Christ’s champion you will rightly dwell among the stars.  
> May that be accepted, I pray, which, after the losses of war,  
> Florus, a servant, restored to a better state.

The meaning of the last distich is obscure, and perhaps the text is corrupt. In the Roman Martyrology I find the name Florus recorded under 22 December: “At Ostia on the Tiber, Saints Demetrius, Honoratus, and Florus, martyrs.” But whether there is anywhere reliable evidence for a consul Florus, or for someone with another name to whom the epigram could apply, is uncertain to me. The final verse of the epigram on Sedulius confirms my conjecture, set out in no. 156 of the *Prolegomena*, that Sedulius’s poems were dedicated to Gelasius by Asterius in this epigram: for the praise of Asterius fits no one else so well, since he says that it contributes more to his merit than the honor of the consulship that he lives on the lips of that priest to whom he was presenting Sedulius’s verses.

1. Who appears to have been the author of this acrostic epigram, Belisarius, has been stated in the *Prolegomena*, no. 163. Different writers transmit this and the following epigram in different orders. In Reg. 1, on the final page, in smaller script after Asterius’s verses “Take, sacred one,” these epigrams appear without any title: first the epigram of Belisarius, then that of Liberius. In Reg. 2 and 3 they are likewise written without the authors’ names and in the same order. In Reg. 6, under the heading “Verses of Belesarius the Scholastic,” both epigrams are included, with the same order retained. The same is true in Mabillon, *Veterum Analecta*, p. 386, Paris edition of 1723, and p. 361 of the first octavo edition, vol. I, from an old Corbie manuscript; but in the latter the title is “Acrostic verses of Bellesarius the Scholastic on the poet Sedulius.” Ott. 1 presents only Belisarius’s epigram, “Sedulius of Christ,” without naming its author. Ott. 2 places Liberius’s verses first and adds Belisarius’s verses, but under a single title: “The name of Sedulius the Bishop at the beginning and end of the meter.” Most printed editions preserve this order.

The same order seems to occur in two manuscripts of Barthius; and in one of them the title of this epigram is: “Belisarius’s Anacrostic on Sedulius.” The glosses interpret this as follows: “An acrostic is formed when something is connected from the first letters of the verses. An anacrostic is formed when something is connected from the first and last letters of the verses.” See *Adversaria*, book LIII, chapter 5, where Barthius reports variant readings from two manuscripts and two ancient editions. When a name is formed from the final letters of the verses, the poem is usually called a telestich. Although this kind of poem is scarcely worthy of the grandeur of Latin poetry, it is nevertheless inferred from Cicero, *De Divinatione*, book II, chapter 5, that it was sometimes used by Ennius and that a similar form is found in the Sibylline verses. The Sibyl’s verses concerning judgment—“The sign of judgment,” etc.—which frequently occur among the Fathers and ancient writers, written both in Greek and in Latin, exhibit an acrostic form.

This form was also used by St. Eugenius of Toledo, St. Damasus in “On the Name of Jesus,” St. Columbanus, the monk Ademar in Mabillon’s *Veterum Analecta*, vol. I, Aldhelmus, Optatianus Porphyrius in his *Panegyric on Constantine*, Rabanus Maurus in *In Praise of the Cross*, Abbo, Arnulf of Emmeram, and Sidonius, to whom most writers attribute the arguments prefixed to the comedies of Plautus. An inscription in Fabretti, chapter 9, no. 290, was composed by the same device. Sarazanius indicates several other similar inscriptions in his note on Damasus’s poem VII. See also Browerus’s note on Rabanus, p. 111. Cellarius collated this epigram with the Alm. manuscript, in which *Bellesarius* is written.

2. Two manuscripts of Barthius have *parva*; most manuscripts have *parvae*, which is better, as in the metrical preface, verse 5, it says *modica mensa* (“a modest table”). Most printed editions have *parva*. Sedulius, in the cited passage, writes: “But content with the modest ceremonies of a table.”

3. Ott. 2 has *convivium* (“banquet”); correct to *convivam* (“guest”). Reg. 2 has *caperet*; correct to *carperet*. Barthius’s codex has *cappit et*, from which, Barthius says, someone might perhaps have carved out another reading. In Ott. 2 something similar appears: *non hunc, qui carpis et illud*. I suspect that Belisarius wrote: *non hunc, qui carpserit illud*.

> And always command that your Asterius be remembered,  
> Through whose aid and care these works were published for the people;  
> Although the highest records celebrate him through the ages,  
> Yet it contributes more to merit if he lives upon your lips.

[8]

### Acrostic of Belisarius the Scholastic on Sedulius

> Sedulius, publishing Christ’s miracles in verse,  
> Shines forth, inviting to the ceremonies of a modest table  
> A worthy guest—not one who would pluck at it.

[Col. 0783A]

4. Alm. has *Vix ad*; Reg. 6 likewise, but the sense is lacking. Reg. 2 has *Vix quam*; the true reading is *Vix quod*. Two manuscripts of Barthius and most of ours have *triplici fert*; Reg. 2 has *praefert triplici*. Reg. 1 corruptly reads: *Vix quod nobilium triplici profert aulaea paratu*; the verse is thereby one foot too long. The Lyon Library has *nobilium proferet triplici aula*, against the meter. Most printed editions have *nobilium profert triplici aula*. The author had Sedulius’s preface before his eyes and therefore seems to recognize a threefold preparation on the tables of the noble, since Sedulius says: “There you will find whatever the sea nourishes for eating, whatever the earth creates, whatever flies toward the stars.” Gallandius rightly condemns *profert triplici aura*, for I do not know where he found the word *aura*.

5. Reg. 1 has the erroneous *spondit* for *ponit*. Reg. 2, 5, Alm., Mabillon’s codex, and Ott. 2 have *quod ponet sub*. Barthius’s codex has *ponit subque*. Most printed editions have *quod ponitque sub*. Ott. 2 with Poelman has *quod ponit sub aurea*. This reading should be retained: *ponitque sub* or *ponit subque* was introduced by those who did not want *sub* to be lengthened. Yet I have often shown in my notes on Dracontius and Juvencus that all monosyllables commonly judged short can be lengthened.

6. Reg. 3 has *tot quae aurea*; others have *totque aurea*. Here too *que* in *totque* may perhaps be superfluous; but it may be retained, since in Sedulius’s metrical prologue the jewel-bearing baskets and golden vessels are likewise distinguished.

7. Reg. 1, 3, 6, Ottob. 1, and two manuscripts of Barthius have *Uvida*. Ott. 2 and the printed editions have *Vivida*. Alm. has *Vita*, incorrectly; Mabillon has *Vivi*, no better. Reg. 2 has *pro modica*, or *permodica*; Reg. 3, obscurely even in its abbreviation, has *permodico* or *praemodico*; others have *pro modico*. Two manuscripts of Barthius have *pro modica* and afterward *vita* for *victu*. Two manuscripts of Barthius, Alm., Mabillon’s codex, and all our manuscripts have *prandia*; the printed editions have *gaudia*. These are the moist second-course dishes of the table, of which Sedulius speaks in his metrical prologue. The same second tables are called *modicus victus* (“modest fare”), in comparison with the threefold preparation.

8. Reg. 2 has *Sed quod olus ille*; one manuscript of Barthius has *Sed quod illud vile*; both are corrupt. Some printed editions have *Sed quod olus vilis*, the reading retained by Arntzenius; others, with most manuscripts, have *Sed quod olus vile*, with the final syllable of *vile* lengthened either because of the caesura or because of the two consonants in the following word. That this is the true reading is confirmed by Sedulius’s metrical prologue, verses 15 ff., where a small vegetable is mentioned in the same metaphor. In Alm. the verse is corrupted as follows: *Sed olus vile producit pauperes ortus*.

9. One manuscript of Barthius has *Aut post*; another, with Mabillon and Reg. 1, 3, 6, has *At post*; Reg. 2 has *Ad post*, which points in the same direction. The printed editions have *Ac post*. Ott. 2 corruptly has *Apud dilicias*.

10. In Ott. 2, *Nitimur*, apparently; but this is an error. The Edinburgh edition and some others have *gramen*; Poelman, with the manuscripts, has *germen*. Arntzenius printed *germen*, but says in his notes that *gramen* is more to his liking.

11. One manuscript of Barthius has *Tutum qui nihil est, dum nil est ventre tumescit*; another, with Ott. 1 and Fabricius, has *Tutum quod nihil est dum nil cum ventre tumescit*. Alm. has *sed quod nil est*, and Reg. 2 *sed nil in ventre*; several printed editions likewise have *sed Tantum quod nihil est*. Mabillon’s codex, with Reg. 1, has *Tantum quod nihil est, dum cum nil ventre tumescit*. Reg. 3 and 6 have *Tutum quo nihil est, dum nil cum ventre tumescit*. Ott. 2 has *Tutum quod nihil est, dum convescendo tumescit*. None of these readings is entirely satisfactory, nor can I find what would be satisfactory. Perhaps the following will seem better: *Totum quod nihil est, dum nil cum ventre tumescit*, or *Totum quod nihil est, nihilum dum ventre tumescit*, since the belly sometimes swells without food. From Reg. 2, Mabillon’s codex, and Ott. 2, the more probable reading seems to be: *Tantum quod nihil est, dum convescendo tumescit*—that is, the sprout or vegetable, the poor man’s food, is almost nothing and merely causes swelling, bringing trouble to the limbs and to the suffering—or, conjecturally, flowing—soul. For the following verse is also corrupt. *Tantum quod* is commonly used for “scarcely” or “almost.” Cicero, *Against Verres*, book III, chapter 45: “He scarcely names the man, but records the whole case.” Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 6: “He was born on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, scarcely at sunrise.” See other examples in Tursellinus, *De Particulis*, chapter 192.

12. Reg. 2 has *Insidiis*; others have *Insidias*. Alm., Reg. 1, 3, 6, Mabillon, and Ott. 1 and 2 have *membris movens*, which is metrically impossible. One manuscript of Barthius has *ventrisque movens*. The Edinburgh edition has *membris implens*; Ottob. 2, *membris moveat*; most printed editions, *membrisque movens*. Reg. 2 has *membris, animae*; *movens* or another verb is missing. Alm., Mabillon, Reg. 1, 2, 3, and Ott. 2 have *animaeque ludenti*, which the meter does not allow. Reg. 6 corruptly has *animae qui ludenti*. Ott. 1 has *animae ludenti*, which would make the verse spondaic. The Edinburgh edition has *animaeque vaganti*. Fabricius has *animaeque ruenti*, and Barthius did not note the readings differing from Fabricius’s. Most printed editions have *animaeque luenti*.

13. Mabillon and the Edinburgh edition have *dignatur*; Alm. has *dignatus*; others have *dignantur*. Arntzenius attributes *egeni* to Mabillon and the Edinburgh edition; but Mabillon has *egenis*, which the telestich requires. It should be noted that Arntzenius often slips in the passages he collated.

14. Alm. has *Temptat*; correct to *Temnat*. Poelman corruptly has *divitas* for *divitias*.

15. The manuscripts of Barthius and ours, together with Alm., Poelman, and Fabricius, have *assumptus*; Ott. 1 incorrectly has *assumpsit*. Some printed editions have *assumpto*. Reg. 3 has *quo*; others, *qui*.

16. Poelman and Fabricius have *satiavit*; other printed editions, with all the manuscripts, have *saturavit*.

> Scarcely does a noble hall provide a threefold array,  
> [5] Which it sets beneath the golden roof of its cheerful tribunal:  
> Jewel-bearing baskets and so many golden vessels  
> Bring themselves moist dishes as modest fare.  
> But the cheap vegetable which a poor man’s garden produces—  
> [10] Those who hasten after great delicacies to consume them strive  
> To despise the small shoot of the poor.  
> It is almost nothing, yet it swells while being consumed,  
> Setting snares for the limbs and for the suffering soul,  
> If the poor nevertheless deign to feed on these dishes.  
> Let the mind despise riches and rest content with little,  
> [15] Following the example of the Lord, who, when all had been dismissed,  
> Satisfied five thousand with a modest supply of food.

[Note: In one manuscript of Barthius the author is called not Liberius but Libertus. The inscription reads: “Acrostic of Libertus on Coelius Sedulius,” with the gloss written at the beginning of Belisarius’s verses.]

### Acrostic of Liberius on Sedulius (C)*

> Sedulius, proceeding through cultivated new fields,  
> [5] Then saw places radiant with abundant flowers.  
> He gladly runs through the meadows, in whose grass David,  
> …

4. Two manuscripts of Barthius have *moderantem*. This is related to the error in Ott. 2, *moderantia*. The common reading *modulantem* is supported by many similar examples. Poelman incorrectly has *carmine* for *carmina*.

5. Reg. 2, 3, 6, Mabillon’s codex, one manuscript of Barthius, and Poelman with other ancient editions have *Laudabili psallente viro*, but the metrical rule rejects this, since the second syllable of *Laudabili* is long. Fabricius and most printed editions have *Laudato psallente viro*, which seems to have been corrected conjecturally by someone so that the verse would scan. Arntzenius conjectured *Laudando*. Barthius found in one of his manuscripts *Laudis hoc psallente viro* and suspected from these variations that the passage was corrupt. Reg. 1 reads *Laudis ceu psallente viri*; Ott. 2, *Laudis et psallente viri*. Nor do the manuscripts agree in the remaining words. Some manuscripts and most printed editions have *refluit citharae mel*; Reg. 1 and Ott. 2, with Poelman and other printed editions, have *refluit cithara mel*. Mabillon’s codex and Reg. 6 have *refluunt citharae mel*. Reg. 2 corruptly has *refluunt cicerea mel*; Reg. 3 likewise corruptly has *refluantque cere mel*. I think the reading should be: *Laudes hoc psallente viro, refluit cithara mel*. For the ancients wrote *laudis* for *laudes*. I take *cithara* as an ablative. It would not be bad to read *et*, namely: “and while David sings praises, sweetness flows from the lyre.”

6. Fabricius and some other editions have *grandisono*; the sense, together with the manuscripts and most printed editions, requires *grandisoni*. Ott. 2 has *cantus*; correct to *captus*. Reg. 2 has *pulchri*; read *plectri*. Liberius borrows the word *grandisonus* from Sedulius, book I, verse 18; it is not found among the earlier writers.

7. Many printed editions, especially the more recent ones, have *Utitur*. Two manuscripts of Barthius and all ours, together with Poelman and other old editions, have *Uritur*, which Burmann the Younger supports. In Ott. 2, *et celeri* is an error for *excellere*.

8. Three books of Barthius and Poelman have *lacte*; Reg. 3, *lite*; most manuscripts and printed editions, *late*. Reg. 1, 2, 3, Ott. 2, and Mabillon have *conspexit*; others, *prospexit*. Three books of Barthius and Poelman have *amomos*; the others, *amoenos*. It would be difficult to find *amomus* in the masculine gender. I am inclined to conjecture:

> And once more the sacred grove looked upon its lovely places,  
> Which the river of Christ washes with eternal water.

9. Reg. 3 has *Aeterno*; Reg. 6, *Aeternam*; correct to *Aeterna*. Regarding *fluvios*, I have just said that *fluvius* may be read conjecturally. In manuscripts *us* is often changed into *os*, and the ancients sometimes ended the nominative singular of the second declension in *-os*. In place of *abluït*, Reg. 6 has *adluit*; and perhaps *alluit* (“washes over”) is better than *abluït*. From the diphthong *ae* the first vowel *a* in *aeterna* is taken for the acrostic rule of the poem. The same occurs in the acrostic inscription reported by Muratori, 1903, and by Bonada, class 10, no. 27, in the verse *Aeterno regi*. That inscription concludes:

> Reader, if you happen to seek the names of the holy women,  
> The first letter of every verse will reveal them to you.  
> The granddaughter Taurina placed this sacred title.

The names are Licinia, Leontia, Flavia, and Ampelia. In Belisarius’s verses, by contrast, from the diphthong *ae* in verse 2, *solemnia mensae*, the vowel *e* is taken so that the telestich may be preserved.

10. Reg. 2 and 3 and Mabillon’s codex have *Nam*; better are *Nec*, or, as Reg. 6 gives it, *Non*. Barthius’s books have *torpore* for *torpere*. Poelman has *ductoris*; so too do Barthius’s books, to which Arntzenius wrongly attributes *doctoris*. Ours, with most printed editions, have *doctoris*, which is much better. These words may be compared with those of the letter to Macedonius: “But the torpor of the dull heart,” etc.

11. Barthius’s books have *Non sua*; the acrostic and the sense require *Tunc sua*. Reg. 1, 2, 3, 6, and Mabillon’s codex have *Daviticus dilectus*; Barthius’s books, *Davidicus delectus*. Ott. 2 corruptly has *Davitico dilectra*, corrected to *dilectu*. Most printed editions have *Davidico delectu*. In manuscripts *Daviticus* is often written for *Davidicus*. Likewise *dilectus* is often found in manuscripts for *delectus*, and both forms are correctly written. Perhaps here *dilectus* is not a substantive noun but an adjective, so that *dilectus Davidicus* would mean “beloved Davidic,” though this can scarcely be explained in a satisfactory sense. Either way, the meaning is the same; but *Davidicus delectus* seems the truer reading. He appears to express this more freely from book I, verses 23 ff.: “Why should I, in Davidic things,” etc.

12. Reg. 2, 3, 6, and Mabillon’s codex have *contemnens*; others, with the printed editions, *contempsit*. Sedulius argues against the worshipers of idols in book I, verses 242 ff.

13. Sedulius, book I, verse 343: “And beauty is fixed upon my forehead; beauty and weapons I bear,” etc.

14. Ott. 2 has *numero qui praemia*. Reg. 1, 2, and Mabillon’s codex have *numerosaque praemia*. Reg. 3 corruptly has *numeros atque praemia*. Reg. 6, worse, has *numeros sacri praemia*. The printed editions have *numerosaque praelia*, and Barthius notes no variation in his manuscripts. But *praemia* must be restored: any advantage or benefit is a *praemium*. Lucretius, book V, verse 4: “Who left us such things, won by his own heart and sought-out rewards.” The miracles of Christ, which Sedulius often calls gifts, are indicated by these words.

15. Ott. 2, with the printed editions, has *Ergo his dum*; most of our manuscripts, *Ergo dum sine his*. Many old editions have *decorat sua membra*; two manuscripts of Barthius, Ott. 2, and other printed editions have *decorat sua rura*, to which the error in Reg. 1, *decorat sua sura*, belongs. In Reg. 6 the passage is corrupted as *decoratu erarva*, where I read *decorat vera arva*, which is not to be rejected. Mabillon’s codex is also corrupt, *decorat vera colore*; Reg. 2 and 3 have *decorat vera sua colore*.

16. Reg. 1 has *in*; read *hi*. All the manuscripts, including those of Barthius, and the old printed editions have *garrula*. Poelman, with Reg. 3 and 6 and Mabillon’s manuscript, writes *garula*, so that the first syllable may be shortened. Fabricius and most other editions have *gracili*. Barthius and Burmann the Younger think that *garrula* derives from a gloss. Mabillon has *dicti*; Reg. 2, *dicta*; correct to *ducti*. After Barthius had collated these two poems of Belisarius and Liberius with two manuscripts and two other printed editions, he added some words which I may with greater right employ: “And I rejoice that I have completed this thorny labor.” Some regard such things as pleasing, others as displeasing. I leave my annotations in the middle. In every respect, however, I think it better that such trifles should survive, since even the smallest works of ancient authors ought to be read in the most corrected form possible, as the sources from which all learning descends. Nor is there almost any monument of theirs so slight that one cannot nevertheless learn something from it. For, as that man says, the aim is to be ignorant of nothing ancient.

> He saw David modulating songs in a divinely inspired chant.  
> [5] While that man sang praises, sweetness flowed from the lyre.  
> Captivated by the sweetness of the loud-sounding plectrum,  
> He burns and walks with swift step through the lilies.  
> And again he beheld the sacred, lovely places far and wide,  
> Which the eternal wave washes—the streams of Christ.  
> [10] Nor did he suffer the teacher’s keen mind to remain dull for long.  
> Then the Davidic chosen one sought his own plectrum,  
> Despising the vain divinities of the defiled world.  
> He places the signs of the cross upon his forehead and briefly touches upon your triumphs,  
> O Christ, and samples their numerous rewards.  
> [15] Therefore, while he adorns his fields with varied color,  
> [16] These verses, drawn by a slender lyre, will endure.

### Epigram on the Map of the World Made at the Command of the Emperor Theodosius the Younger

(From the anthology edited by H. Meyer at Leipzig.)

> This splendid work, in which the sum of the world is contained,  
> In which seas, mountains, rivers, straits, harbors, and cities  
> Are marked, so that it may be easy for everyone to know  
> Whatever lies hidden anywhere. The gentle scion, illustrious offspring,  
> [5] Pious through the ages—whom the whole world can scarcely contain—  
> The emperor Theodosius ordered this to be made by his venerable utterance,  
> When he opens the year with three times five consular fasti.  
> We, his suppliant servants, while one writes and another paints it,  
> Within a few months, following the monuments of the ancients,  
> [10] Restore the work for the better and remove the earlier fault,  
> Briefly comprehending the whole world.  
> [12] Yet your wisdom, prince, taught us this.

# DECREE ON BOOKS TO BE RECEIVED AND NOT RECEIVED

Illustrated from unpublished materials. (S)

## NOTICE

It is clear from the *Prolegomena*, nos. 150 ff., into how many and what kinds of difficulties historians and other critical scholars have fallen because of the praise of Sedulius found in the decree on books to be received and not received. This venerable monument of ecclesiastical antiquity is certainly worthy of being illuminated by a learned scholar in a special commentary. As far as lies within my power, I shall take care to present it here, having checked and corrected it against several manuscript copies. Chiffletius published it in his notes on Vigilius of Thapsus’s third short work; Fontaninus in the *Appendix to the Antiquities of Horta*, p. 317; Blanchinus in the *Prolegomena* to vol. IV of Anastasius’s third work; and Mansi in the *Supplement to the Councils*. Equipped with greater resources, I shall also contribute more on the same subject in a more suitable place, moved by the intention of assisting, insofar as I can, the efforts of certain friends who are devoting serious labor at Bologna to composing a history of the Church.

I shall establish three parts. In this first part I transcribe the Roman Council held under Pope Damasus from a Vatican manuscript. In the second I shall examine the Gelasian Decree—attributed by some to St. Damasus—against ancient copies. In the last I shall produce from ancient parchments in the Vatican Library a certain paraphrase of the same Decree that has not yet been published.

## PART ONE

[Note: Although this Council was previously published among the works of St. Damasus in vol. XIII of our *Patrology*, we have nevertheless not hesitated to reproduce it here, enlarged by nearly half and illustrated with the notes of the most learned Arevalus. Editor.]

### Council of the City of Rome Held under Pope Damasus

On the explanation of the Catholic faith.

[Note: In Vatican paper codex 349, quarto, among various miscellaneous items, this Council is found transcribed, as is indicated at the beginning, from the Vatican Library. Holstenius published the first part of the same Council, up to the words “and he will announce it to you,” from Vatican codex 5845. The same Council is found in manuscript Codex D. IV, 23 of the Casanatense Library, p. 46, from the eleventh century, which the Ballerinii mention in their treatise on the antiquity of canonical collections, part II, chapter 11, § 5. Baronius, under the year 69, no. 4, asserts that in his copy of the Cresconian Collection of Canons, p. 236, the Roman Council under Damasus on the apocryphal books is found—by this I understand the canonical Scriptures—from which he quotes certain words, “After all these prophetic books,” etc., through “they consecrated to the Lord,” and observes that these words are repeated in the Gelasian Decree.

In a codex of the Veronese chapter from the ninth or tenth century, under the title “On the Council published in the city of Rome under Pope Damasus,” the words “After all these prophetic books,” etc., are transcribed. It ends: “Council under Pope Damasus.” Constantius, vol. I of the *Roman Pontiffs’ Letters*, col. 503, mentions a codex of the Royal Library of Paris in which the same Council held under Damasus is found. The Florentine Codex of St. Mark, from the tenth century, attributes the first part, up to the words “and he will announce it to you,” to Damasus; thereafter it gives the Gelasian Decree under the name of Gelasius.

The first person, so far as I know, to publish the entire Council under the name of Damasus was Eusebius Amortius, from the Diessen Canon Collection, compiled around the middle of the seventh century and transcribed around the middle of the eighth: vol. II, p. 476, Augsburg edition of the *Elements of Canon Law*, and vol. I, p. 421, Venetian edition of 1763. From this the most learned Francis Anthony Zacharias reprinted it in his work *On the Prohibition of Books*, under the year 379, when the Council is believed to have been held.

There is considerable variation in the manuscripts, as will be evident from the collation. Vatican 1, or no. 349: “Here begins the Council,” etc., as in the title. Vatican 2, or no. 5845: “Here begins … under Damasus. On the explanation of the faith.” Casanatense and Parisian: “Here begins … under Pope Damasus. On the explanation of the faith.” Diessen: “Here begins … under Pope Damasus. On the explanation of the faith.” Florentine: “Council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus. On examples of the faith and on books to be received and not received.”]

It has been said that one must first discuss the sevenfold Spirit who rests in Christ: the Spirit of wisdom.

[Note: This is how Vatican 1 reads, which I follow, since I do not observe its variant. Vatican 2: “It has been said: first one must discuss the Spirit,” etc. Diessen: “It has been said that one must first discuss the sevenfold Spirit who rests in Christ, the Spirit of wisdom.”]

Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24).

The Spirit of understanding: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way, in which you shall walk” (Ps. 31:8).

[Note: Diessen adds *juxta illud* (“according to that passage”) after *intellectus*. The passage is Psalm 31:8, which Vatican 1 reads as does our Vulgate. Vatican 2: “In the way in which you will enter.” Diessen: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in the way in which you shall walk.”]

The Spirit of counsel: “And his name shall be called the angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6).

[Note: Vatican 2 and Diessen add: “And his name shall be called great,” etc.]

The Spirit of strength, as was said above: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

[Note: Diessen: “as above: the power of God,” etc.]

The Spirit of knowledge, because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says.

[Note: Diessen corruptly has: “because of the knowledge of Jesus the Apostle that is imminent in Christ.” The Apostle, in Ephesians 3:19, speaks of “the surpassing knowledge of Christ.”]

The Spirit of truth: “And I am life and truth” (John 14:6).

[Note: Vatican 2: “I am life and truth.” Diessen: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth.”]

The Spirit of fear: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:6).

[Note: Diessen adds “of God” after “fear.”]

The manifold dispensation of the names of Christ is this.

[Note: Vatican 1 has *dissertatio est* (“is a discussion”); this may be the genuine reading. Vatican 2 has *dispensatio est* (“is a dispensation”). Diessen has *dispensatio* without *est*. Casanatense: “Also concerning the manifold dispensation of the names of Christ.” Certain things concerning the names of Christ are noted in the scholion on elegy, verse 104.]

Lord, because he is Christ. Word, because he is the Son of God, because he is the only-begotten of the Father.

[Note: Vatican 2 and Diessen: “Lord, who is also Spirit; Word, because he is God; Son, because he is the only-begotten of the Father.”]

Flesh, because he was born from the Virgin.

[Note: Vatican 2 and Diessen have *Homo* (“Man”); Vatican 1 has *Caro* (“Flesh”).]

Shepherd, because he is the guardian of the sheep.

[Note: Vatican 2 and Diessen add: “Priest, because he offered himself as a burnt offering.” They omit “of the sheep” after “guardian.” Immediately after “guardian,” both codices have “Worm, because he rose again,” which is absent from Vatican 1.]

Mountain, because he is strong. Way, because through him the entrance to life is straight.

[Note: Vatican 2: “Way, because through him the entrance into life is.” Diessen: “Way, because he is straight; because through him there is entrance into life.”]

Lamb, because he suffered.

[Note: Diessen: “because he suffered.” Stone, because he is the angular construction. Vatican 2: “because he suffered. Cornerstone, because he is the construction.”]

Cornerstone, because he is the construction.

Teacher, because he shows life.

Sun, because he is the illuminator.

[Note: Diessen: “because he illuminates.”]

True, because he is from the Father.

Life, because he is the ruler.

[Note: Diessen and Vatican 2: “because he is the creator.”]

Bread, because he is flesh.

Samaritan, because he is guardian and merciful.

Christ, because he is anointed.

Jesus, because he is Savior.

God, because he is from God.

[Note: Diessen and Vatican 2 omit *est* (“is”) after “from God,” which the others include.]

Angel, because he is a messenger.

[Note: Diessen: “because he was sent.”]

Bridegroom, because he is mediator.

Vine, because by his blood we have been redeemed.

[Note: Vatican 2 has *ejus* (“his”) instead of *ipsius* (“his very own”).]

Lion, because he is king.

Rock, because he is the foundation.

[Note: Diessen: “because he is the foundation of the firmament.” Flower, etc.]

Foundation, because he is the firmament.

Flower, because he is chosen.

Prophet, because he reveals the future.

[Note: Diessen: “he revealed.”]

For the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but the Spirit of both Father and Son.

[Note: Diessen omits *enim* (“for”). Perhaps *etiam* (“also”) should be read; for these two words are often confused in manuscripts. Labbeus, vol. II, col. 895, notes in the margin: “Many things show that these words were appended to the preceding material by Holstenius or someone else. For the words which Baronius cites under the year 447, no. 21, from the Cresconian Collection do not cohere with what precedes. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that these words are found attached to the preceding ones in the oldest codices.” Baronius cites these very words under the name of Damasus from the Roman Council—that is, from the text before us—and elsewhere, as I said above, he himself praises them.]

For it is written: “If anyone has loved the world, the Spirit of the Father is not in him.” It is likewise written: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

[Note: The first quotation is from 1 John 2:15, although our Vulgate reads: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him.” What follows is from Paul’s Letter to the Romans 8:9: “But whoever,” etc.; Diessen has “Whoever,” whereas the Vulgate has “But if anyone.”]

Since, then, the Father and the Son have been named, the Spirit is understood—concerning whom the Son himself says in the Gospel: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, and he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.”

[Note: Vatican 2, with Baronius: “The Holy Spirit is understood.” Baronius omits *ipse* (“himself”) before “the Son.” Diessen: “But when he is named by the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is understood, concerning whom he himself,” etc. The Gospel passage is John 15:26: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.” Baronius, with Diessen and Vatican 2, has: “Because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.” The other passage is John 16:15. In Vatican 1 *illi* (“to him”) is corruptly written for *ille* (“he”). In the others *ille* is absent, as in the Vulgate.]

It was also said:

> “Now, however, we must deal with the divine Scriptures: what the universal Catholic Church holds, and what must be avoided.”

[Note: [Col. 0790C] These words, and those that follow, are attributed by the Casanatensis manuscript and another royal manuscript in Paris to Gelasius; the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark agrees with them and, after the words “and will announce it to you,” adds this heading: “Here begins the Decree concerning books to be rejected and received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy very learned bishops in the apostolic see in the city of Rome.” The Ballerinii think that the first part presented thus far belongs to the Roman council under Damasus, but not the remainder. For this preface suggests that apocryphal books are to be discussed; this is what the words “what must be avoided” signify. The learned Zacharias, who assigns the following canon of Scripture to Damasus, restores the connection of this second part with the first and finds it indicated by the words placed at the beginning, “It was said that we must first deal with …,” to which these words correspond: “Now, however, we must deal with the divine Scriptures,” etc. He further observes that the discussion concerns only the divine Scriptures, namely, which should be received into the canon. Finally, he conjectures that after the canon of Scripture in the council of Damasus there was a brief list condemning other books fabricated under the names of the apostles; this list is read in the letter of Innocent I to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in the year 405: “The remaining writings, which circulate under the name of Matthias, or James the Less, or under the name of Peter and John, and which were written by a certain Leucius, or under the name of Thomas, and any others of this kind, you should know are not merely to be rejected but also condemned.” This brief list could easily have been omitted by scribes, since the so-called Gelasian Decree, which was more widely available everywhere, prescribed these and many other matters concerning apocryphal books. I regard these arguments as probable; but one should not cling so firmly to the words “what must be avoided” that one believes they necessarily imply a catalogue of books specifically prohibited. Once the canon of the divine Scriptures has been established, it follows that other writings absent from that canon, even if they bear the names of apostles or prophets, are not to be counted among the divine Scriptures, but should rather be avoided as apocryphal.]

## The Order of the Old Testament Begins

One book of Genesis. One book of Exodus. One book of Leviticus. One book of Numbers.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Diess., “One book of Deuteronomy.”]

One book of Deuteronomy. One book of Joshua son of Nun. One book of Judges. One book of Ruth. Four books of Kings. Two books of Chronicles.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Diess., “One book of the one hundred and fifty Psalms.”]

One book of the Psalter. Three books of Solomon.

[Col. 0791B]

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Diess., “One book of Proverbs,” and shortly afterward “Wisdom” instead of “of Wisdom.”]

One book of Proverbs. One book of Ecclesiastes. One book of the Song of Songs. Likewise, one book of Wisdom. One book of Ecclesiasticus.

## The Order of the Prophets Begins

One book of Isaiah. One book of Jeremiah.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Diess., “together with Cinoth, that is, with his Lamentations.” Vatican manuscript 1 has “together with one Baruch,” and likewise “with his Lamentations.” So too Athanasius, Letter 39, in Labbe, volume II of the Councils, column 1710: “Jeremiah, and with him Baruch, the Threni and Lamentations.” Thereafter Diess. has “Ezekiel … Daniel … Micah … Ambacum” for Abbacuc or Habacuc … “Zephaniah,” etc. After Ambacum, Amortius places Amos in parentheses.]

with one book of Baruch; likewise, together with his Lamentations. One book of Ezekiel. One book of Daniel. One book of Joel. One book of Obadiah. One book of Hosea. One book of Amos.

[Col. 0791C]

One book of Micah. One book of Jonah. One book of Nahum. One book of Habakkuk.

[Col. 0792A]

One book of Zephaniah. One book of Haggai. One book of Zechariah. One book of Malachi.

## The Order of the Historical Books

One book of Job. One book of Tobit. One book of Judith.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Diess. places after the book of Tobit: “Two books of Ezra. One book of Esther. One book of Judith. Two books of Maccabees.”]

One book of Esther. One book of Ezra. Two books of Maccabees.

## The Order of the Scriptures of the New Testament, Which the Holy and Catholic Church Receives

One book of the Gospel according to Matthew. One according to Mark.

[Col. 0792B]

One according to Luke. One according to John.

## The Fourteen Letters of Paul

One to the Romans. Two to the Corinthians. One to the Ephesians. Two to the Thessalonians. One to the Galatians. One to the Philippians. One to the Colossians. Two to Timothy. One to Titus. One to Philemon. One to the Hebrews.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Zacharias, in the place cited, objects to himself that this does not appear to be Damasus’s canon of Scripture, since Saint Jerome, writing to Dardanus in 414, said that the Latin custom did not receive Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews among the canonical Scriptures. He rightly replies that this is to be understood as referring to the custom of certain churches, which, even after the canon of Damasus and the practice of Innocent I, continued not to receive the Letter to the Hebrews as canonical, until the year 419, when the Third Council of Carthage decreed that all should receive the complete canon of the divine Scriptures, which includes the Letter to the Hebrews, with the authority of Pope Boniface and of the Italian council also invoked to confirm this canon. See Labbe, volume II, column 1177. Thus either the decrees of Damasus and Innocent were not issued in such a way as to have the force of law for all churches, or they had not reached the knowledge of certain churches.]

Likewise, one book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle.

[Note: [Col. 0792D] In Diess. there is no mention of the Apocalypse, as may reasonably be conjectured to result from a scribe’s negligence, for it is present in our manuscript. Jerome, in the place cited, testifies that the Apocalypse was received among the Latins in his own time. Zacharias, who saw the Apocalypse omitted in the Diess manuscript, thinks that Damasus may have omitted it because many Greek churches at that time did not receive it, as Jerome states in the cited passage. In the canon of the Third Council of Carthage, as also in the canon of Innocent I in 405, the Apocalypse is included. In the Diess manuscript the Acts of the Apostles are mentioned after the Gospel of John.]

One book of the Acts of the Apostles. Likewise, seven canonical letters. Two letters of the Apostle Peter. One letter of the Apostle James.

[Col. 0793A]

One letter of the Apostle John.

[Note: [Col. 0793B] In the canon of Innocent I and in other canons, these three letters are said to belong to one John the Apostle. In Damasus’s canon, one is assigned to John the Apostle and two to John the presbyter, following the opinion suggested by Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9: “He [John the Apostle] also wrote one letter … The remaining two … are attributed to John the presbyter.” The antiquity of Damasus’s canon is confirmed by this feature.]

Two letters of the other John, the presbyter. One letter of Jude the Zealot.

[Note: [Col. 0793B] Diess. writes *Zelotis*; Vatican manuscript 1, *Zelotes*. Diess. adds: “The canon of the New Testament ends.”]

After these prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic Scriptures, which we listed above and through which the Catholic Church has been founded by God throughout the world, we also thought it necessary to make known that, although the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are, as it were, one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been placed before the other churches by certain synodical constitutions.

[Note: [Col. 0793C] The Cresconian collection has: “The Roman Church, by certain synodical decrees, [is placed] before the others,” etc. Later it has *inquiens* for *inquit*. Below: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”]

It also obtained primacy through the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

The fellowship of the blessed Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also added. He, contrary to what heretics babble, did not suffer martyrdom at a different time from Peter, but, struggling in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero, was crowned with a glorious death at one and the same time and on one and the same day; and together they consecrated the Roman Church mentioned above to Christ the Lord and placed it before all the others throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

[Note: [Col. 0793C] The margin of Vatican manuscript 1 notes: “Anacletus in Letter 3, and Pope Gelasius in his decretal letter.” Gelasius’s decretal letter is the decree to be produced later. The letters of Anacletus are considered spurious. In that third letter, although many words and opinions of this synod are reproduced, the words “as heretics babble” are absent; perhaps they were sewn onto this passage by someone. For some ancient Fathers say that Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom at Rome, indeed on the same day, but not in the same year, as I showed in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 12, *Peristephanon*, verse 5. I now add the *Sacramentary* which Saint Leo Blanchinus falsely attributed to Leo, while others attribute it to Gelasius and some to an anonymous ancient writer, in the preface for the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul: “Thus, by different dispensations gathering one household of Christ, although at a separated time, one recurring day united them forever, and one crown.” Perhaps the heretics are attacked in this council chiefly because they separated Paul from Peter’s fellowship in the place of martyrdom. I would gladly read: “who did not [suffer] in a different place, as heretics babble, but at one time,” or “who did not [suffer] at a different time, as heretics babble, but in one place, on one and the same day,” etc. In the apocryphal Acts of Linus it is reported that Peter and Paul suffered at different places and times. Certain recent heretics still use this weak testimony to deny that Peter was in Rome or was crowned with martyrdom. The words that follow in the council confirm my conjecture: “By their presence and venerable triumph they placed [it] before [the others].” The Cresconian collection in Baronius has: “who did not, as heretics falsely babble, [suffer] at a different time, but on one and the same day,” etc. Shortly afterward it says that they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ; Baronius quotes no more from that collection.]

Thus the Roman Church is the first see of the Apostle Peter, having neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in Peter’s name by Mark, his disciple and evangelist.

[Note: [Col. 0794C] He says that these three sees belong to Peter. In the Gelasian Decree, however, it reads: “in Peter’s name, by Mark his disciple.”]

Peter sent Mark to Egypt, where he preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third honorable see of the blessed Apostle Peter is held at Antioch, where he lived first, before coming to Rome, and where the name of the Christian people, still a new nation, first arose.

[Note: [Col. 0794C] In the Veronese manuscript, in which, as I have said, the council is mutilated and begins with the words “After all the prophetic [books],” etc., it is noted here: “The council under Pope Damasus ends.” Thus the Roman council under Damasus, brought to its conclusion, offers no reason why it should be taken away from Damasus. For the arguments that many advance from chronology prove only that not everything contained in the Gelasian Decree belongs to Damasus, as is obvious in itself. If some manuscripts present not only this council within its own limits but also the entire decree of Gelasius under the name of Damasus, the error arose either because Gelasius took the first part of his decree from this council, as Roman pontiffs often took many things from their predecessors, or because someone elsewhere appended Damasus’s council to Gelasius’s decree concerning books to be received or not received, or because Damasus’s council was appended by someone to Gelasius’s decree concerning books—not divine books—to be received or not received. It was easy for the name of Damasus, known to belong to the first part of the Gelasian decree, to be placed at the head of the entire decree in many manuscripts. More probably, however, I believe that Gelasius himself, composing his decree concerning Scriptures to be received and not received, took its first part from Damasus’s council, making slight alterations, omitting some matters, and adding others. This will be perceived more easily, I think, from the decree itself, which I shall now present.]

The End.

# PARTS TWO AND THREE

## The Gelasian Decree, from Vatican Manuscripts, together with a Paraphrase of the Same Decree

[Col. 0793]

(We reserve this material for a better place among the works of Gelasius, where, if you please, you may read it.)

# SEVERUS THE RHETOR

(From Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, volume IX.)

[Col. 0795]

# PROLEGOMENA

## 1

The name of this writer is circulated in the editions of the poem of which he is the author in the following form: **SEVERUS SANCTUS, that is, ENDELECHIUS the Rhetor**. From this arose differing opinions among learned men concerning the same writer. Tillemont, on the basis of the common edition, judges that the author was Endelechius, who wished to remain concealed under the name Severus Sanctus.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, volume V, page 148.]

Others, on the contrary, think that the words “that is, Endelechius” were plainly added by another hand and that the author’s proper name was Severus Sanctus.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] *Literary History of France*, volume II, pages 56–57.]

From the letters of Saint Paulinus of Nola we learn that he had bonds of friendship with two men, one called Endelechius and the other Sanctus. Concerning the former he writes:

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Paulinus, Letter 28, no. 6.]

> “Another little book belongs among those which I seem to have written to my blessed—that is, Christian—friend Endelechius, although I may be shown not to have published it.”

He mentions the latter in two letters addressed to Sanctus and Amandus, brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Paulinus, Letters 40 and 41.]

From one of these letters it is clear that Sanctus cultivated poetry. He speaks as follows:

> “I rejoice that I have received the hymns I desired. By this gift, holy brother Sanctus, you have reminded me,” etc.

Concerning Endelechius, the holy Father teaches only that, at his prompting, he wrote a panegyric of Theodosius. This work is mentioned by Jerome,

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Jerome, Letter 58, formerly numbered 13, no. 1.]

Gennadius,

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 48.]

and Cassiodorus.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Cassiodorus, *On Divine Literature*, chapter 21.]

From these facts, therefore, one may conclude that Sanctus must be distinguished from Endelechius, contrary to the opinion of the learned men Baronius,

[Note: [Col. 0795C] Baronius, under the year 376, § 8.]

Sirmondus,

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Sirmondus, on book IV, letter 8 of the works of Sidonius, volume I, page 490.]

Rosweydus,

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Rosweydus, on Paulinus’s Letter 9.]

and Fabricius,

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Fabricius, *Latin Bibliography*, volume III, page 278.]

who maintain that the friend of Saint Paulinus wrote the poem under discussion, but nevertheless suppose that there was only one man, named Severus Sanctus Endelechius. This seems less correct, since the passages just cited clearly establish that the holy Nolan bishop knew of two men and distinguished Sanctus from Endelechius.

## 2

Since this is so, I should myself judge that the poem commonly circulated under the name of Severus Sanctus ought rather to be attributed to Sanctus than to Endelechius, who perhaps had two names. For it is he, not Endelechius, whom Paulinus celebrates as distinguished by eloquence of verse. This is the opinion of the learned writers of the *Literary History of France*.

[Note: [Col. 0796C] *Literary History of France*, cited volume, page 57.]

Petrus Pithoeus judged the author of the poem to have been an Aquitanian. He first published it in Paris, toward the end of the sixteenth century, from the manuscript of Elie Vinet, together with little works by the ancient theologians of Gaul; perhaps from the same city of Bordeaux from which Saint Paulinus, his friend, is said to have come.

The occasion for composing the poem was the terrible plague that severely devastated the Pannonian, Illyrian, Belgian, and other peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Severus, *Bucolics*, verses 22–23.]

Saint Ambrose also mentioned it, as Baronius observed:

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Baronius, in the place cited.]

> “No one is more a witness than we are to the heavenly words. For what battles, and what reports of battles, have we heard! … What famine there was everywhere, what plague alike among cattle, human beings, and other animals, so that even those of us who did not endure war were nevertheless made equal to the conquered by pestilence! Therefore, because we are at the setting of the age, certain illnesses of the world precede us. The world’s illness is famine; the world’s illness is pestilence; the world’s illness is persecution.”

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book X, no. 10, works, volume I, page 1506.]

Thus speaks the holy Father. Our Rhetor explains in his elegant eclogue how such a plague could very easily be cured through the sign of the holy cross:

[Note: [Col. 0796C] Severus, cited work, verses 101 ff.]

### THE CALF

> **… Tell me, Tityrus,**
>
> **What god rescued you from these disasters,**
>
> **So that the plague which ravaged the neighboring herds**
>
> **Has touched none of yours?**

### TITYRUS

> **The sign which they say is the cross of God,**
>
> **…**
>
> **This sign, placed upon the middle of their foreheads,**
>
> **Was the sure salvation of all the cattle.**

## 3

From the same poem one may also discover the period in which the author flourished. Tityrus says:

[Note: [Col. 0797B] Severus, *Bucolics*, verses 102 ff.]

> **Christ, who alone is worshiped in the great cities,**
>
> **The glory of the eternal God,**
>
> **Whose only son he is.**

At that time, therefore, while the Christian religion was growing strong, the worship of idols still flourished in the countryside and villages alone. This observation points to the end of the fourth century.

Add to this that Saint Ambrose composed his *Exposition on Luke*, in which he reports as an eyewitness that the plague in question had raged, no earlier than the year 386, as the learned editors of Ambrose’s works, the Bollandists, have established by numerous arguments, following Hermant.

[Note: [Col. 0797B] Hermant, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, book IV, chapter 20.]

[Note: [Col. 0797B] Ambrose, works, volume II, page 1258 ff.]

Moreover, it should not be passed over that our author’s poem had until now been entitled *On the Deaths of Oxen*. This is indeed an absurd title, as Reinesius rightly determined in Schoettgenius.

[Note: [Col. 0797B] Schoettgenius, volume VI of *The Medieval Latin Library of Fabricius*, page 461.]

The poet’s one purpose was to exalt the power of Christ’s cross, whom he everywhere proclaims to be God,

[Note: [Col. 0798B] Severus, cited work, verses 105, 111, 114, 126.]

for by that all-powerful sign the savage plague had been quelled. He also adds that, moved by this miracle, a crowd of pagans enrolled itself in the Christian army.

Thus in his eclogue our poet introduces Aegon, one of the idolatrous shepherds, speaking:

[Note: [Col. 0798B] The same, same place, verse 121.]

> **Tityrus, I delay no longer,**
>
> **But will serve the true religions.**
>
> **Gladly I shall flee my ancient error,**
>
> **For it is deceptive and empty.**
>
> **And now my mind hastens to visit**
>
> **The temples of the supreme God …**

Accordingly, after removing the foolish title that had prevailed until now, we have entitled the poem *On the Power of the Sign of the Lord’s Cross*.

Furthermore, from the time when it was first published by Pithoeus, as we said above, namely in 1586, we know that it was incorporated into the libraries of the ancient Fathers. It was published separately at Frankfurt in 1612 through the care and scholarship of Johann Weitz and Wolfgang Seber; the same edition then appeared again at Leiden in 1715 with a new preface. Finally, Gerhard Outhovius reprinted it at Groningen in 1725 at the end of his book *On the Judgments of Jehovah*, as we learn from Fabricius.

[Note: [Col. 0798B] Fabricius, *Latin Bibliography*, volume III, page 278.]

[Col. 0797]

# VALERIA FALTONIA PROBA, POETESS OF THE CENTO

(From *A Collection of All the Poets*, printed at Pesaro in 1766.)

[Col. 0801]

# PROLEGOMENA

## 1

Valeria Faltonia Proba, wife of Adelphius, the proconsul—whom Thomas de Simeonibus, a distinguished man, carefully distinguishes from Anicia Faltonia Proba, the mother of three consuls—

[Note: [Col. 0801B] Compare the Paris *Ephemerides* for 1694, page 249 ff., and Pagius and Samuel Basnage under the year 395.]

composed around the year 400 a cento from Virgil concerning the creation of the world and the Gospels, expressed with the greatest completeness.

The very learned Justus Fontanini teaches that the poetess of Virgilian centos should be called Faltonia Proba, a citizen of Horta, not Falconia; that she has nothing in common either with Anicia Faltonia Proba—concerning whom Baltellus wrote—

[Note: [Col. 0801B] *Memoirs of Trévoux*, 1608, page 876; in the dissertation on the marble sarcophagus of Probus Anicius and Proba Faltonia in the Roman Vatican church, 1705, octavo.]

or with Valeria Proba, the wife of Adelphius the proconsul.

[Note: [Col. 0801B] *Acts of the Learned*, 1709, page 6; *Memoirs of Trévoux*, 1708, page 1904; *Journal of the Italian Men of Letters*, volume XXIV, page 140 ff.]

Fontanini argues against the equally eminent Thomas de Simeonibus, who maintains that Valeria Faltonia Proba, the wife of Adelphius, composed those centos.

[Col. 0801B]

[Note: [Col. 0801C] Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 5: “Proba, wife of Adelphius the proconsul, a woman placed alone among ecclesiastical men because she was occupied with the praise of Christ, composed a cento about Christ fitted together from Virgilian verses. We do not marvel at her diligence, but we praise her talent. Nevertheless, this little work is read inserted among the apocryphal Scriptures.” Gelasius, distinction 15, chapter 3: “A cento about Christ, joined together from Virgilian verses, is apocryphal.” Add also what is read at the end of a tenth-century manuscript codex of the *Cento*, preserved in the library of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone, not far from Modena, as Bernard de Montfaucon reports in his *Italian Diary*, page 36: “Proba, wife of Adelphius, mother of Olibrius and Alypius, after she had written the war of Constantius—or Constantine—against Magnentius, also wrote this book.”]

These works were written after the year 393, when Honorius was already Augustus and emperor. They were published after the Venetian edition of 1472, in folio,

[Note: [Col. 0802C] The title of that first edition is reported by the distinguished Michael Maittaire in his *Annals of Typography*, page 98: “The Epigram Books of Ausonius, the most eloquent poet; an excerpt from the Cento of Proba, the most illustrious woman, from the poems of Maro, as a testimony to the Old and New Testament; Ovid’s *Consolation to Livia*; Calpurnius’s *Bucolic Poem*; the hymns and other poems of Publius Gregory of Tifernum, Venice, 1472, in folio.”]

and the Roman edition of 1481, in quarto, found in the Barberini Library, by Aldus together with Sulpicius Severus, the Homeric centos, Juvencus, and others, Venice, 1501, in quarto. This edition differs greatly from another, also in quarto, apparently published about the same time without place or year.

It was also published in Paris in 1509, in quarto, by Jean Petit; at Lyon in 1516, with Mantuanus and others; at Oppenheim in 1517; at Frankfurt in 1541, in octavo, under the care of Peter Brubach, together with the Homeric centos and Nonnus.

[Col. 0802A]

Then in Paris by François Estienne in 1543, in octavo; by Henri Estienne in 1578, in duodecimo; and, edited by Julius Roscius, at Rome in 1588, in duodecimo. It was also published together with other Virgilian centos reviewed by Heinrich Meibomius at Helmstedt in 1597, in quarto. I omit other editions, such as the Cologne edition of 1601, in octavo, and those occurring in the libraries of the Fathers.

But above all, the effort of Johann Heinrich Kromayer deserves praise. He published these centos with notes and an index at Halle in 1719, in octavo, marking for each verse the passages of Virgil from which the centos are composed. The distinguished Johann Gottlieb Krause recently announced in the literary journals published in German at Leipzig that a new edition was to be expected from him.

[Note: [Col. 0802B] *German Literary Journal*, Leipzig, 1710, page 1010, and again *New Literary Journal*, 1719, page 33.]

Richard Le Blanc translated Proba’s centos into French, together with Tancred by Filippo Beroaldo, in Paris in 1553, through Robert Messalinus, as Crucimannus reports.

[Note: [Col. 0802B] Page 440 of the *French Library*.]

Likewise, a certain Pomponius, from the same poet, composed among the other leisure works of his style a *Tityrus*—a bucolic poem—in honor of Christ, as Isidore reports.

[Note: [Col. 0802B] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book I, chapter 38.]

Pomponius’s poem did not survive to the present age, but Proba’s centos, dedicated to the emperor Honorius, have often seen the light. They were first published by Aldus in 1501, in quarto.

[Col. 0803]

# THE VIRGILIAN CENTOS OF VALERIA FALTONIA PROBA, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN, AS A TESTIMONY TO THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS

(C, S)

[Col. 0803A]

## Preface

> Long ago, I confess, I wrote of leaders who violated
>
> The sacred treaties of peace,
>
> Whom the dreadful desire to rule held in misery;
>
> Of diverse deaths, the cruel wars of kings,
>
> And kindred battle-lines stained with the blood of parents;
>
> Of famous shields and trophies taken from many an enemy;
>
> Of triumphs that fame had carried, sprinkled with blood;
>
> Of cities so often bereaved of countless citizens.
>
> It is enough to remember those evils.

## Invocation of God

> Now, almighty God, receive, I pray, this sacred poem,
>
> And unloose the speech of your sevenfold Spirit,
>
> And open the innermost chambers of my heart,
>
> So that I may recount all the secrets faithfully, as a prophet.
>
> [Col. 0803B] I have no concern now with seeking the nectar of Ambrosia,
>
> Nor do I wish to summon the Muses from the heights of Aonia.
>
> Let no empty terror persuade me that rocks can speak,
>
> That I should follow the laurel-crowned tripods and empty prophecies,
>
> The quarreling goddesses and defeated household gods.
>
> For there is no labor in extending fame through words
>
> And searching out a small measure of praise among human efforts.

## Statement of What Is to Be Treated

> But, drenched in the Castalian spring and imitating the blessed,
>
> I have drunk, thirsting, draughts of holy peace.
>
> From this I shall begin to sing: present God, raise up my mind.
>
> I shall say that Virgil sang the holy gifts of Christ.
>
> Returning to the beginning, I shall unfold a matter obscure to no one,
>
> If faith exists in the mind, if the Spirit poured through the limbs
>
> Moves the mass and mingles itself through the whole body,
>
> [Col. 0803C] And so far as harmful bodies do not weigh it down,
>
> Nor earthly limbs and dying members dull it.

# PART ONE: ON THE OLD TESTAMENT

## Prayer to God

> O Father, eternal power of human beings and of things,
>
> Grant an easy course, and flow into our minds.
>
> And you, be present, and run through the labor begun with us,
>
> Son of the highest Father, power and heavenly origin,
>
> Whom we worship first and whose deserved honors we renew,
>
> The new generation, every age, has acknowledged.
>
> I sing true gifts; it is enough to have seemed capable.
>
> Long ago, I remember, the monuments of ancient men
>
> Tell everywhere of Moses before all others:
>
> What things are, what they have been, and what things to come are being drawn forth,
>
> [Col. 0803D] All, as the tender sphere of the world was formed.
>
> Happy is the one who has been able to know the causes of things,
>
> [Col. 0804A] Whence comes the race of human beings and cattle, and of winged creatures,
>
> And what monsters the sea bears beneath its marble surface,
>
> And whether fire or mobile moisture contains anything of the kind.
>
> Nor otherwise, at the first beginning of the growing world,
>
> Would I believe that days shone forth or possessed another order.
>
> A greater arrangement of things rises before me,
>
> If antiquity can lend faith to so great a work.
>
> For (I shall confess it) spectacles of trivial things …

I was always singing of horses, arms, and the battles of men,

and in vain wished to practise my work with zeal;

yet, attempting everything, this purpose seemed best to me:

to disclose matters plunged deep in earth and darkness.

And day by day a great enterprise has long been stirring my mind;

it is not content with tranquil rest.

All, be favorable; turn your joyful minds this way—

matrons and men, boys and unmarried girls.

[Col. 0804B]

## On the Creation of the World

In the beginning the Father himself established heaven, earth, and the liquid plains,

and the shining sphere of the moon and the sun’s labors:

you, most brilliant lights of the world, who lead the passing year across heaven.

For there were not yet the fires of the stars, nor the luminous ether;

but black night, borne upon its chariot, held the pole,

and chaos stretched downward into the shadows,

as far as the lofty Olympus of heaven rises toward the ether.

## On the Division of Light from Darkness

Then the almighty Father, whose is supreme power over all things,

removed the dark air and scattered the shadows,

and now divided the sphere between light and darkness.

[Col. 0804C]

He marked all the stars as they glided through the silent heaven,

turning his attentive eyes to see from which quarter they would bring the southern heats,

which side they would turn away from the pole,

and in what direction the oblique order of the constellations would turn itself.

## On the Four Seasons of the Year

After the Almighty saw all things standing beneath a serene sky,

he assigned numbers and names to the stars,

and made the year equal in its four diverse seasons,

with heats, rains, and winds that bring the cold.

And he made these things so that we might learn them by fixed signs.

In spring the earths swell and demand their generative seeds;

in midsummer the threshing floor treads the roasted grain;

autumn produces varied fruits;

and black winter comes, while the Sicyonian berry is crushed in the presses,

and the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.

[Col. 0804D]

From that time onward the ether, made fertile by abundant rains,

nourishes great fruits, mingled with the great body of the world.

[Col. 0805A]

## The First Day

And now dawn was scattering its first light over the new earth,

and driving away the stars, was bringing on the day.

Then the earth began to endure and Nereus to open his seas,

and little by little the things of nature began to assume their forms.

The varied shapes of the sea—the enormous whales—

were sweeping the waters with their tails and cutting through the waves,

and the creatures of the vast ocean were circling its waters.

Now that the sun had poured forth its light,

now that its light had revealed all things,

it exulted and at the same time scattered the bitter dew.

## The Second Day

And now the following day was rising with the first dawn.

The earth poured forth flowers and unfolded all its leaves;

the uncultivated bird-gardens reddened with bloody berries,

subject neither to human rakes nor to anyone’s care.

[Col. 0805B]

## The Third Day

The third light had removed the cold shadow from heaven.

Then the trackless thickets resounded with singing birds,

and the ravens uttered liquid voices through their compressed throats;

nor did the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm.

## The Fourth Day

On the fourth day the earth brought forth from the forests

monsters of many kinds and every sort of cattle,

wandering through the grass without any keeper.

Then—wondrous to see!—the lion first began to brandish his weapons,

then the most savage tiger,

the scaly dragon,

and the lioness with her tawny neck

began to rage, and the great wolves howled.

The remaining herds grazed upon the green grass,

and neither clear springs nor pasture was lacking for the flocks.

[Col. 0805C]

## The Fifth and Sixth Days

Now one day and another had passed,

and the Father, surveying this entire work of divine mind and craftsmanship,

with all things arranged in order,

could not satisfy his mind, but burned with the desire to behold

the lands, the stretches of sea, the deep heaven,

and the race of birds and cattle.

He pondered within himself who would hold the sea and the lands under complete dominion,

and that they should not lie idle upon the earth;

he delighted in lingering over them.

## On the Formation of the First Human Being

While he was pondering such things, a thought suddenly settled upon him.

He drew forth blessed clay and shaped it by pressing it,

immediately making rich soil from the first months of the year.

[Col. 0805D]

And now, unexpectedly, so great an image of divine benevolence came forth:

a new and most beautiful form of man among created things,

with face and shoulders resembling God.

A greater God moves his mind and sends him on to greater works.

## On the Formation of Eve

Then another is sought, yet no one from so great a company

dares approach the man and be called his companion in the kingdom.

Without delay he grants the young man peaceful rest through his limbs

and inclines his eyes into sweet sleep.

And there, in the midst of the darkness of night,

the almighty Father lays bare his ribs and entrails.

From these he took one rib from the young man,

after opening the joints of his side;

and suddenly a wondrous gift arose.

A magnificent sign shone forth with bright light:

[Col. 0806A]
