a distinguished face, and upon a beautiful breast a virgin,

now mature for a husband, now marriageable in the fullness of her years.

A great fear broke his sleep;

he called the bones and limbs “marriage,”

and, stunned by the divine power, pressed her close,

received her in his hand, and clung to her, embracing her right hand.

## That God Blessed the First-Formed Man and Eve

When these things had at last been accomplished,

he who turns the stars of the world gave his command.

At his word the sea pressed down its tranquil waters,

the earth trembled beneath the ground, and lofty heaven fell silent.

“Live happily, amid the cultivated green places

and the blessed dwellings of fortunate groves.

This is your home, this your fatherland;

here is the sure rest from your labors.

For these things I set neither limits nor times.

I have given you dominion without end;

for many years the earth shall suffer neither the rake nor the vine the pruning hook.

[Col. 0806B]

Yet your immortal race shall remain,

and slow old age shall neither weaken the powers of your mind

nor alter its vigor.”

## What Was Forbidden to the First Parents

“But turn your minds to what I shall say.

In the midst, stretching forth its ancient branches,

there stands before your eyes a tree with blessed boughs.

It is not lawful for anyone to disturb it with fire or to fell it with iron;

sacred reverence has never permitted it to be moved.

Whoever plucks sacred fruit from this tree

shall pay the deserved penalty of death.

My sentence does not change.

Let no prudent adviser persuade you

that it is permissible to stain your hands;

let no woman’s voice move you,

nor let violence from anyone overcome you,

if the glory of divine authority awaits you as your due.”

[Col. 0806C]

## The Delights of Paradise

After the Father, to whom the stars of heaven are obedient,

had arranged all things and given his laws,

he displayed from above the shining fields,

the glory of such great works.

Behold, beneath the threshold of the first sun and dawn,

they came to places where soft marjoram

embraced them with flowers and breathed around them its sweet shade.

Here were purple spring and summer in months not its own;

here were clear springs;

here, at the appointed season of heaven,

the sweet honeycombs pressed out their honey.

Here the white poplar overhung a cavern,

and the pliant vines wove their leafy shelters.

The gardens invited bleating sheep among saffron-colored flowers,

within a fragrant grove of laurel,

and the earth itself freely produced everything,

without anyone demanding it.

Fortunate pair—if the perverse mind

of the accursed wife had not been so misguided.

The great aftermath revealed this.

[Col. 0806D]

## The Temptation through the Serpent

And now the accursed day had come through the flower-filled fields.

Behold, the savage enemy, a serpent,

turned seven enormous coils and seven winding spirals.

He was not easy for anyone to look upon,

nor approachable in speech.

With slanting envy he hung from a leafy branch,

breathing forth a viper’s spirit,

whose heart held grievous wars,

wrath, envy, and harmful crimes.

The father himself he hates;

he twists himself into so many faces,

bristles with erect scales,

and, so that no crime or deception might remain unattempted,

he first approached in this manner,

offering himself willingly in speech:

“Tell me,” he said, “virgin—for we inhabit the shaded groves of light,

[Col. 0807A]

we dwell among the couches of the banks

and the fresh meadows watered by streams—

what such great cowardice has entered your hearts?

The fruits lie scattered everywhere beneath their respective trees;

the clear springs are cups, gifts of heaven.

To touch them is forbidden—that alone was lacking from the arrangement.

Who prevents you from testing the hidden causes thoroughly?

Empty superstition! One part of the world has been taken away from you.

If you do not consider my words vain,

I shall be your guide in daring to loosen the sacred laws.

You, my wife, are free to test your courage through prayer.

I shall be your leader, if your will toward me is firm;

we shall build couches and feast upon rich banquets.”

## Eve, Deceived, Deceives the Man

So he spoke; and quicker than his words,

their eyes were directed to the venerable tree whose fruit was held by the law.

They began to prepare a feast,

and polluted everything by their touch.

She especially persisted,

devoted to the destruction that was to come;

she marveled at the unfamiliar leaves and at fruit not her own.

She touched the cause of so great an evil only with the tip of her mouth,

undertaking a greater crime and beginning a greater frenzy.

Alas, the wretched wife placed before him

a shoot from another tree,

and moved his mind with sudden sweetness.

## They See Themselves Naked and Make Aprons for Themselves

Immediately a new light flashed upon their eyes.

But they were terrified by the sudden sight,

and, lingering no longer,

they shaded their bodies beneath the branches with leaves,

making a woven covering;

yet no hope of help was available.

But the Sower of men and gods,

watching with eyes that miss nothing,

had foreseen these things:

the slaughter and the deeds of the tyrant,

and, enraged, knew what the woman could do.

[Col. 0807C]

Immediately he attacked:

“Far away, far away, profane ones!” he cried,

he who strengthens heaven and earth by his divine power.

## Adam Hides Himself

When they saw him advancing from afar and roaring terribly,

they turned in fear and fled backward.

They scattered into the forests,

and secretly sought whatever hollow rocks they could find.

They regretted their undertaking,

did not look again upon the light or the breezes,

and were weary of gazing upon the vault of heaven.

## The Lord Rebukes Adam

Nor was much time in between,

when the frequent sound of approaching footsteps came to their ears.

Then the Father addressed them through the shadows

with these words, and openly rebuked them:

“Wretched man, what such great madness has seized your mind?

What new frenzy is this?

Where are you going now—where are you making for?” he said.

[Col. 0807D]

“Forgetful of your kingdoms, what madness has changed your mind?

Tell me: what such dreadful longing for the light has come upon you, miserable ones?

Hasten your flight and withdraw from the entire grove.

Nor is it permitted you to turn back your steps,

if ever adversity should call you.

A river rushes through the middle,

surrounded by blazing flames;

hissing, it twists the ringing rocks.

It raises globes of flame and licks the stars.”

## Adam Excuses Himself

At this he replied:

“Your image, Father—your mournful image—

has placed me in these regions;

I deserved it, nor do I plead against it,” he said.

“Almighty One, I tremble at the sound of your footsteps

and at your voice,

conscious of my daring deed and of the sinister warning.

The woman bears bitter juices and a sluggish savor.

[Col. 0808A]

She carried deceit and dreadful crime within her breast.

With an unspeakable accusation,

while she raged, the girl doomed to die destroyed the innocent man

by a cruel death.

For she persuaded me—you know it yourself;

no one can deceive you.

As soon as I saw it, I perished;

evil error carried me away,

and we touched with our hands what no tree produces for itself.”

## The Curse of the Serpent

Then the almighty Father spoke from his lofty throne:

“Receive, then, and fix these words of mine in your minds.

And you, first among them, more monstrous in crime than all the others,

whom neither long time nor any compassion softens,

serpent, instigator of crimes,

you shall feed upon evil grasses in idleness,

dragging your broad belly ingloriously.

Withdraw from these places,

with no human being compelling you,

to where there is thin clay

and stony ground amid thickets.”

[Col. 0808B]

## The Curse of Adam

“But for your crime”—he cried—“for such daring deeds,

your whole life shall be worn away by iron.

First, by your skill”—alas, pitiable man!—

you shall work the earth with rakes

and frighten the birds with their noise.

The thistle shall bristle in the fields,

and the prickly paliurus shall rise with sharp spines,

along with burrs, thorns,

and the deceptive herb of poison.

But if you work the soil for a wheat harvest

and sturdy emmer,

you shall wait in vain for a heap of grain,

and, shaken by hunger,

you shall console yourself in the forests with an oak.

Moreover, diseases, grievous old age,

labor, and the pitiless violence of dreadful death

shall come upon you.”

## The Curse of Eve

[Col. 0808C]

“These things shall always be yours as well.

And you, most savage wife,

not unaware of evil,

head and cause of these misfortunes,

a great calamity has been committed by you.

Alas, ruined woman, you do not know,

nor do you see the dangers that will surround you afterward.

Now die, as you deserve,

for this is what you sought with your whole mind.

My sentence, though changed in place, does not yield.”

## Adam and Eve Are Driven from Paradise

Then savage terror surrounded the first young man.

His eyes stiffened;

they could no longer hide themselves in the darkness

or hear and answer familiar voices.

Without delay they hurried away,

and, ordered onward, were driven with rapid steps.

Together they traversed the shadowed paths,

covered the intervening distance,

and left the threshold behind,

weeping and planting their footsteps with equal grief.

Then branches gave them berries for food in the forests,

and stony cornel cherries;

the herbs fed them with roots torn from the ground.

[Col. 0808D]

## Eve Gives Birth to Two Sons

Meanwhile the great sun completed its revolving year.

Ten long months of distress had passed for the mother.

From her came human beings, a hard race.

Then by their skill neither grasses appear in the field nor leaves upon the trees;

yet the grasses dare safely to entrust themselves to the new suns,

and they began to set grapes upon pliant branches

and teach them to grow into moist juice.

## Abel Is Killed by His Brother

Then the twin brothers were burning altars with torches.

Each envied the honor bestowed upon the other.

I shudder to tell it:

one attacked his unwary kinsman,

so close by blood,

and cut him down at their ancestral altars,

polluting with blood the fires he himself had consecrated.

[Col. 0809A]

## After Abel Was Killed, God Became Angry with the Human Race

Then the Father added venom to the black serpents,

shook the honey from the leaves,

withdrew fire,

ordered wolves to prey,

and commanded the sea to move.

He also held back the wines running everywhere through the streams.

Soon labor was added to the grain,

so that rust might consume the stalks

and the sick harvest deny them food.

Then men learned to catch wild beasts in snares

and to deceive them with birdlime.

Want, pressing upon them in harsh circumstances,

stirred the fields and sharpened mortal hearts with cares.

Until gradually the deteriorating, fading age grew worse,

and an iron race raised its hard head over the fields.

The madness of war and the desire for possession followed.

[Col. 0809B]

Justice, departing, left its footprints upon the earth.

Nor was much time in between:

fury and anger drove their minds headlong,

and they rejoiced, drenched in the blood of their brothers.

One man buried his wealth and lay upon his hidden gold,

nor did he pity the needy in compassion

or extend his right hand.

## The Flood

Then the almighty Father, deeply moved to anger from above,

sent himself down from the ether,

poured the earth into waves,

mingling it with the Flood,

and dissolved heaven into Tartarus.

He struck down the fields,

struck down the joyful crops,

and washed away the labor of the oxen.

The ditches were filled,

the hollow rivers rose,

and he gave the entire race of cattle

and the entire race of wild beasts over to death.

## Noah Is Spared

Then, wondrous to say,

he rescued from death the man who was weighty with piety and merit,

who had been most faithful to justice upon the earth,

amid waters rising so high,

so that he might preserve a source

from which to restore a new race.

[Col. 0809C]

## After the Flood, God Gives Laws to Human Beings; the Jews Are Driven by War

After that Flood, the Almighty gave laws

to the fathers whom he called,

and governed the age by great statutes.

Why should I recall the unspeakable slaughters?

Why the deeds of tyrants?

Why hearts that knew not how to be softened by human prayers?

Egypt, the powers of the East,

and the final wars;

the great-hearted leaders

and all the peoples in their order;

how tribe and nation sought the desert,

and the great nation, never forgetful of a man of such great merit.

And the priests who stood beside the altars;

and the pious prophets who fell for freedom.

[Col. 0809D]

The kings roused to war;

the battle lines that filled the shore of the Red Sea;

the weapons with which the king,

while great fury inflamed him,

burned against that noble race,

driving forward a troop of horsemen

and companies flourishing with bronze.

The remaining deeds of the fathers

and the wars fought in their order

I pass over,

and leave them to be remembered by others after me.

# PART TWO. ON THE NEW TESTAMENT

## Invocation to God

Now I return to you and to your purposes,

great Father.

I undertake a greater work:

I approach the predictions of the earlier prophets.

Although the narrow limit of my life will contain it,

the path must be attempted,

by which I too may raise myself from the earth

and carry my name through so many years of fame.

For your offspring descended from high heaven,

and at last the age brought us,

who had long desired it,

the help and coming of God.

When a woman, bearing the face and appearance of a virgin—

wondrous to say!—

gave birth to a child

who was neither of our race nor of our blood.

But because the prophets had sung with terrifying omen

that a man would come,

proud among peoples and lands,

born from an ethereal seed,

who would seize the world by his powers,

whose rule would extend over the Ocean

and whose fame would reach the stars—

[Col. 0810A]

## On the Birth of Jesus Christ

And now the promised day had come,

the time when the source of the divine race

first raised its sacred head.

Sent beneath authority, the power came in bodily form,

and the image of the beloved Father entered into the world,

mingled with God.

[Col. 0810B]

## On the Star and the Magi

Without delay, in the clear region of heaven,

a star, leading a torch,

shone forth with great light.

The nobles recognized God,

and all at once heaped him with gifts

and worshiped the holy star.

Then their manifest faith,

and the renowned name of the Father’s power,

burned to recognize the face of Christ

and the signs that his divine splendor would give.

## Herod Fears Christ after His Birth

At once the report flew to the king,

who raged with a great cry.

Rumor sharpened his great anger,

inflamed his mind,

and reached the ears of the mother.

She, not ignorant of events,

foresaw the deceit and dreadful crime,

and was the first to receive the motions that were to come.

Foreseeing the future,

she secretly ordered the child to be raised,

while anxious cares remained uncertain

and her mind seethed with anger.

## Herod Orders the Infants to Be Killed

But the troubled king ordered the entire future stock and race

to be struck down

and burned in the fires beneath them.

He made many preparations

and sent men to bring back reliable reports.

They did just as they had been ordered,

and were carried along with rapid steps,

filling the city with great terrors.

Immediately voices were heard,

and immense wailing.

The bodies of the infants,

their souls crying before their parents,

were thrown down upon the very threshold.

## The Virgin Flees with Her Son into Egypt

But the mother, terrified—not without cause—

by such great lamentation,

carrying the infant before her in her own hands amid the tumult,

fled and made her way to the full mangers.

There, beneath the roof of a cramped shelter,

she nourished the newborn,

giving her breast to his tender lips.

“These first cradles, child, shall pour flowers for you;

the earth, mingled everywhere with fragrant baccar,

shall gradually produce colocasia together with soft acanthus.””

## Christ Disputes in the Temple among the Elders

And now the end had come,

when the cycle of time was complete,

as soon as the fury subsided

and the raging faces grew calm.

He bore a heavenly origin within him

before the appointed years.

## Everyone Marvels at Christ

He passes through the cities

and among the neighboring peoples.

[Col. 0811A]

The whole youth, pouring out from houses and fields,

gazes upon him as he walks,

with astonished minds hanging upon the sight.

The crowd of mothers marvels:

what spirit is in him,

what face,

what sound of voice,

or what manner of step has he as he walks?

## John’s Testimony concerning Christ

Immediately the prophet—for he was the most reliable witness—

when from afar he saw him beside the secluded, cold river,

said:

“The time has come.

Behold God, behold God,

to whom belongs the greatest authority over things and words.

You shall not be another like him,

fortunate child, to whom the stars of heaven are obedient.

Thus indeed I had conceived in my mind

and believed that it would be.

You come, long awaited one,

the hope and consolation of our people.”

## Christ Is Baptized by John, and the Holy Spirit Descends from Heaven

[Col. 0811B]

When he had spoken these words,

he received the one who came to be plunged into the healing river

and raised him from the gentle waters.

The shallows exulted,

and suddenly a stirred dove flew down

and stood above his head.

Then it suddenly cleft the liquid path,

without moving its swift wings.

## Many Are Baptized with Christ

The entire crowd poured toward the banks,

vying to pour abundant waters over their shoulders.

## A Voice Is Heard from Heaven: “This Is He,” etc.

Then the Father addressed his son with affectionate words:

“My son, my strength,

my great power alone,

my very sweet glory,

who shall return greatly to your father,

from you is the beginning,

in you it ends.

Receive this, my offspring, I bear witness:

wherever the returning sun looks upon both oceans,

you shall see all things turned and ruled beneath your feet,

rejoicing in perfect honor.

You shall rule peoples by your authority,

mothers and men alike.

Long ago, having pitied their inactive spirits,

their hearts unaccustomed to action,

and their helpless ignorance of the way, undertake them with me,

and now accustom them to be called by prayers.””

He had spoken.

The other was preparing to obey the commands of his great father,

intent upon the work and upon the kingdoms to come.

Alas, piety! Alas, ancient faith!

What thanks shall I begin to speak,

if it is permitted to compare small things with great?

For I had no longer any hope of seeing my ancient homeland,

nor hope of freedom,

nor concern for safety.

[Col. 0811C]

## Everything Rejoices at the Lord’s Coming

He was the first to answer me when I asked,

removed the congealed stain,

and left me with a pure ethereal mind,

restoring me to my own kingdoms.

For him, even if I were an exile

and had to travel through flames or across the Syrtes,

through various misfortunes

and a thousand successive weapons,

whatever fate might bring,

I would perform one thing in return for so great a gift,

and build altars with gifts of my own.

At his coming,

the unshorn mountains themselves

cast voices of such great praise toward the stars in joy.

All the valleys respond.

## Christ Is Tempted

At no other time is it necessary

to recall the frenzied evil of the great serpent

and its memorable name.

It even dared—it is said,

though the story has grown dim with the years—

to address the man

and demand the reasons for his coming.

When he saw him advancing toward him across the meadows,

[Col. 0812A]

he stopped and fiercely roared.

Wounded and serpent-like,

he addressed the powerful one in haughty speech:

“Are you truly what you appear to be?

Do you bring me a true message?

What is your race?

From what household do you come?

Why do you approach our threshold?

Speak now—tell me why you come,

for your words declare that you intend to impose laws.

Or which of the young men,

most confident of yourself,

ordered you to enter our houses

and impose a custom of peace?

I do not envy you;

I marvel rather.

Listen further to what I doubt,

and to the thought that now arises in my mind.

There is another house.

Call upon the west winds

and glide on wings,

seeking the lofty roofs,

daring to entrust yourself to heaven,

if indeed the father you mention

is he to whom the stars are obedient.”

## Christ Addresses the Devil

Smiling at him, with tranquil heart, he said—

not ignorant of the prophets

or unaware of the age to come:

“Did you hope, treacherous serpent,

to dissemble even this?

Do not doubt it,

for you see the truth.

Desire, on wings, to follow the lofty stars,

and to hide yourself in the hollow earth.

Where are you rushing, doomed creature?

Do you dare greater things than your strength permits?

Yield to God,

thrown upon the earth with your whole body.”

## The Devil Flees at the Sound of Christ’s Voice

No more was said.

The other, marveling at the venerable gift,

pressed his forehead to the earth

and drove bloody foam from his mouth.

Content with flight,

he hid himself in the blind shadows.

## The Lord Chooses Disciples, and the People Immediately Follow

Meanwhile the report flew through the great cities.

Men gathered,

all sharing one desire:

to follow wherever he wished

to lead them across the sea to the lands.

[Col. 0812C]

Many others as well,

whom obscure fame keeps hidden,

came running with dense tumult,

crowding together in great numbers.

They exulted in spirit.

For the very large crowd surrounded him,

and received him high upon their shoulders.

When he saw them gathered together,

daring to enter battle,

he began,

and inspired them with divine love through his words:

“Learn justice, having been warned,

and come to the aid of the exhausted.

Each of you, men, gladly give according to your means,

and call upon the common God.

Let us follow better things.

Wherever he calls,

let us turn our course.

The first path of salvation is undefiled faith

and a mind conscious of what is right.

Rest is prepared for you

when the appointed age is complete.

For those who alone have lain upon the wealth they discovered,

and while life remained

set aside no share for their own people,

or when a father was beaten,

and fraud was entwined with a client—

[Col. 0812D]

when cold death has separated the soul from their limbs,

they await punishment shut inside.

This is the greatest multitude.

They are driven into the infernal darkness

and pay the penalties of their former evils.

For some, beneath the vast whirlpool,

the defilement of sin is washed away;

for others, it is burned in fire.

Here the turbid whirlpool seethes with mud

and a vast chasm,

and belches forth all the sand of Cocytus.

From here groans are heard,

and savage blows resound;

then the ringing of iron

and chains dragged perpetually,

while the darkness grows denser beneath the covering night.”

## It Is Commanded That Idols Not Be Worshiped

“Moreover, attend with your minds to what I shall say.

From now on I shall not have you worship,

according to ancestral custom,

with slaughtered young cattle,

with images born from trunks and oak,

or with figures fashioned by mortal hands;

nor shall I have you listen to the temples of the gods.

I shall repeat my warning again and again:

it is enough to have perished once.

It will be more useful to remember

the son and the father,

if he is worthy of belief.

But meanwhile time flees—

irretrievable time flees—

and the day of flames

and the hostile power approaches.”

[Col. 0813A]

## On the Coming Judgment

They remained fixed in astonishment.

Without lingering further,

he sang of another, greater judgment

for suffering, sickly mortals,

and announced the grievous wrath:

destruction would come,

and in a vast convulsion of ruin

all things would then be mingled together

in a flashing fire;

the stars would wander through the sky,

and heaven would collapse.

Then a new terror entered the breasts of all,

shaking them.

In silence they saw what was to come.

[Col. 0813B]

## A Certain Man Asked the Lord What He Should Do to Possess Eternal Life

While he was warning them with these dreadful words about the coming,

a boy, marking his face with the first signs of an unbearded youth,

rich in possessions,

flourishing in pursuits and undistinguished leisure,

came forward.

He had five flocks of bleating sheep,

and two herds,

loading his tables with rich banquets.

Immediately he stretched out both eager hands

and, embracing the Lord’s knees,

addressed him in friendly speech:

“O God,

the greatest part of our fame, deservedly yours,

I flee to you

and as a suppliant seek your divine power.

I have accomplished everything

and previously completed all things within my mind.

Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one.

What remains at last?

What further labor could I undertake

to overcome such great trials?

[Col. 0813C]

Receive my pledge and give yours;

it is lawful for me to undertake your commands.”

## The Lord Answers Him

The hero gave him this brief reply:

“O excellent young man in spirit,

cease your prayers.

Do not regret it:

nothing has been left for you, my friend.

I shall add this as well,

if your will toward me is firm.

Learn, boy, to despise wealth,

and shape yourself as worthy of God;

then you will be able to understand what virtue is.

Give your right hand to the wretched,

and do not abandon your brother, as a brother.

If someone hastens to join you in hospitality,

join yourself to the willing man.

Let a chaste household preserve chastity.

Come now:

break your sluggish delays,

and do not be harsh toward those poor in possessions.”

He had spoken.

The other turned his footsteps away at the words,

raising his pale face in an extraordinary manner.

He groaned deeply,

turned his eyes away,

and departed.

[Col. 0813D]

## Christ Mounts a Donkey

Then, urged on against the ribs of a sluggish donkey,

he mounted,

shining in a cloud.

All around him,

mothers, men, and boys

laid down familiar garments,

and gladly touched the rope with their hands.

Now he was approaching the gates,

and entered the temple,

lofty with a hundred columns of ancient cedar,

with a great crowd accompanying him in the middle.

## He Drives the Buyers and Sellers of Christ from the Temple with a Whip

This temple, dreadful amid the woods, was their council-house;

these were the sacred seats

that they worshiped with marvelous honor.

For while he surveyed each thing beneath the vast temple,

[Col. 0814A]

he suddenly shuddered at the sight.

The whip resounded,

and he gestured with his hand,

while at the same time he thundered in a great voice:

“What appearance of crimes,

and what gleaming bronze do I see?

And the name of Caesar?

What madness changes your minds?

These seats belong to us;

here, at the appointed time,

we are accustomed to sit at our fathers’ perpetual tables.”

They stood stunned in spirit,

and a cold tremor ran through their innermost bones.

In fear they abandoned their former tables.

## The Disciples Are in Danger at Sea

Then, when faith in the sea first arose,

the companions guided their ships over the calm depths,

with skill as their master.

One struck across the broad current with a sling,

aiming high;

another drew wet lines through the sea.

After the ships had reached the deep,

and no land appeared any longer,

the ether flashed with frequent fires.

[Col. 0814B]

Suddenly clouds snatched away both heaven and daylight.

The winds rose

and lifted the waves to the stars.

But a sudden cold fear stiffened the blood of the companions.

Their courage fell,

and all at once they gazed toward the harbor in tears.

One voice came from everyone,

uncertain between hope and fear,

whether they believed they would live

or suffer the final extremity,

with death only a little way off,

as sailors endure many such things upon the open sea.

## Christ Walks upon the Waters

Behold, God sensed the sea being stirred by a great roaring,

and the storm being released.

Supreme power is his,

equal to the light winds

and swifter than the river’s waves.

He sought the sea headlong

and ran across the open waters.

Nor was the ship far distant

as he led the way upon his course.

[Col. 0814C]

From far away the companions recognized their king

and, exposing their right hands,

greeted him with a great cry.

When he had touched the high waves

and reached the waters,

then, wondrous and terrible to see,

the waves subsided,

so that the struggle with the oar might cease.

He drove away the gathered clouds

and walked across the sea,

now halfway across,

while the waves had not yet wet his lofty sides.

As he walked through the very midst of the companions in the ship,

behold, the master helmsman himself came to the steering oar.

The mast trembled,

the boat groaned beneath its burden.

The sails fell,

and God settled upon the lofty stern.

At last, rejoicing,

they turned toward the familiar sands.

## On the Lord’s Supper

Meanwhile evening drew nearer

beneath the sloping Olympus of heaven.

Then they restored their strength with food,

lying scattered upon the grass;

they loaded the tables with dishes

and set out cups.

## He Teaches the Sacrament

After the first rest from the meal,

when the tables had been removed,

he himself first renewed the honors to the Father.

He looked up to heaven,

and then silence fell upon their tongues.

He gave grain into their hands

and sweet waters from the springs.

He filled a cup with unmixed wine,

taught the rites of the sacred observance,

mingled prayers with them,

and spoke these words:

## He Foretells That He Will Be Betrayed by One Man

“Listen, leaders,” he said,

“and learn your hopes.

No one from this number will depart

without having been given to me.

The Father’s promises—

your gifts, he says—

remain certain for you, boys,

and no one moves the palm from its appointed order.

[Col. 0815A]

But when the light of tomorrow first returns to the earth,

there will be only one man against me

and against my destruction,

while he offers himself from the midst of our body

for peace.

For the day is near, if I am not mistaken.

Set aside your cares.

That labor will be with me,

and my judgment does not deceive me.

One head will be given for many.”

Having spoken thus,

he fell silent

and gave deep rest to his limbs.

## The Apostles Flee

The companions scattered

and were covered by the dark night.

They turned many harsh matters over

within their sorrowful hearts.

What should they do?

The faces of the man they had seen

remained fixed within their breasts,

as did his words,

and anxious care gave their limbs no peaceful rest.

## Peter’s Complaint to His Fellow Disciples

Then the elder uttered these words from his heart,

pondering many things:

“Where is that God, our teacher, now?

Whom are we following?

Where do you command us to go?

Where are we to establish our dwelling?

O grief,

and glory, the splendor of such great things!

Now there is no delay:

carry us away with you into everything.

We beg you;

do not withdraw yourself from our sight.”

[Col. 0815B]

## The Priests and the People Against Christ

Meanwhile dawn rose

and left the Ocean behind.

Now the priests filled the places far and wide with complaints,

together with the people and the elders.

A murmur was carried through the ranks:

“What kind of people are these?

What barbarous custom does this homeland permit?

They demand punishments with blood,

gathered from every side,

and follow the innocent with a great cry.

The ignoble crowd rages in its hearts.”

## Christ Is Led Away at the Sixth Hour to Be Crucified

[Col. 0815C]

The fiery sun had climbed to the middle of heaven.

Then suddenly the whole people and the elders

demanded that he be summoned

and ordered him to speak:

from what blood was he born?

What did he seek?

What did he himself bring?

As they watched the man’s deeds as prey,

a mixture of grief and amazement

pressed upon the helpless crowd.

The human mind knows nothing!

They competed to mock their captive.

Then they rushed upon the captive from every side with weapons.

A cry rose to heaven,

and suddenly they seized the sacred figure.

With bloody hands they set up an enormous oak,

its branches cut away on every side,

and bound him to it with enormous thorns.

He stretched out his hands,

his feet joined to each other—

a mournful service!

The rest of the young men followed,

all daring an unspeakable crime

and accomplishing what they had dared.

[Col. 0815D]

But he, undaunted, said:

“Why do you bind these chains?

Has such confidence in your own race seized you?

Hereafter you shall pay for what has been committed,

with a punishment unlike this one.”

He continued to recall such things,

and remained fixed in place.

## An Earthquake Occurs, and the Sun Is Darkened

Meanwhile heaven began to be stirred

with a great roaring,

and black night took the color from all things.

The impious ages feared eternal night.

The earth trembled;

the wild beasts fled;

throughout the peoples humble terror prostrated mortal hearts.

Then suddenly the earth uttered a groan,

and all heaven thundered with a crash.

## Christ Descends to the Underworld

[Col. 0816A]

Immediately the thin shades, the dwellers of Erebus,

went forth from the deepest abodes.

The earth and the waters of the sea also gave signs.

The rivers stopped,

and the earths gaped open.

Even the houses themselves were stunned,

as were the innermost Tartarus of death

and the shadowy caverns;

they opened completely.

The sun too, as it rose—

all confess that they know this—

then covered its bright head

with dark, rusty discoloration.

## Christ Rises on the Third Day

Amid these disturbances,

amid such words,

the third light removed the cold shadow from heaven.

Now, retracing his steps,

he was coming toward the upper air,

when suddenly a tomb of enormous mass came before their eyes,

where the lifeless body had been laid,

but neither its bolts nor the guards themselves

could withstand it.

They saw the stones torn away,

the tightly joined sides of the tomb loosened.

A sound arose;

the earth was shaken by the immense weight.

[Col. 0816B]

Horror filled every heart,

and the very silence terrified them.

## Christ Appears to His Disciples behind Closed Doors

Behold, the first songs of birds beneath the high vault.

He entered,

leaving the cavern,

and went forth in triumph,

proud of his spoils.

The earth trembled,

roused by the striking of his feet.

Bearing those wounds,

he thrust himself through the narrow doors.

There he found, to his amazement,

that an immense number of new companions had gathered.

Suddenly he said to them:

“Here I am before you,

whom you seek.

Piety and living courage have conquered the difficult path.

Be alert, men, and flee from all fear.”

## He Instructs the Apostles

This is my return and the triumph you awaited.

This is my great pledge.

O three and four times blessed ones,

what rewards worthy of these praises

do I think can be paid to you?

What gifts can be prepared?

Receive them, then, into your hearts.

The same earth that first brought you forth

from the stock of your parents

shall receive you again

with its fruitful breast.

Call back your courage

and put away your sorrowful fear.

Now preserve yourselves for favorable circumstances.

[Col. 0816C]

## Christ Leaves Peace to the Apostles

For what remains,

rejoicing that all things have been properly accomplished,

wish peace with your hands;

praise peace as you sit,

great-hearted men.

Peace alone is the inviolable pledge.

And as he spoke these words,

he displayed his face and countenance,

his countenance and both hands,

and his breast ravaged by iron.

They joined hand to hand

and rejoiced as they gazed.

Nor is it enough to have seen once; it is pleasant to linger continually,

[Col. 0816D] to match one’s step, and to join right hand to right hand.

## On the Ascension of Christ

When these things had at last been accomplished, he parts the breathing air,

and, carried upward through the yielding atmosphere into the open heaven,

he leaves mortal eyes while still speaking among them.

He enters, surrounded by a cloud—wonderful to relate!

But the glory of the starry heaven receives him upon its throne

and holds his name throughout the eternal ages.

From that time the honor paid to him was celebrated, and succeeding generations

preserved the day, though so many years have now passed away.

Go, honor—go, our glory, glory of such great deeds;

your honor, your name, and your praises shall endure forever.

And do you, kindly one, aid both us and your sacred rites with favorable step,

[Col. 0817A] rites which it is impious to defer though they recur annually. Companions, celebrate this observance of the sacred rites with favor,

and do you yourself keep it, O beloved wife,

[Col. 0818A] and, if descendants deserve it through their devotion,

may they remain steadfast in this pure religious observance.

# APPENDIX TO THE CHRISTIAN POETS OF THE FOURTH CENTURY

[Col. 0817]

## ADMONITION

This appendix contains the works of Ausonius. Why, although he gave his name to Christ, we have separated him from the Christian poets who flourished in the same period will become sufficiently clear from reading his poems: most of them depart rather far from a Christian character, and some even from ordinary modesty; only a few introduce the name of the true God. Whatever seemed to us to suffer from some degree of obscenity, we have more readily passed over, since a chaste and at the same time learned reader could have derived from it nothing but nausea. As for our edition in general, we have taken care, as is customary, to make it as complete and finished in every respect as possible, comparing various editions with one another and borrowing assistance from each. We shall mention especially two of them: one published at Lyon in 1540, in octavo, by Seb. Gryphius; the other contained in the very rich collection printed at Pesaro in 1766, in quarto.

[Col. 0817]

# PROLEGOMENA TO AUSONIUS

## 1. The age and religion of Ausonius

[Col. 0817B]

Decimus Magnus Ausonius, of Bordeaux, a most learned grammarian and rhetorician, but a graceful and ingenious poet, was also devoted to the Christian rites, although he left only rare—certainly, nevertheless, genuine—traces of this in his writings. Promoted by the emperor Gratian, whom, no less than his brother Valentinian, he had instructed in literature, he advanced to the offices of quaestor and praetorian prefect, and in A.D. 379 to the consulship. He died during the reign of Honorius, after A.D. 392.

[Note: [Col. 0817B] Ausonius’s father was Julius Ausonius, of Bazas, a physician to the elder Valentinian. Marcellus Empiricus mentions his medical books. A saying of his is also reported: that blessed is not the man who has what he desires, but the man who does not desire what he does not have. Add Joseph Scaliger in his Life of Ausonius, and Vossius, in his book On Philosophy, p. 103. How good a man that father Ausonius was, his son shows in the Funeral Oration written for him, in which, among other things, he states that he died at the age of ninety. See the complete genealogy appended to the Parentalia, p. 143 of Jacob Tollius’s edition. There was another Ausonius, a sophist, mentioned by Suidas.]

[Note: [Col. 0817B] Olaus Borrichius, a man of great distinction, in his book On the Poets, p. 73, and the learned Cave, the author of the second part of Literary History, p. 100, as well as Christoph Hendreich in the Brandenburg Pandects, vol. I, p. 360, do not hesitate to declare Ausonius a pagan in religion. Indeed, the distinguished scholar Ludovico Antonio Muratori, vol. I of the Anecdota of the Ambrosian Library, p. 114, says that no one doubts that Ausonius was alien to the Christian religion. Borrichius added that for this reason also he was repeatedly rebuked by Pontius Paulinus. And on p. 74: “Paulinus, Ausonius’s pupil, whom he honored as a teacher, but whom, as one hostile to the Christian religion, he sometimes reproved.” Yet the learned man is unquestionably mistaken, together with Vossius, who says on p. 55 of On Latin Poets concerning Ausonius: “He was a pagan poet, as is clear from Paulinus.” Baillet also seems to regard him as a pagan in his Judgments on the Poets, as does Philippe Brietius in his Treatise on Latin Poets. This opinion is no less removed from the truth than the belief—which I see Trithemius had almost persuaded Gaddius to accept—that this same poet had also been a bishop of Bordeaux, vol. I of On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 57. That Ausonius was a Christian, however, without needing to turn to other arguments from his own writings, Paulinus clearly testifies when he writes to him in these words:

“In your love for us there is as great an accord

as there is in the united mind with which Christ is worshiped.”

Gyraldus is therefore more correct in his tenth dialogue On the Poets: “Ausonius certainly was a Christian, as we readily gather from his verses and also from those of his pupil Paulinus; but he was nevertheless too wanton and licentious”—Gyraldus has in mind both certain licentious epigrams, to be cleansed by fire according to the judgment of Caesar Scaliger, and the obscene nuptial cento composed by Ausonius at the request of the emperor Valentinian, who had described a wedding in a similar playful manner—“to be worthy of being numbered among Christians.” Joseph Scaliger likewise writes that Ausonius was sincerely a Christian, book II, chapter 32, of his Ausonian Readings. Add to these Theophilus Raynaudus in the Hoplotheca Against the Blow of Slander, vol. XII, p. 420, and Bayle’s dictionary, second edition. Paulinus, however, reproved Ausonius not as hostile to the Christian religion, but because Ausonius openly disapproved of Paulinus’s religious retirement. Perhaps Paulinus was also displeased to read in Ausonius’s poems certain passages written in a rather “pagan” fashion [ἐθνικώτερον], such as the following in chapter I, On the Professors of Bordeaux:

“And now, whether anything remains after the final fates,

you still live, remembering the age that has perished.

Or whether nothing remains, and long leisure possesses no sensation,

you have lived for yourself; we are gladdened by your fame.”]

Concerning Ausonius, one should consult the Life of Flavius Mallius Theodorus written by Albertus Paulus Rubenius and published by Graevius at Utrecht in 1699, in duodecimo. Joseph Scaliger notes that he had been governor of Africa in book II of his Ausonian Readings, chapter 17, where he also gives other information. Ausonius himself testifies that his consulship fell in the year 1118 from the foundation of the City, corresponding, according to the reckoning of Ausonius—which shifts the Varronian era by thirteen years—to A.D. 379, in epigram 3, p. 93 of Tollius’s edition:

“A thousand years, and twice nine years besides, have flowed

up to the laws bearing the name of the consul Ausonius.”

And in epigram 2:

“Add four to eleven hundred years,

and add eleven to a trieteric cycle;

this will be the sequence from the beginning of eternal Rome.”

[Note: [Col. 0819D] “Eleven and one,” that is, eleven; when four are added to these together with the trieteric cycle, they make eighteen.]

Ausonius arranged the lists of consuls down to A.U.C. 1122, A.D. 382. Hence, in epigram 4:

“Thus far I have set down the lists; if fortune permits, I shall

add more. If not, you who read shall add them.

Do you wish to know who I am? Seek the fourth title from the bottom;

you will read the name of the consul Ausonius.”

But those Ausonian lists of consuls have long since perished.

The distinguished Ez. Spanheim, vol. II of On the Use of Coins, p. 414, says that more judicious critics believe Ausonius to have been a pagan in religion, not a Christian. It is nevertheless more truthful to say that he was devoted to the Christian rites, as undeniable evidence shows, even if we suppose the Paschal Poem and the rophallic verses to belong to another author. I would not, however, agree with Trithemius, who affirms that Ausonius, the bishop of Bordeaux, attended the Council of Trier in A.D. 386, chapter 114 of On Ecclesiastical Writers. There was another Ausonius, a martyr of the eighth century and bishop of Engolisma in Aquitaine; concerning him, see the Acts of the Saints, vol. V, May 22, pp. 131 ff.

## 2. The writings of Ausonius

There exists, first, a Book of Epigrams, preceded by a letter of Theodosius in which he calls Ausonius his father and asks him to send his writings boldly to him, since he would find no less patronage and affection than learned poets and writers once found with Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] This letter seems suspicious without sufficient reason to Mariangelo Accursio and Caspar Barthius, Adversaria XII.12 and LVIII.3, who absurdly conjecture Ascensius to be its author.]

This letter is followed by three prefaces written in verse: one to the emperor Theodosius, another to Syagrius, and a third to Latinus Pacatus Drepanius, whom he calls his son—that is, his pupil.

Second, the *Ephemeris*, or “the business of the entire day,” in various kinds of verse.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] Anyone who reads this will have no doubt that its author was a Christian. See Tollius’s edition, pp. 96, 98 ff.]

Third, the *Parentalia*, in which he commemorates the deaths of his loved ones, as he himself calls them.

Fourth, the *Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux*.

Fifth, the *Epitaphs of the Heroes Who Took Part in the Trojan War*, to which William Canter and others added a garment, or collection, of Greek epigrams on the same heroes, attributed to Aristotle, but, as John Tzetzes notes in his commentary on Hesiod, not to the Stagirite. Ausonius added several other epitaphs, including those of Niobe, Dido, Diogenes the Cynic, and others.

Sixth, the *Monostichs on the Twelve Caesars*, written by Suetonius Tranquillus and dedicated to his son Hesperius, and *Tetrastichs on the Same Caesars*, from Julius Caesar to Elagabalus.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] He had written similar pieces on the remaining emperors down to Theodosius, but the rest of the tetrastichs have perished.]

These have often been published at the end of Suetonius. Ausonius’s tetrastichs on the Caesars also occur in Part I of the *Eulogies* of Joannes Papirius Masson, pp. 147 ff.

Seventh, the *Illustrious Cities*, or *Order of Noble Cities*, was published separately with Hippolytus a Collibus’s work On the Growth of Cities. It also appeared at Poitiers in 1565, together with the commentary of Elias Vinetus.

Eighth, the *Game*, or *Sayings of the Seven Wise Men*, addressed to Latinus Drepanius Pacatus, proconsul.

Ninth, twenty *Idylls*, the first of which is the *Paschal Poem*, addressed to Proculus, beginning:

“Holy solemnities of saving Christ return.”

[Note: [Col. 0819D] Perhaps “addressed to the proconsul,” just as Idyll 8 is a recitation of the consul Ausonius.]

It must not be confused with the spurious *Paschal Oration*, published under Ausonius’s name, in rophallic verses beginning on p. 326:

“Hope, God, establisher of eternal habitation.”

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Rophallic verses are so called because, like a club, their words rise gradually and increase in the number of their syllables, or because the individual words increase by one syllable at a time. Such is Homer’s passage in Iliad 3.182, concerning which see Gellius XIV.6. A *rhopalōtos* cup is mentioned by Dio in his account of Commodus, formed in the shape of a club. In place of “rophallic verses,” some read “euryphallic.” See Bernhard Moneta’s notes on the *Menagiana*, vol. IV, p. 180. Eustathius, in his commentary on Iliad 3.182, Basil edition, gives the following example of a rophallic verse from Homer:

“O blessed son of Atreus, born to your destiny, fortunate and blessed.”]

Most of the seventh idyll, *On Bissula*, and its more licentious portion, has perished. The tenth, or *Mosella*, is extremely elegant and was published separately at Heidelberg in 1619, in folio, with the commentaries of Marquard Freher. See also the learned Conrad Samuel Schurtzfleisch’s Historical-Political Dissertations, pp. 520 ff. The thirteenth is a Virgilian nuptial cento in the Fescennine manner. The piece *Cupid Crucified*, as I call it, occupies the place of the sixth idyll. It was republished with the notes of various scholars at The Hague in 1712, in octavo,

[Note: [Col. 0820D] *Journal des Savants*, 1713, p. 193.]

at the end of the *Vigil of Venus*. Martin Opitz rendered this idyll into German in the fifth book of his *Forests*. The notable passage in this sixth idyll on Cupid crucified, beginning at verse 16, “Semele’s thunderbolts,” and so forth, was elucidated by the distinguished scholars Oudinus and Ravionus de Varennes; *Journal des Savants*, 1718, pp. 197, 205; *Mémoires de Trévoux*, 1717, pp. 1181, 1189. Scaliger commented on the *Gryphus of the Ternary*, or eleventh idyll, in letter 199. Claudius Minos of Dijon also commented on it, as did Franciscus Sylvius Ambianus in 1516, and Franciscus Sanctius Brocensis together with Ovid’s *Ibis*, Salamanca 1506, in octavo. The fifteenth idyll, *On the Uncertainty of Life*, was printed separately with the commentary of Heinrich Vagetius, Hamburg 1637, in octavo. The same idyll appeared with Cato’s *Distichs* and other works in 1500, in quarto. Federicus Jamotius supplied the same idyll with a Greek paraphrase, p. 57 of his *Poems*. Barthius published an elegy on the same subject by a more recent author in *Adversaria* XLV.16. A dissertation on the idyll *On the Good Man*, or the *Pythagorean Lecture* [Πυθαγορικὴ ἀκρόασις], by Magnus Daniel Omeisius, appeared at Altdorf in 1706, in quarto; it contains also much material on Ausonius.

Tenth, an *Eclogary* of various little poems and epigrams, some of which, as in other poems of Ausonius, are adapted from Greek pieces found in Scaliger’s edition and certain others. The Greek epigram of Posidippus, or of Crates the Cynic, which Ausonius adapted and expanded, together with the contrasting epigram of Metrodorus, is found in Book I of the *Greek Anthology of Epigrams*, pp. 27 ff. In the manuscript of Antonio Eparchius, now preserved in the Library of the Most Christian King, the former appears under the name of Heraclitus, while the latter is attributed to Democritus. See Bandurius on the *Constantinopolitan Antiquities*, p. 882. The *Apophthegms of the Wise Men of Greece*, with the scholia of Erasmus, Cato’s *Distichs*, and certain other works, appeared at Frankfurt on the Oder in octavo; the *Paschal Poem*, with Speltinus’s notes, in Speltinus’s collection of poems, Erfurt 1501, in quarto.

Eleventh, a Book of Twenty-Five Letters, like all those already described, in various kinds of verse. Some of the idylls and letters are occasionally preceded by a prose letter.

Twelfth, a Panegyrical Oration to the emperor Gratian, in which he thanks him for the consulship, often published together with the Twelve Panegyrics, as stated above.

Thirteenth, an *Outline of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey*.

Fourteenth, Vinetus’s edition also contains tetrastichs on each month, which Scaliger omitted from his own edition,

[Col. 0821C] but which he published in the *Extracts of Ancient Poets* without the author’s name; P. Pithoeus did the same in his edition of ancient Latin epigrams. In the very ancient Roman Calendar which Peter Lambecius published from a manuscript of the Imperial Library at the end of the fourth book of his commentaries, and which Graevius inserted into volume eight of the *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*, these tetrastichs— which Graevius considers worthy of Ausonius—are each placed beneath an image of the month and beautifully correspond to it. Compare Eustathius, *On the Loves of Ismenus and Ismenias*, book IV, where he describes images of the twelve months painted according to ancient custom.

## 3. Editions of Ausonius’s works

Gesner reports that Ausonius was first published by Aldus, but Laurentius Pignorius, letter 16, says that we owe Ausonius to Matteo Bosso, Angelo Poliziano, and Taddeo Ugoleto. In Beughem’s *Incunabula of Printing* I find mention of a Milanese edition of 1490, which Rosweidus, in his notes on Paulinus’s fourth poem, p. 836, calls the first edition of Ausonius; then there is a Venetian edition of 1496, in folio, with a preface by Giorgio Merula.

[Col. 0822A] There is also an Ausonius printed at Milan in 1497 together with Terentianus Maurus. See the Venetian *Diary*, *Journal of the Italian Men of Letters*, vol. XVII, p. 303. I possess an edition published at Venice in 1501, in quarto, with the preface of Taddeo Ugoleto of Parma, and frequently annotated in the hand of the eminent Andrea Alciati. Certain epigrams were first added to Ausonius from the library of Giorgio Merula of Alexandria. There is also a Paris edition corrected by Milh-Humelberg, printed by Jodocus Badius Ascensius in 1517, in quarto. In the same year Aldus published Ausonius in octavo. I omit the Basel edition of Valentinus Curio, 1523; the Lyon editions printed by Gryphius in 1540, in octavo, and in 1549; the Paris edition corrected by Vinetus and overseen by Vinetus’s friend Jacobus Goupylus in 1551; the Lyon edition of Ludovicus Miraeus, 1557, in octavo; and the Antwerp edition of Theodorus Pulmannus, in smaller format, 1567.

Above all, however, the excellent edition of Ausonius deserves praise, published at Bordeaux in 1575, in quarto, under the care of the learned Aelius Vinetus, together with his commentaries, printed in the same format in 1580, and again after his death in 1590, in quarto.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Vinetus died in 1587. Joseph Scaliger mentions the commentaries of his second edition on p. 403 of his *Letters*, while explaining Ausonius’s *Gryphus of the Ternary* to Nicolas Michaelis: “You know how uncommon the learning is in Ausonius’s poems. In them the *Gryphus of the Ternary* has posed a cross to the better grammarians of our age, although the hidden learning, removed behind a veil of riddles, has eluded the efforts of all. For Sylvius of Amiens struck nothing but ordinary coin. Good Vinetus distrusts not only himself, but also more learned men, even in matters that are clear. And although in the second commentary, recently reworked after his death, he transcribed many of our Ausonian readings into his own discussions, he brought forth nothing that would make Ausonius more familiar to learned men. See also, if you please, Thomas Crenius, *Observations*, part IV, pp. 11 ff., where there is further material relevant to the history of Ausonius’s editions.]

Before Vinetus’s commentaries were published, Joseph Scaliger dedicated to him his two books of *Ausonian Readings*, in 1573; in the final chapter of the second he gives a brief account of the poet’s life. These books were afterwards frequently published with Ausonius, not only at Lyon in 1575, but also by Commelinus in 1588, in octavo, and in the same year, in smaller format, at Geneva, as well as elsewhere repeatedly thereafter, with selected notes of Vinetus and excerpts from the *Adversaria* of Adrian Turnebus and the philological writings of Adrian Junius, William Canter, and Justus Lipsius.

Before Vinetus and Scaliger, Mariangelo Accursio had published discussions of Ausonius, Ovid, and Solinus at Rome in 1524, in folio. Accused of plagiarism because he had claimed for himself the labors of Fabricius Varanius, bishop of Camerino, he rejected the charge with the following oath:

“Whatever gods and men, divine law, faith, and all that is sacred may hear, I affirm with the religious solemnity of an oath—and I wish this to be understood as spoken lawfully and without malicious deceit—that I have never read through, nor even glanced at, the writings of anyone from which the slightest assistance could have been given to redeem or aid our researches. Indeed, I have labored, insofar as it was possible, so that if anything belonging to another should come to my attention even after my own observations had been published, I might immediately remove it from my writings.”

[Col. 0822D] “But if I should swear falsely, then may the pontiff punish the perjury and an evil genius my discussions, to such a degree that, if there is anything good or even moderately good in them, the most ignorant rabble may judge it worse than the worthless and cheaper than trifles; if any rewards of reputation remain, may they fly away on the wind and be borne along by the fickleness of the crowd.”

Ausonius with Joseph Scaliger’s *Ausonian Readings* was published at Geneva in 1608, in duodecimo. Conrad Rittershusius, p. 113, in his notes on Gunther’s *Ligurinus*, mentions his exercises on Ausonius, in which he corrected several passages of Nazarius and other panegyrists. But neither those exercises, nor Caspar Barthius’s observations on Ausonius, nor the notes and variant readings of Heinrich Ernstius, ever saw the light, so far as I know; although some observations of Rittershusius on the *Panegyrics* do exist, as I remember saying above, book II, chapter 22.

[Col. 0824A] Finally, Jacobus Tollius brought this author into print most elegantly at Leiden in 1671, in octavo, with Scaliger’s complete notes, and with the commentary of Marquard Freher on Ausonius’s *Mosella*, which had appeared at Heidelberg in 1619, in folio, as well as selected observations of Accursius—although the title falsely promises them in full—Vinetus, Barthius, Acidalius, J. F. Gronovius, and Joannes Georgius Graevius. Ausonius’s *Mosella* was also illustrated with selected elegies of Tibullus and Propertius by Paulus Duizius, Pont-à-Mousson 1615, in octavo.

# THE EXTANT WORKS OF DECIUS AUSONIUS OF BORDEAUX IN GAUL

[Col. 0823]

## PREFATORY PIECES

### LETTER TO AUSONIUS (C)

[Col. 0823B]

**Theodosius Augustus to Ausonius, his father, greetings.**

My love for you, and my admiration for your talent and learning, which are both exceedingly great, most delightful father, have moved me to set aside the custom ordinarily observed by other princes and to send you a familiar letter in my own hand. I ask you—not by royal right, but by the right of that private affection which exists between us—not to deprive me of reading your writings, which were once known to me but have now, through the passage of time, been forgotten, and which I desire again: not only so that what is familiar may be recalled, but also so that I may receive those works celebrated in famous report.

Whatever you, who love me, may willingly share from the storeroom of your books, do so by following the example of the best authors—men whom you deserved to equal—who vied with one another in presenting their works to Octavian Augustus, ruler of the world, composing many things without end in his honor. Whether he admired them as much as I admire you, I do not know; certainly he did not love them more.

Farewell, father.

### LETTER TO THEODOSIUS (C)

**Ausonius to Theodosius Augustus.**

If golden Ceres should order the farmer to give seed to the earth;

if Gradivus should order the commander to take up arms;

if Neptune should command an unarmed fleet to leave harbor,

it is as right to trust as it is wrong to doubt:

although the sea may rage wildly, and the raw earth

be unfit for seed, and the hand insufficient for war.

Do not doubt a good commander. Mortal affairs seek

counsel. Confidently undertake the commands of God.

The Augustus orders me to write, and asks for my poems,

almost entreating me. Beneath his gentle command lies force.

[Col. 0823D] I have no talent; but Caesar has ordered it—I shall have one.

Why should I deny that I can do what he thinks I can?

He himself arouses my feeble strength; and the same man

who commands also gives pleasure: it is enough that I obey.

It is not safe to refuse a god. Delay born of modesty

is often praised, whenever one hesitates before an equal.

Indeed, poems that have long wished to burst forth

are already preparing themselves without command. Who would not wish to be Caesar’s free man?

[Col. 0824B] May he not bear an unworthy poet and a hundred erasures,

always to be changed by a worse mark.

Only remember that you ordered this, Roman father,

and grant yourself pardon for my faults.

### LETTER TO SYAGRIUS (C)

**Ausonius to his Syagrius, greetings.**

Ausonius is my father. I, who bear the same name,

have written down who I am, what my school, lineage, household,

and homeland are, so that you might know, good man, whoever I may have been,

and honor me in your remembering heart.

Bazas is my father’s birthplace; my mother’s family

comes from the Aedui through her father,

but my mother herself from the waters of the Tarbelli.

I myself was born at Bordeaux: the origin of my lineage

is divided among four ancient cities.

[Col. 0824C] From this source a widely scattered kinship has spread,

so that, as is fitting, many names are derived from our household.

Others take their names by derivation; for us, from the first stock,

not merely kinship-names but names of descent are pleasing.

But I return to the sequence: my father devoted himself to medicine,

one of the disciplines that God has granted.

We turned our attention to grammar, and soon

also touched rhetoric to a sufficient degree.

Nor were the law courts unknown to me; but my care for teaching

was more cultivated, and I earned the title of Grammarian.

It was not so great a title that our glory could rival

Aemilius, Scaurus, or Berytius Probus,

but, when compared with many of our countrymen,

Aquitanian names, I could regard myself as neither inferior nor subordinate.

After the records of three decades had been completed,

[Col. 0824D] I maintained a municipal teaching appointment.

Ordered to enter the golden palaces of Augustus,

I taught the imperial offspring as a grammarian;

soon also as a rhetorician—for my confidence was not

empty, nor was the glory of my judgment without substance.

Let other teachers nevertheless have enjoyed greater fame,

provided that none had a better pupil.

Alcides had Atlas as teacher, and the Aeacid Chiron;

[Col. 0825A] the latter was almost born of Jupiter, the former was Jupiter’s son.

They had Thessaly and Thebes as their ancestral homes;

but this pupil of mine rules throughout the whole world that is his.

I was his companion, quaestor, and prefect—the summit of honors—

for Gaul, Libya, and Latium.

I was the first to receive the fasces and the Latin curule chair,

and became consul, with him as my later colleague.

This is the Ausonius I am. But then do not despise the fact

that I voluntarily prepare you as patron for my poems.

Since you inhabit the seat of my heart, gracious Syagrius,

and dwell in the Ausonius who is another self,

so too you shall be prefaced to my book,

so that it makes no difference whether it is yours or mine.

### LETTER TO LATINUS PACATUS DREPANIUS (C)

**Ausonius to Latinus Pacatus Drepanius, his son.**

[Col. 0825B]

“To whom should I give my charming new little book?”

The poet of Verona once said:

“And at once he gave it to Nepos.”

But whom shall we trust with this unpolished, rough little book,

these jests, trifles, and absurdities, to cherish them in his lap?

I have found him—be silent, anxious verses—whom I have found,

no less learned and more kindly

than the man whom Gaul gave to Catullus.

No one among my dear ones is more precious to me;

the nine Sisters esteem no one more highly

than all others, except Maro.

“You are certainly speaking of Pacatus, Poet.”

He is the man. Fly forth without fear, verses,

and warm your nest safely in his lap.

He will love you; he will wish to protect you.

He will cover what deserves pardon and pass on what is approved.

[Col. 0826B] After his judgment, fear no one else.

[Col. 0825]

# EPIGRAMS (C)

## I. On Augustus

[Col. 0825B]

Powerful Phoebus, master of numbers; Tritonia, ruler of wars;

and you, winged Victory, gliding down from the airy sky—

come and make bright the brow adorned with a double diadem,

bringing garlands, gifts of the toga, and rewards of battle.

Augustus, powerful in war and eloquence, deserves honor twice over:

he doubles his titles, tempering battles with the Muses

and directing the Getic war with Apollo.

Amid weapons and fierce Chuni, and the harmful

Sauromatae, he gives to the bright Muses as much time

as he withholds from war.

Scarcely has he set aside the whistling arrows,

when his hand is carried to the pens of the Muses; he knows no leisure,

and, changing his reed, meditates a song.

[Col. 0825C] But the song is not soft in its measures: it recalls

the dreadful wars of Odrysian Mars and the weapons of the Thracian warrior-woman.

Rejoice, descendant of Aeacus: you are once again celebrated

by a proud poet, and a Roman Homer has fallen to your lot.

## II. On a wild beast killed by Caesar

The wounded beast, which knows not how to yield to the broad blade,

presses on against the bloody weapon of the armed man.

How great a death it suffers from a small wound,

and proves that the hand alone possesses the power of death!

They marvel at the strange event and the sudden ruin;

the wound is sought, and the fresh gash deceives their eyes.

Not content to pass lethally through the struck limbs,

a single arrow joins two deaths.

Since many creatures perish from one common stroke of lightning,

you might think that these wounds too were sent from heaven.

## III. The Danube addresses the Nile

[Col. 0825D]

Ruler of Illyrian waters, second only to you, Nile,

I raise my joyful head from my spring.

I bid the Augusti—the son and the father—be hailed,

whom I nourished among the warlike Pannonians.

Now I wish to run as a messenger to the Euxine Sea,

so that Valens, the gods’ second care, may know

the Suebi have been laid low by slaughter, flight, and flames,

and that the Rhine is no longer a boundary for the Gauls.

[Col. 0826B] And if the river, ebbing in accordance with the law of the sea,

were to flow back toward me, I could bring the defeated Goths here from there.

## IV. The same addresses the same

The Danube, whose head is hidden in the innermost regions,

now flows wholly beneath your dominion.

Where I pour my icy spring among the Suebi,

where I cut through the Pannonian lands laden with empires,

and where, rich in waters, I release my mouths into the Scythian sea,

I bring all rivers beneath your yoke.

The next victory will be granted to Augustus Valens.

Here too, Nile, he will find your springs.

## V. Beneath a marble image of the younger Valentinian

Now we have made you marble at the expense of the treasury; but when

your brother Augustus returns, may you become gold.

## VI. Beneath a painting in which a lion was killed by Gratian with a single arrow

[Col. 0826C]

That the lion suffers death from so slender a reed

is due not to the strength of the iron, but to the strength of the striker.

## VII. On the mother of Augustus

Before all other women, let me nevertheless be called fortunate in this:

whether I gave birth to a god or to a man.

## VIII. An exhortation to modesty

It is said that King Agathocles dined from earthenware

and often loaded a Samian clay sideboard,

although he set dreadful dishes upon jeweled vessels,

mixing wealth and poverty together.

When asked the reason, he replied: “I am king

of Sicily, but I was born of a potter-father.”

[Col. 0826D] Hold fortune in reverence, whoever you are

who suddenly advance from a place of exile to wealth.

## IX. On his own poems

There is play in my little books, but much seriousness also;

the Stoic plays one part, Epicurus another.

So long as the ancient rule of morals remains safe for me,

let my sober Muse play with mingled jests.

## X. Against the adulteress Eumpina

A wanton wife gave poison to her jealous husband,

[Col. 0827A] but did not think that enough had been given for death.

She mixed deadly quantities of quicksilver,

so that the doubled force might bring a swift death.

If anyone separates these, they produce poison.

Who drinks them together will take an antidote.

Thus, while the harmful cups contend with one another,

the deadly poison yielded to the health-giving one.

At once both sought the empty recesses of the belly,

where the slippery passage for discharged food is known.

How kindly the gods care for us! The more cruel wife proves beneficial.

And when the fates will it, two poisons give help.

## XI. Echo to a painter

Fool, why do you attempt to give my face a form, painter,

and trouble a goddess unknown to the eyes?

I am the daughter of air and tongue, the mother of empty

[Col. 0827B] indication, carrying a voice without a mind.

Repeating the final sounds from the end as they perish,

I follow, mocking, words that belong to others rather than to me.

I, Echo, dwell penetrably in your ears;

and if you wish to paint my likeness, paint a sound.

## XII. On the statue of Opportunity and Repentance

Whose work am I? Phidias’s—the man who made the statue of Pallas

and who made Jupiter. I am his third masterpiece.

I am the goddess whom rare people know, and few know as OCCASION.

Why do you stand upon a wheel? I cannot remain in one place.

Why have you winged sandals? I am swift. What Mercury is accustomed to grant—good fortune—I delay when I wish.

Why do you cover your face with hair? I do not wish to be recognized.

But look: the back of my head is bald, so that I may not be seized while fleeing.

Who is the companion joined to you? Let her tell you. Tell me, I ask, who you are.

I am the goddess to whom not even Cicero himself gave a name.

I am the goddess who exacts punishment for what has been done and what has not been done.

So that one may repent, I am called METANOEA.

Now tell me what she does with you. Whenever I have flown away,

she remains; those whom I have passed by retain her.

You too, while you ask and delay by questioning,

will say that I have slipped from your hands.

## XIII. On a hare caught by a sea-dog

Once, as a hare was running along the shore of Trinacria,

a blue sea-dog seized it before the dogs could.

But the hare said: “I am prey to all the creatures of land and sea,

perhaps even to the sky, if the dog holds the stars.”

## XIV. On Pergamus, a runaway copyist who was captured

[Col. 0827D] As sluggish a writer as you are a slow runner, Pergamus,

you fled, and were captured at the very first stage.

Therefore, Pergamus, you endured the marks of writing upon your face,

and your forehead suffered what your right hand had neglected.

## XV. Against the same Pergamus

Pergamus, you were not rightly punished: upon your forehead you underwent

the punishment deserved by your slow hands.

But you, master, restrain the offending limbs.

It is unjust to torture the wrong culprits.

Either inscribe that right hand which refuses to write,

or fetter the runaway feet with the weight of iron.

## XVI. On himself and his wife

When my wife read in my poem the names of Laïs and Glycera,

[Col. 0828A] names of wanton fame,

she said that I was merely playing and joking about false love:

such is her confidence in my honesty.

## XVII. To his wife

Wife, let us live as we have lived, and keep the names

which we first assumed in the marriage chamber;

let no day come that changes us through all the ages;

rather, may I be young for you, and you a girl for me.

Even if I am older than Nestor, and you, rivaling him in years,

surpass the Cumaean Sibyl, Deiphobe,

let us not know what mature old age is.

It is proper to know that life is uncertain, not to count its years.

## XVIII. Against the old drunkard Meroe

He who first gave you your name, Meroe,

gave the name of Hippolytus to the son of Theseus.

For it is divination to compose a name that may be

an indication of fortune, character, or death.

The fates gave you the name Protesilaus

because you were destined to be Troy’s first victim.

They call Idmon a seer, and Iapis a physician;

names anticipate the arts they must learn.

And so with you, Meroe: not because you are dark in complexion,

like the woman born in Meroe beside the Nile,

but because you do not dilute the wine poured into your cup,

being accustomed to drink it unmixed—pure wine indeed.

## XIX. Nemesis, from the Greek

Once the Persians brought me as a stone, to become a trophy

of their war; now I am NEMESIS.

But just as I stand by Greek victors as a trophy,

so, Nemesis, I punish the boastful Persians.

## XX. On the changes of fortune, from the Greek

When he found a treasure, the man who was about to enter death

left behind in triumph the noose by which he had been destined to perish.

But the man who did not find the gold he had hidden in the earth

found the noose, tied it, and perished.

## XXI. The same, in another form

The man who was tying a noose around his neck found gold

and deposited the noose in place of the treasure.

But the man who had hidden the gold, after failing to find it,

fitted around his neck the noose he had found.

## XXII. On Thrasybulus the Lacedaemonian

You receive seven wounds upon your opposing breast;

you are carried above your weapons, Thrasybulus,

but this is not the grief of your father; it is a glory greater than Pitana’s.

It is rare to be able to enjoy so beautiful a funeral.

After his companions had placed him upon the mournful bier,

his great-hearted father spoke these words:

“Weep for others; my son needs no tears—

he is mine, he is such a one, and he is a Lacedaemonian.”

## XXIII. On a Lacedaemonian mother

A Lacedaemonian mother, arming her son with a shield,

said: “With this, or upon this, return.”

## XXIV. Against a certain rich man

A certain man, proud of his wealth and swollen with arrogance,

noble only in words,

[Col. 0829A] scorns the famous names of the flourishing age,

while grasping after ancient pedigrees,

and naming Mars, Remus, and the founder Romulus

as his first ancestors.

He orders these to be covered with Serian silk;

he engraves them upon heavy silver,

branding them into the wax of his doorposts

and the panels of his halls.

I believe that even his father was uncertain,

and that his mother truly was a she-wolf.

## XXV. Antisthenes, the Cynic philosopher

I was the first inventor of Cynicism. What is this reasoning?

They say that Alcides was much earlier.

Once I was second to Alcides, my teacher;

now I am first among the Cynics, and he is a god.

## XXVI. The same
[Col. 0829B]

A disciple better than no one, and a better teacher,

“Into virtue he happened to fall, and into Cynic wisdom” (*Εἰς ἀρετὴν συνέβη, καὶ κυνικὴν σοφίην*).

He who knows both knows that I speak the truth—

“Both the god Alcides and the dog Diogenes” (*καὶ θεὸν Ἀλκείδην, καὶ κύνα Διογένην*).

### XXVII. To Father Liber

“I am Osiris among the Egyptians, Phanaces among the Mysians,

Bacchus among the living, Aidoneus among the dead,

Dionysus, born of fire, two-horned, destroyer of the Titans”  
(*Αἰγύπτου μὲν Ὄσιρις ἐγώ, Μυσῶν δὲ Φανάκης, / Βάκχος ἐνὶ ζωοῖσιν, ἐνὶ φθιμένοις Ἀϊδωνεύς, / Πυρογενὴς, δίκέρως, Τιτανολέτης Διόνυσσος*).

### XXVIII. The Myobarbus of Father Liber, a marble image in our villa bearing the attributes of all the gods

Ogygia calls me Bacchus;

Egypt considers me Osiris;

the Mysians name me Phanaces;

the Indians regard me as Dionysus;

Roman rites call me Liber;

the Arabian people call me Adoneus;

the Lucanian people, Pantheus.

[Col. 0829C]

### XXIX. On a marble Corydon

“Goat, he-goat, wallet, shepherd, staff-bearer, olive tree—

I, Corydon, am one simple stone made from them all”  
(*Αἲξ, χίμαρος, πήρη, ποιμήν, ῥαβδοῦχος, ἐλαίη, / Εἷς λίθος ἐκ πάντων λιτὸς ἐγὼ Κορύδων*).

### XXX. On a statue of Sappho

Sappho of Lesbos, sister joined to the Pierian Muses,

“I am the ninth of the lyric poets, the tenth of the Aonian women”  
(*Εἰμ’ ἐνάτη Λυρικῶν, Ἀονίδων δεκάτη*).

### XXXI. Of the goddess Venus

Born from the sea, received by the earth, brought forth by heaven her father,

mother of the descendants of Aeneas, gracious Venus dwells here.

### XXXII. To his little book about Proculus

[Col. 0829D]

“If it is necessary for you, paper, to suffer moths and decay,

begin to perish before my little verses.”

“I would rather face moths,” you say. You are wise, wretched little book,

since you prefer to undergo the lighter evil.

But I do not wish to waste the leisure of the costly Muse,

which produces a loss of sleep and oil.

It would have been more useful to sleep than to lose sleep

and oil. “You speak well.” But this is my reason:

I am angry with Proculus, whose eloquence is as great

as his rank. He wrote very many things, which he keeps locked away.

I am intent on taking revenge on him, and this revenge lies ready for the poet:

let him who does not publish his own poems read ours.

[Col. 0830A]

It is in his power either to order you to grow young again through cedar oil,

or to command you to become food for harsh worms.

To him I consign the ignoble leisure that remains to us,

whether he reads what I shall give, or conceals it.

### XXXIII. On the name of a certain Lucius, carved in marble

“Lucius” is a single letter, though divided by twin points:

thus the single letter L makes the praenomen.

After it an M has been cut; I think that the M does not appear whole.

Its upper part sprang away, damaged by a fragment of stone.

No one can know from reliable indications whether

a Marius, a Marcius, or a Metellus lies here.

The letters lie broken, their forms truncated and torn;

everything has perished amid confused marks.

Are we surprised that human beings perish? Monuments decay;

death comes even to stones and to names.

[Col. 0830B]

### XXXIV. On Sabina, his wife

Whether you approve the garment woven with Tyrian under-thread,

or prefer the convenience of an inscribed title,

the elegance of the mistress adorns both equally:

Sabina cultivates these twin arts as one.

### XXXV. On the same Sabina

Let the glory of the East praise Achaemenian fabrics;

let Greece weave soft gold into your cloaks.

While fame celebrates Ausonian Sabina no less,

she matches them in skill while sparing great expense.

### XXXVI. On the same Sabina

Those who weave threads also weave poems; poems belong to the Muses,

threads, chaste Minerva, they contribute to you.

But I, Sabina, will not separate things that belong together:

I have inscribed in verse what my hands have woven.

[Col. 0830C]

### XXXVII. On the brothers Chrestus and Acindynus

“Chrestus and Acindynus are brothers, pitiable children”  
(*Χρηστὸς, Ἀκίνδυνος, εἰσὶν ἀδελφεοὶ, οἰκτρὰ δὲ τέκνα*),

both of bad character, bearing false names.

“Neither is this one good, nor is that one harmless”  
(*Οὐδ’ οὗτος χρηστὸς, οὐδ’ οὗτος ἀκίνδυνός ἐστιν*).

A single letter can correct them both.

“If Chrestus should take the alpha, and Acindynus destroy the alpha”
