(*Αἴκεν Χρηστὸς ἕλῃ, Ἀκίνδυνος ἄλφ’ ἀπολέσσῃ*),

this one will become “Dangerous” (*Κίνδυνος*); his brother will be “Worthless” (*Ἄχρηστος*).

### XXXVIII. On the same men

Chrestus and Acindynus are brothers by birth,

but each bears a false name; to make both names true,

let Acindynus give his alpha to Chrestus;

then, remaining without the alpha, each will bear his true name.

### XXXIX. To Philomus the grammarian

Because your library is filled with purchased books,

do you think yourself learned and a grammarian, Philomus?

By the same method, put away strings, plectrums, and lyres.

You have bought everything; tomorrow you will be a lyre-player.

[Col. 0830D]

### XL. On the statue of Rufus, a half-man and speechless rhetorician

“This is the statue of the rhetorician Rufus.” Nothing is truer. It itself is he.

Indeed, it has no tongue, and no brain;

it is stiff, deaf, and blind. Everything is Rufus.

There is one difference: Rufus himself was softer.

### XLI. On a panel on which the image of the rhetorician Rufus was painted

Who painted you speechless, in the image of one who speaks?

Tell me, Rufus. You are silent. Nothing is more like you.

[Col. 0831A]

### XLII. On the same panel

“This is Rufus’s panel.” Nothing is truer. Where is Rufus himself?

“In the chair.” What is he doing? The same as in the panel.

### XLIII. On the same Rufus

Rufus said “REMINISCO” in his verse:

“So *cor* is a verse?” No indeed: Rufus has no heart.

### XLIV. The same

Whoever thinks he can say *REMINISCO* in Latin

would read *COR* where *CO* is written, if he had a heart.

### XLV. On the same Rufus

Rufus, once summoned as a rhetorician to a wedding,

at a crowded banquet, as happens,

to show himself skilled in grammatical art,

spoke these wishes at the wedding:

“May you beget sons of the masculine and feminine gender,

and children of the neuter gender.”

[Col. 0831B]

### XLVI. The image of the rhetorician Rufus

“With a handsome mouth, and a silent mouth. Do you wish to know what I am? I do.”

“The image of Rufus, the rhetorician of Poitiers.”

“I wish he himself could say, ‘This rhetorician is like me.’ He cannot.”

Why? The rhetorician himself is an image of an image.

### XLVII. On the same statue of Rufus

“This is the statue of Rufus the rhetorician.” “If it is made of stone, it is Rufus.”

“Why do you say that?” He himself was always stone.

### XLVIII. On Diogenes the Cynic philosopher

A wallet, barley-cake, cloak, staff, cup: the Cynic’s equipment

was this, but he thinks even it excessive.

For when he saw a herdsman drinking from hollowed hands,

he said, “Why, cup, do I carry you needlessly?”

### XLIX. On Croesus and the same Diogenes

Diogenes the Cynic saw your likeness, King Croesus,

richest of kings, among the dead.

When he stopped at a distance, shaken by a laugh

greater than usual, he said: “Of what use are your riches now,

richest king of kings, when you are

as solitary as I, and even poorer than I?

For whatever I possessed I carry with me;

you, Croesus, carry nothing with you from all those riches.”

### L. To Daedalus concerning Myron’s heifer

[Col. 0831D]

Daedalus, why do you waste vain labor on your art?

Submit me instead to the enclosed Pasiphae.

If you wish to give the real cow its allure, Daedalus,

Myron’s living image of a cow will be yours.

### LI. The same, speaking of herself

You have gone astray, young bull, paying attention to these thighs of ours.

The craftsman’s hand did not give milk to these udders.

### LII. The same

Pasture your herds far from here, please, herdsman,

lest you drive Myron’s bronze cow among the cattle

as though she were breathing.

### LIII. The same

When a calf sees me, it will low. A bull in love will rush upon me.

The shepherd will send me off with his flock.

[Col. 0832A]

### LIV. On the same heifer of Myron

Myron’s bronze cow could have produced a lowing sound,

but she fears wearing away the artist’s genius.

For to fashion something like a living creature is greater than to make it live;

the marvel is not the work of the god, but of the craftsman.

### LV. The same heifer speaking of herself

I had stood as a bronze cow; a heifer was sacrificed to Minerva,

but the goddess transferred the breath she had breathed out here.

Now I am double: part bronze, part living.

This part is said to belong to the craftsman’s hand, that to the goddess.

### LVI. On the same heifer of Myron

Not yet had the sun declined, though already toward evening,

when at last the shepherd was driving his heifers,

leaving his own, and leading me as though I were his own.

### LVII. On the same heifer

A shepherd had happened to lose one heifer

and, ordered to report the number,

complained that I was missing, because I had refused

to follow the others.

### LVIII. Things that changed sex

At Vallebana—an unusual thing, scarcely credible to poets,

but one drawn from true history—

a male bird was transformed into female form,

and a peahen stood before the eyes where there had been a peacock.

Everyone marvels at the monster; but a gentler ewe

stood there, changed from the flock into a tender male.

What makes you dull-witted fools so astonished

at the appearance of a known novelty?

Or do you not read the poems of Naso?

Consus, Saturn’s son, transformed Caenis,

and Tiresias existed with an ambiguous body.

The spring of Salmacis saw the half-male Hermaphroditus.

Pliny saw an Androgynus marrying.

Nor is the recent event at Beneventum in Campania

sufficiently ancient: one of the youths suddenly became a virgin.

Yet I do not wish to summon proofs from old tradition.

Look: I myself have become a woman from a boy.

### LIX. On Achillas, who split open a skull

A smooth skull lay abandoned at a crossroads, unburied,

the baldness of a man already bare of skin.

Others wept; Achillas, unmoved by weeping,

even split it apart with a blow of flint.

[Col. 0832D]

Then the stone, struck from afar, returned as an avenger from the bone

and attacked the forehead and eyes of its author.

Would that the impious hand might direct its blows accurately,

so that the turned-back missiles might strike their author.

### LX. On Alcon the physician and Diodorus the haruspex

The haruspex Diodorus told the sick Marcus

that no more than six days remained to him of life.

But the physician Alcon, more powerful than the gods and the Fates,

immediately proved the haruspex’s prediction false,

and treated the hand of a man who would have survived,

had he not touched it.

For immediately six days perished for Marcus.

### LXI. On a statue of Jupiter and the physician Alcon

Yesterday Alcon touched the statue of Jupiter. It,

although made of marble, suffers the physician’s power.

Look: today, ordered to be moved from the ancient temple,

it is carried out, although it is both a god and a stone.

[Col. 0833A]

### LXII. On Eunomus the physician

Eunomus once said that Gaius, who was sick,

would die. He escaped his fate through fortune, not through the physician.

A little later Eunomus saw him—or thought he saw him—

pale and bearing every appearance of death.

“Who are you?” “Gaius,” he replied. “Are you alive?” He denied it.

“But what are you doing here now?” “I am coming by order of Dis,” he said,

“so that, since I retained knowledge of things and people,

I might summon the physicians.” Eunomus stiffened with terror.

Then Gaius said: “Fear nothing, Eunomus; I and everyone else

who had any sense say that you are no physician.”

### LXIII. On a man with a discordant voice

[Col. 0833B]

You imitate the barking of puppies and the neighing of horses;

you imitate goat herds and wool-bearing flocks

by their bleating; you might say that you also bray like donkeys

when you wish, Marcus, to imitate an Arcadian flock.

You reproduce the crowing of cocks, the exultant throats of ravens,

and every sound possessed by beast and bird.

Although you imitate everything so truly that the imitations seem real,

you cannot produce the sound of a human voice.

### LXIV. From the Greek: “The beginning is half of everything”  
(*ἀρχὴ τὸ ἥμισυ παντός*)

Begin. To have begun is half the work. The other half remains.

Begin that again, and you will complete it.

### LXV. From the Greek: “Grace that is slow is graceless grace”  
(*Ἁ χάρις ἁ βραδύπους ἄχαρις χάρις*)

A favor that is slow is unwelcome. For a favor,

when it hastens to be done, is more gratefully received.

[Col. 0833C]

### LXVI. The same

If you do something good, do it quickly; for a deed done quickly

will be welcome, while a tardy favor makes the favor unwelcome.

### LXVII. On an inept dancer

Fortunate accident mingled with the deceived art.

The actor who danced Capaneus fell.

The same man danced Niobe as a stone, so that then

a spectator would have believed her a real Niobe.

In the role of Canace he seemed much more fortunate than she herself,

because he did not cut open his entrails with a sword.

### LXVIII. On the same man

The same ape danced Daphne and Niobe—

wooden as Daphne, stony as Niobe.

### LXIX. Dodralis potion

*Dodra* comes from *dodrans*. Gather it thus: broth, water, wine,

salt, oil, bread, honey, pepper, herb—nine ingredients.

### LXX. On the same

I am called *dodra*. Why? I contain nine ingredients. What are they?

Broth, water, honey, wine, bread, pepper, herb, oil, salt.

### LXXI. On the same dodra potion

“Dodra is both a drink and a number; I contain honey, wine, oil,

bread, salt, herb, broth, water, pepper”  
(*Δόδρα πότος καὶ ἀριθμός ἔχω, μέλι, οἶνον, ἔλαιον, / Ἄρτον, ἅλας, βοτάνην, ζωμὸν ὕδωρ, πέπερι*).

### LXXII. A beautiful response of a god

[Col. 0834A]

Hylas was skilled in boxing, Phegeus clever in wrestling,

and Lycus famous in the Olympic races;

they consulted Libya’s god Ammon

about whether all could win in the coming contest.

But the god, speaking wisely, said: “Victory will be granted

to you all without question, if you take care

that no one surpass Hylas in boxing,

Phegeus in wrestling, or you, Lycus, in the race.”

### LXXIII. On Narcissus, who was captivated by love of himself

If you desired another, Narcissus, you could possess one.

Now you have an abundance of love; the enjoyment is absent.

### LXXIV. On the same

What would a lover not endure for this beauty—

one who so passionately loves his own image?

### LXXV. On Echo grieving over the death of Narcissus

Echo, whose voice resounds, dies together with you, Narcissus,

exhausted to the final notes of her voice.

Even now, echoing in lament the groan of the dying man,

she loves not even the last words of him who speaks.

### LXXVI. To Apollo concerning Daphne, the fleeing girl

Put away your bow, Paean, and hide your swift arrows:

the maiden is not fleeing from you, but fears your weapons.

### LXXVII. To the bark that covered Daphne

Why do you hurry, envious bark, to cover the girl?

If the maiden is denied to Phoebus, a laurel is owed him.

### LXXVIII. On two sisters of different character

[Col. 0834C]

Delia, we marvel at you—and it is marvelous that you and your sister

are so unlike.

She appears chaste in her chaste dress, although she is not;

you possess nothing of a prostitute except your adornment.

Since you have chaste behavior and she respectable dress,

both your dress and her conduct condemn you.

### LXXIX. On Venus rising from the sea

Behold Cypris, recently risen from the sea’s generative waves,

the work of Apelles’ labor:

as she clasps in her hand the sea-wet hair,

she wrings the foam from both damp locks.

“Now we, Juno and unmarried Pallas,” they say to you, Cypris,

“yield to you and award the prizes of beauty.”

### LXXX. On a beautiful boy

While Nature hesitated whether to make you male or girl,

you became, beautiful boy, almost a girl.

### LXXXI. On a certain Silvius Bonus, who was a Briton

That Silvius Bonus who attacks our poems

has well deserved our couplets: “Briton Bonus.”

### LXXXII. On the same

This is Silvius Bonus. Who is Silvius? This Briton.

Either this Briton is not Silvius, or he is bad.

### LXXXIII. On the same

This Silvius is said to be Bonus, and is also said to be a Briton.

Who would believe that a good citizen had degenerated?

### LXXXIV. On the same

No Briton is good: if Silvius begins

to be simple, let simple Bonus cease to be.

[Col. 0835A]

### LXXXV. On the same

This is Silvius Bonus. But the same Silvius is a Briton.

Believe me, a bad Briton is the simpler explanation.

### LXXXVI. On the same

Silvius, Briton, Bonus: although you admit that he is not a good man,

the Briton cannot be joined to Bonus.

### LXXXVII. On Furippus

Some call you Furippus with a lengthened first syllable,

others Furippus with it shortened.

Choose whichever you prefer: lengthen or shorten the name.

Either will suit you, mad thief.

[Col. 0835B]

### LXXXVIII. Epicurus’ opinion

That which is blessed is free from death and eternal,

and causes trouble neither to itself nor to another.

### LXXXIX. On a lazy man

A healthy lazy man is much worse than a feverish one.

He drinks twice as much and devours double meals.

### XC. On an image of Dido

I am Dido in the face that you see, stranger,

represented with marvelous skill and beauty.

Such was I; but my mind was not as Maro fashioned it,

nor was my life glad with unchaste desires.

[Col. 0835C]

For no Trojan Aeneas ever saw me,

nor did he come to Libya with Iliac fleets.

But, fleeing the furies and the weapons of insolent Iarbas,

I preserved, I confess, my chastity in death,

with a sword driven through my breast;

it was the chaste sword that struck me, not madness

or the cruel pain of wounded love.

Thus it pleases me to have fallen: I lived without wounding my reputation.

Having avenged my husband, I died after founding the city walls.

Envious Muse, why did you spur Maro against me,

so that he might invent the destruction of my chastity?

Readers, believe the historians about me

more than the lying poets who sing of the thefts

and unions of the gods, who profane truth in song

and make the gods resemble human vices.

### XCI. On Faustulus, the short-statured man of Anicius Probinus

[Col. 0835D]

Faustulus, sitting upon an ant as though upon a great elephant,

fell and gave his back to the ground.

Soon he was beaten to death by its kicks,

and, destroyed, could scarcely hold on to life.

Yet he could just speak: “Why do you laugh, malicious Envy,

because I have fallen? Phaethon fell no differently.”

### XCII. On an image of Medea

When Timomachus’ mind wished to paint Medea,

turning in her heart toward the cruel deed against her children,

he exhausted immense labor in opposite directions,

so as to depict the mother’s feeling as uncertain.

Anger lies beneath the tears, and pity is not without anger.

See either one, so that it may be in the other.

[Col. 0836A]

It is enough that she hesitates; for the mother is worthy

of the blood of her children—not your right hand, Timomachus.

### XCIII. On the same woman

Which of you painters represented you, worst of Colchians,

turning the crime against your children over in your cruel mind?

Are you so thirsty to drink the blood of boys

that you refuse to spare them even in a painting of slaughter?

Does a seducer entice you? Is another Jason,

or another Glauce, the cause of your killing?

Why, even in a painting, are you not a barbarian?

For the tenacious wax has grasped the excessive force of your jealousy.

I praise Timomachus because he painted the mother hesitating

over the sword, lest she stain it with her children’s blood.

### XCIV. On a blind man and a lame man

[Col. 0836B]

The lame man, riding upon the blind man, walks on both his feet.

Each takes from the other what he himself lacks.

The blind man supplies the lame man with feet and movement;

the lame man supplies the blind man with eyes in place of feet.

### XCV. The same

He walks while riding upon the blind man, crippled in both feet,

and the two infirmities undertake their duties in turn.

The blind man lends the lame man his feet;

the lame man, in return, gives the blind man eyes instead of feet.

### XCVI. On the rich man and the poor man

The rich man is not rich in possessions; nor is the poor man,

though lacking, unhappy; neither needs the other more.

The rich man needs jewels, the poor man grain.

But since both are in need, the poor man is less needy.

### XCVII. On Penelope

[Col. 0836C]

Untouched by suitors and preserved for so many years,

my kisses were scarcely known even to Telemachus.

Thus my virginity shone for you with mature torches;

and true love burned with jealousy of its master.

Often, as a new woman, I trembled at dreams that lied;

words slipped from me though I had not deserved them.

Yet, waking, I felt unknown pains

and, terrified, tested the dry bed with a trembling hand.

For you, panting and engaged in the final struggles,

indulgent pain obeyed without a voice.

We dared to violate nothing with tooth or claw;

for love fulfilled its covenants in silent peace.

At last I did not call my grandmother with a trembling cry,

[Col. 0836D]

nor did an old nurse, my servant, run first to me.

I myself touched the girls with modest blushes,

confessing the task imposed by tender shame.

### XCVIII. On a grammarian

A grammarian is not happy—and never has been;

nor is anyone happy who is called a grammarian.

But if anyone has ever become happy despite fate,

that person has finally gone beyond the grammarians’ rules.

### XCIX. On the grammarian’s unlucky marriage

Teaching “arms and the man,” and skilled in “arms and the man,”

I did not lead home a wife, but rather arms.

For all day long and throughout every night in succession

she attacks me and my household with quarrels.

As though endowed by Mars with perpetual wars,

she raises arms against me, and no rest is granted.

Now, though I resist, I shall surrender myself,

so that at last she may quarrel because I avoid quarrels.

### C. On Auxilius the grammarian

What utterance of a teacher can be correct

when he pronounces his own name with an error?

You call yourself Auxilius, ignorant teacher:

give the correct case: you are already a solecism.

### CI. On the Theban brothers

Not even in the Stygian realm do the brothers,

the sons of Oedipus, enter into their covenants—ah, miserable men!

For even flames rising from a single pyre

leap apart in opposite directions from their ashes.

Unspeakable young men! whom neither discord leaves free

in the daylight, nor their savage spirit leaves at peace with one another.

Would that they had also been able to divide Thebes itself,

and the boundaries of their kingdoms, as they divide the clouds of ashes!

### CII. On ungrateful people, from Menander

Earth creates nothing worse than an ungrateful human being.

Neighbor, guest, acquaintance, stranger, client,

and every kind of citizen of that sort—

if you readily give help to one who asks,

as soon as you show pity, gratitude perishes.

### CIII. On Demosthenes

If you wish to learn, you will be able to learn many things from the learned.

What you know, make grow in your mind through reflection.

What you have not yet learned, strive to acquire by learning.

[Col. 0837C]

### CIV. On the changing nature of Fortune

Fortune never remains in the same condition.

She is always in motion: she varies and changes her turns,

and overturns the highest into the lowest and raises what has been overturned.

### CV. On Stella

Stella, once you shone among the heavenly gods as the light-bringer;

now, extinguished, you will be an evening star deprived of light.

### CVI. From Menander

Enjoy your possessions as one born mortal; but cherish possessions

as though immortal. In both, destiny must be feared.

### CVII. To a shorthand writer taking dictation with utmost speed

Boy, skilled servant of winged signs,

hasten here.

Open the tablet with its double leaves,

which has abundant power of speech,

completed by single strokes,

so that one voice is finished.

I unroll ample books

and pour forth a torrent of speech,

roaring like dense hail.

Your ears are never confused,

nor is the page occupied.

And with your moving right hand

you fly across the wax.

Now, when I am speaking at greatest length

with circumlocutory elaboration,

you already hold the thoughts of my heart

as words upon the wax.

Would that my mind had been able to think

as swiftly as you have given your swift hand flight:

you anticipate me as I speak.

Who, I ask, who has betrayed me?

Who has already told you those things

that I was thinking of saying?

What winged right hand is practicing

these thefts in the innermost heart?

What order of things is so new

that what the tongue has not yet completed

should come into your ears?

Learning has not provided this;

nor any hand so swift

with its quick-footed shorthand.

Nature has bestowed this gift upon you,

and God has given you this endowment:

to know beforehand what I would say,

and to desire the same thing that I desire.

### CVIII. Ausonius sends greetings to his son Hesperius

Lest the ages of eternal Rome be unknown to you,

from its kings and under the rule of its ancestors,

I have arranged the Fasti and the names of the enduring ages,

scattered here and there through Latin history.

Let this be your reward: receive the nights spent in vigil.

[Col. 0838C]

Our lamp obeys your study.

You too, along the long course of time, join future Januaries

as my page has gathered those of the past.

You now have your father’s example, so that soon

the purple may add you to the Ausonian consuls.

### CIX. Reckoning from the founding of the City to our consulship

Add eleven times one hundred years to four,

and join to it eleven and one beyond the three-year cycle:

this will be the succession of eternal Rome from its origin.

### CX. On the same, to Proculus

When, Proculus, you receive the succession of years

from the eternal city founded by King Quirinus,

you will read that one thousand one hundred and eighteen years

have passed up to the name of the Ausonian consul.

It may happen that, when a lustrum has been added to these,

Proculus will mark the completed Olympiad.

[Col. 0838D]

### CXI. Added at the end of the same book

Thus far I have written the Fasti. If fortune permits, I shall add more.

If not, you who read will add them.

Do you wish to know who I am? Seek the title that is fourth from the bottom;

you will read the name of the Ausonian consul.

[Note: [Col. 0838D] NOTE. In these last four epigrams it may be observed that the author remembers the Fasti he himself arranged. But this little work has been lost.]

[Col. 0839]

## EPHEMERIS, THAT IS, THE BUSINESS OF THE WHOLE DAY (C)

[Col. 0839A]

Morning, already bright, opens the windows;

the wakeful swallow is already chattering in its nest.

You sleep through what is like the first and middle watches of the night,

Parmeno.

Dormice sleep through an entire winter,

but they spare their food. The reason for your sleep is

that you drink much and stretch yourself with an excessive

bulk of fat.

Hence no sound enters your bent ears;

deep sleep presses upon the seat of your mind,

and flashes of light do not trouble

your gleaming eyes.

The fables once invent an annual rest

that remained through the alternation of night and day

for a young man, for whom the Moon prolonged

his sleep.

Rise, trifler, who deserve to be torn by whips.

Rise, lest a long sleep be given you—

one which you do not fear.

Snatch your limbs from the soft bed,

Parmeno.

Perhaps this little song, shaped in Sapphic verse,

persuades you to sleep.

Drive away the measure of Lesbian rest,

sharp Iambus.

### Interlude

Boy, come, rise; give me my shoes

and my linen garment.

Give me whatever clothing there is,

whatever you have already prepared,

so that I may go out.

[Col. 0839C]

Give me the dew of the spring,

so that I may wash my hands,

my mouth, and my eyes.

And see that the shrine is open,

with no external adornment.

Devout words and harmless vows

are sufficient for the divine rite.

I ask for no incense to be burned,

nor honeyed sacrificial cakes;

and I leave the fire-pan of living turf

to vain altars.

I must pray to God,

and to the Son of the supreme God,

the Majesty of one substance,

joined with the Holy Spirit.

And look, I now begin my vows:

[Col. 0839D]

and the thought of the Divinity,

trembling, feels its presence.

Does hope or faith fear anything?

### Prayer

Almighty One, known to me through the worship of the mind alone,

unknown to evil things and unknown to none of the devout,

without beginning or end, older than every age,

than what has been or what will come,

whose form and measure neither mind can grasp

nor tongue express;

whom the Only-begotten alone has the right to see face to face,

to hear as he commands,

and to sit beside the Father’s right hand;

himself the maker of things, himself the very cause of creation,

himself the Word of God, God the Word,

foreknower of the world he was to make,

begotten at the time when time did not yet exist,

brought forth before the dawn and before the ruddy Morning Star

illuminated heaven;

without whom nothing was done, through whom all things were made,

whose throne is in heaven,

to whom the earth is subject as he sits,

and the sea, and the unconquerable chaos of obscure night;

unresting, himself moving all things,

giving life to what is inert;

God with an unbegotten Father,

who, offended by the deceit of a proud people,

called the nations into kingdoms,

to be worshiped through the better offspring of an adopted race;

whom our forefathers were permitted to see,

and, when they saw that divine power, were granted also to see the Father;

who bore our contamination,

and, suffering the cruel mockeries of death,

taught that there is a traversable path back to eternal life;

that not the soul alone returns,

but that one enters the heavenly regions with the whole body,

leaving behind in the empty earth

the hollow mystery of the grave.

Son of the supreme Father, salvation for our age,

to whom the Father entrusted all his own powers,

withholding nothing through envy, full giver of gifts,

open the way to prayers and carry these words to the Father’s ears.

Father, give me a mind unconquered by every crime,

and turn away the serpent’s evil,

the venom that would cause harm.

Let it be enough that the serpent destroyed ancient Eve

and joined deceived Adam to her;

let us, the late seeds of descendants,

whom the age was foretold by truthful prophets,

avoid the snares in which the deadly serpent entangles us.

Open the way that will carry me upward

after the bonds of my sick body,

the pure Milky Way of heaven,

which rises above the wandering clouds of the windy Moon.

By that way the righteous leaders have gone,

and by that way, once snatched away in a four-horse chariot,

whole in body, Elijah penetrated beyond the ether,

with Enoch going before him in his solid body.

Father, grant the hoped-for breath of eternal light,

if I do not swear that stones are gods,

and, looking up to the one altar worthy of reverence,

offer undefiled libations of life;

if I acknowledge you as Father of the Lord and God,

the Only-begotten, and of the Spirit sent by the Two,

who hovered over the watery deep.

Father, grant forgiveness and cleanse my tormented heart,

if I do not seek you through the entrails of beasts

or through spilled blood,

nor conjecture the divine will from secret entrails;

if I abstain from wrongdoing while liable to error,

and if I desire more than I trust to be judged good and pure.

Deign to receive a soul that confesses,

if I curse my decaying limbs,

if I repent in silence,

and if deep fear of my thoughts torments me

and anticipates the late punishments of Gehenna,

while my wounded mind suffers its own ghosts.

[Col. 0841A]

Father, grant that these vows may be ratified by my prayer.

Let me fear nothing and desire nothing;

let me judge that what is enough is sufficient.

Let me desire nothing shameful, nor be a cause of shame to myself.

I will not do to anyone what, at the same time,

I would not wish done to me.

Let me not be harmed by a well-founded charge

or defiled by a doubtful one.

A suspect person seems little different from one truly guilty.

Let there be no power to do evil;

let there be the calm ability to do good.

Let my food and clothing be simple.

Let me be dear to my friends.

And always let me be a father,

without injury to this name;

let me suffer neither in mind nor body.

Let all my limbs perform their functions in peace,

and let no injured part miss anything that it once possessed.

Let me enjoy peace. Let me live secure.

Let me regard no marvels of earth as important.

When my final hour comes,

let a life conscious of its goodness neither fear death nor desire it.

When, by your indulgence, I am seen pure of hidden faults,

I shall despise everything,

when the only pleasure will be to hope for your judgment.

Meanwhile, while it delays its appointed time

and the day lingers,

drive far away the savage serpent

that lies in wait with alluring errors.

These devout vows, trembling with sorrowful guilt,

Christ, commend to the appeasing Father.

Savior, God and Lord, mind, glory, Word,

Son, true from the true, light from light,

remaining with the eternal Father,

reigning through the ages.

Him David’s harmonious songs celebrate in measured music,

and the air resounds with answering voices: Amen.

### Departure

[Col. 0841C]

Enough prayers have been given to God,

although for the guilty the prayer

of the Divinity is never enough.

Boy, give me my public attire:

I must say “Hail”

to my friends, and “Farewell,” which is exchanged.

When four hours have passed [lacuna]

and the sun inclines toward midday,

Sosias must now be summoned.

### Place for issuing invitations

The time for calling the friends is approaching;

we must not delay lunch for ourselves or for them.

Hurry through the neighboring houses, boy.

You know who they are. Return while I speak.

[Col. 0841D]

I have invited five. For six, including the host, make a proper banquet;

if there are more, it is an insult.

He has gone; we are left with Sosias.

### Place for instructing the cook

Sosias, it is time for lunch. The sun has already been hot

for a full fourth hour;

the shadow is turning toward the fifth mark.

Test by tasting whether the prepared dishes are fresh and lively

(for they often deceive).

Shake the boiling pots with moving palms;

dip your swift fingers into the hot broth,

which the moist tongue may lick in repeated passes.

([Much is missing.])

Quadrupeds and birds, or when land creatures

are mixed with sea monsters,

until the clouds, swollen and dispersed by cleansing East Winds,

are held in the clear air.

Now I see the forum, now lawsuits;

now, cheerful, I watch the theater’s procession.

I endure bands of horsemen and slaughters of brigands;

a savage beast tears our faces,

or we rage with the sword in the bloodstained arena.

On foot I walk across the shipwrecking sea;

I leap across straits in my running,

and suddenly fly through the air on wings.

I even suffer unspeakable loves,

the incestuous disgraces of night,

and tragic assemblies in dreams.

Yet there is a refuge whenever peaceful sleep,

breaking the monsters of slumber,

releases me from shame,

and my mind, awake and free of foul images,

consciously passes its hands over the whole bed.

The disgraceful guilt of the marriage-bed withdraws,

and the crimes of fugitive sleep diminish:

I see myself among triumphing crowds, applauding;

then again I am dragged among captive, disarmed Alans.

I gaze upon temples of the gods,

holy doors, and golden palaces,

and seem to recline on Sarian purple;

then soon I sit as a guest in smoky cookshops.

They say that the divine prophet,

under the leaves of an elm,

placed the vain images of idle dreams,

and that there are two gates:

one, through whose ivory arch

it always sends deceptive forms through the air;

the other, made of horn,

which sends forth true visions.

But if we are granted a choice concerning doubtful things,

it is better for faith to be absent from pleasant things

than for vain evils to be feared.

Look, I would now rather be deceived:

provided that sad things always vanish,

I would rather have gone without enjoyments

than tremble at evils.

It is enough, and good enough, if fear is absent.

There are also those who conjecture both tears

and opposing joys,

and draw events out through a varied account.

Go through the slanting regions of heaven,

evil dreams,

where restless wandering storm-clouds disperse the clouds.

Dwell in the lunar poles.

What business have you with my sudden threshold

and the dark chambers of my narrow roof?

Leave me to pass my lazy nights in peace,

until golden Lucifer returns to me in his rosy rising.

But if gentle sleep, undisturbed by any shapes at night,

caresses me in tranquil air,

I dedicate this grove, green with elms in our field,

for you to inhabit as sentries.

[Col. 0841]

## PARENTALIA (C)

### Preface marked in verse

[Col. 0841D]

The names of my beloved, now committed to a proper funeral,

first mourned with tears, I shall now commemorate in verse,

bare, without ornament and without the embellishment of speech.

Funereal honor is enough for the dead.

A dirge sufficiently dutiful toward funeral laments,

lest you silently pass over the yearly offerings,

which Numa consecrated as solemn rites

to the kindred shades,

according as the degree of death or of lineage requires.

This is enough for tombs, enough for the needy earth.

To summon souls by the voice is like a funeral rite.

The buried ashes rejoice to hear their names spoken.

[Col. 0843A]

Inscriptions written on their fronts, as monuments do, command this.

Even he who lacked a grave urn,

when his name has been spoken three times,

will be almost buried.

But you, whoever you are, reader,

who deem my dead worthy of remembrance in mournful elegies,

may you pass through the periods of your life unharmed,

and weep for no deaths before their due time.

### I. Junius Ausonius, father

First among these is my father Ausonius.

Although a son may hesitate about whom to place first,

order commands that he be placed first.

Having, through God’s care, enjoyed

the honor of a peaceful old age,

he lived twenty-two Olympiads.

He saw everything he desired prosper,

and whatever he wished for came to him as he wished.

Not because of excessive indulgence by the Fates,

but because that man’s wishes were so moderate.

His age set him against the seven sages,

whose teaching he cultivated through his character,

so that he might live rather than merely speak

in the art of philosophers,

although he was not unskilled in eloquent talent.

He was also endowed with the rational art

of prolonging human lives through medicine

and extending their allotted time.

Hence this reverence for his completed life remains:

our age granted him this title,

that Ausonius had no one whom he followed,

just as he now has no one who imitates him.

[Col. 0843B]

### II. Aemilia Aeonia, mother

Next, you, mother Aeonia, joined by blood

to a Tarbellian mother and an Aeduian father.

You received every virtue of an obedient wife:

the reputation of chastity, hands skilled at wool-working,

fidelity to your husband, care in raising your children,

dignity combined with gentleness, and cheerful seriousness.

Embracing forever the peaceful spirit of your husband,

you who once lived, warm, in the marriage-bed,

now, having died, warm the tomb.

### III. Aemilius Magnus Arborius, maternal uncle

My dutiful commemoration has called father and mother first;

but to name Arborius third makes me guilty.

To mention him first would be wrong, since he was second after my father;

yet not to place him first is almost wrong.

Moderation must be observed . . . . . . . . . . . . .

before the others, although he will be second after my father.

You were the brother of my mother and my father’s devoted companion,

and to me you were what both father and mother were.

You adorned me, while I was nursing, a boy, a young man, and an adult,

with the arts that it is a pleasure to have learned.

Learned Toulouse, in her Palladian gown, placed you before herself;

Narbonensian Gaul preferred you,

whose tribunal you adorned with the Latin language:

And the forums of the Iberians, and whatever belongs to the Novempopuli.

From here, as your renown grew, you flourished throughout Europe as a skilled rhetorician of Constantinople.

You were learned in a thousand modes, a thousand oracles of speech,

eloquent, swift, and memorable.

When, entrusted to you in my earliest years, I pleased you,

you said that, once I had been born, I was enough for you.

You declared that I, I to you and to our fathers, was a glorious distinction;

you dictated words for my destinies to record.

[Col. 0844A] Therefore farewell, my uncle, who have obtained a seat in Elysium.

These verses I offer you, your gift from the Muses.

### IV. Caecilius Argicius Arborius, grandfather

Devoted page, do not abandon your dutiful task.

After these, let us commemorate our maternal grandfather,

Arborius, a name drawn from the stock of the Aeduici,

who embraced many noble houses:

those of the province of Lugdunum, those of the powerful Aedui,

and those of Vienna beneath the Alpine ridge.

But an adversity too hostile to his family and his proud resources

descended upon him. For both grandfather and father

were proscribed when Victorinus held the imperial power

and was Victor; and sovereignty fell back upon the Tetrici.

Then, as he wandered in exile through lands

where the Aturrus bursts forth,

and the fury of the Tarbelli roars against the Ocean,

[Col. 0844B] fearing the weapons of fortune that had long been raging,

the condition of impoverished Aemilia ensnared him.

Soon, money laboriously acquired in small amounts,

a solace for the weary man, brought relief but not wealth.

You understood the courses of heaven and the stars conscious of fate,

while pursuing your study in concealment.

Nor was the pattern of our life unknown to you—

the pattern that you had placed in sealed tablets;

it was never revealed. But your mother’s attentive care disclosed it,

the care that had concealed it from your fearful grandfather.

When you had completed ninety years of life,

having experienced the weapons that must be feared from the powerful Goddess,

you mourned the son lost after three decades,

wounded and deprived of one eye.

But you said that long consolations sustained you:

[Col. 0844C] that a special honor awaited my destinies.

And now, mingled with the assemblies of the blessed souls,

you certainly know the fates of your grandson.

You perceive that I commemorate you as quaestor,

as prefect, and also as consul,

with an honorific office.

### V. Aemilia Corinthia Maura, grandmother

Now speak of Aemilia, the grandmother, with the grandson’s devoted care:

she was the wife of the Arborius mentioned above.

A playful name was given her: because once she had dark skin,

she was called Maura among her peers.

But she was not dark in spirit, but brighter than a shining swan,

and whiter than untrodden snow.

She was not quick to forgive shameful indulgence;

she kept herself and her household strictly upright.

She, after I had been taken from the cradle and my mother’s breast,

[Col. 0844D] nourished me gently beneath stern commands.

May you, eternal spirits, grant the tranquil ashes of my grandmother quiet,

if I speak pious words.

### VI. Aemilia Hilaria, maternal aunt, devoted virgin

And you, my maternal aunt by degree of kinship but to be remembered

in a mother’s place because of your motherly affection,

Aemilia, who acquired the name Hilaria in the cradle,

because you were cheerful and gracious in the image of a child,

you openly showed yourself to be a true youth, experienced in the medical arts after the manner of men.

Hatred of the female sex was always yours;

and from this grew your love of devoted virginity,

which you practiced for nine times seven years.

The end of your life was also the end of your chastity.

[Col. 0845A] Since you cherished me as a mother with admonitions and affection,

I, your son, render these final funeral rites.

### VII. Cl. Contentus and Julius Calippio, paternal uncles

And recall my paternal uncles in elegiac song:

Contentus, whom the Rutupine earth covers.

Great and varied wealth had been acquired by him,

but, secure under no heir’s name, it perished.

For he was carried off in joyful, still-flourishing years,

and died across the sea, unknown to his brothers.

Julius prolonged his destiny into a long old age,

afflicted by innumerable losses.

He, genial, gracious, and agreeable at a well-spread table,

regarded us as heirs in name alone.

Both were dutiful, alike in countenance, mingling serious matters with jokes;

they did not possess an equal lot in life.

[Col. 0845B] Though separated in tombs, and lying there with honor,

accept this common service of my words: farewell.

### VIII. Attusius Lucanus Talisius, father-in-law

Whoever wishes to celebrate the nobles and the ancient Senate,

and the illustrious genealogies from the origin of Bordeaux,

let him recall you and your family, Lucanus Talisius:

you adorned the ancient ancestors with your character.

Handsome in the dignity of your face, calm in heart, gracious,

a citizen made eminent by eloquent genius.

Spending your whole life in hunting, cultivating the countryside,

and maintaining the elegance of your table, you despised public office.

Desiring to be known among the foremost, you refused to be first,

living apart according to your own judgment.

You wished for me as a son-in-law in my flourishing youth.

[Col. 0845C] To wish for this alone, but not to possess it, was granted you.

The gods above approve vows and, favoring holy merits,

fulfill what good men have desired.

And now, beneath the perpetual honor of the tomb,

you perceive how reverently I remain toward your daughter and toward you:

for, though unmarried, I now discharge these dutiful offices as your son-in-law.

For even though unmarried, I shall never cease to be your son-in-law.

### IX. Attusia Lucana Sabina, wife

Thus far my song has celebrated in pious measures

the dear dead who were mourned with fitting funerals.

Now grief, torments, and the thunderbolt that cannot be touched—

the memorable death of my stolen wife—

are mine.

Noble through ancestors and illustrious in senatorial descent,

Sabina was still more illustrious through her good character.

As a young man, deceived by my years, I first mourned you,

[Col. 0845D] and unmarried I have wept for you through nine Olympiads.

Nor is it permitted me to lull my grief to sleep beneath old age.

For the punishment is always renewed, ever fresh to me.

Others admit the consolations of suffering time.

For me, the long passage of days makes the wounds worse.

I torture my gray hairs, deceived by a life of celibacy;

and the more solitary I am, the more mournfully I live.

The silent house and the cold marriage bed nourish the wound;

so does the fact that I share neither misfortunes nor blessings with anyone.

I grieve if another man’s wife is good; I grieve, conversely,

if she is bad: you are always present to me as the standard.

You come to me as a torment from either side: whether she is bad,

because she is unlike you, or good, because she is like you.

I do not lament wasted wealth or empty pleasures:

[Col. 0846A] I lament that, as a young man, I was robbed of a young wife.

Joyful, chaste, dignified, illustrious in lineage and illustrious in beauty,

the grief and the glory of your husband Ausonius.

You, who were just about to complete four times seven Decembers,

left two children, our pledges.

By God’s favor, as your prayers had desired,

they flourish, heaped with the blessings you wished for.

And I pray that they may prosper; and that, when both survive, our ashes may at last announce this to your ashes.

### X. Ausonius Parvulus, son

I shall not deprive you, my first son, called by my own name,

of the lament you deserve, unwept in remembrance.

As you were preparing, in your earliest murmurs, to complete your first words,

we mourned you at your funeral as a child full of promise.

You were placed in your great-grandfather’s lap for the common burial,

[Col. 0846B] lest you suffer the envy of your own tomb.

### XI. Pastor, grandson through my son

You too, untimely boy, break into the grandfather’s

mature griefs as the bitter sorrow of mourning,

dear Pastor, whose certain hope was a reality,

the third generation of a father from the West.

Your name was given by circumstance: because a pipe first

sang pastoral melody when you were born.

A belatedly understood proof of life’s brevity:

the breath that escapes from blown reeds.

You died, struck by the weight of a discharged roof-tile,

which the craftsman’s hand had thrown from the roof.

This was not the craftsman’s hand; that was the hand of cruel, unerring fate, ready to substitute a guilty person.

[Col. 0846C] Alas, what hopes of mine you shatter, Pastor!

That hurled tile sought my head.

Would that you, more worthy, had mourned the fate of my old age,

and in sorrow had lamented at my funeral.

### XII. Julia Dryadia, sister

If there was any virtue that a prudent woman would wish

to make her own, Dryadia, my sister, shone in this.

Indeed, she possessed many qualities that the stronger sex

and nobility would wish a man to possess.

Sufficiently learned to cultivate life and preserve reputation,

she was learned in good conduct and taught her own as well.

Truth was dearer to her than life; her single care was to know God and love her brother above all others.

She lost her husband while still young; but, serious in character,

she matched an austere old woman in her way of life.

[Col. 0846D] She carried her swift life through six decades,

and died in the house and under the roof where her father had died.

### XIII. Avitianus, brother

Muse, give Avitianus, my brother,

to the funeral lament.

He was younger than I in age, but superior in talent,

and absorbed our father’s arts.

Yet hostile Atropos prevented him

from enjoying the joyful flowering of youth

and crossing beyond the limits of mature age.

Alas, how many ornaments of life!

What cultivation of hope, what grief for the wounded,

do you abandon, my young brother!

[Col. 0847A] Brother in flesh, by the law of birth and blood,

almost a son in affection.

### XIV. Valerius Latinus Euronius, son-in-law

O glory of a noble family, O bitter funeral for me,

Euronius, son-in-law chosen from the cohort of young men,

you were snatched from me in the first flower of youth,

scarcely known as the father of your nursing infant.

Born from the stock of nobles, you preceded even those themselves

from whom the lineage of illustrious nobility arose.

Comely in face, good in character, eloquent, vigorous

in every ability, and outstanding in faithfulness.

This prefecture’s seat, this Illyrian shore,

and the treasury itself, as its dependent, experienced under your direction.

Yet the brevity of your life took none of your praise from you.

Mature in character, you died bitterly in funeral.

### XV. Pomponius Maximus, kinsman

[Col. 0847B]

And you, bound to me as a brother not by blood but in a brother’s place,

Maximus, our mournful song shall celebrate.

For, joined in marriage to my sister,

you left her a widow before she could enjoy the fruit of your years.

Your household alone did not feel this; wounded Bordeaux’s senate,

alas, felt the bitter disaster:

while you were vigorous as its chief magistrate, it declined when you were gone,

and, as you died, it fell into Valentinus.

Alas, why, Maximus, having been torn from us,

will you not enjoy a son, and the fruit and flower of grandchildren?

But you will enjoy them, if a divine portion dwells among the spirits:

and you are permitted to know whatever joys will one day come.

Here too there is a longer enjoyment of happiness:

to have anticipated for a long time what you now share.

### XVI. Veria Liceria, wife of the son of Arborius’ sister

You too, Veria, whether by the name of daughter-in-law or in the place of a daughter,

accept this song of supreme honor.

If your goodness, beauty, reputation, faithfulness,

the obedience of a dutiful wife, and your wool-working hands

were now to be praised, the voice of your great-grandfather Eusebius

would have to be summoned from the deepest realms.

But since he, long ago, has been buried after completing his life,

he has transferred his part to my words:

“Accept the funeral laments for your mourned granddaughter;

she is to be remembered as my Arborius’ wife.

Leaving only small consolations amid great grief,

you abandon a son; and so you torment him more.

[Col. 0847D] But, lest care for your beloved husband be lacking to you,

you now inhabit the monuments joined to your own chamber.

Where the first marriage was celebrated, there is the sorrowful seat of the tomb.

You may be called married there more truly than buried.”

### XVII. Pomponius Maximus Herculanus, son of my sister

Nor let a mournful melody leave unhonored

Herculanus, born of my sister,

whose mature character possessed

a great abundance of praiseworthy qualities.

But it will be more fitting to remember him

than to praise him as dead.

This glory of his mother and mine,

in the season of youthful age,

was struck down by the envious power of fate.

Alas, what fruit, Maximus?

Eloquent, musical, vigorous,

good in mind, great in talent,

swift of foot, handsome in body,

clever of tongue, melodious of voice,

accept the sad gift of your parents—

the lamentable beginning of a complaint—

which your sorrowful uncle,

having composed a funeral song,

offers to you.

### XVIII. Flavius Sanctus, husband of Pudentilla, the sister of my Sabina

You who cultivate jokes and joy, who condemn sadness,

who fear no one and act so that no one fears you;

who ensnare no one with plots and provoke no one with lawsuits,

but live a just, merciful, and wise life:

with pious mouth and good words,

venerate the tranquil spirits and the gentle final rites of Sanctus.

He diligently served in the military without any turmoil,

and enjoyed the prefecture under which the Rutupine land flourished.

His peaceful old age of eighty years

was changed by no worse day.

Therefore pray favorably that, just as were the seasons of his life,

so too Sanctus may spend such leisure among the spirits.

### XIX. Namia Pudentilla, kinswoman

And address Pudentilla in final words,

she who possessed care for reputation and goodness.

Noble, thrifty, virtuous, joyful, chaste, and decorous,

she constantly maintained her marriage with Sanctus.

Safeguarding inviolate the praises of a chaste life,

she managed her own resources while her husband enjoyed leisure.

She did not reproach him for this, nor lower her brow,

because as a woman she alone managed the entire household.

Alas, she died too young, though joyful while her son

and her husband survived, enduring the final fate.

She was once of one mind with our sister Sabina,

and was called my sister by an untroubled title.

Now pious care also recalls her peaceful spirit,

and honors Pudentilla with the dignity of speech.

### XX. Lucanus Talisius [lacuna]. Care for his son

Nor will you, Talisius, my cousin,

the mother’s only hope, young man,

be left unmentioned.

Snatched away in the first years of flourishing age,

you were already a husband and, quickly, a father.

You might think fate had hastened,

lest your father, made a grandfather so soon,

should endure this bitter funeral.

### XXI. Attusia Lucana Talisia and Erminiscius Regulus, kinsmen

Our acquaintance with you, Attusia, was slight,

and none at all with your husband.

But you are the true sister of our Sabina.

And you, Regulus, bear the name of kinsman.

Therefore, since we have received such dear titles,

let us seal them with the service of a mournful poem.

Though we lie far away in Santonic land,

funereal honor reaches the spirits.

### XXII. Severus Censor Julianus, co-father-in-law

Cease, ancient Calpurnian names, Frugi,

to regard this as the peculiar glory of your race.

Let neither Censor Cato alone,

nor Aristides the Just alone,

be pleased by these titles.

Let anyone who was wise,

and who cultivated truth and fidelity,

consider himself your companion, Censor.

You were dignified and gracious, lenient with justice,

learned to join moderation to severity.

You wished to join our households,

though I was neither adopted by you nor connected by blood.

Surely some likeness of your character in us

presented an image of our own nature.

Or perhaps the wheel of fortune was already turning in such a way

that fate might grant weight to such good vows.

[Col. 0849B] If you feel anything among the spirits,

this comforts your mind:

that what you wished to happen

was God’s will.

### XXIII. Paulinus and Dryadia, children of Paulinus and of my sister Megentira

You bore, Paulinus, your father’s name and face;

you were a likeness of your lost parent.

Because of you, the mourning of your wretched mother

had begun to recede, when your appearance offered her a father;

you would restore his character,

and add to his character that eloquence

which your father, Paulinus, lacked.

You are snatched away in joyful, burgeoning years,

and still trouble your mother’s unripe heart.

For we mourn our sister, torn from the marriage chamber—

alas, Dryadia, taken by an untimely death.

[Col. 0849C] We mourn: I above all, who am your mother’s uncle,

and who love you as the offspring of my children.

He died among his mother’s hands and his father’s kisses, far away in the Spanish region.

How tenderly, and as a new flower in your first age,

you were plucked, young man, before your cheeks were purpled!

She had just brought forth four children as a mother in childbirth;

but she has already given twin funerals to the tombs.

Let this separation suffice, father Paulinus.

The remaining offspring is owed to the mother.

### XXIV. Paulinus, son-in-law of my sister

You who love a joyful character and an even disposition,

and who cultivate faith with holy devotion,

venerate the spirit of Paulinus with me, and wet it

with friendly tears, bringing annual offerings.

You were my contemporary, Paulinus, and had taken my sister’s daughter

into marriage: thus you were almost my son-in-law.

Your mother was of Aquitanian stock; your father’s family

was the municipal line of Cossius of Vasates.

Having earned the archives of a prefect,

you were then placed in charge of Libyan accounts,

and received rich rewards.

For Tarraco in Iberia provided you the tribunal of the Corrector,

seeking to become your dependent.

You honored your mother-in-law as a mother;

you could not be regarded as merely a kinsman,

since you occupied the place of a son.

You lived faithfully among harmonious friends,

having completed eighteen Olympiads.

### XXV. Aemilia Dryadia, maternal aunt

You too, Dryadia, my maternal aunt,

born of your sister and almost a son,

I venerate with pious mouth

in mournful measures.

Envious death snatched you from the marriage chamber

and the marital torches,

and changed the marriage bed

into the honor of a funeral bier.

You were learning through me, maternal aunt,

to become a mother.

Therefore now I bring you this sorrowful duty

as a son.

### XXVI. Julia Cataphronia, paternal aunt

And let the Muse share funeral laments

with my paternal aunt Cataphronia.

Unmarried, she cherished the love of devoted virginity

and lived sparingly as an old woman.

To me, as much as she could,

though from a poor estate,

she gave what a mother might give.

Therefore, once commemorated, farewell;

and, called in place of a mother, farewell.

### XXVII. Julia Veneria, paternal aunt

But my paternal aunt Veneria died too soon.

For her I sing brief, measured melodies.

May her gentle ashes flourish above in peace,

and may the swift-footed one approach the silent places of Erebus.

### XXVIII. Julia Idalia, cousin

Idalia too was small,

and bore the name of the Paphian one,

and earned the beauty of Venus.

She was almost a sister to me.

For she was the daughter of my paternal aunt,

whom this funeral lament

celebrates with pious honor.

### XXIX. Aemilia Melania, sister

Aemilia, scarcely known to me as a sister,

accept these complaints,

which my sorrowful elegy owes to your ashes.

Equal in age, childhood joined our cradles, although you were older by one consulship.

But envious Lachesis hastened through the allotted years

and gave a bitter funeral to the spirits.

Sent ahead, therefore, farewell;

and revere the spirits of your parents,

who came in greater and lesser age.

### XXX. Pomponia Urbica, co-mother-in-law, wife of Censor Julianus

As noble in family as she was a woman of ancient character,

Urbica, ennobled by marriage to Censor,

strong in innate virtues and enriched by those

which her husband, father, and mother taught her;

virtues possessed by Tanaquil, by the Pythagorean Theano,

and those displayed, without precedent, at the death of her husband.

And if fate had granted you the power to exchange its decree,

Censor would still be living in our time.

But you too, not long tortured by the age of widowhood,

immediately followed your husband in the desired end.

Now, with mournful laments, we bring you annual rites,

I, Ausonius, your son-in-law, together with your children.

# MEMORIAL OF THE PROFESSORS OF BORDEAUX (C)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0851A]

You too, whom no relationship joined to me,

but fame, and reverence for our beloved homeland,

and devotion to books, and diligent care in teaching,

I shall commemorate—men made famous by their death.

Perhaps this will one day preserve our spirits,

if someone, wishing to be dutiful,

should follow my example.

### I. Tiberius Victor Minervius, orator

First pillar of Bordeaux in speech, Minervius,

second to Quintilian in the rhetorical toga.

Under whose instruction Constantinople and Rome,

and afterward his native city,

were once illustrious,

I do not indeed compete with the majesty of those two cities; but Bordeaux is superior in this one distinction: that it is my homeland.

[Col. 0851B] Let Calagurris continue to claim Fabius as its alumnus;

so long as Bordeaux has a chair, it shall not be inferior.

This city gave a thousand men to the forum;

the senate added twice a thousand to the number,

and purple-bordered togas as well.

I too—but since there is much to say of the praetexta—I shall be silent;

and I shall sing of you concerning yourself,

not from my own position of honor.

If one wishes to compare books of panegyric,

you will have to be counted among the Panathenaics.

Or if one wishes to unfold the fictitious contests of the games,

Quintilian and you hold a contested palm.

A torrent of eloquence was yours;

yet it would roll gold, not also muddy filth.

And the Demosthenic quality

which he himself called “first” three times

flourished in you so strongly

that he himself must yield to you.

Shall I also add the natural gifts of divine generosity,

and mention how retentive your memory was?

Whatever you heard or read once,

you held as though fixed;

so that your ears and books possessed one and the same trust?

We once saw you, in a long contest at the gaming board,

enumerate all the throws that had occurred,

the throws cast in alternating turns

by the rapidly spinning movement of the dice

through the hollowed boards;

you recounted each point with faithful repetition,

what had been cast and what had been recalled

through the long delays.

Your mind was free from all rancor,

your witty tongue full of salt,

with gracious jokes and no quarrel.

Your table was splendid,

but no censor’s rule could condemn it,

nor would Frugi Piso refuse to call it his own.

Sometimes you were powerful in birth and in festive feasting,

but not so as to diminish narrow resources.

[Col. 0851D] Though lacking an heir, after completing twice six decades,

you were mourned by us as both father and young man.

And now, whether anything survives after the final fates,

you still live, remembering the time that has perished;

or whether nothing survives and long leisure has no perception,

you lived for yourself: your fame benefits us.

### II. Latinus Alcimus Alethius, rhetorician

Nor will impious descendants accuse me

of guilty silence, Alcimus,

or consider me less worthy

as a servant of your memory.

Our recent age sets you alone

against the men of earlier times.

The forum’s palm, the glory of the Muses,

a single model in letters—

the letters cultivated by learned Greece at Athens

or by Rome throughout Latium.

Shall I speak of your character and the course of your life,

even to its final limit?

Though renowned for praise and equipped with learning,

you avoided every ambition.

No one was more dignified than you,

or more gracious,

or more generous to the needy;

ready to give assistance if the forum required it,

and devoted to teaching if the school required it.

Those whom you gave to sacred fame

will live throughout the memory of posterity.

You will give Julianus to fame more than

the scepters that he held briefly.

Your books will contribute more to Sallustius

than his consulship added.

You gave your sons the form

of your character, dignity, and eloquence.

Forgive me, offended by the service of my pen.

This is the crime of my love for you:

unable to express what you deserve,

I cultivate my duty with excessive zeal.

Rest peacefully,

and repay the loss of your perishable body

with glory.

### III. Luciolus, rhetorician

Let my mournful elegy recount Luciolus the rhetorician,

my fellow student, then teacher,

and afterward colleague:

an eloquent and learned man,

whether he shaped his utterance in metrical law

or released his beginnings in the rhythms of prose.

Lachesis snatched him from his father in a bitter death,

as he left two children, one of each sex.

No heir could ever have matched his merits,

though now your fame gives joy to the obscure.

Gentle friend, good brother, most faithful husband,

dutiful son—father, I regret that you were such.

Gracious to guests, never shouting at clients,

never speaking sad words to servants.

[Col. 0852D] As you cultivated peaceful manners,

so cultivate tranquil spirits,

and accept from Ausonius this gift:

farewell, my friend.

### IV. Attius Patera Pater, rhetorician

Though you surpassed in age the learned men of earlier times,

Patera, noble in speech,

yet because you flourished in the age immediately before ours,

and I saw you an old man while I was young,

you shall not lack the honor of my mournful elegy,

teacher of powerful rhetoricians.

[Col. 0853A] You were born from the stock of the Druid priests of Bayeux,

if fame does not betray the truth,

and traced your lineage from the temple consecrated to Belenus.

Hence came your family names:

Patera for you—for so they call

the ministers of mystical Apollo.

Your brother and father received their name from Phoebus,

and your son from Delphi.

No one of that age possessed such learning,

nor such a course and full cycle of eloquence.

Memorable, eloquent, with lucid speech,

melodious and cultivated,

moderate in wit, with no bitterness mixed into your jests,

abstemious from wine and food,

joyful, chaste, handsome; even in old age,

[Col. 0853B] your old age was like that of an eagle or a horse.

### V. Attius Tiro Delphidius, rhetorician

Eloquent, learned, swift in tongue and talent,

pleasant in jokes, Delphidius,

be covered by the mournful dirge of your father,

whose rival in praise you were.

Almost from the cradle you began

as a noble poet of the god,

and, wearing the wreath of an Olympian crown,

as a boy you celebrated Jupiter.

Soon afterward, moving rapidly like a sea torrent,

you composed a metrical epic,

so that no one could weave an oration

with equal freedom under the law of verse.

[Col. 0853C] Your eloquence, celebrated in many ways,

was renowned at home and abroad:

whether you cultivated the governor

of a praetorian cohort,

or the judges of provinces,

devoted to protecting clients,

reputations, and the safety of the injured.

Fortunate if you had remained with peaceful letters,

cultivating the work of the Muses,

and if vengeful impulse had not armed itself

with hatreds aroused by great lawsuits,

nor had you raised yourself in the restless palace

of a tyrannical age.

While you were always summoning a remote hope to yourself,

and were disdainful of what lay before you,

preferring to have your own destiny rather than

the good fortune assigned by fate,

you desired many things.

Wandering through every form of office,

and deserving more than you held,

you were therefore, when a grave movement of accusations followed,

given your father’s hardships.

Then, as a rhetorician, but not persevering in teaching,

you disappointed the expectations of parents,

having experienced fewer of God’s evils

because you were carried off in midlife—

through the error of a wayward daughter, and the punishment of an injured wife.

### VI. Alethius Minervius, son, rhetorician

O flower of young men,

the father’s joyful hope:

[Col. 0854A] no secure destiny

was granted to your homeland;

adorned with blessings

that would not endure;

displayed,

and at the same time snatched away,

like grass at the solstice,

rhetorician Alethius.

You, joyful for your homeland Bordeaux,

carried the bright standards

of the cohort

in the age of young manhood.

[lacuna]

[Col. 0854B] And after Patera,

greater than either of them:

you had every advantage of fate

in your earliest years,

as a teacher and instructor

at a time when it would not have been shameful

for you to learn as an adult.

You had already been compared

with your father in the praetexta.

He, through fame and merits,

in the walls of proud Rome,

increased his renown,

not without the bite

of grievous envy.

You abandoned the hopes of your mature flourishing,

and rhetoric without its fruit,

and the noble marriage of your father-in-law,

without peace from your father,

and the wealth of both men,

without their own heir.

[Col. 0854D] Fortune gave you everything too soon,

and snatched it away.

As Horace says in his prophetic utterance:

**NOTHING IS HAPPY  
IN EVERY RESPECT.**

### VII. Leontius the grammarian, surnamed Lascivus

You who cultivate joyful and cheerful manners,

who celebrate feast days, jokes, vows, and play,

remember in an annual dirge

the name of the deceased Leontius.

[Col. 0855A] This man, willing to be called **LASCIVUS**,

a name unworthy of the goodness of his life,

never rejected it, because it was pleasing

to friendly ears.

He attained as much distinction in letters

as is sufficient for a modest chair,

so that he could appear enrolled

among grammarians.

You, always the companion of my youth,

though burdened with more years,

even now grow warm in my marrow,

gentle Leontius.

And it pleases me, with sorrowful care,

to celebrate a mournful song of remembered lament:

an unwelcome gift, yet one owed to you,

[Col. 0855B] in my verse.

### VIII. Greek grammarians of Bordeaux

After these, should I first recall Romulus—

whether he was born at Corinth

or beside the Spercheius—

and Menestheus, likewise sprung from Attic Muses,

among the grammarians?

Their diligence in teaching was common to all;

their reward slight and their speech thin.

But because they taught in our age,

they are to be commemorated.

The third of these was not my teacher;

the others taught me in my earliest years,

so that I would not be ignorant of words

or of speaking,

though without refinement.

[Col. 0855C] For, I believe, a slower understanding

of my mind stood in the way,

and a harmful error of childhood

did not bring me to Greek studies.

May light turf cover you,

and the roof of the tomb defend

your hidden ashes;

but may the inscription of my voice

render you final honor.

### IX. Jucundus, grammarian of Bordeaux, brother of Leontius

And you too, Jucundus, whom they say

rashly usurped a chair,

and whom they think did not deserve

the name of grammarian,

I shall nevertheless summon by name,

simple, good, friendly companion;

Jucundus, dearer for this very zeal,

that although unequal to the noble name,

you loved it:

you are to be commemorated among deserving men.

### X. Latin grammarians and philologists of Bordeaux: Macrinus, Phoebitius, Concordius, Sucuro, Ammonius, Anastasius, grammarian of the Pictavians

[Col. 0855D]

Now, in whatever order

devout honor for my mournful duty

shall suggest each name,

I shall set them forth.

Although humble in birth,

station, and merit,

they nevertheless introduced

the study of grammar

to the rough minds

of the people of Bordeaux.

Let the succession continue.

[Col. 0856A] Let Macrinus be among them,

sober among boys,

and useful to the abilities

of boys.

To him, at the beginning,

my childhood was entrusted.

Nor will I be silent about the old man

Phoebitius by name,

who, as the priest of Belenus,

gained no advantage from that office.

Yet, as was proper,

born from the stock of Druids

of the Armorican people,

he obtained the chair at Bordeaux

through the work of his son.

[Col. 0856B] And you, Concordius,

who, an exile from your homeland,

exchanged a barren chair

for one in another city;

and you, Sucuro,

offspring of a freedwoman,

who gave the first elements

to unformed boys;

and for Anastasius also,

Muse, compose a mournful song,

and remember the grammarian

in a slender elegy.

Born at Bordeaux,

ambition transferred him

and gave him to the Pictavian city.

[Col. 0856C] There, poor, cultivating

a meager food and way of life,

he lost in old age

his slight little glory

both of homeland and of chair.

Small in learning,

harsh in character,

therefore, as he deserved,

he had a slight reputation.

Yet our honor

has commemorated him.

For it is a dutiful act

to commemorate the grammarian

of my homeland,

lest the tomb likewise

[Col. 0856D] cover both his name and his bones.

### XI. To Herculanus, son of my sister, grammarian of Bordeaux

Herculanus, who, departing from my embrace and my school,

offered your uncle hope rather than something to enjoy,

a participant in my school and almost my successor in the chair,

had not the slippery turn of youth cast you headlong,

when you failed to keep to the straight path of the Pythagorean way:

be peaceful, and cherish a dwelling for the quiet spirits;

you have long been counted by me among names joined by kinship.

### XII. Thalassus, Latin grammarian of Bordeaux

Your duty and your name, Thalassus, in your first years,

I heard as a little boy; I scarcely even remember

what your appearance, merit, or parentage may have been.

A later age celebrates nothing about you.

Fame reported only that you were a young grammarian,

and even then so insignificant

that now no trace remains.

Yet because you lived as a teacher in our age,

accept this service of ours: farewell.

### XIII. Citarius Sicalus of Syracuse, Greek grammarian of Bordeaux

And you too, beloved Citarius, shall be remembered,

worthy to be celebrated among good grammarians.

You would have possessed the glory of Aristarchus and Zenodotus

if the ancient honor of the Greeks had continued.

In the poems composed in your earliest years,

the Muse of Simonides of Ceos yields to you.

Born in a Sicilian city, you came as a foreigner to ours,

which you almost restored as a city cultivated by learning.

Having soon obtained a noble and wealthy marriage,

you died without becoming a father,

through the envy of fate.

But we celebrate you dead with mindful honor,

as we cherished you living in the service of friendship.

### XIV. Censorius Atticus Agricius, rhetorician

Equal in eloquence to the foremost, Agricius,

you were placed here later,

because, born and having died in a recent age,

you were deferred for us but not omitted.

In whatever company, you will be remembered in a mournful dirge.

One honor of the tomb is late and previously bestowed.

As lofty as your lineage was,

so great was your glory in speech.

The glory of the Athenaeum, known by the site’s name,

was carried to Nazarius and to the once-famous Patera,

and splendidly cultivated many young men.

Now, with your wife, surviving children, and son-in-law,

you cherish the spirits and monuments of your ancestors.

### XV. Nepotianus, grammarian and likewise rhetorician

Witty, gracious, an old man with a youthful spirit,

whose mind, steeped in no gall but much honey,

mixed nothing bitter into the whole course of life:

Nepotianus, medicine of our hearts,

a sharer in serious matters as in jokes,

silent one, who by silence surpassed Amyclas.

If you were telling a story, not even Ulysses would leave you;

he leaves the singing maidens who sing melodiously.

Upright, chaste, frugal, thrifty, abstemious,

eloquent, yielding to no rhetorician in style,

and a debater even with the Stoic Cleanthes;

knowing Scaurus and Probus in the innermost heart,

and especially mindful of the Epirote Cineas.

Companion, table-fellow, and constant guest—

a guest too little: you were the mover of my mind.

No one gave counsel with a mind so pure,

or concealed the counsel given in a deeper repository.

Renowned for the honor of a praefecture held,

having completed nineteen years of service,

you met death, leaving two children behind,

with much grief, both for your own and for me.

### XVI. Aemilius Magnus Arborius, rhetorician of Toulouse

Among the spirits of my relatives already mourned,

uncle, you must now be remembered among the rhetoricians.

[Col. 0858A] Let piety regard the former work,

and reverence for men’s names the latter,

as a religious duty owed to the homeland.

Let us celebrate twice-deserving Arborius,

a parent with a double honor:

Arborius was his father,

and Argicius his grandfather.

Your father’s lineage was Aeduican;

your mother Maura’s origin was Tarbellic;

both were of noble stock.

A noble and wealthy wife, a household and a school,

and cultivated friendships with princes

fell to you in your youth.

While wealthy Toulouse kept Constantine’s brothers secluded under the pretext of exile, your fame then drove you to Byzantine citadel and Constantinople, the city of the Thracian Propontis.

There, rich in resources and honored by the learned Caesar,

you died, Magnus, while your parents still survived.

But the piety of the prince Augustus

restored you to your homeland,

your ancestral seat, and the monuments of your family.

From here the annual day renews its cause

with tears and a mournful duty,

through its unwelcome religious observance.

### XVII. Exuperius, rhetorician of Toulouse

Exuperius, memorable to me, eloquent without artifice,

grave in step and enormous in words,

handsome in face and, in short, graceful

in movement and bearing,

whose abundance of speech was exceedingly beautiful;

if you received it only through hearing,

it would please you as though inflated;

but if you examined it,

you would know that it produced no solid meaning.

The Palladian toga first revered you at Toulouse,

then drove you away with equal fickleness.

From there Narbo received you.

There, for a great teaching fee, you trained as a rhetorician the boys born of Dalmatian men, bearers of the fateful names of kings, when you were approaching the end of mature life.

[Col. 0858C] They soon acquired the name and honor of Caesar,

gave you the office of governor,

and the Spanish tribunal.

On retiring, you ended your peaceful character

and quiet years in an exceedingly wealthy home at Cahors.

But the rights of your homeland and the origin of your parents

call you back, so that once again

you may restore the name of a rhetorician to Bordeaux.

### XVIII. Marcellus, son of Marcellus, grammarian of Narbo

Nor will I be silent about you, Marcellus, son of Marcellus,

whom your harsh mother drove from city and home.

But powerful fortune soon restored and increased everything.

Narbo first gave your lost homeland back to your father.

The noble host Clarentius, moved by your character,

gave you his outstanding daughter in marriage.

Soon a school, many pupils, and the praetextate youth

gave you the name and wealth of a grammarian.

But fortune never supports an unbroken course,

especially when it has found a man of perverse character.

Yet I must not burden you with this: I have received

the fates that must be remembered;

it is enough to say that everything perished at once.

Yet not even the name—which I do not withhold from you—received …

Among grammarians, of exceedingly slight merit.

### XIX. Sedatus, rhetorician of Toulouse

It would be impious, Sedatus, if I were to leave you unmentioned,

although you obtained the office of teaching abroad.

Our native country is shared by you and me: perhaps powerful

Fate granted you Toulouse as the seat of your school.

There, marriage, children, and a prosperous old age,

[Col. 0859A] and a reputation such as befits a great rhetorician.

Yet your native land, although it leads you back from a foreign region,

recovers you as a citizen when you have died.

And since you had devoted your wandering industry to a divided city,

your place of origin claims its own right over you.

Your offspring now, following their father’s custom,

ennoble Narbo and Rome through their studies.

[lacuna]

Whether it wishes to or not, Fame will bring you back to Bordeaux.

### XX. Staphylius, rhetorician, citizen of Auch

Until now, the law I have observed in commemorating

citizens has been to include those who taught either at home or abroad.

But it is right to join one foreigner to the citizens:

you, Staphylius, born of a stock from Novempopulania.

To me you were both father and uncle: one person in both roles,

[Col. 0859B] the one as Ausonius, the other as Arborius.

A grammarian trained in the manner of Scaurus and Probus, and a most ready rhetorician,

learned in the history of Livy and Herodotus.

Every system of learning was known to you, as much as Varro

contained in his six hundred volumes.

You had a golden mind, persuasive speech, and a calm manner of speaking.

You were neither hesitant nor hurried in delivery.

A beautiful old age, a shining appearance, far from anger and deceit:

this was the fitting goal of your peaceful life.

### XXI. Crispus and Urbicus, grammarians of Latin and Greek

You too, Crispus, will come into the future age,

remembered in my mourning

through the office of the threnos.

[Col. 0859C] You who taught the very young, still unskilled in speech,

the first signs

of the elements of new learning.

Once believed to burn with unmixed wine,

you were thought capable of bringing forth a rival

to the passages of Virgil and Flaccus.

And for you, Urbicus, celebrated in Greek,

though placed after Latin beginnings,

the poem was thus ἐλελίσω—“I have whirled it” or “I have made it roll.”

For you, joined to your companion Crispus,

were accustomed to speak in prose and verse

with the same force;

so that you might recount in speech

the ancient heroes once commemorated

in Homer’s song:

the sweet Plisthenid in particular,

the snow-laden words, as of stormy Dulichium,

and Nestor the king singing
