sweetly spoken words,

words sweetened with the nectar of honeyed speech.

Both were easy in speech, both learned in every kind of poetry,

skilled in the creations of myth (mythōn plasmata) and in history.

Both were of free birth; yet they were men whom it would have been fitting

to deem worthy of attaining distinction through noble fathers.

### XXII. To Victorius, assistant teacher, or junior-schoolmaster

Victorius, devoted to study, mindful, quick, constantly occupied

in unfamiliar books, reading only what is hidden;

to unroll pages eaten by moths and dark with age

was a greater concern for you than ready exercises in study.

What the law of the pontiffs was, what treaties existed, and what ancestral line

once belonged to the sacrificial priests at Cures before Numa;

what Castor had published concerning all the disputed kings, and what

Rhodope had brought forth from the books of her husband;

what the law of the pontiffs was, what ancient ordinances of the Quirites,

what decrees of the senators; what Draco or Solon

had enacted; and what laws Zaleucus had given to the Locrians;

what Minos established under Jupiter, and what Themis established before Jupiter—

these things were better known to you than our Cicero and Virgil,

and than everything contained in Latin history.

Perhaps prolonged reading would have given you even these works,

had Lachesis not hastened your final journey.

Decorated with the honor of my humble chair,

[Col. 0860A] having tasted the slender title of grammarian,

you afterward died in a distant region of Rome,

to which you had crossed from the Sicilian shore.

But now, remembered among the ranks of the noble, rejoice:

your dutiful care has reached your Manes,

if any pious concern reaches the dead.

### XXIII. To Dynamio of Bordeaux, who taught in Spain and died there

Nor shall I deprive you, Dynamio, of a mournful lament,

a fellow citizen and advocate of my homeland.

Your wounded reputation, driven away by the charge of adultery,

was sheltered by little Ilerda in its hiding places.

Your Spanish wife enriched you while you remained concealed;

for there, under an altered name, you were a rhetorician.

You were disguised as a rhetorician under the surname of Flavinius,

so that your guilt might not betray its fugitive.

[Col. 0860C] Although belated affection had restored you to your homeland,

the household at Ilerda soon drew you back again as a settled man.

Whatever your flight and the reputation of your life may have been,

you are joined to me by an old friendship.

And if any perception remains in the hands of the dead,

receive now, true Dynamio, my service after your death.

Although you lie dead in distant regions,

devoted concern commemorates you in mournful elegies.

### XXIV. To Acilius Glabrio, grammarian, junior citizen of Bordeaux

Glabrio, fallen with equal brevity in learning and in life,

I shall commemorate you in mournful elegies.

A name descended from the lineage of noble ancestors:

Glabrio, offspring of the Dardanian Aquilinus.

Once, as a boy, you were my fellow pupil; later,

after I had become a rhetorician, you became a grammarian.

[Col. 0860D] And in the forum a protector of defendants, and a cultivator in the fields,

worthy to enjoy for a long time the goods you had acquired.

Convenient, cheerful, kindly, temperate, so good in giving

advice as in giving it silently,

you leave behind as much honor for your own people as, soon afterward, grief:

snatched away, Glabrio, by a bitter funeral,

leaving wife and children, father and mother—

alas, lost under so many names of relationship!

Mourn for us a long time, never long enough; receive the bitter farewell,

Glabrio, commemorated forever: FAREWELL.

### Coda

Know that those whom you read, drawn from the first section of this book,

were teachers of my homeland.

[Col. 0861A] In the study of grammar, or rhetoric, or both,

it is enough for me to have recalled them after their death.

Praise is the enticement of the living; to call out names alone

with one’s voice will then suffice for their tombs.

Therefore, you who read the sad leisure of our pages,

do not seek eloquence from it, but the service

by which devoted concern performs funeral rites for renowned and learned men,

while it recalls the honors of an outstanding homeland.

### THE POET

Farewell, spirits of illustrious rhetoricians;

farewell, worthy teachers.

[Col. 0862A] If history, or poetic style,

or the forum made any men renowned;

if medical art, or Platonic doctrine,

gave anyone enduring glory;

and if any concern of all the living is pleasing,

and the honor of survivors brings joy,

receive the mournful worship of my song,

a text shaped by tearful lament.

May steadfast ash preserve a place for tombs.

May the memory of their names live,

until that age returns which, by the gift of God the Judge,

is shared by mortals and gods.

[Col. 0861]

## EPITAPHS OF HEROES (C)

### EPITAPHS OF THE HEROES WHO TOOK PART IN THE TROJAN WAR

[Col. 0861B]

#### I. For Agamemnon

King of kings, son of Atreus, avenger of his brother’s wife,

I myself fell by the hands of my wife.

What profit was there in punishing sorrowfully Helen’s abduction,

when Clytemnestra, the avenger of adultery, killed me?

#### II. For Menelaus

Happy Menelaus, to whom the dwelling owed to the gods belongs,

and Elysium, decreed for the pious Manes.

Beloved son-in-law of Tyndareus, beloved of the Thunderer;

avenger of marriage, punisher of adultery;

powerful in eternal life and everlasting youth,

who suffered neither the season of death nor of old age.

#### III. For Ajax

Virtue lies buried together with Ajax, covered by the same tomb,

herself weeping at the funeral mound of my death;

her hair torn and disordered, because the wicked son of Atreus

forced me to yield through his contrived plots.

Now I shall give a purple flower from bright blood,

bearing witness, with a groan, to the crimes of that judgment.

#### IV. For Achilles

The son of Aeacus has not one land alone: his bones are covered

on the Sigean shore, while Larissa burned his hair.

Part of the tomb … [lacuna]

But throughout the whole world … [lacuna] Homer …

#### V. For Ulysses

Here lies Ulysses, son of Laertes.

Read through the Odyssey, wishing to know everything.

#### VI. For Diomedes

Here lies Diomedes, better than his good father,

driven from his ancestral fields by the crime of his wife’s dowry.

He founded Argyripa and Arpi, cities renowned for their men;

more renowned than the new city whose ancient site was his homeland.

#### VII. For Antilochus

Good in counsel and in war—an uncommon combination—

dear to the sons of Atreus, dear also to the sons of Aeacus:

having gained at once the rewards of courage and devotion,

I, Antilochus, died after saving my father Nestor.

This was not the proper order; but he was more justly the survivor,

without whom faithless Troy could not have been captured.

#### VIII. For Nestor

[Col. 0862B] Here I, Nestor, already lavish of a fourth age,

am covered in this tomb, renowned for counsel and eloquence,

whose son was slain, having been offered up in his father’s place,

and who became a father whose son’s wound was still alive.

Alas, why does it please the Fates to arrange life thus—

so long for us, so short for Antilochus?

#### IX. For Pyrrhus

I am buried in the middle of the world, greater in courage than my father,

because, as a boy and a king, I carried off rich spoils.

Orestes, impious before the altars, killed me by treachery.

What wonder? He was already maddened by the slaughter of his mother.

#### X. For Euryalus

Pleuronia considers me not unworthy of this title,

since my household was shared with Diomedes,

Euryalus, and Sthenelus. For I was the third to possess this kingdom;

of it now the tomb is enough.

#### XI. For Guneus

The sea possesses Guneus; the tomb, without his body, possesses his name.

His spirit returns to heaven; his fame remains among men.

All the elements are the great leader’s common tomb:

heaven, earth, sea, and the shores of men.

#### XII. For Protesilaus

The name Protesilaus was assigned to me as a fatal one.

For I was the first of the Danaans to die in the Phrygian war,

boldly entering the Sigean shores with a daring leap,

caught by the snares of deceitful Laertes’ son.

He himself, so that he might not tread upon Trojan soil,

leapt down upon his own shield.

Why do I complain? Even then my Fates were proclaiming such a death,

when my father bestowed this name upon me.

#### XIII. For Deiphobus

Betrayed to punishment through the treachery of the criminal Spartan woman,

and with his body disfigured, Deiphobus

has no tomb except the one that the pious Aeneas

and Maro composed for him in the voice of the one who calls.

#### XIV. For Hector

This is Hector’s tomb: with him his Troy was buried.

Those who perished together are buried together.

#### XV. For Astyanax

Flower of Asia, the sole survivor of so great a race,

a little child, yet already to be feared by the Argives because of his father,

here I lie, Astyanax, thrown down from the Scaean heights.

[Col. 0863A] Alas! The Neptunian walls of Ilium

saw something more cruel than Hector dragged away.

#### XVI. For Sarpedon

I, Sarpedon the Lycian, born of Jupiter, hoped by my father’s divine power

for heaven; but I am covered by this tomb,

mourned with bloody tears. Alas, iron Fates!

And must he suffer grief who has power to prevent it?

#### XVII. For Nastes and Amphimachus

Nastes and Amphimachus, illustrious offspring of Nomion,

once leaders, are now dust and shadow.

#### XVIII. For Troilus

After Hector had been overthrown, Troilus encountered the son of Aeacus

with neither equal gods nor equal strength;

dragged along by the chariots, I am joined to my brother’s honor,

[Col. 0863B] and, on account of his example, my punishment is not grievous.

#### XIX. For Polydorus

Keep far away, stranger, and flee this myrtle, unaware:

it is a crop of spears grown large on my blood.

Pierced by javelins and buried by the very slaughter,

I, Polydorus, am enclosed in this tomb twice over.

The pious Aeneas knows, and you, impious king, know,

that Thracian punishment oppresses me, while Trojan concern covers me.

#### XX. For Euphemus

The land of Troy buried Euphemus, leader of the Cicones,

in the likeness of spear-bearing Mars.

Nor is it enough to cut an inscription into the stone of the tomb:

in addition, they burden its front with the mass of a statue.

Sooner do such things collapse, which are placed there in such accumulation.

[Col. 0863C] Where the adornment is greater, a great ruin lies beneath.

#### XXI. For Hippothous and Pyleus, buried in a garden

The lowest earth holds Hippothous and Pyleus in its embrace.

Their backs above are green with cabbages and mallows.

The cultivation of the garden does not disturb their quiet ashes,

while tender vegetables are tended by a sparing hand.

#### XXII. For Ennomus and Chromius

Here lie Ennomus and Chromius, to whom Mysia was a kingdom,

to whom Alcinous was father and Oceanus an ancestor.

What good does such great nobility do? The more illustrious

their ancestry, the heavier the condition of death.

#### XXIII. For Priam

[Col. 0863D] This is not Priam’s tomb, nor do I lie in this place:

the Danaans tore my head away.

But when I had a mangled funeral without a name,

I fled, father, to the ashes of Hector.

There I found buried my sons, Troy, and Asia,

and whatever of our race lies buried anywhere.

#### XXIV. Again, for Priam

Whoever seeks Priam’s tomb should first read Hector’s.

That tomb is mine, which I myself first gave to my son.

It is at once the common tomb of Hector and his father,

since the ruin of both was joined together.

#### XXV. For Hecuba

I who was once a queen, born of illustrious Dymas,

wife of Priam, mother of Hector,

here I, Hecuba, perished, overwhelmed beneath stones thrown upon me.

But first I avenged myself upon him through the madness of my tongue.

Do not trust kingdoms, offspring, or ancestral stock,

whoever you are who read this σῆμα κυνός—“monument of a dog.”

#### XXVI. For Polyxena

Polyxena of Troy, joined to Achilles’ funeral mound,

I would rather have been covered by no mound at all.

You Achaians do not properly mingle discordant tombs:

this was more a violation than a burial.

## A FEW EPITAPHS OF OTHERS

#### XXVII. For Niobe, buried on Mount Sipylus beside a spring

I was queen of Thebes, but now I am the Sipylean cliff:

I offended the divinities, the children of Leto.

[Col. 0864B] As the joyful and proud mother of twice seven children,

I led as many funerals as I had given birth to.

Nor was this enough for the gods. Surrounded by hard stone,

I lost the appearance of a human body.

But grief, although my vital organs have been obstructed, remains,

and continually waters tears from a pious spring.

Alas, what a deed! Is there such anger in heavenly minds?

The grief still endures; the image of the mother perishes.

#### XXVIII. The same

I was alive. I became flint; then, polished

by the hands of Praxiteles, I, Niobe, live again.

The craftsman’s hands restored everything, but without sensation.

This sensation I did not possess when I offended the gods.

#### XXIX. The same

The tomb contains no dead thing within it.

Nor does the dead man himself have a tomb above.

He himself is his own tomb here, and he is dead.

#### XXX. For Dido

Unhappy Dido, well married to no husband:

when he perishes, you flee; when he flees, you perish.

#### XXXI. For Diogenes the Cynic, on whose tomb there is a dog as its emblem instead of an inscription

Tell me, dog: whose tomb is this? A dog’s. But who is this dog?

Diogenes. Has he died? He has not died, but has departed.

Diogenes, whose provision was a wallet, whose dwelling was a barrel—

has he gone to the Manes? Cerberus forbids him to go.

Where, then? Where the star of the famous Lion burns,

he has now been added to the faithful dog of Erigone.

#### XXXII. On the tomb of a sixteen-year-old matron

[Col. 0864D]

Everything that is desired over a long span of life

Anicia completed before four full lustrums had passed.

As an infant she nursed; as a girl and virgin she grew up.

She married, conceived, gave birth. Now, already a mother, she has died.

Who would accuse death? Who would not accuse it in this

age? In accomplishments she is an old woman; in years, a girl.

#### XXXIII. For Glaucia, cut off by premature death

Already, Glaucia, as a youth twice eight years old,

under the consul, was encircling your tender cheeks.

And already you had ceased to seem a boy—or perhaps a girl—

when your hastened day carried away all your beauty.

But you will not be mingled with the common crowd of the dead,

[Col. 0865A] nor will you, a lamentable shade, fear the Stygian lakes.

Rather, you will go as Cinyras’ Adonis to Persephone,

or you will be Jupiter’s catamite in Elysium.

#### XXXIV. For Callicrateia

I, Callicrateia, mother of twenty-nine, regarded the death of neither sex [the phrasing is uncertain].

But I completed a hundred and five years happily,

with my trembling hand no longer able to bear the staff.

#### XXXV. For a remarkable horse, by order of Augustus

Phosphorus, accustomed to traverse seven circuits victoriously

over the broad course of the clamorous Circus;

driving your first courses from the starting gate without reproach,

brave enough to overtake the horses who had gone before;

it was easy for you to anticipate the swift four-horse chariots:

to conquer even the victors was a higher glory.

Take this inscription as the empty consolation of a tomb,

and go winged toward Elysium and its swift-footed horses.

Let Pegasus run on your right; on your left let Arion,

your companion, go; let Castor give you a fourth horse.

#### XXXVI. On the tomb of a fortunate man

[Col. 0866A]

Sprinkle my ashes with unmixed wine and fragrant nard,

stranger, and add balsams to Punic roses.

An everlasting spring flourishes for me in an urn without tears.

I have exchanged ages; I have not died.

None of the joys of my former life has perished for me—

whether you think I remember everything, or nothing.

#### XXXVII. The empty tomb of Carus

Carus established for himself, his wife, and his children

a common tomb for their late funeral rites.

Now the monument has long stood empty; may this lament

be prolonged, and may each person come in his proper order,

who has been allotted by the law of birth;

and may he who was born first be buried first

through the peaceful course of time.

#### XXXVIII. From a tomb on the Latin Way

[Col. 0866B]

No name, no indication of whom I was born from, no account of where or what I did.

I am mute forever: ash, bones, nothing.

I am not, nor have I been; yet I was born from nothing.

Let me go, and do not reproach me with particulars—you will be such as I am.

[Col. 0865A]

## ON THE TWELVE CAESARS, WRITTEN BY SUETONIUS TRANQUILLUS (C)

Ausonius sends greetings to his son Hesperius.

[Col. 0865B]

Receive the twelve Caesarean princes, under whose reigns

Roman power long ago passed from the consuls to their rule;

each is distinguished by his own single-line verse,

through whose complete series Suetonius once set forth

[Col. 0865C] their names, deeds, lives, and deaths.

### Monostichs on the order of the twelve emperors

First Julius opened the royal palace,

Caesar, and transferred his name to Augustus and the citadel.

After him his stepson Nero Claudius ruled, from whom

Caesar took the surname that the camp had given to Caligula.

Then Claudius possessed the kingdom, after whom savage Nero,

the last of the descendants of Aeneas.

After him came three, and not for three years:

the old man Galba, trusting vainly in an ineffective ally;

soft Otho, degenerate through luxury in his infamous age;

and Vitellius, unworthy both of rule and of dying as a man.

Tenth among these, summoned by fate, was Vespasian.

And after Titus, fortunate in the brevity of his rule, came his

brother, whom Rome called “the Bald Nero.”

### The duration of the reigns of the twelve Caesars

[Col. 0865D]

Julius, as they report, the deified one, ruled for three years.

After ten lustrums Augustus extended his reign by six years,

and Nero Claudius added twice seven to the total.

The third winter brought Gaius’ ravaging period to an end.

Claudius dragged out two full hebdomads, and savage Nero

the same; only one consul was lacking from the total.

Old Galba, wanton Otho, and notorious Vitellius—

[Col. 0866B] the third summer knew you no longer as rulers of Latium,

your deaths hastened by a life worthy of disgrace.

Vespasian filled out the fatal decade for himself.

While Titus ruled, Janus was crowned with a new laurel three times;

fifteen times, while his brother held the savage reins.

### On their deaths

Julius Caesar perished while the senate raged.

Mature old age added Augustus to the gods.

Old Nero, an exile on Capreae, brought his fate to its late conclusion.

The soft Chaerea exacted punishment from Caesar.

Claudius closed out his fate through an ambiguous poison.

The matricide Nero suffered the force of his own sword.

Old Galba died, struck down by savage Otho.

Soon afterward notorious Otho, but one who obtained a glorious death.

The extravagant scepters of killing passed to Vitellius.

A praised reign, a gentle death for Vespasian.

But Titus, the love of the world, was snatched away in his flourishing years.

Late but deserved punishments destroyed his grave brother.

[Col. 0865]

## TETRASTICHS, FROM JULIUS CAESAR TO HIS OWN TIME

[Col. 0865D]

Now I shall set forth both those already mentioned and those who followed

by the lot of kingship, whom the succession of empire contains.

I shall begin with the Deified One and run through all in order,

whom the new history of Rome remembers.

### I. Julius Caesar

The empire, which once customarily belonged to two consuls,

Julius Caesar obtained.

But the brief authority of kingship, held for only three years,

was struck down by the savage faction of the armed toga.

### II. Octavian Augustus

Thereafter Octavian, at once avenger and successor,

also Caesar, but more distinguished by the name Augustus;

his long-lasting power, never violated by uncertainty,

[Col. 0867A] believed that a god had been placed upon the earth.

### III. Tiberius Nero

Having received the first name Tiberius, Nero spent

the first years of youth in a praiseworthy government.

Afterward, shut away alone in the cave of Capreae,

he believes that places conceal what his vices reveal.

### IV. Caesar Caligula

After him Caesar, surnamed from the soldier’s boot,

succeeded, more savage than savage in character:

stained by slaughter and incest, and by every

crime, he surpassed his polluted grandfather.

### V. Claudius Caesar

Claudius, mocked during the private period of his life,

displayed the nature of his character in his reign.

Yet he suffered the crimes of freedwomen and married women;

he was guilty not through doing, but through enduring them.

### VI. Nero

Nero, sixth and last heir of the race of Aeneas,

polluted and brought to an end the Julian sacred line.

As many names as piety has, so many crimes his life also possesses.

Learn them from Tranquillus; I am reluctant to remember them.

### VII. Sergius Galba

Old man, you frustrated hope: as a private citizen you seemed

worthy of gaining the scepter, but in power you proved inferior.

Your reputation was better as a young man; but the fairer order is

to have pleased afterward, after having displeased before.

### VIII. Marcus Otho

Otho, destined to bear a scepter rivaling polluted Nero’s,

was overwhelmed, carried away by a swift death.

Yet he must be praised for his end: by a noble death

he made this one thing honorable—that he died.

### IX. Aulus Vitellius

The lot of life was foul for you and unworthy, Vitellius,

that you should become Caesar. Such are the pleasures of Fate.

Yet the shadow of your reign was brief, because the rewards of kingship

are often obtained by the unworthy, though possessed only by the worthy.

### X. The Deified Vespasian

Attentive in seeking resources, moderate in their prudent use,

Vespasian increases wealth and does not suppress it.

He once transferred to better things, as a private citizen,

a doubtful reputation, rare in others, when he became princeps.

### XI. Titus Vespasian

[Col. 0867D]

Fortunate in rule, fortunate in the brevity of governing,

untouched by civil bloodshed, beloved by the world;

dying, you said that you had one crime;

but we believed that you had none, though you had one against us.

### XII. Domitian

Until now the Flavian race had produced just masters.

Why did the third steal away the two whom it had given?

It is scarcely worth having possessed them, since the gifts of good men

are brief; what has harmed us is mourned forever.

### XIII. Nerva the Tetrarch

Nerva the old man, next after the tyrant’s extinction,

governs the scepters: a prince in name, a father in mind.

The man had no offspring. Adoption imitates offspring,

which one would be glad to have chosen and would wish to have begotten.

### XIV. Trajan

Trajan undertakes the government in vigorous youth,

first in the glory of war, possessing the rest of his father.

Here too, lacking children, he joins to himself by the lot of adoption

one whom you must acknowledge good, though you must deny him equality.

### XV. Aelius Hadrian

Next Aelius entered amid distinguished achievements:

his beginnings and end are marked by a weightier reputation.

He too was childless, and by joining to himself a man destined to provide an example

he showed how far adopted sons surpass those born to one.

### XVI. Antoninus Pius

From then on Antoninus assumed the government; by his calling

and deliberations he was Pius, bearing a name earned by merit.

He had no son by fate; but according to the law of his predecessors,

he received from his country one who would govern the country.

### XVII. Marcus Antoninus

Afterward guardianship was given to Marcus, who bent Plato’s doctrines

toward imperial rule, better than his father Pius.

At his death, having an evil prince as successor,

he harmed his country only in this: that he begot him.

### XVIII. Commodus

Commodus followed, stained by arena combats,

a prince provoking war with a Thracian sword.

At last, paying the penalty with his throat cut,

he confessed through his crimes his mother’s adultery.

### XIX. Helvius Pertinax

Helvius, chosen by the judgment and decision of the senate,

proclaimed prince by decrees, not by factions;

which grieved the faithless cohort; once its error was proved,

because the senate house had yielded to military power.

### XX. Didius Julianus

Thank the gods that Didius did not rejoice in rich spoils,

and that the rewards were quickly taken from the perjured old man.

And you, father Severus, do not shrink from the title of renewer.

Your power does not seize the empire by force, but receives it back.

### XXI. Severus Pertinax

Unwearied, Severus moves his forces from the icy Danube

to take the kingdom from the parricide Didius.

His origin was Punic; but by his courage he proved

that birthplace does not stand in the way when ability has strength.

### XXII. Bassianus Antoninus Caracalla

Unlike your father in courage, and much more unlike him,

whose adoptive name you claim to bear.

Guilty through your brother’s death, punished by a bloody end,

you, Caracalla, became even more an object of the people’s mockery.

### XXIII. Opilius Macrinus

Here was the emperor’s guard; the sword taken up on behalf of Caesar

Macrinus, sluggish, turned against its instigators in slaughter.

Soon he fell together with his son. Let him cease to strike

his treachery with weighty complaints: what he suffers, he deserved.

### XXIV. Antoninus Heliogabalus

Then also did the false names of the Antonines,

which he bore, defile the inner chambers of the Augustan seat?

[lacuna]

(The remainder is missing.)

[Col. 0869]

## THE ORDER OF THE NOBLE CITIES (C)

### I. Rome

[Col. 0869A]

First among cities, golden Rome, home of the gods.

### II. Constantinople and Carthage

Carthage rises beside Constantinople, the earlier city,

not yielding by an entire degree, because it disdains to be called third,

not daring to hope for second place,

which belonged to both of them. Ancient wealth prefers this city;

recent fortune prefers that one. The former was once supreme, the latter now rises,

and, excelling through new merits, overshadows ancient honor;

it forces Elissa to yield to Constantine.

Carthage, now full of shame, accuses the gods,

if even now she must yield, having scarcely endured Rome before.

Let ancient fortune settle your swelling pride.

Go as equals at last, remembering that by divine power

[Col. 0869B] you changed narrow resources and names:

you were Byzantine Lygos; you were Punic Byrsa.

### III. Antioch and Alexandria

Antioch, home of Phoebus’ laurel, is third;

Alexandria, if placed fourth, would wish it.

Both have one rank; the fury of ambition

drives them into rivalry. Both are turbulent with the crowd’s vices

and scarcely sane amid the unhealthy tumult of a mad people.

This city boasts because it is fortified by the Nile,

and deeply embedded in remote places, fertile and safe.

That one because it is set against the treacherous Persians as their rival.

And you too, go as equals, and exalt the name of the Macedonians.

Great Alexander founded you; that city names Seleucus,

whose anchor was a mark of free birth,

as is commonly branded upon the body—a sure sign of lineage.

For throughout the whole succession of his descendants

[Col. 0869C] the natural likeness continued to run.

### IV. Trier

Long has warlike Gaul desired to celebrate

the throne of the city of Trier, which lies near the Rhine

and rests secure in the lap of peace,

feeding, clothing, and arming the strength of the empire.

Broad walls extend across the long hill.

The Moselle flows generously past in a tranquil stream,

carrying distant commerce from every kind of land.

### V. Milan

Everything is remarkable at Milan too: abundance of resources;

countless and cultivated houses, eloquent talents

and cheerful manners among its men; then the appearance of the place,

enlarged by a double wall, and the people’s delight—

the Circus, and the wedge-shaped mass of the enclosed theater;

temples, palatine citadels, and wealthy Mint,

and the district famous beneath the honor of Hercules’ bath,

and all adorned with marble colonnades bearing statues,

and walls enclosed like the rim of a valley—

everything that excels, as though rivaling great forms of construction;

nor does the neighboring closeness of Rome oppress it.

### VI. Capua

Nor shall I be silent about Capua, powerful in sea, adornment, provisions,

luxury, wealth, and its earlier fame,

though Fortune changes her turns; she did not know how to preserve moderation

when the seas were favorable. Now subject to Rome,

then her rival. Remembering loyalty—or perhaps disloyal,

uncertain whether to disdain or honor the senate—

she dared to hope for curule offices under Campanian auspices

and for one of her own men to be consul,

so that she might raise the empire of a divided world.

Indeed, she attacked the mistress of the world and mother of Latium in war,

not trusting leaders in the toga,

having sworn by Hannibal’s arms; and, deceived,

the mad city passed into the enemy’s slavery

under the appearance of a master.

Soon, when both had fallen into decline through shared vices—

the Carthaginians through luxury, Campania through pride—

(alas, pride has never received a stable dwelling!),

that city, once powerful and strong in wealth,

which could adorn heights with equal cones,

rejected into eighth place, scarcely maintains its position.

### VII. Aquileia

This place was not originally ranked here; nevertheless, enlarged by recent growth,

Aquileia is rightly celebrated as ninth among renowned cities,

an Italian colony set against the Illyrian mountains,

famous for its walls and harbor; but still more remarkable for this:

in the final age it welcomed you,

the one for whom, after a full lustrum had passed,

the Greatest One would at last release late punishments,

once under the name of an arms-bearing camp follower.

Happy city, which joyfully witnessed so great a triumph

and punished the Rutupine robber in an Ausonian battle.

### VIII. Arles

Open, welcoming Arles, your twin harbors,

Gallic Rome, Arles, which Narbo Martius and wealthy Vienna

with Alpine settlers inhabit beside you.

You are so cut apart by the swift waters of the Rhône

that you make a central street with a naval bridge.

Through it you receive the commerce of the Roman world,

and do not restrain it; you enrich other peoples and walls—

the peoples whom Gaul and broad-bosomed Aquitania enjoy.

### IX. Mérida

After these, illustrious Mérida, you shall be remembered by me

as an Iberian name, beside which a river flows from the sea,

and to which all Spain lowers its fasces.

Neither Corduba nor Tarraco, strong in its citadel, competes with you,

nor wealthy Bracara, which displays itself in a sea-bay.

### X. Athens

Now let us recall Athens too, with her earth-born fathers,

once the citadel of Pallas and of Consus in their contest,

to whom first came the olive tree, bringer of peace.

She is the whole glory of the eloquent Attic tongue.

From her, through the peoples of Ionia and the Achaean name,

the Greek hand spread and poured itself into a hundred cities.

### XI. Catana and Syracuse

Who could be silent about Catana? Who about fourfold Syracuse—

the former celebrated for the devotion of the burned brothers,

the latter embracing the marvels of spring and river?

The waters, running beneath the salty depths of the Ionian sea,

unite the sweet streams that please them in their chosen dwelling,

mingling the kisses of uncorrupted waters.

### XII. Toulouse

[Col. 0871A]

I shall never leave unmentioned Toulouse, my nurse,

which a vast circuit of baked-brick walls surrounds,

and beside whose flank the Garonne flows in a beautiful stream;

a city cultivated by countless peoples, near

the snowy Pyrenees and the pine-bearing Cévennes,

between the Aquitanian nations and the Iberian name.

Although it has now poured out four cities from itself,

it feels no loss of its exhausted population,

embracing in its bosom all the colonists whom it produced.

### XIII. Narbo

Nor shall you, Martial Narbo, be silent in my poem:

by whose name a province, once spread through an immense kingdom,

held many colonists by the right of dominion.

Where the Allobroges insinuate themselves along the banks toward the Sequani;

[Col. 0871B] where the Alpine peaks exclude the Italians from the borders;

where the Iberians are divided by the Pyrenean snows;

where the Rhône rushes headlong from its father, Lake Geneva;

where the fields of Aquitania press inward beneath the Cévennes,

all the way to the Tectosages and the rustic peoples called Volcae,

the whole region was Narbo. You, first of Gaul,

raise the fasces of the toga-bearing name under a Roman proconsul.

Who could recount your harbors, mountains, and lakes?

Who your peoples, distinguished by their varied clothing and features?

And your temple, once built of Parian marble,

was of such great mass that in former times it would not have been disdained

by Tarquinius, or Catulus again, or that last Caesar

who set up the golden roofs of the Capitol?

The goods of the eastern sea and the Iberian waters enrich you;

the fleets of Libya and the Sicilian deep enrich you;

and whatever is conveyed by rivers and straits in varied courses

sails to you from throughout the world as a κατάπλους—an arrival by sea.

### XIV. Bordeaux

Long ago I condemned my impious silence, because I did not recall you,

my homeland, renowned for Bacchus, rivers, and men,

for the customs and talents of your people, and for your senate of nobles,

[Col. 0872A] among the foremost—as though, conscious of the city’s modest size,

I hesitated to bestow undeserved praises upon you.

There is no shame for us in this. For my home is not on

the barbarous banks of the Rhine, nor in icy Haemus beneath the northern sky.

Bordeaux is my native soil: here the climate is mild,

and the generous kindness of watered earth;

spring is long, winters brief, and leafy ridges lie beneath;
streams that imitate the windings of the sea run warm.

The fourfold plan of its walls is so lofty, with tall towers,

that its elevated summits enter the airy clouds.

You may marvel at the streets laid out within,

at the arrangement of the houses and the broad avenues preserving their name;

then at the gates answering one another along straight crossings,

and at the channel of the fountain river through the middle of the city.

When Father Ocean fills it with his returning tide,

you will watch the whole plain glide along with fleets.

Why should I recall the fountain covered with Parian marble,

boiling like the strait of Euripus—how deep the shade of its waters!

How great the swelling of the river! With what rushing mass

does its steep current fall, confined along its edge

through twelve mouths, never exhausted for the countless uses of the people!

You would wish, king of the Medes, to bring this water to your camps,

when your rivers have failed after their course was consumed:

to carry the waters of this fountain through foreign cities,

as you were accustomed to carry one Choaspes through them all.

Hail, fountain whose source is unknown, sacred, nourishing, everlasting,

glassy, blue-green, deep, sonorous, clear, shadowed.

Hail, genius of the city, drinkable in medicinal draughts,

DIVONA in the language of the Celts, fountain added to the gods.

Aponus is not purer in drink, nor Nemausus in its glassy light,

nor Timavus fuller in its sea-like current.

[Col. 0872C] This final labor will have gathered together famous cities.

And just as illustrious Rome is the head of the number,

so let Bordeaux establish her seat with a twofold summit at this head.

This is my homeland; yet Rome surpasses all homelands.

I love Bordeaux; I revere Rome. In this city I am a citizen,

in both I am consul. Here are my cradle, there my curule chair.

[Col. 0871]

## THE PLAY OF THE SEVEN SAGES

Ausonius, consul, sends greetings to the proconsul Latinus Drepanius Pacatus. (C)

Whether you think these things deserve pardon or recognition,

read through them, Drepanius, with attentive judgment.

I shall be even-tempered under your judgment: whether you think

the poems we have given should be read or concealed.

For the first thing is to have earned your favor, Pacatus;

the next concern will be the defense of modesty.

I can endure the censorship of a severe reader,

and I can be satisfied with modest praise.

The horse knows how to love the sound of an applauded neck;

the fearless horse knows how to endure the slow blows.

Aristarchus the critic and Zenodotus’ standard

sought such cultivation for Homer, the Maeonian.

Therefore place the obeli—the marks of spuriousness—upon false poets.

I shall consider my palms, not my faults.

And what the learned man’s file adds to me

I shall call corrected rather than condemned.

Meanwhile, about to undergo the weight of so great a judgment,

I shall hope to please; if not, at least to remain hidden.

### Prologue

[Col. 0872C]

The Seven Sages, to whom that name was given

by an earlier age and not removed by the age that followed,

come forth today into the orchestra wearing Greek cloaks.

Why are you ashamed, toga-clad Roman,

that such distinguished men will enter the stage?

This should shame us, not the Athenians also,

for whom the theater takes the place of the senate house.

Our public business has been assigned its places by lot:

the Campus for the elections, the senate house for the Conscript Fathers,

the Forum and Rostra for separate groups of citizens.

At Athens and throughout all Greece there is one place

for the deliberation of public affairs,

which luxury established late in our city.

Formerly an aedile would spread out a stage of planks,

raised suddenly without any mass of stone.

So did Muraena and Gallius. I shall speak what is known.

After the powerful, no longer fearing expense,

[Col. 0873A] believed that they had acquired an everlasting name, if once …

A mass of stone constructed on a foundation of rock

Would establish a place for games for all time:

This immense theater grew in wedge-shaped tiers.

Pompey, Balbus, and Caesar

Octavian provided it, vying with one another in expense.

But why am I concerned with these matters? I did not come here

To explain who founded the theaters, who the Forum,

Who the separate sections of the city walls;

But to pass before men worthy of reverence and divine praise,

And to report what they mean.

They are accustomed to announce their own maxims,

Which each of those provident men has anticipated.

You certainly know what they are; but if memory

Closes them away among ancient matters, Ludius will come,

[Col. 0873B]

The interpreter of these sayings, which I hold only imperfectly.

### Ludius

Tradition says that Solon the Athenian inscribed at Delphi,

“Know yourself” (*Γνῶθι σεαυτόν*), which in Latin is *Nosce te*.

Many think this saying belonged to Chilon of Sparta.

They dispute whether it belongs to the Spartan Chilon or not,

Because what is introduced—*ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου*—

Commands: “Look to the end of a long life.”

Many believe that Solon said this to Croesus.

And tradition says that Pittacus of Lesbos said,

“Recognize the opportune moment” (*Γίγνωσκε καιρόν*),

Urging you to know the proper time.

But *kairos* (*καιρός*) here means a seasonable or timely moment.

Bias of Priene said, “Most people are bad” (*οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί*),

Which in Latin is: “Most human beings are bad”;

But understand that he called inexperienced people bad.

[Col. 0873C]

“Practice is everything” (*Μελέτη τὸ πᾶν*) belongs to Periander of Corinth,

Who considers reflection to be everything.

“Measure is best” (*Ἄριστον μέτρον*) was said by Cleobulus of Lindus—

That is, “The best course for everyone is moderation.”

Thales brought forward, “Surety: ruin is at hand” (*Ἐγγύα, πάρεστι δ’ ἄτη*).

He forbids us to make promises, since harm stands ready at hand.

This warning does not please us who lend at interest.

I have spoken. I shall withdraw. The lawgiver Solon is coming.

### Solon

Following Greek custom, I, Solon, come forth upon the stage,

To whom tradition has awarded the palm among the Seven Wise Men.

But tradition is not the strictness of judgment.

Nor do I consider myself first—or last—among you,

Since equality cannot endure rank.

[Col. 0873D]

Long ago the Delphic god rightly commanded the foolish man

Who asked which of the wise men was first

To inscribe their names upon the rounded globe,

So that no one might be first, nor anyone last.

I, Solon, come forth from the middle of their circle.

Whatever I am thought to have said to King Croesus,

Let every class of human beings consider it spoken to itself.

The Greek expression *ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου*—

“Look to the end of a long life”—becomes more extended when explained in Latin:

“I command everyone to look to the end of life.”

Therefore avoid calling anyone wretched or blessed,

For human beings always stand in an uncertain condition.

That is indeed so. If I can, I shall speak briefly.

Was Croesus of Lydia a king or a tyrant?

[Col. 0874A]

He belonged among the blessed, rich beyond measure,

And gave temples to the gods with walls of gold.

He summoned me. I come, obedient to his command,

So that the Lydians might make use of a better king.

He asks me to name a blessed man, if I know one.

I name Telanus, a citizen of no mean standing.

Fighting for his country, he had offered his life.

Croesus dismissed him and asked for another. I found Aglaus,

Who had never crossed the boundaries of his own little farm.

But he, laughing, said, “Where then do you place me,

Who alone am called blessed throughout the whole world?”

I say that the end of life must first be awaited;

Only then may one judge whether happiness remains.

Croesus received my answer with displeasure. But I

Leave the king. He prepares war against the Persians.

[Col. 0874B]

He sets out, is defeated, captured, and surrendered to the king.

[lacuna]

But he, captured, was himself like a funeral procession.

[lacuna]

The flame spread around him on every side,

Rolling smoky globes of heat high into the air.

And almost too late Croesus, in a mighty voice,

Cried, “O truly prophetic man! O Solon, Solon!”

He called Solon’s name three times in a loud cry.

At that voice Cyrus, moved, ordered the fire

To be extinguished all around and the burning pyre destroyed.

And just then a rain poured down from the clouds

And subdued the fire. Croesus was immediately led

Before the king, carried by the hands of attendants.

Asked whom he had meant by naming Solon,

And why he had called upon that name,

[Col. 0874C]

He explained the whole sequence of events to the king.

Cyrus pitied him; seeing the power of fortune,

He praised Solon and counted Croesus among his friends.

He ordered him to remain with him, bound

With golden fetters, for the rest of his life.

I was praised and approved by the testimony

Of two kings, and by both of them.

Let each person consider what was said to one to have been said to himself.

I have now completed the reason for which I came here.

Look—Chilon is coming. Farewell, and applaud.

### Chilon

My loins ache from sitting and my eyes from watching,

As I waited for Solon to withdraw.

Good heavens, how little the Athenians say in so much time!

At last he completed one maxim in three hundred verses

And, looking back at me, went away.

I am Chilon the Spartan, who now come forth.

By the brevity for which we Laconians are known,

I commend our *γνῶθι σεαυτόν*, “Know yourself,”

Which is already inscribed upon the Delphic column.

That labor is difficult, but its fruit is excellent:

To distinguish what you can bear and what you cannot;

To examine, by night and by day, what you do and what you have done,

Even down to the finest point.

All duties—modesty, honor, steadfastness—

Are contained in this; and glory, despised by us,

Is also contained in it.

I have spoken. Farewell, and bear this in mind. I do not wait for applause.

### Cleobulus

[Col. 0875A]

I am Cleobulus, a citizen of a small island,

But the author of a great maxim, by which I am renowned:

“Measure is best” (*Ἄριστον μέτρον*), as they believe I said.

You there, nearest to the orchestra,

In the fourteen seats closest to the steps,

Interpret it: does *Ἄριστον μέτρον* mean

“The best course is moderation”?

You say yes; I thank you. I shall proceed.

In order, your poet seems to have said this very thing here:

“Let nothing be excessive” (*UT NE QUID NIMIS*).

And one of our own sayings, “Nothing in excess” (*μηδὲν ἄγαν*),

Belongs here also.

The sense is the same, whether Italian or Dorian:

There is a measure in speaking, silence, sleep, and waking,

In kindnesses, gratitude, and injury,

In study and in labor. Whatever exists in life

Requires this measure of the finest restraint.

I have spoken. I shall withdraw, so that there may be moderation. Thales is coming.

### Thales

I am Thales of Miletus; “Water” (*AQUAM*) I declared to be the first principle

In the creation of things, as the prophetic poet Pindar did.

[lacuna]

Fishermen drew it from the sea.

For, at the Delian god’s command, they had chosen me:

He had sent this gift to a wise man.

I refused to accept it, but returned it

To be carried to others whom I considered wiser.

Then, after it had been sent through all seven wise men

And sent back again, they returned it to me.

I received it and consecrated it to Apollo.

For if Phoebus commands that a wise man be chosen,

[Col. 0875C]

It is proper to believe not any human being, but a god.

That, then, is who I am. But the reason I came upon the stage

Is that two men before me have made me

The defender of my maxim.

It will displease those who lack prudence,

But not those whom experience has instructed and made knowledgeable.

We say *ἐγγύα, πάρεστι δ’ ἄτη*:

In Latin: “Give your surety; harm is at hand for you.”

I could run through a thousand examples to prove

That guarantors and sureties are answerable for regret.

But I do not wish to name anyone individually.

Let each of you say it to himself and consider inwardly

For how many people giving surety has brought damage and harm.

Nevertheless, may this service remain pleasing to both sides.

Some of you, then, applaud; those offended, applaud me off the stage.

### Bias

[Col. 0876A]

I am Bias of Priene; I said, “Most people are bad” (*οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί*).

I suspect that the Latin version is: “Most are bad.”

I would prefer not to have said, “Truth produces hatred.”

But I called bad the inexperienced and barbarous:

Those who disregard justice, equity, and sacred customs.

For this people surrounding the theater

Is entirely good; the land of our enemies contains

Those whom you think I called “Most people are bad.”

Yet no one can be so bad a judge

That he does not join himself to the side of the good.

Whether he is truly good, or merely wishes to be called so,

He has already fled that hated name, “bad.”

I depart. Farewell, and applaud: most people are good.

### Pittacus

[Col. 0876B]

I am Pittacus of Mytilene, a Lesbian,

Who uttered the maxim, “Recognize the opportune moment” (*Γίγνωσκε καιρόν*).

But this *kairos*, “know the time,” gives this warning:

There is also a *kairos*, the timely moment, as it is called.

In Roman language: “Come at the right time.”

Your comic poet Terence likewise maintains

That timing is the first thing in every matter,

As when the slave Dromo came to Antiphila

Without hindrance, observing the proper moment.

Consider, all of you, how often offense arises

When appropriateness has not been observed.

It is time for me to depart, lest I become troublesome. Applaud.

### Periander

I, Periander, born at Ephyra, come forth here,

Who said, “Reflection is everything” (*Μελέτη τὸ πᾶν*), and approve the saying:

Reflection is everything in what you undertake.

For only the person who considers every business beforehand

Is effective in carrying it out.

Whether circumstances are adverse or favorable,

The comic poet Terence declares that all things must be considered beforehand.

To take office, wage war, or lay it down—

To undertake great, moderate, and even small matters—

One should always deliberate beforehand.

For all are slower in new undertakings

If consideration of the task has been lacking.

There is nothing that requires more careful attention

Than considering what ought to be done; thereafter,

When people do not think, chance rather than judgment governs.

But now I withdraw to the senators. Applaud,

Having deliberated, so that you may care for the commonwealth.

[Col. 0875]

## THE MAXIMS OF THE SEVEN WISE MEN

Explained by Ausonius in seven verses for each.

### Bias of Priene

[Col. 0875D]

What is the highest good? A mind conscious of its own rectitude.

What is the greatest destruction for a human being? Another human being alone.

Who is rich? The person who desires nothing. Who is poor? The miser.

What is the finest dowry of a married woman? A chaste life.

Who is chaste? The woman about whom rumor is afraid to lie.

What is the work of the prudent? When able, to be unwilling to harm.

What belongs especially to the foolish? Being unable to harm, yet wishing to do so.

### Pittacus of Mytilene

He will not know how to speak who does not know how to be silent.

I would rather be approved by one good man than by many bad ones.

A madman envies the fortunate in their prosperity.

A madman laughs at the sufferings of the unfortunate.

Obey the law that you yourself have established as law.

Acquire many friends in prosperity.

Test a few friends in adversity.

### Cleobulus of Lindus

[Col. 0877A]

The more one is permitted, the less one should wish.

Unmerited misery is the object of Fortune’s envy.

No one will long remain fortunate if guilty.

Forgive much in others; nothing in yourself.

Whoever spares the wicked wishes to destroy the good.

Glory is not granted on account of the merits of ancestors.

A shameful reputation is often bestowed upon lesser men.

### Periander of Corinth

The useful never differs from the honorable.

The more anxious a person is, the happier he is.

To wish for death is bad; to fear it is worse.

Make yourself willing to do what is necessary.

Terrible to many, beware of many.

[Col. 0877B]

If fortune favors you, beware of being lifted up.

If fortune thunders, beware of being plunged down.

### Solon of Athens

I say that life is happy only when its fate has been completed.

Let like be joined to like in marriage. Whatever is unlike is discordant.

Honors will never be gifts bestowed by chance.

Reprove a relative secretly; praise him publicly.

It is much nobler to become noble than to be born so.

If one’s lot is fixed by decree, what good will caution do?

If everything is uncertain, what is there to fear?

### Chilon of Lacedaemon

[Col. 0878A]

I do not wish the lesser to fear me, nor the greater to despise me.

Live mindful of death, so that you may be mindful of safety as well;

Overcome all sadness either by courage or by a friend.

If you do something well, it is not right to remember it.

Whatever good things you receive, remember them forever.

A pleasant old age for a human being is one that resembles youth;

That youth is more burdensome which resembles old age.

### Thales of Miletus

Fear to undertake anything shameful when you have no witness.

Life perishes, but the glory of death does not perish.

What you are going to do, do not announce beforehand.

It is a torment to fear what you cannot overcome.

When you rebuke truthfully, you help as an enemy.

When you praise falsely, you harm even as a friend.

[Col. 0878B]

Nothing excessive is enough, lest even this become excessive.

## On the Same Seven Wise Men, from the Greek

I shall set out the homeland, names, and sayings

Of the seven wise men in verse; each shall speak his own line:

Chilon, whose homeland is Lacedaemon: “Know yourself.”

Periander of Corinth: “Control your trembling anger.”

Pittacus, from the people of Mytilene: “Nothing in excess.”

Cleobulus of Lindus says: “The best measure in everything.”

Solon, born at Athens, teaches us to await the end.

Bias of famous Priene says that most people are bad.

Thales, fosterling of Miletus, says: “Flee the surety.”

[Col. 0877]

# IDYLLS

*(C)*

## IDYLL I. Easter Verses, addressed to Proculus

[Col. 0877C]

The sacred festivals of saving Christ return,

And devout initiates celebrate their fasts.

But we, holding perpetual worship within our breast,

Continue the force of our undefiled honors.

Our care for sacred things is annual, our reverence unbroken.

Great Father of the universe, to whom earth, sea, and air,

And Tartarus and the starry region of the painted sky are subject;

Whom the sinful multitude fears,

And whom again the nourishing throng of pious souls

Celebrates with prayers:

You grant this brief course of life and the swift

End of our perishable soul as a gift of eternal life.

You bestow upon the human race the gentle teachings of your laws

And your sacred prophets, and preserve them for posterity,

[Col. 0877D]

Taking pity on Adam in his deception,

Whom Eve, captured by poisons, entangled as her companion

In her seductive errors.

You grant to the earth your Word, O loving Father,

Your Son and your God, wholly like and equal,

Truth from the true, living from a living origin.

He, instructed by your commands, added this one thing:

That the Spirit, who floated upon the watery surface,

Might invigorate sluggish limbs through an immortal washing.

Threefold faith, from one author; certain hope of salvation

Embraces this number through joined virtues.

Such an example is also seen upon earth:

The Augustus who is a father, the begetter of two Augustuses.

He embraces both brother and son with pious divinity,

Shares the kingdom but does not divide what is one,

Alone possessing everything and generously giving everything.

[Col. 0878C]

Therefore, establish these rulers for us, vigorous in threefold piety,

Peaceful governors of the earth and ministers of heaven,

O Christ, as pleasing to the eternal Father.

## IDYLL II. Funeral Poem for His Father, Julius Ausonius

I, Ausonius by name, was not the least skilled in the art of healing;

And if you had known my period, I was the first.

I lived among neighboring cities, with my homeland and household:

My homeland was Vasates, but Bordeaux my hearth.

Both curias and both senates counted me

As excluded from office, though a participant by name.

Neither wealthy nor needy, I lived frugally without meanness.

I always had the same food, clothing, and habits.

I was unready in Latin speech; but the Attic tongue

Was sufficient for the expressions of cultivated eloquence.

[Col. 0878D]

I offered help to all who requested the art I gave freely,

And my service was accompanied by devotion.

I sought to render the judgment of good men concerning me;

Yet I myself was never pleased with myself as my own judge.

The duties owed to many, with differing forms of regard,

I distributed according to persons, merits, and time.

I abstained from lawsuits; I neither increased nor diminished the matter.

No one perished because of my accusation, nor because of my testimony.

I never envied. I rejected desire and ambition.

I considered swearing and speaking falsely equally wrong.

No faction or conspiracy joined me to itself.

I cultivated friendships in a sincere bond.

I knew that the happy person is not one who possesses whatever he wants,

But one who does not desire what fate has not given.

I was not one who intercepted people, nor a chatterer;

I did not enter places whose doors and curtains concealed what was within.

[Col. 0879A]

I did not invent a reputation that could tear apart the lives of good men;

And if I learned the truth, I kept silent.

Anger was far from me; vain hope was far from me; anxious care was far from me;

And false joys in the prosperity of human beings were far from me.

I avoided gatherings and renounced disturbances,

As well as the constantly feigned friendships of rulers.

I never thought it a matter for praise to have committed no offense,

And I preferred good morals to laws.

Quick to become angry, I hastened to bury my emotion;

And I imposed penalties upon myself for my lightness.

For nine lustral periods I had one marriage,

Harmonious and without wrongdoing; we had four children.

The first died while still nursing; the last of my life,

Not unformed in understanding though still immature in age, died at puberty.

[Col. 0879B]

Maximus reached the highest summit of honors,

As prefect of Gaul, Libya, and Latium;

Tranquil, merciful, serene in eyes, voice, and face,

In mind and spirit a father to his own father.

I saw both his son and his son-in-law as proconsuls.

I had certain hope that he himself would become consul.

My daughter possessed the dignity of a married woman.

Her praise was outstanding both as wife and as widow;

She saw the households of her son, her son-in-law, and her grandson

Made illustrious by the multiple honor of them all.

I myself, neither seeking nor rejecting honors,

Am now called prefect of great Illyricum.

This generous indulgence of fortune persuaded me,

With reverence paid to the divine will, to seek departure from life,

So that no day might wound with a fatal bite

The inviolate span of a fortunate life.

I attained this; my prayers were heard. I leave to others

Hope, vows, and fear, lulled into a peaceful end.

Among grieving friends—but I myself was not grieving—

I lay down according to the arrangements for my funeral.

I completed ninety years without a staff, with my whole body

Sound and unimpaired in all its duties.

Whoever reads these words will not disdain to say:

“May your life be such as my wishes were.”

## IDYLL III. Ausonius’ Little Estate

Hail, little inheritance, the kingdom of my ancestors,

Which great-grandfather, grandfather, and father cultivated,

And which he leaves me, now that I am old,

Through his hastened death.

Alas! I had not wished to be able to enjoy it so soon.

It is proper indeed for a son to succeed his father in order;

Yet for the pious it is a more welcome arrangement to be masters together.

Now the labor and cares are mine. Formerly pleasure alone

Belonged to my portion; everything else belonged to my father.

A small inheritance, I admit, but nothing was ever small

To a man of even temper; add also, of a single mind.

I think it right for the estate to depend upon the spirit,

Not for the spirit to depend upon the estate.

Croesus desires everything; Diogenes nothing;

Aristippus scatters gold in the middle of the Syrtes;

All Lydia is not enough of gold for Midas.

For the person whose desire has no limit, possession has no limit.

The measure of wealth is whatever you establish in your mind.

But learn how large this field of mine is; learn me as well,

[Col. 0880A]

And, if you are able, learn yourself too—

Although it is difficult to know oneself: *Γνῶθι σεαυτόν*.

As quickly as we read this, so quickly we neglect it.

I cultivate two hundred *iugera* of land; the vineyard is cultivated

On one hundred *iugera*, and the meadows on half that amount.

The woodland is more than twice as large as the meadows, vineyard, and plowland together.

There are neither too many nor too few cultivators of the land for us.

A spring and a shallow well are nearby, and then a clear river.

This navigable, flowing-back river carries me and brings me back.

The produce stored away for me always lasts two full years.

For the person whose provisions are not abundant, hunger is also ready at hand.

This estate lies neither far from the city nor entirely in the city:

So that I may not suffer from crowds and may enjoy my possessions.

And whenever distaste compels me to change my place,

[Col. 0880B]

I cross over and enjoy the countryside and the city in turn.

## IDYLL IV. An Exhortation to His Grandson Ausonius on the Study of Childhood

### Ausonius to his son Hesperius, greetings

I have sent you in advance for reading a little book which I had composed in play, as an exhortation for my little grandson, your sister’s son. I preferred this to reciting it myself, so that your judgment might be freer, for two reasons usually obstruct it: what our ears hear passes more quickly than what they read, and the sincerity of judgment is burdened by the presence of the person reciting. Now both conditions are intact for you (our modesty does not stand in the way).

But listen, dearest son: I have something to warn you about. If some passages seem arranged with much more polish than truth, and to possess more color than substance, I knowingly allowed them to flow, so that they might be rather pretty than strong, like girls whose mothers try to make them slender by lowering their shoulders and giving them reedlike chests. You know the rest.

It remains for you to say: “Why do you delay my judgment of something which you yourself declare to be faulty?” I shall say, of course, that I am ashamed of such verses in public; I wrote them more for his years than for mine—or perhaps for mine as well: “Old men are twice children” (*δὶς παῖδες οἱ γέροντες*). In short, let your severity be at rest; I am dealing with a child. Farewell, dearest son.

The Muses too have their own games; leisure mixed with song

Is fitting, beloved grandson, and the teacher’s commanding voice

Does not always subject children to harsh exercise.

But fixed times preserve an ordered alternation of rest and study.

It is enough for an attentive boy to have read willingly.

[Col. 0880D]

It is also permissible to pause. “School” is called by a Greek name

So that proper leisure may be granted to the laboring Muses.

The more confidently you know that play follows work in turn,

Learn willingly. We give intervals to soften

The long labor. Childhood’s study grows weary

Unless cheerful holidays vary the stern working days.

Learn willingly, and do not hate, grandson,

The reins of your grim teacher. Never is the teacher’s appearance

So terrible that, once one has become accustomed to it,

His face will remain savage. He may be gloomy with age,

Not cheerful in voice, and threaten harsh quarrels

From his contracted brow;

But never will he be monstrous whose face has become familiar.

The child who rejects his mother will love his nurse’s wrinkles.

Late-born grandchildren, a new care in old age,

Prefer their grandfathers and trembling grandmothers to their fathers.

[Col. 0881A]

Thus Achilles was not frightened by Chiron, tutor of Achilles,

Who was mixed with a Thessalian horse; nor did the pine-bearing Atlas

Frighten the son of Amphitryon;

Rather, each gently soothed his tender pupil with kind words.

You too need not be afraid, although the school

May shout under many blows and the old teacher may wear

A savage expression.

Fear reveals degenerate spirits; but stand firm,

Undaunted, and let neither the cry nor the resounding blows,

Nor fear during the early morning hours, disturb you:

Neither the scepter which the cane brandishes,

Nor the abundant bundle of rods,

Nor the deceptive leather that covers the whip,

Nor your benches boiling with anxious commotion.

Let the pomp of the place and the theater of empty fear be avoided.

In former days your father and mother, following this course,

Caressed my secure old age with peaceful affection.

[Col. 0881B]

You, grandson who bear my name, first in character,

Grant me enjoyment of whatever old age the Fates

May give me as the passing years flow on,

Whether in reality or in hope.

Now I shall see you as a boy, soon in the years of youth,

And already as a man, if fortune so commands; or if

Envy forbids it, I shall nonetheless hope, and my prayers will not fail,

That, mindful always of your father and of me,

You may desire the lofty prizes of the Muses.

May you one day walk eloquently along this road

Which we have traveled before you, and upon which

Your father as proconsul and your uncle as prefect urge you onward.

Read through whatever is memorable. I shall give you private advice.

[Col. 0881C]

The author of the *Iliad*, and the charming beginnings of Menander,

Must be unfolded for you. With the bend and precision of your voice

Bring forth countless rhythms through learned accents.

Impose the emotions as you read. Pausing and division

Increase meaning, and intervals give strength to the inert.

When will such gifts reach my old age?

When will you renew for me, now old, so many poems,

So many histories linked together through the ages,

The comedies and royal curtains,

And the melodious and lyric modes, by your recitation,

And make my dulled senses grow young again?

With you leading, grandson, I shall be permitted to learn again

The measured poems of Horace and the high-sounding path of Maro.

You too, who run through Terence, learned in Latin speech,

Graceful in Terence’s chosen Latin speech, and treading the stage in the close-fitting comic slipper,

Compel my scarcely remembering old age to new dialogues.

Already I join together in a sequence of twelve years

Your deed, Catiline, and the disturbance of Lepidus,

Beginning with Lepidus and Catulus, the events and times of Rome.

Already I read the civil war mixed with the war of Mars,

Which Sertorius, an exile among his Iberian ally, set in motion.

[Col. 0881D]

I give this advice as no inexperienced grandfather,

But one who has tested a thousand minds in teaching.

I myself nourished many during their nursing years;

Fostering them in my lap and loosening their murmurs,

I rescued their tender age from indulgent nurses.

Soon, with gentle instruction and mild fear,

I enticed boys to seek progress through hardships,

So that they might pluck the sweet fruit from a bitter root.

In the same way I led young men, already at the threshold of maturity,

Toward good morals, skills, and vigor in speech,

Although they refused to bear authority upon their necks

And would not offer their faces to bridles.

A difficult balance, hard experience, rare success,

Observed through long familiarity with affairs—

These are needed for a gentle judgment to govern

An untutored youth.

These things I endured until hardship itself

Began to give pleasure and good habit softened labor through use,

Until I was summoned to the pious duties of Augustan discipline

And girded with increased honors of various kinds:

When I was ordered to obey the golden palaces.

May Nemesis stand aside, and may fortune also bear with my jesting.

I presided over the authority while he, clothed in purple bordered with youth,

With scepter and throne, set the rights of a teacher before himself,

And Augustus considered our honors greater than his own.

These he soon produced in lofty and mature advancement:

I was appointed quaestor to the Augustuses, father and son;

I received a double prefecture and the curule chair;

As consul I put on the embroidered robe and painted toga as my rewards,

And was given precedence in my official records.

[Col. 0882B]

As consul and grandfather I sought this great distinction for my grandson,

And I shine as a light before your life.

Although for a long time you could already be considered

Illustrious, adorned, and honored under your father’s name,

A famous honor from us was added nevertheless.

Make sure it does not become a burden: through your own effort,

Climb upward, leaning upon it,

And hope for your own fasces when you are consul.

## IDYLL V. Birthday Poem for the Same Grandson, Ausonius

When, still in your childish years, the diligent care

Of your constant teacher first offered you poems,

And filled your new ears and receptive senses,

So that your corrected tongue might utter

The answering words with a teachable murmur,

We old men added nothing sad,

Lest the care of admonition should injure you

Or spoil sweet tastes with bitterness.

But now, as you flourish in the movement of youth

And can distinguish strength from tenderness,

And seem yourself to be an adviser of morals and speech,

Receive not indeed commands, but the wishes

Of your praying and grateful grandfather,

On the solemn festival of his grandson.

[lacuna]

Grant me by your assent to pass my old age safely,

Restored from the end of fate; and to see festive days

And long-doubted stars, when in my declining years I have almost been given up for dead.

This, beloved grandson, has been gained for me with doubled interest

As your birthday approaches; and this gift of health

Is fuller for me because your honor grows with your youthful years,

And I, already old, now see my grandson as a young man.

[Col. 0882D]

This is the sixth three-year cycle that returns to you from your first year,

Bringing the Ides of September, marked by your birthday,

The nurturing Ides, a day also honored by the divine spirits.

Hecate, daughter of Latona, claims the Ides of Sextilis;

Mercury, joined to the honor of the heavenly gods, claims the Ides of May.

Maro, born long ago, dedicates the Ides of October.

May you celebrate all the Ides in the twelve months,

You who celebrate the Ides of my Ausonius.

Farewell, dearest grandson.

## IDYLL VI. Cupid Affixed to the Cross

### Ausonius to his son Gregorius, greetings

Have you ever seen a painted cloud on a wall? You certainly have, and you remember it. At Trier, in the dining room of Aeolus, this painted scene was executed: women in love affix Cupid to a cross—not women of our own age, who sin voluntarily, but heroic women, who forgive themselves and punish the god, some of whom our Maro lists in the Mourning Fields.

I admired this image for both its appearance and its subject. Finally, I transferred the amazement it inspired into the foolishness of composing poetry. I like nothing in it except the title. But I commend my error to you: we love our blemishes and scars; and not content to have sinned through our own fault alone, we wish them to be loved.

But why do I defend this little eclogue so carefully? I am certain that whatever of mine you know, you will love—the hope I cherish more than that you will praise it. Farewell, and love your father.

[Col. 0883B]

In the fields of air, which Maro’s Muse recalls,

Where a myrtle grove shades lovers in love,

The heroines performed their rites, and each carried

The tokens of her death, just as she had once died,

Wandering through the great forest beneath the hostile light,

Among reeds and heavy-headed poppies,

And silent lakes without stain, streams without murmur.

Along their banks, beneath a misty light, languished

Flowers bearing the names of kings and boys,

Once mourned: Narcissus, the wonderer, and Oebalian Hyacinthus,

Golden-haired Crocus, and Adonis painted with purple,

And Ajax of Salamis, inscribed with tragic lament.

All these, troubled by tears and sorrowful loves,

Repeated the remembered griefs of deaths already suffered,

And summoned the heroines back into the age they had lost.

[Col. 0883C]

Semele, deceived, mourns her lightning-born child,

And, tearing at her scorched cradle through the empty air,

Fans the impotent fire of the simulated lightning.

Caenis, lamenting her unavailing gifts,

Rejoices in her masculine sex but grieves

At being restored to her former shape.

Procris still dries her wounds; she loves

The bloody hand of Cephalus even though it struck her.

The girl from Sestos leaps headlong from the tower,

Bearing a smoking torch.

And manly Sappho threatens a leap

From clouded Leucas,

To perish beneath Lesbian arrows.

Mournful Eriphyle refuses the adornments of Harmonia,

Unfortunate in her son and not fortunate in her husband.

The whole story of Minos’ airy Crete

Also trembles beneath a delicate image, like a painting.

Pasiphae follows the tracks of the snow-white bull.

[Col. 0883D]

Ariadne, deserted, bears a ball of thread in her left hand.

Phaedra, despairing, looks back at the discarded tablets.

This one carries a noose; this one the semblance of a vain crown;

That one is ashamed to have entered the hiding place of the Daedalian heifer.

Laodamia complains, amid empty pleasures, of the two nights

Snatched away from her with her husband, living and dead.

On another side, all savage with drawn blades,

Thisbe, Canace, and Sidonian Elissa shudder.

One carries the sword of a husband, another of a father,

And another that of a guest.

Luna herself wanders there as she once did among the rocks of Latmos,

When, with torch and starry diadem,

The two-horned Moon used to seek the sleep of Endymion.

A hundred other women, recalling the wounds of ancient loves,

Renew their sufferings through sweet and sorrowful complaints.

[Col. 0884A]

Among them, Cupid, heedless, dispersed the shadow

Of dark mist with his whistling wings.

They all recognized the boy and, in a remembered recurrence,

Recognized that they shared the same offender,

Although the wet clouds around him

And the gold-studded belts dimmed

His quiver and the fire of his glowing torch.

Nevertheless they recognized him, and began to brandish

Their empty strength against one enemy,

Who, having found himself in a place not his own,

Was making sluggish flights beneath the dense night.

They hemmed in the cloud he had made,

And, as he trembled and prepared useless refuges,

Dragged him into the midst of the assembled group.

The myrtle most renowned in that sorrowful grove was chosen,

Hated by the gods for its punishments.

There Proserpina had once tortured Adonis,

Who remembered Venus though she had rejected him.

Upon its lofty trunk they hang Love,

His hands tied behind his back, and fetters fastened

Around his feet. Mourning, without restraint in punishment,

Love is affixed to the tree: accused without a crime,

And charged without a judge.

Each woman strives to acquit herself,

So that she may transfer her own guilt to another’s offense.

All bring forward, reproachfully, the tokens of a death they endured.

They consider these weapons, this sweet vengeance:

Each seeks to punish Cupid with the pain by which she herself perished.

One holds a noose; another thrusts forward

The empty likeness of a sword;

Another displays hollow rivers, a jagged cliff,

The insane terror of the sea, and a shoreless ocean.

Some shake flames and threaten with hissing torches

That burn without fire.

Myrrha rends her mature womb in mourning tears,

And hurls at the frightened boy the jewel-like amber

Of her tear-bearing trunk.

[Col. 0884C]

Some, in the guise of women who forgive,

Wish only for playful mockeries:

One so that a slender stylus beneath a pointed tip

May draw out a tender drop of blood,

From which a rose is born;

Or so that mischievous lamps may bring their lights close to the groin.

Even his mother Venus, herself subject to a similar fault,

The kindly goddess, enters that great tumult without fear.

She does not hurry to aid her son when he is surrounded,

Nor multiply his terror or kindle uncertain rages

With bitter goads.

She herself heaps upon her son the disgrace

Of her own crimes: the unseen bonds of her husband,

Which she endured when caught with Mars;

The laughable shape of Hellespontine Priapus

With his shameful organ;

Cruel Eryx; and Hermaphroditus, half male.

Nor is this enough in words.

Golden Venus, with a rose-colored garland,

Strikes the grieving boy, who fears still heavier blows.

[Col. 0884D]

From his soft purple body the close-petalled rose,

Struck repeatedly, squeezed out crimson dew;

Already stained before, it took on an even brighter fiery color.

Then the savage threats fell silent, and the greater vengeance

Seemed criminal beside her own offense,

As Venus was about to become the guilty one.

The heroines themselves intervene,

And each prefers to attribute her death to cruel fate.

Then the pious mother gives thanks that they have yielded

And releases the boy, his guilt forgiven.

Such visions once, in nocturnal forms,

Disturb anxious sleep with empty terror.

After Cupid had endured them through much of the night,

He escaped; when at last the darkness of sleep was dispelled,

He flew up to the gods and escaped through the ivory gate.

## IDYLL VII. Bissula

[Col. 0885A]

### Ausonius to his Paul, greetings

You have prevailed after all, dearest Paul, and penetrated the hidden things of my Muses, whose obscurity concealed their initiatory rites, although you do not break in as a profane intruder. For although I do not count you among that crowd whom Horace bars from entry, each person has his own sacred rites. Ceres does not have the same rites as Liber, even under the same worshipers.

You forced me to bring into the light, still obscure, the poems I had playfully composed about my fosterling, rough and unfinished, for the solace of household song, while they enjoyed freedom and secret security. You desired, plainly, to strip me of my modesty—or to have me reveal to you, against my will, how much authority you possessed over me.

Indeed, you surpassed the persistence of Alexander of Macedon, who, unable to loosen the reins of the fated yoke, cut them, and entered the cave of the Pythia, which it was forbidden to seek.

Use them, therefore, as your own, with equal right but unequal confidence. Your poems, to be sure, need not fear the public; I am ashamed of mine even within myself.

[Col. 0885B]

As you wished, Paul, you have all the verses of Bissula:

Those which I played with to please the little Sueban girl,

Fostering leisure more than pursuing glory.

You, troublesome petitioner, read the songs you insist upon with troublesome persistence.

What you have ground must be eaten by you; so the old proverb commands;

The fetters which the smith himself made, he himself must wear.

### To the reader of this little book

Reader of this slight little book of unfinished song,

Lower your raised eyebrow.

Examine the serious poems with a furrowed brow.

We follow Thymelē.

Bissula will be sung in this little notebook—or Erasinus.

I advise you to drink beforehand.

I write nothing for the fasting; if someone reads my work after drinking,

Let him have sense.

But he will understand it better if he sleeps, and thinks

That these things have been sent to him as dreams.

### Where Bissula was born and how she came into her master’s hands

Bissula, sprung from stock and hearth beyond the frozen Rhine,

Bissula, who knew the Danube at her birth,

Captured by force but freed by force, rules in the delights

Of the man whose prize of war she had been.

Without a mother and in need of a nurse, she did not know her master’s

Authority [the reading *herai* is uncertain] …

Of fortune and homeland she had felt no reproach,
At once free from unaccustomed servitude.

Thus, transformed by Latin advantages, she would remain Germanic  
in face, blue-eyed, and golden-haired.  
Now her tongue makes the girl ambiguous, now her appearance:  
the one proclaims her born of the Rhine, the other of Latium.

### On the same Bissula

Darling, endearment, plaything, love, delight—
