a barbarian girl, yet you surpass the Latin dolls,  
Bissula, the rustic little name of a tender girl,  
rough-sounding to ears unaccustomed to it, but charming to her master.

[Col. 0886A] ### To the painter, on the portrait of Bissula

Bissula can be imitated neither in wax nor by any pigment;  
her natural beauty lends nothing to fictitious art.  
Cinnabar and white lead simulate other girls;  
the hand does not know how to reproduce this harmony of features. Therefore, painter,  
blend crimson roses and mix in lilies;  
let the color that emerges from them be the color of her face.

### To the same

If, painter, you plan to depict my fosterling,  
let rival art imitate the bees of Cecrops.

## IDYLLIUM VIII. Prayer of Ausonius, consul designate, on the day before the Kalends of January, after assuming the fasces

Janus, come; new year, come; come, renewed Sun,  
to behold Ausonius’s Latin curule chair.

What is there now, after the majesty of Augustus,  
that you might admire? That Rome, the house of Quirinus,  
and the shining purple-bordered toga of the Senate  
mark, with this head, their age in the eternal Fasti.

Come, year begun under favorable auspices: grant a truly healthful spring;  
grant breezes warmed by the sun, grant dewy  
solstices under Cancer, and chill Boreas in the hours of September.  
Let subtle cold bite the autumn frosts;  
let summer, moderated in its seasons, cease its excess.  
Let the south wind moisten the seedtime. Let winter be snowy,  
while March, father of the ancient year, is renewed.  
In fragrant May let the new grace of flowers breathe forth;  
let July ripen the crops and temper the sea with easterly winds.  
Let Sirius not increase the fiery heat of Leo.

[Col. 0886C] Let Pomona diversify the tree-grown fruits with varied colors.  
Let autumn soften what summer has ripened,  
and let fruitful winter enjoy the dowry allotted to it.

Let the world keep peace; let no troubled stars rule.  
May no star offend your household, Gradivus,  
that is not favorable to you: neither Cynthia, nor swift Arcas,  
your neighbor to the earth; nor you, Saturn, last  
in your highest circuit. Far removed from Pyrois,  
you will hasten along a tranquil course. Come close together,  
star of life-giving Jupiter, and Venus as Evening Star.  
May Cyllenius sometimes be present, kindly disposed toward guests.

Janus, come; new year, come; come, renewed Sun.

Where France, joined to the Suebi, subdued its enemies  
and strives for obedience, that it may serve with Latin arms;  
where the wandering Sauromatae had joined their bands with the Chuni;  
[Col. 0886D] and where the Getae had attacked the Danube together with their Alan allies—  
from there Victory brings me news on swift wings.

Now Augustus has come, to adorn my honors,  
honoring with office those whom he would have wished to share them.

Janus, come; new year, come; come, renewed Sun.

Sun, extend golden joys to the coming Janus.  
Caesar will succeed Ausonius in office for the year,  
about to wear the fifth purple-bordered toga of Romulus’s honor.

Look how my purple is heaped up—hear this with gentle  
ears, Nemesis—after me Augustus the consul  
deigns to arise. He seems to grant me more  
than to share with me: he ordered our fasces to precede his own.

Janus, come; new year, come; come, renewed Sun.

Bring together the twelve months that will follow through your double gates;  
[Col. 0887A] make the tropic yield to the sun, and then  
make it turn its back, so that the two tropics may vary from star to star,  
and the change may hasten four times through three signs.  
Drive on the summer days, and let the winter delayed  
by night be accelerated by the year promised by Caesar.

If I behold him, then I shall be three and four times blessed;  
then I shall be consul twice, then I shall touch heaven with my crown.

## IDYLLIUM IX. Also a prayer on the Kalends of January

Year begun under favorable auspices, you behold the happy beginnings  
of Ausonius’s consulship. Bring forth, eternal Sun,  
your radiant head; and, brighter than usual,  
with nourishing light raise the purple beam of the eastern dawn.

Year, father of the things that the double-faced month of Janus  
[Col. 0887B] rolls toward wintry December at its icy end,  
come, and as a new year behold the festival of ancient Janus.

Pass through the solemn roads, varying the twelve  
courses of the world through the seasons by their equal signs;  
carry your headlong course through an eternal revolution.  
Thus, Phoebus, carried along the declining sky,  
bring back the moments in their allotted portion of days,  
and, new, restore your light with the winter’s turning.

While the Moon’s monthly horns return thirty times,  
you will rotate her risings and settings with your revolving hand,  
restraining Phoebus’s lawful passage through the signs.

## IDYLLIUM X. The Moselle

I had crossed the swift Nahe beneath a misty sky,  
marveling at the new walls added to the old village—  
where Gaul once matched Latium’s Cannae,  
and swollen, impoverished troops lie scattered over the fields.

From there, setting out along a solitary road through pathless woods,  
and seeing no trace of human cultivation,  
I passed by dry Dumnissus, surrounded everywhere by thirsty lands,  
and Tabernae, rich in perennial springs,  
and fields recently allotted to Sarmatian settlers.  
At last I caught sight, on the borders of the Belgae,  
of Noviomagus, the famous camp of the divine Constantine.

Here the air is purer over the fields; Phoebus, in serene  
light, now opens the purple brightness of a clear Olympus.  
No longer, through interwoven branches joined to one another,  
must the sky be sought, shut out by green darkness;  
but free air does not begrudge those who look upon it  
the liquid radiance and the red sky of transparent day.

When everything, with its pleasing appearance, had drawn me toward the image of my homeland and the cultivated elegance of shining Burdigala, I saw the roofs of country houses raised  
above hanging banks, green hills sacred to Bacchus,  
and the pleasant waters of the Moselle gliding beneath  
with silent murmur.

Hail, river praised by fields, praised by settlers,  
whose walls the Belgae, made worthy of empire, owe to you.  
River planted with vine-covered ridges by fragrant Bacchus,  
most verdant river, planted with grassy banks;  
navigable like the sea; sloping downward into your waters  
like a river; imitating a lake in your glassy depth;  
able to equal streams in their trembling course,  
and surpassing cold springs in your clear drink—  
[Col. 0888A] alone you possess everything belonging to a spring, a stream, a river,  
a lake, and a sea flowing back through a double channel.

You glide along with peaceful waters, suffering neither  
the murmurs of wind nor the struggles of hidden rock.  
You are not forced, because of a ford rising above you,  
to restore your rapid channels; you do not have  
lands standing in midstream that interrupt you.  
Lest an island divide the river and diminish  
the honor of your proper name, you possess no such obstruction.

You have received two routes, and when you flow  
with a following current, so that swift oars strike the agitated shallows;  
and when, along banks where towing never ceases,  
sailors stretch the ropes around their shoulders.

How often you yourself marvel at your turnings in the river  
and think your proper channels flow somewhat too slowly!  
You do not cover your banks with mud-born weeds,  
nor sluggishly drench your shores with filthy muck,  
but sprinkle dry footprints at the outset with clear water.

Go now, and alone cover light surfaces with Phrygian crusts,  
stretching a marble floor through coffered halls.  
But I, scorning what wealth and riches have bestowed,  
will admire the work of nature—not the care of descendants—  
and poverty rejoicing where it luxuriates in its own losses.

Here solid sands spread over the moist shores  
and do not retain the remembered shapes of pressed footprints.  
You are visible through your glassy depth across your smooth surface;  
the river has no hidden place. Just as nourishing air,  
when it opens itself to the gaze beneath the clear sky,  
is revealed to liquid eyes, and peaceful winds do not  
bar the eyes from passing through empty space,  
so we see, far below, through the depths that remain visible,  
and the river’s hidden inner chamber lies open:

[Col. 0888C] when the gentle shallows move, and the flow of the liquid waters  
reveals shapes scattered in the blue light;  
when the lightly furrowed sand ripples with the current;  
when the grasses inclined upon the green bottom tremble.

As grasses stirred beneath natural springs  
endure the quivering waters, so the pebble shines and hides,  
and gravel distinguishes the green moss.

Such a picture is known to the Caledonian Britons  
when the tide lays bare green seaweed and red coral,  
and the white, berry-like beginnings of shells,  
rich delights of men, which beneath the waves  
imitate our jewelry by resembling human ornaments.

No differently, beneath the peaceful, happy shallows of the Moselle,  
grass of a different color reveals mixed pebbles.  
Yet slippery schools of fish, playing among one another,  
tire the eyes that remain fixed upon them with their errant movement.

But it is not permitted to name all the species,  
their slanting movements, the troops that advance  
against the current, nor the names and numerous offspring  
of the whole abundant race. He does not allow it,  
to whom belongs the care of the second lot  
and the guardianship of the trident of the sea.

You, Naiad dwelling on the riverbanks,  
recite the dances of the scaly flock,  
and describe beneath the clear channel  
the schools floating in the blue river.

The scaly chub glitters among the grassy sands,  
its tender flesh stuffed thickly with roe,  
and not destined to endure beyond two periods of three hours.

The starry saler, marked with purple spots,  
and the redo, whose spine harms no one with its point,  
[Col. 0889A] and the smooth shadow, escaping the eyes by its swift swimming.

And you, barbel, harried through the gorges of the winding Saravus,  
where twice three mouths roar among the rocky teeth:  
when you have flowed down into a river of greater fame,  
you exercise your freer swimming, Barbus.

You are better in a worse age; among all creatures that breathe,  
you have received a not inglorious old age.

Nor would I pass you by, Salmon, gleaming with crimson flesh,  
whose wandering strokes of broad tail  
are carried from midstream to the upper waters,  
when a hidden thrust is revealed upon the calm surface.

You, scaly with an armored breast, slippery in the forehead,  
destined to furnish the dishes of an uncertain dinner,  
you endure for a long time without spoiling,  
distinguished by spots on your head; your belly sways  
and your abdomen flows, heavy with fat.

And you, Mustela, caught by the signs of foam  
through Illyria and the pools of the double-named Ister,  
brought into our waters lest the broad rivers  
of the Moselle be deprived of so renowned a fish.

What color of nature painted you? Above, black  
spots mark your back, which a yellow iris surrounds.  
A blue pigment runs along your slippery back.  
Toward the middle of your body you grow thick with fat;  
from there onward, beneath the very end of your tail,  
your dry skin becomes scaly.

Nor will I be silent about you, Perch, delight of tables,  
worthy, among river-born fish, to rival sea fish,  
alone able to contend with the crimson mullets.  
For your taste is not dull, and in your solid body  
the parts cohere in segments,  
but are separated by bones.

[Col. 0889C] Here too is Lucius, who bears a Latin name for laughter,  
a lover of ponds, most hostile to croaking frogs;  
he occupies dark pools with weed and mud.  
He is chosen for no use at tables;  
he seethes in smoky cookshops with an offensive smell.

Who does not know the green tench, the consolation of common people,  
and the bleak, prey for boys’ hooks,  
and the Alausae, the people’s food that crackles on the hearth?

And you, Fario, caught between two species, neither wholly one nor the other,  
not yet a salmon and no longer a saler,  
ambiguous between both in middle age?

You too, Gobio, memorable among the river cohorts,  
no larger than two palms without the thumb,  
very fat, rounded, and especially swollen with an egg-bearing belly;  
and the gudgeon, imitating the long mane of the barbel.

[Col. 0889D] Now you will be celebrated, mighty Silurus,  
the great creature of the waters. I think you a river-dwelling dolphin,  
your back coated as though with Actaean olive oil.  
Thus you glide through the channels, scarcely uncoiling  
the ranks of your long body, defended either  
by shallow waters or by the river’s weeds.

But when you prepare your tranquil passages through the river,  
the green banks, the blue throng of swimmers,  
and the clear waters marvel at you; the current spreads  
through the channel, and waves run forward from the outer edge.

Such was once the whale in the Atlantic depths,  
when it was driven by wind or by its own movement  
toward the shores of the earth: it poured out the displaced sea,  
great waters rose, and the neighboring mountains feared  
that they would diminish.

[Col. 0890A] Yet here, here is the gentle whale of our Moselle,  
far from destruction, and a great honor has been added to the river.

It is enough now to have looked upon the liquid ways,  
the slippery schools of fish, and the many flocks  
that I have counted.

Let the vine-covered spectacles introduce another procession;  
let the gifts of Bacchus attract wandering eyes:  
where the lofty summit, over a long and difficult course,  
causes rocks, sunny ridges, bends, and hollows  
to rise with vines, forming a natural theater.

So the nourishing vintage clothes the Gauranian ridge,  
and Rhodope and Pangaea shine with their own Lyaeus.  
So the Ismarian hill grows green above the Thracian waters.  
So my vineyards paint the yellow Garumna.

For along the highest ridges, stretching to the furthest part  
of the slope, the riverbank is planted with green Lyaeus.

[Col. 0890B] The cheerful laboring crowd and the hurrying farmers  
now hasten at the very summit, now down the mountain’s back,  
vying with one another in foolish shouts. From below, the traveler  
wearing down the banks; from here, the boatman gliding by,  
they sing insults to the late cultivators. The rocks,  
the trembling forest, and the hollow river resound to them.

Nor does the scene of these places delight human beings alone.  
Here I would believe that rustic Satyrs and blue-eyed Naiads  
meet upon the farthest banks,  
while the joyful insolence of goat-footed Pan drives them on,  
and they leap upon the shallows, frightening their trembling sisters  
beneath the water and striking the waves with an untrained lash.

Often, too, Panope, the river nymph, having stolen grapes  
from the middle of the hills, flees  
the lustful Fauns, rustic deities.

[Col. 0890C] It is said that when the sun stood at the middle of its fiery orbit,  
the Satyrs and glassy sisters celebrated their communal dances  
beside the common sea, when the heat, more burning  
because of the secret hours, had withdrawn the human crowd.

Then the Nymphs leap and play in their own waters,  
and submerge the Satyrs in the shallows, emerging  
through their unskilled swimming hands,  
while the Satyrs pursue their slippery limbs  
and caress the liquid waves around their bodies.

But I may not speak of these things as witnessed or known by sight;  
let what is secret remain covered,  
and let the reverence entrusted to its own streams lie hidden.

That beauty may be openly enjoyed when the blue river  
answers the shadowy hill; the liquid river waters  
seem to put forth leaves, and the river seems planted with vine-shoots.

[Col. 0890D] What color belongs to the shallows when Evening Star  
has brought forth the late shadows and the Moselle pours  
from the green mountain? The whole ridge floats  
in rippling movements; the absent vine trembles,  
and the vintage swells in glassy waters.  
The mocking boatman counts the green vines,  
the boatman floating over the waters in his hollow skiff,  
where the image of the hill merges with the river  
and the river joins the boundaries of the shadows.

How sweetly these spectacles celebrate their pageants,  
when oared skiffs contend in midstream  
and enter varied turns, brushing along the green banks  
the swelling shoots among the shorn meadows!

The masters delight in their sterns and bows,  
[Col. 0891A] while they watch the boyish crew moving over the river’s back;  
then they set aside their serious business for amusement:  
new pleasure excludes their old cares.

Such games Liber looks down upon in the Cumaean sea  
when, among the ridges planted with sulfurous Gaurus  
and through the vineyards of steaming Vesuvius, he walks;  
or when Venus, rejoicing in Augustus’s Actian triumphs,  
ordered the wanton Loves to play at savage battles,  
such as the Nile fleets and Latin triremes  
waged beneath the citadels of Apollo at Leucas;  
or when the Euboean boats resounding through Avernus  
reproduce the dangers of Pompey’s Mylasian war,  
the harmless blows of rafts and playful battles  
of a naval spectacle such as blue Pelorus watched,  
while the sea restores itself beneath a green image.

[Col. 0891B] Puberty, the river, and the painted prows of the skiffs  
add no other spectacle to these mischievous youths.

When the sun has drenched them with Hyperion’s heat,  
the river gives back their nautical forms beneath its glassy whirlpool  
and reproduces the shadows of their inverted bodies.

As they frequently make agile movements to right and left  
and alternate their weight with changing oar strokes,  
the wave returns other watery images of the boatmen.  
The nautical youth itself rejoices in its own likeness,  
marveling that deceptive figures return from the river.

Thus, when a girl is about to display her arranged hair,  
and her nurse first brings to her beloved fosterling  
the shining surface of a mirror,  
she gladly enjoys a game she does not recognize  
and thinks she is looking at the form of her sister:  
[Col. 0891C] she gives kisses to the shining metal that cannot return them,  
or pretends to fasten pins, or begins to extend  
her hair toward her brow with moving fingers.

Such is the nautical youth amid the play of shadows,  
enjoying the ambiguous figures of truth and falsehood.

Now, wherever the bank provides easy access,  
a predatory crowd searches the whole depth  
for the fish—alas!—poorly defended in the river’s inner chamber.

Here, far out in midstream, one drags wet nets,  
turning the schools caught in knotted meshes;  
there, where the river flows in a tranquil course,  
another draws floating nets marked with strips of bark.

Another, leaning over the waters beneath the rocks,  
bends the curved tip of a supple rod,  
casting hooks clothed with deadly bait.

[Col. 0891D] When the wandering school, ignorant of the deception,  
has attacked them with open mouths and, deep within their gaping throats,  
has felt the late wounds of the hidden iron,  
as they tremble, the sign appears, and the rod  
nods in agreement with the crisp trembling of the vibrating line.

There is no delay: the boy’s right hand, with a whistling blow,  
snatches the prey as it is jerked out sideways. Breath receives the stroke,  
as once, when whips were cracked through empty air,  
the air rattles and the wind hisses through stirred atmosphere.

The wet captives leap upon the dry rocks  
and fear the deadly weapons of the daylight.  
The strength that remained beneath their own river  
languishes and spends its life breathing our air.

Now the feeble body gives a sluggish flap;  
now the numb tail suffers its final tremors.  
The jaws no longer close; but the gill, exhaling death,  
returns the air swallowed through its openings as mortal breaths.

[Col. 0892A] Thus, when a craftsman’s bellows work the fires,  
the woolen shield, playing among its greasy cavities,  
takes in and restrains the winds through alternate openings.

I myself have seen some fish, trembling at the end of death,  
gather their remaining breath, then, suddenly launched upward,  
throw their bowed bodies headlong into the river beneath  
and regain possession of the waters they had despaired of.

The boy, unaware of the damage, attacks them from above  
and foolishly tries to seize them by swimming after them.

Thus Glaucus of Anthedon, across the Boeotian waters,  
after tasting the deadly grasses of Circe,  
took the herbs plucked from dying fish  
[Col. 0892B] and entered the Carpathian sea as a new inhabitant.

He, skilled with hooks and nets, explorer of the hidden  
Nereus, accustomed to turning the sea-born Tethys,  
swam as a marauder among captive schools.

Such scenes are looked down upon, along the blue waters’ long course,  
by villas hanging from rocks beneath an overhanging summit.  
The winding river divides them in the middle  
and adorns both banks with alternating country houses.

Who would now marvel at the Sestian sea, the waters  
of Nepheleid Helle? Who would marvel at the strait  
of Abydos’s youth? Who at the sea spread out from the Chalcedonian shore,  
the work of the Great King, where the Euripus amid the waves  
prevents the lands of Europe and Asia from joining?

Here there is no dread fury of the strait,  
no savage battle of raging northwest winds. Here one may join  
the commerce of speech and weave conversation  
with alternating pulses.

The kindly shores mingle voices that carry salutations,  
voices and almost hands. Echo, resounding on both sides,  
returns the words, meeting in the middle of the waves.

Who could, retracing the countless forms and appearances,  
display the architectural designs of each estate?

[Col. 0892C] Would the winged Gortynian, builder of a temple, disdain this work—  
he whom his father’s grief drove away when he tried  
to represent the Icarian disaster in gold?

Or Philo of Cecrops? Or he who, praised even by his enemy,  
depicted the famous struggles of the Syracusan war?

Perhaps this place also contains the distinguished labors  
of men and of their works, celebrated in the tenth book of Marcus;  
here the arts of famous Menecrates flourished,  
and the hand admired at Ephesus, or Ictinus  
on Minerva’s citadel, whose owl, smeared with magical pigment,  
attracts every kind of bird and kills it by its gaze.

Perhaps Dinochares, builder of the palace at Ptolemais,  
was responsible here: a square cone rises  
to its summit, and the pyramid itself consumes its own shadows;  
he who once, ordered to suspend Arsinoe in the air  
of the Pharian temple because of an illicit love affair,  
for beneath the roof’s vault the true magnet breathes  
and draws the suspended girl by her iron hair.

It is therefore worthy to believe that these men,  
or men like them, set up such scenes  
in the lands of the Belgae and fashioned lofty villas  
as ornaments of the river.

This one is raised upon the natural height of a rocky bank;  
[Col. 0893A] this one is founded on the projecting ledge of the shore;  
this one turns aside and claims the captured river within its embrace.

That one, holding the hill that projects most fully over the river,  
appropriates easy views across cultivated and rugged ground,  
and, rich, enjoys the prospect of its own lands.

Indeed, a house built on wet meadows at a low elevation  
balances the natural advantages of the lofty mountain  
and, threatening from its high roof to burst into the sky,  
displays a tall tower like the Pharian lighthouse at Memphis.

It is the particular privilege of this house  
to catch fish enclosed in a constructed pool  
among the sunny clearings between the rocks.

Another, leaning upon the highest ridges,  
looks down upon the rivers flowing below,  
already fading from sight.

Why should I mention halls set beside green meadows  
and roofs floating above countless columns?

[Col. 0893B] Why mention the baths, smoking upon a sulfurous foundation,  
when Mulciber, enclosed beneath the boiling covering,  
rolls the flames breathed through the hollow walls  
and gathers vapor exhaled by the heat?

I have seen people exhausted by the abundant sweat of the bath  
grow weary of the pools and the cold basins,  
so that they might enjoy living waters; then, refreshed by the river,  
they struck the cold river with splashing, applauding swimming.

If a visitor came here from the Cumaean shores,  
he would think that Baiae had bestowed upon these places  
an imitation of its Euboean retreats: such cultivation and brilliance  
attract the eye, and pleasure produces no extravagance.

But for me, what end can there finally be  
to describing your blue-green waters  
and commemorating the Moselle as worthy of the sea?

For countless rivers flow broadly into you  
through different mouths, although they could  
have followed different courses; yet they hasten  
to spend their name in yours.

For the Sura, aided by the flow of Pronaea and Nemesis,  
hurries beneath your waters without disgracing you,  
and, intercepted in its course, does you the favor  
of becoming more famous when mingled with your name  
than if it poured its unknown mouth into the ancestral sea.

The swift Gelbis and marble-bright Erubrus hasten  
to kiss you as quickly as possible with their tributary waters.  
Gelbis, famous for its noble fish,  
whirls millstones in a headlong rotation  
and, dragging shrieking saws across smooth marble,  
hears perpetual tumult from either bank.

I pass over the slender Lesura and the thin Drachon,  
nor do I claim the despised streams of the Salmona.

[Col. 0893D] The Saravus, long ago navigable and roaring over the waters,  
calls me with its twisted channel,  
a river that delayed its long course  
so that its weary mouth might roll beneath Augustus’s walls.

Nor is that lesser which, flowing silently through rich fields,  
happily skirts the fertile banks of the Alisontia.  
A thousand others, as each one is driven by its own stronger impulse,  
wish to become yours. Such is the circumference,  
or mass, of the waters hastening toward you.

But if divine Moselle, Smyrna had given you her poet,  
or famous Mantua, the Simois celebrated  
on the shores of Ilium would yield,  
nor would the Tiber dare to place its honors before yours.

Forgive me, mighty Rome. I beg you, let envy  
be driven away and depart, and let Nemesis, unknown  
to the Latin tongue, not be offended. Guard  
the seat of empire and the fathers of Rome.

[Col. 0894A] Hail, great parent of crops and men, Moselle.  
Famous nobles, youth trained in war,  
and eloquence rivaling the Latin tongue adorn you.

Indeed, nature has granted your fosterlings  
both character and a cheerful spirit beneath a serious brow.

Nor does Rome alone display its ancient Catos,  
nor does only one observer of justice and equity,  
Aristides, possess distinction and glorify ancient Athens.

But why, wandering too far with loosened reins,  
overcome by love for you, should I wear away my praises?  
Put away, Muse, your lyre, your strings dismissed in the final song.

There will be a time when the honor of my subject  
will commend me, while I soothe my cares with humble leisure  
and cherish my old age in the sunlight; when I shall sing, person by person,  
the deeds of the Belgae and the famous glories  
of their ancestral character.

[Col. 0894B] The Pierian sisters will spin soft songs for me  
with a delicate thread, and will run through fitting webs  
with a fine woof. Purple too will be granted to my spindles.

Who will then remain unmentioned by me? I shall remember  
peaceful farmers; men skilled in law and eloquent speech,  
a lofty defense for defendants; men whom the senate-house  
saw as the foremost nobles of their municipalities  
and as their proper senate;  
men whose renowned eloquence in the bordered-toga school  
led them to the praises of the ancient Quintilian.

And those who governed their cities and made their tribunal pure  
of bloodshed, illuminating their blameless axes;  
or who governed Italian peoples and the Britons of the north  
under the honorable title of prefect.

And the man who governed Rome, head of affairs,  
and the people and fathers, almost under his first title—although  
[Col. 0894C] he presided over the first offices. At last Fortune hastens  
to undo her error; filling up the rewards she had only partly granted,  
she will now restore the summit of true honor,  
to be sought again by noble descendants.

But for now let the work already begun be unfolded.  
Putting aside the praise of men, let us speak,  
along a joyful course through the green countryside,  
of the fortunate river, and consecrate it in the waters of the Rhine.

Now, Rhine, spread out your blue bays  
and your green-hued robe of glass, and measure out  
the space of your new stream, soon to be enriched  
by your brother’s waters. Nor are rewards in the waters alone:  
you have seen, approaching the walls of the imperial city,  
the joined triumphs of Father and Son—  
the enemy driven out beyond the Nicer, and beyond Lupodunum,  
and beyond the source of the Danube, unknown to Latin annals.

This is the laurel of the war recently overthrown;  
[Col. 0894D] soon it will bring other laurels, and still others. Go on, joined together,  
and drive the purple sea forward along your double course.

Do not fear, most beautiful Rhine, to seem inferior:  
a guest possesses nothing that provokes envy. You will share  
an everlasting name; adopt your brother, secure in your fame.

Rich in waters, rich in nymphs, a giver to both,  
your channel will extend its divisions between twin banks  
and pour common ways through separate mouths.

Strengths will be added—strengths that France, the Chamavi,  
and the Germans will dread; then you will be regarded as the true frontier.

A double name will be added to you from so great a river.  
And since you flow from a single source, you will be called two-horned.

These things I, Ausonius—drawing my people from the origin of the VIVISCI,  
now known through new alliances as a guest of the Belgae—  
[Col. 0895A] Latin in name, but in homeland and house among the remotest Gauls,  
between lofty Pyrene and the farthest regions of Gaul,  
where happy Aquitania tempers its native character—  
boldly sing with little confidence.

It is permitted me to brush the sacred river  
with a thin libation of the Muse.

I do not seek praise; I ask pardon. Many there are,  
nourishing river, who habitually trouble the sacred streams  
of the daughters of Aonia and drain the whole of Aganippe.

But I, according to the measure of the vein of liquid  
that you will grant me, when Father Augustus and his son,  
my greatest concern, send me back to Burdigala,  
my homeland and nest of old age,  
adorned with the Ausonian fasces and the curule honor,  
after the years of completed training,  
will pursue in broader song the praises of the northern river.

I shall add the cities over which you glide  
with your silent channel;  
[Col. 0895B] and the walls that look out upon you from ancient ramparts.

I shall add the places founded for the defense of uncertain affairs—  
not camps now, but granaries for the secure Belgae.

I shall add the fortunate settlers on either bank,  
and you among the labors of men and oxen,  
skirting the banks and cutting through rich fields.

The Liger will not place himself before you, nor the precipitous Axona;  
nor the Matrona, set between the frontiers of Gaul and the Belgae;  
nor the Carantonus itself, flowing backward in the tide  
of the Santoni.

You will surpass the river rolled down from the icy mountain of the Duran.  
Gaul will set the gold-bearing Tarn after you.

And the Aturrus of Tarbelli, rushing wildly and broadly  
over rolling rocks into the purple sea,  
will nevertheless first worship the divinity  
of the lady Moselle.

Horn-bearing Moselle, to be celebrated in foreign lands,  
[Col. 0895C] not only in the places where, at your highest source,  
you raise the golden glory of your bull’s forehead,  
and wherever you draw your winding courses  
through peaceful fields,  
or wherever you release your mouths beneath German harbors:

if any honor wishes to breathe upon the slender Muse,  
if anyone deigns to spend leisure upon these songs,  
you will go into the mouths of men  
and be cherished in joyful song.

The springs and living lakes will know you;  
the blue rivers will know you; the ancient groves,  
the glory of the villages, will know you.  
Druna will know you, and Druentia uncertain among its scattered banks;  
and the Alpine rivers will honor you,  
as will the river that flows through the twin-named city  
and gives the right bank its name, the Rhone.

I shall commend you to the blue-green pools,  
to the great resounding rivers,  
and to the sea-like Garumna.

## IDYLLIUM XI. The riddle of the number three

[Col. 0895D]

### Ausonius sends greetings to Symmachus

A worthless little book lay hidden among my trifles—would that it had remained hidden and had not perished through its own identification, like a shrew. When I had dug it out, like Euclio’s cockerel, from the squalor of dusty paper, I shook it off and read it again; and, like a greedy moneylender, I preferred to seize a bad coin rather than bury it.

Then, reflecting with myself—not that Catullan question, “To whom shall I give my charming new little book?” but the more ἀμαλακώτερον [“more crudely”] and more truthful question, “To whom shall I give that crude, uncharming little book?”—I did not search long. For you came to mind, and if I had the power to choose one person from everyone, I would always choose you.

Therefore I sent you trifles more worthless than Sicilian nonsense, [Col. 0896A] so that when you are doing nothing you may read these, and, so as not to be doing nothing, defend them. Thus this trifling little book, long kept secret but already torn apart by the reading of the crowd, will at last come into your hands.

You will either restore it to life like Aesculapius, or, like Plato with Vulcan’s help, free it from disgrace, if it ought not to attain fame.

The subject of this little absurdity arose during a military expedition, a time which, as you know, allows military license. An invitation was made at my table—not the invitation of the mock banquet, at which one drank in the Greek manner, but that of Flaccus’s ode in which, because of midnight, the new moon, and Murena’s augurate, the astonished poet calls for three cups three times.

At once that poetic itch of mine began carving out this passage on the number three. Since this disease is easily contagious, may the itch also migrate to you, and, after applying the pigment of your correction, may you press on the sponge that will finish the imperfect work of a badly foaming horse.

And so that you may not call me boastful: I finished the verses begun during lunch before dinner—that is, while I was drinking, and a little before I drank. Let the work therefore be judged according to its subject and its time.

But you too should read this somewhat more cheerfully and sweetly: it is unjust to judge a teetotal reader by a poet who was not very sober.

Nor am I unaware that someone will condemn this joke of ours with a sharp nose and wrinkled brow, and deny that I have touched on everything relating to the numbers three and nine. I shall admit that he speaks truth, but I shall justly deny it.

For if he is a good critic, let him think that what I omitted was not forgotten by me but passed over. Then, whatever sort of person he may be, let him consider with himself how much he would not have discovered in these matters if he himself had searched.

Let him also know that I have neither used everything I unearthed nor used properly everything that was offered. How many things concerning three I knowingly neglected: tenses, persons, genders, and degrees; the nine natural meters together with trimeters; the whole of grammar and music; medical books; Hermes three times greatest; the first lover of philosophy; Varro’s numbers; and whatever the profane crowd does not know.

Finally, since it is easy, when he himself has found many things, let him compare himself with me: one who was occupied with one who was at leisure; one who had dined with a teetotaler; my joke and play with his diligence and faultfinding.

For one person can discover more than another; no one can discover everything. If I seem obscure to anyone, defend me before him thus: first, idylls of this kind, unless they are obscure, will amount to nothing; second, the nature of numbers is not a rush, so that it should be without knots.

Finally, if I am obscure even to you, for whom nothing has been either neglected or misunderstood, then indeed I shall be blessed, because I shall attain what I sought: that you should seek me, miss me, and think of me. Farewell.

Drink three times, or three cups as many times; such is the mystical law,  
whether for one drinking three, or multiplying three times three,  
to weave heaven from nine times three odd numbers.

The same legal principle belongs to three as to three times three. Everything lies in these things:  
the form of a man begun, the full completion of childbirth,  
and the one who holds the final end of fate nine times nine.

Three brothers born of Ops; three sisters produced in order (variant: the Fates).

[Col. 0897A] Vesta, Ceres, and Juno: three sisters of the female sex.

From this come Jupiter’s three-forked thunderbolts. From this, Cerberus.  
From this, the Trident; and the triple egg of Helen with her brothers.

Three times new purple filled the threads of Nestor’s life.  
And the crow, longer-lived by as many times three ages.

The stags with bronze feet, which nine times three cycles of ages assemble,  
surpass the three-times-three-age Nestor.  
Phoebus’s bird, whose three ages surpass theirs,  
is itself surpassed by the Gangetic bird, nine times older,  
the bird whose temples shine from a cinnamon nest.

Hecate is threefold; Diana has three faces as a virgin.  
Three Graces, three Fates, a triple voice, three elements;  
three Sirens in Trinacria. Everything is in threes.

[Col. 0897B] Three birds, three demigoddesses, three half-maidens.

Three times three were ordered to compete for the palm  
with the Camenae, singing with mouth, hand, breath, reed, lyre, and voice.

Three are the parts of wisdom; three the Punic wars; three-month  
cycles of years and of the heavens; and through the shadow of night  
triple sentinels keep watch.

The late attendant sings three clear signs  
of the approaching dawn when Mars has been sighted.

And Hercules, conceived on the evening of the tripled night,  
fixed rich spoils, as commanded, upon four times three trophies.

The lyric poets too number as many as the daughters of Mnemosyne,  
whom once the right hand of Phoebus alone possessed:  
but Cithaeron consecrated three times three in bronze,  
through the religious observance of the ancestors, who feared  
that they had neglected six.

Three-night rites are celebrated in the Terentine games,  
like the Trieteric rites of Bacchus, twice born at Thebes.

[Col. 0897C] Three first battles of the Thracians, in three successive wars,  
the sons of Junius sent as offerings to their ancestral tomb.

That bird, too, seeking husbands through three riddles—  
what was two-footed, four-footed, and three-footed, all by itself—  
terrified Aonia: the three-formed Sphinx—a bird in her wings, a lion in her feet, and a maiden in her face.

Threefold divine associations shine in the Tarpeian temple.

Three kinds of arts make human dwellings:  
the art that places stones in walls, that places beams in the roof,  
and that adorns the upper surface with plasterwork.

From this comes Bromius’s four-gallon measure, and from this the Sicilian medimnus.

The practice of calculation explains this by threes, those matters by twice three.

In Physics: the first three are God, the world, and the given form.

Every kind whatsoever is threefold: begetter, female begetter, and begotten.

[Col. 0897D] Through three kinds of triangles the rule proceeds: equilateral, or with two equal sides, or with all sides unequal.

The perfect number joins itself in three parts, so that the same number, gathered in three groups of three, may be resolved through three times three.

Three is first, even, odd, and middle; yet, as three, so also five and seven, it alone divides.

[This numerical passage is textually uncertain.] And, placed whole beneath the point of the center, it distinguishes solid *trientes* as the *coebus* proceeds, separating equal parts from an odd three, and the threefold middle from evens; likewise, when four and six, and twice four, are separated, the same central point remains.

The threefold law, which the four tablets have sanctioned three times: sacred, private, and that which everywhere belongs in common to the people.

[Col. 0898A] There are three kinds of interdiction: whence I may be repelled by force, or where the disputed thing has been, or “of whatever goods.”

Threefold is freedom, and threefold is diminution of status.

There are three kinds of speech: elevated, moderate, and in a slender thread. There are also three forms of healing, each called by its own name: *logos*, *methodos*, and experience.

Medicine too is threefold: to preserve, to prevent, and to cure.

There are three cultivated styles of oratory: the Rhodian, which Rhodes ruled; the Attic, beloved of Actaean Athens; and the Asiatic, which prose drew from the stage to austere benches, imitating in legal cases the rhythms of choruses.

Hence Orpheus’ tripods, because there are three things: earth, water, and flame.

Threefold is the arrangement of the stars: distance, shape, and measure. And the originator of measures is threefold music, mingled with books, hidden among the stars, and made public in theaters.

Martial Rome is threefold: cavalry, plebs, and Senate.

By this number too are the tribunes, from the Sacred Mount.

Three squadrons of horse: three names of the nobler sort.

There are three names for the strings; there are three names for the measure.

Geryon is threefold; the framework of the Chimera is threefold.

Scylla is threefold, composed of three: dog, virgin, and fish.

The Gorgons, the Harpies, and the Erinyes form a band of three.

And the three prophetic women share the name Sibyl:

Their prophetic songs are contained in three books,

Which the guild of fifteen men preserves.

Drink three times. Three is the number above all; three is the one God.

Here too, so that the game may not run through the number in idle fashion,

[Col. 0898C] let it contain three times ten threes, and ten times nine.

## IDYLL XII. The Technopaegnion

### Ausonius sends greetings to his Paulinus

I have sent you the *Technopaegnion*, a useless little work of my idle leisure. Its verses begin with monosyllables and end with monosyllables. Nor did the stony difficulty stop there: the misery of composing was increased by requiring the same monosyllable that was the ending of the final verse to become the beginning of the following one. Say, then, O delay and O punishment, that I have taken care over a vain thing. It is slight and wearisomely disconnected, and becomes entangled, since it is something amounting to nothing—or is caught in the act. Yet I labored so that it might contain something historical or dialectical. For poetic or [Col. 0898D] sophistic lightness was excluded by the necessity of the constraint. In short, there is no reason for you to marvel at it; but with only a few letters added, it is something for which you may feel pity, and which you should not wish to imitate. And if you descend to this level as well, you will incur more annoyance through loss of ingenuity and eloquence than pleasure from the desire to imitate.

Verses begun and ended with monosyllables, so that from the end of one verse one returns to the beginning of the next.

Chance feeds, rules, and destroys the fragile affairs of men.

Chance is uncertain and forever wavering; hope, flattering, cherishes it.

Hope has no limit in time; its boundary is death.

Death, greedy, plunges into the darkness below, which night—

Night, destined to pass, will restore its turn when golden light returns.

[Col. 0899A] Light, granted as a gift of the gods, for which the sun goes before.

The sun, from whom mighty Mars, armed for war, does not hide even through Venus’ theft.

Mars, born of no father, whom the Thracian people worship.

A people unbridled in men, for whom every law rushes into crime.

It is lawful to kill a man in sacrifice; such is the savage custom of the place.

A savage custom of a bold people, whom no law restrains.

Right is the law established by natural authority.

Law, born from human piety, is the sure mind of God.

Mind, which with heavenly perception waters the worthy heart.

A living heart, having the vigor and force of a soul, like the world itself.

Yet there is no force here: it is truly a jest, a thing of nothing.

As the old saying goes, spring follows winter, and here I append a little mischief of similar trifles. These verses end in monosyllables, though their opening is unrestricted, even if their ending is proper. Yet I labored so that, insofar as it could seem possible to indulgent ears, they might sing absurdities, receive tasteless things, and make gaps fit together; finally, that they might possess bitter sweetness, loveliness in what is unlovely, and softness in what is rough. Since all these things are disfigured by an unpleasant subject, kindly reading may make them acceptable. You too may trust me more confidently, since your own works are better. But, to finish by a proverb what we began with a saying: “Mules scratch one another.”

Monosyllables placed only at the end.

Art, rival of the gods, imitator of nature, mother of all things.

Let my game be content to be peaceful; be the guide of the work.

A strict and unlovely law, though unsuited to poetry.

Under so great a judge, speech will nevertheless receive its right.

[Col. 0899C] For glory has been granted even to ridiculous things, unless chance forbids it.

### On the limbs

In children the first tooth indicates the seven-year period.

A stronger voice anticipates the years of puberty.

The forehead of human beings is unconquered by winds and suns.

Hard bone joins the sinew to the flesh.

The restless, lively, smooth, sharp, warm heart throbs.

From it the senses draw their strength, senses which the ruling mind animates.

And the loquacious mouth conveys them into words according to measured law.

How powerful is the blue bile, such a small part of a human being!

How slender the shin, and what a great bodily mass it carries!

[Col. 0899D] Under what weight does the foot guide our journey!

### Disconnected pieces

Often a dowry becomes harmful in marriage if it is too great.

Both sexes are powerful, but the male prevails in authority.

He who acts rightly, not he who dominates, will be king.

Strife troubles friendships and separates treaties.

Begin whatever you do: the first part of a work is equivalent to the whole.

Praise insinuates itself into heaven and inserts the deserving among the gods.

The city is filled both with disciplines and with vices.

In secure cities, the citadel is more fortified than the cities themselves.

Gold has great honor; yet the value of gold is bronze.

A long day is laborious for a man, but night is restful.

[Col. 0900A] The Ethiopian region lacks it: the people are sleepless and restless.

Always, wherever clear light shines in eternal rotation.

### On the gods

There are also monosyllables among the dwellers in heaven. First among the gods is Fas,

Who is Themis to the Greeks. After her comes Rhea, who among the Latins is Ops.

Then comes Dis, brother of Jupiter and Consus, Tartarean.

And his sister and wife, queen of the gods, is Vis.

And the Sun, who as father rides forward in a four-horse chariot.

And Mars, armed for war, who arouses the savage movements of battle,

Whom neither piety nor good Peace ever concerns,

Nor Pan, inhabitant of the woods, to be kept silent, son of Maenalus,

Nor the household spirit, Lar, born of Larunda.

[Col. 0900B] And the sulfurous Nar, overwhelmingly powerful among the Italian rivers.

And Styx, dark as night, which atones for the gods’ perjuries.

Libs, Leuconotos, who crushes the sail-bearing sea.

And Hope, who never abandons the good of uncertain human beings.

### On foods

Nor will I keep silent about our foods, which ancient custom possesses,

Foods to which sea-salt is added as an irritant.

Once the common food of cattle and human beings was the acorn,

Before grain-bearing produce was available in the fields.

Then came emmer, and, from the meal of emmer, the flour used for porridge,

With which the plebs of Romulus once furnished their tables.

From this came food and drink, when the porridge was diluted with water.

[Col. 0900C] Among grains, pepper equals mustard in bite.

And the smooth, rounded lentil from Pelusian seed.

And the nut of five kinds, protected by a double shell.

And what is pleasing as food and drink—the bees’ hard labor: honey.

That liquid of a new nature, whose dregs float at the top.

### On histories

For you, Phoebus, the Oebalian flower has given new consolation.

With another flower, the sacred spring is guilty of Narcissus’ death.

The thunderbolt-like boar was the baleful glory of Adonis’ slaughter.

A Junonian cloud mocks the perjured Lapith.

Parnassian chance also makes sport of the son of Aeacus, the Delphi-dweller.

An ox cuts through the Thracian, Libyan, and Cimmerian seas.

A tree-trunk does not fall without the fate of a Hamadryad.

[Col. 0900D] The Saturnian sickle that generated Venus cut it down.

Dry among Scythian rocks stood a cross for birds.

From it came the blood-red dew from Prometheus’ body.

It sprinkled the crags and created deadly aconite.

When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane became his avenger.

At the tomb of Aeacus’ descendant, Andromache’s daughter-in-law was sacrificed.

In an Argive prison, slow death overtook Philopoemen.

The Armorican Lars, stripped of his spoils, gave the third rich prize.

A poisoned drink brought Hannibal to a late death.

How many undeserving things did deceit give over to death in Asia!

An avenging torch blazed from the Euboean cliffs.

Tros, begotten by Dardanus, stands beside Jupiter’s cup.

A Cretan man was carried through the air on swift wings.

[Col. 0901A] The savage Thracian imposed incestuous force upon you, Philomela.

The Lydian is barbarous, the Getan a slave, the Phrygian effeminate.

The Ligurians are deceitful; the Carian’s position is held in no esteem.

The fleece-bearing Ser combs the forest wool.

The Theban Sphinx with three bodies is famous in portents.

And the female Strix is famous for the cradles of little children.

### On early spring

When the year, from its rising, unlocks spring rich in flowers,

Everything thrives; every grove turns green; the golden countryside shines.

The root-stock is drawn out from the roots, preparing to send forth shade.

Snow, gathered in no dense fall, flows down toward the earth.

The scent of flowers breathes forth, like frankincense, the glory of Mount Lebanon.

### By question and answer

Who is brought to punishment by capital judgment? A surety.

[Col. 0901B] If the dispute concerns money, who will be given? A guarantor.

With whom does the murmillo contend? The evenly matched Thracian.

What name among the virtues belongs to Mercury? Thief.

What vessel is third among the gods’ censers and bowls? A dish.

What land, enclosed by the sea, produced Hippocrates? Cos.

Does a flock or a kingdom trouble Minos’ descendant? A flock.

What besides a cloud was placed upon the Phaeacians? A mountain.

Tell me: when food is absent, who is richer in sleep? The dormouse.

Tell me what makes backs suitable for shields? Glue.

What nominative is formed spontaneously from the ablative? *Spons*.

What four-footed creature is joined to birds in augury? A mouse.

What floats on the sea but does not swim in a river? Pitch.

What contains twice twelve equal parts? An *as*.

If a third part is missing, what remains? A *bes*.

[Col. 0901C] ### On Greek and Latin monosyllabic letters

I am the leader of the elements in Latin studies: Α.

And the final letter is written among Argolic signs: Ω.

I am the Aeolian Heta, and in Latin I have the value of epsilon: Ε.

I stand for what is always a short E in Latin, a Doric sound: Ε.

With this smooth and piercing sound the Attic people say “no”: Ο.

The Roman letter Ο balances both Greek Ω and Ο: Ο.

I am a letter resembling a licked tongue, a full voice commanding: Ι.

Unknown to Cecropian signs, I sound ominously: Υ.

I open Pythagoras’ forked path with ambiguous branches: Y.

Among Greek words I am never seen at the end: Μ.

A lying Zeta, if it rises, becomes the sign read as Ν.

Imitating the Maeander and its wandering bends, I wander: Ξ.

The divided monosyllable of Beta, Italian: Β.

[Col. 0901D] I bear not Delta’s form but its sound, Roman: Δ.

What shape is the hostile yoke? This will produce Π.

If you write P in the Ausonian manner, I shall be the Cecropian letter Ρ.

And Greek Rho will be changed into Latin Ρ.

As the mast carries a yard at its top, so am I: Τ.

This is the breath, bringing life with the lightest exhalation: Η.

This letter was added in Latium only to three names: Κ,

After C had first prevailed in the place of Gamma,

And, repeated as a title in its own right, had given another letter, Q.

When enclosed by two handles together with Iota, it will be read Θ.

In Latium I am the number ten; among the Greeks, Χ.

This is the figure of a crane, extended by Palamedes: Φ.

Once I was Boeotian Cappa; now I am Latin Κ.

With the appearance of a three-horned fork, I am almost last: Ψ.

### Grammar-bashing

You who now screech *elogodaedalia* in an excessively savage manner,

Do you condemn trifles? Certainly not: merchandise has its price.

As Ennius recalls, it fills you with joyful *gau*.

Let the livid mind of human beings cook condensed bile into pus.

Tell me, what do Virgil’s *catalecta* signify? In them he placed the Celts—

The following *tau* is no clearer.

And what is the deadly *min*, badly mixed with its twin?

How can one thing signify command, lawsuit, and Venus?

Is it a foreign word, or a Latin offspring?

Is it laid across the sea in two boats, or is it a bridge?

Virgil called a hedge *sepes* in pastoral poetry; why does Cicero say *seps*?

A familiar word, known to all, if you remember it: *lac*.

Why should the rule condemn it, so that it makes *lact* instead?

[Col. 0902B] Or is *seps*—the deadly Libyan creature—a Roman word?

If a good man is innocent, his opposite is guilty: he is *sons*.

Why does Dis, the Stygian Jupiter, have the name of one rich in possessions?

Whence did the Rudinian say, “the house of the gods, high-sounding heaven”?

And according to whose usage does he add what he builds, *endo suam do*?

Or, speaking of foliage, why does he say *frus* for poplar?

But where am I going? What is the end, the limit, and the boundary?

Be indulgent, Pacatus, a good, learned, and gracious man.

This whole work, scattered like Antiphila’s hair: peace.

## IDYLL XIII. The Nuptial Cento

### Ausonius sends greetings to Paulinus

Read through this too, if it is worth the effort: a trifling little work of no value, which neither labor forged nor care polished, lacking both the sharpness of ingenuity and the maturity that comes from delay. Those who first played with this sort of composition called it a cento. Its only task is to gather scattered pieces from memory and restore what has been torn apart—something you may laugh at more readily than praise. For that reason, if it were offered for sale at a figurine auction, neither Afranius would give a farthing for it, nor would Plautus offer his *Stichus*. I am ashamed to have dishonored the dignity of Virgilian verse with so playful a subject.

But what could I do? It had been commanded; and the strongest kind of command is a request from one who has the power to command—namely the emperor Valentinian, an educated man in my judgment, who had once described a wedding in a game of this kind, in verses well suited to the subject and with festive composition. Wanting to test how far he surpassed us by his rivalry, he ordered us to compose something similar from the same material. You may understand how scrupulous this was for me. I did not wish to be placed above him or below him; for if I yielded, foolish flattery would be exposed to everyone’s judgment, while if I stood out as a rival, I would seem insolent. I therefore undertook it as though reluctant, and successfully retained his favor without offending him by victory.

This was produced in a single day, with an added night of work. Having found it among my rough drafts, I have such confidence in your candor and affection that I have withheld nothing even of what deserves ridicule from your severity. Accept, then, a little work made continuous out of disconnected pieces, one out of diverse things, a jest out of serious matters, and our own out of another’s. In sacred and mythological works, do not be surprised either by the *Thyonian* or the *Virbius*: the former reshaped from Dionysus, the latter from Hippolytus. And if you allow me to teach you, though I myself need teaching, I shall explain what a cento is.

[Col. 0903A] A structure of verse is solidified from various places and from different meanings, so that either two cut-up pieces, or one and the following piece with its middle, may come together in a single verse. To place two whole verses together is inelegant, and three in one sequence is mere nonsense. The arrangement is distributed through all the caesuras admitted by the heroic verse, so that the half-line before the penthemimeral caesura may fit with the remaining anapaest, or a trochaic section with the latter segment, or seven half-feet with a choric anapaest, or whatever remains of the hexameter after a dactyl and a half-foot. You might compare it to the game the Greeks called *ostomachia* (ὀστομαχία, “bone-fight”). The little bones altogether have fourteen geometric shapes. They are equilateral or triangular with extended lines, or have right or oblique angles. They call them isosceles (ἰσοσκελῆ), equilateral (ἰσόπλευρα), right-angled (ὀρθογώνια), and scalene (σκαληνά).

[Col. 0903B] Through various combinations of these little joints, a thousand forms are imitated: an elephant, a beastly boar, a flying goose, a murmillo sitting in armor, a hunter and a barking dog, and even a tower and a cup, along with countless other such figures, which one person variegates more skillfully than another. But the arrangement of the skilled is a marvel; that of the unskilled is ridiculous.

From this statement you will know that I imitated the latter. Thus this little cento, in the manner in which that game is played, joins diverse meanings so that they fit, makes adopted pieces look related, prevents foreign elements from showing through, keeps borrowed pieces from seeming forced, prevents dense passages from bulging beyond measure, and keeps gaps from opening. If all this seems to you to have been done as prescribed, you will say that I have composed a cento; and since I earned advancement under my emperor, you will order me to receive my pay among the assembled ranks. Otherwise, you will have me broken up for bronze, so that, once the heap of verse has been returned to its treasury, the verses may go back to where they came from. Farewell.

Receive these words into your hearts, and turn your joyful minds toward them,

Both endowed with spirit, both distinguished by outstanding arms;

Both flourishing, a lineage unconquerable in war.

And you first—for clear faith shows that you proceed upon the sea

Under greater auspices. Than whom there was none more just,

nor greater in piety, war, and arms.

And you and your son, the second great hope of Rome,

Flower of the ancients, courage of men, my greatest concern,

Bearing your grandfather’s name, and your father’s character and hands.

I sing nothing without command. Each person’s beginnings

Will bring him labor and fortune; it is right for me to undertake what I was ordered.

[Col. 0903D] ### The wedding feast

The awaited day had arrived; and worthy of the wedding-song,

Mothers and men, young people before their parents’ faces,

Gathered together, and reclined upon spread purple.

Servants gave water to their hands and loaded baskets

With gifts of hard-working Ceres; and they brought the roasted

Flesh of fat game, a very long procession of things:

Birds and cattle were not absent, nor swift roe-deer,

nor sheep and unruly kids,

Nor the sea’s creatures, nor fallow deer and fleeing stags.

Before their eyes and among their hands were ripe fruits.

When hunger had been removed and the desire for eating restrained,

[Col. 0904A] They set out great mixing bowls and served Bacchus.

They sing sacred songs, applaud the dances, and recite verses.

Nor is the Thracian priest absent, in his long robe,

Answering the rhythms with the seven divisions of the voice.

From the other side, the double pipe gives its song.

All rest from their work; and everyone, leaving the tables,

Rises. In crowds they run through the joyful doorways,

People and fathers, matrons and boys, alternating their parts,

And roll their voices through the spacious halls; lamps hang

From the golden ceilings.

### Description of the bride as she goes out

At last she comes forth, Venus’ most proper concern,

Now ripe for a husband, now marriageable in the fullness of her years,

Bearing the face and bearing of a maiden. A deep blush

Set fire beneath it and ran hotly across her cheeks;

She rolled her eyes, and burned those who looked upon her.

All the young people poured from houses and fields,

And the crowd of mothers marveled at her; the white footprints

of her white foot; and she had let her hair stream upon the winds.

She wears embroidered garments stiff with a gold under-weft,

The adornment of Argive Helen; and such as golden Venus

Is accustomed to appear among the gods, and of such stature,

Such was her appearance. Joyfully she carried herself thus

To her parents-in-law and sat, leaning high upon the throne.

### Description of the bridegroom as he goes out

From the other side, through the lofty doors, the boy brought himself forth,

the first bloom of unshorn youth marking his face.

An embroidered golden cloak covered him; around it abundant

Meliboean purple ran in a double meander,

And a tunic his mother had woven with soft gold.

His face and shoulders were like a god, and the light of youth was upon him.

As when Lucifer, drenched in the waters of Ocean,

Raises his sacred face into the sky, so did he carry his face,

So his eyes, and madly he hastened toward the doorway.

Love troubles him, and fixes his gaze upon the maiden.

He lightly kissed her and clung to her, embracing her right hand.

### Offering of gifts

Boys come forward and, before the faces of the parents,

Carry gifts: a mantle stiff with figures and gold,

Gifts of gold and ivory in abundance,

A chair, and a painted covering with saffron acanthus.

Great silverware for the tables, a beaded necklace,

[Col. 0904D] And a double crown of gems and gold.

A female slave is given to her, with two children at her breast.

Four young men are assigned to her, and as many unmarried girls;

All with hair shorn according to custom, and around the upper breast

A flexible twisted gold collar.

### Epithalamium for both

Then the mothers, pouring out their eagerness, lead them to the doorway.

But an equal chorus, boys and unmarried girls,

Play and sing songs in unadorned verses.

O woman joined to a worthy husband, most welcome wife,

May you be happy, having experienced the first labors of Lucina.

And, as a mother, receive the mixing cups of Maeonian Bacchus.

Scatter nuts, bridegroom; bind these altars with a ribbon.

Flower of the ancients, courage of men. A wife is led to you,

[Col. 0905A] So that she may spend all her years with you,

In accordance with such merits, and make you a father through beautiful offspring.

Fortunate both, if the gracious gods have any power.

“Live happily,” they said; “run on in harmony, while the steadfast divinity of the Fates unspools the threads.”

## IDYLL XIV. Roses wrongly attributed to Maro, which Jerome Alexander, relying on an ancient manuscript, ascribed to the author

It was spring, and the returning day breathed forth in the saffron morning

Cold that bit gently with a mild sensation.

A sharper breeze had preceded the eastern yoke,

Urging the hot day to arrive early.

I wandered through the watered crossroads of gardens,

Desiring to invigorate myself in the mature day.

[Col. 0905B] I saw hoarfrost congealed across the bending grass,

Hanging there, or standing on the tips of vegetables;

I saw smooth drops play upon the spreading stalks,

Then heavy with the weight of heavenly water.

I saw rose gardens rejoicing in Paestanian cultivation,

Dewy beneath the rising new light.

A rare bud was whitening on frosty shrubs,

Destined to perish at the first rays of day.

You might have wondered whether dawn was stealing the roses’ redness,

Or giving it to them, and whether the rising day dyed the flowers.

One dew, one color, and one morning belonged to two things:

To star and flower, for Venus is mistress of both.

Perhaps one scent as well; but the scent of the star

Diffuses more loftily through the air, while this one exhales nearby.

The goddess of Paphos, common to star and flower,

Commands that they bear the appearance of one purple dye.

A moment made the difference: the moment in which the flowers’ emerging

Buds would separate from one another at equal intervals.

This one grows green, covered by a narrow cap of leaves;

This one is marked by red-purple color on a slender leaf.

This opens the high summit of its first obelisk,

Releasing the point of its purple head.

That one was unfolding the coverings gathered at its crown,

Already planning to count itself among its own leaves.

There was no delay: it opened the beauty of its smiling basket,

Revealing the dense seeds of enclosed saffron.

This one, which just now had shone with the full fire of its hair,

Is abandoned pale by its fallen leaves.

I marveled at the swift plunder of its fleeing life,

And at roses growing old while they were being born.

[Col. 0905D] Look—the pomegranate-red hair of the shining flower also fell away

While I speak, and the earth glitters covered with redness.

One day opens so many forms, such great beginnings, and such varied renewals;

One day brings them to an end.

We complain, Nature, that the grace of flowers is brief:

You snatch away the gifts displayed before our eyes at once.

As long as one day is, so long is the life of roses,

whose youth is pressed hard by old age joined to it.

The one whom the red East saw just now being born,

Returning late in the evening, it saw as an old woman.

Yet it is well that, though destined to perish after only a few days,

One age succeeds another and prolongs its own life.

Gather roses, maiden, while the flower is fresh and your youth is new,

And remember that your own life hastens in the same way.

## IDYLL XV. From the Greek: Pythagorean poem on the ambiguity of choosing a life

[Col. 0906A]

What path of life shall I follow? If the forums are full of turmoil,

If the household is anxious with cares, if household concern follows

Those abroad, if new losses always await the merchant,

If shameful poverty forbids rest,

If labor vexes the farmer, and the terror of shipwreck makes the sea infamous,

If severe punishments await the unmarried life,

And a still more burdensome, vain watchfulness the wary husband;

If the bloody work of Mars, if the shameful profits

Of usury, and swift interest slaughter the poor?

Every age is care; everyone dislikes his own period of life.

Infants at the breast lack understanding; boys endure

Hard beginnings, and young men reckless youth.

Fortune afflicts men through wars, through the sea,

[Col. 0906B] Through anger, ambushes, and chained labors,

Always to be exchanged for heavier ones. Old age itself,

Long awaited and desired by malicious prayers,

Exposes a body liable to countless diseases.

We all commonly despise the present, though it is agreed

That some refuse to become gods. Juturna protests:

“Why did he give eternal life? Why was the condition

Of death taken away?” Thus beneath the Caucasian rock

Prometheus testifies and never ceases to accuse

Jupiter, son of Saturn, because eternal life was given.

Look also at the pursuits of the mind: thus an unhappy concern

for chastity destroyed Hippolytus.

But if it pleases someone to lead a life stained by seductions,

Let him look also at the punishments and crimes of kings:

The incest of Tereus, or the softness of Sardanapalus.

[Col. 0906C] Three Punic wars warn us to avoid treachery.

But destroyed Saguntum forbids us to keep faith.

Live, and always cherish friendships. For this offense

The learned school of Pythagorean philosophers perished.

Fearing this, then, cherish none. For this offense

Timon was once stoned at Athens by the followers of Pallas.

The mind, confronted by ambiguous wishes, is always divided,

And it is not enough for a person to have wished: he rejects what he desired.

It is pleasant to be honored; soon he regrets it, and, in order to rule,

He will wish to serve. Once increased in honor,

He is exposed to envy; eloquent men endure sleepless care.

But the uneducated lack the adornment of life. Be a patron,

And defend defendants; but a client’s gratitude is rare.

Be a client: the patron’s authority is a burdensome role.

A father's hopes press upon him. Soon harsh

anxiety follows his cares. Childless old age is despised,

and one lacking an heir is the prey of the legacy-hunter.

Live sparingly: you will be torn apart by the reputation of greed.

But censure will mark the lavish man more severely.

Everything is opposed to itself through contrary circumstances. Therefore

The best Greek judgment is this: they say that for a human being

It is good not to be born, or, once born, to die quickly.

## IDYLL XVI. On the good man. Pythagorean lecture (Πυθαγορικὴ ἀκρόασις)

A good and wise man, such as Apollo, consulted by many thousands of human beings,

Hardly found one, judges himself and examines himself completely.

Unconcerned with what nobles may bring or what the empty opinion

Of the crowd may bring, he is smooth and round, possessing the likeness of the world,

So that no external stain may settle upon his polished surface.

[Col. 0907A] He considers how long the day will be beneath the constellation of Cancer,

And how long the night stretches beneath the tropic of Capricorn;

He weighs himself in the just examination of the balance,

So that nothing may gape, nothing bulge, and the angle may meet

At equal sides, so that the set-square may deviate in nothing.

Whatever lies beneath must be solid; nor should a blow

Struck by pressing fingers reveal emptiness below.

He does not lower his eyes into sweet sleep

Before he has reviewed everything accomplished during the long day.

“What have I gone beyond? What was done in its time, and what was not?

Why did honor attend that action, or reason attend the other?

What have I left behind? Why did this opinion settle in my mind,

When it would have been better to change it? Pitying the needy,

[Col. 0907B] Why did I feel someone’s grief with a broken mind?

What did I desire, when it would have been good not to desire it?

Why did I, a bad man, prefer utility to honor?

Did I wound anyone by a word, or finally by a look?

Why does nature draw me more strongly than discipline?”

Thus going through all his words and deeds, and reviewing everything

at the coming of evening, offended by what was wrong,

He gives the palm and prizes to what was right.

## IDYLL XVII. Yes and No, Pythagorean (Ναὶ καὶ Οὔ Πυθαγορικόν)

“Yes” and “No”—everyone frequently uses these monosyllabic signs.

When these are removed, nothing remains that human speech can set in motion;

Everything is in them and from them, whether there is business

Or leisure, a crowd or quiet.

Sometimes they oppose one another equally, sometimes separately,

In their pursuits, just as character and temperament

Have found conflict either easy or difficult.

If agreement is reached, there is no delay: “It is, it is.”

If there is dispute, disagreement will follow: “No.”

Hence the forums leap apart with shouting; hence the mad

Quarrels of the Circus; hence the joyful riot of the theater,

Packed in its tiers; and the senate-house also stirs such disputes.

Marriage and children with their fathers sow these words

Of repose among their pursuits, speaking without violating affection.

From here too the school, harmonious with its accepted doctrines,

Conducts its dogmatic disputes in peaceful contest.

Here the whole dialectical crowd of philosophers argues:

“Is there light? Is it therefore day?” They do not agree.

For whenever night-light exists for a person from many torches

Or flashes of lightning, there is light, but it is not the light of day.

[Col. 0907D] Therefore there is “yes” and “no” whenever it must be admitted

That there is light, but not that there is day. A thousand disputes arise from this.

Here a few, and many others pondering such matters,

Gnaw at their furious silences with muffled murmuring.

[Col. 0908A] Such is human life, revolved through two monosyllables!

## IDYLL XVIII. On the ages of animals, Hesiodic

It exceeds ten times nine years by three times two:

the proper span which completes the life of men grown old.

The talkative crow surpasses them by living nine times as long,

And the stag exceeds the crow’s ages four times.

The raven surpasses the swift-footed stag three times;

And the Phoenix, the bird renewed, multiplies the raven ninefold.

You, Hamadryad nymphs, surpass these by a life ten times as long and unending;

yours is the longest life.

These beings contain the limits of the enduring fates of living creatures.

The god who governs hidden eternity knows the remaining periods:

What ages Stilbon revolves, what centuries Phaenon,

[Col. 0908B] What circuits Pyrois possesses, what Jupiter encircles

With kindly fire, and with what return nourishing Venus hastens;

What labors await Phoebe, and how many await the Titan.

Until, when the Great Year has been completed,

The wandering stars return again to their ancient course,

As they had stood arranged from the origin of the world.

## IDYLL XIX. Monostichs on the labors of Hercules

The first labor was the endurance of the Cleonaean lion.

Next, with sword and torch, he crushed the Lernaean Hydra.

Soon the third exertion struck down the Erymanthian boar.

In the fourth he carried off the golden horns of the brazen-footed stag.

In the fifth contest he drove away the Stymphalian birds.

In the sixth he stripped the Thracian Amazon of her belt.

The seventh was the labor expended in the stables of Augeas.

[Col. 0908C] The eighth victory is reckoned in driving out the bull.

Victory over the horses of Diomedes is the ninth.

With Geryon destroyed, Iberia gives the tenth palm.

In the eleventh triumph, the apples of the Hesperides were drawn forth.

Cerberus is the final limit of the last labor.

## IDYLL XX. Discoveries and gifts of the Muses

CLIO, singing deeds, gives back the ages that have passed.

MELPOMENE cries out sadly with tragic wailing.

Comic THALIA delights in playful speech.

EUTERPE urges her sweet-speaking reeds with her breath.

TERPSICHORE moves, commands, and increases emotions with her lyres.

ERATO, holding the plectra, dances with foot, song, and face.

CALLIOPE entrusts heroic songs to books.

[Col. 0908D] URANIA examines the movements of heaven and the stars.

POLYHYMNIA marks everything with her hand and speaks through gesture.

The power of Apollo’s mind moves these Muses everywhere.

Phoebus, seated in the middle, embraces them all.

[Col. 0907]

## ECLOGARIUM. (C)

### On the nature of the libra

[Col. 0907D]

You may wonder that the immense bodies of the world remain,

Surrounded by the lofty circuit of heaven,

And that no flaw interrupts so great a structure.

Receive something more worthy of wonder: the tiniest principles,

Not admitted to our sight,

Are joined together in a sequence of tiny atoms.

[Col. 0908D] But in small things there is something solid, a segment divisible by no one,

From which vigor and strength remain, and the eternal mobility of things,

Never to be overcome by any age.

Human things may be compared with divine ones. Thus

The *as* is solid, since it consists of twelve equal parts,

And yet among the smallest equal parts one force remains.

For if anything is diminished from the number, the whole totters,

And the parts fall when the body has been weakened:

As when someone pulls out the middle stone from a vaulted arch,

Upon which everything rests, all the remaining stones together

Will follow the slope and drag the common ruin from the summit.

The same is true of the *libra*. If an ounce is missing, the whole

Will no longer be an *as*, and, lacking a twelfth, will now bear the name *deunx*.

Nor does it retain the name *dextans* when the *sextans* has been removed.

And the *dodrans*, born from the quarter, will lack its source.

When the third is torn away, it prevents the *bes* from remaining.

Now there will be no *quincunx* for you if you remove the first part.

And what of the *semis*, whose half is the remaining half of the dying *as*,

And whose seventh part of the *libra* is the *septunx*?

The *libra*, then, is whole if it does not totter in any part.

It is the balance of weight, number, character, deeds, and waters;

There is no measure that you do not mark by this name.

[Col. 0909B] The earth, which hangs in the middle of the air, is a *libra*.

And its *libra* restrains the courses of the Sun and Moon.

Libra determines the equal hours of day and night.

Libra keeps the shoreless Caledonian tides within bounds.

You too, remain a sure *libra* for me in my conduct.

### On the nature of a mature childbirth

Everything that we measure through the varied activity of things

Is governed by the stars; to human beings belong only earthly limbs,

While fortune and spirit come from above,

To be governed by the sevenfold chorus. But the golden Sun presides over them,

Having been allotted rule of the shining ether.

Nor does it govern only the periods of our lives,

While we prolong the short span of our anxious age.

It is believed that by its sight it forms hidden births

And the periods of life to be spent in the maternal womb,

And determines the laws of life not yet brought forth.

For when the conception has settled in the generative womb,

There is no doubt that the Sun occupies some sign.

When it has taken its station in the region of the neighboring star,

It pours no light into the adjacent beginnings.

But when, after the months have passed, it climbs,

Its reins turned, toward the third stars in its purple chariot,
