It sends forth a slanting and feeble ray,

Breathing slight movement through inert masses.

In the fourth position the indulgence of the first Sun grows strong.

It also encourages the tender fetus, suffused with light, to grow together.

The radiance flashes with a life-giving tetragonal aspect,

Bright and gently gleaming; in the fifth quarter of the sign

It strikes the startled mother when the child is quickened.

[Col. 0909D] For in the sixth place there is no power, since no rule of a balanced side is marked for Phoebus to protect. But when, in the middle region of the sign-bearing host, the seventh boundary has received the camp of the blazing sun in a direct position, it sees the bonds of the swelling birth already full beneath the complete light; nor, extending the flashes of its sparing light, does the whole crown favor the birth with its entire fire.

Hence that which anticipates Lucina’s appointed labors and senses the straining efforts stealing upon the pregnant woman before the expected prayer of the hastening mother.

But unless, when the seventh star has poured forth its lights, it shall have driven back the resisting bolts of the slow labor, the later sign cannot prevail where the earlier one can. Is this because the aspect of the eighth star, rivaling the sixth, does not know how to form equal-sided figures?

[Col. 0910A] Yet, pressing upon the ninth sign, it relieves the hesitant prayers of mothers, with the following trigon joining its strength. But if difficult Ilithyia prolongs the labor, the tetragon will loosen the bonds of doubtful delay.

## The heavenly signs

Toward the regions of the North are joined the Bears and the Serpent.

After these come Boötes, and likewise the Crown, the Kneeling One fallen forward, the Lyre, the Bird, Cepheus, and Cassiopeia;

the Charioteer and Perseus, the Triangle and the star of Andromeda,

Pegasus and Delphinus, the Arrow, the Eagle, and the Serpent-Bearer.

Next lies the zodiacal belt: twice six signs complete it.

Here are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo,

Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, Capricorn, and the Water-Bearer,

[Col. 0910B] and Pisces. After these, in the southern regions, are

Orion, Procyon, Lepus, blazing Sirius, Argo,

Hydra, Chiron, the Altar, and the great Fish.

The Sea-Monster follows this, together with the streams of Eridanus.

But in addition, seven wandering lights are said to exist:

the Moon and Mercury, Venus and the Sun, and also shining Mars.

Here is Jupiter, whose star shines above all the stars.

Higher than these is Saturn, slower than all the stars.

## The reckoning of the revolving year

The Sun completes ninety-four days and a half

while he passes from one tropic sign to the other,

proceeding from Phryxus’s Ram to the eight-footed Crab.

Within this span occur the summer’s onset and the day’s limit.

[Col. 0910C] Half a day, two days, and nineteen times ten,

from Cancer to the Claws, the Sun completes in a second course

the equal periods of night and day,

the golden Sun mingling the boundaries of autumn and summer.

From there, passing in order through the autumnal months,

he proceeds to the tropic sign of icy Capricorn,

adding eight days, ten times eight more,

and a quarter of a day; in the fifth year this immediately

receives the name of an intercalary month at the end of Numa’s month.

From there, hastening toward the horns of Agenor’s bull,

the golden Sun climbs to the tropic sign of the Bearer of the Fleece,

restraining it with a fixed limit of ninety days.

This will always be your circle through the turning years:

three hundred and sixty-five days.

## On the names of the seven days

[Col. 0910D]

The year has names suited to the seven revolving days;

the same number of wandering planets gave them those names.

The World, rolling them in its tireless revolution,

orders them to wander in the oblique station of the signs.

The radiant Sun possesses the first and highest day.

Next comes the Moon, sister of the Sun’s crown.

The third is assigned to the Titanian light, Mars.

Mercury claims for himself the stars of the fourth day.

The golden stars of Jupiter illuminate the fifth zone.

The life-bringing, nourishing Venus follows as the sixth parent.

The seventh light belongs to Saturn, who surpasses all.

The revolving orbit restores the eighth Sun.

This verse has no author. What ought to be removed from the body on each day.

[Col. 0911A]

“Mercury’s fingernails, Jupiter’s beard, Venus’s hair.”

This must be refuted as follows.

Mercury approves of ever-sharp fingernails in theft,

and does not allow their edge to be blunted at the joints.

A beard is Jupiter’s distinction, hair Venus’s adornment; therefore it is necessary

that neither of them wish removed what each finds pleasing.

Mars loved beardlessness, and the Moon baldness.

They do not forbid the hair of head and cheeks to be cut.

The Sun and Saturn offer no objection to fingernails; therefore

do not remove from the gods this one-line saying.

## On the months and the four seasons of the year

The four following monostichs will tell you

the eternal months and the four seasons of the year.

[Col. 0911B]

March, April, and May are the season of spring.

July, August, and likewise June are summer.

Autumn belongs to September, October, and all of November.

Winter belongs to January, February, and December.

## Monostichs on the months

January, you begin the Roman Kalends.

Numa established the Februa in the neighboring month.

March brought forth the beginnings of the ancient year.

Nourishing Venus claims April, rich in fruit.

May was named from the name of the ancestors, the maiores.

June is nearest to the title of youth.

July enlarges Quintilis with the Caesarian name.

[Col. 0911C] August follows with a Caesarian name.

September, Pomona, makes your autumn rich.

October enriches the fields with a grain-bearing harvest.

November, you hurl the stars into the sea at an untimely hour.

December, you bring on the fruitful winter with festivity.

## Couplets on the same months

January, new month, you give your name to the first month;

January, two-faced, you look upon two seasons at once.

After the worship of the gods above, Februa, in the neighboring month,

Numa gives funeral offerings to the kindred Manes.

March, guardian both of the Roman race and of the year,

you first gave the Latins their seasons, when they had consuls.

The mother of the Aeneadae, Venus, gives April

its neighboring name, for Aphrodite is the companion of Mars.

[Col. 0911D] Maia the goddess, or a greater age—May—

I am uncertain whether either gave you your name;

but each is a worthy founder of the month.

June follows it, to be celebrated with twofold honor,

whether Juno or Juventas gave it its name.

Then comes July, shining with the star of Dione,

holding the fixed season of midsummer.

August follows with a kindred name derived from Caesar,

and is next to him in the order of the year as in descent.

After these the months are linked and mark their number in order:

September, sprinkling the wine-press with Bacchus’s gift;

and October, happy in the time of sowing,

nourishes the hope of the eager farmer;

while November, sinking the customary stars into the sea,

hurls them down, soon to return to their own sky.

[Col. 0912A] December, completing the number and the fruitful festivals,

finishes the year, so that a new year may soon proceed from winter.

## How many days there are in each month

June, April, and November together with September

fill each of their months with thirty days.

To seven months add one day beyond three tens:

to the Kalends of January and March,

and to those which May, July, and August contain,

and to those which October and December, placed at the end, contain.

There will be one month of only twenty-eight days,

which Numa decreed should follow the preceding January.

Thus the year counts three hundred and sixty-five days,

with a quarter added.

## The three divisions of the months

[Col. 0912B]

Lucina renews twice six Kalends in the year,

and Jupiter gives an equal number of Ides to run their course.

The day of the Nones is made by the second day before the eighth.

These are the only three names belonging to a Roman month;

the remaining days are designated by numbers.

## In which months the Nones and Ides fall on which days

Sometimes the fourth day opens the Nones, sometimes the sixth.

The sixth belongs to May, October, and March,

and to July, which brings its season at the solstice.

The rest of the months are furnished with Nones on the fourth day.

The Ides, however, return on the eighth day in every month.

## On which day the Kalends fall in each month

[Col. 0912C]

After the Ides, which each month possesses in its order,

the Kalends return with different numbers, varying—

[lacuna] while they are called again and again,

until at last they advance with the rising of the desired season.

For three times six days and one, the fruitful festival

extends, so that it may summon January, delayed by the new winter.

With this number, and with Numa’s month, the month returns,

and September, fosterling of Bacchus, brings back the beginning of autumn.

July, May, December placed at the end,

and October are recalled one day later.

From there four return with one day fewer,

to which I shall add in number: Sextilis, June, and

April, after which November reaches the penultimate limit.

With three times five days and one, Mars of June,

you are summoned to return and bring back the first beginnings.

With this number the year, turning to its fullness, will be restored.

## Which sign is in each month along the Sun’s course

[Col. 0912D]

Tropic Capricorn establishes the beginning of January.

In the middle of Numa’s month the faithful Water-Bearer stands firm.

The twin Pisces proceed into the season of March.

You behold, Phryxean Ram, the Kalends of April.

May marvels at the horns of Agenor’s Bull.

June sees the Laconians proceeding across the balanced sky.

At the solstice July bears the star of the blazing Crab.

The fiery Lion burns the month of August with its fire.

September, beneath your star, Virgo, makes Bacchus rich.

October balances Libra at the time of sowing.

[Col. 0913A] November, the winter month, orders precipitous Scorpio to advance.

The Archer ends his signs in the middle of December.

The verses of Quintus Cicero concern knowing which sign is prominent in which season; this is also explained above in our verses.

Pisces bring forth the spring streams with dim light.

Aries makes the course of night and day equal.

The horns of Taurus are adorned with flowers that announce the season.

Gemini opens the dry beginnings of summer.

The brilliant Crab already shortens the long lights.

The enfeebling Lion exhales the fierce heat from its mouth.

Afterward, Virgo, shaking herself a little, drives away the vapor that has risen.

Libra, with its star, opens the gates of autumn

and balances the hours of day against those of night.

And the flame of the Scorpion strips the branches of their fruit.

[Col. 0913B] The sluggish Archer shoots cold upon the lands.

Capricorn breathes forth winter, freezing with frost beneath its radiance.

The lofty Water-Bearer follows, sprinkling liquid mist;

the streams of the universe are vigorous above and around it.

On the right and left the Sun’s shining wheel drives

the moving course, and the likenesses of the Moon are carried along.

The twisted Scales rise beneath the eternal gaze of the Dragon.

Between them, shining among the seven stars,

the Great Bear shakes itself, star-studded; Boötes, guarding it,

is late to sink down on the high shore of Ocean together with the light.

## The reckoning from the solstice to the equinox

The Sun, having departed from the mild spring equinox,

after half a day and then a full ninety-four days,

blazing with fiery reins, completes the summer’s appointed course.

[Col. 0913C] From there autumn, balancing the hours of night with equal light,

[uncertain: “eighty-eight goers”], and more than three hours.

[licuna]

From there spring, flowering, returns with reversed reins,

adding two circuits to the earlier [uncertain: “goers”].

## Roman holidays

Now I shall speak of the Apollinean games through the Tiber’s mouths,

and of the hidden rites of the Megalesian Mother.

I shall explain the days of Vulcan, the beginning of the first autumn,

and the Quinquatria of the goddess Pallas;

and the middle Ides, recurring in May and August,

which Mercury and Diana respectively claim for themselves.

I shall recall what rites matrons celebrate in honor of their husbands,

when the first days of Mars have returned.

[Col. 0913D] I shall commemorate the famous Caprotine festivals on the Nones,

when, after the matrons’ stolae have been removed, they cover the serving-women.

Those four also, distributed through the separate regions of the year,

are the solstices and the days equal to the nights.

Nor is it right to leave unmentioned the Regifugium,

the joyful day for Romans after the tyrants were driven from the city.

[Col. 0914A] Do you wish me to speak of the festival of Ops before her sacred rites,

or of the Saturnalia, the festivals of slaves when they serve their masters?

Or of the festivals that return on no fixed days,

when each person worships his own crossroads throughout the streets?

Or of the double worship called the Neptunalia,

and that which they call after Consus and his counsels?

These festivals, celebrated with ships or with chariots,

unite Roman leaders and neighboring commanders.

I shall add the worship and foreign rites of the gods,

the Herculean birthday and the festival of Isis’s ship;

and also the happy Floralia of the wanton theater,

which those who deny that they wished to see them nevertheless desire to watch.

Now the ancient Equiria games are also celebrated.

These are the first names which the Roman Circus bears.

[Col. 0914B] Rome also honors the Dionysiac games under a Latin name,

as Liber dedicates vows to himself.

The plebeian aediles and the curule aediles likewise

celebrate the sacred rites called by the name of the Little Images.

It is known that gladiators fought funeral battles

in the Forum; now the arena claims its own contests:

at the end of December they appease with blood

the heaven-born god who bears the sickle.

## On the lustral contests

Achaea celebrated four ancient games.

Two belong to the gods above, and two are festivals of men.

They are the sacred games of Jupiter, Phoebus, Palaemon, and Archemorus.

Their crowns are pine, apple, olive, and parsley.

## The locations of the contests

[Col. 0914C]

The first, the Olympian games, are celebrated for great Jupiter at Pisa.

Parnassus consecrated the Pythian games to Clarian Phoebus.

Corinth, between two seas, dedicates the Isthmian contests to Portunus.

The Thebans celebrate the funeral Nemean games of Archemorus.

## The founders of the contests

Jupiter first consecrated the festivals of the Olympian crown

and the stadiums of the Argive Circus to the longest races.

Alcides next consecrated the honor of Nemea.

These sacred games, also marked by periods of five years,

were given to Neptune as the Isthmian games, and to Phoebus as the Pythian,

with a double worship of the buried gods and men.

## That the same contests are sacred games and funeral games

[Col. 0914D]

Elis dedicates a mournful honor to Pelops, son of Tantalus.

The Thebans celebrate the five-year Nemean games of Archemorus.

It is known that the Isthmian games were celebrated for the dead Palaemon.

Delphi established the Pythian games to appease the Dragon.

---

[Col. 0913]

# BOOK OF LETTERS (C)

## LETTER I. Ausonius to his father on the birth of a son

[Col. 0913D]

I had believed that nothing could be added to my feelings

to make you, revered father, more dearly loved.

[Col. 0914D] Something has been added—thanks to the gods and to my middle-generation descendant,

who has given our names a double yoke.

My grandson has made you a grandfather; he is likewise my son,

and I am yours: by this child we are both fathers.

Nor does my own filial devotion alone urge me to love you:

[Col. 0915A] I love you now by the name of two fathers.

A new title has been added, by which your dignity may increase:

through it I may teach my son what it means to love his father.

For I seem to have been made your equal, because the little one,

by this name that honors you, ennobles me as well.

And because our ages are alike—for I am nearly your equal in years,

and can take the place of a brother.

Nor is there as much time between our years

as usually separates other men.

I have therefore seen brothers whose births were separated by as many years

as separate ours. Names do not burden age.

Thus beautiful youth joins itself to your old age,

so that what came first may remain, and what has just begun may begin.

And I think it has pleased both generations that neither

should give itself to the other at an unhurried time.

[Col. 0915B] One would flow gently, the other would come without haste,

bearing ripened fruit while the blossom remained.

I testify, best of fathers, that I do not know your years:

I reckon you to have as many as I believe myself to have.

May the child not know this; may the more hasty heir count

wills more carefully than affectionate prayers,

and by a wicked example teach children to grow young,

so that they may not wish to have fathers who are old as well.

But I, born from a father already advanced in years, shall confess

that these times of nearly equal age are dear to me.

I owe you the fact that I was born. Affection for my grandson urges

that another child be added to the father, so that we may honor the grandfather.

You too, my father, rejoice in your doubled titles,

made a grandfather by the name of your firstborn son.

It is little to be a grandfather. May the holy powers of the gods favor us,

and may he become a great-grandfather through his own grandson.

The Fates may be able to prolong old age more generously;

but I think those prayers are surest which are more restrained.

## LETTER II. Father to his son, when he himself had remained at Trier during the tyrannical times and his son had departed from his father

This unfinished and incomplete piece is described as written in scraps.

I owe this history also to our cares, dearest son,

although the anxious lament of sorrowful affairs

was not worthy of a peaceful title.

Already the boats had carried you out upon the sluggish back

of the chilly Moselle, my son, and the hostile river

had separated the kisses and embraces of your grieving father.

I was alone; and although surrounded by a friendly gathering,

[Col. 0915D] I was alone. I offered faithful prayers to the departing vessel,

still seeing you, my son, alone; and I blamed the swift rowers

for their hurried course against the current.

What day was that? That day is not longer than the year

which the learned Meton’s Attic calculation gathered together.

Abandoned, I exercise myself at empty and solitary altars.

Now I cut down the budding leaves of the willows;

now I break grassy couches; and among the green sedges

I smooth slippery tracks with stones laid beneath.

Thus the first light passed; thus the second limit of day;

thus alternating revolution turns the two darknesses;

and so the others; thus the whole year will pass for me,

until your Fates restore me to you as your father.

On these terms I may bargain even with death:

[Col. 0916A] so long as you, my son, survive to honor your father’s end.

## LETTER III. Ausonius to Hesperius

Like a thrush that plunders the olives of Picenum

and fattens its waxen haunches,

or like one who has seized shining grapes from the vines

and hangs from the entangling nets,

which float beneath the evening hours in mist,

or are stretched out in the dewy morning,

such birds, from the winter hedges, wishing themselves to be caught,

we have sent to you,

twice ten of them; for that many the precipitous flight

brought beneath the dim light of the eastern dawn.

Then we joined to them the married ducks

which the neighboring marsh supplied as prey,

oar-footed, ravaging the blue waters with their broad bills,

and red of leg like purple.

Their many-colored feathering painted them in iridescent hues,

and their necks rivaled those of doves.

These dishes have not been stolen from my table.

When you eat, we enjoy them more.

Fare well, that I may fare well.

## LETTER IV. Ausonius orders Theon, a Paganus whom the scepter now fears, to be greeted

What are you doing, placed at the world’s farthest shores,

poet and dweller in the sands? What shore must be plowed

near the end of Ocean and the setting sun,

which a cheap hut confines beneath a reed-thatched roof,

while the tearful farmstead stains it with pitch-black smoke?

What are things doing, and what are the Muses doing, and the guardian Apollo?

These are not Muses born on Helicon or from the horse’s spring,

but those which, from the fertile breast of Clementinus,

breathe alien verse into poets whose minds are empty.

With good reason: for who would prefer his poems to be called his own

when you can cut him down with a carefree laugh?

You should recite these as well, so that they may not press upon our shame;

then your words will truly be able to seem yours.

Yet what sort of life do you lead on the shore of the Meduli?

Do you conduct trade, capturing goods with a lighter coin,

which a heavy auction will soon sell at insane prices?

White balls of tallow, and heavy masses of wax,

Narycian pitch and split papyrus,

[Col. 0916D] and smoking torches, once the lights of country folk?

Or, undertaking greater matters, do you pursue throughout the whole region

the thieves who, fearing you at the edge of the world,

invite you to share in the booty and its division?

Are you merciful, and hating human blood, do you pardon crimes for money,

call theft an error, and impose a price upon driven-off cattle,

passing from judge to accomplice in the crimes?

Or, with your brother, do you surround wandering deer

through pathless thickets, with spots and many a feathered snare?

Or do you drive the course of a foaming boar with shouts,

and support the beast? Yet I advise you always to refuse

to thrust your lightning-fast hunting spears at your enemy from close range.

Take warning from your brother, who, with his garment drawn back,

displays his foul limbs beside the shameful pools,

and exposes his pierced buttocks naked near his anus.

[Col. 0917A] From there the exhibitionist flits about, so that Gedippa

and his Ursinus, the offspring of Jovinus,

and Taurinus may marvel at him, matching him with ancient heroes:

such as the Calydonian victor over the Olenian boar,

or the Attic youth against the Erymanthian monster.

But spare the beasts and avoid the familiar crimes of the woods,

lest you become the offspring of Cinyras

and once again approach Venus as an Adonis to be mourned.

Thus surely you pour your blond hair and snowy arms,

your fiery locks, down over your white neck;

thus, with tender breast and smooth, reedlike belly,

you descend through the rounded curves of your thighs and shining legs,

beautiful from crown to ankles.

[Col. 0917B]

Such was once the plunderer of Aetna, flower-crowned,

when Orcus, emerging from the Stygian furnaces,

carried away the maiden among the dances.

Or, since you avoid hunting because of such dangers,

are you drawn by a passion for fishing? For all the equipment

of the Dumnotini is accustomed to display such treasures:

knotted garments of creatures from the Nerine waters,

spears and slings, and the rustic names of linen,

nets, and hooks clothed in earthly worms.

Do you swell with confidence in these resources? Every house abounds,

rich in spoils from the shore; the wave brings back

the carroco, the deadly stingray, and tender plaice,

burning tunny-fish, and the poorly covered spine of the garfish,

and crows that will not survive beyond two periods of three hours.

Or does it please you to defile with verse the tuneful daughters

of Mnemosyne, whether three or eight sisters?

[Col. 0917C] And since we have come this far, if you wish to know what difference exists

between learning and laughable Muses,

receive a heap of frivolous nonsense,

which you could not unravel even on unfolded sheets,

not even if you were cleansed ten times with Scyllite vinegar

and anticipated the acumen of your Samian Lucumo—

or if your interpreter were present,

the knower of my riddles,

who, when you were told of

the black daughters of Cadmus,

the white daughter of Melon,

the familiar dark cuttlefish,

and the knots of Cuidius,

explained them to you.

Let him be present now; surely, having just been

appointed a leader in letters,

he will immediately explain

what we write as men under arms.

I present to you familiar verses of a poet,

which you know are called hendecasyllables,

but you do not know that they move in three rhythms.

Phalaecus once composed these,

which have the first penthemimeral caesura,

followed by two iambs after a half-foot.

There are others produced by reversed hexameters,

so that the first penthemimeres may be placed first.

Then there is what the bucolic section leaves behind.

There are also those which the maiden Sappho generates,

whose first foot governs them, the second Hippius,

so that an antibacchius closes the choriamb.

[Col. 0918A] But now you will not be able to be taught, Theon;

nor is it proper for me, a teacher of the region,

to teach meters to a plebeian crowd.

But immediately publish what I ask.

I ask for nothing except what is held in books,

and what the barbarous papyri do not conceal.

If you solve this nonsense, poet,

I hand over the whole Vacuna to you at once,

and afterward you will no longer fear being called everywhere:

“This is that false poet Theon,

A bad shop for good poems.”

## LETTER V

Ausonius says “Greetings” to Theon, dear to him,

testing in verse what I wish and what I complain of.

[Col. 0918B] The Moon has renewed the split-hoofed heifers for the third time,

since you are fleeing our house, sweet friend.

I have dragged out ninety days without you, dearest;

add the summer days: for me this is almost double.

Shall I say that nine times ten and ten times nine

days have passed? A quarter of the year has gone.

Besides two thousand one hundred and sixty hours,

I have spent without you—every hour without you is heavy.

The reckoning of the laws, madly counted,

orders defendants to pass away through so many days.

By now I could have walked to Rome and walked back

since only a few thousand miles separate you from me.

Is the reed-built dwelling of the poet Domnotonus worth so much?

Pauliacus would not be such a villa to me.

Or because, on a tablet marked by the physician in combat,

the sum owed to me is recorded—should we not call it in while you are away?

I would rather lose fourteen royal golden Philips,

even if they were worth so much, than lose you, Theon,

hidden so deeply in my innermost being,

by your absence for so long a period.

Therefore either write back now about the Darii mentioned above

and redeem them, so that delay may be free for idleness;

or I shall give you the same number from my own purse,

provided only that I may see the face of my dear friend,

even if he remains poor.

Hurry swiftly to the vessel and spread the winding sails.

The breeze from the Medulline south wind will carry you,

laid out beneath the prepared awnings and lying on your couch,

so that a body of such weight may not be moved.

A single tide will carry you along the shore of Domnotonus

to the harbor of Condates, if only you hasten.

[Col. 0918D] And whenever your winds fail, in their place

order the oar-driven boat to proceed at once.

You will find mule-drawn carriages ready and waiting.

Soon you will possess Lucanus’s villa—[text uncertain].

Learn to compose a verse by altering the name.

Thus you will imitate the poet Lucilius.

## LETTER VI

Ausonius, consul, sends a return greeting to the poet Theon.

You send golden apples, Theon, but leaden poems.

Who would think these forms were made from one mass?

The name is one for both, but there is a difference between them:

you call the fruits “apples,” but the poems “bad.”

Fare well, Theon, whose name is blessed by the gods.

But this *metoche* often denotes a runner.

## LETTER VII. Ausonius to Theon, when he had sent him thirty oysters, indeed large ones, but so few

[Col. 0919A]

I received, beloved Theon, as a countable gift,

oysters rivaling those of Baiae, which the returning tides of the sea

fatten in the sweet waters of the Meduli.

But how many there were, the following monostichs indicate.

As many as a finger counts after wrestling three times with its thumb.

As many as the Geryons were, if they are multiplied by ten.

As many as the counted decades of the Phrygian war, taken three times.

Or as many as the fiery Sun holds months for the Aeolid, taken three times.

As many nights as wandering Cynthia has from her first horns.

As many signs as the Titan traverses one by one in his days.

As many ages as lofty Phaenon passes through in years.

As many years as the Vestal virgin serves,

[Col. 0919B]

and as many years as the Dardanian descendant brought forth in his reign.

As many Priam’s sons as there were, if twice ten are withdrawn.

And twice as many men as guard the Amphrysian destinies.

As many young as the sow beneath the Alban oaks gave birth to.

And as many asses as there are when ninety triens are counted.

Or as many well-fed horses as the Vasatian carriage has.

But if the mind, clogged in the depths of its inward parts,

does not recognize figures shaded by stories

and number concealed in learned riddles,

at least learn to count them in the manner of the common people.

I shall unfold the little sums twisted back upon themselves.

Three tens, I think, and five times six.

Or twice five, then ten and ten.

Or four sixes, and add twice three.

Four sevens, add one and one.

[Col. 0919C] Bring together two tens, and once ten.

Or add three times four to twice nine.

Four eights, from these subtract two.

Two, thirteen times, and once four.

And add six to nine, or eight to seven.

Or join seven to two pairs of eight.

Or, so that I may not weary you with more,

the whole number was thirty.

The mussel joined to shore-dwelling oysters

first made up the dishes for the meal,

a welcome delicacy for the tables of the wealthy,

and a modest expense for poor hearths.

It is not sought here in the shipwrecking open sea,

so that great danger may increase its price;

it is gathered at the first shallow water, after the sea has retreated,

[Col. 0919D]

on a seaweed-covered shore, of like colour.

For it is enclosed in the hollow of a double shell,

which, warmed by the vapors of boiling water,

reveals flesh with milk-white innards.

But its area spreads too widely and at too great a cost.

Make the papyrus field unfold, Muse;

and now let the furrow of the Cnidian reed

not plow through the roads of the split reed,

writing upon the page placed beneath it

with the black daughters of Cadmus.

Or let the sponge, equally across all the verses,

smear the dark cuttlefish over the milk-white surface.

Let us spare the fault of the Dumnotinian household,

lest paper be more costly to me than oysters.

## LETTER VIII

[Col. 0920A]

Ausonius sends greetings to Axius Paulus, the rhetorician.

At last, having struggled free from the gentle restraints of delay,

we have left behind the soft allurements of Bordeaux

and approached the city of the Santones through the neighboring countryside.

If this pleases you, excellent Paulus, approve it.

Let the hoofed mules carry the loaded carriage;

or, if you prefer, leap into a three-horse gig;

or mount a swift pony, or a post-horse with a broken back—

only come quickly now.

For the solemn rites of Easter summon us back,

and delay is not freely available to our idleness.

On your journey bring three thousand epodes,

or the false disputes your school plants.

You will find none with us, because we left there

the old remnants of nonsense seasoned with salt.

## LETTER IX

Ausonius to Paulus

Oysters known at the banquets of the wealthy and for extravagant expense,

protected in different depths of sea,

or stripped by retreating shallows, or submerged beneath rocky

caves and pools of purple shellfish,

which green moss and disfiguring seaweed conceal,

which are cemented together with their shells like joined stones,

which, moved to another place, are soon enclosed in rich mud,

and whose secret moisture nourishes the enclosed mire—

you order me to enumerate them, old companion of mine, Paulus,

accustomed to jest at my playful verses.

I shall undertake it, although such concerns do not trouble an old man

[Col. 0920C]

and ought to be thought worthy of a frugal man.

For I do not seek a feast that satisfies greed, nor a lavish banquet

such as the table of Penelope’s worthless suitors possessed,

or the youth of shining skin at Alcinous’s court.

Nevertheless I shall enumerate them, following reputation and witnesses,

in accordance with the varied tastes of men, who always approve different things.

But the richest beyond all others are those which the Ocean

of the Meduli produces, those which admiration has carried

from Bordeaux to the tables of Caesar,

no less praised by us than the glory of our wine.

Among all oysters these have won the first prize,

all the others yielding to them from a long way off.

Those are rich in their plump flesh, snowy,

and exceedingly tender with sweet juice;

they mingle an ocean flavor touched with delicate salt.

Let whatever comes next be near them—but far less near,

[Col. 0920D]

at a distance: those from the harbor of Massilia,

those which Narbo nourishes for Venus;

those lacking cultivation which the sea of Hellespontine Abydos protects;

those which hang floating from the piles of Baiae;

those covered by Santonic salt water; those known to Genoa;

or those which the river of Eborum protects where it mingles with the sea,

though they lie covered beneath a great retreat of seaweed;

those with rough shells and sweet, rich flesh.

There are also those who praise the oysters of the Armorican sea,

and those which the inhabitant gathers from the Pictonian shore,

and those which the Caledonian tide sometimes wonderfully uncovers.

There are also those which, as recent report tells us, they praise beneath

the shores of Byzantium and in the wild currents of the Propontis,

celebrated under the name of the commander who brought them forward.

[Col. 0921A] I speak of these to you neither as a poet, nor as a historian,

nor as a banqueter who has wandered throughout the whole world,

but from what has been handed down by many—

as is customary whenever an invitation to the right hand of the table

summons gentle Lyaeus with kindly conversation.

These things are not known to me through the common crowd and eating houses,

or through the associations of Plautine parasites;

but because I myself have often adorned some of my own festive days

and in turn attended as a guest,

if perchance it was a friend’s solemn birthday,

or a wedding feast, or the sacred banquets of ancestors returning,

I have heard and remembered good men praising them frequently.

## LETTER X

Ausonius to Paulus

If false poets are ever to be granted any credibility,

and if they do not always smear on fiction,

[Col. 0921B] Paulus, most celebrated fosterling of the Castalian Muses,

once their nursling, now their father,

or grandfather, or older than great-grandfathers, as once was

the little king of Tartessus—

remember that your promises to me must remain inviolate.

Phoebus commands that you speak the truth.

And even if he allows the Pierian sisters to wander,

he himself never twists the spindle [Greek: **ἄλακα**, “spindle,” uncertain].

Do not be reluctant, either, concerning the bond of our agreement;

come swiftly now by oar or wheel.

Where the Garonne, multiplied by the returning course

of its billowing waters, challenges the sea,

or where the gravel of repeated roads, worn smooth,

carries the military road to Blavia.

[Col. 0921C] For in the first days after Easter we long

to visit the countryside.

We are weary of gatherings of people and crossroads filthy with quarrels,

and we see narrow roads seething,

while the assembled crowd ruins the name of the streets.

Echo is repeated in turbulent voices:

“Hold! Strike! Lead! Give! Beware!”

A muddy sow flees, a rabid dog rushes with savage attack,

and mismatched oxen drag the cart.

It does no good to enter the innermost rooms of a house

and hide within; shouts pass through the roofs.

These things, and whatever can offend peaceful manners,

compel us to leave the city walls,

so that the sweet leisure of secluded country life may be revisited,

pleasant with serious trifles.

There you may arrange your own time as you wish;

your right shall be to do nothing, or whatever you want.

If you hasten to these things, come swiftly

with the entire stock of your Muses.

Place dactylics, elegiacs, choriambic verse, epodes,

and the music of the sock and the cothurnus

upon your carriages; for all the equipment

of pious poets is made of paper.

You will find with us, if you wish to use it, a *catenoplia*,

not with Punic but with Greek faith.

[Col. 0922A]

While you think that my verses, hidden with useful and knowing modesty,

are being drawn out by your poem and the words prefixed to it,

you have held them back. For a man who is himself eloquent and musical

and entices forth another’s edition frightens with the advice

by which he urges it on. The listener who wishes to summon a trembling speaker

to speak ought to conceal his own learning;

veteran cleverness should not shake its seasoned weapons against recruits.

Venus perceived this when the prize of beauty had long remained undecided

through an extended judgment. For modestly, as before her father,

she had competed veiled, and equal adornment did not frighten her rivals.

But after the dispute of the goddesses was brought before the shepherd,

when she emerged as she had from the sea, or when she had joined Mars,

she both overwhelmed the judge and crushed the contest of the competitors.

Therefore, unless your madman had delayed my little works,

which you had promised to bring forth, by laboring at them

with no small effort in a trivial matter,

I would long ago, like a bolder vine-shoot,

have driven out a presumptuous bud even into the winter cares,

undertaking the danger of a grave judgment through ill-considered haste.

[Col. 0922B] Finally, as you ordered, I added a dissonant verse, which I think philologists properly call a *colonomon*; not daring to send what had already been recited to you in haste, I sent it after a recent reading of your verses. For you requested this, and I preferred that you,

through your own fault, should stumble twice on the same stone,

while I, whatever the outcome, should blush only once.

## LETTER XI

Ausonius sends greetings to Paulus

See, my Paulus, how foolishly you have provoked one who is unskilled in words,

gaping in expression, inconsistent with his intentions,

without the art of arrangement in verse,

by nature unattractive in jesting and not polished by art,

of diluted wit and sluggish gall,

neither a flat-footed actor from the mime nor a stage-player from comedies.

And unless you were going to read these things sent by me yourself,

you would also laugh at their delivery.

Now, by a more favorable fate, they are fortunate:

what is genuine among us will be adopted among you.

I shall prepare wine with a two-horse wagon

to be carried at the first season to the Santones;

you too, an egg of a sea sparrow,

which the steward now says has been left far away

at the bottom of our native Bigerritan country.

## LETTER XII

[Col. 0922C]

Ausonius to Paulus.

Sharing in the Greek Muse and the Latin Camena,

Ausonius addresses worthy Paulus in bilingual speech.

Muses, what are we doing? Why do we play so foolishly

at empty hopes, growing old in a single day

in the fields of the Santones, where the cold is boundless?

We, the poets, wander cold and rigid.

Inert servants of the tender-haired Pierian women,

frost possesses everything: the freezing of our feet and the chattering of our teeth;

there is no warmth, because we dwell in a snowy land,

and, thinking deeply, we double the cold

with our chilly poems.

But, beginning then with the morning wrath—

[lacuna]

I shall send honey-sweet first-fruits to our Paulus.

Illustrious children of Memory, she who wears the veil,

the nine wordy, lily-crowned maidens:

come then, spin verses for me—a maidenly song.

Set a winged little book before our brows,

[uncertain: “Υματαρ..· στίχον . . . .”]

and fit for Paul a mingled song.

[Col. 0923A] For it is not permitted that I, remaining in this region,

should compose something unworthy of our Muses.

He is my partner in all things, who knows how to handle

our serious matters and our jokes in every kind of arena.

And now, secluded, he lives alone in rural Crebennus;

in a grape-bearing district he has discourse that soothes the heart,

neither agreeable to friends and companions nor suited to any table,

because, as he said, [lacuna] to the enchanting Muses [lacuna].

Enough now, dear Paul: we have tested our labors

both in public causes and in ungrateful assemblies,

in rhetorical games—and nothing came of it.

But now all that youthful sweat has been poured from my limbs;

terrible old age has seized my trembling sight,

and my light purse provides less for expenditure.

For a helpless man does not possess [lacuna].

[Col. 0923B] Clinias, nor the old man [lacuna].

If you are even-tempered, and would prefer to sleep soundly in all things,

there will be forgetfulness of toil, and likewise of poverty.

But this is supremely beautiful: that, at every table everywhere,

with a bowl or with a companion cup of the Muses,

you seek gentle solace for your grieving spirit.

Here will be the fruit of Demeter, rich in shining produce.

There, let food be yours, when you set down wide-mouthed cups

to mix, if you wish, nectar with good wine.

Thus we shall both set our leisure alongside the life we lead,

while circumstances, age, and the sisters’

purple threads are being woven.

## LETTER XIII

### AUSONIUS TO PAUL

Ausonius, consul of the Romans, to Paul, teller of virtue and poet,

hastens to see his friends.

## LETTER XIV

### AUSONIUS TO PAUL

For your sake, my friend, I left the sea-like Garumna.

For your sake I inhabit the fields of the Santones.

Come, then, seek our meeting. If you have the concern

which I have, you will soon enjoy the sight of me.

But hasten as much as your body and age permit:

if I see you safe, I see you soon enough.

If strength has been restored to your unlucky reins,

and mobility has returned to your limbs,

if you revisit the well-watered Pimpleides with joyful Muses,

now a poet and no longer a fire-bearing Automedon,

drive away sleep-bringing old age and the cloud of torpor,

and travel the middle road with vigorous alertness.

But cautiously mount a cisium or a sluggish post-chaise.

Do not be enamored of a carriage or of a spirited horse.

I advise you to avoid the poorly known canterius and petorita.

Nor should you yourself drive the swift mules of Metiscus.

So may the Muses be favorable to you, meditation ready,

and may you be mindful, with the liquid honey of eloquence flowing.

So may Crebennus, who for so many years has been for sale

and has no purchaser, be yours in place of payment.

Nevertheless, so that you may come more quickly and travel more lightly,

leave at home history, mimes, and poems:

a great burden lies in the Muses; so many centuries stored in books,

which scarcely bear their own times, weigh upon ours.

[Col. 0924A] With us you will find a many-shaped multitude of verses,

weavings of grammarians and verbal intricacy,

the heroic dactyl and the song-bearing choriamb,

together with the trailing strains of Thalia’s chorus and Terpsichore.

the Sotadic effeminate verse and both forms of Ionic,

the well-ordered eloquence of Pindaric rhythms,

the limping choliamb and the non-limping trimeter,

eight [books] of Thucydides, nine of Herodotus.

All the illustrious tribes of marvelous rhetorical sages,

everything, if you wish, and more, if you wish.

This greeting I offer you from our books.

Farewell. If you wish me to fare well, come now.

## LETTER XV

### AUSONIUS TO TETRADIUS, GREETING

O Tetradius, who enrich graceful witticisms

with abundant eloquence,

and take care that a composition should not be gloomy and bitter,

deprived of sweetness;

you who temper poetry with gall and honey,

and do not allow the Muses to grow numb,

while likewise avoiding artificial embellishments, things dull in taste,

and things bitter in flavor;

you who surpass the unpolished Camenae of Suessa,

and yield to age, not to style—

why do you avoid me, though I am near the walls of the Santones,

as the Roman youth once fled the Lucanian oxen,

savage again when battle had been renewed?

It is not with the force of a tiger or lion

that I seek you, but with dear affection.

I long to see the face of my fosterling

and to enjoy his desired character.

Once, unwillingly, I swallowed the necessity

of my former absence,

when, bound by the heavy duty of teaching,

Iculisma concealed you from me.

I envied you your remote and solitary place,

where the wealth of the Camenae lay hidden.

But now, when you are among men in numbers and distinction, and not far away,

when you are in flower among them,

and the wind brings our breezes to you

and speech strikes your ears,

why do you, swollen with the arrogant pride of an upturned breast,

scorn me, a poet and consul—

[Col. 0924D] one who loves you, admires you, and longs for your poems—

and, forgetting me, neglect me in deep disdain?

I ought to be chastised according to your example,

unless the steadfast faith of our heart, though you resist,

continues to love.

Farewell. If you wish me to fare well, fly here

with your writing case and your Muses.

## LETTER XVI

### AUSONIUS TO PROBUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM, GREETING

Probus, excellent man, I know that the favor of my promise has been consumed by expectation, because of the delay caused by the antiquarians. Yet in my good fortune I count it a success not to have disappointed you. I sent to your nobility the apologues of Titianus and the chronicles of Nepos as though they were other apologues—for these too are, in fact, of the nature of fables—rejoicing and even boasting that there would be something which, through my diligent effort, might contribute to the education of your children.

Yet to the little book of apologues I preferred a few epodes, outrageously bold through my devotion to you: few, indeed, as I, a talkative man, judge them; but when you have read them, you will think them too numerous. I call your goodwill to bear witness to my modesty: they flowed from me through a sudden impulse of persuasion. For who would have thought over these for long? They will surely prove this by themselves.

May chance grant that, if life is available to me, I may polish some subject from your history, though I am uncultivated; and, even if you do not approve it when read, you will take kindly what has been written. And since I have imitated the madness of Chaerilus, may you pardon me with the magnanimity of Alexander.

These, then, as Plautus says, will meanwhile be the counter-argument to the fables: chatterers and deceivers who, composed to serve honorific praise and to assault the ears, have rushed together.

Farewell, and love me.

### To the Book: That It May Go to Probus

Go, little book, to Sirmium,

and say to my hero—and yours—

“Greetings and very many salutations.”

“Who is this master of ours?”

“You do not know, little book? Or, since you know, do you willingly listen to what gives pleasure?”

“I could say it plainly,

but I shall speak more sweetly by circumlocution,

and enjoy myself by telling it at length.”

I mean the man who, powerful in speech,

surpasses the lesser Atrides by brief and harmonious pleading,

Ulysses’ hailstorms of speech,

honey-flowing Nestor,

and polished Cicero,

who alone, except for three masters,

is first among masters,

and greatest among prefects of the praetorium.

I mean this leader of the Senate,

at once prefect and consul

—for as consul he will be famed forever—

the colleague of the emperor Augustus,

the support of the Roman curule chair,

first in the secondary fasces.

[Col. 0925D] For he will be first of all as consul,

second only to the prince.

This survivor of a golden lineage,

this begetter of golden offspring,

refutes the old man of Ascra,

who proclaimed the whole age to be iron,

who overcomes the injuries of time,

renewer of the Anician stock,

and who adorns, with equal fillets,

the lineage of the Anicii.

I speak of Probus. You know very well

whom no one has named in speech

without first praising him.

Go, little book, and enjoy

[Col. 0926A] unending felicity.

Indeed, ask him, if he permits you,

while continuing your submissive speech:

“Tell us, true offspring of Romulus,

the reason for your name.

Did your character give you this name,

or did the rule of your character

follow after this name?

Or did the supreme arbiter,

who knows the world yet to come,

having created you such in character,

command that you be called by this name—

a name bestowed by praises

and by the testimony of your life?”

Happy little book, whom so great a man

will unroll from his bosom,

and will not complain that his time

is occupied by a pleasant leisure;

to whom, in a thousand variations of voice,

he will grant either a gentle murmur;

for whom the watchful care of his eyes

will deign to make itself free;

whom, with mind and ear attentive,

he will read through, omitting certain passages.

Whatever fortune is yours,

go, little book, and enjoy

unending felicity.

Tell him that I am well and alive.

Tell him that I live according to my pious wish,

praying with holy words

that he whom the curule office gave as colleague next to his son,

the elder Augustus may again perpetuate in his own fasces.

Add this gently:

“Look, Ausonius has sent you apologues

from as far as the banks of the Rhine—

the Italian-named tutor of your Augustus—

Aesopian tales in trimeter,

which Titianus, a craftsman of speech,

translated in a slender style,

composing a pedestrian work.

As the glory of grandfather and father,

shining in mingled blood,

and that of the Probii and Anicii,

was once joined—

as, within the walls of Alba,

the supreme descendant of Aeneas

mingled the Silvii with the Iulii—

so may this child, your offspring,

the flower of Romulus’s flowers,

among his nurse’s little tales

and sleep-inducing lullabies,

learn both to play and to learn

through stories known to the skilled.

And add the prayer which we have conceived

to the God of the pious undertaking:

‘As the emperor Augustus gave Probus

to the college of his son,

so may Gratian join this new Probus

to the future stock.

What I say will be fulfilled.

Merit and fate command it so.’

But now, so that Julius may speak,

receive unwillingly the manner of speech:

the wing-footed dimeter.

And, having said “Hail,” say: “Farewell.””

## LETTER XVII

### To Ursulus, Grammarian of Trier

He sent back to him the New Year’s gifts which the emperor had not given on the Kalends of January.

This was the first pleasant fruit of honor for you:

to receive the auspicious gift from the hand of the Augusta.

The next step, after a long interval, was to keep watch

over the concern of your friend the Quaestor in place of your gifts.

Therefore accept the royal Philip coins intercepted from you,

as many in number as there are two Geryons;

as many as the three pairs together—less one third for the Camena;

and as many as the hours in which you teach,

and the hours in which you remain at home;

as many gates as the Circus opens groaning on one side,

excepting the middle one that opens onto the stadium;

as many feet as bees walk, and as many as Homer’s verses;

as many hours as the sea flows forward or backward;

as many dramas of fables as the man who lies in the heart of Arcadia

brought onto the stage;

or as many joints as a geometric figure of honeycombs

binds together at all the outer and inner points;

as many telioi as are approved first and alone in number;

as many even and odd numbers as he balances in their parts;

six twice over, and two three times, which one man joins together;

which alone has as many doubled within it;

as many as are formed by joined figures placed below and above,

which together count the Hyades and the Pleiades.

[lacuna]

Ursulus, illustrious colleague of Harmonius—

Harmonius, whom Claranus, Scaurus, and Asper,

whom Varro and the elder Crates would have compared with themselves,

who gathered together the torn body of sacred Homer,

and who affixed notes to spurious verses;

the common glory of Cecropia and the Latin Camena,

the only man who blends Chian and Aminnean wine—

## LETTER XVIII

### AUSONIUS TO PONTIUS PAULINUS

Tartessian Calpe had already enclosed the horses of the sun;

the glorious Titan was roaring in the Iberian strait;

the Moon was already shaking her approaching heifers,

so that, like a rival of her brother, she might overcome the darkness with her rays.

Already the birds, and the human race vulnerable to cares,

were soothing themselves with the calm oblivions of tranquil sleep.

The Ides had passed; mid-December was hastening

to join its final hours to the coming Janus.

And the long night was continually bidding the nineteenth day before the Kalends

to be summoned for the festival that must be celebrated.

You do not know, I think, what I wish to say in so many verses;

by my faith, I scarcely understand it myself—yet I have a suspicion.

It was already the first night before the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January

when your very literary letter was delivered to me.

You had appended to it an exceedingly delightful poem,

in which you had condensed into an epitome the three books of Suetonius

which he devoted to kings, with such elegance

that you alone seem to me to have achieved what is contrary to the nature of things:

brevity without obscurity.

In these verses I recognized the following:

Europe and Asia, the two greatest members of the earth,

to which Sallustius hesitantly adds Libya,

attached to Europe so that it may be called a third;

many kingdoms, whose fame has been obliterated,

and whose barbarian names are not handed down by the Roman tongue:

Illibanus, Avelim the Numidian, Vonones the Parthian,

and Caranus, who gave his name to the Pellaean kings.

And Necepsus, who taught the Magi their empty mysteries;

and he who soon reigned without a name, Sesostris.

All this you expressed so skillfully and elegantly,

so rhythmically and sweetly, so close to the nature of Roman accents,

that the dignity of the true and original words nevertheless did not perish.

What should I say now of your eloquence?

I can confidently swear that no one among the Roman youth

can be compared with you in poetic eloquence.

At least, this is how you seem to me.

If I am wrong, I am a father: bear with me,

and do not demand a judgment where affection stands in the way.

Yet although I love you affectionately, I judge sincerely and severely.

Favor me, I ask, frequently with such a gift,

by which I am both delighted and honored.

A honeyed modulation has been added to your poetic art.

For what else are they doing,

he who gave his name to the bold Icarian sea,

and he who sailed with measured course to the Chalcidian heights,

except to call your vigorous and exalted boldness rashness,

and to describe me, prudent and deliberate,

as one whom a son ought to imitate,

endowed with salutary wisdom?

The truth, however, is the opposite.

For you pursue the highest things in such a way that you do not fall;

my old age is satisfied if it merely stands firm.

I dictated these things to you briefly,

immediately after the morning that followed that evening.

For your letter-carrier was pressing me to return the letter.

If I have leisure, it will be an agreeable task

to rave at greater length to you—

to draw you out, and to satisfy myself.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIX

### AUSONIUS TO PAULINUS

The meter so instructed me that you should be first

and precede my name.

Although you are also first in the title of the official registers,

and your curule ivory chair at Rome preceded ours,

and although the poetic palm has long flourished for you,

it is adorned with the ribbon which my palm lacks.

We surpass you only in the honor of long-lived old age.

What does it matter? A crow is not for that reason before a swan.

Nor, because the Gangetic bird lives a thousand years,

does it surpass your hundred eyes, royal peacock.

We yield to your talent as far as we precede you in age.

Our Camena rises to meet your Muse.

Live, farewell, and accumulate as many coming Januarys

as your fathers or ours have joined together.

## LETTER XX

### AUSONIUS TO HIS PAULINUS, GREETING

How greatly you benefited me, Paulinus my son, by taking up, rather than merely conveying, my complaint! Fearing that the oil which you had sent had displeased me, you repeated the gift; and, adding the seasoning of Barcelonian brine, you made the offering still more abundant.

You know that I neither usually can nor usually do call that substance *muriae*, which is the term used by the common people, since the most learned of the ancients, though they disdain Greek words, do not have it in Latin under the designation *garum*. But by whatever name I speak, that liquor is called *sociorum* (“the Allies’ sauce”). Farewell.

Now I shall fill my dishes,

so that that more sparing juice may flood the small plates

at the tables of my ancestors.

What is as lovable and hospitable as this:

that, to make me share in them, you deprive yourself of your delicacies

at the very freshness of their first fruits?

O sweeter than honey, more festive than the charm of grace,

to be embraced by everyone with a father’s affection!

But these and other such proofs of a generous spirit

may perhaps be shown to someone, and at some time, though more rarely.

As for the learning of your letters, the delight of your poems,

your invention and composition, I swear that no one will ever be able to imitate them,

even if he admits that they ought to be imitated.

As for the little work you command, I shall do it.

I shall refine everything with the greatest care;

and although the final touch has been supplied by you,

I shall apply the finishing of excessive polish,

more to spare you than to add anything to what is already complete.

Meanwhile, however, so that your letter-carrier should not return

without a poetic garland, I thought I ought to offer a brief iambic prelude,

while that which you desire from me in heroic meter is being begun.

These verses, however—so may you and Hesperius remain safe—

were poured out in the time of a single brief vigil;

although they will prove this about themselves,

they received no further diligence.

Farewell.

Iambus, faster than Parthian arrows and Cydonian darts,

iambus, swifter than the wings of birds,

more torrential than the force of the rushing Po,

denser than the great violence of sounding hail,

more flashing than the flames of the gleaming thunderbolt,

now fly through the air on the winged sandals of Perseus,

carried by the rich Arcadian hat.

If the true story of Hippocrene is that the winged horse

struck it forth, roaring, with the blow of his hoof,

you, Iambus, were born at that very spring of Pegasus,

and were the first to join meters of new feet.

There, with the nine Muses singing in harmony,

you stirred Delian Apollo to slay the dragon.

Carry this greeting, winged and feather-footed,

to the walls of Paulinus—I mean Hebromagus.

And at once, if he is vigorous with restored strength

and refreshed bodily movement,

soon demand from him a reciprocal greeting.

Do not delay: while I speak, return,

imitating that ancestor of your stock

who flew over the raging Chimera,

burning with triple fire, safe beside the neighboring flame.

Say also “Farewell”; say that a friend,

a neighbor, and your supporter,

the author of your honor and nourisher of your talent,

orders you to say “Hail.”

Say also “teacher,” say “father,” say every

gentle and sacred name of affection.

Having said “Hail,” say “Farewell,” and return at once.

If he asks what I, mature in age and not unskilled,

judge concerning the new writings,

you will say that I do not know,

but that a chariot full of heroic verses is already prepared.

To it I shall yoke, concerning the wanderings of millstones

which roll stones with mechanical weight,

three-footed horses with backs broken by the whip.

Three fellow messengers are to ride in these.

Perhaps he will ask which companions you mean

are to come together. Say:

“I saw the three-knotted dactyl prepared for the tormenting canterius.

The slow-footed spondee went beside him,

the one who delays my course in equal places;

and a companion like me, though always opposed,

neither even nor odd, who is called the trochee.”

Speak these things quickly, and fly off without delay,

bringing back meanwhile some little gift

from the generosity of the musical storehouse.

## LETTER XXI

### AUSONIUS TO HIS PAULINUS, GREETING

Many frequent occasions and opportunities continually create

reasons for gratitude toward you,

and the kindly ease of your nature wins them for me,

Paulinus my son.

For, since you refuse me nothing when I ask,

you sharpen my boldness more than you blunt it,

as you will now experience in the case of Philo,

formerly my steward,

who, having stored at Hebromagus the goods he bought throughout various fields,

is in danger of being prematurely driven out,

although he has been granted lodging by your people.

Unless, at my request, you allow him to use the delay of residence

for his own convenience,

and unless, by providing a *nausos* or any other vessel,

he can bring a little of our grain as far as the town

and promptly free Lucaniacum from want,

the whole household of this learned man will belong not to Cicero’s grain law

but to Plautus’ *Curculio*.

To make this easier for me to obtain,

or to make you fear greater annoyance if you refused,

I sent you a letter composed in iambics and sealed,

so that you might not say that a messenger had been suborned

if he came to you without the evidence of a seal.

I sealed it not, as Plautus says, through wax,

linen, and interpreting letters,

but marked it more distinctly through poetic character,

so that you might regard it as an impressed sign.

Philo, who has managed my estates,

as he himself prefers, an *epitropos*

—for he thinks it a glorious Greek name,

though speech disguises it in the Doric fashion—

asserts our prayers through his complaints,

which I myself, sluggishly, pursue.

You will see him himself, when he stands close by,

an image of his own fortune:

gray, long-haired, shaggy, grim, hunchbacked,

a Terentian Phormio.

[Col. 0931A] Bristling with hair like a rough sea urchin,

or like the subject of my verses.

This man, often deceived by meager harvests,

hating the name of steward,

whether sowing late or far too early,

and through astronomical ignorance

assailing heaven and withdrawing himself from blame,

brought the gods to trial as defendants.

Not an attentive cultivator, not a knowledgeable plowman,

more a purveyor than a storekeeper,

he preferred to conduct business,

accusing the faithless and unproductive earth.

He trades in every market of things for sale.

He borrows on Greek faith.

And, wiser than the seven men of Greece,

he came as the eighth sage.

Now he has prepared wheat with cheese and salt,

and as a new merchant he flourishes.

He visits tenants, farms, villages, and towns,

trading in land and salt.

In boats, small craft, skiffs, barges, and a ship,

he crosses both the Tarn and the Garumna.

And changing profits into losses and losses through fraud,

he enriches himself and impoverishes me.

Now, carried as far as your Hebromagus,

he has established a station for his goods.

[lacuna]

so that from there he may transport them by boat

[lacuna]

for our purposes, as he reports.

[Col. 0931C] I ask this of you briefly, lest I burden you with a guest.

[lacuna]

so that, soon aided by the support of your ship,

as far as the town’s harbor,

he may free Lucaniacum from the famine

of Perusinian and Saguntine grain.

If I receive this favor as a gift granted by you,

I shall honor you before Ceres.

I shall set behind you Triptolemus of old, or Epimenides, as they call him,

or Boulian Buzyges,

behind your name, which must take precedence.

For this gift will become yours.

## LETTER XXII

### AUSONIUS TO PAULINUS, GREETING

The preceding complaint of my letter,

I had believed, Paulinus, might bend you

and that gentle reproach might draw your voice forth.

But you remain steadfast in the law of silence,

as though devoted to sworn sacred rites.

This is not permitted. Are you ashamed

if a friend still lives for you by paternal right

and you remain an obligated heir?

Let such fear trouble the cowardly; but let there be no fear for you.

Boldly retain the custom of sending and receiving greetings.

Or, if a betrayer presses you,

or a more severe censorial investigation is feared,

meet it with ingenuity, by which hidden things are often concealed.

The savage license of a Thracian king

had once made a woman tongueless;

she uttered her complaints through woven threads

and entrusted her crimes to silent cloth.

And the bashful maiden entrusted her shameful loves

to an apple privy to them but unable to speak,

and did not blush before the silent fruit.

A servant entrusted a royal blemish to dug pits,

and the most faithful earth concealed it for a long time.

Then a reed, inspired by the wind, sang it aloud.

Write your signs in milk: the drying parchment

will retain them forever, invisible to the eye;

your writing will be betrayed by ashes.

Or imitate the Lacedaemonian *scytale*:

write continuously upon strips of Pergamene parchment

wrapped around a rounded staff.

When the strip is then unwound,

it will give scattered forms that do not correspond in order,

until it is wound again around a staff of similar shape.

I could show countless ways of concealment

and unlock the clandestine utterances of the ancients,

[Col. 0932B] if you fear being betrayed, Paulinus,

and dread the charge of our friendship.

Let your Tanaquil know nothing of this.

Despise the others; do not disdain to address your father in words.

I am your fosterer, and that first teacher,

the first giver of honors,

the first to lead you into the colleges of the Aonian Muses.

## LETTER XXIII

### AUSONIUS TO PAULINUS, GREETING

We are breaking the yoke, Paulinus,

which a fixed balance had sustained;

a yoke light in its position and bearable for those joined together,

which gentle concord guided with equal reins;

a yoke which, through such a long sequence of rolling years,

no story had ever disturbed, no complaint,

which no grievance had driven from its place,

neither anger nor error,

nor a plausible suspicion, credulous of ill-advised causes,

that composes credible accusations against settled things.

So peaceful, so gentle a yoke,

which both our fathers drew from the beginning of life

to old age,

and which they wished to remain imposed upon their pious heirs

until long time should dissolve the span of life.

And it remained while joyful faith was not troubled

by the effort of preserving the reciprocal duties;

rather, these carried themselves forward spontaneously,

continuing their course without supervision.

Such a gentle yoke would the horses of Mars

take upon their docile necks,

those driven from the stall of savage Diomedes;

and so would the yoked horses that plunged

the lightning-bearing Phaethon into the Po,

when they were unaccustomed to the altered reins of the sun.

We are breaking it, Paulinus, nevertheless.

The fault is not that of both of us,

but yours alone.

For I shall always bear it with an accommodating neck;

I am deprived of a partner in my labors,

nor is it so easy, when an equal partner fails, for one man to bear

the burden formerly carried by two.

It is not courage or strength that fails,

but the condition of bearing it becomes unjust,

when the whole burden falls upon the one left behind

and the weight of another balance is added.

So a sick part of the body draws the healthy body

into contagion;

and although the injury is confined to a small limb,

the whole structure trembles through its countless joints.

Nevertheless, let me be overwhelmed,

so that the faith of an old friend may not fail while I endure,

and so that, mindful and fixed through the ages,

chaste consolations may restore the banished companion.

Impiously, could you separate Theseus from Pirithous,

or sever Euryalus from his companion Nisus?

At your urging, Pylades would have abandoned Orestes;

the Sicilian Damon would not have kept his pledge to Pythias.

What delight for the people, what hopes of the good

would have been cheated of their expected joy?

Everyone was preparing grateful words;

they were already preparing to insert our names

among the ancient friends of a better age.

Pylades was yielding;

the glory of Phrygian Nisus too would have become lesser,

and Damon would have fulfilled his promised pledge.

We are a happier example,

such as great Scipio and the wisdom of long-lived Laelius provided.

We are alike in studies and spirit,

a marvel to all;

and greater still because we were equals despite unequal ages.

I think that the Pellaean leader could more swiftly have loosened

the fatal reins of that yoke,

whose beginnings lay hidden and whose ends

were concealed by each of the two knots.

Surely we have uttered some grand word,

so that avenging Rhamnusian Nemesis might descend

upon excessive hopes;

just as once the avenging goddess of Median war,

suppressing grand words not favorable to the triumphs

of the Arsacid king,

opposed the Cecropid who was preparing to establish

monuments upon the earth,

and Attic Nemesis stood before the Persians,

already about to be fixed beneath a Greek trophy,

even though they had been defeated.

What desire is this that you have to harass Roman nobles?

Proceed through the clouds and black chaos

against your Medes and Arabs.

Let Roman names be far from you.

There seek others against whom to wage war,

where that envy of yours and rusty poison

may turn against breasts suited to your devices.

It is not fitting that Paulinus and Ausonius,

men whom the sacred purple of Quirinus

and the gilded cloak of the trabea have covered,

should yield to the snares of a foreign goddess.

Why do I complain, and pursue the crimes

of the monster of the East?

The bank of the western Tagus, Punic Barcino,

and the snowy ridges of the two-sea Pyrenees injure me.

Perhaps separation from native walls and shores

also separates me from you;

a province divides each of us by its long expanse,

across mountains and another sun,

across rivers and cities,

and across all that stretches between earth and sky:

the waters of the Emeritan Ana

and the broad currents of the Garumna.

If the distance placed a tolerable boundary

in a narrow interval,

although those who wish to be together believe every distance long,

care itself would nevertheless make the places near,

joining what is distant with words in between.

Thus the Santon joins Bordeaux to itself,

then joins Aginnum;

and Aginnum joins to itself the peoples

who cultivate the Aquitanian fields.

So twofold Arelas joins to itself

the Alpine roofs of Vienna

and Narbo at an equal distance; and then,

Martial Narbo, it joins to itself fivefold allied Toulouse.

If this distance were between neighboring walls,

then I would embrace you as suited to my arms,

and the breeze of my speech would breathe upon your ears.

Now, beyond the Alps and the marble Pyrenees,

you have the house of the Caesarean Augusta.

Beside the Tyrrhenian sea lie Tarraco

and Barcino, added above the oyster-bearing waters.

The ridges of Bordeaux separate me;

three rivers in their gathering separate me

from the common crowds.

Between them are leisure,

vine-bearing hills,

a fruitful field rejoicing its farmers,

green meadows,

a grove with shifting shade,

and a populous gathering in a busy village;

and so many estates of mine,

near one another in the district of Noverus,

diversified throughout the whole year by changing seasons,

so that winters may grow warm

and the delicate north winds may breathe subtle coolness

through the raging heats.

But without you no year comes forth

in its pleasing cycle:

spring flees rainy and flowerless;

the summer dog-star burns;

no Pomona changes the flavors of autumn;

and Aquarius, pouring out his waters,

makes winter sorrowful.

Do you recognize your fault, sweetest Pontius?

For my steadfast faith—and never-changing reverence—

for that old Paulinus endures,

as does the concord that once existed

between my father and yours.

If anyone ever found the bow of Ulysses easy to bend,

or the ash of Achilles capable of being hurled

by anyone but its master,

then may Nemesis also loose us

from so long an alliance.

But why, so late, do I turn sad songs into a sorrowful verse?

Why does my spirit not draw near to better hopes?

Let this fear be far away.

We have firm confidence:

if the Father and Son of God

receive the pious words of those who pray,

you can be restored to us by my prayer,

so that we do not mourn the scattered and ravaged household,

torn among a hundred masters,

the realm of the old Paulinus.

You, wandering through the whole length of Spain,

forgetful of old friends and trusting foreign companions—

come running, our glory, my greatest concern,

called by vows, good omens, and prayers.

Hasten while you are young,

while our old age preserves for you

a strength, gratefully bestowed on you, not yet exhausted.

And when will that messenger drive upon my ears?

“Look! Your Paulinus is here:

he is already leaving the snowy towns of the Iberians;

he already occupies the fields of Tarbellic Gaul;

he is already entering the roofs of Hebromagus;

he is already approaching his brother’s neighboring estates;

he is already gliding down the favorable current;

he is already in sight;

the prow is already turned toward the river;

having entered through the celebrated gates of his harbor,

he passes before the whole crowd rushing to meet him;

and, passing his own threshold,

he is already knocking at yours.”

Do we believe this, or do lovers themselves

fashion dreams for themselves?

## LETTER XXIV

### AUSONIUS TO HIS PAULINUS, GREETING

This fourth letter has disclosed to you,

Paulinus, its familiar complaints

and challenges the idle man with gentle speech.

But no pious duty does any page return to me,

inscribing auspicious beginnings in greeting letters.

From where has this unlucky sheet deserved such a rejection?

How long does your silence, in its arrogance, despise it?

Even an enemy receives a greeting from an enemy

through barbarous words;

and “Hail” intervenes in the midst of arms.

Rocks also answer a human being.

Struck from caves, speech returns;

the vocal image of the groves returns.

The shore cliffs cry out;

streams give murmurs;

a hedge browsed by Hyblaean bees whispers.

There is also musical melody along reedy banks;

and the pine’s trembling crown speaks with its own winds.

Whenever the light East Wind has settled upon its sharp leaves,

the songs of Dindyma answer the Gargarian grove.

Nature has given nothing that is mute:

neither the bird of the air nor the four-footed creatures are silent;

the serpent too has its hisses,

and the sea-creature breathes with a thin approximation of a voice.

[Col. 0935A] Cymbals make a sound when struck;

stages resound beneath leaping feet;

drums echo when their stretched hides are struck;

the Mareotic sistrums stir up Isiac tumults;

nor does the bronze of Dodona cease its ringing,

whenever the basins, struck by beating rods,

answer obediently with a measured stroke.

You live as though in silent Oebalian Amyclae,

or as though Egyptian Sigalion sealed your lips.

You persist in silence, Paulinus.

I recognize your modesty,

the fault which continuous silence itself nourishes.

And because you are ashamed to have kept silent so long,

you are pleased not to preserve the reciprocal duties;

long leisure loves its own fault.

What prevents you from writing “Hail” and “Farewell”

in ready brevity,

and entrusting happy notes to little books?

I do not demand that your page weave lengthy verses,

or that you burden your tablets with a manifold discourse.

There was once only one letter by which the Lacedaemonians replied,

and their refusal pleased the angry king.

For brevity is indeed courteous.

So tradition reports that Pythagoras, reborn,

taught when talkative men were scattering many things

in ambiguous words;

he alone, in answer to everything,

would say: “It is,” or “It is not.”

What a certain rule of speech!

For nothing is briefer or fuller than these words:

affirmed, they confirm,

and denied, they refute.

No silent man has pleased anyone;

many have pleased by the brevity of their speech.

But why am I now carried forward

by the spacious foolishness of my own speech?

How close and yet how opposite are the faults:

speaking much and remaining entirely silent.

Neither of us is pleasing.

Nor can affection, which is free,

bear a yoke that is never answered,

or love to put truth behind gentle words.

Have you changed your character, sweetest Paulinus?

Is this caused by the forests of the Vascones,

the snowy lodgings of the Pyrenees,

and forgetfulness of our sky?

What might I not invoke against you deservedly,

land of Iberia?

May the Carthaginians ravage you;

may faithless Hannibal burn you;

may exiled Sertorius return to you,

the seat of war.

Then will Bilbilis, or Calagurris clinging to its crags,

or Hilerda, whose rugged height looks down from its fallen ruins

upon the dry, rushing Sicoris, possess you—

the glory of me and my country, the pillar of the Senate?

Are you establishing your trabea and Latin curule chair there,

Paulinus,

and burying your ancestral honors there?

Who, nevertheless, advised you to keep

such a prolonged silence?

May he there impiously turn his voice to no use:

may no joys invigorate him;

may neither the sweet songs of poets,

nor the modulation of a gentle, bending lament,

nor wild animals, nor sheep, nor birds soothe him;

nor may Echo, hidden in the woodland groves of shepherds,

who cuts short our spoken words,

bring him comfort.

May he inhabit a sad, impoverished, deserted place,

and wander silently across the vaulted slope of the Alps,

like Bellerophon, who, they say,

once deprived of reason,

avoiding the gatherings and footprints of human beings,

wandered through trackless places.

These are my prayers.
