Receive this voice, Muses, Boeotian divinities,

and call the poet back to the Latin Camenae.

## LETTER XXV

### AUSONIUS TO SYMMACHUS
Now I understand what a honeyed thing speech is, how soothing it is, [Col. 0936A] and how persuasive eloquence can be. You persuaded me that the composition of my letter, delivered to you at Capua, was not inhuman. But this lasted no longer than while I was reading your letter, which, as I gape in longing for your flatteries, leads me along as though steeped in nectar’s juice. Once, however, I put down the little sheet and question myself, my wormwood begins to taste again, and I discover the cups smeared round with your honey. But if—as I often do—I return to your letter, I am once more enticed; and again that most pleasant, that flowering address of your discourse vanishes when the reading is laid aside, while the weight of the evidence prevents sweetness from truly residing in it.

This delights me like the coloring of an airy strip of foil, or a painted cloud—no longer than it remains visible: like the little chameleon, which takes its color from the things beneath it. I feel one thing from your letter and another from my own conscience; and you [Col. 0936B] dare to deem me worthy of the praise bestowed upon the most eloquent men? You, I say, address such things to me—*you* who have carried yourself beyond the correction of everyone else? Or does anyone shine so brightly that, compared with you, he does not seem sordid? Who approaches so closely to Aesop’s charm, to the sophistic conclusions of Isocrates, to Demosthenes’ enthymemes, to Ciceronian richness, or to the precision of our own Maro? Who so carefully pursues each individual excellence as you fill them all? For what else are you but a perfection gathered from the genius of every liberal art?

These words, my lord and son Symmachus, I do not fear will seem more flattering than true when spoken of you. You have tested the truthfulness of my mind and words while we were both living in the imperial entourage, though unequal in age: there, where you, a recruit, earned the rewards of old service, while I, already a veteran, undertook the duties of a recruit. In the entourage I was genuine toward you—so do not [Col. 0936C] imagine that, abroad, I compose fables. In the entourage, I say, which covers men’s faces and conceals their minds, there you perceived that I was to you a parent, a friend, and, if anything is dearer than either, dearer still.

But let us leave these matters, lest this recollection seem to approach that fear of Sosia. There is one thing I almost passed over: with what eagerness you added the request that I send you some little didactic work or hortatory discourse. Shall I teach you, when I myself am still in need of teaching—if I were of an age to learn? Or shall I admonish you, vigorous and spirited as you are? By the same effort I might exhort the Muses to sing, the seas to pour forth their waters, the breezes to grow strong, and the fires to grow hot; or, if there is something that nature accomplishes even against our wishes, I would be an unnecessary instigator, goading it on.

One error is enough: that one of my works was published while I regretted it; that [Col. 0936D] good fortune fell into the hands of friends. For if the reverse had happened, not even you would persuade me that I could be pleasing.

Let this be my reply to your letter. I shall abbreviate the other matters that you wish to know. Even so, the letter is already long. I nevertheless put forward Julianus, a familiar member of our household, if you think there is anything to inquire about concerning us. At the same time I ask you, once you have learned the reason for his arrival, to assist the undertaking that you have already supported in part.

Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Note. Symmachus and Paulinus, to whom Ausonius addressed several letters, in turn sent several replies to Ausonius. You may see them either in the preceding volume, in the *Epistolary Works of Symmachus*, or among the Christian poets of the fifth century, in the works of Paulinus.]

[Col. 0937]

# Ausonius’ Address of Thanks to the Emperor Gratian, His Pupil, for the Consulship (C)

[Col. 0937A] I give you thanks, Emperor Augustus. If I could, I would even repay them. But neither does your fortune require a return, nor does ours provide the means of making one. Such abundance belongs to private persons, who may be generous toward one another. As your benefits surpass all others in majesty, so they do not demand repayment. The only thing within our power, therefore, is to give thanks—and to do so in the manner that God loves: with more feeling than words. I give thanks not only in the sanctuary of the imperial utterance, a place where tranquil awe and reverent fear rarely allow the same countenance and spirit, but everywhere: both silently and aloud, among men and alone with myself; both when I speak openly and when I withdraw into meditation; in every place, action, demeanor, and time.

Nor is it surprising that I set no limit to expressing such gratitude, when you do not know how to put an end to conferring honor. What place or day is there that does not remind me of this or a similar thanksgiving? “Remind me”? What ineptitude of sluggish expression! What place, I ask, is there that your benefits do not stir and inflame? None, I say, Emperor Augustus, that does not impress upon me the wondrous image of your veneration.

Not the Palatine, which, although you received it as a place of terror, you have made beloved. Not the Forum, nor the basilicas once filled with business, now filled with prayers—and prayers undertaken for your safety. For under your rule, who is not secure in his own? Not the senate-house, now joyful with honorable decrees, once mournful with anxious complaints. Not the public spaces, in which the meeting of so many joyful people permits no one to offer thanks alone. Not the common privacy of the home. Even the bed given over to rest is made more tranquil by reflection on your benefits.

Sleep, which erases everything, brings your images before me. And this seat of honor, the curule chair, glorious with the ceremonies of imperial office—at whose height you have placed me from what modest station!—whenever I think of it, I am overcome by its greatness and reduced to silence, not ungrateful for your benefits but overwhelmed by them.

You are present everywhere, and now we no longer wonder at the license of the poets who said that everything is full of the god. You surpass hope; you anticipate what is desired; you outrun prayers. Whatever speed of mind seeks, in the likeness of the gods, is preceded by your benefits. It is quicker for you to grant than for us to wish.

I therefore give you thanks, best of emperors. And if anyone assigns this speech of mine, repeated so often in the same words, to the poverty of the speaker, let him try to pursue the same subject: he will be unable to say anything more eloquent.

For thanks are being given to the bravest emperor—not because of the splendor of his majesty and not without evidence. The Danube frontier and the Rhine, pacified in a single year, bear witness to this. To the most generous: the wealthy army displays it. To the most indulgent: the security of human error proves it. To the wisest: the ordered East under such a ruler demonstrates it. To the most dutiful: the richest testimony to this praise is that your father was consecrated with divine honors; your brother was associated with the empire as your equal; your uncle was rescued from the disgrace of war; a son was joined with his father in the college of prefects; and your teacher was chosen for the consulship.

I could go through all your titles: those once bestowed by virtue, those recently granted by fortune, and those which divine indulgence is still considering. I would call you Germanicus because of the surrender of foreign peoples, Alemanicus because of the display of captives, and Sarmaticus because you conquered and forgave. I would connect all the achievements of virtue and the surnames of felicity. But that is another subject, prepared for its own treatment, when it pleases you to indicate, distinctly and briefly, everything we know without pursuing it in detail—just as those who enclose the whole world within the circumference of a single map diminish its size somewhat but lose none of its truth.

For now, however, since this day belongs especially to it, I shall give thanks for the consulship. Yet other dignities press forward and burst into the voice of thanksgiving, declaring that they have a prior claim. So many grades under the title of Count have been accumulated through your promotions, by your merit, while you and your father are emperors. The quaestorship was shared, and the prefecture was entirely your gift; and even the latter does not wish to receive a simple thanksgiving, since it was more generously divided than joined. Because we possess the whole of both offices, neither of us desires his portion separated from the other.

But those matters, as I promised just now, will have the distinctive privacy proper to their own office. My consulship here begs and implores that you allow its dignity to belong exclusively to you, since you have preferred me above all others.

Indeed, the office itself found a further distinction for me: joined in honor with my colleague, a most illustrious man, but preferred in the proclamation of the consulship, I, Emperor Augustus, received this honor through your gift without having traversed the enclosure, the voting field, the ballots, the voting tablets, or the ballot boxes; without having grasped hands, mingled with the crowd of those offering greetings, failed to return the names of friends, or imposed the names of strangers; without having canvassed the tribes, courted the centuries, trembled before the summoned classes, deposited anything with a broker, or made any agreement with a distributor.

The Roman people, the Campus Martius, the equestrian order, the rostra, the voting enclosures, the senate, the senate-house—all these were, for me, one Gratianus.

With complete justice, most Augustus, I can affirm this while preserving the goodwill of all who have ever attained, or will attain, this honor through different kinds of virtue. Each has his own spirit, his own merit, and his own conscience.

With complete justice, I say, I can affirm that I seem to myself set apart from the others. Some are tormented by the futility of their prayers: I did not pray. Others are driven by ambition: I did not seek office. Others secure it through persistence: I did not compel anyone. Others are offered the opportunity: I was not present. Others are helped by wealth: the discipline of the times stood in the way. I did not buy it.

Nor can I boast of self-restraint. I did not possess the means for such restraint. I have tried to establish only one thing, and I cannot even claim that as my own. For it depends upon your judgment whether I deserved it.

You have done this, and you will make others consuls as well, most dutiful Gratianus—but not men of equal claim in military glory. They share with you, as always in labor and usually in dignity, the fellowship of virtue rather than the older fellowship of honor. They are men of ancient nobility; for many things are granted to names, and Rome assigns men their due. They are men renowned for loyalty and approved by their services. Although I do not separate myself from them in number, I distinguish myself from them in respect of the path to honor.

This fourth stage of a new benefit you now determine to confer upon yourself, Augustus: you refer the goodness of your spirit to another’s excellence, and you turn the education of nature—which you owe to God, to your father, and to yourself—more properly, though not more truly, toward another’s advantage.

These are your own words, written by you to me: “You are repaying what you owed, and you still owe what you have repaid.”

O saying of a golden mind, embossed like gold leaf! O nourishment of speech, milk-white, from a most spotless breast! Is anyone so sparing in displaying a benefit? Does anyone declare the weight of his favor to be the force of another’s merit? Does anyone, finally, prefer to call what he grants a payment rather than a gift, as though it were being offered by one under obligation?

Let the old orators, those of Homer’s age, compete with this sentiment: Menelaus, whose speech was drawn out with subtle elegance; the Ithacan leader, like deep hail; and Nestor, already in the third age of his life, drenched in honeyed eloquence. Yet neither would the first speak more harmoniously, he who gathered himself into Laconic brevity; nor the second more intricately, he who piled words into clusters with his thoughts; nor the third more sweetly, whose gentle speech persuaded by soothing rather than by force.

You say that you are repaying what you owed, and that you will owe it when you have repaid it. Young Augustus, the ruler of heaven and of the human race granted you this: that, preferred to the ancients whom you have surpassed even in the elegance of this sentiment, you should surpass in Menelaus the royal dignity proper to him, in Ulysses his wisdom, and in Nestor his old age.

Someone may object: “You have indeed attained these things, but tell us by what merit.” Why burden me, questioner? No one gives an account of fortune. God—and the one nearest to God, who silently distributes gifts by his own judgment and, indignant that judgment of his benefits should stand through human beings—prefers to have a marvel bestowed upon those beneath him.

“By what merit?” you ask. I know of none, except that you, most dutiful emperor, say that you owe it; and that obligation extends very widely. Perhaps you consider this the interest on your education. Perhaps, without interest, you seek the glory of generosity. Perhaps you are relieving yourself of the weight of a promise undertaken. Perhaps you are fulfilling a trust committed to you by your father. Perhaps, with heavenly magnanimity and with ostentation suppressed, you are imitating God’s gift.

You say that you owe it. To whom? When? Under what name? Read the bond. Name the creditor. Let the accounts of receipts and expenditures be compared. You will see that the accounting of this sum has passed elsewhere: God has begun to owe it to you on our behalf.

But what do you owe me, most gracious emperor? Your humanity allows you to be praised by a private title in addition to your royal virtues. What do you owe me—and, conversely, what do I not owe you? Is it perhaps that I taught you? I can more truly turn that back upon myself: I was judged worthy to teach, preferred by your condescension over so many men outstanding in eloquence and learning, so that there might be someone whom you, already girded by mature age, could advance rapidly through every grade of honor by your hastened kindness.

You seemed afraid that my life might fail before you had anything further left to grant me. Cicero, though a consul, denies that he has anything further to desire. But I, now a consul and an old man, shall still confess my longing: Gratianus, I desire to see you more often in this magistracy, so that you alone may equal the six consulships of Valerius Corvus, the seven of Gaius Marius, and the thirteen consulships of Augustus, your namesake.

Your age and fortune can provide you with more consulships, but I am more sparing in counting because you are more generous in granting. You deprive yourself of this honor more often precisely so that you may bestow it upon others.

You know, most learned emperor—for I shall again employ private praise—you know, I say, how the seven and ten consulships of Domitian, which he strung together by envying the advancement of others, were mocked by his own greed, so that this made him arrogant in the pages of his fasti—or rather, of his disgust—and prevented him from being happy.

If a measured—and what is called a golden—moderation ought to govern the ruler’s possession of this honor, what moderation ought private citizens to maintain? What should men of equable spirit maintain? What restraint should old men now exercise toward themselves?

As far as my honors are concerned, I have filled my prayers. Yet you, best emperor, most dutiful emperor, you whom generosity does not weary except when it has ceased; you, most indulgent Gratianus, who are sudden in doing good and unexpected in your character—you will still find something to bestow upon me in this name.

Everyone has understood this; you yourself have arranged the order for us in this way. You are so dear to God that you have already obtained from him what no one prays for, and what we have not yet prayed for is nevertheless attained.

Again, someone may add, either openly in speech or more freely in thought: “Were there not once many teachers of this sort among the ancients? Are you alone the teacher of an Augustus?”

No. I share the office with many, but the example with very few.

I do not wish to criticize the colleagues of Constantine’s time: Caesars were taught. I shall pass over earlier times. Wealthy Seneca, though not a consul, will rightly be charged rather than praised for not educating Nero’s character but arming his cruelty. Quintilian, who received the ornaments of consular rank through Clement, seems to have possessed rather the decorations of a name than the insignia of power. Titianus was a teacher; but that celebrated man grew old in a municipal school, moving between Vesontio and Lugdunum—not indeed in age, but in lowliness.

For me, only the imitation of Fronto is worthy of embrace. Yet the consulship adorned him, as the teacher of an Augustus, without enclosing him in a prefecture. But what sort of consulship was that? A consulship substituted for an ordinary one, interposed for a period of two months and consumed in the sixth part of the year. It must be asked among which consuls so great an orator served his consulship.

Here is another objection someone might make: “So you raise yourself proudly to the height of such an orator?” To anyone asking this I shall answer briefly: “I do not set myself above Fronto; I prefer Gratianus to Antoninus.”

All the cities everywhere that live under the laws celebrate these solemn days: Rome according to custom, Constantinople in imitation, Antioch in luxury, disordered Carthage, Alexandria, the house of lightning; and Trier through the emperor’s favor. Though the places are far apart from one another and from the very author of that favor, their prayers agree.

One Gratianus is on everyone’s lips: emperor in power, victor in virtue, Augustus in holiness, pontiff in religion, father in indulgence, son in age, and both in filial devotion.

I cannot, as Marius says in Sallust, display the images of my ancestors as proof of my nobility; nor can I trace a lineage descended from heroes back to the stock of the gods; nor can I parade unknown wealth and estates scattered beneath royal rule. I can speak only of what is known, rather than advertise it: a homeland not obscure, a family not shameful, an innocent household, an innocence that was not forced, limited resources but enlarged by books and children, frugality without meanness, a liberal intellect, a spirit that was not illiberal, food, clothing, and furnishings clean but not splendid.

If anyone should deem me worthy to be compared with those ancient consuls—apart from the accumulation of military virtues that existed in their time—let him set aside wealth without detracting from diligence.

But since I have long been collapsing beneath the subject matter while giving thanks, you, Gratianus, take over my speech. You, Gratianus, who have gained this name through fortune in such a way that no one could have sought it more truly through ambition.

Nor was Metellus more justly called Pius, when his father was recalled, whereas he would have been impious had his father remained in exile; nor was Sulla more truly Felix—or more fortunate before he was called so—than you, Gratianus, who possess both this name and the surnames of Metellus and Sulla.

You, I say, Gratianus, who earned this not by individual deeds but by your continual, gracious beneficence in acting acceptably; to whom, had it not been handed down from your grandfather, everyone would have added it.

You yourself, I say, give thanks on my behalf—yourself and your virtues. Let goodness give thanks, by which you are generous toward all and constant toward me. Let filial devotion give thanks, by which you govern your world, which you demonstrate in avenging your uncle, increase in protecting your brother, and multiply in honoring your teacher. Let clemency give thanks, which you extend to the human race; generosity, by which you enrich all; courage, by which you conquer; and that golden mind, which you have drawn from the universal God more abundantly than any one man.

Let the voices of all the Gauls give thanks on my behalf, since you have bestowed this honor upon their prefect. I go further—and I do so because you say that you owe it.

Let this voice, which I have taught, give thanks; it is capable of giving thanks best.

For a long time now, as has been said above, I—a man as limited in speech as I am full of gratitude—have been collapsing beneath the subject matter. I have not yet even touched upon those things which not even the most speechless person, unless also the most impious, could suppress, since their excellence is proclaimed by fame and attested by everyone’s joy.

I hesitate to approach matters placed beyond my powers of speaking, lest I be charged either with ingratitude or with the presumption of rashness. Yet since one of these accusations must be faced, I prefer to have my boldness censured rather than my ill will.

You, venerable Augustus, engaged in a great war and under attack by countless thousands of barbarians, protected by the banks of the Danube, conduct the elections for my consulship while armed.

Are these tribunician proceedings being held at Sirmium, or are they like the centuriate proceedings once held under arms? Or are they to be called, as the ancient pontifical proceedings once were, proceedings conducted by a college without the discretion of the multitude of priests? Let them rather be called what you, as chief pontiff, in fellowship with God, have undertaken.

It is not within my talent, most dutiful emperor, to invent such things. They are the words of your letter, by which you magnify in my eyes the authority of the highest divine power and of your own will. For you write as follows:

“When I was considering alone with myself the consuls to be appointed for the coming year—as you know me, and as I ought to act, since I knew your wishes—I referred my decision to God. Obeying his authority, I designated you consul, declared you consul, and proclaimed you first.”

What order of speech could be clearer? What teaching could be more painstaking than to speak in the proper language of the elections, without mixing foreign terms with the names of ancient custom?

Farewell now, voting classes, peoples, prerogatives of the urban tribes, and centuries lawfully recalled. What elections were ever fuller than those in which God supplied the counsel and the emperor the obedience?

And now, most dutiful emperor, lest I offend the height of this sacred audience as a timid interpreter of your words, I shall pass over, almost as though in expiation, the words of your divinity.

“When I was considering,” you say, “the consuls to be appointed for the coming year”: an educated expression and solemn care.

“When I was considering alone with myself”: O depth of profound secrecy! You therefore have a counselor and do not fear a betrayer.

“As you know me”: what could be more intimate?

“And as I ought to act”: what could be more steadfast?

“Since I knew your wishes”: what could be said more graciously?

“I referred my decision to God.” And how could you do this alone, when such a great decision was available to you? Would you have deliberated more fully with the senate, the equestrian order, the Roman people, your army, and all the provinces?

“I referred my decision to God”—not, I believe, so that you might adopt something new, but so that what you wished might become more sacred, since you obeyed his authority, just as you did in consecrating your father, avenging your uncle, and co-opting your brother.

“I designated you consul, declared you consul, and proclaimed you first.” Who taught you these words? I did not know such precise and thoroughly Latin expressions: “I designated,” “I declared,” and “I proclaimed.”

This is not done rashly. Such mature deliberation, distributed through distinct stages, has its own delays. I shall order these letters of yours to be hung up, like an edict, on every pillar and portico where they can be read from the ground. Shall I not be honored by as many statues as there are pages in the little books?

But I hasten toward plainer matters.

For, turning aside from this portion of the letter you sent me, you also descended to ask what sort of robe should be sent to me. You wearied the entire administrative apparatus of your largesses with your concern. Thus, was such painstaking care exercised by you over and above the consulship for me? Was this fortunate care for me?

Arms are clashing in Illyricum. For my sake you distribute throughout the Gauls the garments of civic honor. Wearing a cuirass, you discuss my toga. On the eve of battle, and especially when you are about to fight, you auspiciously and fortunately arrange the ornaments of my palmata robe. For this garment belongs to the consul in peace just as it belongs to the triumphant general in victory.

It is not enough that you ask what sort of trabea should be sent to me: you order that it be brought forth in your presence. Nor are you satisfied that the officials of the treasury should perform their duties according to custom. You yourself choose among many, and once you have chosen, you honor your gifts with the dignity of your words.

“I have sent you a palmata,” you say, “in which the deified Constantine, our parent, is woven.”

How blessed am I, for whose insignia such care is taken! This, plainly, is the embroidered robe—not more splendid because of its gold than because of your words.

But there is much more in its decoration, which I understand because you have taught me. For the name of Augustus shines twice in a single garment. Constantine is woven into the design of the robe; Gratianus is perceived in the honor of the gift.

The great generosity of your benefit was further increased by the questioning of certain people. When asked which consul you would name first, you said that there could be no doubt; and those who were good men with you could not doubt it either.

Nevertheless, those who would gladly have believed my most illustrious colleague, whom the occasion had present, to be preferred, raised their hopes at this statement. Yet, wearying you with what they had understood, they kept asking for clarification.

Then you, as I have been told, hesitated for a short while with that familiar modesty of yours—not uncertain in your judgment, but condemning by your expression and blush the hesitation of those who were flattering their own preference through a mistaken interpretation.

Then you immediately added: “Why do you ask about two designated consuls? What order should there be in their proclamation? Is it any other than the order established by the prefecture?”

O truly fortunate modesty of yours, to which this popular calculation presented itself so wisely! You knew what else you might say, Gratianus, but out of regard for the modesty of certain people you did not wish to say it.

This is a delicate matter for me, and because of the glory I never sought, it is one I must decline. Since I was announced first, it is enough for me to uphold your judgment. Farewell, interpreters of merit.

Nor, most sacred emperor, do I embrace the order of proclamation as some minor benefit. Is this glory unknown to Cicero? “The Roman people,” he says, “made me praetor first and consul first.” From this very judgment it is clear that he considered it more commendable to be placed before one person than before several. For the second person suffers no insult, but the one preferred out of two gains great glory.

This is also reported of Alexander of Macedon. When he had read those Homeric verses in which, Hector having challenged the Greeks, it was decided that one of nine leaders—all eager to fight—should be selected by lot, and when the whole army prayed to Jupiter Optimus Maximus with anxious concentration of its prayers that the lot might permit it to choose Ajax, the son of Tydeus, or Agamemnon himself, the wealthy king of Mycenae, Alexander said: “I would kill the man who named me third.”

O magnanimity of the bravest man! He refused to be named third among nine, where he would certainly have been superior to more men than he would have been subordinate to.

How much embarrassment would the second of two feel here? For in this number there is a choice full of difficult distinction, since, out of all mortals, two are selected and preferred as consuls. Whoever is preferred to the other is preferred not to one person but to everyone.

I know that the ears of those present are now expecting something, and I see on every face the desire forming in their minds. For they suppose that, having touched briefly upon the matters relevant to giving thanks, drawing them out with a rather slender thread, as the saying goes, I ought also to touch upon some of the praises of your majesty.

Although I said that I had set this subject aside and reserved it for another time, they nevertheless urge me now, by gestures and almost by murmurs, to touch upon something. I shall therefore do so, since they compel one who is willing. But, setting aside the greater matters, I shall mention the lesser ones—not hoping to carry them out fully, but so that everyone may understand that I am being asked to provide knowledge of the things that must be praised inwardly, while others must provide the dignity of their expression.

I shall discuss not the extraordinary but the everyday.

From your youth onward, you have never passed a day without worshiping the divine power, both bound by a vow and immediately discharged from it; with clean hands, a pure mind, an undefiled conscience, and—something found in few people—with sincere thought.

Whose departure was ever more auspicious? Whose gait more modest? Whose bearing more restrained? Whose familiar appearance more fitting? Whose military equipment more ready?

In exercising the body, who drove his course so swiftly? Who moved through the wrestling ground so agilely? Who gathered himself for a leap so high? No one hurled javelins with greater reach; no one threw spears more frequently or struck the intended targets more accurately.

We used to wonder at the poet who called the Numidians “unbridled,” and at another poet who had gathered the idea so that he said that in riding there were both whips and instructions for flight, and instructions for stopping. This was obscure to us as we read. We understood it when we saw you draw the bow and release the reins, or urge on a sluggish horse with the whip, or restrain its excessive speed with that same whip.

Those who seemed to have taught you this do not do it themselves. Rather, those who seemed to have taught you are now learning.

In food, whose priestly ritual is more abstinent? In wine, whose old man’s table is more frugal? Within the covered chambers of your dwelling there is no altar more holy than that of Vesta, no chamber more chaste than a pontiff’s, no sacred couch more modest than a flamen’s.

In the duties owed to friends, I do not say that you return equal service: you surpass it. And whenever we take the lead in serving you, you blush with a shame as submissive as the shame that ought to belong to us when we are anticipated by an emperor.

In this seat—which, according to custom, we call the council chamber, but which I regard as your sanctuary—none of your predecessors ever thought more carefully about what ought to be said, arranged what he had thought with greater deliberation, or carried out what he had arranged more promptly.

I would also say something about your oratorical virtues, if I did not fear that I might be flattering you. For Sulpicius was not more incisive in legal cases, nor was the modesty of the elder Gracchus more commendable, nor was the authority of your father more weighty.

What is the tenor of your voice when you speak with animation? What its inflection when you relax? What its moderation when you combine both? Which orator ever expressed, or—what is freer—conceived, joyful matters more delightfully, eloquent matters more elegantly, opposing matters more densely, or densely arranged matters more compactly?

I wish that Xenophon, Attic writer, if the nature of things allowed it, might come into our age—you who offered a panegyric rather than a history for describing the virtues of Cyrus, when you said not what he was but what he ought to be.

If you now entered our times, you would see in our Gratianus what you had not seen in your Cyrus but had desired.

I have marked all these matters, as it were, with pointed strokes. If eloquence were available to me in proportion to my will, I would pursue this abundance, though not copiously, with a style supplied by the greatness of the subject. But this is suited neither to this day nor to this subject.

Those who are going to pronounce the praises of our emperor have here, as it were, a seedbed from which to fill the fields of their speeches. I have touched upon these matters briefly.

And, as everyone knows, I may appear to be the confidential interpreter of familiar knowledge, revealing these domestic matters rather than praising them. Since I have spoken of things known to me and familiar within the court, I could also mention matters celebrated outside it, unless everyone already knew them individually for himself.

I could speak of earlier matters with equal brevity. It is characteristic of a most blameless man to do nothing of which he must be ashamed. But you have never done anything of which you must repent, and you have always offered pardon to those who repent.

It is beautiful to show indulgence to those who are afraid. But through edicts of perpetual goodness you have met everyone’s fears, so that they would not be afraid.

It is magnificent to bestow honors. You have enriched those honored by your generosity.

It is praiseworthy for an emperor to provide easy access to those who approach him and not to plead the excuse of occupation. You encourage those who hesitate to approach; even when their complaints have been laid out, you ask whether anything remains unsaid.

It was a celebrated saying of Titus Caesar that he had lost a day on which he had done no good. But it became celebrated because it was said by the successor of Vespasian, whose excessive thrift and scarcely tolerable severity made his son’s gentleness seem remarkable.

You, born of Valentinian, whose profound goodness, immediate kindness, and measured severity established and preserved the state excellently, understand that you can be most gentle without weakening discipline.

Nor do you provide one particular good on a single day; you multiply age-long acts of indulgence at every moment of every hour.

What sort of act was that one alone concerning the remission of tax arrears? With what accumulated generosity did you carry it out? Which emperor ever granted this to his provinces with more abundant indulgence, protected them with more reliable security, or fortified them with wiser prudence?

Trajan once did something similar, but he retained portions of the debt. The portion of the debt that had been granted did not provide as much pleasure as the bitterness that remained in what had been preserved.

Antonius had also granted remission, but the successor to the empire, not to the benefit, begrudged it and, using the people’s documentary registers and tablets, reclaimed what had been forgiven.

You ordered every document that could be used to demand payment to be publicly burned.

All the cities saw, in their own public places, the conflagration of a salutary fire. The roots of old frauds were burning; the seeds of future frauds were burning. Already the ash had mingled with the dust. Already smoke had enveloped everything in clouds.

And still the debtors, on the pages being burned, delighted to see the strokes of letters and the marks of sestertii alongside the helpful figures of the accounts, remembering that what they feared had been read could still be read.

What could be more indulgent than you, Emperor Augustus? What could be wiser? The good things you grant, you make lasting; the evils you remove, you ensure cannot recur.

These are the benefits of your indulgence toward the provincials. What of those toward our order? What kindness was there toward the soldiers of the Antonines? And, from the cohort of Germanici, friends, and legions, what familiar humanity was there? [The transmitted syntax is uncertain.]

But I do not wish to make your benevolence excel through comparison with others. In you there are abundant examples of goodness and virtue which future generations may wish to follow and which, if the nature of things allowed it, antiquity itself would have wished to claim for itself.

Nevertheless, something must be compared in order that it may be understood by how much our benefits surpass the earlier ones.

Trajan was accustomed to visit sick friends; this is the extent to which his kindness should be praised. You not only visit them but also heal them: you provide attendants, arrange their food, distribute fomentations, add the expense of medicines, console the afflicted, and rejoice with those who recover.

Along how many paths do you advance from that one act of humanity!

When something adverse had occurred to entire legions, as happens in the common experience of war, I saw you go around the tents, ask whether all was well, examine the wounds of the injured, insist that healing remedies be applied, and urge that treatment not cease.

I saw some who were disgusted with food take it when you commended it. I heard you speak words that strengthened them toward recovery; attend to the wishes of individuals; have the baggage of some carried by mules from the imperial household; provide special animals for others; restore to some the services of lost camp-followers; bear the poverty of others at your own expense; cover the nakedness of others with clothing.

You did everything tirelessly and kindly, with the greatest filial devotion and no ostentation. You provided everything to the sick and reproached the healed for nothing.

By this conduct you became dearer to everyone than our own safety, and you deserved to have friends who were devoted, ready, loyal, and destined to remain so forever—friends whom affection rather than fortune brings together.

I shall now conclude my speech, most dutiful Augustus—more by ending my words than my gratitude. For gratitude is perpetual, and, since it cannot be traversed in its full extent, it knows no finishing point.

Nevertheless, with a slight turn, and without going far from you, I shall turn toward God:

Eternal Father of all, himself unbegotten creator and cause of the world, older than its beginning and longer-lived than its end, who have built temples and altars to yourself in the innermost minds of those initiated into you: you implanted in Gratianus, lord of human affairs, such seeds of love for us that, though becoming no slower in his departure, he remembered those he had left behind, illuminated the absent, and preferred them to those present.

Then, because he could not be present at the beginnings of this dignity owing to the distances between places, he hastened to the solemnity of establishing the honor, so that official duty should not be lacking to his benefactions.

For what memory—memory, I say—has ever imagined, even in the bold fictions of the Greeks, such speed of passage?

Pegasus, driven as a winged creature from Lycia, did not pass beyond Cilicia. Cyllarus and Arion grew old between Argos and Nemea. Even the horses of the Dioscuri, on their longest journey, travel across it only when their rider has been changed.

But you, Gratianus, crossed so many boundaries of the Roman Empire, so many rivers and lakes, so many barriers of ancient kingdoms—from Thrace through the whole length of Illyricum, through Venetia, Liguria, and ancient Gaul, beyond the impassable regions of Raetia, along the banks of the Rhine, across the trackless lands of the Sequani and the broad stretches of Germany—in a more rapid passage than our speech can hurry.

You did so without any rest for leisure, or even for sleep or food, through your generous duty, so that you might unexpectedly illuminate your Gauls; so that you might anticipate, though longed for, your consul; so that you might make even Fame herself, who usually precedes the winds, slower than you.

That supreme god, privy to, judge, and author of your empire and counsels, granted this to my old age and to the honor bestowed upon me, so that you might make the curule chair, whose seat you will often adorn; my bordered robe, tinted by the radiance of your purple; and my trabea, made splendid not more by its own gold than by your gift—garments whose dignity was honored by your speech—more illustrious in the Gauls.

You made me your quaestor, your prefect, your prefect as your consul in your praetorium, and—what you still place before all my other titles—your teacher, whom you had proclaimed with a dutiful voice, preferred with just judgment, enriched with generous largesse, and consecrated through the offices of imperial esteem.

*Before Gratianus Augustus.*

[Col. 0947]

**Outlines of the Iliad and Odyssey of Homer**
[Col. 0947A] If we review Homer, the author of the Trojan War, as far as he begins and ends his *Iliad*, we shall show that, beginning with the wrath of Achilles and ending with the burial of Hector, he composed twenty-four books. This is how the work appears to one who looks only at the surface of its first part. Yet this period of the writing occupied not the whole Trojan War, but nearly its final portion. For if one reckons the duration of the siege as ten years, the ninth year, almost at its very end, contains the events worthy of remembrance from Agamemnon’s offense and seizure of Briseis up to Hector’s funeral. The entire sequence of events extends from the causes and origin of that same war to the destruction of the city. Consequently, to those inexperienced in judgment and unfamiliar with composition, many notable events from the beginning of the war up to Achilles’ quarrel may seem to have been omitted, and no fewer events from Hector’s funeral all the way to the destruction of Ilium. The anticipation of these events was especially great because they brought so long a conflict to completion. But so that it might be clear that the divine poet omitted nothing illustrious and that everything which needed to be concluded actually occurred, we have briefly, in the manner of an epitome, retraced the cause and origin of the Trojan War and the preparations, together with what happened in earlier years. The first origin of all these events is the judgment of Paris among the goddesses, and finally the construction of the fleet by which that same Paris sailed to Europe. Then came the abduction of Helen, which ancient opinion divided into two accounts: most believed that Helen, in accordance with Homer’s poetic fiction, was carried off to Troy; others, however, supposed that when Alexander had strayed from his course and had been carried to Egypt, the Egyptian king—an exceptionally scrupulous guardian of justice—learned of the violation of the laws of hospitality and seized Helen, together with those who had accompanied her, took her away from Paris, and restored her to Menelaus only after Ilium had finally been conquered.

## Synopsis of Book I of the *Iliad*

> Tell, goddess, of the anger of Peleus’ son Achilles,
>
> the baneful anger that brought a thousand disasters upon the Achaeans.

Chryses, priest of Apollo, after supplicating Agamemnon for the ransom of his daughter and being shamefully rejected, prays to the god for vengeance. When a grievous plague subsequently breaks out and the Greek army perishes, Achilles summons an assembly, and Calchas is compelled, against his will, to disclose the cause of the disease. Once this is known, Agamemnon is provoked against Achilles. Stirred by anger, Achilles would even have dared to kill the king, had Minerva not prevented him from advancing to the extremity of fury. Agamemnon then removed Briseis, his concubine, in place of Chryseis, who was being returned to her father. Thereupon Thetis, his mother, pitying her son’s tears and humiliation, goes to heaven. Trusting in the support she had once given Jupiter together with Aegaeon, she entreats the supreme god, eager to avenge her son's injury, to allow the Trojans to prevail in the fortunes of war. When Juno learns of this, she is angrily stirred against her husband. But as the quarrel grows and threatens to become ridiculous, it is calmed by Vulcan, who supplies the feast and intervenes as though offering counsel.

## Synopsis of Book II of the *Iliad*

> The heavenly gods and the race of men, vulnerable to cares,
>
> were enjoying the tranquil gifts of obscure sleep.
>
> But restless night did not soothe the sleepless Thunderer,
>
> as he revolved in his heart his excessive plans,
>
> intent on avenging injured Achilles by the slaughter of the Greeks.

Jupiter warns Agamemnon in a dream that the time has come to wage battle and that he should not delay fighting. Agamemnon then summons the leaders to council and explains Jupiter’s command and the appearance of the nocturnal vision. Soon afterward, when the multitude has gathered in assembly, he tests the soldiers’ resolve and urges them, once the war has been abandoned, to return each to his own home. When everyone is already urging departure by sea, Ulysses restrains the shameful retreat. He also strikes the ugly and garrulous Thersites, who is ready with verbal license to insult the heroes, chastising him sharply. At Minerva’s prompting, Ulysses deters everyone from departure. The army then takes food and arms itself. The Trojans likewise draw up their battle line and advance, Iris giving the command. An individual enumeration of the forces follows, listing, in catalog form, the soldiers, ships, commanders, and homelands.

## Synopsis of Book III of the *Iliad*

[Col. 0948D]

> The Argives follow each his own battle line into war,
>
> arranged in cavalry squadrons and infantry wedges.
>
> The Trojans confuse their ranks with their clamorous blare.

Before the army, drawn up for battle, strikes the opposing line, Priam watches from the walls and, with Helen pointing them out, learns about the distinguished men. Then Menelaus is challenged by Alexander to single combat. Despite Agamemnon’s futile attempt to dissuade him, he engages. The two peoples make a pact, confirmed by sacred rites, on the condition that Helen, with her dowry, will follow the victor. But Paris is defeated; when he returns to the city, his wife receives him with a quarrel, and Agamemnon demands that the terms of the treaty be honored.

## Synopsis of Book IV of the *Iliad*

[Col. 0949A]

> Meanwhile Jupiter, together with the ancestral gods,
>
> convenes a council of the heavenly powers concerning the Achaeans.

Jupiter decides that Troy should be destroyed, and Juno’s obstinacy presses him toward this decision. When Minerva hastens to bring it about, she contrives a breach of the treaty and craftily approaches Pandarus, skilled in archery, persuading him secretly to wound Menelaus so that the cause of war may grow more violent. Once this has been done, the Greeks renew the battle, and when the armies meet, the issue is decided by mutual slaughter.

## Synopsis of Book V of the *Iliad*

> Here Tritonian Pallas also fills Tydeus’ son,
>
> once warned, with daring valor; from his helmet
>
> golden flames pour forth, and his shield flashes with streaming fire.
>
> He himself gleams like a rival to the autumnal star.

[Col. 0949B] Diomedes fights valiantly with Minerva’s help. Venus also attempts to aid her son, but withdraws after being wounded. Mars too is wounded and leaves the battle. The encounter between Tlepolemus and Sarpedon follows. Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, is defeated in combat and killed.

## Synopsis of Book VI of the *Iliad*

> The battle lines contend alone, without divine power,
>
> with aid having ceased; empty of assistance, they undertake the labor
>
> and endure fortune through the peril of their own destined fate.

As the Trojans fight with fortune inclining more favorably toward them, the seer Helenus advises that Minerva be appeased. Accordingly, Hecuba, instructed by Hector to carry a peplos into the citadel, fulfills the vows with the mothers. Alexander, rebuked by his brother, proceeds to battle. Glaucus the Lycian and Diomedes the Aetolian meet to fight, but when the contest is about to begin, they remember the hospitality shared by their fathers, exchange weapons, and withdraw.

## Synopsis of Book VII of the *Iliad*

> When he had spoken these words, Hector emerged through the gates.

With the agreement of Minerva and Apollo, Hector challenges the bravest of the Greeks. Since nine leaders are ready to fight, it is decided that the one who will fight should be selected by lot. Ajax son of Telamon engages in single combat, and Hector, struck by a stone, withdraws into the mass of his people. While the contest continues, the herald Idaeus intervenes. Gifts are then exchanged and the battle is brought to an end. Hector presents Ajax with a sword, and Ajax presents Hector with a baldric. At nightfall the armies each withdraw to their own positions. On the following day the burial of the slain is arranged. The Greeks also fortify their naval camp with a ditch and rampart.

## Synopsis of Book VIII of the *Iliad*

> Dawn shone yellow in her saffron chariot.

After the council of the gods has been held, Jupiter declares his decision: each army shall determine the outcome by its own fortune, and none of the gods shall proceed out of hatred to favor one side against the other. He himself withdraws to Mount Ida, from which the Greeks, terrified by the panic he sends among them, are driven in shameful flight to their fortifications and defend themselves with ditch and embankments. Iris terrifies Juno and Minerva, who wish to aid the Greeks, by reminding them of Jupiter’s commands. When battle is broken off because of night, the victorious Trojans establish siege watches on the very field of battle and, lighting many fires, deliberate throughout the night about the conduct of the war.

## Synopsis of Book IX of the *Iliad*

> Meanwhile the Achaeans are held back by the sentries’ watches.

The leaders are summoned by Agamemnon, since the Greeks are both shaken by the previous battle and terrified by what is now threatening them. The king proposes plans for flight and orders preparations for sailing during the night, but Diomedes and Nestor dissuade him. At Nestor’s urging, Ajax and Ulysses are chosen to go to Achilles, promising him magnificent gifts if he will cease his anger and lend his aid to their exhausted cause. But Achilles remains obstinately angry, and the Achaean envoys return unsuccessful, having obtained nothing.

## Synopsis of Book X of the *Iliad*

[Col. 0950B]

> The rest of the host of commanders lay quiet in sleep beside the ships;
>
> only anxious concern tormented Atreus’ son.

Ulysses and Diomedes set out at night to reconnoiter and catch sight of Dolon, who, encouraged by Hector’s promises, had himself gone out to investigate the Greeks’ plans. They compel him to confess everything and kill him on the same spot. From him they learn of the arrival of Rhesus, king of the Thracians; they kill him as well, together with his men, and lead away his horses as both prize and evidence of the raid. They are remarkable for their whiteness and speed, surpassing both snow and winds.

## Synopsis of Book XI of the *Iliad*

> Leaving Tithonus’ saffron chamber, Dawn
>
> spread over the earth, bringing back its labors and toil.

[Col. 0950C] All the Greeks fight splendidly, but without success. Their leaders are wounded, and the battle is entrusted to the undistinguished mass of the army. Achilles, somewhat moved by this affliction of fortune, sends Patroclus to learn the present situation. When Patroclus returns bearing news of the adverse state of affairs, he sees Eurypylus suffering from a wound and, applying the remedies of medical skill, restores him to health.

## Synopsis of Book XII of the *Iliad*

> The son of Actor tends Eurypylus, exhausted by his wound.

The Greeks’ position—or rather their desperate condition—is carried to the extremity of misfortune. Their leaders are wounded, while the rest of the army has either fled or been struck with fear. The Trojans tear down the defenses of the naval camp, cross the rampart, and are encouraged by omens whose outcome is uncertain. Thus part of the wall is torn down by Sarpedon, the gate is shattered by Hector’s stone blow, and battle is joined within the naval camp itself.

## Synopsis of Book XIII of the *Iliad*

> Jupiter drove the Trojans and Hector toward the fleet.

Neptune, moved by pity, comes to aid the Argives in defending their ships. Assuming the appearance of a seer, he urges both Ajaxes into battle and likewise rouses the rest of the multitude by the presence of his majesty. Idomeneus stands out in a splendid contest. The Trojans, already retreating, are rallied and once more drawn together by Hector, and the battle is fought on both sides with tremendous shouting.

## Synopsis of Book XIV of the *Iliad*

[Col. 0951A]

> Although drinking, the shouting shook Nestor
>
> and struck his startled ears with the weight of the tumult.

Juno borrows Venus’ girdle, called the *cestus*, and goes to Jupiter in a secluded part of Mount Ida. Having urged Sleep to plunge him into slumber, she then weakens his wakefulness by the charms of his wife. Neptune takes advantage of Jupiter’s ignorance and restores the fortunes of the Greeks by aiding them more actively; Ajax the Locrian fights more fiercely than the others.

## Synopsis of Book XV of the *Iliad*

> The Trojan youth had already mounted the rampart and ditch,
>
> threatening to burn the captured fleet.

Jupiter, awakened from sleep, sees that the state of the battle has changed and that the Trojans are being driven back, while Neptune is aiding the Greeks. He therefore harshly rebukes Juno and terrifies her with threats delivered through Iris, ordering his brother, who was aiding the Greeks, to cease. He sends Apollo to restore Hector and instructs him to turn fortune in the war back in favor of the Phrygians. Ajax son of Telamon then fights valiantly, and after killing many of the enemy, prevents the fleet from being burned.

## Synopsis of Book XVI of the *Iliad*

> While the Trojans press on with torch and sword
>
> to attack the lofty ship, and the Argive kings strive to defend it,

Achilles pities the Greeks’ condition, now reduced to the extremity of fortune, and allows Patroclus to arm himself in his weapons. Patroclus leads out the Myrmidon army and deceives the terrified Trojans by appearing as Achilles. He drives them, rushing over the rampart and fleeing from one another in blind panic, into the open plain. He then meets and kills Sarpedon. After slaughtering many of the enemy, Patroclus himself is killed by Hector, though he has first been wounded by Euphorbus.

## Synopsis of Book XVII of the *Iliad*

> Nor did Patroclus’ death escape you, Menelaus, son of Actor.

Battle gathers around the slain Patroclus. The two armies struggle: the Greeks to defend the body, the Trojans to seize the corpse for mockery. Menelaus kills Euphorbus, and Hector arms himself with Achilles’ armor as a display of his glorious deed. Antilochus hastens to Achilles as messenger of the disaster, while Menelaus presses on. Later Menelaus himself withdraws with Meriones within the naval fortifications, as the entire burden of war falls upon the two Ajaxes.

## Synopsis of Book XVIII of the *Iliad*

> While the fiery power of Mars rages in the midst of war,

Achilles laments Patroclus’ death in a pitiful manner. His mother addresses him with consoling words, moved by the force of his grief. She promises that his friend will not remain unavenged and that she will bring Vulcan’s armor. Meanwhile Iris is sent by Juno. At her urging, Achilles, though unarmed, goes outside the rampart; the terrified Trojans flee widely, one falling upon another, and fear spreads even farther. At the same time, Vulcan, urged by Thetis, spends the entire night—however long it is—fashioning heavenly armor for the nymph.

## Synopsis of Book XIX of the *Iliad*

> Meanwhile Dawn rose and left Ocean.

Achilles is equipped with heavenly armor through Vulcan’s skill and his mother’s gift. He then summons the leading Greeks to council, lays aside his anger as though it had been annulled, and is enriched before the assembly by the gifts promised by the king. When the soldiers are ordered to take food, he himself abstains. Then he advances into battle with an army hostile and ready for action.

## Synopsis of Book XX of the *Iliad*

> Now they went forth armed from the lofty ships,
>
> as many thousands as ever came from great Mycenae.

With the full forces of both sides intact, battle is joined between the two armies. Then, with Jupiter’s permission, the gods divide their support between the parties. Juno and Minerva fight for the Greeks, and Neptune, Mercury, and Vulcan likewise support them; Apollo with Venus, Diana with her mother, Mars, and Scamander aid the Trojans. Aeneas, having engaged Achilles with the gods and unequal strength against him, is rescued by Neptune, who, although favoring the Greeks, envelops him in a cloud and carries him away.

## Synopsis of Book XXI of the *Iliad*

> He had driven the terrified bands into the river,
>
> in a shameful flight.

After the Trojans have been driven by flight and terror as far as the bed of the Scamander, and no farther space for retreat remains, Achilles defeats twelve Trojan youths in the river itself, swollen beyond its banks, to sacrifice them at Patroclus’ funeral rites. Vulcan burns up the force of the torrent with his fires. When Achilles advances into the plain, the gods openly fight on their separate sides. With the victor pressing on, the Trojan army is driven against the city walls.

## Synopsis of Book XXII of the *Iliad*

> Driven by fear, the Phrygian ranks patrolled the walls.

Hector engages Achilles in single combat. Priam and Hecuba beg him not to fight, but Minerva, appearing in the likeness of Deiphobus, urges him on. Hector is killed, tied to the chariot, and dragged three times around the Trojan walls. His mangled body is then carried to the ships as vengeance for Patroclus and reserved for further punishment at the victor’s anger.

## Synopsis of Book XXIII of the *Iliad*

> Troy is empty of tears; the Argive youth is occupied with games.

Funeral games are celebrated in honor of Patroclus. Diomedes wins with his horses, Ulysses in wrestling and running, and the others surpass one another in their respective contests.

## Synopsis of Book XXIV of the *Iliad*

> Each returns to his own ships when the contest has been dismissed.

Jupiter sends Thetis to her son with instructions to cease raging against the dead and to respect the fates of human beings in a lifeless enemy by restoring the body for burial. At the same command, Iris urges Priam to ransom his dead son with gold. Guided by Mercury, Priam sets out during the night through the enemy’s watches, falls suppliant before Achilles, and, having redeemed his son, mourns and buries him under a public cessation of business.

## Synopsis of Book I of the *Odyssey*

> Tell me, Muse, of the man who, after Troy’s walls were captured,
>
> saw the customs of many men and many cities.

At Jupiter’s will, Minerva descends to Ithaca, assumes the appearance of Mentor, leader of the Taphians, and advises Telemachus to hasten to Nestor and Menelaus, who, having recently returned home, might know something certain about Ulysses. Then Phemius the lyre-player, summoned to the suitors’ banquet, begins a mournful song about the disastrous voyage that scattered the Greeks who had departed from Ilium into various exiles. Penelope withdraws, offended by the Chalcidian subject of so miserable a theme, and urges him to sing something else.

## Synopsis of Book II of the *Odyssey*

> Dawn had brought forth her rosy steeds from Ocean.

Telemachus summons the Ithacan leaders to the assembly. There he complains about the dishonor done to his household and the wasting of his property, and sets out his plans for departure. Antinous opposes him and tries to prevent him from leaving before his mother marries. After this dispute has continued for a long time, the assembly is dissolved. Telemachus goes to the shore without the suitors’ knowledge. Sensing Minerva standing beside him, he makes preparations suitable for the journey, especially at the goddess’s urging, for she deceived both the people and Telemachus himself by assuming the likeness of Mentor. Once the crew has been assembled and the ship launched, Telemachus and Minerva put out from the harbor as evening approached.

## Synopsis of Book III of the *Odyssey*

> Now the sun had brought forth his radiant rising from Ocean.

Telemachus questions Nestor about his father but learns nothing from the man who does not know. Nevertheless, the old man urges him on the following day, together with his son Pisistratus, to proceed to Menelaus. There is no delay: that very night they stay as guests at the town of Pherae, and on the next day travel onward to Lacedaemon.

## Synopsis of Book IV of the *Odyssey*

[Col. 0953D]

> And now they had reached the mighty citadel of Lacedaemon.

Menelaus receives Telemachus and those who had come with him hospitably, and toward evening they learn certain things about Ulysses. On the following day Menelaus explains the entire course of the voyage. He relates that Ulysses is being detained on the island of Ogygia by the promises and charms of the nymph Calypso. Proteus had told him this when Menelaus inquired about the Greek commanders. When the suitors learn of Telemachus’ departure, they prepare and launch a ship, and twenty men chosen from among them sail out. Lying in wait near the island of Asteria, which lies between Ithaca and Samos, they conceal themselves and await an opportunity for their treachery.

## Synopsis of Book V of the *Odyssey*

[Col. 0954A]

> Dawn had left Tithonus in his warm chamber.

Mercury flies to the island of Ogygia so that, terrified by Jupiter’s command, Calypso will allow Ulysses to depart. Ulysses, alone, rashly undertakes the voyage, constructing a raft. On the eighteenth day, when a storm arises because hostile Neptune is angry, the framework of the beams comes apart. Thus reduced to his last hope, he is saved by the merciful goddess Juno through futile swimming efforts; she removes the headscarf from her own head and gives it to the swimmer. With its support he reaches the shore of the Phaeacians.

## Synopsis of Book VI of the *Odyssey*

> Long afflicted, Ulysses had been taking his sleep.

After swimming to the shore of the Phaeacians, Ulysses relieves his exhaustion with sleep. But while the maiden Nausicaa, daughter of King Alcinous, is playing on the shore with her companions, he is awakened from sleep and emerges naked, covering his private parts with a barrier of leaves. When he falls suppliant at the knees of the royal maiden, he arouses a saving compassion through Minerva’s direction. Placed on a wagon and given clothing, he is led, at the urging of the maiden’s modesty, as far as the temple of Minerva outside the city. There he prays to the deity familiar to him with customary reverence.

## Synopsis of Book VII of the *Odyssey*

> The son of Laertes had long been praying to the gods above.

Minerva, transformed into the appearance of a girl, leads Ulysses first into the town and then into the royal palace. When Arete, the wife of Alcinous, learns from his own account where he obtained his clothing, who he is, and by what fortune he was carried there, she tells him to take courage. As evening comes on, he withdraws to rest.

## Synopsis of Book VIII of the *Odyssey*

> Now the sky glows, and Dawn shines in her rosy chariot.

Alcinous learns from Ulysses, in summary, about the hardships of his voyage. He then orders the leaders to assemble in the council and explains the guest’s arrival and the misfortunes of his prolonged wandering. Having summoned Ulysses to the banquet, he orders Demodocus to play the lyre. When Demodocus sings of the Wooden Horse and the destruction of Troy, he draws tears from Ulysses by recalling his former fortunes. Ulysses tries carefully to conceal them, either disguising his expression or wiping them away with his clothing, but he draws everyone’s attention to himself, especially that of the king. When Alcinous learns the reason for his tears, he kindly promises everything and urges him to recount all that he has endured in order.

## Synopsis of Book IX of the *Odyssey*

> Then in turn the Laertian hero speaks.

Four books are devoted to the account of Ulysses’ wanderings. Asked by Alcinous, he recounts the sequence of his many misfortunes: how, after leaving Ilium, he was first carried to the Cicones; how, after storming their city of Ismarus, he departed in flight, having lost many men; how from there he was driven around Cape Malea in Laconia and afterward came to the Lotus-Eaters. Then he proceeded with a single ship to the island of the Cyclopes, which lay near the Lotus-Eaters. Having carefully hidden the ship, he entered the cave of Polyphemus with twelve companions. Polyphemus, having gorged himself on bloody food prepared by slaughtering Ulysses’ companions and then becoming drunk on the wine Ulysses had given him, fell into sleep and was blinded by Ulysses, paying the penalty for his savagery.

## Synopsis of Book X of the *Odyssey*

> We are driven toward Aeolia, the homeland of the winds and our own home.

From there he relates that he was carried to Aeolia and received gifts from Aeolus, king of the winds. After hospitably providing everything, Aeolus also gave him the winds shut up in a leather bag so that he might sail more safely. When Ulysses was already nearing Ithaca, he fell back into sleep. His companions, believing that some wealth was contained in the bag, loosened its bindings while he slept, and the contrary winds carried them back from the very sight of their homeland. From there he was carried to Antiphates and the Laestrygonians. After losing all but one of his ships, he reached the shore of Circe. There, through the magic of the powerful goddess, Eurylochus and the companions sent with him were changed into the forms of beasts. Ulysses himself was destined to suffer the same fate, but Mercury’s intervention enabled him to avoid it; he then compelled the others to be restored to their former appearance through admiration of his courage.

## Synopsis of Book XI of the *Odyssey*

> But after he had come to the ships and the shores of the sea,

Having departed from Circe, he reaches Avernus, a place believed to be the descent to the dead. There, after properly completing the sacred rites, he fills a pit with the blood of victims and does not allow the hovering souls to touch any of the blood until, as Circe had instructed, the seer Tiresias has first tasted it. There he also sees many heroines, whose catalogue he weaves together with much of the charm of ancient tales.

## Synopsis of Book XII of the *Odyssey*

> Now he had left behind him the clear streams of Ocean.

After learning from the seer Tiresias what he needed to know, he returns to Circe and is instructed by her how to avoid the remaining dangers: how to pass the Sirens and their deadly song for sailors; how to sail past Scylla and Charybdis, the famous monsters of the Sicilian strait. After overcoming these dangers only through severe suffering, he reaches Trinacria. There, although the Sun himself forbids it in vain, his remaining companions, driven by hunger, tear apart the unattended herds of the Sun. They are terrified by dreadful omens following their slaughter of the cattle. Soon afterward, as they sail away, all perish together by a thunderbolt, except Ulysses, who clings to a fragment of the keel and, aided by it, swims alone to the island of Ogygia.

## Synopsis of Book XIII of the *Odyssey*

> All fell silent and held their faces fixed in attention.

After he has recounted everything he endured during his many wanderings, Ulysses is honored with many gifts by the leading men of Phaeacia. They equip a ship with oars and everything necessary. While he sleeps, he is carried to Ithaca in a very peaceful voyage. There, while he is resting in his native harbor with all his gifts and unaware of everything, he is set ashore, and the Phaeacians return while he sleeps.

## Synopsis of Book XIV of the *Odyssey*

> He leaves the harbor by the way to which a narrow path leads.

Awakening from sleep, Ulysses recognizes his native harbor and shore with no little agitation of mind. He marvels at how he was brought there, set ashore, and abandoned, and at how he knew nothing of it. He inspects all the gifts and, finding them undamaged, hides them as safely as he can. Strengthened by Minerva’s counsels, he approaches his servant Eumaeus the swineherd in disguise, imitating a shipwrecked beggar. When asked who he is, he says that he is a Cretan and that, while sailing to Egypt, he was carried to Troy. He continues speaking to Eumaeus with the deepest affection, and when evening finally comes with continuous rain, he wraps himself in a cloak. There, turning many thoughts over in his mind, he at last gives himself over to rest.

## Synopsis of Book XV of the *Odyssey*

> Tritonian Pallas came to the Lacedaemonian region.

Telemachus is warned by Minerva in a dream to return home. Rising early from his bed, he asks Menelaus for permission to return. Having obtained it graciously, he goes back to the ship waiting in the Pylian harbor. He sends Pisistratus to the city and to his homeland, while he himself quickly puts out from the shore, taking as his companion in the voyage the Argive seer Theoclymenus, one of those whom Melampus son of Amythaon had instructed. Having avoided the suitors lying in wait, he arrives in his homeland. He orders his companions to make for the harbor, while he himself takes the opposite route toward the countryside and Eumaeus.

## Synopsis of Book XVI of the *Odyssey*

> Eumaeus’ hut was shared by the divine Ulysses.

Telemachus sends Eumaeus to inform his mother of his return. He himself, with Minerva’s approval, recognizes his father, and together they arrange what must be done. Penelope, having learned of her son’s return, goes out to the gathering of the suitors as far as modesty permits. After rebuking those who plotted against her son, she withdraws no less angry than sorrowful.

## Synopsis of Book XVII of the *Odyssey*

> Now the sky glows with Tritonian Pallas in her rosy chariot.

Telemachus recounts the course of his journey to his anxious mother. Ulysses is led into the town with Eumaeus’ assistance. Entering the house where the suitors were feasting, he begs for food, pitiably going around to them. Antinous then treats him outrageously. Penelope invokes curses upon Antinous for his inhuman deed and sends Eumaeus to summon the guest—for so Ulysses represented himself—to her. At that time the guest courteously excuses himself, but promises that he will come toward evening.

## Synopsis of Book XVIII of the *Odyssey*

> Irus appears, known among the people for begging at the crossroads.

While Ulysses begs within his own home, another man, Irus, an Ithacan of equal poverty, approaches him. He was accustomed to asking for handouts at the crossroads. A quarrel therefore begins through rivalry in their shared destitution and proceeds from words to blows, as the suitors encourage the fight to grow more violent and offer as a prize the caul of a goat’s belly. Ulysses wins and throws the half-dead Irus outside the door, addressing him with mocking encouragement. Penelope also asks the suitors to bring her gifts according to each man’s means, testing the devotion of each; the gifts are promptly offered by men eager to please her.

## Synopsis of Book XIX of the *Odyssey*

> In the inner part of the house, Ulysses remained concealed.

Ulysses and Telemachus remove all the weapons from the middle of the house, preparing destruction for the suitors so that nothing would remain by which they could either defend themselves or inflict violence. At Penelope’s summons he then goes to her and, as he had told Eumaeus, falsely claims to be a Cretan. He invents a story that Ulysses had once stayed as his guest. Soon afterward, when his nurse Eurycleia washes his feet as part of her hospitality, she recognizes by touch the scar he had received long ago on Parnassus when he was wounded by a boar’s tusk. From this evidence she recognizes her foster child, but he restrains her from asking or saying anything further.

## Synopsis of Book XX of the *Odyssey*

> Ulysses, embracing the knees of the suitors, was already begging.

While the suitors are feasting, Eresippus throws a beef leg at Ulysses, but misses his aim. Theoclymenus, skilled in divination, prophesies to the Ithacans the destruction threatening the suitors. They mock him at length, and he is expelled from the table and the house as though he were mad.

## Synopsis of Book XXI of the *Odyssey*

> Here Tritonian Pallas gave resolve to Icarius’ daughter.

Ulysses reveals to Eumaeus and Philaetius who he is, trusting in their loyalty and diligence. Once the recognition has occurred, they decide to prepare the slaughter of the suitors at the appropriate time. Ulysses approaches them by a stratagem, proposing that they allow him to try to bend the bow, so that his old-man’s strength may be tested. The prize would be Penelope’s marriage, which had once been promised to whoever could easily bend the bow belonging to Ulysses. But the suitors forbid the beggar and mocker to attempt this, since even such carefully chosen young men had tried in vain. When the others refuse, Telemachus gives Ulysses permission to test it. From this arises the first amazement at his prowess, while the others, ashamed of their own dishonor, blush because the old beggar has exposed their cowardice.

## Synopsis of Book XXII of the *Odyssey*

> Ulysses threw off the filthy clothing from his shoulders.

Taking up a position farther away, Ulysses bends the bow. With all the doors closed so that no avenue of escape would remain, he kills most of the suitors, some drunk with wine, others stunned by the novelty of the event, and still others occupied with whatever thoughts they were entertaining. First of all he pierces Antinous, who had surpassed the others in audacity and insolence. Eumaeus, Telemachus, and Philaetius then take up arms themselves and carry out a splendid slaughter among the panic-stricken men. Once all have been killed, only two are spared: Phemius the lyre-player, who had been employed for service and yet had produced something shameful in Ulysses’ house, and Medon, whose modesty Telemachus also supported, together with those who were with Telemachus. Melanthius, one of Ulysses’ servants, who had always armed the suitors’ insolence, is cruelly killed. Then they kill by hanging twelve maidservants who had shamefully consorted with the suitors. After completing the slaughter, Ulysses lights a fire and purifies the house with sulfur as an atoning rite.

## Synopsis of Book XXIII of the *Odyssey*

> The nurse outstripped the Chalcidian [reading uncertain] with an old woman’s gait.

Eurycleia, the nurse, awakens Penelope from sleep and announces what has happened. Penelope does not rashly believe that the husband who has come to her is really he. She tests whether he is her husband by a particular secret of the bedroom and by the arrangement of the marriage bed, known only to herself and Ulysses. They then come together and spend the entire night in mutual conversation. From this point the elegant retelling of the labors Ulysses endured is gathered together with remarkable artistry.

## Synopsis of Book XXIV of the *Odyssey*

[Col. 0958C]

> The Cyllenian calls the shades to their infernal dwelling.

Mercury drives the souls of the suitors, gathered in a throng after their recent common slaughter, down to the underworld. Then the heroic shades gather around Agamemnon. Astonished at the crowd of young men lying there and at their dense procession in a single line, they learn the reasons for their journey. In the underworld as well, Agamemnon especially praises Ulysses’ courage and Penelope’s chastity, although Agamemnon’s own experience had been different in each of his fortunes. Ulysses goes into the countryside to his father Laertes and, by both the unexpectedness of his return and the account of his deeds, astonishes the old man. Laertes in turn learns from him what hardships he had endured. Soon the fathers of the suitors hurry to avenge the deaths of their sons and, joining counsel with force, descend upon the countryside sooner than expected. But Ulysses, now accompanied by more supporters, routs and puts them to flight. As hatred grows and a greater revolt and tumult are about to be witnessed, Minerva descends to Ithaca at Jupiter’s command. She establishes peace on both sides and settles the passions and movements of the factions by abolishing the memory of the deeds that had been done.
